LESSONS.title: The human brain
LESSONS.hook: A 1.4-kilogram organ with 86 billion nerve cells, running on about the power of a dim light bulb.

sections.key: The brain is about 2% of your body weight but uses about 20% of your energy.
sections.b: The adult brain weighs about 1.3 to 1.4 kilograms, roughly 2% of your body weight, yet it uses about 20% of your energy, even at rest. That is around 20 watts, about the power of a dim light bulb, which is remarkably efficient compared with computers doing far less. It is about 75% water and has the consistency of soft tofu, so it floats in protective fluid inside the skull. It has no pain receptors of its own, which is why some brain surgery can be done while the patient is awake.

sections.key: About 86 billion neurons pass signals across synapses, forming trillions of connections.
sections.b: The brain holds roughly 86 billion nerve cells called neurons, plus a similar number of supporting glial cells. Neurons send electrical signals along their length. They then release chemical messengers called neurotransmitters, such as dopamine and serotonin, which cross tiny gaps called synapses to the next cell. Each neuron can connect with thousands of others, creating an estimated 100 trillion or more connections. Your thoughts, memories and feelings are patterns of activity across these networks.

sections.key: The cerebrum handles thinking, the cerebellum coordination and the brainstem automatic functions like breathing.
sections.b:
The cerebrum is the large, wrinkled outer part. It handles thinking, language, memory, senses and voluntary movement, and its folds pack more surface area into the skull. The cerebellum, tucked underneath at the back, fine-tunes balance and learned movements like riding a bike. The brainstem links the brain to the spinal cord and runs breathing, heart rate, swallowing and sleep cycles.

Each side of the cerebrum has four lobes. The frontal lobes handle planning, self-control and personality, and mature last, in the mid-20s. The parietal lobes process touch and space. The temporal lobes handle hearing, language and memory, and contain the hippocampus. The occipital lobes process vision.

sections.key: People aren't left-brained or right-brained, and we use virtually all of our brain, not 10%.
sections.b:
The brain has two hemispheres joined by a thick bundle of fibres, and each side mostly controls the opposite side of the body. Some functions lean one way; in most people, language is mainly on the left. But the idea of 'left-brained' logical people and 'right-brained' creative ones is a myth. A 2013 study scanning over 1,000 people found no sign that individuals favour one side overall.

Nor do we use only 10% of our brains. Scans show activity across nearly every region over a day, even in sleep, and damage almost anywhere causes noticeable problems. An energy-hungry organ that was 90% idle would make no evolutionary sense. The myth probably grew from misquoted early psychology and survives through movies and self-help marketing.

sections.key: The brain keeps changing with experience throughout life, and exercise, sleep, learning, connection and heart health protect it.
sections.b:
Your brain physically changes with experience, a property called neuroplasticity. Learning strengthens or forms connections between neurons, and the adult brain keeps changing throughout life. London taxi drivers who spent years memorising about 25,000 streets had a larger rear hippocampus than bus drivers on set routes. After a stroke, other areas can sometimes take over lost functions with rehabilitation.

Brain health is tied to overall health. Regular exercise increases blood flow to the brain and is one of the best-supported ways to protect thinking skills with age. Sleep clears waste and consolidates memories. Social connection and learning are linked to lower dementia risk. Managing blood pressure, not smoking and limiting alcohol protect your brain too, and a helmet protects it directly.

quiz.q: What makes the brain's energy use remarkable?
o: It uses about 2% of the body's energy because it is mostly water
It uses about 20% of the body's energy at about 2% of its weight
It uses over half of the body's energy, even when you are at rest
It uses almost no energy when you are resting or asleep
quiz.e: The brain is small but hungry, yet still runs on roughly the power of a dim light bulb.

quiz.q: How do neurons pass messages along a network?
o: Through tiny blood vessels that link neighbouring neurons
Only through the glial cells that surround each neuron
Electrical signals run along cells, then chemicals cross synapses
By a single long fibre joining all 86 billion cells
quiz.e: Neurotransmitters cross the tiny synapse gaps, and each neuron can connect with thousands of others.

quiz.q: Which part of the brain keeps you breathing while you sleep?
o: The cerebrum, which handles thinking and language
The cerebellum, which handles balance
The frontal lobes, which handle planning
The brainstem, which runs automatic functions
quiz.e: The brainstem controls breathing, heart rate and swallowing without any conscious effort.

quiz.q: Why is the claim that we use only 10% of our brains wrong?
o: Scans show activity across nearly the whole brain
Only the left hemisphere is used, which is more than 10%
Scientists measure brain use only during sleep
The extra 90% is used only by creative people
quiz.e: The brain is an expensive organ, and nearly all of it is active over the course of a day.

quiz.q: What does neuroplasticity mean for adults?
o: Brain connections are fixed once childhood is over
Only physical damage can make the brain change
Learning is stored outside the brain's nerve cells
The brain keeps changing with experience throughout life
quiz.e: Learning physically reshapes the brain, and exercise, sleep and social connection help keep it healthy.

LESSONS.push: Two per cent of your weight, yet it claims a fifth of your energy. Why?

LESSONS.title: Why we sleep
LESSONS.hook: You'll spend about a third of your life asleep. Here's what your brain is doing, and how to sleep better.

sections.key: Sleep is active maintenance, running in ~90-minute cycles of light, deep and REM sleep.
sections.b:
You'll spend about a third of your life asleep, roughly 25 years. It's not wasted time: sleep is when your body repairs tissue, regulates hormones, supports your immune system and locks in memories. Every animal studied sleeps, even fruit flies and jellyfish.

Each night runs in cycles of about 90 minutes, moving through light, deep (slow-wave) and REM sleep. Deep sleep dominates the first half of the night and drives physical recovery. REM, when most vivid dreams happen, grows longer towards morning. Your brain is highly active during REM, but most muscles are paralysed so you don't act out your dreams. Miss sleep and your mood, attention and judgement suffer fast.

sections.key: Sleep moves memories into long-term storage and helps clear waste from the brain.
sections.b:
While you sleep, your brain replays the day and strengthens what you learned, moving it into long-term storage. People remember new facts and skills better after sleeping on them than after the same time awake, and deep and REM sleep both play a part. Sleep also aids problem-solving: people are more likely to spot hidden patterns after a night's rest. That's why spaced learning beats an all-night cram.

Sleep may also be cleanup time. A 2013 study in mice found the brain's "glymphatic" system flushes fluid through brain tissue far more actively during sleep. This clears waste, including proteins linked to Alzheimer's. How it applies to humans is still being studied, but it may help explain why chronic poor sleep is linked to cognitive decline.

sections.key: Light sets your body clock, and caffeine blocks the sleep-pressure chemical adenosine for hours.
sections.b:
A master clock in your brain, the suprachiasmatic nucleus, runs a roughly 24-hour circadian rhythm. It controls sleepiness, body temperature and hormones. Light is its main timekeeper: morning daylight starts the day, and as evening falls, melatonin rises to prepare you for sleep. Bright screens late at night can delay that signal. Jet lag and shift work are hard because they force you out of sync with this clock.

Meanwhile, a chemical called adenosine builds "sleep pressure" while you're awake. Caffeine blocks it, masking tiredness. But caffeine has a half-life of about five hours, so half of a 3 pm coffee is still in you at 8 pm. Even if you fall asleep, it can reduce deep sleep, so many experts suggest no caffeine within 8 hours of bed.

sections.key: Most adults need 7-9 hours; regularly getting less has real costs.
sections.b: Most adults need 7 to 9 hours a night, and teenagers need 8 to 10. Very few people genuinely thrive on less than 6. Regularly falling short is linked to poorer concentration, mood and immunity, weight gain, and higher risks of heart disease and diabetes. It's dangerous on the road too: being awake for 17 hours affects driving about as much as a blood alcohol level of 0.05. Surveys suggest many Australians regularly don't get enough.

sections.key: Keep a consistent schedule, get morning light, and keep your bedroom cool, dark and quiet.
sections.b: Consistency matters most: go to bed and wake at similar times every day, weekends included. Get daylight in the morning. Keep your bedroom cool, dark and quiet, and use your bed mainly for sleep. In the hour before bed, dim the lights and follow a wind-down routine. Limit caffeine later in the day, and alcohol at night, which may help you nod off but fragments sleep later. If you regularly struggle to sleep or snore heavily, see a doctor: conditions like sleep apnoea are common and treatable.

quiz.q: Why isn't sleep "wasted time"?
o: It's when your body repairs, regulates hormones and locks in memories
It only rests your muscles
It just saves energy
Most animals don't need it
quiz.e: Sleep is active maintenance: repair, hormone regulation and memory storage all happen overnight.

quiz.q: Why does sleeping between study sessions beat an all-night cram?
o: Sleep strengthens and stores what you learned
You read faster when tired
Cramming builds long-term memory
Sleep erases what you studied
quiz.e: Your brain replays and consolidates new learning during sleep, which is why spaced study works better.

quiz.q: Why can a 3 pm coffee affect your sleep?
o: Half the caffeine can still be in you at 8 pm
Caffeine raises melatonin
It wears off within an hour
It improves deep sleep
quiz.e: Caffeine's half-life is about five hours, so it can linger and reduce deep sleep.

quiz.q: What's a real cost of regularly sleeping too little?
o: Poorer focus and higher risk of heart disease
None once your body adapts
Better concentration
Only feeling tired
quiz.e: Short sleep is linked to poorer concentration and mood, and to higher risks of heart disease and diabetes.

quiz.q: What's the most effective habit for better sleep?
o: Waking and sleeping at consistent times
A nightcap before bed
Sleeping in on weekends
Scrolling to unwind
quiz.e: A consistent schedule, weekends included, keeps your body clock steady.

LESSONS.push: Half of your afternoon coffee is still in you at bedtime. Here's why.

LESSONS.title: How your immune system works
LESSONS.hook: Right now, an army of cells is patrolling your body, learning, remembering and fighting invaders you'll never notice.

sections.key: Your immune system works in layers, and the first is physical barriers such as skin, mucus and stomach acid.
sections.b:
Every day your body meets bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites, called pathogens. Most never make you sick, thanks to your immune system: a network of cells, tissues and organs including the bone marrow, thymus, spleen, lymph nodes and tonsils. It works in layers.

The first layer simply keeps invaders out. Skin is a tough barrier. Mucus traps particles in your airways, and tiny hairs called cilia sweep it out. Tears and saliva contain enzymes that break down bacteria, and stomach acid kills many microbes you swallow. The trillions of friendly bacteria on your skin and in your gut also take up space and resources that harmful microbes would otherwise use.

sections.key: The innate system reacts within hours to anything suspicious, while the adaptive system takes days but targets specific invaders.
sections.b:
If something gets past the barriers, the innate immune system responds within minutes to hours. White blood cells such as neutrophils and macrophages rush in and engulf invaders. Their chemical signals cause inflammation, the redness, heat, swelling and pain around a cut, which brings more blood and immune cells. Fever helps too: a higher temperature makes it harder for many pathogens to multiply and speeds up immune reactions.

The adaptive system is slower, taking days, but highly targeted. B cells make antibodies, Y-shaped proteins that lock onto a specific pathogen. T cells coordinate the response, and killer T cells destroy infected cells directly. Your body can make enough different antibodies to recognise almost any invader.

sections.key: Memory cells let your body respond faster to a repeat invader, and vaccines build that memory without the disease.
sections.b:
After an infection, some B and T cells become long-lived memory cells. If the same pathogen returns, they mount a faster, stronger response, often clearing it before you feel sick. That is why you usually get diseases like chickenpox only once. Flu and common cold viruses keep changing their outer proteins or come in many varieties, so memory cells miss the new versions.

Vaccines give your immune system a safe preview of a pathogen, using a weakened or inactivated form, a piece of it, or instructions for making a piece, as mRNA vaccines do. Smallpox, which killed hundreds of millions of people, was declared eradicated in 1980. When enough people are immune, disease struggles to spread, protecting those who can't be vaccinated: herd immunity.

sections.key: Allergies are overreactions to harmless things, and autoimmune diseases are attacks on the body's own tissues.
sections.b:
The immune system isn't perfect. In allergies, it overreacts to harmless substances like pollen, dust mites or certain foods. Australia has one of the highest rates of food allergy in the world, especially among children. In autoimmune diseases, such as type 1 diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis and coeliac disease, it mistakenly attacks the body's own tissues. Scientists are still unravelling why, but genetics and environment both play roles.

This is also why you can't 'boost' a healthy immune system into overdrive, and wouldn't want to: an overactive one causes problems of its own.

sections.key: Sleep, activity, good food, vaccination and hygiene support immunity, while 'boosting' products mostly don't.
sections.b:
You can support your immune system even if you can't boost it. Regular sleep, physical activity, a balanced diet with plenty of vegetables and fruit, not smoking and moderating alcohol all help it work well. Staying up to date with vaccinations and washing your hands prevent infections in the first place.

Be sceptical of supplements and products that promise to 'boost immunity'. For most people, the evidence is weak. If you get frequent or unusual infections, see a doctor.

quiz.q: Which of these is part of the body's first line of defence?
o: Antibodies made after an infection
Skin, mucus and stomach acid
Killer T cells that destroy infected cells
Memory cells from past infections
quiz.e: Physical and chemical barriers keep most invaders out before any immune cells are needed.

quiz.q: How does the adaptive immune response differ from the innate response?
o: It reacts within minutes to anything, causing inflammation
It relies on skin and mucus to block invaders
It takes days but targets specific invaders
It is the same response, only sped up by fever
quiz.e: Innate defences are fast and general, while adaptive defences are slower and precise.

quiz.q: How do vaccines protect you?
o: They kill germs already in your body
They train the body to remember a germ safely
They permanently replace your white blood cells
They raise body temperature to stop pathogens multiplying
quiz.e: Vaccines train immune memory safely, and widespread immunity also protects those who can't be vaccinated.

quiz.q: What happens in an autoimmune disease?
o: The immune system overreacts to harmless pollen or food
The body stops making antibodies altogether
Memory cells fail to recognise old infections
The immune system attacks the body's own tissues by mistake
quiz.e: Examples include type 1 diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis and coeliac disease.

quiz.q: What does the evidence support for a healthy immune system?
o: Products that promise to boost immunity into overdrive
Good sleep, activity, diet and vaccinations
Avoiding all contact with other people
Large doses of supplements in winter
quiz.e: Everyday habits support immunity, while 'boosting' products have weak evidence for most people.

LESSONS.push: Your body fights invaders you'll never notice. How does it remember them?

LESSONS.title: Nutrition: what the evidence actually says
LESSONS.hook: Ignore the fads. The science of eating well is simpler, and less exciting, than the internet suggests.

sections.key: Nutrition headlines flip because the science is hard, but the big picture is stable: eat a variety of whole foods and limit saturated fat, salt and sugar.
sections.b:
One week coffee is bad for you, the next it's good. Nutrition is genuinely hard to study. We can't lock people in labs for decades, so much evidence is observational, showing links but not always causes. Headlines amplify single small studies, and influencers sell fads.

Yet the big picture is steady. The Australian Dietary Guidelines, based on a large review of evidence, recommend a wide variety from five groups: vegetables and legumes; fruit; mostly wholegrain grain foods; lean meats, fish, eggs, tofu, nuts and legumes; and milk, yoghurt, cheese or alternatives. Limit foods high in saturated fat, added salt and sugars, and limit alcohol. Drink plenty of water. It's not glamorous, but it's backed by a mountain of evidence.

sections.key: Most Australians eat too few vegetables and too little fibre, and eating more plants is the most useful change for most people.
sections.b:
Adults are advised five to six serves of vegetables and two of fruit a day. A serve is about half a cup of cooked vegetables or a cup of salad. Yet fewer than one in ten Australian adults eat enough vegetables. Plant foods provide vitamins, minerals and beneficial plant compounds, and are linked with lower risks of heart disease, stroke and some cancers. For most people, eating more of them is the single most useful change.

They also provide fibre, the part of plant food your body can't fully digest, which is why it helps. Fibre keeps bowels regular, helps you feel full, slows sugar absorption and feeds gut bacteria. Aim for about 25 grams a day for women and 30 for men. Wholegrains, legumes, nuts and seeds are good sources.

sections.key: Ultra-processed foods are linked with poorer health, and the 'per 100 g' column is the fair way to compare packaged products.
sections.b:
Ultra-processed foods are industrially made products, often with ingredients you wouldn't use at home, like flavour enhancers, emulsifiers and modified starches. Think soft drinks, packaged snacks, confectionery and reconstituted meats. They make up around 40% of the energy in the average Australian diet. Large studies link high intakes with higher risks of obesity, heart disease, type 2 diabetes and depression, though scientists still debate why.

On labels, compare similar products using the 'per 100 g' column, since serving sizes vary. Ingredients are listed by weight, so sugar near the top means a lot, and it hides behind aliases like glucose syrup or dextrose. One food Calorie is about 4.2 kilojoules. The Health Star Rating is a quick guide, but not perfect.

sections.key: Most healthy people don't need detoxes, supplements or exactly eight glasses of water, because overall patterns matter more than single foods.
sections.b:
Some popular beliefs don't hold up. 'Detox' products are unnecessary, because your liver and kidneys do that job. Most healthy people eating a varied diet don't need vitamin supplements, though some groups do, such as people who are pregnant or have specific deficiencies; ask a doctor.

There's no need to drink exactly eight glasses of water a day. Fluid needs vary, food provides some, and thirst is a reasonable guide for most healthy adults. And no single 'superfood' transforms your health: patterns matter more than individual foods.

sections.key: Small, lasting changes beat strict diets, and adding good foods works better than only cutting.
sections.b:
The best eating pattern is one you can keep up. Strict diets often fail because they're hard to sustain. Small changes add up: add a vegetable to every meal, swap sugary drinks for water, choose wholegrain bread, keep fruit where you'll see it, cook at home a bit more.

Focusing on what to add, rather than only what to cut, tends to feel better and works well. For personalised advice, especially with a health condition, an Accredited Practising Dietitian is the qualified professional to see.

quiz.q: Why do nutrition headlines so often contradict each other?
o: Researchers rewrite the basic dietary guidelines every single year
Much evidence is observational, and single small studies get amplified
Foods change how they affect the body from week to week
Official guidelines contradict each other in every country
quiz.e: Observational studies show links, not always causes, but decades of research agree on a simple core.

quiz.q: Why is fibre useful even though your body can't fully digest it?
o: It supplies most of the energy the body needs each day
It is broken down into vitamins inside the gut
It feeds gut bacteria and slows sugar absorption
It replaces the water you would otherwise need to drink
quiz.e: Fibre's resistance to digestion is exactly why it supports gut and heart health.

quiz.q: When comparing two similar packaged foods, which figure is the fairest to use?
o: The per-serve column, since brands choose it
The claims on the front of the pack
The kilojoules in the whole packet
The per 100 g column
quiz.e: Serving sizes vary between brands, but per 100 g is a like-for-like measure.

quiz.q: What is true of most healthy people who eat a varied diet?
o: They need a regular detox to clear toxins from the body
They don't need detox products or routine vitamin pills
They must drink exactly eight glasses of water every day
They should build their whole diet around one superfood
quiz.e: Your liver and kidneys already do the detoxing, and overall patterns matter more than single foods.

quiz.q: What approach to eating tends to work best over the long term?
o: A strict diet that cuts out as much as possible
Waiting until you can overhaul everything at once
Small, lasting changes that add good foods
Copying whatever the latest headline recommends
quiz.e: The best pattern is one you can keep up, and adding foods usually feels better than only cutting.

LESSONS.push: Nutrition headlines flip weekly. The evidence behind them barely moves.

LESSONS.title: What exercise does for you
LESSONS.hook: If exercise were a pill, it would be the most prescribed medicine in the world. You need less than you might think.

sections.key: Regular activity lowers the risk of many serious diseases and is an effective part of treating depression.
sections.b:
Regular physical activity lowers the risk of heart disease, stroke, type 2 diabetes, several cancers including bowel and breast cancer, depression, anxiety and dementia. It strengthens bones and muscles, improves sleep and helps manage weight and blood pressure. Researchers often say that if exercise were a pill, it would be the most prescribed medicine in the world.

The mind benefits too. A 2024 review in the BMJ found that walking, jogging, yoga and strength training were effective treatments for depression, especially at higher intensity. Exercise also boosts attention and memory, partly through more blood flow and growth factors in the brain. It complements professional care; talk to your GP if you're struggling.

sections.key: Even short bursts of vigorous activity count, and the talk test shows how hard you're working.
sections.b:
You don't need a gym session for movement to count. The World Health Organization dropped its old rule that activity only counts in blocks of ten minutes in 2020, because the evidence showed every bit helps. A 2022 University of Sydney study tracked more than 25,000 UK adults who didn't exercise. Those who did three or four short bursts of vigorous activity a day, like charging up stairs or running for the bus, had up to 40% lower risk of early death. It was observational, so it can't prove cause.

To judge effort, use the talk test. Moderate: you can talk but not sing. Vigorous: only a few words. One minute of vigorous activity is worth about two of moderate.

sections.key: Exercise alone usually brings modest weight loss but still improves health, and the 10,000-step target came from marketing.
sections.b:
Can you outrun a bad diet? Not easily. In 2012, anthropologist Herman Pontzer found that the Hadza, hunter-gatherers in Tanzania who walk and work physically all day, burned about the same calories as office workers in Europe and the US, once body size was accounted for. He argues the body trims energy spent elsewhere, and many people eat more after exercise. So diet usually matters more for weight, though activity helps keep weight off and improves fitness, blood pressure, blood sugar and mood at any size.

The 10,000-step target traces to a 1960s Japanese pedometer, the manpo-kei ('10,000-step meter'). Benefits begin well below it: about 7,000 steps is linked to far lower risk of early death than 2,000, with gains flattening beyond that.

sections.key: Long, uninterrupted sitting carries health risks, so break it up regularly.
sections.b:
Many of us sit for most of the day: commuting, working and relaxing. Long, uninterrupted sitting is linked with poorer health, somewhat independently of how much you exercise. The guidelines recommend minimising prolonged sitting and breaking it up as often as possible.

Simple habits help. Stand for phone calls, take the stairs, or walk to talk to a colleague instead of emailing. Set a reminder to get up every 30 to 60 minutes, or use a standing desk for part of the day.

sections.key: Choose activities you enjoy, start small, schedule them and make them social.
sections.b:
The best exercise is the one you'll actually do. Choose activities you enjoy, whether that's walking with a podcast, dancing, swimming, gardening, a team sport or lifting weights. Start small, even ten minutes a day, and build gradually to avoid injury and burnout. Schedule it like an appointment.

Exercising with a friend or group makes you more likely to turn up, and exercising outdoors or with others adds benefits from nature and social connection. If you have a health condition or haven't exercised in a long time, check with your doctor first. An accredited exercise physiologist can also help.

quiz.q: What did a 2024 review find about physical activity and depression?
o: Only vigorous team sport had any measurable effect
Exercise made symptoms worse in the short term
It helped anxiety but made no difference to depression
Walking, jogging, yoga and strength training all helped
quiz.e: Exercise can be an effective part of treating depression, especially at higher intensity, alongside professional care.

quiz.q: What was linked with up to 40% lower risk of early death in adults who didn't exercise?
o: Three or four short bursts of vigorous activity a day
Only workouts of ten minutes or longer, done daily
One long weekend session of moderate exercise
Hour-long gym sessions on at least five days a week
quiz.e: Charging up stairs or running for the bus counts, and the old ten-minute rule was dropped in 2020.

quiz.q: What is true about exercise and weight loss?
o: Calories burned rise in direct proportion to activity
Hitting exactly 10,000 steps guarantees weight loss
Exercise alone brings modest loss but still improves health
Exercise has no health benefit unless you lose weight
quiz.e: The body adapts to high activity, yet fitness, blood pressure, blood sugar and mood still improve.

quiz.q: What do the guidelines advise about long periods of sitting?
o: It is harmless as long as you exercise most days
Break it up often, such as every 30 to 60 minutes
It only becomes a concern after the age of 65
Sit for as long as needed, then do one long walk
quiz.e: Prolonged sitting is linked with poorer health somewhat independently of how much you exercise.

quiz.q: What is the best way to build an exercise habit?
o: Begin with intense daily sessions to build momentum
Pick whatever burns the most calories, whether or not you enjoy it
Wait until you have a long block of free time
Choose activities you enjoy, start small and make it social
quiz.e: The best exercise is the one you will actually keep doing.

LESSONS.push: Short bursts of puffing up the stairs may count more than you think.

LESSONS.title: Stress: friend and foe
LESSONS.hook: Stress can sharpen you or wear you down. The difference is how long it lasts and what you do with it.

sections.key: Stress triggers adrenaline and cortisol, which prepare the body for fight or flight.
sections.b: When your brain perceives a threat, whether a snake, a looming deadline or a tense conversation, it triggers the stress response. The adrenal glands release adrenaline, which speeds up your heart and breathing, and cortisol, which releases energy into the bloodstream. Blood flow shifts to your muscles, your senses sharpen and digestion slows. This fight-or-flight response evolved to help our ancestors escape predators. It's fast and powerful, and it still switches on for modern, non-physical threats.

sections.key: Short-term stress can improve performance, but stress that never switches off harms sleep, mood, immunity and heart health.
sections.b:
Stress isn't all bad. Short bursts sharpen focus and energy, which is why a little pressure before an exam or match can help. In 1908, psychologists Yerkes and Dodson described what is now drawn as an inverted U: performance improves with arousal up to a point, then declines. Challenges that stretch you, like learning a skill or exercising, involve a healthy kind of stress.

The trouble comes when the response doesn't switch off. Work pressure, money worries, caring duties or conflict can keep it going for weeks or months. Chronic stress is linked with poor sleep, anxiety, depression, headaches, digestive problems, weaker immunity and a higher risk of high blood pressure and heart disease. It also pushes people towards extra alcohol, junk food and less exercise.

sections.key: Seeing the stress response as your body preparing to perform can make stress more useful and less harmful.
sections.b:
How you think about stress can change how it affects you. In experiments at Harvard, people taught to see their racing heart and fast breathing as their body preparing to perform, rather than as a sign of failure, showed healthier cardiovascular responses and performed better under pressure. Stanford psychologist Kelly McGonigal popularised this 'stress mindset' idea.

It doesn't mean pretending stress is fine. But seeing it as a sign that something matters to you can make it more useful and less harmful.

sections.key: Long slow exhales calm the body, and exercise, sleep, nature and connection are among the best-supported stress relievers.
sections.b:
Breathing is one of the few parts of the stress response you can control directly. Slow breathing with long exhales activates the parasympathetic nervous system, the body's 'rest and digest' mode, lowering heart rate. Try cyclic sighing: two inhales through the nose, the second topping up the lungs, then a long, slow exhale through the mouth. In a 2023 Stanford study, five minutes a day lifted positive mood more than a similar amount of mindfulness meditation, and both reduced anxiety.

Other well-supported relievers are simple. Exercise burns off stress hormones, and good sleep keeps you less reactive. A short walk in nature and time with people you trust help. Limiting caffeine, alcohol and doomscrolling helps too.

sections.key: Tackle the source of stress where you can, and talk to a GP or a support line if it's overwhelming or persistent.
sections.b:
Where you can, tackle the source. Break big problems into small next steps. Write down what's worrying you; getting it onto paper reduces its power. Separate what you can control from what you can't, as the Stoics advised. Set boundaries on work hours and commitments, and ask for help. For money stress, the free National Debt Helpline (1800 007 007) offers confidential financial counselling.

If stress feels overwhelming, lasts for weeks or affects your sleep, work, relationships or health, talk to your GP, who can discuss options including a mental health treatment plan with Medicare-subsidised psychology sessions. Support is also available any time: Beyond Blue on 1300 22 4636 and Lifeline on 13 11 14, which is open 24 hours. Asking early is good sense, not weakness.

quiz.q: What does the stress response do to your body?
o: Slows your heart rate to conserve energy
Speeds up heart and breathing, releasing energy
Shifts blood flow towards digestion
Dulls your senses to avoid distraction
quiz.e: Adrenaline and cortisol prepare the body for fight or flight.

quiz.q: What makes stress harmful rather than useful?
o: A racing heart just before a big presentation
Taking on a challenge that stretches your skills
The response staying on for weeks or months
Brief pressure in the lead-up to an exam
quiz.e: Short bursts can sharpen performance, but chronic stress takes a toll on sleep, mood and heart health.

quiz.q: In Harvard experiments, what helped people perform better under pressure?
o: Suppressing every visible sign of stress
Avoiding the stressful task altogether
Telling themselves that nothing really mattered
Seeing their racing heart as helpful
quiz.e: Viewing the stress response as helpful led to healthier cardiovascular responses.

quiz.q: Why does a long, slow exhale help you calm down?
o: It triggers adrenaline to sharpen your focus and energy
It activates the rest-and-digest system, lowering heart rate
It raises cortisol to release extra energy for action
It speeds up breathing to settle the nervous system
quiz.e: Breathing is one part of the stress response you can control directly.

quiz.q: What should you do if stress lasts for weeks and affects your sleep, work or health?
o: Wait it out, since asking for help signals weakness
Talk to your GP about options such as a treatment plan
Push through on extra caffeine and longer hours
Avoid the source and tell nobody
quiz.e: Asking early is good sense, and Lifeline (13 11 14) is available 24 hours a day.

LESSONS.push: Your racing heart may be doing you a favour. Here's what research suggests.

LESSONS.title: Sun, UV and skin cancer
LESSONS.hook: Australia has one of the highest skin cancer rates in the world. Most of it is preventable, and it's not about the temperature.

sections.key: UV radiation, not heat, causes sunburn and skin cancer, so you can burn on cool or cloudy days.
sections.b:
Australia and New Zealand have the highest melanoma rates in the world. The Cancer Council estimates that about two in three Australians will be diagnosed with skin cancer by age 70. It is our most common cancer, and melanoma, the most dangerous type, kills over a thousand Australians each year. High UV levels, an outdoor lifestyle and a largely fair-skinned population drive the risk, but most skin cancers are preventable.

Sunburn and skin cancer come from ultraviolet (UV) radiation, not heat. You can't see or feel UV. You can burn badly on a cool, cloudy or windy day, because UV passes through cloud and a breeze makes you feel cooler. UV peaks at midday and in summer, but in much of Australia it reaches damaging levels most of the year, including winter in the north.

sections.key: Protect your skin whenever the UV index is 3 or above, using clothing, sunscreen, a hat, shade and sunglasses together.
sections.b:
The UV index measures UV strength on a scale from 0 with no upper limit; 11 and above is extreme. At 3 or above, it can damage skin and protection is recommended, which in much of Australia is most days. The free SunSmart app and the Bureau of Meteorology show daily sun protection times for your location.

Slip, Slop, Slap began in 1981, sung by an animated seagull, and grew into SunSmart with two more steps. Slip on sun-protective clothing. Slop on SPF30 or higher broad-spectrum, water-resistant sunscreen. Slap on a broad-brimmed hat. Seek shade. Slide on sunglasses that meet the Australian standard. No single measure is enough; use them together.

sections.key: Apply plenty of sunscreen 20 minutes before going out and reapply every two hours, because there is no such thing as a safe tan.
sections.b:
Most people apply far less sunscreen than they need and get only a fraction of the protection on the label. Adults need about a teaspoon for each arm, each leg, the front, the back, and the face, neck and ears: roughly 35 millilitres in all. Apply it about 20 minutes before going out. Reapply every two hours, and after swimming, sweating or towelling off. Check the expiry date, and never use it to extend time in the sun.

There is no safe tan. A tan is your skin making extra pigment in response to damage, and every sunburn raises skin cancer risk, especially in childhood and adolescence. Solariums significantly increase melanoma risk, so commercial ones have been banned across Australia since 2015. Fake tan is safer, but gives no UV protection.

sections.key: Most Australians make enough vitamin D from a few minutes of sun, so balance protection with brief exposure.
sections.b:
Sunlight helps your body make vitamin D, which is important for bones and muscles, and the balance matters. In summer, most fair-skinned Australians get enough from just a few minutes of sun on their arms and hands on most days, outside peak UV times.

In winter, in southern parts of Australia where UV is lower, you may need more time outdoors. People with naturally very dark skin need more sun exposure. If you're concerned about your levels, talk to your GP.

sections.key: Check your skin regularly and see a doctor promptly about any new or changing spot.
sections.b:
Skin cancers found early are usually easy to treat. Get to know your skin, including areas you can't easily see, using a mirror or a partner. See a doctor promptly about any new spot, or any spot that changes in size, shape or colour, bleeds, itches or doesn't heal.

The ABCDE guide helps identify suspicious moles: Asymmetry, irregular Border, uneven Colour, Diameter larger than about 6 millimetres, and Evolving, meaning changing over time. When in doubt, get it checked.

quiz.q: Why can you get badly sunburnt on a cool, cloudy day?
o: Clouds concentrate heat onto the skin
UV passes through cloud and isn't about heat
Wind increases the strength of UV
Winter sunlight is always stronger
quiz.e: UV can't be seen or felt, and a cool breeze can make you underestimate it.

quiz.q: When is sun protection recommended?
o: Only when the UV index reaches 11
Only on days above 30 degrees
Only in summer
Whenever the UV index is 3 or above
quiz.e: At 3 or above, UV is strong enough to damage skin, which in much of Australia is most days.

quiz.q: What is the right way to use sunscreen?
o: A thin layer once in the morning is enough with SPF50
Apply plenty beforehand and reapply every two hours
Apply after your skin begins to feel hot
Use it to stay out longer in the sun
quiz.e: Most people apply too little, and sunscreen should never be used to extend time in the sun.

quiz.q: How much sun do most fair-skinned Australians need for vitamin D in summer?
o: An hour of strong midday sun to build up stores
A deep tan topped up at least once a week
A few minutes on most days, avoiding peak UV
None, because sunlight does not help vitamin D at all
quiz.e: Short exposure is enough, and a GP can advise if you're concerned about your levels.

quiz.q: Which of these should prompt a visit to the doctor?
o: A freckle that has looked the same for years
An evenly coloured mole that hasn't changed
A tan line left by clothing
A spot that changes size or colour, or bleeds
quiz.e: Skin cancers found early are usually easy to treat, so when in doubt, get it checked.

LESSONS.push: Australia's skin cancer risk has little to do with heat. Why?

LESSONS.title: Ancient Egypt
LESSONS.hook: A civilisation that lasted 3,000 years, built by a river in the desert.

sections.key: The Nile's yearly floods left fertile soil that supported a civilisation lasting about 3,000 years, from around 3100 BC to 30 BC.
sections.b:
Ancient Egypt grew along the Nile, a ribbon of green through one of the driest deserts on Earth. Each summer, rains far to the south swelled the river and it flooded, leaving rich black silt. Egyptians called their land Kemet, 'the black land', and the desert Deshret, 'the red land'. Reliable harvests of wheat and barley fed a large population and freed people to become builders, scribes, priests and artisans.

Egypt was first unified around 3100 BC, traditionally by a ruler called Narmer or Menes. It lasted about 3,000 years, as the Old, Middle and New Kingdoms with periods of disorder between, until Rome took over after Cleopatra's death in 30 BC. Cleopatra lived closer in time to us than to the building of the Great Pyramid.

sections.key: Pharaohs were god-kings who kept order and balance, called ma'at, and Egyptians preserved the body so the soul could live on.
sections.b:
The pharaoh was seen as a god on earth, a link between people and the divine. His key job was keeping ma'at: cosmic order, truth, justice and balance. Egyptians worshipped hundreds of gods, including Ra the sun god, Osiris god of the afterlife, Isis and jackal-headed Anubis, guardian of the dead.

They believed the soul could live on but needed the body. Mummification took around 70 days. Embalmers removed the brain and most organs, dried the body with natron, a natural salt, and wrapped it in linen. In the afterlife, the heart was weighed against the feather of ma'at; a heart heavy with wrongdoing was devoured by a monster. Tombs held food, furniture and even board games.

sections.key: The Great Pyramid was built for Khufu around 2560 BC, and the evidence points to organised labourers, not slaves.
sections.b:
The Great Pyramid of Giza was built for the pharaoh Khufu around 2560 BC, from roughly 2.3 million stone blocks. It was the tallest human-made structure on Earth for more than 3,800 years. Exactly how it was built is still studied, but ramps, sledges, levers and huge organised workforces were involved.

Archaeologists have found the nearby workers' town, with bakeries, breweries and cemeteries, as well as a papyrus logbook kept by an official who shipped limestone for the pyramid. The evidence suggests the builders were organised, supported labourers, not slaves.

sections.key: Most Egyptians were farmers, women had notable legal rights, and tomb builders staged the earliest known strike around 1150 BC.
sections.b:
Most Egyptians were farmers in mud-brick houses, eating bread, onions, fish and thick, nutritious beer. By ancient standards, women had notable rights: they could own and inherit property, run businesses, sign contracts and go to court. Men and women wore eye make-up, which may have helped against sun glare and eye infections.

The artisans who decorated royal tombs lived in the walled village of Deir el-Medina, near modern Luxor. Many could write, and they left thousands of notes on limestone flakes and broken pottery. Around 1150 BC, under Ramesses III, their grain rations ran weeks late, so they downed tools and staged sit-ins at nearby temples until they were paid. It is the earliest strike on record, on a papyrus now in Turin.

sections.key: Tutankhamun is famous because his nearly intact tomb was found in 1922, and Egypt's legacy runs from calendars to medicine.
sections.b:
Tutankhamun was a fairly minor boy king of the New Kingdom who died at about 19. He is famous because his tomb, discovered by Howard Carter in 1922, was nearly intact, packed with more than 5,000 objects including his solid gold burial mask.

Egypt's legacy runs deep: a 365-day calendar, early medical texts describing injuries and treatments, papyrus, advances in maths and engineering, and some of the world's most recognisable art. It still shapes how we imagine the ancient world.

quiz.q: Why was the Nile so important to ancient Egypt?
o: It protected Egypt from invaders
It was full of gold
Yearly floods left fertile farmland
It connected Egypt directly to China
quiz.e: Reliable harvests fed a large population and freed people to become builders, scribes and artisans.

quiz.q: What was a pharaoh's most important job?
o: Leading the army in every battle
Keeping ma'at: order, truth and justice
Collecting grain from every farmer
Embalming the dead
quiz.e: The pharaoh was seen as a god on earth who held the world in balance.

quiz.q: What does the evidence from the pyramid builders' town suggest?
o: Slaves captured in foreign wars built the pyramid
Only soldiers on leave did the work
The builders were organised, supported labourers
The work was done by volunteer priests
quiz.e: Bakeries, breweries, cemeteries and a logbook point to an organised workforce.

quiz.q: Why did the tomb builders of Deir el-Medina stage the earliest known strike?
o: Their tombs were being robbed
They were forbidden to write notes
Ramesses III cut their working hours
Their grain rations were weeks late
quiz.e: They staged sit-ins at temples until they were paid, around 1150 BC.

quiz.q: Why is Tutankhamun so famous, despite being a fairly minor king?
o: He ruled longer than any other pharaoh
His tomb was found almost fully intact
He built the Great Pyramid
He first unified Egypt
quiz.e: Howard Carter's 1922 discovery included the solid gold burial mask.

LESSONS.push: Cleopatra lived closer to us than to the Great Pyramid. How is that possible?

LESSONS.title: World War II: how it began and ended
LESSONS.hook: The deadliest conflict in human history, and how it still shapes the world you live in.

sections.key: World War II (1939 to 1945) was the deadliest conflict in history, rooted in the aftermath of World War I and the Depression.
sections.b:
World War II ran from 1939 to 1945 and was the deadliest conflict in human history, with an estimated 70 to 85 million deaths, most of them civilians. It drew in most nations, including every great power, and was fought across Europe, Africa, Asia and the Pacific. Around a million Australians served, from a population of about seven million, and nearly 40,000 died.

It grew from the aftermath of World War I. Germany faced harsh terms under the Treaty of Versailles, including lost territory and reparations. Then the Great Depression brought mass unemployment. Adolf Hitler and the Nazis exploited the anger, took power in 1933, built a dictatorship and rearmed. Britain and France tried appeasement, giving in to some demands, such as letting Germany take part of Czechoslovakia in 1938, to keep the peace.

sections.key: Germany's invasion of Poland in 1939 started the war in Europe, and the 1941 attacks on the Soviet Union and Pearl Harbor made it global.
sections.b:
In August 1939 Germany and the Soviet Union signed a pact not to attack each other, secretly agreeing to divide Poland. Germany invaded on 1 September. Britain and France declared war two days later, and Prime Minister Robert Menzies announced that Australia was at war too. Fast tanks and aircraft swept through western Europe, and France fell in June 1940. Britain held out in the Battle of Britain.

In June 1941 Hitler broke the pact and invaded the Soviet Union, opening the war's largest and bloodiest front. In December, Japan attacked Pearl Harbor, bringing in the US, and swept through South-East Asia. Singapore fell in February 1942, with around 15,000 Australians taken prisoner, and Darwin was bombed days later. The main Allies were Britain and its Commonwealth, the Soviet Union and the US; the Axis was Germany, Italy and Japan.

sections.key: The Nazi regime systematically murdered around six million Jews and millions of others, which led to new international law on genocide.
sections.b:
The Nazi regime systematically murdered around six million Jews, about two thirds of Europe's Jewish population, in what is known as the Holocaust or Shoah. Millions of others were also killed, including Roma, disabled people, Soviet prisoners of war, Poles and political opponents.

Victims were shot in mass executions or murdered in death camps such as Auschwitz-Birkenau. The scale and deliberate planning shocked the world. The Holocaust led directly to new international laws on genocide and human rights after the war.

sections.key: Victories at Midway, Kokoda, El Alamein and Stalingrad turned the war, and D-Day opened a western front in 1944.
sections.b:
In 1942 and 1943 the tide turned. The US defeated Japan's navy at the Battle of Midway in June 1942. Australian troops halted the Japanese advance on the Kokoda Track in Papua. British and Commonwealth forces, including Australians, won at El Alamein in Egypt. The Soviet victory at Stalingrad in early 1943 destroyed an entire German army.

On 6 June 1944, D-Day, Allied troops landed in Normandy, France, opening a second front in the west. Germany was now squeezed between Soviet forces in the east and the Western Allies.

sections.key: Germany surrendered in May 1945 and Japan in August, and the war produced the UN, the Cold War, decolonisation and postwar migration to Australia.
sections.b:
Hitler took his own life in Berlin, and Germany surrendered in May 1945. In August the US dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, killing well over 100,000 people, and the Soviet Union declared war on Japan. Japan announced its surrender on 15 August, now Victory in the Pacific Day in Australia, and signed formally on 2 September.

The war reshaped the world. The United Nations was founded in 1945 to prevent another global conflict. The US and Soviet Union became rival superpowers, beginning the Cold War. European empires weakened and many colonies soon gained independence. In Australia, the main alliance shifted from Britain towards the US, and a huge postwar migration program, under the slogan 'populate or perish', brought millions from Europe and later the world.

quiz.q: What was 'appeasement'?
o: A secret alliance between Britain and Nazi Germany
A military build-up by Britain meant to deter Germany
The peace treaty that ended World War I in 1919
Giving in to some of Hitler's demands for peace
quiz.e: Britain and France hoped concessions would avoid another war, but Germany kept expanding.

quiz.q: What turned a European war into a global one in 1941?
o: The fall of France and the Battle of Britain
The invasion of the Soviet Union and Pearl Harbor
The atomic bombing of Japan
The signing of the Treaty of Versailles
quiz.e: The Soviet Union and the US both joined the Allies, and the war spread across Asia and the Pacific.

quiz.q: What was a lasting outcome of the Holocaust for international law?
o: A permanent ban on armies in all of Europe
The immediate end of all colonial empires
A treaty returning Germany to its 1914 borders
New international law on genocide and human rights
quiz.e: The scale of the crimes led directly to new laws on genocide and human rights after the war.

quiz.q: What did the Allied victories at Midway, Kokoda, El Alamein and Stalingrad achieve?
o: They ended the war in the Pacific within months
They halted Axis advances and turned the tide of the war
They brought the United States into the war
They forced Germany to sign a peace treaty
quiz.e: From 1942 and 1943 the Axis advance was stopped, and D-Day opened a second front the next year.

quiz.q: How did the war change Australia?
o: It left the Commonwealth and became a republic soon after
It ended migration to keep jobs for returning servicemen
It broke with the US and allied itself with the Soviet Union
Its main ally became the US, and mass migration followed
quiz.e: The slogan 'populate or perish' drove a huge postwar migration program from Europe and later the world.

LESSONS.push: Around a million Australians served in World War II. What did it change at home?

LESSONS.title: The printing press changed everything
LESSONS.hook: One goldsmith's invention sparked religious revolutions, modern science and, eventually, the idea of news.

sections.key: Gutenberg's press, with reusable movable metal type, replaced slow hand copying around 1440.
sections.b:
Before the mid-1400s, European books were copied by hand, often by monks. One Bible could take a scribe over a year, copying introduced errors, and a library of a few hundred volumes was a treasure. Most people never owned a book, and most couldn't read. Knowledge sat in churches, universities and wealthy homes.

Around 1440, Mainz goldsmith Johannes Gutenberg developed printing with movable metal type. He cast individual letters in a hand mould so they could be arranged into pages, inked, printed and reused. He adapted the screw press used for wine and olive oil and developed an oil-based ink that stuck to metal. His Bible, printed around 1455, is still considered one of the most beautiful books ever made. About 49 copies survive.

sections.key: Movable type was invented in China and used in metal in Korea before Gutenberg, but his system suited Europe's small alphabet.
sections.b:
Printing wasn't new everywhere. China had woodblock printing centuries earlier; the Diamond Sutra, printed in 868, is the oldest dated printed book. Around 1040, Bi Sheng invented movable type from baked clay. Korea was printing with movable metal type by the 1200s, and its Jikji of 1377 is the oldest surviving book printed that way, decades before Gutenberg.

But Chinese writing uses thousands of characters, which made movable type harder to use. Gutenberg's system suited Europe's small alphabet, and combined with a trading economy hungry for books, it spread explosively.

sections.key: Print made books cheap and let ideas spread across Europe in months, which helped fuel the Reformation.
sections.b:
By 1500, presses were running in more than 200 European towns, and historians estimate millions of books had been printed. Prices fell dramatically, so merchants, lawyers and craftspeople could afford books. Ideas that once took years to spread by hand could travel the continent in months, in identical copies. Mistakes could be corrected in the next edition rather than multiplied by tired copyists.

In 1517, German monk Martin Luther wrote his 95 Theses criticising the Catholic Church's sale of indulgences. Thanks to print, his writings spread across Germany quickly, and he became one of the best-selling authors of his time. He translated the Bible into German so ordinary people could read it. The resulting Protestant Reformation split Western Christianity and reshaped Europe for centuries.

sections.key: Print let scientists share and check each other's work and helped more people read, standardising languages and creating newspapers.
sections.b:
Science depends on sharing results so others can check and build on them. Printed books and, later, journals made this possible at scale. Accurate diagrams, maps and tables could be copied exactly, which hand copying never managed. Copernicus's book arguing that the Earth orbits the Sun was printed in 1543, followed by Galileo, Kepler and Newton. The first scientific journals appeared in 1665.

As books got cheaper, more people learned to read. Printers needed consistent spelling and grammar, which helped standardise languages like English and German. Pamphlets, and eventually newspapers from the early 1600s, created a public sphere where ordinary people could debate current events. Governments and churches saw the danger, and censorship followed.

sections.key: Like print, the internet made publishing cheap, spreading both knowledge and misinformation while society slowly adapted.
sections.b:
Historians often compare the printing press with the internet. Both made publishing dramatically cheaper and faster. Both spread knowledge, but also propaganda, scandal and misinformation; early printers churned out sensational pamphlets about witches and monsters. Both shifted power away from traditional gatekeepers and provoked anxious debates about information overload.

It took societies generations to develop norms, like editors, libraries and reputable publishers, to cope with print. We're still working out the equivalent for the internet.

quiz.q: What made Gutenberg's system practical for printing many pages?
o: A single carved wooden block for every page
Hand copying by teams of trained scribes
Paper that was made locally in Mainz
Reusable metal letters arranged into pages
quiz.e: Letters could be arranged, inked, printed and then reused for the next page.

quiz.q: Why did movable type spread explosively in Europe?
o: China had never developed any form of printing
Its small alphabet suited it and traders wanted books
Chinese rulers had banned all printing
Europe had invented it before Korea and China
quiz.e: Chinese writing's thousands of characters made movable type harder to use there.

quiz.q: How did print change the way ideas spread?
o: Ideas spread more slowly but more accurately
Only the Church could afford to publish
Ideas could spread across Europe within months
Books became rarer and more valuable
quiz.e: Cheaper books and fast copying carried ideas such as Luther's across Europe within a short time.

quiz.q: How did print help the growth of science?
o: Results and diagrams could be copied exactly and checked
It replaced experiments with printed theories
It kept new discoveries secret within universities
It made scientific journals unnecessary
quiz.e: Science depends on others checking and building on published results.

quiz.q: What do the printing press and the internet have in common?
o: Both were used only by governments and churches at first
Both reduced misinformation by giving everyone the facts
Both made publishing cheap and spread misinformation as well
Both arrived without any debate about information overload
quiz.e: Both shifted power from traditional gatekeepers and took generations to manage well.

LESSONS.push: Movable type existed in Asia centuries before Gutenberg. So why Europe?

LESSONS.title: The Renaissance
LESSONS.hook: How a handful of Italian cities rediscovered the ancient world and reinvented art, science and what it means to be human.

sections.key: The Renaissance was a revival of ancient learning and art that began in Italy's wealthy, competing city-states.
sections.b:
The Renaissance, French for 'rebirth', was a cultural revival in Europe from roughly the 14th to the 17th century. It began in Italy, especially Florence, and spread to France, the Netherlands, Germany and England. People then felt they were reviving ancient Greece and Rome after a long decline. Historians now see the 'Dark Ages' as less dark than Renaissance writers claimed.

Italy had advantages. Cities such as Florence, Venice and Milan grew rich on trade, banking and manufacturing. Roman ruins were everywhere. Competing city-states used art and architecture to show off their power. And after Constantinople fell to the Ottomans in 1453, Greek scholars fled to Italy with ancient manuscripts.

sections.key: Rediscovered ancient texts inspired humanism, and wealthy patrons like the Medici paid for the art and scholarship.
sections.b:
Scholars hunted through monastery libraries for lost Greek and Roman writing on philosophy, history, science and poetry. This inspired humanism, an outlook celebrating human potential, reason and achievement alongside religious devotion. Humanists believed a well-rounded education in grammar, rhetoric, history and moral philosophy made better citizens. The poet Petrarch, often called its father, helped launch it in the 1300s. Our 'humanities' come from it.

Art needed money, and the Renaissance ran on patronage. The Medici of Florence, bankers, paid artists, architects and scholars for generations. Popes commissioned huge projects, including rebuilding St Peter's Basilica. Guilds and merchants funded church decorations to display piety and status. Fierce competition for commissions pushed standards higher.

sections.key: Linear perspective, anatomy and light and shadow let Renaissance artists paint realistic, deep-looking images.
sections.b:
Around 1415, the architect Filippo Brunelleschi demonstrated linear perspective, a mathematical way of creating the illusion of depth on a flat surface, with lines converging on a vanishing point. Painters quickly adopted it.

Artists also studied anatomy, sometimes by dissecting corpses, to paint realistic bodies, and used light and shadow to create volume. Leonardo da Vinci painted the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper. Michelangelo sculpted David and painted the Sistine Chapel ceiling. Raphael painted The School of Athens.

sections.key: Leonardo da Vinci embodied the 'Renaissance man', a person skilled across many fields.
sections.b:
Leonardo da Vinci was a painter, engineer, anatomist, inventor and scientist. His notebooks, written in mirror script, hold designs for flying machines, armoured vehicles and diving suits, along with remarkably accurate anatomical drawings. He embodies the 'Renaissance man': someone skilled across many fields. The ideal was a cultivated person who could discuss art, science, poetry and politics, not specialise in one thing.

The same curiosity reached practical fields. In 1494 Luca Pacioli, a friend of Leonardo, published the first printed explanation of double-entry bookkeeping, still the basis of accounting today.

sections.key: Renaissance curiosity fed exploration and the Scientific Revolution, and the printing press spread its ideas across Europe.
sections.b:
The Renaissance spirit of questioning and observation spilled into exploration. Mapmakers constantly redrew the world as new reports arrived, and European navigators sailed to the Americas, around Africa and across the Pacific. These voyages brought wealth and knowledge to Europe, but also colonisation, conquest and devastating consequences for Indigenous peoples.

The printing press, arriving in the mid-1400s, spread Renaissance ideas quickly, as books and engravings reached readers across Europe. The period laid foundations for the Scientific Revolution, the Enlightenment and modern ideas about education and individual achievement. You can see its influence in old European cities, and in grand Australian public buildings with columns and domes.

quiz.q: What helped make Italy the birthplace of the Renaissance?
o: A single united government that funded the arts
Trade wealth, Roman ruins and competing city-states
Isolation from trade routes and foreign scholars
A lack of ancient ruins that forced new styles
quiz.e: Rich cities, ancient ruins and rivalry between rulers created a setting for art and learning.

quiz.q: What did humanists believe about education?
o: Only religious study mattered
A broad education made better citizens
Learning should be left to monasteries alone
Ancient texts should be ignored in favour of new writing
quiz.e: Humanism celebrated human potential and reason alongside religious devotion, inspired by ancient texts.

quiz.q: What did linear perspective allow painters to do?
o: Mix and make their colours far more cheaply
Paint large works without needing any sketches
Show the same scene from every side at once
Create the illusion of depth on a flat surface
quiz.e: Lines converging on a vanishing point made flat paintings look deep and realistic.

quiz.q: What is meant by a 'Renaissance man'?
o: A specialist who mastered a single craft
A person skilled in many fields, like Leonardo
Any man who lived in Florence
A patron who funded artists
quiz.e: The ideal was someone who could discuss art, science, poetry and politics.

quiz.q: What was a consequence of the voyages of exploration?
o: Europe stopped trading with the rest of the world
Mapmakers stopped updating their maps of the world
Gains for Europe, but harm to Indigenous peoples
Indigenous peoples in the Americas were largely unaffected
quiz.e: The age of exploration brought both gains for Europe and devastating consequences elsewhere.

LESSONS.push: Why did a handful of Italian cities spark a rebirth of the ancient world?

LESSONS.title: Ancient Rome: from village to empire
LESSONS.hook: How a small town on the Tiber built an empire of tens of millions, and why you still use its words, laws and calendar.

sections.key: Rome grew from farming villages into a republic in 509 BC, designed so no one person could rule alone.
sections.b:
According to legend, twins Romulus and Remus, raised by a she-wolf, founded Rome in 753 BC. In reality it grew from farming villages on hills beside the River Tiber. Kings ruled for centuries. In 509 BC the Romans expelled the last one and founded a republic, where elected officials ran the state. They hated kings so much that the word stayed an insult.

The republic was built to stop anyone grabbing total power. Two consuls were elected each year and could block each other. The Senate, made up of experienced former officials, advised and controlled finances. Citizen assemblies voted on laws. Ordinary plebeians fought long battles with the aristocratic patricians to win more rights. These checks influenced later democracies, and Australia's Senate takes its name from Rome's.

sections.key: Disciplined legions, and a habit of turning defeated enemies into allies and citizens, let Rome rule the Mediterranean.
sections.b:
Over several centuries Rome conquered Italy, then defeated its great rival Carthage in the Punic Wars, including Hannibal, who famously crossed the Alps with elephants. Its armies were disciplined, well organised and relentless. Just as important, Rome turned defeated enemies into allies and eventually citizens, which kept its strength growing.

At its height, around 117 AD under the emperor Trajan, the empire stretched from northern England to Egypt and from Spain to Iraq. Perhaps 60 million people lived under Roman rule.

sections.key: Conquest produced powerful generals; Caesar's rise and murder ended the Republic, and Augustus became the first emperor in 27 BC.
sections.b:
Conquest brought enormous wealth, but also inequality and ambitious generals with loyal armies. In 49 BC Julius Caesar crossed the Rubicon with his army, breaking Roman law and starting a civil war. He won and became dictator for life. Fearing he would become a king, senators stabbed him to death on the Ides of March, 15 March 44 BC. The murder did not save the Republic. It triggered more civil wars.

Caesar's adopted heir Octavian won them and in 27 BC became Augustus, the first emperor, while keeping the trappings of the Republic. His reign began the Pax Romana, about two centuries of relative peace. Later emperors ranged from Trajan and Marcus Aurelius to Caligula and Nero. July and August are named after Caesar and Augustus.

sections.key: Roman engineers built roads, aqueducts and concrete structures so well that some still stand.
sections.b:
Romans were superb engineers. They built more than 80,000 kilometres of paved roads, letting armies, traders and messages move quickly. 'All roads lead to Rome' was nearly literal.

Aqueducts carried fresh water many kilometres into cities, for fountains, public baths and even toilets. Roman concrete was remarkably durable. The dome of the Pantheon, completed around 125 AD, is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world. Good infrastructure was one of the quiet reasons Rome held together for so long.

sections.key: The Western Empire fell in 476 AD, but Rome lives on in language, law, the calendar and the Byzantine Empire.
sections.b:
From the 200s AD the empire faced civil wars, economic trouble, plague and pressure from peoples on its borders, and it split into western and eastern halves. In 476 AD a Germanic general deposed the last western emperor, a teenager called Romulus Augustulus, the date often used for the fall of Rome. The eastern half, later called the Byzantine Empire, survived until the Ottomans captured Constantinople in 1453.

Rome's influence is everywhere. Latin evolved into Italian, Spanish, French, Portuguese and Romanian, and supplies much of English. Roman law shaped European legal systems, and our calendar descends from Caesar's reforms. Christianity, favoured by Constantine in the 300s, spread partly through Roman networks. Senate, republic, citizen and veto are Roman words.

quiz.q: Why did the Roman Republic elect two consuls each year?
o: So each could block the other and no one held total power
So one could command the army while the other ran the temples
So the Senate would always have a clear majority
So a king could share power with elected officials
quiz.e: Rome's republic was built on checks that stopped any one person taking total power.

quiz.q: What helped Rome keep its strength growing as it conquered?
o: Paying foreign mercenaries with captured gold
Turning defeated enemies into allies and eventually citizens
Keeping conquered peoples out of the army
Moving conquered peoples to distant provinces
quiz.e: Rome absorbed the peoples it defeated, which kept its manpower and loyalty growing.

quiz.q: What was the result of Julius Caesar's assassination?
o: The Republic was restored and soon became stronger
Caesar's generals shared power peacefully for decades
More civil wars, then the rise of the first emperor
The Senate abolished the consuls and ruled alone
quiz.e: The murder did not save the Republic; it triggered more civil wars that Augustus eventually won.

quiz.q: Why did Roman roads matter so much to the empire?
o: They were built mainly for chariot races
They let armies, traders and messages move quickly
They marked the borders between provinces
They carried water into the cities
quiz.e: Fast, reliable movement of people and messages helped hold the empire together.

quiz.q: What happened to the eastern half of the Roman Empire after 476 AD?
o: It was conquered within a few years by Germanic generals
It joined the west under Romulus Augustulus
It broke into the Latin-speaking nations of Europe
It survived as the Byzantine Empire for nearly a thousand years
quiz.e: The fall of the west was not the end of Rome; the east endured until 1453.

LESSONS.push: A small town on the Tiber became an empire. Why do you still speak its words?

LESSONS.title: The Black Death
LESSONS.hook: A plague that killed a third to a half of Europe, and accidentally helped end the medieval world.

sections.key: The Black Death, caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, reached Europe in 1347 along trade routes from Central Asia.
sections.b:
In October 1347, trading ships docked at Messina in Sicily. Many aboard were dead or dying. The plague had travelled along trade routes from Central Asia, and within four years it swept across Europe, the Middle East and North Africa. People called it the great mortality; the name Black Death came later.

We now know the cause was the bacterium Yersinia pestis, confirmed by DNA from plague burial pits. It usually spreads by fleas on rats and other rodents. The bubonic form causes painful swollen lymph nodes called buboes. When it reaches the lungs it becomes pneumonic plague, which spreads by coughing and is almost always fatal without treatment. Some historians think human fleas and lice also played a big role.

sections.key: Perhaps a third to a half of Europe died, and without any idea of germs, fear turned into scapegoating.
sections.b:
Historians estimate that 30% to 50% of Europe's people died between 1347 and 1351, with many more lost across Asia and Africa. Some towns lost over half their people and some villages were abandoned. Cities dug mass graves when churchyards filled. Europe's population took around two centuries to recover, and the plague returned in waves for hundreds of years.

No one understood germs. Many believed the plague was God's punishment, and flagellants whipped themselves in public penance. Doctors blamed 'miasma', or poisonous bad air. Terrifyingly, Jewish people were falsely accused of poisoning wells, and Jewish communities were massacred in many towns. It is a grim reminder of how fear in an epidemic can turn into scapegoating.

sections.key: Cities invented quarantine, health boards and travel restrictions, ideas still used in public health today.
sections.b:
Some responses were remarkably modern. In 1377 the city of Ragusa, now Dubrovnik in Croatia, required arriving ships and travellers to isolate for 30 days. Venice and other ports later extended this to 40 days. The word quarantine comes from the Italian quaranta giorni, meaning 40 days.

Cities also set up health boards, isolated the sick in special hospitals and restricted travel from infected areas. Plague still exists in wild rodents in parts of Africa, Asia and the Americas, including the western United States, with a few hundred to a few thousand human cases a year. Today it is treatable with common antibiotics if caught early. Studying the Black Death also helped scientists understand how disease travels along trade routes.

sections.key: With so many workers dead, labour became scarce, wages rose and the feudal system weakened.
sections.b:
The survivors inherited a changed world. With so many workers dead, labour became scarce and valuable. Peasants demanded higher wages and better conditions, and many moved to wherever pay was best.

Landowners and governments tried to freeze wages by law, such as England's Statute of Labourers in 1351. That fuelled anger which later exploded in the Peasants' Revolt of 1381. Over time, the old feudal system, where peasants were tied to a lord's land, weakened. A catastrophe had shifted the balance of power between those who owned land and those who worked it.

sections.key: The plague reshaped art, faith and medicine, and some historians link it to the Renaissance.
sections.b:
Art became preoccupied with death, with images of skeletons dancing with people of every rank. Faith in the Church was shaken because prayer seemed useless. Medicine began, slowly, to rely more on observation.

Some historians argue that higher wages and wealth concentrated in fewer hands helped fund the Renaissance. Others link labour shortages to experiments with labour-saving technology. These links are debated, but the pattern is clear: big historical shocks often have consequences no one could predict at the time. Lessons from the Black Death about how diseases spread became relevant again during COVID-19.

quiz.q: What do scientists now know caused the Black Death?
o: Poisonous bad air known as miasma
A bacterium, usually spread by fleas on rodents
A virus carried by contaminated water
A fungus that grew in stored grain
quiz.e: DNA from plague burial pits confirmed that Yersinia pestis, usually spread by fleas, caused it.

quiz.q: What did many communities do because they did not understand how the plague spread?
o: Blamed scapegoats, including Jewish communities
Closed their markets until the plague had passed
Moved the sick to churchyards outside the town
Taxed travellers to pay for doctors
quiz.e: Without an understanding of germs, fear led to scapegoating and terrible persecution.

quiz.q: What does the word 'quarantine' originally refer to?
o: The 40 days ships were isolated before entering port
A building where the sick were held
The distance travellers had to stay from towns
The 40 doctors on Venice's health board
quiz.e: Quarantine comes from the Italian for 40 days, the isolation period ports imposed on arrivals.

quiz.q: Why did wages rise after the plague?
o: Governments passed laws requiring higher pay
Landowners chose to share their profits with peasants
Labour became scarce because so many workers had died
Peasants were freed from paying rent to lords
quiz.e: With fewer workers, survivors could demand better pay and conditions.

quiz.q: How did the Black Death change faith and medicine?
o: Trust in the Church grew and medicine turned to astrology and prayer
Faith in the Church was shaken and medicine slowly turned to observation
Doctors stopped treating the sick and fled the plague-struck cities
Religion and medicine merged into a single profession of healers
quiz.e: The plague shook old certainties and slowly pushed medicine towards observation.

LESSONS.push: A plague killed up to half of Europe. Its aftermath gave workers more power.

LESSONS.title: The Industrial Revolution
LESSONS.hook: For most of history, almost everyone was a farmer. Then, in about a century, machines changed everything.

sections.key: From about 1760, Britain's coal, capital, colonies and high wages made it the birthplace of machine-powered industry.
sections.b:
For thousands of years most people worked the land, and living standards barely changed from one century to the next. From around 1760 in Britain, that began to change. Machines powered first by water, then by coal-fired steam, replaced hand tools. Production moved from homes into factories. Historians often call it the most important change in human life since farming.

Britain had a combination of advantages: plentiful coal and iron ore, often close together; banks and investors willing to fund new ventures; relatively stable politics; and a large trading empire. High wages and cheap coal made labour-saving machines especially worth inventing. Much of the cotton came from plantations worked by enslaved people in the Americas, a dark foundation of the new wealth.

sections.key: Textile machines like the spinning jenny and water frame created the first factories.
sections.b:
The revolution began in textiles. Inventions like James Hargreaves' spinning jenny (around 1764) and Richard Arkwright's water frame let one worker spin many threads at once. Arkwright's mill at Cromford, opened in 1771, is often called the first modern factory, with workers arriving for set shifts to tend machines.

Output soared and cloth became cheap. For workers, it meant long hours, strict discipline and dangerous machinery. The factory changed how people spent their days as much as what they produced.

sections.key: Smelting iron with coke made iron cheap, and railways from the 1820s made transport dramatically faster.
sections.b:
Traditional ironmaking needed charcoal, and Britain's woodlands were running short. In 1709 Abraham Darby at Coalbrookdale in Shropshire smelted iron with coke, coal baked to drive off impurities. With coal abundant, iron could be made far more cheaply. In 1779 his grandson built the first major cast-iron bridge over the River Severn nearby. It still stands and gave Ironbridge its name. Cheap iron went into engines, machinery, rails and ships.

The Stockton and Darlington Railway opened in 1825. The Liverpool and Manchester Railway in 1830 was the first to run regular passenger services entirely by steam.
