Journeys that took days by horse took hours. Railways even standardised time, because timetables demanded one national time instead of each town's own.

sections.key: Industrial cities were grim at first, but reforms and long-run productivity growth lifted living standards enormously.
sections.b:
People poured from the countryside into cities like Manchester, which grew from a market town into one of the world's first industrial cities. Housing was cramped and poorly built, and cholera spread through contaminated water. Children as young as five or six worked in mills and mines. Reformers pushed back: Britain's Factory Acts from 1833 limited child labour, public health laws brought sewers and clean water, and unions fought for better wages and shorter hours.

Historians debate how quickly ordinary people benefited. For the first generations, wages rose slowly and life expectancy in industrial towns was low. Over the long run, the gains were enormous: goods became cheaper and incomes rose many times over. Much of the rise in living standards since 1800 followed from the technologies that began in those British mills.

sections.key: Industrialisation created modern prosperity and also began the large-scale burning of fossil fuels.
sections.b:
The Industrial Revolution created the modern world: factories, cities, mass-produced goods, railways, the middle class, and eventually electricity, cars and computers.

It also began the large-scale burning of coal, then oil and gas. Carbon dioxide in the atmosphere has risen from about 280 parts per million before industrialisation to over 420 today, driving climate change. The same engine that lifted living standards carries a cost we are still paying. Many argue we are now living through the next great transition, from fossil fuels to clean energy.

quiz.q: Why was Britain well placed to start the Industrial Revolution?
o: The world's largest population of farmers and few towns
Plentiful coal, willing investors, trade and high wages
No competition from any other trading nation
A ban on the use of hand tools in homes
quiz.e: A mix of coal, capital, trade, stability and high wages made machines worth inventing in Britain.

quiz.q: What changed about work when factories like Cromford appeared?
o: Workers owned the machines they used
Cloth became more expensive and rarer
Workers followed set shifts tending machines
Spinning moved from mills back into homes
quiz.e: The factory brought set shifts, discipline and machines, changing how people spent their days.

quiz.q: Why did smelting iron with coke matter?
o: Coke let abundant coal replace scarce charcoal
It made iron lighter so ships could carry more cargo
It removed the need for furnaces in ironworks
It gave workers safer jobs underground in mines
quiz.e: Coke let Britain use its abundant coal to make iron cheaply and at scale.

quiz.q: How did industrial cities eventually improve?
o: Workers moved back to farms in the countryside
Factory Acts, sewers and unions improved conditions
Cholera disappeared on its own over time
Mills stopped employing children voluntarily
quiz.e: Reformers, public health laws and unions pushed back against the worst conditions.

quiz.q: What is the long-term environmental legacy of industrialisation?
o: Carbon dioxide has fallen as factories became more efficient
Coal use ended completely once oil and gas were discovered
Burning fossil fuels raised carbon dioxide from 280 to over 420 ppm
Cities now absorb more carbon than the forests ever did
quiz.e: The same fossil-fuelled growth that raised living standards also drove up carbon dioxide levels.

LESSONS.push: Why did the machine age start in a damp island with plenty of coal?

LESSONS.title: World War I and the ANZACs
LESSONS.hook: The war that was meant to be over by Christmas lasted four years, killed millions and shaped Australia's sense of itself.

sections.key: A single assassination in 1914 became a world war because of rival alliances, huge armies and imperial rivalry.
sections.b:
On 28 June 1914 Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the throne of Austria-Hungary, was shot dead in Sarajevo by Gavrilo Princip, a young Bosnian Serb nationalist. Austria-Hungary blamed Serbia and declared war a month later.

Why did a regional crisis spread? Europe was split into alliance blocs: Germany and Austria-Hungary on one side, France, Russia and Britain on the other. Countries had huge armies and war plans that relied on mobilising quickly. Empires competed for colonies and naval power, and nationalism ran high. Russia backed Serbia, Germany backed Austria-Hungary, and when Germany invaded neutral Belgium to attack France, Britain declared war. As part of the British Empire, Australia was automatically at war.

sections.key: Machine guns, barbed wire and artillery made attack suicidal, while the war introduced gas, tanks, aircraft and submarines.
sections.b:
Everyone expected a short war. Instead, by late 1914 the Western Front was a line of trenches from the Belgian coast to Switzerland. Machine guns, barbed wire and artillery made attacking across 'no man's land' suicidal, and huge offensives gained only a few kilometres at enormous cost. On the first day of the Somme in 1916, the British Army suffered about 57,000 casualties. Soldiers lived with mud, rats, lice, disease and constant shelling.

It was an industrial war with terrible new weapons. Poison gas, first used on a large scale in 1915, caused blindness and suffocation. Tanks appeared in 1916. Aircraft moved from scouting to bombing. German submarine attacks on shipping helped bring the United States into the war in 1917.

sections.key: The ANZACs landed at Gallipoli on 25 April 1915, and Australia, a nation of under five million, lost about 60,000 people in the war.
sections.b:
In 1915 the Allies tried to knock the Ottoman Empire out of the war by seizing the Dardanelles strait. On 25 April, the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps landed at what became known as Anzac Cove. They faced steep cliffs and determined Ottoman defenders. The campaign dragged on for eight months before the Allies withdrew. About 8,700 Australians died. The day of the landing became Anzac Day.

Australia had fewer than five million people, yet about 417,000 men enlisted, all volunteers; two referendums on conscription were narrowly defeated. More than 60,000 died and around 156,000 were wounded, gassed or taken prisoner. Most deaths came on the Western Front, at places like Pozieres, Fromelles and Passchendaele. More than 1,000 Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander men also served, despite discrimination at home.

sections.key: The armistice took effect at 11 am on 11 November 1918, after about 20 million soldiers and civilians had died.
sections.b:
In 1917 Russia collapsed into revolution and left the war, but American troops and resources tipped the balance towards the Allies. Germany's final offensives in 1918 failed, its allies surrendered and its people were starving.

An armistice took effect at 11 am on 11 November 1918, the 'eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month', now marked as Remembrance Day. Around 20 million soldiers and civilians had died. The influenza pandemic that followed killed tens of millions more. Medicine had advanced too, with blood transfusions, better surgery and new understanding of what was then called 'shell shock'.

sections.key: The harsh Treaty of Versailles bred resentment in Germany that helped fuel the rise of Hitler and a second world war.
sections.b:
The 1919 Treaty of Versailles forced Germany to accept blame, give up territory and colonies, limit its army and pay heavy reparations. Australian Prime Minister Billy Hughes was there and fought for Australia to control German New Guinea.

Four empires, the German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian and Ottoman, had collapsed, redrawing maps across Europe and the Middle East. Many Germans resented the treaty bitterly. That resentment helped fuel the rise of Hitler and a second, even deadlier world war just 20 years later. A peace that humiliates the loser can plant the seeds of the next conflict.

quiz.q: Why did the assassination in Sarajevo grow into a world war?
o: Interlocking alliances and war plans pulled in the great powers
Britain and Germany had signed a secret treaty to divide Europe
Germany and Austria-Hungary had already agreed to partition Serbia
The Ottoman Empire demanded that every European power go to war
quiz.e: Alliances, huge armies and rivalries turned a local crisis into a chain reaction.

quiz.q: Why did the Western Front become a long stalemate?
o: Neither side had any artillery
Soldiers were forbidden from leaving the trenches
Machine guns and barbed wire made attacking deadly
Winter weather stopped all fighting for years
quiz.e: Defensive weapons overwhelmed offensive tactics, so huge attacks gained little ground.

quiz.q: What was unusual about Australia's military effort in World War I?
o: Soldiers were conscripted by law from the very first year
About 417,000 volunteered, and conscription was voted down twice
Australian troops fought only at Gallipoli and nowhere else
Only about 50,000 men enlisted, mostly to guard the coast
quiz.e: A small, all-volunteer nation sent hundreds of thousands, and paid a very heavy price.

quiz.q: What does Remembrance Day on 11 November mark?
o: The landing at Anzac Cove
The signing of the Treaty of Versailles
The start of the Battle of the Somme
The armistice of 11 November 1918
quiz.e: The armistice took effect at 11 am on 11 November 1918, and that moment is remembered each year.

quiz.q: How did the Treaty of Versailles help lead to a second world war?
o: It let Germany keep a large army and its overseas colonies
Its harsh terms bred resentment that helped Hitler rise
It handed Germany control over the collapsed Ottoman Empire
It divided Germany permanently into two separate states
quiz.e: Blame, lost territory and heavy reparations fuelled resentment that extremists exploited.

LESSONS.push: They said it would be over by Christmas. It lasted four years. Why?

LESSONS.title: The Cold War
LESSONS.hook: For over 40 years, two superpowers came close to destroying the world without ever fighting each other directly.

sections.key: After World War II the US and Soviet Union became opposing superpowers, and Europe divided into two armed blocs.
sections.b:
The United States and the Soviet Union fought on the same side in World War II, but had little else in common. The US was a capitalist democracy; the USSR was a communist one-party state. As the war ended, Soviet forces controlled Eastern Europe and installed communist governments. In 1946 Winston Churchill warned that an 'iron curtain' had descended across Europe.

Germany was split into a democratic West and a communist East, and Berlin was split too. In 1948-49 the Soviets blockaded West Berlin, and the Western allies supplied the city entirely by air for almost a year. NATO formed in 1949 and the Soviet bloc answered with the Warsaw Pact in 1955. East Germany built the Berlin Wall in 1961 to stop people fleeing west. It stood until 1989.

sections.key: Both sides stockpiled around 70,000 warheads at the peak, relying on mutually assured destruction to prevent war.
sections.b:
The US used atomic bombs in 1945, and the Soviet Union tested its own in 1949. Both sides then raced to build more and bigger weapons, including hydrogen bombs hundreds or even thousands of times more powerful than the Hiroshima bomb. At the peak, in the mid-1980s, there were around 70,000 nuclear warheads in the world.

The strategy was mutually assured destruction, aptly abbreviated MAD. It held that neither side would attack, because it would be destroyed in return. The Cold War, roughly 1947 to 1991, was called 'cold' because the superpowers never fought each other directly. Schoolchildren practised 'duck and cover' drills.

sections.key: The Cuban Missile Crisis brought the world closer to nuclear war than ever, and ended with a deal and a hotline.
sections.b:
In October 1962, US spy planes discovered Soviet nuclear missiles being installed in Cuba, just 145 kilometres from Florida. For thirteen tense days, the world stood on the edge of nuclear war.

President John F. Kennedy ordered a naval blockade of Cuba. Eventually Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev agreed to remove the missiles in exchange for a US promise not to invade Cuba, and a secret deal to remove US missiles from Turkey. Afterwards, a direct hotline was set up between Washington and Moscow, so leaders could talk quickly in a crisis.

sections.key: The superpowers competed through proxy wars, including Vietnam where Australians served, and through the space race.
sections.b:
Instead of fighting each other, the superpowers backed opposing sides in conflicts around the world. The Korean War (1950-53) ended in a stalemate that still divides the peninsula. In Vietnam, the US fought to stop the communist North taking over the South. About 60,000 Australians served there between 1962 and 1973, and 523 died. The war sparked huge protests in Australia, including over conscription. Proxy conflicts also raged in Afghanistan, Angola and Latin America.

The rivalry extended into space. The Soviet Union launched Sputnik, the first satellite, in 1957, and Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space in 1961. On 20 July 1969 Apollo 11 landed on the Moon. Honeysuckle Creek and the Parkes radio telescope helped broadcast those first pictures.

sections.key: Gorbachev's reforms, the Berlin Wall's fall in 1989 and the Soviet collapse in 1991 ended the Cold War, but its legacies remain.
sections.b:
By the 1980s the Soviet economy was struggling. Mikhail Gorbachev, leader from 1985, introduced reforms known as glasnost (openness) and perestroika (restructuring), and signed arms reduction treaties with Ronald Reagan. In 1989 peaceful revolutions swept Eastern Europe, and on 9 November the Berlin Wall opened. Germany reunified in 1990, and on 26 December 1991 the Soviet Union dissolved into 15 countries.

The legacy is all around us. NATO still exists and has expanded. Thousands of nuclear weapons remain, though far fewer than at the peak. Satellites, GPS and the early internet came from the rivalry. Many of today's tensions, from Ukraine to Korea, have roots in Cold War divisions.

quiz.q: Why was the Cold War called 'cold'?
o: It was mostly fought in polar regions
The two sides never fought directly
It happened during unusually harsh winters
Neither side used any weapons
quiz.e: The superpowers confronted each other for decades without direct war between them.

quiz.q: What did the strategy of mutually assured destruction rely on?
o: Each side hiding its weapons from the other
Neither side striking first, as it would be destroyed
One side having far more weapons than the other
Both sides agreeing to scrap their weapons
quiz.e: The certainty of devastating retaliation was meant to deter any first strike.

quiz.q: How was the Cuban Missile Crisis resolved?
o: The US invaded Cuba and seized the missiles
A deal: missiles left Cuba, with no US invasion
Both sides fired a warning missile into the sea
Cuba sent the missiles back to the Soviet Union
quiz.e: A negotiated deal, followed by a hotline, helped both sides step back from the brink.

quiz.q: What is a proxy war?
o: A war fought only in space and at sea
A war fought directly between two superpowers
A war in which allies attack from the sea
A conflict where superpowers back opposing sides
quiz.e: Korea and Vietnam were proxy conflicts where the superpowers backed opposing sides rather than clash directly.

quiz.q: What helped bring the Cold War to an end?
o: A direct war that the US won in 1991
A UN ban on all nuclear weapons
A merger of NATO and the Warsaw Pact
Economic strain and peaceful revolutions
quiz.e: Economic strain and reform, followed by peaceful revolutions, ended the Cold War without a superpower war.

LESSONS.push: Two superpowers came within days of nuclear war and never fired a shot at each other.

LESSONS.title: The world's oldest continuous cultures
LESSONS.hook: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have lived in Australia for tens of thousands of years. Here's what that history includes.

sections.key: Aboriginal people have lived in Australia for at least 50,000 years, and crossed open sea to get here.
sections.b:
Aboriginal people have lived on the Australian continent for at least 50,000 years. Excavations at Madjedbebe in Arnhem Land suggest people may have been there around 65,000 years ago. That makes Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander cultures among the oldest continuous living cultures on Earth. People were here tens of thousands of years before the last Ice Age ended, and long before the pyramids, farming in the Middle East or the first cities.

During the Ice Age, Australia, New Guinea and Tasmania were joined in one landmass called Sahul. Even then, reaching it from South-East Asia meant crossing open sea, making this one of the earliest known deliberate ocean voyages. Over thousands of years, people adapted to rainforests, deserts, coasts, alpine areas and tropical islands.

sections.key: Before 1788, Australia held hundreds of distinct nations with their own languages, laws and customs.
sections.b:
Aboriginal Australia was never one culture. Before British colonisation in 1788 there were hundreds of distinct nations or clan groups, each with its own country, laws, customs and kinship systems. More than 250 languages were spoken, with many dialects.

The Torres Strait Islands, between Cape York and Papua New Guinea, have their own distinct Melanesian cultures. Many Aboriginal words are now part of Australian English, like kangaroo, koala, billabong, yakka and boomerang.

sections.key: Caring for Country, through cultural burning and sophisticated works like Budj Bim, shaped the land for thousands of years.
sections.b:
For Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, Country means much more than land. It includes waters, skies, plants, animals, ancestors and stories, all connected, with responsibilities to care for it. People managed landscapes through cultural burning, sometimes called fire-stick farming: frequent small, cool fires that reduced fuel, encouraged fresh growth and attracted game. Today, fire agencies increasingly work with Traditional Owners to bring it back to reduce bushfire risk.

At Budj Bim in western Victoria, the Gunditjmara people built channels, weirs and ponds to trap and farm short-finned eels, at least 6,600 years ago. It is one of the oldest known aquaculture systems in the world, World Heritage listed in 2019. Stone fish traps at Brewarrina in New South Wales are also thought to be extremely old.

sections.key: Songlines carry maps, laws and knowledge in song, story, dance and art, passed down for thousands of years.
sections.b:
Aboriginal cultures kept knowledge not in books but in song, story, dance and art. Knowledge of seasons, plants, medicine and the night sky was passed down through generations.

Songlines, also called dreaming tracks, trace the journeys of ancestral beings across the land. They work as maps, laws, histories and guides to water and food, and some stretch across the continent, linking many different language groups. Researchers have found that some oral traditions accurately describe events such as rising sea levels at the end of the Ice Age, suggesting stories were passed down accurately for thousands of years.

sections.key: Colonisation brought dispossession and the Stolen Generations; recognition came through the 1967 referendum, Mabo and the 2008 Apology.
sections.b:
In 1788 Britain established a colony at Sydney Cove on the basis that the land belonged to no one, a legal idea called terra nullius. Colonisation brought introduced diseases like smallpox, loss of land and water, frontier violence including massacres, and laws controlling where Aboriginal people could live and work. In the 20th century, governments and churches removed many children from their families. They are known as the Stolen Generations.

Activism brought change. In the 1967 referendum, over 90% of Australians voted to count Aboriginal people in the census and let the federal government make laws for them. The 1992 Mabo decision, brought by Torres Strait Islander Eddie Mabo and others, rejected terra nullius and recognised native title. In 2008 Prime Minister Kevin Rudd delivered a National Apology. Gaps in health and life expectancy remain a national focus.

quiz.q: What does the evidence about the first Australians' arrival suggest?
o: They walked from Asia on dry land all the way
They crossed open sea, a very early voyage
They arrived long after the first cities
They came ashore with the First Fleet
quiz.e: Even with low Ice Age seas, reaching Sahul required open-water crossings.

quiz.q: What is true of Aboriginal Australia before 1788?
o: It was one culture with a single language
Hundreds of nations, each with its own laws
It had no ties to particular places
A few large kingdoms ruled the continent
quiz.e: Aboriginal Australia was never one culture, but hundreds of distinct nations.

quiz.q: What is cultural burning?
o: Burning old villages when people moved on
Setting huge fires to clear land for farming
Small, cool fires that cut fuel and renew growth
Burning ceremonial objects after a death
quiz.e: Cultural burning managed the land and is now being used again to reduce bushfire risk.

quiz.q: What are songlines?
o: Songs sung only for entertainment
Lists of the names of ancestors and elders
Written maps drawn on bark for travellers
Ancestral journeys that carry maps and law
quiz.e: Songlines hold navigation, law and history in song, story, dance and art.

quiz.q: What did the Mabo decision of 1992 do?
o: Gave Aboriginal people the vote
Recognised native title, rejecting terra nullius
Counted Aboriginal people in the census
Delivered an apology to the Stolen Generations
quiz.e: Mabo overturned the idea that Australia belonged to no one before 1788.

LESSONS.push: People crossed open sea to reach Australia far earlier than you might guess.

LESSONS.title: How to negotiate
LESSONS.hook: Salaries, rent, car prices, bedtimes: life is full of negotiations. A few principles reliably change the outcome.

sections.key: Most negotiations are won before they start, by researching the market and setting a target and walk-away point.
sections.b:
Negotiation is simply two or more sides working out an agreement. Whether it is a pay rise, a second-hand car, a phone bill or who does the dishes, you are negotiating. Many people avoid it because it feels awkward, and they leave money on the table. Studies of salary offers find that people who negotiate often get more, and employers generally expect it.

Most negotiations are won before they start. Research the market: what do similar jobs pay, what have similar cars sold for? Decide your target, the outcome you are aiming for, and your walk-away point, the worst deal you will accept. Anticipate the other side's concerns. Preparation gives you confidence and stops you deciding on the spot under pressure.

sections.key: Your BATNA is your best alternative if no deal is reached; the stronger it is, the more confidently you can negotiate.
sections.b:
Your BATNA is your 'best alternative to a negotiated agreement': what you will do if this deal falls through. The term comes from the 1981 book Getting to Yes by Roger Fisher and William Ury, from the Harvard Negotiation Project.

If you have another job offer, your BATNA is strong. If you would be unemployed, it is weak. The stronger your alternative, the more confidently you can push, and the more clearly you will know when to walk away. Improving your BATNA, for example by getting another quote, is often the smartest move you can make.

sections.key: A position is what someone asks for; an interest is why they want it, and asking why uncovers better deals.
sections.b:
A position is what someone says they want. An interest is why they want it.

The classic story: two sisters argue over one orange and finally cut it in half. One eats the fruit and throws away the peel. The other uses the peel for baking and throws away the fruit. If they had asked why, both could have had all they needed. Asking 'What's most important to you here?' uncovers room for creative deals, like a later start date in exchange for a higher salary.

sections.key: Back a researched first offer with a reason, name the other side's feelings, and stay quiet after you make an offer.
sections.b:
The first number on the table tends to anchor the whole conversation. If you have done your research, it often pays to make the first offer, ambitious but defensible, with a reason: 'Similar roles pay $95,000 to $105,000, and I bring X, so I'm looking for $102,000.' If the other side anchors first with an unreasonable figure, calmly re-anchor with your own researched number.

Former FBI negotiator Chris Voss recommends 'labelling': naming the other side's feelings, like 'It sounds like budgets are tight this year.' It shows you are listening and draws out useful information. Ask open questions such as 'How am I supposed to do that?' After making an offer, stop talking. The other person will often fill the silence, sometimes with a better offer.

sections.key: Trade concessions rather than giving ground for nothing, and aim for a deal both sides can live with.
sections.b:
Avoid simply splitting the difference or giving ground for nothing. Every concession should buy something: 'I can do that price if you include delivery.' Look beyond the headline number. In a job negotiation there is leave, flexibility, training, title and start date. Give ground on what is cheap for you but valuable to them, and ask for what is cheap for them but valuable to you.

If the other side feels cheated, they may not follow through or may resent you in a job you will hold for years. Be firm on substance and friendly with people, and get the final deal in writing. Remember your walk-away point: sometimes the best negotiation is the one where you politely say no.

quiz.q: What is your walk-away point?
o: The first number you put on the table
The worst deal you will accept
The other side's best offer
The target outcome you are aiming for
quiz.e: Knowing your walk-away point before you start keeps you from agreeing to a bad deal under pressure.

quiz.q: Why does a strong BATNA help in a negotiation?
o: It lets you push confidently and walk away
It forces the other side to open the bidding
It guarantees you the full amount you ask for
It means you never need to prepare
quiz.e: A good alternative means you do not need this particular deal, which gives you real bargaining power.

quiz.q: In the orange story, what lesson do the two sisters teach?
o: Always split the difference equally between both sides
Always keep your goals hidden from the other side
Asking why can help both get what they need
The person who asks first usually wins every time
quiz.e: Looking at interests rather than positions reveals deals where both sides win.

quiz.q: What should you do right after making an offer?
o: Immediately explain why it could be lower
Fill the silence with extra reasons
Offer a discount to seem friendly
Stop talking and let the other person respond
quiz.e: Silence is uncomfortable, and the other person will often fill it, sometimes with a better offer.

quiz.q: Why should every concession buy something?
o: Any concession shows weakness to the other side
Giving ground for free weakens your position
It keeps the negotiation as short as possible
Other people expect you to refuse every request
quiz.e: Trading concessions keeps the deal balanced and avoids giving value away.

LESSONS.push: Why two sisters fighting over an orange can teach you to negotiate a better salary.

LESSONS.title: How scams work, and how to beat them
LESSONS.hook: Australians lose billions to scams. Scammers aren't targeting the gullible; they're targeting everyone, using the same few tricks.

sections.key: Scams succeed by exploiting emotions like fear, urgency and greed, and the red flags are the same across almost all of them.
sections.b:
Australians reported losing about $2.18 billion to scams in 2025, and many losses go unreported. Scams are not only aimed at the elderly or naive. Young adults are often targeted too, especially through social media, job and investment scams. Scammers succeed not because victims are foolish, but because they exploit fear, urgency, greed, love and the desire to help.

The tell-tale signs are shared. You are rushed: act now or your account will be closed. You are asked to keep it secret. You are asked to pay in unusual ways, such as gift cards, cryptocurrency or a 'safe account'. You are asked for passwords, one-time codes or remote access. The deal seems too good to be true. Any one of these should make you stop.

sections.key: Scammers pretend to be trusted organisations or family, so verify using contact details you find yourself.
sections.b:
Most scams start with impersonation. Scammers pretend to be your bank, the ATO, myGov, Australia Post, a toll company or the police. Texts can even appear in the same thread as genuine messages. A new register means texts from unregistered sender names may now be marked 'Unverified', but scammers keep adapting. In the 'Hi Mum' scam, someone claims to be your child on a new number and urgently needs money.

In remote access scams, a caller says your computer or account is hacked and asks you to install software so they can 'fix' it. In 'safe account' scams, a fake bank officer says your money is at risk and must be moved to an account they control. No genuine bank will ask for either. Hang up and call the organisation using details you find yourself.

sections.key: Investment, romance and job scams promise easy gains or build trust, then demand money; never pay someone you have only met online.
sections.b:
Investment scams cause the biggest losses. They start with fake ads featuring celebrities, or a friendly stranger on social media or a dating app who shares their trading 'success'. Victims see professional platforms with fake profits, are encouraged to invest more, then cannot withdraw. Warning signs are guaranteed high returns, pressure to invest quickly and unlicensed operators. Check ASIC's professional register for an Australian Financial Services licence.

Romance scammers build trust over weeks, often claiming to work overseas or on oil rigs. They avoid video calls, then ask for money. Job scams offer easy money for simple online tasks, then ask you to deposit money to 'unlock' earnings. Never send money to someone you have only met online, and a real job never asks you to pay to work.

sections.key: Slow down, verify independently, talk to someone you trust, and protect your accounts with two-factor authentication and unique passwords.
sections.b:
Australia's National Anti-Scam Centre recommends three steps.

Stop: do not give money or information if you are unsure. Scammers rely on rushing you.

Check: ask yourself whether the message could be fake, and contact the organisation using details from its official website or app, not the message. Talk to someone you trust. A second opinion often breaks the spell.

Protect: act quickly if something feels wrong. Use two-factor authentication and strong, unique passwords to reduce the damage if details leak.

sections.key: If you are scammed, contact your bank straight away, report it, and do not be embarrassed.
sections.b:
If you have been scammed, act fast and do not be embarrassed. It happens to smart people every day. Contact your bank or card provider immediately; they may be able to stop or recover payments. Change compromised passwords.

Report the scam to Scamwatch (scamwatch.gov.au) and cybercrime to ReportCyber (cyber.gov.au). If your identity documents were exposed, contact IDCARE (1800 595 160), a free national support service. Beware of 'recovery' scammers who contact victims promising to get their money back for a fee.

quiz.q: Why do scams succeed against ordinary, intelligent people?
o: Scammers only go after careless people
They exploit emotions like fear and urgency
Victims rarely bother to read their messages
Banks are unable to detect any fraud
quiz.e: Scams work by pressuring emotions, not by exploiting a lack of intelligence.

quiz.q: What should you do if a caller says your bank account is at risk and asks you to move money to a 'safe account'?
o: Move the money straight away to keep it safe
Ask the caller for their employee number
Hang up and ring the bank on a number you find
Install the software to secure your account
quiz.e: No genuine bank asks you to move money to a safe account, so verify independently.

quiz.q: Which is a warning sign of an investment scam?
o: A company that holds an Australian Financial Services licence
A returns forecast that includes some risk
A statement that past results may not continue
Guaranteed high returns and pressure to invest quickly
quiz.e: Guaranteed returns and pressure are classic signs of fraud; check ASIC's register.

quiz.q: What does 'Check' mean in Stop. Check. Protect.?
o: Check your account balance every day this week
Contact the organisation via its official website
Check how many others replied to the message
Reply to the sender to confirm who they are
quiz.e: Independent verification breaks the scammer's control of the conversation.

quiz.q: What is the first thing to do after being scammed?
o: Contact your bank or card provider immediately
Wait to see whether the scammer contacts you again
Pay a recovery service to get the money back
Delete all messages so no one finds out
quiz.e: Fast action gives your bank the best chance to stop or recover payments.

LESSONS.push: Scammers don't target the gullible. They target everyone, using the same few tricks.

LESSONS.title: Stay safe online
LESSONS.hook: A few simple habits stop the vast majority of account takeovers, and most take only minutes to set up.

sections.key: Most attacks are automated and impersonal, so every account has value to criminals.
sections.b:
Many people think, 'Why would a hacker want my stuff?' But most attacks are not personal. Criminals use automated tools to try millions of stolen passwords, send millions of phishing messages and scan for unpatched devices.

Your email account alone can be used to reset passwords for your bank, shopping and social media. Stolen identities are sold and used for fraud. Australia has seen major data breaches, like Optus and Medibank in 2022, exposing millions of people's details. You do not need to be important to be worth attacking. You only need to be reachable.

sections.key: Use long, unique passphrases, never reuse a password, and let a password manager remember them.
sections.b:
Length beats complexity. A passphrase of four or more random words, like 'purple-kettle-marathon-cactus', is easier to remember and much harder to crack than a short jumble like P@ssw0rd1.

The most important rule is never reuse passwords. When one website is breached, attackers automatically try the same email and password on banks, email and shopping sites, a technique called credential stuffing. Your email password matters most of all.

Nobody can remember 100 unique strong passwords. A password manager generates a random one for each site, stores them securely and fills them in. You only remember one strong master password. Built into Apple and Google devices and browsers, managers also help against phishing, because they will not autofill on a fake website.

sections.key: Two-factor authentication means a stolen password is not enough, and the safest response to phishing is to go to the official site yourself.
sections.b:
Two-factor authentication (2FA or MFA) adds a second step when you log in, such as a code from an authenticator app, a text message code, a fingerprint or a security key. Even if someone steals your password, they cannot get in without it. Turn it on for email, banking, myGov, social media and shopping. Authenticator apps are more secure than text messages. Never share a code with anyone who asks for it.

Phishing messages pretend to come from organisations you trust. Warning signs include urgency or threats, generic greetings, odd sender addresses, spelling mistakes and mismatched links, but modern phishing can look flawless. The safest habit: do not click links in unexpected messages. Open the official app or type the address yourself.

sections.key: Automatic updates close known security holes, and regular backups protect you from ransomware and device failure.
sections.b:
Software updates often patch security holes that attackers already know about and actively exploit. The Australian Signals Directorate lists patching applications and operating systems among its most important cyber security strategies. Turn on automatic updates for your phone, computer, browser and apps. Very old phones and routers that no longer receive updates are a risk worth replacing.

Ransomware and device failure can wipe out photos and documents. Back up important files regularly, ideally automatically to the cloud and to an external drive. Lock your devices with a PIN, password or biometrics, and turn on 'find my device'. Public Wi-Fi is less risky now that most websites are encrypted, but avoid banking on unknown networks.

sections.key: Details you post publicly, like birthdays and pet names, help scammers impersonate you or guess security answers.
sections.b:
Scammers and identity thieves piece together information from social media: your birthday, hometown, school, pet's name and holiday dates. These are often the answers to security questions, or useful for impersonation.

Review your privacy settings and limit what is public. Think before posting in real time that you are away from home. Be sceptical of quizzes asking for personal details. If an organisation you use suffers a data breach, change that password and watch for follow-up scams.

quiz.q: Why are ordinary people targeted by hackers?
o: Hackers pick victims by their wealth alone
Only people with famous names are attacked
Attacks are automated and email opens many accounts
Most attacks come from people the victim knows
quiz.e: Automated attacks target everyone, and one compromised email can open many accounts.

quiz.q: Why is reusing a password so dangerous?
o: Reused passwords expire much sooner than others
It slows down your device and your internet
Websites delete reused passwords automatically
One breach lets attackers try it elsewhere
quiz.e: Credential stuffing tries stolen details everywhere, so one breach can become many.

quiz.q: What is the safest response to an unexpected message asking you to log in?
o: Click the link and check the address later
Open the official app or type the address
Reply to ask if the message is genuine
Forward it to contacts to warn them
quiz.e: Going to the real site yourself avoids fake links, however convincing they look.

quiz.q: Why should you turn on automatic updates?
o: They make your device faster each time
They fix security holes criminals exploit
They delete old files to free up space
They replace the need for any passwords
quiz.e: Updates close known holes that criminals actively exploit.

quiz.q: Why can sharing your birthday, school and pet's name publicly be risky?
o: It makes your account harder to recover
It can reveal answers to security questions
Social media sites sell it to your bank
It stops you from using privacy settings
quiz.e: Scammers gather public details to guess security answers and pose as you.

LESSONS.push: A simple habit blocks most account takeovers. Most people never set it up.

LESSONS.title: First aid basics: DRSABCD
LESSONS.hook: The seven steps that could help you save a life. An overview to build confidence, not a replacement for a proper course.

sections.key: Australian first aid follows DRSABCD, starting with checking for danger before you approach anyone.
sections.b:
Knowing what to do in the first few minutes of an emergency can save a life. When someone's heart stops, every minute without CPR sharply reduces their chance of survival, and ambulances can take several minutes or more to arrive.

Australian first aid follows an action plan called DRSABCD, from the Australian Resuscitation Council. This lesson is an overview only. A hands-on course, from organisations such as St John Ambulance or Australian Red Cross, is the best way to learn and practise.

D is Danger. Before rushing in, check for danger to yourself, bystanders and the injured person: traffic, fire, electricity, deep water or aggressive people. You cannot help anyone if you become a casualty yourself. Wear gloves if available.

sections.key: Check whether the person responds, and if they do not, call Triple Zero (000) and send for an AED.
sections.b:
R is Response. Speak loudly and firmly squeeze their shoulders: can you hear me, open your eyes, what's your name, squeeze my hand. If they respond, make them comfortable, check for injuries and monitor them. If there is no response, get help.

S is Send for help. Call Triple Zero (000), or ask a bystander to while you help. From a mobile, 112 also works. Ask for an ambulance and put the phone on speaker. The operator can guide you step by step, including through CPR, so you are not alone. If an AED (defibrillator) is nearby, send someone to get it immediately. Many are listed on apps and found at shopping centres, gyms and sporting clubs.

sections.key: Clear the airway, then look, listen and feel for normal breathing for up to 10 seconds; gasping is not normal breathing.
sections.b:
A is Airway. Look in the person's mouth for anything blocking it, such as vomit, blood, food or loose teeth. If there is something, roll them onto their side and clear it. Then, with the person on their back, gently tilt the head back and lift the chin. For babies, keep the head in a neutral position rather than tilting it.

B is Breathing. Look for the chest rising and falling, listen and feel for breath on your cheek, for up to 10 seconds. Occasional gasping is not normal breathing and can happen in the first minutes after cardiac arrest. If they are breathing normally, place them in the recovery position, on their side with the top leg bent, and watch them until help arrives. If not, start CPR.

sections.key: Start CPR straight away if someone is unresponsive and not breathing normally; speed matters more than perfect technique.
sections.b:
C is CPR, short for cardiopulmonary resuscitation. It combines chest compressions with rescue breaths to keep some oxygen-carrying blood flowing to the brain and heart.

CPR on its own rarely restarts a stopped heart, but it buys precious time until a defibrillator or paramedics arrive. Start as soon as you have found that the person is unresponsive and not breathing normally. Starting quickly matters more than perfect technique. The CPR lesson walks you through exactly how to do it, including rescue breaths and how to adjust for children and babies.

sections.key: An AED analyses the heart rhythm and guides you, so attach it the moment it arrives while CPR continues.
sections.b:
The final D is Defibrillation: an electric shock that can reset a heart whose rhythm has become chaotic. An automated external defibrillator, or AED, is built for untrained bystanders. It analyses the heart rhythm itself and tells you what to do at every step.

Attach it the moment it arrives, keeping CPR going while it is set up. Notice where AEDs are kept at your workplace, gym, sports club or local shops. They are usually marked by a green sign with a heart and lightning bolt. The CPR lesson covers using one step by step.

quiz.q: What should you do first, before approaching an injured person?
o: Start compressions straight away
Move them somewhere more comfortable
Ask them to describe what happened
Check for danger to everyone nearby
quiz.e: You cannot help anyone if you become a casualty yourself.

quiz.q: If a person does not respond when you speak and squeeze their shoulders, what comes next?
o: Call Triple Zero (000) and send for an AED
Give them a drink to help them recover
Wait a few minutes to see if they wake
Carry them to your car to drive them
quiz.e: No response means getting an ambulance and an AED on the way.

quiz.q: Which of these counts as normal breathing?
o: Occasional gasping every few seconds
A chest rising and falling regularly
Snoring at any steady rate
A single deep breath now and then
quiz.e: Gasping can occur after cardiac arrest, so look for regular chest movement rather than occasional gasps.

quiz.q: Why does CPR matter even though it rarely restarts a stopped heart by itself?
o: It replaces the need for an ambulance
It keeps some blood flowing to the brain
It eases the person's pain until help comes
It is only needed for children and babies
quiz.e: CPR buys time, so starting quickly matters more than perfect technique.

quiz.q: What should you do when an AED arrives?
o: Wait for a trained professional to switch it on
Pause CPR until the AED has finished analysing
Attach it straight away and follow its prompts
Use it only on adults, never on children
quiz.e: An AED is designed for bystanders and guides you at each step.

LESSONS.push: Seven letters guide the first minutes of an emergency. Do you know them?

LESSONS.title: Speak with confidence
LESSONS.hook: The nerves never fully go away, even for professionals. These habits make them work for you.

sections.key: Nerves are a natural stress response, and calling them excitement works better than trying to calm down.
sections.b:
Fear of public speaking ranks alongside heights and spiders in many surveys. The racing heart, dry mouth and shaky hands are your fight-or-flight response, releasing adrenaline to prepare you for action. Even seasoned speakers, actors and politicians feel it. The audience notices far less than you think, an effect psychologists call the illusion of transparency.

Don't fight the feeling. Anxiety and excitement feel alike in the body. Harvard researcher Alison Wood Brooks found that people who said 'I am excited' aloud before a speech performed better than those who tried to calm down. Slow breathing, with long exhales, also helps settle the body.

sections.key: Build a talk around one message you can say in a sentence, then give it a simple structure and a story.
sections.b:
Audiences remember surprisingly little. Decide the single message you want them to leave with, and build everything around it. If you can't say it in one sentence, it isn't clear yet. Cut anything that doesn't support it, however interesting. Nobody has ever complained that a good talk finished five minutes early.

A simple structure works almost anywhere: open with a hook such as a question, a surprising fact or a short story; say what you'll cover; make two or three main points; then sum up and finish with a clear takeaway. Stories and concrete examples stick far better than lists of facts, because our brains are wired for narrative.

sections.key: Slides should support you rather than script you: few words, big visuals and one idea each.
sections.b:
Slides should support what you say, not repeat it. People can't read dense text and listen to you at the same time, so they end up doing neither well. Use few words, large fonts, and images or simple charts that make a point at a glance. One idea per slide is a good rule.

Never read your slides aloud. Here is a test: if the projector died, you should still be able to give the talk. If you couldn't, you're relying on the slides too much.

sections.key: Rehearse the whole talk aloud and standing, and record yourself once to spot filler words and rushing.
sections.b:
Reading your notes silently is not practice. Rehearse the whole talk out loud, ideally standing up, at least three times. Time it, because most people run long. Record yourself once on your phone and watch it back. It's uncomfortable, but you'll spot filler words like 'um', 'like' and 'you know', nervous habits like swaying, and the parts where you rush.

Know your opening lines especially well, since that's when nerves peak. After the first minute, most people settle.

sections.key: Slow down, pause, speak to individuals, and treat questions and slips calmly.
sections.b:
Nervous speakers rush. Slow down and pause before an important point, after a question and between sections. A pause feels endless to you but reads as confidence, gives listeners time to think and replaces filler words. Look at real people, one at a time, for a sentence or so, rather than at the back wall or your notes.

In question time, repeat each question so everyone hears it and you gain a moment to think. 'I don't know, but I'll find out' is a fine answer. If you lose your place, pause, glance at your notes and carry on; audiences are almost always on your side. Every talk makes the next easier, so practise at team meetings or a Toastmasters club.

quiz.q: Before a nerve-racking talk, which approach did Alison Wood Brooks's research find helps performance?
o: Telling yourself you feel excited
Telling yourself to calm down
Trying to ignore the nerves completely
Avoiding any mention of the nerves
quiz.e: Anxiety and excitement feel alike in the body, so relabelling the feeling is easier than calming it.

quiz.q: What should a good talk be built around?
o: Every interesting fact you know on the topic
As many main points as will fit in the time
A single message you can state in one sentence
A long list of statistics to prove your case
quiz.e: One clear message gives you something to build on and a reason to cut everything that does not support it.

quiz.q: How can you tell your slides are doing too much of the work?
o: They contain large fonts and a single image
You could not give the talk if the projector died
They show one idea at a time
They use a simple chart to make a point
quiz.e: Slides should support you, so you should be able to carry the talk without them.

quiz.q: Why is it worth recording yourself once while rehearsing?
o: To spot filler words and rushed sections
To avoid ever needing to practise aloud
To memorise the talk word for word
To check how long slides take to load
quiz.e: Watching yourself back shows habits you cannot notice while speaking.

quiz.q: What does a deliberate pause do for a speaker?
o: It signals you have lost your place
It sounds confident and replaces filler words
It makes the audience lose interest
It lets nerves build up before the next point
quiz.e: A pause feels long to you but reads as confidence and gives listeners time to think.

LESSONS.push: Calming down before a talk is harder than it sounds. Try this instead.

LESSONS.title: How to really listen (and be heard)
LESSONS.hook: Most arguments aren't about what they seem to be about. Better communication starts with listening.

sections.key: Most people listen to reply; active listening means full attention, reflecting back and asking open questions.
sections.b:
In most conversations we're waiting for our turn, planning a response or relating everything back to ourselves. Author Stephen Covey put it simply: most people listen with the intent to reply, not to understand. The other person can tell, and feeling genuinely heard is one of the most powerful things you can give someone.

Active listening is a set of simple skills. Give full attention: phone away, eye contact, no interrupting. Reflect back what you heard in your own words: 'So you're frustrated because you felt left out of the decision?' Ask open questions starting with what, how or tell me. And resist jumping in with solutions; people often want to be understood before they want advice.

sections.key: Naming a feeling calms a conversation, and 'I' statements raise problems without triggering defensiveness.
sections.b:
Simply naming what someone seems to feel, like 'That sounds really stressful', tends to lower the temperature. Brain-imaging research by psychologist Matthew Lieberman found that putting feelings into words reduced activity in the amygdala, a region involved in threat responses. Validation says 'your feelings make sense', not 'you're right'.

When raising a problem, how you start matters. 'You never help around the house' is an attack, so the other person defends themselves. An 'I' statement describes your experience instead: 'I feel overwhelmed when I do the dishes every night on my own. Could we take turns?' The formula: I feel [emotion] when [specific situation], because [why it matters]. Could we [request]? It focuses on behaviour and needs, not character.

sections.key: Criticism, contempt, defensiveness and stonewalling predict relationship breakdown, and each has an antidote.
sections.b:
Psychologist John Gottman studied thousands of couples and identified four patterns he called the four horsemen, because they predict relationship breakdown. Criticism attacks the person rather than the behaviour. Contempt, including sarcasm, eye-rolling and mockery, is the most damaging of all. Defensiveness means making excuses and refusing responsibility. Stonewalling is shutting down and withdrawing.

The antidotes: complain without blame, express appreciation, take responsibility for your part, and take a break to calm down. Appreciation matters because Gottman found that stable couples have around five positive interactions for every negative one during conflict.

sections.key: When flooded with emotion, pause for at least 20 minutes and agree a time to return.
sections.b:
When an argument escalates, your heart rate climbs and your body floods with stress hormones. In this state, called flooding, it's very hard to think clearly or listen, and people say things they regret.

Gottman's research suggests taking a break of at least 20 minutes and doing something calming, not rehearsing your arguments. Agree on a time to come back to the issue. Pausing isn't avoiding the problem; it gives both of you the chance to discuss it productively.

sections.key: Give feedback as Situation, Behaviour, Impact, and build good communication from small habits.
sections.b:
Feedback lands better when it's specific. The Situation–Behaviour–Impact model is simple. Describe the situation: 'In this morning's meeting…'. Describe the specific behaviour, not your interpretation: '…you interrupted Sam twice while she was presenting…'. Then the impact: '…and she didn't finish her point, so we missed her idea.' Then ask for their view. Give praise the same way; specific praise tells people what to repeat.

Small habits help too. Keep your phone out of sight, since research suggests even a visible phone can make conversations feel less close. Remember details people tell you. And when you get it wrong, a sincere, specific apology without a 'but' goes a long way.

quiz.q: Which of these is a key part of active listening?
o: Planning your reply while they talk
Offering advice as soon as they pause
Reflecting back what you heard in your own words
Keeping your phone nearby in case you need it
quiz.e: Reflecting back shows you understood and lets them correct you if you did not.

quiz.q: Which of these is an 'I' statement?
o: You never help out with the dishes at all
I feel overwhelmed when I do all the dishes
Why can't you ever do your fair share?
You always leave everything for me to do
quiz.e: An 'I' statement describes your experience and need, which makes defensiveness less likely.

quiz.q: What is the recommended antidote to criticism?
o: Withdrawing and waiting until it blows over
Using sarcasm to lighten the mood a little
Listing all the other person's past mistakes
Raising the behaviour without blaming the person
quiz.e: Criticism attacks character, so the fix is to raise the specific behaviour without blame.

quiz.q: Why take a break of at least 20 minutes during a heated argument?
o: It gives you time to plan stronger arguments
It lets stress hormones settle so you can think
It shows the other person you are winning
It lets you avoid the issue until it fades
quiz.e: Flooding makes clear thinking and listening very hard, so calming down comes first.

quiz.q: In the Situation–Behaviour–Impact model, what should you describe for the 'Behaviour' step?
o: What you think the person intended
What kind of person you believe they are
What you would like them to do next
What the person actually did or said
quiz.e: Specific, factual behaviour is easier to hear than a judgement about character.

LESSONS.push: Most of us listen only to reply. What changes when you do the opposite?

LESSONS.title: Time management that works
LESSONS.hook: You can't make more time. But you can stop losing it to the wrong things.

sections.key: The Eisenhower matrix sorts tasks by urgency and importance, and the biggest gains come from protecting important-but-not-urgent work.
sections.b:
In a 1954 speech, US President Dwight Eisenhower quoted a former college president: 'I have two kinds of problems, the urgent and the important. The urgent are not important, and the important are never urgent.'

The Eisenhower matrix sorts tasks into four boxes. Urgent and important: do it now, such as a crisis or deadline. Important but not urgent: schedule it, such as exercise, planning, relationships and learning. Urgent but not important: delegate or minimise, such as most interruptions and many emails. Neither: drop it. Most people live in the urgent boxes. The biggest gains come from protecting time for the important-but-not-urgent work.

sections.key: Work expands to fill the time you allow, and we underestimate how long tasks take, so set tight limits and add a buffer.
sections.b:
In 1955, historian C. Northcote Parkinson wrote that 'work expands so as to fill the time available for its completion.' Give yourself a week for a report and it takes a week. Timeboxing, setting a fixed block for a task, uses this to your advantage. Decide what 'good enough' looks like first, so perfectionism doesn't swallow the extra time.

Psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky named the planning fallacy: we underestimate how long tasks take, even when similar ones ran long before. We imagine the best case and forget interruptions. The Sydney Opera House was due to open in early 1963 and opened in 1973, ten years late and hugely over budget. Check how long similar tasks really took, then add a buffer, often 50% or more.

sections.key: Schedule important work in your calendar and protect it from interruptions, because multitasking is just costly task-switching.
sections.b:
A to-do list tells you what to do, not when. Time blocking means scheduling tasks in your calendar as if they were meetings: 9 to 10.30 am, write proposal. It shows how much time you really have and reduces decision fatigue. Put demanding work in your peak energy hours, often the morning, and leave buffer blocks for the unexpected.

Multitasking is mostly a myth. The brain switches between demanding tasks rather than doing both at once, and each switch costs time and attention. Research on interruptions suggests it can take many minutes to refocus on a complex task. Batch small tasks like emails into set times and turn off non-essential alerts. An hour of uninterrupted work can beat a distracted afternoon.

sections.key: If a task takes less than two minutes, do it now, and keep everything else in one trusted list.
sections.b:
David Allen, author of Getting Things Done, suggests a simple rule: if a task takes less than two minutes, do it immediately instead of writing it down or putting it off. Reply to the quick email, file the document, book the appointment. It stops small tasks piling up into a mental burden.

Allen's broader insight is that your mind is for having ideas, not holding them. Capture every other task in one trusted list or app so your brain can stop trying to remember everything.

sections.key: A short weekly review sets your priorities, and every yes is a no to something else.
sections.b:
Once a week, often Friday afternoon or Sunday evening, spend 20 to 30 minutes reviewing. Look at what you finished, what's still open and what's coming up. Clear your inboxes and notes into your task list. Choose your three most important priorities for the week ahead and block time for them. It stops tasks slipping through the cracks and turns vague stress into a plan.

Then protect those priorities. Every yes is a no to something else, so ask what a new commitment will replace. You can decline politely: 'Thanks for thinking of me, but I can't take that on right now.' Some people use a rule: if it's not a clear yes, it's a no.

quiz.q: In the Eisenhower matrix, what should you do with important but not urgent tasks?
o: Drop them
Delegate them
Do them instantly
Schedule them
quiz.e: Exercise, planning and learning rarely feel urgent, so they only happen if you schedule them.

quiz.q: Why is it wise to add a buffer to your time estimates?
o: We picture the best case and miss interruptions
Most tasks are finished faster than expected
Deadlines are rarely enforced in practice
Longer estimates make the work more enjoyable
quiz.e: The planning fallacy makes us underestimate, even when we know similar tasks ran long.

quiz.q: What really happens when you 'multitask' on demanding work?
o: You complete both tasks at full quality
You switch between them and lose time each switch
You finish both tasks in half the usual time
Your brain handles both tasks fully in parallel
quiz.e: The brain switches rather than doing two demanding things at once, so batching and quiet blocks work better.

quiz.q: What does the two-minute rule say?
o: Take a two-minute break from work every hour
Reply to every email within two minutes of receiving it
If a task takes under two minutes, do it now
Work on any single task for two minutes at a time
quiz.e: Doing quick tasks immediately stops them piling up into a mental burden.

quiz.q: Why ask what a new commitment will replace before agreeing to it?
o: Because it makes you look more organised
Because every yes is a no to something else
Because new commitments are always unimportant
Because declining is rude
quiz.e: Your time is limited, so saying no to lesser things makes room for what matters most.

LESSONS.push: The Sydney Opera House opened ten years late. Your to-do list has the same flaw.

LESSONS.title: Cooking fundamentals
LESSONS.hook: You don't need recipes to cook well. You need to understand salt, fat, acid, heat and a few core techniques.

sections.key: Good cooking rests on salt, fat, acid and heat, and salt works best added in stages while you taste.
sections.b:
Recipes are useful, but confident cooks understand principles. Chef and author Samin Nosrat boiled good cooking down to four elements in her book Salt Fat Acid Heat: salt enhances flavour, fat carries flavour and creates texture, acid balances and brightens, and heat transforms food. Once you understand them, you can improvise and rescue a bland dish. The best habit is to taste as you go.

Salt makes food taste more like itself and reduces bitterness. Season in stages, because salt added early has time to penetrate. Salt pasta water generously. Salting meat 40 minutes to a day ahead keeps it juicy and seasoned. Still moderate your overall salt intake; much of it comes from processed foods.

sections.key: Butter burns early because of its milk solids, so match the fat to the job.
sections.b:
Different fats suit different jobs. Butter tastes wonderful, but its milk solids start to burn at around 150°C. For high-heat searing, add it near the end or use ghee, clarified butter with the milk solids removed, which copes with far more heat. Neutral oils such as peanut or canola suit woks and deep-frying.

Smoke point isn't the whole story. Laboratory studies, including Australian research, have found extra virgin olive oil among the most stable oils under heat, likely helped by its natural antioxidants. Fat also builds texture: cold butter rubbed into flour makes flaky pastry. And never pour used oil down the sink, where it sets and clogs pipes.

sections.key: Tough, collagen-rich cuts turn tender with long, gentle, moist cooking, while lean cuts suit fast, hot cooking.
sections.b:
Choosing the right heat starts with the cut. Lean, tender cuts such as fillet, loin and chicken breast have little connective tissue. They suit quick, hot methods like grilling and pan-frying, and dry out if cooked too long.

Hard-working muscles such as beef shin, chuck, brisket and lamb shoulder are full of collagen, a tough connective protein. Cooked gently in liquid for hours, collagen slowly melts into gelatine, giving meat that falls apart and a silky sauce. Keep a braise at a bare simmer, not a rolling boil, which tightens the muscle fibres and dries the meat. If a stew is still tough, it usually needs more time, not more heat.

sections.key: Read the recipe and prepare everything before heating the pan, then master a few flexible meal templates.
sections.b:
Mise en place is French for 'everything in its place', and it separates calm cooks from frantic ones. Before any heat goes on, read the whole recipe, then wash, chop, measure and line up every ingredient. Chef Anthony Bourdain called it the religion of all good line cooks. It matters most for fast cooking like stir-fries, and reading ahead catches surprises such as meat that needs marinating overnight.

Rather than collecting hundreds of recipes, master a few templates. Stir-fry: hot pan, protein, vegetables, a sauce of soy, garlic, ginger and something sweet or sour. Tray bake: vegetables and protein roasted with oil, salt and spices at about 200°C. Soup: soften onion and garlic, add vegetables, stock and beans, simmer. And eggs. Swap freely and taste as you go.

sections.key: Meat keeps cooking after leaving the heat, and pasta is best finished in the sauce with some starchy water.
sections.b:
Food doesn't stop cooking when it leaves the heat. The hot outer layers push heat inward, so a steak's centre climbs a few more degrees as it sits, and a big roast more. This carryover cooking is why cooks pull meat slightly early. Resting also keeps meat juicier. Rest a steak about five minutes and a roast ten to twenty, loosely covered with foil. A meat thermometer removes the guesswork.

For pasta, stir well in the first minute or two, when it is stickiest; oil in the water doesn't help. Stop when it's al dente, tender with a slight bite. Scoop out a cup of cooking water, then finish the pasta in the pan with the sauce and splashes of that starchy water so it turns glossy and clings.

quiz.q: Why is it better to season in stages and salt meat well ahead of cooking?
o: It makes the food cook noticeably faster
It draws most of the fat out of the meat
Early salt has time to penetrate the food
It kills the bacteria on the food surface
quiz.e: Early salt works its way into the food, so it tastes seasoned all the way through.

quiz.q: Why is ghee better than butter for high-heat searing?
o: Ghee contains much more salt than butter
Ghee has no milk solids to burn early
Ghee is mostly water, so it stays cooler
Butter always tastes bitter when heated
quiz.e: Removing the milk solids lets ghee handle far more heat before it burns.

quiz.q: Why do cuts like beef shin and chuck suit long, slow cooking?
o: Their collagen slowly melts into gelatine
They contain almost no connective tissue
They cook faster than fillet
Slow cooking adds extra protein
quiz.e: Gentle, moist heat melts collagen into gelatine, making tough cuts tender.

quiz.q: Why should you read the recipe and prepare all ingredients before turning on the heat?
o: It lets the oven preheat for much longer
It avoids a mid-cook scramble and surprises
It makes the finished dish much healthier
It reduces how much salt you need to add
quiz.e: Mise en place keeps you calm, especially in fast cooking where there is no time to chop.

quiz.q: Why do cooks take a steak off the heat slightly before it reaches the target temperature?
o: The steak shrinks if it is cooked fully
Resting only works on undercooked meat
Carryover cooking keeps heating the centre
The pan must cool down before serving
quiz.e: Heat from the outer layers keeps moving inward after the meat leaves the pan.

LESSONS.push: Four simple elements sit behind almost every good meal. Can you name them?

LESSONS.title: Home maintenance basics
LESSONS.hook: Ten minutes a month and a few checks a year prevent the expensive, and dangerous, problems. Renters, this is for you too.

sections.key: Know where your water main, switchboard and gas shut-off are, and test your safety switches every three months.
sections.b:
The time to find your water shut-off valve is not when a pipe has burst. Locate three things now: the water main tap, usually near the water meter at the front of the property; the switchboard and main switch; and, if you have gas, the meter and its shut-off valve. Show everyone in the household, and keep a working torch you can find in the dark.

A safety switch, or residual current device (RCD), cuts power in a fraction of a second if electricity leaks, for example through a person. Test it every three months by pressing the 'T' button; power to those circuits should cut off, then flip the switch back up. If it doesn't trip, call a licensed electrician.

sections.key: Test smoke alarms monthly, replace them every 10 years, and clear dryer lint every load.
sections.b:
Working smoke alarms save lives, and they're required by law in Australian homes. Test each one monthly by pressing the test button, and vacuum dust from the vents occasionally. Replace alarms that are 10 years old or more; the date is usually printed on the alarm.

Fire services recommend photoelectric alarms, ideally interconnected so they all sound together, in bedrooms, hallways and on every level. Rules differ by state; Queensland, for example, is phasing in interconnected photoelectric alarms in every bedroom.

Clear the clothes dryer's lint filter every load, because lint build-up is a common cause of house fires.

sections.key: Check for hidden leaks with your water meter, fix drips early, and keep moisture and gutters under control.
sections.b:
A dripping tap can waste thousands of litres a year, and a hidden leak can cause major damage. To check, turn off every tap, note the water meter reading, wait an hour without using water and check again. If it has moved, you have a leak. Watch for damp patches, bubbling paint, musty smells or high bills, and replace worn silicone around showers and baths.

Mould thrives on moisture and poor airflow. Run the bathroom exhaust fan during and after showers, open windows, dry clothes outside and fix leaks promptly. Large or recurring mould may mean a hidden leak that needs a professional.

Clean gutters before storm and bushfire seasons: blocked ones overflow into roofs and walls, and dry leaves are an ignition risk from embers.

sections.key: Electrical, gas and most plumbing work needs a licensed tradesperson, and homes built before 1990 may contain asbestos.
sections.b:
Plenty of jobs are fine to DIY: painting, changing tap washers, patching small holes, assembling furniture. But electrical work, gas fitting and most plumbing must be done by licensed tradespeople in Australia, for good safety reasons.

Be especially careful when renovating homes built before 1990, which may contain asbestos in walls, eaves, floors and roofing. Disturbing it can release deadly fibres. If you're not sure, get it tested before drilling, cutting or sanding. Check the roof for loose tiles or sheets after big storms from the ground, with binoculars, rather than climbing up. And always check for underground services through Before You Dig Australia before digging.

sections.key: Renters should report repairs in writing, because urgent repairs must be fixed quickly.
sections.b:
If you rent, most repairs are the landlord's responsibility, but you need to report them. Always report problems in writing, such as by email, and keep copies.

Every state distinguishes urgent repairs, like a burst water pipe, gas leak, dangerous electrical fault or broken hot water system, which must be fixed quickly, from general repairs, which must be done within a reasonable time. Take dated photos at the start of your lease for your condition report. Your state's tenancy authority has free guides and advice.

quiz.q: How should you test a safety switch (RCD)?
o: Press the test button every three months
Flip the main switch off once a year
Unplug every appliance in the house monthly
Call an electrician to test it every month
quiz.e: A regular test confirms the switch will cut power in a fraction of a second when needed.

quiz.q: How often should you test a smoke alarm, and when should you replace it?
o: Test yearly and replace after 20 years
Test monthly and replace after 10 years
Test weekly and replace after 2 years
Test only when it beeps and replace after 5
quiz.e: Alarms are tested monthly and wear out, so those 10 years or older should be replaced.

quiz.q: How can you check for a hidden water leak?
o: Listen at the walls for dripping sounds
Turn off all taps and watch the water meter
Wait for the next water bill to arrive
Check whether the gutters are clear
quiz.e: If the meter moves when nothing is using water, water is escaping somewhere.

quiz.q: Why take extra care when renovating a home built before 1990?
o: The wiring in these homes is always unsafe
It may contain asbestos, deadly if disturbed
The home must be inspected by council first
Older homes cannot be painted or patched
quiz.e: If you are unsure, get materials tested before drilling, cutting or sanding.

quiz.q: How should a renter report a repair problem?
o: Mention it in passing at the next inspection
Wait until the lease ends to raise it
Tell your neighbours and wait for a reply
In writing, such as by email, keeping copies
quiz.e: A written record shows you reported it and when, which matters if repairs are delayed.

LESSONS.push: Do you know where your water main is? Better to find out before a leak.

LESSONS.title: Car basics everyone should know
LESSONS.hook: A few simple checks keep you safer, save money on fuel and repairs, and stop you being stranded on the side of the road.

sections.key: Check tyre pressure monthly when cold using the car's placard, and replace tyres worn to the tread indicators.
sections.b:
Tyres are your only contact with the road, so they matter enormously for braking and handling. Check the pressure at least once a month and before long trips, when the tyres are cold. The correct pressure is on a placard, usually inside the driver's door or fuel flap, not the maximum printed on the tyre. Under-inflated tyres wear faster, increase fuel use and can overheat; over-inflated tyres reduce grip.

Tread channels water away so the tyre grips wet roads. In most of Australia, the legal minimum is 1.5 millimetres. Raised bars in the grooves, called tread wear indicators, show when it's time to replace the tyre. Look for cracks, bulges or uneven wear, and know where your spare and jack are.

sections.key: Red warning lights mean stop safely and investigate, amber means get it checked, and fluids need regular checks.
sections.b:
Dashboard warning lights follow a colour code. Red means a potentially serious problem, such as oil pressure, engine temperature, brake or battery warnings: stop when it's safe and investigate. Amber or orange means attention soon, such as the check engine, low tyre pressure or ABS lights. Green or blue lights are just information. Your owner's manual explains every symbol.

Every month or so, with the engine cold and the car on level ground, check the oil on the dipstick; it should sit between the minimum and maximum marks. Check the coolant in the overflow reservoir, but never open a radiator cap on a hot engine, as scalding liquid can spray out. Check brake fluid and top up the washer fluid. A sudden drop in any fluid can mean a leak.

sections.key: Follow the logbook service schedule, expect a battery to last about three to five years, and consider roadside assistance.
sections.b:
Your logbook sets out when the car needs servicing, usually by time or distance, such as every 12 months or 15,000 kilometres. Regular servicing replaces oil and filters, checks brakes and belts, and catches problems when they're cheaper to fix. In Australia you don't have to use the dealer to keep your new-car warranty, as long as the service follows the manufacturer's specifications and uses suitable parts. Keep records; they help resale value.

Car batteries typically last three to five years, often less in hot climates. A sluggish start and dim lights are warning signs. Roadside assistance, through motoring clubs like the RACQ or NRMA, some insurers or new-car warranties, covers breakdowns, flat batteries and lockouts. If you break down, pull over as far off the road as possible and turn on your hazard lights.

sections.key: Smooth driving, correct tyre pressure and less weight all cut fuel use.
sections.b:
How you drive makes a big difference to fuel use. Accelerate smoothly, look ahead to avoid unnecessary braking and keep to steady speeds. Driving at 110 km/h uses noticeably more fuel than at 90 or 100.

Correct tyre pressure, removing roof racks when not in use and clearing heavy junk from the boot all help. Fuel prices in many Australian cities follow a regular cycle, and fuel price apps and state government websites show where it's cheapest nearby.

sections.key: After a crash, stop, switch on hazard lights, check for injuries, call 000 if needed and exchange details.
sections.b:
If you're in a crash, you must stop. Turn on your hazard lights, check yourself and others for injuries, and call Triple Zero (000) if anyone is hurt, if there's a danger such as fire or leaking fuel, or if a driver leaves without exchanging details.

Exchange names, addresses, registration numbers and insurance details with the other drivers. Take photos of the scene and damage. Don't admit fault at the scene. Reporting requirements to police vary by state, so check your own state's rules.

quiz.q: Where do you find the correct tyre pressure for your car?
o: The maximum figure printed on the tyre wall
A sign at the nearest service station
On the placard inside the door or fuel flap
It is the same for almost every car
quiz.e: The placard gives the pressure for your car, while the tyre wall shows only the tyre's maximum.

quiz.q: What does a red dashboard warning light usually mean?
o: Stop safely and check what is wrong
The headlights have been left on
A routine service is due next year
It is only there for information
quiz.e: Red signals a potentially serious fault, while amber means get it checked soon.

quiz.q: In Australia, what is needed to keep your new-car warranty when servicing?
o: Every service must be done at the dealer
Servicing only matters in the first year
Only the manufacturer's own parts may be used
Service to the manufacturer's specifications
quiz.e: You can choose where to service, provided the work follows the manufacturer's schedule and specifications.

quiz.q: Which habit helps cut fuel use?
o: Accelerating hard and braking late
Driving smoothly at steady speeds
Leaving a roof rack on all year
Running with under-inflated tyres
quiz.e: Smooth driving, correct tyre pressure and less weight all reduce the fuel you burn.

quiz.q: What should you do straight after a crash?
o: Leave quickly to avoid blocking traffic
Admit fault so the matter is settled quickly
Stop, switch on hazard lights, check injuries
Wait a day before contacting the other driver
