quiz.e: You must stop, make the scene safe, check for injuries, call 000 if needed and exchange details.

LESSONS.push: The number printed on your tyre isn't the pressure you should use.

LESSONS.title: How compound interest works
LESSONS.hook: Interest that earns interest. It's the most powerful force in personal finance, working for you or against you.

sections.key: Compound interest pays interest on your original money plus the interest already earned, so growth snowballs.
sections.b:
Interest is the price of money: what a bank pays you for your savings, or a lender charges you for borrowing. Simple interest is paid only on your original amount, the principal. Compound interest is paid on the principal plus the interest you've already earned. Your money earns money, and then that money earns money too. The same maths applies to investments that reinvest their returns.

Put $10,000 in an account paying 5% a year and leave the interest in. After one year you have $10,500. In year two you earn 5% on $10,500, so you gain $525 and have $11,025. The extra $25 is interest on interest. After 10 years you'd have about $16,300; after 20, about $26,500; after 30, about $43,200, more than four times the original, without adding a dollar.

sections.key: Compound growth starts slowly and accelerates, so starting early often matters more than how much you invest.
sections.b:
Growth curves upward, gently at first, then steeply. In the example above, the first 10 years added about $6,300, while the last 10 added about $16,700 from the same $10,000. Many people give up in the early years, just before the curve bends upwards.

Here's a famous comparison at a 7% annual return. Alex invests $5,000 a year from age 25 to 35, then stops: $50,000 in total. Sam starts at 35 and invests $5,000 every year until 65: $150,000 in total. At 65, Alex has more than Sam despite contributing a third as much, because Alex's money had an extra decade to compound. It's never too late to start, but small amounts started early are extraordinarily powerful.

sections.key: Divide 72 by the annual interest rate to estimate how many years it takes money to double.
sections.b:
A handy shortcut: divide 72 by the annual rate to estimate how many years it takes to double your money. At 6%, it doubles in about 12 years. At 9%, about 8 years. At 2%, a typical savings rate in some years, about 36 years.

It works in reverse too: to double your money in 10 years, you'd need a return of about 7.2%. The rule is an approximation, but it's accurate enough for rates between about 2% and 15%.

sections.key: Compounding also makes high-interest debt grow fast, so paying it off is a guaranteed return.
sections.b:
Compounding is just as powerful in reverse. Credit cards in Australia often charge around 20% interest a year. By the rule of 72, an unpaid balance would roughly double in under four years. Paying only the minimum each month can stretch a modest debt over a decade or more, costing far more in interest than the original purchase.

That's why paying down high-interest debt is often one of the best 'returns' you can get: it's a guaranteed saving at that rate.

sections.key: Compare accounts by effective annual rate, and remember that fees and inflation compound too.
sections.b:
Interest can be added annually, monthly or even daily. The more often it's added, the sooner it earns interest itself. At 5%, monthly compounding gives an effective annual return of about 5.12%, against 5% for yearly compounding. When comparing savings accounts, look for the effective annual rate, and watch for 'bonus' rates that only apply if you meet conditions each month.

Anything expressed as a yearly percentage compounds, including costs. A super or investment fund charging 1% more in fees each year doesn't sound like much, but over 30 years it can cut your final balance by tens of thousands of dollars. Inflation compounds too, shrinking what your money can buy. So start early, be patient, keep fees low and pay off expensive debt.

quiz.q: What makes compound interest different from simple interest?
o: The interest rate is always much higher
You earn interest on your earlier interest too
Interest is paid just once, at the start
The interest is always completely tax-free
quiz.e: Interest added to the balance starts earning interest itself, which makes growth snowball.

quiz.q: Why did Alex, who invested for only ten years, end up with more than Sam?
o: Alex's money had an extra decade to grow
Alex earned a higher rate of return than Sam
Sam stopped investing at the age of 55
Alex invested larger amounts every year
quiz.e: Time in the market is a more powerful ingredient than the total amount contributed.

quiz.q: Using the rule of 72, roughly how long does money take to double at 8%?
o: 6 years
12 years
9 years
72 years
quiz.e: Divide 72 by the rate: 72 ÷ 8 gives about 9 years.

quiz.q: Why is an unpaid 20% credit card balance so dangerous?
o: It stays the same size if left alone
It roughly doubles in under four years
The interest rate falls each year
Interest is only charged on new purchases
quiz.e: Compounding works in reverse on debt, so high rates grow balances quickly.

quiz.q: Why can a 1% yearly fee on a super fund cost tens of thousands of dollars over 30 years?
o: Fees are only charged once, at the very start
Fees come out yearly, and the lost growth compounds
Fees apply only to the original deposit you made
Fees are all refunded to you at retirement
quiz.e: Costs expressed as a yearly percentage compound just like returns do.

LESSONS.push: Alex invested for ten years and stopped. Sam invested for thirty. Who won?

LESSONS.title: How the stock market works
LESSONS.hook: What you're actually buying when you buy a share, why prices jump around, and how ordinary people build wealth with it.

sections.key: A share is a small slice of ownership in a company, bought and sold on exchanges like the ASX.
sections.b:
A share, or stock, is a small slice of ownership in a company. If a company has a million shares and you own 1,000, you own 0.1% of it, including a claim on 0.1% of its future profits. Companies sell shares to raise money without borrowing, and shareholders can usually vote on big decisions. If the company does well, your slice becomes more valuable; if it fails, it can become worthless.

A stock exchange is a marketplace where shares are traded. Australia's main one is the ASX, formed in 1987 from the merger of earlier state exchanges. Most trading is electronic. A company's first public sale of shares is an initial public offering, or IPO. After that, investors trade with each other, and the company doesn't get the money from those trades.

sections.key: Prices follow supply and demand driven by expected profits, and crashes are a normal part of investing.
sections.b:
If more people want to buy than sell, the price rises. Underneath, buyers are betting on future profits. Prices react to earnings, scandals, interest rates and the economy. In the short term, fear and excitement drive them; in the long run, they tend to follow real profits.

A rising market is a bull market, and a fall of 20% or more from a peak is a bear market. Markets fell sharply in 1987, in the 2008–09 financial crisis, and in early 2020, when the ASX lost over a third of its value in about a month. Broad markets have historically recovered, though it can take years, and past performance guarantees nothing.

sections.key: Investors earn from capital gains when prices rise and from dividends, which come with franking credits in Australia.
sections.b:
There are two main ways to make money from shares. If the price rises and you sell for more than you paid, that's a capital gain. And many companies pay part of their profits to shareholders as dividends, usually twice a year in Australia.

Australian companies often attach franking credits to dividends. They represent company tax already paid, and can reduce the tax you owe. Reinvesting dividends to buy more shares is a powerful way to compound growth.

sections.key: Index funds spread risk cheaply, and long-term diversified investing differs from day trading and tips.
sections.b:
An index tracks a group of stocks. The ASX 200 tracks the 200 largest companies on the ASX; the S&P 500 tracks 500 large US companies. An index fund, often an exchange-traded fund (ETF), simply buys every company in an index, giving you a tiny slice of hundreds of businesses at low cost. Most professional fund managers fail to beat their index over the long term, once fees are included.

Holding a broad index fund for decades is very different from day-trading or chasing tips on social media. Studies consistently find most day traders lose money over time, after costs. Invest for the long term, diversify, keep fees low, don't try to time the market, and never invest money you might need soon. This is general information, not personal advice; a licensed adviser can help.

sections.key: Listed companies must announce price-sensitive news promptly, and trading on inside information is a serious crime.
sections.b:
A fair market needs everyone to have access to the same important information. Under the ASX's continuous disclosure rules, a listed company must immediately announce anything a reasonable person would expect to affect its share price materially, such as a big new contract, a profit downgrade or a takeover offer. If news is about to break, the company can ask for a trading halt so no one trades on half the story.

Buying or selling shares using price-sensitive information that isn't public, or tipping someone else off, is insider trading. It's a serious crime in Australia, carrying up to 10 years' jail, and the corporate regulator, ASIC, investigates suspicious trades.

quiz.q: What does owning a share mean?
o: You have lent money to the company
You own a small part of the company
You work for the company
You are guaranteed a fixed return
quiz.e: A share is a slice of ownership, so you share in the company's success or failure.

quiz.q: In the long run, what do share prices tend to follow?
o: Media headlines
Changes in the mood of investors each day
The company's real profits
The number of shares traded each week
quiz.e: Fear and excitement move prices in the short term, but over time profits matter most.

quiz.q: What do franking credits attached to an Australian dividend represent?
o: A fee charged each time you buy shares
Company tax already paid, which offsets your tax
A bonus paid out by the exchange itself
The price you originally paid for the shares
quiz.e: Franking credits stop company profits being taxed twice in the hands of shareholders.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of an index fund?
o: It guarantees you will beat all fund managers
It lets you own a slice of many businesses cheaply
It removes all risk of losing money
It lets you predict future market crashes
quiz.e: Buying the whole index spreads risk across many companies while keeping fees low.

quiz.q: What is insider trading?
o: Buying shares through a licensed broker
Owning shares in the company where you work
Buying shares in every company in an index
Trading on secret price-sensitive information
quiz.e: Markets stay fair only if no one profits from information that others cannot see.

LESSONS.push: Why a company doesn't receive a cent when you buy its shares on the market.

LESSONS.title: What inflation really is
LESSONS.hook: Why a dollar buys less every year, what the Reserve Bank does about it and what it means for your money.

sections.key: Inflation is the general rise in prices, measured in Australia by the Consumer Price Index.
sections.b:
Inflation is the general rise in prices across the economy over time. When inflation is 3%, something that cost $100 last year costs about $103 today, so each dollar buys a little less. Individual prices move around; petrol might jump while TVs get cheaper. Inflation is about the overall level. Over decades it adds up: something that cost $1 in 1990 costs well over $2 today.

The Australian Bureau of Statistics tracks a 'basket' of goods and services a typical household buys, from bread and petrol to rent and haircuts. The change in its cost is the Consumer Price Index, or CPI. Each item is weighted by household spending, so housing counts for far more than tea. Since late 2025, the ABS has published a complete CPI every month, replacing the quarterly figure as the headline measure.

sections.key: Inflation comes from demand outstripping supply or rising costs, and extreme cases become hyperinflation.
sections.b:
Demand-pull inflation happens when people and businesses want to buy more than the economy can produce, so sellers raise prices. Cost-push inflation happens when the cost of making things rises, such as wages, energy or shipping, and businesses pass it on. The surge after COVID-19 was both: supply chains were disrupted and energy prices spiked while demand bounced back. Australia's inflation peaked at 7.8% in late 2022.

Extreme, runaway inflation is hyperinflation, often defined as prices rising more than 50% in a month. It usually happens when governments print money to pay debts. In Germany in 1923, people carted cash around in wheelbarrows. Zimbabwe's peaked in 2008, and it went on to print a 100 trillion dollar note.

sections.key: The RBA aims for 2–3% inflation, raising interest rates to cool it, because a little inflation is healthier than falling prices.
sections.b:
Why not aim for zero? A little inflation gives central banks room to cut rates in a downturn. Deflation, a general fall in prices, can be damaging: people delay purchases, businesses cut jobs and debts become harder to repay. Japan struggled with low growth and deflation for years.

The Reserve Bank of Australia aims to keep inflation between 2% and 3%, focusing on the 2.5% midpoint. Its main tool is the cash rate, which flows through to mortgage, loan and savings rates. When inflation is too high, the RBA raises rates. Borrowing becomes dearer, mortgage holders have less to spend, businesses invest less and demand cools. When the economy is weak, it cuts rates. Changes take a year or more to fully work through.

sections.key: Inflation hurts savers earning low interest and people whose pay lags prices, and can help borrowers.
sections.b:
Inflation doesn't hit everyone equally. Savers lose out when inflation runs higher than the interest they earn, because their money's buying power shrinks. People on fixed incomes, or whose wages rise slower than prices, see their living standards fall. Borrowers with fixed debts can benefit, because the real value of what they owe shrinks over time.

Economists talk about 'real' figures, meaning adjusted for inflation. A 4% pay rise with 5% inflation is actually a 1% real pay cut.

sections.key: You can soften inflation by earning more than it on savings and investments, and by reviewing your pay and bills.
sections.b:
You can't control inflation, but you can soften its effect. Keep an emergency fund in a high-interest savings account rather than a zero-interest transaction account. For long-term money, investments like shares and property have historically outpaced inflation over long periods, though with more risk.

Review your pay regularly, since employers may not raise it automatically. And shop around on big recurring bills like insurance, energy and phone plans, which often creep up when you stay with the same provider.

quiz.q: What does the Consumer Price Index measure?
o: The change in cost of a basket of everyday goods
The total value of all shares on the market
The interest rate on overnight loans between banks
The total size of the national economy
quiz.e: CPI tracks a weighted household basket, and its change is the headline measure of inflation.

quiz.q: What is demand-pull inflation?
o: Prices rising because production costs have fallen
Prices rising as people want more than is made
Prices falling because of weak consumer spending
Prices that are set directly by the government
quiz.e: When demand outstrips supply, sellers raise prices.

quiz.q: How does the Reserve Bank usually respond to high inflation?
o: By cutting taxes across the economy
By setting prices directly for shops
By raising interest rates to cool demand
By printing more money for the banks
quiz.e: Higher rates make borrowing dearer, so spending and demand cool.

quiz.q: You get a 4% pay rise while inflation is 5%. What is your real pay change?
o: About −1%
quiz.e: Real figures adjust for inflation, so a pay rise below inflation is a real cut.

quiz.q: Why keep an emergency fund in a high-interest savings account rather than a zero-interest transaction account?
o: The interest offsets some of inflation's bite
It means the money is not taxed at all
It protects the money from every kind of risk
It makes the money easier to spend each day
quiz.e: Money earning nothing loses buying power every year that prices rise.

LESSONS.push: A 4% pay rise can still leave you worse off. Here's how.

LESSONS.title: Budgeting that actually works
LESSONS.hook: A budget isn't a diet for your money. It's a plan that gives every dollar a job, and it takes about 20 minutes to set up.

sections.key: A budget is a plan for your money, and the first step is tracking where it currently goes.
sections.b:
A budget is simply a plan: deciding in advance where your money goes instead of wondering afterwards where it went. It's not about never spending on fun; it's about spending on what matters to you. Surveys consistently find money is one of the biggest sources of stress for Australians, and knowing your numbers replaces vague anxiety with a plan.

Start with reality. Most banking apps sort your spending into categories automatically. Look back over one to three months. Many people are surprised by the total of small regular purchases: coffees, takeaway, delivery fees and forgotten subscriptions. Don't judge yet; just get the facts. Include irregular costs like car rego, insurance and Christmas by dividing the yearly cost by 12.

sections.key: Aim for about 50% of after-tax income on needs, 30% on wants and 20% on savings and extra debt repayments.
sections.b:
A simple starting framework, popularised by US senator and former Harvard professor Elizabeth Warren, is the 50/30/20 rule. About 50% of after-tax income goes on needs: rent or mortgage, groceries, utilities, transport and insurance. About 30% goes on wants: eating out, entertainment, hobbies and holidays. And 20% goes on savings and paying down debt faster.

In high-cost cities, needs often take more than half, so treat the numbers as a guide and adjust them to fit your life.

sections.key: Automatically move savings out on payday and build an emergency fund of three to six months of essentials.
sections.b:
The most effective budgeting habit is automation. Set up an automatic transfer to a separate savings account on payday, before you can spend it. Money you never see in your everyday account is much easier not to spend. Many Australians use 'buckets': separate accounts for bills, everyday spending, savings goals and emergencies.

Life guarantees surprises: a car repair, a vet bill, a job loss. An emergency fund turns crises into inconveniences. A common target is three to six months of essential expenses in an easy-access, high-interest savings account. That sounds like a lot, so start with a smaller goal like $1,000. Without a buffer, surprises tend to land on a credit card, where they grow.

sections.key: The avalanche method saves the most interest, while the snowball builds momentum.
sections.b:
Credit cards often charge around 20% interest, so paying one off is like earning a guaranteed 20% return. Two popular methods: with the avalanche, you pay the minimum on everything and throw extra money at the debt with the highest interest rate, which saves the most money. With the snowball, you clear the smallest balance first, building momentum through quick wins.

Be wary of buy now, pay later services too. They're convenient, but missed payments bring fees and they make it easy to overspend.

sections.key: Review recurring bills each year, allow fun money, and check in monthly to keep your budget going.
sections.b:
The easiest savings are often recurring costs you've stopped noticing. Cancel subscriptions you don't use. Once a year, compare your energy, insurance, internet and phone plans; loyalty is rarely rewarded, and switching can save hundreds of dollars. The Australian Government's Energy Made Easy site compares electricity and gas offers for free (in Victoria, use Victorian Energy Compare).

The best budget is one you'll keep. Include guilt-free fun money, or you'll eventually rebel. Check in monthly for 15 minutes. Give your savings a purpose, like a holiday or house deposit, and expect imperfect months. This is general information, not personal financial advice; the National Debt Helpline (1800 007 007) offers free help if debts feel overwhelming.

quiz.q: What is the first step in building a budget?
o: Cutting all discretionary spending
Opening a new bank account
Buying shares
Tracking where your money currently goes
quiz.e: Seeing the facts, including small regular costs, shows where a plan is needed.

quiz.q: In the 50/30/20 rule, what is the 20% for?
o: Rent and groceries
Savings and paying down debt faster
Eating out and holidays
Tax
quiz.e: Needs take about 50%, wants about 30%, and the remaining 20% builds your future.

quiz.q: What does 'pay yourself first' mean?
o: Buy yourself a treat on payday
Pay bills late to keep cash on hand
Move savings out automatically on payday
Ask for a raise before paying anyone
quiz.e: Money moved out on payday is far easier not to spend.

quiz.q: Which debt payoff method saves the most interest?
o: Snowball, smallest balance first
Avalanche, highest interest rate first
Minimum payments only
Newest debt first
quiz.e: Targeting the highest rate first cuts the interest you pay, while the snowball trades some savings for motivation.

quiz.q: Why should a budget include some guilt-free fun money?
o: Lenders expect fun spending in every budget
Without it you will eventually rebel against it
Fun spending raises your credit score over time
Fun spending lowers the tax that you pay
quiz.e: The best budget is one you will actually keep.

LESSONS.push: A budget isn't a diet for your money. Here is what it is instead.

LESSONS.title: Superannuation explained
LESSONS.hook: It's probably your second-biggest asset after a home, and most people barely look at it. Ten minutes here could be worth tens of thousands.

sections.key: Super is money set aside from your pay and invested for retirement, and your employer must add to it on top of your wages.
sections.b:
Superannuation, or super, is money set aside during your working life and invested to support you in retirement. It became compulsory for most employees in 1992, and Australia's system now holds more than $4 trillion, one of the largest retirement savings pools in the world.

Your employer must pay a percentage of your ordinary earnings into your fund on top of your wages. This Super Guarantee rose to 12% on 1 July 2025. On a $70,000 salary, that is $8,400 a year. Check your payslips and fund account to confirm it is arriving, and report unpaid super to the ATO. Self-employed people aren't covered, so they make their own contributions.

sections.key: Super is invested, so over 40 years or more compounding does much of the work, even though balances dip in some years.
sections.b:
Your super isn't sitting in a bank account. Your fund invests it in a mix of Australian and international shares, property, infrastructure, bonds and cash. Most people stay in their fund's default 'balanced' or 'growth' option, often a MySuper product.

Because the money stays invested for 40 years or more, compounding does enormous work: much of your final balance comes from investment returns, not from contributions. Balances will fall in some years when markets drop, but this is a very long game, and the simple idea is small amounts, invested steadily, growing into a large sum. Because it is locked away until retirement, it is also protected from being spent early.

sections.key: A fee difference of 0.5% or 1% a year compounds into tens of thousands of dollars less at retirement.
sections.b:
Fees are charged as a dollar amount, a percentage of your balance, or both. A difference of just 0.5% or 1% a year sounds tiny. Over a working lifetime, though, it can mean tens of thousands of dollars less in retirement, because fees compound just as returns do.

The ATO's free YourSuper comparison tool lets you compare MySuper products by fees and past returns. The regulator, APRA, also tests these products each year, and funds that fail the performance test must tell their members. Compare your fund against others at least occasionally, rather than leaving it untouched for decades.

sections.key: Keep one fund rather than several to avoid duplicate fees and premiums, and check the insurance inside it before closing any account.
sections.b:
Many people end up with several super accounts from different jobs, each charging fees and often insurance premiums. Since 2021, your existing fund is generally 'stapled' to you and follows you to new jobs, which helps. Link the ATO to your myGov account to find all your accounts, including lost super, and consolidate them online in minutes.

Most funds automatically include life cover (paid to your beneficiaries), total and permanent disability cover and sometimes income protection. Premiums come out of your balance. It can be good value, but check the amounts suit you. Before closing an account, check whether it holds insurance you want, as that cover ends when the account closes. Nominate your beneficiaries too; a binding nomination gives more certainty.

sections.key: Super is taxed lightly and locked away until you reach preservation age (60) and retire, or turn 65.
sections.b:
Super is taxed lightly to encourage saving. Employer contributions are generally taxed at 15%, below most people's income tax rate, and investment earnings are generally taxed at no more than 15%, though extra tax is planned for very large balances. You can add extra through salary sacrifice or personal contributions you claim as a tax deduction, up to an annual cap. Lower-income earners may qualify for government co-contributions.

You can generally access super once you reach preservation age (60 if born on or after 1 July 1964) and retire, or at 65 even if you keep working. Early access is allowed only in narrow cases such as severe financial hardship. Be wary of anyone offering early release; illegal schemes bring heavy penalties. Check the ATO website for current limits.

quiz.q: What does the Super Guarantee require employers to do?
o: Deduct super from your wages and keep it
Pay super only to senior full-time employees
Add a share of your pay to super on top of wages
Match any extra amount that you choose to save
quiz.e: The Super Guarantee is paid on top of wages, which is why checking your payslips and fund account matters.

quiz.q: Why can a super balance grow so large over a working life?
o: Decades of investing let compounding do the work
Employers pay it in one lump sum at retirement
Balances can never fall in value over time
It earns a fixed rate set by the government
quiz.e: Decades of investing and compounding mean much of the final balance comes from returns, not contributions.

quiz.q: Why do small differences in super fees matter so much?
o: Fees are a one-off cost taken at retirement
They compound over decades into a big gap
They are always tax deductible, so cost nothing
Higher fees guarantee higher returns
quiz.e: A small yearly fee difference compounds over a working lifetime into a large gap at retirement.

quiz.q: What should you check before closing an extra super account?
o: Whether the ATO has approved the closure
Whether it holds insurance you want to keep
Whether your employer agrees
Whether the fund is stapled to you
quiz.e: Insurance inside an account ends when it closes, so check the cover before consolidating.

quiz.q: When can most people generally access their super?
o: Whenever they like once they turn 40
At preservation age if retired, or at 65
Only after the age of 75, never earlier
Straight after any period of financial difficulty
quiz.e: Super is locked away until a condition of release, usually retiring after reaching preservation age or turning 65.

LESSONS.push: Your second-biggest asset is one you probably never look at. Here's why it matters.

LESSONS.title: How tax works in Australia
LESSONS.hook: The pay rise that 'pushes you into a higher bracket' won't leave you worse off. Here's how income tax actually works.

sections.key: Income tax is the government's biggest source of revenue and funds health, education, welfare, defence and more.
sections.b:
Income tax is the Australian Government's biggest source of revenue. It funds services like Medicare and hospitals, schools and universities, the pension and other welfare payments, defence, roads and much more. Other taxes include the 10% GST on most goods and services, company tax, and excise on fuel, alcohol and tobacco.

The financial year runs from 1 July to 30 June, and the Australian Taxation Office, the ATO, collects the money.

sections.key: Each tax rate applies only to the income inside its bracket, so a pay rise never reduces your take-home pay.
sections.b:
Australia's income tax is progressive: the more you earn, the higher the rate on the extra dollars. For residents in 2026-27, the first $18,200 is tax-free. Then 15% applies up to $45,000, 30% up to $135,000, 37% up to $190,000, and 45% above that. The 15% rate is legislated to fall to 14% from July 2027. Most people also pay a 2% Medicare levy.

A common myth says a pay rise can 'push you into a higher bracket' and leave you worse off. It can't. If you earn $136,000, only the $1,000 above $135,000 is taxed at 37%. Your marginal rate is the rate on your next dollar; your average rate is always lower.

sections.key: Your employer withholds tax from each pay, and your tax return settles the difference at year's end.
sections.b:
If you're an employee, your employer withholds tax from each pay under the Pay As You Go (PAYG) system and sends it to the ATO. They use your tax file number and whether you claim the tax-free threshold, which you should normally claim from only one job at a time.

After the financial year ends, your tax return works out exactly what you owed. If too much was withheld, you get a refund; if too little, you pay the difference. If you lodge it yourself, it is due by 31 October. Most people use myTax in myGov, where income, bank interest and private health details are pre-filled, but you are still responsible for what you lodge. It is worth waiting a few weeks after 30 June for pre-filling to complete.

sections.key: A deduction saves you your marginal tax rate on the amount claimed, and only expenses you paid, linked to earning income and backed by records qualify.
sections.b:
Deductions reduce your taxable income. You can generally claim work expenses such as tools, uniforms with a logo, professional memberships and some work-from-home costs. The ATO's three golden rules: you must have spent the money yourself and not been reimbursed; it must directly relate to earning your income; and you need a record, like a receipt. A $100 deduction saves $100 multiplied by your marginal tax rate, not $100.

Other taxes matter too. GST is built into prices, though basic food, most health care and education are GST-free. Profit from selling an investment such as shares attracts capital gains tax, with a 50% discount if you held it over a year; your main home is generally exempt. HECS-HELP debts are repaid through the tax system once your income passes a threshold.

sections.key: Keep your records for five years and treat unexpected ATO contact with suspicion, because tax scams are common.
sections.b:
Keep receipts and records for five years, since the ATO can review your return. Use official sources like ato.gov.au for rates and rules, which change regularly. Capital gains rules in particular may change, so check before you sell.

Be very wary of scams. Fake ATO texts, emails and calls that threaten arrest or demand payment in gift cards or cryptocurrency are common. The ATO won't threaten you with immediate arrest or ask for payment that way. If unsure, don't use the contact details in the message; contact the ATO using the number on its official website. This is general information only, and a registered tax agent can advise on your situation.

quiz.q: What is the Australian Government's biggest source of revenue?
o: GST
Company tax
Fuel excise
Income tax
quiz.e: Income tax is the biggest source of revenue, funding services such as health, education, welfare and defence.

quiz.q: You get a pay rise that takes you into the next tax bracket. What happens?
o: Only dollars above the threshold are taxed higher
All of your income is taxed at the higher rate
Your take-home pay can fall below what it was
The higher rate applies from the next financial year
quiz.e: Each rate applies only to income within its bracket, so a pay rise always increases take-home pay.

quiz.q: What happens when your tax return is processed after PAYG withholding?
o: You always owe the ATO extra tax
You get a refund or pay the difference
Your employer pays any shortfall itself
The withheld tax is never adjusted again
quiz.e: PAYG is an estimate; the return works out exactly what you owed and settles the difference.

quiz.q: Which is one of the ATO's golden rules for claiming a deduction?
o: Your employer must sign off on it first
The amount must be over $1,000 in total
You must keep a record, like a receipt
It must be an expense you were reimbursed for
quiz.e: You need to have spent the money yourself, tie it to earning income and keep a record.

quiz.q: An unexpected message says it is from the ATO and demands payment in gift cards. What should you do?
o: Pay quickly to avoid being arrested
Reply with your tax file number to check
Phone the ATO on the number from its website
Call back on the number in the message
quiz.e: The ATO never threatens arrest or demands gift cards, so verify through official contact details.

LESSONS.push: A pay rise can't push you into a worse position because of tax brackets. Here's the maths.

LESSONS.title: How credit scores work
LESSONS.hook: A three- or four-digit number can decide whether you get a loan, and at what rate. Here's how to see yours for free.

sections.key: A credit score boils your credit history into one number that lenders use to judge how likely you are to repay.
sections.b:
When you apply for a loan, credit card, phone plan or sometimes even a utility account, the provider checks your credit history to judge how likely you are to repay. A credit score boils that history into a single number. A higher score suggests lower risk, which can mean easier approval and sometimes better interest rates. A low score doesn't mean rejection everywhere, but it can limit your options.

In Australia, credit reports are kept by credit reporting bodies, mainly Equifax, Experian and illion. Each calculates its own score on its own scale: Equifax uses 0 to 1,200, while Experian and illion use 0 to 1,000. So your score can differ between them.

sections.key: Your credit report lists your accounts, applications and up to 24 months of repayment history, plus defaults that can stay for years.
sections.b:
Your credit report includes personal details, the credit accounts you hold and their limits, and every time you've applied for credit, called an enquiry. It also includes up to 24 months of repayment history, showing whether you paid on time each month.

Defaults, which are overdue debts of $150 or more that a lender has reported, can also appear, along with bankruptcies and similar insolvency records. These generally stay on your report for years. Lenders may check one or more of the credit reporting bodies when you apply, and each may hold slightly different information.

sections.key: Paying on time is the biggest help, while late payments, defaults and many applications in a short time lower your score.
sections.b:
The single biggest factor is paying bills and loan repayments on time, every time. Setting up direct debits for at least the minimum payment helps avoid accidental misses. Keep credit card limits no higher than you need, since lenders consider your total available credit, not just what you've used. A long, steady history of well-managed accounts also works in your favour.

Missing repayments, especially by more than 14 days, can show up in your history. Defaults are more serious and can stay on your report for five years even after you pay them. Many credit applications in a short period can lower your score, because it can look like financial stress. Buy now, pay later became regulated as credit in 2025, so providers may now check and report to credit bureaus.

sections.key: You can get a free credit report from each bureau every three months and have errors corrected free of charge.
sections.b:
You have the right to a free credit report from each credit reporting body every three months, and also if you've been refused credit recently. Request it directly from Equifax, Experian and illion, and look for the free option, as some services try to sell paid subscriptions. Checking your own report doesn't hurt your score. Do it once a year, and before applying for a big loan like a mortgage.

Reports sometimes contain mistakes, such as a debt that isn't yours or a default already paid. Ask the bureau or the lender to correct it, free of charge. If it isn't resolved, complain to the Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA). Be wary of 'credit repair' companies that charge large fees; legitimate negative information can't simply be removed.

sections.key: Unexpected enquiries or unknown accounts can signal identity theft, and you can ask bureaus to ban access to your credit file.
sections.b:
Identity thieves sometimes use stolen details to apply for credit in your name, which damages your report. Warning signs include enquiries you didn't make or accounts you don't recognise, which is another reason to check your report regularly.

If you think your identity has been stolen, you can ask the credit reporting bodies to place a ban on your credit file, stopping anyone accessing it for 21 days (extendable). IDCARE, a free national service, can help you respond. Guard your licence, passport and Medicare details carefully.

quiz.q: What is a credit score for?
o: It sets the interest rate on your savings
It summarises your history so lenders can judge risk
It shows your yearly income to the ATO
It guarantees approval for any loan
quiz.e: A credit score boils your history into one number lenders use to assess risk.

quiz.q: Which of these can appear on your credit report?
o: Your employer's name only
Your account balances at the supermarket
Your bank account PINs
Up to 24 months of repayment history
quiz.e: Reports include accounts, enquiries, repayment history over 24 months and defaults.

quiz.q: What is the single biggest thing you can do to help your score?
o: Apply for several cards at once
Pay bills and repayments on time, every time
Close all your accounts
Raise your credit limits as far as possible
quiz.e: On-time payments are the biggest factor, and setting up direct debits helps avoid accidental misses.

quiz.q: What should you do if your report shows a debt that isn't yours?
o: Ask the bureau or lender to correct it, free
Pay a credit repair company to fix it
Pay the debt off so that it vanishes
Wait for it to disappear after a month
quiz.e: Errors can be corrected free of charge, and unresolved complaints can go to AFCA.

quiz.q: You suspect your identity has been stolen. What can you request?
o: A new tax file number
A bigger credit limit
A ban on your credit file
A lower credit score
quiz.e: A ban stops anyone accessing your credit file for 21 days (extendable), limiting fraudulent applications.

LESSONS.push: Your credit score can differ at three bureaus. Here's why, and how to see them free.

LESSONS.title: How home loans work
LESSONS.hook: Over a 30-year loan, you can pay more in interest than you originally borrowed. Understanding a few features can save you tens of thousands.

sections.key: Early repayments are mostly interest, so over 30 years the interest can exceed the amount you borrowed.
sections.b:
A home loan, or mortgage, is money borrowed to buy a property, which serves as security: if you can't repay, the lender can sell it to recover the debt. Most Australian loans run for 25 to 30 years. You repay the principal (the amount borrowed) plus interest.

Take a $500,000 loan at 6% over 30 years. The monthly repayment is about $3,000, and you'd repay around $1.08 million, roughly $580,000 of it interest. Early on, most of each repayment goes on interest and only a small slice reduces the principal. As the balance falls, that shifts. Because the sums are large and the timeframe long, small differences in rates and features matter enormously.

sections.key: Borrowing more than 80% of a property's value usually means paying lenders mortgage insurance, which protects the lender, not you.
sections.b:
Your deposit is the share of the price you pay yourself. Lenders look at the loan-to-value ratio (LVR): a $600,000 loan on a $750,000 home is an 80% LVR.

If you borrow more than 80%, lenders usually charge lenders mortgage insurance (LMI), which can cost thousands or tens of thousands of dollars. LMI protects the lender, not you. Government schemes such as the Home Guarantee Scheme can let eligible first-home buyers purchase with a smaller deposit without paying LMI.

sections.key: Variable rates move with the market, while fixed rates give certainty for a set period but limit flexibility.
sections.b:
A variable rate moves up or down over time, usually following the Reserve Bank's cash rate. A fixed rate stays the same for a set period, often one to five years, giving certainty about repayments.

Fixed loans often limit extra repayments and can charge break fees if you exit early. Many people split their loan, part fixed and part variable, to balance certainty and flexibility. When a fixed period ends, the loan usually rolls onto a variable rate, often not the lender's best one, so plan ahead for that date.

sections.key: Offset balances and extra repayments cut the balance you pay interest on, saving years and tens of thousands of dollars.
sections.b:
An offset account is a transaction or savings account linked to your loan. Its balance is subtracted from your loan balance when interest is calculated. With $30,000 in offset against a $500,000 loan, you pay interest on only $470,000. Every dollar in offset effectively 'earns' your mortgage rate, tax-free. A redraw facility lets you take back extra repayments you've made.

Interest is calculated on the outstanding balance, so every extra dollar repaid removes all the interest it would have attracted. On the $500,000 example, an extra $200 a month from the start would cut about four and a half years off and save roughly $100,000. Paying half the monthly amount fortnightly also helps, because it adds up to one extra monthly payment each year.

sections.key: Compare loans using the comparison rate and features, and challenge your lender, because existing customers are often charged more than new ones.
sections.b:
Advertised rates can hide fees, so Australian lenders must also show a comparison rate, which combines the interest rate with most fees in a single figure. Compare features too: offset, redraw, extra repayments and fees. Brokers can compare many lenders for you; they're usually paid by the lender and must act in your best interests by law. Also check how much you can comfortably afford, not just how much a lender will offer.

Banks often give their best rates to new customers while existing ones drift onto higher rates, sometimes called the loyalty tax. Every year or two, check what new customers are offered, call your lender and ask for a better rate, or consider refinancing. Even a 0.3% cut on $500,000 saves about $1,500 a year. This is general information only.

quiz.q: Early in a long home loan, where does most of each repayment go?
o: Paying down the principal
Fees and insurance
Interest
Stamp duty
quiz.e: Early repayments are mostly interest, which is why extra repayments in the early years are so powerful.

quiz.q: Who does lenders mortgage insurance protect?
o: The borrower
The lender
The real estate agent
The government
quiz.e: LMI covers the lender's risk when you borrow more than 80% of the property's value, though you pay for it.

quiz.q: What usually happens to a fixed-rate loan when the fixed period ends?
o: It usually rolls onto a variable rate
It is automatically repaid in full
It stays fixed at the same rate for life
It is refinanced to the cheapest lender
quiz.e: After a fixed period the loan usually rolls to a variable rate, so plan ahead and compare your options.

quiz.q: What does an offset account do?
o: Fixes your interest rate for a set term
Lowers the balance you are charged interest on
Pays your council rates and insurance
Reduces the size of your deposit
quiz.e: Money in offset is subtracted from your loan balance for interest, saving interest at your loan rate.

quiz.q: What does a comparison rate include?
o: Only the headline interest rate
The interest rate plus most fees
The property price and stamp duty
Your credit score
quiz.e: The comparison rate combines the interest rate with most fees to show the true cost more clearly.

LESSONS.push: Over 30 years you can repay more than double what you borrowed. Here is how to cut it.

LESSONS.title: Index funds and ETFs
LESSONS.hook: The boring, low-cost way to invest that beats most professional fund managers over time.

sections.key: An index fund buys every company in an index in proportion to its size, rather than trying to pick winners.
sections.b:
Most investment funds are actively managed: professionals try to pick shares that will beat the market. An index fund does something simpler. It buys every company in a market index, like the ASX 200 or the S&P 500, in proportion to its size, and just holds them. You don't try to beat the market; you are the market.

The first index fund for ordinary investors was launched in 1976 by John Bogle, founder of Vanguard. Critics called it 'Bogle's folly'. It turned out to change investing.

sections.key: After fees, most active funds underperform their index over 10 to 15 years, because the average investor can only earn the market return.
sections.b:
It seems obvious that experts should beat a fund that simply buys everything. But studies such as S&P's SPIVA reports find that most actively managed funds underperform their benchmark index over 10 to 15 years, once fees are counted. Before costs, the average investor earns the market return, so after higher costs, the average active investor must do worse. It's also very hard to identify in advance which managers will be the lucky few who win.

In 2007, Warren Buffett bet $1 million that an S&P 500 index fund would beat a selection of hedge funds over 10 years. By the end of 2017, the index fund averaged about 7% a year, the hedge funds about 2%.

sections.key: Low fees are one of the few things investors control, and they compound over decades.
sections.b:
Index funds are cheap because they don't pay teams of analysts to pick stocks. Broad index funds and ETFs often charge between about 0.03% and 0.3% a year, while active funds commonly charge 1% or more. That gap looks small, but it is taken from your balance every year, whether markets rise or fall.

On a $100,000 investment over 30 years, earning 6% a year after fees instead of 7% leaves you with about $187,000 less. You can't control market returns, but you can control costs. Check the fee on any fund before you buy it, since it is one of the few numbers you can know in advance.

sections.key: An ETF trades on the exchange like a share and can give you a slice of thousands of companies, including overseas ones.
sections.b:
An exchange-traded fund, or ETF, is bought and sold on the stock exchange like a share. Many track an index, so one unit gives you a slice of hundreds or thousands of companies. You can buy them through any online broker, often with small amounts. There are ETFs for Australian shares, global shares, bonds, property and more. Some are narrow or complex, like those chasing a single theme or using leverage; broad, simple ones suit most long-term investors.

Australian shares make up only about 2% of world markets, and the ASX is dominated by banks and miners. Global funds add diversification and industries like technology that are smaller here. Some ETFs hold a mix of shares and bonds in one fund, rebalancing automatically.

sections.key: Regular investing and staying invested beat trying to time the market, and shares suit money you won't need for years.
sections.b:
Nobody reliably predicts short-term market moves, and some of the best days often come shortly after the worst, so jumping in and out can mean missing the recovery. Many investors use dollar-cost averaging: investing a fixed amount regularly, which buys more units when prices are low and fewer when they're high. Time in the market beats timing the market.

Shares suit money you won't need for at least five to seven years, because markets can fall sharply in the short term. First build an emergency fund and clear high-interest debt. Your super is probably already invested in shares. This is general information; ASIC's Moneysmart has free guides, and a licensed adviser can help.

quiz.q: What does an index fund do?
o: Picks a handful of shares it expects to win
Trades frequently to chase short-term gains
Buys only government bonds
Holds all the companies in an index
quiz.e: An index fund simply holds the whole index rather than trying to beat it.

quiz.q: Over 10 to 15 years, how do most active funds perform against their index after fees?
o: Most beat it comfortably
Most underperform it
They match it exactly
Results are always random
quiz.e: The average investor earns the market return before costs, so higher costs push most active funds behind.

quiz.q: Why do low fees matter so much for long-term investors?
o: Costs compound over decades and cut returns
Fees are fully refunded when you sell up
Lower fees always guarantee higher returns
Fees only matter during the first year
quiz.e: Investors can't control returns but can control costs, which compound just as returns do.

quiz.q: What is an ETF?
o: A government savings bond
A type of superannuation fund
A bank term deposit
A fund that trades like a share
quiz.e: ETFs trade like shares, and broad ones can give you a slice of thousands of companies.

quiz.q: What is dollar-cost averaging?
o: Waiting for the perfect time to invest
Investing a fixed amount at regular intervals
Converting savings into foreign currency
Selling when prices fall
quiz.e: Regular fixed investments remove the need to time the market and buy more units when prices are low.

LESSONS.push: Experts are paid to beat the market. Most of them can't. Find out why.

LESSONS.title: Supply and demand: why things cost what they do
LESSONS.hook: Why avocados are cheap one month and pricey the next, why concert tickets vanish in minutes, and why rents keep rising.

sections.key: In a market, prices carry information about scarcity and desire, coordinating millions of people without a central planner.
sections.b:
Every price you see is a signal. In a market economy, prices aren't set by a central planner; they emerge from millions of decisions by buyers and sellers. A high price signals that something is scarce or much wanted, encouraging producers to make more and buyers to use less. A low price signals the opposite.

Economist Friedrich Hayek argued this is one of the market's most remarkable features: prices coordinate the actions of millions of people who've never met and don't know why things changed.

sections.key: Generally, lower prices mean people buy more and producers sell less, and other factors can shift either one.
sections.b:
Demand describes how much people want to buy at different prices. Generally, the lower the price, the more they buy. That's the law of demand. Demand also shifts for other reasons: income, tastes, the price of alternatives, expectations and population. When avocado toast became a café trend, demand for avocados rose at every price.

Supply describes how much sellers will produce at different prices. Higher prices encourage more supply, because producing becomes more profitable. Supply shifts with costs, technology, weather and the number of producers. After Cyclone Larry wiped out Queensland banana crops in 2006, banana prices soared to around $12 or more a kilogram.

sections.key: The market price tends to settle where the amount buyers want equals the amount sellers offer.
sections.b:
Put supply and demand together and the price tends to settle where the amount buyers want equals the amount sellers offer. Economists call this the equilibrium.

If the price is above it, sellers have unsold stock and cut prices. If it's below it, buyers compete for too few goods and prices rise. This constant push and pull explains everyday price changes: strawberries are cheap in peak season when supply floods in, and dear in the off-season when they're scarce.

sections.key: Elasticity measures how much demand changes with price, and essentials like petrol are inelastic because people keep buying them.
sections.b:
Some things you'll buy almost regardless of price, at least in the short term, like petrol to get to work, electricity or essential medicines. Demand for these is called inelastic.

Other things you can easily skip or swap, like a particular brand of chips or a restaurant meal, so demand is elastic: a price rise sends buyers elsewhere. Elasticity explains why governments tax items like tobacco and fuel, which people keep buying, and why businesses fight so hard over competitive products.

sections.key: When prices stay below the level where supply meets demand, or supply can't keep up, shortages, sell-outs and rising rents follow.
sections.b:
In March 2020, Australians rushed to buy toilet paper. Demand spiked while supply couldn't adjust overnight, and supermarkets kept prices steady and set purchase limits instead. Production never ran short; fear drove the surge, and shelves refilled within weeks.

Tickets for a hugely popular artist are often priced below what fans will pay, so they sell out in minutes and scalpers resell them higher. Some sellers now use dynamic pricing, raising prices with demand. Several Australian states cap ticket resale prices.

Housing is a supply story. If new homes don't keep pace with population growth, because of land, planning rules, costs or labour shortages, prices and rents climb. Low vacancy rates give landlords more pricing power.

quiz.q: What does a high price usually signal in a market?
o: That something is scarce or much wanted
That a planner has set it too low
That producers should make less
That buyers should use more
quiz.e: Prices carry information: high prices signal scarcity or strong desire, encouraging more supply and less use.

quiz.q: A cyclone destroys most of the banana crop. What typically happens to prices?
o: They fall because fewer people buy
They stay roughly the same
They rise because supply drops
They are fixed by the government
quiz.e: A supply shock without a fall in demand pushes prices up, as bananas showed after Cyclone Larry.

quiz.q: What is the equilibrium price?
o: The highest price a seller can charge
A price set by the government
The cost to make the item
The price where demand equals supply
quiz.e: Prices above equilibrium leave stock unsold and prices below leave buyers short, pushing toward the middle.

quiz.q: Why is demand for petrol in the short term usually inelastic?
o: People need it and keep buying
It has many cheap substitutes
People buy more when prices rise
Its price never changes
quiz.e: Essentials with few quick alternatives keep selling even at higher prices, which is why governments tax them.

quiz.q: What tends to happen when housing supply doesn't keep up with demand?
o: Prices fall
Vacancy rates rise
Prices and rents rise
Nothing changes
quiz.e: When supply lags demand, prices and rents climb, and building more homes where people want to live helps.

LESSONS.push: Why were bananas $12 a kilo, and tickets gone in minutes? One idea explains both.

LESSONS.title: The alien intelligence of octopuses
LESSONS.hook: An animal that thinks with its arms, tastes with its suckers, changes colour while colour-blind and escapes from aquariums.

sections.key: Octopuses evolved intelligence separately from vertebrates, so studying them shows the different ways a mind can be built.
sections.b:
Octopuses are molluscs, related to snails and clams. Our last common ancestor with them was probably a small worm-like creature that lived over 500 million years ago. That means octopus intelligence evolved completely independently of ours.

Philosopher Peter Godfrey-Smith, who spent years diving with octopuses off the New South Wales coast, describes them as the closest thing we'll meet to an intelligent alien. Studying them helps scientists understand what minds are, and the different ways they can be built.

sections.key: An octopus has about two thirds of its neurons in its arms, and its suckers can taste what they touch.
sections.b:
An octopus has around 500 million neurons, similar to a dog. But about two thirds are in its eight arms, not its central brain. Each arm has its own cluster of neurons that can process information and control movement semi-independently. An arm can explore a crevice and decide to grab something while the central brain focuses elsewhere. Even a severed arm can react to touch and grasp food for a while.

A common octopus has up to around 2,000 suckers, each packed with chemical receptors, so octopuses 'taste' what they touch. In 2020, researchers described receptors that let them detect chemicals on surfaces and identify prey hidden in cracks without seeing it.

sections.key: Octopuses have three hearts, blue copper-based blood and no bones, so they can squeeze through any gap larger than their beak.
sections.b:
Octopuses have three hearts. Two pump blood through the gills; the third pumps it around the rest of the body. That third heart stops when the octopus swims, which is partly why they tire quickly and prefer crawling. Their blood uses a copper-based protein called haemocyanin to carry oxygen, which makes it blue, and it works well in cold, low-oxygen water.

They also have no bones. Their only hard part is a parrot-like beak, so they can squeeze through any gap larger than it. In 2016, an octopus named Inky escaped from New Zealand's National Aquarium through a gap in his tank, crossed the floor and slid down a drainpipe into the sea.

sections.key: Octopuses change colour and texture in a fraction of a second using pigment cells, despite appearing to be colour-blind.
sections.b:
Octopuses can change colour, pattern and even skin texture in a fraction of a second. Thousands of pigment cells called chromatophores, each controlled by tiny muscles and nerves, expand or shrink to show colour. Other cells reflect light to create shimmering or white effects, and muscles raise bumps and spikes to mimic rocks or seaweed.

Remarkably, octopuses appear to be colour-blind, having only one type of light receptor. Scientists are still working out how they match colours so well.

sections.key: Octopuses solve problems and use tools, yet most live only one to two years and many die after breeding.
sections.b:
Octopuses can learn to unscrew jar lids, even from the inside, navigate mazes and recognise individual humans, sometimes squirting water at people they dislike. In Indonesia, veined octopuses have been filmed carrying coconut shell halves and assembling them into portable shelters, a rare example of tool use by an invertebrate. Off New South Wales, gloomy octopuses live in small communities nicknamed Octopolis and Octlantis.

Yet most octopuses live only one to two years, and many species breed once and then die. One deep-sea octopus was seen brooding her eggs for four and a half years, the longest known of any animal. Why evolve a big, costly brain for so short a life? It remains a mystery.

quiz.q: Why is octopus intelligence so interesting to scientists?
o: It evolved separately from ours
It is identical to a dog's
It evolved from our direct ancestors
It only exists in the deep sea
quiz.e: Octopus minds evolved separately from ours, showing there are different ways to build a mind.

quiz.q: Where are most of an octopus's neurons found?
o: In its central brain
In its eyes
In its eight arms
In its three hearts
quiz.e: About two thirds of an octopus's neurons are in its arms, which can act semi-independently.

quiz.q: Why can an octopus squeeze through such small gaps?
o: Its skeleton folds up
It has no bones, only a hard beak
Its arms are detachable
Its blood thins out
quiz.e: With no bones, an octopus can pass through any gap larger than its beak.

quiz.q: How can an octopus change its skin colour so quickly?
o: By eating different foods
By seeing colour through three types of receptor
By stretching and shrinking pigment cells
By absorbing ink from the water
quiz.e: Pigment cells controlled by muscles and nerves expand or shrink within a fraction of a second.

quiz.q: How long do most octopuses live?
o: About 10 years
One to two years
About 25 years
More than 50 years
quiz.e: Despite their intelligence, most octopuses live only one to two years, which puzzles scientists.

LESSONS.push: Three hearts, blue blood and most of its neurons in its arms. Meet an alien mind.

LESSONS.title: Why bees matter
LESSONS.hook: About a third of what we eat depends on pollinators. Australia has around 2,000 native bee species most people have never noticed.

sections.key: About three quarters of leading food crops benefit from animal pollination, and bees are the most important pollinators.
sections.b:
Many flowering plants can't make fruit or seeds unless pollen moves between flowers. Wind does the job for some, like wheat and rice, but many rely on insects that visit flowers for nectar and carry pollen with them. Bees are the most important. The UN Food and Agriculture Organization estimates that about three quarters of the world's leading food crops benefit at least partly from animal pollination.

Almonds depend almost entirely on bees; Australia's almond industry hires hundreds of thousands of beehives each year. Apples, cherries, blueberries, avocados, melons and pumpkins also rely heavily on them. We wouldn't starve without pollinators, but diets would be less varied and nutritious, and many foods would cost much more.

sections.key: European honey bees live in large organised colonies and communicate food locations through the waggle dance.
sections.b:
The honey bee most people know isn't native to Australia; European honey bees were introduced in 1822. A hive can hold tens of thousands of bees: one queen who lays eggs, a few hundred male drones, and thousands of female workers who build comb, feed young, guard the hive and forage. Making about half a kilogram of honey may take around two million flowers.

When a forager finds good flowers, she returns and performs a 'waggle dance'. The angle of her waggle run relative to vertical shows the food's direction relative to the Sun, and its length shows distance. Other bees follow and fly straight there. Karl von Frisch decoded the dance and shared the 1973 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

sections.key: Australia has around 2,000 native bee species, mostly solitary, and some can pollinate in ways honey bees cannot.
sections.b:
Australia has around 2,000 native bee species, many still not formally described. Most are solitary: each female builds her own nest in the ground, in wood or in plant stems, and doesn't live in a hive.

The blue-banded bee pollinates tomatoes by 'buzz pollination', vibrating flowers to shake pollen loose, something honey bees can't do. About a dozen species are social stingless bees, found mainly in warmer areas, which make small amounts of tangy 'sugarbag' honey that Aboriginal people have long harvested.

sections.key: Bees face habitat loss, pesticides, disease and climate change, and the varroa mite now threatens honey bees in Australia.
sections.b:
Bees face many pressures: loss of flowering habitat, some pesticides, diseases and parasites, and climate change shifting when flowers bloom.

The varroa mite, a parasite that has devastated honey bee colonies worldwide, was detected in Newcastle, NSW, in 2022. Australia had been the last inhabited continent free of it. After a major effort, authorities concluded in 2023 that eradication was no longer feasible, and the focus shifted to managing it. Native bees aren't affected by varroa but face their own habitat pressures.

sections.key: Flies, birds, bats and even possums pollinate too, and a backyard with varied flowers, water and nesting spots helps them all.
sections.b:
Bees aren't the only pollinators. Hoverflies, beetles, moths and butterflies all move pollen. Honeyeaters and lorikeets pollinate banksias, grevilleas and eucalypts, flying foxes carry pollen across the landscape at night, and the honey possum feeds almost entirely on nectar and pollen.

You can help even on a balcony. Plant a variety of flowers, especially native ones, so something blooms across the seasons. Herbs like lavender, basil and rosemary attract bees. Avoid spraying pesticides on flowering plants, leave a shallow dish of water with pebbles, and provide bare ground or a simple 'bee hotel' of drilled wood blocks for native solitary bees.

quiz.q: Why would our food supply change without pollinators?
o: Wheat and rice would be the first to vanish
Many fruit, nut and veg crops would suffer
Food would become much cheaper overnight
Our diets would stay exactly the same
quiz.e: Staples like wheat survive without them, but many crops depend heavily on pollinators.

quiz.q: What does the honey bee waggle dance communicate?
o: A threat approaching the hive
How healthy the queen is today
Whether storms are on the way
Direction and distance to food
quiz.e: The angle shows direction relative to the Sun and the length of the waggle shows distance.

quiz.q: What can a blue-banded bee do that honey bees can't?
o: Produce large amounts of honey
Communicate through a waggle dance
Buzz flowers to shake pollen loose
Live in hives of tens of thousands
quiz.e: Buzz pollination by native bees such as the blue-banded bee suits flowers honey bees can't work.

quiz.q: What changed for Australia's honey bees in 2022?
o: Varroa mite was found in Australia
Honey bees became a native species
Australia banned all beekeeping
Native bees died out across the country
quiz.e: Varroa arrived in Australia, and by 2023 the focus moved from eradication to managing it.

quiz.q: Which action best helps pollinators at home?
o: Spraying flowers with pesticide
Planting varied flowers for every season
Removing every outdoor water source
Paving over any bare ground
quiz.e: A variety of flowers, water and nesting spots supports a range of pollinators year-round.

LESSONS.push: Australia has about 2,000 native bee species, and most of them make no honey.

LESSONS.title: Australia's 'deadly' animals, in perspective
LESSONS.hook: Snakes, spiders, sharks and crocs get the headlines. The numbers tell a very different, and reassuring, story.

sections.key: Australia's wildlife has a fearsome reputation, but familiar animals like horses and cattle cause more deaths than snakes or spiders.
sections.b:
Australia has a fearsome reputation: venomous snakes, deadly spiders, box jellyfish, crocodiles and sharks. It's true that many of the world's most venomous snakes live here. But a study of hospital and coronial data from 2000 to 2013 found that only about 20 to 30 people died from animal-related causes each year, and most weren't from the animals you'd expect.

Horses and cattle caused more deaths than any wild animal, through falls, kicks and crushing. Bees and wasps, through severe allergic reactions called anaphylaxis, caused about as many as snakes. Familiar animals cause more harm than exotic ones simply because we're around them so much more.

sections.key: Antivenom, fast care and pressure immobilisation first aid mean snakebite and spider-bite deaths are now very rare.
sections.b:
Australia has some of the most venomous snakes in the world, including the inland taipan and the eastern brown snake. Yet on average only about two people die from snakebite each year, thanks to antivenom, fast emergency care and good first aid. First aid is the pressure immobilisation technique: call 000, keep the person still, wrap a firm bandage over the bite and up the whole limb, then splint it. Don't wash the bite, cut it or use a tourniquet. Most bites happen when people try to catch or kill snakes.

No one has died from a confirmed spider bite since the funnel-web antivenom arrived in 1981; redback antivenom has existed since the 1950s. For a suspected funnel-web bite, use the same first aid and call 000.

sections.key: Drowning kills far more people than sharks or crocodiles, but stingers, crocodiles and rips are real risks that call for swimming only at safe, patrolled places.
sections.b:
Shark attacks get enormous media attention, but fatal attacks in Australia average only a few a year, while millions of people swim and surf. Around 300 people drown in Australia each year across all waterways. Saltwater crocodiles in the north are genuinely dangerous, causing roughly one or two deaths a year, usually when people ignore warning signs. Stay well back from the water's edge in croc country.

Box jellyfish and tiny irukandji are a serious risk in tropical waters, roughly October to May, and box jellyfish stings can be fatal. Swim at patrolled beaches, in stinger nets and wear a stinger suit. For a box jellyfish sting, call 000 and pour vinegar over it for at least 30 seconds; for bluebottles, use hot water instead. Always swim between the flags.

sections.key: Magpies swoop only to protect nests in spring, so stay calm, walk away and protect your head and eyes.
sections.b:
Every spring, some Australian magpies swoop people who come near their nests. It's usually the male protecting his chicks, for about six weeks. Most swoops are warnings, but they can cause eye injuries.

Avoid known swooping areas if you can, walk rather than run, and wear a hat and sunglasses. Cyclists should dismount and walk through. Research suggests magpies can recognise individual human faces, and they may be less likely to swoop people who've been kind to them.

sections.key: Australia's biggest outdoor dangers are drowning, heat, sun and roads, not wildlife.
sections.b:
Australia's big outdoor killers are far less exotic: drowning, road crashes, extreme heat and, over the long run, skin cancer from UV. Heatwaves kill more Australians than any other natural hazard.

So respect the wildlife, learn basic snakebite first aid and heed croc and stinger warnings. But the habits that save the most lives are ordinary ones: swimming between the flags, being sun smart, staying hydrated in heatwaves and driving safely. Fear tends to follow what is dramatic, so it helps to match your caution to the real risks.

quiz.q: Why do horses and cattle cause more deaths than snakes in Australia?
o: People are around them far more often
Their venom is stronger than snake venom
They live mainly in remote bushland
They are far harder to treat after injury
quiz.e: Familiar animals cause more harm than exotic ones because we're around them far more.

quiz.q: What is the correct first aid for a snakebite?
o: Wash the bite, apply a tourniquet and wait
Cut the bite open and suck out the venom
Keep still, bandage the limb and call 000
Apply ice, then walk to the car for help
quiz.e: Pressure immobilisation slows venom spreading; avoid washing, cutting or tourniquets.

quiz.q: What kills far more Australians in or near water than sharks?
o: Drowning
Stingrays
Crocodiles
Box jellyfish
quiz.e: Around 300 people drown each year, so swimming between the flags is the most important habit.

quiz.q: A magpie swoops you in spring. What is the best response?
o: Run as fast as you can
Walk away calmly and shield your head
Swing at the bird to scare it off
Stand still and stare it down
quiz.e: Swoops are protective warnings; walk, don't run, and shield your head.

quiz.q: Which natural hazard kills the most Australians?
o: Bushfires
Floods
Cyclones
Heatwaves
quiz.e: Heatwaves, along with drowning, road crashes and UV, are far bigger risks than wildlife.

LESSONS.push: Snakes, spiders and sharks get the fear. The real risks are far more ordinary.

LESSONS.title: The strange story of English
LESSONS.hook: Why is English spelling so chaotic? Why do we eat 'beef' from a 'cow'? Blame invaders, printers and a mysterious vowel shift.

sections.key: English began with Germanic tribes in the 5th century, then borrowed hundreds of everyday words from Viking settlers.
sections.b:
English began in the 5th century, when the Angles, Saxons and Jutes crossed the North Sea and settled in Britain. Their Old English would be unreadable to most of us; the epic poem Beowulf looks almost foreign. But many basic words come from it: house, water, bread, eat, sleep, mother, love, and 'English' itself, from the Angles.

From the late 700s, Viking raiders and then settlers arrived. Old Norse was related to Old English, so the two mixed easily. English borrowed hundreds of everyday words, including sky, egg, knife, window, skin, husband, law and even the pronouns they, them and their. Many 'sk' words, like skirt, are Norse; the older shirt survived beside it with a different meaning.

sections.key: After the Norman Conquest, French flooded English, especially words of law, government and the food of the rich.
sections.b:
In 1066, William of Normandy conquered England, and for around 300 years the ruling class spoke Norman French. English survived among ordinary people but absorbed around 10,000 French words, especially to do with power: government, parliament, court, judge, jury, crime, army and nobility.

This created a class divide that still shows in food. The animals, tended by English-speaking peasants, kept English names like cow, pig and sheep, while the meat served to French-speaking nobles took French names: beef, pork and mutton.

sections.key: English pronunciation shifted after spelling had started to settle, so many spellings are fossils of older speech.
sections.b:
Between roughly 1400 and 1700, English went through the Great Vowel Shift, a major change in how long vowels were pronounced. 'Bite' had sounded like 'beet' and 'house' like 'hoose'.

But spelling, influenced by printing's arrival in England in 1476, was starting to settle during this time, so many words kept spellings that matched older pronunciation. Printers, some of them Dutch, added quirks too. Words like 'knight', where the k and gh were once pronounced, are fossils of older English. Samuel Johnson's influential dictionary of 1755 later helped standardise meanings and spellings.

sections.key: English keeps adding words from other languages and from writers like Shakespeare, which gives it a huge vocabulary.
sections.b:
William Shakespeare's works contain the first recorded uses of many words and phrases still common, though some were probably already in speech: 'the be-all and end-all', 'heart of gold', 'a foregone conclusion', 'the green-eyed monster' and 'wear my heart upon my sleeve'. The 1611 King James Bible popularised phrases like 'the salt of the earth'.

English is also a magpie language. Latin and Greek gave thousands of scientific words. Trade and empire brought shampoo, bungalow and pyjamas from Indian languages; tea and ketchup from Chinese; algebra and coffee via Arabic; tsunami and emoji from Japanese; chocolate and tomato from Nahuatl, the language of the Aztecs. That is why English has several words for similar ideas.

sections.key: Australian English developed its own accent and words, and English now has far more second-language speakers than native ones.
sections.b:
Australian English developed from the mix of accents brought by convicts and settlers, mainly from southern England and Ireland, and soon sounded distinct. It borrowed around 400 words from Aboriginal languages, including kangaroo, koala, wombat, dingo, billabong, yakka and boomerang. It loves shortening words: arvo, brekkie, servo, barbie, ambo. Spelling mostly follows British conventions, and the Macquarie Dictionary, first published in 1981, records it.

Today around 1.5 billion people speak English, but only about 380 million as a first language. It dominates international business, science, aviation and the internet, a result of British colonial history and later American influence. English keeps changing, and dictionaries add hundreds of new words each year.

quiz.q: Why do pronouns like 'they' and 'them' exist in English?
o: They were borrowed from Old Norse settlers
They came from Norman French
They were invented by Shakespeare
They were taken from Latin
quiz.e: Close contact with Old Norse speakers gave English hundreds of everyday words, including they, them and their.

quiz.q: Why do we call cow meat 'beef' but the animal a 'cow'?
o: Beef is an Australian word for the meat
French-speaking nobles ate it and named it
It comes from a Viking word for meat
The meat used to be imported from abroad
quiz.e: English-speaking farmers kept English animal names, while the French-speaking elite named the meat.

quiz.q: Why is English spelling so inconsistent with pronunciation?
o: Sounds changed after spelling began to settle
Printers chose spellings at random
Spelling was never written down
Reformers made it harder on purpose
quiz.e: The Great Vowel Shift changed sounds while spelling stayed, leaving old spellings like 'knight'.

quiz.q: Why does English have such a huge vocabulary?
o: It was designed by a committee
It has borrowed words from many languages
It avoids using synonyms wherever possible
It only uses words with Latin roots
quiz.e: Trade, empire and contact meant English kept borrowing words, often giving several words for similar ideas.

quiz.q: Which of these English words comes from an Aboriginal language?
o: Parliament
Beef
Shampoo
Kangaroo
quiz.e: Australian English borrowed around 400 words from Aboriginal languages, such as kangaroo and billabong.

LESSONS.push: Why do we eat beef from a cow? Blame a conquest nearly a thousand years old.

LESSONS.title: Cognitive biases: the shortcuts that fool you
LESSONS.hook: Your brain makes the same mistakes again and again, in ways psychologists can predict. Once you know them, you'll spot them everywhere.

sections.key: Cognitive biases are predictable errors caused by fast, automatic mental shortcuts.
sections.b: Your brain handles far more information than it can weigh carefully, so it uses mental shortcuts called heuristics. Usually they work well: you don't calculate the odds before crossing a quiet street. But in some situations the same shortcuts cause the same mistakes, again and again.
