Psychologists call these systematic errors cognitive biases. Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman popularised the idea in the 1970s, and Kahneman later won a Nobel Prize in economics. In his 2011 book Thinking, Fast and Slow, he described System 1, which is fast, automatic and gives you a gut feeling, and System 2, which is slow and tiring, like multiplying 17 by 24. Most biases are System 1 jumping to conclusions that lazy System 2 never checks.

sections.key: We seek out evidence that backs our existing views, and most of us overrate our own abilities.
sections.b: We notice, search for and remember information that supports what we already believe. Type 'is coffee bad for you' and you'll find reasons to worry; type 'benefits of coffee' and you'll feel reassured. Social media amplifies this by showing more of what we already engage with. That's confirmation bias, and it's why facts alone rarely change minds. Overconfidence is its partner. In a classic 1981 study of US and Swedish drivers, most rated themselves safer than the median driver, which can't be true for everyone. In 1999, David Dunning and Justin Kruger found that the lowest scorers on logic and grammar tests overestimated themselves most, though researchers still debate how much of that is a statistical quirk. We also underestimate how long projects take, even when we've been late before.

sections.key: The first number you hear anchors your estimates, and vivid examples make rare events seem likely.
sections.b: The first number you hear pulls later judgements towards it, even when it's irrelevant. That's anchoring. In a famous experiment, people spun a rigged wheel that landed on 10 or 65, then estimated the percentage of African countries in the United Nations. Those who saw 65 guessed much higher. A 'was $199' tag makes $129 feel like a deal, a $90 bottle makes the $45 wine seem reasonable, and the first salary mentioned often sets the range. The availability heuristic works differently: we judge how likely something is by how easily examples come to mind. Plane crashes are vivid, so many people fear flying more than driving, though driving is far more dangerous per kilometre. Shark attacks make headlines; drownings rarely do.

sections.key: Losses feel roughly twice as strong as equal gains, and sunk costs wrongly keep us committed.
sections.b: Losing feels worse than gaining the same amount feels good. Research suggests losses weigh roughly twice as heavily, so most people refuse a coin flip that wins $100 or loses $100. It explains why people hold falling investments hoping to 'get back to even', why free trials work, and why 'Last chance' sells. A sunk cost is money, time or effort already spent and gone. The sunk cost fallacy lets it drive your next decision: sitting through a terrible movie because you paid, a company funding a failing project after spending millions, or staying in a hated job because of the years invested. Only the future matters. Ask: 'If I were starting fresh today, would I choose this?'

sections.key: You can't switch biases off, but seeking disconfirming evidence and checking base rates can catch them.
sections.b: You can't switch biases off, and knowing about them doesn't make you immune. But you can build habits that catch them. Before a big decision, look for evidence against your view and ask: what would convince me I'm wrong? Write down your own estimate before hearing anyone else's number. Ask how you'd feel if the choice were framed as a gain instead of a loss. Check base rates, meaning how often something actually happens out of how many, rather than trusting vivid stories. For plans, look at how long similar projects really took. Small speed bumps like these give your slow, careful System 2 a chance to step in.

quiz.q: Why do cognitive biases occur?
o: Random slips of attention that differ for every person
Fast mental shortcuts that mislead everyone the same way
A lack of intelligence in people who choose badly
Slow, deliberate reasoning that overcomplicates choices
quiz.e: Biases are systematic: shortcuts that usually work sometimes mislead everyone in the same way.

quiz.q: Why do facts alone rarely change someone's mind?
o: We forget most information within minutes of reading it
We trust new information more when it comes from strangers
We notice and remember evidence that suits our beliefs
We judge every claim by how many people have shared it
quiz.e: Confirmation bias filters what we notice, so ask what would convince you that you're wrong.

quiz.q: A shop puts a 'was $199' tag beside a $129 price. Which bias is at work?
o: Loss aversion, because the shopper fears losing the deal
Availability, because the higher price is easy to remember
Confirmation, because the shopper wants the item to be cheap
Anchoring, because the first number sets the benchmark
quiz.e: The first number you see becomes a reference point that shapes later judgements of value.

quiz.q: Why should the money already spent on a failing project not decide whether to continue?
o: It is gone whichever way you decide, so look ahead
Past spending suggests the project is likely to succeed
Stopping early always costs more than continuing
Earlier effort should count double in later decisions
quiz.e: A sunk cost can't be recovered, so ask whether continuing is worth it from here.

quiz.q: Which habit helps counter your own biases before a big decision?
o: Go with the most vivid example you can recall
Look for evidence against your view and check base rates
Hear other people's estimates before forming your own
Decide quickly while your gut instincts are strong
quiz.e: Deliberate speed bumps give slow, careful System 2 thinking a chance to catch System 1 errors.

LESSONS.push: Your mistakes are more predictable than you think. Psychologists can name them.

LESSONS.title: The psychology of persuasion
LESSONS.hook: Most attempts to persuade you pull on the same few levers. Once you see them, you can't unsee them.

sections.key: Robert Cialdini found that most persuasion relies on a few principles that trigger fairly automatic responses.
sections.b: In 1984, psychologist Robert Cialdini published Influence after studying salespeople, fundraisers and advertisers, even taking jobs undercover to learn their techniques. He found that most persuasion relies on a handful of principles that trigger fairly automatic responses. These shortcuts usually serve us well: following experts or returning favours is often sensible. The trouble is that anyone who knows the shortcuts can trigger them on purpose. In 2016 he added a seventh principle, unity, which appears later in this lesson. Knowing the principles helps you persuade honestly and notice when someone is pushing your buttons.

sections.key: We feel obliged to repay favours, and once we make a small commitment we tend to stay consistent with it.
sections.b: Reciprocity is a deep social rule: we feel obliged to return favours, even for an uninvited gift. Free supermarket samples, a 'complimentary' drink before a sales pitch and charity letters with a small gift all rely on it. Restaurants that bring mints with the bill tend to get slightly bigger tips. Consistency works alongside it. Once we commit to something, especially publicly or in writing, we want to act consistently. Salespeople use the 'foot in the door': get a small yes, like signing a petition or starting a free trial, and a bigger yes becomes more likely. The defence isn't refusing every gift. It's accepting without feeling you owe. You can use consistency yourself: writing down a goal or telling a friend makes you likelier to follow through.

sections.key: When unsure, we copy what others do and defer to credible experts, and both instincts can be faked.
sections.b: When we're unsure, we look at what others are doing. That's why a busy restaurant beats an empty one, and why reviews, star ratings and 'bestseller' labels work. In one well-known hotel study, a card saying most guests reused their towels beat a card about saving the environment. Social proof is strongest when the people are similar to us, but crowds can be wrong, and fake reviews and bought followers exploit this instinct. Authority works similarly: we follow credible experts and also the symbols of expertise, such as uniforms, titles and lab coats. Ads feature people who look like doctors or scientists for a reason. Ask two questions: is this person truly an expert in this topic, and do they gain if I agree?

sections.key: We say yes to people we like or see as one of us, and rarity or urgency makes offers seem more valuable.
sections.b: We say yes more easily to people we like, and we like people who are similar to us, pay us compliments and cooperate with us. That's why salespeople look for common ground ('You're from Brisbane too?'), and why products are sold through friends at parties. Unity goes further: we're more easily influenced by people we see as part of 'us', such as family, a team or a hometown. Scarcity makes things seem more valuable when they're rare or running out: 'Only 3 left', 'offer ends tonight'. It ties to loss aversion, since missing out feels like losing something, and it cuts your thinking time. Treat urgency as a signal to slow down. Genuine bargains rarely vanish overnight, and a seller who won't let you sleep on it is telling you something.

sections.key: All seven principles can be used ethically; the line is crossed when the pressure is manufactured.
sections.b: All seven principles can be used honestly. If you give something first, show real reviews, cite real expertise, offer genuine value and set a true deadline, you're persuading ethically. The line is crossed when the pressure is manufactured: fake scarcity, bought reviews, borrowed authority. When you're on the receiving end, separate the person from the deal. Would this offer still look good if a stranger you didn't warm to were making it? And for your own persuasion, try a simple test: would you be comfortable if the other person knew exactly what you were doing? Knowing the levers protects you from them and makes you a more honest persuader.

quiz.q: Why can anyone use persuasion principles to trigger a yes on purpose?
o: They only work on people who have never heard of them
They rely on long arguments that people check carefully
They trigger quick shortcuts that usually serve us well
They work only when the persuader is a genuine expert
quiz.e: Because the responses are quick and automatic, anyone who knows them can trigger them deliberately.

quiz.q: A free sample at the supermarket mainly works through which principle?
o: Reciprocity: we feel obliged to repay what we're given
Scarcity: we want what is rare or running out
Authority: we defer to credible experts
Liking: we agree with people who are similar to us
quiz.e: Even an uninvited gift creates a sense of debt, but you can accept one without owing anything.

quiz.q: Why did the 'most guests reused their towels' card work better in the hotel study?
o: People respond more strongly to appeals about the environment
People feel obliged after receiving a free gift
People defer to hotel staff in uniform
People copy what others like them are doing
quiz.e: Social proof is strongest when we're unsure and the people we copy seem similar to us.

quiz.q: What is a sensible response to 'Only 3 left, offer ends tonight'?
o: Buy quickly, because genuine bargains vanish fast
Treat the urgency as a signal to slow down and think
Assume the offer is a scam and walk away
Ask whether the seller seems friendly and familiar
quiz.e: Scarcity cuts thinking time, and a genuine bargain rarely disappears once you take a day to decide.

quiz.q: What separates ethical persuasion from manipulation?
o: Whether the pressure is real or manufactured
Whether the persuader uses any of the seven principles
Whether the other person ends up saying yes
Whether the persuader is an expert in the topic
quiz.e: The principles themselves are neutral; faking scarcity, reviews or expertise is what crosses the line.

LESSONS.push: Seven levers sit behind most of the yeses you give. Can you spot them?

LESSONS.title: Classical and operant conditioning
LESSONS.hook: Why does your heart jump when your phone buzzes? Blame a Russian scientist, his dogs and a man who trained pigeons.

sections.key: Classical conditioning is learning to link a neutral signal with something that naturally triggers a response.
sections.b: Around 1900, Russian physiologist Ivan Pavlov was studying digestion in dogs, work that won him a Nobel Prize in 1904. He noticed something odd: the dogs began drooling before food arrived, at the sight of the assistants who fed them or the sound of their footsteps. Their bodies had learned to predict food. He then paired a neutral sound, such as a metronome or buzzer, with food. At first the sound meant nothing. After repeated pairings, the sound alone made the dogs salivate. In the jargon, the food is an unconditioned stimulus because it naturally causes drooling, and the sound becomes a conditioned stimulus because it works only after learning. That's classical conditioning.

sections.key: Many everyday reactions are conditioned cues, and they fade through extinction when the cue stops predicting the outcome.
sections.b: Feel a jolt when your phone buzzes? Get hungry at the rustle of a chip packet? Feel tense in a dentist's waiting room before anything happens? Your brain has linked a cue with an outcome. Advertisers pair products with upbeat music and happy scenes, hoping the feeling rubs off on the brand, and a bad experience in a lift can make lifts frightening for years. These links can fade. If Pavlov kept sounding the buzzer without food, the drooling gradually stopped. This is extinction, the basis of exposure therapy, one of the most effective treatments for phobias: meeting the feared cue repeatedly in safe conditions teaches the brain it no longer predicts danger. Extinguished responses can return after a break, called spontaneous recovery, which is why old fears and habits resurface.

sections.key: Operant conditioning shapes behaviour through consequences: reinforcement makes it more likely, punishment less.
sections.b: In the 1930s, American psychologist B. F. Skinner studied how consequences shape behaviour. Using boxes with levers and food dispensers, he trained rats to press levers and pigeons to peck keys, and even taught pigeons a simple version of ping-pong. Classical conditioning links signals; operant conditioning teaches which actions pay off. Reinforcement makes a behaviour more likely and punishment makes it less likely. 'Positive' means adding something and 'negative' means removing it. A treat for a sitting dog is positive reinforcement. A seatbelt beep that stops when you buckle up is negative reinforcement. Being scolded for running late is positive punishment; a parking fine or lost screen time is negative punishment. Rewarding what you want generally works better and lasts longer than punishing what you don't.

sections.key: Rewards that arrive unpredictably, on a variable schedule, create the most persistent behaviour.
sections.b: Skinner found that rewards given unpredictably, on a variable schedule, produce the most persistent behaviour. If a pigeon gets food every tenth peck, it pecks steadily. If food arrives after a random number of pecks, it pecks relentlessly, and keeps going long after the food stops. It's the logic of poker machines and social media feeds: you never know when the next reward is coming, so you keep checking. It's also why Golden Lessons in this app appear at random.

sections.key: Pair habits with immediate rewards, remove the cues for habits you don't want, and watch for variable rewards.
sections.b: You can use conditioning deliberately. Pair a habit you want with something you enjoy, like only listening to a favourite podcast while exercising. Reward yourself immediately after the behaviour, not days later. Notice the cues that trigger habits you don't want, like the phone on your bedside table, and remove or change them. And be aware of variable rewards in the apps you use: turning off notifications breaks the cue, and moving apps off your home screen adds friction to the loop.

quiz.q: Why did Pavlov's dogs begin to salivate at the buzzer?
o: The buzzer itself naturally causes drooling in dogs
They had learned that the sound predicted food
Loud noises trigger digestion in all animals
They were rewarded with extra food for drooling
quiz.e: Repeated pairing taught the dogs to link a neutral signal with food, which is classical conditioning.

quiz.q: How does exposure therapy help with a phobia?
o: It rewards the person for avoiding the feared cue
It erases the memory of the original bad experience
It punishes the fear response until it stops
Repeated safe contact shows the cue is harmless
quiz.e: Extinction happens when a cue keeps appearing without the feared outcome.

quiz.q: A seatbelt beep stops once you buckle up. What is this?
o: Negative reinforcement: removing something unpleasant rewards the behaviour
Positive punishment: adding something unpleasant discourages the behaviour
Negative punishment: removing something pleasant discourages the behaviour
Positive reinforcement: adding something pleasant rewards the behaviour
quiz.e: 'Negative' means taking something away, and reinforcement means the behaviour becomes more likely.

quiz.q: Why do social media feeds keep people checking?
o: Rewards arrive on a fixed schedule that people learn to expect
Punishments for not checking build up over time
Rewards arrive unpredictably, which makes the behaviour persistent
Each check delivers the same reward, so it never gets dull
quiz.e: Variable rewards produce the most persistent behaviour because the next one could come at any time.

quiz.q: Which step helps break a phone habit triggered by cues?
o: Keep the phone close as a reward for resisting it
Mute notifications and move apps off the home screen
Delay rewards for good behaviour by several days
Check it at random times so it feels less habitual
quiz.e: Removing or changing cues and adding friction weakens the loop that drives the habit.

LESSONS.push: Why your heart jumps when your phone buzzes, and what pigeons have to do with it.

LESSONS.title: How habits really work
LESSONS.hook: Around 40% of what you do each day happens on autopilot. Here's how to take control of the autopilot.

sections.key: Habits run on a loop of cue, routine and reward, and about 40% of daily actions are habitual.
sections.b: Studies that asked people to log their day found roughly 40% of actions were repeated almost daily, in the same place, often while thinking about something else. Habits free your conscious mind, but bad habits run on the same autopilot, which is why willpower alone so often fails. Researchers describe a habit as a loop. A cue triggers it: a time, place, feeling, person or preceding action. The routine is the behaviour itself. The reward makes the brain want to repeat the loop. Finishing a coffee (cue) leads to checking your phone (routine), which delivers a hit of novelty (reward). Charles Duhigg popularised this model in The Power of Habit, and James Clear expanded it in Atomic Habits.

sections.key: In one study, habits took 66 days on average to feel automatic, with a range from 18 to 254 days.
sections.b: You may have heard that habits take 21 days. That figure doesn't come from habit research. In a 2009 study at University College London, volunteers chose a new daily behaviour, like drinking water with lunch or doing sit-ups before dinner. On average it took 66 days for the behaviour to feel automatic, but the range was huge, from 18 to 254 days depending on the person and the habit. Encouragingly, missing a single day didn't derail progress. Consistency matters more than perfection.

sections.key: Tie a new habit to a specific cue and shrink it until it's almost too easy to skip.
sections.b: Vague intentions like 'I'll exercise more' rarely stick. Specific plans work better: 'I will do X at time Y in place Z.' Habit stacking attaches a new habit to an existing cue: 'After I pour my morning coffee, I'll write down three priorities.' Design your surroundings too: the book on your pillow, the running shoes by the door. Then cut friction, the biggest enemy of a new habit. Start ridiculously small: one push-up, one page, two minutes of tidying. The point isn't the push-up; it's becoming someone who shows up every day. For bad habits, add friction instead: log out of social media, keep snacks in a high cupboard, leave your credit card out of shopping accounts. Habits follow the path of least resistance.

sections.key: Immediate rewards strengthen habits, and bad habits are best replaced by keeping the cue and reward but swapping the routine.
sections.b: The benefits of fitness or savings arrive months or years later, and our brains value distant rewards little. So add an immediate one: tick a calendar box and watch the chain grow, pair the habit with something you enjoy, or transfer $5 to a 'treat' account each time you skip takeaway. Streaks work for this reason, which is why this app has one. To break a bad habit, replace it. Work out what reward it gives you. Is afternoon snacking about hunger, boredom or a break from work? Keep the cue and reward but change the routine, such as a five-minute walk and chat at the 3 pm slump. Or remove the cue: people who quit smoking often change routines linked to cigarettes, like the morning coffee spot.

sections.key: Habits stick best when they reflect who you want to be, not just a target to hit.
sections.b: Goals are useful for direction, but they end: you run the marathon, then stop running. Habits that last are often tied to identity. 'I'm trying to quit smoking' is weaker than 'I'm not a smoker.' 'I want to read more' is weaker than 'I'm a reader.' Every time you do the behaviour, you cast a small vote for that identity. Start with who you want to become, then choose the tiny daily actions that person would take, and let the results follow.

quiz.q: In the habit loop, what is the cue?
o: The behaviour you carry out
The payoff that makes you repeat it
The trigger that starts the loop
The plan you write to change it
quiz.e: A cue starts the loop, the routine is the behaviour, and the reward makes you want to repeat it.

quiz.q: What did the 2009 University College London study find about forming habits?
o: It took around 21 days for nearly everyone
It took about a week if you never missed a day
It took over a year, and one missed day reset progress
It took about 66 days on average, with a huge range
quiz.e: Habit formation varies widely, and missing a single day didn't derail progress.

quiz.q: Which plan is most likely to build a new habit?
o: 'I'll try to get more organised this year'
'After my coffee, I'll write down my priorities'
'I'll do it whenever I feel motivated'
'I'll start big next Monday with an hour a day'
quiz.e: Attaching a new habit to an existing cue, and starting small, makes it easy to begin.

quiz.q: Why add an immediate reward to a habit like saving or exercise?
o: Benefits come late, and brains undervalue them
Immediate rewards make long-term benefits larger
Brains value distant rewards more than near ones
Rewards only matter when breaking bad habits
quiz.e: Satisfaction has to arrive right after the behaviour to strengthen the loop.

quiz.q: Why is 'I'm a reader' stronger than 'I want to read more'?
o: A specific target gives clearer feedback on progress
Naming a goal publicly adds pressure to finish
Identity keeps going after a goal is reached
Goals only work for short-term behaviours
quiz.e: Each action casts a vote for the person you want to become, so the habit outlasts any single target.

LESSONS.push: Everyone quotes 21 days to form a habit. The real research says otherwise.

LESSONS.title: Why we procrastinate
LESSONS.hook: Procrastination isn't laziness or poor time management. It's an emotion problem, and that's good news.

sections.key: Procrastination is mainly about avoiding unpleasant feelings, not poor time management.
sections.b: Around one in five adults describe themselves as chronic procrastinators, and nearly everyone does it sometimes. It's tempting to blame laziness or poor organisation, but research by psychologists such as Tim Pychyl and Fuschia Sirois suggests otherwise. Procrastination is mostly about emotions. We delay tasks that make us feel bored, anxious, confused, overwhelmed or insecure, because putting them off gives instant relief. That's a short-term fix with a long-term cost, and the relief rewards the delay, turning it into a habit. The good news is that an emotion problem can be worked on.

sections.key: We favour rewards now over later, and fear of imperfect work makes delaying feel safer than starting.
sections.b: Economists call it present bias: rewards now feel much bigger than rewards later, so a finished report next week can't compete with scrolling right now. Brain-imaging studies even find that thinking about our future selves looks more like thinking about a stranger, so we hand future-us the hard work as if it were somebody else's problem. Perfectionism adds fuel. Many procrastinators care a lot. If a task feels like a test of your ability, starting risks proving you're not good enough, and delay protects your self-image with a ready excuse: 'I only did badly because I left it too late.' Lower the stakes of starting. Allow a terrible first draft, 'version zero'. Perfection is for the end, never the beginning.

sections.key: Dread is worst before you begin, so commit to a tiny, concrete first step.
sections.b: Dread is usually worst before you begin, and it often fades once you start. So make starting tiny: commit to two minutes, one paragraph, or just opening the document and writing the heading. You may stop after that, but you often won't, partly because unfinished tasks tend to stay on your mind. Even if you stop, you've broken the avoidance loop. Make tasks concrete too. 'Do tax' or 'Plan the wedding' is vague, so your brain can't picture the first step. Turn it into a next action that starts with a verb: 'Find last year's tax return', 'Email three venues for quotes'. Productivity writer David Allen calls this the 'next action'. Small steps feel less threatening and build momentum.

sections.key: Short timed work blocks and a distraction-free environment work better than relying on willpower.
sections.b: Willpower is unreliable, especially when you're tired, so shape your time and surroundings instead. The Pomodoro Technique, created by Francesco Cirillo in the late 1980s and named after a tomato-shaped kitchen timer, means 25 minutes on one task, then a 5-minute break, with a longer break after four rounds. A deadline 25 minutes away is easy to face, and the break is a reward. Timeboxing goes further: put the task in your calendar like an appointment, removing one more decision. Then design out distraction. Put your phone in another room, since even face-down it can pull at your attention. Use website blockers, close extra tabs, work somewhere you associate with focus, and tell someone what you'll finish by when.

sections.key: Self-compassion after procrastinating reduces future procrastination.
sections.b: Beating yourself up feels like it should help, but it usually makes things worse, because guilt is another unpleasant feeling to avoid. In a study of university students, those who forgave themselves for procrastinating before their first exam procrastinated less before the next one. Self-compassion isn't letting yourself off the hook; it's treating yourself like a friend who stumbled. Acknowledge it, work out what made the task feel hard, and choose the next small step. Then take it.

quiz.q: According to the research, what is procrastination mostly about?
o: Laziness and a basic lack of ambition
Avoiding unpleasant emotions like boredom
Poor skill at planning and scheduling time
Having too little to do each day
quiz.e: Delay gives instant relief from bad feelings, which rewards the avoidance and builds the habit.

quiz.q: Why can perfectionism lead to procrastination?
o: Perfectionists don't care how the task turns out
Starting early makes a task seem too easy
Delay protects your self-image and offers an excuse
High standards make people finish tasks too quickly
quiz.e: If starting risks proving you're not good enough, delay feels safer; a terrible first draft lowers the stakes.

quiz.q: Why commit to just two minutes of a dreaded task?
o: Dread is worst before you begin and often fades after
Two minutes is long enough to finish most tasks outright
It shows the task was never really important to you
Short sessions use far less willpower than long ones
quiz.e: Starting breaks the avoidance loop and shows you the task is survivable.

quiz.q: How does the Pomodoro Technique make a task easier to face?
o: It sets a full-day deadline that reduces stress
It removes breaks so momentum is never lost
It works best when you decide what to do on the spot
A short deadline is easy to face and the break a reward
quiz.e: Short timed blocks make starting less daunting, especially when you've decided when to work.

quiz.q: What helped students procrastinate less before their next exam?
o: Criticising themselves harshly for the delay
Forgiving themselves for the earlier delay
Ignoring the delay and not thinking about it
Promising themselves to work much harder
quiz.e: Guilt is another feeling to avoid, whereas self-compassion makes it easier to take the next small step.

LESSONS.push: Putting things off isn't about time. It's about a feeling you're avoiding.

LESSONS.title: The memory palace
LESSONS.hook: The 2,500-year-old technique memory champions use to remember almost anything, and how to build your own tonight.

sections.key: The memory palace, or method of loci, works by borrowing our strong memory for places.
sections.b: The memory palace, or method of loci ('loci' is Latin for places), dates back to ancient Greece. Legend says the poet Simonides stepped out of a banquet moments before the hall collapsed, then identified the unrecognisable victims by remembering where each had sat. Roman orators such as Cicero and Quintilian later described walking through an imagined building, each room holding the next point of a speech. It works because human brains evolved to remember places and routes. You can probably walk through your childhood home in your mind, yet struggle to recall ten random words from yesterday. The method borrows that spatial memory to store lists, numbers and abstract facts. The hippocampus, central to navigation, is also central to forming new memories.

sections.key: Choose a familiar route of distinct spots, then place a vivid, exaggerated image at each one.
sections.b: Pick a place you know well, such as your home or your walk to the shops, and choose about ten distinct spots in a fixed order: front door, hallway mirror, lounge, TV, kitchen bench, fridge, back door. Always walk it in the same direction and rehearse it until you can list the spots easily. Then turn each item into a vivid image at a spot. The stranger and more exaggerated, the better. To remember 'milk, eggs, batteries', picture a giant cow blocking the front door, eggs exploding against the hallway mirror and batteries fizzing and sparking over the lounge. Add sound, smell and movement. Ordinary images fade; absurd ones stick, because the brain notices what's surprising or emotional.

sections.key: Recall by walking the route in your mind, and turn abstract ideas into concrete images first.
sections.b: To recall the list, walk the route in your mind and see what's waiting at each spot. Because the route is fixed, you get the order for free and can even recall the list backwards. An empty spot tells you exactly which item you've forgotten, which is handy for speeches. The first attempts feel slow and silly, but with practice, placing an image takes a few seconds. For abstract ideas, convert them into something you can picture: for 'rising costs', imagine a price tag growing into a balloon and lifting off the couch. For names, 'Rose' becomes a rose and 'Barker' a barking dog. Memory athletes turn digits into images too, such as 1 = a candle and 2 = a swan.

sections.key: In a 2017 study, six weeks of training more than doubled recall of a 72-word list.
sections.b: Yes. Competitive memory athletes use the method to memorise shuffled decks of cards in under a minute and thousands of digits of pi. In a 2017 study published in the journal Neuron, ordinary volunteers trained with the technique for 30 minutes a day over six weeks. Their recall of a 72-word list more than doubled, and their brain connectivity shifted to resemble that of memory champions. Four months later, much of the improvement was still there.

sections.key: Use memory palaces for shopping lists, speeches and names, and add spaced review to keep them long term.
sections.b: Everyday uses include shopping lists, the key points of a presentation, a set of instructions, the order of topics in an exam essay, or the names of people at a meeting. You can build several palaces from places you know: your gym, your parents' house, your favourite cafe. The technique helps you get information in. To keep it for months, combine it with spaced review, walking through the palace again a day later, then a few days later, then a week later.

quiz.q: Why does the memory palace work so well?
o: It trains the brain to read much faster
It borrows our strong memory for places
It replaces memory with written notes at each spot
It works only for lists of familiar objects
quiz.e: Brains evolved to remember places and routes, so linking facts to places makes them stick.

quiz.q: What makes an image stick at a spot in your palace?
o: Being ordinary, realistic and easy to picture
Being tiny, plain and barely noticeable
Being strange, exaggerated and multi-sensory
Being the same image reused at each spot
quiz.e: The brain pays attention to what is surprising or emotional, so absurd images outlast ordinary ones.

quiz.q: How do you remember an abstract idea like 'rising costs'?
o: Convert it into a concrete image, then place it at a spot
Repeat it aloud until it feels familiar
Write it on a list beside the route
Skip it, since palaces suit only physical objects
quiz.e: Anything can be remembered once it becomes a picture you can place along the route.

quiz.q: What did the 2017 Neuron study show about memory training?
o: Only memory champions could benefit from the method
Memory gains vanished within a week
Recall improved slightly but brain connectivity didn't change
Six weeks of practice more than doubled recall of a 72-word list
quiz.e: Ordinary volunteers improved a lot, and much of the gain remained four months later.

quiz.q: How can you keep palace-stored information for months?
o: Use a brand-new palace each time you review
Combine it with spaced review over several days
Review it once, right after building the palace
Add more spots to the route each time you recall
quiz.e: The palace gets information in; spaced review is what keeps it there.

LESSONS.push: An ancient trick more than doubled ordinary people's recall in six weeks.

LESSONS.title: Mnemonics, chunking and how memory works
LESSONS.hook: Simple tricks that make information stick, from ROY G BIV to phone numbers, and the science of why they work.

sections.key: Memory has three stages, and working memory holds only about four meaningful chunks at a time.
sections.b: Remembering has three stages. Encoding gets information in, storage keeps it there, and retrieval gets it back out. Most 'bad memory' is really poor encoding: you never properly paid attention, like forgetting a name seconds after hearing it because you were planning what to say. Mnemonics mostly help encoding by making information meaningful, and they give you a hook for retrieval. Working memory, the mental scratchpad, is also surprisingly small. In 1956, psychologist George Miller suggested it holds 'seven, plus or minus two' items. More recent research by Nelson Cowan and others puts the true limit nearer four meaningful chunks. That's why you can lose a phone number between reading it and dialling it.

sections.key: Grouping information into meaningful chunks multiplies what you can hold.
sections.b: The way around the limit is chunking: grouping items into meaningful units. 0412345678 is ten items, but 0412 345 678 is three chunks. FBICIAABC is nine letters, but FBI, CIA, ABC is three familiar acronyms. Chess masters can recall a whole board at a glance, but only if the pieces are in positions from real games, because they see patterns rather than individual pieces. Chunking is one reason experts seem to have super memories: their knowledge lets them group new information into bigger chunks.

sections.key: Acronyms, first-letter sentences, rhyme and rhythm compress or cue information so it's easier to recall.
sections.b: Acronyms turn a list into a single word: ROY G BIV gives the rainbow's colours, and many first-aid courses teach DRSABCD for the emergency action plan. When the letters don't form a word, make a sentence: 'My Very Educated Mother Just Served Us Noodles' gives the planets in order from the Sun. Silly or personal sentences stick best, so make your own. Rhyme and rhythm add extra cues. 'Thirty days hath September, April, June and November' has helped people for centuries, and advertising jingles stick for decades. Many people learned the alphabet through a song and still hum it to find a letter. Setting a list or sequence of steps to a familiar tune or beat can help.

sections.key: Linking new information to what you know, and asking why, deepens memory.
sections.b: The more connections a memory has, the easier it is to find. Link new facts to things you know: Canberra sounds like 'can, bra', so picture a bra in a can. Even better is elaboration: ask why and how something is true and explain it in your own words. Thinking about meaning builds much stronger memories than simply repeating. The keyword method applies this to foreign vocabulary. The Spanish 'pato', meaning duck, sounds like 'pot', so picture a duck wearing a pot on its head. In 1975, Richard Atkinson and Michael Raugh tested it on Russian vocabulary, and learners using it remembered far more words than those who simply rehearsed. It also works for names, like noticing that Rose has rosy cheeks, and for medical terms.

sections.key: Drawing a word or idea, even badly, makes it more memorable than writing it out.
sections.b: One of the simplest memory boosters is to draw what you want to remember. In 2016, researchers at the University of Waterloo in Canada gave volunteers lists of simple words and about 40 seconds for each, asking them either to draw the word or to write it out repeatedly. Drawn words were remembered far better, in some experiments about twice as often, and artistic skill made no difference. Drawing seems to work because it combines thinking about meaning, making a picture and moving your hand. Quick sketches in the margins of your notes, or a rough diagram of a process, can turn a forgettable page into a memorable one.

quiz.q: Why can you lose a phone number between reading it and dialling it?
o: Phone numbers are stored in the wrong memory stage
Retrieval can't begin until the number is written down
Working memory holds only about four chunks at a time
Working memory holds up to twenty items briefly
quiz.e: Working memory is a small scratchpad, which is why grouping information into chunks helps.

quiz.q: Why is 0412 345 678 easier to hold in mind than 0412345678?
o: Grouping gives three chunks instead of ten separate items
Spaces make each digit larger in memory
Spaced digits move straight into long-term memory
Repeating the number is easier with spaces
quiz.e: Chunking packs several items into one meaningful unit, so you can hold more at once.

quiz.q: What is the benefit of an acronym such as ROY G BIV?
o: It compresses a list into one memorable item
It puts the colours in alphabetical order
It removes the need to learn the list at all
It works only for lists of colours
quiz.e: Acronyms and first-letter sentences give you one hook that unlocks the whole list.

quiz.q: Which approach builds the strongest memory of a new fact?
o: Explaining why it's true in your own words
Repeating it silently several times in a row
Copying it out word for word on paper
Reading it again at the end of the day
quiz.e: Thinking about meaning and linking facts to what you know gives a memory more connections.

quiz.q: What did the University of Waterloo drawing studies find?
o: Only skilled artists remembered drawn words well
Written words were remembered about twice as often
Drawing helped regardless of artistic skill
Drawing helped only with very long lists
quiz.e: Drawing combines meaning, imagery and movement, so even rough sketches help.

LESSONS.push: You can hold about four things in mind at once. Here's how to fit in more.

LESSONS.title: The placebo effect
LESSONS.hook: A sugar pill can make you feel better. Even when you know it's a sugar pill.

sections.key: A placebo has no active ingredient, yet expectation can trigger real brain chemistry and relieve symptoms.
sections.b: A placebo is a treatment with no active ingredient: a sugar pill, a saline injection or even a fake procedure. The word is Latin for 'I shall please'. The placebo effect is the real improvement people often feel after receiving one, and it is essential in research: if people on a real drug don't improve more than those on a dummy, the drug isn't doing much. It isn't imaginary. Brain imaging shows that people expecting pain relief release endorphins, the body's natural painkillers, and in one classic experiment a drug that blocks endorphins also blocked the placebo's relief. Expectation changes how the brain processes pain, nausea and fatigue. But placebos work on symptoms we perceive, not underlying disease: a sugar pill won't shrink a tumour or cure an infection.

sections.key: Details like price, form and a warm clinician strengthen placebo effects, which can even work when patients know the pill is a placebo.
sections.b: Strangely, the details matter. In studies, expensive placebos relieved pain better than cheap ones, two pills beat one, injections beat pills, and colour can play a role too. Fake surgery can be surprisingly powerful. A warm, confident, attentive practitioner boosts the effect: in one irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) study, patients improved more with an attentive practitioner than with a brisk, impersonal one. Then comes the strangest part. In a 2010 Harvard study, people with IBS received pills openly labelled as placebos, 'like sugar pills', and were told such pills had helped through mind-body processes. They still reported significantly more improvement than a group given no pills. Later studies found similar results for chronic back pain and fatigue. The ritual of treatment and the expectation it creates may work even without deception.

sections.key: Negative expectations cause real symptoms, and the body can learn to respond to a cue paired with a drug.
sections.b: The placebo effect has a dark twin, the nocebo effect: people who expect side effects often get them, even from a dummy pill. Placebo groups in drug trials commonly report headaches, fatigue and nausea, especially after reading a long list of possible side effects. In a 2020 UK trial of people who had stopped statins because of side effects, much of the discomfort they reported on statins also appeared when they took placebo tablets. Expectations can also be learned. In 1975, psychologist Robert Ader paired saccharin-sweetened water with an immune-suppressing drug in rats; later the sweet water alone suppressed their immune responses. In small trials with children taking ADHD medication, pairing each dose with a placebo pill let researchers cut the real dose while keeping much of the benefit.

sections.key: Sham-surgery trials have shown that some common operations work no better than a placebo procedure.
sections.b: Surgery carries a powerful placebo effect of its own, which only trials using sham operations can reveal. In a 2002 US study of keyhole knee surgery for osteoarthritis, patients who received only skin incisions reported as much improvement in pain and function over two years as those who had the full operation. A 2013 Finnish trial found much the same for a common keyhole operation on worn knee cartilage in middle-aged people. A 2014 review found that in about half of sham-controlled surgical trials, the real operation did no better than the fake. Results like these have led guidelines to advise against routine keyhole knee surgery for osteoarthritis.

sections.key: Expectations affect how you feel, but don't swap proven treatments for placebos.
sections.b: The placebo effect shows the mind has real influence over how we experience symptoms, especially pain, nausea and fatigue. Positive expectations, trusted care and good routines can genuinely help you feel better. But it's no substitute for effective treatment, and products that rely on it often exploit it. When judging any remedy, ask whether it has been tested against a placebo in a blinded trial. If not, you can't know whether it's doing anything beyond what belief and time would do. For any health concern, talk to a doctor or other qualified health professional.

quiz.q: What shows the placebo effect is more than imagination?
o: Placebos reliably cure the underlying disease
Placebo relief appears only in people faking symptoms
Placebos change nothing measurable in the brain
Blocking endorphins also blocks the relief
quiz.e: Expectation alters how the brain handles pain, though it won't cure an infection or shrink a tumour.

quiz.q: What did the 2010 Harvard study find about open-label placebos?
o: IBS patients improved knowing the pills were placebos
Placebos worked only when patients were deceived
Patients improved no more than the group given no pills
Only pills described as real medicine had any effect
quiz.e: The ritual of treatment and the expectation it creates can work without deception.

quiz.q: What is the nocebo effect?
o: Negative expectations causing real symptoms
A placebo that works better than the real drug
A drug side effect that appears only after months
Relief that comes from a caring practitioner
quiz.e: Expectations shape how we feel in both directions, which is why long side-effect lists matter.

quiz.q: What did sham-surgery trials of keyhole knee operations show?
o: Fake surgery produced no improvement at all
The real operation was always far better in results
Fake surgery worked about as well as the real thing
Fake surgery caused more harm than good overall
quiz.e: Surgery has a strong placebo effect, which only sham-controlled trials can separate from the real one.

quiz.q: What is a sensible way to judge a remedy?
o: Assume any remedy that makes you feel better works
Ask whether it beat a placebo in a blinded trial
Swap proven treatments for placebos when symptoms are mild
Treat expectations as having no effect on symptoms
quiz.e: Without a placebo-controlled trial, you can't tell what belief and time alone would have done.

LESSONS.push: Some people improve on pills they know are fake. Here's what that means.

LESSONS.title: How to make better decisions
LESSONS.hook: Practical tools from psychology and economics for the choices that actually matter.

sections.key: Decide small, reversible choices quickly and aim for 'good enough', saving careful thought for one-way doors.
sections.b: We make thousands of decisions a day, and treating them all seriously is exhausting. A useful filter, popularised by Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, asks whether a decision is a 'one-way door' or a 'two-way door'. One-way doors, like selling a house or quitting a career, are hard to reverse and deserve careful thought. Two-way doors, like trying a new gym or ordering a dish, can be undone, so decide quickly and learn. Most are two-way. Psychologist Barry Schwartz adds two styles: maximisers hunt for the very best option, while satisficers set criteria and pick the first option that meets them. Maximisers sometimes land better outcomes, such as higher starting salaries, but feel less satisfied and more regretful. For most choices, define 'good enough' first, then stop when you find it.

sections.key: Too many options can stall decisions, so narrow them fast and count the opportunity cost of what you give up.
sections.b: In a famous 2000 study, shoppers who saw 24 jams were more likely to stop but far less likely to buy than those who saw 6. Later research found choice overload isn't universal; it depends on how complex the options are and how clear your preferences are. Still, when faced with too many options, narrow them fast: pick your top two or three criteria, drop anything that fails them, and compare only the finalists. Then count the opportunity cost, the value of the best alternative you give up. A $60,000 car costs more than $60,000; it also costs what that money could have become, or the holiday you won't take. An evening of scrolling costs the book not read or the friend not called. Asking 'What else could I do with this?' makes invisible costs visible.

sections.key: Writing out and weighting factors, the 10/10/10 test and the outsider view reduce the pull of the loudest emotion.
sections.b: Working memory holds only a few items, so decisions juggled in our heads get dominated by whichever factor feels loudest. Writing helps. Charles Darwin famously listed the pros and cons of marriage before proposing. Better still, weight each factor from 1 to 5 by how much it matters, and score how well each option performs. You needn't follow the numbers blindly, but the process often reveals what you really care about. Emotions in the moment can also hijack decisions, so try the 10/10/10 test suggested by writer Suzy Welch: how will I feel about this in 10 minutes, 10 months and 10 years? Or take the outsider view and ask, 'What would I tell my best friend to do?' We often reason more wisely about other people's problems.

sections.key: Decide in advance what would make you stop or rethink, so sunk costs don't trap you later.
sections.b: Many decisions go wrong not at the start but months later, when we keep pushing on after the evidence has turned, partly because of the time and money already spent. Brothers Chip and Dan Heath, in their 2013 book Decisive, suggest setting tripwires: before committing, write down the signals that would make you stop or reconsider. 'If the renovation runs 20% over budget, we pause and rethink.' 'If this job still feels wrong in six months, I start looking.' Drawing the line while you're calm makes it far easier to act later, when pride and money already spent are urging you to keep going.

sections.key: Good decisions can have bad outcomes because of luck, so judge the process rather than the result.
sections.b: Former poker champion Annie Duke warns against 'resulting': judging a decision by how it turned out. A good decision can have a bad outcome because of luck, and a reckless one can work out fine. If you drive home drunk and arrive safely, it was still a bad decision. Instead, judge the process: did you have reasonable information, consider alternatives and think about risks? Keeping a simple decision journal, noting what you decided and why, helps you learn from both luck and skill over time.

quiz.q: What should you do with a 'two-way door' decision?
o: Deliberate for weeks, because every choice is final
Treat it with the care you'd give to selling a house
Decide quickly, since it can be undone
Put it off until every option is known
quiz.e: Save careful thought for hard-to-reverse choices and act fast on the rest.

quiz.q: Why ask 'What else could I do with this money or time?'
o: It shows which option has the lowest price
It reduces the number of options automatically
It proves the first option was the best
It reveals the opportunity cost you'd overlook
quiz.e: The real cost of a choice includes the best alternative you give up.

quiz.q: What does the 10/10/10 test help you separate?
o: Hard facts from mere opinions
Short-term feeling from long-term value
Risky options from safe options
Your values from friends' opinions
quiz.e: Asking how you'll feel in 10 minutes, 10 months and 10 years loosens the grip of the moment.

quiz.q: What is a tripwire in decision-making?
o: A signal set in advance to stop or rethink
A deadline after which you must commit
A penalty for changing your mind
A reason to continue no matter what the evidence shows
quiz.e: Setting the line while calm makes it easier to act when sunk costs and pride urge you on.

quiz.q: What is 'resulting'?
o: Repeating a decision that worked last time
Delaying a decision until the results are known
Judging a decision only by its outcome
Blaming bad luck for every poor outcome
quiz.e: Luck affects outcomes, so judge whether you used good information, alternatives and risk thinking.

LESSONS.push: Some decisions deserve weeks; most deserve minutes. How do you tell which?

LESSONS.title: How evolution works
LESSONS.hook: No designer, no plan, just time, variation and small differences adding up over millions of years.

sections.key: Natural selection acts on genetic variation between individuals, which comes from mutations and reshuffled genes.
sections.b: In 1859, Charles Darwin published On the Origin of Species, arguing that living things change over generations through natural selection. His voyage on HMS Beagle stopped in Sydney and Hobart in 1836. Alfred Russel Wallace, working in South-East Asia, reached the same idea independently, and their work was presented together in 1858. It became the foundation of modern biology. The raw material is variation. No two individuals are exactly alike: some giraffes have longer necks, some moths are darker, some bacteria resist a drug. Much of it comes from genes passed to offspring. New variation arises from mutations, small random changes in DNA, and from the reshuffling of genes in sexual reproduction. Most mutations are neutral or harmful, but occasionally one helps.

sections.key: Traits that suit an environment spread because their owners leave more offspring; 'fittest' doesn't mean strongest.
sections.b: Every species produces more offspring than can survive. A cod can release millions of eggs, and even slow-breeding elephants would overrun the planet if every calf lived. So individuals compete for food, mates and safety. Those whose traits suit their environment are slightly more likely to survive and have young. Over many generations, helpful traits become more common. That's natural selection: simple, relentless and unguided. 'Survival of the fittest', a phrase coined by philosopher Herbert Spencer, is often misunderstood. It doesn't mean the strongest survive. 'Fittest' means best suited to a particular environment: perhaps the best camouflaged, the most cooperative or the one needing the least food. A trait that helps in one place can hurt in another, and evolution has no goal. It keeps whatever works well enough, right now.

sections.key: Peppered moths and antibiotic-resistant bacteria show natural selection working within human lifetimes.
sections.b: Peppered moths in England were mostly pale, speckled like lichen on tree bark. During the Industrial Revolution, soot killed the lichen and blackened the trees. Within decades, dark moths became far more common around industrial cities, because birds spotted and ate pale moths more easily. When clean-air laws cut pollution in the late 20th century, pale moths bounced back. Bacteria evolve even faster, sometimes reproducing every 20 minutes. When antibiotics kill most bacteria in an infection, any with a lucky mutation survive and multiply, and repeating this produces resistant 'superbugs'. That's why doctors say to take antibiotics exactly as prescribed and not for viral infections like colds. Insects evolving resistance to pesticides works the same way.

sections.key: Fossils, DNA, anatomy and observed change all independently support evolution.
sections.b: Evolution is supported by several independent lines of evidence. Fossils show changing life forms through time, including transitional species like early whales with legs. DNA comparisons show how closely species are related; humans and chimpanzees share roughly 98 to 99 per cent of their aligned DNA sequence. Anatomy reveals shared designs, like the same bones in a human arm, a bat wing and a whale flipper. And we observe evolution directly in bacteria, insects and even Darwin's finches in the Galapagos.

sections.key: Earth is about 4.5 billion years old, and humans share common ancestors with all life.
sections.b: Earth is about 4.5 billion years old, and life appeared at least 3.5 billion years ago. That's enough time for small changes to add up to the enormous variety of life today. Humans didn't evolve from modern chimpanzees; we share a common ancestor that lived roughly 6 to 7 million years ago. Our own species, Homo sapiens, appeared in Africa around 300,000 years ago. Go back far enough and every living thing, from koalas to mushrooms, shares a common ancestor.

quiz.q: Where does the variation that natural selection works on come from?
o: Traits an individual builds up through effort and passes on
Genetic differences from mutations and gene reshuffling
Changes organisms choose to suit their environment
Copying useful traits from other species
quiz.e: Genetic variation arises by chance; selection then favours what happens to work.

quiz.q: What does 'survival of the fittest' really mean?
o: Those best suited to their setting leave more young
The strongest individuals always win every contest
Species steadily improve towards a fixed goal
Animals fight each other until one remains
quiz.e: Fitness is about suiting a particular environment, and evolution has no goal or direction.

quiz.q: Why did dark peppered moths become common near industrial cities?
o: Birds ate pale moths more often on sooty trees
Pollution made individual moths turn darker
Birds preferred to eat dark moths
Dark moths migrated in from the countryside
quiz.e: Selection shifted the population as dark moths survived and reproduced more than pale ones.

quiz.q: Which is an independent line of evidence for evolution?
o: DNA comparisons showing species are unrelated
Fossils showing life forms staying constant
Observations of species that never vary
Shared bones in a human arm, a bat wing and a whale flipper
quiz.e: Fossils, DNA, anatomy and direct observation each point to the same conclusion.

quiz.q: What is true of humans and chimpanzees?
o: Humans evolved from the chimpanzees living today
We share an ancestor from about 6 to 7 million years ago
Chimpanzees evolved from early human ancestors
Our two lineages split only 300,000 years ago
quiz.e: Related species descend from shared ancestors rather than from one another.

LESSONS.push: Evolution isn't only ancient history. You can watch it happen in weeks.

LESSONS.title: Water is weird
LESSONS.hook: The most ordinary liquid on Earth breaks almost every rule in chemistry, and life depends on it.

sections.key: Water's bent, polar molecules cling together through hydrogen bonds, which explains most of its oddness.
sections.b:
A water molecule is one oxygen atom bonded to two hydrogens, in a bent shape like a wide 'V' with an angle of about 104.5 degrees. Oxygen pulls the shared electrons towards itself, so the oxygen end is slightly negative and the hydrogen ends slightly positive. That uneven charge makes water polar, a bit like a tiny magnet.

The positive hydrogen of one molecule is attracted to the negative oxygen of its neighbour. These weak links are called hydrogen bonds, and they form and break trillions of times a second. Without them, water would boil at around minus 80°C, and Earth would have no liquid oceans.

sections.key: Ice floats because freezing locks molecules into an open lattice about 9% less dense than liquid water, so lakes freeze from the top.
sections.b:
Most substances are densest as solids: solid wax sinks in melted wax. Water does the opposite. When it freezes, hydrogen bonds lock the molecules into an open, hexagonal lattice that takes up more space. Ice is about 9% less dense than liquid water, so it floats. That's why pipes burst in freezing weather and why icebergs show only about a tenth of their bulk above the surface. Water is actually densest at about 4°C.

Floating ice forms an insulating lid, so the water beneath stays liquid and fish and plants survive the winter. If ice sank, many lakes would freeze solid. This quirk has helped life persist through ice ages.

sections.key: Water absorbs and releases heat slowly, and evaporating it carries heat away, moderating climates and cooling your body.
sections.b:
Water has a very high heat capacity: it takes a lot of energy to warm up and releases it slowly as it cools. That's why the sea is still cold in early summer and warm in autumn, and why coastal Sydney is milder than inland Dubbo. The oceans absorb enormous amounts of heat, moderating global climate. Your body, about 60% water, uses the same property to hold a steady temperature.

Turning liquid water into vapour also takes a lot of energy, because hydrogen bonds must be broken. When sweat evaporates, it carries heat away. That's why a breeze feels good, and why humid days feel worse: moist air slows evaporation. Evaporative coolers, common in drier parts of Australia, work the same way.

sections.key: Hydrogen bonds give water an elastic surface and let it climb narrow tubes, which helps plants lift water to their leaves.
sections.b:
At the surface of water, molecules are pulled inwards by their neighbours below, creating a kind of elastic skin called surface tension. It's strong enough for water striders to walk on ponds and for a carefully placed paper clip to float.

The same sticky pull lets water climb up narrow tubes, a process called capillary action. It's part of how plants draw water from their roots up to their leaves.

sections.key: Because it's polar, water dissolves more substances than almost any other liquid, which is why life's chemistry happens in it.
sections.b:
Because it's polar, water pulls apart and surrounds many charged or polar molecules, dissolving them. It dissolves more substances than almost any other liquid, which is why it's called the universal solvent. It carries nutrients in your blood, minerals from rocks into rivers, and salt into the sea. It's also why water is so hard to keep pure.

Nearly every chemical reaction that keeps you alive happens in water, which is why scientists searching for life elsewhere start by looking for it.

quiz.q: Why do water molecules cling to each other so strongly?
o: Positive hydrogens attract neighbouring negative oxygens
Their oxygen atoms are bonded tightly to each other
They are held together by a thin film of dissolved salt
They are pulled together by the Earth's magnetic field
quiz.e: Water's uneven charge creates hydrogen bonds between neighbouring molecules.

quiz.q: Why does ice float on liquid water?
o: Freezing removes some of the water's mass
Cold water always rises above warmer water
Its molecules lock into a more open pattern
Tiny pockets of trapped air hold it up
quiz.e: The open hexagonal lattice makes ice about 9% less dense than liquid water.

quiz.q: Why do humid days feel hotter than dry days at the same temperature?
o: Humid air is always warmer than dry air
Sweat evaporates more slowly, cooling you less
Moist air blocks sunlight from your skin
Water vapour makes your body produce more heat
quiz.e: Evaporation carries heat away, and moist air slows it down.

quiz.q: Why can a water strider walk across a pond?
o: Its body is less dense than the water
Constant wind holds it up off the surface
Water near the surface is denser than below
Hydrogen bonds create an elastic skin on the surface
quiz.e: Molecules at the surface pull inwards, forming surface tension.

quiz.q: Why does water dissolve so many different substances?
o: Its warm temperature breaks most substances apart
Its polar molecules surround and separate other molecules
Its low weight lets other substances slip through it
Its acidity eats away at most other materials
quiz.e: Water's polarity lets it surround and separate many other molecules.

LESSONS.push: Water breaks the rules of chemistry. One quirk keeps lakes alive through winter.

LESSONS.title: Quantum mechanics, simply
LESSONS.hook: The physics of the very small breaks every everyday rule. Yet it's the most tested theory in science, and it runs your phone.

sections.key: Quantum mechanics describes atoms and particles, is among the most precisely tested theories in science, and underpins modern electronics.
sections.b:
Quantum mechanics describes how things behave at the scale of atoms and particles such as electrons and photons. At that size, everyday ideas of cause and effect stop working the way you'd expect. It sounds like science fiction, yet it's one of the most precisely tested theories in science, with predictions confirmed to many decimal places.

It's also practical. Without it, we'd have no transistors, computer chips, lasers, LEDs, solar panels or MRI machines. Your phone runs on it.

sections.key: Energy comes in fixed packets called quanta, and electrons in atoms can only have certain energy levels.
sections.b:
In 1900, Max Planck found that the colours of light from hot objects only made sense if energy is given off in tiny fixed amounts, which he called quanta. In 1905, Albert Einstein showed that light itself comes in packets, now called photons, to explain how light knocks electrons out of metal. That work, not relativity, won him his Nobel Prize.

In 1913, Niels Bohr proposed that electrons in an atom have only certain energy levels, like rungs on a ladder rather than a ramp. Jumping between them gives off exactly the right amount of light. That's why each element glows in its own set of colours, which astronomers use to work out what distant stars are made of. A 'quantum leap' is actually incredibly tiny.

sections.key: Electrons and light act like particles in some experiments and like waves in others, and detecting the path destroys the wave pattern.
sections.b:
Light and matter behave like particles in some experiments and like waves in others. In the famous double-slit experiment, electrons are fired one at a time at a barrier with two narrow slits. Each electron lands as a single dot on the screen behind, like a particle.

Over time, though, the dots build up a striped interference pattern, which only waves make, as if each electron passed through both slits at once. Try to detect which slit each electron goes through, and the pattern disappears.

sections.key: Quantum theory predicts probabilities, and nature itself limits how precisely you can know a particle's position and momentum together.
sections.b:
Quantum mechanics doesn't say exactly what a particle will do. It gives probabilities. Before it's measured, a particle can be in a 'superposition' of several possible states at once. Measuring it produces one definite result, with odds the theory predicts precisely. Schrödinger's cat, both alive and dead until the box is opened, was meant to show how strange this seems when scaled up.

In 1927, Werner Heisenberg showed you can't know a particle's exact position and momentum at the same time. This isn't a flaw in our instruments; it's built into nature. It's also why atoms don't collapse: an electron squeezed into the nucleus would have enormous uncertainty in its momentum, so it spreads out in a cloud instead.

sections.key: Entanglement and tunnelling are confirmed quantum effects, and quantum computers aim to exploit superposition for certain hard problems.
sections.b:
Two particles can become entangled, so that measuring one tells you about the other, however far apart they are. Einstein called it 'spooky action at a distance' and doubted it, but experiments have confirmed it repeatedly, and that work won the 2022 Nobel Prize in Physics. Tunnelling lets particles pass through barriers they classically shouldn't cross. It helps power the Sun's fusion and is used in some computer memory.

The first quantum revolution gave us transistors and lasers. A second is under way. Quantum computers use qubits, which can be in superpositions of 0 and 1, to tackle problems such as simulating molecules for new medicines. They're still experimental and error-prone. Australia is a notable player, with research groups in Sydney, Melbourne and Brisbane.

quiz.q: Why does quantum mechanics matter in everyday life?
o: It explains why heavy objects fall faster than light ones
It underpins technology like transistors and lasers
It predicts the weather with great accuracy
It describes how planets orbit the Sun
quiz.e: Quantum physics is behind the electronics and medical scanners we rely on.

quiz.q: What does a 'quantum leap' mean in physics?
o: A huge, sudden advance in energy
A particle travelling faster than light
A slow drift of energy between atoms
A tiny jump between fixed energy levels
quiz.e: The everyday phrase is misleading: a physical quantum leap is incredibly tiny.

quiz.q: What happens to the striped pattern in the double-slit experiment if you detect which slit each electron uses?
o: The pattern gets sharper
The pattern disappears
The electrons stop landing on the screen
The stripes turn into a single wide band of light
quiz.e: Detecting the path forces particle-like behaviour, so the wave pattern vanishes.

quiz.q: What does the uncertainty principle say?
o: Position and momentum can't both be known exactly
Scientists can't trust their instruments at small scales
Measurements always disturb the apparatus too much to use
Particles have no properties at all
quiz.e: The limit is built into nature, not caused by poor instruments.

quiz.q: What have experiments on entangled particles shown?
o: Particles can be cloned perfectly
Linked particles stay correlated however far apart
Information can be sent faster than light
Particles lose their link after a few seconds
quiz.e: Entanglement is real and repeatedly confirmed, even though Einstein doubted it.

LESSONS.push: An electron fired alone can still build a wave pattern. How is that possible?

LESSONS.title: Climate change: the basics
LESSONS.hook: The physics has been understood since the 1800s. Here's what's actually happening, what it means for Australia and what's being done.

sections.key: Greenhouse gases trap heat that would otherwise escape to space, and the physics has been understood for over a century.
sections.b:
Sunlight warms the Earth's surface, which then gives off heat as infrared radiation. Gases such as water vapour, carbon dioxide (CO₂) and methane absorb some of that infrared and send it back down, like a blanket. This natural greenhouse effect is essential: without it, Earth's average temperature would be around minus 18°C instead of about 15°C. The problem is thickening the blanket.

This isn't new science. In 1856, Eunice Foote showed that a glass cylinder of CO₂ heated up more in sunlight than one of ordinary air. John Tyndall measured how gases absorb heat in 1859, and in 1896 Svante Arrhenius calculated that burning coal could warm the planet.

sections.key: Humans have raised CO₂ from about 280 to over 420 ppm, and its chemical signature shows it comes from fossil fuels.
sections.b:
Since the Industrial Revolution, humans have burned vast amounts of coal, oil and gas, and cleared forests. Atmospheric CO₂ has risen from about 280 parts per million to over 420, higher than at any time in at least 800,000 years, based on air bubbles trapped in Antarctic ice. We know the extra carbon comes from fossil fuels because it carries a distinctive isotope signature.

Globally, the biggest sources are electricity and heat, industry such as steel and cement, transport, agriculture, land clearing and buildings. Methane, from livestock, landfill and gas leaks, is a powerful short-lived gas. In Australia, coal-reliant electricity has historically been the largest source, and emissions per person are among the highest in the developed world.

sections.key: The world has warmed about 1.3 to 1.4°C, and Australia about 1.5°C since 1910, as land warms faster than the oceans.
sections.b:
The global average surface temperature has risen by roughly 1.3 to 1.4°C since the late 1800s, and the last decade was the warmest on record. In 2024, the global average for a single year exceeded 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels for the first time.

Australia's climate has warmed by about 1.5°C since national records began in 1910, according to the Bureau of Meteorology and CSIRO. Land warms faster than oceans, which is why Australia's figure is higher than the global average. Global sea level has also risen by more than 20 centimetres since 1900, and the rate is increasing.

sections.key: Australia faces more extreme heat, longer fire seasons, warmer and more acidic oceans, and coral bleaching.
sections.b:
For Australia, the effects include more frequent and intense heatwaves, and longer, more dangerous bushfire seasons in the south and east. Some areas get heavier downpours, while the south-west and south-east get less cool-season rain.

The oceans around Australia have warmed and become more acidic, which stresses marine life. During marine heatwaves, when seawater stays unusually hot for days or weeks, corals expel the algae that feed them and turn white. The Great Barrier Reef has suffered several of these mass bleaching events since 2016. Rising seas also add to the risk of flooding along low-lying coasts.

sections.key: Countries aim to keep warming well below 2°C, and cheap renewables are making the shift achievable.
sections.b:
In the 2015 Paris Agreement, nearly every country agreed to keep warming well below 2°C and pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5°C. Scientists say that needs steep emissions cuts this decade and net zero, where remaining emissions are balanced by removals, around mid-century. Every fraction of a degree matters: 2°C instead of 1.5°C means more extreme heat, more species loss and far more damage to coral reefs.

Solutions are scaling quickly. Solar power's cost fell by roughly 90% in the 2010s. Australia has more than four million rooftop solar systems, among the most per person in the world, and renewables provide around 40% of its electricity. Individuals help most through big choices: how they power and heat their homes, how they travel and how they vote.

quiz.q: Why is the natural greenhouse effect important?
o: Earth would average about minus 18°C without it
It protects Earth from ultraviolet radiation
It stops the oceans from evaporating
It produces the oxygen we breathe
quiz.e: Greenhouse gases keep Earth habitable; the problem is thickening the blanket.

quiz.q: How do scientists know the extra CO₂ comes from fossil fuels?
o: Satellites photograph it leaving smokestacks
It is measurably warmer than natural CO₂
It carries a distinctive isotope signature
It appears only over cities
quiz.e: Fossil carbon has a chemical fingerprint that shows up in the air.

quiz.q: Why has Australia warmed by more than the global average?
o: Land warms faster than oceans
Australia sits closer to the Sun
Its coastline traps extra heat
Its cities are unusually large
quiz.e: The global average includes oceans, which warm more slowly than land.

quiz.q: What has happened to the Great Barrier Reef during recent marine heatwaves?
o: It has grown faster than before
It has moved to cooler waters
It has had several bleaching events
It has been unaffected so far
quiz.e: Warmer seas stress corals, causing bleaching events since 2016.

quiz.q: Why does the gap between 1.5°C and 2°C of warming matter?
o: It would make little noticeable difference anywhere
It would mostly affect only the polar regions
It would slightly cool the surface of the oceans
It brings more extreme heat, species loss and reef damage
quiz.e: Every fraction of a degree adds to the harm, which is why the Paris goals are so tight.

LESSONS.push: Without greenhouse gases Earth would sit near minus 18°C. So what has changed?

LESSONS.title: Antibiotics and superbugs
LESSONS.hook: A mouldy dish in 1928 changed medicine forever. Now the bugs are fighting back.

sections.key: Before antibiotics, minor infections could be fatal; penicillin was discovered by accident in 1928.
sections.b:
Before antibiotics, a scratch from a rose thorn, an infected tooth or a farm cut could turn into a fatal infection. Pneumonia, tuberculosis, meningitis and infections after childbirth killed huge numbers of people. Surgery was risky largely because of infection afterwards, and in World War I infected wounds killed many soldiers who would survive today.

In September 1928, Alexander Fleming returned from holiday to his London laboratory and found that a dish of Staphylococcus bacteria had been contaminated by a mould. Around the mould, the bacteria had died. It was Penicillium, and he named the substance penicillin. But he struggled to purify it, and for about a decade it stayed a laboratory curiosity.

sections.key: Adelaide-born Howard Florey and his team turned penicillin into a usable medicine in the 1940s.
sections.b:
The breakthrough came at Oxford University, led by Howard Florey, who was born in Adelaide, with biochemist Ernst Chain and a talented team including Norman Heatley. Around 1940, they purified penicillin, showed it cured infected mice and then treated the first human patients.

With American help, production was scaled up massively during World War II, saving countless wounded soldiers. Fleming, Florey and Chain shared the 1945 Nobel Prize in Medicine.

sections.key: Antibiotics attack structures bacteria have and human cells lack, so they do nothing against viruses.
sections.b:
Antibiotics attack features bacteria have but human cells don't. Penicillin and its relatives stop bacteria building their cell walls, so they burst. Others block the tiny machines bacteria use to make proteins, or interfere with how they copy their DNA. They can also affect helpful gut bacteria, which is why they sometimes upset the stomach.

Viruses are different. They have no cell walls or protein-making machinery of their own; they hijack your cells instead. So antibiotics do nothing against colds, flu, COVID-19 or most sore throats and coughs. Taking them for a cold won't help you recover faster, and it exposes your body's bacteria to the drug, which can help resistance develop. Antivirals and vaccines are the tools for viruses.

sections.key: Overusing antibiotics lets resistant bacteria survive and spread, producing superbugs that kill over a million people a year.
sections.b:
Every time antibiotics are used, bacteria that happen to survive can multiply and spread their resistance, even swapping resistance genes with other bacteria. Overuse in humans and animals speeds this up. The result is superbugs: infections that some or most antibiotics can no longer treat.

A major study estimated that in 2019, drug-resistant bacterial infections directly caused about 1.27 million deaths worldwide. Fleming himself warned in his 1945 Nobel lecture that misuse could lead to resistance.

sections.key: Take antibiotics only when prescribed, exactly as directed and never shared, while scientists search for new ones.
sections.b:
