They hide their odds from regulators
quiz.e: On average, players get back less than they spend, which is how the operators profit.

quiz.q: Why are surprising coincidences so common?
o: Fate tends to arrange them for us
Many possible pairs make a match likely
Our memories record every event exactly
Rare events repeat on a fixed schedule
quiz.e: With 23 people, there are so many pairs that a shared birthday is more likely than not.

quiz.q: What was wrong with the '1 in 73 million' figure in Sally Clark's trial?
o: It was too generous to the defence team
It came from a source with no qualifications
It was based on badly out-of-date figures
It was flawed and answered the wrong question
quiz.e: Confusing the direction of conditional probability led to a wrongful conviction.

quiz.q: Which risk deserves insurance according to this lesson?
o: A rare but unaffordable loss, like a fire
A likely small loss, like a scratched phone
Any loss with a 50% chance of happening
A loss you could easily cover yourself
quiz.e: Insurance suits catastrophic losses you can't absorb, not minor ones.

LESSONS.push: A roulette wheel hit black 26 times. Why did betting on red cost millions?

LESSONS.title: How statistics can mislead
LESSONS.hook: The numbers can be true and still tell a false story. Here's how to spot the tricks.

sections.key: Accurate statistics can still mislead, and the median is often more representative than the mean when data is skewed.
sections.b:
Most misleading statistics aren't lies; the numbers are accurate. The deception is in what's included, what's left out, how it's compared and how it's shown. The 1954 book How to Lie with Statistics by Darrell Huff became a bestseller because its tricks were so common. Most still are.

The 'average' usually means the mean: add everything up and divide. But extremes drag the mean around. If a billionaire walks into a café, the mean wealth of the customers soars, though nobody else got richer. The median, the middle value when everything is lined up, is often more representative for skewed data like incomes and house prices. When someone quotes an average, ask which one.

sections.key: Percentages and graphs can make small changes look dramatic through framing, truncated axes and convenient timeframes.
sections.b:
If an interest rate rises from 4% to 5%, that's one percentage point but a 25% increase. If support for something rises from 10% to 15%, that's 5 percentage points, or a 50% increase. Both are correct, and people choose whichever sounds more impressive. A 200% increase in something rare might mean going from 1 case to 3.

Graphs mislead too. The classic trick is a truncated y-axis: starting at 95 instead of 0 makes a small change look like a leap. A convenient start and end date can make a trend look up or down. Two lines on different scales can seem connected. Check the axis labels, starting point and timeframe before reacting.

sections.key: A statistic is only as good as its sample, and looking only at survivors or self-selected respondents distorts the picture.
sections.b:
A statistic is only as good as its sample. Online polls anyone can vote in attract people with strong opinions and can be flooded by campaigns. In 1936, the Literary Digest polled millions, drawing largely on car owners and telephone directories, and predicted a landslide defeat for Roosevelt. He won by a landslide. A well-designed random sample of around 1,000 is usually far more accurate than a huge biased one.

Survivorship bias is similar. In World War II, the US military studied returning bombers to decide where to add armour. Statistician Abraham Wald noted they only saw planes that survived: the areas without holes, like the engines, were where hits brought planes down. Studying only successful businesses or old buildings still standing makes the same mistake.

sections.key: A trend in every subgroup can reverse when the groups are combined, so how data is grouped can change its story.
sections.b:
Sometimes a trend that appears in every subgroup reverses when the data is combined. In a well-known 1973 case, the University of California, Berkeley appeared to admit men at a higher rate than women overall.

But when researchers looked department by department, women were admitted at similar or higher rates in most departments. The overall gap arose because women applied more often to highly competitive departments.

The lesson: how data is grouped can completely change its story.

sections.key: When you meet a striking statistic, ask who collected it, how, compared with what, and what is left out.
sections.b:
When you meet a striking statistic, ask: Who collected it, and do they have an agenda? How was the sample chosen, and how big was it? Is it an average, and which kind? Is it a relative or absolute change? Compared with what, and over what time period? What's left out?

Reputable sources, like the Australian Bureau of Statistics, publish their methods so you can check.

You don't need to be a mathematician to ask good questions about numbers.

quiz.q: Why are median house prices usually reported instead of the mean?
o: A few extreme sales skew the mean
The median is always the higher figure
The mean is too hard to calculate
Almost all houses sell for the same price
quiz.e: For skewed data, the middle value is more representative than one pulled around by extremes.

quiz.q: A rate rises from 10% to 15%. How can this be described?
o: Only as a 5% increase in the rate
Only as a 50 percentage point rise
As 5 percentage points or 50% more
As a 150% increase in the rate
quiz.e: Both descriptions are correct, so check which one is being used and why.

quiz.q: Why was the Literary Digest's two-million-strong poll so wrong?
o: Voters changed their minds after polling
Its sample skewed to car and phone owners
It asked leading questions of voters
It surveyed voters in only one state
quiz.e: A huge biased sample is worse than a small, well-designed random one.

quiz.q: What does Simpson's paradox show?
o: Averages are always misleading
Small samples are the most reliable
Percentages should never be compared
Trends can reverse when groups combine
quiz.e: How data is grouped can completely change the story it tells.

quiz.q: Which question helps you judge a striking statistic?
o: How large and colourful is the chart?
How many news sites have repeated it?
Who collected it, and what is missing?
Does the number sound impressive?
quiz.e: Source, method, comparison and omissions reveal how a true number can tell a false story.

LESSONS.push: Every number in the story was true, and the story was still false.

LESSONS.title: How to spot misinformation
LESSONS.hook: False stories spread faster than true ones. Professional fact-checkers use a few simple habits you can copy in 30 seconds.

sections.key: False stories spread faster than true ones, driven by people responding to emotion rather than by bots.
sections.b:
A major 2018 MIT study of millions of tweets found that false news spread further, faster and deeper than true news, and was about 70% more likely to be retweeted. People, not bots, were mainly responsible. False stories tend to be more novel and emotionally charged, triggering surprise, fear or disgust, which is what makes us share them.

If a post makes you instantly furious, frightened or triumphant, slow down. Misleading content is often engineered to provoke emotion, because emotion bypasses careful thinking. Watch especially for content that confirms what you already believe about people you disagree with. The stronger your reaction, the more worth spending 30 seconds checking.

sections.key: Misinformation is false information shared in good faith, while disinformation is spread deliberately to deceive.
sections.b:
Misinformation is false or misleading information shared by people who believe it, like a relative forwarding a fake health tip. Disinformation is false information spread deliberately to deceive, for profit, politics or to cause chaos.

There's also malinformation: true information used out of context to mislead, like an old photo presented as happening today.

Much of what spreads online is a mix: a kernel of truth wrapped in exaggeration or missing context. It isn't only 'other people' who fall for it. It's designed to exploit everyone's instincts.

sections.key: Stop, investigate the source, find better coverage and trace claims to the original, and judge a source by what others say about it.
sections.b:
Digital literacy expert Mike Caulfield developed a four-step method called SIFT. Stop: pause before reacting or sharing. Investigate the source: who's behind this, and what's their expertise and agenda? Find better coverage: see what trusted outlets or fact-checkers say. Trace claims, quotes and media to their original context. Most checks take under a minute.

When Stanford researchers compared professional fact-checkers, historians and students evaluating websites, the fact-checkers were fastest and most accurate. Their secret was lateral reading: rather than scrolling the site itself, they opened new tabs and searched for what others said about the source. Professional-looking sites and official-sounding names are easy to fake. What independent sources say is much harder to fake.

sections.key: Reverse image search and independent fact-checkers can reveal where a photo or claim really came from.
sections.b:
Photos and videos are often real but taken out of context: an old flood picture reshared as a new disaster, or footage from another country. A reverse image search, using tools like Google Lens or TinEye, can reveal where and when an image first appeared. For video, screenshot a key frame and search that. Clues like signs, shop names, number plates, weather and which side of the road cars drive on can confirm where it was taken.

Independent fact-checkers investigate viral claims and publish their evidence, including AAP FactCheck in Australia, and Full Fact and Snopes internationally. Search the claim plus 'fact check'. 'Prebunking', learning manipulation techniques like fake experts and emotional language in advance, helps people resist misinformation. You're doing that right now.

sections.key: Listening, asking questions and sharing good sources works better than mocking or lecturing someone who believes misinformation.
sections.b:
When friends or family share misinformation, mocking or lecturing usually backfires, making people defend their views harder. It's more effective to stay curious and respectful: ask where they heard it and what would change their mind.

Share a reliable source privately rather than correcting them in public. Explaining how a manipulation technique works can be more persuasive than arguing about the specific claim.

And model good behaviour yourself: when you share something that turns out to be false, correct it openly.

quiz.q: Why do false stories tend to spread faster than true ones?
o: Bots are mainly responsible for sharing them
They're novel and emotional, so people share them
They're written by professional journalists
Platforms promote them on purpose
quiz.e: People, not bots, drive the spread, and emotion makes content shareable.

quiz.q: What distinguishes disinformation from misinformation?
o: It is always shared by accident
It is shared only by automated bots
It is only ever about politics
It is spread deliberately to deceive
quiz.e: Misinformation is shared by people who believe it; disinformation is intended to mislead.

quiz.q: What is lateral reading?
o: Opening new tabs to check the source
Reading a website very quickly from top to bottom
Checking a site's design for professionalism
Counting references on the page
quiz.e: What independent sources say about a site is much harder to fake than its appearance.

quiz.q: How can you check where a viral photo came from?
o: Run a reverse image search on the picture
Check how many people have shared it
Judge whether the picture looks professional
Ask whoever posted it where it came from
quiz.e: Reverse image search can show when and where an image first appeared.

quiz.q: What works best when a friend shares misinformation?
o: Mocking the claim in front of others
Lecturing them with a long list of facts
Staying curious and sharing a source privately
Ignoring it and never raising the subject
quiz.e: Mocking or lecturing makes people defend their view harder.

LESSONS.push: Fact-checkers spot a fake site faster by leaving it. Here's how.

LESSONS.title: Stoicism today: an ancient philosophy goes viral
LESSONS.hook: Footballers, generals and millions of readers have rediscovered a 2,300-year-old philosophy. Here's where it shows up now, and what people get wrong about it.

sections.key: Once confined to classics departments, Stoicism became one of the most popular philosophies of the 21st century.
sections.b: For most of the 20th century, Stoicism lived in university classics departments. Then it spread fast. In 2009 the American philosopher William Irvine published A Guide to the Good Life, pitching Stoicism as a practical philosophy for ordinary people. In 2014 the marketer turned writer Ryan Holiday released The Obstacle Is the Way, its title adapted from a line of Marcus Aurelius. A daily newsletter, a podcast and more books followed. Massimo Pigliucci's How to Be a Stoic and Donald Robertson's How to Think Like a Roman Emperor added to the boom. The ancient teachers themselves appear in later lessons.

sections.key: Athletes and soldiers value Stoic calm, but critics warn that endurance without expression can mean burying pain.
sections.b:
Sport has embraced Stoicism. Holiday's book, about treating setbacks as raw material, spread through American football. Staff at the New England Patriots reportedly read it in their 2014 season, which ended in a Super Bowl win, and Seattle Seahawks coach Pete Carroll and general manager John Schneider are said to have passed it around too. Athletes can't control referees, injuries or weather, and dwelling on them wastes energy.

Military culture prizes endurance and calm under fire. Former US general and defence secretary Jim Mattis has described carrying Marcus Aurelius's Meditations on deployments. The philosopher Nancy Sherman, in Stoic Warriors (2005), admired this but warned that prizing calm over fear and grief can push people to bury pain. Veterans, she argues, need room to feel and talk, not just endure.

sections.key: Toughing it out in silence is not the Stoic philosophy, and the ancient Stoics sought help constantly.
sections.b:
Psychologists separate capital-S Stoicism, the philosophy, from small-s stoicism: hiding feelings, enduring pain without complaint and insisting on handling everything alone. Studies link small-s stoicism with people, especially men, delaying a visit to the doctor or help for their mental health, including research on men in rural Australia.

The irony is that the ancient Stoics constantly sought counsel. Seneca's letters show one friend helping another through fear, illness and grief, and Stoic students trained with teachers. The 'stiff upper lip' isn't the goal either. Despite its British image, the phrase's earliest known use is in an American newspaper in 1815. Seething behind a brave face is not the Stoic work, which happens in how you think about events. If you're ignoring chest pain or struggling in silence, see a doctor or ask for help early.

sections.key: Critics say pop-Stoicism can shrink a rich philosophy into emotional armour and hustle culture.
sections.b:
Not everyone welcomes the revival. Critics use the jokey term 'broicism' for online versions that sell Stoicism to ambitious young men as a kit of cold showers, grinding and never showing feelings. The classicist Donna Zuckerberg's 2018 book Not All Dead White Men documented how parts of the online 'manosphere' borrowed Stoic writers to justify contempt for women and emotion.

Others argue that a narrow focus on your own reactions can slide into shrugging at injustice, although the ancient Stoics insisted on public duty. Pop versions also drop the Stoic idea of a rational, ordered universe, which made acceptance make sense to the ancients. Whether the ethics works without it is still debated.

sections.key: Stoic Week and a small personal experiment can show whether Stoic practices help you, though the results are not proof.
sections.b:
In 2012 classicists, philosophers and psychotherapists at the University of Exeter ran a trial: could ordinary people benefit from living like a Stoic for a week? Stoic Week became an annual event, usually in October. Tens of thousands have joined. Participants typically report higher life satisfaction and fewer negative emotions afterwards. Treat that with care: they are keen volunteers, many drop out before the final survey, and there's no comparison group.

You can run your own experiment. Each evening for a week, rate your calm, mood and coping from 1 to 10. Each morning, try one practice from the Stoic practices lesson. Then see which helped. Simply paying attention to your mood can lift it, so treat the results as a personal guide, not proof.

quiz.q: How did books like Irvine's and Holiday's change Stoicism's reputation?
o: They presented it as a practical philosophy for ordinary people
They argued it should stay a subject for classics scholars
They replaced it with a new modern doctrine
They treated it mainly as a form of religion
quiz.e: Stoicism moved from classics departments to bestseller lists once it was pitched as practical guidance for everyday life.

quiz.q: Why has Stoicism appealed to athletes?
o: It promises to remove all nerves before a match
It says focus on what you can't control wastes energy
It teaches that winning matters more than anything
It forbids talking about injuries with teammates
quiz.e: Referees, injuries and weather are out of an athlete's hands, so Stoic focus on what you can influence suits performers under pressure.

quiz.q: How does everyday small-s stoicism differ from the ancient Stoics on seeking help?
o: Both agree that handling problems alone is best
The ancient Stoics avoided teachers, while modern people seek them
Small-s stoicism delays help, but the Stoics constantly sought counsel
Small-s stoicism encourages help, while the Stoics discouraged it
quiz.e: Silent toughness is linked with putting off help, yet Seneca's letters and Stoic teaching show the Stoics relied on others.

quiz.q: What is a common criticism of modern pop-Stoicism?
o: It focuses too heavily on ancient physics
It is too complicated for beginners to follow
It requires joining a formal organisation
It can shrink into emotional armour
quiz.e: Critics say 'broicism' strips out the philosophy's concern for duty, community and a rational universe.

quiz.q: Why should Stoic Week's positive results be treated with care?
o: It had keen volunteers and no comparison group
Stoic Week lasted for only one day
Only a few dozen people ever took part
No one was asked how they felt afterwards
quiz.e: Without a comparison group, the improvements can't be pinned on Stoic practice alone.

LESSONS.push: The ancient Stoics asked for help constantly. So why do we think they didn't?

LESSONS.title: Three ways to decide what's right
LESSONS.hook: Would you pull the lever? Philosophy's three big approaches to right and wrong, and how they help with real decisions.

sections.key: Consequentialism judges actions by their results, and utilitarianism aims for the greatest good for the greatest number.
sections.b:
Ethics, or moral philosophy, asks how we should live and act. Most of the time our instincts work fine: don't steal, keep promises, help people in need. But instincts can conflict, and some decisions in medicine, business, technology and our own lives are genuinely hard. Three approaches dominate: consequentialism, deontology and virtue ethics.

Consequentialism says the right action has the best consequences. Its most famous form, utilitarianism, was developed by Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill: act to produce the greatest wellbeing for the greatest number. It is practical and impartial, since everyone counts equally, and it underpins policy like cost-benefit analysis in health funding. Australian philosopher Peter Singer is a leading modern advocate.

sections.key: Pure consequence-counting can seem to justify terrible acts, which is why most people resist it.
sections.b:
Imagine a surgeon with five patients who will die without organ transplants, and a healthy visitor whose organs could save them all. Pure consequence-counting seems to say: sacrifice the visitor. Almost everyone recoils.

The approach has other problems. It demands that we predict consequences, which is often impossible, and it can seem to ignore justice, rights and promises. Defenders respond that, in practice, respecting rights usually produces the best outcomes anyway. Still, the surgeon case shows why many people feel that results cannot be the whole story.

sections.key: Deontology holds that some actions are right or wrong in themselves, but strict rules can clash or give absurd results.
sections.b:
Deontology, from the Greek for 'duty', says some actions are right or wrong in themselves, whatever the consequences. Lying, killing innocent people and breaking promises are wrong even if they'd produce good results. Immanuel Kant argued we should act only on principles we could want everyone to follow, and treat people as ends in themselves, never merely as means. That explains why sacrificing the visitor is wrong: it uses him as a tool. Human rights reflect this thinking.

Rules have problems too. Kant argued you shouldn't lie even to a murderer asking where your friend is hiding, which strikes most people as absurd. Duties can also conflict. Many modern deontologists allow that duties can sometimes be outweighed, but deciding when is the hard part.

sections.key: Virtue ethics asks what kind of person to be, building virtues that sit between extremes.
sections.b:
Virtue ethics, going back to Aristotle in ancient Greece, shifts the question from 'What should I do?' to 'What kind of person should I be?' It focuses on developing good character traits, or virtues, like honesty, courage, compassion, fairness and wisdom.

Aristotle argued that virtues sit between extremes: courage lies between cowardice and recklessness, and generosity between stinginess and extravagance. Good people develop practical wisdom, the ability to judge what each situation needs, through experience and habit. Instead of a formula, virtue ethics offers a standard to grow towards.

sections.key: Our intuitions draw on both consequences and duties, so use all three lenses on hard decisions and notice where they disagree.
sections.b:
In the famous trolley problem, a runaway tram will kill five people unless you pull a lever to divert it onto a track where it will kill one. Most people say pull it. But if the only way to stop the tram is to push a large person off a bridge, most refuse, though the numbers are identical. Our intuitions draw on both consequences and duties.

So don't pick one theory. Try three lenses. Consequences: who is affected, and how? Duties: am I respecting rights and keeping commitments? Character: what would a person I admire do? Often all three agree. When they don't, the tension shows what is at stake, which is where good judgement begins. A quick test: would you be comfortable if the decision appeared on the front page?

quiz.q: What does utilitarianism say makes an action right?
o: It follows strict rules whatever the outcome
It brings the greatest wellbeing overall
It expresses the virtues of a good person
It is approved by those in authority
quiz.e: Utilitarianism judges actions by their results, counting everyone's wellbeing equally.

quiz.q: Why does the surgeon and visitor case trouble pure consequentialism?
o: Surgeons rarely have enough patients to compare
It seems to justify harming an innocent person
It shows that predicting outcomes is always easy
It proves that rights never matter in medicine
quiz.e: Counting only outcomes can endorse acts that almost everyone sees as deeply wrong.

quiz.q: According to deontology, why is sacrificing the healthy visitor wrong?
o: It would be too expensive to organise
It uses him merely as a tool for others
It would not actually save the five
It has never been tried in practice
quiz.e: Treating people as ends in themselves, never merely as means, rules out using one person as a tool.

quiz.q: What question does virtue ethics put at the centre?
o: Which choice gives the best results?
Which rule applies here?
What do the laws say?
What kind of person should I be?
quiz.e: Virtue ethics focuses on developing character traits like honesty and courage, guided by practical wisdom.

quiz.q: What does the difference between the lever and bridge versions of the trolley problem reveal?
o: Most people ignore numbers when deciding
Most people refuse to make any choice at all
Our intuitions draw on both consequences and duties
Everyone agrees on the right answer to ethical dilemmas
quiz.e: The same numbers feel different because we weigh duties as well as outcomes.

LESSONS.push: Saving five by pulling a lever feels right. Saving five by a push does not. Why?

LESSONS.title: Plate tectonics
LESSONS.hook: The ground beneath you is moving. Australia is drifting north faster than your fingernails grow.

sections.key: Earth's outer shell is split into plates that move a few centimetres a year, enough to reshape the planet over millions of years.
sections.b: Earth's outer shell, the lithosphere, isn't one solid piece. It's broken into several major plates and many smaller ones, fitting together like a cracked eggshell. They ride on the asthenosphere, a layer of hot rock that is solid but flows extremely slowly, like very stiff putty. The plates move a few centimetres a year, roughly as fast as fingernails grow. Over millions of years, that is enough to open oceans and build mountain ranges. Plate tectonics also shapes life: mountains alter climates, opening and closing oceans separate species, and carbon is recycled over long timescales, helping keep Earth habitable.

sections.key: Wegener proposed drifting continents in 1912, and seafloor spreading with magnetic stripes confirmed plate tectonics in the 1960s.
sections.b:
In 1912, German meteorologist Alfred Wegener proposed that the continents were once joined in a supercontinent he called Pangaea, meaning 'all lands'. Coastlines of South America and Africa fit like jigsaw pieces, matching fossils and rocks appear on continents now separated by oceans, and signs of ancient glaciers turn up in today's tropics. But he couldn't explain what moved the continents, and most geologists rejected the idea for decades.

The proof came from the ocean floor. In the 1950s and 60s, scientists mapped a vast underwater mountain range down the middle of the Atlantic. Rocks on either side carried mirror-image magnetic stripes, recording reversals in Earth's magnetic field as new crust formed and spread outwards. By the late 1960s, plate tectonics was geology's unifying theory.

sections.key: Plates pull apart, collide or slide past each other, while hotspots leave volcano chains as plates drift over them.
sections.b:
Most geological action happens at plate boundaries. Where plates pull apart, magma rises to form new crust, as along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge and through Iceland. Where they collide, an ocean plate may dive beneath another (subduction), making trenches and volcanoes, or two continents crumple into mountains like the Himalayas. Where they slide past each other, you get faults like California's San Andreas.

Some volcanoes sit far from any edge. A hotspot is where unusually hot rock rises from the mantle and melts through the plate above. The plate moves on while the hotspot stays roughly put, leaving a chain of volcanoes that grow older with distance, like the Hawaiian Islands. Eastern Australia's Cosgrove track, identified in 2015, runs over 2,000 kilometres from central Queensland to Victoria, the longest known on any continent.

sections.key: Australia is moving north at about 7 centimetres a year, fast enough that its map coordinates had to be updated.
sections.b:
The Australian plate is one of the fastest-moving continental plates, heading north-north-east at about 7 centimetres a year. It has been moving north since it split from Antarctica tens of millions of years ago. The movement is so large that Australia's national datum, used by GPS, had to be shifted by about 1.8 metres to catch up. If current movement continues, Australia is expected to collide with parts of South-East Asia in perhaps 50 million years.

Pangaea wasn't the first supercontinent, and it won't be the last. Geologists have found evidence of several earlier ones, and plate movements suggest the continents will gather again in perhaps 200 to 250 million years. Names proposed include Amasia and Pangaea Ultima.

sections.key: Australia sits in the middle of a plate, so big earthquakes are rarer than on plate edges, but they do happen.
sections.b:
Because Australia sits in the middle of its plate, far from boundaries, large earthquakes are much rarer than in New Zealand or Indonesia. But stresses from the plate's movement still cause quakes.

The 1989 Newcastle earthquake, magnitude 5.6, killed 13 people and caused billions of dollars of damage. In 2021, a magnitude 5.9 quake near Mansfield in Victoria was felt as far away as Sydney and Adelaide. Geoscience Australia records many earthquakes across the country every year, most too small to feel.

quiz.q: How can plates that move only a few centimetres a year reshape the planet?
o: Their speed increases sharply every century
The movement adds up over millions of years
They are pushed along by ocean tides
Each plate moves in short, violent bursts
quiz.e: Fingernail-speed movement, sustained for millions of years, is enough to open oceans and build mountains.

quiz.q: What finally confirmed that the seafloor is spreading and continents move?
o: Satellite photographs of the world's coastlines
Mirror-image magnetic stripes in seafloor rocks
Fossils found in rocks from desert regions
The shapes drawn on ancient sailors' maps
quiz.e: The matching magnetic stripes recorded new crust forming and spreading outwards.

quiz.q: Why does a hotspot leave a chain of volcanoes rather than a single one?
o: The hotspot wanders around the globe
The plate drifts over a fixed hotspot
Earthquakes push the volcanoes sideways
Each volcano splits in two as it ages
quiz.e: The Hawaiian Islands and Australia's Cosgrove track both formed as a plate drifted over a fixed source of heat.

quiz.q: Which way is the Australian plate moving, and how fast?
o: South-west at about 7 centimetres a year
North-north-east at about 7 centimetres a year
North-north-east at about 70 centimetres a year
South-east at about 70 centimetres a year
quiz.e: Australia is heading north-north-east, one of the fastest continental plates.

quiz.q: Why are large earthquakes rarer in Australia than in New Zealand?
o: Its rock is harder than anywhere else
Australia is mid-plate, far from the boundaries
Quakes here are always too deep to feel
Plate movement stopped there long ago
quiz.e: Most big quakes occur at plate edges, but stress inside a plate can still cause them.

LESSONS.push: Australia is moving north faster than your fingernails grow. Where is it headed?

LESSONS.title: Droughts and flooding rains: Australia's weather
LESSONS.hook: Why Australia swings between drought and flood, and what El Niño and La Niña actually mean.

sections.key: Australia is the driest inhabited continent, with rainfall that swings between drought and flood.
sections.b:
Dorothea Mackellar's 1908 poem My Country described 'a land of sweeping plains... of droughts and flooding rains'. She was right. Australia is the driest inhabited continent, and its rainfall varies more from year to year than almost anywhere else. Long droughts, like the Millennium Drought from about 1997 to 2009, can be broken by devastating floods, like those in Queensland in 2010-11.

Much of Australia lies between about 20 and 35 degrees south, where sinking dry air creates belts of high pressure, the same kind of belt that makes the Sahara and Kalahari. High pressure means clear skies. The land is also flat, with few high mountains to force moist air upwards, and much of the interior is far from the sea. So about 70% is arid or semi-arid, and most people live near the wetter coast.

sections.key: El Niño tends to make eastern Australia drier and hotter, while La Niña tends to make it wetter, with more floods.
sections.b:
The biggest driver of year-to-year rainfall in eastern Australia is the El Niño-Southern Oscillation, or ENSO, a pattern in the tropical Pacific Ocean. Normally, trade winds pile warm water near Australia and Indonesia, which fuels rain clouds.

During El Niño, the winds weaken and warm water spreads east towards South America. The rain moves with it, so eastern Australia often gets drier conditions, hotter days and higher bushfire risk. La Niña is the opposite. Stronger trade winds pile even more warm water near Australia, bringing more evaporation, cloud and rain to eastern and northern Australia, and a higher chance of floods and cyclones. Three La Niña years in a row from 2020 to 2022 brought record floods to parts of New South Wales and Queensland.

sections.key: The Indian Ocean Dipole and the Southern Annular Mode steer rainfall across southern and western Australia.
sections.b:
The Indian Ocean has its own pattern, the Indian Ocean Dipole, or IOD: a difference in sea temperature between the western and eastern Indian Ocean. In a positive IOD, cooler water near Australia means less moisture and often drier conditions for southern and central Australia in winter and spring. A negative IOD tends to bring more rain. In 2019 a strong positive IOD combined with other factors to produce extreme drought and heat, setting the stage for the Black Summer bushfires.

The Southern Annular Mode describes the movement of the westerly winds circling Antarctica. When they and their cold fronts shift south, southern Australia gets less winter rain. When they shift north, more storms reach Melbourne, Adelaide and Perth. The westerlies have tended to sit further south in recent decades, contributing to declining winter rainfall in south-west Western Australia.

sections.key: Bushfires need fuel, dry conditions, heat and wind, and wet La Niña years can grow extra fuel that later dries out.
sections.b:
Bushfires need fuel, dry conditions, heat and wind, plus an ignition source like lightning. Wet La Niña years can grow extra grass and scrub, which then dries out and provides more fuel. Hot, dry winds ahead of cold fronts create the most dangerous fire weather.

Australia's Fire Danger Rating system, updated in 2022, has four levels: Moderate, High, Extreme and Catastrophic. The Black Summer fires of 2019-20 burned more than 24 million hectares. Climate change is making dangerous fire weather more frequent.

sections.key: The Bureau of Meteorology's long-range outlooks help farmers, water managers and emergency services plan, and you should know your own local risks.
sections.b:
The Bureau of Meteorology monitors ENSO, the IOD and the Southern Annular Mode, and publishes long-range outlooks showing the chances of wetter or drier, warmer or cooler conditions over the coming months. These help farmers decide what to plant, water authorities plan storage and emergency services prepare.

For everyday life, it's worth knowing your local risks, whether flood, fire, cyclone or heat. Have an emergency plan, and follow warnings through the official apps of your state emergency services.

quiz.q: Why is so much of Australia dry?
o: Sinking dry air, flat land and few mountains
It has no oceans nearby to supply moisture
Its winds only ever blow from the interior
It sits too far north for storms to form
quiz.e: High pressure at these latitudes brings clear skies, and the flat, far-from-sea interior gets little rain.

quiz.q: What does La Niña usually bring to eastern Australia?
o: Drought and a higher bushfire risk
More rain and a higher risk of floods
Cooler oceans and clear skies
Weaker trade winds across the Pacific
quiz.e: Stronger trade winds pile warm water near Australia, bringing more evaporation, cloud and rain.

quiz.q: What happens to southern Australia's winter rain when the westerly winds and cold fronts shift south?
o: It tends to decline
It tends to increase sharply
It switches to summer
It is unaffected
quiz.e: Fewer rain-bearing fronts reach the south, as seen in declining winter rainfall in south-west Western Australia.

quiz.q: How can wet La Niña years raise later bushfire risk?
o: Extra grass grows, then dries out as fuel
Lightning stops, so fires burn unchecked
Rain makes the soil hotter during summer
Wet years raise the Fire Danger Rating automatically
quiz.e: Bushfires need fuel as well as dry, hot, windy conditions, and a wet year can grow more fuel.

quiz.q: What do the Bureau of Meteorology's long-range outlooks show?
o: The exact weather on a given day months ahead
The chances of a wetter or drier season ahead
Only the risk of cyclones each season
Which suburbs will flood next season
quiz.e: Outlooks give probabilities, which help farmers, water authorities and emergency services plan ahead.

LESSONS.push: Why does a warm patch of the Pacific decide whether Queensland floods?

LESSONS.title: Gödel: The Truths No Proof Can Reach
LESSONS.hook: In 1931 a young Austrian logician proved that no single set of rules can capture every truth about numbers. Here is what he really showed, and what people wrongly think he showed.

sections.key: Hilbert hoped to rebuild mathematics as a formal system that was complete, consistent and mechanically checkable.
sections.b: Königsberg, September 1930. David Hilbert, the leading mathematician of his age, ends a radio address with a defiant line: 'We must know, we will know.' His programme aimed to rebuild mathematics as a formal game of symbols, with axioms as starting positions and rules of inference as legal moves. Two properties mattered most. The system should be complete, so every statement could be proved or disproved. And it should be consistent, never proving both a statement and its negation. Ideally, consistency would itself be proved with simple, finite reasoning nobody could doubt. The day before Hilbert's speech, at a conference in the same city, a quiet young Austrian named Kurt Gödel briefly announced a result that would make this dream impossible.

sections.key: Any consistent, mechanically listable system strong enough for basic arithmetic contains true statements it can neither prove nor disprove.
sections.b:
Gödel's first incompleteness theorem says that if a system's axioms can be listed mechanically, it is consistent, and it handles ordinary addition and multiplication, then some statement can be neither proved nor disproved. The system is incomplete. Truth and provability come apart.

Gödel gave every symbol, formula and proof a unique number, so arithmetic could talk about its own proofs. A diagonal construction, a rigorous cousin of the liar paradox, produced a sentence G equivalent to 'G has no proof in this system'. If the system proved G, it would be proving something false. So a consistent system cannot prove G, which is exactly what G says. Hence G is true. Adding G as an axiom does not help: the theorem applies again to the enlarged system.

sections.key: A consistent system strong enough for arithmetic cannot prove its own consistency.
sections.b:
Gödel's second theorem is like asking a witness to vouch for their own honesty. The reasoning behind the first theorem can be carried out inside the system, so it can prove 'if I am consistent, then G is true'. If it could also prove 'I am consistent', it would prove G, which we know it cannot. So a consistent system of this kind cannot prove its own consistency.

This was the sharpest blow to Hilbert, whose hope was to establish the consistency of all mathematics using a small, trustworthy fragment. Consistency proofs remain possible, but only by assuming something stronger. In 1936 Gerhard Gentzen proved arithmetic consistent, using a principle of transfinite induction that reaches beyond arithmetic itself.

sections.key: The theorems are precise technical results, not proof that truth is relative or that mathematics is broken.
sections.b:
Gödel gets quoted in support of almost anything, from God to the limits of minds. Most of this is a stretch. The theorems apply only to formal systems meeting specific conditions. Some useful systems escape entirely: arithmetic with addition but no multiplication, known as Presburger arithmetic, is complete and decidable.

Incompleteness does not mean mathematics is inconsistent or unreliable; everyday mathematics carries on untroubled. Nor does it say some truths are forever unknowable, since a statement unprovable in one system may be provable in a stronger one. The argument that Gödel shows minds are not machines, pressed by John Lucas and Roger Penrose, remains heavily disputed, partly because humans cannot verify their own consistency either.

sections.key: No algorithm can decide whether every program halts, and real mathematical questions turn out to be independent of the standard axioms.
sections.b:
In 1936 Alan Turing tackled Hilbert's question of whether a mechanical procedure can decide if any statement is provable. He invented the Turing machine and used a diagonal argument like Gödel's. Suppose a program could check whether any program halts. Build a contrary program that asks the checker about itself and does the opposite. Contradiction. So no general halting checker can exist, and incompleteness follows quickly.

The continuum hypothesis, about whether an infinite size lies between the whole numbers and the real numbers, was shown by Gödel in 1940 and Paul Cohen in 1963 to be neither provable nor disprovable from the standard ZFC axioms. Goodstein's theorem is true yet unprovable in Peano arithmetic. Mathematics is an open landscape, where choosing axioms is an act of judgement.

quiz.q: What did Hilbert hope to achieve for mathematics?
o: A complete and consistent system, checkable by finite reasoning
A guarantee that every open problem would be solved this century
A system with axioms that nobody could ever write down
A proof that mathematics ultimately rests on human opinion
quiz.e: Hilbert's dream of a complete, provably consistent foundation is what Gödel's theorems ruled out.

quiz.q: According to the first incompleteness theorem, what must a consistent, mechanically listable system capable of basic arithmetic contain?
o: A finished proof of its own consistency
A contradiction hidden among its axioms
A statement it cannot prove or disprove
A finite list of all true statements
quiz.e: Such a system is incomplete: some true statement, and its negation, both remain unprovable.

quiz.q: What does the second incompleteness theorem show?
o: Mathematics contains hidden contradictions
Every system can prove its own consistency
No system can ever be shown consistent
Such a system cannot prove itself consistent
quiz.e: A system cannot certify itself, though a stronger system can prove its consistency.

quiz.q: Which of these is a correct statement about incompleteness?
o: It proves that human minds cannot be machines
It shows that all mathematical knowledge is uncertain
It shows some truths are unknowable in any system
Presburger arithmetic, without multiplication, is complete
quiz.e: The theorems need enough arithmetic strength, so weaker systems like Presburger arithmetic escape them.

quiz.q: What does Turing's halting problem show?
o: Every program eventually comes to a stop
No algorithm can decide whether every program halts
Computers cannot run programs that loop forever
Any program can be tested by running it long enough
quiz.e: Turing's diagonal argument shows that no general halting checker can exist, which is closely tied to incompleteness.

LESSONS.push: In 1931 a young logician showed no rule set can prove every truth. How?

LESSONS.title: Thinking Like Bayes
LESSONS.hook: A test that is 90 per cent accurate says you have a rare disease, yet your real chance of having it is about one in twelve. Understanding why will change how you weigh every piece of evidence.

sections.key: A prior is the probability you give a hypothesis before weighing new evidence, and Bayes' theorem flips evidence back to cause.
sections.b:
Thomas Bayes, an eighteenth-century Presbyterian minister, worked on a problem in probability that few cared about. He died in 1761 without publishing it. His friend Richard Price found the essay, edited it and sent it to the Royal Society, which published it in 1763. If we know how likely some evidence is given a cause, how likely is the cause given the evidence? Bayes' theorem is the rule for flipping the arrow.

Your phone buzzes at 3 am saying you've won a luxury car. You already hold a strong opinion: almost certainly a scam. That is your prior, the probability you give a hypothesis before the new evidence. Ignoring priors doesn't make you objective; you've just assumed one unexamined. State it openly, ground it in frequencies, and stay willing to revise it.

sections.key: Evidence matters only to the extent it is more probable under one hypothesis than another, so posterior odds equal prior odds times the likelihood ratio.
sections.b:
A dog barks in the night. Is it a burglar? That depends on two numbers, not one. How likely is barking if there is a burglar, and how likely if there is not? If your dog barks at every possum, both numbers are high and the bark tells you little.

The ratio between them, the likelihood ratio, measures the strength of the evidence. Evidence ten times more probable under one hypothesis shifts the odds tenfold. Bayes' theorem in its tidiest form says posterior odds equal prior odds multiplied by the likelihood ratio. This exposes a trap: evidence that fits your theory perfectly is worthless if it would have appeared just as readily had your theory been false.

sections.key: When a condition is rare, most positive results can be false even from a fairly accurate test, and independent results accumulate step by step.
sections.b:
Suppose a disease affects 1 per cent of people. A test detects it in 90 per cent of those who have it, and wrongly flags 10 per cent of those who do not. You test positive. Most people guess your chance of being ill is around 90 per cent.

Now imagine 1,000 people tested. Ten have the disease and 9 test positive. Of the 990 healthy people, 99 also test positive. So only 9 of 108 positives are genuine: about 1 in 12, or 8 per cent. It still raised your risk from 1 in 100 to 1 in 12.

Today's conclusion becomes tomorrow's prior. A second independent positive lifts the odds to 9 to 11, or 45 per cent, and a third to about 88 per cent.

sections.key: Ignoring how common something is to begin with is one of the most widespread reasoning errors.
sections.b:
Psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky studied a classic puzzle. In a city, 85 per cent of cabs are Green and 15 per cent are Blue. A witness to a hit-and-run says the cab was Blue, and tests show the witness identifies colours correctly 80 per cent of the time. Most people conclude the cab was probably Blue. The correct answer is about 41 per cent, because there are so many more Green cabs for the witness to mistake.

Ignoring how common something is in the first place is called base-rate neglect. Gerd Gigerenzer has shown the error often shrinks when problems are posed as natural frequencies, such as '9 out of 108 people', rather than as percentages.

sections.key: A claim with a tiny prior needs evidence with an enormous likelihood ratio before it becomes believable.
sections.b:
In 2011 physicists on the OPERA experiment reported neutrinos that appeared to travel faster than light. Many physicists suspected an error, and a poorly connected fibre-optic cable was eventually found among the faults. That caution was Bayes, not closed-mindedness. A claim that contradicts well-tested knowledge has a tiny prior, so the evidence needs a huge likelihood ratio to lift it. A surprising measurement is far more likely to come from a hidden mistake than from overturned physics.

Carl Sagan popularised the slogan 'extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence'. The flip side: a prior of exactly zero can never be raised by any evidence, so wise thinkers keep even unlikely ideas slightly open.

quiz.q: What is a prior in Bayesian thinking?
o: Your probability for a hypothesis before the new evidence
The probability of the evidence if the hypothesis is false
The final conclusion reached after weighing all evidence
The number of tests that have been carried out so far
quiz.e: A prior is your honest starting point, grounded in background frequencies and open to revision.

quiz.q: What does the likelihood ratio measure?
o: How confident you were before you saw the evidence
How strongly evidence favours one hypothesis over another
The percentage of people who have a given condition
How many separate tests have been carried out so far
quiz.e: It compares how probable the evidence is under each hypothesis, which sets how far the odds shift.

quiz.q: In the lesson's example (1 per cent prevalence, 90 per cent detection, 10 per cent false positives), what is the chance a positive tester has the disease?
o: About 90 per cent
About 50 per cent
About 1 per cent
About 8 per cent
quiz.e: Of 108 positives per 1,000 people, only 9 are true positives, so the chance is 9 in 108: about 8 per cent, or 1 in 12.

quiz.q: In the cab problem, why is the probability the cab was Blue only about 41 per cent?
o: The witness was probably lying about the colour
There are many more Green cabs to mistake for Blue
Blue cabs are much harder to see at night
The witness was right only half of the time
quiz.e: The high base rate of Green cabs produces many false 'Blue' identifications.

quiz.q: Why does an extraordinary claim need extraordinary evidence?
o: Its tiny prior means only a huge likelihood ratio can lift it
Scientists distrust any new idea as a matter of principle
Surprising measurements turn out to be right most of the time
Evidence counts for less the more often it is repeated
quiz.e: A single surprising result is more likely a hidden mistake than overturned physics.

LESSONS.push: A positive result from a 90 per cent accurate test. Why the odds still favour you.

LESSONS.title: Arrow's Impossibility: Why No Vote Is Perfectly Fair
LESSONS.hook: Three friends, three restaurants, and a majority that goes round in circles. In 1951 an economist proved that this tangle can never be fully untied by any ranked voting system.

sections.key: Majority preferences can form a loop even when every individual voter is perfectly consistent.
sections.b:
Three friends are choosing dinner. Ana ranks pizza, then sushi, then tacos. Ben ranks sushi, then tacos, then pizza. Cara ranks tacos, then pizza, then sushi. Pizza beats sushi two to one. Sushi beats tacos two to one. Surely pizza beats tacos? No: Ben and Cara prefer tacos, so tacos wins two to one. The group's majority preference runs in a circle, even though each person is entirely rational.

The Marquis de Condorcet, a French mathematician and philosopher, described this in 1785, and it bears his name: the Condorcet paradox. It means 'the will of the majority' can be incoherent, and whoever controls the order of head-to-head votes can steer the result.

sections.key: With three or more options, no ranked voting rule can meet all of Arrow's basic fairness conditions at once.
sections.b:
In 1951 the American economist Kenneth Arrow asked: could any rule at all turn individual rankings into a sensible group ranking? He proposed minimal conditions. Unrestricted domain: voters may rank options any way they like. Unanimity: if everyone prefers A to B, so does the group. Independence of irrelevant alternatives: the group's choice between A and B depends only on how voters rank A against B, not on a third option C. Non-dictatorship: no single voter always decides. The group ranking must also be a proper ordering, without circles.

Arrow's theorem states that with at least three options, no rule satisfies all of these. Any method meeting the first three must be a dictatorship. He shared the 1972 Nobel memorial prize in economic sciences with John Hicks.

sections.key: A candidate who cannot win can still change who does, which is what independence of irrelevant alternatives forbids.
sections.b:
Independence of irrelevant alternatives sounds abstract until you meet a spoiler. Under first past the post, used in British and United States elections, each voter marks one candidate and the most votes wins. Suppose 45 per cent prefer a conservative candidate, while 55 per cent prefer one of two progressive candidates, splitting 35 to 20. The conservative wins, even though a majority might have preferred either progressive. The minor candidate did not win but changed who did.

Commentators have argued that minor candidates swung close contests, such as Ralph Nader in Florida in the 2000 US presidential election, though such claims rest on assumptions about how his supporters would otherwise have voted. Spoilers push people towards tactical voting, abandoning their favourite to avoid a worse result.

sections.key: Preferential voting softens the spoiler problem but, as Arrow predicts, cannot remove every paradox.
sections.b:
Since 1918, members of the federal House of Representatives have been elected by preferential voting, known overseas as instant-runoff or ranked-choice voting. Voters number every candidate in order. If no one has an absolute majority of first preferences, the candidate with the fewest votes is excluded and their ballots flow to the next preference, repeating until someone passes 50 per cent.

This largely tames the classic spoiler: a Greens or independent voter can rank a favourite first without wasting the vote. The Senate uses a different, proportional method, the single transferable vote. Arrow's theorem still applies, though. Preferential voting can violate independence of irrelevant alternatives, and it can eliminate a broadly liked centrist who would beat every rival head to head, simply because they attracted too few first preferences.

sections.key: Arrow's result can be sidestepped, at a cost, and shows that the voting rule itself is a political choice.
sections.b:
Arrow's theorem has escape hatches, each with a price. If preferences are single-peaked, arranged along a left to right line, Duncan Black showed majority rule produces no cycles and the median voter's favourite wins. Score or approval methods fall outside Arrow's framework because they use more information than rankings, but they raise new dilemmas, such as how generously to rate a second choice. Gibbard's theorem shows any deterministic method choosing among three or more outcomes is either dictatorial or, in some situations, rewards tactical voting.

Elections aren't rigged by mathematics. Rather, 'the will of the people' is not always a single, well-defined thing waiting to be measured; the voting rule helps construct it. So choosing a rule is a genuine political decision. No system is perfectly fair, but some are fairer in the situations that actually occur.

quiz.q: What does the Condorcet paradox show?
o: Individual voters usually hold circular preferences themselves
Majority preferences can loop even when each voter is consistent
Majority rule always selects the best available option
Two-candidate elections frequently end in a tied result
quiz.e: Each friend's ranking is consistent, yet the pairwise majorities loop around.

quiz.q: With three or more options, a rule meeting unrestricted domain, unanimity and independence of irrelevant alternatives must be what?
o: Proportional
A dictatorship
Preferential
Random
quiz.e: Arrow proved these conditions together force one voter's preferences to decide every outcome.

quiz.q: What is a spoiler candidate?
o: A candidate who cannot win but changes who does
A candidate who wins with fewer votes than a rival
A candidate caught breaking electoral rules
A candidate who withdraws before polling day
quiz.e: A minor candidate can split a vote and hand victory to someone a majority did not prefer.

quiz.q: How does preferential voting largely tame the spoiler effect?
o: It bans minor candidates from appearing on the ballot
A favourite can be ranked first without wasting the vote
It limits every voter to one choice of candidate
It guarantees minor parties a fixed share of seats
quiz.e: Excluded candidates' ballots transfer to later preferences, though Arrow's theorem still applies.

quiz.q: What does Arrow's theorem imply about choosing a voting system?
o: Democratic voting can never really work in practice
A perfect system exists but is yet to be discovered
Every system has trade-offs, so the choice is political
Voting rules make no real difference to results
quiz.e: Systems fail in different situations, so designers must choose which flaws to accept.

LESSONS.push: Three friends, three dinners, and a majority that votes in circles.

LESSONS.title: The Hard Problem of Consciousness
LESSONS.hook: Science can map the neurons that fire when you taste coffee. Explaining why that firing feels like anything at all may be the deepest unsolved puzzle there is.

sections.key: Explaining the brain's functions is hard work, but explaining why they come with felt experience is a different kind of problem.
sections.b:
In 1994, at a conference in Tucson, Arizona, a young Sydney-born philosopher named David Chalmers drew a line that still shapes the field. Questions about how the brain discriminates stimuli, integrates information, focuses attention and reports its states are the 'easy problems'. They may take centuries, but they are easy in principle, because explaining a function means describing a mechanism. The hard problem is different: why is all this processing accompanied by experience at all? He set this out in a 1995 paper.

Bite into a lemon. Beyond the chemistry, there is the sharp quality of sourness itself. Philosophers call such felt qualities qualia: the redness of red, the ache of a headache. Whether qualia exist in the robust sense some intend is disputed, but there is something to explain.

sections.key: If a scientist who knows every physical fact about colour still learns something on seeing red, not all facts may be physical.
sections.b:
In 1974 the philosopher Thomas Nagel asked what it is like to be a bat, which builds a picture of the world from echoes. We could learn every fact about bat neurophysiology and still not know what echolocating feels like. Objective science describes the world from no point of view, while experience seems tied to one.

In 1982 the Australian philosopher Frank Jackson imagined Mary, a brilliant scientist who has lived in a black and white room and knows every physical fact about colour vision. On leaving, she sees red for the first time. If she learns something new, not all facts are physical. Jackson later changed his mind and defended physicalism. Critics say Mary gains a new ability, or a new way of grasping an old fact.

sections.key: If a physical duplicate without experience is genuinely possible, physical facts alone would not settle the facts about consciousness.
sections.b:
Picture your exact physical duplicate, atom for atom, who walks, talks, laughs at jokes and insists it is conscious, yet has no inner experience. Philosophers call such a being a zombie. Nobody claims zombies exist. The question is whether they are conceivable without contradiction.

Chalmers argues they are, and that if a zombie world is even possible in principle, then physical facts alone do not fix the facts about consciousness, so physicalism is false. Opponents attack each step. Some deny zombies are truly conceivable once consciousness is understood. Others grant they seem conceivable but deny this shows they are possible, just as water once seemed conceivably distinct from H2O before chemistry showed they are the same.

sections.key: Physicalism, dualism, panpsychism and illusionism give sharply different answers, and none commands a consensus.
sections.b:
Physicalism holds that consciousness is ultimately physical, and that the explanatory gap reflects the limits of our concepts. Its roots include the identity theory developed in Adelaide in the 1950s by U. T. Place and J. J. C. Smart.

Dualism holds that experience involves something non-physical, whether a separate substance, as Descartes proposed, or irreducible mental properties, a view Chalmers has defended. Panpsychism, revived by thinkers such as Galen Strawson and Philip Goff, suggests that some simple form of experience is a fundamental feature of matter, which raises the puzzle of how tiny experiences combine into a unified mind. Illusionism, argued by Keith Frankish and in related form by Daniel Dennett, claims phenomenal consciousness as we conceive it does not exist; our brains merely represent themselves as having it.

sections.key: Questions about consciousness shape real decisions in medicine, animal welfare and artificial intelligence.
sections.b:
Doctors must judge whether patients in unresponsive states retain awareness, and brain imaging studies have suggested that some do. Animal welfare law depends on which creatures can suffer, and some jurisdictions now formally recognise animals such as octopuses and crabs as sentient. As artificial intelligence grows more fluent at describing inner lives, we need principled ways to ask whether anything is felt behind the words, a question no major theory can yet settle.

Theories such as global workspace theory and integrated information theory make testable predictions, and researchers have begun pitting them against each other in organised experiments. Yet even a perfect map of the neural correlates of consciousness might leave Chalmers' question standing: why does any of this activity feel like something at all?

quiz.q: According to Chalmers, which of these is the hard problem?
o: Explaining how the brain focuses and directs attention
Explaining why brain processing comes with experience
Explaining how people report their own mental states
Mapping every neuron that fires during an experience
quiz.e: The easy problems concern functions; the hard problem asks why any of it is felt.

quiz.q: If Mary learns something new on seeing red for the first time, what does the argument conclude?
o: Not all facts are physical facts
Colour vision cannot be studied scientifically
Mary must have been told the wrong facts about colour
Seeing colour depends on the brain's use of echoes
quiz.e: Critics reply that she gains a new ability or way of grasping an old fact, not a non-physical fact.

quiz.q: What is a philosophical zombie?
o: A person in a deep coma
A being that behaves like us but is built from different materials
A creature that has experiences but cannot act
A physical duplicate of a person with no inner experience
quiz.e: A zombie matches you atom for atom and in behaviour but has no experience at all.

quiz.q: Which position holds that some simple form of experience is a fundamental feature of matter?
o: Illusionism
Identity theory
Panpsychism
Substance dualism
quiz.e: Panpsychists treat experience as basic to the physical world, then face the puzzle of how it combines.

quiz.q: Which real-world question depends on how we understand consciousness?
o: Whether a patient in a vegetative state is aware
How fast a medicine is absorbed by the body
Which materials make the strongest chip circuits
How much a hospital should charge for a scan
quiz.e: Medicine, animal welfare and artificial intelligence all depend on knowing when experience is present.

LESSONS.push: You can map every neuron that fires when you taste coffee. Why does it feel like anything?

LESSONS.title: Ergodicity and the Maths of Ruin
LESSONS.hook: A bet can make the average player richer every round while making almost every actual player poorer. Understanding why is one of the most important ideas in all of risk.

sections.key: A bet can have a positive average payoff and still be ruinous to keep taking, because the crowd's average is not one person's path.
sections.b:
A stranger offers a coin game. Heads, your wealth rises by 50 per cent. Tails, it falls by 40 per cent. Half the time you gain 50, half the time you lose 40, so on average you gain 5 per cent per flip. Yet if you play repeatedly with everything you own, you will almost certainly end up nearly broke.

The trap is a quiet assumption: that the average across many people tells you what happens to one person across time. Ten thousand people flipping once gain 5 per cent in total, the ensemble average. One person flipping ten thousand times follows the time average. A system is ergodic when these agree. Wealth compounds, multiplying rather than adding, so it is not. Physicist Ole Peters argues economics went astray by treating such situations as ergodic.

sections.key: Because gains and losses multiply, one win and one loss leave you 10 per cent poorer.
sections.b:
Start with 100 dollars. Flip heads and you have 150. Flip tails and you fall to 90, because 40 per cent of 150 is 60. Reverse the order and 100 becomes 60, then 90. One win plus one loss multiplies your wealth by 1.5 times 0.6, which is 0.9. A typical pair of flips costs you 10 per cent.

Over a hundred flips, a typical player sees roughly fifty heads and fifty tails, leaving about 0.9 to the power of 50 of their stake: around half of one per cent. Meanwhile the ensemble average is 1.05 to the power of 100, about 131 times the stake. That average is real, but propped up by a tiny number of astronomically lucky players while nearly everyone else is ruined.

sections.key: No reward justifies a repeated bet with a chance of ruin, because ruin ends the game permanently.
sections.b:
Suppose someone offers you a fortune to play one round of Russian roulette with a six-chamber revolver. Across a crowd, five in six walk away rich, so the ensemble looks attractive. But one person who keeps accepting survives ten rounds with probability five sixths multiplied by itself ten times, roughly 16 per cent. Play long enough and death becomes a certainty.

Any strategy with even a small probability of total loss, repeated often enough, eventually meets that loss. Ruin is an absorbing state: once you are bankrupt, dead or banned from the table, you cannot use the good outcomes that would have followed. The average never gets to rescue you.

sections.key: The Kelly criterion maximises long-run growth and usually says to bet far less than everything, which makes ordinary caution look sensible.
sections.b:
In 1956 John Kelly, a researcher at Bell Labs, worked out how a gambler with an edge should size bets to make wealth grow fastest over time. He maximised the expected logarithm of wealth, which captures compounding. In our coin game, staking everything gives a typical growth rate of about minus 5 per cent per flip. Stake a quarter of your wealth each flip, and a typical player grows roughly 0.6 per cent per flip. The same favourable odds become an engine of wealth simply by betting smaller. Bet more than Kelly and growth falls.

This also defends ordinary caution against the charge of loss aversion. A 50 per cent loss needs a 100 per cent gain to recover, so deep drawdowns cost more than they seem.

sections.key: Before asking how much you can gain, ask whether any path leads to ruin, and remove it.
sections.b:
The practical moral is simple to state and hard to live by: survive first, then optimise. A business that grows quickly on heavy debt may look brilliant in average conditions, yet a single bad year can wipe it out. An investor using leverage can be right about the long run and still be forced to sell at the bottom.

Warren Buffett's well known first rule, don't lose money, is usually read as a joke, but in a non-ergodic world it is close to a mathematical principle. Diversification, insurance, emergency savings and modest position sizes all trade a little expected gain for a large reduction in the chance of ruin. This is general information, not financial advice, but the idea holds: you only get the long run if you stay in the game.

quiz.q: When is a system called ergodic?
o: When its outcomes follow a normal distribution
When its ensemble average equals its time average
When every player has the same starting wealth
When gains and losses are always equal in size
quiz.e: In ergodic systems, averaging across many people gives the same answer as following one person through time.

quiz.q: Starting with 100 dollars, what do you have after one heads (+50 per cent) and one tails (-40 per cent), in either order?
o: 100 dollars
110 dollars
95 dollars
90 dollars
quiz.e: Gains and losses multiply: 1.5 times 0.6 equals 0.9, so 100 becomes 90.

quiz.q: Why is ruin worse than just a very bad outcome?
o: It is usually taxed far more heavily than other losses
It is an absorbing state, so you cannot play on
It always happens more often than models predict
It only ever affects people who borrow to invest
quiz.e: Once ruined you cannot take part in later good outcomes, so averages cannot rescue you.

quiz.q: What does the Kelly criterion aim to maximise?
o: The expected value of each individual bet
The chance of winning each single bet
The size of the biggest single win possible
The long-run growth rate of your wealth
quiz.e: Kelly maximises the expected logarithm of wealth, which is the fastest long-run compound growth.

quiz.q: Which approach reflects the idea of surviving first?
o: Using heavy debt to chase the highest average return
Holding savings and insurance and keeping bets modest
Staking everything on the best average payoff
Ignoring rare events because they seldom happen
quiz.e: These habits give up a little expected gain for a large reduction in the chance of ruin.

LESSONS.push: A fair coin game with a positive average that still ruins almost everyone.

LESSONS.title: Fat Tails and Power Laws
LESSONS.hook: Some quantities behave politely, clustering around an average. Others are ruled by rare giants. Mistaking one kind of world for the other is how sensible people get blindsided.

sections.key: In some domains no single observation moves the total much, while in others one observation can dominate everything.
sections.b:
Fill a stadium with a thousand randomly chosen adults and weigh them. Add the heaviest person on Earth and the average barely changes. Repeat with wealth. Add one of the world's richest people and they may hold most of the stadium's total wealth. The average now describes nobody.

The writer and former trader Nassim Nicholas Taleb popularised this thought experiment, and named the two worlds. Mediocristan is the land of the bell curve: height, weight, calorie intake, a dentist's income. No single observation changes the total meaningfully. Extremistan is the land of power laws: wealth, book sales, pandemic deaths, financial losses. One observation can dwarf the rest. A useful test: is the quantity physically constrained, or can it scale? A baker can only bake so many loaves, but a book can be copied without limit.

sections.key: The normal distribution makes extreme events so rare that they are effectively impossible, which is dangerous when applied to the wrong quantities.
sections.b:
The normal distribution, the familiar bell curve, describes things like human height, measurement errors and many test scores. It arises when an outcome is the sum of many small, independent influences, none of which dominates.

Its tails thin out astonishingly fast. Each extra standard deviation from the mean makes an event dramatically rarer, so events many standard deviations out become vanishingly unlikely. That is why you will never meet an adult three metres tall. Under a bell curve, averages and past samples are trustworthy guides. The danger begins when this model is applied to quantities that do not come from many small independent influences, such as market prices, which can move together in a panic.

sections.key: In a power law, extremes become rarer only slowly, so giants keep appearing and a small minority of causes drive most of the effect.
sections.b:
In a power law, the probability of exceeding some size falls away as a power of that size. Instead of plunging like a bell curve, the tail declines gently, which is why it is called fat. Earthquakes follow such a pattern: each step up in magnitude is roughly ten times rarer yet releases about thirty times more energy. When the tail is fat enough, the variance can be infinite, and with a fatter tail still, even the average is undefined.

Economist Vilfredo Pareto noticed in the late nineteenth century that a small share of people held most of the wealth. The 80/20 rule is a loose rule of thumb inspired by his work, not a law of nature. In such domains, the outliers are the story.

sections.key: A black swan is a rare, high-impact event that seems obvious only in hindsight, and fat-tailed domains generate them naturally.
sections.b:
Europeans once treated 'all swans are white' as safe, until explorers found black swans in Western Australia. Taleb borrowed the image for his 2007 book The Black Swan: outliers that carry extreme impact and are rationalised afterwards as predictable.

Consider a turkey, fed generously every day for a thousand days. Each meal increases its statistical confidence that humans are benevolent, right up until the day before a festive feast. Its confidence peaks when the risk is greatest. On Black Monday in October 1987, the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell more than 20 per cent in a single day, a move that standard bell-curve models treated as nearly impossible. They were describing the wrong world.

sections.key: In fat-tailed domains, focus less on predicting extremes and more on capping your downside so no single shock can ruin you.
sections.b:
If extreme events cannot be forecast reliably, change your exposure to them. First, distrust averages and standard deviations in fat-tailed domains, and ask what the worst plausible case would do to you. Second, never assume the biggest loss in your data is the biggest loss possible: the next record may be far larger. Third, cap your downside, through diversification, insurance and avoiding heavy debt, so no single shock can ruin you. Taleb also advocates a barbell approach, combining very safe holdings with a small amount of exposure to large positive surprises.

This is general information, not financial advice. The deeper habit is to ask of any risk, 'Which world am I in?' because the right strategy in Mediocristan can be fatal in Extremistan.

quiz.q: In the stadium thought experiment, why does adding a billionaire change things so much more than adding the heaviest person?
o: Billionaires are far rarer than very heavy people
Weight is measured much less accurately than wealth
Wealth can scale without limit, but body weight cannot
The stadium holds more wealthy people than heavy ones
quiz.e: Weight is physically bounded, but wealth can scale so far that one person dominates the total.

quiz.q: When does a normal distribution typically arise?
o: When a few very large shocks dominate the result
When many small, independent influences add together
When the same pattern repeats at every scale
When the average of the data is undefined
quiz.e: The bell curve emerges from many small independent contributions, none of which dominates.

quiz.q: What makes the tail of a power law 'fat'?
o: Extremes fade slowly, so giants keep turning up
Extremes become impossible beyond a certain size
Most observations sit very close to the average
Every observation is about the same size
quiz.e: The gently declining tail means very large events remain surprisingly likely, so averages mislead.

quiz.q: What is the lesson of Taleb's turkey?
o: Animals learn nothing useful from past experience
Confidence from past data can peak just before disaster
Rare events nearly always give clear warning signs
Gathering more data always removes the danger
quiz.e: The turkey's confidence grows daily and is highest right before the event it never saw coming.

quiz.q: What is a sensible response to fat-tailed risks?
o: Predict the biggest event and plan only for that
Assume the largest past loss is the largest possible
Cap your downside so no single shock can ruin you
Rely on the average to judge the risk
quiz.e: Since extremes can't be forecast reliably, limit your exposure to them through diversification, insurance and low debt.

LESSONS.push: Add one person to a stadium and the average weight barely moves. Try it with wealth.

LESSONS.title: The Evolution of Cooperation
LESSONS.hook: Why would selfish players ever learn to trust each other? A puzzle about two prisoners, and a computer tournament in the 1980s, revealed a surprisingly hopeful answer.

sections.key: In the prisoner's dilemma, each player's best individual move leaves both worse off, and that stable trap is called a Nash equilibrium.
sections.b:
Two suspects are held in separate cells. Each can betray the other or stay silent. If both stay silent, both serve a short sentence. If you betray and your partner stays silent, you go free. If both betray, both serve a long sentence. Whatever the other does, betrayal is better for you: it either sets you free or spares you the worst outcome. So two rational prisoners both betray, and both end up worse off.

The mathematician John Nash showed this mutual betrayal is an equilibrium. It is stable not because it is good, but because neither player can escape it alone. The game was devised around 1950 by Merrill Flood and Melvin Dresher at RAND, and Albert Tucker gave it the prisoner story. The same trap appears in arms races, price wars and shared fishing grounds.

sections.key: When players expect to meet again, cooperation can become the rational choice, especially if the end is uncertain.
sections.b:
Everything changes when the game repeats. If you will face the same partner tomorrow, betraying today may cost you their cooperation for weeks. The political scientist Robert Axelrod called this the shadow of the future: the longer and more certain the relationship, the more cooperation pays.

There is a catch. If both players know exactly when the final round occurs, logic says to betray in that round, since no future remains. Then the second last round becomes the last, and the argument unravels backwards to the first move. This is called backward induction. So cooperation is most robust when the end is uncertain or distant. Open-ended relationships, like those between neighbours or long-term trading partners, sustain trust best.

sections.key: In Axelrod's computer tournaments, the simplest strategy, Tit for Tat, beat far more elaborate rivals.
sections.b:
Around 1980, Axelrod invited game theorists, economists, psychologists and others to submit programs for a round-robin of the repeated prisoner's dilemma. Some entries were elaborate, trying to model opponents or exploit their weaknesses.

The winner was the shortest program submitted: Tit for Tat, entered by the mathematical psychologist Anatol Rapoport. Its rule was almost childishly simple. Cooperate on the first move, then copy whatever the other player did last time.
