Margaret Sixel, born in South Africa and building her career in Australia, edited George Miller's Mad Max: Fury Road (2015) and won the Academy Award for Best Film Editing. She kept the key action in the centre of the frame from shot to shot, so even quick cuts stay readable. Try counting the cuts in a scene and see how many slip by.

quiz.q: What is the main lesson of the Kuleshov effect?
o: An actor's face has no effect on how audiences feel
Audiences always see the same emotion in the same face
A shot's meaning depends heavily on the shots around it
Neutral expressions are the hardest to edit
quiz.e: The same face seemed to show hunger, grief or desire depending on what it was cut with.

quiz.q: How did digital editing change the craft compared with cutting film by hand?
o: Footage could be rearranged instantly and versions saved
Editors no longer had to choose which shots to show
Films could no longer follow the 180-degree rule
Cuts became impossible to hide from the audience
quiz.e: Digital tools made trying alternatives fast, though many editors say the craft of choosing what to show and when has not changed.

quiz.q: Why do editors often cut on action?
o: It makes scenes cheaper to film on set
It lets actors skip the difficult movements
It breaks the 180-degree rule on purpose
Motion draws the eye across, hiding the join
quiz.e: Cutting mid-movement keeps the viewer's attention on the action, so the cut goes unnoticed.

quiz.q: Why does breaking an editing rule work as a technique?
o: Audiences cannot tell any editing rules exist
Audiences know the rules, so a break stands out
The rules only apply to silent films
Rules have no real effect on how stories feel
quiz.e: Jump cuts felt raw in 1960 because audiences were used to smooth continuity.

quiz.q: What did Walter Murch rank first in judging a good cut?
o: Perfect continuity between every pair of shots
The speed and pace of the cuts across a film
The emotion that the cut makes the viewer feel
Clear plot progress at every moment
quiz.e: If a cut makes you feel the right thing, a small continuity slip will not matter.

LESSONS.push: Every cut steers what you feel. Why the best editing is the kind you never notice.

LESSONS.title: The colourful history of paint
LESSONS.hook: Some colours were once worth more than gold. Others were made from snails, insects or even Egyptian mummies. The story of pigments is a story of trade, chemistry, danger and luck.

sections.key: Ochre, a clay coloured by iron oxides, is one of humanity's oldest pigments and is still used today.
sections.b:
Pick up a lump of red or yellow earth, grind it to powder, mix it with water or fat, and you have paint. Ochre, a clay coloured by iron oxides, is among the oldest pigments people used. Humans were collecting and processing it tens of thousands of years ago, and it appears in ancient rock art worldwide.

In Australia, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have used ochre for a very long time, for painting rock, bark and bodies, and in ceremony. Some sources were highly valued and traded over long distances. Heating yellow ochre turns it red, a trick early people seem to have discovered. Earth colours such as raw sienna and burnt umber remain on every artist's palette today.

sections.key: Ultramarine from lapis lazuli and Tyrian purple from sea snails were so costly and laborious that they signalled status and power.
sections.b:
The finest medieval and Renaissance blue came from the mines of Badakhshan in what is now Afghanistan, where lapis lazuli was dug from the mountains. Grinding the stone gave a dull greyish powder, so craftspeople kneaded it in a dough of wax and resin and washed out the pure blue particles. The result, ultramarine, meaning 'from beyond the sea', could cost more than gold by weight. Contracts sometimes specified how much a painter had to use, and it was often kept for the robes of the Virgin Mary.

The city of Tyre, in today's Lebanon, became famous for a dye from murex sea snails. Each snail yields a tiny amount, so the dye needed vast numbers and smelled awful. In ancient Rome, a purple stripe marked senators, and emperors claimed the deepest purple for themselves.

sections.key: Many of history's loveliest pigments, including lead white and arsenic greens, were poisonous.
sections.b:
Many old pigments were dangerous. Lead white, the main white paint for centuries, was toxic, and painters who handled it often risked lead poisoning. In 1775 the Swedish chemist Carl Wilhelm Scheele made a vivid green from copper and arsenic. Scheele's green, and the related emerald green, became fashionable in the nineteenth century for wallpapers, clothing and even sweets. They released arsenic as they aged or got damp, harming the people who lived with them.

Then there was mummy brown, a rich paint made from ground-up Egyptian mummies and sold by colourmakers until the twentieth century. Some artists were horrified when they learned what it contained. Modern artists' paints are far safer, and labels warn about the few hazardous pigments still sold.

sections.key: Accidental discoveries like Prussian blue and mauveine, plus the portable paint tube, transformed painting in the 1700s and 1800s.
sections.b:
Around 1706 in Berlin, a colourmaker trying to make red ended up with deep blue, apparently because an ingredient was contaminated. Prussian blue, cheaper than ultramarine, became one of the first modern synthetic pigments, used in painting, printing and engineers' blueprints.

In 1856 eighteen-year-old William Henry Perkin, a London chemistry student, tried to make the malaria drug quinine from coal tar. He failed, but noticed a purple residue that dyed silk beautifully. He called it mauveine and started a business. Mauve became a craze and helped launch the synthetic dye industry.

In 1841 John Goffe Rand, an American portrait painter in London, patented a collapsible metal paint tube with a screw cap. Paint became portable, making it easier to paint outdoors, as the French Impressionists often did.

sections.key: New pigments such as YInMn blue and Vantablack keep appearing, and some spark arguments over who may use them.
sections.b:
The search for new colours has not ended. In 2009 a team led by chemist Mas Subramanian at Oregon State University was experimenting with materials for electronics when a sample came out of the furnace a brilliant blue. Named YInMn blue after yttrium, indium and manganese, it was the first new inorganic blue pigment in about two centuries, and it is very stable.

In 2014 a British company announced Vantablack, a coating of tiny carbon tubes that absorbs almost all visible light, making objects look like holes in space. When the sculptor Anish Kapoor obtained exclusive rights to use it in art, other artists protested. The artist Stuart Semple responded by releasing his own pink paint that anyone could buy except Kapoor.

quiz.q: How can ochre be turned into paint?
o: By heating it in a furnace until it melts
By grinding it and mixing it with water or fat
By soaking it in vinegar and straining it
By kneading it in wax and resin for weeks
quiz.e: Ochre needs only grinding and a binder, which is why people have used it for tens of thousands of years.

quiz.q: Why was ultramarine so expensive?
o: It was made from huge numbers of sea snails that had to be collected
Painters were banned by law from using it on ordinary works
Its stone came from distant mines and needed long processing
It was produced only in tiny amounts by accident in laboratories
quiz.e: Lapis lazuli from distant Badakhshan needed a long extraction process, so it could cost more than gold.

quiz.q: Why were Scheele's green and emerald green dangerous?
o: They contained lead that built up in painters' bodies
They were made from ground-up Egyptian mummies
They faded quickly and caused skin burns
They released arsenic as they aged or got damp
quiz.e: These fashionable greens harmed people who lived with them by releasing arsenic.

quiz.q: How did the collapsible paint tube change painting?
o: It made paint portable, so artists could paint outdoors
It made paint cheaper by using new synthetic dyes
It let artists mix any colour without needing pigments
It swapped oil paint for water-based ink
quiz.e: Portable paint helped artists such as the Impressionists capture changing outdoor light.

quiz.q: What was notable about YInMn blue's discovery?
o: Ground from a rare blue stone mined in Afghanistan
It appeared by accident during electronics research
Created deliberately to imitate the colour of ancient Tyrian purple
Designed from the start to absorb almost all visible light
quiz.e: Found by accident while testing electronic materials, it was the first new inorganic blue in about two centuries. Chemistry can still produce new colours by chance.

LESSONS.push: Some colours were once worth more than gold, and one was made from mummies.

LESSONS.title: The Great Wave and the floating world
LESSONS.hook: A giant wave curls like a claw over three tiny boats while Mount Fuji sits calmly in the distance. This Japanese print is one of the most famous images on Earth. Here is the world that made it.

sections.key: Ukiyo-e were affordable woodblock prints celebrating the urban pleasures of Edo-period Japan.
sections.b:
During the Edo period, from 1603 to 1868, Japan was largely closed to the outside world and ruled from Edo, today's Tokyo. As cities grew, prosperous merchants and artisans built a lively popular culture of theatre, teahouses, fashion and pleasure districts. The word 'ukiyo' once meant a sorrowful, fleeting world in a Buddhist sense, but came to mean the 'floating world' of urban entertainment, enjoyed for the moment.

Ukiyo-e, pictures of the floating world, showed that culture. Early ones were paintings, but woodblock prints made them affordable to ordinary townspeople. Popular subjects included kabuki actors, celebrated beauties and courtesans, legendary heroes and, later, landscapes and travel scenes. They were the posters and celebrity photos of their day.

sections.key: A ukiyo-e print was made by a publisher, designer, carver and printer working together, using many blocks.
sections.b:
We usually name a single artist, but a ukiyo-e print was a team product. The publisher came up with the project, paid for it and sold the results. The designer, the artist we remember, drew the image in ink on thin paper. A skilled carver pasted that drawing face down onto a block of cherry wood and carved away everything except the lines, destroying the original in the process. Extra blocks were carved for each colour.

A printer then brushed water-based ink onto each block in turn and pressed damp paper onto it by hand with a flat pad called a baren. Small notches called kento made sure each colour lined up precisely. A single print could need a dozen or more blocks.

sections.key: From 1765 reliable registration allowed full-colour prints, launching a golden age of ukiyo-e.
sections.b:
Early woodblock prints were black and white or had a few colours added by hand. In 1765 the artist Suzuki Harunobu and his collaborators produced prints using many separate colour blocks, made possible by the reliable registration system. These full-colour prints were called nishiki-e, or 'brocade pictures', because their rich colours reminded people of luxurious woven silk.

They kicked off a golden age. Kitagawa Utamaro became famous for elegant portraits of women, often close-up half-length figures. Toshusai Sharaku produced striking, almost caricature-like portraits of kabuki actors in a career of less than a year, before vanishing from the record. Prints were produced in large editions and sold in shops, many relatively cheaply, part of the everyday visual life of the city.

sections.key: Hokusai's Great Wave, made around 1831, and Hiroshige's atmospheric travel series turned landscape into a popular print subject.
sections.b:
Katsushika Hokusai, born in 1760, worked for roughly seven decades and changed his name around thirty times. Around 1831 he designed Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji. Its most famous image, Under the Wave off Kanagawa, now called The Great Wave, shows boats dwarfed by a towering wave whose foam breaks into claw-like fingers, with Fuji small in the distance. It uses Prussian blue, an imported synthetic pigment cheaper and more lasting than earlier blues. Thousands of copies were probably printed.

His younger rival Utagawa Hiroshige became famous for gentler, atmospheric landscapes. His 1830s series The Fifty-three Stations of the Tokaido followed the road from Edo to Kyoto through rain, snow and dusk, part souvenir and part journey for those who could not travel. Soft colour gradations, made by wiping the ink on the block, put viewers in the scene.

sections.key: Japanese prints inspired a European craze called Japonisme, shaping Van Gogh, Monet, Degas and Cassatt.
sections.b:
In the 1850s Japan was forced to open its ports to foreign trade, and Japanese goods flowed into Europe. A popular story says a French artist found Hokusai's sketches used as packing around porcelain; it may be partly legend, but prints certainly arrived in large numbers. Japonisme swept through Western art and design. Artists admired bold flat colour, strong outlines, unusual high or low viewpoints and off-centre compositions, which differed from Europe's realistic perspective.

Van Gogh and his brother Theo collected hundreds of prints in Paris, and Vincent painted copies of two Hiroshige prints with his own intense colours. Monet's collection still hangs at Giverny, and his Japanese-style footbridge appears in his garden paintings. Degas and Cassatt borrowed the cropped, off-centre compositions. The floating world helped shape modern Western art.

quiz.q: What made ukiyo-e affordable to ordinary townspeople?
o: Artists painted each one by hand very quickly
The government paid for every print
Many copies could be printed from the same blocks
They were printed on cheap imported paper
quiz.e: Printing in large editions turned images of the floating world into everyday goods.

quiz.q: Why was a print a team product rather than one person's work?
o: The designer carved and printed every block alone
The publisher drew the image and sold the paintings
Each colour was painted by a separate artist
Four specialists each handled a different stage
quiz.e: The artist we remember was only one of four people whose skills made a print.

quiz.q: What allowed full-colour nishiki-e prints from the 1760s?
o: A registration system that kept colour blocks aligned
The import of European printing presses
Hand-painting every print after it was printed
Switching from woodblocks to copper plates
quiz.e: Kento notches let printers align a dozen or more blocks precisely.

quiz.q: How did Hiroshige's prints differ from Hokusai's Great Wave?
o: Using only black ink with no colour at all in the final prints
Gentler and more atmospheric, with weather and soft colour fades
Showing mainly kabuki actors in dramatic close-up portraits
Printed in only a few copies for wealthy private collectors
quiz.e: Hiroshige's rain, snow and soft gradations of colour made viewers feel they stood in the scene.

quiz.q: What did European artists admire in Japanese prints?
o: Realistic perspective drawn carefully from life in the studio
Heavy shading and dark backgrounds in the Renaissance manner
Bold flat colour, strong outlines and unusual viewpoints
Detailed portraits of European royalty and their courts
quiz.e: These ideas differed from the Renaissance tradition of realistic perspective, and shaped modern Western art.

LESSONS.push: A tiny Mount Fuji sits behind the world's most famous wave. Meet the team that made it.

LESSONS.title: Art forgery: the con artists who fooled the experts
LESSONS.hook: One forger sold a fake Vermeer to a Nazi leader. Another was caught by a single tube of white paint. The history of art forgery is full of daring tricks, and it raises a surprisingly hard question: why does a fake matter?

sections.key: Han van Meegeren invented new 'Vermeers' and used baked synthetic resin to fake the hardness of age.
sections.b:
In May 1945 Dutch police arrested painter and dealer Han van Meegeren after a 'Vermeer' was traced from the collection of the senior Nazi Hermann Goring. His defence was astonishing: it was not a national treasure, because he had painted it himself. Disbelieving investigators had him paint a new 'Vermeer' under supervision. In 1947 he was convicted of forgery and fraud, not collaboration, and sentenced to a year in prison, but died before serving it. To some Dutch people he was a folk hero.

He invented religious scenes, as some experts thought Vermeer had an early religious phase. He reused genuine seventeenth century canvases and mixed pigments with phenol-formaldehyde resin, the material of Bakelite, then baked the painting hard. Rolling the canvas created cracks, and he rubbed ink into them. In 1937 an expert hailed his Supper at Emmaus.

sections.key: Wolfgang Beltracchi faked 'lost' works and their paperwork, and was caught by an anachronistic pigment.
sections.b:
German forger Wolfgang Beltracchi may have been even more ambitious. Instead of copying known paintings, he created works that might plausibly have existed, often filling gaps where a real artist's painting was recorded in a catalogue but lost. Just as important was the paperwork. He and his wife invented a story that the pictures came from her grandfather's collection, and faked an old photograph of her posing as her own grandmother in front of several forgeries.

For years the works passed through auction houses and dealers, sometimes selling for millions. His undoing was science. One painting supposedly from 1914 contained titanium white, a pigment not yet available to artists then. In 2011 he was sentenced to six years in prison.

sections.key: Laboratories test whether materials could really be old, while connoisseurs and provenance can be fooled by hopeful stories.
sections.b:
Today suspicious paintings are examined like crime scenes. Many pigments have known invention dates, so an impossible colour is a giveaway. X-rays reveal hidden layers, infrared shows the underdrawing, and tree-ring dating estimates when panel wood was cut. Nuclear tests in the 1950s and 1960s spiked carbon-14 in the atmosphere, so plants grown afterwards carry a modern signature that old materials do not.

Before laboratories, authenticity rested on connoisseurs, who knew an artist's hand like a friend's handwriting. That still matters, but experts can be swayed by what they hope to find, and by a convincing provenance, the history of ownership. A large scandal at New York's Knoedler gallery, which closed in 2011, showed that convincing paperwork and confident dealers could carry fakes into major collections.

sections.key: Australia has had disputes over authenticity, and imitation Aboriginal art harms artists, so buy through community art centres or reputable dealers.
sections.b:
Australia has not escaped. A Brett Whiteley fraud case saw a conviction in 2016 overturned on appeal the following year, showing how hard forgery is to prove in court.

Aboriginal art faces its own problems. Because it is popular with tourists and collectors, cheap imitations with no connection to the communities and cultures they copy have been widespread. This harms artists and misrepresents their culture. Many Aboriginal art centres now supply certificates and keep careful records of who made each work.

If you are buying, it helps to look for works sold through community art centres or reputable dealers. The Indigenous Art Code is a voluntary industry code worth checking.

sections.key: Forgery makes us ask what we value in art: the achievement, the connection to the maker, or only how it looks.
sections.b:
Here is the puzzle. When experts believed Van Meegeren's Supper at Emmaus was a Vermeer, they found it profound. Once exposed, the same canvas seemed clumsy to many viewers, and its value fell dramatically. The paint did not change, so what did?

One answer is that we value art partly as an achievement: a genuine Vermeer is a particular person solving particular problems in seventeenth century Delft, and a forgery fakes that history. Another is that an artwork carries a connection to its maker, like a letter in someone's own handwriting.

Fraud also causes real harm to buyers and to an artist's reputation, since fakes can distort what we think an artist was like. Forgery makes us ask what we really value in art.

quiz.q: Why did Van Meegeren mix his paint with synthetic resin and bake the painting?
o: To make the colours brighter than old paintings
To keep the canvas from cracking in storage
To make the painting waterproof for shipping
To harden fresh paint so it seemed centuries old
quiz.e: Baking the resin hardened the paint so it behaved like centuries-old work.

quiz.q: What exposed Beltracchi's forgery of a painting supposedly from 1914?
o: Titanium white, a pigment not yet available
A witness who saw him painting it
A misspelt signature on the canvas
An inventory error in the auction catalogue
quiz.e: Titanium white was not yet available to artists in 1914, a scientific giveaway that no story could explain.

quiz.q: Why is provenance a target for forgers?
o: A convincing history can make a fake seem genuine
Laboratories can test nothing except provenance
Auction houses never check ownership records
It lets forgers avoid period materials altogether
quiz.e: A plausible history of ownership can make experts see what they hope to find.

quiz.q: Which step helps when buying Aboriginal art?
o: Choosing whichever work is cheapest at a market
Buying from any tourist stall you pass
Buying via community art centres or reputable dealers
Avoiding certificates because they are unreliable
quiz.e: Art centres keep careful records of who made each work, protecting both buyers and artists.

quiz.q: What does the Van Meegeren story suggest about how we value art?
o: Only the physical paint and canvas matter
Forgeries are always easy for experts to spot
A work's value stays the same once exposed as fake
We value achievement, not only appearance
quiz.e: The same canvas lost value once it was no longer a genuine Vermeer, though the paint was unchanged.

LESSONS.push: One forger was caught by a single pigment that did not yet exist. Which one?

LESSONS.title: Opera, explained: drama at full volume
LESSONS.hook: Opera combines music, theatre, poetry, costume and spectacle, and its singers fill huge halls without microphones. Here is how the most extravagant art form began and how to enjoy it.

sections.key: Opera began in Italy around 1600 in an attempt to recreate sung Greek drama, and public opera houses made it popular.
sections.b:
In the late 1500s scholars, poets and musicians in Florence, the Florentine Camerata, became fascinated by Greek tragedy. They believed, partly correctly, that Greek plays were sung or chanted, and tried setting drama to music with a single voice singing clearly over simple accompaniment. This led to the first operas around 1600. The earliest still regularly staged is Monteverdi's L'Orfeo, first performed in Mantua in 1607, retelling the myth of Orpheus in the underworld.

Early operas were for princes at court. In 1637 the first public opera house opened in Venice, and anyone with a ticket could attend. Audiences chatted, ate and played cards. Baroque stars included castrati, male singers castrated before puberty, a cruel practice that died out in the nineteenth century.

sections.key: A few terms, such as libretto, recitative and aria, make opera much easier to follow.
sections.b:
A little vocabulary helps enormously. The libretto, meaning 'little book', is the opera's text, written by a librettist, while the composer writes the music. Many operas begin with an overture, an orchestral piece that sets the mood before the curtain rises.

Much of the story moves forward in recitative, singing close to the rhythms of speech, often lightly accompanied, where plot and conversation happen. Then the action pauses for an aria, a solo song in which a character expresses feelings at length, where singers show off.

Duets, trios and larger ensembles let several characters sing at once, sometimes each with different words and emotions, something spoken theatre cannot easily do. The chorus represents crowds, soldiers, villagers or spirits.

sections.key: A small group of composers, from Mozart to Puccini to Wagner, wrote the operas most often staged today.
sections.b:
Mozart, writing in the 1780s and early 1790s, gave opera human characters: The Marriage of Figaro, Don Giovanni and The Magic Flute. In the early nineteenth century Rossini, Bellini and Donizetti perfected bel canto, 'beautiful singing', with dazzling vocal agility. Verdi (Rigoletto, La Traviata, Aida) and Puccini (La Boheme, Tosca, Madama Butterfly) combined thrilling melodies with intense drama, and remain among the most performed. They make good starting points.

Richard Wagner wanted opera as a total work of art. His four-opera Ring cycle takes around fifteen hours. Short musical themes, leitmotifs, represent characters and ideas, a technique film composers borrowed. His Bayreuth theatre, opened in 1876, hid the orchestra and darkened the hall, helping create modern quiet, dark audiences. His antisemitic writings make him a troubling figure.

sections.key: Trained opera voices cut through an orchestra with breath control and a concentration of energy around three thousand cycles per second.
sections.b:
An opera singer may need to be heard over dozens of players in a theatre seating a couple of thousand people, without a microphone. Part of the answer is training: years developing breath control and an efficient, open throat.

Another part is acoustics. Researchers have found that trained classical singers, particularly men, often produce a concentration of energy at high frequencies, around three thousand cycles per second, sometimes called the singer's formant. An orchestra is comparatively quiet in that range, and human ears are especially sensitive to it, so the voice carries over the instruments.

Voices are classified by range, high to low: soprano, mezzo-soprano and contralto for women, and tenor, baritone and bass for men. Composers write roles for particular voice types.

sections.key: Australia produced the sopranos Nellie Melba and Joan Sutherland, and surtitles now make opera easy to follow.
sections.b:
Australia has a proud opera tradition. Helen Porter Mitchell, born in Melbourne in 1861, took the stage name Nellie Melba in honour of her home city and became one of the world's most celebrated sopranos. Peach Melba and Melba toast were named after her.

Joan Sutherland, born in Sydney in 1926, became a superstar of bel canto opera, nicknamed La Stupenda. The main opera theatre at the Sydney Opera House bears her name.

Today Opera Australia is the national company, and state companies perform around the country. If opera seems intimidating, remember that most performances show translated text as surtitles above the stage, a practice that spread from the 1980s, so you can follow every word.

quiz.q: Why did the Florentine Camerata create the first operas?
o: They wanted to replace church music with theatre
They were hired to entertain the public in Venice
They were trying to invent a cheaper type of theatre
They wanted to recreate ancient Greek drama as sung
quiz.e: Setting drama to music with a clear single voice led to opera around 1600.

quiz.q: What happens in an aria?
o: A character sings at length about their feelings
The plot moves quickly in speech-like singing
The orchestra plays alone before the curtain rises
The chorus sings as a crowd
quiz.e: Recitative moves the plot, while arias pause it so a character can express emotion.

quiz.q: What are leitmotifs in Wagner's operas?
o: Spoken introductions given before the start of each act
Short musical themes that represent characters, objects or ideas
Large choruses that represent crowds, soldiers or spirits
The printed list of characters in the libretto
quiz.e: Leitmotifs let the orchestra comment on the drama, a technique film composers later borrowed.

quiz.q: Why can an opera singer be heard over an orchestra?
o: Hidden microphones built into the theatre walls and stage floor
Singing louder than every instrument at all pitches at once
Training, plus energy at high frequencies where the orchestra is quieter
The orchestra is told to play softly whenever the singer enters
quiz.e: The singer's formant sits where orchestras are weaker and ears are most sensitive.

quiz.q: How can newcomers follow opera sung in another language?
o: The orchestra plays a summary first
Singers pause to speak a translation
The audience must learn the language
Translated text appears above the stage
quiz.e: Surtitles, common since the 1980s, make every word easy to follow.

LESSONS.push: Singers fill huge halls without microphones. The secret is partly in the physics of sound.

LESSONS.title: Why every piano is slightly out of tune
LESSONS.hook: Ancient thinkers noticed that beautiful harmonies follow simple number ratios. Then musicians discovered those ratios don't quite fit together. The compromise they reached shapes every song you hear.

sections.key: Pleasing musical intervals correspond to simple ratios, which you can test by pressing a guitar string.
sections.b:
Legend credits Pythagoras with noticing that musical harmony follows numbers, though the story of him hearing blacksmiths' hammers is almost certainly myth. The basic discovery is real, and you can test it on a guitar. Pluck an open string, then press it at the halfway point and pluck again: the note is an octave higher, because the vibrating length has halved and the frequency has doubled, a ratio of 2 to 1.

Press a third of the way along, so two thirds vibrates, and you get a perfect fifth, a ratio of 3 to 2, the interval at the start of many familiar tunes. A ratio of 4 to 3 gives a perfect fourth, and 5 to 4 a major third. Simple ratios sound smooth and stable together.

sections.key: Notes in simple ratios share overtones and produce little beating, so they sound calm and clear.
sections.b:
A string or voice sounds a note at its main frequency and also at whole-number multiples of it, faint higher tones called overtones that give each instrument its colour. If two notes are in a simple ratio, many of their overtones line up exactly.

When two tones are close but not quite matched, they interfere and produce a regular wobble in loudness called beating. Play two notes that differ by two cycles per second and you hear the sound pulse twice a second. Piano tuners listen for exactly these beats, slowing or speeding them to set each interval. Simple ratios produce little beating, so they sound calm and clear.

sections.key: Stacking twelve pure fifths overshoots seven octaves by the Pythagorean comma, so no keyboard can have every interval pure.
sections.b:
Here is the snag. Start on C and go up by a pure fifth to G, then D, then A, and keep going. After twelve fifths you have passed through every note and should land on a C, seven octaves above where you began. But the numbers disagree. Twelve pure fifths multiply out to about 129.7 times the starting frequency, while seven octaves give exactly 128.

The gap is the Pythagorean comma. Musicians measure intervals in cents, with 100 cents in a modern semitone and 1200 in an octave, and the comma is about 23.5 cents, roughly a quarter of a semitone. It is a mathematical fact: no keyboard can have all its fifths and octaves perfectly pure at once.

sections.key: Earlier tunings made some keys sweet and others unusable, and well temperaments made every key playable with its own character.
sections.b:
Pythagorean tuning kept fifths pure, but its major thirds sounded harsh. Renaissance musicians adopted meantone temperaments, narrowing the fifths so the common major thirds came out pure or nearly so. The leftover error piled up in one fifth that howled, called the wolf fifth. Nearby keys sounded lovely, but distant keys were sour or unusable, and changing key could mean retuning.

By the late seventeenth and early eighteenth centuries, musicians wanted every key. Well temperaments spread the comma unevenly, so no interval howled, though common keys stayed sweeter and remote keys more tense, giving each key its own flavour. In 1722 Bach completed the first book of The Well-Tempered Clavier, twenty-four preludes and fugues, one in every major and minor key. Scholars still debate his tuning, but it was probably not modern equal temperament.

sections.key: Modern pianos split the octave into twelve equal steps, trading pure intervals for freedom, while singers and other cultures make different choices.
sections.b:
Equal temperament divides the octave into twelve exactly equal semitones, each a frequency ratio of the twelfth root of two, about 1.0595. Zhu Zaiyu in China worked it out in the late 1500s, as did Simon Stevin in Europe. It became the piano standard in the nineteenth century, and every key now sounds the same. The price is that almost every interval is slightly impure. Fifths are about two cents narrow, but major thirds are about fourteen cents wider than the pure 5 to 4 ratio, a shimmer our ears accept as normal.

Choirs and string quartets tune thirds by ear so harmony rings. Tuners stretch piano octaves a little wider because stiff strings run sharp. Concert pitch sets the A above middle C at 440 cycles per second. Gamelan and Arabic music use scales that fall between piano keys.

quiz.q: What happens when you press a guitar string exactly halfway along?
o: The note drops an octave in pitch
The note becomes a perfect fifth higher
The note rises an octave in pitch
The note stays the same but quieter
quiz.e: Halving the vibrating length doubles the frequency, a 2 to 1 ratio.

quiz.q: Why do notes in simple ratios sound smooth together?
o: They are always played at exactly the same volume
They are made without any overtones at all
They always come from the same single string
Their overtones line up, so there is little beating
quiz.e: Matching overtones and few wobbles give a calm, clear sound.

quiz.q: Why can't a keyboard have every fifth and octave perfectly pure?
o: Pure fifths are too quiet to hear on a piano
Octaves are too wide to fit on one keyboard
The comma is only an old measuring error
Twelve pure fifths overshoot seven octaves slightly
quiz.e: The numbers disagree: twelve pure fifths are about 129.7 times the starting frequency, but seven octaves are exactly 128.

quiz.q: What was the advantage of well temperaments over meantone?
o: Every interval became perfectly pure in all keys
Every key became playable, each with its own flavour
They removed the need to tune keyboards at all
They made every distant key sound just like C
quiz.e: No interval howled, so composers could write in any key, each with its own flavour.

quiz.q: What is the trade-off of equal temperament?
o: Every interval is pure, but few keys are usable
Only one key can be played on a given piano
Any key works, but most intervals are slightly impure
Pianos must be retuned whenever the key changes
quiz.e: Freedom to change key comes at the cost of slightly impure intervals, such as wide major thirds.

LESSONS.push: Every piano is slightly out of tune, on purpose. Here is the maths behind it.

LESSONS.title: Sikhism: the faith of the free kitchen
LESSONS.hook: Walk into any gurdwara in the world and someone will offer you a hot meal, no questions asked. Here is the faith behind that open door.

sections.key: Langar, the free communal meal served at every gurdwara, is Sikh equality put into practice.
sections.b:
Picture a vast hall at the Golden Temple in Amritsar, India. Rows of people sit cross-legged on long mats: farmers, tourists, businesspeople, the very poor. Volunteers ladle out dal, vegetables and fresh roti. Nobody pays, and nobody is asked their religion or caste. On a busy day the kitchen serves tens of thousands of meals.

This is langar, the free community kitchen found at every gurdwara, or Sikh place of worship. Sitting together on the floor is deliberate, because it puts everyone at the same level. For Sikhs, langar is not charity handed down from above. It is a practical way of living out equality.

sections.key: Guru Nanak taught one formless God, honest work and sharing, and rejected caste and empty ritual.
sections.b:
Sikhism began in Punjab with Guru Nanak, born in 1469. Tradition says he vanished into a river for three days and returned saying, 'There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim.' Sikhs read this as a call to look past labels to a shared humanity and one God. His teachings rejected empty ritual and the caste system. The word Sikh means learner or disciple.

Sikhs believe in one formless God, expressed in the phrase Ik Onkar, 'One Creator'. The aim of life is to move from ego towards God. Three practices help: Naam Japna (remembering God), Kirat Karni (earning an honest living) and Vand Chakna (sharing what you have).

sections.key: After ten human Gurus, the scripture itself, the Guru Granth Sahib, became the eternal Guru.
sections.b:
Guru Nanak was followed by nine more human Gurus over roughly two centuries. The fifth, Guru Arjan, compiled the hymns of the Gurus and of some Hindu and Muslim saints into a single scripture.

Before his death in 1708, the tenth Guru, Gobind Singh, made a remarkable decision: there would be no more human Gurus. The scripture, the Guru Granth Sahib, would be the eternal Guru. It is treated with deep respect. In a gurdwara it rests on a raised platform under a canopy, someone waves a whisk over it, and at night it is carried ceremonially to its own resting room. Visitors cover their heads and remove their shoes.

sections.key: Initiated Sikhs keep five articles of faith, and shared surnames reject caste.
sections.b:
In 1699, at the spring festival of Vaisakhi, Guru Gobind Singh created the Khalsa, a community of initiated Sikhs committed to discipline, courage and defending the vulnerable. Members keep the Five Ks: kesh (uncut hair), kara (a steel bracelet), kanga (a small wooden comb), kachera (a cotton undergarment) and kirpan (a small ceremonial blade, a symbol of standing against injustice).

Uncut hair is covered by a turban, or dastaar, which many Sikhs see as a commitment to faith and dignity. Many Sikh men take the surname Singh (lion) and many women Kaur (often 'princess'). Shared surnames reject caste, since regional surnames often revealed it.

sections.key: Sikhs have lived in Australia since the 1800s, and many gurdwaras take langar to disaster-hit communities.
sections.b:
Sikhs are not newcomers to Australia. In the 1800s, Punjabi men worked here as hawkers and farm labourers, travelling the bush selling goods from carts. The coastal town of Woolgoolga in northern New South Wales became home to a Punjabi farming community, and one of Australia's earliest gurdwaras was built there in the late 1960s.

Sikhism is now one of the fastest growing religions in the country, with more than 200,000 people identifying as Sikh in the 2021 census. Worldwide there are around 25 to 30 million Sikhs, most of them in Punjab. Many Australian gurdwaras cook langar for communities hit by bushfires and floods, carrying the free kitchen into new places.

quiz.q: Why do people sit together on the floor to eat langar?
o: It keeps the hall cleaner
It puts everyone at the same level
It is a rule for visitors only
It saves money on furniture
quiz.e: Sitting side by side is deliberate: langar is a practical way of living out equality, not charity from above.

quiz.q: What does the Sikh practice of Kirat Karni ask of a person?
o: To fast each week
To make a pilgrimage
To earn an honest living
To avoid all possessions
quiz.e: Kirat Karni, honest work, sits alongside remembering God and sharing with others as the core Sikh practices.

quiz.q: What did Guru Gobind Singh decide about the line of Gurus?
o: The scripture would be the eternal Guru
His eldest son would lead for life
A council would choose each Guru
The Golden Temple would become the Guru
quiz.e: He ended the line of human Gurus, so the Guru Granth Sahib is treated as the living Guru.

quiz.q: Why do many Sikhs use the shared surnames Singh and Kaur?
o: They are required by law for all Sikhs in India
They show the trade a family has worked in
They mark the village a Sikh family came from
They reject caste, which many surnames revealed
quiz.e: Shared surnames were another way of rejecting caste, since surnames in the region often revealed it.

quiz.q: How do many Australian gurdwaras carry the langar tradition today?
o: By running cooking classes for visiting tourists
By selling meals to raise money for the temple
By cooking free meals after bushfires and floods
By holding langar only on major festival days
quiz.e: Cooking langar for disaster-hit communities extends the free kitchen beyond the gurdwara walls.

LESSONS.push: Why a free hot meal is waiting at every Sikh temple, and what it says about equality.

LESSONS.title: Shinto: Japan's way of the kami
LESSONS.hook: Japan is dotted with more than 80,000 shrines, marked by bright red gates. Behind them sits a tradition with no founder, no single holy book and a world full of spirits.

sections.key: Shinto is Japan's native tradition of honouring kami, sacred powers found in nature, places and ancestors.
sections.b:
A tall vermilion gate of two posts and two crossbeams stands at the edge of a forest. This is a torii, the boundary between the everyday world and sacred ground. Beyond it lies a Shinto shrine, home to a kami.

Shinto, 'the way of the kami', is Japan's oldest religious tradition. It has no founder, no single scripture and no fixed list of beliefs. Kami means a god, a spirit or simply something that inspires awe. One might live in Mount Fuji, an old tree, a waterfall or a boulder wrapped in a rope with paper streamers. Others are mythological figures or honoured ancestors. 'Eight million kami' means countless, not an exact number. Kami are neither all-powerful nor perfectly good, so Shinto is about keeping a respectful relationship with them.

sections.key: Japan's ancient chronicles tell how the islands were created and how laughter coaxed the sun goddess from her cave.
sections.b:
Japan's oldest surviving books, the Kojiki (712) and Nihon Shoki (720), record its myths. The deities Izanagi and Izanami stir the ocean with a jewelled spear, and brine dripping from its tip forms the first island. They give birth to the islands of Japan and many kami. When Izanami dies, Izanagi follows her to the land of the dead and flees in horror. Washing himself clean, he gives rise to new kami, including the sun goddess Amaterasu.

Upset by her storm god brother Susanoo's pranks, Amaterasu hides in a cave and the world goes dark. The other kami hang a mirror outside, and Ame no Uzume performs a comic dance that makes them roar with laughter. Curious, Amaterasu peeks out, sees her own radiance in the mirror and is drawn into the open. Light returns.

sections.key: Shinto treats impurity as spiritual dirt that can be washed away, so visitors purify before approaching the kami.
sections.b:
A central idea in Shinto is purity. Impurity, called kegare, is not quite the same as sin. It is more like spiritual dirt that comes from contact with death, illness or wrongdoing, and it can be washed away.

At the entrance to most shrines is a stone basin with wooden ladles. Visitors rinse their left hand, then their right, then their mouth. At the main hall they often toss a coin into a box, bow twice, clap twice, make a wish or prayer, and bow once more. Priests perform larger purification rituals, waving a wand of paper streamers. Visitors can buy omamori charms for luck or safe driving, and omikuji, paper fortunes tied to racks if the news is bad.

sections.key: Japan's most sacred shrine, at Ise, is rebuilt every twenty years because Shinto treats renewal as sacred.
sections.b:
The Grand Shrine of Ise, dedicated to Amaterasu, is the most sacred site in Shinto. Its main buildings are made of plain cypress wood with thatched roofs. Every twenty years they are carefully rebuilt on a neighbouring plot, and the old ones are taken down. The most recent rebuild was in 2013.

The tradition has continued, with some interruptions, for well over a thousand years. It keeps carpentry skills alive across generations and expresses the idea that renewal and freshness are sacred. It also raises a puzzle: is a building that is constantly rebuilt very new or very old? Western ideas of preserving original materials do not quite fit, and visitors often find that question as memorable as the shrine itself.

sections.key: Most Japanese people mix Shinto and Buddhist customs, and Shinto today is mainly festivals, seasonal rituals and respect for nature.
sections.b:
Ask Japanese people whether they are religious and many will say no, yet most take part in Shinto customs. Millions visit shrines in the first days of the New Year, babies are often presented at a shrine, and weddings may follow Shinto rites. Funerals, however, are usually Buddhist.

For centuries Shinto and Buddhism were blended, until the government separated them in the 1860s. From then until 1945, a nationalist form called State Shinto promoted the emperor as divine. After the Second World War, Emperor Hirohito publicly rejected the idea that he was a living god, and Japan's new constitution separated religion and the state. Today Shinto is mostly about community festivals, seasonal rituals and respect for nature.

quiz.q: What does the phrase 'eight million kami' suggest?
o: An exact count of the spirits
That kami are countless
The number of shrines in Japan
The number of ancient emperors
quiz.e: The phrase means countless: kami are found everywhere, in nature, places and ancestors.

quiz.q: How was Amaterasu drawn out of her cave?
o: Her brother apologised to her
An earthquake split the cave open
The emperor ordered her to leave
Laughter made her curious about the noise
quiz.e: The kami's laughter at the comic dance made Amaterasu peek out, and the mirror drew her fully into the open.

quiz.q: How does Shinto understand impurity, or kegare?
o: As spiritual dirt that can be washed away
As a sin that cannot be forgiven
As a punishment sent by the kami
As a sign of a weak faith
quiz.e: Kegare comes from contact with death, illness or wrongdoing, and rituals such as rinsing at the basin cleanse it.

quiz.q: Why is the Grand Shrine of Ise rebuilt every twenty years?
o: Termites steadily destroy the wooden frames
Each new emperor orders a shrine of his own
Floods damage the shrine every generation
Renewal and freshness are considered sacred
quiz.e: Rebuilding keeps both the buildings and the craft skills fresh, expressing the Shinto idea that renewal is sacred.

quiz.q: How do most Japanese people treat Shinto and Buddhism today?
o: They must choose only one
They take part in both without conflict
They practise neither of them
They follow Buddhism on holidays
quiz.e: Shrine visits and weddings are often Shinto, while funerals are usually Buddhist, and few see a contradiction.

LESSONS.push: A sacred shrine in Japan is demolished and rebuilt every twenty years. Why?

LESSONS.title: The Dreaming: law, land and story
LESSONS.hook: For tens of thousands of years, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have carried knowledge in story, song and country. 'Dreamtime' barely begins to describe it.

sections.key: The Dreaming is a living system of law, belief and knowledge, and 'Dreamtime' is only a clumsy English label for it.
sections.b:
Many Australians first meet Aboriginal spirituality through the word 'Dreamtime', imagined as a magical era long ago. That misses a great deal. The Dreaming links creation, law, kinship, land and daily responsibility. It explains how the world came to be, and it tells people how to live and how to care for country. Australia's First Peoples have lived here for at least 50,000 years. There is no single version: each nation has its own beliefs and words.

Anthropologists popularised 'Dreamtime' in the late 1800s, translating an Arrernte word. Many Aboriginal people find it clumsy, because it suggests something imaginary when these beliefs describe what is most real. The Anangu speak of Tjukurpa, and the Warlpiri of Jukurrpa. In the 1950s W. E. H. Stanner called it an 'everywhen': ancestral events continue to shape the present.

sections.key: Ancestral beings shaped the land and remain present in it, so country is family, history and law at once.
sections.b:
In many Dreaming accounts, ancestral beings travelled across a formless or sleeping land, and their actions created its features. A waterhole may mark where an ancestor rested, a ridge where one lay down, a rock formation where a battle took place.

These beings took many forms: animals, plants, people, stars, and powerful figures like the Rainbow Serpent. Its stories appear in different ways across much of the continent and are often tied to water and fertility.

Because ancestors are believed to remain present in the land, country is not just scenery or property. It is family, history and law all at once. Many Aboriginal people speak of belonging to country, rather than country belonging to them.

sections.key: Songlines are sung routes across the land that carry stories, law and practical knowledge.
sections.b:
The journeys of ancestral beings are often remembered as songlines, sometimes called Dreaming tracks. A songline can stretch hundreds or even thousands of kilometres, crossing the lands of many nations. Each group holds responsibility for its own section of the song.

Singing the verses in order works like a map. It names waterholes, landmarks and food sources in sequence, which could help people travel safely through dry country. Songlines also carry law, kinship rules and seasonal knowledge, and some follow patterns in the stars. Researchers studying memory are keenly interested in how songs, places and stories together can hold huge amounts of information without writing. For the custodians, though, songlines are first and foremost sacred.

sections.key: Some Dreaming knowledge is restricted, and sharing it needs the right authority.
sections.b:
A key point for outsiders is that Dreaming knowledge is not public property. Some stories are open, often told to children and visitors. Others are restricted to people who have gone through certain ceremonies, or are known as men's business or women's business and kept within those groups. Certain sites are sacred and should not be photographed or entered.

Rights to tell a story, paint its designs or sing its songs belong to particular custodians, who inherit that responsibility through kinship. This is why respectful books, galleries and tourism operators work with traditional owners and seek permission. It is also why this lesson does not retell specific sacred stories: the respectful way to hear them is from the people who hold them.

sections.key: The Dreaming is not in the past: it guides decisions like the Uluru climb closure and lives on in ceremony, art and language.
sections.b:
At Uluru, Tjukurpa is present for the Anangu traditional owners, and the climbing route has deep spiritual significance. For decades signs asked tourists not to climb, and many did anyway. After the park was handed back to Anangu ownership in 1985 and leased to the national parks agency, the joint management board voted to end the climb. It closed permanently in October 2019. Visitors now walk around the base, where guides share stories that are open to the public.

Colonisation caused enormous harm, including dispossession, language loss and the removal of children. Yet ceremony, song and story survive, and communities are reviving languages. Since the 1970s, painters from Papunya in the Western Desert have shared permitted aspects of their Dreamings through acrylic art. When you hear a Welcome to Country, you hear a very old relationship with land.

quiz.q: Why do many Aboriginal people find 'Dreamtime' a clumsy translation?
o: It suggests something imaginary, not real
It was invented by a single nation
It refers only to children's stories
It is too old-fashioned to use
quiz.e: The Dreaming is a living framework of law and belief, not a fantasy confined to the distant past.

quiz.q: What does it mean to say Aboriginal people belong to country?
o: They are legally tied to one house
They must never leave their home
Country is family, history and law
They own land in the European sense
quiz.e: Because ancestors remain present in the land, country carries kinship, history and responsibility.

quiz.q: What is one practical function of a songline?
o: It records colonial property boundaries
It names landmarks and waterholes in order
It sets the dates of ceremonies each year
It counts how many people live nearby
quiz.e: Sung in order, a songline names places and resources along a route, helping people navigate dry country.

quiz.q: Why might a respectful book avoid retelling certain Dreaming stories?
o: Every nation tells exactly the same stories
Most of the stories have been lost over time
Some knowledge belongs to particular custodians
Stories about country are only meant for children
quiz.e: Rights to share a story belong to specific custodians, so the respectful way to hear one is from them.

quiz.q: What guided the decision to close the Uluru climb in 2019?
o: A government plan to build a new road
Anangu law and the site's spiritual meaning
A rockfall that made it unsafe to climb
Advice from a tourism marketing review
quiz.e: For the Anangu, Tjukurpa makes the route sacred, and the joint management board voted to end the climb.

LESSONS.push: Why 'Dreamtime' is an English word that barely begins to describe Aboriginal law and land.

LESSONS.title: Gilgamesh: the world's oldest great story
LESSONS.hook: A tyrant king, a wild man from the steppe and a desperate quest to cheat death. Written on clay over 3,000 years ago, Gilgamesh still feels startlingly modern.

sections.key: Gilgamesh was rediscovered on clay tablets from Nineveh, and its hero may have been a real king of Uruk.
sections.b:
In 1872 George Smith, a young assistant at the British Museum, was piecing together broken clay tablets from the ruins of Nineveh in modern Iraq. In the cuneiform script he found a flood, a man who built a boat and a bird sent to look for land. It looked strikingly like Noah's story. The tablets came from the library of the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal, from the 600s BCE, and held the Epic of Gilgamesh.

Gilgamesh was probably based on a real king of Uruk, one of the first great cities, who may have reigned around 2700 BCE, though there is no direct proof. He grew into a legend, two thirds god and one third human. Sumerian poems about him came first, around 2100 BCE, and were later woven into a Babylonian epic of twelve tablets.

sections.key: The gods create Enkidu to balance a proud Gilgamesh, and their friendship leads them into heroic deeds that cost a life.
sections.b:
Gilgamesh is magnificent but arrogant, and he oppresses the people of Uruk. The gods answer their cries by creating Enkidu, a wild man who lives among the animals of the steppe. Shamhat brings him into human society, and he learns to eat bread, drink beer and wear clothes. When Enkidu confronts Gilgamesh, the two wrestle fiercely. Neither wins, and the struggle becomes a deep friendship.

Seeking lasting fame, they travel to the Cedar Forest and kill its guardian, Humbaba, with help from the sun god Shamash. The goddess Ishtar proposes marriage to Gilgamesh, and he rudely refuses. She sends the Bull of Heaven to ravage the land, and the heroes slay it too. The gods take note: one of the friends must die for these offences, and the lot falls on Enkidu.

sections.key: Enkidu's death makes Gilgamesh face his own mortality, and the epic becomes a meditation on it.
sections.b:
Enkidu falls ill and dies after days of suffering, and Gilgamesh is shattered. He refuses to let his friend be buried until, in a famously grim detail, a worm falls from Enkidu's nose. The mighty king suddenly understands that he too will die.

This is the emotional heart of the epic, and it is why Gilgamesh feels so human more than 3,000 years later. He tears off his fine clothes, dresses in animal skins and wanders the wilderness, consumed by grief and terror. His question is one every reader recognises: is there any way to escape death? He sets out to find the one man said to have been granted eternal life.

sections.key: Utnapishtim survived a flood sent by the gods and was granted immortality, a story that parallels the biblical flood.
sections.b:
After a long journey, including crossing the waters of death, Gilgamesh reaches Utnapishtim, a wise man who lives with his wife at the edge of the world. Utnapishtim tells his story. The gods decided to destroy humanity with a flood, but the god Ea secretly warned him to build a huge boat and load it with his family, craftsmen and animals.

The storm raged for days. When it ended, the boat came to rest on a mountain. Utnapishtim released a dove, a swallow and then a raven, which did not return because it had found land. Grateful, he made an offering, and the gods granted him and his wife immortality. Scholars still discuss how this story relates to the biblical flood.

sections.key: Gilgamesh cannot cheat death, but the epic suggests our work, cities and stories can outlast us.
sections.b:
Utnapishtim challenges Gilgamesh to stay awake for a week, and the exhausted king immediately falls asleep. Out of kindness, Utnapishtim tells him of a plant at the bottom of the sea that restores youth. Gilgamesh ties stones to his feet, dives down and gets it.

On the way home, while he bathes in a pool, a snake slithers up and eats the plant, shedding its skin as it goes. Gilgamesh weeps. He returns to Uruk empty-handed, and the epic ends with him showing a companion the city's mighty walls and brickwork. The message many readers take is that we cannot live forever, but our work, our cities and our stories can outlast us.

quiz.q: How do many historians view Gilgamesh?
o: As a god who was invented from nothing
As a Greek hero later adopted by Assyria
As a character first written in the 1800s
As a legend likely based on a real king
quiz.e: King lists name Gilgamesh as a ruler of Uruk, so he is part history, part myth and part great literature.

quiz.q: Why do the gods decide that Enkidu must die?
o: He killed Humbaba and the Bull of Heaven
He refused to leave the steppe
He stole the plant of youth from the sea
He broke a promise to the goddess Ishtar
quiz.e: The heroes' killing of the Cedar Forest guardian and the Bull of Heaven offended the gods.

quiz.q: What sends Gilgamesh on his quest for eternal life?
o: A prophecy from the goddess Ishtar
A command from the council of gods
Grief for Enkidu and fear of his own death
A dream about a coming flood
quiz.e: Enkidu's death forces the king to face his own mortality, which is the emotional heart of the epic.

quiz.q: What did the raven's failure to return show Utnapishtim?
o: That the bird had died at sea
That it had found dry land
That the gods were angry
That the flood was starting again
quiz.e: A bird that did not come back meant the waters had gone down enough for it to find land.

quiz.q: What message do many readers take from the ending of the epic?
o: The gods always reward the brave
Youth can be restored by diving deep
Our work, cities and stories can outlast us
Kings should never travel
quiz.e: Gilgamesh cannot live forever, but the walls of Uruk stand as a legacy that endures.

LESSONS.push: A tablet found in 1872 told a flood story older than the Bible's. Who was its hero?

LESSONS.title: The great flood stories
LESSONS.hook: Noah's ark is famous, but it is one of many. From Mesopotamia to India, Greece and China, cultures have told of a world drowned and begun again.

sections.key: Flood stories appear across cultures because floods were a shared fear, and a fresh start gives a story room for big questions.
sections.b:
Imagine rain that does not stop, rivers that swallow fields, then a single boat afloat on an endless sea. Versions of this image appear around the world: Noah's ark in the Hebrew Bible, flood heroes in Mesopotamia, a warning fish in Hindu tradition, and Greek, Chinese and many Indigenous stories. For believers, some carry deep religious meaning. For historians, the pattern raises questions about shared memories and borrowed stories.

Early civilisations grew along rivers and coasts, where floods threatened lives yet fed fertile soil. A flood also wipes the slate clean, so it lets a tradition ask who deserves to survive and why. The survivors start a new world, so the stories are as much about hope as destruction.

sections.key: The oldest written flood stories come from ancient Mesopotamia, where river floods were a very real fear.
sections.b:
The earliest known written flood stories come from Mesopotamia, the land between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers in modern Iraq. A Sumerian account tells of a king named Ziusudra who survives a flood.

A Babylonian poem, the Atrahasis epic, explains that the gods sent the flood because humans had become too numerous and noisy, disturbing their rest. The wise Atrahasis is secretly warned by the god Enki and builds a boat. The same story appears in the Epic of Gilgamesh, where the survivor is called Utnapishtim.

These tablets date back to roughly the early second millennium BCE. On flat land beside bursting rivers, a catastrophic flood was a very real fear.

sections.key: Genesis and the Mesopotamian accounts share a shape but differ in message: moral judgment and a promise.
sections.b:
In Genesis, shared by Judaism and Christianity, with a version in the Quran where Noah is called Nuh, God sees the earth filled with violence and sends a flood. The righteous Noah survives with his family and pairs of animals. Afterwards he sends out a raven and a dove, and the dove returns with an olive leaf. God makes a covenant never again to destroy the earth by flood, with the rainbow as its sign.

When George Smith translated the Gilgamesh flood tablet in 1872, readers saw close parallels: a divine warning, a great boat, animals, a landing on a mountain, birds and a sacrifice. Many scholars think both draw on a shared regional tradition. But in Mesopotamia many quarrelsome gods act for seemingly petty reasons. In Genesis one God responds to wrongdoing and ends with a promise.

sections.key: Hindu, Greek and Chinese flood stories each add their own twist.
sections.b:
In Hindu tradition, the first man, Manu, finds a tiny fish that asks for protection. He cares for it as it grows huge, and it turns out to be the god Vishnu in his fish form, Matsya. The fish warns of a flood and tows Manu's boat to safety.

In Greek myth, Deucalion and his wife Pyrrha survive a flood sent by Zeus, then repopulate the world by throwing stones over their shoulders, which become people.

Chinese tradition tells of Yu the Great, who succeeded where his father had failed. Instead of building dams to block the water, Yu dug channels to guide it to the sea. The Chinese story is less about divine punishment and more about wise human effort.

sections.key: Some flood stories may preserve real memories of coastlines drowned as seas rose after the last Ice Age.
sections.b:
Could some flood stories remember real events? At the end of the last Ice Age, melting ice sheets raised global sea levels by well over 100 metres, a process that largely ended around 7,000 years ago. Coastlines around the world moved inland.

In Australia, researchers including linguist Nicholas Reid and geographer Patrick Nunn have studied Aboriginal stories from many coastal areas that describe the sea rising and land being lost. They argue that some may preserve memories from that time. Others have proposed that a sudden flooding of the Black Sea inspired ancient legends, though that idea remains debated.

These theories are interesting but not settled, and none of them proves or disproves any particular religious account.

quiz.q: Why does a flood make such a useful story setting?
o: It resets the world, so big questions can be asked
It was the only disaster early peoples feared
It always proves that a historical event occurred
It was borrowed from one single ancient culture
quiz.e: A flood resets the world, so stories can explore why bad things happen and who deserves to survive.

quiz.q: According to the Atrahasis epic, why did the gods send a flood?
o: Humans had stopped making sacrifices
A king had insulted the sun god
Humans had become too numerous and noisy
The rivers needed refilling
quiz.e: In Atrahasis, the gods are disturbed by the noise of an overpopulated humanity.

quiz.q: What is a key difference between Genesis and the Mesopotamian flood accounts?
o: Only Genesis has a boat that lands on a mountain
Genesis has one God, wrongdoing and a promise
Only the Mesopotamian versions mention animals
Genesis has no birds, unlike Mesopotamian tales
quiz.e: Mesopotamian versions feature many gods with sometimes petty motives, while Genesis centres on one God, wrongdoing and a covenant.

quiz.q: How did Yu the Great tame the flood in Chinese tradition?
o: By building much taller dams
By praying to a dragon king
By building a huge wooden ark
By digging channels to guide the water
quiz.e: Yu succeeded by channelling the water, where his father's dams had failed.

quiz.q: What might some Aboriginal coastal stories remember, according to researchers?
o: A tsunami from a distant volcano
Seas rising after the last Ice Age
A comet striking the ocean
A great flood of the Murray
quiz.e: Researchers argue some stories may preserve memories of coastlines lost as seas rose after the last Ice Age.

LESSONS.push: Many cultures tell of a drowned world and a fresh start. What are they remembering?

LESSONS.title: Zoroastrianism: the fire and the choice
LESSONS.hook: Once the faith of Persian empires, now held by a small community, Zoroastrianism asks every person to pick a side in a cosmic battle between good and evil.

sections.key: Zoroastrians pray in the presence of fire as a symbol of purity, and the faith traces back to the prophet Zarathustra.
sections.b:
In the Iranian city of Yazd, a flame burns in a large metal vessel inside a fire temple. According to the community, it has been kept alight for many centuries by priests who add sandalwood and recite prayers. Outsiders sometimes call Zoroastrians 'fire worshippers', but that is a misunderstanding. Fire is a symbol of purity, light and the divine, and prayers are said in its presence rather than to it.

The faith takes its name from Zarathustra, known to the Greeks as Zoroaster. Scholars disagree about when he lived, from around 1500 BCE to about 600 BCE. His hymns, the Gathas, are the oldest part of the Avesta, the Zoroastrian scripture. In them he speaks directly to God, asking about justice, truth and how to live.

sections.key: Zoroastrians see a world split between good and evil, and every person freely chooses a side.
sections.b:
Zoroastrians worship one supreme God, Ahura Mazda, the Wise Lord, who is entirely good. Opposed to him is Angra Mainyu, the destructive spirit, the source of evil, sickness and death. The world is a struggle between asha, truth and right order, and druj, the lie. Scholars debate whether this is dualistic or monotheistic, but Zoroastrians generally call their faith monotheistic. Evil is not part of God's nature, and it will ultimately be defeated.

Because the world is a battleground, every choice counts. People are not born sinful. They have free will and strengthen the good through honest, kind and hard-working lives and care for earth, water and fire. The motto is good thoughts, good words, good deeds. Young people are initiated at the navjote, receiving a sacred cord, the kusti, which many retie several times a day with prayers.

sections.key: Zoroastrian tradition teaches judgment after death and a final renewal of the world, ideas that may have shaped other faiths.
sections.b:
Zoroastrianism has a vivid picture of what happens after death. Tradition teaches that on the third night after a person dies, the soul crosses the Chinvat Bridge. For the righteous, the bridge is wide and they pass to the House of Song, a paradise. For the wicked it narrows like a blade, and they fall into a place of suffering.

At the end of time, a saviour figure called the Saoshyant will appear, the dead will be raised, evil will be defeated and the world will be renewed in perfection. Many scholars think these ideas of individual judgment, heaven and hell, resurrection and a final saviour influenced Judaism, Christianity and Islam, though the extent of that influence is still debated.

sections.key: Zoroastrianism was tied to Persian power for over a thousand years, then shrank to a minority after the Arab conquest.
sections.b:
Zoroastrian beliefs were bound up with Persian power for over a thousand years. Inscriptions of the Achaemenid king Darius the Great, who ruled from about 522 BCE, credit his rule to Ahuramazda, a form of Ahura Mazda. The Sasanian empire, from the 200s CE, made Zoroastrianism its official religion, with a powerful priesthood and grand fire temples.

Many people believe the Magi who visit the infant Jesus in the Gospel of Matthew were Zoroastrian priests, as magi was a term for that priestly class, though the Gospel does not say so directly. After the Arab conquest of Persia in the 600s CE, Islam gradually became the majority faith, and Zoroastrians became a shrinking minority in their homeland. Today they number only in the low hundreds of thousands worldwide.

sections.key: Parsis, descendants of Zoroastrians who migrated to India, are a small but influential community.
sections.b:
According to tradition, a group of Zoroastrians left Persia and sailed to the coast of Gujarat in India, perhaps around the 700s to 900s CE, seeking freedom to practise their faith. Their descendants are called Parsis, meaning Persians. Many later settled in Mumbai, where Parsis became prominent in business, law and philanthropy. The Tata family is a famous example, and the rock star Freddie Mercury, born Farrokh Bulsara, came from a Parsi family.

Traditionally Parsis placed the dead in Towers of Silence to be exposed to vultures, to avoid polluting earth or fire, though this is changing. The community is small and ageing, and debates about intermarriage and conversion are lively. Iran's festival of Nowruz has Zoroastrian roots.

quiz.q: How do Zoroastrians understand their sacred fire?
o: As a god to be worshipped
As a weapon against evil spirits
As a way to cook offerings
As a symbol of purity and the divine
quiz.e: Fire symbolises purity, light and divine presence; prayers are said before it, not to it.

quiz.q: Why does every choice matter in Zoroastrian teaching?
o: People are born sinful and must be saved
People freely choose a side in the struggle
Fate has already decided every outcome
Only priests can influence the outcome
quiz.e: People have free will, so honest, kind actions strengthen the side of good in the struggle against evil.

quiz.q: What happens at the Chinvat Bridge, according to tradition?
o: The sacred fire is first lit
Souls are judged after death
Young people are initiated
Kings are crowned
quiz.e: The bridge widens for the righteous and narrows like a blade for the wicked.

quiz.q: How did Zoroastrianism's position change after the 600s CE?
o: It spread across Europe as a major faith
It was replaced by the Greek religion
It grew stronger as Persia was conquered
It shrank from an empire faith to a minority
quiz.e: After the Arab conquest, Islam became the majority faith, leaving Zoroastrians a minority in their homeland.

quiz.q: Who are the Parsis?
o: Descendants of Zoroastrians who moved to India
Priests who tend the fire temples of Iran
A medieval Persian dynasty of Muslim rulers
Followers of a breakaway Islamic sect in Iran
quiz.e: Parsis descend from Zoroastrians who, by tradition, sailed from Persia to Gujarat.

LESSONS.push: Zoroastrians pray beside fire, not to it. What do they see in the flame?

LESSONS.title: Daoism: the way of water
LESSONS.hook: A short ancient book, a sage who may never have existed and the idea that doing less can achieve more. Daoism has shaped Chinese life for over 2,000 years.

sections.key: Daoism uses water as an image of quiet strength and points to the Dao, the unnameable pattern behind all things.
sections.b:
Watch a river carve a canyon. Water does not fight the rock. It flows around it and, over time, wears down stone. The Daodejing, Daoism's most famous text, praises water again and again: it benefits all things without competing, and nothing can withstand it.

Daoism is one of China's great traditions, alongside Confucianism and Buddhism, and is both a philosophy and an organised religion. Dao means 'way'. It is the source of the universe and the natural pattern by which it unfolds. The Daodejing opens by saying the Dao that can be spoken of is not the eternal Dao: words can point towards it but never capture it. The Dao is no god issuing commands. It is more like the grain of the universe. The wise person learns to recognise its patterns and move with them.

sections.key: Tradition credits Laozi with the Daodejing, but most historians think it was compiled from earlier sayings.
sections.b:
Tradition credits the Daodejing to Laozi, whose name means 'Old Master'. A famous legend says he was a record keeper at the royal court of the Zhou dynasty. Weary of the decline of society, he rode west on a water buffalo to leave China. At the border pass, a gatekeeper recognised his wisdom and begged him to write down his teachings.

Laozi wrote a short book of about five thousand characters, handed it over and was never seen again.

Most historians today think the Daodejing was compiled from earlier sayings, probably around the 300s or 400s BCE, and that Laozi may be partly or wholly legendary. The book is now one of the most translated texts in the world.

sections.key: Wu wei means acting in harmony with circumstances, effortlessly and without strain, not doing nothing.
sections.b:
One of Daoism's central ideas is wu wei, often translated as 'non-action' but better understood as effortless or natural action. It does not mean being lazy. It means acting in harmony with circumstances rather than forcing them, like a skilled swimmer who uses the current instead of thrashing against it.

A story from the Zhuangzi, another key Daoist text, describes a cook who carves an ox so skilfully that his knife never dulls, because he follows the natural spaces between the joints. Daoist writing applies the same idea to rulers: the best leaders govern so lightly that people barely notice them. Modern ideas about being in the 'flow' echo this ancient thought.

sections.key: Zhuangzi's playful stories invite us to hold our fixed ideas about reality lightly.
sections.b:
The second great Daoist thinker, Zhuangzi, lived around the 300s BCE and wrote with humour and imagination. In his most famous passage, he dreams he is a butterfly, fluttering happily with no idea he is Zhuangzi. Then he wakes and is unmistakably himself. But now he wonders: was he Zhuangzi dreaming of being a butterfly, or a butterfly now dreaming of being Zhuangzi?

The story is less a riddle to solve than an invitation to hold our fixed ideas lightly. Zhuangzi loved stories that turn conventional values upside down: useless trees that survive because no carpenter wants them, and outcasts who turn out to be wiser than kings. His book remains one of the most enjoyable works of ancient philosophy.

sections.key: Yin and yang are complementary forces, and Daoist ideas live on in religion, tai chi and popular culture.
sections.b:
Yin, the dark, receptive side, and yang, the bright, active side, are not good and evil but complementary forces, each holding a seed of the other. The idea is older than Daoism, yet the yin yang symbol is one of its emblems.

Around the 100s CE, Daoism developed as an organised religion, with priests, temples, festivals and immortals such as the Eight Immortals. Some Daoists sought long life through meditation, breathing, diet and alchemy, and some elixirs contained toxic mercury, with deadly results.

Tai chi, practised in parks around the world, draws on Daoist ideas about balance and qi. Traditional Chinese medicine and feng shui share similar ideas. In China, people often blend Confucian, Buddhist and Daoist teachings. The core message travels well: slow down, notice nature and stop forcing things.

quiz.q: Why does the Daodejing keep returning to the image of water?
o: It shows gentle strength that wears down stone
It warns about the danger of floods
It stands for the wealth of the emperor
It represents the cycle of the seasons
quiz.e: Water benefits all things without competing, and over time nothing can withstand it.

quiz.q: What do most historians think about the Daodejing?
o: It was written in one night at a border pass
It was compiled from earlier sayings
It was written by Confucius himself
It was copied from an Indian text
quiz.e: The Laozi story is a famous legend, but the book was likely assembled from older material.

quiz.q: What is the best description of wu wei?
o: Refusing to work at all
Strict obedience to rulers
Fasting for a long life
Acting naturally, without strain
quiz.e: Wu wei is effortless action, like the cook whose knife follows the natural spaces in the ox.

quiz.q: What is the point of Zhuangzi's butterfly dream?
o: To prove that dreams predict the future
To invite us to hold our fixed ideas lightly
To argue that waking life is worthless
To warn that dreaming is dangerous
quiz.e: The story questions how certain we can be about reality rather than offering a puzzle with an answer.

quiz.q: How do Daoists view yin and yang?
o: As good and evil locked in permanent war
As two rival gods competing for worship
As complementary forces that keep balance
As heaven and hell in the afterlife
quiz.e: Yin and yang are not moral opposites but complementary forces.

LESSONS.push: A sage who may never have existed, and a book that says doing less can achieve more.

LESSONS.title: Māui and the myths of Polynesia
LESSONS.hook: He fished up islands, slowed the sun and stole fire. Māui, the trickster demigod, is a hero across thousands of kilometres of Pacific Ocean.

sections.key: Māui is a clever, underestimated demigod whose stories are told across Polynesia, from Aotearoa to Hawaiʻi.
sections.b:
Picture the vast triangle of Polynesia. It runs from Aotearoa New Zealand in the south-west to Hawaiʻi in the north and Rapa Nui, or Easter Island, in the east. Island peoples with shared ancestral roots tell stories of the same mischievous hero: Māui, a clever, cheeky, slightly reckless demigod whose adventures explain features of the world.

In a well-known telling, Māui was born early and his mother, Taranga, wrapped him in her topknot and cast him into the sea. Seaweed and jellyfish protected him, and a sky ancestor raised him. As a boy he returned to announce himself to his surprised family. He begins as an outsider who must prove himself, as the youngest of several brothers.

sections.key: Māori tradition says Māui hauled up the North Island like a giant fish, using a magical hook.
sections.b:
