The most famous Māui story in Aotearoa tells how he hid in the bottom of his brothers' canoe when they went fishing. Far out to sea, he revealed himself and lowered a magical hook made from the jawbone of his grandmother, Murirangawhenua. He caught something enormous and hauled it up: a vast fish, which became the North Island.

Its Māori name, Te Ika a Māui, means the fish of Māui. His brothers began hacking at the fish before it had settled, which is said to explain the North Island's mountains and valleys. The South Island is often known as Te Waka a Māui, his canoe, and Stewart Island as Te Punga a Māui, its anchor stone.

sections.key: Māui slowed the sun to lengthen the day and tricked the fire goddess, leaving fire hidden in certain trees.
sections.b:
The sun once raced across the sky so fast that people lacked daylight to fish, farm and cook. Māui and his brothers plaited strong ropes, went to where the sun rose and snared it. Māui beat it with his grandmother's jawbone until it agreed to travel more slowly. In Hawaiian tradition, a similar feat happens on Haleakalā, 'house of the sun', on Maui.

In another story, Māui put out the village fires and visited the fire goddess Mahuika, who kept fire in her fingernails. He tricked her into giving up nail after nail until one was left. She threw it at him, setting the land ablaze. Māui called on rain, and the last sparks escaped into certain trees, such as the kaikōmako. That is why rubbing sticks of those woods together makes fire.

sections.key: Māui's bid to win immortality for humans fails, and the story asks listeners to accept mortality.
sections.b:
Māui's final adventure is his most daring. He wanted to defeat death itself, so that people could live forever. Death was personified by Hine nui te pō, the great woman of the night, a guardian of the underworld.

Māui planned to crawl through her body while she slept, which would reverse the course of death. He took birds with him and warned them to keep quiet. But as he crawled, the sight was so comical that a little fantail, the pīwakawaka, burst into laughter. Hine nui te pō woke and crushed Māui, and so all people remain mortal.

Like Gilgamesh, the hero fails to escape death, and the story asks listeners to accept mortality as part of life.

sections.key: Polynesian myths are living culture, tied to Māori genealogy, the new year of Matariki and debates about how they are portrayed.
sections.b:
These stories are not museum pieces. Many Māori trace their whakapapa, or genealogy, back through gods and ancestors, so myths and family history are deeply connected. Māori creation traditions describe the sky father Ranginui and earth mother Papatūānuku, pushed apart by their son Tāne to let light into the world.

Matariki, the Māori new year marked by the rising of the Pleiades star cluster, became a New Zealand public holiday in 2022. Māui reached a global audience in Disney's 2016 film Moana. Many people enjoyed it, while some Pacific voices criticised the way Māui was portrayed and argued that sacred figures should be depicted with care. That debate shows how much these stories still matter to the people who own them.

quiz.q: What pattern do Māui's stories share?
o: An underestimated outsider proves himself
A king defeats a rival island
A farmer is rewarded for patience
A priest is tested by the gods
quiz.e: Māui begins as an overlooked outsider, so his triumphs are all the sweeter.

quiz.q: How does the story explain the North Island's mountains and valleys?
o: A volcano shaped the fish when it landed
The fish was dragged across the sea floor
The hook tore deep gashes into the land
His brothers hacked at the fish too soon
quiz.e: The brothers cut into the great fish before it settled, creating its mountains and valleys.

quiz.q: Why can people make fire by rubbing sticks of certain woods?
o: The last sparks hid in certain trees
The sun gave fire to the forest
Māui buried fire beneath the trees
Rain trapped fire in the soil
quiz.e: When Māui called rain to quench the flames, the final sparks hid in trees such as the kaikōmako.

quiz.q: What does Māui's failure to defeat death ask listeners to do?
o: Look harder for a way to cheat death
Avoid trying to trick the gods
Accept mortality as part of life
Treat the night with greater fear
quiz.e: Like Gilgamesh, Māui cannot escape death, and the story invites acceptance of it.

quiz.q: Why are Māori myths described as living culture?
o: They are mainly kept in written archives
They are performed only for visitors
They have been replaced by newer tales
They link to Māori genealogy and identity
quiz.e: Myth and family history are connected, so the stories remain part of identity today.

LESSONS.push: He fished up an island and slowed the sun. How did a trickster end up mortal?

LESSONS.title: Your skin: the organ you wear
LESSONS.hook: It is waterproof, self-repairing, temperature-controlled and covered in sensors, and you are wearing it right now. Meet the most underrated organ you have.

sections.key: Skin is your largest organ, covering about two square metres and packed with touch sensors, especially in the fingertips.
sections.b:
Lay an adult's skin flat and it would cover roughly two square metres, about the area of a single bed, and weigh several kilograms. It is the body's largest organ. It keeps water in and germs out, shields you from sunlight, helps control temperature, makes vitamin D and heals itself after cuts.

It is also a sensor. Specialised nerve endings respond to light touch, vibration, pressure, stretching, heat, cold and damage. They are not spread evenly. Fingertips, lips and tongue are packed with receptors, while your back has far fewer, which is why it is hard to tell whether one or two pencil points are pressing on it. Fingerprint ridges form before birth and help with grip and fine texture. Even identical twins have different fingerprints, because small variations in the womb shape the ridges.

sections.key: The epidermis is a thin barrier of dead, keratin-filled cells that is replaced roughly monthly.
sections.b:
Skin has three layers. The epidermis is thin, but it faces the world. Its top is flattened dead cells packed with tough keratin, forming a waterproof, germ-resistant barrier. Beneath it, the dermis is woven from collagen and elastin fibres that give strength and stretch, and holds blood vessels, nerve endings, hair roots and sweat glands. The fat layer below cushions you, stores energy and holds in heat. Eyelid skin is delicate, while the soles of your feet are thick.

At the base of the epidermis, cells divide constantly and are pushed upwards, filling with keratin and dying on the way. The journey takes roughly a month, so you grow a new outer skin many times a year. A popular claim says most household dust is dead skin, but much indoor dust comes from outside.

sections.key: Melanin gives skin its colour and some protection from ultraviolet light, and a tan is a sign of damage.
sections.b:
Cells called melanocytes at the bottom of the epidermis make a pigment called melanin. People of all skin tones have broadly similar numbers of melanocytes. What differs is how much melanin they make and what type. More melanin, especially the darker form, gives deeper skin tones and stronger natural protection against ultraviolet radiation.

When skin is exposed to the sun, melanocytes ramp up production. That is a tan: a sign skin has been damaged and is trying to defend itself. Scientists think skin colour varies so much because our ancestors lived under very different levels of sunlight, balancing protection from UV against the need to make vitamin D. In a high-UV country like Australia, sun protection matters for everyone.

sections.key: Skin cools you by sweating and by widening blood vessels, and goosebumps are a leftover from furrier ancestors.
sections.b:
On a hot Brisbane afternoon, your skin becomes a cooling system. Millions of sweat glands release watery sweat, and as it evaporates it carries heat away. Blood vessels near the surface widen, so warm blood sends heat out, which is why your face flushes. In the cold the reverse happens: vessels narrow to keep warmth near your core.

A second type of sweat gland, found mainly in the armpits and groin, releases a thicker sweat. It is odourless at first, and the smell comes from skin bacteria breaking it down.

Goosebumps are made by tiny muscles that pull hairs upright. In furry animals this traps insulating air or makes them look bigger. In us, it is mostly a curious leftover.

sections.key: Much of what looks like ageing skin is sun damage, so sun protection is the most useful habit.
sections.b:
As we age, skin makes less collagen and elastin, grows thinner and holds less moisture, which is why wrinkles and sagging appear. But much of what people think of as ageing skin is actually sun damage. Compare the skin on someone's forearm with the inner upper arm and the difference can be striking.

Australia has some of the highest rates of skin cancer in the world, so sun protection is the single most useful habit: shade, clothing, a broad-brimmed hat, sunglasses and sunscreen, especially when the UV index is 3 or above. Getting to know your own skin and checking for new or changing spots is also worthwhile. This is general information, not medical advice, so for any concern see a doctor or visit healthdirect.

quiz.q: Why is it hard to tell whether one or two pencil points are touching your back?
o: The back has far fewer touch receptors
Back skin contains no nerve endings
The brain ignores signals from the back
Pencil points are too blunt to feel
quiz.e: Receptors are unevenly spread: fingertips, lips and tongue are packed with them, while the back has far fewer.

quiz.q: Why is the surface of your skin such an effective barrier?
o: It is a living layer of fat cells
It is dead cells filled with keratin
It is a thick layer of collagen
It is shed and replaced daily
quiz.e: Flattened dead cells filled with keratin form a waterproof, germ-resistant barrier that is renewed about monthly.

quiz.q: What is a tan?
o: More melanin made in response to sun damage
The skin storing extra vitamin D for later
New skin cells forming faster than usual
Dead skin cells darkening at the surface
quiz.e: A tan is a defence response, a sign that UV has damaged the skin.

quiz.q: How does sweat cool your body?
o: Salt in sweat absorbs heat
Sweat glands remove heat from blood directly
As sweat evaporates, it carries heat away
Sweat blocks warmth from the sun
quiz.e: Evaporation takes heat from the skin, while widened blood vessels bring warm blood close to the surface.

quiz.q: Much of what people call ageing skin is actually caused by what?
o: Dry air
Washing too often
Sun damage
Poor diet alone
quiz.e: Sun damage drives many visible signs of ageing, which is why sun protection is the most useful habit.

LESSONS.push: It weighs several kilograms and replaces itself every month. Meet your biggest organ.

LESSONS.title: How breathing works
LESSONS.hook: You will take around 20,000 breaths today without thinking about any of them. Here is the clever machinery that keeps the air moving.

sections.key: Breathing runs on autopilot via the brainstem, and the diaphragm does the work of drawing air in.
sections.b:
You breathe roughly 12 to 20 times a minute, almost none of them by choice. Breathing runs automatically yet can be taken over by will: you can hold your breath, sing a long note or blow out candles. When you stop paying attention, the brainstem quietly takes control back. Every breath delivers oxygen your cells need to release energy from food, and removes the carbon dioxide they produce.

Lungs have no muscles of their own. The diaphragm, a dome of muscle beneath them, contracts and flattens, while rib muscles lift the ribcage. The chest enlarges, pressure inside drops below the air outside, and air flows in. Breathing out at rest is mostly passive: the diaphragm relaxes and elastic lungs spring back. In hard exercise, neck, chest and belly muscles help. Hiccups are sudden spasms of the diaphragm.

sections.key: Branching airways end in hundreds of millions of air sacs, where oxygen enters the blood and carbon dioxide leaves it.
sections.b:
Air passes the voice box, travels down the windpipe and splits into two main branches, one per lung, which divide again and again like an upside-down tree. The smallest twigs end in tiny air sacs called alveoli. There are hundreds of millions, giving the lungs an enormous surface. The right lung has three lobes, the left only two, leaving room for the heart. The nose warms, moistens and filters the air.

Each alveolus is wrapped in hair-thin capillaries. Oxygen crosses into the blood and latches onto haemoglobin in red blood cells, while carbon dioxide moves out. Inhaled air is about 21 per cent oxygen, and exhaled air still has roughly 16 per cent. That leftover oxygen is one reason rescue breaths during CPR can help someone who is not breathing.

sections.key: The urge to breathe comes mainly from rising carbon dioxide, not falling oxygen, which makes hyperventilating before swimming underwater dangerous.
sections.b:
Hold your breath and the urge to breathe becomes overwhelming. Surprisingly, that urge is not mainly caused by running low on oxygen. Sensors in the brainstem and major arteries track carbon dioxide in the blood, which also changes its acidity. When carbon dioxide rises, they push you hard to breathe.

This carries a safety lesson. Some swimmers and divers hyperventilate before going underwater, blowing off carbon dioxide so they can stay down longer. The urge to breathe is delayed, but oxygen keeps falling, and a person can black out without warning. This is a known cause of drowning, even among strong swimmers, so hyperventilating before breath-holding in the water is dangerous and should be avoided.

sections.key: Mucus and tiny beating hairs sweep dust and germs out of your airways, and smoke damages that defence.
sections.b:
Every day you breathe in dust, pollen, smoke particles and microbes. Your airways are lined with sticky mucus that traps particles, and with millions of microscopic hair-like structures called cilia. The cilia beat in coordinated waves, moving mucus up to the throat, where it is usually swallowed without you noticing. Scientists sometimes call this the mucociliary escalator.

Coughing and sneezing are the emergency backups, blasting out irritants at high speed. Cigarette smoke damages and slows the cilia, which is one reason people who smoke often develop a persistent cough: the body must cough up what the escalator can no longer clear. Bushfire smoke is also hard on airways, so on smoky days it makes sense to follow local health advice.

sections.key: Slow, steady breathing can calm you, and regular exercise trains the muscles that move and use oxygen.
sections.b:
Breathing is closely tied to the nervous system. When you are anxious, breathing tends to become fast and shallow, and when you are relaxed it slows down. The link works in both directions, so deliberately slowing your breath, especially with a long, unhurried breath out, can help many people feel calmer.

Exercise does not grow new lung tissue, but it trains the breathing muscles, the heart and the muscles that use oxygen, so everyday activity feels easier. Lung function naturally declines a little with age, and smoking speeds that decline sharply. Breathlessness that is new, sudden or worsening deserves attention. This lesson is general information rather than medical advice, so if you are worried about your breathing, talk to a doctor or check healthdirect, and in an emergency call triple zero.

quiz.q: What happens when the diaphragm contracts?
o: It pushes up and squeezes the lungs
It flattens and enlarges the chest
It closes the windpipe to hold air
It pumps oxygen into the blood
quiz.e: Flattening lowers the pressure in the chest, so air flows in.

quiz.q: Why does the left lung have fewer lobes than the right?
o: It is damaged at birth
It is used only during exercise
It holds the voice box
It leaves room for the heart
quiz.e: The left lung has two lobes rather than three, making space for the heart.

quiz.q: Why is hyperventilating before breath-hold swimming dangerous?
o: It fills the lungs with water
It postpones the urge to breathe
It raises carbon dioxide too high
It makes the heart stop suddenly
quiz.e: Blowing off carbon dioxide postpones the warning signal, so a swimmer can black out without feeling the need to surface.

quiz.q: What job do the cilia in your airways do?
o: Absorb oxygen into the blood
Produce the sound of your voice
Sweep mucus up towards the throat
Warm the air to body temperature
quiz.e: Cilia beat in waves to move mucus and trapped particles out of the airways, and smoke slows them.

quiz.q: How can deliberately slowing your breath help?
o: It can help many people feel calmer
It grows new lung tissue
It removes the need for exercise
It cures breathlessness
quiz.e: Breathing and the nervous system influence each other, so a long, unhurried breath out can calm you.

LESSONS.push: You breathe about 20,000 times a day. The urge to breathe isn't what you think.

LESSONS.title: Hormones: the body's chemical messengers
LESSONS.hook: A tiny drop of the right chemical can make your heart race, your stomach growl or a child grow taller. Hormones are the body's slow but powerful postal service.

sections.key: Hormones are chemicals released into the blood that change how distant cells behave.
sections.b:
Nearly step on a snake on a bush track and your heart pounds within seconds. Nerves start that response almost instantly, but hormones help drive it. A hormone is a chemical messenger made in one place and carried in the blood to cells elsewhere, where it changes what they do. Only cells with the matching receptor respond, like a letter only the right key can open.

Nerves are like phone calls: fast, targeted and brief. Hormones are more like a broadcast: slower to arrive, but able to reach the whole body and keep working for minutes, hours or even years. The word comes from a Greek term meaning to set in motion, popularised by physiologist Ernest Starling in 1905.

sections.key: Most hormone levels are held steady by negative feedback, directed by the hypothalamus and pituitary.
sections.b:
Glands that release hormones straight into the blood make up the endocrine system: the thyroid, the adrenal glands on top of the kidneys, the pancreas, and the ovaries or testes. Fat tissue, the gut, the heart and the kidneys release some too. In the brain, the hypothalamus monitors the body and signals the pea-sized pituitary, often called the master gland, which tells other glands to speed up or slow down.

Levels stay steady through negative feedback, like a thermostat. When thyroid hormone falls, the signals urge the thyroid to make more. When it rises enough, they ease off. The thyroid needs iodine, and since 2009 iodised salt has been required in most commercial Australian bread to top up intake.

sections.key: Adrenaline gives an instant boost, while cortisol manages longer-term energy and follows a daily rhythm.
sections.b:
When you get a fright, your adrenal glands release adrenaline, also called epinephrine. It quickens the heart, widens the airways, sends more blood to the muscles and releases stored fuel, preparing you to fight or flee.

The adrenals also make cortisol, often labelled the stress hormone, though that undersells it. Cortisol helps regulate blood sugar, blood pressure, inflammation and energy use. It follows a daily rhythm too, typically rising in the early morning to help you wake and falling towards night. Short bursts of these hormones are normal and useful. Problems are more likely when stress is intense and long-lasting, which is one reason sleep, exercise and rest matter for the whole body.

sections.key: Insulin controls blood sugar, and its discovery in Canada in the early 1920s transformed type 1 diabetes.
sections.b:
After a meal, sugar enters your blood. The pancreas releases insulin, which signals cells in the muscles, liver and fat to take that sugar in, bringing blood levels back down. Between meals, another hormone, glucagon, does the reverse.

In type 1 diabetes, the immune system destroys the cells that make insulin. Before the 1920s, that meant a grim and usually short life. In 1921, Frederick Banting and Charles Best, working with colleagues at the University of Toronto, extracted insulin. In early 1922 a teenage boy, Leonard Thompson, became the first person treated with it, and his condition improved. Within a few years insulin was being produced on a large scale, saving countless lives.

sections.key: Ghrelin, leptin, melatonin and oxytocin shape appetite, sleep and connection, and hormone problems need a GP.
sections.b:
Ghrelin, made mainly in the stomach, tends to rise before meals and stirs up hunger. Leptin, released by fat tissue, helps tell the brain how much energy is stored. Melatonin, from the pineal gland, rises as light fades and signals that it is time for sleep, which is why bright screens late at night can make it harder to drift off.

Oxytocin plays key roles in childbirth and breastfeeding and is involved in bonding. It is nicknamed the love hormone, but its effects are complex and depend on context, so the nickname oversimplifies. Hormone problems can cause vague symptoms such as tiredness or weight changes. This is general information, not medical advice. A GP can arrange tests, and healthdirect is a reliable starting point.

quiz.q: How do hormones mainly reach their target cells?
o: Along nerve fibres
Carried in the bloodstream
Through the air we breathe
Through the lymph nodes only
quiz.e: Hormones are released into the blood and act on cells that have the matching receptor.

quiz.q: How does negative feedback keep thyroid hormone steady?
o: Rising levels turn off the signal for more
Low levels shut the thyroid down completely
The adrenal glands take over production
Levels rise until the thyroid is exhausted
quiz.e: Like a thermostat, low levels prompt more hormone and high enough levels turn the signals down.

quiz.q: What is cortisol's role beyond being a stress hormone?
o: It makes the heart race within seconds
It helps manage energy over a daily rhythm
It only works during a sudden fright
It tells the thyroid to release more hormone
quiz.e: Cortisol manages longer-term energy and typically rises in the morning and falls towards night.

quiz.q: What does insulin do after a meal?
o: Releases stored sugar into the blood
Makes the stomach feel empty and hungry
Signals cells to take in blood sugar
Raises the heart rate and blood pressure
quiz.e: Insulin helps cells absorb sugar, bringing blood sugar levels back down.

quiz.q: Why can bright screens late at night make it harder to sleep?
o: They raise ghrelin and cause hunger
They make the pineal gland release adrenaline
They stop leptin signalling the brain
They delay the evening rise of melatonin
quiz.e: Melatonin rises as light fades, so bright light late at night can hold back the signal for sleep.

LESSONS.push: A drop of the right chemical can make a child grow. How does it find its target?

LESSONS.title: The liver: your chemical factory
LESSONS.hook: Quietly tucked under your ribs is an organ that stores fuel, builds proteins, breaks down toxins and can even regrow itself. Meet the liver.

sections.key: The liver can regenerate after part is removed, which makes living donor transplants possible.
sections.b:
In Greek myth, Prometheus stole fire from the gods and was chained to a rock. Each day an eagle ate his liver, and each night it grew back. Whether or not the storytellers knew it, they picked exactly the right organ.

The liver is famous among doctors for its ability to regenerate. If a large part is removed, the remaining tissue can grow and restore much of the organ's size and function within weeks to months. That is what makes living donor liver transplants possible: part of a healthy adult's liver can be given to someone else, and both pieces can grow. Few organs can do anything like it.

sections.key: The liver receives blood straight from the gut and stores sugar as glycogen to keep blood sugar steady.
sections.b:
Your liver sits in the upper right of your abdomen, behind the lower ribs. At around one and a half kilograms, it is the largest solid organ inside the body. Most of its blood arrives through the hepatic portal vein, straight from the stomach and intestines, so nearly everything you absorb passes through the liver first.

After a meal, with help from insulin, the liver links surplus sugar into glycogen for storage. Hours later, as blood sugar dips, it breaks glycogen down and releases sugar, keeping your brain fuelled overnight. In a long fast it can make new sugar. It also packages fats and makes cholesterol. It is both pantry and kitchen.

sections.key: The liver makes clotting proteins and bile, and recycles old red blood cells into bilirubin.
sections.b:
The liver makes most of the clotting factors that stop bleeding after a cut. It also produces albumin, the most abundant blood protein, which keeps fluid inside blood vessels. So a struggling liver can cause easy bruising or swollen legs. Doctors check liver function with a blood test.

It also makes bile, a greenish-yellow fluid stored in the gallbladder. Bile breaks fat into tiny droplets, a bit like washing-up liquid on a greasy pan, so enzymes can digest it. Bile carries away bilirubin, a yellow substance made from old red blood cells. Gut bacteria change it further, giving poo its brown colour. If bilirubin builds up in the blood, skin and eyes turn yellow, a sign called jaundice.

sections.key: The liver changes harmful substances, including ammonia and alcohol, into forms the body can remove.
sections.b:
Breaking down proteins releases ammonia, which is harmful to the brain at high levels. The liver converts it into urea, a much safer substance that the kidneys flush out in urine. The liver also alters many medicines, hormones and foreign substances so they are easier to excrete.

Alcohol is a major example. The liver breaks it down at a fairly fixed pace, often estimated at around one standard drink an hour, and nothing such as coffee or a cold shower speeds it up. It is also why detox teas and cleanses are unnecessary for healthy people: the liver and kidneys already do this job continuously, and do it well.

sections.key: Liver problems often cause no symptoms early on, so prevention and checks matter.
sections.b:
The liver has few pain nerves and plenty of spare capacity, so it can be quite damaged before you feel unwell. Fat build-up in the liver is now common, often linked with being overweight, type 2 diabetes and inactivity. It frequently causes no symptoms at first and can often improve with changes to diet, activity and weight.

Heavy drinking and viral hepatitis are other major causes of damage. Australia offers vaccination against hepatitis B, and effective treatments now exist for hepatitis C. This is general information, not medical advice. If you have concerns about your liver, your GP can arrange simple blood tests, and healthdirect offers reliable background.

quiz.q: Why are living donor liver transplants possible?
o: Humans are born with two livers
The liver is not essential for life
Liver tissue is never rejected by the body
The liver can regrow after part is removed
quiz.e: Part of a healthy liver can be donated and both portions can regrow.

quiz.q: Why does the liver store sugar as glycogen?
o: It can release the sugar again between meals
It turns the sugar into bile for digestion
It sends sugar straight to the kidneys
It keeps sugar away from the brain and muscles
quiz.e: The liver releases sugar from glycogen when blood sugar dips, fuelling the brain overnight.

quiz.q: What gives poo its typical brown colour?
o: Undigested fibre from food
Bilirubin, changed by gut bacteria
Stomach acid mixing with food
Iron left over from red meat
quiz.e: Bilirubin from recycled red blood cells leaves in bile and is changed by gut bacteria.

quiz.q: What does the liver convert toxic ammonia into?
o: Glycogen
Cholesterol
Urea
Albumin
quiz.e: Ammonia becomes urea, which the kidneys remove in urine.

quiz.q: Why can liver damage go unnoticed for a long time?
o: It only ever affects the skin and eyes
It has few pain nerves and spare capacity
Doctors cannot test for liver damage
Damage to it always heals completely
quiz.e: Early liver problems often cause no symptoms, so checks and prevention matter.

LESSONS.push: An ancient Greek myth hid a surprisingly accurate fact about one organ.

LESSONS.title: Your kidneys: the body's master filters
LESSONS.hook: Two fist-sized organs filter your entire blood supply many times a day, balancing water, salt and acid with exquisite precision.

sections.key: Your kidneys filter around 180 litres of fluid a day but make only about one and a half litres of urine.
sections.b:
Each kidney is about the size of a fist, yet together they receive about a fifth of the blood your heart pumps. Every day they filter something like 180 litres of fluid, enough to fill a large bathtub. A typical adult makes only around one and a half litres of urine, so the kidneys reclaim about 99 per cent of it.

The working unit is the nephron, and each kidney has roughly a million. In its glomerulus, a tangle of capillaries, blood pressure pushes water and small molecules through a fine filter while blood cells and most proteins stay behind. Along the tube that follows, cells take back sugar, salts, amino acids and most of the water, and add extra wastes. What remains becomes urine.

sections.key: A hormone from the brain tells the kidneys how much water to save, which is why urine colour changes.
sections.b:
Work outdoors in the Pilbara all day without drinking enough and your urine turns darker and smaller in volume. Drink plenty on a cool day and it turns pale and plentiful. The kidneys are following instructions.

When your blood becomes too concentrated, sensors in the brain trigger the release of antidiuretic hormone, also called vasopressin, from the pituitary gland. It makes the final parts of the nephron more permeable to water, so more is reabsorbed and urine becomes concentrated. Alcohol suppresses this hormone, partly why drinking makes people urinate more and can leave them dehydrated. Urine colour is a rough guide to hydration, though some vitamins, foods and medicines change it too.

sections.key: The kidneys help set blood pressure, balance acidity, signal red blood cell production and activate vitamin D.
sections.b:
Sodium and potassium must stay in a narrow range for nerves and muscles, including the heart. The kidneys fine-tune both. When blood flow to them falls, they release renin, starting a chain of reactions that narrows blood vessels and makes the body retain salt and water. More fluid means higher pressure, and several common blood pressure medicines act on this pathway.

The kidneys also remove acid and hold onto bicarbonate, a natural buffer. When their oxygen falls, as at altitude or after blood loss, they release erythropoietin (EPO), telling the bone marrow to make more red blood cells. EPO is a vital medicine, but was notoriously misused as a doping drug. They also complete the activation of vitamin D, needed to absorb calcium for healthy bones.

sections.key: Kidney stones form when minerals crystallise in urine, and chronic kidney disease often shows no early symptoms.
sections.b:
Kidney stones are hard deposits that form when minerals in urine, most often calcium combined with oxalate, become concentrated enough to crystallise. A small stone may pass unnoticed, but one moving down the narrow tube to the bladder can cause sudden, severe pain that many rank among the worst they have experienced. Dehydration is a common contributor, which matters in hot parts of Australia.

Long-term diabetes and high blood pressure are two leading causes of chronic kidney disease. Because the kidneys have so much reserve, it often causes no symptoms until a lot of function is lost. Simple blood and urine tests can pick it up early, when steps to protect the kidneys work best.

sections.key: People can live well with one kidney, and dialysis or a transplant can replace failed kidneys.
sections.b:
With so much spare capacity, most people can live a normal life with just one kidney, which is why living kidney donation is possible. The first successful kidney transplant took place in Boston in 1954, between identical twins, which avoided the problem of rejection.

When both kidneys fail, a person needs dialysis, where a machine or the lining of the abdomen filters the blood, or a transplant. In Australia you can register as an organ and tissue donor through the Australian Organ Donor Register, run by Services Australia, and it is important to talk about your wishes with family. This is general information, not medical advice. For kidney health questions, see your GP or healthdirect.

quiz.q: Roughly what share of the filtered fluid do the kidneys take back?
o: About 10 per cent
About half
About 75 per cent
About 99 per cent
quiz.e: Of roughly 180 litres filtered daily, only about one and a half litres leaves as urine.

o: It suppresses antidiuretic hormone
It blocks the filters in the kidneys
It stops the bladder from emptying
It makes the kidneys hold onto more salt
quiz.e: With less antidiuretic hormone, the kidneys save less water and more urine is produced.

quiz.q: What does erythropoietin (EPO) from the kidneys do?
o: Dissolves kidney stones in urine

Activates insulin in the pancreas

quiz.e: When oxygen in the kidney is low, EPO signals the bone marrow to boost red blood cell production.

quiz.q: Why can chronic kidney disease go unnoticed for years?
o: It only affects the bladder and ureters
It is painless because stones are absent
The kidneys have so much spare capacity
Blood and urine tests cannot detect it
quiz.e: Large spare capacity hides early damage, so simple blood and urine tests help catch it sooner.

quiz.q: Why was the first successful kidney transplant, in 1954, between identical twins?
o: Twins have unusually large kidneys
It avoided the problem of rejection
The law required relatives to donate

quiz.e: Identical twins are genetically matched, so the recipient's immune system did not reject the organ.

LESSONS.push: They filter a bathtub of fluid daily, then take almost all of it back.

LESSONS.title: Your microbiome: the trillions living inside you
LESSONS.hook: You are not just you. Your gut is home to a vast, bustling community of microbes that digest food you cannot, train your immune system and may even chat with your brain.

sections.key: Your gut hosts trillions of microbes, and the old claim that they outnumber your cells ten to one is wrong.
sections.b:
Your large intestine is like a rainforest: warm, dark and teeming. It hosts trillions of microorganisms, mostly bacteria, along with archaea, fungi and viruses. Together they are the gut microbiota, and their combined genes are the microbiome. Hundreds of species may live in one gut, in a mix so individual it is compared to a fingerprint. Most are long-term residents that are helpful or harmless, weighing perhaps a couple of hundred grams, about a mango.

For decades, people repeated that microbes outnumber human cells ten to one, based on a rough 1970s estimate. In 2016, researchers recalculated it as closer to one to one, with tens of trillions of each. Catchy statistics can outlive their evidence.

sections.key: Gut microbes ferment fibre that human enzymes cannot digest, producing useful short-chain fatty acids.
sections.b:
We lack the enzymes to break down many types of dietary fibre, such as those in legumes, oats, wholegrains, vegetables and fruit. That fibre reaches the large intestine largely intact, where microbes ferment it. This produces gases, which explains the noisy consequences of a big serve of baked beans, and short-chain fatty acids.

One of these, butyrate, is a key fuel for the cells lining the colon. Short-chain fatty acids also appear to influence inflammation and metabolism elsewhere in the body. Gut bacteria help make some vitamins too, including vitamin K. In a real sense, eating fibre is a way of feeding the microbes that help feed you.

sections.key: The microbiome starts forming at birth, helps train the immune system and crowds out harmful invaders.
sections.b:
A baby's gut is thought to be largely free of microbes before birth. Colonisation begins during and after delivery, from the mother, the environment and early feeding. Vaginal and caesarean births tend to start with different communities, though the differences seem to narrow over time. Breast milk contains sugars the baby cannot digest but certain beneficial bacteria can.

Much of the body's immune tissue sits along the gut. Germ-free laboratory animals develop abnormal immune systems, suggesting microbes help train it. A diverse community also provides colonisation resistance: it takes up space and resources, making it harder for harmful bacteria to settle in. The microbiome becomes adult-like within a few years, then keeps responding to diet, illness, travel, medicines and age.

sections.key: Faecal transplants can cure one stubborn infection, while gut-brain research is promising but early.
sections.b:
The most dramatic proof that gut microbes matter is faecal microbiota transplantation. It sounds unappealing, but for people with recurring Clostridioides difficile infections, often triggered by antibiotics, screened stool from a healthy donor can restore a healthy community and has proved remarkably effective.

Researchers are also exploring the gut-brain axis, the network of nerves, hormones and immune signals linking gut and brain. Animal studies suggest microbes can influence behaviour and mood, and human studies have found associations with various conditions. But association is not cause, and much of this work is early. Be wary of headlines claiming a particular bacterium causes or cures complex conditions. The science is fascinating, but still unfolding.

sections.key: A varied diet rich in plant fibre is the best-supported way to support a diverse microbiome.
sections.b:
The best-supported advice is not exotic. Eat a wide variety of plant foods, such as vegetables, fruit, legumes, wholegrains, nuts and seeds, to provide the range of fibres that different microbes thrive on. Fermented foods such as yoghurt, kefir and kimchi contain live microbes and may increase diversity, though more research is needed. Probiotic supplements vary greatly in evidence depending on the strain and condition, and many claims run ahead of the science.

Antibiotics are life-saving when needed, but they can kill helpful bacteria and sometimes cause diarrhoea, so use them only when appropriate. This is general information, not medical advice. Talk with your GP or an accredited practising dietitian about specific gut concerns.

quiz.e: The famous ten to one figure was revised to roughly one to one, with tens of trillions of each.

quiz.e: Fermenting fibre yields short-chain fatty acids, including butyrate, a key fuel for colon cells.

quiz.q: What does colonisation resistance mean?

quiz.e: A healthy microbial community occupies space and resources, crowding out invaders.

Repeat C. difficile gut infections
Short-sightedness in children

quiz.e: Screened donor stool can restore a healthy gut community and clear recurring C. difficile.

o: Taking any probiotic supplement
Avoiding all fibre

quiz.e: A range of plant fibres feeds different microbes, whereas probiotic claims often run ahead of the science.

LESSONS.push: You may carry about a mango's weight of microbes. The famous count of them is wrong.

LESSONS.title: Why we age: the biology of growing old
LESSONS.hook: Some tortoises seem barely to age, while mice are old at three. What is actually happening inside our cells as the years go by, and why did evolution let it happen at all?

sections.key: Ageing is a build-up of damage and declining repair, which evolution does little to prevent.
sections.b:
The body is not a car slowly wearing out. It constantly repairs itself: cells are replaced, proteins recycled and damaged DNA fixed, often thousands of times a day in a single cell. Ageing seems to happen as damage accumulates faster than repair can keep up, and as the repair systems themselves weaken. Ageing is also the biggest single risk factor for heart disease, many cancers and dementia.

Why hasn't evolution removed it? Biologists including Peter Medawar and George Williams noted that most wild animals die young, so natural selection is strong in youth and weak in later life. A gene harming only in old age is barely selected against, and one that helps us grow fast and breed early may be favoured despite later damage, an idea called antagonistic pleiotropy.

sections.key: Telomeres, the protective caps on chromosomes, tend to shorten as cells divide.
sections.b:
Telomeres are repeating stretches of DNA at the ends of chromosomes, often compared to the plastic tips on shoelaces. Each time most cells divide, the telomeres shorten, because the copying machinery cannot fully copy the very ends. When they become too short, the cell typically stops dividing or dies.

In the 1960s, Leonard Hayflick showed that normal human cells grown in the laboratory divide only a limited number of times, now called the Hayflick limit. An enzyme called telomerase can rebuild telomeres and is active in some cells, such as certain stem cells. Many cancer cells switch it on, which helps them divide indefinitely. That link shows why simply boosting telomerase is not a safe anti-ageing shortcut.

sections.key: Senescent cells stop dividing but linger, releasing inflammatory signals that can harm nearby tissue.
sections.b:
When cells are damaged or their telomeres run short, some enter a state called senescence. They stop dividing, which helps prevent damaged cells turning cancerous. But they do not always die. They can linger and release inflammatory chemicals that disturb surrounding tissue, earning the nickname zombie cells.

Normally the immune system clears them, but with age they seem to build up in many tissues. The low-grade chronic inflammation that tends to rise with age, called inflammaging, may be partly driven by them. In mice, clearing senescent cells has improved some measures of health. Drugs designed to do this, called senolytics, are being tested in people, but it is too soon to know whether they will be safe and useful.

sections.key: Researchers group the causes of ageing into interconnected hallmarks, so no single pill can halt it.
sections.b:
In 2013, scientists proposed a widely cited framework of nine hallmarks of ageing, later expanded. They include DNA damage, shortening telomeres, changes in how genes are switched on and off, faulty protein folding, faltering mitochondria (the cells' energy producers), senescent cells, exhausted stem cells and altered communication between cells. Chronic inflammation is often added too.

Crucially, these processes are interlinked. Damaged mitochondria can produce harmful molecules that damage DNA, which can push cells into senescence, which drives inflammation, which harms stem cells. Ageing looks less like a single cause and more like a web of problems feeding one another. That complexity is one reason no single pill or treatment has been shown to halt human ageing.

sections.key: Ageing can be slowed in some animals, but for people only well-established habits are proven to help.
sections.b:
The naked mole-rat, a small burrowing rodent, can live over 30 years, many times longer than a mouse, with few signs of ageing for most of its life. Greenland sharks are estimated to live for centuries, and some tortoises have passed a hundred years. In the laboratory, genetic changes, certain drugs and reduced calorie intake without malnutrition have extended the lifespan of worms, flies and mice. Translating this to people is harder: trials take decades, and mouse results often fail to carry over.

No supplement has been proven to slow human ageing. The evidence supports regular activity including strength training, not smoking, limited alcohol, a plant-rich diet, sleep, sun protection and social connection. This is general information, not medical advice; ask your GP about health checks.

quiz.q: Why has evolution not eliminated ageing?
o: Ageing helps species evolve faster
Old animals are needed to teach the young
Natural selection is weak late in life
Evolution has not had enough time
quiz.e: Because most wild animals die young, genes with late harmful effects are poorly weeded out.

quiz.q: Why is boosting telomerase not a safe anti-ageing shortcut?
o: Telomerase shortens telomeres
Many cancer cells switch it on
It is only found in neurons
It stops all cell division
quiz.e: Telomerase rebuilds telomeres, but cancer cells exploit it to keep dividing.

quiz.q: Why are senescent cells nicknamed zombie cells?
o: They only appear in the body after death
They come back to life after dying
They linger and release inflammatory signals
They attack the brain and nerves
quiz.e: Senescent cells stop dividing yet persist, disturbing surrounding tissue with inflammatory chemicals.

quiz.q: What is the key idea behind the hallmarks of ageing?
o: Linked processes feed into each other
Ageing has one single main cause
Ageing can be stopped with one drug
Ageing affects only the skin
quiz.e: The hallmarks are interconnected, making ageing a web of problems rather than a single cause.

quiz.q: Why is it hard to test anti-ageing treatments in humans?
o: Ethics rules ban research on adults
There are no long-lived animals to compare
Human lives are long, so trials take decades
Ageing cannot be measured at all
quiz.e: Long human lifespans make trials slow, and mouse results often fail to translate.

LESSONS.push: Some animals barely age. What does that say about why we do?

LESSONS.title: The science of pain
LESSONS.hook: Pain feels like a simple signal from an injury, but it is really the brain's best guess about danger. That surprising idea changes how we understand hurt.

sections.key: Pain is produced by the brain and does not always match the amount of tissue damage.
sections.b:
A case reported in the British Medical Journal in 1995 describes a builder who jumped onto a 15 centimetre nail. It went straight through his boot and he was in agony, needing strong pain relief. When doctors removed the boot, the nail had passed between his toes without touching his foot. Other people suffer serious injuries in emergencies or sport and feel little at first.

Pain is not a direct readout of damage. It is something the brain produces to protect you from what it judges to be a threat. Nerve endings called nociceptors detect potential harm, such as intense pressure, heat, cold or chemicals from damaged tissue, and signal the spinal cord and brain. That detection, nociception, is not the same as pain.

sections.key: The brain weighs context, attention, expectations and emotions when deciding how much something hurts.
sections.b:
Warning signals do not simply switch pain on. Many brain regions weigh them against context, memories, attention, mood and expectations. That is why the same injury can feel very different in different situations. A paper cut on a stressful day may sting more than a scrape in an exciting footy match. Anxiety and fear tend to amplify pain, while distraction and feeling safe can reduce it.

Stub your toe and you often feel a sharp first jolt, then a duller throb, as faster and slower nerve fibres deliver their messages in turn. In phantom limb pain, people feel pain in an amputated limb because the brain's map of the body still includes it. All pain is real, whatever its source.

sections.key: The nervous system actively turns pain up or down, through spinal gates and natural opioid-like chemicals.
sections.b:
Bang your elbow and you rub it without thinking. In 1965, Ronald Melzack and Patrick Wall proposed gate control theory: circuits in the spinal cord act like a gate, letting more or fewer pain signals through. Touch and pressure signals can partly close it, which is why rubbing helps. The details have been revised, but the idea that the nervous system actively modulates pain remains influential.

In the 1970s, scientists found brain receptors for opium-derived drugs like morphine, because the body makes its own, including endorphins (endogenous plus morphine). They dampen pain during stress, injury and exercise and play a role in some placebo effects. Opioid medicines are powerful but can cause dependence, so Australia regulates them tightly.

sections.key: Chronic pain can persist after healing as the nervous system becomes more sensitive.
sections.b:
Acute pain is the short-term pain of an injury and usually fades as tissue heals. Chronic pain generally means pain lasting longer than about three months, and it is common. Australian health organisations estimate around one in five adults lives with it.

In many cases the nervous system itself has changed, becoming more sensitive so it produces pain more easily, a process called central sensitisation. The alarm system has become overprotective, sounding off even when the danger is small or gone. This does not mean the pain is imagined. Treating chronic pain often takes more than looking for ongoing damage, and may need to address the nervous system's sensitivity as well.

sections.key: Modern pain care often combines movement, education, sleep and psychological strategies with medicines.
sections.b:
Understanding pain as a protective output of the brain has changed how many people are treated. For persistent pain, care often combines several elements: graded physical activity that gradually builds confidence and capacity, good sleep, stress management, and pain education that explains how the nervous system works. Psychological therapies can help reduce fear and restore valued activities.

Medicines still have a place, but for many types of chronic pain, relying on them alone tends to work less well than a combined approach. Australian researchers have been prominent in pain education. This is general information, not medical advice. If you live with pain, talk to your GP. healthdirect and Painaustralia are helpful starting points.

quiz.e: The nail missed his foot entirely, yet he felt intense pain, showing pain is produced by the brain.

quiz.e: Pain depends on how the brain weighs the signal against context, so fear amplifies it and distraction can reduce it.

quiz.e: Touch and pressure signals can reduce pain-related signals passing through the spinal cord.

quiz.e: In central sensitisation the nervous system's alarm becomes overprotective, a common feature of chronic pain.

quiz.q: Why does modern care for persistent pain often combine several approaches?
o: Medicines alone often work less well
Medicines are never part of care
Pain is imagined and needs only reassurance
Rest alone cures most chronic pain
quiz.e: Movement, sleep, education and psychological strategies address the sensitive nervous system as well as the pain.

LESSONS.push: A nail passed through a boot and missed the foot, yet he screamed in pain.

LESSONS.title: The hidden psychology of prices
LESSONS.hook: Why does almost everything cost $9.99, and why does a menu include a dish nobody orders? Prices are quietly designed to steer your choices.

sections.key: Prices ending in 9 feel cheaper because we weigh the first digit most, and a high first price anchors our judgement.
sections.b:
A price of $4.99 is only one cent under $5, yet it feels like four dollars and something. This is the left-digit effect: we read left to right and give the first digit extra weight. Sales data show prices ending in 9 can lift demand, though it varies by product. Luxury shops often use round prices like $500 instead, because a price that looks discounted can make an expensive item feel cheap.

The first number you see also works as an anchor. A jacket marked Was $400, now $199 feels cheap whether or not anyone paid $400. In 1970s experiments, Tversky and Kahneman showed estimates were nudged by a number from a spun wheel. In Australia, was prices must be genuine, and the ACCC has acted against misleading ones.

sections.key: Adding an unattractive option can make another option look like a bargain.
sections.b:
Behavioural economist Dan Ariely described an old subscription offer from The Economist: web access for $59, print for $125, or print plus web for $125. Nobody sensible picks print alone when the bundle costs the same, so why include it? Because it makes the bundle look like a steal.

When Ariely tested the offer on students, most chose the bundle. When he removed the print-only option, far more chose the cheaper web-only deal. This is called the decoy effect. You will see it in cinema popcorn sizes, coffee cups and phone plans, where a middle option is priced to push you towards the largest one.

sections.key: Many businesses charge different customers different prices for almost the same product.
sections.b:
Two people sitting side by side on a plane may have paid wildly different fares. Economists call this price discrimination, and it is often legal. The aim is to charge each customer close to what they are willing to pay.

Airlines do it with booking dates and flexible tickets. Cinemas do it with cheap Tuesday sessions. Software companies offer student discounts, because students have little money now but may become loyal paying customers. Coupons and loyalty apps work similarly: people who collect points or hunt for codes tend to be more price sensitive, so they get a lower price while everyone else pays full price. The product barely changes, but the price fits the customer.

sections.key: Free feels different from cheap, and small regular payments hurt less than one large one.
sections.b:
Zero is special. Shoppers often choose a free item over a better deal that costs a little, because free removes any sense of risk or loss. Freemium apps are free to download and earn money from the few users who pay for extras. Free shipping thresholds work too: if delivery is free over $50 and your cart is at $43, many people add something rather than pay a few dollars postage.

Paying also hurts a little, more with cash than cards and less still when money leaves automatically. That is why subscriptions have spread. $15 a month feels lighter than $180 a year, and inertia keeps people paying for services they rarely use. Review your bank statement every few months and cancel anything you would not sign up for again today.

sections.key: Knowing these techniques helps you compare the real cost of things.
sections.b:
None of these techniques are secret, and once you know them they lose some power. A useful defence is unit pricing. Large Australian supermarkets must display unit prices, such as the cost per 100 grams, which makes it easier to compare a big pack with a small one, or a brand with a home brand.

Another defence is to decide what something is worth to you before you see the price tag, so an anchor cannot do your thinking for you. The ACCC has also cracked down on drip pricing, where extra fees appear only at the end of a purchase. If a price seems misleading, the ACCC website explains your rights and how to report it.

quiz.q: What is the left-digit effect?

Giving the first digit extra weight
Rounding all prices up in your head
quiz.e: We read prices left to right, so $4.99 feels closer to $4 than to $5.

quiz.q: In The Economist example, what did the print-only option do?
o: It was the most popular choice
It acted as a decoy for the bundle

quiz.e: Nobody wanted print-only, but its presence pushed people towards the bundle.

quiz.e: Price discrimination fits the price to the customer, and discounts can build future loyalty.

quiz.q: Why does $15 a month feel lighter than $180 a year?
o: It costs less in total over the year

quiz.e: The total is identical, but small regular payments feel less painful and are easy to forget.

quiz.q: How does unit pricing help shoppers?

quiz.e: Unit prices like cost per 100 grams let you compare different pack sizes fairly.

LESSONS.push: Why does a menu include a dish that almost nobody orders?

LESSONS.title: Why we pay more for a name
LESSONS.hook: In blind taste tests, people often cannot tell their favourite cola from its rival. So why will they happily pay more for the logo?

sections.key: Brands began as marks of ownership and now act as mental shortcuts that reduce the risk of a bad choice.
sections.b:
Long before logos, farmers burned marks into the hides of cattle to show whose they were. The modern brand grew out of the Industrial Revolution, when goods travelled far from their makers. Buy flour from a neighbour and you knew who to blame if it was bad. If it came from a distant factory, a trusted name on the packet did that job. In 1876 the Bass brewery's red triangle became the first trade mark registered under a new British law.

Brands also act as mental shortcuts. A large supermarket stocks thousands of products, so a familiar name lets you assume the product will match last time. Much of what a brand sells is confidence, which is why travellers often pick a global chain over an unknown local cafe.

sections.key: Knowing the brand can literally change how something tastes to us.
sections.b:
In the 1970s Pepsi ran the Pepsi Challenge, a marketing campaign built on blind taste tests in which many people preferred Pepsi. Yet Coca-Cola stayed the bigger seller. In 2004, neuroscientists explored why.

When people tasted the drinks without knowing which was which, their preferences were fairly evenly split. When told they were drinking Coke, more said they preferred it, and brain scans showed extra activity in areas linked to memory and emotion. The brand was not just a label on the can. A lifetime of advertising, memories and associations had become part of the experience of drinking it. Brands work partly in our heads, and that is still real to us.

sections.key: Some brands are bought mainly to tell others something about us.
sections.b:
In 1899 the economist Thorstein Veblen coined the phrase conspicuous consumption for wealthy people spending lavishly to display status. Luxury brands still trade on this idea. A handbag with a famous logo holds the same things as an unbranded one, but it also sends a message. For some luxury goods, raising the price can even increase demand, because the high price is part of the appeal. Economists sometimes call these Veblen goods.

Signalling is not only about wealth. People choose brands to show they are outdoorsy, ethical, sporty or creative. A sticker on a laptop or a logo on a pair of runners can quietly announce which group you feel you belong to.

sections.key: Brands that become the everyday word for a product can lose their legal protection.
sections.b:
Escalator, thermos and trampoline all began as brand names. People came to use them for any product of that type, and in some countries the owners lost exclusive rights to the name. Courts call this genericide. In the United States, Otis lost its trade mark on escalator in 1950.

Companies fight to avoid this fate, which is why some insist on phrases like Band-Aid brand adhesive bandages. In Australia, Esky is a registered trade mark, even though many people use it for any portable cooler. The irony is painful for owners: becoming a household word is the ultimate marketing success, yet it can wipe out the legal value of the name.

sections.key: Home brands show shoppers will switch when quality is close, and a brand's trust can be lost quickly.
sections.b:
Own brands once had a plain, cheap reputation. When Aldi arrived in Australia in 2001, it built its business largely on own-label products sold at low prices. Coles and Woolworths expanded their own ranges in response. Many home brand items come from similar factories to branded goods, sometimes the same manufacturers. Well-known brands must now justify higher prices with quality, innovation or emotional appeal, not familiarity alone.

Because a brand is really a reputation, it is fragile. Decades of trust can be damaged by one scandal, unsafe product or misleading conduct, and sales and share prices can fall sharply. Some brands recover by acting quickly and honestly. For shoppers, the lesson is to check whether a product earns its extra price.

quiz.q: Why did brands become more important during the Industrial Revolution?
o: Governments banned unbranded goods
Goods travelled far from their makers
Factories could not print labels before then
Cattle farming increased
quiz.e: When buyers no longer knew the maker personally, a trusted name filled the gap.

quiz.q: What did the 2004 cola study suggest?
o: Coke and Pepsi are chemically identical
Nobody can taste the difference between colas
Blind tests always favour the bigger brand
Knowing the brand shifted people's preferences
quiz.e: When people knew they were drinking Coke, more preferred it and their brains responded differently.

quiz.q: What did Thorstein Veblen mean by conspicuous consumption?
o: Buying only what you truly need
Always choosing the cheapest option
Spending lavishly to display status

quiz.e: Spending designed to show off wealth is a form of signalling, and luxury brands still trade on it.

quiz.q: What is genericide?

A price war between rival home brands
Destroying unsold stock to hold prices
A brand name becoming the generic word
quiz.e: Names like escalator lost legal protection after becoming the common word.

quiz.q: Why must well-known brands now work harder to justify higher prices?
o: Many shoppers will switch to home brands
Home brands are always lower quality
Advertising costs have fallen sharply
Supermarkets have stopped stocking brands
quiz.e: Own-label products showed that many shoppers will switch when quality is close enough.

LESSONS.push: People often cannot tell colas apart blind. So what are they paying for?

LESSONS.title: Moats: why some companies stay on top
LESSONS.hook: Most successful businesses attract copycats that eat away their profits. A few seem untouchable for decades. The difference is what investors call a moat.

sections.key: A moat is any lasting advantage that stops rivals from competing away a company's profits.
sections.b:
Picture a medieval castle full of treasure. The treasure is a company's profits, and every competitor would love to storm the walls. Investor Warren Buffett popularised the idea that the best businesses are protected by a wide economic moat.

In ordinary markets, high profits are a signal to others. If a cafe makes a fortune, new cafes open next door, prices fall and profits shrink back to normal. Economists call this competition doing its job. A moat interrupts that process, letting a company earn unusually high returns for many years. Spotting a real moat is hard, and mistaking temporary success for a lasting advantage is one of the most common errors in business and investing.

sections.key: Network effects and switching costs keep customers with a company even when a rival is better or cheaper.
sections.b:
A telephone is useless if you are the only owner, and more useful with every new person who joins. This is a network effect. Card payment networks are a classic case: shops accept a card because customers carry it, and customers carry it because shops accept it. A better rival struggles to get everyone to switch together, which helps explain why digital markets end up dominated by one or two giants, and why regulators watch them closely.

Switching costs work differently. Moving a large company's accounting software means years of records, trained staff and connected systems. Changing banks means updating direct debits. Businesses deepen these costs with loyalty schemes and bundles. When convenience turns into dependence, a company has the most power over price.

sections.key: Cheaper production, patents, licences and trusted brands can all protect a company's profits.
sections.b:
Some companies win by producing more cheaply than rivals. A huge retailer can negotiate lower supplier prices, spread advertising across thousands of stores and fund efficient logistics. Economists call these economies of scale. Location can matter too: a quarry near a city has a lasting advantage, because rock is heavy and costly to transport. But a rival's cleverer method can erase a cost advantage.

Other moats are intangible. A patent gives an inventor exclusive rights for a limited time, usually up to 20 years, in exchange for disclosing how the invention works. Drug revenues can fall sharply when a major patent expires and cheaper generics arrive. Government licences can limit a market to a few operators. A trusted brand can allow higher prices, though familiarity alone does not guarantee pricing power.

sections.key: Technology and changing habits can drain even the widest moat.
sections.b:
History is full of companies that looked unbeatable. In the late 2000s Nokia sold more mobile phones than anyone, and BlackBerry was the device of choice for business. Within a few years touchscreen smartphones with app stores had pushed both aside.

Newspapers once held a powerful moat in classified advertising: to sell a car or find a job, you went to the paper with the most readers. The internet drained that moat remarkably quickly. These stories show moats are not permanent. They need constant maintenance and are vulnerable to shifts that make the old advantage irrelevant. A company that grows complacent behind its walls may not notice the water level falling.

sections.key: Asking what would stop a well-funded rival copying this business is a simple test of any company.
sections.b:
You can use moat thinking on any business, from a local bakery to a global tech giant. Ask: if a well-funded competitor tried to copy this company tomorrow, what would stop them? If the honest answer is not much, high profits are unlikely to last.

Analysts look for evidence such as steady returns on capital over many years, loyal customers and the ability to raise prices without losing sales. A great company is not automatically a great investment if its share price already reflects all that strength. This is general information rather than financial advice, and moneysmart.gov.au has helpful guidance if you are thinking about investing.

quiz.q: In business, what is an economic moat?
o: A large reserve of spare cash
A legal ban on all new competitors
A water supply contract for a factory
A lasting edge that protects profits
quiz.e: A moat is any durable advantage that stops rivals eroding a company's profits.

quiz.q: Why do card payment networks have strong network effects?
o: Shops and cardholders each need the other
They are all owned by the government
They charge shops and users no fees
They hold patents on plastic cards
quiz.e: Each side of the network makes it more valuable to the other, so rivals struggle to break in.

quiz.q: What usually happens when a major drug patent expires?
o: The drug must be withdrawn from sale
Cheaper generics arrive and sales can fall
Prices rise sharply as demand grows
The company gets a permanent licence
quiz.e: Patents are temporary, so competition arrives when they expire.

quiz.q: What lesson do Nokia and BlackBerry illustrate?
o: Brands never matter in the end
Big companies always stay on top
Moats can be drained by new technology
Phones are always a bad business
quiz.e: Both lost their dominant positions when touchscreen smartphones changed the market.

quiz.q: What is a simple test for whether a business has a moat?
o: Whether its founder is famous or wealthy
Whether it advertises more than rivals
Whether its share price has risen lately
Whether anything stops a rival copying it
quiz.e: If the honest answer is not much, high profits are unlikely to last.

LESSONS.push: Why do a few companies stay on top for decades while copycats circle?

LESSONS.title: Kodak and the innovator's dilemma
LESSONS.hook: In 1975 a young Kodak engineer built the world's first digital camera. Nearly four decades later, Kodak filed for bankruptcy. How does a company invent the future and still lose it?

sections.key: Kodak made photography easy, but its profits came mostly from film and processing that every photo needed.
sections.b:
In the 1880s George Eastman set out to make photography simple enough for anyone. His first Kodak camera came loaded with film; when the roll was finished you posted the whole camera back, and the company developed the pictures and returned it reloaded. The slogan was You press the button, we do the rest. Kodak became a household name, and for much of the twentieth century dominated the US film market, employing tens of thousands at its peak.

Its model resembles razors and blades. Cameras sold cheaply, while the real money came from film, chemicals, paper and processing. Margins were high, but the whole company, from factories to managers' bonuses, was built around chemistry. Anything that threatened film threatened its profits.

sections.key: Kodak invented the digital camera but had little reason to push it.
sections.b:
In 1975 Kodak engineer Steven Sasson built a prototype digital camera. It was about the size of a toaster, weighed several kilograms and took around 23 seconds to record a single black and white image, at about 0.01 megapixels, onto a cassette tape. Viewing it required a special playback system and a television.

Sasson later recalled that managers found it interesting but were unsure why anyone would want to look at photos on a TV. That reaction was reasonable at the time, as the technology was crude and expensive. The problem was what happened over the following decades, as digital improved rapidly while Kodak's core business still depended on film.

sections.key: Successful companies often ignore new technologies because they look small and unprofitable at first.
sections.b:
In 1997 Harvard professor Clayton Christensen published The Innovator's Dilemma. Studying industries such as computer disk drives, he saw a pattern. Well-run companies listened to their best customers and improved existing products. New technologies usually began worse, cheaper and aimed at small or unfashionable markets. Sensible managers ignored them, since they offered lower profits and the main customers did not want them.

But the new technology kept improving until it was good enough for everyone, and by then the old leaders were too far behind. Christensen called this disruption. The painful insight is that leaders did not fail through stupidity. They failed by doing what good managers are trained to do.

sections.key: Kodak did move into digital, but digital could never replace the profits of film.
sections.b:
Kodak was not blind to digital. It invested heavily, held valuable patents and for a time was one of the leading sellers of digital cameras in the United States. But digital cameras were a competitive hardware business with thin margins, nothing like the steady profits of film.

Then smartphones made separate cameras unnecessary for most people. Photos were shared online rather than printed, so the processing business shrank too. Kodak cut tens of thousands of jobs and sold divisions, but filed for bankruptcy protection in the United States in January 2012. It later emerged as a much smaller company focused on commercial printing and other specialised areas.

sections.key: Fujifilm survived by reusing its chemical know-how, and the same pattern of disruption keeps repeating.
sections.b:
Japan's Fujifilm faced the same collapse in film sales yet survived far better. Its leaders asked what else the company was good at. Making film involves sophisticated chemistry, including handling collagen and preventing fading from oxidation. Fujifilm applied it to medical imaging, pharmaceuticals, specialised materials and skincare, and bought other businesses to speed the change. Both companies saw digital coming; the difference lay partly in how willing each was to treat its old core business as temporary.

The pattern repeats. Blockbuster reportedly had the chance to buy a young Netflix around 2000 and declined, then filed for bankruptcy in 2010. A useful question: is there a cheaper, simpler product experts dismiss as not good enough, but which keeps improving each year?

quiz.q: Why was Kodak's business built around film rather than cameras?
o: Film and processing were bought again and again
Cameras were too complicated to build cheaply
Rivals held the patents on camera bodies
Customers rarely bought film after the first roll
quiz.e: Like razors and blades, the recurring sales of film drove the profits.

quiz.q: Why did Kodak's managers show little enthusiasm for the 1975 digital camera?
o: It was invented by a rival company
It was crude and few saw a use for it
It broke down every time it was used
It was too cheap to be profitable
quiz.e: The prototype was bulky and slow, so the reaction seemed reasonable at the time.

quiz.q: According to Clayton Christensen, why do good companies often miss disruptive technologies?
o: Their managers are not paying attention
They cannot afford new technology
Governments shield them from rivals
New products start out worse and smaller
quiz.e: Disruptive products begin small and unattractive, so sensible managers focus elsewhere.

quiz.q: Why could digital cameras not replace Kodak's film profits?
o: Digital cameras were too costly to sell
Kodak held no useful digital patents
Digital was a thin-margin hardware business
Few people wanted digital photos
quiz.e: Even as a leading digital seller, Kodak could not recreate film's high margins, and smartphones then removed the need for cameras.

quiz.q: How did Fujifilm survive the decline of film?
o: By raising the price of its film
By using its chemistry skills elsewhere
By merging with its rival Kodak
By dropping chemistry completely
quiz.e: Fujifilm moved into medical imaging, materials and skincare, among other areas.

LESSONS.push: The world's first digital camera was built inside the company it later helped sink.

LESSONS.title: Ford, Toyota and the art of making things
LESSONS.hook: Two car companies, half a world apart, changed how almost everything is made, from your phone to your runners. Their ideas still shape factories, hospitals and offices today.

sections.key: Ford's moving assembly line cut Model T build time from over 12 hours to about an hour and a half.
sections.b:
In the early 1900s cars were hand-built toys for the wealthy. Henry Ford wanted one ordinary families could afford. His 1908 Model T was simple and tough, but making it cheap meant building it faster than anyone had. His engineers broke the work into small, repeatable tasks, borrowing the overhead lines of Chicago meatpacking plants, where carcasses moved past workers who each made one cut. Ford reversed the idea: instead of taking something apart, put a car together.

In 1913 Ford's Highland Park plant in Michigan introduced a moving assembly line. The car travelled past workers who each repeated one task. Assembly time for a Model T chassis fell from over 12 hours to about an hour and a half. Prices fell, and by the 1920s millions were on the road, for years only in black.

sections.key: Ford doubled typical wages to cut the high turnover caused by gruelling, repetitive line work.
sections.b:
The line had a human cost. The work was monotonous and exhausting, and many workers quit soon after starting, so Ford was constantly hiring and training new people. In 1914 the company announced five dollars a day for many workers, roughly double the typical factory wage, along with a shorter working day. Crowds of job seekers gathered outside the factory.

The policy came with conditions, and the company inspected aspects of some workers' private lives. Still, it cut turnover sharply and helped create a workforce that could afford the very cars it was building. Mass production had arrived, and factories around the world rushed to copy it.

sections.key: Toyota's just-in-time system makes parts only as they are needed, to eliminate waste.
sections.b:
After World War II, Toyota faced the opposite situation to Ford. Japan was recovering from devastation, money was scarce, and the market wanted many types of vehicle in modest numbers. Huge runs of identical cars, backed by enormous stockpiles of parts, did not fit.

Engineers led by Taiichi Ohno developed the Toyota Production System, aiming to eliminate waste of every kind: overproduction, waiting, unnecessary movement, defects and excess inventory. Ohno later said he drew inspiration from American supermarkets, which restock shelves only as customers take items away. The result was just in time. Each step pulls parts from the step before only when it needs them, often signalled by simple cards called kanban. This keeps stockpiles small and exposes problems quickly.

sections.key: Letting any worker stop the line, and improving constantly, fixes root causes before defects multiply.
sections.b:
Toyota's second idea is jidoka, or automation with a human touch. Machines stop when something goes wrong, and workers can pull a cord, called an andon, to halt the line when they spot a defect. To outsiders this seemed crazy, because stopping a production line is expensive. But fixing the cause immediately prevents thousands of faulty cars being built later.

Toyota also encouraged kaizen, or continuous improvement. Workers on the factory floor were expected to suggest ways to make their own jobs safer, simpler and less wasteful. One well-known technique is the 'five whys': ask why something happened, then ask why again about each answer, until you reach the root cause rather than the surface symptom.

sections.key: Lean thinking spread widely, but running with minimal inventory leaves supply chains vulnerable to shocks.
sections.b:
By the 1980s Toyota's cars had a strong reputation for reliability, and Western carmakers studied its methods closely. A 1990 book, The Machine That Changed the World, helped spread the label 'lean production'. Lean ideas now run through hospitals, software companies, warehouses and government offices. Agile software teams, for example, borrow its small batches and quick feedback.

But lean has limits. Holding little inventory works when supply chains run smoothly and fails when they break. After the 2011 earthquake and tsunami in Japan, and again during COVID-19, shortages of parts such as computer chips halted car production around the world. Many companies now hold larger buffers of critical components. The deeper lesson is that how work is organised can matter as much as the technology.

quiz.q: What made Ford's 1913 assembly line so much faster?
o: Skilled craftsmen built each car by hand in turn
The car moved past workers who each repeated one task
Workers walked around a stationary car fitting parts
Customers chose from a wide range of colours
quiz.e: Bringing the work to the worker, in small repeated tasks, cut chassis assembly from over 12 hours to about an hour and a half.

quiz.q: Why did Ford introduce the five dollar day?
o: To let workers choose their own hours
To match the wages every other factory already paid
To reduce turnover and create customers
To replace the assembly line with craft work
quiz.e: Gruelling line work made workers quit, and better pay reduced turnover while creating customers for the product.

quiz.q: What does 'just in time' mean in Toyota's system?
