The loading is removed after you have held hospital cover continuously for 10 years. Some exceptions exist, including for people who arrived in Australia later in life. Extras-only cover does not count towards avoiding the loading.

sections.key: Use the government's comparison site, compare like with like, and review your cover each year.
sections.b:
Insurers have thousands of policies, and names alone tell you little. The government website privatehealth.gov.au, managed by the Commonwealth Ombudsman, lets you compare policies from all registered funds, and every policy has a standard information statement summarising what it covers. Commercial comparison sites can help, but they may not list every fund.

You can switch funds. If you move to an equivalent level of hospital cover you generally will not serve the same waiting periods again, though upgrades may attract new ones. Review your cover each year, especially when life changes, such as planning a family or retiring. If you have a dispute with your fund, the Commonwealth Ombudsman can help, free of charge. A tax agent can help you apply the tax rules to your situation.

quiz.q: What is a main reason Australians hold private hospital cover?
o: It is needed to enrol in Medicare
It is compulsory for all residents
Choice of specialist and sooner elective surgery
It removes every cost in public hospitals
quiz.e: Medicare already covers public hospital care, so private cover is mainly about choice and timing.

quiz.q: Which hospital tier must cover every clinical category?
o: Gold
Silver
Bronze
Basic
quiz.e: Gold must cover all categories, while lower tiers cover fewer, so check the treatments you might need.

quiz.q: What is the effect of choosing a higher excess?
o: Shorter waiting periods for claims
Extras cover with no annual limits
Higher premiums and no hospital bill
A lower premium but a bigger bill
quiz.e: A higher excess trades a cheaper premium for more out-of-pocket cost at the time of care.

quiz.q: Under Lifetime Health Cover, what loading applies for each year over 30 that you wait to take hospital cover?
o: 2 per cent
1 per cent
5 per cent
10 per cent
quiz.e: The 2 per cent per year loading, capped at 70 per cent, rewards joining earlier and drops away after 10 years of continuous cover.

quiz.q: How can you fairly compare policies from all registered funds?
o: Ask a single fund to rank its rivals
Use the government site privatehealth.gov.au
Compare tier names only
Choose the lowest premium regardless of cover
quiz.e: The government site lists all registered funds with standard information statements so you can compare like with like.

LESSONS.push: Why waiting past 30 to join a health fund can cost you for years after.

LESSONS.title: Cleaning smarter: the science of stains
LESSONS.hook: Hot water can set a bloodstain for good, and vinegar can wreck a marble benchtop. Learn what is really happening when you clean, and you will clean faster with fewer products.

sections.key: Detergent molecules grab grease with one end and water with the other, so grease rinses away.
sections.b:
Rinse a greasy frying pan under the tap and the water simply beads and runs off, leaving the oil behind. Oil and water do not mix, which is why plain water is a poor cleaner. Soaps and detergents solve this with molecules called surfactants. One end of each is attracted to water, and the other end to oil and grease.

When you scrub, millions of these molecules surround tiny droplets of grease, oily tails pointing in and water-loving heads pointing out. The grease is wrapped in little parcels that rinse away. Warm water helps because it softens fats, and scrubbing helps because it breaks grime into smaller pieces for the surfactants to grab.

sections.key: Clean top to bottom and dry to wet, and clean before you disinfect, because disinfectants work poorly through grime.
sections.b:
Wipe the bench until it gleams, then dust the rangehood and watch crumbs drift onto it. Professionals avoid this with two rules. Work top to bottom, so gravity carries dirt onto areas not yet cleaned. Work dry to wet: dust and vacuum before you mop, because wet cloths turn loose dust into smeared mud. Spray a product and leave it for a few minutes, since many cleaners need contact time to loosen grime.

Cleaning with detergent and water lifts off dirt, grease and most germs. Disinfecting uses chemicals to kill the rest, but disinfectants work poorly through grime, so clean first. Most must stay wet for several minutes, so check the label. Ordinary cleaning is enough for most of the home. Save disinfecting for high risk spots, such as benches after raw meat and toilets.

sections.key: Acids dissolve mineral deposits and alkalis cut grease, but neither suits every surface.
sections.b:
The chalky white crust on a shower screen in a hard water area is mostly alkaline mineral deposit. A mild acid such as white vinegar or citric acid dissolves it. Greasy kitchen grime responds better to alkaline products such as bicarbonate of soda or dishwashing detergent. Knowing this saves you buying a cupboard full of special sprays.

It also protects your surfaces. Acids etch natural stone such as marble and limestone, leaving dull patches, so use a pH neutral cleaner there.

Mixing vinegar with bicarb, a popular online trick, mostly cancels them out. The fizz is carbon dioxide, and what remains is largely salty water. Use each separately, for the job it does best.

sections.key: Mixing bleach with ammonia or acids can release toxic gases.
sections.b:
Some cleaning mistakes leave streaks. Others put people in hospital. Bleach, which contains sodium hypochlorite, is the most dangerous product to combine. Mixed with ammonia, found in some glass and multipurpose cleaners, it releases chloramine gases. Mixed with acids, including vinegar and some toilet and descaling cleaners, it can release chlorine gas. Both irritate the eyes and lungs and can cause serious breathing problems. Even mixing two brands of toilet cleaner can be risky if you do not know what is in them.

The safe habits are simple. Use one product at a time, rinse between products, keep products in their original labelled bottles, and open a window. If someone feels unwell after exposure, call the Poisons Information Centre on 13 11 26.

sections.key: Protein, tannin, grease and dye stains each need a different approach, and heat can set them for good.
sections.b:
Protein stains, such as blood, egg, milk and sweat, need cold water first, because heat cooks the proteins and bonds them to the fibres. Enzyme pre-treatments then break them down. Tannin stains, such as tea, coffee, wine and fruit juice, usually respond to prompt rinsing and laundry detergent, though some need an oxygen bleach soak. Grease needs dishwashing liquid rubbed in before a warm wash. Dye stains, such as ink, are hardest and may need specialist removers.

On a fresh spill, resist scrubbing, which pushes the stain deeper. Blot from the outer edge towards the centre. Test any product on a hidden spot first, and rinse it out afterwards. Check the stain has gone before using a dryer or iron, as heat can fix a faint stain permanently.

quiz.q: How do detergent molecules remove grease?
o: They make water heavier than oil
They dissolve the surface the grease sits on
One end holds grease, one holds water
They freeze the grease so it cracks off
quiz.e: Surfactants wrap grease in little parcels that water can carry away.

quiz.q: Why should you clean a surface before disinfecting it?
o: Cleaning makes disinfectant smell nicer
Disinfectants work poorly through grime
Disinfectant damages clean surfaces
Cleaning is only needed on floors
quiz.e: Grime shields germs from disinfectant, so detergent and water come first.

quiz.q: What is the best choice for cleaning a marble benchtop?
o: White vinegar
Citric acid
A vinegar and bicarb mix
A pH neutral cleaner
quiz.e: Acids etch natural stone such as marble, leaving dull patches.

quiz.q: What can happen if bleach is mixed with vinegar?
o: It can release chlorine gas
It becomes a stronger, safer disinfectant
The two simply cancel each other out
It turns into plain water
quiz.e: Bleach mixed with acids can release chlorine gas, so use one product at a time.

quiz.q: Why should a bloodstain be treated with cold water first?
o: Cold water is more acidic
Hot water dissolves the fabric dye
Cold water contains more oxygen
Heat cooks the protein into the fibres
quiz.e: Heat sets protein stains, so start cold and use an enzyme pre-treatment.

LESSONS.push: Hot water can set a bloodstain for good. Here's the chemistry behind it.

LESSONS.title: Laundry done right
LESSONS.hook: Shrunken jumpers, pink socks and towels that smell faintly of damp are all avoidable. A few habits will make your clothes last longer and your washing cheaper.

sections.key: Read the care label, sort your washing, and prepare each load before it goes in.
sections.b:
Flip a shirt inside out and you will find a small label of symbols. Most people ignore it, which is how a favourite wool jumper ends up fitting a child. The tub shows washing, with a number or dots for maximum temperature and a hand for hand washing. The triangle is bleaching, the square drying, the iron ironing, and a circle alone means dry cleaning. A cross through any symbol means do not.

Sort whites, lights and darks, since one new red t-shirt can turn a load of undies pink. Wash new dark items alone for the first few washes, when excess dye is most likely to run. Empty pockets, zip up zips, and put delicates in a mesh bag. Turn dark clothes and prints inside out.

sections.key: Cold washing saves energy, and more detergent or a packed drum does not mean cleaner clothes.
sections.b:
Most of the energy a washing machine uses on a warm or hot cycle goes into heating the water. Modern detergents are designed to work well in cold water, so for everyday loads a cold wash is usually enough and costs much less. Save warm or hot washes for greasy stains, towels and bedding, if the care label allows.

More detergent does not mean cleaner clothes. Too much does not rinse out properly, leaving clothes stiff, dull and itchy, and residue can build up in the machine and cause smells. Follow the dose on the pack.

Clothes also need room to move. For a front loader, leave a hand's width at the top of the drum. Tiny half loads waste water and electricity.

sections.key: Line drying is cheap and gentle; dryers are convenient but harder on fabric.
sections.b:
Australia's sunshine makes the clothesline one of the best appliances in the house, and it costs nothing to run. Sunlight helps freshen whites, though strong sun can fade dark and bright colours, so hang those inside out or in the shade. Hang clothes by their strongest seams to cut down on ironing. Dry knitted wool flat on a towel, because hanging it wet can stretch it out of shape.

Clothes dryers are handy on wet days, but heat and tumbling are the main causes of shrinkage and wear, and dryers use a lot of electricity. Heat pump dryers use considerably less than standard vented ones. Clean the lint filter every single load. Built-up lint makes the dryer work harder and is a recognised fire risk.

sections.key: Leave the door open, clean the seal and run a hot maintenance wash to stop musty smells.
sections.b:
If clean washing smells musty, the problem may be the machine. Front loaders have rubber door seals that trap water, lint and detergent, creating a cosy home for mould and bacteria. After each wash, leave the door and detergent drawer slightly open so the inside can dry. Wipe the seal regularly, checking the folds for hair, coins and grime.

Every month or so, run an empty hot wash, using a washing machine cleaner if you like. Many machines have a dedicated drum clean cycle. Clean the filter too, if it is accessible, following the manual. Take wet clothes out promptly. Washing left sitting in the drum for hours is a fast route to that damp, sour smell.

sections.key: Some laundry mishaps can be partly reversed if you act quickly, but felted wool cannot be undone.
sections.b:
Even careful people end up with a pink load now and then. If dye has run, do not put the clothes in the dryer. Rewash them straight away in cold water, or use a supermarket colour run remover, following the instructions and checking the care labels first. White items can often be soaked in an oxygen bleach solution.

Shrunken wool is harder. Heat and agitation lock wool fibres together in a process called felting, which is permanent. Soaking the garment in lukewarm water with a little hair conditioner and gently stretching it while damp can sometimes win back a little size, but there are no guarantees.

For stubborn smells in towels and sportswear, a hot wash with less detergent, plus thorough drying in the sun, often does more than adding fragrance.

quiz.q: When are new dark clothes most likely to run dye?
o: After about a year of wear
Only in cold water
Only when line dried
In the first few washes
quiz.e: Excess dye is most likely to run early on, so wash new dark or bright items on their own.

quiz.q: Where does most of the energy go in a warm or hot wash?
o: Heating the water
Spinning the drum
Running the display
Pumping water out
quiz.e: Heating is the big cost, so cold washes for everyday loads save a lot of energy.

quiz.q: How often should you clean a clothes dryer's lint filter?
o: Once a year
Every load
Only when it smells
Every month
quiz.e: Built-up lint makes the dryer work harder and is a recognised fire risk.

quiz.q: Why do front loaders develop musty smells?
o: Cold water breeds mould in the pipes
Detergent attracts insects into the drum
The door seal traps water and lint
Spinning too fast dries out the drum
quiz.e: Leaving the door open, wiping the seal and running a hot maintenance wash keep the machine fresh.

quiz.q: Why is shrunken wool so hard to fix?
o: The wool's dye has faded
The fibres have locked together
The wool has partly dissolved
The care label was wrong
quiz.e: Heat and agitation permanently lock wool fibres together, so any fix recovers only a little size.

LESSONS.push: Why one red t-shirt can turn a whole load pink, and how to stop it.

LESSONS.title: Cutting your power and water bills
LESSONS.hook: Your energy bill is a story about heat: heating rooms, heating water and keeping food cold. Read it properly and you can find real savings without living in the dark.

sections.key: Bills combine a daily supply charge with a price per kilowatt hour, and heating, cooling and hot water are the big users.
sections.b:
Look past the total on your electricity bill. The daily supply charge is a fixed amount you pay just to be connected. The usage charge is a price per kilowatt hour (kWh), the unit your meter counts. One kWh is a 1,000 watt appliance running for an hour. Time of use plans charge more at peak times. Watch your average daily use as you make changes.

People often start by unplugging phone chargers, which is like skipping a mint while buying a new car. In most Australian homes, heating and cooling are the biggest users, then water heating, then fridges, dryers and pool pumps. To find big users, multiply wattage by hours. A 2,400 watt heater running five hours a night uses 12 kWh.

sections.key: Reverse cycle air conditioners, sensible thermostat settings and draught sealing cut the biggest costs.
sections.b:
A reverse cycle air conditioner is a heat pump. Rather than turning electricity directly into heat, it moves heat from outside to inside. It can deliver several units of heat for each unit of electricity, which typically makes it far cheaper to run than a plug-in bar or fan heater.

Thermostat settings matter too. Australian energy agencies commonly suggest around 18 to 20 degrees in winter and 25 to 27 in summer, and each extra degree adds noticeably to running costs. Heat or cool only the rooms you use. Seal draughts around doors and windows with weather strips and door snakes. Close curtains on winter nights, and block summer sun with external shading, which works better than internal blinds.

sections.key: Shorter showers, efficient showerheads, a well-set fridge and switching off standby devices are easy wins.
sections.b:
Every hot shower costs you twice: once for the water and again to heat it. A showerhead with a good Water Efficiency Labelling and Standards (WELS) star rating uses less hot water, and cutting a shower by a couple of minutes adds up over a year. Fix dripping hot taps quickly and wash clothes in cold water.

Your fridge runs all day, so keep it at around 3 to 4 degrees and the freezer around minus 18. Check the door seals by closing the door on a sheet of paper to see if it holds, and leave space behind for air. An old second fridge in the garage can be surprisingly expensive to run.

Walk through your home at night and count the glowing standby lights. Switch off consoles and spare devices at the wall.

sections.key: Leaks, toilets and gardens are where hidden water waste usually hides.
sections.b:
A toilet with a slow leak into the bowl can waste a large amount of water without anyone noticing. Test yours by adding a few drops of food colouring to the cistern and waiting about 15 minutes without flushing. If colour appears in the bowl, the cistern is leaking and needs repair. Most plumbing repairs need a licensed plumber.

Use the half flush button where you have one. Run dishwashers and washing machines only when full, and look for good WELS star ratings when buying them. Outside, water the garden early in the morning or in the evening so less is lost to evaporation, and use mulch to keep soil moist. Check local water restrictions and rebates.

sections.key: Compare appliance ratings and energy plans regularly, and ask about concessions or hardship help.
sections.b:
The Energy Rating Label shows a star rating and an estimated yearly energy use in kWh, the best number for comparing models of a similar size. A cheaper appliance with a poor rating can cost more over its life than a pricier efficient one.

Many households stay on the same plan for years and pay more than they need to. Compare plans every year or so. The government's Energy Made Easy website, energymadeeasy.gov.au, compares offers in most states and territories, and Victoria has its own Victorian Energy Compare site. Ask your retailer if they have a better plan.

If you hold a pension, health care or other concession card, ask about energy concessions. If you are struggling to pay, contact your retailer early about hardship programs. This is general information only.

quiz.q: Which usually uses the most energy in an Australian home?
o: Phone chargers
Heating and cooling
LED lighting
The television
quiz.e: Target the large loads first, because small devices and lighting are usually a smaller share.

quiz.q: Why is a reverse cycle air conditioner cheap to heat with?
o: It runs on gas
It only heats one small spot
It moves heat in from outside
It switches off every hour
quiz.e: As a heat pump, it delivers several units of heat for each unit of electricity used.

quiz.q: How can you check a fridge door seal?
o: Shine a torch around the inside
Measure the fridge with a tape measure
Listen closely to the motor running
Close the door on paper to test its grip
quiz.e: If the paper slides out easily, the seal is not gripping and the fridge is wasting energy.

quiz.q: How can you test a toilet cistern for a leak?
o: Add food colouring to the cistern and wait
Flush it three times in quick succession
Pour a cup of vinegar into the bowl
Turn off the water main for a week
quiz.e: If colour appears in the bowl after about 15 minutes, the cistern is leaking.

quiz.q: Which figure on an Energy Rating Label is most useful for comparing similar-sized models?
o: The brand name and logo
The price tag on the shelf
Yearly energy use in kWh
The number of settings
quiz.e: A cheaper appliance with a poor rating can cost more over its life than a pricier efficient one.

LESSONS.push: Your energy bill is a story about heat. Here's how to read it properly.

LESSONS.title: DIY basics: your toolkit and first fixes
LESSONS.hook: Hanging a mirror, patching a hole and fixing a sticking door are well within reach. Knowing which jobs to leave to a licensed tradie is just as important.

sections.key: A small set of quality tools, with safety gear, handles most household jobs.
sections.b:
You do not need a shed full of gear to look after a home. A good starter kit fits in one toolbox. Include a claw hammer, screwdrivers with both flat and Phillips heads, a tape measure, a spirit level, a utility knife with spare blades, pliers and an adjustable spanner.

A cordless drill driver is the single most useful power tool, since it both drills holes and drives screws. Add a stud finder, a pencil, sandpaper, a putty knife and a selection of screws and wall plugs. Safety gear belongs in the kit too: safety glasses, gloves and a dust mask. Buy decent quality basics rather than a giant bargain set of flimsy tools, and keep everything together so you are not hunting for the hammer every time.

sections.key: Protect yourself, watch for asbestos in older homes, and leave electrical, gas and most plumbing work to licensed tradies.
sections.b:
Most DIY injuries come from ordinary moments: a slip on a ladder, a chip of masonry in the eye. Wear safety glasses whenever you drill, hammer or cut, and keep three points of contact on ladders. Remove the battery before changing bits or blades.

In homes built or renovated before 2004, some materials may contain asbestos, including some wall and ceiling sheeting, eaves and vinyl floor tiles. You cannot identify it by looking, so do not drill, cut or sand anything you suspect, and get it tested.

In every state and territory, electrical wiring work, including replacing a power point, must be done by a licensed electrician. Gas fitting needs a licensed gasfitter, and most plumbing needs a licensed plumber. Unlicensed work can be dangerous, illegal and may affect your insurance.

sections.key: Before drilling, picture what lies behind the wall: studs, pipes and cables, and choose the right fixing.
sections.b:
Most Australian homes have plasterboard walls fixed to timber or steel studs, commonly spaced about 450 or 600 millimetres apart. Pipes and electrical cables also run inside. Cables often travel straight up or down from power points and switches, so avoid drilling directly above or below them.

A stud finder with cable detection helps, but it is not foolproof, so drill carefully and stop if you hit something unexpected. For heavy items such as shelves, mirrors and wall mounted televisions, screw into the studs where possible. Where there is no stud, use plasterboard anchors rated for the weight, as an ordinary screw will simply pull out. Brick and concrete walls need a masonry drill bit and wall plugs.

sections.key: Fill, sand and paint small holes, and fix most squeaks and sticks by tightening screws or lubricating hinges.
sections.b:
For small holes and dents in plasterboard, press ready mixed filler into the hole with a putty knife and scrape it level. Many fillers shrink as they dry, so a second thin coat may be needed. Once dry, sand gently, wipe off the dust and paint to match. Holes bigger than a coin need a self adhesive mesh patch first. Renters should check their lease before making holes.

A squealing door usually needs lubricant on the hinge pin. If a door sticks, check the hinges before reaching for a plane, as loose screws let it sag. If a screw just spins, pack the hole with matchsticks and wood glue, snap them off flush, and drive the screw back in. Crooked cabinet doors usually have adjustable hinges.

sections.key: Fresh silicone around baths and showers keeps water out and mould away.
sections.b:
Look at the sealant where your bath or shower meets the wall. If it is black with mould, cracked or peeling, water can seep behind it and damage the wall and floor. Resealing is a satisfying weekend job.

Cut away the old sealant with a sharp blade or a removal tool, clean the joint thoroughly and let it dry completely. Apply masking tape on either side for a clean edge, then run a steady bead of mould resistant bathroom silicone along the gap. Smooth it with a wet finger or a shaping tool and peel the tape away straight away. Let it cure for the time stated on the tube before using the shower. Good ventilation afterwards keeps the new seal fresh for longer.

quiz.q: Which power tool is described as the most useful for a starter kit?
o: A small angle grinder
A handheld circular saw
A cordless drill driver
A cordless nail gun
quiz.e: A drill driver both drills holes and drives screws, so it covers the most jobs.

quiz.q: What should you do with a material you suspect contains asbestos?
o: Sand it lightly to check
Leave it alone and get it tested
Drill a small test hole
Paint over it and drill as normal
quiz.e: Asbestos cannot be identified by looking, so avoid disturbing it until it has been tested.

quiz.q: Where are cables commonly found inside a wall?
o: Only in the ceiling space
Diagonally across the middle of the wall
Straight up or down from power points
Only in walls beside windows
quiz.e: Avoid drilling directly above or below power points and switches.

quiz.q: What is a quick fix for a hinge screw that just spins?
o: Hit the screw in with a bigger hammer
Take the door off and leave it off
Spray the screw with lubricant oil
Pack the hole with matchsticks and glue
quiz.e: The wood fills the stripped hole so the screw can grip again.

quiz.q: Why reseal a bath or shower when the sealant is black, cracked or peeling?
o: Water can seep in and damage the wall
It makes the bath hold more water
It lets the shower run hotter
It removes the need for ventilation
quiz.e: Fresh mould resistant silicone keeps water out of the wall and floor.

LESSONS.push: In some countries you can rewire your own switches. Why not in Australia?

LESSONS.title: Gardening basics for Australian conditions
LESSONS.hook: Australian gardens face old soils, fierce sun, sudden downpours and long dry spells. Work with these conditions and even a beginner can grow something wonderful.

sections.key: Australia spans many climate zones, so your local climate and your own patch decide what grows and when.
sections.b:
A planting guide written for Melbourne will lead a Darwin gardener badly astray. Australian gardens range from tropical to subtropical, temperate, arid and cool highland climates, and what to plant and when depends on yours. Zone maps help, and a local nursery is a goldmine of practical advice.

Then study your own patch. In the southern hemisphere, north facing areas get the most sun, while south facing spots stay shadier and cooler. Watch where sun falls in the morning and afternoon, which areas stay soggy after rain, and where wind whips through. Most fruiting vegetables need at least six hours of direct sun a day. Matching plants to the spot is half the battle won.

sections.key: Test your soil's texture and pH, add organic matter, and feed with care because many natives dislike phosphorus.
sections.b:
Squeeze a handful of moist soil. Sandy soil feels gritty and drains fast but holds few nutrients. Clay feels sticky and forms a ribbon, holding nutrients but waterlogging easily. Loam sits in between. Many Australian soils are ancient and low in nutrients, especially phosphorus. A cheap pH kit shows whether soil is acidic or alkaline; many plants prefer around 6 to 7. Almost every soil improves with compost or well rotted manure.

More fertiliser is not always better. Too much can burn roots and wash into waterways. Many natives, such as grevilleas, banksias and waratahs, evolved in low phosphorus soils and can be harmed by ordinary fertilisers, so use a product labelled for natives. Vegetables are hungry feeders and benefit from compost and balanced fertiliser.

sections.key: Deep, infrequent watering grows stronger roots, and a layer of mulch saves water and suppresses weeds.
sections.b:
A quick sprinkle every evening trains roots to stay near the surface, where they dry out fast. Watering deeply and less often encourages them down into cooler, moister soil. Push a finger a few centimetres into the soil, and if it is damp, wait. Water early in the morning, at the soil rather than the leaves. Drip irrigation delivers water right where it is needed. Some dry soils repel water, so a wetting agent helps. Follow your local water restrictions.

Mulch is any material spread over the soil, such as pea straw, sugar cane mulch or wood chips. A layer of roughly 5 to 7 centimetres slows evaporation, steadies soil temperature, smothers weed seeds and feeds the soil as it breaks down. Keep it clear of stems and trunks, because constant moisture can cause rot.

sections.key: Choose plants suited to your area, avoid local weeds, and handle potting mix carefully because it can carry Legionella.
sections.b:
Local native plants are one of the easiest ways to build a garden that copes with your climate and feeds native birds and insects. Avoid plants listed as weeds in your area. Some popular garden plants have escaped into bushland and caused serious damage, so check your council or state weed lists before buying.

A safety note surprises many people: potting mix and compost can carry Legionella bacteria, which can cause a serious lung infection. Australian potting mix bags carry a warning for this reason. Open bags carefully away from your face, dampen the mix to reduce dust, wear gloves and a mask, and wash your hands afterwards. Wear gloves when gardening generally, and keep your tetanus vaccination up to date. This is general information, not medical advice.

sections.key: Start small with easy crops, and plant them in the right season for your climate zone.
sections.b:
Few things taste better than a tomato still warm from the vine. The secret to a successful first edible garden is starting small, perhaps one raised bed or a few large pots in a sunny spot.

Herbs such as parsley, basil, mint and chives are forgiving starters, though mint spreads aggressively and is best kept in a pot. Leafy greens such as lettuce and silverbeet grow quickly, so you can pick leaves within weeks. Cherry tomatoes are generally easier than large varieties.

Plant in the right season for your climate zone, using a local planting calendar, since planting tomatoes in winter in Hobart will end in disappointment. Water consistently, mulch well, and visit your garden often, because catching pests and problems early makes them far easier to fix.

quiz.q: In the southern hemisphere, which part of your garden usually gets the most sun?
o: South facing areas
North facing areas
Shaded corners by the fence
All areas get equal sun
quiz.e: North facing spots get the most sun, so match plants to the light each area receives.

quiz.q: Why can ordinary fertilisers harm grevilleas and banksias?
o: They give the soil too little nitrogen
They make the soil far too acidic
These plants evolved in low phosphorus soils
They attract pests to the new growth
quiz.e: Use a product labelled for natives, or skip fertiliser for these plants.

quiz.q: Why is deep, infrequent watering better than a daily sprinkle?
o: It uses more water overall
It encourages deeper, tougher roots
It keeps leaves wet overnight
It helps weeds establish
quiz.e: Shallow watering keeps roots near the surface, where they dry out fast in hot weather.

quiz.q: Why do Australian potting mix bags carry a health warning?
o: They contain traces of asbestos
They are highly flammable
They contain traces of lead
They can carry Legionella bacteria
quiz.e: Open bags carefully, dampen the mix, and wear gloves and a mask.

quiz.q: What is the best way to start a first edible garden?
o: Start small with easy crops, in the right season
Plant every vegetable at once for variety
Choose crops regardless of the season
Begin with the hardest plants for a challenge
quiz.e: A small, well-matched start builds skills and avoids disappointment.

LESSONS.push: Why a fertiliser that helps your veggies can kill a banksia.

LESSONS.title: Moving house without the chaos
LESSONS.hook: Moving house is often ranked among life's most stressful events. A plan that starts weeks ahead turns moving day from a frantic scramble into a long, tiring but manageable day.

sections.key: Book removalists early, compare written quotes and declutter before you pack.
sections.b:
The worst time to find every removalist booked is the week before you move, especially at the end of the month or around school holidays, when demand peaks. Once you know your date, get at least two or three written quotes. Ask whether the price is fixed or hourly, what is included, whether they offer transit insurance, and read the fine print about stairs, long carries and heavy items like pianos. If you plan to move yourself, book the trailer or truck now and line up some strong friends.

Start decluttering too. Every item you sell, donate or recycle is one less thing to pack, carry, unpack and pay to move. Begin with spare rooms, sheds and cupboards.

sections.key: Use small boxes for heavy things, label every box by room, and keep a first night box with you.
sections.b:
A large box full of books can be far too heavy to lift safely. The professional rule is simple: heavy items go in small boxes, and light bulky items in large ones. Wrap fragile items individually, stand plates on their edges, and fill gaps with towels or paper. Label every box on the side as well as the top, with the destination room and a few words on the contents. Photograph the cables behind your television before unplugging them.

Pack one first night box last and keep it with you in the car. Include toilet paper, soap, a towel, chargers, medication, a change of clothes, sheets, a kettle, snacks, a torch and basic tools. Add pet supplies or a toy if needed. Keep documents, keys and valuables with you too.

sections.key: Redirect mail, notify key organisations, and arrange utility connections and disconnections ahead of time.
sections.b:
Missing one organisation can mean lost mail or a missed bill. Australia Post offers a paid mail redirection service, which catches anything you forget. Update the Australian Electoral Commission, the ATO, Medicare and Centrelink, much of it through myGov. Your state transport authority needs your new address for your licence and registration, usually within a set number of days. Then work through your bank, super fund, insurers, employer, doctor, schools and subscriptions. Car and home or contents premiums can change with your suburb.

About two weeks out, arrange electricity and gas connection at the new address and disconnection at the old one. Compare plans while you are switching. Book internet early, as it can take longest. On moving day, photograph the meter readings at both properties.

sections.key: Clean thoroughly and compare against your entry condition report to protect your bond.
sections.b:
For renters, the bond is often the biggest sum tied up in a move, and the condition report is the key to getting it back. Before you leave, read the entry condition report you completed when you moved in, and use it as a checklist.

Clean thoroughly, including the oven, rangehood filters, windows, skirting boards and bathroom grout, and remove all rubbish. Fix any damage you caused, beyond fair wear and tear, which is the normal deterioration expected from everyday living. Take dated photos and videos of every room after cleaning. Attend the final inspection if you can, and return all keys and remotes on time. If you and the landlord disagree about the bond, your state's tenancy authority or tribunal can help. This is general information, so check your state's rules.

sections.key: Supervise loading, then do the safety basics and set up beds before anything else.
sections.b:
On moving day, be at the old property early to guide the removalists, pointing out fragile items and anything that is not coming. Do a final walk through every room, cupboard and the garden shed before you leave.

At the new place, direct boxes to the right rooms using your labels, and check furniture for damage before signing anything. Do the safety basics before unpacking: find the water main, the switchboard and the gas meter, test the smoke alarms, and make sure doors and windows lock.

Assemble beds first, so that whatever else happens, everyone has somewhere to sleep. Unpack the kitchen and bathroom next. Do not expect to finish in a weekend. Unpack a few boxes a day, and introduce yourself to the neighbours.

quiz.q: When is demand for removalists usually highest?
o: Midweek during the winter months
At month's end and school holidays
Early on Monday mornings
In the middle of the month
quiz.e: Book early, because peak times fill up and leave you with few options.

quiz.q: Why should books go in small boxes?
o: Large boxes always cost more
Books must stay visible in transit
Heavy large boxes hurt backs and split open
Small boxes are easier to label
quiz.e: Heavy items go in small boxes and light bulky items in large ones.

quiz.q: Why photograph meter readings on moving day?
o: The utility company requires a photo to connect
It is needed to claim your bond
It helps the removalists
It gives you evidence if a bill looks wrong
quiz.e: Photos at both properties protect you from disputed final bills.

quiz.q: What helps most in getting a renter's bond back?
o: A clean checked against the entry report
Leaving before the final inspection
Repainting the walls in a new colour
Keeping a spare key for the landlord
quiz.e: The entry report, a thorough clean and dated photos show the property's condition.

quiz.q: What should you do at the new home before unpacking?
o: Hang pictures and paint the walls
Find the water main and test smoke alarms
Rearrange the furniture in each room
Unpack every box in the lounge room
quiz.e: Safety basics come first, then beds, then the kitchen and bathroom.

LESSONS.push: Why one big box of books can wreck your back, and how to pack smarter.

LESSONS.title: Keeping pests out of your home
LESSONS.hook: Cockroaches, mice and termites are not signs of a dirty house so much as an inviting one. Take away what they need, and most pests simply go elsewhere.

sections.key: Pests come for food, water and shelter, so remove those and block the ways in.
sections.b:
Every pest is looking for the same three things: food, water and shelter. Crumbs under the toaster, open cereal, pet food left out overnight and a dripping tap add up to a five star resort for a cockroach. The best pest control is unglamorous. Store food in sealed containers, wipe benches, empty bins often, and rinse recyclables. Fix leaks, reduce clutter and cardboard, and treat chemicals as a second line of defence.

Then seal the way in. A house mouse can squeeze through a gap about the width of a pencil. Fit door seals, seal gaps around pipes and cables, and use steel wool or metal mesh in rodent holes, since mice chew softer materials. Repair flyscreens, trim branches touching the house, and store firewood off the ground and away from the walls.

sections.key: Baits that insects carry home usually work better than surface sprays.
sections.b:
If you switch on the kitchen light at night and small brown cockroaches scatter, you may have German cockroaches, a common indoor species that breeds quickly in warm kitchens. Surface sprays kill the insects you can see, but most of the population hides in cracks and behind appliances.

Gel baits and bait stations usually work better, because cockroaches eat the bait and spread it to others in their hiding places. Place baits where they shelter, such as behind the fridge, and keep cleaning so the bait is the most tempting food around.

Ants are similar. Follow the trail to find where they enter, wipe it away with soapy water, and use ant baits rather than sprays, which can scatter the colony.

sections.key: Snap traps are effective, while poison baits can harm pets and wildlife.
sections.b:
Droppings in the pantry, gnawed packets and scratching in the ceiling at night are the classic signs of rodents. Once you have removed food and sealed entry points, traps are an effective way to deal with those already inside. Set snap traps along walls, where rodents prefer to run. Bait them with a little peanut butter and check them daily, wearing gloves.

Poison baits are widely sold but have downsides. Poisoned rodents may die inside walls and smell, and pets, owls and other wildlife that eat them can be poisoned too. If you use baits, use lockable bait stations and follow the label exactly. Wet droppings with disinfectant before cleaning them up, rather than sweeping or vacuuming dry.

sections.key: Termite damage can be costly and is often excluded from home insurance, so watch for signs and call a licensed pest manager.
sections.b:
Termites, often called white ants, can hollow out a house's timber for months before anyone notices. In much of Australia they are a serious threat, and termite damage is often excluded from home insurance, so check yours. Warning signs include mud tunnels, called leads, running up walls or foundations, timber that sounds hollow when tapped, and bubbling paint.

If you find termites, do not disturb or spray them, because they may simply move elsewhere in the house. Call a licensed pest manager. To lower your risk, keep garden beds, mulch and stored timber away from the house's edges, do not let soil cover weep holes in brick walls, fix leaks, and keep any subfloor well ventilated. Inspections, commonly recommended yearly, catch problems early.

sections.key: Remove standing water weekly, and read the label every time you use a pesticide.
sections.b:
In warm weather, mosquitoes can go from egg to biting adult in as little as a week or so, and they need only a small amount of still water. A forgotten bucket, blocked gutter or plant saucer can produce hundreds. Once a week, tip out standing water, including pet bowls and birdbaths. Clean gutters and screen rainwater tank inlets and overflows. Flies breed in rotting food and animal waste, so keep bins sealed. Mosquitoes can spread diseases in parts of Australia, so check health advice when travelling.

Pesticides kill living things, so read the label every time. Store them in original containers, locked away, never in drink bottles. Call a licensed pest manager for termites, large infestations or roof cavities. Possums are protected natives, so call a licensed wildlife remover.

quiz.q: What are the three things pests are looking for in a home?
o: Light, warmth and noise
Paint, timber and plastic
Food, water and shelter
Darkness, cold and silence
quiz.e: Removing food, water and shelter is the most effective and least glamorous pest control.

quiz.q: Why do gel baits often beat sprays for cockroaches?
o: They kill on contact faster
Roaches carry bait to hidden ones
They smell much nicer to roaches
They never wear out or expire
quiz.e: Sprays kill what you can see, but baits reach the hidden population in cracks and behind appliances.

quiz.q: Why can poison baits be a problem?
o: They never actually kill rodents
They attract even more mice
They are harmless to local wildlife
Pets and wildlife can be poisoned too
quiz.e: Traps are effective and avoid the risk to pets and owls, while poisoned rodents can also die inside walls.

quiz.q: What should you do if you find active termites?
o: Leave them alone and call a pest manager
Spray them with insecticide immediately
Break open the mud leads to look inside
Pour boiling water on the mud leads
quiz.e: Disturbing or spraying termites can send them elsewhere in the house.

quiz.q: How often should you tip out standing water to stop mosquitoes breeding?
o: Once a year
Every three months
About once a week
Only in winter
quiz.e: Mosquitoes can develop from egg to adult in about a week, and they need only a little still water.

LESSONS.push: A pencil-width gap is all a mouse needs. Where else is your home open?

LESSONS.title: Declutter and organise your home
LESSONS.hook: Most of us use a small fraction of what we own, while the rest quietly costs us space, time and calm. Here is a practical way to clear it out and keep it clear.

sections.key: We overvalue what we own, so clutter is not a character flaw, and the fix is to start small.
sections.b:
Hold up a mug you never use and ask if you would buy it today. Often the answer is no, yet it stays. Psychologists call part of this pull the endowment effect: our tendency to value things more simply because we own them. Add 'just in case' thinking, guilt over money spent, gifts and busyness, and clutter grows quietly. It is not a character flaw. It is the result of things coming into a home faster than they leave.

Decluttering the whole house in a weekend is a recipe for piles and giving up. Pick one small space you can finish in 15 to 30 minutes, such as the cutlery drawer or bathroom cabinet. Start with low emotion areas like the linen cupboard. Leave photos and inherited items for later.

sections.key: Sort items into keep, donate, sell or rubbish, then move the other boxes out promptly.
sections.b:
Clear your chosen space completely, then sort each item into keep, donate, sell, or rubbish and recycling. Ask: have I used this in the past year? Would I buy it again? Do I have another that does the job? Return only the keep items. Then deal with the other boxes promptly, or you are just moving clutter from room to room. Put rubbish out that day, list sale items within the week, and put donations in your car boot.

Only donate usable items, since charity shops spend heavily disposing of what they cannot sell, and never leave goods outside closed shops. Take old electronics, batteries, paint and chemicals to council e-waste points or collection days, not the household bin. Wipe your personal data from old phones and computers first.

sections.key: Keep the best few sentimental items and let photos hold the memories of the rest.
sections.b:
A box of your children's drawings, your grandmother's tea set or decades of birthday cards can feel impossible to sort, because they are not really about the objects. They are about people and moments.

Some strategies help. Choose the very best examples and display or store them properly, so they are honoured rather than buried in a cupboard. Photograph items you want to remember but do not need to keep, such as artwork or bulky souvenirs. Remind yourself that the memory lives in you, not in the object, and that letting go of an item is not letting go of a person.

Give yourself permission to come back later. You do not need to make every sentimental decision in one sitting.

sections.key: Give everything a home, store things by how often you use them, and declutter before you buy storage.
sections.b:
Once you have cleared the excess, organising is far easier because you are arranging fewer things. The golden rule is that everything needs a home: a specific place it lives and returns to. Store things where you use them, and by how often you use them. Daily items belong at waist to eye height, while the Christmas decorations can live on the highest shelf.

Group similar items together so you can see what you have and avoid buying duplicates. Clear containers and labels help everyone find things and put them back. Use vertical space with shelves and hooks. And resist buying storage before decluttering. New containers often just let you keep more clutter, more neatly hidden.

sections.key: Small daily habits, such as a nightly reset and one in, one out, stop clutter creeping back.
sections.b:
A tidy home is not a one-off project. It is a set of small habits. Try a ten minute reset each evening, putting things back in their homes so you wake to a clear kitchen and lounge.

Use a one in, one out rule for categories that tend to grow, such as clothes, shoes, mugs and toys: when something new arrives, something old leaves. Deal with paper as soon as it arrives, recycling junk mail straight away and keeping a single spot for bills and letters that need action.

Pause before buying, perhaps waiting a day or two on non-essential purchases, and ask where the item will live. Keep a donation bag in a wardrobe so letting go is easy. Revisit problem areas every few months.

quiz.q: What is the endowment effect?
o: Buying more of an item when prices fall
Valuing things more because we own them
Forgetting what we already own
Preferring new things to old things
quiz.e: This pull is one reason clutter builds up, and it is normal rather than a character flaw.

quiz.q: What is the most important step after sorting with the four box method?
o: Storing the boxes in the hallway
Sorting everything a second time
Moving the other boxes out promptly
Buying new storage containers
quiz.e: A box of donations left in the hallway for months is just clutter moved from room to room.

quiz.q: How can you honour a sentimental item you do not need to keep?
o: Photograph it, as the memory lives in you
Keep it hidden in a box just in case
Throw it out without a second thought
Keep every item, however many there are
quiz.e: Letting go of an item is not letting go of a person.

quiz.q: Where should everyday items be stored?
o: On the highest shelf in the house
In a box out in the garage
At waist to eye height
Wherever there happens to be space
quiz.e: Store by how often you use things, so daily items are easy to reach and rarely used ones go up high.

quiz.q: What does the one in, one out rule mean?
o: Only one person can tidy at a time
Clean one room each day of the week
Buy one storage box for each room
A new arrival means an old item leaves
quiz.e: It keeps the flow of things into your home balanced with the flow out.

LESSONS.push: Why a mug you never use stays, and what that says about how we value things.

LESSONS.title: Doing your own tax return, step by step
LESSONS.hook: Every year millions of Australians lodge a tax return from their couch in under an hour. Here is how to do it calmly, claim what you are entitled to, and keep the records that protect you if the ATO comes asking.

sections.key: A self-lodged tax return is generally due by 31 October, but wait until your income statement is marked 'tax ready'.
sections.b:
The Australian financial year runs from 1 July to 30 June. If you lodge your own return, it is generally due by 31 October. A registered tax agent can often give you extra time, provided you are on their books before that date.

Don't rush in on 1 July. Your employer, bank and health fund are still sending their information to the ATO. Wait until your income statement in myGov is marked 'tax ready', usually late July or August, and most of your details will be waiting for you. This lesson is general information, not tax advice, so check your situation at ato.gov.au.

sections.key: myTax pre-fills much of your return, but you should check every figure against your own records.
sections.b:
The simplest way to lodge is myTax, the ATO's free online return. Create a myGov account, then link the ATO as a service. You prove who you are with questions about a past notice of assessment, your bank account or a payment summary, or with a digital ID. Turn on two-step sign-in and never share your login.

Salary, tax withheld, bank interest and health insurance details then fill in automatically. Treat that as a starting point, not a guarantee. Compare it with your payslips and add anything missing: a second job, side hustle, dividends or foreign income. The ATO matches data from many sources, so omissions are often caught later, with interest and penalties.

sections.key: You can claim a work expense only if you paid for it, it directly relates to earning your income, and you have a record.
sections.b:
Deductions reduce your taxable income, so it is tempting to be generous. The ATO's rules boil down to three tests. First, you spent the money yourself and were not reimbursed. Second, the expense relates directly to earning your income, not private life. Third, you have a record to prove it.

If something is partly for work and partly personal, like a phone or laptop, you can claim only the work share. Ordinary commuting, everyday clothes and childcare are generally not deductible. The ATO publishes occupation guides, from nurses to tradies, spelling out what people in each job can usually claim.

sections.key: Keep digital records as you go, and hold them for five years from the day you lodge.
sections.b:
The best time to organise tax records is the moment you buy something, not the following October. Photograph each work receipt into one folder, or use the free myDeductions tool in the ATO app. It lets you snap receipts and log car trips and expenses through the year, then upload them to myTax.

Generally you must keep records for five years from the date you lodge. For working from home, the ATO expects evidence of the hours you actually worked, such as a timesheet, roster or diary, not a rough guess made up at year's end. The methods and rates are reviewed from time to time, so check the current rules.

sections.key: Read your notice of assessment line by line, and fix any mistake by amending the return.
sections.b:
When you submit, myTax shows an estimate of your refund or the amount you owe. The ATO then issues a notice of assessment in your myGov inbox. Read it rather than just checking the bottom line. It shows your taxable income, the tax on it, any Medicare levy, study loan repayments and credits for tax withheld. If you owe money and can't pay by the due date, contact the ATO early, as they can often arrange a payment plan.

If you find an error, you can amend through myTax, usually within two years of your notice of assessment. For complex affairs, a registered agent can be worth the fee, and you can check one on the Tax Practitioners Board register at tpb.gov.au. You, not the agent, are responsible for what your return says.

quiz.q: If you lodge your own tax return, when is it generally due?
o: 30 June
31 August
31 October
31 December
quiz.e: A self-lodged return is generally due by 31 October, though waiting for 'tax ready' data makes lodging easier.

quiz.q: Why should you check prefilled figures in myTax before lodging?
o: Prefill can miss income or contain errors
The ATO charges for each change
Prefill is always accurate, so checking is optional
Only payslips need to be checked, not bank records
quiz.e: Prefill is a starting point, and left-out income is often caught later with interest and penalties.

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of the three tests for claiming a work deduction?
o: You spent the money and were not reimbursed
The expense directly relates to earning your income
You have a record to prove it
The item cost more than a set minimum amount
quiz.e: The tests are about who paid, the link to earning income, and having a record, not a minimum cost.

quiz.q: Generally, how long should you keep your tax records?
o: One year from purchase
Until you receive your refund
Ten years from purchase
Five years from when you lodge
quiz.e: Records are generally kept for five years from the date you lodge, and storing them digitally as you go makes that easy.

quiz.q: Where can you check that a tax agent is registered?
o: The Fair Work Ombudsman
The Tax Practitioners Board
Services Australia
The agent's own website
quiz.e: The Tax Practitioners Board register is the official check, and you remain responsible for your return either way.

LESSONS.push: Most of your tax return fills itself in. The risk sits in what it leaves out.

LESSONS.title: Super housekeeping: find, combine and check your fund
LESSONS.hook: Many Australians have super scattered across funds they barely remember, each quietly charging fees. A once-a-year check-up can tidy it up, but there are traps to look out for before you hit 'combine'.

sections.key: Old super accounts keep charging fees, so it pays to find them even though stapling now slows new duplicates.
sections.b:
Picture someone who worked at a café, then a retail chain, then an office. Before the rules changed, each employer could open a new default super account. Each one may charge administration and investment fees, and sometimes insurance premiums, nibbling at small balances.

Since late 2021, stapling means your existing fund generally follows you to a new job unless you choose otherwise. But old accounts don't vanish by themselves. The quickest way to see them all is myGov, with the ATO linked: it lists every account in your name, plus lost super and unclaimed super held by the ATO. This is general information, not financial advice.

sections.key: Rolling an account into another fund normally ends its insurance, so compare cover before you combine.
sections.b:
This is the trap that catches people. Many super accounts include default insurance: cover if you die or become totally and permanently disabled, and sometimes income protection. When you roll an account into another fund, the old cover normally ends. If your health has changed since you joined, you may struggle to get equivalent cover elsewhere.

Before consolidating, download the insurance details for each account and compare the type of cover, the amounts and the cost. Cover in an account that has stopped receiving contributions can also be switched off after a period of inactivity unless you ask to keep it. Decide deliberately, rather than letting a rollover decide for you.

sections.key: Some accounts are worth keeping, and once you choose, consolidating through myGov is free and simple.
sections.b:
Defined benefit funds, common in older public sector and some corporate schemes, calculate your benefit by formula rather than balance, so leaving can mean giving up valuable entitlements. Some employers also pay into a specific fund with cheaper fees or tailored insurance. Funds can no longer charge exit fees, but investments may be sold and re-bought during a transfer, and your money can be out of the market for a few days.

Once you have chosen a fund, select the accounts and the receiving fund in myGov, and the request is sent electronically. Transfers take days to weeks. Check that old accounts show zero, tell your employer which fund to use, and avoid anyone charging to 'find your lost super'. The official tools are free.

sections.key: Compare funds on long-term net returns after fees, using the ATO's YourSuper tool.
sections.b:
A single account is tidy, but it should also be a good one. The ATO's YourSuper comparison tool ranks MySuper products, the default options most people are in, by fees and net returns over several years.

Under the annual performance test, products that underperform a benchmark must write to their members to say so, and repeat failures can be closed to new members. If you get one of those letters, take it seriously.

Compare long-term returns after fees, not one good year, and check that the investment mix suits how long you have until retirement. Fees that look small as a percentage can add up to a large sum over decades, thanks to the same compounding that grows your balance.

sections.key: Super does not automatically follow your will, so nominate beneficiaries and review your super yearly.
sections.b:
Super is generally held in trust, so it does not automatically follow your will. Most funds let you nominate who receives your balance and any insurance payout if you die. A valid binding nomination generally directs the trustee to pay the people you name, while a non-binding one is only a guide.

Some binding nominations lapse after a set period unless renewed, and marriage, separation or a new child can make an old nomination wrong. Set a yearly reminder to check contributions, fees, insurance, investment option and beneficiaries. Moneysmart.gov.au has plain-language guides to every step.

quiz.q: What does 'stapling' mean in Australian super?
o: Your existing fund generally follows you to a new job
The government merges all your accounts
You must change funds with every job
Your employer picks a new fund each year
quiz.e: Stapling keeps your existing fund with you, which slows the creation of duplicate accounts.

quiz.q: What is a key risk of rolling an old super account into another fund?
o: Your tax file number is cancelled
Its insurance normally ends
You lose access to myGov
Your employer stops paying super
quiz.e: Cover in the old account normally ends on rollover, so compare insurance before you combine.

quiz.q: Why might someone keep a defined benefit fund rather than roll it over?
o: It always charges the lowest possible fees
It cannot be seen or found in myGov at all
The benefit uses a formula that can be valuable
It pays the highest interest rate on savings
quiz.e: A formula-based benefit can be worth more than the account balance, so leaving may mean giving it up.

quiz.q: What must happen when a MySuper product fails the annual performance test?
o: The ATO refunds all fees
The fund must notify its members
Members are automatically moved
Nothing, it is just kept private
quiz.e: Underperforming products must notify members, and repeat failures can be closed to new members.

quiz.q: Why is a beneficiary nomination important?
o: It lowers your fees
It increases your insurance
It is needed to make contributions
Super may not follow your will
quiz.e: Super is held in trust, so a valid nomination guides who receives it if you die.

LESSONS.push: You may own super accounts you've forgotten, and they may be quietly costing you.

LESSONS.title: Switching providers: beating the loyalty tax
LESSONS.hook: Staying with the same provider for years can quietly cost you. A little comparison, a phone call and a calendar reminder can trim your household bills without changing how you live.

sections.key: Long-term customers often pay more than new ones, so check your deals once a year.
sections.b:
Picture two neighbours with identical houses and habits. One signed up with an energy retailer a decade ago and never looked again. The other compares plans each year. The first often pays noticeably more, because a discount expired or cheaper plans arrived that they never moved to. This pattern, sometimes called the loyalty tax, shows up across energy, phone, internet and insurance. Providers rely on inertia.

The fix is not constant switching. Choose one month, perhaps around tax time, and review every regular bill in a single sitting. Start with your latest bills: usage, daily supply charge, rates, any time-of-use pricing and your solar feed-in tariff.

sections.key: Use the free government comparison sites, and look past headline discounts.
sections.b:
For electricity and gas, use free government comparison sites rather than commercial ones that may be paid by retailers. In New South Wales, Queensland, South Australia, Tasmania and the ACT, the Australian Energy Regulator runs Energy Made Easy at energymadeeasy.gov.au. In Victoria, use Victorian Energy Compare. Western Australia and the Northern Territory have different market arrangements, with fewer choices in many areas.

Enter your usage or upload a bill to see plans at your address. In many states retailers must show how offers compare with a government reference price. Look past headline discounts: conditional discounts that vanish if you pay late can make a plan dearer than it looks.

sections.key: Switching is usually painless, and you should match phone and internet plans to what you actually use.
sections.b:
Changing energy retailers usually involves no physical work. The same poles, wires and meter supply you, and only the company billing you changes. The new retailer arranges the transfer. Check for exit fees and contract end dates. You can usually keep your mobile number, and month-to-month plans leave you free to go. Sometimes just telling your provider you are thinking of leaving gets you a better plan.

Many people pay for more mobile data or home internet speed than they use. Check your usage in your provider's app, then choose a plan with a modest buffer. On the NBN, typical evening speeds matter more than maximums. Cancel streaming services and subscriptions you no longer use.

sections.key: If paying bills is hard, ask early for the hardship team, and check what concessions you can get.
sections.b:
If paying bills is becoming hard, act before disconnection notices arrive. Energy retailers must have hardship programs, which can include payment plans, advice on cutting usage and protection from disconnection while you take part. Telcos have financial hardship policies too. Ask for the hardship team by name.

State and territory governments offer energy concessions and rebates to eligible people, such as pensioners, healthcare card holders and some low-income households. These are not always applied automatically, so check your state government's website. Services Australia can tell you which cards and payments you may qualify for. The free National Debt Helpline, on 1800 007 007, connects you with a financial counsellor who can negotiate with providers for you.

sections.key: Complain to the provider first, then take unresolved problems to the free ombudsman.
sections.b:
Billing errors, surprise fees and botched transfers do happen. Contact the provider, explain the problem clearly and ask for a complaint reference number. Keep notes of every call, including the date and the name of the person you spoke with.

If the problem isn't fixed, you can go to an independent ombudsman for free. For phone and internet, that is the Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman. For energy and water, most states have their own energy and water ombudsman scheme, so check which applies in your state. Ombudsmen can investigate and, in many cases, require providers to fix the problem or pay compensation. This is general information; check moneysmart.gov.au and your state's consumer affairs website.

quiz.q: What does the 'loyalty tax' refer to?
o: A government tax on long-term customers
A fee charged for switching providers
Loyal customers often paying more than new ones
A discount for staying with one provider
quiz.e: Providers rely on inertia, so a yearly check keeps you off outdated, pricier plans.

quiz.q: Which site does the Australian Energy Regulator run for comparing energy plans in several states?
o: Victorian Energy Compare
Energy Made Easy
myGov
YourSuper
quiz.e: Energy Made Easy is a free government comparison site, unlike commercial sites that may be paid by retailers.

quiz.q: What usually happens physically when you switch electricity retailer?
o: A new meter must be installed
Your power is cut off for a day
Nothing, only the billing company changes
An electrician must visit to reconnect you
quiz.e: The poles, wires and meter stay the same, so switching is usually painless.

quiz.q: If you are struggling to pay an energy bill, what should you ask for?
o: The retailer's hardship team
A new meter
A higher discount on late payments
To be disconnected
quiz.e: Hardship programs can include payment plans and protection from disconnection, and asking early gives you more options.

quiz.q: Where can you take an unresolved phone or internet complaint for free?
o: The Australian Financial Complaints Authority
The Australian Taxation Office
The Fair Work Ombudsman
The Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman
quiz.e: Complain to the provider first, then escalate to the free, independent ombudsman.

LESSONS.push: Two identical homes, two very different bills. The gap has a name.

LESSONS.title: Making an insurance claim that sticks
LESSONS.hook: You pay premiums for years hoping you never need them. When something finally goes wrong, how you handle the first days of a claim can make a real difference to the outcome.

sections.key: Know your policy, sum insured and excess before you need to claim, because underinsurance is common.
sections.b:
The best time to prepare for a claim is a quiet weekday, long before a storm or break-in. Download your product disclosure statement, the long document that sets out what your policy covers, and read the sections on exclusions and how claims work.

Check your sum insured for home and contents. Underinsurance is common, because people guess the value of their belongings and fall well short. Many insurers offer online calculators for rebuilding or replacement costs. Film each room and store the video in the cloud, along with receipts for expensive items. Note your excess, the amount you pay towards each claim. This is general information, not advice; read your own policy.

sections.key: Prevent further damage if it is safe, and photograph everything before you clean up.
sections.b:
Imagine coming home to water pouring through the ceiling. Safety comes first: turn off water or power if it is safe, and call emergency services if anyone is in danger. Policies generally expect reasonable steps to prevent further damage, such as a tarp or an emergency plumber, and those costs are often covered.

Before you throw anything away, photograph and film the damage, including serial numbers and brand labels. Keep damaged items until the insurer says you may dispose of them. After a car crash, exchange names, contact details, registrations and insurer details, photograph the scene, collect witness details and don't admit fault, as that is for insurers to work out. Report theft to police and record the event number.

sections.key: Notify your insurer promptly, keep a written log, and be completely honest.
sections.b:
Contact your insurer as soon as practical, through their app, website or claims line. Delays can complicate a claim, especially if damage worsens. You will receive a claim number; write it on every document and email.

Start a simple claim log on paper or in a notes app. Record the date and time of every call, who you spoke to and what was agreed. Follow up important calls with a short email confirming what was said.

Be honest and accurate in everything you tell the insurer. Exaggerating a claim, even slightly, can give the insurer grounds to refuse it or cancel your policy, and it can have serious legal consequences.

sections.key: You can get your own quotes, and a cash settlement usually ends the insurer's responsibility for repairs.
sections.b:
For larger claims, the insurer may send an assessor or ask for quotes from builders. You can generally supply your own quotes, and it is reasonable to ask for a copy of the assessor's report.

Insurers may offer to manage repairs through their own builders, or offer a cash settlement. Cash can seem attractive, but check that it would cover the real cost of fixing the damage with a licensed tradesperson. Once you accept it, the insurer usually has no further responsibility for the repairs. Ask how the figure was calculated. Keep receipts for temporary accommodation and emergency costs, as some policies cover these up to a limit.

sections.key: Ask for decisions in writing with reasons, then complain internally before going to AFCA.
sections.b:
Insurers that subscribe to the General Insurance Code of Practice commit to keeping you updated, deciding within set timeframes and explaining their reasons. If your claim is denied, ask in writing for the decision, the policy wording relied on and any reports used. Sometimes a refusal rests on a misunderstanding that extra evidence, like a receipt or tradesperson's report, can fix.

If you still disagree, make a formal written complaint, use the word 'complaint', and say what outcome you want. Most complaints should get a response within about 30 calendar days. If you are unhappy or hear nothing, lodge a complaint with the Australian Financial Complaints Authority at afca.org.au. It is free for consumers and independent of insurers, and its decisions can bind the insurer.

quiz.q: Why is it worth checking your sum insured before anything goes wrong?
o: It lowers your excess automatically
Underinsurance is common and costly
It cancels policy exclusions
It is needed to lodge a tax return
quiz.e: People often guess their belongings' value and fall short, so checking in advance avoids a nasty surprise.

quiz.q: What should you do before throwing away damaged items?
o: Nothing, throw them out quickly
Sell them online to recoup some money
Repair them yourself before photographing
Photograph them and wait for the insurer's OK
quiz.e: Evidence and damaged items let the insurer assess the claim, so document first and discard later.

quiz.q: Why is exaggerating a claim, even slightly, a bad idea?
o: It can lead to a refused claim or cancelled policy
It only delays the payment by some weeks
It lowers your excess on later claims
It is overlooked if you keep a claim log
quiz.e: Honesty protects both your claim and your policy, and a log keeps your account accurate.

quiz.q: What is a risk of accepting a cash settlement?
o: You must pay tax on all of it at once
Your excess doubles on future claims
The insurer usually owes no further repairs
All your other policies are cancelled
quiz.e: Check the amount covers the real repair cost first, because accepting usually ends the insurer's obligation.

quiz.q: Where can you take an insurance dispute after the insurer's internal process?
o: The Fair Work Ombudsman
The Tax Practitioners Board
The Australian Taxation Office
The Financial Complaints Authority
quiz.e: AFCA, the Australian Financial Complaints Authority, is free for consumers and independent of insurers, and it follows a written internal complaint.

LESSONS.push: What you do in the first hours after damage can decide how a claim ends.

LESSONS.title: Comparing loans: the real cost of borrowing
LESSONS.hook: The interest rate in the ad is only part of the story. Fees, terms, balloon payments and add-ons can turn a cheap-looking loan into an expensive one. Here is how to read the numbers like a lender.

sections.key: Compare loans by the total amount repayable, because the headline rate ignores fees.
sections.b:
Two car loans are advertised side by side. One has a lower rate; the other has no upfront fee. Which is cheaper? You can't tell from the rates alone. True cost is interest plus every fee: establishment, monthly account, early repayment and late fees. The most useful single number is the total you will repay over the life of the loan. Ask lenders for it directly.

Lenders advertising rates on many consumer loans must show a comparison rate, which rolls most fees into one percentage. But it is based on a standard example loan. If yours is smaller or shorter, fixed fees weigh more and your real cost can be higher. It also excludes some costs, such as late fees. Treat it as a guide. This is general information, not credit advice.

sections.key: Secured loans usually cost less but put an asset at risk, and fixed rates trade flexibility for certainty.
sections.b:
A secured loan uses an asset, often the car you are buying, as security, so the lender can repossess it if you default. Because the lender's risk is lower, secured loans generally have lower rates than unsecured ones.

A fixed rate stays the same for the term, which makes budgeting easy, but fixed loans often charge break costs or limit extra repayments. A variable rate can rise or fall, but variable loans frequently allow extra repayments without penalty, which can save significant interest if you plan to pay off early.

Ask each lender three questions: can I make extra repayments, can I pay out the loan early, and what will each cost? The answers can matter as much as the rate.

sections.key: Smaller repayments from longer terms or balloon payments usually mean more interest overall.
sections.b:
Lenders and car dealers advertise the weekly repayment, because it feels affordable. Two common ways to shrink it are a longer term and a balloon payment. A balloon, also called a residual, is a large lump sum due at the end of the loan.

Because part of the debt is pushed to the end, you pay interest on a bigger balance for longer, so the total cost rises. When the balloon falls due, you need the cash, or must refinance, or sell the car, which may by then be worth less than you owe. Longer terms work the same way: smaller repayments, more total interest. Always compare loans on total cost, not the weekly repayment.

sections.key: Get your own quote before accepting dealer finance, and question any add-on insurance.
sections.b:
Car yards and big retailers often offer finance on the spot. It is convenient, but easy to focus on the car and skip comparing. Get pre-approval or a quote from your own bank or credit union before you shop. It gives you a benchmark and strengthens your hand.

Watch for add-ons bundled into the loan, such as gap insurance, extended warranties or loan protection insurance. Sold this way, they have historically been poor value for many buyers, and when financed you pay interest on them too. Recent rules restrict how some add-on insurance can be sold, including a deferred sales period, but you can still simply say no. Ask for the price of the car and the loan separately.

sections.key: Lenders must check a loan is not unsuitable, and you should compare offers side by side before deciding.
sections.b:
Under responsible lending laws, licensed lenders must make reasonable inquiries about your income, expenses and needs, and must not offer an unsuitable loan, such as one you could repay only with substantial hardship. Be truthful. Each formal application is usually recorded on your credit report, so ask about eligibility checks first. Avoid payday lenders where possible. People on low incomes may qualify for the No Interest Loan Scheme.

For each offer, write down the amount, term, rate, comparison rate, every fee, extra-repayment rules and any balloon, plus the total repayable. Ask whether you could cope if income fell or rates rose. Then sleep on it: 'today only' pressure is a warning sign.

quiz.q: When might your real cost be higher than the comparison rate suggests?
o: When you make every single repayment on time
When your loan is smaller or shorter than the example
When the loan carries no fees of any kind at all
When the interest rate is variable, not fixed
quiz.e: The comparison rate uses a standard example loan, so a smaller or shorter loan can cost more than it shows.

quiz.q: Why do secured loans generally have lower rates than unsecured ones?
o: An asset backs it, lowering the lender's risk
They never carry any establishment fees
They are always fixed rate loans for the term
Government schemes subsidise the interest
quiz.e: Security lowers the lender's risk, but it means you could lose the asset if you default.

quiz.q: What is a balloon payment?
o: A monthly account fee charged by the lender
A refund paid out at the end of the loan
A large lump sum due at the end of the loan
A penalty charged for paying the loan early
quiz.e: Balloons shrink repayments but raise total interest, and the lump sum still has to be found later.

quiz.q: What is a smart step before accepting car yard finance?
o: Accept the add-ons to secure the deal
Sign the same day to lock in the deal
Judge it by the weekly repayment alone
Get your own quote or pre-approval first
quiz.e: A benchmark from your own bank lets you judge whether the dealer's offer is actually good.

quiz.q: Under responsible lending laws, what must licensed lenders do?
o: Approve every application that meets a minimum
Make reasonable inquiries about your situation
Offer the lowest rate available in the market
Avoid looking at your credit report
quiz.e: Lenders must check your income, expenses and needs, which is why truthful applications protect you.
