LESSONS.hook: Within a generation of 1788, visitors noticed that children in the colony sounded different. Here is how a new way of speaking English took shape.

sections.key: The Australian accent formed surprisingly quickly among the first colonial children.
sections.b:
The First Fleet that arrived in 1788 carried people from all over Britain and Ireland: Londoners, rural English, Irish convicts, Scots and more. Their parents spoke a jumble of dialects. But children growing up together in Sydney did what children everywhere do: they copied each other more than their parents.

By the 1820s, visitors were already remarking that native born children, sometimes called currency lads and lasses, spoke differently. Linguists call this dialect levelling. When many accents mix, the strongest regional quirks tend to drop out and a new shared accent emerges. That is why Australian English is fairly uniform across a huge continent.

sections.key: Many everyday Australian words were borrowed from Aboriginal languages.
sections.b:
When Captain Cook's expedition was stranded near what is now Cooktown in 1770, the crew recorded a word that sounded like 'kangaroo' from the local Guugu Yimithirr people. It became one of the most famous loanwords in the world. After 1788, settlers in Sydney borrowed more words from the Dharug language, including 'dingo', 'wombat' and 'koala'. 'Boomerang' also came from a Sydney area language, and 'billabong' is thought to come from Wiradjuri.

Hundreds of Australian place names, from Wagga Wagga to Kakadu, have Aboriginal origins too. Before colonisation there were around 250 Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander languages, many with several dialects. Many are now endangered, and communities are working to revive them.

sections.key: Australians shorten words and add 'o' or 'ie', and it signals friendliness, not laziness.
sections.b:
Ask an Aussie what they did this arvo and you might hear that they stopped at the servo, grabbed a sanga and caught up with a rello. Australian English is famous for diminutives: shortened words with an ending added. The two big endings are 'ie' or 'y', as in 'brekkie', 'barbie' and 'sunnies', and 'o', as in 'arvo', 'ambo', 'smoko' and 'bottle-o'. There are a great many of these forms.

Despite the stereotype, they are not about laziness. Research suggests they often signal friendliness, informality and shared identity. Notice how 'ambo' sounds warmer than 'paramedic'.

sections.key: Classic expressions often have surprising origins, and Australian accents vary along a spectrum more than by region.
sections.b:
'Dinkum' appears in English regional speech in the 1800s, where it seems to have meant work or a fair share of work. In Australia it came to mean genuine, and 'fair dinkum' became a catchphrase. A popular story says it comes from Chinese miners saying 'ding kum' for real gold, but there is no good evidence for this.

In the 1960s, linguists Alexander Mitchell and Arthur Delbridge recorded thousands of school students and described three broad accent types. 'Broad' is the stereotypical outback sound, heard in the voice of Steve Irwin. 'Cultivated' is closer to British pronunciation and was once common among radio announcers. 'General', in between, is what most Australians speak. These are points on a scale, and cultivated has become much rarer.

sections.key: Vocabulary differs by state, and the idea that Australians mumble to keep out flies is a myth.
sections.b:
Accents are fairly uniform, but vocabulary is another story. What you wear to the beach depends on your state: 'bathers' is common in Victoria, South Australia and Western Australia, 'togs' in Queensland, and 'swimmers' or 'cossie' in New South Wales. A slice of fried potato in batter is a 'potato cake' in Melbourne and a 'potato scallop' in Sydney. Processed sandwich meat is 'devon', 'fritz', 'polony' or 'Belgium sausage' depending on where you grew up.

An old myth says Australians speak with half closed mouths to keep out flies, or that the accent comes from lazy or drunk convicts. Linguists reject this. Every accent is the result of speech drifting over time. Australian English sits alongside British, American and Indian English as a major variety. A humorous 1965 book, Let Stalk Strine, popularised the jokey name 'Strine'.

quiz.q: Why did a distinct Australian accent form so quickly?
o: Convicts deliberately invented a secret accent for privacy
Children copied each other, not their parents' dialects
The settlers brought one shared accent over from Britain
Aboriginal languages replaced English pronunciation
quiz.e: Mixed accents level out when children grow up together, leaving a shared new accent.

quiz.q: Which Australian word came from the Guugu Yimithirr people?
o: Kangaroo
Dingo
Wombat
Billabong
quiz.e: The word recorded near Cooktown in 1770 became one of the world's best-known loanwords.

quiz.q: What do words like 'arvo' and 'brekkie' usually signal?
o: Laziness and careless speech habits
A formal, official style of language
A lack of education among speakers
Friendliness, informality and identity
quiz.e: Diminutives often mark a relaxed, warm relationship between speakers.

quiz.q: What is the likely truth about the origin of 'fair dinkum'?
o: It comes from a Chinese miners' phrase for real gold
It was invented by advertisers in the 1960s
It probably comes from a British dialect word
It comes from a Dharug word for honest
quiz.e: The popular 'ding kum' story has no good evidence behind it.

quiz.q: What explains the 'half closed mouth' idea about the Australian accent?
o: It is true, and it began with the first convicts
It is a myth; the accent came from ordinary sound change
It is caused by the heat and flies of the climate
It was recorded by linguists in the 1960s
quiz.e: Australian English follows the same rules of sound change as any other variety.

LESSONS.push: Within a generation of 1788, visitors noticed colonial children sounded different. Why?

LESSONS.title: The secret history of punctuation
LESSONS.hook: Ancient Romans wrote without spaces, commas or full stops. The marks we now take for granted were invented one by one, often by monks and printers.

sections.key: Ancient Greek and Latin were usually written as one unbroken stream of letters.
sections.b:
Imagine reading a book where every line looked like THISISHOWMOSTANCIENTTEXTSLOOKED. Much ancient Greek and Latin was written like this, which scholars call scriptio continua. There were no spaces between words, no lower case letters and very little punctuation. It worked because reading was usually done aloud, often by trained readers who prepared a text in advance, much as an actor studies a script.

The reader worked out where words and sentences broke by sounding them out. To us it seems maddening, but to a skilled Roman reader it was normal. Punctuation, as we know it, began as helpful notes for performers, telling them where to pause and breathe.

sections.key: Dots at different heights marked pauses, and early medieval monks gave us spaces between words.
sections.b:
Around 200 BCE, Aristophanes of Byzantium, who worked at the great library in Alexandria, is credited with a simple system. He placed dots at different heights beside the text. A low dot marked a short pause, a middle dot a slightly longer one and a high dot the end of a complete thought. The short section was a 'komma', Greek for a piece cut off, and the complete thought was a 'periodos', a full circuit. Those words became our comma and period. Many writers ignored the system.

The space between words may be the most important mark of all. From around the 7th century, Irish and Anglo-Saxon scribes copying Latin began leaving gaps, because Latin was foreign to them and spaces made it easier to read. Spaces also helped make silent reading more common.

sections.key: Venetian printers gave us the semicolon, and printing house style became many of our rules.
sections.b:
When printing spread across Europe in the late 1400s, punctuation became more consistent, because thousands of copies came from the same set of type. One of the most influential printers was Aldus Manutius in Venice. In the 1490s his press printed a work by the scholar Pietro Bembo that used the semicolon, a mark that became popular across Europe. Aldus is also associated with italic type and with the elegant small books that were the paperbacks of their day.

Printers needed rules so that compositors setting type would make the same choices, and over time they settled on many conventions we still follow. Much of what we call correct punctuation began as a printing house's house style.

sections.key: The apostrophe arrived in English in the 1500s and has caused confusion ever since.
sections.b:
The apostrophe came into English in the 16th century, borrowed from French and Italian printing, where it marked missing letters, as in 'don't' for 'do not'. Its use for possession, as in 'the dog's bone', developed gradually and was not fully settled until around the 1700s and 1800s.

Even then, awkward exceptions remained, such as 'its' for possession and 'it's' for 'it is', which still trip up careful writers. The so-called greengrocer's apostrophe, as in 'banana's $3 a kilo', is a much mocked error, but it shows how slippery the rules are. Some place names have dropped the apostrophe altogether, and Australian naming authorities generally prefer place names without it, as in Kings Cross.

sections.key: New marks spread only when many people adopt them at once, and texting is giving old marks new meanings.
sections.b:
In 1962, American advertising executive Martin Speckter proposed the interrobang, a question mark and exclamation mark merged into one symbol, for startled questions such as 'You did what?' It had brief fame and appeared on some typewriters, but never entered everyday writing. Punctuation spreads only when many writers, printers and readers adopt it together, so the core marks have changed little in centuries.

Send a friend a text that says 'Fine.' and they may worry you are upset. In casual messaging, the full stop at the end of a short message can look deliberate, and some research suggests readers find such messages less sincere. Exclamation marks often signal warmth. This is not decline. It is punctuation adapting to make meaning clear.

quiz.q: Why could ancient texts be written without spaces or punctuation?
o: Ancient readers could not read very quickly
Spaces had not been invented as a concept in any language
Writers did not care whether anyone could read it
Reading was usually aloud, by trained readers
quiz.e: Early punctuation began as notes to help performers know when to pause.

quiz.q: What was the purpose of the dots at different heights?
o: They separated words from each other
They showed which words were borrowed
They marked pauses of different lengths
They marked questions and exclamations
quiz.e: The names 'komma' and 'periodos' became our comma and period.

quiz.q: What was the effect of adding spaces between words?
o: It made manuscripts longer and harder to copy
It made text easier to read and silent reading common
It made reading aloud more necessary
It had no effect until the invention of print
quiz.e: Spaces meant readers no longer needed to sound out text to find the words.

quiz.q: Why did punctuation become more consistent after the late 1400s?
o: Printers needed fixed rules for identical copies
Governments passed laws about punctuation
Scribes were banned from copying books
Schools began teaching punctuation rules
quiz.e: Many conventions we call correct began as printing house style.

quiz.q: Why have new punctuation marks like the interrobang rarely caught on?
o: Publishers refused to print them
They were too hard to type on keyboards
Readers prefer text without punctuation
Many writers must adopt them at once
quiz.e: Marks succeed through widespread adoption, which is hard to arrange.

LESSONS.push: Ancient Romans read aloud for a reason. The marks we use today began as stage directions.

LESSONS.title: How the detective story was invented
LESSONS.hook: From a murder in a Paris apartment to Sherlock Holmes and Agatha Christie, the whodunnit has a surprisingly short and lively history.

sections.key: Edgar Allan Poe set the pattern for the detective story in 1841 with 'The Murders in the Rue Morgue'.
sections.b: In 1841, the American writer Edgar Allan Poe published 'The Murders in the Rue Morgue'. Two women are found brutally killed in a Paris apartment that seems impossible to enter or leave. The police are baffled. Then an eccentric amateur, C. Auguste Dupin, solves the case by pure reasoning, noticing clues everyone else missed. The answer is famously bizarre: an escaped orangutan. Poe wrote only three Dupin stories, but they set the pattern. There is a brilliant, slightly odd detective, a less clever friend who narrates, a puzzling crime and a final explanation that makes everything click. Almost every fictional detective since owes something to Dupin.

sections.key: Detective fiction rose alongside modern police forces, crowded cities and a faith in careful observation.
sections.b: It is no accident that detective stories appeared in the 1800s. London's Metropolitan Police was founded in 1829, and in 1842 it set up a small detective branch. Big cities were full of strangers, and crime became something to investigate with evidence, not simply punish. Newspapers fed public fascination with real murder cases. At the same time, science was teaching people that careful observation could reveal hidden truths. The fictional detective captured that spirit. He, and later she, was a kind of scientist of crime, bringing order and reason to the chaos of the modern city. Readers found that deeply reassuring, and many still do.

sections.key: Sherlock Holmes became the world's most famous detective, yet a Melbourne novel outsold his first adventure.
sections.b:
In 1887, a young doctor named Arthur Conan Doyle introduced Sherlock Holmes and Dr Watson in A Study in Scarlet. Holmes was partly modelled on Joseph Bell, an Edinburgh medical teacher who could deduce a patient's job from small details. Stories in The Strand Magazine from 1891 made him a sensation. When Doyle killed him off in 1893, readers cancelled their subscriptions, and Holmes returned in 1903.

A year before Holmes appeared, Fergus Hume, a lawyer raised in New Zealand, published The Mystery of a Hansom Cab in Melbourne. It sold far more copies than Doyle's first Holmes novel, though Hume reportedly sold the rights cheaply and saw little profit.

sections.key: Golden Age writers promised readers a fair chance to solve the crime before the detective did.
sections.b:
Between the world wars, the puzzle mystery peaked. Agatha Christie's first novel, The Mysterious Affair at Styles, appeared in 1920 and introduced the Belgian detective Hercule Poirot. Dorothy L. Sayers, Margery Allingham and New Zealand's Ngaio Marsh were also leading writers. Their books often featured country houses, a closed group of suspects and a body in the library.

The central idea was fair play: every clue the detective used had to be shown to the reader too. In 1929 Ronald Knox published a tongue-in-cheek list of rules, including no supernatural forces and no undiscovered poisons. In 1930 many of these writers formed the Detection Club in London, promising to play fair.

sections.key: American hardboiled writers took the detective out of the drawing room, and crime fiction has kept branching since.
sections.b: Not everyone loved tidy country house puzzles. In 1920s and 1930s America, Dashiell Hammett and Raymond Chandler created hardboiled detectives: tough, weary private investigators in corrupt cities like San Francisco and Los Angeles. Their stories were less about clever clues and more about violence, money and moral compromise. Chandler's Philip Marlowe became the model for countless film noir heroes. Since then, crime fiction has split into police procedurals, psychological thrillers, Scandinavian noir and rural Australian crime, from Arthur Upfield to Kerry Greenwood and Jane Harper. Yet the basic appeal remains. A crime throws the world out of balance, and a detective who notices what others miss puts it right.

quiz.q: What basic pattern did Poe's Dupin stories establish for detective fiction?
o: A police chief, a confession and a chase through the city streets
An odd genius, a narrating friend and a puzzle solved by reasoning
A secret society, a stolen treasure and a final duel at dawn
A grieving widow, a haunted house and a ghost who names the killer
quiz.e: Poe's formula of a brilliant detective, a narrating friend and a clever solution still shapes the genre.

quiz.q: Why did detective fiction emerge in the 1800s?
o: Printing had only just been invented and publishers needed new stories
Crime had disappeared, so readers turned to imaginary cases
Governments paid authors to write stories that encouraged obedience
Cities, police and a faith in observation made crime-solving feel modern
quiz.e: Crowded cities, new police detectives and respect for science made the reasoning detective a fitting hero.

quiz.q: What did the success of The Mystery of a Hansom Cab show?
o: A Melbourne crime novel could outsell Holmes's first adventure
Australian readers preferred stories set overseas
Crime fiction could only succeed through magazine serials
Holmes's first novel was an instant bestseller worldwide
quiz.e: Hume's Melbourne-set novel was a huge success in Australia and Britain, outselling Doyle's first Holmes novel.

quiz.q: What did 'fair play' mean for Golden Age mystery writers?
o: The murderer always had to be caught within a single day
The detective had to be a police officer, never an amateur
Every clue the detective used had to be shown to the reader too
The victim had to be someone the reader disliked
quiz.e: Fair play turned the mystery into a game in which a sharp reader could solve the case first.

quiz.q: How did hardboiled crime fiction differ from the country house puzzle?
o: It removed the detective and let the police solve everything
It focused on violence, money and moral compromise in corrupt cities
It was set entirely in small English villages
It gave readers every clue so they could solve the case first
quiz.e: Hammett and Chandler swapped tidy puzzles for weary investigators in morally murky cities.

LESSONS.push: Where did the whodunnit begin? A Paris apartment, and a very odd culprit.

LESSONS.title: The dark origins of fairy tales
LESSONS.hook: Before Disney, Cinderella's stepsisters cut off parts of their feet to fit the slipper. Fairy tales have a long, strange and sometimes gruesome history.

sections.key: Fairy tales began as spoken folk tales, and Cinderella-type stories have been told around the world for well over a thousand years.
sections.b:
Long before anyone wrote them down, fairy tales were told aloud, by grandparents at the fire, by workers passing the time and by nurses to children. They were not just for kids. Adults told tales of clever peasants, cruel stepmothers and magical helpers to entertain each other and pass on lessons. Because the tales lived in memory, they changed with each teller and crossed borders. Folklorists catalogue thousands of tale types in the Aarne-Thompson-Uther index.

Cinderella is a good example. The Greek writer Strabo recorded the story of Rhodopis, whose sandal an eagle dropped in an Egyptian king's lap. A 9th-century Chinese tale tells of Ye Xian, helped by a fish's bones, who loses a golden shoe.

sections.key: Charles Perrault turned folk tales into polished stories with morals for the French court.
sections.b: In 1697, Charles Perrault, a member of the French Academy, published a small book of tales that included 'Cinderella', 'Sleeping Beauty', 'Little Red Riding Hood' and 'Puss in Boots'. He polished folk tales for fashionable readers at the court of Louis XIV, adding wit and ending each tale with a little moral in verse. Perrault gave us the pumpkin coach and the glass slipper. His Red Riding Hood ends badly: the wolf eats her, and no woodcutter arrives. The moral warns young women about smooth-talking men. Earlier, in the 1630s, the Italian writer Giambattista Basile had published his own collection, including early versions of Cinderella and Sleeping Beauty.

sections.key: The Grimms collected German tales to preserve a national culture, but their sources were not simple peasants.
sections.b:
In 1812, the German scholars Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm published the first volume of their Children's and Household Tales. They were language experts who wanted to preserve what they saw as the authentic voice of the German people, at a time when Germany was divided and occupied by Napoleon's France.

Their image of peasants telling ancient tales is a little misleading. Many storytellers were educated, middle-class young women, some of French Huguenot descent, who already knew Perrault's tales. One prized source, Dorothea Viehmann, was a tailor's widow with a vast memory for stories. The brothers revised the collection repeatedly, and the final edition of 1857 held around 200 tales.

sections.key: The Grimms removed sexual hints from later editions but kept the violence that punished wickedness.
sections.b:
The first Grimm edition was not a children's book, and parents complained. So Wilhelm in particular reworked the tales for family reading. Sexual hints went. In the first 'Rapunzel', the witch discovers the prince's visits when Rapunzel innocently remarks that her clothes are getting tight around her waist. Later editions changed this to a harmless slip of the tongue. Evil mothers were often turned into stepmothers, to protect the ideal of motherhood.

Violence mostly stayed, because it punished wickedness. In the Grimms' Cinderella, the stepsisters cut off a toe and a heel to fit the slipper, and at the wedding, birds peck out their eyes.

sections.key: Andersen invented his own melancholy tales, and fairy tales endure because they handle big themes in simple shapes.
sections.b:
Hans Christian Andersen mostly invented new tales, starting in 1835: 'The Little Mermaid', 'The Ugly Duckling', 'The Emperor's New Clothes' and 'The Snow Queen'. In his original 'Little Mermaid', the prince marries someone else. She refuses to kill him to save herself and dissolves into foam, becoming a spirit of the air. Many readers see Andersen's own loneliness in his stories.

Fairy tales keep returning because they deal with growing up, injustice, luck and courage. In 1976 Bruno Bettelheim argued that their frightening parts help children face fears safely, though his ideas are debated. A 2016 study suggested some tales may be thousands of years old, though such estimates are uncertain.

quiz.q: Why do very similar fairy tales appear in many different countries?
o: Every country copied them from one printed book
Travelling merchants sold the same pamphlets everywhere
Spoken tales changed with each teller and crossed borders
Each culture invented identical plots by pure coincidence
quiz.e: Oral tales travelled with people and changed as they were retold, so related versions turn up worldwide.

quiz.q: What did Perrault typically add when he retold folk tales?
o: Wit, polish and a short moral in verse
Long descriptions of the tale's historical setting
Gruesome details to frighten children into obedience
Alternative endings chosen by the reader
quiz.e: Perrault refined folk tales for the French court and closed each with a moral.

quiz.q: How did the Grimms' sources differ from the popular image?
o: They were all illiterate farmers who had never heard printed stories
They were professional actors from travelling theatres
They were children who made up the stories themselves
Many were educated young women who knew Perrault's tales
quiz.e: The Grimms' storytellers often knew printed tales, so the 'pure peasant voice' is partly a myth.

quiz.q: What did later Grimm editions change, and what did they keep?
o: They removed the violence but kept the sexual content
They removed sexual hints but kept most of the violence
They kept both unchanged to stay true to the sources
They removed both and ended every tale happily
quiz.e: Wilhelm cleaned up sexual content for families, but violence stayed because it punished wickedness.

quiz.q: What set Hans Christian Andersen's tales apart from the Grimms'?
o: He translated them word for word from Italian
He wrote only comic tales with cheerful endings
He collected them from German villagers
He mostly invented his own stories
quiz.e: Andersen was an original author, and his tales were often melancholy.

LESSONS.push: Cinderella's story is older than you think, and the slipper wasn't always glass.

LESSONS.title: Frankenstein and the birth of science fiction
LESSONS.hook: A teenager, a stormy summer and a ghost story contest produced one of the most influential novels ever written.

sections.key: Frankenstein began in 1816, when a volcanic eruption's cold, stormy summer trapped young writers indoors.
sections.b:
In April 1815, Mount Tambora in what is now Indonesia exploded in one of the largest eruptions in recorded history. Its ash and gases cooled the global climate, and Europe's 1816 became the year without a summer, with cold, rain and failed harvests. That June, a group of young English writers stayed near Lake Geneva: the poet Lord Byron at the Villa Diodati, and nearby Percy Bysshe Shelley, eighteen-year-old Mary Godwin, her stepsister Claire Clairmont and Byron's doctor, John Polidori. Trapped indoors, they read ghost stories aloud, and Byron proposed that each write one.

Mary struggled for days. Polidori's effort became The Vampyre in 1819, which helped shape the vampire as an elegant aristocrat.

sections.key: Mary Shelley, from a radical family, wrote Frankenstein before she was twenty-one after a vivid waking vision.
sections.b:
After listening to Byron and Percy discuss whether life could be artificially created, Mary had what she later called a waking dream. She pictured a pale student kneeling beside a thing he had put together, watching it stir into life, then fleeing in horror. She described this in an introduction to the 1831 edition, so it is her own account, years later.

Mary was the daughter of two radical thinkers: Mary Wollstonecraft, author of A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, who died shortly after her birth, and the philosopher William Godwin. Frankenstein was published anonymously in January 1818, when she was twenty. Many reviewers assumed the author was a man.

sections.key: The novel drew on real experiments in which electricity made dead tissue move.
sections.b: Frankenstein was not pure fantasy. In the 1780s, the Italian scientist Luigi Galvani made the legs of dead frogs twitch using electricity, which led to the term galvanism. His nephew Giovanni Aldini went further. In London in 1803, he applied electric currents to the body of an executed criminal, making the face grimace and a hand rise, to the alarm of onlookers. Many people wondered whether electricity might be the spark of life itself. Mary Shelley knew about these debates. In the novel, Victor Frankenstein is deliberately vague about his methods, but a scientist using cutting-edge knowledge to cross a forbidden line came straight from the science of her day.

sections.key: In the novel, Frankenstein is the scientist, and the creature is eloquent, lonely and rejected.
sections.b: Anyone who knows Frankenstein only from films may be surprised by the book. First, Frankenstein is the scientist, Victor. The creature is never given a name. Second, he is no grunting brute. Abandoned by his horrified creator, he teaches himself to speak and read by secretly watching a family through a gap in a cottage wall. He reads Milton's Paradise Lost and compares himself to both Adam and Satan. When he confronts Victor, he speaks with great eloquence about his loneliness and the cruelty he has suffered, and asks Victor to make him a companion. Victor's refusal sets off the tragic final events. The real horror of the book is rejection.

sections.key: Frankenstein is often called the first science fiction novel because its monster comes from science, not magic.
sections.b:
Frankenstein grew out of the Gothic tradition of haunted castles, which began with Horace Walpole's The Castle of Otranto in 1764. But Mary Shelley did something new. Her monster was made not by a curse or spell but by a scientist using knowledge and method. The writer Brian Aldiss argued this makes it the first true science fiction novel, a view many critics share. The subtitle, The Modern Prometheus, points to the myth of the Titan who stole fire from the gods. Her question was new: what responsibility do creators have for what they make?

The 1931 Universal film with Boris Karloff, and Jack Pierce's flat-topped makeup, turned the creature into a mostly silent icon.

quiz.q: What set the stage for the ghost story contest that produced Frankenstein?
o: A plague closed the Swiss borders and stranded them
A publisher offered a prize for the best horror story
A fire destroyed their lodgings and forced them to share one room
A volcanic eruption cooled the climate and kept the group indoors
quiz.e: Tambora's eruption caused the cold, wet 1816 summer that trapped the writers indoors.

quiz.q: How did Mary Shelley later describe the origin of her story's central image?
o: As a true story told by a doctor she met in Geneva
As a waking dream of a student and his creature
As a newspaper report she had read years earlier
As a dream she had as a small child
quiz.e: Her waking-dream account, written years later in 1831, is a famous but personal origin story.

quiz.q: Why did people in Mary Shelley's day find her premise believable?
o: Surgeons had already revived people after death
Chemists had created living cells in laboratories
Experiments with electricity had made dead tissue move
Doctors had built working mechanical limbs
quiz.e: Galvani's and Aldini's electrical experiments made the idea of electricity as the spark of life seem plausible.

quiz.q: How does the creature in the novel differ from the film version?
o: He is eloquent and teaches himself to speak
He is a mindless brute who never learns to speak
He is a spirit that only the scientist can see
He is a cheerful helper who is welcomed by all
quiz.e: The novel's creature is eloquent and lonely, so the real horror is rejection.

quiz.q: Why do many critics call Frankenstein the first science fiction novel?
o: Its monster is created through scientific method rather than magic
It was the first novel to be set in outer space
It predicted the exact technology used in modern laboratories
It was the first novel written by a woman
quiz.e: By replacing curses with science, Shelley asked what creators owe to what they make.

LESSONS.push: The famous monster has no name, and he's far more articulate than the films let on.

LESSONS.title: How children learn to talk
LESSONS.hook: By around age four, most children have mastered the basics of a staggeringly complex grammar without a single lesson. How do they do it?

sections.key: Babies tune in to language before birth, then narrow their hearing to the sounds that matter.
sections.b:
Language learning starts earlier than most people think. In late pregnancy, a baby hears muffled sounds with their rhythm intact. Newborns prefer their mother's voice and the rhythm of the language they heard in the womb. Research comparing French and German babies suggests newborns' cries may carry traces of that melody.

In the first months, babies can tell apart speech sounds from almost any language, including contrasts their parents cannot hear. That fades. Research led by Janet Werker found that by around 10 to 12 months, babies lose sensitivity to differences their language does not use. This is specialisation, which makes learning words easier. It also helps explain why adults often struggle with sounds their own language lacks, such as Japanese speakers hearing the difference between English 'r' and 'l'.

sections.key: Most children follow a broadly similar path from babbling to words to sentences, at their own pace.
sections.b: Around six or seven months, many babies begin babbling, repeating syllables like 'bababa' or 'dadada'. Deaf babies exposed to sign language babble with their hands in a similar rhythm, which suggests babbling is about language, not just mouth practice. First words usually arrive around the first birthday, though the range is wide. Words then come slowly. Often in the second year, many children go through a vocabulary burst, adding new words at a rapid pace. Two-word phrases like 'more milk' and 'daddy gone' appear, followed by longer sentences. By around four, most children speak in complex sentences. Every child is different, so these ages are general guides, not strict deadlines.

sections.key: Errors like 'goed' and 'mouses' show children are working out rules, not just copying.
sections.b: One of the most charming signs of language learning is also one of the most revealing. A child who once said 'went' may suddenly say 'goed'. A child who said 'mice' may switch to 'mouses'. Parents sometimes worry, but this is progress. The child has discovered a rule, add '-ed' for the past or '-s' for plurals, and is applying it everywhere, even to exceptions. Linguists call this overregularisation. Nobody taught the child 'goed', and they almost certainly never heard an adult say it. They invented it from the pattern. Over time, children relearn the exceptions, and 'went' returns. The mistakes show that children are not just copying. They are building a system.

sections.key: Scientists still debate how much language is built in, but children can even create new languages.
sections.b:
In the 1950s and 1960s, Noam Chomsky argued that children could not learn language's complex rules from the limited, messy speech they hear, so humans must have an inborn capacity, sometimes called universal grammar. Michael Tomasello and others argue that general thinking skills, such as spotting patterns and reading intentions, plus huge practice, are enough. Most scientists agree humans have some special readiness, but disagree on how much.

In the late 1970s and 1980s, new schools in Nicaragua brought together deaf children who had lived isolated lives. In playgrounds and on buses they began signing, and a shared language formed. Later, younger children made it more systematic. Children can create and refine language.

sections.key: Back-and-forth conversation, shared reading and play do more for young children's language than flashcards or apps.
sections.b: Research suggests what matters most for young children is back-and-forth conversation, not flashcards or apps. Responding to a baby's babbles, naming things in everyday routines, asking questions and waiting for answers all help. Reading together is especially valuable, because books contain words and sentence types that rarely come up in daily chat. Many people find the singsong voice adults use with babies, sometimes called parentese, a little silly, but studies suggest it helps babies pay attention to speech. Children raised with two or more languages are not confused by them, and bilingualism is common worldwide. This is general information. For milestones, see raisingchildren.net.au, and if you have concerns, talk to your GP, child health nurse or a speech pathologist.

quiz.q: Why do babies lose the ability to hear sound differences their language doesn't use?
o: Their brains specialise in the sounds that matter to them
Their ears slowly lose sensitivity to quiet sounds
They stop paying attention to unfamiliar voices
They forget sounds that are rarely spoken at home
quiz.e: Narrowing is a specialisation: the brain commits to the sounds of the language around it.

quiz.q: What does the babbling of deaf babies exposed to sign language suggest?
o: Babbling has nothing to do with later speech
Deaf babies learn language faster than hearing babies
Babbling is about language, not just mouth practice
Babbling only develops when parents copy it
quiz.e: Manual babbling shows babbling is a language skill that can take any form.

quiz.q: Why is a child saying 'goed' instead of 'went' a sign of progress?
o: The child is copying exactly what adults say
The child has learned a rule and applies it everywhere
The child has forgotten how to speak properly
The child is being careless about pronunciation
quiz.e: Overregularisation shows children build a system of rules instead of simply copying.

quiz.q: What did the Nicaraguan deaf children show about language?
o: Children cannot learn a language without formal teaching
Sign languages are simpler than spoken languages
Older children learn language better than younger ones
Given the chance, children can create and refine a new language
quiz.e: Nicaraguan Sign Language emerged among children and became more systematic with each younger group.

quiz.q: What helps young children's language most, according to research?
o: Educational apps played alone on a screen
Flashcards drilled daily from birth
Back-and-forth conversation and shared reading
Hearing only one carefully chosen language
quiz.e: Responsive conversation, shared reading and play give children the practice language growth needs.

LESSONS.push: Children invent words they've never heard. What their mistakes reveal.

LESSONS.title: The hidden shapes of stories
LESSONS.hook: Is there really only a handful of plots in the world? Writers and scientists have long tried to map the hidden structures beneath the stories we love.

sections.key: Thinkers from Aristotle to Freytag described plot as a chain of causes that rises and falls.
sections.b:
Think of almost any film you have enjoyed. Someone wants something, obstacles appear, things get worse, then there is a turning point and a resolution. It feels natural, but people have tried to describe the pattern for over two thousand years. In his Poetics, in the 4th century BCE, Aristotle observed that a good tragedy has a beginning, a middle and an end, and its events follow from one another by necessity or probability. A plot is a chain of causes, not a list of events.

In 1863 the German critic Gustav Freytag drew drama as a five-part pyramid: introduction, rising action, climax, falling action and catastrophe or resolution. It fits tragedies like Hamlet well, but suits many modern stories less well.

sections.key: Joseph Campbell argued that hero myths around the world share one pattern, though critics say he picked examples that fit.
sections.b: In 1949 the American scholar Joseph Campbell published The Hero with a Thousand Faces. Drawing on myths from many cultures, he argued that hero stories often follow a similar path, which he called the monomyth. A hero leaves the ordinary world after a call to adventure, often helped by a mentor. The hero crosses into an unfamiliar world, faces trials and a great ordeal, gains a reward or insight, and returns home transformed. Campbell became enormously influential in Hollywood. George Lucas has said his work shaped Star Wars, and screenwriters later popularised the pattern as a practical template. Critics argue Campbell picked examples that fit and ignored many that do not, but the idea remains widely used.

sections.key: Schemes that sort stories into a few types are useful for spotting patterns but can hide as much as they reveal.
sections.b:
In 2004 the British journalist Christopher Booker published The Seven Basic Plots, arguing that stories fall into types such as overcoming the monster, rags to riches, the quest, comedy, tragedy and rebirth. Others propose anywhere from three to over thirty. Jaws and David and Goliath really are both about overcoming a monster. But critics say the categories are so broad that almost anything fits.

Kurt Vonnegut drew stories as lines on a graph, with good fortune up and bad fortune down. In 2016 US researchers analysed the emotional words in over 1,000 works of fiction and reported six basic emotional arcs. Like all such studies, it is open to debate.

sections.key: The conflict-driven Western plot is one model among many.
sections.b: Most of these models come from European and American traditions and assume stories are driven by conflict between a hero and an obstacle. Other traditions work differently. A classical structure from Chinese poetry, later used in Japanese and Korean storytelling and often called kishotenketsu in Japanese, has four parts: introduction, development, a twist and a conclusion that brings the parts together. The twist need not be a conflict, just a surprising new angle. Aboriginal storytelling traditions are often closely tied to land and place, and many stories connect to particular sites and to responsibilities for Country, rather than following one hero's arc. These differences remind us that the Western plot is one model among many.

sections.key: Knowing story shapes helps readers notice craft and gives writers useful questions.
sections.b: Knowing these patterns does not mean every story must follow them. Many great books play with structure: they start at the end, tell events out of order, or refuse a tidy resolution. But understanding the common shapes is useful. As a reader, it helps you notice why a story feels satisfying or why it drags. As a writer, it gives you questions to ask: what does the main character want, what stands in the way, and what changes by the end? Psychologists have also found that people tend to remember information better when it is told as a story with causes and consequences. That may be why the same shapes keep appearing, from campfire tales to streaming series. We seem to think in stories.

quiz.q: What was Aristotle's key point about plot?
o: A plot should contain as many surprises as possible
Events should follow from one another as a chain of causes
The ending of a story should always be a happy one
A plot should be built around a single hero's journey
quiz.e: A plot is a chain of causes, not just a list of events.

quiz.q: What is a common criticism of Campbell's monomyth?
o: He chose examples that fit and ignored many that did not
He used only stories from modern Hollywood films
He claimed hero stories had no shared features
He argued every story must end in tragedy
quiz.e: The hero's journey is a useful template, but it was built from selected examples.

quiz.q: Why do critics doubt schemes of 'seven basic plots'?
o: Nobody has ever managed to count the types of story
Every scheme agrees on the same number of plots
They only describe stories written before 1800
The categories are so broad that almost anything fits
quiz.e: Broad categories reveal some patterns but can hide what makes individual stories different.

quiz.q: How does kishotenketsu differ from the Western conflict-driven arc?
o: It has no ending and leaves the story unresolved
It always features a single hero fighting an enemy
Its twist can be a new angle rather than a conflict
It consists of exactly seven stages of struggle
quiz.e: Four-part structures show a story can be satisfying without conflict at its centre.

quiz.q: How can knowing story structure help a writer?
o: It guarantees that readers will enjoy the finished story
It suggests questions about what a character wants
It means every story should follow the same pattern
It removes the need for original ideas in a story
quiz.e: Structure is a tool for asking good questions, not a rulebook that every story must obey.

LESSONS.push: Are there really only a handful of stories? A few thinkers say so.

LESSONS.title: The power of doubling
LESSONS.hook: Fold a sheet of paper 42 times and, in theory, it would reach past the Moon. Doubling is the simplest pattern in maths, and the one our brains are worst at imagining.

sections.key: Doubling one grain across 64 squares produces more wheat than the world could grow in centuries.
sections.b: An old legend says the inventor of chess was offered any reward by a delighted ruler. He asked for something that sounded modest: one grain of wheat on the first square, two on the second, four on the third, doubling each time across all 64 squares. The ruler laughed and agreed. He should not have. By square 11 the pile holds 1,024 grains, still only a handful. By square 21 it passes a million. The final square alone needs about 9.2 quintillion grains, and the whole board adds up to 18,446,744,073,709,551,615 grains, which is 2 multiplied by itself 64 times, minus one. The world would need many centuries of harvests to grow that much.

sections.key: Fold paper 42 times and, in theory, the stack would pass the Moon, yet our intuition expects steady growth.
sections.b:
Take a sheet of paper about 0.1 millimetres thick. Each fold doubles it. After 20 folds, if that were possible, it would be about 105 metres tall. After 30 folds it would pass 100 kilometres, reaching the edge of space. After 42 folds it would stand about 440,000 kilometres high, past the Moon's average distance of about 384,000. In reality each fold needs far more paper. In 2002 the American student Britney Gallivan folded a very long strip 12 times, a record.

Our intuition is built for adding. Thirty steps of one metre cover 30 metres. Thirty steps doubling in length would total over a million kilometres, nearly 27 times around the Earth. Researchers call this 'exponential growth bias'.

sections.key: With doubling, most of the change comes at the end, and the rule of 72 estimates doubling time.
sections.b:
A lily patch doubles in area every day and covers the pond on day 48. On what day was it half covered? Many say day 24, but it is day 47. Four days before the end, only about 6 per cent is covered. Early on the numbers look tiny, and by the time the problem is obvious, few doublings remain. That is why acting a few days sooner matters so much early in an outbreak.

To estimate doubling time, divide 72 by the yearly percentage growth. At 6 per cent, it takes about 12 years. Credit card debt charging 20 per cent would double in under four years if unpaid. This is general information, not financial advice; moneysmart.gov.au has free calculators.

sections.key: Repeated halving shrinks things just as dramatically, which is how scientists date ancient remains.
sections.b: Doubling has a mirror image: repeated halving. Radioactive carbon-14 has a half-life of about 5,730 years: in that time, half of any sample decays into nitrogen. After another 5,730 years, half of what is left has gone, leaving a quarter. After ten half-lives, about 57,000 years, less than a thousandth of the original remains. Living things constantly take in carbon, so their carbon-14 level stays steady while they are alive. When they die the clock starts ticking, and by measuring how much is left, scientists can date bones, wood and charcoal back to roughly 50,000 years. Halving also explains why the amount of a medicine in your blood fades in steps rather than all at once.

sections.key: Real-world doubling hits limits and bends into an S-shaped curve.
sections.b:
If a single bacterium dividing every 20 minutes kept going unchecked, its descendants would outweigh the entire Earth in about two days. That never happens, because food runs out, waste builds up and space fills. Real growth usually follows an S-shaped curve: slow at first, then explosive, then levelling off. Mathematicians call this logistic growth.

Technology shows the same pattern. In 1965 the engineer Gordon Moore noticed that the number of components on a chip was doubling regularly, and in 1975 he revised this to roughly every two years. Moore's law powered the computer revolution, though progress has slowed as parts approach the size of atoms. The lesson is to spot doubling early, and to ask what limit will eventually stop it.

quiz.q: Why does the chessboard reward grow so enormous?
o: Each square adds ten more grains than the one before
Later squares are physically larger and hold more
Each square doubles the one before, so totals explode late
The ruler counted the grains incorrectly at the end
quiz.e: Repeated doubling starts slowly but reaches astronomical numbers within 64 steps.

quiz.q: Why does our intuition struggle with doubling?
o: We cannot picture numbers larger than a thousand
We always overestimate how big small numbers are
We assume that fast growth will stop very quickly
We are used to adding steady amounts, not multiplying
quiz.e: Exponential growth bias makes us underestimate how fast repeated doubling grows.

quiz.q: In the lily pond puzzle, why is the pond half covered on day 47?
o: One more doubling fills the pond the next day
The lilies grow much more slowly at the start of the month
The lilies stop growing altogether after day 24
Half of the lilies die off again every night
quiz.e: With doubling, the last step does as much as all earlier steps combined, so warnings come late.

quiz.q: What does the half-life of carbon-14 let scientists do?
o: Make living things stay young for longer
Estimate the age of bones, wood and charcoal
Predict exactly when a person will die
Measure the speed of light in a vacuum
quiz.e: Because carbon-14 decays at a known rate, the amount left works as a clock for ancient remains.

quiz.q: Why do real-world things not double forever?
o: Limits such as food and space slow the growth
Doubling is mathematically impossible beyond ten steps
Growth always stops after exactly one year
Nature punishes any fast growth immediately
quiz.e: Real growth levels off as it meets limits, so ask what will stop a doubling pattern.

LESSONS.push: Fold a sheet of paper 42 times and, in theory, it passes the Moon. How?

LESSONS.title: The Monty Hall problem: the puzzle that fools almost everyone
LESSONS.hook: Three doors, one car, two goats. Should you switch? The right answer is simple to state, hard to believe, and once had people with maths doctorates writing angry letters.

sections.key: Your first pick is right only a third of the time, so switching wins two-thirds of the time.
sections.b:
Imagine a game show with three closed doors: a car behind one, goats behind two. You pick door 1. The host, who knows where the car is, always opens another door to reveal a goat, say door 3, and offers a switch to door 2. Most people feel it is 50 to 50. The puzzle is named after Monty Hall, host of the American show Let's Make a Deal, and the statistician Steve Selvin posed it in 1975.

Your first pick is the car one time in three. Then switching loses. Two times in three you picked a goat, and the host must open the only other goat door, so the last door hides the car. Switching wins two thirds of the time.

sections.key: Thousands of readers, including academics, insisted the correct answer was wrong.
sections.b: In 1990 a reader sent the puzzle to Marilyn vos Savant, who wrote the 'Ask Marilyn' column in Parade, a US magazine read by millions. She replied that you should switch, because switching wins two thirds of the time. The reaction was extraordinary. She received thousands of letters, many from people with doctorates, many telling her she had made an embarrassing mistake. She was right. The puzzle even troubled Paul Erdős, one of the most prolific mathematicians of the twentieth century. According to a well-known account, he refused to accept the answer until he was shown a computer simulation of the game played many times over. Expertise does not protect anyone from a strong but faulty intuition.

sections.key: Scaling the puzzle up to a hundred doors makes the right answer feel obvious.
sections.b: If the answer still feels wrong, imagine 100 doors, with a car behind one and goats behind the other 99. You pick door 37. Your chance of being right is just 1 in 100. Now the host, who knows where the car is, opens 98 of the other doors, every one revealing a goat, and leaves just one other door closed: door 74. Would you stick with door 37 or switch to door 74? Almost everyone now feels the pull to switch, and they are right. Your door still has its original 1 in 100 chance. The host has carefully avoided the car while opening 98 doors, so door 74 carries the remaining 99 in 100. The three-door game works the same way, with smaller numbers.

sections.key: Switching helps only because the host knows where the car is and never reveals it.
sections.b: There is a subtle condition hidden in the puzzle. The host knows where the car is, always opens a goat door and always offers the swap. Change those rules and the answer changes. Suppose the host has no idea where the car is and opens one of the other two doors at random. Sometimes he will reveal the car and spoil the game. But in the games where he happens to reveal a goat, your chances really are 50 to 50, and switching makes no difference. The difference is information. A knowing host's choice is limited by where the car is, so his action tells you something useful. A random host's choice tells you nothing extra. Many heated arguments about the puzzle are really about which rules apply.

sections.key: Our intuition counts the options left and assumes they are equally likely, so list every starting case instead.
sections.b:
More than 70 years before the game show, the French mathematician Joseph Bertrand described a similar trap in an 1889 book. One box holds two gold coins, one two silver and one a gold and a silver. You pick a box at random and draw a gold coin. Is the other coin gold? Most say one half, but it is two thirds. Three gold coins could have been drawn, and two of them sit in the gold box.

Intuition counts the options left and assumes they are equally likely. Instead, list every equally likely starting situation and follow each through. Or experiment: play 30 rounds of Monty Hall with cups and a friend as host, always sticking, then 30 always switching. Switching will usually come out well ahead.

quiz.q: Why does switching doors win two thirds of the time?
o: The host secretly moves the car after you have chosen
The two remaining doors are equally likely to hide the car
Doors on the left win more often than doors on the right
Your first pick is usually wrong, so the other door usually wins
quiz.e: Opening a goat door concentrates the two-thirds chance that you were wrong onto the one remaining door.

quiz.q: What does the reaction to Marilyn vos Savant's answer show?
o: Mathematicians cannot understand basic probability
Magazine columns are unreliable sources of maths
Expertise does not protect against faulty intuition
The answer depends on the person's qualifications
quiz.e: Even people with doctorates trusted their intuition over the correct reasoning.

quiz.q: Why does the 100-door version make switching feel obvious?
o: The host opens doors at random, so any remaining door could win
Your door keeps its 1 in 100 chance and the last door carries 99 in 100
Every door left closed has an equal chance once the host finishes
The host has hidden the car behind the door you first chose
quiz.e: Scaling up shows how the host's careful choices concentrate probability on the remaining door.

quiz.q: What happens if the host opens a door at random and happens to reveal a goat?
o: Switching and sticking are equally likely to win
Switching still wins two thirds of the time
Sticking now wins two thirds of the time
The game must be replayed from the start
quiz.e: The host's knowledge supplies the information, so a random choice changes the answer.

quiz.q: What is a reliable way to check an unintuitive probability?
o: Count only the options still left in front of you
Trust your first instinct about which feels likelier
List every starting case and follow each through
Ask someone who has already played the game once
quiz.e: Listing every starting case, or simply playing many rounds, reveals what intuition misses.

LESSONS.push: Three doors, one car. Why professional mathematicians got this wrong.

LESSONS.title: Fractals: the infinite detail of coastlines, ferns and clouds
LESSONS.hook: How long is a coastline? The honest answer is 'it depends on your ruler', and that puzzle opened the door to a whole new kind of geometry.

sections.key: The more finely you measure a jagged coastline, the longer it gets.
sections.b: Try measuring a rocky coastline on a map with dividers set to 100 kilometres. You cut across bays and headlands and get one number. Set the dividers to 10 kilometres and you follow more of the wiggles, so the total grows. Walk the shore with a one-metre ruler, tracing around every rock, and it grows again. In the mid twentieth century the English scientist Lewis Fry Richardson noticed this when comparing published lengths of coasts and borders, which often disagreed. In 1967 Benoit Mandelbrot built on this in a famous paper titled 'How Long Is the Coast of Britain?'. His point was that for shapes like coastlines, length is not a fixed property. It depends on the scale you measure at.

sections.key: Fractals are shapes whose rough detail reappears at smaller scales, and branching fractals help nature reach everywhere.
sections.b:
A fern frond is made of smaller leaflets shaped much like the whole frond. A floret of romanesco broccoli looks like a miniature of the whole head. This is self-similarity, and shapes with rough detail across many scales are called fractals, a word Mandelbrot coined in 1975 from the Latin fractus, meaning broken. In nature the repetition is imperfect and limited, but it appears in river networks, trees, lightning and clouds.

Branching solves practical problems. Your windpipe splits again and again, ending in hundreds of millions of tiny air sacs, packing tens of square metres of surface for oxygen into your chest. Blood vessels branch so almost every cell sits near a capillary.

sections.key: The Koch snowflake has an infinitely long edge around a finite area, and its dimension lies between 1 and 2.
sections.b:
In 1904 the Swedish mathematician Helge von Koch described a startling shape. Start with an equilateral triangle. On the middle third of each side, add a smaller triangle pointing outwards, turning each side into four shorter pieces. Repeat on every piece, forever. Each round multiplies the outline's length by four thirds, so the edge grows without limit. Yet the area settles at exactly eight fifths of the starting triangle's.

Scale a line up by three and you get three copies; a square gives nine. A Koch side gives four, so its dimension is the power of three that makes four: about 1.26. Mandelbrot estimated about 1.25 for Britain's rugged west coast, while smoother coastlines came out closer to 1.

sections.key: A one-line rule, repeated by a computer, produces a shape of endless complexity.
sections.b: The most famous fractal comes from a very short rule. Start with zero. Square it and add a fixed number, called c. Then take the result, square it and add c again, over and over. For some values of c the numbers stay small forever. For others they rush off towards infinity. The numbers involved are complex numbers, which can be plotted as points on a flat plane. Colour every point that stays small black, and you get the Mandelbrot set, named after Benoit Mandelbrot, who studied it using computers at IBM around 1980. Its boundary is endlessly intricate. Zoom in anywhere along the edge and you find spirals, seahorse shapes and tiny copies of the whole set.

sections.key: Fractal ideas now help create film landscapes, design antennas and describe rough surfaces.
sections.b: Computer graphics pioneers realised that repeatedly adding smaller random bumps to a shape produces convincing mountains, coastlines and clouds. Fractal techniques helped create a computer-generated planet surface for the 1982 film Star Trek II: The Wrath of Khan, and similar ideas still build landscapes in films and video games. Some mobile phone antennas use fractal-like shapes, which let a compact antenna work across a wide range of frequencies. Scientists use fractal dimension to describe the roughness of surfaces, the branching of blood vessels in medical scans and the sprawl of growing cities. Mandelbrot himself applied fractal thinking to financial markets, arguing that prices are wilder and more prone to sudden jumps than standard models assume.

quiz.q: Why does a coastline's measured length keep growing as the ruler gets shorter?
o: A shorter ruler follows more of the bays and wiggles
Coastlines slowly lengthen as the sea erodes them
Maps always shrink the true distance by a fixed amount
Shorter rulers are less accurate
quiz.e: For rough shapes, length depends on the scale you measure at.

quiz.q: What is self-similarity?
o: A shape that looks identical from every direction
Detail that reappears in smaller copies
A pattern that repeats at exactly the same size
A smooth shape with no rough edges
quiz.e: Ferns, romanesco and river networks echo their whole shape in smaller parts.

quiz.q: What is surprising about the Koch snowflake?
o: Its area is infinite while its edge is short
It is the same shape as a circle
It becomes smooth after enough repetitions
Its infinite edge encloses a finite area
quiz.e: An endless boundary can still wrap around a limited area.

quiz.q: What defines the Mandelbrot set?
o: Points that lie along a perfectly smooth curve
Numbers that grow larger with every single step
Values of c for which the repeated rule stays small
The outline of one particular rocky coastline
quiz.e: A tiny rule, repeated by a computer, produces endlessly detailed structure.

quiz.q: How have fractal ideas been used in technology?
o: To remove the roughness from natural surfaces
To make computers faster by shrinking their screens
To measure exactly how long a coastline is
To make realistic landscapes and compact antennas
quiz.e: Repeated rough detail suits natural-looking graphics and compact, wide-ranging antennas.

LESSONS.push: How long is a coastline? The honest answer changes with your ruler.

LESSONS.title: The seven bridges puzzle and the maths of networks
LESSONS.hook: In the 1700s, people in a Prussian city wondered whether they could stroll across all seven of its bridges exactly once. The answer started a branch of maths that now guides your phone's maps.

sections.key: A local puzzle about crossing seven bridges once each launched a new kind of maths.
sections.b: The city of Königsberg, in what was then Prussia, sat on the River Pregel. The river split around two islands, and seven bridges linked the islands to each other and to the two riverbanks. Residents enjoyed a puzzle: could you walk through the city and cross every bridge exactly once? You could start and finish anywhere, but no swimming, no boats and no turning back halfway across a bridge. Nobody could find a route, but nobody could prove none existed. In 1736 the Swiss mathematician Leonhard Euler, then working in St Petersburg, took up the problem. His answer to this small local puzzle launched a whole new field. Königsberg is now Kaliningrad, part of Russia.

sections.key: Euler ignored distances and shapes, and showed that a route using every line once needs zero or two odd points.
sections.b:
Euler threw away almost everything about the map. Bridge lengths and island shapes made no difference. Only which land areas connected, and by how many bridges, mattered. He shrank each land area to a point and each bridge to a line. Today this diagram is called a graph, with nodes (points) and edges (lines). This focus on connections grew into graph theory.

Think about passing through a place mid-walk: you arrive by one bridge and leave by another, so bridges are used in pairs. Only the start and end can have an odd number. In Königsberg, one island had five bridges and the other three areas had three each. Four odd points made the walk impossible.

sections.key: The same rule solves pen-and-paper puzzles and tells you where to start.
sections.b:
Try drawing a house, a square with both diagonals and a triangular roof, without lifting your pen or retracing a line. Count the lines at each corner. The top corners of the square have four each and the roof peak has two. The two bottom corners have three each. Exactly two odd points means it can be done, but only by starting at one bottom corner and finishing at the other. Start anywhere else and you get stuck.

Much of old Königsberg was destroyed in the Second World War, and several bridges were lost or replaced. With the bridges standing today, only two land areas have an odd number, so a walk crossing each exactly once is now possible.

sections.key: Graphs describe road maps, the internet and social networks, where short chains link surprisingly distant people.
sections.b:
A road map is a graph, with intersections as points and roads as lines labelled with distances or times. When your phone suggests the fastest route, it is searching a vast graph. A classic method was devised by the Dutch computer scientist Edsger Dijkstra in 1956, reportedly in about 20 minutes at a café. Electricity grids, web links and the internet are graphs too.

Social networks are graphs of people. In the 1960s Stanley Milgram asked volunteers to pass letters towards a target in Boston through acquaintances. Those that arrived took around six steps, though many never arrived. In 1998 Duncan Watts and Steven Strogatz showed that mostly local friendships plus a few long-range links make 'small worlds'. A 2016 Facebook analysis found users about 3.6 steps apart on average.

sections.key: Any map can be coloured with four colours so that no neighbours match, a fact first proved with a computer.
sections.b: In 1852 a young British graduate, Francis Guthrie, was colouring a map of England's counties and noticed he never needed more than four colours to keep neighbours different. Could any map, however complicated, manage with four? Turn the map into a graph, with regions as points and shared borders as lines, and it becomes a question about networks. The problem resisted proof for over a century. In 1976 Kenneth Appel and Wolfgang Haken at the University of Illinois finally proved it, but only by having a computer check nearly two thousand special cases, far too many for a person to do by hand. Some mathematicians were uneasy about a proof no human could fully check. Today the theorem is accepted, and computer-assisted proofs are a normal tool.

quiz.q: What was the Königsberg bridge puzzle?
o: How to build an eighth bridge across the river
Which bridge was the longest in the city
Whether one walk could cross all seven bridges once
How to cross the river without using any bridge
quiz.e: The puzzle looked trivial but needed a new kind of reasoning to settle.

quiz.q: What made the Königsberg walk impossible?
o: There were too many bridges to cross in a single day
Four areas had odd bridge counts, and at most two are allowed
Some of the bridges were too narrow to walk across
The islands had no bridges connecting them to the banks
quiz.e: A route using every line once needs zero or two points with an odd number of lines.

quiz.q: Where must you start to draw the house shape without lifting your pen?
o: At one of the two corners with three lines
At the peak of the roof, which has two lines
At either top corner of the square, with four lines
Anywhere at all, because every starting point works
quiz.e: Only the two odd points can serve as the start and end of the route.

quiz.q: What did Watts and Strogatz explain about social networks?
o: Every person knows exactly six other people directly
Friendships form at random across the whole world
Larger networks always have longer chains between people
Local friendships plus a few long links bring everyone close
quiz.e: A few long-range links are enough to create a small world.

quiz.q: Why were some mathematicians uneasy about the proof of the four colour theorem?
o: The proof relied on an unproven guess about maps
A computer checked far too many cases for a person
The proof used colours that cannot be printed
The result was later shown to be false
quiz.e: The theorem is accepted, and computer-assisted proof is now a normal tool.

LESSONS.push: A Prussian walking puzzle that no one could solve, and why that mattered.

LESSONS.title: Check digits: the hidden maths that catches typos
LESSONS.hook: Mistype one digit of a card number online and the website often knows instantly, before it has contacted any bank. The secret is a single extra digit doing some clever arithmetic.

sections.key: One extra digit, calculated from the others, lets a computer detect the most common typing mistakes.
sections.b:
Every day, millions of long numbers are typed, read aloud, copied and scanned. People make predictable mistakes. A well-known 1969 analysis by the Dutch mathematician Jacobus Verhoeff found that the most common slip by far is getting a single digit wrong, such as typing 7 for 1. Next is swapping two neighbouring digits, so 58 becomes 85. The cheap fix is one extra digit whose only job is to check the others.

Simple version: make all digits add to a multiple of 10. For 2 4 7 3, the sum is 16, so the check digit is 4, giving 24734. If someone types 24834, the sum is 21 and the error shows. But swap two digits, as in 27434, and the sum is unchanged.

sections.key: Barcodes weight alternate digits by 1 and 3, which also catches most swapped digits.
sections.b: Look at the barcode on a packet in your pantry. The 13-digit number beneath it, called an EAN-13, ends in a check digit. The recipe multiplies the first 12 digits alternately by 1 and 3, adds the results, and picks the final digit that brings the total to a multiple of 10. Because neighbouring digits carry different weights, swapping them usually changes the total, and the system spots it. The one blind spot is swapping two neighbouring digits that differ by exactly 5, such as 1 and 6. Many Australian products have barcodes starting with 93, a prefix GS1 assigned to Australia, though it shows where a company registered, not where a product was made.

sections.key: The old ten-digit ISBN used division by 11 to catch every single wrong digit and every neighbouring swap.
sections.b: The older 10-digit ISBN multiplied the first digit by 10, the second by 9, and so on down to the check digit, multiplied by 1. The total must divide exactly by 11. For 0-306-40615-2, the first nine digits give 0 + 27 + 0 + 42 + 24 + 0 + 24 + 3 + 10 = 130. Adding the check digit 2 gives 132, which is 12 times 11. Because 11 is a prime number, this system catches every single wrong digit and every swap of neighbouring digits. Sometimes the check digit has to be 10, which is written as an X. Since 2007, books have used 13-digit ISBNs that follow the barcode recipe.

sections.key: Card numbers use the Luhn formula to catch typos, and Australian ABNs have a built-in check too.
sections.b:
Card numbers end in a check digit from the Luhn formula, created by IBM engineer Hans Peter Luhn and patented in 1960. From the right, double every second digit starting next to the check digit, add together the digits of any two-digit result (8 doubled is 16, so 7), then add everything. A valid number totals a multiple of 10. That is how a payment page flags a mistyped number instantly. But the check is public and easy to satisfy, so it says nothing about whether a card is real, active or yours.

The ABN has 11 digits and a published check: after adjusting the first digit, each digit gets a weight and the total must divide by 89. Overseas, IBANs use division by 97.

sections.key: Error-correcting codes repair damaged data, which is why scratched QR codes can still scan.
sections.b: A check digit can tell you something is wrong, but not what. Error-correcting codes add enough carefully designed extra information to repair mistakes. In the late 1940s the American mathematician Richard Hamming, frustrated that his weekend computer jobs kept failing because of errors, devised codes that could find and fix a flipped digit automatically. Later codes, such as Reed-Solomon codes from 1960, protect data on CDs, in deep space communications and in QR codes. A QR code can be printed with different levels of protection, and at the highest level it can still be read even if around 30 per cent of it is damaged or covered. Behind everyday convenience sits some elegant mathematics.

quiz.q: Which errors are most common when people type numbers?
o: Missing the final digit, then repeating a digit
Reversing the whole number, then adding zeros
Swapping the first and last digits
A single wrong digit, then swapped neighbouring digits
quiz.e: Check digits are designed around the mistakes people actually make.

quiz.q: Why do barcodes weight digits alternately by 1 and 3?
o: Swapped neighbouring digits then change the total
It makes the barcode shorter and cheaper to print
It means the number can only be read by machines
It makes the total always come out as an odd number
quiz.e: Different weights make the order of neighbouring digits matter.

quiz.q: Why does the old ISBN system catch every neighbouring swap?
o: The check digit is always the sum of the other digits
Alternating weights of 1 and 3 make any swap show
Division by the prime 11, with weights, exposes any swap
Every ISBN is checked by a person before printing
quiz.e: The prime modulus and weights mean any single error or neighbour swap breaks the arithmetic.

quiz.q: What does the Luhn check on a card number tell you?
o: That the card is genuine and currently active
Only that it was probably typed correctly
That the account holder has enough money to pay
That the card belongs to the person who is using it
quiz.e: Luhn catches accidents, not fraud, because the method is public and easy to satisfy.

quiz.q: How do error-correcting codes go beyond check digits?
o: They only detect mistakes and cannot repair anything
They make stored data impossible to damage
They add enough extra information to repair damaged data
They remove any need to scan the code at all
quiz.e: Extra structured information lets QR codes and CDs recover from scratches and damage.

LESSONS.push: Mistype a card number and the site knows instantly. One extra digit does it.

LESSONS.title: Benford's law: why so many numbers start with 1
LESSONS.hook: In many tables of real-world numbers, from river areas to company accounts, almost a third begin with the digit 1. The pattern is real, it can be explained, and it has helped auditors spot cooked books.

sections.key: Benford's law was spotted twice, first in worn logarithm books and later in thousands of real-world numbers.
sections.b:
Before calculators, scientists looked up logarithms in thick books of tables. In 1881 the astronomer Simon Newcomb noticed that the early pages, covering numbers starting with 1, were far more worn than the later ones. People were looking up numbers beginning with 1 much more often than those beginning with 9. His short note was largely forgotten.

In 1938 the physicist Frank Benford, working at General Electric, noticed the same thing independently. He collected more than 20,000 numbers from around 20 very different sources, including river areas, city populations, physical constants and magazine figures. The same lopsided pattern appeared again and again, and it now carries his name.

sections.key: In data that follow Benford's law, about 30 per cent of numbers start with 1 and fewer than 5 per cent start with 9.
sections.b:
You might expect each leading digit, 1 to 9, to turn up about 11 per cent of the time. In data that follow Benford's law, they don't. About 30.1 per cent of numbers start with 1. Around 17.6 per cent start with 2, 12.5 per cent with 3 and 9.7 per cent with 4.

The share keeps falling: 7.9 per cent for 5, 6.7 for 6, 5.8 for 7 and 5.1 for 8, down to just 4.6 per cent for 9. The formula uses logarithms: the chance of a leading digit d is the base 10 logarithm of one plus one divided by d.

sections.key: Anything that grows by multiplying spends the most time starting with 1 and the least starting with 9.
sections.b:
Imagine a town of 100 people growing by 10 per cent a year. Doubling to 200 takes a little over seven years, all spent starting with a 1. Going from 200 to 300 takes a little over four. Going from 900 to 1,000, a rise of just 11 per cent, takes about a year, and then it must double again to escape the 1s.

Populations, prices, investments and revenues grow by multiplying, so they linger on low leading digits. The pattern also holds in any units: convert dollars to yen, or kilometres to miles, and it stays the same. In 1961 Roger Pinkham showed that any law of leading digits independent of units would have to be Benford's law.

sections.key: Benford's law fits numbers spread across many orders of magnitude, not data stuck in a narrow range or assigned by people.
sections.b:
Benford's law is not a law of nature that every list must obey. It works best for numbers that spread across several orders of magnitude, say from tens to tens of thousands, and that arise from natural processes or from combining other numbers.

It fails for data stuck in a narrow range. Adult heights in centimetres almost all start with 1, because nearly everyone is between 100 and 199 centimetres tall. It also fails for numbers that people assign, such as phone numbers, postcodes and lottery numbers, and for prices deliberately set at points like $9.99 or $49. Before applying the law to any data set, ask whether there is a good reason to expect it to fit at all.

sections.key: Benford's law is a screening tool that flags where to look, and misusing it can dress up a hunch as mathematics.
sections.b:
People who invent numbers tend to spread first digits fairly evenly, because that feels random. Real financial data, such as invoices, often follow Benford's law closely, so the gap is a useful screening tool. Mark Nigrini helped popularise it in auditing in the 1990s. A deviation does not prove fraud and often has an innocent explanation, such as many identical fees.

It is also easy to misuse. After the 2020 US election, online posts claimed some vote counts broke the law and proved fraud. Statisticians replied that precinct totals cluster in a narrow range, so no fit was expected. Always ask whether the data should fit the pattern first.

quiz.q: What did the worn pages in the logarithm books suggest?
o: Early pages were printed on weaker paper than later ones
Numbers starting with 1 were looked up far more often
Scientists preferred to work with smaller numbers
Logarithm tables were written in a confusing order
quiz.e: Heavier wear on the early pages hinted that numbers starting with 1 turn up more often.

quiz.q: In data that follow Benford's law, roughly how often does a number start with 1?
o: About 11 per cent of the time
About 50 per cent of the time
About 30 per cent of the time
About 5 per cent of the time
quiz.e: Instead of an even 11 per cent, the digit 1 leads about 30 per cent of the time.

quiz.q: Why does a steadily growing quantity so often start with the digit 1?
o: Growth lingers longest while the leading digit is 1
Growth always stops once the leading digit reaches 9
The digit 1 is easier for people to record
Every quantity begins life at exactly 1
quiz.e: Growing through the leading-1 range takes far longer than growing through the leading-9 range, so low digits dominate.

quiz.q: Which data would you not expect to follow Benford's law?
o: River areas, which span many orders of magnitude
Adult heights in centimetres, which cluster narrowly
Company revenues, which range from small to huge
City populations, which vary widely in size
quiz.e: Data confined to a narrow range, or assigned by people, gives no reason to expect the pattern.
