quiz.q: What does an auditor's Benford test result actually tell them?
o: Where to look more closely, without proving fraud
That the accounts are definitely fraudulent
That every invoice has been checked and approved
That the company's profits are higher than reported
quiz.e: A deviation is a flag for closer inspection, not proof, because innocent explanations are common.

LESSONS.push: Look at the first digit of any real-world number. One digit shows up far too often.

LESSONS.title: Nature's geometry: hexagons, spirals and bubbles
LESSONS.hook: Bees build hexagons, sunflowers count in Fibonacci numbers and soap bubbles solve maths problems in an instant. Nature is full of geometry, and there are good reasons why.

sections.key: Hexagons enclose a given area with the least wall, so bees save wax by building them.
sections.b:
Honeycomb is made of near-perfect hexagons. Only three regular shapes fit together on a flat surface with no gaps: triangles, squares and hexagons. Of these, hexagons enclose a given area with the shortest total wall. For cells of equal area, a square needs about 7.5 per cent more perimeter than a hexagon, and a triangle about 22 per cent more.

Bees must eat honey to make wax, so saving wax saves energy. Around 300 CE Pappus of Alexandria praised bees for their geometric wisdom. The stronger claim, that hexagons beat every possible way of dividing a flat surface into equal areas, was only proved in 1999, by the mathematician Thomas Hales. It is known as the honeycomb conjecture.

sections.key: Seed heads often show two sets of spirals with neighbouring Fibonacci numbers, but it is a tendency, not a rule.
sections.b:
Look closely at a large sunflower and you will see seeds in two sets of spirals, one clockwise and one anticlockwise. Count them and you often get neighbouring Fibonacci numbers, such as 34 and 55, or 55 and 89. Pinecones, pineapples and daisy centres show smaller pairs, like 8 and 13.

The pattern is common rather than universal. A large citizen science project published in 2016, inspired by Alan Turing's interest in sunflowers, counted the spirals on hundreds of seed heads. A sizeable minority did not fit simple Fibonacci patterns. Nature leans strongly towards these numbers, but it is not an unbreakable rule.

sections.key: Each new seed sits about 137.5 degrees from the last, which packs seeds evenly and creates the spirals as a side effect.
sections.b:
A sunflower head grows from the centre, adding seeds one at a time, each at a fixed angle from the one before. If that angle were a simple fraction of a turn, such as a quarter, seeds would line up in four straight spokes with big gaps between them.

The angle that best avoids lining up is about 137.5 degrees, called the golden angle. It is linked to the golden ratio, the number that resists approximation by simple fractions more than any other. With it, seeds fill the head evenly and pack in as many as possible. The spirals we see, and their Fibonacci counts, are a side effect of that efficient packing, and computer models reproduce them from this one rule.

sections.key: Surface tension pulls soap films into the smallest possible surface, and bubble foams obey fixed angles.
sections.b:
Blow a single soap bubble and it becomes a sphere. For any amount of air, a sphere has the smallest possible surface, and surface tension pulls the soap film as tight as it can go.

When bubbles cluster in a foam, they follow rules set out by the Belgian physicist Joseph Plateau in 1873. Soap films always meet in threes, at equal angles of 120 degrees, and the edges where films meet always come together in fours, at about 109.5 degrees.

Dip a wire frame into soapy water and the film often forms the smallest surface spanning it, instantly solving a problem that can take pages of calculation. The architect Frei Otto used soap film models to design light, curving roofs.

sections.key: Shells grow in self-similar spirals, while the square-cube law is why giant ants cannot exist.
sections.b:
A snail or nautilus cannot remodel its shell, so it adds material at the open end and each turn is a scaled-up copy of the last. The result is close to a logarithmic spiral, which keeps its shape however far you zoom. Jacob Bernoulli called it the 'marvellous spiral' and asked for it on his gravestone, though the mason carved the wrong kind. Claims that the nautilus follows the golden ratio do not survive careful measurement.

Geometry also limits size. Double an ant's length, width and height and its leg strength rises four times, but its weight rises eight. Galileo described this square-cube law in 1638, which is why elephants have stout legs. Slowly cooling lava cracks at angles near 120 degrees into columns, as at the Giant's Causeway and Organ Pipes National Park near Melbourne.

quiz.q: Why do bees build hexagonal cells?
o: Hexagons enclose an area with the least wall, saving wax
Hexagons are the only shape that can be built without gaps
Bees cannot build any other shape
Hexagonal cells store more honey per bee
quiz.e: Of the shapes that tile a flat surface, hexagons need the shortest wall, which saves wax and energy.

quiz.q: What is true of Fibonacci spirals in sunflowers?
o: They are common, but not universal
They appear only in sunflowers
Every sunflower follows them exactly
They have never been measured
quiz.e: Counts of hundreds of seed heads showed a strong tendency but not a universal rule.

quiz.q: Why do spirals appear in a sunflower head?
o: Each seed is placed along a pre-drawn spiral
The seeds are pushed outwards by the wind
A side effect of packing seeds at the golden angle
The spirals form only as the flower dries
quiz.e: One simple rule, a turn of about 137.5 degrees per seed, produces both even packing and the spirals.

quiz.q: Why does a single soap bubble become a sphere?
o: Air always rushes towards the bubble's centre
Soap films cannot bend into other shapes
Gravity pulls the bubble into a ball
A sphere has the least surface for its volume
quiz.e: Surface tension pulls the film as tight as possible, and a sphere is the tightest shape.

quiz.q: Why can't an ant simply be scaled up to giant size?
o: Its legs would grow faster than its body
Its weight grows faster than the strength of its legs
Larger insects cannot breathe air at all
Its brain would shrink as its body grew
quiz.e: Weight scales with volume but leg strength with cross section, so larger bodies struggle to support themselves.

LESSONS.push: Honeycomb is hexagonal, and bubbles meet at exact angles. What do they know about maths?

LESSONS.title: Why an hour has 60 minutes: a history of counting
LESSONS.hook: We count in tens, tell the time in sixties and buy eggs by the dozen. Each habit is a fossil from a different civilisation's way of counting, and together they tell a story more than 40,000 years long.

sections.key: Tally marks are the most natural counting system, and people have been cutting them for tens of thousands of years.
sections.b:
Long before writing, people may have kept count by cutting marks into bone. The Lebombo bone, a baboon leg bone found in a cave in the mountains between South Africa and Eswatini, carries 29 notches and is more than 40,000 years old. The Ishango bone, found in what is now the Democratic Republic of the Congo and thought to be around 20,000 years old, bears groups of notches that some researchers read as deliberate number patterns.

Nobody can be sure what these marks meant. But tally marks, one for each thing, are the most natural counting system there is. People still use them today, often grouping strokes in fives, to keep score or count votes by hand.

sections.key: Most of the world counts in tens because of our fingers, though some cultures counted in twenties.
sections.b:
Most of the world counts in tens, and the reason is probably at the end of your arms. The word digit comes from the Latin digitus, meaning finger or toe. Counting in tens means that once you reach ten, you start a new group.

Not every culture stopped at the fingers. Counting fingers and toes gives base 20, which the Maya used. Traces survive in modern languages: French says quatre-vingts, literally 'four twenties', for 80, and English speakers once commonly used 'score' for 20, as in Lincoln's 'four score and seven years ago'. Some communities in Papua New Guinea traditionally counted by pointing to a sequence of body parts, running up one arm, across the head and down the other.

sections.key: The Babylonians' base 60 and the dozen are why we have 60 minutes in an hour and 24 hours in a day.
sections.b:
About 4,000 years ago, scribes in Mesopotamia, in what is now Iraq, did sums in base 60. It divides evenly by 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 12, 15, 20 and 30, which makes fractions easy. Greek astronomers later borrowed it from the Babylonians, which is why an hour has 60 minutes and a circle 360 degrees. One Babylonian tablet gives the square root of 2 in base 60, accurate to about six decimal places.

Twelve matters too. The Egyptians divided day and night into 12 hours each, the root of our 24 hour day. We buy eggs by the dozen, and a dozen dozen, 144, is a gross. Before 1966 Australia had 12 pence in a shilling.

sections.key: Roman numerals worked for recording numbers but were awkward for arithmetic.
sections.b:
The Romans wrote numbers with letters: I for 1, V for 5, X for 10, L for 50, C for 100, D for 500 and M for 1,000. Symbols are added together, so 27 is XXVII, and a smaller symbol placed before a larger one is usually subtracted, so 4 is IV and 90 is XC.

You still see Roman numerals on clock faces, at the end of film credits and in the names of monarchs and Super Bowls. Many clocks show 4 as IIII rather than IV. The system worked well for recording, but it is awkward for arithmetic. Try multiplying XLVIII by XIV. Romans calculated on counting boards, moving small stones. The Latin word for a pebble, calculus, gives us the word calculate.

sections.key: Place value and zero, from India, made written arithmetic fast, and binary later suited computers.
sections.b:
Our numerals grew out of India, where by around the sixth century CE mathematicians wrote numbers with ten symbols, including zero, and a digit's value depended on its place. In 347, the 3 means three hundreds; in 734, three tens. Al-Khwarizmi wrote about it in the ninth century, and his name gives us 'algorithm'. In 1202 Fibonacci championed it in Europe, though it took centuries to win out.

Binary uses just 0 and 1, each place worth double the last, so 13 is 1101. Leibniz published an account in 1703. It suits computers because a switch is off or on. Decimal time, with 10 hours a day, was suspended in France in 1795.

quiz.q: What are tally marks?
o: A system of symbols that depends on place value
One mark for every item that is counted
Letters used in place of numbers
A way of counting only in groups of twenty
quiz.e: Tally marks match one mark to one item, and are still used today, often in groups of five.

quiz.q: Why do most people count in tens?
o: Ten is the only number that divides into 100
Ancient kings ordered it to be used
Ten is the largest number a person can remember
Our ten fingers probably gave us the system
quiz.e: Counting on our fingers is the likely source, and the word digit comes from the Latin for finger.

quiz.q: Why was Babylonian base 60 so convenient?
o: Sixty has only two divisors, which keeps sums simple
Sixty divides evenly by many numbers
Sixty was the biggest number they could write
Sixty is easier to write than ten
quiz.e: Sixty has so many divisors that thirds, quarters and fifths are simple to handle.

quiz.q: What was a weakness of Roman numerals?
o: They could not record numbers above 100
They had no way to show large values
They were awkward for multiplication
They were too slow to write down at all
quiz.e: The system suited recording numbers, but calculations were done on counting boards instead.

quiz.q: What made Indian numerals so useful for arithmetic?
o: Place value, with zero to fill gaps
Each number had its own unique symbol
They used only the digits 1 and 2
They had separate symbols for each power of ten
quiz.e: Place value and zero let ten symbols write any number and made written sums fast and reliable.

LESSONS.push: Why does an hour have 60 minutes? The answer goes back about 4,000 years.

LESSONS.title: Shells, silver and plastic: a history of money
LESSONS.hook: Money is one of humanity's strangest inventions: a shared story that strangers agree to believe. Here's how it went from clay tablets to tap and go.

sections.key: Money probably began as a way of keeping score of debts, not as a fix for awkward barter.
sections.b:
The textbook story says a baker wants shoes, the shoemaker wants fish, and nobody can trade until someone invents money. It has been told since Adam Smith's day. But anthropologists have struggled to find any society that ran on everyday barter. In small communities, people shared, gave gifts and kept informal track of who owed whom. Barter mostly showed up between strangers, or where money had collapsed, such as prisoner of war camps where cigarettes became currency.

David Graeber made the argument famous in his 2011 book Debt: The First 5,000 Years. Credit and obligation probably came before coins, not after. Money began as a way of keeping score.

sections.key: One of money's oldest jobs is as a unit of account, a shared measuring stick for value.
sections.b:
More than 4,000 years ago in Mesopotamia, in what is now Iraq, scribes pressed marks into wet clay to record who owed what. Temples and palaces collected grain, managed workers and lent out goods, so they needed a common yardstick. They settled on weights of silver, measured in shekels, alongside measures of barley. A farmer might owe a debt valued in silver but pay it in grain at harvest, while the silver stayed locked in the temple.

One of money's oldest jobs is as a unit of account. Paying with a physical object came later.

sections.key: A ruler's stamp turned a lump of metal into something people could trust without weighing it.
sections.b:
People have used remarkable things as money. Cowrie shells circulated for centuries across parts of Africa and Asia because they were durable, hard to fake and easy to count. On the island of Yap, people used huge carved stone discs called rai, some too heavy to move, so ownership changed by community agreement while the stone stayed put.

The first stamped coins appeared in Lydia, in what is now western Turkey, around the 600s BC. Made of electrum, a natural mix of gold and silver, they were stamped by the state to vouch for their weight. A ruler's stamp turned a lump of metal into something people could trust without weighing it.

sections.key: Paper money works because of the promise and belief behind it, not the paper itself.
sections.b:
Heavy iron and copper coins were a nuisance, so merchants in Sichuan, China, began depositing coins for paper receipts. In the Song dynasty, around the early 1000s, the government issued official paper money. In Europe, paper money grew out of goldsmiths and banks writing receipts for gold deposits, which were passed around as payment. It works only if people believe it can be spent, and Chinese dynasties learned that printing too many notes made them lose value. The paper wasn't valuable; the promise was.

In colonial New South Wales, coins were so scarce that rum acted like a currency. In 1813 Governor Macquarie had a hole punched out of Spanish silver dollars, making two coins, the holey dollar and the dump, which stayed in the colony. Australia went decimal in February 1966.

sections.key: Modern money works because enough people agree that it does, and most of it is now digital.
sections.b:
By the late 1800s many leading economies were on the gold standard, with paper money swappable for a fixed amount of gold. After the Second World War, currencies were linked to the US dollar, which was convertible to gold, until President Nixon ended that in 1971. Since then most money has been fiat: valued because governments declare it legal tender, accept it for taxes, and central banks try to keep it stable.

Australia issued the world's first polymer banknote in 1988. Yet cash is shrinking as people tap cards and phones, and most money is now numbers in accounts. Bitcoin, launched in 2009, tried to work without a central issuer, though its price swings wildly. Money works because enough people agree that it does.

quiz.q: What does the evidence suggest about how money began?
o: Credit and obligation probably came before coins
Coins were invented to replace everyday barter
Governments first created money to collect taxes
Money began when traders swapped shells for grain
quiz.e: Anthropologists find little evidence of everyday barter, suggesting money began as a record of debts.

quiz.q: What is a 'unit of account'?
o: A coin stamped with a ruler's face
A shared measuring stick for comparing value
A weight of silver kept in a temple
A receipt exchanged for a deposit of gold
quiz.e: Mesopotamian scribes used silver weights and barley to compare very different goods and debts.

quiz.q: What did a stamp on early Lydian coins provide?
o: Trust in the coin's weight without having to weigh it
Protection from forgers using other metals
Proof that the coin was made of pure gold
A guaranteed fixed exchange rate for foreign traders
quiz.e: The state's stamp vouched for the weight, so people could use the coin on trust.

quiz.q: Why does paper money have value?
o: The paper is made from rare materials
It can always be swapped for gold
People believe the promise that it can be spent
Banks will swap it for silver on request
quiz.e: The note itself is cheap; its worth rests on belief in the promise behind it.

quiz.q: What is fiat money?
o: Money backed by a fixed amount of gold
Money made from precious metals such as silver
Currency declared legal tender by a government
Digital money issued without any central bank
quiz.e: Since the gold link ended, most money works through legal tender status and public trust.

LESSONS.push: Most of today's money isn't paper or coin. What is it, and why do we trust it?

LESSONS.title: How banks create money out of thin air
LESSONS.hook: When a bank approves a home loan, it doesn't hand over someone else's savings. It creates brand new money with a few keystrokes.

sections.key: When a bank approves a loan, it creates a new deposit that didn't exist a moment earlier.
sections.b:
Imagine a couple borrowing $600,000 for a house. Most people assume the bank passes along other customers' savings. Not quite. When the loan is approved, the bank records a loan the couple owes it, and a matching deposit paid to the seller's account. That deposit didn't exist a moment earlier. It is brand new money, spendable like any other in a bank account.

The Bank of England explained this in a 2014 article, 'Money creation in the modern economy', and the Reserve Bank of Australia describes it the same way. Most money in the economy is created like this.

sections.key: Most everyday money is bank deposits, which are promises from banks rather than cash in a vault.
sections.b: The balance in your banking app is not cash in a vault with your name on it. It is a promise from your bank to pay you, an IOU you can use to make payments. When you tap your card, the bank moves that promise to someone else's account. These deposits count as part of the money supply, and they dwarf physical cash. Banknotes are issued by the Reserve Bank, and coins by the federal government and made by the Royal Australian Mint. But most day to day money is bank deposits, so private banks create most of a modern country's money, under rules set by public authorities.

sections.key: Banks lend first and deposits follow, so the amount of money depends heavily on how much people want to borrow.
sections.b: Many textbooks describe a money multiplier: savers deposit money, the bank keeps a fraction in reserve and lends the rest, which is deposited and lent again. It isn't completely wrong, because lending ripples through the system. But central banks have said it gets cause and effect backwards. Banks don't usually wait for deposits. They lend when they find creditworthy borrowers, and the deposits are created in the process. Afterwards, they manage the consequences, such as holding enough reserves to settle payments with other banks. So the amount of money depends heavily on how much people and businesses want to borrow.

sections.key: Repaying loans destroys money, so the money supply grows or shrinks with lending.
sections.b:
Repaying a loan does the opposite of taking one. When the couple makes a mortgage repayment, their deposit and the loan balance both fall, and that money effectively vanishes. The money supply grows when new lending outpaces repayments and can shrink when people rush to pay down debt, as in some economies after the 2008 financial crisis. A surge in lending pumps new money into houses, cars and businesses, which can push prices up.

What limits lending? Banks need borrowers likely to repay, because bad loans cost money. APRA requires them to hold enough capital and liquid assets. Funding costs interest. And when the RBA raises its cash rate, fewer people borrow and less money is created. It is a powerful but imprecise lever.

sections.key: Banks hold only a small share of assets as ready cash, so a loss of trust can cause a run.
sections.b:
Banks hold only a small portion of assets as ready cash and reserves. That's fine, because depositors don't all want their money on the same day. But if people fear a bank is in trouble, they may rush to withdraw, and the fear becomes self fulfilling. This is a bank run. Customers queued outside Northern Rock in Britain in 2007, and in 2023 depositors pulled billions from Silicon Valley Bank in hours, largely through phone apps. Australia's Financial Claims Scheme protects deposits up to a set limit per person per bank; check the current figure at fcs.gov.au.

None of this means banks print free money, since every loan carries risk and must be repaid. This is general information, not financial advice; see moneysmart.gov.au.

quiz.q: What happens when a bank approves a home loan?
o: It moves money from another customer's savings account
It prints notes and delivers them to the seller
It records the loan and creates a matching new deposit
It borrows the full amount from the Reserve Bank first
quiz.e: The loan and a brand new deposit are recorded together, so lending creates money.

quiz.q: What is the balance you see in your banking app?
o: Cash held in a vault with your name on it
A share of the bank's gold reserves
A record of the notes you have deposited
A promise from your bank to pay you
quiz.e: Deposits are IOUs from the bank, and they make up most of the money we use.

quiz.q: What have central banks said about the money multiplier story?
o: It is exactly right and describes how all lending works
It gets cause and effect backwards, as loans create deposits
It applies only to coins and banknotes held by banks
It proves banks must wait for deposits before lending
quiz.e: Banks usually lend first, creating deposits in the process, rather than waiting for savings.

quiz.q: What happens to money when a loan is repaid?
o: It moves to the Reserve Bank's account as a reserve
It is stored by the bank as extra savings for later
It is lent out again straight away to new borrowers
It is effectively destroyed as deposit and loan both fall
quiz.e: Repayments shrink both the deposit and the loan, so repaying debt reduces the money supply.

quiz.q: Why can a bank run happen even at a healthy bank?
o: Banks keep all deposits as cash that can be stolen
Banks hold little ready cash, so fear can feed itself
Regulators order healthy banks to close without warning
Banks lose the ability to lend after any withdrawal
quiz.e: If many depositors withdraw at once, fear itself can push a bank into trouble.

LESSONS.push: When a bank lends you money, where does it come from? The answer surprises most people.

LESSONS.title: Hyperinflation: when money stops working
LESSONS.hook: Imagine your wages losing half their value before you can spend them. In Weimar Germany and Zimbabwe, that nightmare became daily life.

sections.key: Hyperinflation devours money's value until people stop trusting money at all.
sections.b:
In the autumn of 1923, a German worker might be paid twice a day and hurry out at lunchtime to buy food before prices rose again. Photographs show children building towers from bundles of banknotes, and people reportedly burned money because it was cheaper than firewood. By November 1923, one US dollar was worth about 4.2 trillion German marks. Lifetime savings were wiped out, and a pension that once supported a comfortable retirement could barely buy a loaf of bread.

This was hyperinflation. Normal inflation slowly nibbles away at money's value. Hyperinflation devours it, until people stop trusting money altogether.

sections.key: A common definition of hyperinflation is prices rising at least 50 per cent in a month.
sections.b:
Inflation is a general rise in prices over time. Central banks such as the Reserve Bank of Australia aim to keep it low and steady, at around 2 to 3 per cent a year. Hyperinflation is a different beast. A common definition, from the economist Phillip Cagan in the 1950s, is prices rising at least 50 per cent in a month. At that pace prices more than double every couple of months and rise well over a hundredfold in a year.

In the worst cases it is far faster. Hungary after the Second World War holds the record: in July 1946 prices were doubling roughly every 15 hours. Episodes like this are rare, but they have happened on almost every continent.

sections.key: Hyperinflation usually starts when a government pays its bills by creating money, then feeds on itself.
sections.b:
Almost every hyperinflation starts with a government in deep trouble. It owes more than it can raise through taxes or borrowing, so it has the central bank create money. In 1923 French and Belgian troops occupied Germany's industrial Ruhr after Germany fell behind on war reparations. Germany backed passive resistance there, paying striking workers with newly printed money while output collapsed. When more money chases fewer goods, prices climb, the government needs more money, and it prints faster. The cycle feeds itself.

Psychology speeds it up. If people expect money to be worth less tomorrow, they spend wages at once and shops raise prices early. Economists call this rising velocity of money. People turn to barter, foreign currency, land or gold. Once trust is lost, it is very hard to win back.

sections.key: Zimbabwe's hyperinflation ended when people abandoned the local currency for foreign money.
sections.b:
One of the best known modern examples was Zimbabwe. During the 2000s, farm production collapsed after controversial land seizures, exports fell, and heavy government spending was increasingly funded by creating money. By 2008 inflation was so extreme that official statistics stopped being reliable, with estimates running into the billions of per cent a year.

The central bank issued ever larger notes, culminating in a 100 trillion Zimbabwean dollar note, which soon became a collector's novelty. In 2009 the country effectively gave up on its own currency, and people began using foreign money such as the US dollar and the South African rand. Prices stabilised almost immediately once that happened.

sections.key: Hyperinflations can end quickly when credibility returns, but the damage lasts and falls hardest on savers.
sections.b:
Hyperinflations can end quickly. Germany's ended in late 1923 with a new currency, the Rentenmark, strict limits on issuing it, and efforts to balance the budget. Within weeks prices steadied. The pattern repeats: a new or foreign currency and a government that stops printing to fund itself. The key is credibility, which is one reason many countries give central banks independence from day to day politics.

The damage lasts. It hits savers, pensioners and people on fixed incomes hardest, while those with debts, land or foreign currency may come out ahead. Historians debate how much 1923 contributed to the turmoil that followed, though many say the Great Depression did more. It did shape Germany's later caution about inflation, and so the European Central Bank.

quiz.q: What distinguishes hyperinflation from normal inflation?
o: It affects only the prices of food and fuel
It destroys trust in money, so trade breaks down
It lasts a few days and then stops by itself
It is caused by too little money in circulation
quiz.e: Normal inflation erodes value slowly, while hyperinflation wrecks confidence in money itself.

quiz.q: By one common definition, what rate counts as hyperinflation?
o: Prices rising at least 5 per cent in a year
Prices rising at least 10 per cent in a month
Prices rising at least 50 per cent in a month
Prices doubling every ten years
quiz.e: A 50 per cent monthly rise means prices more than double every couple of months.

quiz.q: Why does printing money to pay bills feed hyperinflation?
o: Rising prices raise its costs, so it prints even faster
Printing money lowers prices by increasing supply
People save more when there is more cash around
Banks lend less once the government prints money
quiz.e: Prices climb, costs rise, and more printing follows, so the cycle feeds itself.

quiz.q: What happened in Zimbabwe once people used foreign currencies?
o: Inflation became even worse
Prices stabilised almost immediately
The 100 trillion dollar note became widely used
Production collapsed further straight away
quiz.e: Abandoning the failing currency for foreign money removed the source of the price spiral.

quiz.q: What is the crucial ingredient in ending a hyperinflation?
o: Credibility: belief that the new money holds value
A much larger supply of banknotes in circulation
Higher taxes on everyone who still has savings
Barter for everyday goods and services instead
quiz.e: Strict, visibly enforced rules let people trust that the new money will keep its value.

LESSONS.push: In 1923 a German worker rushed out at lunch to spend wages. What was she afraid of?

LESSONS.title: Bubbles and manias: when prices lose their minds
LESSONS.hook: Tulip bulbs, South Sea shares and internet start ups have all sold for wildly more than they were worth. Why do sensible people keep getting swept up?

sections.key: A bubble is a price far above what an asset's future income or use could justify, kept up by hopes of selling higher.
sections.b:
Picture a street where house prices have doubled in two years. People who've never invested start buying, not to live there, but because they're sure prices will keep rising. That's the feeling of a bubble.

Economists define it roughly as a period when an asset's price climbs far above what its future income or usefulness could justify, kept aloft mainly by people expecting to sell to someone else at a higher price. This is the 'greater fool' theory: you don't need something to be worth the price, as long as someone more optimistic will pay more later. Bubbles are notoriously hard to spot for certain while they are happening.

sections.key: Early bubbles in tulips and South Sea shares show how hype can lift prices far above worth, though tulip mania was probably exaggerated.
sections.b:
In the Dutch Republic in the 1630s, rare tulips with streaked petals became status symbols. Some bulbs reportedly sold for more than a skilled worker earned in years, and traders bought contracts for bulbs still in the ground. The market collapsed in February 1637. Charles Mackay's 1841 book made it the ultimate tale of collective madness, though historians such as Anne Goldgar argue it involved fewer people and less economic damage than the legend suggests.

In 1720 the South Sea Company, set up in 1711 and mainly managing government debt, offered to take over much of Britain's national debt for its shares. The price rose roughly tenfold in months, then collapsed that year. Thousands lost fortunes, reportedly including Isaac Newton. In France, John Law's Mississippi scheme also boomed and burst.

sections.key: Modern bubbles in tech shares and US housing ended in crashes with wide consequences.
sections.b:
In the late 1990s, investors poured money into almost any company with '.com' in its name, many with little revenue and no profits. The technology heavy Nasdaq index soared, then fell by roughly three quarters between 2000 and 2002. Some companies, like Amazon, survived and thrived; many others vanished.

A few years later came the US housing bubble. Easy lending, including loans to people unlikely to repay, pushed house prices up across much of America. When prices began to fall from around 2006, defaults rose and losses spread through banks worldwide, contributing to the global financial crisis of 2008. Australia was cushioned more than many countries, but felt the shock too.

sections.key: Many bubbles follow a familiar path from real innovation, through euphoria, to panic selling.
sections.b:
The economists Hyman Minsky and Charles Kindleberger described a pattern many bubbles follow. It begins with a displacement, something genuinely new, such as railways, the internet or a new financial product. Early investors make real money. Credit expands, more people pile in, and rising prices seem to prove the optimists right.

Then comes euphoria, when caution is mocked and people say 'this time is different'. Some insiders quietly sell. Prices wobble, borrowers who bought with debt are forced to sell, and selling feeds more selling until panic sets in. The shape is familiar across centuries, from canal shares in the 1790s to recent crypto crazes.

sections.key: Intelligent people join bubbles because of social proof, rising prices, career pressure, easy credit and real innovation.
sections.b:
Intelligent, experienced investors have joined in. Watching neighbours get rich is powerful social proof. Rising prices create their own story, since each gain seems to confirm the last. Professionals may follow the crowd, as being wrong with everyone is safer for a career than being wrong alone. Easy credit magnifies gains and losses. And there's often a genuine innovation underneath: railways and the internet really did change the world.

Why not sell at the top? Almost nobody can reliably tell where it is, and calling a bubble too early can cost as much as too late. Many experts suggest not putting everything into one hot asset, being wary of borrowing to speculate, and being sceptical when everyone says prices can only go up. This is general information, not financial advice; see moneysmart.gov.au.

quiz.q: What best describes a financial bubble?
o: A price far above an asset's worth, held up by hopes of resale
A steady rise in prices driven by growing company profits
A sharp fall in prices after bad news about the economy
A period when interest rates are unusually low for years
quiz.e: Bubbles rest on expecting to sell to someone else at a higher price, not on the asset's real value.

quiz.q: What do historians such as Anne Goldgar say about tulip mania?
o: It ruined the whole Dutch economy for decades
It never happened and was invented later on
It was smaller and less damaging than the legend
It was caused mainly by a shortage of bulbs
quiz.e: The legend is memorable, but the evidence suggests the episode was smaller than the popular story.

quiz.q: What happened as US house prices began falling from around 2006?
o: Banks made large profits from the cheaper homes
Lenders eased their standards even further at once
Defaults rose and losses spread to banks worldwide
Prices recovered fully within a few weeks
quiz.e: Falling prices and rising defaults hit banks and helped trigger the 2008 global financial crisis.

quiz.q: What typically happens in the euphoria stage of a bubble?
o: Prices fall as investors become more careful
Regulators step in and ban all new borrowing
Insiders buy heavily to hold prices up
Caution is mocked and 'this time is different'
quiz.e: Rising prices make caution look foolish, which draws in more buyers.

quiz.q: Why can't investors simply sell at the top of a bubble?
o: Selling is not allowed during a boom
Almost nobody can reliably tell where the top is
Prices always fall before the top is reached
Banks refuse to process trades near the peak
quiz.e: Prices can stay high for years, so calling the peak is extremely hard, even for experts.

LESSONS.push: Smart people have lost fortunes in every bubble in history. Why do they keep joining in?

LESSONS.title: Opportunity cost: the hidden price of every choice
LESSONS.hook: Everything you choose to do means something else you didn't. Economists call that missing alternative the opportunity cost, and it changes how you see every decision.

sections.key: Opportunity cost is the value of the best option you gave up, even when no money changes hands.
sections.b: Say you've got a free Saturday and $100, and spend both at a music festival. The ticket price is obvious, but what else did that day cost? Perhaps a beach trip with friends, a shift that would have paid $200, or a lazy day of rest. Economists call the value of the best option you gave up the opportunity cost. It matters because every choice involves a trade off, even when no money changes hands. The festival might still be right. The point is not guilt, but seeing clearly what you're choosing between, rather than only noticing the price tag.

sections.key: Nothing is truly free: free things are paid for with data, taxes, attention or time.
sections.b: The saying 'there's no such thing as a free lunch' was popularised by Milton Friedman. It dates back to American saloons that offered free food to customers who bought drinks; the cost was built into the price of beer. The same logic applies widely. A free app may be paid for with your data and attention. A free park was paid for with taxes, and the land could have been used for housing. Your own time is never free, because an hour scrolling is an hour not spent sleeping, exercising or talking to someone you love. Recognising hidden costs doesn't mean refusing free things. It means knowing what you're trading.

sections.key: Time only runs one way, so the real cost of many choices is what else those hours could give you.
sections.b: Money can be earned again, but time only runs one way, so it's a key place to think about opportunity cost. Should you spend two hours driving across town to save $20? It depends on what else those hours could give you. Studying for a qualification means giving up income or leisure now for higher earnings or more satisfying work later. A big cost of university for many students is not the fees but the wages they could have earned instead. None of these choices has a universal right answer. Opportunity cost turns a vague feeling into a clearer question: is this the best use of my time?

sections.key: Count the unseen alternatives, and ignore sunk costs that are gone whatever you decide.
sections.b:
In 1850 Frederic Bastiat told the parable of the broken window. A boy smashes a shop window, and onlookers say at least the glazier gets work. Bastiat asked about the unseen: the shopkeeper would have spent that money elsewhere, perhaps on shoes, so the shoemaker loses what the glazier gains, and the town is a window poorer. When someone says a project will create jobs, ask what the money would otherwise have done.

Sunk costs work the other way. If you paid $150 for a concert ticket but you're sick and it's pouring, that $150 is gone whether you go or not. The only question is whether the night out beats staying home now. Throwing good resources after bad to avoid admitting a loss is the real waste.

sections.key: Use opportunity cost on decisions that matter by naming the realistic next best alternative.
sections.b:
Textbooks illustrate opportunity cost with 'guns and butter': with limited workers and materials, more military spending means fewer civilian goods. Budgets work the same way. Funding a hospital, road, tax cut or defence program means not spending that money elsewhere, or borrowing and paying interest later. Asking 'compared with what?' is a powerful question in politics.

Taken too far, the idea could make life miserable, as if every coffee should have been invested. It works best for decisions that matter: a job offer, a big purchase, a windfall, or whether to keep pouring effort into something that isn't working. Before a significant choice, name the realistic next best alternative out loud. You'll choose with open eyes, and sometimes rest or fun is the best use of your time.

quiz.q: What is the opportunity cost of attending the festival in this example?
o: Only the price of the ticket and nothing else
The value of the best alternative, such as a paid shift
The combined value of every other way to spend the day
The money you would have saved by staying home
quiz.e: Opportunity cost is the single best option you gave up, not just the price you pay.

quiz.q: Why is a 'free lunch' not really free?
o: The food is always of poorer quality than paid meals
Someone always demands a favour in return later
Saloons simply lose money on every meal they serve
The cost is hidden elsewhere, such as in drink prices
quiz.e: The saloon recovered the lunch cost through the price of beer, so the cost was hidden, not absent.

quiz.q: Why might driving two hours to save $20 be a poor choice?
o: Bargains usually turn out to be poor quality
Those hours may be worth more spent elsewhere
Petrol always costs more than the amount saved
Savings under $50 are never worth any effort
quiz.e: Time only runs one way, so the question is what else those hours could provide.

quiz.q: What should you do about a sunk cost, like a non-refundable ticket?
o: Go anyway so the money is not wasted
Add its price to the cost of staying home
Ignore it and weigh only what happens from here
Ask friends whether they would go instead
quiz.e: The money is gone either way, so only the future costs and benefits should affect your decision.

quiz.q: What is a good habit for a significant decision?
o: Name the realistic next best alternative first
Always choose the cheapest option available
Weigh opportunity cost on every small purchase
Avoid dwelling on trade-offs until afterwards
quiz.e: Naming what you give up helps you choose with open eyes, without second-guessing every small choice.

LESSONS.push: Every choice has a price you never see on the receipt. Here's how to spot it.

LESSONS.title: Externalities: the costs nobody pays for
LESSONS.hook: When a factory pollutes a river, someone pays the price, just not the factory or its customers. That gap is one of the biggest ideas in economics.

sections.key: An externality is a cost or benefit that lands on people outside the transaction, so the price misses it.
sections.b:
It's 7am on Sunday, and your neighbour fires up a petrol leaf blower. They get a tidy driveway. You get a ruined sleep in. Your lost rest doesn't appear on their bill, so it doesn't factor into their decision.

Economists call this an externality: a side effect of an activity that falls on people outside the transaction. Externalities can be negative, like noise, pollution or congestion, or positive, like a neighbour's beautiful garden. Markets match prices to costs and benefits. When some sit outside the price, markets can produce too much of the harmful stuff and too little of the helpful, often called a market failure.

sections.key: Pigou proposed taxing harm to match its cost, while Coase showed bargaining can also solve it when talking is cheap.
sections.b:
In his 1920 book The Economics of Welfare, Arthur Pigou noted that the private cost of an activity can differ from its social cost, which includes harm to others. A factory owner pays for fuel and wages, not for the coughing downwind. His solution: tax the harm by the damage it causes, so the price reflects the true cost. Such charges are called Pigouvian taxes, and economists across much of the political spectrum like them.

In 1960 Ronald Coase argued taxes aren't always the answer. If rights are clear and bargaining is cheap, the parties might negotiate: neighbours pay for filters, or the factory compensates them. The catch, as Coase stressed, is that bargaining is often costly. You can't negotiate with millions affected by air pollution, so governments usually step in.

sections.key: Positive externalities mean people may do too little of what benefits others, which is why governments support them.
sections.b:
Externalities aren't all bad news. When you get vaccinated, you lower your own risk but also make it harder for disease to spread to others, including people who can't be vaccinated. Education ripples out to employers, colleagues and the wider community. A beekeeper's bees pollinate nearby orchards without sending the orchardist a bill.

The problem is the mirror image of the negative kind: because people don't capture all the benefits, they may do less of the good thing than society would like. That's one reason governments subsidise or provide things such as vaccination programs, schooling and research. Debate continues about exactly how much support is justified, but the economic logic is widely accepted.

sections.key: Shared resources can be overused when each user gains and everyone shares the cost, but communities can manage them.
sections.b:
In 1968 the ecologist Garrett Hardin popularised the 'tragedy of the commons'. Imagine a pasture open to all herders. Each gains from adding another cow, while the cost of overgrazing is shared by everyone, so the pasture ends up ruined. Overfishing is a classic example: each boat has an incentive to catch more before others do.

Hardin thought the only solutions were government control or private ownership. Elinor Ostrom disagreed. She studied fisheries, forests and irrigation systems around the world and found that many communities manage shared resources successfully with their own local rules, monitoring and penalties. In 2009 she became the first woman to win the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences, shared with Oliver Williamson.

sections.key: Charges, deposits and permits try to make people pay for harm, and the key question is always who bears the cost.
sections.b:
Pigou's idea shows up in daily life. London introduced a congestion charge in 2003, and Stockholm and Singapore have similar schemes. Container deposit schemes, now in every Australian state and territory, put a small refundable value on bottles and cans. Carbon pricing charges for emissions through a tax or a cap and trade system where companies trade permits. Australia had a carbon price from 2012 until 2014, and the topic remains politically contested.

Externalities are everywhere: each extra car slows everyone on a busy road, and a loud phone call costs train passengers their peace. Many are handled by manners and norms. A useful question: who gets the benefit, who bears the cost, and do they line up? When they don't, trouble usually follows.

quiz.q: Why does the leaf blower example show an externality?
o: The noise costs you, not the person making it
The blower is an expensive item to buy and run
Both neighbours benefit from the tidy driveway
The noise is a cost only the owner bears
quiz.e: A cost falling on someone outside the transaction is an externality, and it is not in the price.

quiz.q: What does a Pigouvian tax aim to do?
o: Raise as much revenue for government as possible
Make prices reflect the full social cost of harm
Ban the harmful activity completely and permanently
Compensate people who suffer the harm
quiz.e: Taxing harm by its damage makes producers and buyers account for costs they would otherwise ignore.

quiz.q: Why might people do too little of something with positive externalities?
o: They cannot keep all the benefits for themselves
Governments usually tax activities that help others
The benefits are always too small to measure
People tend to dislike activities that help others
quiz.e: Because others share the benefit, individuals undervalue the activity compared with society.

quiz.q: What did Elinor Ostrom find about shared resources?
o: They are always ruined unless government controls them
They must be sold to private owners to survive
Many communities manage them well with local rules
Overuse cannot happen where users know each other
quiz.e: Her studies showed that monitoring and local rules can prevent the tragedy of the commons.

quiz.q: What do container deposit schemes do?
o: Tax drinks to pay for rubbish collection
Ban plastic bottles from all supermarkets
Put a refundable value on bottles and cans
Charge shops a fee for every bottle sold
quiz.e: A small refundable deposit gives people a reason to return containers rather than discard them.

LESSONS.push: Who pays for the noise, the smoke and the traffic? Often, not the person making it.

LESSONS.title: Incentives: why rewards so often backfire
LESSONS.hook: Offer people a reward and they'll respond, just not always the way you hoped. Here's why clever incentives can go spectacularly wrong.

sections.key: People respond to what is actually rewarded, not what the designer meant.
sections.b:
In 1902 French colonial authorities in Hanoi faced rats in the city's new sewers, and plague made it urgent. They offered a small bounty for every rat killed, paid on presentation of a tail. Soon officials noticed rats running around without tails. People were cutting off tails for the reward and releasing the rats to breed. The historian Michael Vann found reports of rat farming too.

The scheme did what it paid for, not what it meant. People respond to what is actually rewarded, not what the designer intended. It's one of the most important and most forgotten lessons in economics.

sections.key: An incentive is anything that makes an action more or less attractive, and careless design invites gaming.
sections.b:
If there's one sentence many economists would put on a T shirt, it's 'people respond to incentives'. An incentive is anything that makes an action more or less attractive: a price, a bonus, a fine, a deadline, even praise or embarrassment. Raise the price of something and people tend to buy less of it.

Many responses are what policymakers want. Australia's container deposit schemes and rooftop solar incentives have changed behaviour on a large scale. The trouble comes when incentives are designed carelessly, because people are quick to find the easiest path to a reward, whether or not it achieves the actual goal.

sections.key: When a measure becomes a target, people game it and it stops being a good measure.
sections.b:
In 1975 the economist Charles Goodhart observed that statistics used to guide policy tend to break down once they become targets. Marilyn Strathern later summed it up: 'When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.'

A call centre rewarding short call times may find staff hanging up on difficult customers. A hospital judged on waiting times may find creative ways to reclassify waits. Schools judged on test scores can end up teaching to the test. There's an old Soviet era joke about a nail factory: given a target by weight, it made a few giant useless nails; given a target by number, it made millions of tiny ones. Whatever gets measured gets gamed.

sections.key: A small fine can turn a moral duty into a price, and money can crowd out other motives.
sections.b:
In a 2000 study, Uri Gneezy and Aldo Rustichini looked at Israeli day care centres where parents were often late. Some introduced a small fine, and lateness rose. The paper's title, 'A Fine Is a Price', gives the reason: late pick-up had meant imposing on a teacher's goodwill, but now it felt like a service parents could buy. When the fines were removed, lateness stayed high. A cheap financial incentive had replaced a social one, and the old norm didn't return.

Money can crowd out other motives. In 1970 Richard Titmuss argued that paying for blood could undermine the civic duty of voluntary donors. Researchers debate how strong this is, and payment raises effort in many settings. But people are also motivated by pride, fairness and belonging. Australia's Lifeblood relies on unpaid volunteers.

sections.key: Good incentive design rewards the true goal, expects gaming, and remembers that trust and pride are incentives too.
sections.b:
Moral hazard is an insurance term: if someone else bears the cost when things go wrong, people may be less careful. A driver with comprehensive insurance might park carelessly. A bank expecting a rescue might make riskier loans, keeping profits and passing losses to taxpayers, a worry after 2008. Insurers use excesses so customers share part of every claim. It can be managed, not eliminated.

Australia's banking Royal Commission, which reported in 2019, heard many examples of staff chasing commissions and sales targets at customers' expense. To design better incentives, reward the true goal rather than an easy proxy, imagine how a cynical person might game it and close those loopholes, and use several measures. Pride, trust and fairness are incentives too. Ask the rat tail question: what am I really paying for?

quiz.q: What went wrong with the Hanoi rat bounty?
o: Nobody wanted to hunt rats for the money
Officials refused to pay out for the rat tails
People bred rats and cut off tails for cash
The bounty was too large for the city to afford
quiz.e: The reward was for tails, so people found cheaper ways to produce tails than to reduce rats.

quiz.q: What does 'people respond to incentives' mean?
o: People always do exactly what designers hope for
Only cash rewards can ever change behaviour
Incentives work on businesses but never on individuals
Rewards and penalties change behaviour, often unexpectedly
quiz.e: People take the easiest path to a reward, whether or not it serves the real goal.

quiz.q: What does Goodhart's law warn about?
o: Statistics can never be collected accurately
A measure turned into a target stops being a good one
Targets always improve the quality of services
Large organisations should avoid all measurement
quiz.e: Once people are judged on a number, they work on the number rather than the goal behind it.

quiz.q: Why did the day care fine increase lateness?
o: The fine was bigger than parents could afford
Teachers refused to accept the fine money
Parents were never told that the fine existed
Lateness started to feel like a service to buy
quiz.e: The fine replaced a social obligation with a cheap financial one, and the norm didn't return.

quiz.q: What is a sound rule for designing better incentives?
o: Set one clear measure as a strict target
Reward the real goal, not an easy proxy
Offer the biggest bonus the budget allows
Remove every penalty for poor outcomes
quiz.e: Rewarding the real goal leaves fewer easy loopholes for people to exploit.

LESSONS.push: A bounty on rat tails produced more rats. What does that say about rewards?

LESSONS.title: Smith, Marx, Keynes and Hayek: the great economic debate
LESSONS.hook: Four thinkers shaped how the modern world argues about markets, governments and fairness. Their ideas still echo in every budget and election.

sections.key: Adam Smith argued that specialisation and trade create wealth, with self-interest kept in check by competition and rules.
sections.b:
In 1776 Adam Smith opened The Wealth of Nations with a pin factory. One worker alone might make one pin a day, and certainly not twenty. Ten workers splitting the job into specialised steps could make around 48,000. Specialisation plus trade, he argued, was the engine of prosperity.

A butcher or baker feeds us out of self-interest, not kindness, and competition steers that self-interest towards serving others. He used the phrase 'invisible hand' only once in the book. Smith was no cheerleader for business: he distrusted merchants conspiring to raise prices, criticised monopolies, and backed public spending on defence, justice, infrastructure and some basic education. He had also written The Theory of Moral Sentiments (1759), on how sympathy underpins morality.

sections.key: Karl Marx argued that owners profit from the value workers create beyond their wages, and that capitalism is prone to crisis.
sections.b:
Decades later, Karl Marx looked at the same industrial world and saw crowded slums, long hours and child labour. In The Communist Manifesto (1848, with Friedrich Engels) and the first volume of Capital (1867), he argued that capitalism rested on conflict between those who owned factories and those who worked in them.

Workers, he claimed, produced more value than they were paid, and owners kept the difference as profit. He predicted repeated crises and eventual overthrow. His ideas inspired socialist movements and later communist states, whose record of repression and economic failure has been heavily criticised. Many historians still credit him with sharpening questions about power, inequality and economic change.

sections.key: Keynes argued that in a slump, governments should spend more or cut taxes to restart demand, even if that means borrowing.
sections.b:
In the Great Depression of the 1930s, mass unemployment lasted for years, and advice to wait for markets to correct themselves looked hopeless. In The General Theory (1936), John Maynard Keynes offered a different diagnosis: an economy can get stuck with too little total spending, or demand.

When households and businesses are frightened, they cut back. That cuts other people's incomes and causes more cutbacks. In such times, he said, governments should step in, spending more or cutting taxes to restart demand, even if it means borrowing. He had earlier written the much quoted line 'In the long run we are all dead', a jab at those who said things would sort themselves out eventually.

sections.key: Friedrich Hayek argued that prices carry scattered knowledge that no central planner could ever gather.
sections.b:
Keynes's great rival was the Austrian-born economist Friedrich Hayek. In The Road to Serfdom (1944), he warned that heavy government planning could gradually erode personal freedom. His most influential idea came in a 1945 essay, 'The Use of Knowledge in Society'.

Useful knowledge, Hayek pointed out, is scattered among millions of people. A farmer knows the weather on her land, and a shopkeeper knows what customers want this week. No central planner could gather it all. Prices act like a vast communication system. If tin becomes scarce, its price rises, and people everywhere economise on tin without needing to know why. Markets, in this view, are a way of coordinating knowledge.

sections.key: Each thinker saw something real, and today's mixed economies argue mainly about the balance between markets and government.
sections.b:
After the Second World War, Keynesian ideas shaped policy across much of the West, including Australia, with governments aiming for full employment. The 1970s changed that. Oil shocks helped trigger stagflation, high inflation combined with high unemployment, which many Keynesian models struggled to explain. Milton Friedman, who argued that 'inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon', gained influence.

From the 1980s, many governments, Australia's included, floated currencies, deregulated finance and gave central banks the job of controlling inflation. After 2008, Keynesian stimulus returned. Today almost every developed economy is a mixed economy, and most political arguments are about the balance: how much to tax, spend and regulate, and how to share the gains from growth.

quiz.q: What did Smith's pin factory example show?
o: Splitting a job into steps multiplies output
Small workshops always outperform big factories
Merchants should set prices without competition
Workers produce most when each works alone
quiz.e: Specialisation and trade, Smith argued, are the engine of prosperity.

quiz.q: According to Marx, where did owners' profits come from?
o: Clever investment in gold and other metals
The value workers created beyond their wages
Government subsidies paid to industry owners
Trade with distant colonies and empires
quiz.e: Marx argued owners kept the gap between the value workers created and their wages as profit.

quiz.q: Why did Keynes want governments to spend during a slump?
o: Fear makes people spend less, which cuts incomes
Markets always correct themselves within a year
Government debt never causes any problems
Higher taxes always make people save more
quiz.e: Falling demand can feed on itself, so Keynes argued governments should restart it.

quiz.q: What did Hayek say prices do?
o: They reveal which products are morally valuable
They carry scattered knowledge to people who need it
They stay fixed unless planners change them
They only reflect what producers spend
quiz.e: Prices coordinate the knowledge of millions of people, which no planner could gather.

quiz.q: How are most developed economies, including Australia's, best described?
o: Wholly planned and directed by government
Completely free of regulation and public spending
Mixed, combining private markets and public services
Based on gold coins rather than paper currency
quiz.e: Most political argument is about the balance within a mixed economy, not about choosing one extreme.

LESSONS.push: Four thinkers, one pin factory, and an argument still shaping every budget.

LESSONS.title: Tardigrades: the toughest animals on Earth
LESSONS.hook: Smaller than a full stop, the eight-legged 'water bear' can survive being dried out for years, frozen solid and even exposed to open space.

sections.key: Tardigrades are microscopic, eight-legged animals found almost everywhere, from backyard moss to the polar regions.
sections.b:
Scrape moss off a garden wall, soak it in water and look through a microscope. You may see a plump creature lumbering along on eight stubby, clawed legs. This is a tardigrade. Most are well under a millimetre long, and the largest reach only about a millimetre and a half.

A German pastor called one a 'little water bear' in 1773, and the name stuck. Tardigrada means 'slow steppers'. More than 1,300 species are known. They live in moss, lichen, soil, fresh water and ocean sediments, from mountaintops to the deep sea and the poles. Most feed by piercing plant cells, algae or other tiny animals with sharp mouthparts.

sections.key: Tardigrades survive drying out by shrivelling into a dormant 'tun' in which their metabolism almost stops.
sections.b:
A tardigrade's watery home can vanish in one hot afternoon. As the moss dries, many species pull in their head and legs, lose almost all their body water and shrivel into a little barrel called a tun. Their metabolism slows until it can barely be detected. This state is called cryptobiosis, meaning 'hidden life'.

In a tun, a tardigrade can wait out drought for years. When water returns, it rehydrates and starts walking again within minutes to hours. In one well-known case, Japanese researchers revived tardigrades from Antarctic moss that had been frozen for more than 30 years, and one went on to lay eggs.

sections.key: Tardigrades' extreme tolerance applies mainly to the dried tun state, so their real talent is switching life off and on.
sections.b:
In laboratory experiments, dried tardigrades have survived chilling to within a degree or so of absolute zero and brief heating above the boiling point of water. They have endured pressures several times greater than the deepest ocean trench, and radiation doses hundreds of times higher than would kill a person.

It is easy to conclude they are indestructible, but they are not. Most of these feats apply only to dried tuns, and often only for short periods. An active, hydrated tardigrade is a fairly delicate animal, and long exposure to warm temperatures can kill it. Their real superpower is not toughness but the ability to switch life off and on.

sections.key: Dried tardigrades were the first animals known to survive open space, but the Moon is probably not now home to any.
sections.b:
In 2007 a European experiment launched dried tardigrades into low Earth orbit on an uncrewed Russian satellite. For about ten days they sat outside the spacecraft, exposed to vacuum and cosmic radiation. Back on Earth, many were rehydrated and recovered, and some went on to reproduce. Those that also faced unfiltered ultraviolet light from the Sun fared far worse, though a few survived. It was the first time any animal was known to survive open space.

In 2019 an Israeli lunar lander carrying dried tardigrades crashed on the Moon. Later laboratory tests, firing tardigrades from a gun, suggested the impact was probably too violent for them to survive.

sections.key: Special tardigrade proteins protect cells from drying and DNA damage, and may one day help store medicines without refrigeration.
sections.b:
Drying normally destroys cells, because proteins unfold and membranes tear. Brine shrimp flood their cells with a protective sugar, trehalose, but many tardigrades make little of it. Instead, researchers have found proteins unique to tardigrades that seem to form a gel and then a glass-like solid as the cell dries, holding delicate molecules in place. Another protein, Dsup ('damage suppressor'), binds DNA and appears to shield it. Human cells given the Dsup gene suffered noticeably less X-ray damage in the lab.

This could matter: many vaccines need refrigeration, which is hard in remote places such as the outback. But the work is at an early stage and may take many years. You can meet tardigrades yourself by soaking moss in water overnight and scanning it under a simple microscope.

quiz.q: What does the name Tardigrada mean?
o: Moss dwellers
Slow steppers
Tiny survivors
Water bears
quiz.e: Tardigrada means 'slow steppers', a nod to their lumbering walk.

quiz.q: What happens to a tardigrade in the dried tun state?
o: Its metabolism slows to almost nothing
It lays eggs, then dies in the drought
It grows a hard shell around its body
It keeps feeding slowly on dust particles
quiz.e: In cryptobiosis the animal loses nearly all its water and its metabolism almost stops, until water returns.

quiz.q: Which statement about tardigrade toughness is most accurate?
o: They are indestructible in every state
Active tardigrades survive boiling indefinitely
They tolerate extremes mainly when dried
They survive cold but never heat or radiation
quiz.e: The extreme feats mostly apply to dried tuns, so their real talent is switching life off and on.

quiz.q: What did the 2007 orbit experiment show?
o: Dried tardigrades survived open space, and some bred
Tardigrades cannot survive any amount of radiation
Tardigrades survived on the Moon for many years
Hydrated tardigrades coped best with the vacuum
quiz.e: Dried tardigrades were the first animals known to survive direct exposure to open space.

quiz.q: What does the protein Dsup appear to do?
o: Help them digest their prey
Make their cells glow in the dark
Protect their DNA from damage
Speed up how fast they reproduce
quiz.e: Dsup binds to DNA and seems to protect it, which is why it interests radiation researchers.

LESSONS.push: Smaller than a full stop, it can switch life off for years. Meet the water bear.

LESSONS.title: Mangroves: forests at the edge of the sea
LESSONS.hook: Muddy, smelly and buzzing with life, mangroves are trees that drink salt water, breathe through snorkels and quietly protect Australia's coasts.

sections.key: Mangroves are a mix of salt-tolerant trees and shrubs that grow where tropical and warm coasts meet the tide.
sections.b:
Walk a mangrove boardwalk at low tide and you hear snapping shrimp, popping air bubbles in the mud and crabs scuttling into holes. Twice a day, the sea floods in over the roots.

Mangroves are not one kind of plant but a mix of trees and shrubs from different families, each adapted to life where land meets salt water. They grow along sheltered tropical and warm coastlines worldwide. Australia has around 40 species and one of the largest areas of mangrove forest of any country, across the north and down both the east and west coasts. Around Darwin, Cairns and the Gulf of Carpentaria, they form vast, dense forests.

sections.key: Mangroves cope with salt by filtering or excreting it, and breathe and stand firm in airless mud using specialised roots.
sections.b:
Salt water kills most plants by drawing water out of their cells. Many mangroves filter salt out at the roots. Others take it in and then expel it: the grey mangrove, Australia's most widespread species, pushes salt out through glands in its leaves, and you may taste crystals on a leaf's underside. Some store salt in old leaves or bark and shed them. This costs energy, so growth is often slower in very salty places.

Mangrove mud has almost no oxygen. Grey mangroves send up pencil-like roots called pneumatophores that act as snorkels, taking in air through tiny pores at low tide. Red mangroves stand on arching prop roots. These tangles also anchor the trees and slow the water, so sediment settles and builds the shoreline.

sections.key: Many mangroves germinate on the parent tree, then drop or float away as seedlings that can drift for weeks or months.
sections.b:
Most plants drop seeds and wait for them to sprout. Many mangroves do something closer to giving birth. The seed germinates while still on the parent tree, growing into a seedling called a propagule. In some species these look like long green cigars or pens dangling from the branches.

When ready, the propagule drops. If the tide is out, it may lodge in the mud and start growing straight away. If the tide is in, it floats off and can drift for weeks or even months before washing up somewhere suitable. This head start helps the young plant establish where waves and tides would sweep away an ordinary seed. It is also how mangroves have spread along coastlines and between islands across the tropics.

sections.key: Mangroves shelter young fish, protect shorelines from waves and lock away large amounts of carbon in their muddy soils.
sections.b:
Calm water and tangled roots make an ideal nursery. Young fish and prawns hide from predators while feeding on fallen, decaying mangrove leaves. Barramundi, mud crabs, mangrove jack and banana prawns all depend on mangroves for part of their lives. Birds use them too. The rotten egg smell is not a sign of trouble: it comes from bacteria breaking down organic matter in oxygen-poor mud, part of the recycling that makes the system so productive.

Mangroves also act as a natural sea wall, absorbing wave and storm surge energy. Their waterlogged mud buries dead material, building deep, carbon-rich soil. Per hectare, these 'blue carbon' ecosystems can store several times more carbon than many land forests. Clearing them can release it.

sections.key: Clearing, development and climate extremes threaten mangroves, which are protected by law in Australia.
sections.b:
Worldwide, large areas of mangroves have been cleared for shrimp farms, ports, housing and farmland. Australia's are in better shape than many, but not immune. In late 2015 and early 2016, mangroves along roughly 1,000 kilometres of the Gulf of Carpentaria died back over a few months, affecting thousands of hectares.

Scientists linked the event to drought, high temperatures and a temporary drop in sea level during a strong El Niño. Some areas have since begun to recover. Mangroves are protected by law in Australian states and territories. In Queensland, for example, they are protected marine plants, and damaging them without approval is an offence, so check local rules before trimming any. The simplest way to appreciate them is from a boardwalk.

quiz.q: Roughly how many mangrove species does Australia have?
o: About 5
About 40
About 400
About 4,000
quiz.e: Australia has around 40 mangrove species across its northern, eastern and western coasts.

quiz.q: What are pneumatophores?
o: Seeds that float away on the tide
Leaves that store excess salt
Snorkel-like roots that take in air
Roots that store water underground
quiz.e: These pencil-like roots poke out of the mud and pass air to the buried roots.

quiz.q: What is a mangrove propagule?
o: A seedling that grows on the parent tree
A salt gland on the underside of a leaf
A root that props up the trunk in mud
A fruit that crabs bury in the mud
quiz.e: Many mangroves germinate while still attached, then drop or float away as ready-made seedlings.

quiz.q: Why can the rotten egg smell of a mangrove forest be a good sign?
o: It shows bacteria recycling matter in the mud
It means the trees are slowly dying of disease
It keeps predators away from young fish
It comes from salt crystals on the leaves
quiz.e: The smell comes from bacterial breakdown in the mud, part of what makes the ecosystem so productive.

quiz.q: What was linked to the 2015 to 2016 mangrove dieback in the Gulf of Carpentaria?
o: A major cyclone and a large oil spill
Drought, heat and a drop in sea level
Grazing by introduced feral goats
A fungal disease carried by birds
quiz.e: Scientists linked the dieback to drought, high temperatures and a sea level drop during a strong El Niño.

LESSONS.push: These trees drink seawater and breathe through snorkels. Here's how.

LESSONS.title: Plants that eat animals
LESSONS.hook: Snapping traps, sticky tentacles and slippery pitchers: some plants have turned the tables on the animal world, and Australia is a hotspot for them.

sections.key: Carnivorous plants eat animals mainly to gain nitrogen and phosphorus that their poor soils lack.
sections.b:
Picture a peat bog: soggy, acidic and sunlit, with soil that holds almost no nitrogen or phosphorus. Most plants struggle there. Carnivorous plants thrive, because they trap and digest insects and other small creatures, absorbing the minerals the soil lacks.

They still make their own food from sunlight, like any green plant. Prey is more of a fertiliser supplement than a main meal. There are several hundred species, and the habit has evolved independently several times in unrelated plant groups, a sign of how useful it is in poor soils. Each group came up with its own kind of trap, from snapping jaws to sticky glue to water-filled pits.

sections.key: A Venus flytrap counts touches before snapping shut, while pitcher plants rely on slippery, fluid-filled cups.
sections.b:
The Venus flytrap grows wild only in a small area of North and South Carolina. Its trap is a pair of hinged lobes with a few trigger hairs. One touch does nothing. A second touch within about 20 seconds snaps it shut in a fraction of a second. This counting stops the plant wasting energy on raindrops. A struggling insect keeps brushing the hairs, which seals the trap and releases digestive juices. Digestion takes several days, and each trap can open and close only a limited number of times.

Pitcher plants use a passive trap: a deep cup of digestive fluid with a slippery rim. Insects tumble in and cannot climb out. Australia has native Nepenthes pitcher plants in far north Queensland.

sections.key: Sundews trap prey with sticky droplets and Australia is a world centre of sundew diversity, while bladderworts suck in prey in a split second.
sections.b:
Sundews look covered in morning dew, but each tentacle's droplet is sticky glue. A landing insect is held fast, and in many species the tentacles bend inward to press it against the leaf, where enzymes digest it. Australia is one of the world's great centres of sundew diversity, especially the south-west of Western Australia. Some are tiny pygmy sundews no bigger than a coin, and many survive dry summers as underground tubers.

Bladderworts, which live in water or wet soil, pump water out of tiny bladders to create low pressure. When a water flea brushes a trigger hair, a trapdoor opens and the bladder sucks it in within a tiny fraction of a second, one of the fastest movements known in plants.

sections.key: The Albany pitcher plant grows wild only in a small region of south-west Western Australia and is the only species in its family.
sections.b:
Australia has a true original: the Albany pitcher plant. It grows wild only in a small coastal region of south-west Western Australia. It is so distinctive that it is the only species in its plant family.

Its small, hairy pitchers sit at ground level, catching mostly ants and other crawling insects.

Plants like this are specialists of nutrient-poor wetlands and heaths, so they are vulnerable when those places change. Draining swamps, clearing land, adding fertiliser and suppressing the natural fires that keep competing plants in check can all push them out. Their striking looks also attract collectors, and poaching is a serious problem for the Venus flytrap and some Nepenthes species. Never dig carnivorous plants up from bushland.

sections.key: Carnivorous plants need rainwater, poor soil and bright light, and should never be fed meat or fertiliser.
sections.b:
Carnivorous plants break most gardening rules. Ordinary potting mix and fertiliser can burn their roots. Most are grown in peat moss or a substitute mixed with sand or perlite. Tap water often contains enough dissolved minerals to harm them over time, so use rainwater or distilled water, and many types like to sit in a shallow tray of it. Most need plenty of bright light.

Resist feeding them pieces of meat, which can rot in the trap, and avoid triggering flytraps for fun, since every closure uses energy. Outdoors, they usually catch all the insects they need. Buy plants from reputable nurseries that propagate their own stock, not plants that may have been taken from the wild.

quiz.q: Why do carnivorous plants catch animals?
o: They cannot make food from sunlight
To get nutrients that poor soils lack
To protect their flowers from pests
To collect water during long droughts
quiz.e: Prey supplies nitrogen and phosphorus, a bit like fertiliser, while sunlight still provides their food.

quiz.q: What makes a Venus flytrap snap shut?
o: Any single touch anywhere on the leaf
Bright sunlight warming the open trap
Two touches to its hairs within seconds
Warm air from an animal's breath
quiz.e: Counting touches stops the plant wasting energy on raindrops and debris.

quiz.q: Which part of Australia is a major centre of sundew diversity?
o: Tasmania's wet west coast
The treeless Nullarbor Plain
Central Australia's red desert
South-west Western Australia
quiz.e: South-west Western Australia has an exceptional variety of sundews.

quiz.q: What is special about the Albany pitcher plant?
o: It is wild only in south-west Western Australia
It is the largest pitcher plant in the world
It grows wild across all of northern Australia
It catches mostly flying insects, such as moths
quiz.e: It is found wild only in a small coastal region, and is the only species in its family.

quiz.q: What water is best for most carnivorous plants?
o: Tap water mixed with fertiliser
Rainwater or distilled water
Bore water high in minerals
Bottled mineral water from a spring
quiz.e: Dissolved minerals in tap water can harm plants adapted to nutrient-poor conditions.

LESSONS.push: Some plants eat animals, and Australia has some of the strangest.

LESSONS.title: Masters of disguise: how animals hide
LESSONS.hook: A bird that becomes a broken branch, a fish that looks like seaweed, a cuttlefish that changes its skin in a blink: inside nature's art of hiding.
