sections.key: Camouflage is about defeating the eyes and brain of the observer, using behaviour and shape as well as colour.
sections.b:
At dusk in an Australian park, you might walk right past a tawny frogmouth. By day this bird sits motionless on a branch, its mottled grey and brown feathers matching the bark. If it senses danger, it stretches, points its beak upward, narrows its eyes to slits and freezes, looking just like a broken stump.

The disguise works because of the whole package: colour, shape and stillness. That is the heart of camouflage. It is not just about being the right colour. It is about defeating the eyes and brain of whoever is looking, whether a hungry predator or prey to be ambushed. Over millions of years, animals have evolved many ways to do it.

sections.key: Animals hide by matching their background, using countershading to cancel shadows, and breaking up their outline with bold patches.
sections.b:
The simplest strategy is background matching, as with a grasshopper on dry grass. But light comes from above, so a body's top is bright and its belly shadowed, which makes it look solid. Many animals counter this with countershading: darker on top, paler underneath. It cancels the shadow, flattening the body. Many fish, sharks and dolphins use it. From above, dark backs blend with the deep water; from below, pale bellies blend with the bright surface.

Our brains are good at spotting outlines, so another strategy is to destroy them. Disruptive colouration uses bold contrasting patches across the body's edges, so the eye sees separate shapes, not one animal. In the First World War, ships were painted in dazzle stripes to confuse submarine crews judging their speed and direction.

sections.key: Masquerade works by looking like a boring or inedible object, such as a twig, leaf or seaweed, rather than by hiding.
sections.b:
Some animals are perfectly visible but go unnoticed because they look like something boring or inedible. This is called masquerade. Stick insects look like twigs, and many sway as if in the wind. Leaf insects have fake veins and even nibbled edges. Some caterpillars and spiders look like bird droppings, which few predators want to eat.

One of the most beautiful examples lives in southern Australia's cool waters. The leafy seadragon, a relative of seahorses, is covered in leaf-like flaps of skin and drifts slowly through kelp and seagrass, looking like floating seaweed. It is the marine emblem of South Australia, and divers can stare at weed for a long time before realising it is looking back.

sections.key: Harmless animals can copy dangerous ones, and cuttlefish change colour in under a second using pigment sacs controlled by nerves.
sections.b:
Dangerous animals often advertise with warning colours, such as the yellow and black of wasps. Predators learn to avoid them, which lets harmless species cheat. Hoverflies cannot sting but look like wasps: Batesian mimicry. When several dangerous species share a warning pattern, it is Müllerian mimicry. The mimic octopus of Southeast Asia can change its shape and movement to resemble a flatfish, a lionfish or a sea snake.

Cuttlefish skin holds thousands of elastic pigment sacs called chromatophores, each wrapped in muscles controlled directly by nerves. Stretching or squeezing them changes colour and pattern in well under a second, and bumps on the skin can match rough rock. Most appear colour-blind, yet match colours well. At Point Lowly, near Whyalla, small male giant cuttlefish have been seen posing as females to slip past larger rivals.

sections.key: Camouflage evolves through natural selection, as predators and prey keep driving each other to improve.
sections.b:
Camouflage is a product of natural selection. Individuals that are slightly harder to spot are more likely to survive and pass on their genes, while predators with sharper eyes catch more food. The result is an ongoing arms race.

A classic example is the peppered moth in England. During the Industrial Revolution, soot darkened tree trunks, and a dark form of the moth, once rare, became common in industrial areas because birds found the pale moths easier to spot. After clean air laws cut pollution in the twentieth century, the pale form became common again.

Today camouflage faces new challenges, as climate change shifts the timing of seasons. In some places, animals that turn white for winter are now sometimes stranded in white coats on brown, snowless ground.

It freezes and looks like a broken stump
It quickly changes its feather colour
It flies off into the dense grass
quiz.e: Colour, shape and stillness together make it look like a broken stump.

quiz.q: What is countershading?

Changing colour with the seasons
Copying the look of a dangerous animal
Having dark stripes across the eyes
quiz.e: A pale belly cancels the shadow that would otherwise make a body look solid.

quiz.q: What is masquerade in camouflage?

Looking like something a predator ignores
Copying the warning colours of wasps
Changing colour within a few seconds
quiz.e: Masquerading animals stay visible but are mistaken for sticks, leaves, seaweed or droppings.

quiz.q: What lets cuttlefish change colour so quickly?
o: Hormones slowly released into the blood
Bacteria that live in their skin
Pigments absorbed from the food they eat
Pigment sacs worked by nerves and muscles
quiz.e: Stretching or squeezing the sacs changes their colour and pattern in well under a second.

quiz.q: Why did dark peppered moths become common in industrial England?
o: Soot darkened trunks, so birds saw pale moths first
Dark moths breed faster in every condition
Birds always prefer to eat dark moths
Pollution changed the colour of individual moths
quiz.e: Natural selection favoured whichever form was harder for predators to see.

LESSONS.push: A bird that becomes a broken branch. How animals vanish in plain sight.

LESSONS.title: The hidden kingdom of fungi
LESSONS.hook: The mushroom you see is just the tip of the iceberg. Below ground, fungi feed forests, recycle the dead and sometimes grow into some of the largest living things on Earth.

sections.key: Fungi are a kingdom of their own that digest food outside their bodies and are more closely related to animals than to plants.
sections.b:
After autumn rain, mushrooms seem to appear overnight. It is tempting to see them as odd little plants, but fungi are something else. They cannot make food from sunlight. Instead, they release digestive enzymes into their surroundings and absorb the nutrients that are broken down. Their cell walls are made of chitin, the tough material in insect shells, not plant cellulose. Genetic studies show fungi are more closely related to animals than to plants.

The kingdom includes yeasts, moulds, mushrooms, rusts and lichen partners. Around 150,000 species have been named, but the true total is estimated in the millions, and in Australia most fungi are thought to be undescribed.

sections.key: A mushroom is only the fruiting body, and the real fungus is a network of fine threads called mycelium that can grow enormous.
sections.b:
A mushroom is to a fungus roughly what an apple is to an apple tree: a temporary structure for spreading spores. The main body of most fungi is the mycelium, a web of microscopic threads called hyphae that spread through soil, wood or leaf litter. A teaspoon of healthy soil can hold a startling length of them.

Mycelium can grow enormous. In an Oregon forest, a single honey fungus spreads through the soil across nearly ten square kilometres, and is thought to be thousands of years old. It is often described as one of the largest living organisms on Earth. Above ground, you would notice only the occasional clump of honey-coloured mushrooms and some unhealthy trees.

sections.key: Most land plants trade sugars for water and nutrients with mycorrhizal fungi, though claims about forests 'talking' go beyond the evidence.
sections.b:
Most healthy plants have fungi wrapped around or inside their roots. These partnerships, mycorrhizas ('fungus root'), are formed by the large majority of land plants. The fungus's fine threads reach much further than roots, gathering water and nutrients such as phosphorus and nitrogen. In return, the plant gives the fungus sugars from photosynthesis. Some Australian orchids cannot even germinate without the right fungus.

In 1997 Suzanne Simard and colleagues suggested carbon could move between trees through shared fungal networks, and the 'wood wide web' idea took off. Networks linking roots are real, but how much they move between trees, and whether it helps, is still debated. A 2023 review argued the evidence for some popular claims, such as 'mother trees', was weaker than often suggested.

sections.key: Fungi break down tough dead wood and leaves, returning nutrients to the soil that keep ecosystems running.
sections.b:
Without fungi, forests would be buried in their own dead wood. Wood is hard to digest because it contains lignin, a complex material that stiffens plant cell walls. Few organisms can break lignin down efficiently, and white rot fungi are among the best.

As fungi, bacteria and small animals break down logs, leaves and dead animals, they release nitrogen, phosphorus and other nutrients back into the soil. A rotting log in Australian bushland may look like waste, but it is a busy recycling plant and a home for beetles, frogs, lizards and small mammals. That is one reason many land managers now leave fallen timber on the ground rather than tidying it away.

sections.key: Fungi give us food and medicines but can also be deadly, so never eat wild mushrooms you cannot identify with certainty.
sections.b:
You probably ate fungi today. Baker's yeast releases carbon dioxide to make bread rise, and yeasts ferment beer and wine. Penicillium moulds make the blue veins in some cheeses, and koji mould makes soy sauce, miso and sake. In 1928 Alexander Fleming noticed a Penicillium mould killing bacteria on a dish, which led to penicillin. Cyclosporine, used to prevent organ rejection, also came from a fungus.

But the chytrid fungus has caused declines in hundreds of frog species worldwide, including in Australia. The death cap mushroom, introduced and found around Canberra and Melbourne, has caused deaths here, and cooking does not make it safe. This is general information: never eat wild mushrooms unless an expert has identified them, and if you suspect poisoning, call the Poisons Information Centre on 13 11 26.

quiz.q: Which group are fungi more closely related to?
o: Plants
Algae
Animals
Bacteria
quiz.e: Genetic studies show fungi are closer to animals than plants, and they feed by absorbing digested food.

quiz.q: What is a mushroom, compared with the whole fungus?
o: A temporary structure that spreads spores
The main feeding body, found underground
A poison produced by the fungus itself
The root system that anchors the fungus
quiz.e: The mushroom is the fruiting body, while the mycelium underground is the main body of the fungus.

quiz.q: What is the fairest summary of the 'wood wide web' idea?
o: Studies have completely disproved the whole idea
Trees are proven to share messages and warnings
Fungal networks are real, but claims outrun the evidence
It only holds in tropical rainforests, not elsewhere
quiz.e: Networks linking plant roots exist, but how much they matter between trees is still debated.

quiz.q: Why are fungi important in forests?
o: They break down dead wood and return nutrients
They stop fallen logs from decaying for years
They fix nitrogen from the air for the trees
They make food from sunlight for the forest
quiz.e: White rot fungi and other decomposers keep nutrients cycling through ecosystems.

quiz.q: If you suspect mushroom poisoning in Australia, who should you call?
o: Your local council's rangers or parks team
A gardening club or plant nursery helpline
The Poisons Information Centre on 13 11 26
No one, as cooking makes wild mushrooms safe
quiz.e: Cooking does not make poisonous mushrooms safe, so seek expert help straight away.

LESSONS.push: The mushroom is only the fruit. What's underneath may be among the largest living things.

LESSONS.title: Ants: the superorganism
LESSONS.hook: There may be around 20 quadrillion ants on Earth. Individually simple, together they farm, build, wage war and solve problems no single ant could.

sections.key: Ants are astonishingly abundant, with about 20 quadrillion alive, weighing more than all wild birds and mammals combined.
sections.b:
Sit on almost any patch of Australian ground for a few minutes and an ant will find you. In 2022, researchers combined hundreds of studies and estimated about 20 quadrillion ants on Earth, roughly two and a half million per person. Together, they estimated, ants weigh more than all wild birds and wild mammals combined.

More than 14,000 species have been named, and many more await description. Australia is especially rich, with well over a thousand known species. Ants live almost everywhere except the coldest places, from rainforest canopies to the hottest deserts, and they shape their environments by moving soil, spreading seeds and eating other insects.

sections.key: An ant colony works like a single organism, with queens that reproduce and female workers who do everything else, guided by chemical signals.
sections.b:
A typical colony is a family. At its heart are one or more queens, whose job is laying eggs. Almost all the ants you see are workers, which are female and usually do not reproduce. Males appear only to mate, and die soon after. Workers divide the jobs of caring for young, building and defending the nest, and foraging. Biologists call the colony a superorganism, with workers a little like cells in a body.

No ant is in charge. They communicate mainly with pheromones. A forager that finds food lays a scent trail home. Shorter routes are reinforced faster, because round trips are quicker, so the colony settles on efficient paths without a plan. This emergent behaviour has inspired 'ant colony optimisation' in computing.

sections.key: Some ants farm fungus or herd sap-sucking insects for honeydew, practising agriculture long before humans did.
sections.b:
Humans began farming roughly 12,000 years ago, but some ants have been doing it for tens of millions of years. Leafcutter ants of Central and South America do not eat the leaves they carry. They chew them into a pulp to feed a fungus in underground gardens, and the fungus becomes their food. Their nests can hold millions of ants.

Other ants are herders. They protect aphids and scale insects from predators and collect honeydew, the sugary liquid these insects excrete. If you see ants running over a plant covered in scale insects, that is this partnership in action. Some ants even carry their insect 'livestock' to fresh plants to feed.

sections.key: Honeypot ants store nectar in their swollen bodies, while green tree ants build nests by gluing leaves together with larval silk.
sections.b:
In the arid centre, honeypot ant workers called repletes are fed so much nectar and honeydew that their abdomens swell into amber balls the size of a small grape. They hang from the ceilings of underground chambers as living food stores for lean times. Aboriginal people have long dug them up as a sweet food.

In the tropical north, green tree ants, also called weaver ants, build nests by pulling leaves together. Some workers hold the leaves in place while others carry larvae, whose silk glues the leaves together. Green tree ants are also a traditional bush food, and many people describe their taste as sharp and lemony.

sections.key: Bull ants and jack jumpers can trigger serious allergic reactions, and invasive ants can devastate wildlife and farms.
sections.b:
Most ants are harmless, but bull ants and jack jumpers deserve respect. Their sting is painful. For a minority who are allergic, especially to jack jumper venom, it can cause life-threatening anaphylaxis. Jack jumper allergy is well known in Tasmania. This is general information, not medical advice: difficulty breathing, facial or throat swelling, or collapse need urgent help, so call 000. People with known allergies should follow their doctor's plan.

Invasive ants are among the world's most damaging pests. Red imported fire ants were found in Brisbane in 2001 and have been the target of eradication ever since. On Christmas Island, yellow crazy ants formed supercolonies and killed millions of red crabs. If you suspect fire ants, report them to the national fire ant program or your state biosecurity agency.

quiz.q: According to a 2022 estimate, how do ants compare with wild birds and mammals by weight?
o: Ants weigh far less than wild birds alone
Ants weigh about the same as wild mammals
Ants outweigh wild birds and mammals combined
Ants weigh about half as much as mammals
quiz.e: Ants are so numerous that their combined weight exceeds that of all wild birds and mammals.

quiz.q: How do ant colonies tend to find efficient routes to food?
o: Shorter trails collect pheromone scent faster
The queen plans each route in advance
Workers vote on the best route at the nest
They follow the position of the sun only
quiz.e: Round trips on shorter routes are quicker, so scent trails strengthen there first, with no leader needed.

quiz.q: Why do leafcutter ants carry leaves into their nests?
o: To eat them straight away
To feed a fungus they farm
To block the nest entrance
To feed herds of aphids
quiz.e: They grow fungus in underground gardens, a form of farming that predates humans by millions of years.

quiz.q: What do honeypot ant repletes do?
o: Guard the nest from intruders
Sew leaves together with silk
Store nectar in swollen bodies
Farm fungus in underground gardens
quiz.e: Repletes act as living food stores for the colony in lean times.

quiz.q: What should you do if you suspect red imported fire ants?
o: Dig up the nest to inspect it closely
Report it to your state biosecurity agency
Ignore them, as they are mostly harmless
Move the nest out to nearby bushland
quiz.e: Reporting helps eradication efforts against a damaging invasive species.

LESSONS.push: Twenty quadrillion ants may outweigh every wild bird and mammal. How?

LESSONS.title: Eucalypts: trees built for fire
LESSONS.hook: Gum trees define the Australian landscape. Their oils, bark and hidden buds tell the story of a continent shaped by fire.

sections.key: Eucalypts are more than 800 mostly Australian species that dominate the country's forests and have adapted to both drought and fire.
sections.b:
Step into the bush after rain and you may catch the clean scent of eucalyptus oil. Botanists group the eucalypts into three closely related genera: Eucalyptus, Corymbia (many bloodwoods and the spotted gums) and Angophora. Together they include more than 800 species, almost all native to Australia, with a few in New Guinea and nearby islands.

They dominate roughly three-quarters of Australia's native forests and grow in almost every environment, from snowy mountains to the dry inland. As the continent dried out and fire became more common, eucalypts became extraordinarily good at living with both drought and flame.

Forms vary widely: shrubby mallees grow as clumps of stems a few metres tall, while mountain ash is the world's tallest flowering plant, with one Tasmanian tree, Centurion, about 100 metres high.

sections.key: Eucalyptus leaves hold aromatic oils that deter most animals and make eucalypt forests burn fiercely in extreme weather.
sections.b:
Hold a eucalyptus leaf to the light and you may see tiny translucent dots. These are oil glands. The aromatic oils protect the leaves from many insects and animals. Only specialists, such as koalas, some possums and certain insects, cope with large amounts. People have long used eucalyptus oil in cleaning products and cold remedies.

The oils are also flammable, and on hot days some of these compounds evaporate from the leaves. Together with other natural chemicals released by the trees, they are thought to contribute to the blue haze that gives the Blue Mountains near Sydney their name. That volatility helps explain why eucalypt forests can burn so fiercely in extreme weather. Bark varies too: stringybarks are fibrous, ironbarks are hard and furrowed, and smooth-barked gums shed their outer layer each year.

sections.key: Many eucalypts survive fire by resprouting from buds protected under their bark or from a woody base called a lignotuber.
sections.b:
A few months after a bushfire, blackened eucalypt trunks become covered in soft green and red shoots. Many eucalypts have epicormic buds, dormant buds hidden beneath thick bark along the trunk and branches. Fire may kill the leaves, but the insulated buds survive and sprout once the danger has passed, rebuilding the canopy far faster than a seedling could.

Many species also have a lignotuber, a woody swelling at the base of the trunk, partly underground, packed with buds and food reserves. If the whole tree above ground is destroyed, it can resprout from this lump. Mallees are a classic example, regrowing from their lignotubers again and again after fire.

sections.key: Mountain ash is usually killed by intense fire and relies on seed, so fires returning too soon can destroy its forests.
sections.b:
Not all eucalypts resprout. Mountain ash and its relative alpine ash are usually killed by intense fire. Instead, they bet on seed. Their gumnuts release seeds in huge numbers after the heat of a fire. The seeds fall onto nutrient-rich ash in full sunlight, and a dense, even-aged forest springs up.

This works well when big fires come at long intervals. The danger is fires returning too often. Young mountain ash take many years, often around two decades, to produce plenty of seed. If a young forest burns again before then, there may be no seed left, and the forest can be replaced by shrubs or other species.

sections.key: Aboriginal people have managed the land with fire for tens of thousands of years, and large gums can drop limbs without warning.
sections.b:
Fire in Australia is not only a natural force. Aboriginal people have used it as a land management tool for tens of thousands of years. Cultural burning typically uses cooler, smaller fires at chosen times to create a patchwork of burnt and unburnt country, reducing fuel and encouraging fresh growth. Many practices were disrupted after colonisation, and more land managers now work with Aboriginal rangers to restore them. The Black Summer fires of 2019 and 2020 showed how hotter, drier conditions make fire seasons more dangerous.

Eucalypts are also planted worldwide, for timber and pulp, though some places criticise their water use and fire risk. At home, river red gums and other large eucalypts can shed big limbs suddenly, earning the nickname 'widowmaker', so avoid camping or parking under them.

quiz.q: Roughly what share of Australia's native forests are dominated by eucalypts?
o: About one-tenth
About one-quarter
About three-quarters
Almost none
quiz.e: Eucalypts dominate roughly three-quarters of Australia's native forests.

quiz.q: Why can eucalypt forests burn so fiercely in extreme weather?
o: Their flammable leaf oils vaporise in the heat
Their wood holds water that turns to steam
Their leaves are always dry and brittle
Their thin bark catches alight easily
quiz.e: The same oils that deter animals are volatile and flammable.

quiz.q: What are epicormic buds?
o: Seeds stored inside woody gumnuts for years
Flowers that open only after heavy rain
Tiny oil glands scattered through the leaves
Dormant buds under bark that sprout after fire
quiz.e: Insulated by bark, these buds survive fire and rebuild the canopy quickly.

quiz.q: Why can frequent fires threaten mountain ash forests?
o: Repeated fire makes their bark too thick
Young trees may burn before setting seed
Fire makes their seeds too heavy to spread
They resprout too slowly from lignotubers
quiz.e: Mountain ash relies on seed, and young trees take around two decades to produce plenty.

quiz.q: Why do some large gums carry the nickname 'widowmaker'?
o: Their leaf oil is poisonous to people
Their roots can crack nearby houses
They can drop large branches suddenly
They attract dangerous snakes at night
quiz.e: Big limbs can fall without warning, so avoid camping or parking beneath them.

LESSONS.push: Australia's gum trees are built to burn and regrow. Here's the trick.

LESSONS.title: Animals that cheat ageing
LESSONS.hook: A shark born before Captain Cook sailed, a rodent that barely seems to age, a jellyfish that turns back its own clock: what nature's longest lives reveal about growing old.

sections.key: Some animals live for centuries, and their ages can be read from growth layers, raising the question of why ageing happens at all.
sections.b:
In 2006, scientists dredging the seabed off Iceland pulled up an ordinary-looking clam. It was frozen on board as routine, so it was already dead when researchers counted the growth rings in its shell, much like tree rings, and realised it was extraordinary. The ocean quahog, nicknamed Ming, was about 507 years old, alive since around the start of the 1500s.

Ming is one of the oldest individual animals whose age has been reliably measured. Its story raises a big question: if some animals live for centuries, why do others, including us, age and die on a much shorter schedule?

sections.key: Evolutionary theory says ageing happens because natural selection weakens later in life, so safer lives should evolve slower ageing.
sections.b:
Ageing is an evolutionary puzzle. Why would natural selection allow bodies to wear out? Biologists such as Peter Medawar and George Williams developed an influential answer. In the wild, most animals die young from predators, disease, accidents or starvation. Genes that cause problems late in life are rarely 'seen' by natural selection, because few individuals live long enough for them to matter. Some genes that help early, for example by boosting reproduction, might even cause harm later.

A related idea, the 'disposable soma' theory, says bodies invest in reproduction rather than perfect long-term repair. It predicts that animals facing less outside danger should age more slowly. Many long-lived species fit that pattern.

sections.key: Greenland sharks and bowhead whales may live for centuries, and naked mole-rats show no rising risk of death with age.
sections.b:
The Greenland shark lives in cold North Atlantic and Arctic waters. Sharks lack bony growth rings, so in 2016 researchers used radiocarbon dating on eye lenses, which form before birth and do not change. They estimated the largest shark was around 400 years old, with a wide margin of uncertainty, making it the longest-lived vertebrate known. Bowhead whales may live more than 200 years, and old harpoon tips from the 1800s have been found in whales caught in modern times.

The pink, almost hairless naked mole-rat of East Africa has lived over 30 years in captivity, where a mouse lives two or three. A study found its risk of dying did not seem to rise with age, unlike almost every other mammal. It also very rarely gets cancer.

sections.key: Some simple animals, like the 'immortal jellyfish' and hydra, show little or no sign of ageing, so ageing is not an unbreakable law.
sections.b:
A tiny jellyfish, Turritopsis dohrnii, is nicknamed the immortal jellyfish. When injured, stressed or old, it can transform back into an earlier life stage, a polyp attached to the seabed, and grow into a new jellyfish. In principle, it could repeat this many times. In practice, individuals still die from predators and disease, so it is not truly immortal.

The freshwater hydra, a small relative of jellyfish, also appears to show little or no ageing. Stem cells constantly renew its body, and in laboratory studies hydra did not show the usual rise in death rate over time. These animals suggest ageing is not an unbreakable law of biology.

sections.key: Big, long-lived animals resist cancer through extra defences, but there is no proven shortcut to a much longer human life.
sections.b:
Cancer starts when a cell picks up harmful mutations and divides out of control. So animals with more cells, living longer, should get more cancer. Yet large animals do not seem to have higher rates than small ones, a puzzle called Peto's paradox. Elephants have around 20 copies of the TP53 gene, which helps trigger the death of damaged cells, while humans have one pair. Bowhead whales appear unusually good at repairing DNA.

These animals give researchers real leads. But they do not yet translate into treatments that extend human life, and many anti-ageing products lack good evidence. This is general information, not health advice. The well-tested basics, such as not smoking, staying active, sleeping well and eating well, remain best supported.

quiz.q: How was the age of Ming the clam worked out?
o: Counting growth rings in its shell
Radiocarbon dating of its eye lens
Measuring how heavy its shell was
Reading its age from its DNA length
quiz.e: Shell growth layers record age, much as tree rings do.

quiz.q: According to evolutionary theory, which animals should evolve to age more slowly?
o: Those facing more danger from predators
Those facing less danger from outside
Those that start breeding the earliest
Those that have the smallest bodies
quiz.e: If few individuals die young, late-life problems face stronger selection, so slower ageing evolves.

quiz.q: What is unusual about the naked mole-rat's risk of dying?
o: It drops sharply after the age of two
It doubles with every year of life
It is higher than any other rodent's
It does not seem to rise with age
quiz.e: Unlike almost every other mammal, its risk of death appears not to climb with age.

quiz.q: Why is the 'immortal jellyfish' not truly immortal?
o: It can still die from predators and disease
It ages in the same way as other jellyfish
It is unable to return to the polyp stage
It lives for only a few days at most
quiz.e: Reversing its life stage does not protect it from being eaten or sickened.

quiz.q: What is Peto's paradox?
o: Small animals always outlive much larger animals
Big animals get no more cancer despite more cells
Cold-water animals always age much faster
Jellyfish can reverse their whole life cycle
quiz.e: Big animals seem to have evolved extra defences, such as more TP53 copies or better DNA repair.

LESSONS.push: A clam was alive before Shakespeare was born. What do long lives teach us?

LESSONS.title: The trolley problem: would you pull the lever?
LESSONS.hook: A runaway tram, five people on the track and one lever in your hand. This simple puzzle has become one of the most argued-about scenarios in moral philosophy, and it now shapes how we think about self-driving cars.

sections.key: The trolley problem asks whether it is right to divert a runaway tram so it kills one person instead of five.
sections.b:
Picture yourself beside a railway line. A tram with failed brakes is hurtling towards five workers who cannot get out of the way. You stand next to a lever. Pull it, and the tram swings onto a side track, where it will kill one worker instead. Do nothing, and five people die.

Most people say they would pull the lever. But the puzzle is not really about trams. It is a carefully built thought experiment, a stripped-down scenario that isolates one question so we can examine our moral instincts. Do the numbers alone matter, or does how a death comes about matter too?

The British philosopher Philippa Foot introduced it in 1967, and Judith Jarvis Thomson later named it and invented many variations.

sections.key: When saving five means pushing one person to their death, most people's answer flips even though the arithmetic is identical.
sections.b:
Thomson's most famous variation puts you on a footbridge above the track. There is no lever. The only way to stop the tram is to push a very large stranger off the bridge into its path. His body would halt it, saving five, but he would die.

The arithmetic is identical: one life for five. Yet in surveys, most people who would pull the lever say they would not push the man. Many find pushing deeply wrong, even if they struggle to explain why. That gap makes the puzzle so productive. If the numbers are the same, something else must be driving our judgement, and philosophers have spent decades working out what it is, and whether it should count.

sections.key: Consequentialists judge actions by their outcomes, so they favour saving five in both versions, though critics say this could justify terrible acts.
sections.b:
One family of answers is consequentialism: the rightness of an action depends on its results. The best-known version, utilitarianism, associated with Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill, aims for the greatest overall wellbeing. In the lever case, five deaths are worse than one, so you should pull.

A consistent consequentialist may say the same about the footbridge, arguing our reluctance to push is a gut reaction, not a moral insight. Defenders note the approach is impartial and takes every life equally seriously. Critics reply that if outcomes are all that matter, it could justify terrible things, such as harvesting one healthy patient's organs to save five others, which almost everyone rejects.

sections.key: Some thinkers argue people must never be used merely as a means, and the doctrine of double effect separates intended harm from foreseen side effects.
sections.b:
A rival tradition, linked to Immanuel Kant, holds that people must never be treated merely as a means to an end. Pushing the man uses his body as a tool to stop the tram, which looks like exactly that. Pulling the lever is different: the one worker dies as a side effect of redirecting the threat, not as the means of stopping it.

This is the heart of the doctrine of double effect, which traces back to the medieval thinker Thomas Aquinas. It says causing harm as a foreseen side effect can sometimes be permissible when causing the same harm intentionally would not. Critics question whether that distinction can carry so much moral weight.

sections.key: Emotion and reasoning both shape moral choices, and self-driving cars have turned the thought experiment into a real design question.
sections.b:
Around 2001, Joshua Greene and colleagues scanned people's brains as they considered trolley dilemmas. Up-close, personal harms like pushing seemed to trigger stronger emotional responses, while impersonal cases like the lever invited calculation. Greene proposed a 'dual process' account in which both systems compete. Some later studies have questioned how well the results hold up, and philosophers ask whether the emotion tracks something real.

Then came autonomous vehicles. Someone must decide in advance what software does when a crash is unavoidable. The 2018 Moral Machine project from MIT collected millions of responses worldwide. It found broad agreement on sparing more lives and humans over animals, but regional differences on other questions. Engineers stress that real crashes are rarely neat dilemmas, and avoiding collisions is the goal.

quiz.q: What is the trolley problem designed to test?
o: Whether numbers alone decide right, or the manner of a death counts too
How well people understand tram safety, brakes and track signals
Which railway design is cheapest to build and maintain over decades
Whether people can follow instructions quickly under time pressure
quiz.e: The scenario isolates one question so we can examine our moral instincts.

quiz.q: In the footbridge version, how do most people respond compared with the lever version?
o: They are more willing to act
They are less willing to act
They respond exactly the same
They refuse to answer
quiz.e: Though the numbers are identical, most people who would pull the lever would not push the man.

quiz.q: What does a consequentialist mainly use to judge whether an action is right?
o: The intentions of the actor
Religious rules
Its outcomes
Tradition
quiz.e: Consequentialists weigh results, so saving five usually beats saving one.

quiz.q: What does the doctrine of double effect say?
o: Every action has two equal effects, one good and one bad
Two wrongs together can sometimes make a right
Only the second effect of an action counts morally
Foreseen harm can be allowed where intended harm would not
quiz.e: It separates harm used as a means from harm that is a foreseen side effect.

quiz.q: What did the Moral Machine project find?
o: Broad agreement on sparing more lives, but regional differences
Near-total agreement worldwide on every question it asked
Most people wanted cars to ignore pedestrians entirely
Engineers rejected the idea of the experiment completely
quiz.e: It showed shared intuitions about numbers but disagreement on other trade-offs.

LESSONS.push: Five lives or one, and why pushing feels different from pulling a lever.

LESSONS.title: The ship of Theseus: what makes you the same person?
LESSONS.hook: Replace every plank of a ship, one by one, and is it still the same ship? This ancient puzzle leads straight to one of the most personal questions in philosophy: what makes you, you, over a lifetime of change?

sections.key: If every part of an object is gradually replaced, it is unclear whether it is still the same object.
sections.b:
The Greek writer Plutarch, around the turn of the second century, told of the ship in which the hero Theseus was said to have sailed home from Crete. The Athenians kept it for generations, removing old timbers as they decayed and fitting new ones. Philosophers used it in arguments about growth: some said it stayed the same ship, others that it did not.

Carry the process to the end, with not one original plank left. Is it still Theseus's ship? If yes, what makes it so? If no, at which plank did it stop being the original? Neither answer is as comfortable as it first seems.

sections.key: Rebuilding the ship from the old planks shows that 'the same thing' bundles features, such as history and material, that can come apart.
sections.b:
In the 1600s the English philosopher Thomas Hobbes added a complication. Suppose someone collected every old plank as it was removed and later reassembled them, in order, into a ship. Now there are two. One sits in the harbour, continuously maintained, with no original material. The other is built entirely of the original timbers.

Which is the ship of Theseus? Both have a strong claim: one has continuity of history and use, the other continuity of material. Our everyday idea of 'the same thing' bundles features that usually travel together but can come apart.

sections.key: Because your body and mind keep changing, the puzzle becomes the problem of personal identity, which asks what makes you the same person over time.
sections.b:
You are a bit like that ship. Many of your cells are replaced over time, from skin to blood to the lining of your gut, although some, including most neurons in the brain, can last a lifetime. Your beliefs, tastes and memories change even more. The child in your earliest photos shares little with you in material, knowledge or personality, yet you feel certain that child was you.

Philosophers call this the problem of personal identity. It matters for everyday things, like holding someone responsible for a promise or a crime, and for deeper ones, like what it would mean to survive.

sections.key: Locke tied identity to memory, but Reid's brave officer showed that memory alone breaks the logic of 'same as'.
sections.b:
In the late 1600s John Locke argued that a person is a thinking being who can consider itself as itself at different times. You are the same person as someone in the past if you remember that person's experiences from the inside, not because you share a body. That explains why memory loss feels so frightening.

Nearly a century later, Thomas Reid offered the brave officer. A boy is flogged for stealing; as an officer he remembers the flogging; as a general he remembers being the officer but has forgotten the flogging. On Locke's view the general is the officer and the officer is the boy, yet the general is not the boy. Later philosophers repaired the theory with overlapping chains of memory and psychological connection.

sections.key: Buddhist non-self and Parfit's teleporter both suggest that what matters is continuity of mind, not an unchanging core self.
sections.b:
Long before Locke, Buddhist thinkers took another route. In the Questions of King Milinda, the monk Nagasena asks the king whether his chariot is the axle, the wheels, the frame or the reins. None alone is the chariot, nor is it separate from them: 'chariot' names parts working together. Likewise 'Nagasena' names a changing combination of body, feelings, perceptions and mental activity, with no unchanging core. This idea, anatta or non-self, is central to many Buddhist traditions.

In 1984 Derek Parfit imagined a teleporter that destroys you and builds an exact copy on Mars. Is that you? He concluded there may be no fact of the matter, and that psychological continuity matters more than identity. Many philosophers disagree.

quiz.q: What difficulty does the ship of Theseus puzzle raise?
o: Whether old wooden ships were stronger than modern ones
Whether an object stays the same after all its parts are replaced
Whether a ship can be repaired without losing its value
Whether the planks of an old ship can ever be counted
quiz.e: The puzzle asks what makes an object the same thing when none of its original material remains.

quiz.q: What does Hobbes's rebuilt ship reveal about the idea of 'the same thing'?
o: It bundles features like history and material that can split
It depends only on how old the original material is
It always follows what the original builder intended
It is settled by whichever of the two ships is larger
quiz.e: Two ships each match part of 'sameness', so the idea turns out to bundle several features.

quiz.q: Why does the ship puzzle apply to people?
o: Our bodies stay fixed while only our thoughts change
We change in body and mind, yet feel we are the same person
Every part of the brain is replaced every single year
People are legally treated as new people each decade
quiz.e: Because we change in body and mind, we need an account of what keeps a person the same over a lifetime.

quiz.q: What was Reid's objection to Locke's memory view?
o: Memory is always accurate, so identity never changes in any way
It makes A the same as B and B as C, but A not the same as C
Anyone who forgets nothing is no longer counted as a person
Memory belongs to the body and cannot be a feature of the mind
quiz.e: Memory links can fail to chain together, which breaks the basic logic of 'same as'.

quiz.q: What is the Buddhist idea of non-self, as in the chariot example?
o: A person is a soul that moves between bodies unchanged
A person is defined only by their role in society
A person is simply whatever their memory records
A person is a changing bundle of parts with no fixed core
quiz.e: Like 'chariot', 'self' is a name for parts working together, not a separate fixed thing.

LESSONS.push: Replace every plank of a ship, and is it still the same ship? Are you?

LESSONS.title: Descartes: I think, therefore I am
LESSONS.hook: What if everything you believe is a dream, or a trick? René Descartes set out to doubt everything he possibly could, and what was left became one of the most famous sentences ever written.

sections.key: Descartes set out to clear away every doubtful belief and rebuild knowledge on a foundation that could not be doubted.
sections.b:
In the winter of 1619, a young Frenchman named René Descartes was stuck in Germany, serving with an army. By his own account, he spent a day alone in a stove-heated room, thinking. Despite an excellent education, he felt much of what he had learned was uncertain. Admiring the step-by-step certainty of geometry, he resolved to clear away every belief that could be doubted and see what solid ground remained.

In his Meditations of 1641 he began with the senses. A tower looks round from far away and square up close; a straight stick looks bent in water. A source that has fooled you once is not safe to trust fully. This was a tool for one quiet hour of reflection, not a way to live as a sceptic.

sections.key: Descartes asked how we could know we are not dreaming, or being fooled by a powerful deceiver.
sections.b:
Descartes then raised a stronger worry. He had often dreamed he was sitting by the fire in his dressing gown when he was actually asleep in bed. Is there any sure sign that separates waking life from a vivid dream? If not, even the scene in front of him might be unreal.

Finally he imagined an evil demon, supremely powerful and cunning, devoting all its energy to deceiving him about everything, perhaps even simple sums. Modern philosophers have updated the demon into a brain in a vat, fed false experiences by scientists, an idea that inspired films such as The Matrix. The question is the same: can you prove this is not happening to you right now?

sections.key: Even if he is deceived about everything else, Descartes must exist in order to be deceived: I think, therefore I am.
sections.b:
Here Descartes found his foothold. Suppose the demon deceives him about everything. Still, to be deceived, he must exist. To doubt, he must be thinking. However far the doubt is pushed, it cannot reach the fact that there is a doubter.

In the Meditations he put it as 'I am, I exist', which must be true whenever he thinks it. In his earlier Discourse on the Method of 1637, written in French, he used the form that became famous, usually rendered in Latin as cogito, ergo sum: I think, therefore I am. The early Christian thinker Augustine had made a similar point more than a thousand years earlier, arguing that if he was mistaken, he must exist to be mistaken.

sections.key: Descartes tried to rebuild trust in the world through God and argued that mind and body are distinct, but both steps drew sharp criticism.
sections.b:
Knowing only that you exist is a lonely position. Descartes argued that his idea of a perfect being could only come from a perfect God, who would not deceive him, so clear and distinct perceptions could be trusted. Critics noted the Cartesian circle: he seems to use clear ideas to prove God, then God to guarantee clear ideas.

His method also led to dualism. He could doubt having a body but not that he was thinking, so mind must be a different kind of thing from body. From 1643 Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia pressed him: if the mind is not physical, how can it move an arm? He suggested the pineal gland in the brain, an answer few found satisfying. Most philosophers and scientists today reject his dualism.

sections.key: Descartes made the question of what we can know for certain central to modern philosophy, and his method of careful doubt still helps.
sections.b:
Descartes died in Stockholm in 1650, not long after moving there at the invitation of Queen Christina of Sweden. By starting from the individual mind and asking what it can know for certain, he put epistemology, the study of knowledge, at the centre of philosophy for centuries. Later thinkers such as John Locke and David Hume answered him by stressing experience over pure reason.

He also helped shape modern science and gave us coordinate geometry, the familiar x and y axes, called Cartesian coordinates. Even people who reject his conclusions use his method: when in doubt, slow down, question your assumptions and ask what you really have good reason to believe.

quiz.q: What was Descartes trying to do with his method of doubt?
o: Persuade people to stop trusting their senses in daily life
Prove that geometry was less reliable than experience
Clear away doubtful beliefs to find a certain foundation
Show that all earlier scholars were equally wrong
quiz.e: The doubt was a tool to find out what could survive the strongest possible doubt.

quiz.q: What point does the evil demon thought experiment make?
o: Evil demons are the best explanation for vivid dreams
Waking life is always clearly different from dreaming
Experience alone cannot prove we are not being deceived
Simple sums are the one thing we can never doubt
quiz.e: If a deceiver could fake everything, no sensation alone proves the world is as it seems.

quiz.q: Why can't even the demon deceive Descartes about his own existence?
o: To be deceived, he must exist and be thinking
The demon is not powerful enough to fool him
His senses confirm to him that he has a body
Mathematics alone proves that he must exist
quiz.e: Doubting or being deceived requires a thinker, so 'I think, therefore I am' survives the doubt.

quiz.q: What is the Cartesian circle objection?
o: He proves God exists by relying only on the senses
He proves God from clear ideas, then clear ideas from God
He first doubts his own existence and then proves it
He relies on his dreams to prove the world is real
quiz.e: The argument seems to assume what it needs to prove.

quiz.q: How does Descartes's method still help us today?
o: By slowing down and asking what we have good reason to believe
By teaching us to distrust every source of information
By proving that reason is more reliable than experience
By showing that certainty is always easy to reach
quiz.e: His lasting contribution is a habit of careful, reasoned doubt.

LESSONS.push: A man in a warm room tried to doubt everything. One sentence survived.

LESSONS.title: Epicurus: the surprising philosophy of pleasure
LESSONS.hook: Today 'epicurean' suggests fine wine and rich food. But Epicurus, the philosopher behind the word, lived simply in a garden, ate bread and water, and taught that the secret of happiness was needing less.

sections.key: Around 306 BC Epicurus founded a simple school in a garden near Athens that valued friendship and welcomed women and enslaved people.
sections.b:
Today 'epicurean' suggests fine dining, but Epicurus lived simply. Born on the Greek island of Samos in 341 BC, he later bought a house with a garden near Athens, and his followers became known as the Garden. Ancient sources say it welcomed women and enslaved people, who were usually excluded from philosophical schools. Members lived simply and valued friendship above all; Epicurus is reported to have called it the greatest thing wisdom provides.

The ancient biographer Diogenes Laertius says Epicurus lived mainly on bread and water, and once asked a friend to send a little pot of cheese so he could have a feast whenever he liked.

sections.key: Epicurus taught that pleasure is the goal of life, but he meant mainly freedom from pain and worry.
sections.b:
Epicurus held that pleasure is the beginning and end of a happy life. His enemies, ancient and modern, presented that as an invitation to indulge. But he defined pleasure in a particular way. The highest pleasure was a calm state of body and mind: freedom from physical pain, called aponia, and freedom from mental disturbance, called ataraxia.

A banquet might bring a burst of enjoyment, followed by a hangover, debt or jealousy. A simple meal with friends, eaten without anxiety, could bring deeper and more lasting contentment. In his Letter to Menoeceus, he says explicitly that by pleasure he does not mean the pleasures of the profligate.

sections.key: Epicurus sorted desires into natural and necessary, natural but unnecessary, and empty ones that can never be satisfied.
sections.b:
A practical tool at the heart of Epicureanism is a way of sorting desires. Some are natural and necessary, like food, shelter and friendship. These are easy to satisfy and bring real peace. Some are natural but not necessary, like fancy food: fine to enjoy when they come along, but not worth chasing.

A third kind he called empty or vain, like the desire for fame, power or limitless wealth. These are dangerous because they have no natural limit. However much you get, there is always more to want, so they breed endless anxiety. The lesson sounds strikingly modern. Advertising and social media often work by turning unnecessary desires into what feel like needs.

sections.key: Epicurus argued that fear of the gods and of death is needless, because nature runs on atoms and death ends all sensation.
sections.b:
Epicurus built his ethics on the atomism of Democritus: everything is made of indivisible atoms moving through empty space. Thunderstorms, earthquakes and disease have natural causes. He did not deny that gods existed, but argued that perfectly happy beings would not bother to punish or reward humans.

Death was next. In the Letter to Menoeceus he says death is nothing to us, since good and bad lie in sensation and death ends sensation. When we exist, death is not present; when death is present, we do not exist. The Roman poet Lucretius, in On the Nature of Things, added that we do not fear the endless time before we were born, so why fear the time after? Critics reply that what we dread is losing the good things life would have held.

sections.key: Epicureans condensed their teaching into a four-part remedy for anxiety and advised a quiet life, which drew both admiration and criticism.
sections.b:
Later followers condensed the teaching into the tetrapharmakos, or fourfold remedy, found in the writings of Philodemus. Commonly translated: don't fear god, don't worry about death, what is good is easy to get, and what is terrible is easy to endure. The last line reflects Epicurus's view that intense pain tends to be brief while lasting pain is usually bearable, which may seem too optimistic for chronic illness. Treating philosophy as medicine for the mind echoes modern therapy.

Epicurus also advised 'living unnoticed', away from politics, which he saw as breeding fear and rivalry. The Stoics and Cicero called this selfish. Yet Thomas Jefferson called himself an Epicurean late in life. The question stays fresh: what do you actually need to be content?

quiz.q: How did Epicurus actually live?
o: Lavishly, hosting grand banquets for his followers
Alone, avoiding all friendships and all visitors
In public life, advising the leaders of Athens
Simply, on bread and water, among friends in a garden
quiz.e: The man whose name suggests luxury treated a little cheese as a feast.

quiz.q: What did Epicurus mean by pleasure?
o: The intense enjoyment of food, wine and entertainment
Winning honour and lasting respect from others
Taking in as many new experiences as possible
Mainly freedom from physical pain and mental disturbance
quiz.e: The highest pleasure, for Epicurus, was calm of body and mind, not indulgence.

quiz.q: Why did Epicurus see empty desires, such as for fame or limitless wealth, as dangerous?
o: They always damage the health of the body
They can never be shared with close friends
They have no natural limit, so they breed anxiety
They are impossible for anyone to feel naturally
quiz.e: Because there is always more to want, they can never be satisfied.

quiz.q: What was Epicurus's argument that death is nothing to us?
o: The soul is judged after death and then rewarded or punished
Death is painful but brief, and so it is bearable for most people
Good and bad lie in sensation, and death ends all sensation
Fear of death keeps people honest and so is useful to society
quiz.e: When death is present, we do not exist, so death cannot harm us.

quiz.q: Why did the Stoics and Cicero criticise the Epicureans?
o: They said Epicureans ate far too lavishly
They thought they believed in far too many gods
They called them selfish for neglecting civic duty
They said they spent too much time in politics
quiz.e: Epicurus's advice to avoid public life looked to critics like a neglect of civic duty.

LESSONS.push: The man behind 'epicurean' lived on bread, water and a little cheese.

LESSONS.title: Ubuntu: I am because we are
LESSONS.hook: A person is a person through other people. This idea from southern Africa helped guide a nation through its transition from apartheid, and it offers a challenge to the way many Western philosophies picture the self.

sections.key: Ubuntu is a southern African idea that we become fully human through our relationships with others.
sections.b:
In many parts of southern Africa, a common greeting translates roughly as 'I see you', and the reply as 'I am here'. The exchange hints at a philosophy in which existence is affirmed through recognition by others. It is often summed up in the word ubuntu, found in Nguni languages such as isiZulu and isiXhosa, with related words across many Bantu languages.

Ubuntu is usually translated as 'humanness' or 'humanity towards others', and captured in the isiZulu saying umuntu ngumuntu ngabantu: 'a person is a person through other persons'. It is not one written theory by a founding philosopher. It is a living ethical outlook, carried in proverbs, customs and everyday expectations, which thinkers have more recently set out systematically.

sections.key: Ubuntu treats personhood as something achieved through relationships, not simply possessed by an isolated individual.
sections.b:
Many influential Western philosophies start with the individual. Descartes began with a single mind doubting everything; social contract theorists imagined separate individuals agreeing to form a society. Ubuntu starts elsewhere, treating people as fundamentally bound up with one another. On many accounts, personhood is not just a biological fact but something you grow into by how you treat others.

In everyday speech in some communities, a person who behaves cruelly or selfishly may be said to lack ubuntu, or even to be 'not a person', meaning not living up to what a human should be. The Kenyan-born philosopher John Mbiti put a related African communal outlook in 1969: 'I am, because we are; and since we are, therefore I am.'

sections.key: Ubuntu values generosity, hospitality and compassion, and judges actions by whether they promote harmonious relationships.
sections.b:
In practice, ubuntu is associated with sharing with those in need, welcoming strangers, respecting elders, and repairing damaged relationships rather than simply punishing. A frequently told illustration is a traveller passing through a village, who would expect to be offered food and water without having to ask.

The American-born philosopher Thaddeus Metz, who works in South Africa, has tried to state its core precisely. On an ubuntu view, he suggests, right actions respect and promote harmonious relationships, where people identify with one another and act for each other's good. Wrong actions are unfriendly or divisive. That makes ubuntu different from both rule-based and outcome-based ethics: the focus is the quality of relationships.

sections.key: Ubuntu shaped South Africa's transition from apartheid, from the Truth and Reconciliation Commission to the abolition of the death penalty.
sections.b:
Ubuntu became internationally known during South Africa's transition to democracy. The 1993 interim Constitution said there was 'a need for ubuntu but not for victimisation'. Archbishop Desmond Tutu, who chaired the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, explained his approach through ubuntu. The commission offered amnesty to some perpetrators who fully disclosed politically motivated crimes, and gave victims a public platform. Tutu argued that dehumanising others diminishes the oppressor too, and that healing requires restoring relationships. Some victims felt justice was sacrificed.

In 1995, in S v Makwanyane, the Constitutional Court ruled the death penalty unconstitutional. Several judges cited ubuntu as valuing life and dignity and favouring reconciliation over retribution. Critics say the concept is too broad to guide judges clearly.

sections.key: Critics call ubuntu vague or romanticised, and it is one strand in a wider tradition of African philosophy.
sections.b:
Ubuntu has thoughtful critics, including African philosophers. Some say it has become a slogan, used in corporate training until it means little more than 'teamwork'. Others warn against romanticising a single 'African' worldview across hundreds of cultures. A deeper worry concerns rights: if personhood depends on community, what protects dissenters or people marginalised by their own communities? Defenders reply that ubuntu condemns treating anyone as less than human. Kwame Gyekye proposed a 'moderate communitarianism' giving both community and individual rights their due.

Other African philosophers include Kwasi Wiredu, who urged 'conceptual decolonisation', and Henry Odera Oruka, who recorded the reasoning of local sages. Ubuntu leaves a question worth asking: how much of who you are was made by other people?

quiz.q: What does the isiZulu saying umuntu ngumuntu ngabantu mean?
o: A person is a person through other persons
A person is stronger when alone
A leader is a leader through the law
A person is defined by their ancestors
quiz.e: Ubuntu holds that we become fully human through our relationships with others.

quiz.q: How does ubuntu differ from philosophies that start with the isolated individual?
o: It denies that individual people exist at all
It sees personhood as grown through relationships
It holds that personhood is purely biological
It says community matters only to the village elders
quiz.e: For ubuntu, being a person is an achievement of relationship, not a private possession.

quiz.q: According to Thaddeus Metz, what makes an action right on an ubuntu view?
o: It produces the greatest total happiness
It respects and promotes harmonious relationships
It follows a fixed rule without exception
It benefits the person who acts on it
quiz.e: Ubuntu focuses on the quality of relationships rather than rules or outcomes alone.

quiz.q: How did Tutu's Truth and Reconciliation Commission reflect ubuntu?
o: Reliance only on trials and harsh punishment of every offender
An effort to erase the past from the nation's public memory
Immediate legal immunity for every perpetrator without disclosure
Amnesty for full disclosure, plus a public voice for victims
quiz.e: Tutu argued that healing requires restoring relationships, not only punishment.

quiz.q: What is one criticism of ubuntu raised by African philosophers?
o: It has no real connection to everyday life or ordinary expectations
It places too much emphasis on the individual rights of each person
It rejects every form of community and shared responsibility
It may be vague or romanticised, and may pressure dissenters to conform
quiz.e: Critics worry the concept can become a slogan or fail to protect individuals.

LESSONS.push: Ubuntu says you are a person only through other people. What does that change?

LESSONS.title: Philosophy's golden age in the Islamic world
LESSONS.hook: Between Ancient Greece and the European Renaissance, some of the boldest philosophy on Earth was written in Arabic. Meet the thinkers who preserved Aristotle, argued about cause and effect, and imagined a man floating in the air.

sections.key: From the late 700s, scholars under the Abbasid caliphs translated Greek philosophy and science into Arabic, and argued with it.
sections.b:
In the late 700s and 800s, under the Abbasid caliphs based in Baghdad, a remarkable translation movement got under way. Scholars, many of them Christians fluent in Greek and Syriac, translated Aristotle, Plato's ideas as passed down by later writers, and Greek medicine, astronomy and mathematics into Arabic. Wealthy patrons paid well. Baghdad's House of Wisdom is often associated with the movement, although historians debate how far it was a formal academy rather than a palace library.

Much of this learning was scarcely read in Western Europe at the time. It became part of a lively intellectual culture stretching from Central Asia to Spain. Thinkers did not just preserve these texts; they argued with them.

sections.key: Al-Kindi and al-Farabi set out to show how Greek philosophy related to Islamic belief and to politics.
sections.b:
Al-Kindi, working in Baghdad in the 800s, is often called 'the philosopher of the Arabs'. He argued that truth should be welcomed whatever its source, even foreign peoples, and that philosophy and revelation pointed in the same direction.

A generation or two later, al-Farabi, who probably came from Central Asia, became so respected as an interpreter of Aristotle that he was called 'the Second Teacher'. He wrote on logic, music and especially politics. Inspired partly by Plato's Republic, he described a 'virtuous city' led by a wise ruler who would guide citizens towards true happiness. His work shaped how later thinkers connected philosophy, religion and the good society.

sections.key: Avicenna distinguished essence from existence and imagined a floating man to argue that we know our own existence directly.
sections.b:
Ibn Sina, known in Europe as Avicenna, was born around 980 near Bukhara, in today's Uzbekistan. By his own account he mastered most sciences by eighteen. His Canon of Medicine served as a medical textbook in Europe for centuries. In philosophy, he distinguished what a thing is, its essence, from the fact that it exists: you can understand a unicorn without knowing whether any exist. He argued for a necessary being, whose essence includes existence, identified with God.

His best-known thought experiment imagines a person created in mid-air, blindfolded, limbs apart, with no sensations. Would they know they exist? Avicenna said yes, taking this to show the self is distinct from the body. It resembles Descartes's argument six centuries later. Critics question whether imagining yourself without a body shows you could exist without one.

sections.key: Al-Ghazali questioned whether we ever observe necessary cause and effect, and Averroes defended philosophy in reply.
sections.b:
Not everyone welcomed the philosophers' confidence. In the late 1000s, Abu Hamid al-Ghazali wrote The Incoherence of the Philosophers, attacking Avicenna and others. His most striking argument concerned causation. When cotton touches fire, it burns. But we observe only that burning follows contact, never a necessary connection. He concluded that God directly creates each event, usually in regular patterns, so miracles are possible. Centuries later David Hume made a similar observation for very different reasons.

In the 1100s, in Córdoba, the judge and physician Ibn Rushd, or Averroes, replied with The Incoherence of the Incoherence. He argued that religious law itself encouraged capable people to study nature through reason. His commentaries on Aristotle became so influential in Latin translation that Thomas Aquinas called him simply 'the Commentator'.

sections.key: This tradition linked Greek, Jewish, Christian and Muslim thinkers and did not end in the 1100s.
sections.b:
This was not only a Muslim story. The Jewish philosopher Moses Maimonides, born in Córdoba and later working in Egypt, wrote his Guide for the Perplexed in Arabic, engaging closely with Aristotle and Islamic philosophy. Christian scholars in Spain translated Arabic works into Latin, feeding the rise of medieval European universities.

Ibn Tufayl wrote a philosophical novel about a boy raised alone on an island who reasons his way to deep truths. It may have been known in Europe by the time of Robinson Crusoe.

It is also a myth that Islamic philosophy ended in the 1100s. It continued to flourish, especially in Persia, with thinkers such as Mulla Sadra in the 1600s. These debates on reason, faith and the self belong to everyone's intellectual history.

quiz.q: What did the Abbasid-era translators help achieve?
o: Greek philosophy was replaced by entirely new Arabic ideas
Greek texts were kept hidden from most scholars and readers
Greek learning was absorbed into Arabic thought and debated
Works were produced mainly in Latin for a European audience
quiz.e: Scholars did not just preserve Greek works; they engaged with and debated them.

quiz.q: What did al-Kindi argue about truth?
o: Welcome truth from any source; philosophy and revelation agree
Truth should come only from scholars of one's own people
Truth cannot be reached through human reason or philosophy
Foreign ideas should be avoided because they mislead believers
quiz.e: Al-Kindi held that truth is truth wherever it comes from.

quiz.q: What does Avicenna's floating man suggest?
o: The body is the whole of what a person really is
A person without sensations would still be self-aware
Thinking is impossible without constant sensory input
People can never be sure that they exist at all
quiz.e: He took this to show that the self is something distinct from the body.

quiz.q: What did al-Ghazali claim about cause and effect?
o: We see burning follow contact, but never a necessary link
Natural laws are fixed and can never be questioned by anyone
Fire never causes burning, because cotton cannot burn at all
Causes are plainly visible to any careful observer of nature
quiz.e: His point was that we see sequence, not necessity, which left room for miracles.

quiz.q: Why is it a myth that Islamic philosophy ended in the 1100s?
o: It was replaced by the Greek philosophy it had once translated
It continued to flourish, for instance in 1600s Persia
It moved entirely to Europe and disappeared from the Islamic world
It was banned across the region by the caliphs of the period
quiz.e: Philosophical debate in the Islamic world carried on for centuries after Averroes.

LESSONS.push: Some of history's boldest philosophy was written in Arabic. Meet the thinkers.

LESSONS.title: Hume's problem: why trust that the sun will rise?
LESSONS.hook: You are sure the sun will rise tomorrow. But can you prove it? David Hume's simple question about learning from experience has troubled philosophers and scientists for nearly three centuries, and a black swan from Western Australia became its mascot.

sections.key: Hume asked what justifies our expectation that the future will resemble the past, a question about induction.
sections.b:
In 1739 a young Scottish philosopher, David Hume, published A Treatise of Human Nature, which he later said 'fell dead-born from the press'. In it, and in a 1748 book, he asked a question that seems almost silly. Why do we believe the sun will rise tomorrow? Because it always has. But we have only observed the past. Our confidence rests on an assumption that nature will keep behaving as it has.

There are two kinds of reasoning. In deduction, true premises guarantee the conclusion. Induction moves from observed cases to rules or predictions, so the conclusion could still be false. Science, medicine and crossing the road depend on it. Hume did not say stop using it. He asked whether we can justify it without assuming what we are trying to prove.

sections.key: Any argument that induction works seems to rely on induction itself, which is circular.
sections.b:
Hume's argument runs roughly like this. A justification for induction must be either a deductive proof or an argument from experience. It cannot be deductive, because there is no contradiction in imagining the future being different: you can coherently picture the sun failing to rise, or bread ceasing to nourish.

So it must come from experience. But that argument would be: induction has worked in the past, so it will work in the future. That is itself inductive, so it assumes the very thing in question. Hume concluded that our expectations come not from reason but from custom or habit. After seeing one event follow another many times, the mind simply comes to expect it. This, he thought, is how human nature works. It is now called the problem of induction, and it remains famously unsolved.

sections.key: Russell's chicken and Australia's black swans show how expectations built on past experience can fail.
sections.b:
Bertrand Russell gave a grim illustration in 1912. A chicken is fed every day by the farmer and comes to expect food whenever he appears. One day, the farmer wrings its neck instead. Its past experience was real, but it misled the chicken completely.

A more cheerful example comes from Australia. For centuries Europeans used 'black swan' for something impossible, because every swan they had seen was white. In 1697 the Dutch explorer Willem de Vlamingh's expedition recorded black swans on a river in Western Australia, which they named the Swan River. A rule supported by countless observations was overturned by one. The black swan is now a common emblem of the limits of induction.

sections.key: Popper said science advances by trying to falsify bold theories, while Goodman's 'grue' showed that choosing which patterns to trust is itself puzzling.
sections.b:
The philosopher Karl Popper, in work first published in 1934, agreed that induction cannot be justified but argued science does not need it. Scientists do not prove theories by piling up confirming cases. They propose bold conjectures and try to refute them. One genuine black swan falsifies 'all swans are white', and that is deduction. Surviving theories are simply the best we have so far. Critics reply that we still rely on tested theories to predict the future, which brings induction back.

In 1955 Nelson Goodman defined 'grue' as green if first observed before some future date, and blue otherwise. Every emerald observed so far is both green and grue, so the evidence seems to support opposite predictions. We should project green, but why? The hard part is knowing which patterns count.

sections.key: Responses to Hume remain debated, but his lesson is to hold beliefs with confidence proportional to the evidence.
sections.b:
Many responses to Hume have been tried. Some use probability and Bayesian reasoning to show how evidence should raise or lower our confidence, though critics say these methods still need assumptions about the world. Others take a pragmatic line: if any method can predict the future, induction will, so it is our best bet. Some argue that demanding a non-circular justification is unreasonable, since the most basic forms of reasoning cannot all be proved without using themselves.

Immanuel Kant said that reading Hume woke him from his 'dogmatic slumber'. Whatever view you take, Hume's lesson is practical: hold general beliefs with confidence proportional to the evidence, and stay open to the black swan.

quiz.q: What is the problem of induction?
o: We cannot observe anything at all about the past or present
Deduction always leads to false conclusions about the world
Science cannot make any predictions without perfect knowledge
Our trust in the future rests on assuming nature stays as it was
quiz.e: Experience alone cannot guarantee that the future will resemble the past.

quiz.q: Why is any argument for induction circular?
o: It relies on a deductive proof that turns out to be invalid
It depends on a contradiction that appears in picturing the future
It says induction worked before, which itself relies on induction
It rests entirely on memories that are often unreliable
quiz.e: Using induction to justify induction assumes the very thing in question.

quiz.q: What do the chicken and the black swan show?
o: Animals reason about the future better than people do
Observation is always misleading and should never be trusted
A pattern from many observations can fall to a single one
Rules drawn from experience are never useful in practice
quiz.e: Expectations built on past experience can fail, so induction has limits.

quiz.q: How did Popper respond to Hume?
o: Induction can be proved correct if enough data is collected
Theories that survive testing are thereby proven true
Science advances by trying to falsify bold theories
Science should avoid making any predictions about the future
quiz.e: A single counterexample can refute a theory by deduction, with no need for induction.

quiz.q: What practical lesson does Hume leave us?
o: Match confidence to the evidence and stay open to surprises
Never trust any belief about the future, however well supported
Treat habit as a better guide than any available evidence
Stop using induction altogether in your daily life and work
quiz.e: We cannot do without induction, but we should hold its conclusions with humility.

LESSONS.push: You are sure the sun will rise tomorrow. Can you prove it? A swan says no.

LESSONS.title: The veil of ignorance: designing a fair society
LESSONS.hook: Imagine designing the rules of society without knowing whether you would be born rich or poor, healthy or sick. John Rawls's thought experiment reshaped debates about justice, and drew powerful critics who saw things very differently.

sections.key: John Rawls asked which rules people would choose for society if they did not know their own place in it.
sections.b:
Imagine you are about to be born into a society, but you do not know who you will be. You might be born into wealth or poverty, with great talents or a serious disability, into a majority or a minority. Before you find out, you help choose the basic rules: how wealth is shared, which freedoms are protected, how opportunities are distributed.

This is the heart of the most famous thought experiment in modern political philosophy, set out by John Rawls in his 1971 book A Theory of Justice. Rawls called it the original position, with a 'veil of ignorance' hiding your sex, class, abilities, religion and idea of a good life. If you do not know whether you will be rich, you cannot rig the rules for the rich. The principles that emerge should be acceptable from every position.

sections.key: Rawls argued for equal basic liberties and for allowing inequality only if it benefits the least advantaged.
sections.b:
Rawls argued that people behind the veil would choose two principles. First, everyone gets an equal right to the most extensive basic liberties compatible with the same for others, such as free speech and conscience. These rank above the second principle. Second, inequalities are acceptable only if positions are open to all under fair equality of opportunity, and if they work to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged. That last part is the difference principle.

It does not demand equal incomes. Paying some people more, say to encourage training, can be justified if it lifts up the worst-off. Rawls thought people would reason cautiously, focusing on the worst outcome: a 'maximin' strategy, maximising the minimum. The economist John Harsanyi argued that rational people would instead maximise average wellbeing.

sections.key: Robert Nozick argued that justice depends on how holdings came about, not on matching a pattern of distribution.
sections.b:
Rawls's most famous critic was his Harvard colleague Robert Nozick, whose 1974 book Anarchy, State, and Utopia defended a libertarian view. A distribution is just, he argued, if people acquired their holdings fairly and transferred them voluntarily, whatever pattern results.

He illustrated this with the basketball star Wilt Chamberlain. Suppose society begins with a distribution you consider perfectly fair, and then a million fans each happily pay a small sum to watch Chamberlain play. He becomes rich, and the pattern is upset. Yet every step was voluntary. How could the result be unjust? Nozick concluded that maintaining any fixed pattern would require continual interference in free choices, and that redistributive taxation risks treating people's labour as a resource others may claim.

sections.key: Communitarians, feminists and capability theorists challenged Rawls from different directions.
sections.b:
