Criticism came from other angles too. Communitarians, such as Michael Sandel in a 1982 book, argued that the people behind the veil are 'unencumbered selves', stripped of the loyalties, traditions and communities that make us who we are.

The feminist philosopher Susan Moller Okin argued that Rawls had not taken justice within the family seriously enough, even though families shape children's opportunities so profoundly.

The economist and philosopher Amartya Sen, with the philosopher Martha Nussbaum, developed the capabilities approach. They argued that justice should focus less on resources and more on what people can actually do and be, since people with different needs convert the same income into very different lives.

sections.key: The veil of ignorance remains a practical fairness test, since you can test any rule by asking whether you would accept it without knowing which side of it you would end up on.
sections.b:
Rawls refined his views over the following decades, notably in Political Liberalism in 1993, which asked how people with deeply different religious and moral beliefs can share a stable, fair society. His work and the responses to it frame much of today's argument about tax, welfare, health care and opportunity, across the political spectrum.

Even people who reject his conclusions often find the veil of ignorance a useful thinking tool. When debating a policy, from school funding to disability support, ask: would I accept this rule if I did not know which side of it I would end up on? That question does not settle every disagreement, and reasonable people still reach different answers. But it pushes us to see a society from more than our own seat.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of the veil of ignorance?
o: To hide facts about economics from decision makers
To strip away bias so rules are fair from every position
To make sure everyone shares the same talents and wealth
To let the majority choose whichever rules it prefers
quiz.e: If you do not know your place, you cannot rig the rules in your own favour.

quiz.q: What does the difference principle allow?
o: Equal incomes for every person, whatever their role or effort
Inequalities only if they benefit the least advantaged
Any inequality at all that helps to grow the economy
Inequalities that reward the most talented people most
quiz.e: Inequality is justified only when it makes the worst-off better off than they would otherwise be.

quiz.q: What point does Nozick's Wilt Chamberlain example make?
o: Athletes should be paid less than other kinds of workers
Wealth should always be divided equally across a society
Fans should not be allowed to pay for entertainment
Voluntary exchanges break any set pattern of distribution
quiz.e: Nozick held that justice depends on how holdings came about, not on matching a pattern.

quiz.q: What was Sandel's communitarian objection to the veil?
o: It gives too much weight to the role of the family
It ignores the need for economic growth in a society
It hands people far too many liberties to choose from
It imagines 'unencumbered selves' stripped of their loyalties
quiz.e: Communitarians argue we cannot understand people apart from their communities.

quiz.q: How can the veil of ignorance be used in everyday debate?
o: Choose the rule that is favoured by the largest number of people
Choose the rule that would benefit you and your family most
Ask whether you would accept a rule without knowing your side
Set aside the views of those who are directly affected by it
quiz.e: It is a thinking tool for testing fairness, not a way to settle every disagreement.

LESSONS.push: Design a society without knowing who you will be in it. What would you choose?

LESSONS.title: The invisible gorilla: why we miss what's in front of us
LESSONS.hook: Half the people in a famous experiment failed to notice a gorilla walking through a basketball game. They weren't careless. They were human, and so are you.

sections.key: When we focus hard on one thing, we can miss something huge and obvious.
sections.b:
In 1999, psychologists Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris made a short video of students passing basketballs. Viewers were asked to count the passes made by the team in white shirts. Partway through, a person in a gorilla suit strolls into the middle of the game, thumps their chest and walks off. It is on screen for several seconds. Roughly half the viewers never saw it.

When told afterwards, many refused to believe it until they watched again, and some accused the researchers of swapping the tape. The study has been repeated many times with similar results. The lesson is unsettling: we do not see everything our eyes are pointed at.

sections.key: Attention picks out a small slice of what reaches your eyes, so we can miss unexpected objects and even big changes.
sections.b:
It feels as though we take in a whole scene in rich detail, like a camera. We do not. Your eyes send the brain more than it can process, so attention acts like a spotlight, picking out what seems relevant and leaving the rest dim. Psychologists call failing to notice an unexpected object while focused on something else inattentional blindness, a term popularised by Arien Mack and Irvin Rock. The missed object is in plain view. What is missing is attention turning light into conscious experience.

A close cousin is change blindness. In a 1998 study by Simons and Daniel Levin, pedestrians giving directions had the researcher swapped for a different person behind a passing door. Around half did not notice. Film continuity errors work the same way.

sections.key: Expertise sharpens what you look for, which can blind you to what you don't expect.
sections.b:
You might think trained professionals would be immune. In a 2013 study, Trafton Drew, Melissa Vo and Jeremy Wolfe asked radiologists to search lung scans for small nodules that can signal cancer. In the final case, the researchers had inserted a small image of a gorilla, many times larger than a typical nodule. About four in five radiologists did not report it, even though eye tracking showed most had looked directly at the spot.

This does not mean radiologists are bad at their job. They were brilliantly tuned to find nodules, and that is the point. Expertise tells you where to look and what to look for, and anything outside that search template can slip by unseen.

sections.key: On the road, inattentional blindness can be deadly, and hands-free calls do not remove the risk.
sections.b:
Road safety researchers have a name for a common type of crash: 'looked but failed to see'. A driver pulls out of a side street and hits a motorcyclist or cyclist, then insists they checked and the road was clear. Often they are telling the truth as they experienced it. Their attention was tuned to cars, so a smaller, less expected vehicle did not register.

Research by David Strayer and colleagues has found that phone conversations make this worse, and that hands-free calls are still distracting, because the problem is divided attention, not just your hands. Australian road rules on phones vary by state, so check your state transport authority, but the psychology is the same everywhere.

sections.key: Selective attention is a useful filter, and since knowing about it doesn't switch it off, the answer is building habits and systems.
sections.b:
Selective attention is what lets you function at all. Imagine reading this sentence while consciously processing every sound, the feel of your clothes and every object in your peripheral vision. Filtering lets you hold a conversation in a noisy cafe. The cost is that it sometimes throws out something important. People told about the gorilla in advance nearly always see it, but in a later Simons variation, those who knew the original gorilla were no better at spotting other unexpected changes.

So confidence is not evidence. When driving, make a deliberate second look for bikes, motorbikes and pedestrians. For important work, use checklists or a second pair of eyes. Allow that two honest people can see different things. The gorilla is always there somewhere; build systems that catch it.

quiz.q: What did the gorilla experiment show?
o: Focused attention can hide something large and obvious
Most people have poor eyesight without glasses
People can count and notice everything at once
Gorillas are easy to spot in a crowd of players
quiz.e: We do not see everything our eyes are pointed at when attention is elsewhere.

quiz.q: What causes inattentional blindness?
o: The object is hidden from view by other objects in the scene
Attention does not turn what reaches your eyes into awareness
The eyes fail to receive light from the object in the first place
Viewers are not paying any attention to the scene at all
quiz.e: The missed object is in plain view; what is lacking is attention, not light.

quiz.q: Why did most radiologists miss the gorilla in the scan?
o: Their expertise tuned them to nodules, so a gorilla slipped by
They were not looking at that part of the scan at all
They are generally poor at finding the nodules they search for
They did not take the research task seriously enough
quiz.e: Expertise directs attention, and unexpected items outside the search template can be missed.

quiz.q: Why are hands-free calls still risky for drivers?
o: The phone signal interferes with the car
The problem is divided attention, not only the hands
Hands-free kits are poorly made and often faulty
Drivers tend to talk louder on hands-free calls
quiz.e: Attention, not hand position, is the limited resource.

quiz.q: What helps most with the limits of selective attention?
o: Know about the gorilla and you'll always spot it
Build habits and systems such as checklists and second looks
Concentrate harder on everything at the same time
Trust your confidence that you would have noticed
quiz.e: Awareness alone doesn't switch the effect off, so we build in safeguards.

LESSONS.push: Half of viewers missed a gorilla in plain sight. Experts did too.

LESSONS.title: Cognitive dissonance: why we twist the facts to feel better
LESSONS.hook: When reality clashes with what we believe or what we've done, something has to give. Surprisingly often, it isn't the belief.

sections.key: A doomsday group whose prophecy failed gave psychologists a view of how people defend a belief.
sections.b:
In 1954, a small group in the American Midwest believed a flood would destroy much of the world on 21 December, and that a flying saucer would rescue the faithful beforehand. Some members quit jobs and gave away possessions. Unknown to the group, several new members were researchers working with psychologist Leon Festinger.

They watched as midnight passed with no spaceship and no flood. Rather than abandon the belief, the leader announced that the group's faith had saved the world, and some members began seeking publicity and recruits for the first time. Festinger and colleagues described the episode in the 1956 book When Prophecy Fails. It illustrated an idea Festinger would soon make famous.

sections.key: Holding clashing thoughts creates discomfort that we are driven to reduce, often by changing beliefs rather than behaviour.
sections.b:
In 1957 Festinger published A Theory of Cognitive Dissonance. When we hold two beliefs, or a belief and an action, that conflict, we feel an uncomfortable tension. A smoker who knows smoking kills experiences it every time they light up.

That discomfort motivates us to restore consistency, and there are only a few ways. We can change our behaviour, by quitting. We can change our belief, by deciding the risks are exaggerated. Or we can add thoughts that soften the clash, such as 'my grandfather smoked and lived to ninety' or 'everyone dies of something'. Changing behaviour is often the hardest option, so the mind quietly reaches for the others.

sections.key: After a hard decision or a costly effort, we tend to value what we chose or suffered for more.
sections.b:
Dissonance is thought to be strongest after a hard decision. If you agonised between two similar cars and bought one, you may suddenly notice how good your choice is and how flawed the other was. In 1956 Jack Brehm had people choose between two appliances they liked equally; the chosen item tended to rise in their ratings, the rejected one to fall. Later researchers noted a statistical problem with this design, and corrected studies often find a smaller effect. In a 1968 racetrack study, punters who had just placed a bet were more confident of winning.

The same logic gives effort justification. In a 1959 study, Elliot Aronson and Judson Mills found that people who endured an embarrassing initiation rated a dull group more highly. It helps explain fierce loyalty after hazing, and why people stay with failing projects.

sections.key: The theory is influential, but classic experiments deserve more caution than textbooks usually give them.
sections.b:
The most famous dissonance study is a 1959 experiment by Festinger and James Carlsmith. Students did an hour of dull tasks, then were paid one dollar or twenty to tell the next participant it was fun. The one dollar group later rated the task as more enjoyable. The explanation: twenty dollars was reason enough to lie, one dollar was not, so they decided the task wasn't so bad. Replications of this kind of finding have been mixed, so it deserves caution.

The theory has always had critics. In the 1960s Daryl Bem argued that we simply infer our attitudes from our behaviour. Others suggested the real driver is protecting our self-image as a good, sensible person. The doomsday study is also questioned. Most psychologists still accept that people often rationalise, but treat specific classic experiments cautiously.

sections.key: Noticing your own defensiveness can help you think more honestly, and offering others a face-saving way to change their mind works better than cornering them.
sections.b:
The practical value of dissonance theory is self-awareness. When you feel defensive, irritated or eager to explain something away, a cherished belief may have met an inconvenient fact. Pausing to ask 'what would change my mind?' helps. So does separating your identity from your opinions: being wrong about a decision does not make you foolish.

In relationships, remember that others feel dissonance too, so cornering someone with evidence often makes them dig in. Offering a face-saving way to change their mind works better. There is a famous anecdote from Benjamin Franklin, who said he won over a rival by asking to borrow a rare book. Helping you, perhaps, made the rival like you more.

quiz.q: What did the failed doomsday prophecy illustrate?
o: Believers always give up their belief when proven wrong
Groups quickly forget failed predictions and move on
People may defend a belief harder when reality contradicts it
Prophecies about the end of the world usually come true
quiz.e: The group reinterpreted the failure rather than abandoning the belief.

quiz.q: What is cognitive dissonance?
o: The inability to make any decision between two close options
The feeling of complete certainty that follows a decision
The discomfort of clashing beliefs or actions, which we try to ease
The fear of being found wrong in front of other people
quiz.e: The tension motivates us to restore consistency, often by changing beliefs.

quiz.q: What is 'effort justification'?
o: Spending effort to justify our decisions to other people
Rewarding people strictly in proportion to their effort
Valuing something more because of the effort it cost us
Avoiding tasks that would require too much effort
quiz.e: Admitting we suffered for something worthless creates dissonance, so the mind upgrades the prize.

quiz.q: What does the lesson say about the classic dissonance experiments?
o: They deserve more caution than textbooks give them
They have all been conclusively proven by replication
They have all been fully rejected by later researchers
They are the only real evidence for the whole theory
quiz.e: Science updates its beliefs, and some famous findings have not replicated cleanly.

quiz.q: What works best when helping someone change their mind?
o: Cornering them with evidence
Offering a face-saving way to change it
Repeating the facts more loudly
Pointing out their earlier mistakes
quiz.e: People feel dissonance too, and being cornered makes them dig in.

LESSONS.push: A prophecy failed on schedule. Its believers got stronger. Why?

LESSONS.title: Impostor feelings: when success feels like a fluke
LESSONS.hook: You got the job, passed the exam or won the award, and you're quietly waiting to be found out. You are in very good company.

sections.key: Many capable people secretly believe they don't deserve their success, a pattern named in 1978 as the impostor phenomenon.
sections.b:
Picture a doctor newly qualified, a manager freshly promoted, or a student who topped the class. From the outside they look confident. Inside runs a different story: 'I got lucky. Any day now, someone will realise I don't know what I'm doing.' This feeling of being a fraud despite clear evidence of competence is widely known as impostor syndrome.

The concept was introduced in 1978 by American psychologists Pauline Rose Clance and Suzanne Imes, working with high-achieving women who credited luck or charm rather than ability. Note the word phenomenon, not syndrome. It is not a mental illness or a diagnosis. It describes thoughts and feelings many ordinary, healthy people experience at times. Later research found it in men as well, across many professions and cultures.

sections.key: Impostor feelings are clearly widespread, but claims such as '70 per cent' have murky origins.
sections.b:
You may have seen claims that 70 per cent of people experience impostor feelings. That figure is repeated often, but its origins are murky. A 2020 systematic review led by Dena Bravata found reported rates from under ten per cent to over eighty per cent, depending on who was studied and how it was measured.

The honest conclusion is that nobody knows the exact figure, but impostor feelings are very common, particularly during transitions such as starting university, a new job or a promotion. They seem especially frequent among people who are among the first in their family or community to reach a particular position, and in competitive fields where everyone around you seems brilliant.

sections.key: Overpreparing or procrastinating, then explaining success away, keeps the doubt alive.
sections.b:
Clance described a self-sustaining loop sometimes called the impostor cycle. Faced with a task, a person feels anxious and doubtful. They respond in one of two ways: by overpreparing, working far longer than necessary, or by procrastinating, then working frantically at the last minute.

The task goes well. But instead of concluding 'I'm good at this', they explain the success away. If they overprepared, it was only the extra effort. If they procrastinated, it was luck. Either way, the success does not count as evidence of ability, so the doubt is ready and waiting for the next task. Breaking the cycle often starts with noticing how you explain your wins, and whether you would accept that explanation from a friend.

sections.key: Impostor feelings come from how success is interpreted, often in competent people, and sometimes from real signals in the environment.
sections.b:
Impostor feelings are sometimes described as the opposite of the Dunning-Kruger effect, the idea that people with low skill overestimate themselves. The comparison is catchy but loose. People with impostor feelings are usually genuinely competent. Expertise can even feed the feeling: the more you learn, the more you see how much you don't know, while beginners may be blissfully unaware of the gaps.

Some researchers also criticise the 'syndrome' label for putting all the focus on individuals. If you are the only person like you in a room, hear subtle comments questioning whether you belong, or never see anyone with your background in senior roles, feeling out of place may be a reasonable response to real signals. Leaders should ask what the environment is communicating, not just tell people to be more confident.

sections.key: Talking about it, keeping a record of evidence and finding mentors help you see your achievements more accurately.
sections.b:
Several simple habits loosen the grip of impostor feelings. Talk about it: hearing that respected colleagues feel the same is powerfully reassuring. Keep a record of positive feedback, results and things you have learned, and reread it when doubts flare. Separate feelings from facts by asking, 'What evidence would convince me I'm competent?' and checking whether it already exists. Accept that not knowing everything is normal at every level. Mentors can tell you what 'good' looks like in your field.

If self-doubt is persistent, affecting your sleep or mood, or stopping you from going for opportunities, it is worth speaking to your GP. This is general information, not personal advice, and healthdirect and Beyond Blue have useful resources.

quiz.q: Why is 'impostor phenomenon' the more accurate term than 'syndrome'?
o: It only affects people working in certain kinds of jobs
It is a pattern of thoughts and feelings, not a diagnosis
It affects only women, and never affects men in any field
It is a clinical condition that always requires treatment
quiz.e: Many ordinary, healthy people experience impostor feelings at times.

quiz.q: What does research say about how common impostor feelings are?
o: Exactly 70 per cent of people experience them at some time
They are rare outside the medical and legal professions
They affect fewer than one in ten people in any group
Reported rates vary hugely, so the exact figure is unknown
quiz.e: Rates range from under ten to over eighty per cent depending on who and how it was measured.

quiz.q: What keeps the impostor cycle going?
o: Failing at nearly every task the person attempts
Avoiding every challenging piece of work altogether
Receiving too much praise from colleagues and managers
Explaining success away as effort or luck rather than ability
quiz.e: If success never counts as evidence of ability, the doubt returns with the next task.

quiz.q: Why can expertise feed impostor feelings?
o: Experts get far less feedback than beginners do
Experts are usually less skilled than they appear
The more you know, the more you see what you don't
Beginners always know more about their own gaps
quiz.e: Feeling unsure can reflect a realistic understanding of how complex the work is.

quiz.q: Which habit helps loosen impostor feelings?
o: Avoid any situation where other people might judge your work
Work far longer than necessary on every single task
Keep a record of your wins and reread it when doubts flare
Keep the feelings to yourself rather than talking about them
quiz.e: Evidence of competence is easier to see when you record it and review it.

LESSONS.push: You earned the job, so why does it feel like a fluke? Most people feel it.

LESSONS.title: The spotlight effect: nobody's watching as closely as you think
LESSONS.hook: That embarrassing stumble, the stain on your shirt, the awkward thing you said: you're replaying it all night. Everyone else has already forgotten.

sections.key: People overestimate how much others notice them, a bias called the spotlight effect.
sections.b: In a 2000 study, psychologist Thomas Gilovich and colleagues at Cornell University had students wear a T-shirt with a large picture of Barry Manilow, a singer then considered deeply uncool. Each wearer walked briefly into a room of peers filling in questionnaires, then left. Asked how many people had noticed the shirt, they guessed about half. In reality, only about a quarter could say who was on it. The researchers called this the spotlight effect: we believe we are noticed, for better or worse, far more than we really are.

sections.key: We judge how we look to others from our own intense inner view and don't adjust enough, while observers read mistakes in context and move on.
sections.b:
You are the one person you can never escape. You feel every flush of embarrassment and replay every clumsy sentence in high definition. When guessing what others see, you start from that inner view and adjust, but researchers argue we don't adjust nearly enough. Everyone else is busy with their own spotlight.

Studies by Kenneth Savitsky, Nicholas Epley and Gilovich found people who committed a minor blunder in front of others expected harsher judgement than observers gave. Observers see the wider context and remember their own slips. While you rerun your blunder at 2 am, the witnesses have most likely moved on.

sections.key: We overestimate how visible our nerves are, and learning this makes speakers calmer and better.
sections.b:
A close cousin is the illusion of transparency: believing our inner states show more than they do. In late 1990s experiments, liars overestimated how many people would catch them, and people tasting a foul drink overestimated how obvious their disgust was. A speaker may feel a pounding heart and wobbling voice and assume the audience sees terror. Usually they see someone mildly nervous.

There is good news. In a 2003 study by Savitsky and Gilovich, students told about this illusion felt less anxious and gave speeches that observers rated better than those of students who were simply reassured. Knowing the bias breaks the loop of worry feeding worry.

sections.key: After conversations, people underestimate how much the other person liked them.
sections.b:
The same pattern shapes friendships. In 2018, Erica Boothby, Gus Cooney and colleagues paired strangers for conversations, then asked each person how much they liked their partner and how much they thought their partner liked them. Consistently, people underestimated how much they were liked. The researchers called this the liking gap.

After a chat, we pick over our own awkward moments, while our partner was busy worrying about theirs. The gap appeared in lab studies, among university students getting to know their housemates and in a workshop setting. Many of us leave conversations more pessimistic than we should be, which can make us hesitate to follow up and build new friendships.

sections.key: Remembering that others notice and judge you less than you fear frees you to speak up and try new things.
sections.b:
The spotlight effect can keep us quiet in meetings or stop us trying a new dance class or wearing something different. Knowing about it offers practical freedom. Before turning down an opportunity because you fear looking foolish, remember the Barry Manilow shirt: far fewer people will notice than you imagine, and fewer still will care tomorrow.

When you replay a mistake, ask how much you remember of someone else's similar slip last week. Probably very little. After meeting someone new, assume they liked you more than your inner critic suggests, and consider sending that follow-up message. The people around you are not your audience. They are the stars of their own shows.

quiz.q: In the Barry Manilow T-shirt study, how did the wearers' guesses compare with reality?
o: Wearers guessed about half noticed; about a quarter could say who was on it
Wearers guessed a quarter noticed; about half could say who was on it
Wearers guessed nobody noticed; nearly everyone could say who was on it
Wearers guessed almost everyone noticed; and almost everyone had
quiz.e: People overestimate how much others notice them, which is the spotlight effect.

quiz.q: Why do we tend to overestimate how closely others are watching us?
o: We rely on other people's reactions and adjust too much
We start from our own intense inner view and don't adjust enough
We assume strangers are paying close attention to everyone
We forget our own mistakes and notice theirs
quiz.e: Our inner experience feels vivid to us, while others are mostly absorbed in themselves.

quiz.q: What happened when students were told about the illusion of transparency before giving a speech?
o: They felt more anxious but spoke for longer
They felt less anxious and their speeches were rated better
They felt calmer but their speeches were rated no better
They avoided speaking altogether
quiz.e: Knowing your nerves are less visible than you fear helps break the cycle of worry.

quiz.q: What does the liking gap show?
o: People tend to underestimate how much a new partner liked them
People tend to overestimate how much a new partner liked them
People tend to like strangers less than their friends
People tend to like others less as a conversation goes on
quiz.e: We dwell on our own awkward moments, so we leave conversations more pessimistic than we should be.

quiz.q: What is a sensible response to fearing you'll look foolish?
o: Avoid situations where you might make a mistake
Remember that others notice less and forget faster
Apologise at length to everyone who might have noticed
Assume the people around you are judging closely
quiz.e: Few people notice your slips, and fewer remember them, so the fear is usually bigger than the risk.

LESSONS.push: You think everyone saw your slip. A famous T-shirt study says they didn't.

LESSONS.title: Deja vu and other glitches of memory
LESSONS.hook: That eerie sense that you've lived this exact moment before. Is it a glimpse of the future, a past life, or something stranger and more ordinary?

sections.key: Deja vu is a strong sense of familiarity combined with the awareness that it is wrong.
sections.b:
You walk into a cafe you have never visited, and everything feels oddly known: the light, the clatter of cups, the conversation next door. For a few seconds you feel certain you have lived this moment, while knowing you can't have. The French phrase means 'already seen'. Surveys suggest roughly two thirds of people have experienced it. It is most common in teenagers and young adults, becomes less frequent with age, and has been linked with tiredness and stress.

What makes it special is the clash: part of your mind says 'I know this' while another says 'no, you don't'. Psychologist Chris Moulin argues this clash is the heart of the experience.

sections.key: A new scene can feel familiar because its layout matches one you've forgotten, but the sense of knowing what comes next is an illusion.
sections.b:
Psychologist Anne Cleary at Colorado State University proposed that deja vu can occur when a new scene resembles something in your past that you can't consciously recall. In virtual reality experiments, new scenes with a similar spatial layout to earlier ones were more likely to trigger deja vu when people could not recall the earlier scene. That unfamiliar cafe may share its arrangement of tables, windows and counter with a room you forgot years ago.

Many people also feel they can predict what comes next. In a 2018 test, participants felt sure which way to turn, but their predictions were no better than chance. The premonition is a feeling, not foresight.

sections.key: Deja vu may be your brain's error-checking at work, a sign of a healthy memory system.
sections.b:
Researchers can trigger something like deja vu in the lab. People hear related words such as bed, pillow, night and dream, but never the word sleep. Asked if they heard a word starting with 's', they know they did not, yet 'sleep' feels oddly familiar.

In a study presented in 2016, Akira O'Connor and colleagues scanned brains during these moments. Activity showed up mainly in frontal areas involved in decision-making and conflict, rather than in the memory hubs. One interpretation is that deja vu reflects the brain checking its memories for errors. If so, it may be a sign of a healthy memory system doing its job.

sections.key: Occasional deja vu is harmless, but very frequent or prolonged episodes with other symptoms are worth a GP visit.
sections.b:
For most people, deja vu is harmless and occasional. It does have a known link with temporal lobe epilepsy, where some people experience intense deja vu as an aura, a warning sensation at the start of a seizure. Surgeons stimulating parts of the temporal lobe during operations have also triggered deja vu-like feelings, which helped researchers pin down where the sensation arises.

Signs that it might need checking include happening very often, lasting a long time, or coming with blank spells, strange smells or tastes, or confusion. This is general information rather than medical advice. If you are concerned, talk to your GP. healthdirect also has information.

sections.key: Deja vu has an opposite, jamais vu, and together with tip-of-the-tongue states it shows memory is an active, self-monitoring process.
sections.b:
Deja vu has a stranger opposite called jamais vu, 'never seen': the sense that something you know well, such as a familiar word or face, suddenly seems foreign. You can trigger a version by writing a common word like 'door' over and over until it looks wrong. In 2023, Chris Moulin, Akira O'Connor and colleagues won an Ig Nobel Prize, the award for research that first makes people laugh and then think, for studying this.

Another familiar glitch is the tip-of-the-tongue state, when you are sure you know a name but can't retrieve it, often recalling its first letter or number of syllables. Together, these quirks reveal memory as a busy, self-monitoring process, not a simple recording.

quiz.q: What distinguishes deja vu from an ordinary false memory?
o: It only ever happens during vivid dreams
You feel familiarity while knowing it can't be right
It only happens in places you have really visited
It happens only once or twice in a lifetime
quiz.e: Deja vu is the clash between a feeling of knowing and the awareness that the feeling is wrong.

quiz.q: According to Anne Cleary's research, what can trigger deja vu?
o: Strong sunlight in a place you have never been
Hearing your own name called out in a crowd
A new scene whose layout matches one you've forgotten
Eating a food you haven't tasted in many years
quiz.e: A familiar spatial layout can create real familiarity even when you can't recall its source.

quiz.q: What might deja vu say about your memory?
o: A sign that your memory is starting to fail
A sign your brain is checking its memory for errors
A sign that you have lived the moment before
A sign that you are probably dreaming now
quiz.e: Brain scans suggest deja vu involves decision and conflict areas, consistent with a memory system checking itself.

quiz.q: Which situation suggests deja vu might be worth discussing with a GP?
o: It happened once during a holiday last year
It tends to come with tiredness and stress
It is frequent or long-lasting, or brings confusion
It happens in a place like somewhere you've been
quiz.e: Frequent or prolonged deja vu with other symptoms can be linked with temporal lobe epilepsy, so get it checked.

quiz.q: What is jamais vu?
o: Remembering a vivid scene from a past life
Seeing the very same scene twice in one day
A familiar word or face suddenly seeming foreign
Forgetting most of a dream on waking up
quiz.e: Jamais vu is the opposite of deja vu and shows memory is an active, self-monitoring process.

LESSONS.push: Two thirds of us have felt it, yet it may be your brain doing its job.

LESSONS.title: Boredom: the feeling we'll do almost anything to escape
LESSONS.hook: Given the choice between sitting quietly with their thoughts and giving themselves an electric shock, many people chose the shock. What is boredom trying to tell us?

sections.key: Many people find being alone with their thoughts so unpleasant that they would rather give themselves a mild electric shock.
sections.b:
In studies published in 2014, psychologist Timothy Wilson and colleagues at the University of Virginia asked people to sit alone in a plain room for about six to fifteen minutes with nothing to do but think. No phone, no book, no pen. Many found it unpleasant.

In one version, participants had first been given a mild electric shock, and many said they would pay money to avoid feeling it again. Yet when left alone with a button that would deliver the same shock, about two thirds of men and a quarter of women pressed it at least once. One participant pressed it 190 times. The result raised a question: what exactly is boredom?

sections.key: Boredom is the discomfort of wanting to engage but being unable to, and it works as a signal to change course.
sections.b:
Boredom is not the same as having nothing to do. You can relax happily on a beach, and you can be bored stiff in a meeting while busy. In 2012, psychologist John Eastwood and colleagues defined it as 'the aversive experience of wanting, but being unable, to engage in satisfying activity'. The mind is ready to be used, but the situation, perhaps too easy, too hard or meaningless, offers nothing to capture it.

Many researchers now see boredom as a useful emotion, like hunger or pain. Andreas Elpidorou describes it as a regulatory signal that nudges us towards goals that matter. It is not laziness or a moral failing.

sections.key: Some mind-wandering time may help creativity, but boredom is not a guaranteed booster.
sections.b:
A popular idea says boredom makes us more creative. In a 2014 study, Sandi Mann and Rebekah Cadman had some participants copy numbers from a phone book. Afterwards, they thought of more uses for a pair of plastic cups than people who had not been bored. The theory is that when the world is dull, the mind wanders and makes unexpected connections.

It is an appealing finding, but the studies have been small and results across experiments have been mixed. Some mind-wandering time may help creativity, but treating boredom as a guaranteed creativity booster goes beyond the evidence.

sections.key: How we respond to boredom matters, and reaching for a screen may silence the signal without satisfying it.
sections.b:
People differ in how often they get bored. Since Richard Farmer and Norman Sundberg developed a Boredom Proneness Scale in 1986, researchers have found that easily bored people report more attention problems, impulsive behaviour and low mood. Boredom proneness has also been linked with gambling, overeating and substance use, perhaps because these offer quick stimulation. These are associations, not proof that boredom causes the problems.

Smartphones offer an instant escape from even a few seconds of boredom. If boredom signals us to seek something meaningful, endless scrolling may silence the signal without satisfying it. Whether phones make us more bored overall is not settled, but a mindless scroll rarely leaves people refreshed.

sections.key: When bored, ask what is missing (challenge, meaning, novelty or control) and respond, or sometimes just let yourself be bored.
sections.b:
If boredom is a signal, listen to it. Ask what is missing: challenge, meaning, novelty or control. A task that is too easy can become a game, such as beating your previous time. A task that is too hard may need breaking into smaller steps. If something feels pointless, connect it to a goal you care about.

It is also worth occasionally letting yourself be bored without escaping, such as walking without headphones or sitting with a cup of tea and no screen. Many people find that ideas, plans and solutions surface in those quiet gaps. Boredom, used well, can be the start of something interesting.

quiz.q: What did the 2014 study find about being alone with one's thoughts?
o: Many found it unpleasant, and some chose to shock themselves
Most found it relaxing and wanted more time alone
Most preferred reading to sitting, but none chose a shock
Few found it unpleasant, and nobody chose a shock
quiz.e: Many people dislike unoccupied time enough to pick a mild shock over quiet thinking.

quiz.q: How do researchers now often view boredom?
o: As a sign of laziness or weak willpower
As a signal that your activity isn't engaging you
As a feeling that only happens with nothing to do
As a harmless feeling that serves no purpose
quiz.e: Like hunger, boredom nudges us to change course towards something more meaningful.

quiz.q: How strong is the evidence that boredom boosts creativity?
o: Conclusive, backed by many large and careful studies
Mixed, from small studies, so 'guaranteed' overstates it
Disproved by every single experiment run so far
Strong, but only for physical rather than mental tasks
quiz.e: Mind-wandering may help, but results are mixed, so boredom is no guaranteed creativity booster.

quiz.q: Why might constant phone scrolling leave us restless?
o: It satisfies the need for meaningful activity too well
It makes us feel bored for the rest of the day
It mutes the signal without giving us anything real
It stops our minds from wandering completely
quiz.e: A mindless scroll escapes the feeling without answering what the signal was asking for.

quiz.q: What is a useful response to boredom?
o: Distract yourself immediately every time
Treat boredom as a personal failing
Do whatever seems easiest in that moment
Ask what is missing and adjust the task
quiz.e: Identifying whether challenge, meaning, novelty or control is missing lets you fix the mismatch.

LESSONS.push: Many people chose an electric shock over sitting quietly. What does that say?

LESSONS.title: The paradox of choice: can more options make us less happy?
LESSONS.hook: Twenty-four jams, hundreds of streaming shows, dozens of super funds. More choice sounds like freedom, so why does it sometimes leave us stuck?

sections.key: A famous study found shoppers stopped for a big jam display but bought far more from a small one.
sections.b:
In a California supermarket, psychologists Sheena Iyengar and Mark Lepper set up a tasting booth for gourmet jams. Some days it offered 24 flavours, others just six. The big display drew more shoppers to stop. But when it came to buying, the result flipped: about three per cent of those at the large display bought a jar, against about thirty per cent at the small one. Published in 2000, it was cited in business books, TED talks and marketing meetings.

In 2004, Barry Schwartz built on it in The Paradox of Choice, arguing that beyond a point, more options leave us less satisfied: more regret, higher expectations and more self-blame.

sections.key: Later research found choice overload is not a general law: it depends on how hard the options are to navigate.
sections.b:
As researchers tried to repeat choice overload experiments, the picture grew messier. In 2010, Benjamin Scheibehenne, Rainer Greifeneder and Peter Todd pooled about fifty experiments. On average, the effect of the number of options was close to zero. Some studies found overload, some found more options led to more buying, and many found no difference.

A 2015 analysis by Alexander Chernev, Ulf Bockenholt and Joseph Goodman found overload was more likely when options were complex and hard to compare, decisions were difficult or time-pressured, or people had no clear preferences. If you already love apricot jam, a huge range is no problem. One striking study is a starting point for science, not the final word.

sections.key: Satisficers, who choose the first option that is good enough, tend to be happier than maximisers who must find the best.
sections.b:
Economist Herbert Simon coined 'satisficing': choosing the first option that meets your standards rather than searching for the absolute best. Schwartz and colleagues contrasted satisficers with maximisers, who feel they must examine every option. In a 2002 study, high maximisers reported more regret and less happiness and life satisfaction.

A later study of university graduates found maximisers tended to land jobs with higher starting salaries, but felt less satisfied with them. Being a satisficer does not mean having low standards. It means knowing what is good enough for you, then stopping, rather than chasing a perfect option that may not exist.

sections.key: Overload bites hardest on big, complex decisions like super, where people often delay or accept the default.
sections.b:
Choice overload matters most for complex decisions such as insurance, energy plans and retirement savings. Research by Iyengar and colleagues on American retirement plans found that as the number of investment funds offered rose, participation tended to dip slightly. When overwhelmed, people often delay or accept the default.

In Australia, many workers never actively choose a super fund, and their contributions go into a default fund, which is part of why rules about default products matter. This is general information, not financial advice. To compare super funds, energy plans or insurance, government tools such as Moneysmart and the ATO's YourSuper comparison tool can narrow the field.

sections.key: Decide what matters first, limit your search, satisfice on small decisions and stop shopping once you've chosen.
sections.b:
You can protect yourself from the downsides of abundant choice. First, decide what matters before you look: write down two or three must-haves and ignore options that fail them. Second, limit your search, perhaps to three options or a time limit. Third, for small decisions such as toothpaste or tonight's show, deliberately satisfice: pick something good enough and move on.

Fourth, once you have chosen, stop shopping around, because constantly checking alternatives keeps regret alive. Finally, use trusted recommendations and comparison tools to do some of the sorting. You don't have to experience every option to enjoy choice.

quiz.q: What did the jam study find?
o: More shoppers bought from the 24-flavour display than the six-flavour one
Shoppers stopped at the big display but far fewer bought there
Shoppers ignored both displays equally
Shoppers preferred tasting to buying at both displays
quiz.e: The large display attracted attention but about three per cent bought, against about thirty per cent at the small display.

quiz.q: What did pooling about fifty choice overload experiments show?
o: More choice always lowers how much people buy
The average effect of options on buying was close to zero
More choice always raises how much people buy
Choice overload disappears when people are experts
quiz.e: The jam finding is real for some situations, but 'more choice is bad' is not a general law.

quiz.q: What does being a satisficer mean?
o: Having low standards for what you will accept
Choosing at random and never looking back
Examining every option to find the very best
Picking the first option that meets your standards
quiz.e: Satisficers know what is good enough for them, which tends to bring more satisfaction and less regret.

quiz.q: What do people often do when overwhelmed by a complex decision like choosing a super fund?
o: Compare every available fund in detail
Choose the most expensive option
Ask a friend to decide
Delay or accept the default
quiz.e: Overwhelmed people often postpone or accept defaults, which is why comparison tools and default rules matter.

quiz.q: Which habit best protects against choice overload?
o: Keep browsing alternatives after you've chosen
Decide your must-haves first and limit your search
Always look at every option
Choose the most popular item without checking
quiz.e: Clear criteria and a limited search keep the options manageable.

LESSONS.push: 24 jams or six? Why a famous supermarket result is more complicated than it looks.

LESSONS.title: Willpower: what the marshmallow test really tells us
LESSONS.hook: A child, a marshmallow and a promise of two if they can wait. It became psychology's most famous test of self control, and the real story is more interesting than the legend.

sections.key: The marshmallow test began as a study of strategies for delaying gratification, and was later spun into a story about predicting success.
sections.b:
In the late 1960s and early 1970s, psychologist Walter Mischel and colleagues ran experiments at a Stanford University nursery school. A child sat at a table with a treat such as a marshmallow, pretzel or biscuit. If they waited until the researcher returned, they got two treats. If not, they could ring a bell and eat the single treat straight away. Some children gobbled it immediately; others squirmed, sang or covered their eyes.

Mischel's original aim was to learn which strategies helped children delay. A 1990 follow-up of teenagers found longer waiters scored higher on the SAT. The legend grew, though the samples were small and drawn from a privileged university community.

sections.key: In a larger, more diverse sample, the link between waiting and later success was half as strong and mostly disappeared after accounting for family background.
sections.b:
In 2018, Tyler Watts, Greg Duncan and Haonan Quan revisited the idea with a much larger, more diverse sample of several hundred children. Waiting longer at age four was linked with better academic achievement at fifteen, but only about half as strongly as in the original.

More importantly, once they accounted for family background, home environment and early cognitive skills, the link shrank substantially and much of it disappeared. A lot of what the test seemed to measure might reflect a child's circumstances rather than a stable inner trait of willpower. The test still tells us something, but far less than the legend implied.

sections.key: Whether waiting makes sense depends on trust: children who had been let down by an adult waited far less.
sections.b:
A 2013 study by Celeste Kidd and colleagues at the University of Rochester added a twist. Before the marshmallow test, children were promised better art supplies. For one group, the researcher returned with them. For the other, the researcher came back empty-handed with an apology. Children who had met a reliable adult waited, on average, around four times longer.

If you grow up where promises are often broken and resources can disappear, grabbing what you can now may be a sensible strategy, not a lack of self-control. Decisions about waiting depend on trust and circumstance, not only on character.

sections.key: The idea that willpower is a limited resource that drains like a battery has largely failed to replicate.
sections.b:
Ego depletion was another hugely influential idea. In a 1998 study, Roy Baumeister and colleagues asked hungry participants to resist freshly baked cookies and eat radishes instead. The radish eaters then gave up sooner on an unsolvable puzzle than the cookie eaters. The conclusion was that willpower is a limited resource, like a muscle that tires.

Hundreds of studies followed. Then in 2016, a coordinated replication across more than twenty labs and over two thousand participants found an effect close to zero. A later large project led by Kathleen Vohs, one of the original proponents, also found at most a very small effect. The strong willpower-battery version is now widely doubted.

sections.key: Self-control works best through strategies like removing temptations, if-then plans and habits, and kindness after lapses.
sections.b:
Mischel's original research was about strategies. Children who distracted themselves, looked away or imagined the marshmallow as a fluffy cloud waited longer than those who stared at it. A 2012 study by Wilhelm Hofmann and colleagues found people with high self-control reported fewer temptations overall. They arranged their lives so they rarely had to resist. Angela Duckworth stresses situational strategies: remove temptations and make good choices easier.

Peter Gollwitzer's if-then plans help too: 'If I want a snack after dinner, I will have fruit.' So do habits and kindness after lapses, since harsh self-criticism can make people quit. Self-control depends on strategies, environments and trust, all of which can change.

quiz.q: What was the original aim of Mischel's marshmallow experiments?
o: To predict which children would succeed in life
To find which strategies help children delay
To test if children prefer sweet or savoury treats
To measure each child's intelligence
quiz.e: The prediction story came later; the original work was about the strategies that help children wait.

quiz.q: What did the 2018 replication suggest about waiting time and later achievement?
o: The link was stronger than in the original
The link halved, and mostly vanished after adjustment
There was no link at all, even before adjusting
The link held only for wealthy families
quiz.e: Much of what the test measured seems to reflect circumstances rather than a fixed trait of willpower.

quiz.q: Why did children who had been let down by the researcher wait less?
o: They disliked the treats
They didn't understand the instructions
They had less reason to trust the payoff
They were naturally less patient
quiz.e: Where promises are broken, taking the sure thing now can be a sensible choice.

quiz.q: What did large replications find about ego depletion, the idea that willpower runs down like a battery?
o: A strong effect confirmed by every lab
An effect close to zero in large replications
An effect found only in young children
An effect that reversed in older adults
quiz.e: Multi-lab replications failed to find the strong willpower-battery effect.

quiz.q: What do people with high self-control seem to do?
o: Resist temptations through constant effort
Avoid all treats and enjoyment
Arrange their lives to face fewer temptations
Rarely feel any desires at all
quiz.e: Self-control is often about smart design of your environment rather than raw strength.

LESSONS.push: The famous marshmallow test says less than the legend claims. Here's what it shows.

LESSONS.title: Floods: if it's flooded, forget it
LESSONS.hook: Floodwater that looks shallow and calm can sweep a car off the road in seconds. Here is how floods catch people out, and how to stay on the right side of the water.

sections.key: If it's flooded, forget it: floodwater hides depth, damage and current, and cars and people are easily swept away.
sections.b:
Picture a country road after heavy rain, brown water covering a dip for twenty metres. You know this road, and it looks barely ankle-deep. But floodwater is murky. You can't see how deep it is, whether the road has washed away, or what lies beneath. Driving into floodwater is one of the most common ways people die in Australian floods, which is why emergency services say: if it's flooded, forget it.

A car is a sealed box of air. In a few tens of centimetres of water it starts to float and the tyres lose grip, so a current can sweep it away. Fast-flowing water around knee height can knock an adult off their feet. Never drive, walk, ride or swim through floodwater.

sections.key: Floods come as slow river rises, flash floods or storm surge, so find out which could affect your home and routes.
sections.b:
Australia's rivers can rise slowly over days or explode in minutes. Riverine floods build as rain upstream drains into big catchments, giving hours or days of warning. Flash floods follow intense downpours, often in hilly or built-up areas, where drains overflow and creeks rise almost instantly. Storm surge from cyclones can flood low-lying coastal land.

Find out whether your home, work or regular routes are at risk. Many councils publish flood maps, and state emergency service websites explain local risks. Notice small clues too: a street called Creek Road, a low dip on the way to school, or a causeway with depth markers. Trust those markers.

sections.key: Check warnings through official channels, and prepare a plan and kit on a sunny day.
sections.b:
The Australian Warning System has three levels: Advice (an incident has started, stay up to date), Watch and Act (conditions are changing, act now) and Emergency Warning (you are in danger, act immediately). The Bureau of Meteorology issues flood watches and warnings. Check your state emergency service website and app, the Bureau, and local ABC radio. Don't wait for a warning if water is rising around you.

The best time to prepare is on a sunny day. Plan where you would go and how, without crossing flooded roads. Pack a kit with a torch, battery radio, medicines, document copies, chargers and water. Plan early for pets and livestock. Store valuables up high, and check what your insurance covers, because flood cover is not automatic. For non-life-threatening help, call the SES on 132 500.

sections.key: Evacuate early; if trapped and in danger, call 000, move to the highest safe point and wait for rescue.
sections.b:
If authorities tell you to evacuate, go, and go early. Roads can be cut long before water reaches your door, and leaving late often means crossing rising water in the dark. If you are trapped and your life is in danger, call Triple Zero (000). Move to the highest safe point of the building with a phone, torch and warm clothes, and wait for rescue rather than trying to swim out.

Never let children play in floodwater or stormwater drains, which can suck people in. Floodwater can carry sewage, chemicals, sharp debris and displaced snakes and spiders, so avoid touching it and wash well if you do. This is general information; follow your state emergency service's advice.

sections.key: Returning after a flood brings new hazards: electrical, gas, structural, contaminated food and water, and emotional strain.
sections.b:
When floodwater recedes, new hazards appear. Only return home when authorities say it is safe. Power lines may be down, and any appliance or wiring that has been underwater should be checked by a licensed electrician before use. If you smell gas, leave and call for help. Walls and floors may be weakened, and mud can hide broken glass, nails and animals.

Wear gloves, sturdy boots and long sleeves while cleaning, and wash your hands often. Throw out any food that touched floodwater, and check with your council or water authority before drinking tap water. Floods are emotionally exhausting, so check on neighbours and ask for help yourself.

quiz.q: Why is driving through floodwater so dangerous?
o: Floodwater is always electrified
Depth is hidden and cars can float
Cars are easily damaged by splashes
Four-wheel drives always sink
quiz.e: Murky water hides depth and road damage, and a car can float in a few tens of centimetres.

quiz.q: Which type of flood can arise almost instantly after an intense downpour?
o: Riverine flood
Flash flood
Storm surge
Slow catchment flood
quiz.e: Flash floods hit quickly where drains overflow and creeks rise fast, while riverine floods give more warning.

quiz.q: What does an Australian Warning System 'Watch and Act' mean?
o: An incident has started; stay informed
Conditions are changing; act now
You are in danger; act immediately
The danger has passed; stay alert
quiz.e: Watch and Act sits between Advice and Emergency Warning.

quiz.q: If authorities tell you to evacuate, what should you do?
o: Wait to see how high the water gets
Wait until dark when the roads are quieter
Drive through shallow water to save time
Leave early, before roads are cut
quiz.e: Leaving late often means crossing rising water in the dark.

quiz.q: What should you do with food that touched floodwater?
o: Wash it and eat it
Throw it out
Cook it thoroughly
Freeze it
quiz.e: Floodwater can carry sewage and chemicals, so contaminated food should be discarded.

LESSONS.push: Floodwater that looks like ankle depth can hide a lot. Here is what.

LESSONS.title: Surviving a heatwave
LESSONS.hook: Heatwaves do not burn houses or wash away roads, yet they are one of Australia's deadliest natural hazards. Here is how heat harms the body, and how to stay safe when the mercury soars.

sections.key: Heatwaves are among Australia's deadliest natural hazards, and the harm happens quietly, mostly to vulnerable people.
sections.b:
A bushfire or cyclone is obviously dangerous. A heatwave is different. The sky is blue and most people just feel uncomfortable. Yet Australian emergency and health agencies often describe heatwaves as having caused more deaths than any other natural hazard in the country's recorded history.

Much of the harm happens quietly, indoors, to older people living alone or people with health conditions whose bodies can't cope with days of heat. Hot nights make it worse, because the body never recovers. The Bureau of Meteorology publishes heatwave forecasts rating events as low-intensity, severe or extreme. When severe or extreme is forecast, it is time to plan.

sections.key: Sweating cools you only with enough water and dry air, and older people, babies, outdoor workers and those with health conditions are most at risk.
sections.b:
Your core temperature sits around 37 degrees. When you heat up, skin blood vessels widen and you sweat, and evaporating sweat carries heat away. This needs enough body water and air dry enough for evaporation. In humid conditions sweat just drips off. If you lose fluid without replacing it, the system falters and your heart works harder.

Heat can affect anyone, including fit people working hard outdoors, but some need extra care: older people, who may not feel thirst, babies and young children, pregnant women, people with heart, kidney, lung or diabetes conditions or certain medicines, outdoor workers, and people who can't escape the heat. Check on vulnerable neighbours and relatives, ideally daily.

sections.key: Drink water regularly, avoid the midday heat, keep your home cool and plan ahead before summer.
sections.b:
The basics work. Drink water regularly, even before you feel thirsty, and go easy on alcohol and very sugary drinks. If your doctor limits your fluids, ask what to do in hot weather. Do errands and exercise in the cooler morning or evening. Wear light, loose clothing and a hat.

At home, close curtains and blinds on sunny windows early, and open windows when it cools outside. Fans help, but in very high temperatures may not be enough. A cool shower, a damp cloth on the neck, or a few hours in an air-conditioned library can help. Before summer, check fans and air conditioners work, store medicines as labelled, and make a list of people to check on.

sections.key: Never leave children, vulnerable adults or animals in a parked car, even briefly.
sections.b:
On a warm day, the inside of a closed car can quickly become far hotter than the air outside, often by tens of degrees. Much of the rise happens in the first few minutes, and leaving a window slightly open does very little. Children are especially vulnerable because their bodies heat up faster than adults' and they can't get themselves out. Pets are at serious risk too.

The rule is simple: never leave children, vulnerable adults or animals in a parked car, not even for a quick dash into a shop. If you see a child or animal locked in a hot car and distressed, call Triple Zero (000) straight away. Make a habit of checking the back seat every time.

sections.key: Heat exhaustion needs cooling and rest; heatstroke, with confusion or collapse, is an emergency requiring a Triple Zero call.
sections.b:
Signs of heat exhaustion include heavy sweating, pale skin, weakness, dizziness, headache, nausea and fainting. Move the person somewhere cool, lay them down, loosen clothing, cool them with water and fans, and give small sips of water if fully alert. If they don't improve quickly, seek medical help.

Heatstroke is more serious and can be fatal: the body's cooling has failed. The person may be confused, slur words, collapse, have a seizure or lose consciousness, and their skin may be hot and dry or sweaty. Call Triple Zero (000) immediately. While waiting, cool them with water, wet sheets, fans and cold packs at the armpits, groin and neck. Give no drinks to someone not fully conscious. This is general information; healthdirect (1800 022 222) can help.

quiz.q: Why are heatwaves described as a 'quiet' hazard?
o: They rarely cause any serious harm
They only affect people in remote areas
The harm happens quietly, often indoors
They only happen during the night
quiz.e: There is no visible destruction, yet heat strains bodies, especially those of older people living alone.

quiz.q: Why can sweating fail to cool you in humid conditions?
o: Humans stop sweating when it is humid
Sweat is hotter in humid air than in dry
Humid air contains much less oxygen
Sweat can't evaporate, so it just drips off
quiz.e: Sweat cools only when it evaporates, which needs dry air and enough body water.

quiz.q: Which is a good heat-safety habit?
o: Exercise at midday
Drink water before you feel thirsty
Rely only on a fan in extreme heat
Drink alcohol to stay hydrated
quiz.e: Regular drinking, avoiding midday heat and keeping the home cool all reduce risk.

quiz.q: Does leaving a car window slightly open make it safe to leave a child inside?
o: Yes, but only for up to ten minutes
Yes, as long as it is parked in shade
Yes, if the child is old enough to cope
No, it does very little; never leave anyone
quiz.e: Cars heat quickly, mostly in the first few minutes, and a cracked window barely helps.

quiz.q: What should you do if someone shows signs of heatstroke such as confusion or collapse?
o: Give them a large drink and wait
Let them sleep it off in a quiet room
Wait to see if they improve soon
Call Triple Zero (000) and start cooling
quiz.e: Heatstroke can be fatal and needs emergency help plus active cooling.

LESSONS.push: It's quieter than a bushfire, yet heat has a grim record in Australia.

LESSONS.title: Home fires: alarms, escape plans and kitchen fires
LESSONS.hook: A house fire can make a home deadly in a matter of minutes. A working smoke alarm and a practised escape plan are the two things most likely to get everyone out alive.

sections.key: Smoke is what kills in house fires, so a working smoke alarm giving early warning is vital.
sections.b:
Real house fires are not like films. Modern homes are full of synthetic materials such as foam couches, plastics and carpets that burn hot and fast and release thick, toxic smoke. A room can become deadly within a few minutes. Smoke, not flames, is usually what kills, filling the air with poisonous gases like carbon monoxide and blocking your sight. Many fatal fires happen at night. You can't rely on smelling smoke to wake you.

Australian states and territories require smoke alarms, but rules differ; Queensland is moving to interconnected photoelectric alarms in every bedroom, hallway and level. Test monthly, clean vents, and replace alarms about ten years old. Check your state fire service website.

sections.key: Plan two ways out of every room, practise it, and in a fire get low, get out, stay out and call 000.
sections.b:
At 2 am you won't have time to think. Draw a floor plan and mark two ways out of each room, usually a door and a window. Make sure security screens and deadlocks open quickly from inside. Choose a meeting place outside, such as the letterbox. Practise with everyone, including children, once or twice a year, and teach children to get out, not hide under beds.

In smoke, get low and crawl to the nearest safe exit. Feel a closed door with the back of your hand; if hot, use another way. Close doors behind you. Once out, call 000 and stay out. Never go back for pets or belongings. If clothes catch fire: stop, drop, cover your face and roll.

sections.key: Never throw water on a pan fire: turn off the heat and smother it, or get out and call 000.
sections.b:
The kitchen is where many house fires start, often when someone leaves food cooking and gets distracted. Fire services say it neatly: keep looking while cooking.

If a pan of oil or fat catches fire, never throw water on it. Water sinks under the hot oil, flashes into steam and can blast burning oil across the kitchen. Instead, if it is safe, turn off the heat and smother the flames by sliding a lid or fire blanket over the pan, then leave it covered until completely cool. Don't carry the burning pan outside. A fire blanket near the kitchen exit is cheap and easy to use. If the fire is spreading or you're unsure, get everyone out, close the door and call Triple Zero (000).

sections.key: Keep heaters a metre from anything flammable, maintain dryers and power boards, and treat damaged lithium-ion batteries as a fire risk.
sections.b:
Winter brings more house fires as heaters, electric blankets and dryers work harder. Keep heaters at least a metre from curtains, bedding, clothes and furniture, and turn them off when you leave the room or go to bed. Check electric blankets for frayed cords before winter. Clean the dryer lint filter every use. Avoid overloading power boards, and never cover them with rugs.

A newer worry is lithium-ion batteries in e-bikes, e-scooters and power tools. Damaged or poor-quality batteries can overheat and burn fiercely. Use the supplied charger, avoid charging bulky batteries overnight or near your exit path, and stop using any battery that is swollen, hot or damaged.

sections.key: Cool a burn under cool running water for 20 minutes, cover it loosely, and call 000 for serious burns.
sections.b:
If someone is burned, Australian first aid advice is clear: cool the burn under cool running water for 20 minutes. This helps even if some time has passed. Remove jewellery and clothing from the area unless stuck to the skin. Do not use ice, butter, toothpaste or creams.

After cooling, cover the burn loosely with plastic cling wrap or a clean non-stick dressing, and keep the person warm. Call Triple Zero (000) for burns that are large, deep, on the face, hands, feet, groin or airway, caused by chemicals or electricity, or on a child or older person. This is general information only. A proper first aid course teaches these skills hands-on and is one of the best investments a household can make.

quiz.q: What usually kills people in house fires?
o: Flames
Smoke and gases
Falling furniture
Collapsing roofs
quiz.e: Smoke fills the air with poisonous gases like carbon monoxide and blocks vision, so early warning matters.

quiz.q: If you encounter smoke while escaping, what should you do?
o: Run upright to the door as quickly as possible
Get low and crawl to the nearest exit
Open every window first
Go back for your pets
quiz.e: The air is cleaner and cooler near the floor.

quiz.q: What should you do if a pan of oil catches fire?
o: Throw cold water over the pan
Carry the pan outside to cool
Fan the flames to blow them out
Turn off the heat and smother it
quiz.e: Smother it with a lid or fire blanket. Water turns to steam under hot oil and spreads burning oil across the kitchen.

quiz.q: Which is a safe lithium-ion battery habit?
o: Charge bulky batteries overnight near your exit
Use the supplied charger; retire damaged ones
Keep using a hot battery if it still works
Cover chargers to keep them warm
quiz.e: Damaged or poor-quality batteries can overheat and burn fiercely.

quiz.q: How should you first treat a burn?
o: Press ice directly on it
Rub on butter or toothpaste to soothe it
Cool it under running water for 20 minutes
Cover it tightly with a bandage straight away
quiz.e: Cooling under running water for 20 minutes is the recommended first aid, even if some time has passed.

LESSONS.push: A house can turn deadly in minutes, and flames aren't the main reason.

LESSONS.title: Get ready: your emergency kit and household plan
LESSONS.hook: When disaster strikes, the decisions you make in the first hour matter most. A little planning on a quiet weekend can make those decisions almost automatic.

sections.key: Planning in calm conditions lets you act quickly in an emergency, so start by learning your local risks.
sections.b:
Imagine your phone buzzes at midnight with an emergency warning and you have half an hour. Where are the car keys? What about the dog, the medicines and the passports? Stress makes clear thinking hard. The Australian Red Cross and state emergency services urge every household to plan ahead so you do the thinking once, in calm conditions.

Start with your risks. Northern coasts face cyclones and storm surge, river towns face floods, bushland edges face fire, and cities face heatwaves, storms and outages. Almost everyone could face a house fire. Check council and emergency service websites, and ask long-term neighbours who remember past events.

sections.key: A household plan sets out when you'll leave, where you'll go, how you'll get there and how you'll stay in contact.
sections.b:
A plan doesn't need to be complicated. It should answer a few questions. When will you leave, and what triggers that decision? Where will you go: friends or relatives in a safer area, or an evacuation centre? How will you get there, and what is your backup route if roads close?

How will family members contact each other if phones are down or you're split up? Many families choose one contact person in another area. Write key numbers on paper too, in case your phone dies. The Australian Red Cross offers free planning tools, including its Get Prepared app. Share the plan with everyone in the household and review it each year.

sections.key: Keep water, food, power and medicine supplies together, and plan early for pets because they can delay evacuation.
sections.b:
An emergency kit is a collection of supplies stored together. A common guideline is about three litres of drinking water per person per day for at least three days, plus food needing no cooking or refrigeration. Add a torch, battery radio, first aid kit, power bank, cash, medicines, glasses and anything needed for babies, older relatives or people with a disability. Keep document copies in a waterproof bag or saved securely online. Check the kit every six months.

People have delayed evacuating because of pets. Microchip them, keep a photo on your phone, pack food, leads and a carrier, and find out which shelters take animals. Move horses and livestock early.

sections.key: Know your state's emergency apps and sites, use official sources, and keep a battery radio for outages.
sections.b:
Reliable information can decide whether you leave in time. Australia uses a national warning system with three levels: Advice, Watch and Act, and Emergency Warning. Each state and territory has its own emergency websites and apps, so find yours before you need them.

The Bureau of Meteorology provides weather and flood warnings, and ABC local radio is an official emergency broadcaster that often keeps going when other services fail. A battery or wind-up radio helps if power and mobile networks go down. Be careful with social media: it spreads local news quickly, but rumours and old photos circulate too. Check official sources before acting, and if your life is in danger, call Triple Zero (000).

sections.key: Neighbours are often the first helpers, and strong local connections help communities cope and recover.
sections.b:
In many Australian disasters, the first people to help were neighbours, not police or firefighters. They checked on older residents, shared generators, moved livestock and offered spare rooms. Strong local connections are linked to communities coping and recovering better.

Build them simply: swap phone numbers, find out who might need help to evacuate, and join a local community or volunteer group. If you have a medical condition or disability, tell trusted neighbours what support you may need. Recovery can take months or years, and stress and grief are normal. The Australian Red Cross, councils and recovery centres can help. This is general information, so follow official advice for your area.

quiz.q: Why do emergency organisations urge households to plan ahead?
o: Disasters are certain every year
Plans are required by law
Warnings are never issued
Stress makes clear thinking hard
quiz.e: Doing the thinking once, in calm conditions, lets you act quickly when it matters.

quiz.q: Which question should a household plan answer?
o: Which insurer is cheapest
The trigger for when you will leave
What the weather was last year
Which neighbour has the biggest car
quiz.e: Plans should cover trigger, destination, route and how to contact each other.

quiz.q: What is a common guideline for drinking water in a kit?
o: One litre per household a day
Three litres per person per day
Half a litre per person for one day
Whatever fits in the car
quiz.e: Water is the core of a kit, with food needing no cooking or refrigeration.

quiz.q: Why keep a battery or wind-up radio?
o: Radios are required in kits by law
Radios save phone data
It keeps working if networks fail
It replaces the need for warnings
quiz.e: ABC local radio often keeps broadcasting when other services fail.

quiz.q: Who are often the first people to help in a disaster?
o: Police and firefighters
Neighbours
Insurers
Government ministers
quiz.e: Strong local connections help communities cope and recover.

LESSONS.push: At midnight with half an hour to leave, what would you grab first?

LESSONS.title: Severe storms and cyclones
LESSONS.hook: Every year, wild storms and tropical cyclones tear roofs off, drop trees on cars and cut power to thousands of homes. Knowing what to do before and during one can keep your family safe.

sections.key: Australia faces severe thunderstorms and tropical cyclones, and cyclone categories describe wind only, not total danger.
sections.b:
On a hot spring afternoon in south-east Queensland or western Sydney, towering clouds can drop giant hail, flatten fences and flood streets in under an hour. Severe thunderstorms happen across most of Australia. In the tropical north the bigger threat is the tropical cyclone, which forms over warm ocean water. The cyclone season runs from November to April.

The Bureau of Meteorology rates cyclones from Category 1 to 5, with Category 3 and above called severe. But the category describes only wind. A weaker cyclone can still be deadly through flooding rain, which can spread hundreds of kilometres inland, or storm surge. Cyclones can also strengthen rapidly or change direction, so don't relax at 'only' a low category.

sections.key: Storm surge, a sea-level rise pushed by wind and low pressure, can force evacuation even from well-built homes.
sections.b:
When a strong cyclone nears a coast, powerful winds push ocean water toward the shore, and the low air pressure at its centre lets the sea bulge upward. The result is a storm surge: sea level well above normal high tide, topped with large waves. If it arrives at high tide, it can flood low-lying coastal suburbs, roads and caravan parks. Around the world, surge has caused many of the deadliest cyclone disasters.

In Australia, authorities may order people in surge zones to evacuate even if their homes are well built, because the threat is water, not wind. If you live near the coast in cyclone country, find out whether you are in a storm surge zone.

sections.key: Before storm season, clear gutters, trim branches, check the roof and plan to secure loose items.
sections.b:
Much storm damage comes from flying debris and falling trees. Before the season, clean gutters and downpipes, trim overhanging branches (use a qualified arborist for large trees) and check the roof. List loose items such as trampolines, outdoor furniture, bins and pot plants to secure or bring inside when a warning is issued.

In cyclone areas, residents often fit shutters or protect windows, and learn whether their home was built to modern cyclone standards. Keep your emergency kit stocked, fill vehicles with fuel, and charge phones and power banks when a warning comes. Park cars under cover or away from trees if hail is forecast. For storm damage that is not life-threatening, call the SES on 132 500.

sections.key: Shelter in the strongest, windowless part of the building, beware the calm eye, and go indoors when you hear thunder.
sections.b:
