The French thinker Montesquieu made the case in The Spirit of the Laws (1748): liberty is at risk when one body both makes and enforces laws, or when judges are not separate from rulers. His reading of England was imperfect, but his argument shaped modern democracies.

sections.key: The United States separates its three branches strictly and builds in checks and balances.
sections.b:
The framers of the United States Constitution in 1787 took Montesquieu seriously. They placed Congress, the President and the Supreme Court in separate articles and kept their members apart: the President does not sit in Congress, and members of Congress cannot serve in the cabinet. They added checks and balances so each branch can restrain the others. The President can veto bills, Congress can override a veto with a large enough majority, the Senate must approve many appointments, and the courts can strike down laws that breach the Constitution.

Supporters say this makes power hard to abuse. Critics say it can make government slow and prone to deadlock when rival parties control different branches.

sections.key: Australia's Constitution separates the courts firmly but deliberately fuses Parliament and the executive.
sections.b:
Australia's founders borrowed from two traditions. From the United States came a written Constitution with separate chapters: Chapter I covers Parliament, Chapter II the executive and Chapter III the courts. From Britain came the Westminster system of responsible government, where ministers must sit in Parliament and answer to it. Section 64 says a minister must become a senator or member of the House within three months. So Parliament and the executive overlap heavily: the government is formed by whoever holds the confidence of the House of Representatives.

What keeps this in check is that ministers can be questioned in Parliament every sitting day, can lose the House's confidence, and must face voters at regular elections.

sections.key: The High Court has insisted that federal judicial power stays with real courts, and judges are protected from removal.
sections.b:
Where Australia is strict is the judiciary. In the landmark 1956 Boilermakers' Case, the High Court ruled that a federal body could not combine judicial power, such as deciding legal guilt and punishment, with non-judicial functions like setting wages through arbitration. Judicial power under Chapter III must be exercised by courts, and courts should not be handed tasks that compromise their independence. Later cases extended some protection to state courts too, because they can exercise federal power.

Judges are also protected in other ways. Federal judges can be removed only by the Governor-General after both houses of Parliament ask, on grounds of proved misbehaviour or incapacity, and their pay cannot be cut while they hold office.

sections.key: Many familiar parts of Australian politics are checks on power, and every democracy strikes its own balance.
sections.b:
Once you know what to look for, checks appear everywhere. The Senate rejecting or amending a bill is one house checking another. Senate estimates hearings, where officials are grilled on spending, are Parliament checking the executive. A court ruling a government decision unlawful is the judiciary checking the executive. Auditors-General, ombudsmen and anti-corruption commissions add more, and a free press and the right to vote act as checks from outside government.

There is no perfect division. Separate power too strictly and government can grind to a halt. Concentrate it and those in charge may escape accountability. Britain relies heavily on convention, the United States has rigid separation, and Australia sits between. People tend to value checks more when their side is out of power.

quiz.q: Why does splitting government into three branches protect against abuse?
o: It guarantees that decisions are made quickly
No one group can make, enforce and judge the rules
It ensures all branches are run by the same party
It removes the need for regular elections
quiz.e: If one group held all three powers, it could write, enforce and judge its own rules.

quiz.q: What is a common criticism of the strict American separation of powers?
o: Courts are barred from reviewing any laws
The President also sits in Congress
Congress is unable to pass any bills
Rival parties can deadlock the government
quiz.e: Strict separation and checks make power hard to abuse, but can also stall decisions.

quiz.q: How does Australia differ from the United States on Parliament and the executive?
o: Ministers must sit in Parliament, so the two overlap
The Prime Minister is barred from entering Parliament
Ministers are appointed by the High Court judges
Ministers cannot be questioned in Parliament at all
quiz.e: Australia's Westminster system fuses the two, and ministers answer to Parliament.

quiz.q: What did the High Court decide in the 1956 Boilermakers' Case?
o: Federal judges must be elected by the public
Parliament may overrule any court decision
Courts alone can exercise federal judicial power
States are not allowed to have their own courts
quiz.e: The case set a strict separation of federal judicial power from other functions.

quiz.q: Which is an example of Parliament checking the executive?
o: A court hearing a criminal trial
Senate estimates hearings about spending
A newspaper publishing an editorial
A citizen lodging a tax return
quiz.e: Estimates hearings let senators scrutinise how government departments spend money.

LESSONS.push: Why Australia's government is deliberately tangled, except for its courts.

LESSONS.title: The Dismissal: Australia's 1975 constitutional crisis
LESSONS.hook: On 11 November 1975 the Governor-General removed an elected Prime Minister from office. Half a century later, Australians still argue about whether it was a constitutional necessity or a step too far.

sections.key: On 11 November 1975 the Governor-General dismissed Prime Minister Gough Whitlam, the only time this has happened federally.
sections.b: Just after one o'clock on 11 November 1975, Gough Whitlam arrived at Government House in Canberra expecting a routine meeting. Governor-General Sir John Kerr instead handed him a letter terminating his commission. Within hours, Kerr had appointed Opposition Leader Malcolm Fraser as caretaker Prime Minister. That afternoon, on the steps of Parliament House, Kerr's official secretary read the proclamation dissolving both houses. Whitlam, standing behind him, told the crowd: 'Well may we say God save the Queen, because nothing will save the Governor-General.' It is the only time a Governor-General has dismissed a federal Prime Minister. To see why, go back several weeks to a fight over money.

sections.key: The crisis began when the Opposition-controlled Senate deferred the budget bills, helped by two non-Labor Senate appointments.
sections.b:
Governments need Parliament to approve spending through appropriation bills, called supply. Without it, money for public servants and services eventually runs out. Whitlam's Labor government, elected in 1972 and re-elected in 1974, controlled the House but not the Senate. In 1975 it faced controversies, the worst being the Loans Affair, in which ministers sought a very large overseas loan through unconventional channels. In October the Coalition, led by Fraser, used its Senate numbers to defer the supply bills until Whitlam called an election. He refused, arguing a government's survival should depend on the House, not the Senate.

Those numbers were themselves controversial. Two Labor Senate vacancies, in New South Wales and Queensland, were filled by non-Labor appointees, breaking the usual convention. The states acted within their legal powers.

sections.key: Kerr used the Crown's reserve powers, concluding that a government without supply must go to an election.
sections.b:
Section 64 of the Constitution says ministers hold office during the Governor-General's pleasure, and section 61 gives the Governor-General executive power. Normally these are used only on the Prime Minister's advice. But the Governor-General also has reserve powers that can be used in rare cases without advice. Kerr concluded that a government unable to obtain supply should either advise an election or be dismissed. He sought the view of Chief Justice Sir Garfield Barwick, who advised in writing that dismissal was within his power.

Kerr did not warn Whitlam. He later said he feared Whitlam would ask the Queen to remove him first. Fraser was commissioned on condition he obtain supply and advise a double dissolution, which happened that same afternoon.

sections.key: Voters gave the Coalition a landslide in December 1975, yet serious scholars still disagree about the dismissal.
sections.b:
The dismissal unleashed fierce emotion. Protesters gathered outside Parliament House, and Labor's slogan became a call to maintain the rage. The House passed a no-confidence motion in Fraser, but Parliament was dissolved before the Speaker could tell the Governor-General. At the 13 December 1975 election, the Coalition won a large majority in both houses. Supporters called it the people's endorsement. Critics said victory could not prove the method was proper.

Supporters argue the Senate may reject money bills, a government that cannot pay its bills cannot govern, and the voters should decide. Critics argue the Senate should not bring down a government the House backs, Kerr should have warned Whitlam, and an unelected official should not remove an elected Prime Minister. Some also question whether Barwick should have advised at all.

sections.key: The crisis led to a constitutional change, a likely new convention, and later revelations from the Palace Letters.
sections.b:
In 1977 voters approved a referendum requiring a replacement senator to come from the same party as the senator who left, closing the loophole exposed in 1975. No Opposition since has blocked supply in the same way, and many observers think a new convention has formed against it. The episode also fed later debates about whether Australia should become a republic.

In 2020, after a High Court case brought by historian Jenny Hocking, the National Archives released Kerr's correspondence with the Queen's private secretary, known as the Palace Letters. They showed Kerr had discussed the reserve powers with the Palace beforehand, but did not tell the Queen in advance of his decision.

quiz.q: What made 11 November 1975 unusual?
o: Parliament voted to dissolve itself in protest
The Queen personally removed the Prime Minister
A Governor-General dismissed an elected Prime Minister
The Prime Minister resigned during a national emergency
quiz.e: Kerr's dismissal of Whitlam is the only time a Governor-General has removed a federal Prime Minister.

quiz.q: What triggered the 1975 crisis?
o: The Senate deferring the government's supply bills
A High Court ruling against the government
A failed referendum on the Senate
The Prime Minister's resignation
quiz.e: Without supply, the government's money would eventually run out.

quiz.q: What did Kerr conclude about a government that cannot obtain supply?
o: It could keep governing until the money ran out
It should wait for the High Court to decide
It should ask the Queen to settle the dispute
It should either advise an election or be dismissed
quiz.e: Kerr used the reserve powers on that reasoning, after Barwick advised he had the power.

quiz.q: What is a main argument made by critics of the dismissal?
o: The Constitution gives the Senate no power over money bills
An unelected official should not remove an elected leader
The Constitution forbids any election during a crisis
The supply bills had already been passed by both houses
quiz.e: Critics say the decision let an unelected Governor-General override an elected government.

quiz.q: What did the 1977 referendum change?
o: It made Australia a republic with an elected president
It abolished the Governor-General's reserve powers
It made replacement senators come from the same party
It ended the Senate's power to block money bills
quiz.e: This closed the casual vacancy loophole exposed in 1975.

LESSONS.push: He expected a routine meeting. Hours later, Australia had a new Prime Minister.

LESSONS.title: Mabo and the end of terra nullius
LESSONS.hook: In 1992 a man from a tiny island in the Torres Strait changed the foundations of Australian land law. The Mabo decision overturned a legal fiction that had stood since 1788 and reshaped the national conversation about who owns the country.

sections.key: Eddie Mabo discovered that Australian law gave his family's island land to the Crown, on the fiction that the continent had no owners.
sections.b:
Mer, or Murray Island, is a small volcanic island in the eastern Torres Strait. For generations the Meriam people have tended gardens there, with plots passed down through families under their own laws. Eddie Koiki Mabo grew up on Mer and later worked on the mainland, including as a gardener at James Cook University in Townsville. In the 1970s academics there told him that under Australian law his family's land belonged to the Crown. To Mabo this made no sense.

The law rested on a fiction often called terra nullius, Latin for land belonging to no one: that the continent in 1788 had no recognisable system of ownership. A 1971 case, Milirrpum v Nabalco, brought by Yolngu people, accepted they had a sophisticated system of law but ruled it gave no property rights recognised by Australian law.

sections.key: The Mabo case took a decade and included an earlier High Court win over Queensland.
sections.b: In 1982 Eddie Mabo and four other Meriam people, including David Passi and James Rice, began a High Court case claiming their traditional land rights on Mer. In 1985 the Queensland Government passed a law declaring any such rights had been wiped out when the islands were annexed in 1879. In 1988, in Mabo No 1, the High Court struck that law down because it was inconsistent with the federal Racial Discrimination Act. The main case then returned to fact-finding, with weeks of evidence about Meriam customs and land holding. It was gruelling, expensive and slow. Eddie Mabo died of cancer in January 1992, months before the final decision.

sections.key: On 3 June 1992 the High Court recognised native title by six judges to one, but with limits.
sections.b:
On 3 June 1992, in Mabo v Queensland No 2, the High Court ruled six judges to one that the Meriam people held native title to most of the land on Mer. More broadly, it held that Australia's common law recognises native title, reflecting the rights of Indigenous peoples under their traditional laws and customs. The judges rejected the idea that the land belonged to no one as a basis for denying those rights, calling it out of step with history and modern values.

But the decision set limits. Valid government acts, such as granting freehold, can extinguish native title, and it survives only where a group has kept up its connection with the land.

sections.key: Parliament created a claims system in 1993, and native title varies by place and usually sits alongside other people's rights.
sections.b:
The decision raised urgent questions. After negotiating with Indigenous leaders, industry and the states, the Keating government passed the Native Title Act 1993. It confirmed existing titles, set up a claims process and created the National Native Title Tribunal; the Federal Court decides or approves claims. After the 1996 Wik decision found pastoral leases did not necessarily extinguish native title, the Howard government passed major amendments in 1998.

Native title does not threaten suburban backyards, because freehold generally extinguishes it. What it includes depends on a group's traditional laws and the rights already over the land. Sometimes it means exclusive possession. More often it is shared rights to camp, hunt, fish, hold ceremonies or be consulted, alongside pastoralists, miners or the public. Proving a claim can be very hard for peoples forcibly moved off their country.

sections.key: Mabo changed Australian law and remains a landmark in debates about history and reconciliation.
sections.b:
Reactions were sharply divided in the 1990s. Some business groups and politicians warned of uncertainty for mining and farming, while many Indigenous advocates felt the system that followed gave them too little. Over time, native title has been recognised over a large share of the continent, often through negotiated agreements rather than courtroom battles, though the rights involved vary greatly.

The anniversary of the judgment, 3 June, is now marked as Mabo Day. It closes National Reconciliation Week, which begins on 27 May, the date of the 1967 referendum. Eddie Mabo did not live to see his victory, but his name marks the moment Australian law formally recognised that the land had owners long before 1788.

quiz.q: What did Mabo's case challenge?
o: The idea that Queensland could not make its own laws
The idea that the High Court could hear land claims
The idea that the continent had no owners in 1788
The idea that freehold land could ever be sold
quiz.e: The terra nullius fiction treated the land as belonging to no one, so Indigenous peoples had no legal title.

quiz.q: Why did the High Court strike down Queensland's 1985 law in 1988?
o: It clashed with the Racial Discrimination Act
It had not received the Governor's assent
It breached the constitutional right to vote
It applied only to land used for mining
quiz.e: The 1988 decision cleared the way for the main case to continue.

quiz.q: What did the 1992 decision conclude about native title?
o: Australian courts can never recognise it at all
It automatically overrides all freehold owners
It applies only on islands of the Torres Strait
It exists, but freehold grants can extinguish it
quiz.e: The court recognised native title but accepted it can be extinguished by valid government acts.

quiz.q: What generally happens to native title on freehold land?
o: It overrides the freehold owner
It is generally extinguished
It is shared equally
It becomes a lease
quiz.e: Freehold grants generally extinguish native title, so it does not threaten suburban backyards.

quiz.q: Why is Mabo remembered as a turning point?
o: It abolished all pastoral leases
It gave Indigenous people ownership of the whole continent
It formally recognised that the land had owners before 1788
It made Queensland a federal territory
quiz.e: The decision overturned the idea that the land belonged to no one.

LESSONS.push: A gardener's question about his family's land changed Australian law.

LESSONS.title: The Nuremberg trials and the birth of international criminal law
LESSONS.hook: In 1945 the leaders of a defeated regime were put on trial before the world for crimes so vast there were barely words for them. The Nuremberg trials invented much of modern international law, and their critics raised questions we are still answering.

sections.key: In 1945 the Allies chose to put surviving Nazi leaders on trial in Nuremberg rather than simply execute them.
sections.b:
On 20 November 1945, twenty-one men sat in a wooden dock in a Nuremberg courtroom, among them Hermann Göring, once Hitler's designated successor, and Rudolf Hess, the former deputy leader. Much of the city lay in ruins. Its Palace of Justice had survived with a prison attached, and Nuremberg had hosted the Nazi Party's huge rallies. Interpreters translated proceedings simultaneously into four languages, a novelty then.

Some Allied leaders, at times including Winston Churchill, favoured simply shooting top Nazis. Others, especially in the United States, argued a trial would test the evidence, let the accused defend themselves and build a public record. In August 1945 the United States, Britain, France and the Soviet Union signed the London Charter, creating the International Military Tribunal.

sections.key: The tribunal judged conspiracy, crimes against peace, war crimes and crimes against humanity.
sections.b:
The London Charter set out the charges. Crimes against peace covered planning and waging wars of aggression. War crimes covered breaches of the laws of war, such as murdering prisoners or civilians in occupied territory. Crimes against humanity covered murder, extermination, enslavement, deportation and persecution of civilians. A count of conspiracy tied these together.

Crimes against humanity were especially important, because they reached acts a government committed against its own people, which traditional international law had largely ignored. A related word was also coming into use. In 1944 the Polish-Jewish lawyer Raphael Lemkin had coined 'genocide' for the deliberate destruction of a people. It was mentioned at Nuremberg, and in 1948 the United Nations adopted a convention against it.

sections.key: Most defendants were convicted, three were acquitted, and following orders was no excuse.
sections.b:
The prosecution relied heavily on the Nazis' own documents, including orders, minutes and reports, and on film shot by Allied troops in liberated concentration camps. Survivors and former officials testified. The trial lasted almost a year. On 1 October 1946, twelve defendants were sentenced to death, including Martin Bormann, tried in his absence. Seven received prison terms, from ten years to life. Three were acquitted, which showed the judges were not simply backing the prosecution.

The tribunal rejected the defence of superior orders: following orders could reduce a sentence but did not excuse a crime. Göring took his own life the night before the executions, which were carried out on 16 October 1946.

sections.key: Critics argued the trials were victors' justice and applied some laws retrospectively.
sections.b: Even at the time, serious people had doubts. The most common criticism was victors' justice: only the defeated were tried, while Allied actions such as the area bombing of German cities were never examined. The Soviet Union's presence was awkward, since it had invaded Poland in 1939 alongside Germany, and its prosecutors tried to blame the Katyn massacre of Polish officers on the Germans, though the Soviets were responsible. The tribunal did not convict on that charge. Others argued crimes against peace were not clearly crimes when committed, breaching the principle that no one should be punished under a law made after the fact. Defenders replied that aggression had already been outlawed by treaty and that the atrocities were crimes under any civilised legal system.

sections.key: The trials established that individuals can answer for state crimes and led to the International Criminal Court, though enforcement remains uneven.
sections.b:
Other trials followed. The Tokyo tribunal tried Japanese leaders, with Australian judge Sir William Webb as president. American courts at Nuremberg held twelve further trials, and the doctors' trial produced the Nuremberg Code on ethical medical research. The Cold War then froze the project until the 1990s, when the United Nations created tribunals for the former Yugoslavia and Rwanda. Countries adopted the Rome Statute in 1998, and the permanent International Criminal Court began work in The Hague in 2002. Australia ratified the Statute that year.

Nuremberg's lasting principle is that individuals, even heads of state, are personally responsible for the gravest crimes. Enforcement remains hard: courts depend on states to arrest suspects, and the United States, China and Russia are not ICC members.

quiz.q: Why did some Allied leaders favour a trial over summary executions?
o: It would be cheaper and quicker than executions
It would test the evidence and leave a public record
Allied treaties required trials for all prisoners
German law required its leaders to be tried
quiz.e: A courtroom could test evidence, let the accused defend themselves and create a record that could not easily be denied.

quiz.q: What made crimes against humanity especially significant?
o: It applied only to soldiers on the battlefield
It replaced the existing laws of war entirely
It covered only economic crimes such as looting
It covered a government's acts against its own people
quiz.e: Traditional international law had largely ignored how states treated their own citizens.

quiz.q: How did the tribunal treat the defence of following superior orders?
o: It was no excuse, but could lessen a sentence
It was accepted as a complete defence
It was accepted only for low-ranking staff
It was ruled irrelevant even to sentencing
quiz.e: Following orders could mitigate punishment but did not remove guilt.

quiz.q: What is the criticism known as victors' justice?
o: All of the judges were German citizens
The trials were held entirely in secret
Only the losing side was put on trial
Every defendant was found not guilty
quiz.e: Allied conduct, such as area bombing, was never examined.

quiz.q: What is Nuremberg's lasting principle?
o: Only states, never individuals, can be put on trial
Even heads of state can be held personally responsible
Following orders removes all personal responsibility
Courts can arrest suspects without any state help
quiz.e: Acting for a government is no shield, though enforcement still depends on states.

LESSONS.push: The Nuremberg judges acquitted three men. What that said about the trial.

LESSONS.title: Votes for women: how Australia led the world
LESSONS.hook: In the 1890s, a colony on the edge of the British Empire did something almost no government on Earth had done: it let women vote and stand for parliament. The story of how Australian women won the vote is full of determined campaigners, giant petitions and some uncomfortable exceptions.

sections.key: Campaigners won attention with enormous petitions, public meetings and relentless lobbying.
sections.b: In 1891 Victorian campaigners presented parliament with a petition so long it was rolled up like a carpet. The Monster Petition carried around 30,000 signatures, gathered door to door by women across the colony. It did not succeed straight away, but it showed that huge numbers of ordinary women wanted a say. Similar petitions spread across the colonies in the 1880s and 1890s. Campaigners held public meetings, wrote to newspapers and lobbied members of parliament one by one. Many also belonged to the Woman's Christian Temperance Union, which campaigned against alcohol abuse and saw the vote as a way for women to protect their families and communities.

sections.key: In 1894 South Australia became the first place in the world to let women both vote and stand for parliament.
sections.b:
New Zealand gave women the vote in national elections in 1893, the first self-governing country to do so. South Australia followed in December 1894 and went further: women could both vote and stand for parliament, a world first. Mary Lee, an Irish-born widow, had campaigned for years, and a petition of more than 11,000 signatures reached parliament in 1894. Opponents hoped adding the right to stand would make the bill too radical to pass. It backfired. South Australian women first voted in 1896.

Opponents said politics was too rough for women, or that wives would copy their husbands. Supporters said women paid taxes and obeyed the laws, so deserved a say.

sections.key: The Commonwealth Franchise Act 1902 gave most women the federal vote but excluded most Aboriginal people.
sections.b: When the colonies federated in 1901, the new Parliament had to decide who could vote. The Commonwealth Franchise Act 1902 gave women the right to vote and stand for federal Parliament on the same terms as men, making Australia one of the first nations to do so. But the Act also excluded most Aboriginal people, and people from Asia, Africa and the Pacific Islands other than New Zealand, unless they were already entitled to vote in their state. In practice, many Aboriginal people were denied the vote for decades. They gained the clear right to enrol for federal elections in 1962, and enrolment and voting became compulsory for them, as for everyone else, in 1984.

sections.key: Women could stand long before they were elected in numbers, and the first federal women arrived only in 1943.
sections.b:
Catherine Helen Spence, a South Australian writer and reformer, made history in 1897 by standing for the convention that drafted the Constitution, Australia's first female political candidate. At the 1903 federal election, four women stood, the first in the British Empire to contest a national parliament. The best known, Vida Goldstein, ran for the Senate in Victoria and won tens of thousands of votes but was not elected. The others were Selina Anderson, Nellie Martel and Mary Moore-Bentley.

Western Australia gave women the vote in 1899, and Victoria was the last state, in 1908. Edith Cowan became the first woman elected to an Australian parliament in 1921, in Western Australia. Federally it took until 1943: Enid Lyons (United Australia Party) and Dorothy Tangney (Labor). Women remained a small minority for decades.

sections.key: Australia's early start is a point of pride, and a reminder that rights are often won only in part.
sections.b:
Australia's suffrage story is often told as a simple triumph, and there is real reason for pride. A young democracy on the far side of the world helped lead a global change that took many countries, including Britain and the United States, decades longer. Yet the same laws that welcomed many women into political life shut out most Aboriginal women and men. Rights are rarely won all at once.

Today voting is compulsory for adult citizens, and you can check your enrolment on the Australian Electoral Commission's website. Every ballot you cast uses a right people campaigned for, petition by petition, for decades.

quiz.q: What did the Monster Petition show politicians?
o: That most women opposed voting
That only wealthy women cared about politics
That huge numbers of ordinary women wanted a say
That petitions were illegal in Victoria
quiz.e: Around 30,000 signatures, gathered door to door, could not be ignored.

quiz.q: What did South Australia's 1894 law achieve that was a world first?
o: Compulsory voting for all adults
Votes at 18 for women and men
Paid wages for members of parliament
Letting women vote and stand for election
quiz.e: New Zealand gave women the vote in 1893, but South Australia also let them stand.

quiz.q: Who was largely excluded by the Commonwealth Franchise Act 1902?
o: Most Aboriginal people
Women over 30
Landowners
People born in Britain
quiz.e: Most Aboriginal people were denied the federal vote unless already enrolled in their state.

quiz.q: How quickly did women win seats once they could stand?
o: Women won many seats straight after 1902
It took four decades to elect a woman federally
No woman has ever won a seat federally
Women held half of parliament by 1910
quiz.e: Winning the vote came long before women were elected in significant numbers.

quiz.q: Why is the suffrage story not a simple triumph?
o: Women were not allowed to vote federally until 1962
Voting was banned in most colonies
The same laws shut out most Aboriginal women and men
Only men could stand for parliament until 1943
quiz.e: Rights are rarely won all at once, and the 1902 Act excluded most Aboriginal people.

LESSONS.push: A petition so long it was rolled like a carpet. How Australian women won the vote.

LESSONS.title: The social contract: why we agree to be governed
LESSONS.hook: Why should anyone obey the government? For nearly four centuries, philosophers have answered with a powerful thought experiment: imagine life with no rulers at all, then ask what deal reasonable people would strike.

sections.key: Hobbes argued that without a powerful ruler, life would be a constant war of fear and conflict.
sections.b:
Picture waking to find no police, courts, laws or government. Nothing would stop a stronger neighbour taking your food or home. This imagined situation is the 'state of nature', the starting point of the social contract: the idea that governments are legitimate because the governed, in some sense, agree to them, trading some freedom for security and order.

Thomas Hobbes lived through the English Civil War. In Leviathan (1651) he argued that people in a state of nature would be roughly equal in their ability to harm one another, and constantly suspicious. The result: a war of every person against every person, with no farming, industry or arts, and life 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short'. The only escape was a single sovereign strong enough to keep the peace. Even a harsh ruler beat chaos.

sections.key: Locke argued that people have rights before government exists, and governments that violate them lose legitimacy.
sections.b:
John Locke painted a gentler picture. In Two Treatises of Government (around 1689) he argued that even in a state of nature people are bound by a natural law forbidding harm to others' life, health, liberty or possessions. People form governments not to escape chaos but to protect these rights more reliably, with impartial judges and enforcement.

That changes everything. A government built to protect rights can lose its legitimacy by violating them, and people may then resist and replace it. His ideas about consent and natural rights echoed in the American Declaration of Independence in 1776, which speaks of unalienable rights to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness.

sections.key: Rousseau argued that a legitimate society makes its own laws according to the shared common interest.
sections.b: Geneva-born Jean-Jacques Rousseau took the idea in another direction. His book The Social Contract (1762) opens with the line usually translated as 'Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains.' He thought existing societies had corrupted people and entrenched inequality. A legitimate society, he argued, is one where citizens collectively make their own laws, guided by the general will: what is genuinely in the common interest, not just the sum of private wants. In obeying such laws, people would in effect obey themselves. His ideas inspired democratic and revolutionary movements, especially in France. Critics worried the general will could be twisted to justify forcing people to conform.

sections.key: Critics point out that no real person ever agreed to the social contract.
sections.b:
The obvious objection is that no one ever signed anything. You were born into a country with laws already in place. In the 18th century the Scottish philosopher David Hume argued that most governments began in conquest or usurpation, not agreement. Some theorists replied that by staying and accepting a country's benefits, you give tacit consent. Hume answered that this is like saying a man carried aboard a ship while asleep consents to the captain because he could leap into the ocean.

Later critics, including some feminist scholars, argued that historical versions of the contract quietly excluded women and colonised peoples from the agreement altogether.

sections.key: Rawls revived the social contract as a test of fairness, and its questions still run through modern political debate.
sections.b:
In 1971 the American philosopher John Rawls revived the idea in A Theory of Justice, not as history but as a test of fairness. Imagine designing a society from behind a veil of ignorance, not knowing whether you would be rich or poor, talented or not, or which gender, race or religion you would have. Rawls argued you would choose equal basic liberties and accept inequality only if it benefits the least advantaged. In 1974 his Harvard colleague Robert Nozick countered that people's rights to what they have earned strictly limit what a state may redistribute, defending a much smaller government.

These debates echo in arguments over taxes, welfare and trading freedom for safety. When someone claims authority over you, ask whether the people affected could genuinely agree to it.

quiz.q: Why did Hobbes think people should accept a powerful ruler?
o: Rulers always protect natural rights
It prevents constant fear and conflict
Citizens could then vote on every law
It guarantees equal wealth for everyone
quiz.e: Hobbes thought only a powerful sovereign could prevent a war of all against all.

quiz.q: According to Locke, what can people do if a government violates their natural rights?
o: Nothing, since all rule is legitimate
Only petition the monarch
Resist and replace it
Leave the country
quiz.e: Locke tied legitimacy to protecting rights, so violating them could forfeit it.

quiz.q: What did Rousseau mean by the general will?
o: What is in the common interest, not private wants
Whatever a majority wants at any given moment
The decisions of one wise and fair king
The combined wishes of the wealthiest citizens
quiz.e: For Rousseau, obeying laws made in the common interest means citizens obey themselves.

quiz.q: What point did Hume make with his ship comparison?
o: Strong captains are needed to run a ship
Citizens should be free to emigrate at will
Governments are best run like businesses
Staying is not consent if leaving is unrealistic
quiz.e: Hume doubted that tacit consent showed genuine agreement.

quiz.q: What is Rawls's veil of ignorance designed to test?
o: How much ordinary people know about politics
Which rules people pick not knowing their place
Whether voters are well informed before elections
How secret ballots keep each vote private
quiz.e: Not knowing your position pushes you to choose principles that are fair to everyone.

LESSONS.push: Imagine no government at all. Philosophers use that to ask why we obey.

LESSONS.title: Auroras and space weather
LESSONS.hook: The southern lights are a solar storm hitting Earth's invisible shield, and the same storms can knock out power grids and drag satellites from the sky.

sections.key: Auroras are light shows high in the atmosphere, triggered by the solar wind streaming from the Sun.
sections.b:
On the night of 10 May 2024, people across southern Australia stepped outside to find the sky glowing pink and green. The aurora australis, or southern lights, was seen far further north than usual during one of the strongest geomagnetic storms in about two decades. Auroras usually hang around the polar regions, in curtains, arcs and rays roughly 100 to several hundred kilometres up. Their northern twin is the aurora borealis.

Both begin at the Sun. Its corona, over a million degrees, boils into space as the solar wind, charged particles streaming outward at hundreds of kilometres per second and usually reaching Earth in a few days. Solar activity rises and falls over roughly 11 years. The latest maximum, around 2024 to 2025, is why so many Australians saw auroras.

sections.key: Earth's magnetic field deflects most of the solar wind and funnels some particles towards the poles.
sections.b: Earth is protected by a magnetic bubble, the magnetosphere, generated by molten iron churning in the outer core. The solar wind squashes it on the Sun-facing side and stretches it into a long tail on the other. Most of the solar wind flows around it. But magnetic field lines dip into the atmosphere near the magnetic poles, and energy stored in the magnetosphere can drive charged particles down along them. That is why auroras form in rings, called auroral ovals, around both magnetic poles. When the solar wind is calm, the southern oval sits over Antarctica and the Southern Ocean. When the Sun hits hard, the ovals expand towards the equator, and Tasmania and the mainland get a show.

sections.key: Different gases at different heights glow different colours when struck by incoming particles.
sections.b: An aurora is a little like a neon sign. Fast particles slam into atoms and molecules of air, giving them energy, which they release as light. The colour depends on which gas is hit and how high up it is. Oxygen around 100 to 250 kilometres up gives the most common colour, a vivid green. Higher still, where the air is extremely thin, oxygen can glow deep red, which is why great storms often paint the top of the sky crimson. Nitrogen adds blues and purples, often along the lower edges. Our eyes are poor at colour in dim light, so a faint aurora can look pale grey. A camera gathering light for several seconds often reveals colours you couldn't see.

sections.key: Solar flares and coronal mass ejections can cause geomagnetic storms that disrupt power, satellites, radio and navigation.
sections.b:
When tangled magnetic fields near sunspots snap and reconnect, they release enormous energy. A solar flare is an intense flash of radiation reaching Earth in about eight minutes. A coronal mass ejection (CME) is a vast cloud of magnetised gas, billions of tonnes of it, usually arriving one to three days later. If its magnetic field lines up the right way, it can spark a geomagnetic storm. The largest on record, the Carrington Event of 1859, sent auroras far into the tropics and made telegraph systems spark and fail.

In March 1989 a storm induced currents in Quebec's power grid, and millions lost electricity for hours. In February 2022, SpaceX lost dozens of new Starlink satellites after a modest storm increased drag on them. Storms can also scramble radio and GPS.

sections.key: Your best chance in Australia is a dark, clear, moonless night with a low southern horizon during a strong storm.
sections.b:
Tasmania is Australia's aurora capital, but strong storms can bring displays to Victoria, South Australia, southern New South Wales and southern Western Australia. Get well away from city lights, ideally somewhere with a clear, low southern horizon such as a beach or hilltop. A cloudless, moonless night helps enormously. Auroras can appear at any time of year, often around the middle of the night, and can surge and fade within minutes, so patience pays.

Sign up for alerts from the Bureau of Meteorology's space weather service, which also watches the Sun and issues warnings, or follow local aurora groups online. Bring warm clothes and a camera set to night mode or long exposure. Even a faint glow can photograph in vivid colour.

quiz.q: What is the solar wind?
o: Air currents in Earth's upper atmosphere
Moonlight reflected back towards the Earth
Gas escaping from Earth out into space
Charged particles streaming out from the Sun
quiz.e: The Sun's hot corona constantly leaks charged particles that flow outward through the solar system.

quiz.q: Why do auroras mostly appear near the poles?
o: The cold air there makes gases glow brightly
The magnetic field steers particles to the poles
The Sun only shines on the polar regions
There is much more oxygen at the poles
quiz.e: Magnetic field lines dip into the atmosphere near the magnetic poles, so auroras form in ovals around them.

quiz.q: What usually produces the most common green colour in auroras?
o: Nitrogen in the air near the ground
Water vapour in the clouds overhead
Oxygen roughly 100 to 250 kilometres up
Carbon dioxide in the lower air
quiz.e: Energised oxygen atoms at those heights release green light.

quiz.q: Why did SpaceX lose dozens of Starlink satellites in February 2022?
o: A geomagnetic storm increased their drag
They were struck by a passing meteor shower
They ran out of fuel before reaching orbit
They collided with other satellites in orbit
quiz.e: Storms heat and expand the upper atmosphere, dragging down satellites in very low orbits.

quiz.q: What gives the best chance of seeing the southern lights?
o: A well-lit city rooftop just after sunset
A dark, moonless night with a clear southern view
A cloudy night at a busy, well-lit lookout
A bright full-moon night facing north
quiz.e: Dark skies, a clear southern view and a strong storm give the best odds.

LESSONS.push: A solar storm lit Australian skies in 2024. The same storms can pull satellites down.

LESSONS.title: Shooting stars and meteorites
LESSONS.hook: Most shooting stars are specks of dust smaller than a grain of rice, yet a few space rocks survive the fall and carry chemistry older than the Sun.

sections.key: A shooting star is a speck of space rock or dust burning up in the atmosphere, and it lands as a meteorite only if part survives.
sections.b:
Lie on your back somewhere dark for half an hour and you will probably see a few shooting stars. Despite the name, they have nothing to do with stars. Each one is a piece of rock or dust, often no bigger than a grain of sand, hitting the atmosphere at roughly 11 to 72 kilometres per second. It heats the air so violently that it vaporises and makes the air glow, usually 70 to 100 kilometres up.

Astronomers use three words. A meteoroid drifts in space. A meteor is the glowing streak. A meteorite is any piece that survives and lands on the ground.

sections.key: Meteor showers happen when Earth passes through trails of dust shed by comets, at the same point in its orbit each year.
sections.b:
On most nights you might see a handful of random meteors an hour. On certain dates each year the count jumps, sometimes to dozens an hour. These are meteor showers, and they arrive like clockwork because Earth crosses the same streams of debris at the same point in its orbit. Most streams were shed by comets as they swung past the Sun.

Halley's Comet, for example, feeds two showers: the Eta Aquariids in May and the Orionids in October. The meteors seem to fly out from one point, the radiant, and the shower is named after the constellation it sits in. It is a perspective effect, like parallel railway lines appearing to meet in the distance.

sections.key: From Australia, the Eta Aquariids in May and the Geminids in December are among the best showers to watch.
sections.b:
Some famous showers favour the north. The Perseids in August are low or invisible from much of Australia. Southern observers do better with the Eta Aquariids, peaking in early May, whose radiant rises higher in our pre-dawn sky. The Geminids, peaking around the middle of December, are among the richest showers of the year. Unusually, they come from an asteroid called Phaethon rather than a comet.

For any shower, get away from city lights, let your eyes adjust for at least 20 minutes and lie back to take in as much sky as possible. Counts are usually best after midnight, when your side of Earth faces forward into the debris stream.

sections.key: Most meteorites are stony, some preserve material older than the Sun, and very large impacts leave craters.
sections.b:
Meteorites come in three families. Stony ones are the most common, and many are chondrites containing round grains formed in the dust cloud that built the planets about 4.6 billion years ago. Iron meteorites are metal chunks, thought to come from the cores of shattered asteroids. Stony-iron ones mix both.

On 28 September 1969 a meteorite broke up over Murchison in Victoria. It contains amino acids, the building blocks of proteins, and grains older than the Sun itself.

Very large rocks barely notice the air and blast out craters, like the 880-metre Wolfe Creek Crater in Western Australia. In 2013 a roughly 20-metre object exploded over Chelyabinsk, Russia, and flying glass injured around 1,500 people.

sections.key: A real meteorite is usually unusually heavy, often magnetic and has a thin, dark, glassy crust, but most suspected finds are Earth rocks.
sections.b:
Australia's deserts are excellent meteorite hunting grounds. Dark rocks stand out on pale ground, and the dry climate slows weathering. Curtin University's Desert Fireball Network uses cameras to photograph bright fireballs so their landing spots can be calculated and fragments recovered.

If you think you have found one, look for a rock that feels unusually heavy for its size, often attracts a magnet and has a thin, dark, glassy crust from melting during its fall. Real meteorites rarely have bubbly holes. Most candidates turn out to be iron-rich Earth rocks or industrial slag, nicknamed meteorwrongs. State museums can often identify specimens, and in some states meteorites legally belong to the state, so check the rules before selling one.

quiz.q: Which description fits a meteorite?
o: The glowing streak seen in the night sky
A space rock that survives and lands on Earth
A small rocky body drifting through space
The glowing tail of a comet near the Sun
quiz.e: A meteorite is the part of a space rock that survives the fall and reaches the ground.

quiz.q: Why do meteor showers return on the same dates each year?
o: Comets cross the sky on a strict yearly timetable
The Moon sheds dust at the same point each year
Earth passes through the same debris trails each year
Old satellites all burn up together on set dates
quiz.e: Showers repeat because Earth's orbit takes it through the same debris streams each year.

quiz.q: Why are the Eta Aquariids a better choice than the Perseids for Australian viewers?
o: They come from a much larger comet than most
They can only be seen from tropical latitudes
They are always brighter than any other shower
Their radiant sits higher in the pre-dawn sky
quiz.e: A shower is only as good as its radiant is high, and the Perseids sit mostly in the northern sky.

quiz.q: What makes the Murchison meteorite scientifically valuable?
o: It contains amino acids and grains older than the Sun
It is made almost entirely of pure iron and nickel
It formed from a large piece broken off the Moon
It is the largest meteorite ever found on Earth
quiz.e: Murchison preserves ancient material, including organic building blocks and pre-solar grains.

quiz.q: Which clue suggests a rock might be a real meteorite?
o: It floats in water and feels remarkably light
It is full of bubbly holes and gas pockets
It feels heavy and has a thin, dark, glassy crust
It crumbles easily into a chalky white powder
quiz.e: Heavy weight and a melted dark crust are typical of real meteorites, while bubbly holes suggest slag.

LESSONS.push: Most shooting stars are smaller than a grain of rice. So what lands?

LESSONS.title: Neutron stars and pulsars
LESSONS.hook: Imagine squeezing more than the mass of the Sun into a ball the size of a city, then spinning it hundreds of times a second.

sections.key: A neutron star packs more mass than the Sun into a ball about 20 kilometres across, left behind when a massive star's core collapses.
sections.b:
A neutron star is about 1.4 times the mass of the Sun, yet only around 20 kilometres across, roughly the size of a large city. A teaspoon of its material would weigh something like a billion tonnes on Earth. Its surface is thought to be incredibly smooth, with mountains only millimetres tall. Beneath it, matter is crushed so tightly that most electrons and protons have merged into neutrons.

The core of a massive star fuses elements until it makes iron, which cannot release energy by fusion. Gravity wins, and the core collapses in a fraction of a second. The outer layers rebound in a supernova. A lighter core becomes a neutron star; a heavier one becomes a black hole.

sections.key: Pulsars are spinning neutron stars whose beams sweep past Earth like a lighthouse, and the first was spotted in 1967 by a postgraduate student.
sections.b:
In 1967 Jocelyn Bell, a postgraduate student at Cambridge, noticed a bit of "scruff" on chart paper from a new radio telescope. It was a signal pulsing with astonishing regularity, about every 1.3 seconds. The team half jokingly labelled it LGM-1, for "little green men". More pulsing sources elsewhere made an alien explanation very unlikely. The 1974 Nobel Prize in Physics went to her supervisor Antony Hewish and Martin Ryle, an omission many scientists consider unfair.

The sources were rapidly spinning neutron stars. A collapsing core spins faster as it shrinks, like a skater pulling in their arms. Magnetic fields channel beams of radiation from the poles, and each time a beam crosses Earth, telescopes record a pulse. The fastest known spins over 700 times a second.

sections.key: Magnetars are neutron stars with the strongest magnetic fields known, capable of colossal outbursts.
sections.b:
Some neutron stars have magnetic fields far more extreme than usual. Magnetars are estimated to have fields up to around a thousand trillion times stronger than Earth's. As a magnetar's crust shifts under these enormous stresses, it can unleash sudden bursts of X-rays and gamma rays.

In December 2004 a giant flare from a magnetar called SGR 1806-20, on the far side of our galaxy, was so powerful that it measurably disturbed Earth's upper atmosphere. Astronomers now suspect that some magnetars are behind fast radio bursts, brief and extremely energetic flashes of radio waves detected from across the universe.

sections.key: When two neutron stars merge, they forge heavy elements such as gold and platinum.
sections.b:
Many neutron stars live in pairs, spiralling slowly towards each other. In 1974 Russell Hulse and Joseph Taylor found a binary pulsar whose orbit shrank exactly as Einstein's theory predicts if the pair radiates gravitational waves. It earned a Nobel Prize in 1993.

On 17 August 2017, detectors caught the gravitational waves of two neutron stars colliding about 130 million light-years away. Telescopes worldwide, including in Australia, watched the glowing aftermath, called a kilonova. Its light carried the signature of freshly made heavy elements. Astronomers estimate that mergers like this have produced a significant share of the universe's gold, platinum and other heavy metals, possibly including some of the gold in your jewellery.

sections.key: Millisecond pulsars keep time almost as well as atomic clocks, so astronomers use them to test physics and detect gravitational waves.
sections.b:
Some millisecond pulsars tick with a regularity that rivals atomic clocks. Australia has played a big role in studying them, and CSIRO's Parkes radio telescope, Murriyang, has discovered a large share of all known pulsars.

By timing dozens of pulsars over many years, astronomers watch for tiny shared shifts in when their pulses arrive. In 2023, several international teams, including the Parkes Pulsar Timing Array, reported evidence of a faint background of very long gravitational waves rippling through the galaxy, likely produced by pairs of supermassive black holes.

Pulsars have even been proposed as a galactic GPS. The plaques on the Pioneer probes and the Voyager records already carry a map of the Sun's position relative to 14 pulsars, a cosmic return address.

quiz.q: What is left behind when a massive star's core collapses and the outer layers explode?
o: A white dwarf about the size of Earth
A neutron star or, if heavier, a black hole
A fresh star about the size of the Sun
A cloud of thin gas with no dense core
quiz.e: The mass of the collapsing core decides whether a neutron star or a black hole remains.

quiz.q: Why do pulsars appear to pulse?
o: They swell and shrink every few seconds
Clouds of dust regularly pass in front of them
They switch on and off like a signal beacon
Beams from their poles sweep across Earth as they spin
quiz.e: Pulsars shine steadily, but their tilted beams sweep past us like a lighthouse.

quiz.q: What sets magnetars apart from other neutron stars?
o: They have the strongest magnetic fields known
They are the largest neutron stars
They spin faster than any other star
They are made mostly of iron
quiz.e: Magnetars have extreme magnetic fields that can trigger huge bursts of X-rays and gamma rays.

quiz.q: What did the 2017 neutron star merger help show?
o: Neutron stars are mostly made of iron
Mergers can forge heavy elements like gold
Gravity travels much slower than light
Neutron stars are always found alone
quiz.e: The kilonova's light carried the signature of freshly made heavy elements.

quiz.q: Why are millisecond pulsars useful to astronomers?
o: They are bright enough to see by eye at night
They give out enough heat to warm planets
They keep time as precisely as cosmic clocks
They point astronomers towards alien life
quiz.e: Their near-perfect timing lets astronomers spot tiny shifts such as passing gravitational waves.

LESSONS.push: Squeeze a star into a city, spin it hundreds of times a second. What then?

LESSONS.title: Gravitational waves: hearing the universe
LESSONS.hook: A century after Einstein predicted them, scientists caught a ripple in space itself that had travelled for over a billion years from two colliding black holes.

sections.key: Gravitational waves are ripples in spacetime from accelerating masses, so faint that even colliding black holes barely disturb Earth.
sections.b:
Drop a stone into a pond and ripples spread outward. In 1916 Albert Einstein realised his theory of general relativity predicted something similar in space itself. Mass and energy curve spacetime, and when massive objects accelerate, especially in close orbits, they send out ripples at the speed of light. A passing wave stretches space in one direction and squeezes it in the other, including the space you occupy.

But spacetime is extraordinarily stiff. The first wave measured changed the length of a four-kilometre detector arm by about a thousandth of the width of a proton. Einstein doubted anyone could ever measure it. Before then, the only evidence was indirect: a neutron star pair, found in 1974, spiralling together at just the rate expected.

sections.key: LIGO detects the tiny stretching of space by watching for laser beams falling out of step along two four-kilometre arms.
sections.b:
The Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory, LIGO, has two detectors in the United States, at Hanford in Washington state and Livingston in Louisiana. Each is shaped like a giant L, with two arms four kilometres long.

A laser beam is split in two and sent down both arms, bouncing off mirrors before the beams are recombined. Normally they cancel out perfectly. If a gravitational wave passes, one arm stretches while the other shrinks, the beams fall out of step and a flicker of light appears. Two widely separated detectors help rule out local disturbances such as trucks or earthquakes. Europe's Virgo and Japan's KAGRA have since joined, helping pinpoint sources in the sky.

sections.key: In September 2015 LIGO caught waves from two black holes merging about 1.3 billion years ago, a century after Einstein's prediction.
sections.b:
On 14 September 2015, just days after the upgraded detectors switched on, both LIGO sites recorded the same signal, milliseconds apart. Turned into sound, it rose in pitch and volume and ended in a sudden chirp. It came from two black holes, each about 30 times the mass of the Sun, merging 1.3 billion years ago. In the final fraction of a second, roughly three Suns' worth of mass became gravitational waves, briefly outpowering all the stars in the observable universe combined.

The discovery was announced in February 2016, almost a century after Einstein's prediction. Rainer Weiss, Barry Barish and Kip Thorne won the 2017 Nobel Prize in Physics for it.

sections.key: Australian researchers helped build LIGO's technology and analyse its data, and now work together through OzGrav.
sections.b:
Australia has been part of the gravitational wave story for decades. Researchers at the Australian National University, the University of Western Australia, the University of Adelaide and other institutions developed technologies used in LIGO, including precise laser and optics techniques and ways to reduce quantum noise in the measurements. Australians were among the authors of the discovery papers.

Today many of these researchers belong to OzGrav, the ARC Centre of Excellence for Gravitational Wave Discovery, which works on detecting signals, analysing data and following up events with telescopes. Australia's Southern Hemisphere position helps, since it covers parts of the sky that northern telescopes cannot see well.

sections.key: A 2017 neutron star merger was seen in both gravitational waves and light, confirming gravity travels at the speed of light.
sections.b:
Black hole mergers produce gravitational waves but little or no light. Neutron star collisions are different. On 17 August 2017, LIGO and Virgo picked up a merger about 130 million light-years away. About 1.7 seconds later, a space telescope recorded a burst of gamma rays from the same region, and within hours telescopes worldwide were watching the debris. This was the birth of multi-messenger astronomy: studying one event through different signals.

The near-simultaneous arrival of light and gravitational waves after 130 million years confirmed that gravity travels at the speed of light to extraordinary precision, and ruled out several alternative theories of gravity.

Detections are now routine, with hundreds of candidates so far. Future instruments, such as ESA's planned LISA, will listen for slower waves.

quiz.q: Why is it so hard to detect gravitational waves?
o: Spacetime is so stiff that effects are tiny
They travel far more slowly than light
They can only be produced inside black holes
They are absorbed by Earth's atmosphere
quiz.e: Only the most violent events make waves, and by arrival they stretch a four-kilometre arm by less than a proton's width.

quiz.q: How does LIGO detect a gravitational wave?
o: By watching distant stars wobble in the sky
By listening with microphones in orbit
By weighing distant objects very precisely
By spotting laser beams that fall out of step
quiz.e: A passing wave stretches one arm and squeezes the other, so recombined laser beams no longer cancel.

quiz.q: What produced the first gravitational waves ever detected, in 2015?
o: A supernova in our own galaxy
Two black holes merging
The Big Bang itself
The Sun's magnetic field
quiz.e: The signal came from two roughly 30-solar-mass black holes spiralling together and merging.

quiz.q: What is OzGrav?
o: An Australian detector built in the outback
A satellite launched by an Australian agency
An Australian gravitational wave research centre
A NASA mission to search for black holes
quiz.e: OzGrav brings Australian researchers together to detect and analyse gravitational waves.

quiz.q: What did the 2017 neutron star merger confirm?
o: Black holes give off bright light
Gravitational waves are too weak to detect
Neutron stars are extremely rare
Gravity travels at the speed of light
quiz.e: Gravitational waves and gamma rays arrived about 1.7 seconds apart after 130 million years.

LESSONS.push: A ripple in space itself crossed 1.3 billion years to reach us. What made it?

LESSONS.title: Ocean moons: hidden seas of the outer solar system
LESSONS.hook: Some of the best places to look for alien life may be dark oceans hidden beneath the ice of moons orbiting Jupiter and Saturn.

sections.key: Several icy moons hide liquid oceans, kept from freezing by tidal heating as their planet's gravity flexes them.
sections.b:
Out past Mars, sunlight is weak and the surface of Jupiter's and Saturn's moons sits well below minus 100 degrees Celsius. Yet spacecraft show that several of these moons appear to hide global oceans of liquid water beneath shells of ice. Europa may hold more water than all of Earth's oceans combined.

How does water stay liquid? Mainly through tidal heating. These moons follow slightly oval orbits around giant planets, so the pull of gravity changes and squeezes and stretches them. Like a paperclip bent back and forth, they warm by friction. Jupiter's Io is the extreme case, the most volcanically active world in the solar system. Gentler heating, plus heat from radioactive elements in the rock, appears enough to keep oceans liquid under kilometres of ice.

sections.key: Europa's cracked, young ice shell covers a salty ocean that probably touches a rocky seafloor where chemistry could support life.
sections.b:
Europa is slightly smaller than our Moon, but its surface is bright white ice crisscrossed by reddish brown cracks, with very few craters. That means the surface is young and constantly reshaped.

In the late 1990s NASA's Galileo spacecraft measured how Europa disturbed Jupiter's magnetic field, and the best explanation was a salty, electrically conducting ocean under the ice. The ice shell is thought to be several to a few dozen kilometres thick, over an ocean perhaps around 100 kilometres deep.

Crucially, that ocean probably sits on a rocky seafloor. Water and rock could react chemically there, as they do around hydrothermal vents in Earth's deep oceans, where life thrives without sunlight.

sections.key: Saturn's tiny moon Enceladus sprays its ocean into space, and Cassini flew through the plumes and sampled them.
sections.b:
Enceladus is only about 500 kilometres across, small enough to fit within the width of Victoria, so scientists expected little. Then in 2005 NASA's Cassini spacecraft spotted jets of water vapour and ice grains erupting from long cracks near its south pole, nicknamed tiger stripes. The plumes feed one of Saturn's rings.

Cassini later flew straight through them, essentially tasting an alien ocean. It found water, salts, carbon dioxide, ammonia and organic molecules. Tiny silica grains hinted at hot water reacting with rock on the seafloor, and later analysis found phosphorus, an essential ingredient for life on Earth. Enceladus appears to tick many boxes for habitability: liquid water, chemical energy and the right raw materials.

sections.key: Titan has methane lakes over a likely water ocean, while Ganymede, the largest moon, probably hides a salty ocean too.
sections.b:
Saturn's Titan is bigger than Mercury and the only moon with a thick atmosphere, mostly nitrogen. At around minus 180 degrees Celsius, water is rock-hard, but methane and ethane flow as liquids. Titan has clouds, rain, rivers and seas of liquid hydrocarbons. In 2005 Europe's Huygens probe parachuted through the orange haze and landed on a damp plain strewn with rounded ice pebbles. Measurements suggest a water ocean lies deep below.

Jupiter's Ganymede is the largest moon in the solar system and the only one known to generate its own magnetic field. Hubble observations of its shifting auroras suggest a salty ocean beneath the surface. Callisto may have one too, and oceans are suspected further out, including Triton and Pluto.

sections.key: New missions are heading to these moons, and old spacecraft were deliberately destroyed to avoid contaminating them.
sections.b:
If buried oceans are common, liquid water may be far more widespread in the universe than on sunlit rocky planets like Earth, greatly increasing the number of places life could arise.

Several spacecraft are on their way. ESA's JUICE, launched in 2023, will study Jupiter's icy moons and eventually orbit Ganymede. NASA's Europa Clipper, launched in 2024, will make dozens of close flybys of Europa. NASA's Dragonfly, a nuclear-powered rotorcraft, is planned to fly between sites on Titan in the 2030s.

Scientists take great care not to contaminate these worlds with Earth microbes, a principle called planetary protection. That is why Galileo was deliberately plunged into Jupiter in 2003, and Cassini into Saturn in 2017, as their fuel ran low.

quiz.q: What mainly keeps these moons' oceans from freezing?
o: Strong sunlight warming their frozen surfaces
Thick greenhouse atmospheres trapping heat
Heat from tidal flexing by their planet's gravity
Warmth radiated from the giant planet's surface
quiz.e: Tidal flexing generates heat inside the moon, helped by radioactive heat from rock.

quiz.q: Why is Europa's ocean especially interesting for life?
o: Its water is warm enough to be boiling
It probably meets rock where chemistry can happen
It is exposed directly to the Sun's light
It is made mostly of methane and ethane
quiz.e: Water reacting with rock could give chemical energy, as at Earth's hydrothermal vents.

quiz.q: What did Cassini discover at Enceladus?
o: A thick nitrogen atmosphere like Titan's
Active lava volcanoes like those on Io
Rings of its own that surround the moon
Jets of water and ice near its south pole
quiz.e: Cassini sampled the plumes and found water, salts and organic molecules.

quiz.q: What are Titan's lakes and seas made of?
o: Liquid methane and ethane
Liquid water and salts
Molten rock and metal
Liquid carbon dioxide
quiz.e: At around minus 180 degrees Celsius water is frozen solid, but methane and ethane can flow.

quiz.q: Why was Cassini deliberately sent into Saturn in 2017?
o: To measure the composition of Saturn's core
To clear the orbit for a newer spacecraft
To avoid contaminating moons that might host life
Because debris had damaged its instruments
quiz.e: Planetary protection means avoiding Earth microbes reaching worlds that could be habitable.

LESSONS.push: Some of the best places to look for alien life are dark seas under ice.

LESSONS.title: Space junk: the litter problem in orbit
LESSONS.hook: Tens of thousands of dead satellites and rocket parts are racing around Earth faster than bullets, and once in 1979 a big piece landed near Esperance.

sections.key: Earth is ringed by dead satellites, rocket stages and fragments travelling so fast that even tiny pieces cause serious damage.
sections.b:
Since Sputnik in 1957, much of what has gone up has stayed there. Space junk includes dead satellites, used rocket stages, lost tools, flakes of paint and fragments from explosions and collisions. Agencies track tens of thousands of pieces larger than about a softball, and estimates suggest around a million pieces bigger than a centimetre, plus many millions smaller. Most sits in low Earth orbit, the busy region used by the International Space Station.

To stay up there, an object travels at about 28,000 kilometres per hour, many times faster than a rifle bullet. At that speed even a fleck of paint carries surprising energy, and Space Shuttle windows were replaced after being chipped. The ISS has extra shielding and regularly fires its engines to dodge tracked debris.

sections.key: Accidental collisions and deliberate missile tests create debris clouds, raising the risk of a runaway chain reaction known as Kessler syndrome.
sections.b:
On 10 February 2009 a working Iridium satellite hit a dead Russian satellite, Kosmos 2251, about 790 kilometres above Siberia. It was the first known accidental collision between two intact satellites and created well over a thousand trackable fragments.

In 1978 NASA scientist Donald Kessler warned that if debris became dense enough, collisions would create more fragments, causing more collisions in a cascade. This is the Kessler syndrome, and in its worst form some orbits could become too risky to use for generations.

Some clouds were made on purpose. In 2007 China destroyed its own weather satellite with a missile, creating over 3,000 trackable fragments, the largest single event on record. In 2021 Russia did the same, forcing ISS crew to shelter. Since 2022 several countries, including Australia, have pledged not to hold such tests.

sections.key: Most debris eventually sinks and burns up, but large objects sometimes reach the ground, including in Australia.
sections.b:
Thin traces of atmosphere slowly drag on objects in low orbit, so they sink and eventually burn up on re-entry. Large, sturdy parts can survive.

In July 1979 the American space station Skylab broke apart over the Indian Ocean and scattered debris around Esperance in Western Australia. Nobody was hurt, and the local shire famously fined NASA $400 for littering. An American radio host eventually paid it decades later.

In 2022, pieces of a SpaceX capsule's trunk landed on farms in the Snowy Mountains of New South Wales. Today operators often steer big spacecraft down over a remote part of the South Pacific near Point Nemo, the place furthest from land, nicknamed the spacecraft cemetery.

sections.key: Thousands of new internet satellites bring faster connections but make orbit busier and astronomy harder.
sections.b:
The number of active satellites has soared, mainly because of megaconstellations: huge fleets of small satellites providing internet from low orbit. SpaceX's Starlink alone has launched many thousands, and others are building their own. These networks bring fast internet to remote areas, including outback Australia, and are designed to fall out of orbit within a few years once retired.

But more satellites mean more close approaches, and operators must perform large numbers of avoidance manoeuvres. Astronomers have raised another concern: sunlit satellites leave bright streaks across telescope images and can interfere with radio observations. Darker coatings and sunshades have been tried, but the growing traffic is changing how scientists plan their observations.

sections.key: The first fix is not to make more mess: rules now push operators to remove satellites after use, while capture technologies are tested.
sections.b:
International guidelines have long asked operators to remove satellites from busy low orbits within 25 years of the end of a mission. In 2022 the United States regulator set a stricter five-year rule for satellites it licenses. Rocket stages are increasingly designed to burn up quickly, and satellites carry fuel to lower themselves at the end of their lives.

Removing existing junk is harder, because every piece is moving fast and tumbling. Japan's Astroscale has flown missions that approached and inspected a discarded rocket stage, and European projects are developing robotic arms and nets to catch dead satellites. In Australia, the Australian Space Agency works with industry on space situational awareness, tracking objects to help keep orbits safe.

quiz.q: Why can even a tiny fleck of paint damage a spacecraft in low orbit?
o: It is made of very dense metal
It is heated by sunlight
It is magnetic and sticks to hulls
It moves at about 28,000 km/h
quiz.e: At orbital speed, even tiny pieces carry a great deal of energy.

quiz.q: What is the Kessler syndrome?
o: An illness astronauts can develop in orbit
A chain reaction of collisions
A rule for retiring satellites
A type of satellite engine
quiz.e: Each collision makes more fragments, which cause more collisions, and some orbits could become unusable.

quiz.q: What usually happens to debris in low orbit over time?
o: It drifts out into deep space
It stays in the same orbit forever
Drag slowly pulls it down so it burns up
It is collected by passing satellites
quiz.e: Thin traces of atmosphere drag on objects in low orbit until they re-enter.

quiz.q: Why are astronomers concerned about megaconstellations?
o: They block sunlight from reaching Earth
Sunlit satellites streak telescope images
They warm the upper atmosphere
They change the Moon's orbit
quiz.e: Reflected sunlight from many satellites interferes with astronomical observations.

quiz.q: What is the first and simplest fix for the space junk problem?
o: Retiring satellites promptly after use
Firing missiles at the debris
Moving every satellite to a higher orbit
Pausing all rocket launches
quiz.e: Prevention, such as retiring satellites promptly, is easier than removing tumbling junk.

LESSONS.push: A rubbish fine sent to NASA from a small Australian shire. What was dumped?

LESSONS.title: How we measure the universe
LESSONS.hook: No one has ever stretched a tape measure to a star, yet we know distances across billions of light-years. The trick is a ladder of clever steps.

sections.key: Astronomers measure space in light-years, the distance light travels in a year, using a chain of methods called the cosmic distance ladder.
sections.b:
Light covers about 300,000 kilometres every second. Even so, sunlight takes about eight minutes to reach us, and light from Proxima Centauri, the nearest star beyond the Sun, takes over four years. So astronomers use the light-year: the distance light travels in a year, about 9.5 trillion kilometres. It is a distance, not a time.

That has a fascinating consequence. Look at a star a thousand light-years away and you see light that left it a thousand years ago. Looking further means looking back in time.

No single method works for everything. Astronomers built a chain of techniques, each checked against the last, called the cosmic distance ladder.

sections.key: Nearby distances come from timing radar and laser echoes, and nearby stars from parallax, their apparent shift as Earth orbits the Sun.
sections.b:
The first rung is our own neighbourhood. Knowing the speed of light, we can bounce signals off objects and time the echo. Radar off Venus, Mars and asteroids fixes the solar system's scale; the Earth to Sun distance, the astronomical unit, is about 150 million kilometres. Lasers fired at reflectors left by Apollo astronauts give the Moon's distance to within millimetres, and show it drifting away a few centimetres a year.

Next comes parallax. Hold a thumb at arm's length and look with one eye, then the other: it seems to jump against the background. Astronomers use two positions of Earth, six months apart. A nearby star shifts slightly against distant ones, and geometry turns that shift into a distance. Friedrich Bessel first managed it in 1838; the Gaia spacecraft has since measured over a billion stars.

sections.key: Henrietta Leavitt's discovery that a Cepheid's pulse rate reveals its brightness let Hubble show that Andromeda is a separate galaxy.
sections.b:
Parallax only works nearby. Beyond it, astronomers need standard candles: objects of known true brightness.

In the early 1900s Henrietta Swan Leavitt of Harvard Observatory studied the Small Magellanic Cloud, visible from Australia. She found that Cepheid variables, stars that brighten and dim rhythmically, follow a pattern: the slower the pulse, the brighter the star. So a Cepheid's rhythm reveals its distance.

In the 1920s Edwin Hubble used this to settle whether spiral nebulae lay inside the Milky Way. Cepheids in Andromeda showed it was a separate galaxy, about 2.5 million light-years away. The known universe grew from one galaxy to billions.

sections.key: Type Ia supernovae are bright enough to measure distances across billions of light-years and revealed that the universe's expansion is speeding up.
sections.b:
Cepheids are not bright enough to see in very distant galaxies. For those, astronomers use Type Ia supernovae. These are thought to occur when a white dwarf, the dense remnant of a star like the Sun, is pushed over a critical limit and blows apart.

Because they explode in a fairly consistent way, their peak brightness can be worked out. That makes them standard candles visible across billions of light-years.

In 1998 two teams used them to discover that the universe's expansion is speeding up, not slowing down. One team was led by Brian Schmidt, working at the Australian National University's Mount Stromlo Observatory near Canberra. He shared the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics with Saul Perlmutter and Adam Riess.

sections.key: Redshift reveals the distance of the most remote galaxies, but two ways of measuring the expansion rate disagree.
sections.b:
At the top of the ladder is redshift. As the universe expands, light is stretched to longer, redder wavelengths. The further away a galaxy is, the faster it recedes and the redder its light, a relationship known as Hubble's law. Once the ladder is calibrated, redshift tells astronomers roughly how far away a galaxy is.

But there is a puzzle. Measuring today's expansion rate with the ladder of Cepheids and supernovae gives a noticeably higher answer than calculating it from the faint afterglow of the Big Bang, the cosmic microwave background.
