Cognitive scientists Steven Sloman and Philip Fernbach describe knowledge as a community effort. No one understands how to make a pencil from scratch. Because we can look things up or ask someone, community knowledge feels like ours.

sections.key: Asking people to explain how a policy would work, rather than why they support it, exposes gaps and softens extreme views.
sections.b:
Many of us hold firm opinions on complex issues such as tax, health systems or climate policy while knowing little about how the proposals would work. In a 2013 study, Fernbach and colleagues asked people in the United States to rate their understanding of political policies, then explain in detail how those policies would work. Afterwards, people rated their understanding lower and their views tended to become less extreme.

Simply listing reasons for their position didn't have the same effect. Reasons let you stay on familiar ground. Mechanisms force you to confront the gaps. Asking someone to explain the how, rather than defend the why, can make a heated conversation calmer.

sections.key: Explaining something out loud or in writing reveals the gaps in your understanding, so hold complex views a little more loosely.
sections.b:
You can turn the illusion into a learning tool. Before you decide you understand something, explain it out loud as if teaching a curious twelve year old. The method is often linked to physicist Richard Feynman. Wherever you stumble or reach for jargon, you have found a gap. Fill it, then try again. Writing works even better, because vague ideas look obviously vague on paper.

None of this means you should feel embarrassed about not knowing how a zip works. Relying on others is sensible. The lesson is calibration. When you feel very certain about something complex, ask whether you could explain how it works to a sceptical friend. If not, hold your view more loosely. Listen to people who disagree, and be ready to say, 'I'm not sure; let me find out.'

quiz.q: What happened when people tried to explain how everyday objects work?
o: Their ratings went up afterwards
Their ratings went down afterwards
Their ratings stayed the same
Only experts changed their ratings
quiz.e: Trying to explain exposes the gap between feeling you understand and actually understanding.

quiz.q: What does the bicycle drawing test show?
o: Cyclists never make mistakes when drawing bikes
Drawing skill predicts engineering skill
Using something is not knowing how it works
Most people have never seen a bicycle closely
quiz.e: Everyday knowledge is mostly useful shortcuts, not a detailed blueprint.

quiz.q: Why does the illusion of explanatory depth arise?
o: People deliberately pretend to know more than they do
Modern devices are too complex for anyone to use
Memory fails for details we learned as children
The mind keeps rough outlines and leans on others
quiz.e: Because details are available in the world or from others, borrowed knowledge feels like our own.

quiz.q: What made people's views less extreme in the 2013 policy study?
o: Explaining in detail how a policy would work
Listing reasons for supporting their position
Reading opposing arguments from other voters
Being asked to rate their confidence higher
quiz.e: Explaining mechanisms forces you to confront the gaps, whereas listing reasons keeps you on familiar ground.

quiz.q: What is a good way to find the gaps in your understanding?
o: Re-read the material until it feels familiar
Compare how confident you feel with a friend
Explain it aloud as if teaching a curious child
Look up the topic and decide you understand it
quiz.e: Where you stumble or reach for jargon is where your real understanding ends.

LESSONS.push: Could you explain a zip? Most people's confidence disappears within a sentence.

LESSONS.title: Science or pseudoscience? How to tell the difference
LESSONS.hook: Astrology, crystal healing and a revolutionary new diet can all sound scientific. A few sharp questions reveal which ideas are willing to be proven wrong.

sections.key: A claim is scientific if some observation could show it to be false, so a theory that fits every possible result tells you nothing.
sections.b:
In Vienna after the First World War, young Karl Popper was surrounded by bold ideas. Einstein's relativity made a risky prediction: starlight passing the Sun should bend by a specific amount. In 1919, expeditions led by Arthur Eddington measured starlight during a solar eclipse and supported Einstein. The theory could have failed, and it didn't. Some popular theories of psychology and history, by contrast, explained every possible outcome. Popper saw that as a weakness.

His answer to the problem of separating science from non-science was falsifiability. 'All swans are white' is falsifiable: one black swan breaks it, and Europeans found black swans in Western Australia. 'Invisible fairies tend my garden but leave no trace' isn't. Falsifiable doesn't mean false, just testable. Ask what would prove an idea wrong.

sections.key: Pseudoscience looks scientific but is vague, relies on anecdotes, makes excuses when tests fail and rarely changes.
sections.b:
Pseudoscience is dressed up to look scientific without behaving like science. It shows familiar warning signs. Claims are vague, so they can't easily be checked. Evidence comes mainly from testimonials and anecdotes rather than controlled studies. Scientific words such as 'quantum', 'energy' and 'frequency' are borrowed for glamour without precise meaning. When a test fails, excuses appear: the sceptic's negative energy interfered. The idea hasn't changed for decades despite new evidence. Critics are dismissed as closed-minded. And there is often something to buy.

No single sign proves an idea is bogus, but when several appear together, look much more carefully before you believe or spend.

sections.key: When astrologers were tested under blind conditions, they did no better than guessing.
sections.b:
Astrology makes claims that can, in principle, be tested: your birth chart is said to reveal your personality. In a 1985 study in the journal Nature, physicist Shawn Carlson ran a double-blind test with astrologers who had agreed to the method in advance. They were given birth charts and asked to match each to the correct personality profile from a small set of options. Their success rate was about what guessing would produce.

Other studies have looked for links between star signs and personality or career and generally found nothing meaningful. Astrology can still be enjoyable, a prompt for reflection or a bit of fun. But as a scientific claim about how people work, it hasn't passed the test.

sections.key: Australia's 2015 NHMRC review found no reliable evidence that homeopathy works for any health condition.
sections.b:
Homeopathy was developed in Germany around 1800 by Samuel Hahnemann. Its central idea is that a substance causing symptoms can cure similar symptoms when heavily diluted, and that more dilution makes it stronger. Many remedies are diluted so far that, statistically, not one molecule of the original substance is likely to remain.

In 2015, Australia's National Health and Medical Research Council published a major review of the evidence. It concluded there were no health conditions for which there was reliable evidence that homeopathy was effective. The council warned that choosing it over proven treatments may put health at risk.

This is general information rather than medical advice. Talk to a doctor, and healthdirect is a reliable starting point for health questions in Australia.

sections.key: Science earns trust by testing and correcting itself, and being mocked by experts proves nothing: evidence is what vindicates an idea.
sections.b:
Science gets things wrong all the time. What makes it different is that it has ways of finding and fixing errors. Studies are checked by experts, results are repeated by independent teams, and failed ideas are revised or dropped. For decades, doctors thought stomach ulcers were mainly caused by stress. Perth researchers Barry Marshall and Robin Warren showed that a bacterium, Helicobacter pylori, played a central role. Marshall even swallowed a culture to prove the point. Doctors were sceptical, but evidence won, and the pair received the 2005 Nobel Prize.

Fringe promoters often say 'they laughed at Galileo'. But for every rejected idea later proven right, vast numbers were rejected because they were wrong. Galileo was vindicated by his observations, not by being mocked. Being an outsider is fine. Avoiding tests isn't.

quiz.q: What makes a claim scientific, according to falsifiability?
o: It has never been disproved
A test could show it to be false
Many experts say it is true
It uses careful technical terms
quiz.e: A testable claim sticks its neck out, while one that fits every result tells you nothing.

quiz.q: Which is a common warning sign of pseudoscience?
o: Excuses appear when a test fails
Claims are checked by independent teams
Ideas change as new evidence arrives
Results are shared openly for review
quiz.e: Blaming failed tests on negative energy or poor conditions protects an idea from ever being proven wrong.

quiz.q: What did the 1985 test of astrologers find?
o: They matched most charts correctly
They did better with longer profiles
Their matches were no better than chance
Some star signs were matched accurately
quiz.e: Under double-blind conditions agreed in advance, astrologers could not do better than chance.

quiz.q: What did Australia's 2015 review conclude about homeopathy?
o: It worked for minor conditions only
It matched standard treatment for some illnesses
It worked best at higher dilutions
No condition had reliable evidence it works
quiz.e: The review found no reliable evidence of effectiveness and warned against replacing proven treatments.

quiz.q: Why doesn't 'they laughed at Galileo' show an idea is right?
o: Galileo was never actually opposed
Many rejected ideas really were wrong
Experts are never wrong about new ideas
Ideas rejected by experts are always false
quiz.e: Marshall and Warren, like Galileo, won on evidence rather than on being doubted.

LESSONS.push: Some ideas are built so they can never be wrong. Here's the test that exposes them.

LESSONS.title: Seeing patterns in random noise
LESSONS.hook: Shuffle a playlist and the same artist plays three times in a row. Rigged? Probably not. Randomness is far lumpier than our brains expect.

sections.key: Real randomness contains streaks and clusters that feel deliberate.
sections.b:
Ask one group to invent 100 coin tosses and another to actually toss a coin 100 times. Teachers who run this trick can usually spot the fakes. Invented sequences switch between heads and tails too often and avoid long runs. Real tosses often include a streak of five or six of the same result, because over 100 tosses such runs are quite likely.

Our intuition says random things should look evenly spread, like sprinkles on a cake. In reality, randomness is clumpy. Rain falls unevenly, stars cluster and buses arrive in bunches. When we see a clump, our brains shout 'pattern', even when chance alone would produce it.

sections.key: Londoners saw a targeting pattern in V-1 strikes, but statistics showed it was chance.
sections.b:
During the Second World War, German V-1 flying bombs fell on London. Many residents were convinced the strikes were targeted, because some neighbourhoods were hit repeatedly while others were spared. Rumours spread that German spies lived in the spared areas.

In 1946, a British actuary named R. D. Clarke divided a section of south London into hundreds of equal squares and counted the hits in each. The counts closely matched what you would expect if the bombs had landed at random. The clusters that felt so meaningful were just the natural clumping of chance. This is now called the clustering illusion, and it still shapes how people read crime maps, disease outbreaks and accidents.

sections.key: Drawing the target after the shots makes any pattern look impressive.
sections.b:
Imagine a cowboy firing randomly at a barn. Afterwards, he paints a bullseye around the tightest group of holes and declares himself a sharpshooter. This joke names the Texas sharpshooter fallacy: finding a cluster first, then treating it as if it had been predicted.

It happens whenever people search lots of data, spot an interesting clump and forget how many other places they looked. A town might seem to have an unusual number of a particular illness. But there are thousands of towns and many kinds of illness, so somewhere, by chance, a striking cluster will appear. Investigators take such reports seriously, and some turn out to be real. Many, though, prove to be painted bullseyes.

sections.key: Our brains expect pattern, so we see faces in noise and distrust true randomness.
sections.b:
In 1976, the Viking 1 spacecraft photographed a hill on Mars that looked startlingly like a human face. Later, sharper images showed an ordinary eroded mesa. Seeing meaningful images in random shapes, especially faces, is called pareidolia. It probably reflects how vital it has been to recognise friends, enemies and emotions quickly.

The reverse also happens. Users have complained that music shuffles weren't random because songs by one artist played close together. Many apps now adjust shuffle so an artist doesn't repeat, because genuine randomness feels suspicious. Likewise, many people feel that 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 could never win a lottery, though it is exactly as likely as any other combination.

sections.key: Decide what you're looking for first, check it in fresh data, and stay humble both ways.
sections.b:
Ask how many chances there were for a pattern to appear. A one in a million coincidence is likely in a country of millions. Decide what you are testing before you look, as scientists do by registering their plans in advance. Then check whether the pattern holds in fresh data. A real effect should reappear; a random clump usually won't.

Be humble in both directions. For decades, researchers called basketball's 'hot hand' an illusion. In 2018, Joshua Miller and Adam Sanjurjo found a statistical bias in the original analysis and argued a modest effect may exist after all. 'It's just randomness' can be a mistake too.

quiz.q: How do invented 'random' coin sequences usually differ from real ones?
o: They contain far more long streaks
They switch sides too often
They contain only heads or only tails
They are identical to real sequences
quiz.e: Real randomness is clumpier than we expect, so people invent sequences that look too evenly mixed.

quiz.q: What did the analysis of V-1 strikes on London show?
o: The hits closely matched a random pattern
The bombs targeted wealthy suburbs
Most bombs missed London entirely
The bombs followed the line of the Thames
quiz.e: Clusters that felt deliberate were just the natural clumping of chance.

quiz.q: What is the Texas sharpshooter fallacy?
o: Shooting at targets that are too far away
Believing every marksman is accurate
Drawing the target after the shots land
Ignoring evidence from small towns
quiz.e: A cluster found after searching the data proves little, because you didn't predict it first.

quiz.q: Why do music apps often adjust shuffle so an artist doesn't repeat?
o: Truly random lists are too hard to code
Repeated songs slow the streaming service
Storage limits stop an artist repeating
True randomness feels rigged to listeners
quiz.e: We expect random to look evenly mixed, so real randomness often feels suspicious.

quiz.q: What is a sound way to test a suspicious pattern?
o: Search until you find a striking cluster
Check whether it holds up in fresh data
Trust it if it feels convincing
Dismiss every pattern as chance
quiz.e: A real effect should show up again; a random clump usually won't.

LESSONS.push: Shuffle your playlist and the same artist plays three times running. Rigged?

LESSONS.title: Regression to the mean: why extremes don't last
LESSONS.hook: A footballer has a dream season, then a so-so one. A new treatment seems to cure your worst week. Often the real cause is a quiet statistical force.

sections.key: Praise seemed to make pilots worse and criticism seemed to make them better.
sections.b:
The psychologist Daniel Kahneman told of teaching Israeli air force flight instructors. One objected that praise works better than punishment. When he praised an excellent manoeuvre, he said, the next attempt was usually worse. When he shouted at a bad one, the next was usually better.

Kahneman realised the instructor saw something real but drew the wrong conclusion. An unusually good flight is partly skill and partly luck, and luck tends not to repeat. So the next attempt is likely to be closer to average, whatever the instructor says. The same goes for unusually bad flights. The praise and shouting were mostly irrelevant. This pattern is called regression to the mean.

sections.key: Any result that mixes skill and luck drifts back towards average after an extreme.
sections.b:
Think of any performance as skill plus luck. Skill is fairly stable. Luck bounces around randomly. When you pick out an extreme result, the very best or worst, you are partly selecting for skill and partly for unusually good or bad luck. Next time the skill remains, but the luck is likely to be more ordinary, so the result moves back towards typical.

Crucially, no cause is needed. Nobody got lazy or complacent. The more luck matters, the stronger the pull to average. Pure skill wouldn't regress; pure luck would regress completely.

Francis Galton noticed it in the 1880s: very tall parents tended to have tall children, but on average not quite as tall. It describes groups, not destiny.

sections.key: Many famous 'curses' are just regression in disguise.
sections.b:
People joke about the Sports Illustrated cover jinx: athletes on the American magazine's cover often seem to slump soon after. Similar talk follows big award winners and players who sign large contracts.

But think about when someone lands on a cover. It is usually after a remarkable stretch, often their best ever, which almost certainly involved some good luck. The following season is likely to be closer to their usual level, which looks like a slump by comparison. No curse required.

The same logic applies to businesses praised after a record year, fund managers who topped the charts and restaurants that have just won an award. Picking people at their peak practically guarantees an apparent decline afterwards.

sections.key: People often seek treatment at their worst and improve anyway, so trials need control groups.
sections.b:
When are you most likely to try a new remedy for back pain, a headache or a cold? Usually when symptoms are at their worst. Many conditions naturally fluctuate, so after a bad patch things are likely to improve somewhat, whatever you do. If you took a remedy at the peak, it will seem to have worked.

That is a major reason researchers use control groups. In a well designed trial, some patients get the treatment and others get a placebo or standard care, and both groups are chosen in the same way. Regression affects both equally, so only a genuine difference between them shows a real effect. This is general information, so speak to a health professional about your own situation.

sections.key: Expect extremes to look less extreme next time, and ask what would have happened anyway.
sections.b:
Imagine cameras installed at the intersections with the most crashes last year. Next year, crashes there fall. Success? Partly, perhaps. But some sites topped the list through an unusually unlucky year and would have improved anyway. Road safety researchers account for this by comparing treated sites with similar untreated ones, or by using several years of data. The trap also appears in schools, where extra help goes to the lowest scorers, and in workplaces, where struggling teams get a new manager.

So when something is chosen for being extreme, expect it to look less extreme next time, and ask what would have happened without the intervention. Kahneman's instructors weren't wrong about what they saw, only about why.

quiz.q: Why did the flight instructor's criticism seem to work?
o: Criticism motivates people more than praise does
Trainees tried harder out of fear of him
Poor flights were usually followed by average ones
Shouting helped him give clearer instructions
quiz.e: Extreme results tend to be followed by more ordinary ones, whatever anyone says in between.

quiz.q: Which kind of activity shows the strongest regression to the mean?
o: One where luck plays a big role
One based purely on skill
One with no measured results
One done only once
quiz.e: The more luck matters, the more an extreme result is likely to fall back towards average.

quiz.q: Why might an athlete slump after appearing on a magazine cover?
o: The cover really does bring a curse
Fame always destroys an athlete's focus
The cover came after an unusually lucky peak
Athletes stop training after the photo shoot
quiz.e: Picking people at their peak practically guarantees an apparent decline afterwards.

quiz.q: Why do medical trials use control groups?
o: To make each trial cheaper to run
Because placebos cure most illnesses
To check the doctors rather than the drug
To show what improvement happens anyway
quiz.e: People often treat themselves at their worst and improve anyway, so a fair comparison is essential.

quiz.q: Why might crashes fall at camera sites even without cameras?
o: Drivers stop using those intersections afterwards
Sites were chosen after unusually bad years
Crash figures are never recorded accurately
The cameras were fitted at random sites
quiz.e: Selecting the worst spots builds in some improvement through regression alone.

LESSONS.push: Praise a great performance and the next is worse. Scold a bad one and it improves.

LESSONS.title: Berkson's paradox: when filtering creates false patterns
LESSONS.hook: Why do the best restaurants seem to be in the worst locations, and why do attractive dates seem more likely to be rude? The answer is a sneaky trick of selection.

sections.key: Looking only at hospital patients can create links between diseases that don't exist outside.
sections.b:
In 1946, the American statistician Joseph Berkson pointed out a puzzle in medical research. Among hospital patients, two unrelated conditions could appear linked, found together more or less often than in the general population.

The reason was how patients got into the data. People are admitted because they have one condition or another, or both. Studying only hospital patients filters the population by those very conditions, and that filtering alone can create a statistical relationship that doesn't exist in the wider world. This is now called Berkson's paradox. It is a cousin of selection bias, and once you know it, you spot it in dating, hiring, restaurants and headlines.

sections.key: If you only date people who are kind or attractive, those traits will seem to clash.
sections.b:
The mathematician Jordan Ellenberg popularised this example. Suppose someone will only date a person who is reasonably kind, reasonably attractive, or both. In the general population, imagine kindness and looks are unrelated.

Now look only at the people this person actually dates. Anyone neither kind nor attractive has been filtered out. Among those left, the attractive ones only needed to clear one bar, so many aren't especially kind. The kind ones are often not especially attractive. Within this group, looks and kindness seem to be opposites, and it feels as though attractive people are more likely to be rude. Nothing about the people changed. The filter created the pattern.

sections.key: Selecting on a combination of two traits manufactures a relationship between them.
sections.b:
Picture a square scatter plot with talent along one axis and charm along the other. If the traits are unrelated, the dots fill the square evenly, with no tilt.

Now add a rule: only people whose talent plus charm exceeds a certain total are admitted. Draw a diagonal line across the lower left corner and remove every dot beneath it. The remaining dots now slope downwards. Among those who passed, the most talented tend to be less charming, and the most charming less talented. A negative correlation has appeared from nowhere.

That is the essence of the paradox. It also explains why great food can seem to hide in awkward locations: a restaurant in a bad spot survives only if the food is excellent.

sections.key: Filtering or controlling for something influenced by two factors can create a false link between them.
sections.b:
Researchers call a variable influenced by two other factors a 'collider'. Filtering on it, or statistically controlling for it, can create a misleading link between those factors.

A well-known puzzle involves birth weight. Babies of smokers tend to be lighter, and low birth weight raises risk. Yet among only low birth weight babies, some studies found those born to smokers did slightly better. Smoking wasn't protective. Low birth weight can come from smoking or from other, often more serious problems, so comparing within that group mixed very different situations.

The same trap appears in admissions. Among admitted students, a weak school record must be offset by a strong entrance test, so the test may seem to predict nothing. Hiring shows it too, and in early COVID-19 studies of only tested or hospitalised patients.

sections.key: Always ask how the cases in a dataset got there.
sections.b:
The key defence is a simple question: how did these cases end up in front of me? If the group was selected on the very traits you're comparing, be suspicious of any pattern within it.

Your social circle, your newsfeed, a hospital ward, a list of successful companies and the people you have dated are all filtered samples. Patterns within them may be produced by the filter rather than the world. When possible, look at a broader, unfiltered group. When that isn't possible, be careful about drawing big conclusions.

Data never simply speaks for itself. It always arrives through some process, and understanding that process is half the work of understanding the data.

quiz.q: Why did hospital data suggest links between unrelated conditions?
o: Doctors recorded the data incorrectly
Hospitals themselves cause disease
Admission filtered patients by those conditions
The diseases were highly contagious
quiz.e: Studying only admitted patients filters the population by the very conditions being compared.

quiz.q: In the dating example, why do kindness and attractiveness seem opposed?
o: Those lacking both traits were filtered out
Attractive people really are less kind
Kindness makes people look less attractive
Dating apps hide kinder people from view
quiz.e: Within a filtered group, each trait can excuse a lack of the other, which creates a false trade-off.

quiz.q: What happens when you remove the lower left corner of an unrelated scatter plot?
o: The dots spread out more evenly
The remaining dots slope downwards
The dots form a neat circle
The correlation becomes perfectly positive
quiz.e: Selecting on a combined total manufactures a negative relationship between the two traits.

quiz.q: What is a 'collider' in research?
o: A type of particle accelerator
A large randomised trial
A variable that causes everything else
A variable influenced by two other factors
quiz.e: Filtering or controlling for a collider can create a false link between its two causes.

quiz.q: What is the best first question to ask of a surprising pattern in a dataset?
o: How big is the dataset?
Who paid for the study?
How did these cases get selected?
Is the result significant?
quiz.e: If the sample was selected on the traits you're comparing, the filter may have created the pattern.

LESSONS.push: Why do the best restaurants seem to hide in the worst spots? Blame the filter.

LESSONS.title: Your heart and blood
LESSONS.hook: Your heart beats about 100,000 times a day, pushing blood through tens of thousands of kilometres of vessels.

sections.key: The heart is a fist-sized pump with four chambers, serving two circuits.
sections.b:
Your heart sits in the middle of your chest, tilted slightly left, and is about the size of your fist. Its cardiac muscle resists fatigue. At rest it beats 60 to 100 times a minute, around 100,000 times a day. A natural pacemaker, the sinoatrial node, triggers each beat.

The heart has two upper atria that receive blood and two lower ventricles that pump it out. The right side sends oxygen-poor blood to the lungs to pick up oxygen. The left side pumps oxygen-rich blood to the whole body, so its ventricle has the thickest wall. Four one-way valves keep blood moving the right way, and their closing makes the 'lub-dub' a doctor hears.

sections.key: Arteries carry blood away, veins return it, and capillaries exchange oxygen and waste.
sections.b:
Arteries have thick, elastic walls to handle the pressure of each beat; the pulse in your wrist is an artery stretching. They branch into capillaries, so narrow that red blood cells pass in single file, where oxygen and nutrients move into tissues and waste moves out. Veins return blood at lower pressure, using one-way valves and squeezing leg muscles. Laid end to end, an adult's vessels would stretch tens of thousands of kilometres.

Blood pressure, like 120/80, is the force on artery walls: the top number as the heart beats, the bottom between beats. Persistently high pressure often has no symptoms but damages arteries, so regular checks from a GP or pharmacy matter.

sections.key: Blood is plasma carrying red cells, white cells and platelets.
sections.b:
An adult has about five litres of blood. Just over half is plasma, a yellowish liquid carrying nutrients, hormones, salts and proteins.

Red blood cells, made in bone marrow, carry oxygen using haemoglobin, an iron-rich protein that makes blood red. Their flattened disc shape gives more surface area and lets them squeeze through tight capillaries. White blood cells, far fewer in number, fight infection. Platelets are cell fragments that clump together to plug wounds and start clotting.

Red blood cells live about 120 days, and your body replaces them at roughly two million every second.

sections.key: Matching the markers on red cells makes transfusions safe.
sections.b:
Red blood cells carry markers called antigens. The ABO system sorts blood into groups A, B, AB and O, and the Rh factor adds positive or negative. Blood with markers your immune system doesn't recognise can trigger a dangerous reaction, so blood is carefully matched.

O negative can be given to almost anyone in an emergency, so it is always in demand. AB positive people can usually receive red cells from any group.

In Australia, donations are collected by Australian Red Cross Lifeblood. One donation is split into parts, such as red cells, plasma and platelets, so it can help several patients.

sections.key: Coronary arteries feed the heart itself, and healthy habits keep them clear.
sections.b:
The heart can't feed itself from the blood inside its chambers. Coronary arteries, wrapped around its surface like a crown, supply its muscle. Over decades, fatty plaque can narrow them. If a plaque ruptures, a clot can block the artery, starving the muscle beyond it of oxygen. That is a heart attack, and fast treatment saves muscle.

Heart disease is a leading cause of death in Australia. Key risks include smoking, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, diabetes, inactivity and too much alcohol. Exercise, plenty of plants and less salt help. Adults 45 and over (30 for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people) can ask a GP for a Heart Health Check. For chest pain or pressure, pain spreading to the arm, jaw or back, or breathlessness, call 000.

quiz.q: Where does the right side of the heart send blood?
o: To the brain and spinal cord
To the legs and feet
To the lungs
To the stomach and gut
quiz.e: The right side sends oxygen-poor blood to the lungs; the left pumps oxygen-rich blood to the body.

quiz.q: Why is high blood pressure worth checking regularly?
o: It often causes damage without any symptoms
It always causes a noticeable headache
It only happens during the night
It is extremely rare in younger adults
quiz.e: Because it rarely feels like anything, regular checks are how it is found.

quiz.q: What makes blood red?
o: Pigment dissolved in the plasma
A dye made by white blood cells
Colour released by platelet fragments
Iron-rich haemoglobin inside red cells
quiz.e: Red cells carry oxygen using haemoglobin, which gives blood its colour.

quiz.q: Why is blood carefully matched before a transfusion?
o: Blood expires within a few hours
Mismatches can cause an immune reaction
Every donor's blood is chemically unique
Hospitals only accept paired donors
quiz.e: Antigens on red cells decide compatibility, which is why group and Rh factor matter.

quiz.q: What causes a heart attack?
o: A blocked artery cutting off oxygen
The heart running out of stored blood
A burst vein inside the lungs
The natural pacemaker switching itself off
quiz.e: Heart muscle depends on its coronary arteries, so a blockage means muscle begins to die.

LESSONS.push: Your heart beats about 100,000 times today, and never once asks permission.

LESSONS.title: How digestion works
LESSONS.hook: From first bite to final exit, your food travels through several metres of tubing and takes a day or more. Here's what happens along the way.

sections.key: Digestion starts with chewing and saliva, then the stomach churns food with acid.
sections.b:
The digestive tract is a long tube from mouth to anus, often quoted as about nine metres in an adult. Chewing breaks food up, and saliva, about half a litre to one and a half litres a day, contains amylase, which starts turning starch into sugar. That's why bread tastes slightly sweet if chewed long enough. Waves of muscle contraction, called peristalsis, push food down the oesophagus, even if you're upside down.

The stomach is a stretchy muscular bag that churns food with hydrochloric acid, which kills many microbes, and pepsin, which starts digesting protein. Mucus protects its lining, which renews every few days. After a few hours, the thick liquid called chyme is released gradually into the small intestine.

sections.key: Most digestion and absorption happens in the small intestine, with help from the liver and pancreas.
sections.b:
Despite its name, the small intestine is the longest part of the tract, several metres long and a few centimetres wide. Bile from the liver breaks fat into droplets, and pancreatic enzymes break down carbohydrates, proteins and fats into sugars, amino acids and fatty acids. Millions of finger-like villi, covered in even smaller microvilli, give a huge surface area to absorb nutrients into the blood.

Blood from the gut goes first to the liver, which processes nutrients, stores energy as glycogen and removes toxins, including alcohol. The largest internal organ, it can regenerate remarkably. The pancreas also makes insulin, which helps cells absorb sugar.

sections.key: The large intestine absorbs water and hosts trillions of gut bacteria.
sections.b:
What's left, mostly fibre, water and bacteria, passes into the large intestine, or colon, about 1.5 metres long. Here water and salts are absorbed, turning liquid waste into solid stool, which can take a day or more.

The colon is home to trillions of bacteria, the gut microbiome. They ferment fibre, produce some vitamins such as vitamin K, and help train the immune system. Fermenting fibre also makes short-chain fatty acids that help nourish the colon lining.

Researchers are actively studying links between the microbiome and health, though many popular claims go beyond current evidence.

sections.key: Hormones and nerves between gut and brain tell you when to eat and when to stop.
sections.b:
Your gut and brain talk constantly, through hormones and the vagus nerve. An empty stomach releases ghrelin, which increases hunger. As you eat, the stomach stretches and the intestine releases hormones that signal fullness. Fat tissue releases leptin, which helps regulate appetite over the longer term.

These signals take time to register, which is one reason eating quickly makes it easier to overeat. Short sleep and stress also affect appetite; short sleep, for example, is linked to stronger hunger.

The gut even has its own vast network of nerves, sometimes called the second brain.

sections.key: Common gut problems overlap, so see a GP, and fibre and plants keep digestion healthy.
sections.b:
Reflux, where acid flows back into the oesophagus, causes heartburn; large meals, lying down after eating and alcohol worsen it. Many adults make less lactase after childhood, so dairy may cause bloating. Coeliac disease, an immune reaction to gluten, affects roughly 1 in 70 Australians, and most don't know they have it. Irritable bowel syndrome causes pain and changed bowel habits without visible damage. Symptoms overlap, so see a GP rather than cutting out foods on your own.

Most Australians eat less fibre than recommended. Vegetables, fruit, legumes and whole grains keep you regular and feed healthy bacteria. Seek advice about persistent bowel changes, blood in stool or unexplained weight loss. Free bowel cancer screening kits are available from age 45.

quiz.q: What is peristalsis?
o: Chewing food into smaller pieces
Muscle waves that push food along
The acid that breaks down food
An enzyme that digests starch
quiz.e: Muscle waves push food through the oesophagus and gut, even when you're upside down.

quiz.q: Where does most nutrient absorption happen?
o: The small intestine
The stomach
The large intestine
The mouth
quiz.e: Its villi and microvilli create a huge surface for absorbing nutrients into the blood.

quiz.q: What do gut bacteria in the large intestine do?
o: Make bile to help digest fats
Produce insulin to manage sugar
Ferment fibre and make vitamins
Absorb most of the body's protein
quiz.e: The microbiome ferments fibre, makes vitamins such as K and helps train the immune system.

quiz.q: Why does eating quickly make overeating easier?
o: Fast eating stretches the stomach less
Fullness signals take time to register
Ghrelin stops working altogether
The vagus nerve switches off
quiz.e: Gut and brain signals need time, so slowing down lets fullness catch up.

quiz.q: Why see a GP about ongoing gut symptoms before cutting out foods?
o: Many gut conditions share the same symptoms
Food never plays any part in gut problems
Only surgery can diagnose gut conditions
Fibre is the cause of most gut disease
quiz.e: Reflux, coeliac disease, intolerances and IBS look alike, so a proper diagnosis comes first.

LESSONS.push: Your food takes a day or more to travel several metres inside you. What happens?

LESSONS.title: Muscles and bones
LESSONS.hook: Your skeleton is living tissue that rebuilds itself constantly, and your muscles are the engines that move it.

sections.key: Bones are living tissue that supports you, protects organs and constantly rebuilds.
sections.b:
Babies are born with around 270 to 300 bones or bony pieces, many of which fuse as they grow, leaving about 206 in adults. More than half your bones are in your hands and feet. The femur is the largest; the stapes in the middle ear, about the size of a grain of rice, is the smallest.

Bone isn't dead and dry. It has blood vessels and nerves, and it's made of flexible collagen hardened with calcium and phosphate. Osteoclasts break down old bone and osteoblasts build new bone, so your skeleton is gradually renewed. Marrow makes blood cells, and bones store calcium. Weight-bearing exercise makes bones denser; long bed rest or spaceflight makes them lose mass.

sections.key: Joints, cartilage and tendons let bones move smoothly.
sections.b:
Where bones meet, joints allow movement. Hinge joints, like the knee and elbow, bend mainly one way. Ball-and-socket joints, like the hip and shoulder, rotate in many directions. The shoulder is the most mobile joint, which is also why it dislocates more easily.

Smooth cartilage covers bone ends and synovial fluid lubricates them. Cartilage has no blood supply, so it heals poorly, and its wear is part of osteoarthritis. Ligaments connect bone to bone; tendons connect muscle to bone. The Achilles tendon, at the back of the ankle, is the body's strongest.

sections.key: Muscles only pull, so they work in opposing pairs, with fast and slow fibres.
sections.b:
You have over 600 skeletal muscles. Protein filaments, actin and myosin, slide past each other when a nerve signal arrives, shortening the muscle. Muscles can only pull, so they work in pairs: to bend your elbow the biceps contracts while the triceps relaxes. Working muscles make heat, which is why shivering warms you.

Slow-twitch fibres resist fatigue and power posture, walking and long-distance running. Fast-twitch fibres are quick and powerful but tire sooner, suiting sprinting and heavy lifting. Your mix is partly genetic, and training can't completely change it, but endurance work improves stamina and strength training thickens fibres.

sections.key: Broken bones heal in stages, first a soft callus and then new hard bone.
sections.b:
When a bone breaks, bleeding forms a clot around the break. Within days, cells lay down a soft callus of cartilage and fibrous tissue that bridges the gap. Over the following weeks, osteoblasts replace it with a harder bony callus, and over months the bone is remodelled towards its original shape.

Many simple fractures in adults take roughly six to eight weeks to heal enough for normal use, though full remodelling takes longer. Children heal faster. Casts and splints hold the pieces in line so they knit correctly. Smoking slows bone healing noticeably.

sections.key: Strength and weight-bearing exercise, with calcium and vitamin D, protect muscle and bone at any age.
sections.b:
From your 30s or 40s, muscle mass slowly declines; in older age this is called sarcopenia. Bone density also falls, especially in women after menopause, raising the risk of osteoporosis, where bones break easily. Weak muscles make falls more likely, a major cause of injury in older Australians. Strength training and weight-bearing exercise, like walking or stair climbing, build muscle and bone at any age, even in the 80s and 90s.

Bones need calcium, from dairy, leafy greens, canned fish with bones and fortified foods, and vitamin D, made by skin from sunlight, so balance sun protection with exposure. Muscles need protein across the day. Adults should do muscle-strengthening activity on at least two days a week. A GP can check your bone health.

quiz.q: What do osteoblasts do?
o: Break down old bone
Make blood cells
Build new bone
Connect muscle to bone
quiz.e: Osteoclasts clear old bone while osteoblasts build new, so the skeleton is constantly renewed.

quiz.q: What connects muscle to bone?
o: Tendons
Ligaments
Cartilage
Marrow
quiz.e: Ligaments link bone to bone; tendons link muscle to bone.

quiz.q: Why do muscles work in pairs?
o: It keeps the body symmetrical
They can only pull, not push
It saves energy
Single muscles tire instantly
quiz.e: One muscle pulls a joint one way, and its partner pulls it back.

quiz.q: What happens first when a bone breaks?
o: A clot forms around the break
Hard bone forms straight away
The marrow rebuilds the whole bone
The cartilage is cleared out entirely
quiz.e: Healing runs in stages: clot, soft callus, hard bony callus, then remodelling.

quiz.q: What helps build muscle and bone at any age?
o: Resting more as the years pass
Taking supplements and staying still
Avoiding impact and heavy loads
Strength and weight-bearing activity
quiz.e: Muscle and bone respond to load, even in people in their 80s and 90s.

LESSONS.push: Your skeleton is alive and rebuilding itself right now. Here's how to help it.

LESSONS.title: How your senses work
LESSONS.hook: You have far more than five senses. And every one of them is your brain's interpretation, not a direct window on the world.

sections.key: Beyond the classic five, we also sense body position, balance, temperature, pain and internal states.
sections.b:
The idea of five senses goes back to Aristotle. Scientists now count many more, depending on how you define a sense. Proprioception tells you where your limbs are without looking, which is how you can touch your nose with your eyes closed. The vestibular system in your inner ear senses balance and motion. Separate receptors detect temperature and pain. Interoception reports your internal state, like hunger, thirst, a full bladder or a racing heart.

All of them work the same basic way: specialised receptor cells convert physical signals into nerve impulses that the brain interprets.

sections.key: The eye focuses light onto the retina, where rods and cones turn it into nerve signals.
sections.b:
Light enters through the cornea and lens, which focus it onto the retina at the back of the eye. The iris adjusts the pupil to control how much light gets in.

The retina holds about 120 million rods, which work in dim light but don't see colour, and about 6 million cones, which detect colour in three types, roughly sensitive to red, green and blue. Cones are packed into a small central spot, the fovea, which gives your sharpest vision.

The image on the retina is upside down; the brain flips it. Each eye also has a blind spot where the optic nerve leaves, which your brain fills in.

sections.key: Fluid-filled structures in the inner ear turn sound and movement into nerve signals.
sections.b:
Sound waves vibrate the eardrum. Three tiny bones amplify the vibrations and pass them to the cochlea, a fluid-filled spiral about the size of a pea. Thousands of hair cells bend with the vibrations, different parts responding to different pitches. Young people typically hear from about 20 to 20,000 vibrations per second, and the upper limit drops with age. Loud noise can permanently damage hair cells, which don't regrow in humans.

Next to the cochlea, three semicircular canals sense head rotation as fluid lags behind and bends hair cells, and tiny crystals shift with gravity. When these disagree with vision, as when reading in a car, you may get motion sickness. Spinning makes you dizzy because the fluid keeps moving.

sections.key: Smell links straight to emotion and memory, while touch receptors are unevenly spread.
sections.b:
Taste and smell detect molecules. Taste buds, mostly on the tongue, are replaced every week or two, which is why a burnt tongue recovers. Humans have around 400 types of smell receptor, and combinations let us tell apart far more odours than once believed. Smell signals travel almost directly to brain areas for emotion and memory, which is why a scent can instantly bring back a place. Sudden loss of smell is worth mentioning to a doctor.

Skin has receptors for light touch, pressure, vibration, stretch, heat, cold and pain. Fingertips and lips are packed with them, so the brain's touch map, the 'homunculus', has huge hands and lips. Many receptors adapt quickly, so you stop noticing your clothes. People born unable to feel pain often suffer serious injuries unknowingly.

sections.key: The brain interprets sensory data, so perception is construction, and protecting senses matters.
sections.b:
Your brain combines information from different senses, fills gaps and makes predictions. In the McGurk effect, watching lips say one sound makes you hear another. Expectations change taste: the same wine can taste better when people are told it's expensive. Some people have synaesthesia, such as seeing colours when hearing music. Perception is an active construction, not a camera recording.

Protect what you have. Australia's strong sun makes sunglasses and hats worthwhile, as UV contributes to cataracts. Regular eye tests can catch glaucoma before you notice vision loss. A common workplace guide treats noise averaging 85 decibels over eight hours as the limit before protection is needed; earbuds at high volume count. See a doctor promptly about sudden loss of smell, hearing or vision, or new dizziness.

quiz.q: What is proprioception?
o: Sensing balance and head movement
Detecting changes in temperature
Sensing limb position without looking
Sensing hunger and thirst
quiz.e: It is one of many senses beyond the classic five, and lets you touch your nose with eyes closed.

quiz.q: What do the cones in the retina detect?
o: Colour, in three types
Dim light and shadow
Movement at the edges

quiz.e: Rods handle dim light without colour; cones, packed in the fovea, give sharp colour vision.

quiz.q: Why is loud noise so harmful to hearing?
o: It permanently blocks the ear canal
It harms hair cells that can't regrow
It stretches the ear canal wider
It causes lasting inner ear infections
quiz.e: Cochlear hair cells don't regrow in humans, which is why hearing protection matters.

quiz.q: Why can a smell instantly bring back a memory?
o: Nose cells keep a copy of each memory
The eyes process smells alongside sight
Smell signals link closely to memory areas
Taste buds record every meal you eat
quiz.e: Smell has an unusually direct route into the brain's emotion and memory centres.

quiz.q: What does the McGurk effect show?
o: Hearing is more reliable than sight
Lip reading is almost impossible
Sound travels faster than light
What you see can change what you hear
quiz.e: The brain blends senses and fills gaps, so perception is built rather than recorded.

LESSONS.push: You can touch your nose with your eyes shut. Which sense lets you?

LESSONS.title: How neurons talk
LESSONS.hook: Every thought, memory and movement comes down to cells sending electrical and chemical messages. Here's how they do it.

sections.key: A neuron receives signals through dendrites and sends them along an axon, often insulated with myelin.
sections.b:
A neuron has three main parts. Branching dendrites receive signals. The cell body combines those inputs. A long, thin axon carries the output away, sometimes over a metre, like those from your lower spine to your toes. Many axons are wrapped in myelin, a fatty insulating layer that speeds signals up enormously; the signal jumps between small gaps in the myelin.

The brain has around 86 billion neurons, a figure from careful cell-counting studies, plus a similar number of supporting glial cells. Oligodendrocytes make myelin in the brain and spinal cord, and Schwann cells do so elsewhere. Astrocytes help feed neurons, and microglia clear debris and prune unused synapses. Glia means 'glue', but they take an active part.

sections.key: Neurons fire an all-or-nothing pulse called an action potential.
sections.b:
A resting neuron keeps a small voltage across its membrane, about minus 70 millivolts, by pumping ions in and out. When enough input pushes it past a threshold, channels open, sodium rushes in, and a spike of voltage, the action potential, races down the axon. Potassium flows out to reset it.

It's all-or-nothing: a neuron either fires or it doesn't. Stronger stimuli make neurons fire more often, not more strongly. Signals in thin, unmyelinated fibres crawl at about a metre per second, while in myelinated axons they can travel over 100 metres per second.

sections.key: Neurons pass signals across gaps with neurotransmitters that excite or inhibit.
sections.b:
Most neurons don't quite touch. Between them is a synapse, far narrower than a human hair. When an action potential arrives, the axon releases neurotransmitter molecules from vesicles. They cross in a fraction of a millisecond and bind to receptors on the next neuron, making it more or less likely to fire. Then they are broken down or recycled. The brain has an estimated 100 trillion or more synapses.

Glutamate is the main excitatory neurotransmitter and GABA the main inhibitory one. Each neuron adds up both to decide whether to fire. Too much excitation can cause seizures. Alcohol and some sedatives enhance GABA, slowing reactions. Dopamine and serotonin act more like volume controls, tuning whole networks.

sections.key: Connections between neurons strengthen with use, which is the basis of learning.
sections.b:
In 1949, psychologist Donald Hebb proposed that when one neuron repeatedly helps another fire, the connection strengthens. It is often summarised as 'neurons that fire together, wire together'. In 1973, researchers reported long-term potentiation in the hippocampus, a memory hub, where repeated stimulation made synapses stronger for hours or longer.

Practice physically strengthens pathways, adding receptors and even new connections, while unused connections can weaken and be pruned. This is how skills and memories are built, and why regular practice and review beat a single long session.

sections.key: Many conditions involve faults in neurons, myelin or neurotransmitters, and signals can now be decoded.
sections.b:
In multiple sclerosis, the immune system attacks myelin, slowing signals. Parkinson's disease involves loss of dopamine-producing neurons. Alzheimer's disease damages synapses and neurons and involves abnormal protein build-ups. Many medicines act at synapses; some antidepressants, for example, affect how serotonin is recycled.

Because neurons communicate electrically, activity can be recorded and decoded. Brain-computer interfaces place sensors near the motor cortex and translate firing patterns into commands. In trials in the early 2000s, people with paralysis learned to move a cursor by imagining moving a hand. Melbourne company Synchron's Stentrode is threaded up the jugular vein beside the motor cortex, avoiding open brain surgery. In a small Australian trial, recipients with motor neurone disease used it to text, shop and bank online. It is still experimental.

quiz.q: What does the axon do?
o: Receives signals from other neurons
Carries signals away from the cell body
Stores memories for the long term
Insulates the cell with a fatty layer
quiz.e: Dendrites receive, the cell body combines, and the axon sends the output.

quiz.q: What is special about an action potential?
o: It is all-or-nothing
It grows stronger with a stronger stimulus
It travels at the same speed in every fibre
It is purely a chemical signal
quiz.e: Stronger stimuli make neurons fire more often, not more strongly.

quiz.q: What is GABA's main role in the brain?
o: It is the main excitatory neurotransmitter
It makes myelin
It carries signals along axons
It is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter
quiz.e: Inhibition balances excitation, and too little inhibition can lead to seizures.

quiz.q: What does 'neurons that fire together, wire together' describe?
o: Seizures spreading across the brain
Neurons merging into one cell
Connections strengthening with use
Sleep clearing waste
quiz.e: Repeated activity strengthens synapses, which is why regular practice and review work.

quiz.q: What does multiple sclerosis involve?
o: Loss of dopamine neurons
The immune system attacking myelin
A build-up of abnormal proteins
Failure of the synapse's vesicles
quiz.e: Damaged myelin slows or blocks signals, causing numbness, weakness or vision problems.

LESSONS.push: Your thoughts run on a signal that is either fully on or fully off.

LESSONS.title: Dopamine, serotonin and friends
LESSONS.hook: Pop culture calls dopamine the 'pleasure chemical' and serotonin the 'happy chemical'. The truth is more interesting.

sections.key: Brain chemicals work through many receptors, so labels like 'happy chemical' mislead.
sections.b:
Neurotransmitters carry signals between neurons across tiny gaps. Hormones travel through the blood to distant organs, over seconds to days. Some, like adrenaline, act as both. Each chemical affects many systems, depending on which receptors and brain regions are involved; dopamine alone has five main receptor types. So labels like 'the happy chemical' are misleading. You also can't measure your brain's levels with a blood test.

Still, a few key players help explain motivation, mood, stress and how many medicines and drugs work.

sections.key: Dopamine drives wanting and learning, and serotonin is more complex than 'the happy chemical'.
sections.b:
Research by Kent Berridge and others suggests dopamine is more about wanting than liking: motivation, anticipation and learning which actions bring rewards. Its neurons fire when a reward beats expectations and dip when it falls short. Unpredictable rewards, like slot machines or notifications, tap this system powerfully. Dopamine loss in Parkinson's disease affects movement.

About 90% of the body's serotonin is in the gut, where it helps regulate digestion. It affects mood, sleep and appetite. The idea that depression is simply low serotonin is now considered too simple; a widely publicised 2022 review found no consistent evidence for it, though some researchers disputed how it was reported. Antidepressants help many people, probably through more complex effects. Decide on medication with a doctor.

sections.key: Oxytocin shapes bonding in context, while adrenaline and cortisol prepare you for threat.
sections.b:
Oxytocin is made in the hypothalamus and released by the pituitary. It triggers contractions in childbirth and milk release, and is involved in bonding. But it's no simple 'love hormone': some studies found it can increase closeness to one's own group while increasing defensiveness towards outsiders, and early findings that nasal sprays boost trust haven't reliably replicated.

In a threat, adrenaline rapidly raises heart rate and breathing and sharpens alertness. Cortisol, released more slowly by the adrenal glands, raises blood sugar and helps you cope over hours. It normally peaks soon after waking. Both are life-saving in short bursts, but chronic stress is linked to poor sleep, weakened immunity, weight gain and higher risk of heart disease and depression.

sections.key: Endorphins ease pain, and melatonin is a timing signal for night rather than a knockout pill.
sections.b:
Endorphins are the body's own opioids, released during injury, intense exercise and laughter. They help explain why people sometimes feel little pain right after a serious injury. The 'runner's high' was long credited to endorphins, though endocannabinoids also play a big role. Opioid drugs like morphine act on the same receptors, which is why they relieve pain so powerfully and can be addictive and dangerous in overdose.

Melatonin comes from the pineal gland and is controlled by a master clock in the hypothalamus that responds to light. It rises as darkness falls and drops in the morning. Bright, blue-rich light at night can suppress it. It is mainly used for jet lag and sleep timing problems. In Australia it is a pharmacy or prescription medicine, so ask a pharmacist or GP.

sections.key: Brain chemicals work as systems, so be sceptical of quick fixes that promise to hack them.
sections.b:
Popular advice promises to boost or reset one chemical, from 'dopamine detox' to foods that raise serotonin. Brain chemistry doesn't work that simply, and there is little evidence for most such claims.

The principles behind them can still be sensible. Cutting back on constant notifications can make everyday activities feel more rewarding. Regular exercise, daylight, good sleep and time with people you care about all support mood and stress resilience.

If low mood, anxiety or stress persists for weeks, talk to a GP, who can discuss options including therapy and medication.

quiz.q: Why is 'the happy chemical' a misleading label?
o: Chemicals have no effect on mood
Only hormones ever affect the brain
Blood tests can read brain levels
Each acts via many receptors and regions
quiz.e: Effects depend on which receptors and regions are involved, so single-job labels oversimplify.

quiz.q: What does research suggest dopamine is mostly about?
o: Wanting and learning from rewards
The feeling of pure pleasure
Setting the body's sleep timing
Moving food through the gut
quiz.e: Dopamine neurons fire when a reward beats expectations, teaching the brain to repeat what worked.

quiz.q: What did a widely publicised 2022 review find about serotonin and depression?
o: Low serotonin clearly causes depression
No consistent evidence for that simple link
Serotonin alone reliably cures depression
Serotonin has no role in the body
quiz.e: Depression is more complex than one low chemical, so treatment decisions belong with a doctor.

quiz.q: Why can chronic stress be harmful?
o: Adrenaline eventually stops working for good
It shuts down the pituitary gland entirely
Long-term high cortisol is linked to heart disease
It pushes endorphins to unsafe levels
quiz.e: Stress hormones help in short bursts, but weeks or months of elevated cortisol take a toll.

quiz.q: What is melatonin best described as?
o: A strong sedative that knocks you out
A fast-acting stress hormone from the adrenals
A body-clock signal that rises at night
A natural painkiller released in exercise
quiz.e: It tells the body it is night, which is why it is used for jet lag and timing problems.

LESSONS.push: Dopamine isn't the pleasure chemical. Its real job is far more interesting.

LESSONS.title: Why we dream
LESSONS.hook: You spend about six years of your life dreaming. Scientists still debate why, but they've learned a lot about how.

sections.key: REM sleep, with vivid dreams, was discovered in the early 1950s when eyes were seen darting beneath sleepers' lids.
sections.b:
In the early 1950s, Eugene Aserinsky, a student in Nathaniel Kleitman's Chicago sleep lab, wired sleepers to an old brainwave machine, starting with his eight-year-old son, Armond. Several times a night the pens traced bursts of rapid, jerky eye movements while the brain looked almost awake. He first suspected a faulty machine. In 1953 he and Kleitman published their discovery of rapid eye movement, or REM, sleep.

A few years later William Dement woke volunteers at different moments. Roused from REM, most described vivid dreams; at other times, far fewer did. Dreams do occur outside REM, but they tend to be shorter and less story-like.

sections.key: Most dreams are forgotten quickly, and those we recall are mostly familiar and emotional.
sections.b:
Most people dream several times a night but remember few dreams. Brain chemistry during sleep, including low noradrenaline, seems to make storing dreams hard. Waking during or just after a dream helps recall. Writing dreams down immediately, lying still with eyes closed for a moment, and intending to remember all improve it.

Psychologist Calvin Hall began systematically cataloguing dream reports in the mid-20th century, and his coding system is still used. Dreams are less bizarre than we assume: they often feature familiar people and places and recent worries. Fear, anxiety and frustration are common. Being chased, falling, flying and being unprepared for an exam recur across cultures. Reading in dreams is often difficult and unstable, perhaps because language areas work differently in REM.

sections.key: Theories range from wish fulfilment to emotional processing, and dreaming may serve several functions.
sections.b:
Sigmund Freud's The Interpretation of Dreams, published in late 1899 though dated 1900, argued dreams disguise hidden wishes, a theory few scientists accept today. In 1977, activation-synthesis proposed dreams are the brain making sense of random brainstem activity. Others suggest dreams consolidate memories or rehearse responses to threats, as Finnish researcher Antti Revonsuo argued in 2000.

Sleep researcher Matthew Walker and others suggest REM acts as 'overnight therapy', processing emotional memories while stress chemicals like noradrenaline are low. Some studies find people react less intensely to emotional images after sleep, though findings are mixed. In PTSD, nightmares can replay trauma. Imagery rehearsal, rewriting a nightmare's ending while awake and rehearsing it, can reduce nightmares.

sections.key: Lucid dreamers can signal from REM sleep, and animals show REM-like sleep and memory replay.
sections.b:
In a lucid dream, you know you're dreaming. In the 1970s and 80s, researchers including Keith Hearne and Stephen LaBerge showed it was real: sleepers signalled with pre-agreed eye movements while recordings confirmed REM. Around half of people report at least one lucid dream, but frequent ones are rare. Daytime reality checks ('am I dreaming?') and setting an intention before sleep may help.

REM-like sleep has been found in mammals and birds, with signs in some reptiles and octopuses. We can't ask animals what they experience. But in a 2001 study, patterns of hippocampal neurons firing as rats ran a maze were replayed during their REM sleep. Whether animals experience anything like human dreams is unknown.

sections.key: Occasional nightmares are normal, but frequent ones or acted-out dreams deserve medical advice.
sections.b:
Nightmares are common, especially in children and stressful times. Frequent, distressing ones may be linked to anxiety, trauma, some medications, alcohol or sleep disorders. Sleepwalking and sleep talking usually happen in non-REM sleep, not during dreams.

REM sleep behaviour disorder, where people act out dreams because muscle paralysis fails, is uncommon but important to diagnose, as it can be an early sign of Parkinson's disease and related conditions.

Regular sleep hours and a calm wind-down routine help sleep overall. If nightmares or sleep problems are affecting your life, a GP can help or refer you to a sleep specialist.

quiz.q: What did waking sleepers during REM show?
o: Almost none recalled anything
They all described identical dreams
Most described vivid dreams
They were fully awake and alert
quiz.e: REM is strongly linked with vivid dreaming, though dreams occur outside it too.

quiz.q: How can you remember dreams better?
o: Write them down at once
Sleep in for longer
Move around straight after waking
Avoid thinking about them
quiz.e: Dream memories fade fast, so capturing them straight away improves recall.

quiz.q: Why might REM sleep help with emotional memories?
o: It deletes the unpleasant ones for good
It may process them while stress chemicals are low
It strengthens them so they feel more intense
It has no link to emotion of any kind
quiz.e: This 'overnight therapy' idea suggests REM takes the sting out of experiences, though evidence is mixed.

quiz.q: How did researchers show lucid dreaming was real?
o: By interviewing sleepers each morning
By hypnotising sleepers in the lab
By scanning volunteers while awake
Sleepers signalled with eye movements
quiz.e: Signals from verified REM sleep proved dreamers could be aware they were dreaming.

quiz.q: Which sleep behaviour usually happens outside dreaming?
o: Sleepwalking and sleep talking
Nightmares
Acting out dreams in REM behaviour disorder
Lucid dreaming
quiz.e: These occur mostly in non-REM sleep, unlike REM sleep behaviour disorder where paralysis fails.

LESSONS.push: A student wired up his own eight-year-old son, and found a hidden stage of sleep.

LESSONS.title: The mystery of consciousness
LESSONS.hook: Why does it feel like something to be you? Science can map the brain in astonishing detail, yet this question remains unsolved.

sections.key: Consciousness is subjective experience: there is something it is like to be you.
sections.b:
Right now you are experiencing colours, sounds, thoughts and feelings. In his 1974 essay 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?', philosopher Thomas Nagel argued that a creature is conscious if there is something it is like to be that creature. A bat navigating by echolocation presumably has experiences, but ones we may never be able to imagine.

Scientists can show which brain processes accompany experiences. Explaining why there is any experience at all, rather than just information processing in the dark, is extraordinarily hard.

sections.key: Chalmers called the question of why brain activity comes with subjective experience 'the hard problem'.
sections.b:
In the mid-1990s, Australian philosopher David Chalmers split the puzzle in two. The 'easy problems' cover how the brain processes information, directs attention and controls behaviour. They are not actually easy, but they are the kind science knows how to tackle.

The 'hard problem' asks why any of this is accompanied by subjective experience. Chalmers illustrated it with a philosophical zombie: a being physically identical to you, but with no inner experience. Some philosophers think the problem will dissolve with more knowledge. Others think it reveals a deep gap in our understanding.

sections.key: Researchers compare brain activity with and without awareness, and find that much processing stays unconscious.
sections.b:
Neuroscientists look for the neural correlates of consciousness: the minimal brain activity needed for a specific experience. In binocular rivalry, each eye sees a different image, yet people consciously see only one at a time, switching back and forth. Comparing brain activity when the same image is seen or not seen shows that much processing is unconscious.

In blindsight, people with damage to the visual cortex can point to objects they insist they cannot see. Consciousness also shifts with state: it fades in deep sleep and vanishes under general anaesthesia, which doctors use safely every day but still don't fully understand. Meditation and psychedelics alter it too.

sections.key: The leading theories disagree, and none has decisive evidence.
sections.b:
Global Workspace Theory, from Bernard Baars and Stanislas Dehaene, says information becomes conscious when it is broadcast widely across the brain. Integrated Information Theory, from Giulio Tononi, ties consciousness to how much a system integrates information. A large 'adversarial collaboration' tested both, with mixed results, and some researchers questioned whether the second counts as science at all.

Illusionists, influenced by Daniel Dennett, argue that inner experience is a trick the brain plays. Panpsychists, such as Philip Goff, suggest consciousness is a basic feature of matter. Most scientists sit in between: consciousness arises from brain activity, but how is unknown.

sections.key: Judging who or what is conscious shapes medicine, animal welfare and how we treat AI.
sections.b:
This is not just an armchair puzzle. In a landmark 2006 study, brain scans showed an apparently unresponsive patient following instructions, such as imagining playing tennis. Later studies found similar hidden awareness in a minority of such patients. Anaesthetists work to prevent awareness during surgery.

The 2012 Cambridge Declaration said many animals, including mammals, birds and octopuses, have the brain structures needed for consciousness. A 2024 New York declaration saw a realistic possibility in reptiles, fish and some invertebrates. The UK recognised octopuses, crabs and lobsters as sentient in a 2022 law. Whether AI could ever be conscious remains deeply uncertain. Staying curious, and humble, is the honest position.

quiz.q: What does it mean for a creature to be conscious, in Nagel's sense?
o: There is something it is like to be that creature
It can process information and respond to its surroundings
It can sense the world with tools such as echolocation
It has a brain large enough to reason about itself
quiz.e: Consciousness is about subjective experience, not about processing information or having particular senses.

quiz.q: Why is the 'hard problem' harder than the 'easy problems'?
o: It needs brain scanners that have not yet been invented
It involves processes too fast for experiments to measure
It asks why brain processing comes with any experience at all
It deals with behaviour that cannot be studied in animals
quiz.e: The easy problems explain function and behaviour; the hard problem asks why any of it feels like something.

quiz.q: What does blindsight show?
o: Damaged visual cortex heals when people point at objects
The brain can guide actions using sights a person is not aware of
People can see in the dark by using their other senses
Conscious vision depends only on the eyes, not the brain
quiz.e: Pointing accurately at objects people say they cannot see shows that vision and conscious experience can come apart.

quiz.q: What is the state of the leading theories of consciousness?
o: One theory has been proven and the others rejected
All of them agree that consciousness is an illusion
Experiments have shown it exists in all matter
None is settled, and a major test gave mixed results
quiz.e: Competing theories remain open, and each has serious critics.

quiz.q: Why does the question matter beyond philosophy?
o: Who is aware affects patient care, animal welfare and AI
It decides which brain scans doctors are legally allowed to use
It has been solved, so only the practical details remain
It matters mainly for choosing which animals can be farmed
quiz.e: Who or what can be aware influences end-of-life care, animal protection laws and how societies treat future AI.

LESSONS.push: You can map every neuron, yet no one can say why it feels like anything.

LESSONS.title: What atoms are made of
LESSONS.hook: Everything you can touch is made of atoms, and atoms are almost entirely empty space.

sections.key: The idea of atoms is ancient, but solid evidence came only in the last two centuries.
sections.b:
The Greek thinker Democritus proposed around 400 BC that matter is made of tiny, uncuttable particles; atomos means 'uncuttable'. For two thousand years this stayed a guess, and Aristotle's view that matter is continuous won out.

Around 1808, English chemist John Dalton revived the idea with evidence: elements combine in fixed proportions by weight, which made sense if they came in discrete units. Even then, many scientists treated atoms as a handy bookkeeping device. In 1905, Albert Einstein explained Brownian motion, the jittery dance of tiny particles in water, giving strong evidence that atoms really exist. Jean Perrin's experiments soon confirmed it.

sections.key: Atoms are far too small to see with light, and each has a tiny dense nucleus of protons and neutrons.
sections.b:
Atoms are roughly 0.1 to 0.5 nanometres across; a nanometre is a millionth of a millimetre. Hundreds of thousands of carbon atoms side by side would just span a human hair, and one grain of table salt holds around a billion billion atoms. Light microscopes cannot show them, because atoms are smaller than the wavelength of visible light. In 1989, IBM researchers spelled out their logo with 35 xenon atoms.

J.J. Thomson discovered the electron in 1897. Around 1909, Geiger and Marsden, working under New Zealand-born Ernest Rutherford, fired alpha particles at gold foil; a few bounced almost straight back. In 1911 Rutherford concluded that atoms have a tiny, dense, positive nucleus. James Chadwick found its neutral neutrons in 1932.

sections.key: Atoms are almost entirely empty space, yet matter feels solid because electrons repel each other.
sections.b:
If an atom were the size of a football stadium, the nucleus would be about the size of a pea. More than 99.9% of an atom's mass sits in that nucleus, while nearly all its volume is space where electrons might be found. Quantum physics describes electrons as fuzzy clouds of probability, not tiny planets on neat orbits.

So why can't your hand pass through a table? Electrons repel other electrons, and a quantum rule called the Pauli exclusion principle stops them crowding into the same state. When you 'touch' something, your atoms never actually touch the object's atoms. What you feel is electromagnetic repulsion across a tiny gap.

sections.key: Protons define the element; neutron counts create isotopes, and unstable ones decay at a steady rate.
sections.b:
Every atom with one proton is hydrogen; six protons, carbon; eight, oxygen; 79, gold. That count, the atomic number, fixes the element. Atoms of one element can carry different numbers of neutrons. These versions, called isotopes, behave almost identically in chemistry but differ in mass and stability.

Carbon-12 makes up about 99% of natural carbon. Carbon-14 is radioactive: its unstable nucleus breaks down by releasing a beta particle (other isotopes release alpha particles or gamma rays). Each radioactive isotope has a half-life, the time for half a sample to decay. Carbon-14's is about 5,730 years, which allows radiocarbon dating of once-living material up to about 50,000 years old. Uranium-238's is about 4.5 billion years, which helps date rocks and the Earth. Many smoke alarms contain a trace of americium-241.

sections.key: Outer electrons decide how atoms bond, and protons and neutrons are themselves made of quarks.
sections.b:
Chemistry is mostly about electrons. Atoms are most stable with a full outer shell, so they share, give away or take electrons to form bonds. Sodium readily gives up its single outer electron and chlorine readily takes one, forming table salt. Carbon, with four outer electrons, shares them in long chains and rings, forming the backbone of every living thing. Helium's shell is already full, so it barely reacts, making it safe for party balloons.

Deeper still, protons and neutrons are made of quarks, bound by the strong force. A proton has two 'up' quarks and one 'down'; a neutron has one up and two down. Electrons, as far as we know, are not made of anything smaller.

quiz.q: What finally turned atoms from a useful idea into accepted fact?
o: Ancient Greek arguments about uncuttable particles
Photographs taken with the first light microscopes
Evidence from chemistry and from jittery particles in water
Aristotle's reasoning that matter is continuous
quiz.e: Dalton's chemistry and Einstein's explanation of Brownian motion gave real evidence where the Greeks had only a guess.

quiz.q: Why can't ordinary light microscopes show individual atoms?
o: Atoms are smaller than the wavelength of visible light
Atoms move too fast for any lens to focus on
Atoms are too widely spaced to appear in one view
Atoms are invisible in every kind of light
quiz.e: Light cannot resolve anything smaller than its own wavelength, so other tools were needed.

quiz.q: If atoms are mostly empty space, why can't your hand pass through a table?
o: The nuclei of the two sets of atoms collide and bounce apart
The empty space in solids is filled with an invisible gas
Gravity locks the atoms of the table tightly together
Electrons repel one another, and quantum rules keep them apart
quiz.e: Solidity is the feel of electromagnetic repulsion across tiny gaps, not atoms touching.

quiz.q: What decides which element an atom belongs to?
o: Its number of neutrons
Its number of protons
Its number of electron shells
Its total mass alone
quiz.e: The atomic number, the count of protons, fixes the element; different neutron counts just make isotopes.

quiz.q: Why does helium barely react with other atoms?
o: Its outer electron shell is already full
It has no electrons to share or take
Its nucleus is too heavy to take part in bonds
Its electrons are all in the nucleus
quiz.e: Atoms bond to reach a full outer shell, and helium starts with one.

LESSONS.push: A table is mostly empty space. So why can't your hand pass through it?

LESSONS.title: The periodic table
LESSONS.hook: One chart organises every element in the universe, and when it was invented, it predicted elements nobody had found yet.

sections.key: Mendeleev's table left gaps for undiscovered elements, and their predicted properties proved right.
sections.b:
