By the 1860s, chemists knew about 60 elements but had no pattern linking them. Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev wrote each element's properties on cards and arranged them by atomic weight, grouping similar behaviour in columns. Legend says the answer came in a dream. His crucial move was boldness: he left gaps for undiscovered elements and described them, calling them eka-aluminium, eka-silicon and eka-boron.

Gallium (1875), scandium (1879) and germanium (1886) matched his predictions closely. When gallium's first density disagreed, he suggested the sample was impure, and a remeasurement proved him right. Today the table is ordered by atomic number, the count of protons, as Henry Moseley showed in 1913 using X-rays.

sections.key: Each column, or group, holds elements with the same number of outer electrons, so they behave alike.
sections.b:
Each row, or period, begins a new shell of electrons, and the table has seven periods. Each column, or group, holds elements with the same number of outer electrons, which is why they behave alike.

Group 1, the alkali metals such as sodium and potassium, are so reactive they are stored under oil and fizz or explode in water. Group 17, the halogens such as fluorine and chlorine, are highly reactive non-metals; chlorine compounds disinfect swimming pools. Group 18, the noble gases helium, neon and argon, barely react at all. Argon makes up almost 1% of the air you breathe.

sections.key: Most elements are metals, and the crowded middle holds the industrial workhorses.
sections.b:
More than three-quarters of elements are metals: usually shiny, good conductors, and easy to hammer or draw into wire. Mercury is the only metal liquid at room temperature. Non-metals such as carbon, oxygen and the halogens cluster on the right. Between them, the metalloids silicon and germanium have mixed properties; silicon's controllable electrical behaviour underpins computer chips.

The wide central block holds the transition metals, including iron, copper, gold and platinum, many making coloured compounds and useful catalysts. The lanthanides, with scandium and yttrium, are the rare earths. Most aren't especially rare, just hard to find in concentrated, mineable deposits. Neodymium makes powerful magnets for wind turbines and electric cars, and Australia mines rare earths at Mount Weld in Western Australia.

sections.key: Symbols often come from Latin names, and the heaviest of the 118 elements are made in labs.
sections.b:
Some symbols reveal Latin names: Na for sodium (natrium), K for potassium (kalium), Fe for iron (ferrum), Au for gold (aurum), Pb for lead (plumbum, which gives us 'plumber'). The Swedish village of Ytterby lent its name to four elements. Curium, einsteinium and mendelevium honour scientists. IUPAC approves new names.

Almost all elements up to uranium (92) occur naturally; technetium and promethium are found only in tiny traces. Heavier ones are made by smashing atoms together. Element 118, oganesson, completed the seventh row, named in 2016 with nihonium, moscovium and tennessine. Superheavy atoms last milliseconds or less. Physicists suspect an 'island of stability' where some might last longer, and labs are chasing elements 119 and 120.

sections.key: Light elements came from the Big Bang; heavier ones were forged in stars and stellar explosions.
sections.b:
Hydrogen, helium and a little lithium formed in the first few minutes after the Big Bang, about 13.8 billion years ago. Stars then fuse lighter elements into heavier ones, building carbon, oxygen and more up to iron, where fusion stops releasing energy.

Elements heavier than iron form mainly in extreme events, such as supernova explosions and collisions between neutron stars. A neutron star merger observed in 2017 was seen producing heavy elements, probably including gold and platinum. The calcium in your bones and the iron in your blood were made inside stars that died before the Sun was born. As Carl Sagan put it, we are made of star stuff.

quiz.q: Why did Mendeleev's table convince chemists it reflected something real?
o: It listed every element in the order they were discovered
It predicted unknown elements that were later found
It was the first table to include more than 100 elements
It placed every element at exactly its measured weight
quiz.e: Accurate predictions of gallium, scandium and germanium showed the pattern was real.

quiz.q: Why do elements in the same group behave alike?
o: They have the same number of outer electrons
They have the same atomic weight
They were discovered around the same time
They have the same number of neutrons
quiz.e: Outer electrons drive chemical behaviour, so each column shares similar reactions.

quiz.q: Why are rare earth elements hard to supply, despite most not being especially rare?
o: They break down soon after being mined
They are found only in a few laboratories
Most are used up in making magnets
They rarely form rich, mineable deposits
quiz.e: Scarcity here is about finding mineable concentrations, not about total abundance.

quiz.q: Why are the heaviest elements known only in tiny amounts?
o: They exist only on distant planets we can't reach
They react with air and quickly vanish
Only a few atoms are made, and they decay fast
Their atoms break apart when they are weighed
quiz.e: Superheavy nuclei are unstable and last milliseconds or less before decaying.

quiz.q: Where did the iron in your blood come from?
o: It formed minutes after the Big Bang
It was forged in stars that died long ago
It was fused inside the Sun itself
It was created as the Earth cooled
quiz.e: Fusion in stars builds elements up to iron, and dying stars scattered them into space.

LESSONS.push: A chemist described three unknown elements before anyone had found them.

LESSONS.title: Chemical reactions
LESSONS.hook: Cooking, rusting, burning, breathing. Chemical reactions rearrange atoms into new substances, and they're happening in you right now.

sections.key: In a reaction, atoms rearrange into new substances, and none are created or destroyed.
sections.b:
In a chemical reaction, bonds break and new bonds form, producing substances with different properties. Hydrogen and oxygen are gases, yet burning hydrogen in oxygen makes water. In the 1770s and 1780s, French chemist Antoine Lavoisier used careful weighing to show that mass is conserved. A burning log seems to vanish, but most of its atoms go into the air as carbon dioxide and water vapour.

Chemists write this as equations: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. Numbers in front count molecules, and numbers after a symbol count atoms. Because atoms are never created or destroyed, an equation must balance: here, four hydrogen and two oxygen atoms on each side. That lets chemists calculate exactly how much of each ingredient they need.

sections.key: Chemical changes create new substances, and they either release energy or absorb it.
sections.b:
Melting ice or dissolving sugar are physical changes: the substance stays the same, and the change is often reversible. Chemical changes, like rusting or baking a cake, create something new. Clues include a new colour or smell, gas bubbles, light or heat, or a solid forming. Evaporate salt water and you get the salt back, so dissolving is physical. You can't un-bake a cake.

Breaking bonds takes energy; forming bonds releases it. Exothermic reactions release more than they absorb and give off heat, like burning fuel or iron oxidising in hand warmers. Endothermic reactions draw in heat, like photosynthesis storing sunlight in sugar. Even exothermic reactions often need a spark to start, called activation energy.

sections.key: Heat, concentration, surface area and catalysts all make reactions go faster.
sections.b:
Reactions happen when particles collide with enough energy. Heating makes particles move faster and collide harder. As a rough rule, many reactions go about twice as fast for every 10°C rise, one reason refrigeration slows food spoiling. Higher concentration or pressure means more frequent collisions.

Smaller pieces offer more surface area, which is why fine flour or coal dust can explode while a sack of flour won't. Catalysts speed reactions without being used up, by offering an easier pathway. Your car's catalytic converter turns toxic exhaust gases into less harmful ones, and enzymes are the biological catalysts running your body.

sections.key: Oxidation, losing electrons often to oxygen, drives rusting, burning and the way your cells make energy.
sections.b:
Oxidation once meant combining with oxygen. Now it means losing electrons, and its partner, reduction, means gaining them; the two always happen together.

Rusting is slow oxidation of iron into iron oxide, needing oxygen and water. Salt speeds it up, so cars in coastal towns rust faster. Galvanising coats steel in zinc, which corrodes first and protects the iron beneath. Burning is fast oxidation, releasing heat and light. Your cells use controlled oxidation too: cellular respiration combines glucose with oxygen to release energy step by step, producing the carbon dioxide you breathe out.

sections.key: Reversible reactions settle into equilibrium, and pushing that balance gave us synthetic fertiliser.
sections.b:
Many reactions run both ways. In a closed container they reach equilibrium: forward and reverse reactions happen at the same rate, so amounts stop changing even though molecules keep reacting. In 1884, Henri Le Chatelier described how such a system shifts to partly counteract any disturbance. Haemoglobin picks up oxygen in your lungs, where it is plentiful, and releases it in tissues, where it is scarce.

In the early 1900s, Fritz Haber and Carl Bosch combined nitrogen from air with hydrogen to make ammonia. Because the reaction is reversible, they used high pressure, high temperature and an iron catalyst to push it towards ammonia quickly enough to be practical. It helps feed around half the world's population, but uses much energy, mostly from natural gas. Haber also developed chemical weapons in World War I: chemistry can serve good or harm.

quiz.q: Why must a chemical equation balance?
o: Molecules always have to join in pairs
Atoms are only rearranged, never created or lost
Energy must be identical before and after
Products must always be half gas, half solid
quiz.e: Reactions only rearrange atoms, so the atom count must match on both sides.

quiz.q: Which of these is a chemical change?
o: Melting ice
Boiling water
Baking a cake
Dissolving sugar in water
quiz.e: Baking creates new substances and cannot be reversed, while the others only change form.

quiz.q: Why can fine flour dust explode when a sack of flour won't?
o: Smaller particles expose far more surface area to react
Dust is always hotter than the flour in a sack
Fine flour contains a different chemical from coarse flour
Air pushes sack-sized flour apart
quiz.e: More exposed surface means more collisions, so reactions run much faster.

quiz.q: What happens when iron rusts?
o: It dissolves completely in water
It burns quickly and gives off flame
It reacts with salt and nothing else
It slowly reacts with oxygen and water
quiz.e: Rusting is slow oxidation; salt only speeds it up.

quiz.q: Why does the Haber-Bosch process use high pressure, heat and a catalyst?
o: To stop the nitrogen from escaping into the air
To push a reversible reaction towards ammonia, quickly
To turn the ammonia into a liquid fuel
To make the reaction safe for workers
quiz.e: Controlling the equilibrium and speed made ammonia practical and fertiliser affordable.

LESSONS.push: A burning log seems to vanish. Where do its atoms actually go?

LESSONS.title: Acids and bases
LESSONS.hook: From lemon juice to stomach acid to drain cleaner, acids and bases are everywhere, and the pH scale measures them.

sections.key: Acids release hydrogen ions in water, bases accept them, and indicators show which is which.
sections.b:
When acids dissolve in water, they release hydrogen ions (H+). Acids taste sour, like lemons, vinegar and yoghurt, and strong ones corrode metals and burn skin. Bases remove hydrogen ions or release hydroxide ions (OH−); those that dissolve in water are called alkalis. They often feel slippery and taste bitter, like soap. Never taste unknown chemicals: strong bases like drain cleaner are as dangerous as strong acids.

Indicators change colour with acidity. Litmus turns red in acid and blue in base. Red cabbage juice is red-pink in acid, purple near neutral and green or yellow in strong bases. Hydrangeas act as living indicators: blue flowers in acidic soil, pink in alkaline.

sections.key: The pH scale runs from 0 to 14, each step is tenfold, and your body holds blood pH within a narrow range.
sections.b:
pH measures how acidic or basic a solution is, usually from 0 to 14. Pure water is neutral at 7. Lemon juice is about 2, stomach acid about 1.5–3.5, coffee about 5, blood about 7.4, seawater about 8.1 and bleach 12–13. The scale is logarithmic: pH 3 is ten times more acidic than pH 4 and a hundred times more than pH 5. Danish chemist Søren Sørensen introduced it in 1909.

Your stomach makes hydrochloric acid to digest protein and kill microbes, while a layer of mucus stops it digesting the stomach itself. Your blood must stay between about 7.35 and 7.45, as shifts outside that range can be life-threatening. Your lungs and kidneys adjust it constantly, partly through how much carbon dioxide you breathe out.

sections.key: Strong acids split fully into ions; strong is not the same as concentrated, and acids and bases neutralise each other.
sections.b:
Strong and weak don't mean concentrated and dilute. A strong acid, like hydrochloric acid, splits almost completely into ions in water. A weak acid, like the acetic acid in vinegar, releases only a small fraction. Concentration is how much acid is dissolved in the water, so a very dilute strong acid can be gentler than a concentrated weak one. Among bases, sodium hydroxide (some drain cleaners) is strong; ammonia is weak.

An acid and a base neutralise each other, forming water and a salt. Antacid tablets neutralise excess stomach acid. Farmers spread lime on acidic soils, common in parts of Australia. Baking soda reacts with acidic ingredients, releasing carbon dioxide bubbles that make cakes rise.

sections.key: Small pH shifts matter: acid dissolves tooth enamel, and the oceans are slowly becoming less alkaline.
sections.b:
Tooth enamel starts to dissolve below about pH 5.5. Frequent sugary drinks, which mouth bacteria turn into acid, and acidic drinks like soft drink and juice can harm teeth. Saliva helps by neutralising acid between meals.

The oceans absorb roughly a quarter of the carbon dioxide humans emit. It forms carbonic acid in seawater, lowering pH. Average surface ocean pH has fallen from about 8.2 to about 8.1 since the industrial revolution. Because the scale is logarithmic, that means roughly 30% more hydrogen ions. The oceans are not acidic yet; they are becoming less alkaline. That makes it harder for corals, oysters and some plankton to build shells and skeletons from calcium carbonate, adding pressure on reefs like the Great Barrier Reef.

sections.key: Many cleaners are strong acids or bases, and some become dangerous when mixed.
sections.b:
Many household cleaners are acids or bases. Descalers and some toilet cleaners are acidic. Oven cleaners, drain cleaners and ammonia sprays are alkaline, as is household bleach, which contains sodium hypochlorite.

Never mix cleaning products. Bleach with acidic cleaners can release chlorine gas, and bleach with ammonia releases toxic chloramine gases; both can badly damage the lungs. Keep chemicals in their original labelled containers, out of reach of children, and wear gloves with strong products. If a chemical is swallowed or splashed in the eyes, rinse with water and call the Poisons Information Centre on 13 11 26, or 000 in an emergency.

quiz.q: Which description fits an acid?
o: It removes hydrogen ions and tastes sweet
It never reacts with metals
It releases hydrogen ions in water
It always has a pH above 7
quiz.e: Acids release H+ ions in water, while bases accept them or release hydroxide ions.

quiz.q: How does a solution at pH 3 compare with one at pH 4?
o: It is ten times more acidic
It is three times more acidic
It is slightly less acidic
It is neutral
quiz.e: The pH scale is logarithmic, so each step is a tenfold change.

quiz.q: What makes an acid 'strong' rather than just concentrated?
o: It has a very large amount dissolved in the water
It splits almost completely into ions in water
It tastes more sour than any weak acid
It reacts only with other acids
quiz.e: Strength is about how fully an acid ionises; concentration is how much is dissolved.

quiz.q: Why is ocean acidification a concern if the oceans remain slightly alkaline?
o: It makes seawater too acidic to swim in
It turns the ocean a darker colour
It stops the oceans absorbing carbon dioxide
Lower pH hampers corals and oysters building shells
quiz.e: Even a small pH drop means about 30% more hydrogen ions, stressing shell-building life.

quiz.q: Why should you never mix bleach with other cleaning products?
o: They can release toxic gases, such as chlorine
The mixture becomes a strong sweet-smelling base
It makes both cleaners lose their strength
The mixture may freeze inside the container
quiz.e: Bleach mixed with acids or ammonia produces gases that can badly damage the lungs.

LESSONS.push: Your blood stays within a hair's breadth of one pH. What holds it there?

LESSONS.title: The chemistry of cooking
LESSONS.hook: Every time you cook, you're running chemistry experiments. Understanding them makes you a better cook.

sections.key: Maillard browning needs proteins and sugars, and caramelisation needs only sugar; both start at high temperatures.
sections.b:
The Maillard reaction creates hundreds of flavour compounds and a brown colour when food with proteins and sugars is heated. It runs quickly above about 140°C, so it happens in a hot pan or oven but not in boiling water, which stays near 100°C. It gives seared steak, toast, roasted coffee and bread crusts their richness. French chemist Louis-Camille Maillard described it in 1912. Pat meat dry and don't crowd the pan: surface water and trapped steam keep it too cool to brown.

Caramelisation needs sugar alone and starts around 160°C for table sugar, producing amber colour and complex, slightly bitter flavour. Fructose caramelises at a lower temperature. Caramel goes from golden to burnt in seconds; starting with a little water heats it more evenly.

sections.key: Heat unfolds proteins and swells starch, and that changes the texture of food.
sections.b:
Egg white is mostly water plus folded proteins. Heat makes them unfold, called denaturation, then tangle into a solid network. White begins to set around 62–65°C, and yolk thickens at roughly 65–70°C, which is how chefs make firm whites and runny yolks. Overcook and the network squeezes out water, turning rubbery; the grey-green ring around an overboiled yolk is iron sulfide. Acid can denature proteins too: ceviche 'cooks' fish in citrus juice.

Starch granules absorb water and swell when heated, called gelatinisation, which is how cornflour thickens gravy. On cooling, the chains realign and squeeze out water, called retrogradation. This is the main reason bread goes stale, fastest at fridge temperatures, so keep bread at room temperature or freeze it.

sections.key: Cutting cells open lets enzymes meet oxygen or sulfur compounds, which browns fruit and makes you cry.
sections.b:
Slicing an apple, banana or avocado lets an enzyme, polyphenol oxidase, meet oxygen, turning natural polyphenols into brown pigments. It is harmless, and you can slow it. Lemon or lime juice lowers the pH, which the enzyme dislikes, and its vitamin C undoes the first step. Chilling slows it, blanching destroys the enzyme, and pressing cling wrap onto guacamole keeps air out. An avocado stone only protects the flesh it touches.

Cutting an onion mixes enzymes with sulfur compounds, making a volatile gas, syn-propanethial-S-oxide, which irritates nerves in your eyes so tears flow. To cry less, chill the onion and use a sharp knife, which crushes fewer cells. Garlic's pungent allicin forms only once a clove is cut or crushed.

sections.key: An emulsifier lets droplets of oil stay suspended in water, as in mayonnaise.
sections.b:
Oil and water don't mix, because water molecules cling to each other and push oil away. An emulsion suspends tiny droplets of one liquid in the other. Mayonnaise is oil droplets in egg yolk and lemon juice or vinegar, held stable by lecithin in the yolk, an emulsifier with one end that attracts water and one that attracts oil.

Milk and butter are natural emulsions too. Vinaigrettes separate because they lack a strong emulsifier; a spoonful of mustard helps hold them together. If mayo 'breaks', slowly whisk it, a little at a time, into a fresh yolk and it can usually be rescued.

sections.key: Salt, acid and fat shape flavour, and knowing what each does helps you fix a dish.
sections.b:
Salt does more than make food salty. It suppresses bitterness, enhances other flavours, draws moisture out of vegetables such as eggplant and cabbage, and in brines helps meat hold its juices by changing how proteins behave. Salting pasta water seasons the pasta from within.

Acid, from lemon, vinegar, wine or tomatoes, brightens flavours and balances richness. Fat carries many flavour compounds, which is why low-fat versions can taste flat. Use this to fix dishes: if food tastes flat, it may need salt; if it is heavy or dull, a squeeze of lemon often helps; if it is too sour, a pinch of sugar can balance it.

quiz.q: Why should you pat meat dry and avoid crowding the pan before searing?
o: Dry meat absorbs more oil from the pan
Steam and surface water keep the meat cool
Crowding makes the pan heat up unevenly
Water prevents the sugars from forming
quiz.e: Maillard browning needs a surface well above 100°C, and moisture holds it down.

quiz.q: What happens to egg white when it is heated?
o: Its proteins unfold and form a solid network
Its water boils away, leaving a dry shell
Its sugars caramelise and turn it solid
Its fats melt, then harden as it cools
quiz.e: Heat denatures the proteins, turning clear liquid into firm, opaque white.

quiz.q: Why does lemon juice slow browning in cut fruit?
o: It seals the surface from the air with an oily film
It destroys the enzyme completely
It dries out the surface of the fruit
Its acid and vitamin C interfere with the enzyme
quiz.e: Acid and vitamin C interfere with the enzyme chemistry that turns polyphenols brown.

quiz.q: Why does mayonnaise hold together when a plain vinaigrette separates?
o: Oil mixes fully with water when it is whisked hard
Lecithin in egg yolk acts as an emulsifier
Vinegar is heavier than lemon juice
Cold oil is thicker than warm oil
quiz.e: An emulsifier has an end attracting water and an end attracting oil, keeping droplets suspended.

quiz.q: A dish tastes heavy and dull. What is a sensible fix?
o: Add a squeeze of lemon to brighten it
Add more fat to carry the flavour
Cook it longer to concentrate it
Stir in a pinch of baking soda
quiz.e: Acid balances richness, while a lack of salt makes food taste flat.

LESSONS.push: Why does a seared steak taste richer than a boiled one? It's chemistry.

LESSONS.title: Newton's laws of motion
LESSONS.hook: Three simple rules explain why seatbelts save lives, rockets fly, and a heavy trolley is hard to stop.

sections.key: Objects keep doing what they are doing unless an outside force acts on them.
sections.b:
Newton's great book began with a question. In 1684, Edmond Halley asked what path a planet follows if the Sun's pull weakens with the square of the distance. Newton answered at once: an ellipse. The work grew into the Principia, published in 1687 and paid for by Halley. It set out three laws still used to design cars, bridges, rollercoasters and spacecraft.

The first law says an object at rest stays at rest, and a moving object keeps moving in a straight line at the same speed, unless an outside force acts on it. The more mass, the more inertia. Friction hides this on Earth, so for centuries people believed motion needs a constant push. In a crash, the car stops but your body keeps moving forward: that is why seatbelts and airbags save lives.

sections.key: Force equals mass times acceleration, so more force or less mass means more acceleration.
sections.b:
The second law says force equals mass times acceleration: F = ma. Push an empty shopping trolley and it speeds up easily; push a full one with the same force and it barely moves. A loaded truck needs far more braking force than a car. Force is measured in newtons: one newton accelerates one kilogram by one metre per second, every second, roughly the weight of a small apple.

Acceleration happens only when forces are unbalanced. Friction resists surfaces sliding and is essential for tyres to grip and for you to walk. Air resistance, or drag, rises rapidly with speed, so driving faster uses more fuel. A skydiver speeds up until drag balances their weight, reaching about 200 km/h belly-down.

sections.key: For every action there is an equal and opposite reaction, acting on different objects.
sections.b:
When you push on something, it pushes back just as hard in the opposite direction. When you jump, you push down on the Earth and it pushes you up. The Earth moves too, but immeasurably little because its mass is so huge.

A rocket pushes exhaust gases backwards at high speed, and they push the rocket forwards. It needs no air to push against, which is why rockets work in space. The two forces act on different objects, so they don't cancel out. The recoil of a gun and the kick of a fire hose are the same law at work.

sections.key: Momentum is mass times velocity, and spreading a change in momentum over more time reduces the force.
sections.b:
Momentum is mass times velocity, so a slow truck can carry as much as a fast, much lighter car. In a collision the total momentum stays the same, merely shared differently. That is why Newton's cradle keeps clicking, and a cue ball can stop dead while the ball it hits rolls on.

Changing momentum takes a force applied over time, so stretching out the time reduces the force. Crumple zones lengthen a collision, lowering the force on passengers. Bending your knees when landing from a jump, or a cricketer drawing their hands back to catch a ball, does the same.

sections.key: Circular motion needs a force towards the centre, and the same few laws explain sport, travel and space.
sections.b:
Moving objects travel in straight lines, so anything moving in a circle needs a constant pull towards the centre: centripetal force. For a car on a corner it is tyre friction; for the Moon, Earth's gravity; for washing in a spinning machine, the drum wall. The outward 'fling' you feel is not a real force. It is your inertia trying to carry you straight on.

A footballer's kick accelerates the ball (second law). A swimmer pushes water back to move forward (third law). Engineers use the laws for safer car seats and helmets, and NASA still uses them for most spacecraft trajectories. Newton said he saw further by standing on the shoulders of giants, among them Galileo and Kepler.

quiz.q: What problem do seatbelts solve in a crash?
o: The car tends to roll over on impact
You get pushed backwards off the seat
Your body keeps moving forward as the car stops
The car's momentum spreads evenly to you
quiz.e: Inertia keeps you moving, so the belt supplies the force that stops you with the car.

quiz.q: You push a full trolley and an empty one with the same force. What happens?
o: The full one accelerates less, as it has more mass
Both accelerate equally because the force is the same
The full one accelerates more because it has more inertia
Neither moves unless the force doubles
quiz.e: F = ma means that, for the same force, more mass gives less acceleration.

quiz.q: Why can rockets work in space where there is no air?
o: They push against the thin gas that fills space
They use the Sun's pull to move them along
Their engines work only while they are in the atmosphere
Exhaust is pushed back and pushes the rocket forward
quiz.e: Action and reaction need no medium; the exhaust and the rocket push on each other.

quiz.q: How do crumple zones reduce injuries in a crash?
o: They stop the car's momentum from changing at all
They lengthen the collision time, lowering the force
They make the car heavier so it stops sooner
They absorb the crash by removing the car's mass
quiz.e: A given change in momentum over more time needs less force.

quiz.q: What is the outward 'fling' you feel when a car turns a corner?
o: Your inertia trying to carry you straight on
A real force pushing you towards the outside
Centripetal force pulling you outwards
Friction between you and the seat
quiz.e: The only real force is the inward one; your body simply resists changing direction.

LESSONS.push: Why a loaded truck is so hard to stop, and what a seatbelt really does.

LESSONS.title: Gravity
LESSONS.hook: It holds you to the ground, keeps the Moon in orbit and shapes galaxies. It's also the weakest force in nature.

sections.key: Every mass attracts every other mass, with a pull that grows with mass and falls with distance squared.
sections.b:
Newton realised the force pulling an apple down is the same one holding the Moon in orbit. His law of universal gravitation, published in 1687, says every object attracts every other, with a force that increases with their masses and decreases with the square of the distance between them. Double the distance and gravity drops to a quarter; triple it and it drops to a ninth.

In 1798, Henry Cavendish measured the tiny pull between lead balls in his laboratory, which allowed Earth's density and mass to be calculated. You are gravitationally attracting the device in your hand right now, just very, very weakly.

sections.key: Objects fall at the same rate without air resistance, and weight changes with gravity while mass does not.
sections.b:
Aristotle taught that heavy objects fall faster, and for almost 2,000 years few checked. Around 1600 Galileo showed otherwise, most likely by rolling balls down ramps rather than, as legend says, dropping them from the Leaning Tower of Pisa. Heavier objects feel a stronger pull but also resist acceleration more, so the effects cancel exactly. In 1971, Apollo 15 astronaut David Scott dropped a hammer and a falcon feather on the airless Moon, and they landed together.

Your mass, how much matter you contain, is the same everywhere. Your weight, the force of gravity on that mass, is not. On the Moon, with about one-sixth of Earth's gravity, a 70 kg person would read about 12 kg on Earth scales; on Mars about 26 kg. Near Earth's surface, falling objects speed up by about 9.8 m/s every second.

sections.key: Orbiting is falling around a planet, and gravity's change with distance stretches whole moons.
sections.b:
Newton imagined firing cannonballs from a mountaintop faster and faster, until one curved down exactly as fast as Earth's surface curved away. It would fall forever without landing: an orbit. The International Space Station, about 400 km up at roughly 28,000 km/h, circles Earth about every 90 minutes. Astronauts float not because gravity is absent, since it is about 90% as strong there, but because they and the station fall together. Geostationary satellites orbit about 36,000 km up, keeping pace with Earth's rotation.

Because gravity weakens with distance, a planet pulls harder on a moon's near side than its far side. Jupiter's tides melt the interior of Io, the most volcanically active world in the solar system. In 1992 Jupiter tore Comet Shoemaker-Levy 9 into more than 20 pieces, which hit the planet in 1994.

sections.key: Gravity is the weakest force, yet it always attracts and adds up, and Einstein described it as curved spacetime.
sections.b:
Gravity is by far the weakest of nature's four fundamental forces. A small fridge magnet holds itself up against the pull of the entire Earth. Between two protons, electric repulsion is roughly 10^36 times stronger. Yet gravity rules the cosmos because electric charges, positive and negative, mostly cancel in bulk matter, while gravity only attracts and keeps adding up across unlimited distances.

Newton admitted he couldn't explain how gravity acts across empty space. In 1915, Einstein's general relativity said massive objects curve space and time, and other objects follow those curves. So gravity isn't instant: if the Sun vanished, Earth would circle its empty position for about eight minutes. In 2017, gravitational waves and light from a neutron star collision arrived within two seconds of each other after 130 million years, confirming gravity travels at light speed.

sections.key: Gravity constantly loads your bones, muscles and spine, and it varies slightly across Earth.
sections.b:
In orbit, without the constant load of weight, astronauts can lose around 1% of bone density in weight-bearing bones each month. They exercise about two hours a day to limit muscle and bone loss. Their spines lengthen, making them a few centimetres taller, and fluids shift towards the head, giving a puffy face.

On Earth, gravity squeezes your spinal discs through the day, so you are slightly taller in the morning. Gravity isn't uniform either: because of Earth's spin and bulging equator, you weigh about 0.5% less at the equator than at the poles.

quiz.q: If you double the distance between two masses, what happens to the gravitational pull?
o: It drops to a half
It drops to a quarter
It stays the same
It drops to a tenth
quiz.e: Gravity falls with the square of distance, so double the distance gives a quarter of the force.

quiz.q: Why do a hammer and a feather fall together on the Moon?
o: Extra mass brings extra pull and extra inertia
The Moon's gravity affects feathers more strongly
Heavier objects are always pulled less by gravity
The hammer is slowed down by lunar dust
quiz.e: Pull and resistance to acceleration both scale with mass, so all objects fall at the same rate.

quiz.q: Why do astronauts float aboard the International Space Station?
o: Gravity is almost absent at that height
The station spins fast enough to cancel gravity
They and the station are in continuous free fall
Space itself pushes objects upwards
quiz.e: Gravity there is about 90% as strong; orbiting is continuous falling.

quiz.q: Why does gravity dominate the cosmos despite being the weakest force?
o: It is stronger than electricity at very short range
It acts instantly, unlike the other forces
Its strength grows as objects move apart
It only attracts, so its effects keep adding up
quiz.e: Electric charges cancel in bulk matter, but gravity always adds.

quiz.q: Why do astronauts lose bone density in orbit?
o: Space radiation dissolves the minerals in bone
Their bones lack the constant load of weight
They breathe less oxygen than on Earth
Their bodies stop making blood
quiz.e: Bones respond to load, which is why astronauts exercise about two hours a day.

LESSONS.push: Gravity is the weakest force in nature. So why does it shape galaxies?

LESSONS.title: Energy: what it is and where it goes
LESSONS.hook: Energy can't be created or destroyed, only changed from one form to another. Almost all of it on Earth started in the Sun.

sections.key: Energy is the ability to do work, and it changes form without ever being created or destroyed.
sections.b:
Energy is what makes things happen. Physicists define it as the capacity to do work, applying a force over a distance. Kinetic energy is the energy of motion. Potential energy is stored, like water behind a dam or a stretched rubber band. There are also chemical, thermal, electrical, light, sound and nuclear forms. Energy is measured in joules, named after English brewer and physicist James Joule; Australian food labels use kilojoules.

Energy is never created or destroyed. In the 1840s, Joule showed that a set amount of mechanical work always produces the same amount of heat. Riding downhill turns potential into kinetic energy; braking turns it into heat in the pads. When we 'waste' energy, we convert it into forms less useful to us.

sections.key: Kinetic energy rises with the square of speed, so doubling speed quadruples it.
sections.b:
Kinetic energy equals half the mass times the speed squared. Double your speed and your kinetic energy quadruples. A car at 60 km/h carries four times the energy of the same car at 30 km/h. The brakes, or in a crash the vehicle and the people inside, must absorb all of it.

That is why braking distances grow so quickly with speed, and why lower limits in busy areas, like 40 km/h school zones, save lives. Small increases in speed matter more than they feel.

sections.key: Every conversion wastes some energy as heat, which spreads out and becomes less useful.
sections.b:
Old incandescent bulbs turned only about 5% of electricity into light; LEDs use roughly 75–80% less electricity for the same light. Petrol engines turn roughly 20–30% of fuel energy into motion, while electric motors manage around 90%. Muscles convert only about a quarter of the energy they use into movement, the rest becoming heat, which is why exercise warms you up.

Heat pumps, including reverse-cycle air conditioners, seem to beat the rules, but they move heat rather than make it, delivering three or more units of heat per unit of electricity. The underlying principle is the second law of thermodynamics: energy tends to spread out and become less concentrated, which is why perpetual motion machines are impossible.

sections.key: Most energy on Earth comes from the Sun, which gets its own from converting mass.
sections.b:
Plants capture sunlight through photosynthesis, feeding almost every food chain. Coal, oil and gas are the remains of ancient plants and marine organisms, so they are stored ancient sunlight. Wind comes from the Sun heating Earth unevenly; hydro depends on rain, which depends on the Sun evaporating water. Sunlight striking Earth in an hour or two carries about as much energy as humanity uses in a year. The exceptions are nuclear energy, geothermal heat and tidal energy, which comes mainly from the Moon's gravity.

The Sun runs on E = mc², Einstein's 1905 finding that mass is a form of energy. Fusion converts about four million tonnes of the Sun's mass into energy every second. One gram of matter, fully converted, would release roughly the energy of 20,000 tonnes of TNT.

sections.key: Power is the rate of using energy, in watts, and your body runs on food energy in kilojoules.
sections.b:
Power is how fast energy is transferred: one watt is one joule per second. A kettle might draw 2,000 watts or more, a laptop about 50 and a phone charger 5–20. Electricity bills charge in kilowatt-hours: 1,000 watts for an hour, like running a small heater. The biggest home users are heating and cooling, hot water, clothes dryers and pool pumps, and standby power adds up. Energy Rating Label stars and full dishwasher loads help cut bills.

Your body is an energy converter too. One food calorie is about 4.2 kilojoules, and Australian labels use 8,700 kilojoules a day as a reference for an average adult, though needs vary. Even at rest, your brain uses about a fifth of your energy.

quiz.q: What does the law of conservation of energy say?
o: Energy is gradually used up as machines run
Moving objects create new energy as they speed up
Heat is a form that cannot change into anything else
Energy changes form, but the total stays the same
quiz.e: When we say energy is 'wasted', it has simply become a less useful form such as heat.

quiz.q: What happens to a car's kinetic energy if its speed doubles?
o: It quadruples
It doubles
It stays the same
It increases by half
quiz.e: Kinetic energy depends on speed squared, which is why small speed increases matter.

quiz.q: Why do heat pumps seem to beat the efficiency rules?
o: They create extra energy from the air
They move existing heat instead of making it
They run on a hidden second power source
They store heat from the previous day
quiz.e: Delivering three or more units of heat per unit of electricity doesn't break conservation, because the heat is moved.

quiz.q: Why are coal, oil and gas described as stored sunlight?
o: They were formed by sunlight heating rocks directly
They are replenished by fresh sunlight each year
They come from ancient life that captured sunlight
They absorb sunlight from the air as they burn
quiz.e: Photosynthesis stored sunlight as chemical energy, then the remains were buried for millions of years.

quiz.q: What does one kilowatt-hour measure?
o: Using 1,000 watts for one hour
The power of any appliance at one moment
Using 1,000 watts for one second
The energy in 1,000 kilojoules of food
quiz.e: Bills charge for energy over time, so power multiplied by hours matters.

LESSONS.push: Double your speed and you quadruple your energy. Here's why it matters.

LESSONS.title: How electricity works
LESSONS.hook: Flick a switch and the lights come on. Behind that is a flow of electrons, a power station, and a grid spanning a continent.

sections.key: Current is the flow of charge; individual electrons move slowly, but the push travels very fast.
sections.b:
In metals like copper, some outer electrons are free to wander between atoms. When a battery pushes them, they drift through the wire as an electric current. Individual electrons move very slowly, often less than a millimetre per second, but the push travels at a large fraction of light speed, like pushing water into a full pipe. Copper is used for most wiring because it conducts well and costs far less than silver, the best conductor.

Static electricity is charge that builds up rather than flows. Rub a balloon on your hair and electrons move to the balloon, so it clings to walls. Lightning is the same on a colossal scale: ice particles colliding in storm clouds separate charge until a discharge leaps to the ground, heating the air to around 30,000 degrees. Thunder is that explosive expansion.

sections.key: Voltage pushes, current flows and resistance opposes, and current needs a complete circuit.
sections.b:
Voltage, in volts, is the electrical pressure pushing charge around a circuit. Current, in amps, is the charge flowing per second. Resistance, in ohms, is how strongly a material opposes flow. Georg Ohm's 1827 law says voltage equals current times resistance. Voltage times current gives power in watts. Australian household supply is 230 volts, against about 120 in North America.

Current flows only around a complete loop, and a switch breaks or connects it. In a series circuit one failure stops everything, like some old Christmas lights. In a parallel circuit each component has its own path, as in house wiring, so one broken appliance doesn't cut power to the rest.

sections.key: Most electricity comes from spinning magnets near coils, and AC lets us send it over long distances.
sections.b:
In 1831, Michael Faraday found that moving a magnet near a coil of wire produces a current. Almost all power stations use this: something spins a turbine connected to a generator. Coal and nuclear plants boil water for steam, gas plants mostly use hot combustion gases, and wind and hydro spin turbines directly. Solar panels turn light directly into electricity in silicon, with no moving parts.

Grids use alternating current, which completes 50 cycles a second (50 hertz) in Australia. In the 1880s, Edison championed direct current and Tesla and Westinghouse championed AC. AC won because transformers raise its voltage for long-distance transmission, then lower it for homes. High voltage means lower current, and less energy wasted as heat in the wires. Some very long or undersea cables, like Basslink, use high-voltage DC.

sections.key: Supply must match demand every second, and batteries and rooftop solar are changing the grid.
sections.b:
Australia's main grid, the National Electricity Market, links Queensland, New South Wales, the ACT, Victoria, South Australia and Tasmania. It stretches around 5,000 km, one of the longest interconnected systems in the world. Western Australia and the Northern Territory run separate systems.

Because electricity is hard to store at scale, supply must match demand every moment, and operators balance it around the clock. Big batteries, pumped hydro schemes like Snowy 2.0, and rooftop solar are changing how the grid works. In South Australia, rooftop solar has at times supplied most of the state's demand, while evenings, when solar fades and households cook and run heaters, remain the peak.

sections.key: Current through the body is what harms, so water, damaged cords and overloaded boards are key hazards.
sections.b:
It is the current through the body that makes shocks dangerous, not voltage alone, and wet skin has much lower resistance, so far more current flows. Keep appliances away from baths, sinks and pools. Never use damaged cords, and don't overload power boards or plug them into each other.

Fuses and circuit breakers cut power when too much current flows. Safety switches (RCDs) detect current leaking to earth, perhaps through a person, and cut power in a fraction of a second. Test them with their test button regularly; many authorities suggest every three months. Fixed wiring in Australia must be done by a licensed electrician. If someone is being electrocuted, don't touch them: switch off the power if it's safe, then call 000. Stay at least eight metres from fallen power lines and treat them as live.

quiz.q: Electrons drift slowly, so why does a light come on instantly?
o: Electrons speed up to light speed once the switch closes
The push travels through the wire extremely fast
The light stores energy and releases it on demand
Electrons are already waiting inside the bulb
quiz.e: Like pushing water into a full pipe, the effect moves far faster than each electron.

quiz.q: Why does house wiring use parallel circuits?
o: One broken appliance doesn't cut off all the others
They make the voltage higher for each appliance
They need less copper than series wiring
They let current flow in both directions at once
quiz.e: In series, one broken component breaks the loop for everything.

quiz.q: Why is electricity sent over long distances at high voltage?
o: High voltage makes the electricity travel much faster
Transformers can only work at high voltage
High voltage turns alternating current into direct current
Higher voltage means lower current and less heat loss
quiz.e: Transformers make AC practical for transmission, then lower the voltage for homes.

quiz.q: Why must electricity supply match demand every moment?
o: Generators cannot be turned off once started
Power lines hold only a few seconds of electricity
Electricity is hard to store at scale
Homes use exactly the same amount all day
quiz.e: Big batteries and pumped hydro are growing, but operators still balance the grid around the clock.

quiz.q: What does a safety switch (RCD) do?
o: Limits the voltage in your home to a safe level
Detects leaking current and cuts power in an instant
Stops lightning from reaching your wiring
Turns off power only when a wire overheats
quiz.e: RCDs cut the power in a fraction of a second, which is why you should test them regularly.

LESSONS.push: Electrons crawl through a wire, yet the light comes on instantly. How?

LESSONS.title: Light and colour
LESSONS.hook: Light is the fastest thing in the universe, it's both a wave and a particle, and colour doesn't exist without a brain to see it.

sections.key: Light travels at about 300,000 kilometres per second, and nothing with mass can match that speed.
sections.b:
Light moves at 299,792 kilometres per second in a vacuum, usually rounded to 300,000. In one second it could circle the Earth about seven and a half times. Moonlight takes about 1.3 seconds to reach us, sunlight about 8 minutes and 20 seconds, and light from Proxima Centauri, the nearest star beyond the Sun, over four years.

So when you look at distant stars, you're looking into the past: their light left years, centuries or millennia ago. Light slows down in glass and water, but nothing with mass can ever reach its speed in a vacuum.

sections.key: Visible light is a narrow band of the electromagnetic spectrum, which runs from radio waves to gamma rays.
sections.b:
Light is electromagnetic radiation, a travelling wave of electric and magnetic fields, as Scottish physicist James Clerk Maxwell showed in the 1860s. Visible light is only a narrow band, with wavelengths of about 400 to 700 nanometres.

Longer wavelengths include infrared, which you feel as heat, then microwaves and radio waves. Shorter ones include ultraviolet, which causes sunburn, then X-rays and gamma rays. They're all the same kind of thing, differing only in wavelength and energy.

Some animals sense beyond our range. Bees see ultraviolet patterns on flowers that are invisible to us, and some snakes detect the infrared glow of warm-blooded prey.

sections.key: Light bends when it changes material, and different colours bend by different amounts, which splits white light into a rainbow.
sections.b:
Smooth surfaces such as mirrors and still water reflect light at the same angle it arrives, which is why you see clear images in them. When light passes from one material into another, such as air into water, it changes speed and bends. This is refraction. It makes a straw look broken in a glass and a pool look shallower than it is. Lenses in glasses, cameras and eyes use it to focus light, and optical fibres use total internal reflection to carry internet data across oceans.

In the 1660s, Isaac Newton split sunlight with a prism, then recombined it, showing that white light is a mixture. Violet bends most and red least. Raindrops do the same job: light enters, reflects off the back and bends again on the way out. You see a rainbow with the Sun behind you.

sections.key: Objects look coloured because they absorb some wavelengths and reflect others, and your brain turns the signals into colour.
sections.b:
A banana looks yellow because it reflects mostly yellowish wavelengths and absorbs the rest. A black T-shirt absorbs most light, so it heats up in the sun. The sky is blue because air molecules scatter short blue wavelengths far more than red, a process called Rayleigh scattering. At sunrise and sunset light crosses far more air, so blue is scattered away and reds and oranges remain. Clouds look white because their larger droplets scatter all colours equally.

Colour itself is made by your brain. Your eyes have three types of cone cell, and the brain compares their signals. That's why screens make almost any colour from red, green and blue dots, and why magenta, which matches no single wavelength, still looks real. About 8% of men and 0.5% of women of Northern European descent have some colour vision deficiency.

sections.key: Light behaves as both a wave and a stream of particles called photons, and lasers put its waves in step.
sections.b:
In the early 1800s, Thomas Young shone light through two narrow slits and saw bands of light and dark, as overlapping water waves would make. That was strong evidence for a wave. But in 1905 Einstein explained the photoelectric effect, where light knocks electrons out of metal, by treating light as particles, later called photons. He won the 1921 Nobel Prize for this, not for relativity. Light acts as both, depending on how it's measured, a puzzle at the heart of quantum physics.

A laser produces waves of one wavelength, marching in step, in a narrow beam. Einstein predicted the process in 1917 and Theodore Maiman built the first working laser in 1960. Lasers now read barcodes, carry data, cut steel and reshape corneas. Powerful pointers can damage eyes and are restricted in Australia.

quiz.q: What does it mean to look at a distant star?
o: You see light that left it centuries ago or more
You see the star exactly as it is right now
You see light that has slowed to a crawl in space
You see heat that has not yet turned into light
quiz.e: Light takes time to travel, so distant stars are seen as they were in the past.

quiz.q: How does visible light relate to infrared and ultraviolet?
o: They are unrelated kinds of energy with different sources
Infrared and ultraviolet are particles, while light is a wave
They exist only in space, never on Earth's surface
All are the same kind of wave, differing in wavelength and energy
quiz.e: The whole electromagnetic spectrum is one kind of wave, and visible light is a narrow band of it.

quiz.q: What did Newton show by splitting sunlight with a prism?
o: Prisms add colour to light that was colourless
Violet light travels faster than red light in space
White light is a mixture of colours that can be recombined
Sunlight is mostly invisible infrared radiation
quiz.e: Colours bend by different amounts, so a prism separates white light and a second prism recombines it.

quiz.q: Why is the sky blue?
o: The sky reflects the colour of the oceans below
Air molecules scatter blue light more than red
Blue is the true colour of sunlight at midday
Dust in the air absorbs every colour except blue
quiz.e: This is Rayleigh scattering, and at sunset the blue is scattered out of the longer light path.

quiz.q: What does light's behaviour in different experiments suggest?
o: It acts as wave or particle, depending on the test
It is purely a wave and never behaves as particles
It is purely a stream of particles, never a wave
It switches nature depending on who is observing it
quiz.e: Interference patterns show wave behaviour, while the photoelectric effect shows particle behaviour.

LESSONS.push: Colour isn't out in the world at all. So where does it come from?

LESSONS.title: Einstein's relativity, simply
LESSONS.hook: Moving clocks run slow, space bends, and your head ages faster than your feet. Relativity is strange, and it's been confirmed again and again.

sections.key: The speed of light is the same for every observer, however they are moving, and that single fact upends our ideas of time.
sections.b:
If you throw a ball forward at 20 km/h on a train doing 100 km/h, someone on the platform sees it move at 120 km/h. Light doesn't work that way. In 1887, Michelson and Morley tried to detect Earth's motion through a supposed 'ether' that carried light waves. They found nothing: light's speed came out the same in every direction.

Light always travels at about 300,000 km per second, whether you move towards it or away. In 1905, Albert Einstein, then a 26-year-old clerk at the Swiss patent office in Bern, took this as a basic law and followed it to astonishing conclusions.

sections.key: Moving clocks run slow and moving objects shorten along their direction of travel, which is why nothing with mass can reach light speed.
sections.b:
If light's speed is fixed for everyone, time must give. A clock moving relative to you runs slower from your point of view: time dilation. At everyday speeds the effect is tiny but measurable. In 1971, atomic clocks flown around the world on airliners differed from ground clocks by billionths of a second, as predicted. Muons, created when cosmic rays hit the upper atmosphere, should mostly decay before reaching the ground, yet many arrive, because their clocks run slow.

Fast-moving objects also contract along their direction of motion, though travellers notice nothing. Near light speed, each extra push takes more and more energy, and reaching it would take infinite energy. The Large Hadron Collider pushes protons beyond 99.999999% of light speed, but never to it.

sections.key: A twin who travels near light speed and returns is younger than the twin who stayed home, because only the traveller changes reference frames.
sections.b:
Imagine one twin staying on Earth while the other flies to a distant star and back at close to light speed. On return, the traveller is younger, perhaps by years. It seems paradoxical, since each twin sees the other moving. But the situations aren't symmetrical. The traveller accelerates, turns around and comes back, changing reference frames. The Earth twin doesn't.

The effect is real on small scales. Astronauts on the International Space Station, moving at about 28,000 km/h, age a few thousandths of a second less than people on Earth over a six-month mission.

sections.key: Space and time form one fabric called spacetime, and in general relativity mass curves it, which we feel as gravity.
sections.b:
In 1908, Einstein's former teacher Hermann Minkowski showed that relativity treats space and time as one four-dimensional fabric: spacetime. Observers in motion slice it into 'space' and 'time' differently, so they can disagree about whether two distant events were simultaneous, and neither is wrong. There is no universal 'now'.

General relativity, completed in 1915, covered gravity. Einstein realised that free fall feels exactly like floating without gravity, which he called the happiest thought of his life. Mass and energy curve spacetime, and objects follow the curves. As John Wheeler put it, spacetime tells matter how to move; matter tells spacetime how to curve. The theory explained a drift in Mercury's orbit and predicted that light bends around massive objects. Arthur Eddington's 1919 eclipse expeditions confirmed it, making Einstein famous overnight.

sections.key: Curved spacetime bends light and slows clocks, and GPS satellites must correct for both effects every day.
sections.b:
A massive galaxy cluster can act as a giant lens, bending and magnifying the light of objects far behind it. Einstein worked this out in 1936 but thought it would never be seen. The first lensed quasar was found in 1979, and the James Webb telescope now uses lensing to study galaxies too faint to see otherwise. A perfect alignment smears the background object into an Einstein ring. Relativity also predicts that a spinning mass drags spacetime around with it, which NASA's Gravity Probe B measured around Earth, reporting in 2011.

Gravity slows time too: clocks run faster where gravity is weaker, so your head ages slightly faster than your feet. GPS satellites gain a net 38 microseconds a day from both effects. Uncorrected, positions would drift by about 10 kilometres daily.

quiz.q: What was so strange about the speed of light?
o: It depends on how fast the light source is moving
It is the same for every observer, however they are moving
It increases when you move towards the light
It changes with the direction of Earth's travel
quiz.e: Michelson and Morley found no difference in any direction, and Einstein took constant light speed as a law.

quiz.q: Why can't anything with mass reach the speed of light?
o: It would take infinite energy to reach it
Air friction slows every object before it gets there
Gravity pulls fast objects back towards the Earth
Fast objects shrink until they vanish from view
quiz.e: Accelerators get protons extremely close to light speed, but extra energy mostly adds energy rather than speed.

quiz.q: Why does the travelling twin return younger?
o: Space travel slows the ageing of every living thing
Each twin sees the other ageing faster, so they cancel out
The Earth twin ages faster because gravity is stronger
Only the traveller accelerates, turns and changes reference frames
quiz.e: The twins' situations are not symmetrical, so the traveller returns younger.

quiz.q: In general relativity, what is gravity?
o: A force carried between objects by an invisible ether
A property found only in very large objects
The effect of mass and energy curving spacetime
Light pressure pushing objects towards each other
quiz.e: Objects follow curves in spacetime, and starlight bending past the Sun in 1919 supported the idea.

quiz.q: Why do GPS satellites need relativity corrections?
o: Their orbits are too elliptical to calculate
Their clocks run at different rates, causing drift
Their radio signals are slowed down by the atmosphere
Phones cannot read signals from fast-moving objects
quiz.e: Without correction, positions would drift by about 10 kilometres a day.

LESSONS.push: Your head ages faster than your feet. Here's why your phone map relies on it.

LESSONS.title: Polynesian navigators
LESSONS.hook: Without compasses or charts, Polynesian voyagers settled the vast Pacific, reading stars, swells and birds to find specks of land in an ocean.

sections.key: Polynesian voyagers settled a vast triangle of Pacific islands, reaching some of the last places on Earth settled by humans.
sections.b:
The Polynesian triangle runs from Hawai'i in the north to Aotearoa New Zealand in the south-west and Rapa Nui (Easter Island) in the south-east. Each side is thousands of kilometres long, and most of the inside is open ocean dotted with tiny islands. Finding them meant aiming for targets a few kilometres wide. New Zealand was one of the last major places on Earth settled by humans, around 1250 to 1300 AD.

The story begins with the Lapita culture, named after a site in New Caledonia and known for its stamped pottery. About 3,000 years ago, Lapita people reached Fiji, Tonga and Samoa, where Polynesian culture and languages took shape. After a pause of over a thousand years, voyaging resumed about 1,000 years ago and spread people across the triangle.

sections.key: Double-hulled canoes carried whole families, plants and animals on deliberate voyages of settlement.
sections.b:
Polynesians sailed large double-hulled canoes: two hulls joined by a deck, with sails woven from pandanus leaves. The hulls were shaped with stone adzes and lashed together with coconut-fibre cord, with no metal at all. The canoes were stable and fast, and could carry dozens of people along with taro, breadfruit, coconuts, pigs, dogs and chickens.

These weren't accidental drifts. Genetic, linguistic and archaeological evidence shows deliberate, planned voyages of settlement. Navigators often sailed into the prevailing winds, so the trip home would be downwind and a return stayed possible.

sections.key: Master navigators memorised a star compass of where stars rise and set, and used it to hold a course through the night.
sections.b:
A master navigator memorised a 'star compass': the points on the horizon where many stars rise and set. As one star climbed too high to be useful, the next along the same path took its place through the night. Stars passing directly overhead revealed latitude, so a navigator could sail to the right latitude and then run along it to an island. By day they used the Sun and the steady direction of the ocean swells.

This knowledge was passed down orally over many years of apprenticeship, often within families, and guarded carefully.

sections.key: Navigators used swells, seabirds, clouds and water colour to find land that lay beyond the horizon.
sections.b:
Swells travel long distances in steady directions. Skilled navigators felt them through the hull, even lying down, and noticed how islands bent and reflected them. Seabirds such as terns and noddies fly out to sea to fish in the morning and back to land at dusk, pointing the way. Because they range only a few dozen kilometres, they effectively widen each island into a much bigger target.

Clouds pile up over islands, a greenish tinge under them can reveal a lagoon, and floating plants and water colour offered more clues.

In 1769, the Ra'iatean priest and navigator Tupaia joined James Cook's Endeavour at Tahiti. He guided the ship through nearby islands and helped draw a chart of more than 70, which scholars still debate how to read. He also helped Cook speak with Māori, and died in Batavia in 1770.

sections.key: The 1976 voyage of Hōkūle'a proved traditional navigation works, and wayfinding is now being taught again.
sections.b:
For much of the twentieth century, some Western scholars doubted that Polynesians navigated deliberately, suggesting they drifted by accident. In 1976, the double-hulled canoe Hōkūle'a, about 19 metres long, sailed some 4,000 kilometres from Hawai'i to Tahiti in roughly a month. Its navigator was Mau Piailug of Satawal in Micronesia, using no instruments. The voyage proved the methods worked and sparked a revival across the Pacific.

Piailug trained Hawaiian navigators such as Nainoa Thompson, breaking with tradition to share knowledge beyond his own people so it would survive. Hōkūle'a sailed around the world from 2014 to 2017.

Polynesians probably reached South America too: the sweet potato grew across Polynesia before Europeans arrived, and a 2020 genetic study found contact with Native Americans around 1150 to 1230.

quiz.q: What made settling the Polynesian triangle such a feat?
o: Islands were close together and easy to see
Voyagers used compasses and metal tools
Tiny islands lay far apart across open ocean
Settlers followed a chain of large islands
quiz.e: Navigators had to find targets a few kilometres wide in a vast ocean, and they did.

quiz.q: What does the evidence say about Polynesian settlement voyages?
o: They were mostly accidental drifts that happened to succeed
They were planned, deliberate voyages carrying families and crops
They were short trips between neighbouring islands
They relied on metal-hulled boats and early charts
quiz.e: Genetic, linguistic and archaeological evidence shows deliberate voyages, often sailing into the wind.

quiz.q: What was a 'star compass'?
o: Memorised horizon points where stars rise and set
A metal instrument for measuring latitude at sea
A chart carved on the deck of a canoe
A song that listed the names of every island
quiz.e: Knowing where stars rise and set let a navigator hold a course all night.

quiz.q: How did seabirds help navigators find land?
o: They sing louder as a canoe nears an island
They follow canoes in order to share food
They sleep on the water far from any island
Some fly out to fish and return to land at dusk
quiz.e: The birds' daily range effectively widens each island into a bigger target.

quiz.q: What did Hōkūle'a's 1976 voyage to Tahiti show?
o: Polynesians must have drifted there by accident
Only metal ships could cross the open Pacific
Traditional navigation without instruments really works
Canoes need modern charts to find distant islands
quiz.e: It answered doubters and sparked a revival of traditional wayfinding.

LESSONS.push: They crossed the Pacific with no compass or charts. How did they find land?

LESSONS.title: Marco Polo and the Silk Road
LESSONS.hook: A young Venetian travelled to the court of Kublai Khan and wrote the book that made Europe dream of the East.

sections.key: The Silk Road was a web of land and sea routes that carried goods, ideas and diseases between China and the Mediterranean.
sections.b:
The Silk Road wasn't one road but a web of land and sea routes across Central Asia, the Middle East and India, active from around the 100s BC. The name is modern, coined by German geographer Ferdinand von Richthofen in 1877.

Silk, spices, porcelain, horses, glass and paper travelled along it, usually through many traders' hands, so few people ever travelled its whole length. Ideas moved too: Buddhism spread from India to China, and papermaking moved west. So did disease, including, eventually, the Black Death in the 1300s.

sections.key: The Mongol Empire made travel across Asia safer than ever, which let Europeans reach China.
sections.b:
In the 1200s, Genghis Khan and his successors built the largest contiguous land empire in history, stretching from Korea to Eastern Europe. The conquests were brutal, and resisting cities were often destroyed. But once established, the Mongols protected trade routes and travellers, ran relay stations for messengers and tolerated many religions, a period sometimes called the Pax Mongolica.

This allowed European merchants and missionaries to travel all the way to China, now ruled by Genghis's grandson, Kublai Khan.

sections.key: Marco Polo left Venice at 17 and spent years at Kublai Khan's court, describing a China richer than Europe.
sections.b:
Niccolò and Maffeo Polo, Venetian merchants, had visited Kublai Khan in the 1260s. In 1271 they set out again, taking Niccolò's 17-year-old son Marco. The journey through Persia, Central Asia and the Gobi Desert took about three and a half years. Venice was a wealthy trading republic, so the Polos were adventurous but not unusual.

According to Marco, Kublai took a liking to him and sent him on missions across China. He described paper money accepted across the empire, black stones burned for heat (coal), a postal relay of thousands of horses, and cities like Hangzhou that dwarfed Venice. Kublai ruled from Khanbaliq, on the site of Beijing, with a summer palace at Shangdu, the 'Xanadu' of later poetry. Some claims about his own importance were probably exaggerated.

sections.key: Marco Polo's stories, dictated in a Genoese prison, became one of the most famous travel books ever.
sections.b:
After about 17 years in China, the Polos wanted to go home, but Kublai was reluctant. Their chance came when the Mongol princess Kököchin needed an escort to Persia to marry its ruler. They sailed from southern China around 1291, via Sumatra, Sri Lanka and India. The voyage took about two years and many died. Her intended husband had died, so she married his son. The Polos reached Venice in 1295.

Marco was captured in a war with Genoa, probably around 1298. In prison he told his stories to Rustichello da Pisa, a writer of romances, who wrote them in French. Hand-copied in many versions, the book has no single original. In Italy it became 'Il Milione', perhaps for his 'million' tall tales. Marco died in Venice in 1324.

sections.key: Most historians accept that Marco Polo went to China, and his book inspired explorers like Columbus.
sections.b:
Sceptics note that the book omits the Great Wall, tea and foot binding, and that Chinese records don't name him. Supporters reply that the Great Wall people picture was built later, under the Ming; that he mixed mainly with Mongols; and that he gave accurate details, such as salt production, paper money and the princess's voyage, which a Persian source also records. Most historians accept that he went, even if some stories were embellished.

The Travels shaped European images of Asia for centuries, and the 1375 Catalan Atlas drew on it. Columbus owned a heavily annotated printed copy, which survives in Seville. When the Mongol Empire fragmented and the Ottomans rose, overland trade became harder, pushing Europeans towards sea routes and the Age of Discovery. Venice's airport bears his name.

quiz.q: What was the Silk Road?
o: A single paved highway across Central Asia
A canal system built by the Roman Empire
A route used only to carry silk cloth
A network of trade routes from China westward
quiz.e: Goods, ideas such as Buddhism, and diseases such as the Black Death all travelled along it.

quiz.q: Why could Europeans travel to China in the 1200s?
o: Chinese emperors invited all foreign visitors
Sea routes had replaced the dangerous overland ones
The Mongols protected trade routes and travellers
Venice had made peace with every Asian power
quiz.e: The Pax Mongolica made travel across Asia safer than before.

quiz.q: What astonished Marco Polo's European readers about China?
o: Printed Bibles and Christian cathedrals
Paper money, coal and enormous cities
Steam engines and tall glass towers
Roman-style roads and stone aqueducts
quiz.e: He described a China far richer than Europe, though he probably exaggerated his own role.

quiz.q: How did Marco Polo's book come to be written?
o: He told his stories to a writer while in prison
He wrote it himself during his years in China
Kublai Khan's scribes dictated it to him
His father published a diary after Marco died
quiz.e: Rustichello da Pisa wrote down the tales, and hand copying left no single original.

quiz.q: What do supporters of Marco Polo say about the missing Great Wall?
o: Mongol guards had hidden it from foreign visitors
It was too small to be worth mentioning
Floods had destroyed it before he arrived
The famous wall was built later, by the Ming
quiz.e: His accurate details, such as salt production and the princess's voyage, suggest he did go.

LESSONS.push: A teenage merchant's son left for China, then came home with tales Europe doubted.

LESSONS.title: Columbus, da Gama and the Age of Discovery
LESSONS.hook: In a few decades, European sailors reached India by sea and crossed the Atlantic, connecting the world, with enormous and often devastating consequences.

sections.key: Europeans sought sea routes to Asia to reach valuable spices directly and cut out the middlemen.
sections.b:
Spices such as pepper, cinnamon, nutmeg and cloves were hugely valuable in Europe, used to flavour food, make medicines and display wealth. They arrived overland through Middle Eastern and Venetian middlemen who raised prices at every step. After the Ottomans took Constantinople in 1453, the eastern Mediterranean trade was even more firmly in others' hands.

Portugal and Spain, on Europe's Atlantic edge, wanted direct sea routes. Religion also drove them: spreading Christianity and rivalry with Muslim powers. So did the simple hope of fortune and fame.

sections.key: Better ships, instruments and steady Portuguese exploration of Africa made long ocean voyages possible.
sections.b:
The Portuguese caravel was small, light and, with triangular lateen sails, could sail closer to the wind. Larger carracks carried more cargo. The magnetic compass, used in China first and in Europe by about 1200, showed direction under cloud. The astrolabe and quadrant measured the Sun or Pole Star, giving latitude. Longitude could only be estimated until marine chronometers arrived in the 1700s.

Prince Henry 'the Navigator' sponsored voyages down Africa's west coast from the 1420s, though he didn't sail himself. Crews learned the Atlantic's winds, including swinging far out to sea to catch favourable winds home. Ships traded gold, ivory and, tragically, enslaved Africans. In 1488, Bartolomeu Dias rounded the southern tip of Africa, proving a sea route to the Indian Ocean, before his exhausted crew forced him back.

sections.key: Columbus reached the Caribbean in 1492 because he badly underestimated Earth's size, not because people thought it was flat.
sections.b:
Genoese sailor Christopher Columbus believed he could reach Asia by sailing west. He badly underestimated Earth's size (educated Europeans already knew it was round), and experts rejected his plan for years. Backed by Queen Isabella and King Ferdinand of Spain, he sailed in 1492 with the Santa María, Pinta and Niña and reached the Bahamas on 12 October, landing on an island home to the Taíno people. Believing he'd reached Asia, he called the inhabitants 'Indians'.

He made four voyages, and his governorship of Hispaniola was notoriously brutal, even by the standards of his time.

sections.key: The 1494 Treaty of Tordesillas divided new lands between Spain and Portugal, and da Gama reached India by sea in 1498.
sections.b:
Columbus's return sparked a dispute over who owned new lands. In 1494, Spain and Portugal signed the Treaty of Tordesillas, drawing a north-south line through the Atlantic: lands to the west went to Spain, to the east to Portugal. It later gave Portugal a claim to Brazil, reached by Pedro Álvares Cabral in 1500, which is why Brazilians speak Portuguese. Amerigo Vespucci's voyages convinced many that a 'New World' had been found, and a 1507 map named it America.

Following Dias, Vasco da Gama left Lisbon in 1497, rounded Africa and, guided by a local pilot from East Africa, reached Calicut, India, in 1498. Scurvy killed many crew, but the spices were worth many times the voyage's cost. Portugal built a trading empire from East Africa to Indonesia, often using violence against established merchants.

sections.key: Contact between hemispheres moved crops, animals and diseases around the world, with enormous and often devastating human costs.
sections.b:
In 1972, historian Alfred Crosby named the Columbian Exchange: the transfer of plants, animals, people and diseases between the Americas and the rest of the world. Potatoes, maize, tomatoes, chillies and cacao went east, transforming diets from Ireland to China. Horses, cattle, wheat, sugar cane and coffee went west. Smallpox and measles, to which Indigenous Americans had no prior exposure, devastated communities, and populations fell perhaps 90% in some regions within about a century.

Inhabited continents were now linked by regular trade. Silver from Potosí, in modern Bolivia, flowed to Europe and China, and from 1565 Spanish galleons crossed the Pacific from Mexico to Manila. Demand for plantation labour drove the Atlantic slave trade, which carried about 12 million Africans across the ocean. Historians now often prefer 'contact' or 'encounter' to 'discovery', since these lands were already home to millions.

quiz.q: Why did Europeans want direct sea routes to Asia?
o: To buy valuable spices without paying many middlemen
To escape plague by settling distant islands
To find new farmland for crowded European towns
To avoid paying taxes to the Roman Church
quiz.e: Overland middlemen raised prices at every step, so a sea route promised big profits.

quiz.q: What did Bartolomeu Dias's 1488 voyage prove?
o: The Atlantic Ocean had no western shore
The world was round rather than flat
Africa had no gold or ivory worth trading
A sea route to the Indian Ocean existed
quiz.e: He rounded the southern tip of Africa before his exhausted crew forced him back.

quiz.q: What did Columbus get wrong?
o: He believed the Earth was flat
He expected to meet no people at all
He underestimated the Earth's size
He expected a voyage of more than a year
quiz.e: Educated Europeans already knew the Earth was round, and experts rightly doubted his plan.

quiz.q: What did the Treaty of Tordesillas do?
o: It ended a long war between Spain and England
It split new lands between Spain and Portugal
It gave the Pacific Ocean its name
It banned the trade in enslaved people
quiz.e: The line later gave Portugal a claim to Brazil, which is why Brazilians speak Portuguese.

quiz.q: What was the Columbian Exchange?
o: A swap of crops, animals and diseases across oceans
A Spanish bank that paid for Columbus's voyages
A trade treaty that set taxes on spices
A fleet that carried silver from Potosí to Europe
quiz.e: It transformed diets worldwide, and spread diseases that devastated Indigenous Americans.

LESSONS.push: Columbus knew the Earth was round. So what did he get badly wrong?

LESSONS.title: Magellan: the first voyage around the world
LESSONS.hook: Five ships and about 270 men set out in 1519. Three years later, one battered ship and 18 survivors limped home. They had sailed around the planet.

sections.key: Magellan set out in 1519 to reach the Spice Islands by sailing west, with a multinational fleet of five ships.
sections.b:
Ferdinand Magellan was an experienced sailor who had fought for Portugal in India and South-East Asia. After falling out with Portugal's king, he offered his services to Spain. He proposed reaching the Spice Islands, the Moluccas in modern Indonesia, by sailing west around South America. Under the Treaty of Tordesillas, he argued, the islands might fall on Spain's side of the line. The young King Charles I, later Emperor Charles V, backed him.

In September 1519, five ships left Sanlúcar de Barrameda: the Trinidad, San Antonio, Concepción, Victoria and Santiago, with about 270 men of many nationalities.
