As Allied armies advanced, the SS forced prisoners on brutal 'death marches'. Soviet troops reached Auschwitz on 27 January 1945, now International Holocaust Remembrance Day. Survivors were often sick and starving, their families murdered and their homes taken. Hundreds of thousands lived for years in displaced persons camps before emigrating to Israel, the United States, Australia and elsewhere.

sections.key: Trials and the new crime of genocide aimed to hold perpetrators to account, and remembering helps us notice early warning signs.
sections.b:
From 1945 to 1946, surviving Nazi leaders were tried at Nuremberg for crimes including crimes against humanity; twelve were sentenced to death. Further trials followed, though many perpetrators were never punished. In 1961 Israel tried Adolf Eichmann, a key organiser of the deportations. Polish-Jewish lawyer Raphael Lemkin coined the word genocide in 1944, and the United Nations made it a crime under international law in 1948.

Many survivors rebuilt their lives in Australia, and Melbourne's Jewish Holocaust Centre was founded by survivors in 1984. Denial persists despite overwhelming evidence. We remember because a modern, educated society did this step by step, with laws and ordinary officials, while many looked away. The lesson is to notice dehumanising language, scapegoating and the quiet removal of rights.

quiz.q: Which description of the Holocaust is accurate?
o: A famine that struck Jewish communities during the war
Nazi Germany's organised murder of about six million Jews
A series of battles between rival armies in Poland
A wave of violence confined to Germany in 1938
quiz.e: The Holocaust killed around two-thirds of Europe's Jews, and millions of other victims also died.

quiz.q: What is one of the Holocaust's most important lessons about how it happened?
o: It began suddenly with mass killing
It was hidden from the public entirely
It was done only by soldiers on the front
It escalated gradually as few objected
quiz.e: Discrimination, laws and then violence each tested public reaction before the next step.

quiz.q: What was the purpose of the 1942 Wannsee Conference?
o: To negotiate a peace settlement with the Allies
To coordinate the murder of all European Jews
To decide how to feed people in the ghettos
To put Nazi leaders on trial for war crimes
quiz.e: The meeting coordinated the 'Final Solution' as extermination camps were built in occupied Poland.

quiz.q: What did the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising and the Oneg Shabbat archive show?
o: Jews resisted by fighting and by keeping records
Jews had no means of organised resistance
The Allies liberated Warsaw in April 1943
Most bystanders actively helped to rescue Jews
quiz.e: Resistance took many forms, even though most people remained bystanders.

quiz.q: Why does remembering the Holocaust matter, according to the lesson?
o: It proves modern societies cannot be brutal
It helps us spot early warning signs
It shows laws never protect anyone
It is only relevant to Europe
quiz.e: It was carried out by a modern society through laws and officials, so early warning signs matter.

LESSONS.push: It did not begin with killing. How ordinary steps led somewhere terrible.

LESSONS.title: The end of empires
LESSONS.hook: In 1945, European empires ruled a large share of the world's people. Within about three decades, most colonies had become independent nations.

sections.key: World War II weakened the European empires and made old-style colonial rule hard to defend.
sections.b: In the early 20th century, Britain's empire covered about a quarter of the world's land. France, the Netherlands, Belgium and Portugal also held vast colonies. World War II weakened these powers economically and militarily, and damaged their prestige: Japan had defeated European forces across Asia, capturing Singapore from Britain in 1942. Colonised peoples who had fought for the Allies asked why freedom should apply to Europe but not to them. The 1941 Atlantic Charter had promised people the right to choose their own government, and the new United States and Soviet superpowers both opposed old-style empires.

sections.key: India won independence in 1947 at the cost of partition, while colonies that met resistance fought wars of independence.
sections.b:
India's movement, led by Mahatma Gandhi and Jawaharlal Nehru, used mass nonviolent protest, such as the 1930 Salt March. A weakened Britain decided to leave quickly. In August 1947 it partitioned the subcontinent into mostly Hindu India and mostly Muslim Pakistan, with hastily drawn borders. Around 15 million people moved, and hundreds of thousands to two million died in violence.

Where colonial powers resisted, wars followed. Indonesia fought the Netherlands until 1949, backed by Australian waterside workers who refused to load Dutch ships. Vietnam defeated France at Dien Bien Phu in 1954. Algeria's war against France (1954 to 1962) killed hundreds of thousands. Britain brutally suppressed the Mau Mau uprising in Kenya. Portugal held on to Angola and Mozambique until a 1974 revolution at home.

sections.key: Africa's rapid independence, led by 17 nations in 1960, left new states with artificial borders and fragile institutions.
sections.b:
Ghana became the first sub-Saharan British colony to gain independence in 1957. In 1960, the Year of Africa, 17 nations followed, and Harold Macmillan told South Africa's parliament that a 'wind of change' was blowing. White-minority rule lasted in Zimbabwe until 1980 and apartheid South Africa until 1994.

New nations inherited problems. Colonial borders, drawn by Europeans during the Scramble for Africa after the 1884–85 Berlin Conference, grouped rival groups together or split peoples apart. Colonial economies exported raw materials like cotton, cocoa, copper and rubber rather than building local industry. Some colonies had very few university graduates to run a government. India and Botswana built lasting democracies; others suffered civil wars, coups or dictatorships, sometimes backed by Cold War superpowers. Historians debate colonial legacies versus later choices.

sections.key: Many new nations tried to stay out of the Cold War, and Papua New Guinea became independent from Australia in 1975.
sections.b:
The United States and Soviet Union courted new nations with aid and weapons. In 1955, leaders from 29 Asian and African countries met at Bandung in Indonesia to oppose colonialism. In 1961 the Non-Aligned Movement was founded in Belgrade by leaders including Nehru, Nasser, Sukarno and Tito. The 1956 Suez Crisis, when Britain and France failed to retake the canal from Egypt under American pressure, showed how far the old powers had declined.

Closer to home, Australia administered Papua from 1906 and later governed German New Guinea under League of Nations and then United Nations mandates. The combined territory became independent as Papua New Guinea on 16 September 1975, under Michael Somare. Samoa (1962), Nauru (1968) and Fiji (1970) also gained independence. The United Nations now has 193 members, up from 51 in 1945.

sections.key: The end of empire still shapes languages, borders, migration and politics, and some questions remain open.
sections.b: Imperial history is still visible everywhere. English, French, Spanish and Portuguese are spoken across continents because of it. The Commonwealth of Nations, a voluntary association of mostly former British territories, has over 50 members, including Australia. Britain returned Hong Kong to China in 1997, and Timor-Leste, abandoned by Portugal in 1975 and then occupied by Indonesia, became independent in 2002. The UN still lists around 17 'non-self-governing territories'. New Caledonia, a French territory near Australia, voted against independence in referendums in 2018, 2020 and 2021. Debates continue about apologies, reparations and returning museum artefacts.

quiz.q: Why were European empires harder to maintain after World War II?
o: The war made their colonies richer than Europe
The superpowers wanted old-style empires to grow
The war left them weaker and less respected
Colonised peoples had stayed out of the war
quiz.e: Weakened powers, Japanese victories and promises of self-government undermined colonial rule.

quiz.q: What was one result of the hasty partition of the Indian subcontinent in 1947?
o: A vast migration and widespread violence
A calm, orderly exchange of populations
The creation of a single united state
A lasting military alliance with Britain
quiz.e: Hastily drawn borders led to around 15 million people moving and many deaths.

quiz.q: Why did many new African nations struggle after independence?
o: They had large numbers of trained civil servants
They were left free of all Cold War pressure
They inherited awkward borders and weak industry
They had no neighbouring countries to trade with
quiz.e: Borders, weak institutions and export economies were colonial legacies, though historians debate their weight.

quiz.q: What was the aim of the Non-Aligned Movement?
o: To avoid choosing sides in the Cold War
To join the Soviet bloc together
To restore European colonial rule
To form a single military alliance
quiz.e: Leaders from Asia and Africa wanted cooperation and independence from both superpowers.

quiz.q: Which example shows that the end of empire is not fully finished?
o: The Commonwealth voted to expel Australia
All UN territories became independent by 1975
New Caledonia has voted on independence from France
Hong Kong stayed under British rule after 1997
quiz.e: The UN still lists territories that are not self-governing, and debates over empire's legacy continue.

LESSONS.push: In 1960 alone, seventeen African countries became independent. Why then?

LESSONS.title: The civil rights movement
LESSONS.hook: Bus boycotts, sit-ins and marches. How ordinary people used nonviolent protest to dismantle legal segregation in America, and inspired Australians too.

sections.key: After slavery, southern states enforced segregation, until the Supreme Court ruled segregated schools unconstitutional in 1954.
sections.b: After the Civil War ended slavery in 1865, southern states passed Jim Crow laws segregating Black and white Americans in schools, transport, restaurants and hospitals, and used poll taxes, literacy tests and intimidation to stop Black citizens voting. Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) approved 'separate but equal', though Black facilities were far worse. Lynchings terrorised Black communities. NAACP lawyers led by Thurgood Marshall spent years challenging school segregation. In Brown v. Board of Education (1954), the Supreme Court unanimously ruled separate schools inherently unequal. Many southern states resisted, and in 1957 the Little Rock Nine needed federal troops to escort them into a high school in Arkansas.

sections.key: Disciplined nonviolent action, from the Montgomery boycott to the March on Washington, turned local struggles into a national cause.
sections.b:
In December 1955, Rosa Parks, an experienced activist and secretary of the local NAACP branch, refused to give up her bus seat to a white passenger in Montgomery, Alabama, and was arrested. Black residents boycotted the buses for 381 days, walking or sharing carpools, until the Supreme Court ruled bus segregation unconstitutional. A 26-year-old minister, Martin Luther King Jr., emerged as a leader.

Then came sit-ins at lunch counters from February 1960 and the 1961 Freedom Riders, who were violently attacked. In 1963, Birmingham police turned fire hoses and dogs on young protesters, shocking the nation on television. In August, around 250,000 people joined the March on Washington, where King gave his 'I Have a Dream' speech.

sections.key: Landmark laws ended legal segregation, but by the late 1960s some activists rejected nonviolence and King was assassinated.
sections.b:
President Lyndon B. Johnson pushed through the Civil Rights Act of 1964, banning segregation in public places and discrimination in employment. In March 1965, state troopers attacked peaceful marchers at Selma, Alabama, on 'Bloody Sunday'. The Voting Rights Act followed, outlawing literacy tests and sending federal officials to register voters; in Mississippi, Black registration jumped from under 10% to around 60% within a few years.

Not everyone shared King's strategy. Malcolm X argued for the right to self-defence, and from 1966 'Black Power' called for pride, self-reliance and political power. King broadened his focus to poverty and the Vietnam War before he was assassinated on 4 April 1968. A week later, Congress passed the Fair Housing Act.

sections.key: In 1965, Charles Perkins led students through NSW to expose segregation against Aboriginal people, helping build support for the 1967 referendum.
sections.b: Inspired by the American movement, University of Sydney students led by Charles Perkins toured country towns in NSW by bus in February 1965. Perkins, an Arrernte and Kalkadoon man, became one of the first Aboriginal university graduates in 1966. The students surveyed living conditions and exposed segregation at swimming pools, clubs, cinemas and shops. In Moree, where Aboriginal children were barred from the town pool, and in Walgett, they faced angry crowds. The publicity helped build support for the 1967 referendum, in which about 90.8% of Australians voted to count Aboriginal people in the census and let the federal government make laws for them.

sections.key: The movement ended legal segregation, but gaps and debates about equality, voting and policing continue.
sections.b: The civil rights movement transformed American law and politics. Black elected officials, rare in the South in 1965, now number in the thousands, and in 2008 Barack Obama was elected the first Black president. Yet gaps in wealth, health, schooling and incarceration rates remain large. In 2013 the Supreme Court struck down a key part of the Voting Rights Act, and later protests, such as those after the murder of George Floyd by a police officer in 2020, echoed earlier struggles. The movement's methods, patient organising, boycotts, legal challenges and disciplined nonviolent protest, are still studied by campaigners worldwide.

quiz.q: What did the Supreme Court decide in Brown v. Board of Education?
o: Segregated schools were acceptable if equal
Schools could choose their own policy
Only private schools had to integrate
Segregated public schools were unconstitutional
quiz.e: The Court ruled separate schools inherently unequal, overturning Plessy's reasoning for public education.

quiz.q: What did the 381-day Montgomery bus boycott show?
o: Boycotts almost never change anything
Disciplined nonviolent mass action can win change
Change comes only through armed violence
Courts will never rule against segregation
quiz.e: Black residents refused the buses until the Supreme Court ruled bus segregation unconstitutional.

quiz.q: Why did television coverage matter to the movement?
o: It removed the need for further marches
It made new laws pass without any debate
It ended the violence in the South at once
It made local struggles a national issue
quiz.e: Images like Birmingham's fire hoses and dogs shocked a national audience into backing reform.

quiz.q: What did the Voting Rights Act of 1965 achieve?
o: It lowered the voting age to 18 nationwide
It banned literacy tests and sent in registrars
It ended segregation in public schools
It gave Black Americans the vote in 1865
quiz.e: Black voter registration in the South rose dramatically after the Act.

quiz.q: What was the aim of the 1965 Australian Freedom Ride?
o: To campaign for an Australian republic
To protest against the war in Vietnam
To open new schools in outback towns
To expose racial discrimination in NSW towns
quiz.e: Its publicity of segregation at pools and clubs helped build support for the 1967 referendum.

LESSONS.push: A seamstress's arrest, a 381-day boycott and a law that changed a nation.

LESSONS.title: The First Fleet and colonisation
LESSONS.hook: In 1788, eleven ships arrived in Sydney Cove. For Britain it was a new colony; for the land's Aboriginal owners, it was an invasion.

sections.key: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples had lived in Australia for more than 50,000 years before Europeans arrived.
sections.b: When Europeans arrived, Australia was home to hundreds of distinct Aboriginal nations and more than 250 languages, with Torres Strait Islander peoples to the north. Archaeologists agree people have lived here for more than 50,000 years, and excavations at Madjedbebe in Arnhem Land suggest about 65,000, though that date is still debated. Aboriginal peoples managed the land with fire, fish traps and trade networks, and lived by complex systems of law, kinship and knowledge. Dutch sailors had mapped parts of the coast from 1606, and James Cook charted the east coast in 1770, claiming it for Britain despite its people.

sections.key: Britain founded a penal colony after losing its American colonies, and the First Fleet arrived at Sydney Cove in January 1788.
sections.b:
Britain had shipped around 50,000 convicts to its American colonies until the American Revolution ended that option in the 1770s. Harsh laws made minor thefts serious crimes, and prisons and hulks overflowed. In 1786 the government chose Botany Bay as a penal colony. Strategic interests, such as a Pacific base and timber and flax for the navy, may also have played a part. Captain Arthur Phillip became first governor.

The First Fleet left Portsmouth on 13 May 1787 with eleven ships and roughly 1,400 people, about 750 of them convicts. It called at Tenerife, Rio de Janeiro and Cape Town. Botany Bay proved unsuitable, so Phillip moved to Port Jackson, and on 26 January 1788 raised the British flag at Sydney Cove.

sections.key: The colony nearly starved at first, then grew as convicts built new lives and free settlers arrived.
sections.b:
Few convicts had farming skills. Crops failed in poor, sandy soils, cattle strayed, and supplies were delayed; the store ship Guardian never arrived after hitting an iceberg in 1789. Rations were cut severely. The Second Fleet arrived in 1790 with hundreds of convicts dead or dying from neglect. A smallpox epidemic in 1789 devastated Aboriginal communities around Sydney. Only in the mid-1790s did Hawkesbury River farms ease food shortages.

About 162,000 convicts were transported to Australia between 1788 and 1868. Well-behaved convicts could earn a 'ticket of leave', and many emancipists became farmers, merchants and builders. Governor Lachlan Macquarie (1810 to 1821) championed them. Free settlers arrived in growing numbers from the 1820s, and many Australians today have convict ancestors.

sections.key: Early relations with the Eora mixed curiosity and kidnapping, then settlement brought a century of frontier conflict.
sections.b:
Relations with the Eora began with some curiosity but deteriorated as colonists took fish, land and water. Hoping to learn the language, Phillip had Aboriginal men captured, including Arabanoo and, later, Bennelong. Bennelong escaped, then chose to return, and sailed to England with Phillip in 1792. In 1790 Phillip was speared at Manly but did not retaliate.

Britain treated the land as terra nullius in practice and made no treaties. As colonists took land for farming and grazing, Aboriginal people resisted, and frontier conflict continued for over a century. Pemulwuy led resistance around Sydney until he was killed in 1802. Massacres occurred across the country; after Myall Creek in 1838, seven colonists were hanged, a rare punishment. Disease, violence and loss of land caused catastrophic population decline.

sections.key: For many Australians 26 January is a national holiday, and for many Aboriginal people it marks the beginning of dispossession.
sections.b: The anniversary of the First Fleet's landing gradually became a national holiday, observed on 26 January by all states and territories only from 1994. For many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, it marks the beginning of dispossession. On 26 January 1938, the 150th anniversary, Aboriginal activists including William Cooper, Jack Patten and William Ferguson held a Day of Mourning in Sydney, and the date has been a day of protest ever since. Today Australians hold a range of views: some celebrate, some mourn, some want the date changed. Understanding these perspectives is part of understanding Australian history.

quiz.q: Which statement about Australia before 1788 is supported by the evidence?
o: People had lived here for over 50,000 years
Australia was uninhabited before Cook's voyage
Only one Aboriginal language was spoken here
People lived here for only a few thousand years
quiz.e: Hundreds of nations with complex law and land management predated colonisation.

quiz.q: Why did Britain establish a penal colony in Australia?
o: It had just discovered gold there
It wanted a trade route to India
America no longer took its convicts
Its jails had plenty of spare room
quiz.e: The American Revolution ended transportation there, and Britain's prisons and hulks were overflowing.

quiz.q: Why did the early colony nearly starve?
o: Poor soils, few farmers and late supplies
The Eora refused to trade fish with them
Governor Phillip refused to ration food
Too many free settlers arrived at once
quiz.e: Poor soils, little farming skill and late supplies left the colony short of food for years.

quiz.q: What did the Myall Creek massacre trial show?
o: Frontier violence ended soon after 1838
The courts regularly punished such killings
Colonists were rarely punished for such killings
No Aboriginal people were harmed in the colonies
quiz.e: Seven colonists were hanged, but massacres across the country mostly went unpunished.

quiz.q: Why do many Aboriginal people mark 26 January as a day of protest or survival?
o: It marks the beginning of dispossession
It celebrates the end of transportation
It was chosen by the 1967 referendum
It honours the Second Fleet
quiz.e: The date has been protested since the 1938 Day of Mourning, and Australians hold a range of views.

LESSONS.push: Why Britain chose a faraway continent for its convicts, and what it cost.

LESSONS.title: The gold rushes
LESSONS.hook: In the 1850s, gold transformed Australia almost overnight, nearly tripling its population and sparking its most famous rebellion.

sections.key: Gold finds in 1851 triggered rushes that nearly tripled Australia's population and made Melbourne rich.
sections.b: In February 1851, Edward Hargraves found gold near Bathurst in New South Wales. Within months, richer finds followed in the new colony of Victoria, at Ballarat, Bendigo and Mount Alexander. Shepherds, clerks, sailors and shopkeepers abandoned their jobs, and some ships in Melbourne's harbour were left stranded when their crews deserted. People poured in from Britain, Ireland, Europe, the United States and China. Australia's non-Indigenous population grew from about 430,000 in 1851 to over 1.1 million by 1861. Gold wealth paid for public buildings, railways and banks, and Melbourne earned the nickname 'Marvellous Melbourne' by the 1880s. Many newcomers brought ideas about democracy.

sections.key: Digging was hard and mostly unrewarding, and Chinese miners faced heavy discrimination.
sections.b:
Diggers lived in tents and bark huts, using picks, shovels, pans and cradles to wash gold from dirt. As surface gold ran out, they sank deep shafts, and later companies crushed quartz with machinery. Supplies were expensive and diseases like dysentery spread. A few struck it rich, like the 72-kilogram 'Welcome Stranger' nugget found at Moliagul in 1869. Most found little, and many made their fortunes by selling supplies, food and services to diggers.

By the late 1850s, around 40,000 Chinese people were in Victoria. Resentment led to violent attacks, like the Buckland River riot in 1857 and the Lambing Flat riots in NSW in 1860–61. Colonies imposed special taxes on Chinese arrivals, so many ships landed at Robe in South Australia instead. This hostility fed into the later White Australia policy.

sections.key: The 1854 Eureka Stockade rebellion over licence fees and voting rights helped win democratic reforms.
sections.b:
Miners paid an expensive monthly licence, 30 shillings at first, whether they found gold or not, and police conducted brutal 'licence hunts'. Diggers had no vote. Anger boiled over at Ballarat in 1854 after a hotel keeper was acquitted of killing a miner. Led by Peter Lalor, miners swore allegiance to the Southern Cross flag and built a rough stockade. Early on 3 December 1854, soldiers and police attacked; the fight lasted about 15 minutes, and around 30 people died, mostly miners.

Public sympathy swung behind the miners. Melbourne juries refused to convict 13 men charged with treason. The licence was replaced with a cheap miner's right that came with a vote, and Victoria introduced the secret ballot in 1856, which became known worldwide as the 'Australian ballot'.

sections.key: Gold rushes continued for decades, most famously in Queensland and Western Australia.
sections.b: Gold fever did not end with the 1850s. Finds at Gympie in 1867 helped rescue Queensland from debt, and the Palmer River rush in the 1870s drew thousands of Chinese miners to Cape York. In 1892 Arthur Bayley and William Ford found gold at Coolgardie in Western Australia, and in 1893 Paddy Hannan's find at Kalgoorlie started another stampede. Water was so scarce that engineer C. Y. O'Connor designed a pipeline of over 500 kilometres from near Perth, completed in 1903. The WA rush multiplied that colony's population, and many eastern miners there helped sway it towards joining Federation.

sections.key: Gold built cities and democracy, but at a heavy cost to Aboriginal peoples and the land.
sections.b: The rushes left grand streetscapes in towns like Ballarat, Bendigo and Beechworth, and Sovereign Hill in Ballarat recreates goldfields life for visitors. They also sped up the dispossession of Aboriginal peoples, such as the Wadawurrung around Ballarat and the Dja Dja Wurrung around Bendigo, whose lands and waterways were overrun and damaged. Digging and sluicing stripped forests and choked creeks with silt. Gold remains important: Australia is one of the world's largest gold producers, with much of it mined in Western Australia. In an old goldfields town, look for the Chinese joss houses, mullock heaps and ornate banks.

quiz.q: How did the gold rushes change Australia?
o: The population halved as many people left
Population nearly tripled and wealth grew
The colonies became noticeably poorer
Only Sydney felt any effect at all
quiz.e: Newcomers and gold wealth turned convict and pastoral colonies into a richer, more diverse society.

quiz.q: Who often made the most reliable fortunes on the goldfields?
o: Diggers who found large nuggets
Officials collecting licence fees
Farmers who left their land
Shopkeepers supplying the diggers
quiz.e: Most diggers found little, while suppliers earned steady profits.

quiz.q: How were Chinese miners treated on the goldfields?
o: They were welcomed and given free licences
They faced riots and special taxes
They were banned from every goldfield
They were given the best claims
quiz.e: Heavy discrimination, including riots and special taxes, fed into the later White Australia policy.

quiz.q: What drove the Eureka rebellion?
o: A shortage of gold in the Ballarat creeks
Competition from Chinese miners on claims
A government ban on digging near Ballarat
Costly licences, harsh policing and no vote
quiz.e: After Eureka, juries refused to convict and the miner's right came with a vote.

quiz.q: What is the main environmental cost of the rushes noted in the lesson?
o: Rainfall decreased across Victoria
Forests were stripped and creeks silted up
Ocean currents shifted along the coast
Every native animal was removed
quiz.e: Gold built cities and democracy but also damaged land and dispossessed Aboriginal peoples.

LESSONS.push: Ships sat abandoned in Melbourne's harbour as crews left for the goldfields.

LESSONS.title: Federation: how Australia became a nation
LESSONS.hook: Until 1901, 'Australia' was six separate British colonies with their own armies, stamps and tariffs. Then they voted to unite.

sections.key: Before 1901 the six colonies acted like separate countries, and defence, trade and identity pushed them together.
sections.b: By the late 1800s, New South Wales, Victoria, Queensland, South Australia, Western Australia and Tasmania each had their own parliament, laws, defence forces and postage stamps. They charged tariffs on goods crossing borders, and different railway gauges meant passengers and cargo changed trains at Albury. Britain still controlled foreign affairs. Supporters argued a united nation could defend itself better as powers expanded in the Pacific, and free trade would help business after the severe depression of the early 1890s. A national government could control immigration, a goal tragically tied to keeping Australia 'white'. By the 1890s most colonists were Australian-born, and identity grew through painters like Tom Roberts and poets like Henry Lawson and Banjo Paterson.

sections.key: Sir Henry Parkes drove the idea, ordinary citizens revived it, and voters approved the Constitution in referendums.
sections.b:
NSW Premier Henry Parkes, the father of Federation, called for a national government in his 1889 Tenterfield speech and chaired an 1891 convention that drafted a constitution. Momentum stalled, then ordinary citizens revived it: at Corowa in 1893, a proposal was made for the people to elect delegates to a new convention. Edmund Barton and Alfred Deakin were key figures.

Unusually, the Constitution was approved by voters in each colony. A first round in 1898 fell short in NSW, and after changes a second round passed in 1899. Western Australia joined last, in 1900. Only some could vote: in most colonies, women and many Aboriginal people were excluded. Queen Victoria gave royal assent in July 1900.

sections.key: The Commonwealth began on 1 January 1901 and divided power between the federal government and the states.
sections.b:
The new nation was proclaimed in Centennial Park, Sydney, before a crowd of perhaps 60,000 or more, and Edmund Barton became the first prime minister. Parliament met in Melbourne until Canberra, a compromise between Sydney and Melbourne designed by Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin, was ready in 1927. One of its first laws was the Immigration Restriction Act, the foundation of the White Australia policy.

The Constitution divided powers. The federal government handles defence, foreign affairs, trade, immigration and currency, mostly listed in section 51; states keep schools, hospitals, police and roads. A High Court settles disputes. The Senate gives each original state equal representation. Changing the Constitution needs a majority of voters nationally and in a majority of states, which is why only 8 of 45 proposals had passed by 2023.

sections.key: Federation made Australia a pioneer of votes for women while excluding most Aboriginal people.
sections.b: In some ways the new nation was a democratic pioneer. South Australia had given women the vote and the right to stand for parliament in 1894, a world first for standing. The Commonwealth Franchise Act of 1902 gave most women the right to vote and stand in federal elections, making Australia one of the first countries to do so. But the same Act excluded most Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, and not all Aboriginal Australians gained the federal vote until 1962. New Zealand took part in early federation talks and is even mentioned in the Constitution, but chose not to join.

sections.key: Knowing which level of government is responsible helps you get things done.
sections.b: Federation still shapes daily life. Australians vote in federal, state or territory and local elections, and local councils, though important, are not mentioned in the Constitution; referendums to recognise them failed in 1974 and 1988. The ACT and Northern Territory are territories, not states, so the federal parliament can override their laws, and each elects two senators, while each state elects twelve. When you have a problem, it helps to know who is responsible: Centrelink, passports and Medicare are federal; public hospitals, schools, driver licences and police are state matters; bins, local roads and building permits usually belong to councils.

quiz.q: What practical problem did different railway gauges cause between colonies?
o: Trains ran faster across colonial borders
Tickets became cheaper across the borders
Passengers and goods changed trains at borders
Rail travel was banned between colonies
quiz.e: Separate rules, tariffs and gauges showed the case for a single national system.

quiz.q: What made Australia's Constitution unusual for its time?
o: Voters in each colony approved it by referendum
It was imposed by the British Parliament alone
It was drafted by the colonial armies
It was approved by the colonial governors only
quiz.e: Ordinary citizens helped revive Federation and then voted to approve the Constitution.

quiz.q: Why have so few referendum proposals succeeded?
o: They need the personal approval of the Queen
They require a majority vote in the Senate only
They need a national majority and most states
They must be passed by every state parliament
quiz.e: Only 8 of 45 proposals had passed by 2023 because of this 'double majority' requirement.

quiz.q: Who could vote in federal elections after the 1902 Act?
o: Most women, but not most Aboriginal people
All adults, including all Aboriginal people
Men only, until women won the vote in 1962
Most Aboriginal people, but not most women
quiz.e: Australia was a pioneer for women's votes, yet the same Act excluded most Aboriginal people.

quiz.q: Who is generally responsible for public hospitals and schools?
o: The federal government
Local councils
State governments
The High Court
quiz.e: Knowing which level of government handles an issue helps you find the right help.

LESSONS.push: Australia once had six sets of rules, stamps and tariffs. Then came 1901.

LESSONS.title: Post-war Australia: migration and change
LESSONS.hook: 'Populate or perish.' After 1945, millions of migrants, the end of White Australia and new recognition of First Nations rights reshaped the country.

sections.key: After the 1942 bombing of Darwin, Australia launched a mass immigration programme that brought about three million people by the mid-1970s.
sections.b: The Japanese bombing of Darwin in 1942 convinced Australian leaders that a small population was a danger. They wanted more people for defence and industry. Immigration Minister Arthur Calwell's slogan was 'populate or perish', and a Department of Immigration was created in 1945. Australia first accepted about 170,000 displaced people from war-torn Europe. Large numbers of British, Italian, Greek, Dutch, German and Maltese migrants followed. Many British arrivals paid just ten pounds for the voyage, earning the nickname 'Ten Pound Poms'. Between 1945 and the mid-1970s, roughly three million migrants arrived, many of them to work on nation-building projects.

sections.key: The Snowy Scheme was built by workers from over 30 countries and became a symbol of post-war ambition and multicultural Australia.
sections.b: The biggest of those projects was the Snowy Mountains Hydro-Electric Scheme. Built between 1949 and 1974, it has 16 major dams, seven power stations and about 145 kilometres of tunnels. It diverts water from the Snowy River westward through the mountains, generating electricity and supplying irrigation water to the Murray and Murrumbidgee river systems. More than 100,000 people from over 30 countries worked on it, many of them recent migrants who had been on opposite sides in the war. More than 100 workers died during construction. It became a symbol of post-war ambition and an emerging multicultural society, and it is still a major source of renewable electricity.

sections.key: The White Australia policy was dismantled between the 1950s and 1973, and migration became far more diverse.
sections.b: Since 1901, the White Australia policy had restricted non-European immigration. Officials could set a 50-word dictation test in any European language, designed to be failed. The policy eased gradually. The Colombo Plan brought thousands of Asian students to Australian universities, the test was abolished in 1958, and the Holt government loosened restrictions in 1966. In 1973, the Whitlam government removed race as a factor in immigration selection. The Fraser government accepted tens of thousands of Vietnamese refugees in the late 1970s and 80s. Multiculturalism became official policy and SBS television began in 1980. Today about 30% of Australians were born overseas, roughly half have a parent who was, and over 300 languages are spoken at home.

sections.key: The 1967 referendum was a powerful symbol that later underpinned land rights, which Mabo then transformed by recognising native title.
sections.b: The 1967 referendum removed two discriminatory references from the Constitution: one excluded Aboriginal people from population counts, and the other stopped the Commonwealth making laws for them. About 90.8% voted yes, the highest result of any referendum. It did not give Aboriginal people citizenship or the vote, which they already had in law federally from 1962. Instead it was a symbol of support that later underpinned land rights and heritage laws. Activism grew. Gurindji stockmen led by Vincent Lingiari walked off Wave Hill in 1966, first over pay and then over land, and in 1975 Gough Whitlam poured soil into Lingiari's hand. The Tent Embassy rose in Canberra in 1972. In 1992, months after Eddie Mabo's death, the High Court's Mabo decision rejected terra nullius and recognised native title.

sections.key: Australia has faced its history through the Bringing Them Home report, the 2008 Apology and the failed 2023 Voice referendum, while debate continues.
sections.b: The 1997 Bringing Them Home report documented the Stolen Generations, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children forcibly removed from their families by governments and churches. It estimated that between one in three and one in ten children were taken between 1910 and 1970. About 250,000 people walked across Sydney Harbour Bridge for reconciliation in 2000, and Kevin Rudd delivered a formal National Apology in February 2008. The 2017 Uluru Statement from the Heart called for a First Nations Voice. A 2023 referendum on a Voice to Parliament was defeated, with about 60% voting no, and debate about treaties and truth-telling continues. Wider change came too: equal pay decisions in 1969 and 1972, the Sydney Opera House in 1973, no-fault divorce in 1975, and Medicare in 1984.

quiz.q: Why did Australian leaders push for a much bigger population after World War II?
o: Fear of invasion, as shown by Darwin, made defence a priority
Gold discoveries created a shortage of workers in the mines and towns
Britain required Australia to take a fixed number of migrants each year
Farmland had been abandoned and needed new settlers to farm it
quiz.e: The wartime scare of invasion convinced leaders that Australia needed more people to defend and build the country.

quiz.q: What made the Snowy Mountains Scheme a symbol of post-war Australia?
o: It was a ski resort built to attract tourists from overseas
Workers from over 30 countries, many recent migrants, built it
It was the first project funded entirely by private investors
It was built almost entirely by Australian-born workers
quiz.e: The Snowy Scheme showed post-war ambition and a society being reshaped by migrants.

quiz.q: How did the Whitlam government change immigration in 1973?
o: It brought back the dictation test for some applicants
It capped migration from Asia at a fixed number
It removed race as a factor in immigration selection
It limited entry to refugees only
quiz.e: Removing race from selection in 1973 ended the last formal pillar of White Australia.

quiz.q: What did the 1967 referendum actually do?
o: Gave Aboriginal people citizenship for the first time in Australia
Gave Aboriginal people the right to vote in federal elections
Returned traditional lands to Aboriginal owners across the country
Removed two discriminatory references from the Constitution
quiz.e: The 1967 vote was a symbol of national support and a legal step, not the moment Aboriginal people gained citizenship or the vote.

quiz.q: What did the Bringing Them Home report document?
o: Aboriginal children denied access to schooling in remote areas
Children forcibly removed from their families by governments and churches
Land taken from Aboriginal communities for mining and farming
British child migrants sent to Australia after the war
quiz.e: The report documented the Stolen Generations, a key part of the reckoning with Australia's past.

LESSONS.push: Fear of invasion reshaped who Australians are. Here's how it unfolded.

LESSONS.title: Psychology's most famous experiments
LESSONS.hook: Prisons in basements, marshmallows and fake patients. The studies everyone's heard of, and what they really showed.

sections.key: Famous studies deserve scrutiny, because psychology's replication crisis showed that striking findings often don't hold up when repeated.
sections.b: Some psychology experiments became famous because they told a striking story: that ordinary people can turn cruel, or that a child's self-control predicts their future. They shape textbooks, films and how people think about human nature. But since the early 2010s psychology has faced a 'replication crisis'. In a major 2015 project, teams repeated 100 published studies and got clearly similar results in well under half of them. Good signs in research include large samples, pre-registered methods (a public plan made in advance), shared data and results that independent teams reproduce. Looking closely at famous studies teaches two lessons at once: what they suggest about people, and how careful good science needs to be.

sections.key: The Stanford prison experiment and Rosenhan's fake-patient study are now widely doubted.
sections.b: In 1971, Philip Zimbardo turned a Stanford basement into a mock prison, with male student volunteers randomly assigned as guards or prisoners. Some guards became cruel and the study stopped after six days. It was long used to argue that situations alone turn good people bad. Later investigations found guards were encouraged to be tough and some behaviour was performed for the researchers. A 2002 BBC prison study saw no guard tyranny. In 1973, David Rosenhan reported that eight healthy people went to 12 US psychiatric hospitals claiming to hear voices saying 'empty' and 'hollow'. All were admitted and stayed about 19 days. In 2019, journalist Susannah Cahalan found details that didn't match his notes, and she could trace only two of the pseudopatients.

sections.key: The marshmallow test's link to later success mostly faded once family background was accounted for.
sections.b: In the late 1960s and 1970s, Walter Mischel offered preschoolers at a Stanford nursery a choice: one treat now, or two if they waited alone for up to about 15 minutes. Follow-ups years later suggested children who waited longer did better at school, making it a famous story about willpower. But a larger 2018 replication with a more diverse group of children found a much weaker link, and most of it disappeared after accounting for family income and home background. Another study found children waited far less when an adult had just broken a promise to them. Waiting less can be a rational choice when promised rewards don't always arrive.

sections.key: Little Albert and Harlow's monkeys taught lasting lessons, but their harm to subjects shows why research ethics rules exist.
sections.b: Two classics show why ethics rules exist. John B. Watson and Rosalie Rayner wanted to show that fear could be learned. They struck a steel bar behind an infant, known as Little Albert, whenever he reached for a white rat. Soon he cried at the rat and seemed wary of similar furry things. It supported classical conditioning in humans, but it involved one child, was poorly documented, and his fear was never removed. Even his identity is debated. In the 1950s, Harry Harlow raised infant rhesus monkeys with two artificial mothers: bare wire with milk, or soft cloth without. The babies clung to the cloth mother and visited the wire one mainly to feed. Attachment isn't just about food. But isolated monkeys were badly harmed, fuelling debate about animal research.

sections.key: Loftus's findings on misleading questions have been repeated many times, so ask how many took part and whether anyone replicated a study.
sections.b: Not every famous study has crumbled. In 1974, Elizabeth Loftus and John Palmer showed people a film of a car crash, then asked how fast the cars were going when they 'smashed' or 'hit' each other. The 'smashed' group gave higher estimates. A week later, about a third of them said they had seen broken glass, compared with roughly one in seven of the 'hit' group. There was none. Research on misleading questions has been repeated many times and has changed how police are advised to interview witnesses. Classical conditioning and the spacing effect also replicate well. When you hear 'a study shows', ask how many people took part, whether anyone has repeated it, and whether the story sounds a little too neat.

quiz.q: What does psychology's 'replication crisis' mean for famous studies?
o: Most famous studies were exposed as deliberate fraud
Psychologists stopped running experiments on people
Many findings didn't hold up when others repeated them
Nearly all famous findings were confirmed when repeated
quiz.e: Repeating studies showed that striking findings are not always reliable, which is why replication matters.

quiz.q: Why do many psychologists now treat the Stanford prison experiment as a cautionary tale?
o: Its guards were all trained and experienced prison officers
Guards were encouraged to be tough and some played a part
The volunteers were too tired after six days to behave naturally at all
A later study using the same basement prison reversed its results completely
quiz.e: Guards were nudged towards cruelty, so the study cannot show that situations alone turn good people bad.

quiz.q: What did the larger 2018 marshmallow replication find?
o: A stronger link between waiting and later success in life
That no child was able to wait longer than a single minute
That children waited longer when promised even bigger rewards
A much weaker link, mostly explained by family background
quiz.e: Much of the apparent link between waiting and success reflected children's backgrounds, not willpower alone.

quiz.q: What did Harlow's monkeys show about attachment?
o: Babies bond with whoever feeds them
Babies want comfort and contact, not only food
Babies show no preference between caregivers
Babies prefer isolation to contact
quiz.e: The babies clung to the soft cloth mother, showing attachment depends on comfort as well as food.

quiz.q: What did Loftus and Palmer's 'smashed' versus 'hit' wording show?
o: Witnesses to car crashes always remember speeds accurately
The wording of a question can change what people remember seeing
Memories cannot be changed after a week has passed
People remember violent events better than calm ones
quiz.e: Leading questions can alter memory, a finding that has been repeated many times.

LESSONS.push: The studies everyone knows may be less solid than the story suggests.

LESSONS.title: Personality: the Big Five
LESSONS.hook: Forget star signs and most online quizzes. Psychologists measure personality with five traits, and they predict real things about your life.

sections.key: Decades of research settled on five broad personality spectrums, remembered as OCEAN, that stay stable on retest and predict real outcomes.
sections.b: When people describe themselves and others, the words cluster into a few broad dimensions. Decades of research across many cultures settled on five: openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness and neuroticism, remembered as OCEAN. Each is a spectrum, not a box, and most people sit near the middle on most traits. The model grew from the lexical hypothesis: if a difference matters, languages will have words for it. In 1936, Gordon Allport and Henry Odbert found about 18,000 English words describing people. Statistics boiled them down to the same five clusters, and questionnaires built in the 1980s and 90s are still used. Scores stay similar on retest and predict real outcomes, from job performance to health. Some researchers argue for a sixth factor, honesty-humility.

sections.key: Conscientiousness is among the best personality predictors of success and health, and introversion is not the same as shyness.
sections.b: People high in openness love new ideas, art, travel and abstract thinking; lower scorers prefer the familiar and practical. Openness is linked to creativity and, on average, more liberal attitudes. Conscientiousness means being organised, reliable and hardworking. It is among the best personality predictors of success at school and work, and it is linked to better health and a longer life, perhaps because conscientious people exercise, avoid risks and follow medical advice. Very high levels can tip into perfectionism and inflexibility. Extraverts are talkative, energetic and energised by company, and tend to feel more positive emotion. Introverts prefer quieter settings and recharge alone. That differs from shyness, which is anxiety about social judgement.

sections.key: Neither end of a trait is simply good or bad, and high neuroticism is a tendency, not a diagnosis.
sections.b: Agreeableness describes kindness, trust, modesty and cooperation. Highly agreeable people avoid conflict and put others first; lower scorers are more competitive, sceptical and blunt. Neither end is simply good: a negotiator, critic or auditor may benefit from lower agreeableness. People high in neuroticism, or low in emotional stability, feel stress, worry, sadness and irritation more often and more intensely. Low scorers stay calm under pressure. High neuroticism is linked to a higher risk of anxiety and depression, but it isn't a diagnosis, and its caution can help, such as noticing risks others miss. Exercise, good sleep and cognitive behavioural therapy can help manage it. If worry or low mood is affecting daily life, a GP is a good first step.

sections.key: Traits predict life outcomes and are partly heritable, but they shift gradually, with people tending to mature over time.
sections.b: Personality isn't destiny, but it adds up. A well-known 2007 review by Brent Roberts and colleagues found that traits predicted how long people live, divorce and career success about as well as family income or intelligence did. Conscientiousness predicts job performance in most occupations, and lower neuroticism and higher agreeableness go with more satisfying relationships. Each link is modest for one person, but the patterns are consistent. Twin studies suggest roughly 40-60% of the variation between people is linked to genes, yet personality isn't fixed. From young adulthood to middle age, people tend to become more conscientious and agreeable and less neurotic, the 'maturity principle'. Specific goals and repeated practice can shift traits gradually.

sections.key: Myers-Briggs forces either-or types and often gives different results on retest, so a Big Five test is a more accurate mirror.
sections.b: The Myers-Briggs Type Indicator was developed in the 1940s by Katharine Cook Briggs and her daughter Isabel Briggs Myers, based on Carl Jung's ideas. It sorts people into 16 types, like INTJ or ESFP, and is popular in workplaces. But psychologists criticise it. It forces people into either-or categories when most sit near the middle, and many people get a different type when retested weeks later. Star signs don't predict personality at all in studies. If you're curious, a free Big Five test from a university research site is a more accurate mirror.

quiz.q: Why are the Big Five traits described as spectrums?
o: People swap between opposite traits from day to day
Each trait is scored only as high or low
Most people sit near the middle of each scale
Only people with extreme personalities have these traits
quiz.e: Each trait is a scale, and most people sit near the middle on most of them.

quiz.q: How does introversion differ from shyness?
o: Introverts dislike all people, while shy people enjoy company
Introverts are anxious about judgement, while shy people recharge alone
There is no real difference between the two, as they mean the same
Introverts recharge alone, while shy people fear social judgement
quiz.e: Introversion is about where you recharge, while shyness is about fear of being judged.

quiz.q: What does high neuroticism mean?
o: A diagnosed anxiety disorder needing treatment
Being unusually calm and steady under pressure
A tendency to feel stress and worry more often
Having little concern for other people's feelings
quiz.e: Neuroticism describes a tendency towards stronger negative emotion, and it can come with useful caution.

quiz.q: What is the 'maturity principle'?
o: Personality traits are fixed by around age 25 and rarely change
People become more neurotic as they approach middle age
Mature people score highly on every one of the five traits
People tend to grow more conscientious and calmer with age
quiz.e: Personality changes gradually, and the typical direction is towards more conscientiousness and calm.

quiz.q: Why do psychologists criticise Myers-Briggs?
o: Its either-or types often change on retest
It is too new to have been studied by researchers
It sorts people according to their star signs
It measures only one trait of personality
quiz.e: Most people sit near the middle on traits, so forced types are unreliable and often shift on retest.

LESSONS.push: Your star sign says nothing, but five traits say a surprising amount.

LESSONS.title: First impressions
LESSONS.hook: People judge your trustworthiness from your face in a tenth of a second. Here's what drives snap judgements, and how accurate they are.

sections.key: We form impressions of faces in about a tenth of a second, and they can sway real decisions such as votes.
sections.b: In a 2006 study, Princeton researchers Janine Willis and Alexander Todorov showed people unfamiliar faces for just 100 milliseconds. Their ratings of trustworthiness, likeability, attractiveness and competence were very similar to ratings made with no time limit. More time mainly made people more confident, not different. The amygdala, a brain region that detects threats, also responds to untrustworthy-looking faces when people aren't judging at all. In a 2005 study, people shown pairs of faces of winning and losing US congressional candidates for about a second picked the one who looked more competent; that candidate had actually won about 70% of the time. There is little evidence such faces make better politicians, so voters who know little may simply be swayed by appearance.

sections.key: One good trait, or one early word like 'warm', can colour everything else we assume about a person.
sections.b: If someone is good-looking, we tend to assume they are also kinder, smarter and more competent. This is the halo effect, named by Edward Thorndike in 1920 after army officers rated soldiers good in one respect as good in almost everything. It works in reverse too, the 'horns effect'. It shows up in job interviews, school marking and even courtrooms, which is why many employers use structured interviews and blind marking. In 1946, Solomon Asch found that swapping one word in a trait list, 'warm' for 'cold', dramatically changed how people imagined someone. In 1950, Harold Kelley's students expecting a 'rather warm' guest lecturer rated him more favourably. What we hear before meeting someone can shape the impression before they speak.

sections.key: We judge warmth first and competence second, and you can signal both through simple, genuine habits.
sections.b: Susan Fiske and colleagues suggest we size people up on two dimensions: warmth (do they mean well towards me?) and competence (can they act on it?). Warmth is usually judged first, because intentions matter most for our safety. Warm but less competent earns pity; competent but cold, envy; both, admiration. You can't control your face, but you can control a lot. A genuine smile, open posture, using people's names and real interest in the other person signal warmth quickly. Clear, confident speech signals competence. Be on time, match the setting's dress norms, make comfortable eye contact and put your phone away.

sections.key: Some snap judgements are surprisingly accurate, but face-based judgements of character are often wrong and shaped by stereotypes.
sections.b: Some snap judgements hold up. In 'thin-slicing' research by Nalini Ambady and Robert Rosenthal, strangers watching short silent clips of university teachers predicted end-of-semester student ratings surprisingly well. People can also guess extraversion fairly accurately from brief encounters. But face-based judgements of trustworthiness or competence often don't match reality, and they are heavily shaped by stereotypes about gender, race, age and attractiveness. A 'baby face', with large eyes and a round face, tends to make people seem warmer and more naive, though it has nothing to do with character. Different photos of the same person can also produce very different impressions.

sections.key: Early information shapes how we read everything after it, so impressions are hard to change and best treated as a guess.
sections.b: Early information shapes how we interpret everything after it, the primacy effect. In a classic finding by Solomon Asch, people told someone is 'intelligent, industrious, impulsive, critical, stubborn and envious' viewed them more positively than people given the same words in reverse order. We then tend to notice information that confirms our view and explain away what doesn't, a form of confirmation bias. Our impressions can even change how we treat people, which changes how they behave back, making the impression seem correct. That's why it usually takes much more evidence to change an impression than to form one. Notice your own snap judgement, ask what it's based on, and give people a second chance. The first impression is a guess, not a verdict.

quiz.q: What did Willis and Todorov find about judging faces?
o: People needed several seconds before their ratings settled
Longer viewing made the ratings far more accurate
Snap ratings closely matched ratings with no time limit
Ratings differed completely from one viewer to the next
quiz.e: Snap judgements of faces form almost instantly, and more time mainly adds confidence.

quiz.q: What is the halo effect?
o: Trusting people who happen to share your opinions
Judging people more harshly when you are tired
Forgetting everything about someone except their face
Assuming other good qualities from one appealing trait
quiz.e: One positive trait, such as good looks, can lead us to assume other good qualities without evidence.

quiz.q: Which dimension do we usually judge first, and why?
o: Competence, because ability matters most for getting things done
Warmth, because someone's intentions matter most for our safety
Status, because rank decides who we should obey
Age, because older people are more trustworthy
quiz.e: We first ask whether someone means well, then whether they can act on it.

quiz.q: Why can face-based snap judgements mislead us?
o: They are shaped by stereotypes more than by character
They take so long that we forget the first look
They are always accurate for adults but not children
They depend entirely on how well we know the person
quiz.e: Appearance cues such as a baby face and stereotypes can bias our judgements without telling us about character.

quiz.q: Why does it usually take more evidence to change an impression than to form one?
o: People forget what they first learned about someone
Early information shapes how we read later information
Impressions are usually correct, so they rarely need changing at all
New information is always less reliable than old information
quiz.e: The primacy effect and confirmation bias make early impressions stubborn.

LESSONS.push: You judge a stranger's face in a tenth of a second. How reliable is that?

LESSONS.title: Conformity: why we follow the crowd
LESSONS.hook: Would you say a clearly shorter line was longer, just because everyone else did? In a famous experiment, many people did.

sections.key: In Asch's experiment, about three-quarters of people went along with a group's clearly wrong answer at least once.
sections.b: In the early 1950s, Solomon Asch asked American college students to judge which of three lines matched a reference line, a task so easy that people alone almost never erred. But each participant sat in a group whose other members were secretly working with the experimenter, and on certain rounds they all gave the same wrong answer aloud. About three-quarters of participants went along with the wrong answer at least once, and overall about a third of responses on those rounds matched the group. Yet about a quarter never conformed at all. Many who conformed later said they doubted their own eyes.

sections.key: We conform to fit in and because we assume the group knows more, and both are often sensible.
sections.b: Psychologists distinguish two pressures. Normative influence is wanting to fit in and avoid rejection: we go along in public even when we privately disagree, as many of Asch's participants did. Informational influence is believing the group has better information, especially in unfamiliar situations: if everyone is hurrying out of a building, you probably should too. Both are often sensible. Humans evolved in small groups where exclusion could be dangerous, and copying others is a fast, cheap way to learn what's safe and how to behave. Brain imaging studies suggest that learning your opinion differs from the group's triggers activity in regions linked to detecting errors, so standing apart feels uncomfortable. The details are still debated.

sections.key: A single ally breaks the group's pull, and a lone dissenting voice matters more than it seems.
sections.b: In Asch's variations, when just one other person gave the correct answer, conformity fell to a small fraction of its usual level. Even an ally who gave a different wrong answer broke the group's spell, because the participant was no longer alone. Group size mattered only up to a point: conformity rose as the group grew to three or four people, then levelled off, so a crowd of fifteen wasn't much more persuasive than a handful. Answering privately, in writing, also reduced conformity a great deal. The lesson: a lone dissenting voice matters more than it seems.

sections.key: Social proof can spread good or bad behaviour, and how much people conform varies across cultures.
sections.b: Marketers use social proof constantly: 'bestseller', star ratings, queues outside restaurants and laugh tracks on sitcoms. In a well-known 2008 study, hotel guests reused towels more when a card said most guests in that room had done so. Governments use the same idea, for example by telling people most others pay their tax on time. It can spread good behaviour, but also fads, panic buying and misinformation, as the toilet paper rush in 2020 showed. A 1996 review by Rod Bond and Peter Smith of over 130 Asch-style studies from 17 countries found higher conformity in collectivist cultures than in individualist ones like Australia, the United States or the UK. Conformity in the US also appeared to have fallen since the 1950s.

sections.key: Following norms usually helps, but when a group is mistaken, speaking up calmly may help someone else do the same.
sections.b: Conformity is not fixed. In 1980, Stephen Perrin and Christopher Spencer repeated the line task with British science and engineering students and found almost no conformity, suggesting Asch's results were partly 'a child of its time', shaped by 1950s America. Other repeats found conformity again, so context matters. Most of the time, following norms keeps society running: queuing, driving on the left, keeping quiet in a library. The danger comes when the group is mistaken or doing harm, and nobody wants to be first to say so. In meetings, ask people to write down their views before any discussion, so early speakers don't sway the rest. If you disagree, say so calmly and clearly. You may be the ally someone else is waiting for.

quiz.q: What happened in Asch's line experiment?
o: Almost everyone followed the group's wrong answer on every round
Hardly anyone ever followed the group's wrong answer
Only participants unsure of the lines followed the group
About three-quarters went along with the group at least once
quiz.e: Even on an easy task, most people conformed at least once, though many stayed independent.

quiz.q: What is informational influence?
o: Going along in public to avoid rejection while disagreeing privately
Going along because you believe the group knows more than you do
Changing your view after reading the news
Copying others only when a situation is certain
quiz.e: Informational influence is trusting the group's knowledge, especially when a situation is uncertain.

quiz.q: What most reduced conformity in Asch's variations?
o: Making the group much larger
Offering participants a reward for accuracy
Making the comparison lines easier to see
Having one other person give the correct answer
quiz.e: A single ally breaks the group's pull, so one dissenting voice matters.

quiz.q: Why does a hotel card saying most guests reuse their towels work?
o: People treat others' behaviour as a guide
People are afraid of being fined
People dislike reading environmental messages
People enjoy being observed by staff
quiz.e: Social proof makes us use others' behaviour as evidence of what's right.

quiz.q: How can a team stop early speakers from swaying everyone in a meeting?
o: Let the most senior person speak first
Ask people to write down their views before any discussion
Hold the meeting with as large a group as possible
Take a vote by show of hands straight away
quiz.e: Writing views privately first reduces the pull of the group, as Asch's private answers did.

LESSONS.push: Would you doubt your own eyes if everyone else disagreed? Many people did.

LESSONS.title: Obedience: the Milgram experiments
LESSONS.hook: Ordinary people were told to give electric shocks to a stranger. Most kept going. What this tells us, and doesn't, about obeying authority.

sections.key: Milgram set out to test how far ordinary people would obey an authority figure who told them to hurt someone, and experts badly underestimated it.
sections.b: In 1961, Nazi official Adolf Eichmann was on trial in Jerusalem, claiming he had only followed orders. That year, Yale psychologist Stanley Milgram began studying how far ordinary people would obey an authority who asked them to hurt someone. He recruited men from New Haven through newspaper ads and paid them about four dollars. Volunteers played 'teacher' and were told to shock a 'learner' for each wrong answer, in 15-volt steps up to 450 volts. The learner was an actor who received no shocks but protested, screamed and then fell silent. If the teacher hesitated, a stern experimenter used scripted prompts, ending with 'You have no other choice, you must go on.' Psychiatrists predicted perhaps one in a thousand would go all the way.

sections.key: In the best-known version, about 65% went to the maximum shock, apparently seeing themselves as carrying out an authority's wishes.
sections.b: In the most famous version, 26 of 40 men, about 65%, continued to the maximum shock. Many were visibly distressed: sweating, trembling, stuttering, laughing nervously and pleading to stop, yet continuing. Some asked who would take responsibility if the learner was hurt, and were told the experimenter would. Milgram concluded that ordinary people can do terrible things when they feel an authority has taken responsibility. He called this the agentic state, where people see themselves as instruments carrying out someone else's wishes rather than acting on their own.

sections.key: Distance, closeness and social support changed obedience dramatically, and knowledge helped nurses resist a doctor's order.
sections.b: Milgram ran around 20 variations, and small changes made big differences. When orders came by phone, full obedience fell to just over 20%. When the teacher had to press the learner's hand onto a shock plate, it fell to about 30%. When two other 'teachers', actually actors, refused to continue, only about 10% went all the way. Moving the study from prestigious Yale to a run-down office building lowered obedience only to just under half. In 1966, Charles Hofling had an unknown 'doctor' phone nurses and order a dose twice the labelled maximum, against hospital rules. Of 22 nurses, 21 were stopped on their way to give it. A 1977 study with a familiar drug, where nurses could consult colleagues, saw almost all refuse.

sections.key: The study raised ethical problems and its interpretation is debated, but the core finding has held up reasonably well.
sections.b: The study caused participants serious stress, and today's ethics rules wouldn't allow it in its original form. Australian psychologist Gina Perry, studying Milgram's archives, found the experimenter sometimes went off script and pushed harder than reported, and some participants doubted the shocks were real. Alex Haslam and Stephen Reicher argue people continued not from blind obedience but because they identified with the scientific goal, since direct orders like 'You have no other choice' tended to make people stop. Milgram also ran a version with 40 women and found the same 65%. In 2009, Jerry Burger stopped at 150 volts, where the learner first demands release, and about 70% were willing to continue. A 2017 Polish study found similar results.

sections.key: Harmful acts often come from ordinary people in pushing situations, so institutions build checks, and one person refusing makes it easier for others.
sections.b: Milgram's work reminds us that harmful acts often come from ordinary people in situations that push them, not only from monsters. That's why institutions build in checks: militaries teach that clearly illegal orders must be refused, hospitals encourage nurses to question doctors, airlines train junior pilots to challenge captains, and workplaces set up whistleblower protections. It helps to notice when you're telling yourself 'it's not my responsibility'. The variation where others refused is the hopeful part: one person saying no, out loud, makes it much easier for everyone else in the room to do the same.

quiz.q: How did experts' predictions compare with what Milgram found?
o: Experts expected about two-thirds to obey, and they were right
Experts expected half to refuse at the first protest
Experts expected very few to go all the way, but about 65% did
Experts expected everyone to obey, and most did not
quiz.e: People, including experts, underestimated how far ordinary participants would go under authority.

quiz.q: What does the 'agentic state' describe?
o: Feeling free to choose your own actions
Acting on a strong personal grudge
Following a plan you designed yourself
Acting as an instrument of an authority
quiz.e: When people feel an authority holds responsibility, they can act against their own conscience.

quiz.q: Which change most reduced obedience in Milgram's variations?
o: Offering the teachers a lot more money
Making the learner's screams much louder
Two other 'teachers' refusing to go on
Using a younger experimenter
quiz.e: Seeing others refuse cut full obedience to about 10%, showing the power of social support.

quiz.q: Why do some researchers question the idea of blind obedience in Milgram's study?
o: The learner really did receive the shocks
All participants refused the very first order
The experiment was never repeated anywhere in the world
People may have identified with the scientific goal
quiz.e: Debate continues over interpretation, though the core finding has largely held up.

quiz.q: What is the hopeful lesson of the variation where others refused?
o: One person saying no makes it easier for others to do the same
Nobody can ever resist an authority figure alone
Groups always make better moral decisions than individuals
Orders should always be given and followed in writing
quiz.e: A single refusal, said out loud, can break the pressure to obey for everyone else.

LESSONS.push: How far would you go if a calm authority told you to continue?

LESSONS.title: The bystander effect
LESSONS.hook: When someone needs help, a crowd can make each person less likely to act. Understanding why could make you the one who does.

sections.key: The Kitty Genovese '38 witnesses' story was badly exaggerated, but it led psychologists to study when and why people help.
sections.b: In March 1964, Kitty Genovese was murdered outside her apartment in Queens, New York. Two weeks later, The New York Times reported that 38 neighbours had watched and done nothing, and the story shocked the world. Later investigations found the report was badly exaggerated. Far fewer people saw the attack, many only heard noises they didn't understand, at least one person called police, and a neighbour went down and held her as she was dying. But the story, true or not, prompted psychologists John Darley and Bibb Latané to study carefully when and why people help.

sections.key: Crowds stop us helping through pluralistic ignorance, where everyone looks calm, and diffusion of responsibility, where everyone assumes someone else will act.
sections.b: In a 1968 experiment, students filled in questionnaires as smoke poured through a vent. Alone, about three-quarters reported it. With two strangers, actors told to ignore it, only about 1 in 10 did. Afterwards, many said they'd decided it was steam or harmless. This is pluralistic ignorance: everyone looks calm, so everyone concludes nothing is wrong. In another 1968 study, participants heard a student apparently having a seizure. Those who thought they were the only listener almost always went for help, about 85% before the seizure ended. Those who thought four others could also hear helped less often and more slowly, with only about a third acting that fast. This is diffusion of responsibility: everyone assumes someone else will act.

sections.key: Helping needs five decisions, and everyday pressures such as being in a hurry can matter more than good values.
sections.b: Darley and Latané described a chain of decisions: notice the event, interpret it as an emergency, decide it's your responsibility, know what to do, and decide to help. Crowds interfere at every step. We're distracted, we look to others to judge how serious it is, we assume someone else will act, and we fear embarrassment if we've misread things. First aid training helps at the 'know how' step. In a 1973 study by Darley and Daniel Batson, seminary students walked to give a talk, some on the Good Samaritan, and passed a man slumped in a doorway, groaning. Only about 10% of those told they were running late stopped, against about 63% of those with time to spare. The talk's topic made little difference.

sections.key: The effect is weaker in obvious emergencies, and real-world footage shows someone usually steps in.
sections.b: A 2011 review led by Peter Fischer combined more than 50 bystander papers, covering over 7,000 people. It confirmed the bystander effect but found it weaker when an emergency was clearly dangerous, such as a violent attack. In obvious danger, other bystanders become physical backup rather than a reason to hold back. And a large 2019 study led by Richard Philpot analysed surveillance footage of about 200 public disputes in the UK, the Netherlands and South Africa. In around 90% of incidents at least one bystander stepped in, and more bystanders meant a higher chance someone would help. On real streets, people are more helpful than the Genovese story suggests.

sections.key: If you need help, point at one person and give them a task, and if you're a bystander, don't treat others' calm as proof nothing is wrong.
sections.b: If you need help, don't just shout into the crowd. Point at one person: 'You in the blue shirt, call 000.' That removes the ambiguity and hands responsibility to one person. If you're a bystander, remind yourself that others' calm isn't evidence nothing is wrong: they may be waiting for you. Ask the person if they're okay, and if in doubt, call 000. A first aid course, offered widely in Australia, builds the confidence to act. Research suggests that simply learning about the bystander effect makes people more likely to help, so you're already better prepared.

quiz.q: What did later investigations find about the Kitty Genovese '38 witnesses' story?
o: It was accurate in every detail
It was exaggerated, and some neighbours helped
It was invented and no murder took place
It showed that nobody called the police
quiz.e: The story was exaggerated, but it still sparked valuable research on helping.

quiz.q: Why did most students with calm actors in the room not report the smoke?
o: They did not notice the smoke at all
They were told to stay seated
Others looked calm, so they assumed all was well
They wanted to finish the questionnaire first
quiz.e: Pluralistic ignorance means that when everyone seems calm, we assume there is no emergency.

quiz.q: What mattered more than the topic of the talk in whether seminary students stopped to help?
o: How long they had studied theology
Whether they were walking alone or in pairs
Whether they believed they were running late
How loudly the man groaned
quiz.e: Everyday pressures such as being rushed can outweigh good values in whether we help.

quiz.q: What did the 2019 surveillance study find about real public disputes?
o: Bystanders almost never intervened
Someone intervened in about 90% of incidents
Only police officers intervened
Larger crowds always made things worse
quiz.e: More bystanders mean more potential helpers, so real streets are kinder than the myth suggests.

quiz.q: What is the best way to get help from a crowd?
o: Call out to the whole crowd as loudly as possible
Wait quietly for someone to notice
Film the situation to prove what happened
Point at one specific person and give them a clear task
quiz.e: Naming one person removes ambiguity and gives them responsibility.

LESSONS.push: A crowd can make each person less likely to help. Here's how to beat that.

LESSONS.title: Groupthink
LESSONS.hook: Smart people in a room together can make spectacularly bad decisions. Here's how it happens and how to stop it.

sections.key: In groupthink, the wish for agreement is so strong that members stop questioning ideas, as happened at the Bay of Pigs.
sections.b: William Whyte coined the term in 1952, and psychologist Irving Janis developed the theory in his 1972 book 'Victims of Groupthink'. In groupthink, members care so much about agreement and loyalty that they stop questioning ideas, ignore warnings and fail to consider alternatives. Each person may have private doubts but stays quiet, assuming everyone else is on board. In April 1961, President John F.
