Primes were a curiosity for over 2,000 years before securing the internet. Imaginary numbers, once seen as a trick, are essential in electrical engineering and quantum physics. In 1960 Eugene Wigner called this 'the unreasonable effectiveness of mathematics'.

quiz.q: Why do sunflower seed spirals often follow Fibonacci numbers?
o: The plant counts the numbers on purpose
It is a coincidence of petal count
Fibonacci planted the first sunflowers
Efficient packing as the plant grows
quiz.e: The pattern comes from efficient packing, not magic.

quiz.q: What was the key step India added to the idea of zero?
o: Using a placeholder for an empty position
Using zero only in calendars
Treating zero as a true number
Rejecting negative numbers
quiz.e: Placeholders existed earlier, but treating zero as a true number came from India.

quiz.q: Why do primes matter for online security?
o: Multiplying primes is easy; recovering them is hard
Primes are easy to guess from short passwords
Primes can be divided evenly by any number
Every encryption key is made from an even prime
quiz.e: RSA relies on this one-way difficulty.

quiz.q: What is the best summary of the golden ratio in art and nature?
o: It was used to design the Parthenon and the Mona Lisa
It appears exactly in the spiral of a nautilus shell
It is interesting, but many claims are myths
It is exactly 1.5 and is found in all great art
quiz.e: Many claims rest on after-the-fact measurements that happen to fit.

quiz.q: What does Hilbert's Hotel show about infinity?
o: An infinite hotel can never be full
A full hotel can still fit one more
Infinity is the largest whole number
Adding a guest always removes one
quiz.e: Infinity behaves strangely: everyone shifts up one room and room 1 is free.

LESSONS.push: Pythagoras may not have proved his own theorem. What else is misattributed in maths?

LESSONS.title: Germ theory: the idea that saved millions
LESSONS.hook: For most of history, doctors blamed disease on bad air. Then a handful of stubborn scientists proved that invisible living things were to blame.

sections.key: For centuries disease was blamed on foul air, which pointed people at smell rather than the real cause.
sections.b:
For centuries, the leading explanation for epidemics was miasma: foul, poisonous air rising from rubbish, swamps and sewage. Malaria literally comes from the Italian for 'bad air'. The theory wasn't entirely foolish. Filthy places really were more dangerous, and cleaning up cities did reduce disease. But it pointed people at the smell rather than the cause.

Doctors went from post-mortems to childbirth without washing, and nobody suspected that the real killers were too small to see.

sections.key: Microbes were seen in the 1670s, but proving they cause disease needed careful experiments.
sections.b:
In the 1670s, Dutch cloth merchant Antonie van Leeuwenhoek ground tiny, powerful lenses and looked at pond water, rainwater and scrapings from his own teeth. He saw swarms of moving 'animalcules' and became the first person to describe bacteria.

Yet for almost 200 years few connected them with illness. Many scientists believed microbes arose spontaneously from decaying matter, so they seemed a result of rot, not a cause of sickness. In the 1860s Louis Pasteur boiled broth in flasks with long, swan-shaped necks. Air could get in, but dust and microbes were trapped. The broth stayed clear while the neck was intact; tilt the flask so broth touched the dust, and it quickly spoiled. This helped overturn spontaneous generation.

sections.key: Semmelweis and Snow showed that handwashing and clean water cut deaths, before anyone fully understood why.
sections.b:
In 1847, Hungarian doctor Ignaz Semmelweis noticed far more mothers died of childbed fever in a Vienna maternity ward run by doctors and students than in the midwives' ward. When a colleague died after cutting himself during an autopsy, with similar symptoms, Semmelweis suspected doctors carried 'cadaverous particles' from corpses. He made staff wash their hands in chlorinated lime, and deaths fell to around 1 to 2%. Colleagues rejected his ideas, and he died in an asylum in 1865.

In 1854 cholera hit Soho, London. John Snow suspected contaminated water, mapped the deaths and found them clustered around a Broad Street pump. Nearby brewery workers, who drank beer, were largely spared. The pump handle was removed and the outbreak, already waning, ended. His work is often called the birth of modern epidemiology.

sections.key: Pasteur and Koch turned germ theory into proof by linking specific microbes to specific diseases.
sections.b:
Pasteur showed that microbes spoil wine and milk, giving us pasteurisation, which uses gentle heat to kill them. Later he developed vaccines, including one for rabies in 1885.

German doctor Robert Koch turned germ theory into hard proof. In 1876 he showed that a specific bacterium caused anthrax in animals. In 1882 he identified the bacterium behind tuberculosis, then one of Europe's biggest killers, and soon afterwards the cause of cholera. Koch's postulates set a logical test: the germ should be found in every case of the disease, grown in pure culture, cause the disease in a healthy host, and be recovered again. His techniques, such as growing bacteria on solid plates, are still used.

sections.key: Antiseptic surgery and handwashing for about 20 seconds with soap remain frontline defences against infection.
sections.b:
In the 1860s, even a successful operation often ended in death from infection. Glasgow surgeon Joseph Lister read Pasteur's work and reasoned that germs entered wounds. From 1867 he used carbolic acid on instruments, dressings and wounds, even spraying it into the air during operations. Infection and death rates on his wards fell sharply. Many mocked him, but by the 1880s antiseptic surgery was spreading. Listerine (1879) was named in his honour, though Lister had no part in it.

Germ theory's simplest lesson is still powerful. Soap and water remove germs and break apart the fatty coat of some viruses. Scrub for about 20 seconds, including backs of hands, between fingers and under nails, then dry well. Wash before eating, after the toilet, after blowing your nose and after caring for someone sick. Alcohol-based sanitiser is a good backup.

quiz.q: Why was the miasma theory unhelpful even though cleaning up cities reduced disease?
o: It claimed that disease was caused by germs
It blamed all disease on poor diet alone
It pointed people at the smell, not the real cause
It told doctors to wash their hands often
quiz.e: Cleanup helped, but miasma ignored the invisible microbes actually responsible.

quiz.q: What did Pasteur's swan-necked flasks help show?
o: Microbes arrive on dust from the air
Microbes can only live in boiled broth
Broth always spoils after it is boiled
Air is never needed for any life
quiz.e: Broth stayed clear until the trapped dust touched it, which overturned spontaneous generation.

quiz.q: What did John Snow's mapping of cholera deaths suggest?
o: Foul air from the brewery caused the outbreak
Drinking beer was the main cause of illness
Contaminated water from one pump was spreading it
The disease was inherited within local families
quiz.e: Deaths clustered around the Broad Street pump, pointing to water rather than miasma.

quiz.q: What did Koch's postulates provide?
o: A method for making vaccines
A test linking one germ to one disease
A way to heat milk safely
A rule for dividing hospital wards
quiz.e: They helped turn germ theory into proof that a particular microbe causes a disease.

quiz.q: What is the recommended way to wash hands to remove germs?
o: Give them a quick rinse under cold water
Use sanitiser only and never use soap
Wash them only before you eat meals
Scrub with soap and water for 20 seconds
quiz.e: Soap and a thorough scrub remove germs and break apart the coat of some viruses.

LESSONS.push: Doctors once blamed foul air for plague. Who finally proved otherwise?

LESSONS.title: Vaccines: history, science and safety
LESSONS.hook: One idea, tested on a boy in an English village in 1796, went on to wipe a disease that killed hundreds of millions off the face of the Earth.

sections.key: Variolation was risky, and Jenner's 1796 cowpox experiment gave the world its first vaccine.
sections.b:
Smallpox killed about 30% of those infected and scarred many survivors. People noticed survivors rarely caught it twice, so healers in China, India and the Ottoman Empire practised variolation: giving healthy people material from smallpox sores, usually causing a milder, protective infection. Lady Mary Wortley Montagu helped popularise it in England from 1721. It worked, but some patients died and could spread smallpox to others.

In 1796, English doctor Edward Jenner tested a rural belief that milkmaids who caught mild cowpox escaped smallpox. He scratched cowpox material from milkmaid Sarah Nelmes into the arm of eight-year-old James Phipps. Weeks later the boy resisted smallpox. It would never pass an ethics committee today. The word vaccine comes from vacca, Latin for cow.

sections.key: Smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980, and polio has been eliminated from most of the world.
sections.b:
Smallpox killed an estimated 300 million people in the 20th century alone. A global campaign led by the World Health Organization tracked down every case. The last natural infection occurred in Somalia in 1977, and in 1980 smallpox was declared eradicated, the first human disease ever wiped out.

Polio, which paralysed many thousands of children each year, was next. Jonas Salk's vaccine passed a huge 1954 field trial involving over a million American children and reached Australia in 1956. Australia was declared polio-free in 2000, and wild polio now survives in very few countries.

sections.key: Vaccines show the immune system a harmless imitation of a germ, using weakened or killed germs, single pieces, or genetic instructions.
sections.b:
Every vaccine shows the immune system something that looks like a germ without causing the disease. Live attenuated vaccines, such as measles, mumps and rubella (MMR), use weakened germs. Inactivated vaccines, like most flu shots, use killed germs. Subunit vaccines use one piece of the germ, such as a protein, and toxoid vaccines, like tetanus, use a harmless version of a toxin. Newer mRNA vaccines, used against COVID-19, deliver temporary instructions for cells to make one harmless protein.

The HPV vaccine, which prevents several cancers, was developed at the University of Queensland.

sections.key: COVID-19 vaccines were quick because steps overlapped, not because safety trials were skipped, and monitoring continues after approval.
sections.b:
Vaccines face the same phased human trials as other medicines. Pfizer's Phase 3 trial enrolled over 40,000 volunteers and, with the virus spreading widely, reached a clear answer within months. Time was saved by overlapping phases, by governments paying for doses early, and by regulators reviewing data as it arrived. Australia's TGA gave provisional approval in January 2021.

Trials of thousands can't catch side effects affecting one person in 100,000, so monitoring continues. Australians can report suspected side effects to the TGA, and AusVaxSafety surveys people afterwards. In 2021 a very rare clotting condition was linked to the AstraZeneca vaccine, and advice changed to prefer other vaccines for younger adults. Clinics ask you to wait about 15 minutes because severe allergy, though rare, can occur.

sections.key: Herd immunity protects people who can't be vaccinated, and the claimed link between vaccines and autism came from a fraudulent, retracted paper.
sections.b:
When enough people are immune, an infected person meets too few vulnerable people to keep the disease spreading. This herd immunity protects newborns, people having cancer treatment and others who can't be vaccinated. Measles is extremely contagious, so about 95% of people need to be immune, and it returns quickly when coverage slips.

The most damaging myth began with a 1998 paper by Andrew Wakefield linking MMR to autism. It was found fraudulent, retracted in 2010, and Wakefield lost his medical registration. Large studies, including one of over 650,000 Danish children, found no link, and vaccines don't overload the immune system. Check your records on the Australian Immunisation Register and ask your GP what you need.

quiz.q: Why was variolation risky?
o: It gave only a few weeks of protection
It used cowpox, which often caused severe illness
It used real smallpox, which could kill or spread
It needed a dozen doses over several years
quiz.e: Variolation used material from smallpox sores, so it could kill the patient or pass smallpox to others.

quiz.q: What does it mean to say smallpox was eradicated?
o: It was wiped out as a natural infection worldwide
It was cured in everyone who had caught it
It stopped in Europe but continued elsewhere
It was controlled only in wealthy countries
quiz.e: Eradication means the disease no longer occurs naturally anywhere, which has happened to only one human disease.

quiz.q: How does an mRNA vaccine work?
o: It injects a weakened live virus
It contains killed whole germs
It carries a harmless version of a toxin
It gives cells brief instructions for a protein
quiz.e: mRNA vaccines teach the immune system using a single harmless protein that your own cells briefly make.

quiz.q: Why does safety monitoring continue after a vaccine is approved?
o: Approval lasts only a few years by law
Trials of thousands can miss very rare effects
Vaccines change once they leave the factory
Phase 3 trials never test for safety
quiz.e: Very rare side effects only show up once millions of people are vaccinated, so monitoring carries on.

quiz.q: Why do about 95% of people need to be immune to stop measles outbreaks?
o: Measles vaccines wear off within a year
Measles spreads only in crowded schools
Measles is extremely contagious
Immune people can still spread it forever
quiz.e: The more contagious a disease, the higher the share of people who must be immune to protect the community.

LESSONS.push: We have wiped out exactly one human disease. A cow played a part.

LESSONS.title: Anaesthesia and the rise of modern surgery
LESSONS.hook: Until 1846, the best surgeon was the fastest one, because patients were awake for every cut.

sections.key: Before anaesthesia, speed was a surgeon's greatest skill; ether's public demonstration on 16 October 1846 changed surgery forever.
sections.b:
Before the 1840s, surgery meant being held down, fully awake. Alcohol, opium and a leather strap to bite on were about all that was offered. Operations were mostly amputations, removing surface lumps and draining abscesses, because opening the chest or abdomen was almost always fatal. Speed was everything: London surgeon Robert Liston was famous for removing a leg in under three minutes.

Georgia doctor Crawford Long used ether from 1842 but didn't publish for years. On 16 October 1846 in Boston, dentist William Morton gave ether to a patient while a surgeon removed a lump from his neck. The patient felt no pain, and the news spread worldwide within months. By mid-1847 ether was used in the Australian colonies. The word anaesthesia, 'without sensation', was suggested around then.

sections.key: Chloroform made anaesthesia popular, but infection kept killing patients until Lister introduced antisepsis and surgeons adopted asepsis.
sections.b:
In 1847 Scottish obstetrician James Young Simpson and colleagues tested chemicals on themselves and found chloroform worked. It was faster than ether but could stop the heart. Critics called pain in childbirth natural, until Queen Victoria accepted chloroform from John Snow, also famous for tracing cholera, for the birth of Prince Leopold in 1853.

Anaesthesia solved pain but not infection. Sleeping patients allowed longer operations, yet many died afterwards from infected wounds. From 1867 Joseph Lister used carbolic acid to kill germs (antisepsis). Surgeons then moved to asepsis: keeping germs out in the first place, with steam-sterilised instruments, gowns and masks. Rubber gloves arrived in the 1890s, partly because William Halsted's nurse had skin irritated by harsh antiseptics.

sections.key: Modern general anaesthesia combines several drugs for unconsciousness, pain relief and muscle relaxation, with constant monitoring.
sections.b:
Today's general anaesthesia is a careful balance of several drugs rather than one gas on a cloth. One drug, often propofol, brings on unconsciousness quickly. Others block pain. Muscle relaxants, first used in the 1940s and derived from the arrow poison curare, keep the body still. Because these relaxants also stop breathing, a machine breathes for the patient.

The anaesthetist monitors heart rhythm, blood pressure, oxygen levels and exhaled carbon dioxide throughout. In Australia, anaesthetists are specialist doctors who train for many years after medical school.

sections.key: Local, regional and sedation techniques, and keyhole surgery, let many procedures happen with less risk, pain and recovery time.
sections.b:
General anaesthesia is only one option. Local anaesthetic, like a dentist's injection, numbs a small area. Regional anaesthesia numbs more: an epidural or spinal block can numb everything from the waist down, so many caesarean births happen with the mother awake. Nerve blocks numb a whole arm or leg. Sedation, used for procedures like colonoscopies, relaxes you and often leaves little memory without full unconsciousness.

Keyhole surgery (laparoscopy) uses a few cuts of roughly 5 to 12 millimetres, gas to inflate the abdomen, and a thin camera. The first laparoscopic gallbladder removal was in Germany in 1985. Patients usually have less pain, smaller scars and shorter hospital stays.

sections.key: Follow fasting instructions and tell your anaesthetist about all medicines, past reactions and family history.
sections.b:
Anaesthesia is now very safe. In countries like Australia, deaths caused by anaesthesia are very rare, and rarer still in otherwise healthy people. You can help keep it that way. Follow fasting instructions exactly, because food in the stomach can be inhaled into the lungs. Tell your anaesthetist about all medicines, including supplements and herbal products, any past reactions, and any family history of problems with anaesthesia, as some serious reactions run in families.

After a general anaesthetic, don't drive, sign legal documents or make big decisions for at least 24 hours. Ask your doctor or anaesthetist about anything that worries you.

quiz.q: Why was speed so important for surgeons before the 1840s?
o: Operating theatres had to be shared
Patients were awake and in agony
Instruments rusted quickly
Surgeons were paid per operation
quiz.e: With no anaesthesia, every extra second was suffering, so the fastest surgeon was the best.

quiz.q: What is the difference between antisepsis and asepsis?
o: They mean exactly the same thing
Antisepsis uses heat; asepsis uses chemicals
Antisepsis kills germs; asepsis keeps them out
Asepsis came first, antisepsis later
quiz.e: Lister killed germs with carbolic acid; asepsis later prevented them reaching the wound at all.

quiz.q: Why does a machine breathe for a patient under general anaesthesia?
o: Anaesthetic drugs always damage the lungs
It keeps the patient's body temperature steady
It stops the patient from waking suddenly
Muscle relaxants also stop the breathing muscles
quiz.e: The relaxants that keep the body still also paralyse the breathing muscles, so a machine takes over.

quiz.q: How can a caesarean birth happen with the mother awake?
o: A spinal or epidural numbs the lower body
Sedation erases all pain permanently
The baby is delivered through keyhole cuts
General anaesthetic wears off within minutes
quiz.e: Regional anaesthesia numbs a large part of the body without making you unconscious.

quiz.q: Why must you follow fasting instructions before a general anaesthetic?
o: Food makes anaesthetic drugs stronger
It helps you lose weight before surgery
Stomach contents can enter the lungs
Digestion raises your temperature
quiz.e: Under anaesthesia, food in the stomach can be inhaled, so fasting protects your lungs.

LESSONS.push: Before 1846, the best surgeon was the fastest. What changed in one Boston theatre?

LESSONS.title: Pandemics: from plague to COVID-19
LESSONS.hook: Every few generations a new disease sweeps the world. History shows how they spread, what stops them, and why the next one is a question of when, not if.

sections.key: An epidemic is a surge in one region, a pandemic spreads across the world, and an endemic disease is constantly present.
sections.b: These three words describe how widespread a disease is, not how deadly. An epidemic is a sudden rise in cases above normal levels in a particular area. A pandemic is an epidemic that spreads across several countries or continents, affecting large numbers of people. An endemic disease is always present at a fairly steady level in a region, like malaria in parts of Africa or the common cold everywhere. A disease can move between categories. Many experts expect pandemic diseases to settle into endemic ones as immunity builds, as happened with the descendants of the 1918 flu strain.

sections.key: The Black Death killed perhaps a third to a half of Europe, and the 1918 flu killed an estimated 50 million people, mostly young adults.
sections.b:
Plague is caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, mainly spread by fleas on rats. The Black Death reached Europe in 1347 and killed perhaps a third to a half of its people within about five years. Quarantine comes from the Venetian practice of isolating ships for 40 days, quaranta giorni. In 1900, plague in Sydney killed more than 100 people, prompting mass rat catching and slum clearance around The Rocks.

The 1918 flu, misleadingly called the Spanish flu, killed an estimated 50 million people, unusually including healthy young adults. Australia's strict maritime quarantine delayed its arrival until early 1919, but it still killed roughly 12,000 to 15,000 Australians. Schools and theatres closed, and masks were required in some states.

sections.key: HIV treatment now allows long lives, and COVID-19 vaccines were ready within a year.
sections.b:
AIDS was recognised in 1981, and HIV identified in 1983. It spreads through blood, sexual contact and from mother to child, and has killed over 40 million people. Australia's 1980s response is widely praised: governments worked with affected communities, introduced needle and syringe programs early, and ran bold campaigns like the 1987 Grim Reaper ad. Since 1996, combination treatment has allowed long lives, and people with an undetectable viral load don't transmit HIV sexually.

The WHO declared COVID-19 a pandemic on 11 March 2020 and later estimated about 15 million excess deaths in 2020 and 2021. Australia closed its border and used lockdowns, testing and tracing, with far fewer deaths per person than many countries. Effective vaccines were ready within a year. The emergency ended in May 2023.

sections.key: Diseases spread through air, touch, water, food, blood or animals, and the R number shows whether an outbreak will grow or shrink.
sections.b:
Germs travel by droplets and airborne particles (flu, COVID-19), contaminated hands, water and food (cholera), blood and sexual contact (HIV), or mosquitoes (dengue). Most new diseases are zoonotic, jumping from animals to people. Hendra virus, first identified in Brisbane in 1994, passes from flying foxes to horses and occasionally to humans.

Epidemiologists track the reproduction number, R: the average number of people each case infects. Measles has an R0 around 12 to 18, seasonal flu around 1 to 2. If R is above 1, cases grow exponentially; with R of 2, one case becomes over a thousand within ten generations. Below 1, the outbreak shrinks. Vaccines, masks, testing and isolation all work by pushing R down.

sections.key: Preparedness means surveillance, stockpiles and fast vaccine development, plus everyday habits like staying home when sick.
sections.b:
Experts agree another pandemic is likely; the questions are when and what. Governments prepare by watching for unusual outbreaks, sharing data internationally, stockpiling masks, medicines and equipment, and building the capacity to make vaccines quickly. After COVID-19, Australia set up a national Centre for Disease Control to coordinate this work.

Individuals matter too. Stay home when you're sick, wash your hands, cover coughs, keep your vaccinations up to date, and keep a small supply of basics at home. In an outbreak, follow official health advice from sources like Healthdirect and your state health department rather than social media rumours.

quiz.q: What is the difference between an epidemic and a pandemic?
o: A pandemic is always the deadlier of the two
A pandemic spreads across many countries
An epidemic only ever affects animals
There is no difference between the two
quiz.e: The words describe how widely a disease has spread, not how deadly it is.

quiz.q: How did Australia delay the 1918 flu reaching its shores?
o: Strict maritime quarantine
Vaccinating arriving passengers
Closing all schools in 1917
Rationing food and fuel
quiz.e: Isolating arriving ships held the virus off until early 1919.

quiz.q: What has combination treatment since 1996 made possible for people with HIV?
o: A complete cure within a year
Long, healthy lives with ongoing treatment
Lifelong protection from a single dose
Immunity passed on to their children
quiz.e: HIV still has no cure, but treatment now controls it so well that people live long lives.

quiz.q: If the R number is below 1, what happens to an outbreak?
o: It grows exponentially
It stays exactly the same
It becomes a pandemic
It shrinks over time
quiz.e: When each case infects fewer than one other person on average, the outbreak fades.

quiz.q: Where should you look for guidance during an outbreak?
o: Posts that are widely shared online
Advice passed on by friends and family
Official advice such as Healthdirect
Advice remembered from past outbreaks
quiz.e: Official health advice is accurate and updated as the situation changes.

LESSONS.push: The word quarantine means forty. Find out why, and what stops a pandemic.

LESSONS.title: Clinical trials: how we know what works
LESSONS.hook: Your neighbour swears a supplement cured her. A trial of 10,000 people says it does nothing. Here's why the trial wins.

sections.key: James Lind ran an early controlled trial in 1747, and modern drugs pass through Phase 1, 2 and 3 trials, approval and Phase 4 monitoring.
sections.b:
In 1747, naval surgeon James Lind faced sailors dying of scurvy aboard HMS Salisbury. He gave 12 sick sailors on the same diet different treatments in pairs: cider, vinegar, seawater, a spicy paste, diluted sulfuric acid, or two oranges and a lemon daily. The citrus pair recovered dramatically within about a week. The navy took about 50 years to issue citrus juice.

Medicines are tested in the lab, then in people. Phase 1 gives it to 20 to 100 volunteers to check safety and dose. Phase 2 asks a few hundred patients if it works. Phase 3 compares it with a placebo or best current treatment in hundreds to thousands. A regulator such as Australia's TGA then reviews it, and Phase 4 monitors wide use. Roughly 1 in 10 drugs entering Phase 1 is approved.

sections.key: Randomly assigning people to groups makes the groups alike, so differences in results are due to the treatment.
sections.b: In a randomised controlled trial, a computer or similar process decides who gets the treatment and who gets the comparison. This matters enormously. If doctors chose, they might unconsciously give the new drug to healthier or more hopeful patients, making it look better than it is. Randomisation spreads age, fitness, genes, habits and countless unknown factors evenly between groups, so any difference in outcomes can fairly be blamed on the treatment. The 1948 British trial of the antibiotic streptomycin for tuberculosis is widely regarded as the first modern randomised controlled trial.

sections.key: Blinding and placebo groups strip out expectations and natural recovery, revealing the true effect of a treatment.
sections.b:
Expectations shape results. Patients who know they got the new drug may feel better, and doctors who know may judge them more generously. In a double-blind trial neither patients nor the researchers assessing them know who got what until the end, which is why trial tablets often look identical. Blinding isn't always possible, as you can't hide surgery, but good trials use it where they can.

People also improve through the placebo effect, natural recovery and the extra attention of being in a study. A placebo group captures all of that, so a drug's real effect is the difference between the groups. Where an effective treatment exists, giving sick people a dummy is unethical, so new treatments are compared with the best current one. Australian ethics committees review trials, and participants give informed consent.

sections.key: Personal stories can't separate a treatment's effect from natural recovery, placebo and coincidence.
sections.b:
'It worked for me' feels convincing, but stories are unreliable evidence. Many illnesses, like colds and back pain, get better on their own, and people usually try remedies when symptoms are at their worst, so almost anything taken then seems to work. This is regression to the mean. We remember the hits, forget the misses, and rarely hear from people a remedy failed.

Even large observational studies can mislead. Studies once suggested hormone replacement therapy protected women's hearts, but a large trial published in 2002 found it didn't, and slightly increased some risks.

sections.key: A single trial can be a fluke, so look for systematic reviews, and check any headline for who was studied, how many, and the absolute risk.
sections.b:
The strongest evidence comes from systematic reviews, which gather every good trial on a question, sometimes pooling the numbers in a meta-analysis. The Cochrane Collaboration, founded in 1993, produces many. But exciting results are more likely to be published than null ones, a problem called publication bias, so trials are now registered before they start, for example on the Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry.

When reading a headline, ask: was it in humans, or mice or cells? How many people? A randomised trial, or only a link? Is risk absolute? 'Doubles your risk' may mean 1 in 10,000 to 2 in 10,000. Who funded it? Healthdirect is a reliable Australian source, and talk to your doctor or pharmacist before changing treatment.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of a Phase 1 trial?
o: To compare a drug with the best existing treatment
To monitor a drug after approval
To check safety and find a dose in a small group
To test the drug on thousands of patients
quiz.e: Phase 1 asks first whether a medicine is safe, in a small group, and at what dose.

quiz.q: Why are participants randomly assigned to groups?
o: So the groups are alike apart from treatment
To make the trial cheaper to run
So doctors can pick the healthiest patients
To keep the results secret from everyone
quiz.e: Random assignment spreads known and unknown factors evenly, so the treatment is the main difference.

quiz.q: In a double-blind trial, who doesn't know which group each patient is in?
o: Only the patients taking part
Only the doctors treating them
Only the regulator and the funder
Patients and the assessing researchers
quiz.e: Hiding group membership from everyone assessing results prevents expectations skewing them.

quiz.q: Why can 'it worked for me' mislead?
o: Personal stories are nearly always invented
Illnesses often improve on their own anyway
Remedies never work outside trials
Memory records every detail accurately
quiz.e: Natural recovery, placebo and coincidence can all look like a remedy working.

quiz.q: A headline says a supplement 'shrinks tumours'. What is most worth checking?
o: How much the supplement costs
Whether it is sold in pharmacies
Whether it was tested in people
How many times the story was shared
quiz.e: Results in mice or cells often do not carry over to people.

LESSONS.push: Your neighbour's cure may be real, or coincidence. Here's how we tell.

LESSONS.title: How music works
LESSONS.hook: Every song you love is just air, pushed back and forth in careful patterns. Here is how those patterns become music.

sections.key: Sound is a pressure wave, and pitch is how we hear its frequency: faster vibrations sound higher.
sections.b:
A vibrating guitar string squeezes and stretches the air beside it. That pressure wave travels at about 343 metres per second, roughly a kilometre every three seconds, and nudges your eardrum. Tiny bones pass the movement to the cochlea, where hair cells turn it into nerve signals.

Pitch depends on frequency, measured in hertz (Hz). A healthy young ear hears roughly 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz, and the upper limit falls with age. Orchestras tune to the A above middle C at 440 Hz. Double any frequency and you get the same note an octave higher, so the next A is 880 Hz. That's why men and women singing the 'same' tune are often an octave apart without noticing.

sections.key: Timbre, the colour of a sound, comes from the mix of overtones above the main note.
sections.b: A piano and a violin can play exactly the same pitch and still sound completely different. The reason is timbre, or tone colour. Almost no instrument produces a single pure frequency. Alongside the main note, the fundamental, it produces fainter overtones at higher frequencies, often simple multiples of the fundamental. Each instrument has its own recipe of overtones, plus its own way of starting and fading a note: the sharp strike of a piano hammer, the smooth swell of a bowed string. Your brain reads that recipe instantly, which is how you can recognise a familiar voice from a single word.

sections.key: The beat is the steady pulse, rhythm the pattern over it, and a melody is a shape of pitches that balances repetition and surprise.
sections.b:
The beat is the pulse you tap your foot to, and tempo is its speed in beats per minute. A slow ballad sits around 60 to 80, while much dance music runs at about 120 to 130. Beats group into bars, commonly four beats, though waltzes use three. Rhythm is the pattern of long and short sounds over that pulse. Humans are unusually good at locking onto a beat; few other animals do, though some parrots have been filmed bobbing in time.

A melody is a line of notes your brain hears as one shape. Good melodies repeat short motifs so you can follow them, then vary them to stay interesting. Most move in small steps with occasional leaps, build to a high point, and settle back 'home', one of music's strongest pulls.

sections.key: A scale is the set of notes a piece draws on, and notes with simple frequency ratios sound smooth together.
sections.b:
Most Western music divides each octave into 12 equal steps called semitones, the white and black keys on a piano. A scale is a chosen subset. The major scale uses seven, the do-re-mi from school. The pentatonic scale uses five and appears in folk music from Scotland to China to West Africa. Indian classical and Arabic music use pitches between the piano's keys.

Harmony is notes sounding together. Consonant combinations sound smooth and stable; dissonant ones sound tense. Consonant intervals have simple frequency ratios: an octave is 2 to 1, and a perfect fifth, the interval opening many fanfares, is 3 to 2. Much of music's drama comes from building tension with dissonance, then resolving it to a consonant chord.

sections.key: Major chords tend to sound bright and minor chords darker, partly from acoustics and partly from learning.
sections.b: Listeners raised on Western music usually hear major chords as bright or happy and minor chords as darker or sad. The difference is small: in a minor chord, the middle note is one semitone lower. Why it matters so much is still debated. Some researchers point to acoustics, and to similarities with the way sad speech is lower and flatter. Others stress learning, since the association varies between cultures and eras. Context counts too: a minor key at a fast tempo can sound energetic rather than sad. Next time a song moves you, listen for where the key or tempo changes.

quiz.q: If a note vibrates at 440 Hz, what is the frequency of the same note one octave higher?
o: 220 Hz
660 Hz
880 Hz
quiz.e: Doubling a frequency raises the note by one octave.

quiz.q: Why does a violin sound different from a piano playing the same note?
o: They travel at different speeds of sound
Each has a different mix of overtones
The violin's note is always louder
Pianos can play only pure frequencies
quiz.e: Each instrument adds its own recipe of overtones above the main note.

quiz.q: What do good melodies usually balance?
o: Repeated ideas with enough variation
Constant leaps with no repeated ideas
One note held from start to finish
Total repetition with no change at all
quiz.e: Repetition helps you follow a tune, and variation keeps it interesting.

quiz.q: What is the frequency ratio of a perfect fifth?
o: 2 to 1
5 to 4
9 to 8
3 to 2
quiz.e: Simple ratios like 3 to 2 make waves line up neatly, which sounds smooth.

quiz.q: Why do minor chords tend to sound sad to many listeners?
o: They are always played more slowly
Scientists proved it is purely acoustic
A mix of acoustics and cultural learning
Minor chords contain no consonant notes
quiz.e: Both sound and learned associations seem to play a part, and tempo and context matter too.

LESSONS.push: Every song is air pushed back and forth. Why do some patterns feel like music?

LESSONS.title: The world of instruments
LESSONS.hook: Blow, bow, pluck, strike or switch it on: every instrument ever made uses one of a handful of tricks to shake the air.

sections.key: Instruments are classified by what vibrates: a solid body, a skin, a string, air, or electricity.
sections.b: In 1914, musicologists Erich von Hornbostel and Curt Sachs published a system for sorting instruments by what actually vibrates. Idiophones vibrate their whole body, like bells, rattles and xylophones. Membranophones use a stretched skin, like most drums. Chordophones use strings, from the harp to the guitar. Aerophones vibrate a column of air, like flutes, trumpets and the didgeridoo. A fifth group, electrophones, was added later for instruments that make sound electronically. Museums still use this system because it works for instruments from any culture, not just the European orchestra.

sections.key: Stringed instruments use a hollow body to amplify a quiet string, and the piano is a stringed instrument whose strings are struck.
sections.b:
A vibrating string moves very little air, so stringed instruments use a hollow wooden body to resonate and amplify it. Players change pitch by string length (a finger on the neck shortens it), tension (tuning pegs) and thickness (heavier strings sound lower). Violins, cellos and double basses are bowed, with horsehair coated in rosin to grip. Guitars, harps and lutes are plucked.

The piano is a stringed instrument too. Before it, the harpsichord plucked strings at much the same volume however hard you pressed. Around 1700 in Florence, Bartolomeo Cristofori built keys that threw leather-covered hammers at the strings, so pressing harder made a louder note. Pianoforte means 'soft-loud'. Today's piano has an iron frame and 88 keys.

sections.key: Woodwinds use a reed or an edge to start the air vibrating; brass players buzz their lips.
sections.b: Wind instruments set a column of air vibrating inside a tube, and the tube's length sets the pitch. Woodwinds start the vibration in two main ways. A flute player blows across an edge, like blowing over a bottle. Clarinets and saxophones use a single cane reed, and oboes and bassoons use a double reed. Covering holes changes the tube's effective length. Brass players buzz their lips into a cup-shaped mouthpiece, and valves or a slide add extra tubing to lower the pitch. The family is defined by the lips, not the metal: the saxophone is brass-coloured, but it is a woodwind.

sections.key: Percussion is probably the oldest family, while electronic instruments make sound from electrical signals.
sections.b:
Percussion instruments are struck, shaken or scraped, and are probably the oldest family, since clapping and hitting sticks need no technology. Some are untuned, like snare drums, cymbals and shakers. Others have definite pitches, like timpani, xylophones and the steel pans of Trinidad and Tobago, invented in the twentieth century from oil drums.

The theremin, invented by Leon Theremin around 1920, is played without touching it: your hands near two antennas change its pitch and volume. In the 1960s Robert Moog's synthesisers let musicians shape sounds with knobs and cables. Australia's CSIRAC, one of the first stored-program computers, played music in the early 1950s. Since 1983, MIDI has let keyboards and computers talk to each other, so a laptop can stand in for a studio.

sections.key: The yidaki is a Yolŋu instrument with ceremonial meaning, so buy from and learn from Aboriginal makers and teachers.
sections.b:
The instrument most Australians call the didgeridoo is the yidaki to the Yolŋu people of north-east Arnhem Land, with other names elsewhere. It is traditionally a eucalyptus branch hollowed by termites. Players buzz their lips for a deep drone and use circular breathing, breathing in through the nose while pushing air out from the cheeks. Rock art suggests it has been played for at least a thousand years. 'Didgeridoo' is not an Aboriginal word and probably imitates the sound.

It accompanies ceremony, and its rhythms can link to clans, places and stories. Protocols on making and playing it differ between communities; in some it is a men's role. Buy from Aboriginal-owned makers and art centres, and learn the protocols from Aboriginal teachers.

quiz.q: In the Hornbostel-Sachs system, what is a drum with a stretched skin?
o: An idiophone
A membranophone
A chordophone
An aerophone
quiz.e: Membranophones make sound from a vibrating stretched skin.

quiz.q: What does the hollow body of a stringed instrument do?
o: It keeps the strings in tune
It resonates and amplifies the strings
It lets the strings vibrate for longer
It removes the need for a bow
quiz.e: A string alone moves little air, so the body makes the sound much louder.

quiz.q: Which family does the saxophone belong to, and why?
o: Brass, because it is made of metal
Percussion, because its keys click
Strings, because it has a curved body
Woodwind, because it uses a reed
quiz.e: Instruments are grouped by how the sound starts, not by what they are made of.

quiz.q: Why are percussion instruments thought to be the oldest?
o: Clapping and hitting sticks need no technology
They are made of the oldest materials
Orchestras developed them first
They can play more pitches than other instruments
quiz.e: Anyone can make rhythm with hands and sticks, so percussion predates other instruments.

quiz.q: What is a respectful way to get a yidaki?
o: Make your own from a hardware-store pipe
Buy a cheap copy from a souvenir shop
Order a mass-produced one online
Buy from Aboriginal-owned art centres
quiz.e: The yidaki has ceremonial meaning, so supporting Aboriginal makers and teachers shows respect.

LESSONS.push: A saxophone is not a brass instrument. Here is how instruments are really sorted.

LESSONS.title: A guide to classical music
LESSONS.hook: Three centuries, three giants and a lot of music that still turns up in films, ads and ringtones. Here is how to find your way in.

sections.key: 'Classical music' usually means the Western art music tradition, grouped into broad periods that explain how a piece sounds.
sections.b: In everyday speech, 'classical music' means the tradition of Western art music written for orchestras, choirs, soloists and small ensembles over roughly the last four centuries. Historians divide it into periods: the Baroque, about 1600 to 1750; the Classical period, about 1750 to 1820, which confusingly gives the whole tradition its name; and the Romantic period, about 1820 to 1900. Then came a burst of twentieth-century experiment. The dates are rough, since composers did not wake up in a new era. Knowing the periods helps you hear why a piece sounds the way it does.

sections.key: Baroque music is ornate and driven by a steady bass, and Bach was its master of counterpoint.
sections.b:
Baroque music is busy, decorated and driven by a continuous bass line, often a cello with a harpsichord filling in chords. Opera was born in Italy around 1600, and the concerto flourished. Vivaldi's The Four Seasons (1725) paints spring birdsong and winter ice in four violin concertos. Handel's Messiah, first performed in Dublin in 1742, is still sung by Australian choirs every Christmas.

Johann Sebastian Bach (1685 to 1750) was better known as an organist than a composer. He wrote more than a thousand works, including the Brandenburg Concertos and the Mass in B minor. His gift was counterpoint: several independent melodies played at once that fit together, as in a fugue. His music fell from fashion until Mendelssohn revived the St Matthew Passion in 1829.

sections.key: The Classical period prized clarity and balance, and Mozart wrote over 600 works in just 35 years.
sections.b:
After the dense layers of the Baroque, composers turned to clarity: a clear melody over simpler accompaniment, in balanced phrases. The piano replaced the harpsichord. This was the age of the symphony and the string quartet. Haydn wrote more than 100 symphonies and is often called the father of both. Sonata form, which presents two contrasting themes, develops them and brings them back, shaped instrumental music for 150 years.

Mozart (1756 to 1791) toured Europe as a child prodigy from age six. In 35 years he wrote over 600 works, including 41 symphonies and operas like The Marriage of Figaro and The Magic Flute. He died in Vienna working on his Requiem. The film Amadeus popularised a murderous rivalry with Salieri that historians don't support.

sections.key: Beethoven kept composing as he went deaf and opened the door to the Romantics, who used bigger orchestras for intense emotion.
sections.b:
Beethoven (1770 to 1827) began losing his hearing in his late twenties and was almost completely deaf by his final years. In 1802 he wrote a despairing letter, the Heiligenstadt Testament, yet kept composing. His Fifth Symphony opens with perhaps the most famous four notes in music, and his Ninth (1824) added singers to its finale. His music was more personal and dramatic than that of earlier composers.

Romantic composers valued feeling and imagination over balance. Orchestras and pieces grew larger, often linked to stories or landscapes. Chopin wrote intimate piano music, Tchaikovsky the ballets Swan Lake and The Nutcracker, Wagner operas of four or five hours. Dvořák and Grieg drew on folk music. Today's sweeping film scores grow out of this era.

sections.key: Start with short, famous pieces, listen actively, then try hearing an orchestra live.
sections.b: You don't need training to enjoy classical music. Start with short, well-known pieces: a movement of Vivaldi's The Four Seasons, Mozart's Eine kleine Nachtmusik, the opening of Beethoven's Fifth, or Tchaikovsky's Nutcracker suite. Many are free on streaming services and on radio such as ABC Classic. Listen actively the first time, with no phone, and notice what repeats and what changes. If a piece grabs you, explore more by the same composer. Then try it live: the Sydney, Melbourne and other state symphony orchestras run affordable concerts, and hearing a full orchestra in person is a different experience from headphones.

quiz.q: What does knowing the main periods of classical music help you do?
o: Hear why a piece sounds the way it does
Date any piece to the exact year
Skip the older music entirely
Predict which composer wrote a new work
quiz.e: Each period has a recognisable style, which helps explain what you are hearing.

quiz.q: What is counterpoint, the technique Bach mastered?
o: Playing one simple melody very quickly
Several independent melodies at once
Using only drums and other percussion
Singing a tune with no accompaniment
quiz.e: In a fugue, one theme enters again and again in different voices, all fitting together.

quiz.q: What do historians say about the story that Salieri murdered Mozart?
o: It is confirmed by Salieri's letters
It was proven in a Viennese court
Mozart himself accused Salieri
There is no good evidence for it
quiz.e: The murderous rivalry was popularised by the film Amadeus, not by evidence.

quiz.q: What happened to Beethoven's music as he went deaf?
o: He gave up composing and only conducted
He wrote only short pieces for piano
He kept composing in a more personal style
He stopped writing for orchestras
quiz.e: His late works, such as the Ninth Symphony, broke conventions and opened the door to Romanticism.

quiz.q: What is a good way to start exploring classical music?
o: Begin with the longest operas
Start with short, famous pieces
Read up on every period first
Avoid anything recorded after 1900
quiz.e: Short, familiar pieces and active listening are an easy, free way in.

LESSONS.push: Where to start with classical music, and which story about Mozart is a myth.

LESSONS.title: From blues to hip hop
LESSONS.hook: Almost every song on your playlist can trace its family tree back to the blues, and to a few machines that changed how music was heard.

sections.key: The blues grew from African American communities in the US South around the turn of the twentieth century and shaped almost everything after.
sections.b: The blues emerged in African American communities in the southern United States in the late 1800s and early 1900s, drawing on work songs, field hollers and spirituals rooted in the experience of slavery and its aftermath. Its most famous structure, the 12-bar blues, repeats a pattern of three chords over twelve bars, and its 'blue notes' bend slightly below the standard pitches of a Western scale. Musicians such as W.C. Handy, Bessie Smith and Robert Johnson helped spread it. The blues shaped jazz, rhythm and blues, rock and roll, soul and much of the popular music that followed.

sections.key: Recording turned music from a live-only event into something anyone could own, replay and even build in the studio.
sections.b:
For most of history, you could only hear music when someone played it in front of you. In 1877 Thomas Edison demonstrated the phonograph, recording sound on a tin foil cylinder. Gramophone discs followed, then 1920s radio, bringing music into millions of homes. Records fixed a performance permanently, so one recording, not the written song, became the version people loved.

After the Second World War, magnetic tape made editing easy, and multitrack recorders let musicians layer parts. The long-playing record (1948) held about twenty minutes a side, encouraging whole albums. By the late 1960s the studio was an instrument. Cassettes and the 1979 Walkman made music mobile; CDs, MP3s and, from the late 2000s, streaming followed.

sections.key: Rock and roll combined blues, country and gospel in the 1950s, made the electric guitar central and was marketed to teenagers.
sections.b: In the 1950s, rock and roll fused rhythm and blues with country and gospel, driven by a strong backbeat on beats two and four. Black musicians such as Chuck Berry, Little Richard and Sister Rosetta Tharpe were central to its sound, and Elvis Presley became its biggest star. The electric guitar, amplified to compete with drums, became its signature instrument. It was also a social shift: marketed directly to teenagers, who now had money to spend. In the 1960s, British bands such as the Beatles and the Rolling Stones sent it back across the Atlantic, reshaped.

sections.key: Hip hop began at 1970s Bronx block parties, and house and techno grew from disco in 1980s Chicago and Detroit.
sections.b:
Hip hop grew from 1970s Bronx block parties among African American and Caribbean-born young people; a 1973 party where DJ Kool Herc played is often cited as its start. DJs extended funk drum breaks by switching between two turntables, and MCs rhymed over the top. Its four elements are DJing, MCing, breakdancing and graffiti, and sampling fragments of old recordings became central. It grew into one of the world's best-selling genres, including a strong Australian scene.

Disco built music around a steady four-on-the-floor kick drum. When it faded in the US, Black and gay club scenes kept experimenting. In the mid-1980s Chicago gave rise to house and Detroit to techno, built on cheap drum machines and synthesisers like the Roland TR-808 and TB-303, fuelling the rave scene.

sections.key: Australia has produced rock, pop and Indigenous-language hits, and following a genre's family tree is the best way to find more music you love.
sections.b:
Johnny O'Keefe's Wild One (1958) was an early Australian rock and roll hit. AC/DC formed in Sydney in 1973 and its 1980 album Back in Black is among the best-selling ever. Kylie Minogue went from Neighbours to pop stardom with The Loco-Motion in 1987. Yothu Yindi's Treaty (1991), sung partly in the Yolŋu language Gumatj, became a national hit, and Mandawuy Yunupingu was Australian of the Year for 1992. Countdown and triple j launched countless careers.

Almost every genre borrows from earlier ones. Look up who influenced an artist you like, and check credits for who wrote, produced and sampled each track. Support live venues, community radio and triple j Unearthed.

quiz.q: What is the 12-bar blues?
o: A song that lasts exactly 12 minutes
A repeating three-chord pattern over 12 bars
A scale with twelve different notes
A style for twelve-string guitar only
quiz.e: The 12-bar pattern is the blues' most famous structure and underpins much popular music.

quiz.q: How did recording change the way people knew songs?
o: Songs became permanently shorter
One recording became the known version
Live music disappeared completely
Only radio stations could play music
quiz.e: Records fixed a performance for good, so listeners came to know a specific version.

quiz.q: Who was rock and roll marketed to?
o: Older fans of big-band jazz
Regular classical concert-goers
Teenagers with money to spend
Studio engineers and technicians
quiz.e: Rock and roll was a social shift as well as a sound, aimed straight at young people.

quiz.q: What did early hip hop DJs do with funk records?
o: Played the records backwards at parties
Replaced the singer with a live choir
Slowed every record to half speed
Extended drum breaks using two turntables
quiz.e: Looping the drum breaks gave MCs a continuous beat to rhyme over.

quiz.q: How can you find new music you are likely to love?
o: Listen only to current chart hits
Follow the family tree of influences
Avoid anything older than ten years
Shuffle randomly and never check credits
quiz.e: Almost every genre borrows from earlier ones, so influences lead to more music you will enjoy.

LESSONS.push: Most songs on your playlist share one ancestor. Trace the family tree back.

LESSONS.title: Music and the brain
LESSONS.hook: Music gives you no food, shelter or money, yet it can make your skin tingle and bring back memories you thought were lost. Why?

sections.key: Music engages hearing, movement, memory and emotion at once, and stirs feeling by mimicking speech and playing with expectation.
sections.b:
There is no single music centre in the brain. Sound areas decode pitch and timbre, movement regions track the beat (hence the foot tapping), memory areas recognise familiar tunes, and emotional and reward systems respond to how it feels.

Music can make us sad, joyful or calm within seconds. One explanation is that it borrows the cues of emotional speech: happy music is faster, higher and brighter, sad music slower, lower and softer. Another is expectation. Your brain constantly predicts what comes next, and composers delay, confirm or surprise those predictions to create tension and release. Some features travel across cultures: people can often tell a lullaby from a dance song even in an unfamiliar tradition.

sections.key: Musical chills come with unexpected moments, and the brain releases dopamine both at the peak and in anticipation of it.
sections.b:
A shiver or goosebumps at a key moment, called frisson, often arrives with something unexpected: a sudden change in volume, a new voice, a surprising chord after a long build-up. Not everyone gets chills, and some studies suggest people high in openness to experience report them more often.

A 2011 McGill University study used brain scans on people listening to music that gave them chills. At peak pleasure, the striatum, part of the reward system that also responds to food, released dopamine. A different part of the striatum released it in the seconds before the peak, in anticipation. That helps explain why a favourite song's build-up can feel almost as good as the moment itself.

sections.key: Music is tightly tied to memory, especially songs from our teens and early twenties.
sections.b: A few notes of an old song can transport you to a particular summer, car trip or school dance. Music is closely bound up with autobiographical memory and tends to be tied to emotion, which helps memories stick. Studies consistently find that people remember and feel most strongly about music from their teens and early twenties, part of a wider pattern psychologists call the reminiscence bump. That's one reason many adults feel the best music was made when they were young. Songs also make words easier to remember, which is why children learn the alphabet with a tune.

sections.key: Musical memory often survives in dementia, and personally meaningful music can improve mood and connection but does not cure.
sections.b:
Carers have long noticed that people with dementia, including some who struggle to recognise family, can still sing along to songs from their youth. Musical memory seems to rely partly on brain areas affected relatively late in some forms of dementia, such as Alzheimer's disease.

Music does not cure dementia or reverse its progress. But there is reasonable evidence that personally meaningful music can lift mood, reduce agitation and help people connect with those around them. Many Australian aged-care homes now use personalised playlists, and registered music therapists work in hospitals and care settings.

sections.key: The Mozart effect was small, brief and hard to repeat, and evidence that learning an instrument boosts general intelligence is mixed.
sections.b:
In 1993 a short paper in Nature reported that students who listened to ten minutes of a Mozart sonata did slightly better on a spatial reasoning task for the next 10 to 15 minutes. Media turned this into 'Mozart makes babies smarter', and in 1998 Georgia's governor proposed a classical CD for every newborn. Later studies struggled to repeat it; enjoyable music can briefly lift mood and alertness, and Mozart has no special power.

Children who learn instruments often do better at school, but families who pay for lessons differ in many ways. Randomised studies are mixed, and reviews find little broad gain in intelligence. Practice does improve listening, timing and coordination. Learn an instrument because you want to play.

quiz.q: Which features tend to make music sound happy?
o: Slower, lower and softer
Faster, higher and brighter
No beat or rhythm at all
Only notes in minor keys
quiz.e: Happy music borrows the cues of excited speech: faster, higher and brighter.

quiz.q: What did the 2011 McGill study find about dopamine and music?
o: Released at the peak and in anticipation
Music switched off dopamine release
It was released only while people slept
Only classical music triggered any release
quiz.e: Anticipation of a musical peak is itself rewarding, which is why the build-up feels so good.

quiz.q: Music from which stage of life do people tend to remember most strongly?
o: Early childhood, before age five
Middle age
The most recent year
The teens and early twenties
quiz.e: This pattern is called the reminiscence bump.

quiz.q: What can personally meaningful music do for people with dementia?
o: Reverse the progress of the disease
Restore recognition of family permanently
Lift mood and help with connection
Replace the need for other care
quiz.e: Music can help wellbeing and connection, though it does not cure dementia.

quiz.q: What is the best explanation for the original 'Mozart effect' result?
o: Mozart's music rewires the brain
Enjoyable music briefly lifted mood
The students were all trained musicians
It was found only in young children
quiz.e: The effect was small and short-lived, with no special power in Mozart.

LESSONS.push: Music gives no food or shelter, yet it can raise goosebumps. What is going on?

LESSONS.title: Why every culture tells myths
LESSONS.hook: Floods that drown the world, gods who build the sky from a giant's skull, heroes who leave home and come back changed. Almost every people on Earth has told stories like these. Here's why.

sections.key: To scholars, a myth is a traditional, often sacred story about gods or origins that explains the world, backs customs and gives a community its identity.
sections.b:
In everyday speech a myth is something untrue, like goldfish having three-second memories. Scholars use the word differently. The Greek mythos simply meant 'story'. A myth is a traditional story, often sacred to its tellers, about gods, ancestors and how things came to be, set in a time before ordinary time. Calling a story a myth says nothing about whether it is true.

Myths answer the big questions: where did the world come from, why do we die, why are there seasons? Anthropologist Bronisław Malinowski, studying the Trobriand Islanders in the early 1900s, argued myths work like a 'charter' that backs a society's rules, rituals and land ownership. They teach what counts as brave, shameful or sacred, and knowing them marks you as belonging.

sections.key: Creation myths follow a few recurring shapes, and flood stories appear across cultures, most famously in the Epic of Gilgamesh.
sections.b:
Creation stories take a handful of shapes. In the Babylonian Enuma Elish, Marduk defeats the sea goddess Tiamat and splits her body into sky and earth. In many Native American traditions, an animal dives to the bottom of a primeval sea and brings up mud that becomes land. In a Chinese story, the giant Pangu hatches from a cosmic egg and his body becomes mountains, rivers and stars. In Genesis, God creates by speaking.

In 1872, George Smith of the British Museum translated a tablet from Nineveh telling of Utnapishtim, who builds a boat to survive a world-destroying flood and sends out birds to find land. It closely parallels Noah's story and is older than any surviving Genesis text. Greece has Deucalion and Pyrrha; India has Manu. Early civilisations grew up beside flood-prone rivers, which may help explain why.

sections.key: Myths are sacred stories of gods, legends are set in the human past, folktales entertain, and Propp found Russian fairy tales share 31 plot functions.
sections.b:
Folklorist William Bascom's 1965 scheme sorts stories three ways. Myths are held sacred and true, feature gods and are set in the remote past. Legends are set in the historical world and may have a real person at their core, like King Arthur or Ned Kelly. Folktales, like Cinderella, are told for entertainment and could happen anywhere. The lines blur.

In 1928, Vladimir Propp analysed 100 Russian fairy tales and found 31 recurring plot 'functions', such as the hero leaving home, being tested, receiving a magical helper and defeating the villain. Not every tale uses all of them, but those that appear always come in the same order. He found just seven character roles. Screenwriters and game designers still borrow his checklist.

sections.key: The Dreaming is not old mythology but a living system of law, knowledge and responsibility to Country.
sections.b: It would be wrong to file Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander knowledge under 'mythology' as though it belonged to the past. For many Aboriginal peoples, the Dreaming is a living framework of law, kinship, ceremony and responsibility to Country. It tells how ancestral beings shaped the land, its creatures and its people, and it continues in the present. Each nation has its own words and knowledge: the Anangu of Uluru, for example, speak of Tjukurpa. Knowledge is carried in song, dance, art and songlines across the land, and some of it is restricted to particular people. Stories belong to their custodians and shouldn't be retold without permission.

sections.key: Myths live on in our language, films and psychology, and reading them well means asking what question each story answers.
sections.b:
Myths never went away. Marvel's Thor and the Percy Jackson books borrow gods and monsters directly. Psychology names ideas after them, like the Oedipus complex. We still speak of the Midas touch, a nemesis, a siren song, or being caught between Scylla and Charybdis.

When you meet a myth, ask what problem it is solving, who told it, and when. Compare versions, since most myths survive in several. Notice what it says about the values of its tellers. And remember that what is 'just mythology' to one person may be sacred, living belief to someone else.

quiz.q: How do scholars use the word 'myth'?
o: A story that has been proven false
A traditional, often sacred story
Any story written for young children
An account of a real battle
quiz.e: Calling a story a myth describes its kind and job, not whether it is true.

quiz.q: In many Native American creation stories, how does land appear?
o: An animal fetches mud from the sea floor
A god creates it simply by speaking
A giant's body becomes the mountains
A goddess is split into sky and earth
quiz.e: Creation myths recur in a few shapes, and the earth-diver is a common one in Native American traditions.

quiz.q: What most clearly separates a legend from a myth?
o: Legends are always completely true
Legends are told only to children
Legends only ever feature the gods
Legends are set in human history
quiz.e: Myths belong to a sacred remote past, while legends sit in human history.

quiz.q: Why is it misleading to call the Dreaming mythology?
o: It was only invented in the 1900s
It is only about the stars and sky
It is a living system of law and Country
It contains no real stories at all
quiz.e: For many Aboriginal peoples the Dreaming continues in the present as law and responsibility.

quiz.q: What helps when you meet a myth from another culture?
o: Deciding fast whether it is true or false
Asking what problem the story solved
Hunting for the one original version
Ignoring what it says about its tellers
quiz.e: Context and comparing versions show what a story meant to those who told it.

LESSONS.push: Calling a story a myth doesn't mean it's false. What scholars actually mean.

LESSONS.title: The gods of Olympus
LESSONS.hook: Jealous, vain, passionate and powerful: the Greek gods behaved like the most dramatic family you've ever met, and they left their names all over our language.

sections.key: In Hesiod's Theogony the universe begins with Chaos, and Zeus wins power by defeating his father Cronus and the Titans.
sections.b:
The fullest Greek account of the gods is the Theogony, a poem by Hesiod from around 700 BC. First came Chaos, a yawning emptiness, then Gaia (Earth), who bore Uranus (Sky). Their children were the Titans. Uranus trapped them inside the Earth, so Gaia gave her youngest son Cronus a sickle, and he overthrew his father. In Greek myth, sons topple fathers.

Warned that his own child would overthrow him, Cronus swallowed each baby. His wife Rhea saved Zeus by hiding him on Crete and handing Cronus a stone in baby clothes instead. Zeus freed his siblings and won a ten-year war against the Titans. Most were locked in Tartarus, while Atlas was condemned to hold up the sky.

sections.key: The twelve Olympians each ruled a domain, yet they showed human flaws such as jealousy, vanity and revenge.
sections.b:
The winning gods lived on Mount Olympus, Greece's highest peak at nearly 2,920 metres. The usual twelve are Zeus (king and thunder), Hera (marriage), Poseidon (sea and earthquakes), Demeter (harvest), Athena (wisdom and crafts), Apollo (music, prophecy and healing), Artemis (the hunt), Ares (war), Aphrodite (love), Hephaestus (the blacksmith), Hermes (the messenger) and Dionysus (wine), though some lists include Hestia, goddess of the hearth. Hades ruled the underworld.

These gods were immortal but far from perfect. Zeus pursued countless lovers, and Hera took furious revenge. In Ovid's telling, the weaver Arachne boasted she was better than Athena and was turned into a spider. The lesson for mortals: never show hubris, the arrogant pride that challenges the gods.

sections.key: Greek myths explained why humans have fire, why the world holds suffering and why there are seasons.
sections.b:
The Titan Prometheus stole fire from the gods for humans. Zeus chained him to a rock, where an eagle ate his liver every day. Zeus also sent Pandora, the first woman, with a jar that released evils into the world and kept only hope inside. It was a jar, not a box: the box crept in through a translation slip in the 1500s.

The seasons had their own story. When Hades carried off Persephone, her mother Demeter's grief made the crops fail. Because Persephone had eaten pomegranate seeds in the underworld, she must spend part of every year there, and the earth goes barren while she is away.

sections.key: Greek religion centred on rituals, festivals and oracles rather than a single holy book or creed.
sections.b:
The Greeks had no single holy book and no fixed creed. Religion was about doing things properly: offering sacrifices, pouring wine for the gods, keeping festivals and honouring your city's patron god, as Athens honoured Athena in the Parthenon.

People also sought guidance from oracles. The most famous was at Delphi, where a priestess called the Pythia spoke for Apollo. Cities and kings sent envoys to ask her advice before wars and colonising expeditions, and her answers were famously ambiguous. The myths themselves came in many versions, told by different poets and playwrights, and nobody expected them all to agree.

sections.key: Rome renamed the Greek gods, and those names live on in our planets, weekdays and everyday words.
sections.b:
Rome identified its own gods with the Greek ones and absorbed their stories. Zeus became Jupiter, Hera became Juno, Poseidon became Neptune, Ares became Mars, Aphrodite became Venus, Hermes became Mercury, Athena became Minerva, Artemis became Diana, Hephaestus became Vulcan and Cronus became Saturn. Europe learned much of its mythology through Latin, so the Roman names stuck: they are on the planets, and Saturday is Saturn's day.

Everyday words hide the myths too. Panic comes from Pan, the goat-legged god of the wild, whose shout could terrify travellers. An echo recalls the nymph Echo, who could only repeat the last words spoken to her. Titanic means huge, like the Titans, cereal comes from Ceres (the Roman Demeter) and volcano from Vulcan's forge. Nike is named for the goddess of victory.

quiz.q: How did Zeus escape being swallowed by his father Cronus?
o: Rhea gave Cronus a stone in baby clothes
He turned himself into an eagle
Atlas carried him away to the underworld
Gaia hid him deep inside the Earth
quiz.e: Cronus swallowed the stone, and Zeus grew up in hiding on Crete before freeing his siblings.

quiz.q: What do the stories of the Greek gods show about them?
o: They were immortal but had human flaws
They were perfect models of good behaviour
They never took sides in human affairs
They punished only those who broke laws
quiz.e: The gods were jealous, vain and vengeful, which is why hubris was the great warning to mortals.

quiz.q: Which Greek myth explained the changing seasons?
o: Prometheus stealing fire from the gods
Pandora letting evils out of her jar
Atlas being condemned to hold up the sky
Persephone's yearly stay in the underworld
quiz.e: While Persephone is away, Demeter's grief leaves the earth barren.

quiz.q: What was central to ancient Greek religion?
o: Studying one sacred holy book
Rituals, festivals and oracles
Agreeing on one fixed creed
Avoiding all contact with the gods
quiz.e: Religion was about doing things properly, and nobody expected the myths to agree.

quiz.q: Where does the word 'panic' come from?
o: The Titan Prometheus and his fire
The nymph Echo and her voice
The goddess Athena and her owl
The god Pan and his terrifying shout
quiz.e: Many English words, including panic, echo, cereal and volcano, trace back to Greek and Roman myth.

LESSONS.push: Saturday carries a god's name, and so do the planets. Which gods are in your week?

LESSONS.title: Greek heroes and their flaws
LESSONS.hook: They slew monsters, outwitted giants and sailed to the ends of the world. Yet many Greek heroes were undone by something inside themselves.

sections.key: A Greek hero was usually part divine and chased glory through extraordinary deeds, but was not necessarily a good person.
sections.b:
The Greek word heros did not simply mean a good person. Heroes were extraordinary figures of the distant past, often with one divine parent, who performed deeds beyond ordinary humans. What drove them was kleos, glory: the fame that would keep their names alive after death. Many were violent, proud or reckless.

Heroes were also worshipped. People across Greece made offerings at shrines and tombs believed to belong to heroes, hoping for their protection. Poets and playwrights retold their stories for centuries, which is why most exist in several, sometimes contradictory, versions.

sections.key: Heracles, son of Zeus, performed twelve labours as penance after Hera drove him mad.
sections.b:
Heracles, called Hercules by the Romans, was the son of Zeus and a mortal woman, Alcmene. That earned him the lifelong hatred of Zeus's wife Hera, who drove him into a madness in which he killed his own wife and children.

To atone, he served King Eurystheus and performed twelve labours. He strangled the Nemean lion, whose hide no weapon could pierce, and killed the many-headed Hydra. He cleaned the filthy Augean stables in a day by diverting two rivers, and dragged Cerberus, the three-headed guard dog, up from the underworld. After his death, he was taken up to live among the gods.

sections.key: Perseus beat Medusa by watching her reflection, and Theseus killed the Minotaur but forgot his sails and lost his father.
sections.b:
Perseus, son of Zeus and Danaë, was sent to fetch the head of Medusa, a Gorgon whose gaze turned anyone to stone. Aided by Athena's polished shield, winged sandals and a cap of invisibility, he cut off her head by watching only her reflection. On the way home he rescued Andromeda from a sea monster.

Theseus, an Athenian prince, volunteered to be among the seven young men and seven young women Athens sent to King Minos of Crete to feed the Minotaur, a half-bull monster in the Labyrinth. Ariadne gave him a ball of thread, so he killed the monster and followed the thread out. But he forgot to change his ship's black sails to white. His father Aegeus, thinking him dead, leapt into the sea, which is still called the Aegean.

sections.key: Jason needed the sorceress Medea to win the Golden Fleece, while Odysseus relied on cunning rather than strength.
sections.b:
Jason was set an impossible task to reclaim his throne: bring back the Golden Fleece from Colchis, at the eastern end of the Black Sea. He gathered the Argonauts, named after their ship the Argo. In Colchis, the sorceress Medea fell in love with him and helped him yoke fire-breathing bulls and get past the dragon guarding the fleece. Years later he left her for a Corinthian princess, and in Euripides' play Medea her revenge is terrible.

Odysseus won by brains, not brawn. Tradition credits him with the wooden horse that got Greek soldiers inside Troy. Returning home to Ithaca disguised as a beggar, he was recognised only by his old dog Argos. Then he strung the great bow no suitor could manage.

sections.key: Achilles chose a short, glorious life, and Aristotle said the tragic hero falls through a flaw or error, often driven by hubris.
sections.b:
Achilles, son of the mortal king Peleus and the sea goddess Thetis, was the greatest Greek warrior at Troy. A prophecy gave him a stark choice: a long, obscure life at home or a short one with undying glory. He chose glory. In the Iliad, grief over the death of his companion Patroclus drives him back into battle to kill the Trojan prince Hector. His vulnerable heel comes from later writers, not Homer.

In his Poetics, Aristotle said the ideal tragic hero is admirable but falls through hamartia, closer to 'error' than 'flaw'. Oedipus, who unknowingly kills his father, is the classic case. Pride, or hubris, is often the trigger, and the fall brings pity, fear and catharsis. Heroes are most interesting when their strengths and weaknesses are the same thing.

quiz.q: What mainly drove a Greek hero to act?
o: A sense of duty to the law
Kleos, glory that outlives death
Obedience to their local king
A wish for a long, quiet life
quiz.e: Heroes sought lasting fame, and many were violent, proud or reckless along the way.

quiz.q: Why did Heracles perform his twelve labours?
o: To win the hand of a princess
To become king of Athens
To atone for killing his own family
To free the Titans from Tartarus
quiz.e: Hera's hatred drove him mad, and the labours were his penance.

quiz.q: How did Perseus avoid being turned to stone by Medusa?
o: He wore a blindfold the whole time
He looked only at her reflection
He struck while she was sleeping
He was immune as a son of Zeus
quiz.e: Looking only at her reflection let him strike without meeting her gaze.

quiz.q: How did Jason succeed in winning the Golden Fleece?
o: He defeated the dragon alone with his sword
He tricked the king with a wooden horse
With help from the sorceress Medea
With a ball of thread from Ariadne
quiz.e: Medea's magic let him yoke the fire-breathing bulls and get past the dragon.

quiz.q: According to Aristotle, how does a tragic hero fall?
o: Through a pure accident that could not be avoided
Through an error or flaw, often driven by hubris
Through the plotting of a wicked enemy
Through a lack of courage in battle
quiz.e: The hero is admirable but brought down by hamartia, which is closer to 'error' than to a moral flaw.

LESSONS.push: Greek heroes slew monsters, yet many fell to their own flaws. Which ones?

LESSONS.title: Odin, Thor and the end of the world
LESSONS.hook: A one-eyed god who hanged himself for wisdom, a thunder god in a wedding dress, and a prophecy that the gods themselves will die. Norse myth is wilder than the movies.

sections.key: Most Norse myths survive in two Icelandic collections from the 1200s, written by Christians centuries after the conversion.
sections.b:
The Norse peoples of Scandinavia told their myths aloud, so most of what we know was written down later in Iceland, which officially adopted Christianity around the year 1000.
