quiz.e: Without the dance, audiences could focus on the score's power, and it became a classic.

LESSONS.push: A ballet premiere in 1913 caused an uproar. A year later, the same music was cheered.

LESSONS.title: The Bauhaus: the school that designed the modern world
LESSONS.hook: A German art school lasted only fourteen years before the Nazis shut it down. Yet its ideas are in your kitchen chairs, your fonts and the buildings you walk past every day.

sections.key: Walter Gropius founded the Bauhaus in 1919 to unite art and craft, so students learned both principles and hands-on skills.
sections.b: In 1919, just after the First World War, the architect Walter Gropius founded a school in Weimar, Germany, by merging an art academy with a school of arts and crafts. He called it the Staatliches Bauhaus, roughly meaning state house of building. Gropius believed the old split between fine artists and craftspeople was harmful. Painters looked down on furniture makers, while industry churned out poorly designed products. At the Bauhaus, students learned artistic principles and hands-on skills in workshops for metal, wood, textiles, pottery, printing and more. The long-term goal was building, bringing all the arts together. Germany was poor and divided, and the school hoped to help shape a better society.

sections.key: Every student began with a preliminary course that stripped away old habits and explored materials, shape and colour.
sections.b: New students first took the preliminary course, developed by Johannes Itten and later run by László Moholy-Nagy and Josef Albers. The aim was to unlearn old academic habits and experiment directly with materials. Students explored the textures of wood, glass, paper and metal, studied contrasts of light and dark, and built structures from folded paper. Albers later became famous for his studies of how colours change depending on their neighbours. The painters Paul Klee and Wassily Kandinsky taught theories of form and colour. It was one of the most remarkable teaching staffs ever gathered.

sections.key: Bauhaus workshops designed simple objects for industry, but women who were promised equality were steered towards weaving.
sections.b:
The school shifted from handcraft towards designing prototypes for industry. Marianne Brandt designed teapots and lamps. Marcel Breuer designed a tubular steel armchair in the mid 1920s, later called the Wassily chair, inspired by the steel tubes of his bicycle. Herbert Bayer designed clean lower case typefaces. Many Bauhaus designs are still made today.

The school officially welcomed women, and in its first year more women than men applied. Leaders worried, and many women were pushed towards weaving. They turned that limitation into an achievement: under Gunta Stölzl, the first female master, the weaving workshop became one of the most commercially successful, and Anni Albers developed new textiles. Brandt broke into metalwork.

sections.key: Pressure from conservative politicians, then the Nazis, forced the Bauhaus from Weimar to Dessau and Berlin, and closed it in 1933.
sections.b:
Conservative politicians in Weimar saw the Bauhaus as foreign, left-wing and a waste of public money, and cut its funding. In 1925 it moved to Dessau, where Gropius designed an icon of modern architecture, completed in 1926: a glass curtain wall, flat roofs and linked wings. Gropius stepped down in 1928, followed by Hannes Meyer and, from 1930, Ludwig Mies van der Rohe. The Weimar and Dessau buildings are now UNESCO World Heritage sites.

The Nazis attacked it as un-German and communist. After they won control of Dessau's council in 1932, the school was forced out. Mies tried to continue in Berlin, but police raided it, and the staff closed it in 1933. Jewish and left-wing members suffered persecution, and some were killed in the Holocaust.

sections.key: Bauhaus teachers spread its ideas across the world, though the phrase 'form follows function' came from Louis Sullivan.
sections.b:
In fourteen years the school had perhaps 1,250 students, a small number for such influence. Its closure scattered its ideas worldwide. Gropius taught at Harvard, and Mies led the architecture school at what became the Illinois Institute of Technology, designing glass and steel towers that defined the modern skyline. Moholy-Nagy founded the New Bauhaus in Chicago in 1937. Josef and Anni Albers taught at Black Mountain College in North Carolina. Bauhaus-trained architects helped build the White City of Tel Aviv, now a World Heritage site.

A common myth credits the Bauhaus with the slogan form follows function, but it came from the American architect Louis Sullivan in the 1890s. Still, it suits the Bauhaus well.

quiz.q: What was Gropius's central aim for the Bauhaus?
o: To train only architects for the German government
To teach painting as a pure art, apart from industry
To unite fine art and craft, working towards building
To keep painters and craftspeople in separate schools
quiz.e: He thought the split between artists and craftspeople was harmful and wanted all the arts brought together.

quiz.q: What was the purpose of the preliminary course?
o: To unlearn old habits and explore materials
To teach students to copy old masters exactly
To choose which students would become teachers
To train students in business and printing
quiz.e: It cleared away academic habits so students could experiment directly with materials.

quiz.q: How did the weaving workshop become important at the Bauhaus?
o: It was chosen as the school's only industrial workshop
Women steered into it made it a commercial success
It was led by Gropius, who preferred textiles
It replaced metalwork once funding ran out
quiz.e: A limit placed on women became an achievement under Gunta Stölzl, the first female master.

quiz.q: Why did the Bauhaus close in 1933?
o: Its funding ended soon after the First World War
Its students all emigrated to the United States
Gropius sold the Dessau building to the council
Nazi pressure and a police raid led staff to close it
quiz.e: Attacked as un-German and left-wing, it was forced out of Dessau in 1932 and closed in Berlin.

quiz.q: What is true of the slogan 'form follows function'?
o: It predates the Bauhaus but suits its ideas well
Gropius coined it in his 1919 manifesto
It was the school's official motto from 1919
Mies adopted it after leaving Germany
quiz.e: It came from the American architect Louis Sullivan in the 1890s, so it is often wrongly credited to the Bauhaus, though it fits the school's ideas.

LESSONS.push: The Bauhaus lasted fourteen years, yet its ideas are probably within arm's reach of you.

LESSONS.title: How music learned to be written down
LESSONS.hook: For most of history, music lived only in memory. The squiggles, lines and dots that now let anyone read a song were invented bit by bit over a thousand years.

sections.key: For most of history, music was passed on by ear and memory, and early notation systems were limited or lost.
sections.b: Every culture has made music, but very few wrote it down with precise pitches and rhythms. Melodies were learned by listening and copying. Some ancient societies did develop notation. A clay tablet from the city of Ugarit, in modern Syria, dating to around 1400 BCE, contains instructions for a hymn, and the ancient Greeks used letter symbols for pitch. But these systems were limited or lost. In medieval Europe, the church's huge repertoire of chant, now often called Gregorian chant, was learned by heart. Training a singer to know it all could take many years.

sections.key: Neumes only reminded singers of a melody's shape, until lines showing exact pitch, promoted by Guido of Arezzo, let anyone read an unheard tune.
sections.b:
From around the ninth century, scribes added little marks called neumes above the Latin words in chant books. They showed whether the melody rose or fell, but not exactly how high or how long. They were memory aids: a singer who had never heard a chant could not learn it from neumes alone. Gradually, scribes placed them at different heights, so position hinted at pitch.

Around 1030, the Italian monk Guido of Arezzo championed notes on horizontal lines, each representing a fixed pitch, with letters that became clefs. Singers could now read a melody they had never heard, and Guido claimed young singers could learn in a short time what once took years. Music could travel on parchment alone.

sections.key: The syllables used to sing scales come from the first syllables of lines in a Latin hymn that Guido used as a teaching tool.
sections.b:
Guido also gave singers a memory trick. He used a Latin hymn to Saint John the Baptist in which each of the first six lines began one step higher than the last. The first syllables of those lines were ut, re, mi, fa, sol and la. By learning the hymn, students fixed the sound of each step in their minds.

Over the centuries, ut was replaced in most countries by do, which is easier to sing. A seventh syllable, si, was added later, and in the nineteenth century English teachers changed it to ti so every syllable began with a different letter. This system, called solfège, is still used to teach singing around the world.

sections.key: As composers wrote for several voices at once, note shapes were invented to show how long each note lasts.
sections.b: Showing pitch was only half the problem. As composers wrote for several voices singing different lines at once, called polyphony, singers needed to know exactly how long each note lasted so they stayed together. In the thirteenth century, theorists such as Franco of Cologne set out rules in which the shape of a note indicated its duration. This system, called mensural notation, developed over the following centuries. Notes gradually changed from black squares and diamonds to the round open and filled heads used today. Bar lines became common only in the seventeenth century. Time signatures, rests and ties followed.

sections.key: Printed music from 1501 spread compositions across Europe, and notation is only one way to record music.
sections.b:
Copying music by hand was slow and expensive. In 1501, the Venetian printer Ottaviano Petrucci published the Odhecaton, generally regarded as the first book of polyphonic music printed with movable type. Printed music spread compositions across Europe and created a market of amateurs who bought music to play at home.

Staff notation is not universal. Renaissance lute players used tablature, which shows where to put the fingers rather than which notes sound, as modern guitar tabs do. India, China, Indonesia and other traditions have their own systems, and many jazz, folk and popular musicians learn by ear. Notation struggles to capture subtle timing, tone colour and improvisation. In the twentieth century, some composers used graphic scores of drawings and instructions.

quiz.q: How was the huge repertoire of medieval church chant mostly learned?
o: By heart, which took singers many years
From printed books given to every singer
From detailed staff notation on parchment
By copying a single teacher's written lessons
quiz.e: Without precise notation, music depended on memory and teachers, so training took years.

quiz.q: What did Guido of Arezzo's staff make possible?
o: Printing music with movable type
Recording exactly how long each note lasts
Reading a melody you had never heard before
Singing in several voices at once
quiz.e: Lines representing fixed pitches meant a singer no longer needed a teacher to learn each chant.

quiz.q: Where do the syllables ut, re, mi, fa, sol and la come from?
o: The names of six medieval musical instruments
The first syllables of lines in a Latin hymn
The first six letters of the Greek alphabet
The names of six saints in a medieval calendar
quiz.e: Each line of the hymn began one step higher, so learning it fixed the sound of each step.

quiz.q: Why did composers need ways to notate rhythm?
o: To help singers hide mistakes during performance
To let audiences read the music while listening
To replace the staff with a simpler system
To keep voices singing different lines together
quiz.e: Polyphony only works if every singer knows how long each note lasts, so note shapes showed duration.

quiz.q: What does guitar tablature show?
o: Where to put the fingers on the strings
The sounding notes, written on a staff
Only the length of each chord in a piece
How loudly to pluck each string in turn
quiz.e: Tablature shows finger positions rather than which notes sound, as Renaissance lute notation did.

LESSONS.push: Where do do, re and mi come from? A medieval monk had a clever memory trick.

LESSONS.title: Vermeer: the mystery of light
LESSONS.hook: Barely three dozen paintings, almost no letters, no surviving drawings. Johannes Vermeer painted quiet rooms full of light, and art detectives are still arguing about how he did it.

sections.key: Vermeer left only about 34 to 37 paintings and almost no personal records, so much about him is guesswork.
sections.b:
Johannes Vermeer was baptised in Delft, in the Dutch Republic, in 1632. His father was a weaver who also dealt in art, and Johannes took over the business. He married Catharina Bolnes, from a Catholic family, in 1653, and they had a large family. He joined the painters' guild and later served as one of its heads.

Yet he left no diaries, no letters about his art and no drawing that can confidently be attributed to him. Nearly everything known comes from legal and financial documents. Scholars attribute only about 34 to 37 surviving paintings to him, and some attributions are disputed. He seems to have worked very slowly, perhaps finishing only a few a year.

sections.key: Vermeer's quiet interiors are famous for the subtle way they capture daylight from a window on the left.
sections.b:
A striking number of Vermeer's paintings show a quiet room lit by a window on the left. The figures are usually one or two women, reading letters, pouring milk, playing music or weighing pearls. A local collector, Pieter van Ruijven, appears to have bought many of them, which may have let Vermeer work carefully.

He watched how daylight behaves. In The Milkmaid, the whitewashed wall is full of subtle shifts, tiny nail holes and marks. Shadows are not just darker; they pick up colour from nearby surfaces. Tiny dots of light paint suggest sparkle on bread, metal or fabric. They resemble the blurred highlights of an out-of-focus lens, which has fuelled debate about his methods.

sections.key: Vermeer used costly ultramarine freely, even in shadows, which is puzzling for an artist who died in debt.
sections.b:
Natural ultramarine was made from lapis lazuli, a semi-precious stone mined in what is now Afghanistan. It cost more than many other pigments, and many painters saved it for important details, such as the robes of the Virgin Mary.

Vermeer used it remarkably freely. It appears in the blue and yellow headscarf of the Girl with a Pearl Earring and in the apron of The Milkmaid. Technical studies have also found ultramarine mixed into shadows and underlayers, where it helps create cool, luminous tones. Such lavish spending is puzzling for an artist who ended his life in debt. It remains part of the mystery of his methods and his finances.

sections.key: Some argue Vermeer used optical aids, but there is no documentary proof, and genius still shaped every choice.
sections.b:
A camera obscura is a darkened box or room in which a lens projects an image of the outside scene onto a surface. The device was known in Vermeer's day. Delft was home to the microscope pioneer Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, later trustee of Vermeer's bankrupt estate, though nothing suggests they discussed optics.

In 2001 the historian Philip Steadman argued that the geometry of several Vermeer rooms fits a camera obscura, and David Hockney suggested Old Masters used optical aids. In the 2013 documentary Tim's Vermeer, inventor Tim Jenison used a lens and mirror to produce a strikingly close copy of The Music Lesson without painting training. Critics reply that possible is not proven. No document mentions Vermeer owning such a device, and composition, colour and mood still demanded his skill.

sections.key: Vermeer died in debt, was largely forgotten for two centuries, and was revived by a French critic.
sections.b:
In 1672 France invaded the Dutch Republic and the art market collapsed. Vermeer's income dried up. He died in December 1675, aged 43, leaving his family deeply in debt. His widow later said the stress of financial ruin had contributed to his death.

Over the following centuries his name faded, and some paintings were sold under other artists' names. In the 1860s the French critic Théophile Thoré-Bürger published enthusiastic articles about him and helped restore his reputation. Since then his fame has soared. The Girl with a Pearl Earring is now one of the best-known paintings in the world, and a major Vermeer exhibition in Amsterdam in 2023 sold out completely.

quiz.q: What makes Vermeer unusual for a famous painter?
o: He left few paintings and almost no personal records
He signed every work with a detailed diary entry
He painted hundreds of works for a busy market
He kept careful letters explaining his methods
quiz.e: Only about 34 to 37 paintings survive and almost no personal records, so much about him is inferred.

quiz.q: What detail shows how closely Vermeer observed daylight?
o: Plain white walls with no variation at all
Shadows that pick up colour from nearby surfaces
Light that always comes from the right
Figures lit by candles rather than windows
quiz.e: His shadows and whitewashed walls hold subtle colour shifts, showing close study of how daylight behaves.

quiz.q: Why is Vermeer's lavish use of ultramarine puzzling?
o: The pigment was cheap and easy to buy in Delft
He used it only for the robes of the Virgin Mary
It was costly, yet he used it freely despite debts
Studies found he never used it in shadows at all
quiz.e: Ultramarine was expensive, so his generous use sits oddly with his money troubles.

quiz.q: What is the fair conclusion about Vermeer and the camera obscura?
o: A surviving receipt proves he bought one in Delft
It is possible but unproven, and skill still mattered
Experts agree he never used any optical aid at all
Leeuwenhoek personally taught him how to use one
quiz.e: Showing that a method is possible does not prove he used it, and no document mentions such a device.

quiz.q: Why did Vermeer's reputation revive in the 1860s?
o: His paintings were found under other names in Delft
A French critic wrote enthusiastically about him
The Dutch art market recovered after the invasion
His widow published his private letters
quiz.e: After two centuries of fading, critic Thoré-Bürger's articles helped restore his reputation.

LESSONS.push: Barely three dozen paintings survive, and nobody agrees how he made them.

LESSONS.title: Jainism: the path of harming nothing
LESSONS.hook: Some monks sweep the ground before every step so they won't crush an insect. Behind that gesture lies one of the world's oldest and most demanding ideas: that every living thing has a soul.

sections.key: Jainism is an Indian religion built on non-violence, self-discipline and freeing the soul.
sections.b:
Jainism grew up on the Ganges plain of northern India, in the same restless era as the Buddha. Its most famous teacher, Mahavira, is usually dated to the sixth or fifth century BCE. Jains do not call him the founder, though. In their tradition he is the twenty-fourth and last Tirthankara of our age, a "ford-maker" who crossed the river of rebirth and showed others the way. His predecessor, Parshvanatha, is widely accepted by historians as a real figure who lived a few centuries earlier.

Today there are roughly four to five million Jains, mostly in India, with communities in Britain, North America, East Africa and Australia.

sections.key: Jains believe souls exist in all living things and are weighed down by karma, a fine matter that clings to them.
sections.b:
At the heart of Jain teaching is the jiva, the soul. Every soul is by nature perfectly knowing, perceiving and blissful. The problem is karma. In many religions karma is a moral law of cause and effect. In Jainism it is an extremely fine substance that clings to the soul whenever we act with passion, greed or violence.

That build-up keeps the soul trapped in the cycle of birth and death. Souls are found not only in humans and animals but in plants, and even in tiny beings in earth, water, fire and air. The goal of life is to stop new karma attaching and to burn away the old, until the soul rises free.

sections.key: Ahimsa, or non-violence, is the central Jain value and covers diet, daily habits, words and thoughts.
sections.b:
Because so many beings have souls, the Jain duty not to harm reaches further than in almost any other tradition. Jains are strict vegetarians. Many also avoid root vegetables such as onions, garlic and potatoes, because pulling them up kills the whole plant and the small creatures in the soil. Traditionally many avoid eating after sunset, when insects could fall unseen into food.

Monks and nuns may carry a soft brush to clear the ground before they sit or walk, and some wear a cloth over the mouth to avoid harming tiny beings in the air. Harsh speech and hateful intentions count as harm too, so ahimsa is a discipline of the mind as much as the body.

sections.key: Anekantavada teaches that truth has many sides and no single viewpoint captures all of it.
sections.b:
One of Jainism's most admired ideas is anekantavada, often translated as "many-sidedness". Reality is complex, Jain philosophers argued, and any statement about it is true only from a particular standpoint. To illustrate this, Jains, like Buddhists and Hindus, tell the story of the blind men and the elephant. One touches the trunk and says an elephant is like a snake. Another feels a leg and says it is like a tree. Each is partly right and wrong to think he has the whole truth.

Jain logicians built this into a careful system for qualifying statements with words like "in some respect". Many modern Jains see it as a partner to ahimsa: intellectual humility as a form of non-violence.

sections.key: Two branches differ over monastic dress, yet Jain ideas of non-violence shaped Gandhi and still inspire charity.
sections.b:
Monks and nuns take five great vows: non-violence, truthfulness, not stealing, chastity and non-possession. How far to take non-possession helped split Jainism in two. Digambara ("sky-clad") monks go naked and hold that women must be reborn as men to reach liberation. Svetambara ("white-clad") monks and nuns wear simple white robes, and the tradition teaches that women can be liberated. Lay Jains follow gentler versions of the vows.

Jain temples are known for carved marble, as at Dilwara and Ranakpur. The festival of Paryushana ends with the words "Micchami Dukkadam", roughly "may my wrongs be forgiven". Gandhi, raised in Gujarat, counted the Jain thinker Shrimad Rajchandra among his guides. Jain communities also fund hospitals for animals and birds, including one in Old Delhi.

quiz.q: How do Jains regard Mahavira?
o: As the founder who started Jainism from scratch
As a god who grants wishes to worshippers
As the last Tirthankara, or ford-maker
As a famous disciple of the Buddha
quiz.e: In Jain tradition Mahavira is the twenty-fourth and last Tirthankara of our age, not the founder.

quiz.q: How does Jainism picture karma?
o: As a fine substance that clings to the soul
As a purely moral law with no physical effect
As a reward given by a creator god
As something that affects only humans
quiz.e: Karma is pictured as extremely fine matter that attaches to the soul through passion, greed and violence.

quiz.q: Why do many Jains avoid root vegetables?
o: They are thought to be unclean
Uprooting them kills the plant and soil life
They are said to grow only in the dark
Monks are forbidden all vegetables
quiz.e: Harm to any living being counts, so uprooting a plant and the creatures around it is avoided.

quiz.q: What does the blind men and elephant story illustrate?
o: Each view holds part of the truth
Only the man at the trunk was right
Animals see reality better than us
No truth can ever be known at all
quiz.e: Anekantavada holds that each standpoint is partly right, so no one should claim the whole truth.

quiz.q: What helped divide Jainism into two main branches?
o: Whether Jains should eat meat
How far to take the vow of non-possession
Disagreement over Mahavira's birthplace
A war between two royal families
quiz.e: Digambara monks give up even clothing, while Svetambara monks and nuns wear simple white robes.

LESSONS.push: Some monks sweep the path before each step. The reason is older than it sounds.

LESSONS.title: Ireland's gods, heroes and fairy mounds
LESSONS.hook: Before St Patrick, Ireland had shining gods who vanished into the hills, a hero who could fight an army alone, and a giant who supposedly built a causeway to Scotland.

sections.key: Most Irish myths survive only because medieval Christian scribes wrote them down, and they reshaped them as they did.
sections.b:
The pre-Christian Irish left no written scriptures. Poets and druids, trained for years, carried genealogies, laws and tales in memory. What we have comes mostly from manuscripts copied by monks between roughly the eighth and fifteenth centuries, long after Ireland became Christian.

That makes the stories wonderful but tricky. The scribes preserved them with affection, yet they also reshaped them, turning old gods into ancient kings and fitting Irish history into a biblical timeline. Scholars sort the tales into groups: the Mythological Cycle, the Ulster Cycle, the Fenian Cycle and the Cycles of the Kings.

sections.key: The Tuatha Dé Danann were Ireland's old gods, remembered in the Book of Invasions as a magical people who retreated into the hills.
sections.b:
The medieval Lebor Gabála Érenn, the "Book of the Taking of Ireland", tells of Ireland settled in waves: Cessair and Partholón, then Nemed, then the Fir Bolg, each struggling against the monstrous Fomorians. Then came the Tuatha Dé Danann, magical beings who arrived wrapped in mist, and finally the Milesians, ancestors of the Irish. Compiled largely in the eleventh century, it is legend, not a record of real migrations.

Many scholars see the Tuatha Dé as former gods. The Dagda owned a cauldron that never ran empty. Lugh, master of every craft, led them to victory over the Fomorians. Brigid, linked with poetry and healing, lives on as St Brigid. The Morrígan, goddess of war, could become a crow. When the Milesians won, the Tuatha Dé withdrew into the sídhe, the ancient mounds, and became the fairy folk of folklore.

sections.key: The boy hero Cú Chulainn earned his name by killing a guard dog, then held back an army single-handed.
sections.b:
The boy Sétanta, nephew of King Conchobar of Ulster, arrived late to a feast at the smith Culann's house. Culann's ferocious guard dog attacked him, and he killed it. Seeing the smith's grief, the boy offered to be his hound until a new one was raised. So he became Cú Chulainn, "Culann's Hound".

In battle he could be seized by a terrifying frenzy, the ríastrad, which twisted his body into a monstrous shape. In the epic Táin Bó Cúailnge, the "Cattle Raid of Cooley", Queen Medb of Connacht invades Ulster to seize a prize bull. The Ulster warriors lie helpless under a curse, so the teenage Cú Chulainn holds back her army alone, fighting a long series of duels at a river ford.

sections.key: Bound by conflicting geasa, Cú Chulainn tied himself to a standing stone to die on his feet.
sections.b:
Irish heroes lived under geasa, sacred prohibitions that could not be broken without disaster. Cú Chulainn was bound never to eat dog meat, yet also never to refuse hospitality. Before his last battle, three old women offered him dog meat, and either choice meant breaking a geis. Weakened, he fought on.

Mortally wounded, he tied himself to a standing stone so that he could die on his feet, facing his enemies. They dared not approach until a crow, the sign of the Morrígan, landed on his shoulder. A bronze statue of the dying Cú Chulainn stands in Dublin's General Post Office as a memorial to those who fought in the 1916 Easter Rising.

sections.key: Fionn gained wisdom from the Salmon of Knowledge, while tales of Lir's children and Oisín explore time and loss.
sections.b:
The Fenian Cycle follows Fionn mac Cumhaill and his war band. As a youth he served a poet who had spent seven years trying to catch the Salmon of Knowledge. Told to cook it but not taste it, Fionn burnt his thumb, sucked it, and gained all its wisdom. Later folklore made him a giant who built the Giant's Causeway as a road to Scotland, a playful tale about land formed by cooling lava.

In the Children of Lir, a jealous stepmother turns four children into swans for nine hundred years. When the spell breaks, they age and die. Fionn's son Oisín rides to Tír na nÓg, the Land of Youth. After what seems three years, he visits home and finds three hundred have passed. Touching the ground, he ages instantly.

quiz.q: Why are Irish myths tricky to treat as pure pre-Christian belief?
o: Monks wrote them down and reshaped them
They were composed by Victorian folklorists
They survive only as spoken tales today
They were carved in stone by the druids
quiz.e: Monks preserved the tales but turned gods into kings and fitted them into a biblical timeline.

quiz.q: What happened to the Tuatha Dé Danann after the Milesians won?
o: They sailed back across the sea to Spain
They were wiped out in a final battle
They withdrew into the mounds as fairy folk
They became the first Irish Christian saints
quiz.e: The old gods retreated into the sídhe, which is how they became the fairy folk of later folklore.

quiz.q: How did Sétanta become Cú Chulainn?
o: He won the Cattle Raid of Cooley
He killed a guard dog, then took its place
He was cursed by Queen Medb
He was adopted by the smith's family
quiz.e: After killing Culann's dog, he offered to serve as the smith's hound, earning the name.

quiz.q: Why was Cú Chulainn doomed before his last battle?
o: He lost his weapons while crossing a river
Each choice would break one of his sacred vows
His own army deserted him on the eve of battle
Heavy snow blocked every road to the battlefield
quiz.e: Eating dog meat or refusing hospitality each broke a geis, so either choice meant disaster.

quiz.q: What happens to Oisín when he touches the ground in Ireland?
o: He returns safely to Tír na nÓg
He is turned into a swan
He ages at once into an old man
He is turned into a standing stone
quiz.e: Three hundred years had passed in Ireland, and touching the ground let that time catch up with him.

LESSONS.push: A hero who held off an army tied himself to a stone. Why wouldn't they approach?

LESSONS.title: King Arthur: how a legend was built
LESSONS.hook: There may never have been a King Arthur. Yet over a thousand years, writers in Wales, England and France assembled Camelot, the Round Table and the Holy Grail piece by piece.

sections.key: Arthur's story grew from very thin records in the obscure centuries after Roman rule ended in Britain.
sections.b:
Roman authority in Britain collapsed in the early fifth century. Over the next two hundred years, Anglo-Saxon groups settled much of what became England, while Britons held out in the west and north. Written records are extremely thin, which is why legends could flourish.

A British monk, Gildas, writing in the sixth century, described a British victory over the Saxons at Mount Badon. Tellingly, he never mentions Arthur. The earliest possible reference is in a Welsh poem, Y Gododdin, which praises a warrior as brave, "though he was no Arthur". Its date is uncertain and the line may be a later addition. From these faint traces, a towering figure would grow.

sections.key: Early Welsh texts present Arthur as a war leader, though historians doubt there is enough evidence to prove he existed.
sections.b:
Around 830, the Latin Historia Brittonum, traditionally linked to a monk named Nennius, listed twelve battles fought by Arthur, a "leader of battles", ending at Badon. Some sites are impossible to locate, and one passage has him carrying an image of the Virgin Mary into combat.

A later Welsh chronicle, the Annales Cambriae, records Badon and also Camlann, "in which Arthur and Medraut fell". Medraut would become the treacherous Mordred. Early Welsh poems and tales show a different Arthur, leading heroes against giants, witches and a monstrous boar. Most historians now think there is not enough evidence to say whether a real Arthur existed, though the debate continues.

sections.key: Geoffrey of Monmouth's History turned Arthur into a conquering king and gave the story its famous outline.
sections.b:
The Arthur most people know was launched by Geoffrey of Monmouth, a cleric in Oxford. His History of the Kings of Britain, completed around 1136, claimed to be translated from an ancient British book, a claim most scholars doubt.

Geoffrey gave Arthur a dramatic life. Merlin's magic lets Uther Pendragon visit Igerna at Tintagel, and Arthur is conceived. As king, Arthur defeats the Saxons, conquers much of Europe and challenges Rome itself. While he is away, his nephew Mordred seizes the throne and Guinevere. Arthur returns, kills Mordred and is mortally wounded, then carried to the island of Avalon to be healed. The book was a medieval sensation, surviving in more than two hundred manuscripts.

sections.key: French writers added the Round Table, Lancelot, Camelot and the Holy Grail, shifting focus to the knights.
sections.b:
Writers across the Channel dressed Geoffrey's warrior king in courtly fashion. In 1155 the Norman poet Wace retold the history in French verse and introduced the Round Table, where no knight could claim the place of honour. Later, Chrétien de Troyes shifted attention from Arthur to his knights. He gave us the earliest surviving story of Lancelot's love for Guinevere, and first mentioned Camelot.

Chrétien's unfinished Perceval, from the 1180s, introduced a mysterious graal, a serving dish carried in a procession. He died before explaining it. Soon Robert de Boron identified the Grail as the vessel of the Last Supper, and later romances made the quest a spiritual test that most knights failed. Only the pure Galahad, Lancelot's son, achieves it.

sections.key: Malory fixed the English legend in 1485, and Arthur keeps returning because each age reshapes him.
sections.b:
In 1191, monks at Glastonbury Abbey announced they had found the grave of Arthur and Guinevere. The abbey needed funds and pilgrims after a fire, and many historians suspect the find was staged. It still tied Avalon to Glastonbury. Nearly three centuries later, Sir Thomas Malory, who wrote at least part of his work in prison, gathered the French and English stories into one English prose narrative. William Caxton printed it in 1485 as Le Morte d'Arthur, and it became the main source for later English retellings.

Legend said Arthur would return in Britain's hour of need, and he has. Tennyson made him a model of Victorian duty. T. H. White used him to think about power after two world wars. Arthur stands for the hope of a just ruler, and the sadness when good kingdoms fall.

quiz.q: Why could Arthur legends flourish in the centuries after Rome?
o: Written records from the period are extremely thin
Roman historians wrote detailed biographies of him
Anglo-Saxons recorded every battle
Gildas named Arthur at Badon
quiz.e: With so few records, there was little to contradict the growing stories.

quiz.q: What do most historians conclude about a real Arthur?
o: He was certainly a Roman general in Britain
There is not enough evidence to say either way
Gildas confirms he led the British at Badon
Geoffrey of Monmouth certainly invented him
quiz.e: The early sources are thin and contradictory, so the question remains open.

quiz.q: What did Geoffrey of Monmouth's book do for the legend?
o: Showed Arthur was only a Welsh folk hero
Proved the stories were invented by French poets
Gave Arthur a dramatic life as a conquering king
Replaced Arthur with Lancelot
quiz.e: Geoffrey's history launched the Arthur most people know, from Merlin and Uther to Mordred and Avalon.

quiz.q: How did the Grail change in the romances?
o: From a mysterious dish to the vessel of the Last Supper
From the vessel of the Last Supper to a mysterious dish
From a royal crown to the vessel of the Last Supper
From a mysterious dish to a mythical sword
quiz.e: Chrétien introduced a mysterious dish, and Robert de Boron made it Christ's Last Supper vessel.

quiz.q: Why does the Arthur legend keep returning?
o: Historians keep finding new graves
Each age reshapes him for itself
Malory's book has never gone out of print
Living kings still claim descent from him
quiz.e: Authors from Tennyson to White reused Arthur to explore duty, power and hope.

LESSONS.push: The Round Table and Camelot were added by French poets. Was there ever a king?

LESSONS.title: The great pilgrimages
LESSONS.hook: Every year millions of people walk, pray and queue for days to reach a single sacred place. Pilgrimage is one of the oldest things humans do, and it is booming.

sections.key: Pilgrimage joins an outer journey to an inner one, and the hardship is often part of the point.
sections.b:
A pilgrimage is a journey to a place believed to be holy. People make it to fulfil a duty, give thanks, ask for healing or forgiveness, honour the dead, or simply be near something sacred.

Almost every major tradition has sites: Jerusalem for Jews, Christians and Muslims; Mecca for Muslims; the Ganges for Hindus; Bodh Gaya, where the Buddha is said to have awakened, for Buddhists; the Golden Temple at Amritsar for Sikhs. The hardship is often part of the point. Walking long distances, fasting or sleeping rough strips away daily comforts, and many pilgrims say the road changes them as much as the destination.

sections.key: The Hajj is a once-in-a-lifetime duty for able Muslims, where rich and poor stand dressed alike.
sections.b:
The Hajj, one of the Five Pillars of Islam, is a duty for every Muslim who is physically and financially able. It takes place over several days in the month of Dhu al-Hijjah, and in recent years has drawn between one and a half and two and a half million pilgrims.

Before arriving, pilgrims enter a state of ritual purity called ihram. Men wear two plain, unstitched white cloths, so rich and poor stand alike before God. Pilgrims circle the Kaaba seven times anticlockwise. The most important moment is a day standing in prayer on the plain of Arafat. They also throw pebbles at pillars in Mina, remembering Abraham's rejection of temptation. Eid al-Adha follows, celebrated by Muslims worldwide.

sections.key: Hindu pilgrims bathe in the Ganges at the Kumbh Mela, and many hope to die or be cremated in Varanasi.
sections.b:
Hindu tradition says gods and demons churned the cosmic ocean for amrita, the nectar of immortality. Drops spilled from the pot, or kumbha, at four places: Prayagraj, Haridwar, Ujjain and Nashik. The Kumbh Mela rotates among them, and the largest gatherings, at Prayagraj, draw tens of millions over several weeks. Pilgrims believe bathing at auspicious times washes away sins. Organisers build a temporary city with roads, bridges, hospitals and police stations. UNESCO recognised the festival in 2017.

Varanasi, on the Ganges, is among the world's oldest continuously inhabited cities and is Shiva's city. Many Hindus believe dying there, or having ashes placed in the river, brings moksha, release from rebirth. Cremation fires at Manikarnika ghat burn day and night.

sections.key: The Camino de Santiago and Japan's Shikoku circuit show how walking journeys of faith have endured for centuries.
sections.b:
According to tradition, the remains of St James were discovered in north-western Spain in the ninth century, and a cathedral rose at Santiago de Compostela. Medieval pilgrims walked from all over Europe along the Camino. The scallop shell became their symbol, and yellow arrows still guide walkers. Hundreds of thousands now arrive each year; those who walk the final 100 kilometres, or cycle 200, can receive a certificate called the Compostela.

On Japan's island of Shikoku, a loop of about 1,200 kilometres links 88 Buddhist temples, honouring the monk Kūkai. Pilgrims, called henro, wear white and carry a staff said to represent Kūkai walking beside them. Walking it takes one to two months. Locals offer pilgrims gifts of food or money, a custom called osettai.

sections.key: Cheaper travel has made pilgrimage bigger, bringing safety and crowding problems, but the need for special places remains.
sections.b:
Cheaper travel has transformed pilgrimage. Journeys that once took months now take hours, and numbers have grown enormously. That brings pressure. Saudi Arabia allocates Hajj places by country through a quota and has built vast infrastructure to move crowds safely, yet crushes and extreme heat remain serious dangers at crowded sites. Popular Camino routes face overcrowding, and towns worry about housing and daily life.

New kinds of pilgrimage have appeared too. Many Australians and New Zealanders travel to Gallipoli for Anzac Day dawn services, and visitors file past the graves of musicians and writers. Whether religious or not, people still seem to need special places where they feel connected to something larger than themselves.

quiz.q: What role does hardship play in pilgrimage?
o: It shows that the journey has failed
It is avoided by most modern pilgrims
It is often part of the journey's purpose
It is added only by modern organisers
quiz.e: Walking, fasting and sleeping rough are often part of the point, and the road itself changes pilgrims.

quiz.q: Why do male Hajj pilgrims wear plain white unstitched cloths?
o: Rich and poor stand dressed alike before God
It marks who has completed the Hajj before
They must be easy to spot in crowds
It shows which country they come from
quiz.e: The simple dress of ihram removes signs of wealth and status.

quiz.q: What do many Hindus believe about Varanasi?
o: It may be visited only once in a lifetime
Dying there is believed to bring moksha
Only ascetics may bathe in its waters
It was founded after the Kumbh Mela
quiz.e: Release from the cycle of rebirth is believed to follow death in the holy city, or having ashes placed in the Ganges.

quiz.q: What does the staff carried by a Shikoku henro represent?
o: The monk Kūkai walking beside them
A permit from the temples
The distance of 88 temples
The scallop shell of Santiago
quiz.e: The staff stands for Kūkai himself, which is why hats say 'we two, travelling together'.

quiz.q: What problem has cheaper travel brought to pilgrimage?
o: Far fewer people now choose to take part
Crowding and safety risks at popular sites
Sites have lost their religious meaning
Journeys now take far longer than before
quiz.e: Numbers have grown enormously, bringing dangers such as crushes and heat, and strain on local towns.

LESSONS.push: Why male Hajj pilgrims, rich or poor, all wear the same plain white cloth.

LESSONS.title: Día de Muertos: a festival for the dead
LESSONS.hook: Each year at the start of November, families across Mexico build glowing altars and lay paths of orange petals so that their dead can find the way home. It is a celebration, not a horror show.

sections.key: Día de Muertos is a family celebration of love and remembrance, not a spooky festival.
sections.b:
Día de Muertos, the Day of the Dead, is often lumped in with Halloween because the dates are close and both involve skulls. The spirit is very different. Halloween plays with fear; Día de Muertos is about love and remembrance.

Families believe their departed relatives return for a short visit, and the living prepare to welcome them as honoured guests. The main days are 1 and 2 November. In many places the first day honours children who have died, sometimes called los angelitos, the little angels, and the second honours adults. Customs vary greatly from region to region, and Indigenous communities often keep some of the most distinctive traditions.

sections.key: The festival blends Indigenous Mexican ways of honouring the dead with Catholic feast days.
sections.b:
Long before the Spanish arrived, peoples of Mesoamerica, including the Aztecs, held ceremonies honouring the dead. Death was seen as part of a cycle rather than a final end, and the Aztec underworld, Mictlan, was ruled by Mictlantecuhtli and his consort Mictecacihuatl.

After the Spanish conquest in the sixteenth century, missionaries promoted the Catholic feasts of All Saints' Day and All Souls' Day on 1 and 2 November. Over centuries, local practices and Catholic customs wove together. Historians debate how much of today's festival comes directly from pre-Hispanic religion, since some features developed much later. What is clear is that the result is uniquely Mexican, neither simply Indigenous nor simply European.

sections.key: An ofrenda is a home altar of photographs, favourite foods and objects that welcomes returning souls.
sections.b:
The heart of the celebration is the ofrenda, an altar built in homes, and sometimes in schools, offices and public squares. It usually has several tiers covered in cloth and decorated with papel picado, delicate tissue paper cut into patterns.

Photographs of the dead take pride of place, along with things they loved in life: a favourite dish, a bottle of tequila, cigarettes, sweets, toys for children. Candles light the way, and copal incense perfumes the air. Many families include water to quench the souls' thirst after their long journey, and salt for purification. Building the ofrenda is a family task, and telling stories about the people pictured is part of the point. Remembering keeps the dead present.

sections.key: Orange marigolds, sweet bread and cheerful sugar skulls express the idea that death comes to everyone and can be met with a smile.
sections.b:
The flower of the season is the cempasúchil, a vivid orange marigold whose name comes from the Nahuatl language. Its strong colour and scent are believed to guide souls, and families scatter petals in paths from the street, or the cemetery, to the altar.

Bakeries fill with pan de muerto, a soft, sweet bread often flavoured with orange blossom and decorated with strips of dough shaped like bones. Sugar skulls, calaveras de azúcar, are moulded from sugar and decorated with coloured icing, sometimes with a person's name across the forehead. They are cheerful and bright rather than morbid. They express a familiar attitude: death comes to everyone, so it may as well be met with a smile.

sections.key: The festival mixes warm graveside vigils with joking skeletons, and UNESCO recognised it in 2008.
sections.b:
In many towns, families clean and decorate graves with marigolds, candles and offerings, and some keep vigil through the night. On Janitzio island in Lake Pátzcuaro, Purépecha fishermen cross the lake in canoes carrying lights. The mood is warm and social, closer to a family reunion than a funeral.

Skeletons dressed as living people have long mocked the powerful in Mexico. In the early 1910s, printmaker José Guadalupe Posada etched a skeleton woman in a grand feathered hat, mocking Mexicans who imitated European fashion. Diego Rivera placed her in his 1947 mural, and she became La Catrina. UNESCO listed the festival in 2008. The film Spectre (2015) invented a Mexico City parade, which the city then staged for real, and Pixar's Coco (2017) spread the ofrenda worldwide.

quiz.q: How does Día de Muertos differ from Halloween?
o: It welcomes the dead home with love
It is meant to frighten children
It is held on 31 October each year
It is a festival only for children
quiz.e: The festival is a family celebration of remembrance, not a spooky one.

quiz.q: How did today's festival take shape?
o: It was created in the twentieth century for tourists
It came entirely from Spanish Catholic practice
It is a direct copy of Aztec ceremonies
Indigenous and Catholic customs blended
quiz.e: Local traditions and Catholic feast days blended into something uniquely Mexican.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of the water and food on an ofrenda?
o: To raise money for the local church
To refresh the returning souls
To be left out for wandering animals
To decorate the altar and nothing more
quiz.e: Favourite foods and water for thirst honour the dead, and telling stories keeps them present.

quiz.q: What attitude do cheerful sugar skulls express?
o: Dread of the dead returning each year
Death is a subject best kept hidden
Death comes to all, so meet it with a smile
Only the wealthy should be remembered
quiz.e: The bright skulls reflect an acceptance of death rather than morbidity.

quiz.q: What was the original point of the skeleton that became La Catrina?
o: To warn children to stay away from graves
To mock those who copied European fashion
To celebrate the wealthiest families of the city
To honour the victims of the Revolution
quiz.e: Posada's skeleton in a feathered hat satirised Mexicans copying European style and forgetting their roots.

LESSONS.push: Why Mexican families lay a path of orange petals for the dead to follow.

LESSONS.title: The Bahá'í Faith: one God, one humanity
LESSONS.hook: Born in nineteenth-century Persia amid persecution and exile, the Bahá'í Faith teaches that all the great religions come from the same source. One of its temples stands among the gum trees of Sydney's northern beaches.

sections.key: The Bahá'í story begins in 1844, when a young Persian merchant declared a new age and was later executed.
sections.b:
In 1844, in the Persian city of Shiraz, a young merchant named Siyyid ‘Alí-Muhammad declared himself the Báb, meaning "the Gate". He taught that a new era of revelation was beginning and that he was preparing the way for a far greater messenger. His message spread quickly, and so did opposition from religious and political authorities. Thousands of his followers were killed.

The Báb was imprisoned and, in 1850, executed by firing squad in Tabriz. Bahá'í accounts say the first volley only cut the ropes binding him, and a second regiment carried out the execution. Bahá'ís regard him as a messenger of God in his own right and the forerunner of their faith's founder.

sections.key: The founder, Bahá'u'lláh, spent about four decades as a prisoner and exile, writing the faith's central texts.
sections.b:
Mírzá Husayn-‘Alí, born in 1817 to a noble Persian family, followed the Báb and took the title Bahá'u'lláh, "the Glory of God". In 1852 he was thrown into a notorious underground prison in Tehran, the Black Pit, where Bahá'ís believe he first received the revelation of his mission.

He was banished to Baghdad, then Constantinople, Adrianople and finally the prison city of Akka, in what is now Israel. In 1863, in a Baghdad garden called Ridván, he announced he was the messenger the Báb had foretold. He wrote thousands of tablets and several books. He died in 1892 near Akka, where his shrine is the holiest place on Earth for Bahá'ís.

sections.key: Bahá'ís believe one God has revealed truth in stages through messengers suited to their times.
sections.b:
A central teaching is that there is one God, who has revealed truth to humanity in stages. Messengers such as Abraham, Moses, Krishna, Zoroaster, the Buddha, Jesus and Muhammad are seen as teachers from the same divine school, each bringing guidance suited to their age. Their spiritual truths are eternal, while their social laws suited particular times and places.

The Báb and Bahá'u'lláh are the most recent messengers, though not the last; Bahá'ís believe revelation will continue in the far future. This leads them to treat other religions with deep respect, seeing divisions as the result of human interpretation rather than of the founders' teachings.

sections.key: Bahá'ís teach the oneness of humanity and govern themselves through elected councils with no clergy or campaigning.
sections.b:
If there is one God and one unfolding religion, Bahá'ís reason, there is one human family. From this come principles that sounded radical in the nineteenth century: equality of women and men, universal education, and ending prejudice of race, class, nation or religion. True science and true religion cannot conflict, since both seek truth. Bahá'u'lláh also called for world peace, global governance and an international auxiliary language.

There are no priests or ministers. Since 1963 the faith has been governed by the Universal House of Justice, a nine-member council in Haifa. Communities elect nine-member spiritual assemblies with no nominations, candidates or campaigning: each voter prays and writes the names of those best suited to serve. Life centres on the Nineteen-Day Feast, as the calendar has nineteen months of nineteen days.

sections.key: Bahá'í Houses of Worship are open to everyone, yet Bahá'ís still face persecution in Iran, where the faith began.
sections.b:
Bahá'í Houses of Worship are nine-sided, crowned with a dome, and open to everyone. Services are simple readings and prayers from many faiths' scriptures, often sung by a choir without instruments, with no sermons. The lotus-shaped temple in New Delhi, completed in 1986, is one of India's most visited buildings. Sydney's, in bushland at Ingleside, was dedicated in 1961. The faith's holy places in Haifa and Akka were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2008.

The faith has spread to almost every country, with followers estimated in the millions. In Iran, though, Bahá'ís are the largest non-Muslim minority and their religion is not recognised. Since 1979, hundreds have been executed and many imprisoned, barred from university or stripped of property, according to the United Nations and human rights groups. Bahá'ís have responded without violence.

quiz.q: What did the Báb teach about his own role?
o: That he was the final messenger of God
That he would found a state in Persia
That he was a forerunner of a greater one
That all earlier religions were false
quiz.e: He announced a new era and said he was preparing the way for a far greater messenger.

quiz.q: Where do Bahá'ís believe Bahá'u'lláh first received his revelation?
o: In the underground Black Pit prison in Tehran
In the garden of Ridván in Baghdad
On Mount Carmel, overlooking the bay of Haifa
At his final home near the city of Akka
quiz.e: He was imprisoned in 1852, and Bahá'ís believe the revelation came to him there.

quiz.q: What does progressive revelation say about other religions?
o: Earlier teachers were largely mistaken
They share one source, suited to each age
Only the newest religion has any truth
Their spiritual truths are now out of date
quiz.e: Messengers are seen as teachers in one school, so Bahá'ís respect other religions.

quiz.q: How are Bahá'í assemblies elected?
o: By open campaigns and speeches
By appointment from a senior priest
By drawing lots among local adults
By secret ballot, with no candidates
quiz.e: There are no nominations, candidates or campaigning; each voter prays and writes names.

quiz.q: How are Bahá'ís treated in Iran, the faith's birthplace?
o: They are recognised as the main religion
They face persecution and are not recognised
They hold most senior government posts
They are protected as an official minority
quiz.e: The government does not recognise the faith, and many Bahá'ís have been executed or imprisoned.

LESSONS.push: A faith born in a Persian prison now has a temple among Sydney gum trees.

LESSONS.title: Enuma Elish: Babylon's war in heaven
LESSONS.hook: Long before Genesis was written down, Babylonians told how the world was made from the split body of a sea goddess. Their creation epic is also a brilliant piece of political propaganda.

sections.key: Enuma Elish is the Babylonian creation epic, and it tells how one god became king of all the others.
sections.b:
Ancient Mesopotamian texts were known by their first words, and this one begins "Enuma elish", meaning "When on high". It opens in a world before the sky or earth had names, when nothing existed but water. The poem fills seven clay tablets written in Akkadian cuneiform.

Most surviving copies date from the first millennium BCE, but the poem is older. Many scholars think it was composed in the late second millennium BCE, perhaps in the reign of Nebuchadnezzar I (twelfth century BCE), though others argue for earlier dates. It is not a neutral account of creation.

In the mid-nineteenth century, excavations at Nineveh uncovered Ashurbanipal's library, and tablets reached the British Museum. In 1876 George Smith published a translation as The Chaldean Account of Genesis.

sections.key: The first gods were born from fresh water and salt water, and their noisy descendants led to Marduk's birth.
sections.b:
In the beginning were two primal beings: Apsu, the fresh water beneath the earth, and Tiamat, the salty sea, often imagined as female and sometimes linked with a sea dragon. Their waters mingled, and generations of gods were born.

The younger gods were noisy and restless, and their racket disturbed Apsu's rest. He resolved to destroy them, despite Tiamat's protests. The wise god Ea discovered the plot, cast a spell that put Apsu to sleep, killed him and built his home upon Apsu's body. There, in that freshwater dwelling, Ea and his wife Damkina had a son: Marduk, a dazzling god with four eyes and four ears, mightier than all his elders.

sections.key: Tiamat created monsters for vengeance, and Marduk agreed to fight her only if he became supreme.
sections.b:
Tiamat at first refused to harm her children, but after Apsu's death other gods urged her to strike back. She gave birth to an army of monsters, including serpents with venom for blood, dragons, scorpion-men and raging demons. She chose Kingu as her new husband and commander, and fastened to his chest the Tablet of Destinies, which gave its holder supreme authority over the universe.

The other gods were terrified. Ea and then the sky god Anu went out to face her and turned back. Finally the assembly turned to young Marduk. He agreed to fight on one condition: if he won, his word would decide destinies, and he would be supreme among the gods.

sections.key: Marduk slew Tiamat and built the ordered cosmos from the two halves of her body.
sections.b:
Armed with a bow, a mace, a net and the winds, Marduk rode out in a storm chariot. When Tiamat opened her mouth to swallow him, he drove in an evil wind that swelled her body, then shot an arrow that split her heart. He caught her helpers in his net and took the Tablet of Destinies from Kingu.

Then he began to build. He split Tiamat's body in two like a fish for drying, raising one half to form the sky and laying out the other as the earth. From her eyes flowed the Tigris and Euphrates. He set the stars and constellations, fixed the calendar, and gave the moon its phases. The cosmos was ordered from the body of chaos.

sections.key: Humans were made from a rebel god's blood to serve the gods, and the epic promoted Babylon's own god, Marduk.
sections.b:
With the world built, someone had to do the endless labour of maintaining it. The gods blamed Kingu for the rebellion and put him to death. From his blood Ea fashioned humankind, given the gods' work so the gods could rest. People exist to serve the gods by tending temples and offering food. The gods built Babylon and its temple, the Esagila, for Marduk.

The epic raised Marduk, Babylon's patron, above older gods, mirroring the city's rise, and was recited at the Akitu new year festival. When the Assyrians adopted it, some versions replaced Marduk with their god Ashur. Genesis likewise opens with primeval waters and a separation of sky from earth. Some scholars link the Hebrew tehom, "the deep", to Tiamat, though how much the biblical writers knew is debated.

quiz.q: Why is Enuma Elish not a neutral account of creation?
o: It was written by a foreign historian
It covers only the creation of animals
It makes one god king of all the others
It was copied from the Book of Genesis
quiz.e: The poem explains creation while elevating Marduk to supreme rule.

quiz.q: What triggered Apsu's decision to destroy the younger gods?
o: They had stolen his Tablet of Destinies
They were so noisy he could not rest
They had refused to bow down to him
They plotted to overthrow Tiamat
quiz.e: Their racket disturbed Apsu, and the plot that followed led to his death and Marduk's birth.

quiz.q: What condition did Marduk set before fighting Tiamat?
o: That he would rule and decide destinies
That Ea would fight beside him
That the gods build him a temple first
That Kingu be spared
quiz.e: Marduk's price for risking battle was supremacy among the gods.

quiz.q: How did Marduk make the sky and earth?
o: By drawing them from a primal egg
By splitting Tiamat's body in two
By pouring out the waters of Apsu
By casting the Tablet of Destinies down
quiz.e: He halved her body like a fish for drying, making one half the sky and the other the earth.

quiz.q: What does the Assyrians' swap of Marduk for Ashur suggest?
o: Marduk had been forgotten across Mesopotamia
The epic was a claim about whose god rules
Ashur had always been the god of Babylon
The Assyrians could not read Akkadian
quiz.e: Swapping the national god suggests the epic was read as a claim about who rules.

LESSONS.push: Babylon's creation story makes the world from a goddess's body, and a political point.

LESSONS.title: The Aztec gods and the Fifth Sun
LESSONS.hook: The Mexica believed they lived under the fifth sun the gods had made, and that it moved only because gods had given their lives. Their religion was built around keeping it in the sky.

sections.key: The people we call the Aztecs called themselves the Mexica and founded Tenochtitlan on a lake island.
sections.b:
The name "Aztec" was popularised much later. The builders of Tenochtitlan called themselves the Mexica, and their name lives on in Mexico. In their own tradition, they migrated south from a homeland called Aztlan, guided by their patron god Huitzilopochtli. He promised they would know their new home when they saw an eagle perched on a cactus growing from a rock.

They found that sign on a marshy island in Lake Texcoco, where they founded Tenochtitlan, traditionally in 1325. The eagle on the cactus is now at the centre of Mexico's flag. Within two centuries the island had become one of the largest cities in the world, linked to the shore by causeways.

sections.key: The Mexica believed the world had been destroyed four times, and the present Fifth Sun began when gods sacrificed themselves.
sections.b:
In Mexica cosmology, time moved in great ages called Suns, each a separate creation that ended in catastrophe. In one widely told version, the first world was destroyed by jaguars, the second by winds, the third by a rain of fire and the fourth by a flood. Accounts differ, since our sources were written after the Spanish conquest. The Fifth Sun, Nahui Ollin, was also destined to end, many believed, in earthquakes.

After the fourth world, the gods gathered in darkness at Teotihuacan. Proud Tecciztecatl lost his nerve four times; humble, sickly Nanahuatzin leapt into the fire and rose as the sun. Ashamed, Tecciztecatl followed. A god threw a rabbit into his face, dimming him into the moon. Even then the sun would not move until the other gods gave their lives.

sections.key: The Templo Mayor honoured both war and rain, while Quetzalcoatl and Tezcatlipoca were rival creator gods.
sections.b:
At the heart of Tenochtitlan stood the Templo Mayor, a stepped pyramid topped by two shrines. One honoured Huitzilopochtli, the Mexica's patron god of the sun and war. The other honoured Tlaloc, an ancient god of rain and fertility. Together they represented war and agriculture, the twin foundations of the empire. Huitzilopochtli was born fully armed, defeated his siblings who plotted against his mother Coatlicue, and cast his dismembered sister Coyolxauhqui down the hill.

Quetzalcoatl, the Feathered Serpent, was linked with wind, learning and the morning star. His rival Tezcatlipoca, the "Smoking Mirror", was a powerful god of night, fate and sorcery. In one cycle of tales they alternately create and destroy the earlier Suns.

sections.key: Because gods died to set the sun moving, the Mexica believed humans owed a debt repaid in offerings and blood.
sections.b:
Mexica sacrifice followed from their myths. The gods gave their lives to create and power the Fifth Sun, so humans owed a debt that had to be repaid. Worshippers offered incense, food, flowers and their own blood, drawn with cactus spines or bone points.

Most dramatically, priests sacrificed human beings, many of them war captives, at ceremonies across the ritual year. Spanish accounts of the scale were sometimes exaggerated, and historians long debated them, but archaeology has confirmed that sacrifice was real and significant. Since 2015, excavations in Mexico City have uncovered parts of the Huei Tzompantli, a great rack and tower built with the skulls of hundreds of individuals, near the Templo Mayor.

sections.key: The story that the Mexica thought Cortés was Quetzalcoatl is now widely doubted, but much of their culture survived.
sections.b:
Hernán Cortés conquered Tenochtitlan in 1521, with tens of thousands of Indigenous allies. A famous story claims the emperor Moctezuma believed Cortés was the returning Quetzalcoatl. Many historians now doubt this, since it appears mainly in sources written decades after the conquest, shaped by Spanish and Indigenous writers trying to explain what had happened. One tale has Quetzalcoatl departing east, promising in some versions to return.

The Mexica religion was suppressed, its temples demolished and a cathedral built near the ruins. Yet much survived. In 1978 electricity workers in Mexico City uncovered a huge carved stone of the dismembered Coyolxauhqui, leading to the full excavation of the Templo Mayor. More than a million and a half people in Mexico still speak Nahuatl, the Mexica language.

quiz.q: What sign told the Mexica where to found their city?
o: A river flowing into a great lake
An eagle perched on a cactus on a rock
A jaguar crouched on a stone pyramid
A rabbit marked on the moon's face
quiz.e: Huitzilopochtli's promised sign appeared on an island in Lake Texcoco, and it is now on Mexico's flag.

quiz.q: What did the Mexica believe about the Fifth Sun?
o: It was certain to last for all time
It was made by humans to honour the gods
It began in divine sacrifice and could fail
It had already ended in a great flood
quiz.e: The world was seen as fragile, and the sun only moved because gods gave their lives.

quiz.q: What did the twin shrines of the Templo Mayor represent?
o: Two rival kings of the empire
War and farming
Day and night as opposing forces
The Spanish and the Mexica peoples
quiz.e: Huitzilopochtli stood for sun and war, and Tlaloc for rain and fertility.

quiz.q: Why did the Mexica believe in sacrifice?
o: Humans owed a debt to gods who died
Spanish priests required it
It was only used for entertainment
Gods demanded it as punishment for old crimes
quiz.e: Offerings and blood repaid the gods who gave their lives to power the Fifth Sun.

quiz.q: Why do many historians doubt the claim that Moctezuma thought Cortés was Quetzalcoatl?
o: Quetzalcoatl never existed in Mexica myth
It appears mainly in much later sources
Cortés rejected it in his own letters
Moctezuma never actually met Cortés
quiz.e: The tale comes from later accounts shaped by writers explaining the conquest.

LESSONS.push: Why the Mexica thought the sun itself needed their help to rise.

LESSONS.title: The orishas: Yoruba gods of two continents
LESSONS.hook: From the cities of south-western Nigeria to the beaches of Brazil and the streets of Havana, millions of people honour the orishas, divine forces of thunder, rivers, iron and the sea.

sections.key: Yoruba religion centres on a distant creator and the orishas, divine forces who govern nature and life.
sections.b:
The Yoruba are one of Africa's largest ethnic groups, numbering tens of millions, mostly in south-western Nigeria and neighbouring Benin and Togo. Their traditional religion, Ìṣẹ̀ṣe, recognises a supreme creator, Olodumare, who is vast and distant and not usually approached directly.

Instead, people relate to the orishas, divine beings who act as intermediaries and govern particular forces of nature and areas of life. Some are seen as forces present since creation, others as deified ancestors and kings. There is also àṣẹ, the vital power that makes things happen, flowing through gods, people, words and objects. Today many Yoruba are Christian or Muslim, but traditional practice and its influence remain strong.

sections.key: In Yoruba tradition the orisha Obatala helped make dry land at Ile-Ife, the sacred city.
sections.b:
One widely told creation story begins with the world as water and marsh. Olodumare sends the orisha Obatala down from the sky on a golden chain, carrying a snail shell full of earth and a bird, often described as a hen or cockerel. Obatala pours out the earth, and the bird scratches and scatters it, spreading dry land.

In some versions Obatala becomes drunk on palm wine and falls asleep, and his rival Oduduwa completes the task. Obatala is also said to shape human bodies from clay, and some traditions explain disabilities as the result of his drunkenness. His followers therefore avoid palm wine and protect people with disabilities. The place where land first appeared is Ile-Ife, still regarded as sacred.

sections.key: Each orisha has its own domain, symbols and devotees, from Ogun's iron to Oshun's sweet waters.
sections.b:
The orishas are vivid personalities. Obatala, associated with white cloth and coolness, stands for purity, wisdom and calm judgement. Ogun, orisha of iron, tools and war, is honoured by blacksmiths, hunters and, today, drivers and mechanics. Shango, lord of thunder and lightning, is remembered as a fiery king of Oyo, and his symbol is a double-headed axe.

Oshun, orisha of sweet waters, love, beauty and fertility, is linked with the Osun River, and her sacred grove at Osogbo is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Yemoja is a great mother associated with water. Eshu, or Elegba, the trickster messenger, guards crossroads, carries offerings, and must be honoured first in many ceremonies.

sections.key: Ifá divination uses 256 patterns, each tied to memorised verses, to guide decisions.
sections.b:
Facing a serious decision, illness or trouble, a person may consult a babalawo, a priest of Ifá. Ifá is linked with Orunmila, the orisha of wisdom and destiny. The babalawo casts a divining chain, or manipulates sacred palm nuts, to produce one of 256 possible patterns called odu.

Each odu is associated with a large collection of memorised verses, stories and proverbs. The priest recites them, and priest and client together interpret which passage speaks to the situation, often followed by recommended offerings. Training takes many years. UNESCO has recognised Ifá divination as part of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, and its verses are treasured as a vast store of Yoruba history, values and wisdom.

sections.key: Enslaved Yoruba people carried the orishas to Cuba and Brazil, where Santería and Candomblé grew.
sections.b:
During the Atlantic slave trade, especially in its final decades, large numbers of Yoruba people were taken to the Americas, particularly Cuba and Brazil. Forbidden from openly practising their religion and pressured to become Catholic, many found ways to keep the orishas alive. Each orisha came to be linked with a Catholic saint of similar imagery: Shango with St Barbara, whose symbols include lightning, and Oshun with Cuba's Virgin of Charity. Scholars debate how far this was disguise and how far blending.

From this grew Santería (Lucumí) in Cuba and Candomblé in Brazil, with drumming, dance, possession and initiation. Yemoja became Yemayá in Cuba and Iemanjá in Brazil, queen of the sea. On 2 February crowds in Salvador carry gifts to the sea for her, and many Brazilians toss flowers into the waves on New Year's Eve.

quiz.q: How do Yoruba people usually relate to the creator Olodumare?
o: Through the orishas as intermediaries
By offering sacrifices every morning
By consulting only the Ifá priests
Directly, in daily personal prayer
quiz.e: Olodumare is distant and not usually approached directly, so people turn to the orishas.

quiz.q: What did Obatala's bird do in the creation story?
o: Carried the first sun into the sky
Scattered the earth to spread dry land
Led him on the path to Ile-Ife
Released the golden chain from above
quiz.e: Obatala poured out earth from a snail shell, and the bird spread it into dry land.

quiz.q: Which orisha is honoured by blacksmiths and mechanics?
o: Oshun
Shango
Ogun
Yemoja
quiz.e: Ogun is the orisha of iron, tools and war, so metalworkers and now drivers honour him.

quiz.q: How does an Ifá priest give guidance?
o: By predicting the future from the stars
By reading lines on the client's palm
By applying a written code of law
By reciting verses tied to a cast pattern
quiz.e: Each of the 256 odu has memorised verses, and priest and client interpret which fits the situation.

quiz.q: Why were orishas linked with Catholic saints in the Americas?
o: Church officials assigned saints to orishas at random
Orishas shared imagery or qualities with certain saints
Catholic missionaries had already adopted the orishas
Yoruba priests first learned of the saints in Africa
quiz.e: Similar symbols, like Shango's lightning and St Barbara's, let the orishas live on under pressure.

LESSONS.push: How a West African religion survived slavery and now fills Brazil's beaches each New Year.

LESSONS.title: How the Bible became a book
LESSONS.hook: The Bible was not written at once, nor agreed on in a single meeting. It grew over a thousand years, and Christians still do not all have the same list of books.

sections.key: The Bible is a library of writings from many authors, and different communities keep different official lists, called canons.
sections.b:
The word Bible comes from the Greek ta biblia, "the books". It is a library, not a single work, holding law, history, poetry, prophecy, proverbs, letters and visions. Most of it was written in Hebrew and Greek, with some Aramaic, over a span usually put at more than a thousand years.

A canon is the official list of books a community accepts as scripture, from a Greek word for a measuring rod. The Jewish Bible has 24 books. Protestant Bibles have 66, Catholic Bibles 73, and Eastern Orthodox and Oriental churches more again. Even chapters and verses are late additions: chapters date from the thirteenth century, New Testament verse numbers from 1551.

sections.key: The Hebrew Bible took shape in three parts, with the Torah recognised first and the Writings settled last.
sections.b:
Jewish scripture is called the Tanakh, an acronym of its three parts: Torah (the Teaching, the five books of Moses), Nevi'im (the Prophets) and Ketuvim (the Writings, including Psalms, Proverbs and Job). Scholars generally think the Torah was recognised as authoritative first, probably by around the fifth or fourth century BCE, then the Prophets.

The Writings stayed open longer. Rabbinic texts record debates over whether Ecclesiastes and the Song of Songs belonged, and the list seems to have been broadly settled in the early centuries CE. Protestant Old Testaments hold the same material, counted as 39 books rather than 24 because Samuel, Kings and the twelve minor prophets are divided differently.

sections.key: Christian Bibles differ because of extra books in the Greek Septuagint, which Protestants, Catholics and Orthodox treat differently.
sections.b:
From the third century BCE, Greek-speaking Jews in Alexandria translated their scriptures into Greek. A legend says seventy-two scholars finished in seventy-two days, hence the name Septuagint, from the Latin for seventy. The Greek collections also held books outside the Jewish canon, such as Tobit, Judith, Sirach and Maccabees. Early Christians mostly read Greek and used it widely.

Catholics call these extra books deuterocanonical, and Protestants call them the Apocrypha. In 1534 Martin Luther placed them in a separate section, useful but not equal to scripture. In 1546 the Council of Trent affirmed them as canonical. Orthodox churches accept more again, and the Ethiopian Orthodox canon is largest, usually counted at around 81 books.

sections.key: Scrolls found near Qumran from 1947 pushed the manuscript record of the Hebrew Bible back about a thousand years.
sections.b:
In 1947 Bedouin shepherds exploring caves near Qumran, on the north-western shore of the Dead Sea, found jars holding ancient scrolls. Over the next decade around 900 manuscripts, mostly fragments, were recovered from eleven caves. Dating mainly from the third century BCE to the first century CE, they include copies or fragments of every Hebrew Bible book except Esther.

Until then, the oldest complete Hebrew Bible manuscripts were medieval, such as the Leningrad Codex of about 1008 CE. The Great Isaiah Scroll, roughly a thousand years older, proved remarkably close to the medieval text. Other scrolls show variant versions, revealing that some books still circulated in more than one form.

sections.key: No single council chose the New Testament; the list formed gradually, and the claim that Nicaea decided it is a myth.
sections.b:
Paul's letters, usually dated to the 50s CE, are the earliest New Testament writings. Most scholars date the four gospels to roughly 70 to 100 CE. By around 200 CE the gospels and Paul's letters were widely accepted, while Hebrews, James, 2 Peter, Jude and Revelation stayed disputed longer. The Shepherd of Hermas was read in some churches but left out.

A popular claim, spread by novels such as The Da Vinci Code, says Constantine and the Council of Nicaea in 325 CE picked the books. There is no evidence for it. Nicaea dealt with the nature of Christ, the date of Easter and church discipline. In 367 CE Athanasius wrote the earliest known list matching today's 27 books, and councils at Hippo (393) and Carthage (397) endorsed similar lists.

quiz.q: What is a canon of scripture?
o: The oldest surviving manuscript of a text
An official list of books a community accepts
A translation of scripture into another language
A commentary explaining difficult passages
quiz.e: A canon is a community's official list of accepted books, and different communities settled on different canons.

quiz.q: Which part of the Hebrew Bible was recognised as authoritative first?
o: The Writings
The Prophets
The Apocrypha
The Torah
quiz.e: The Torah was recognised first, then the Prophets, while the Writings stayed open the longest.

quiz.q: Why do Catholic and Protestant Bibles differ in length?
o: Catholics include extra books from the Greek Septuagint
Protestants added later gospels to their New Testament
Catholics left out several of Paul's letters
Protestants added books found at Qumran
quiz.e: Extra books in the Greek Septuagint became a lasting point of difference between Christian traditions.

quiz.q: What did the Great Isaiah Scroll show?
o: Isaiah was rewritten in the Middle Ages
Isaiah was originally written in Greek
Its wording closely matched medieval copies
Isaiah was not part of the Hebrew Bible
