Around 1974 he remembered Spencer Silver's light adhesive and realised it could make the perfect bookmark: it would stay in place but peel off without tearing the page.

He began coating paper with the glue and experimenting. Soon he noticed an even bigger use. When he wrote a note on a sticky bookmark and stuck it on a report for a colleague, it worked as a message that stayed attached without damaging the document underneath.

sections.key: Early test sales flopped until people were given free samples and tried the notes for themselves.
sections.b:
Even with a working product, success was not guaranteed. In 1977 3M test marketed the notes in four American cities as Press 'n Peel, and sales were disappointing. Customers had never seen anything like it and could not imagine why they needed it.

Instead of giving up, the company changed tactics. In 1978 it flooded Boise, Idaho, with free samples, an effort later nicknamed the Boise Blitz. Once office workers actually used the notes, they wanted more, and a large majority of those surveyed said they would buy them. Renamed Post-it Notes, the product launched across the United States in 1980 and in other countries soon after. Today it is sold in well over a hundred countries.

sections.key: The famous canary yellow came from scrap paper that happened to be nearby, not from careful design.
sections.b:
Many famous product features are carefully designed. The colour of the Post-it Note was not. According to the company's own telling, the team working on early versions used scrap paper that happened to be yellow, borrowed from a neighbouring laboratory. The colour stuck, in more ways than one, and canary yellow became the signature.

It also proved practical, because a bright yellow square stands out on a desk, a computer screen or a page of black and white text. Today the notes come in a rainbow of colours, sizes and shapes, but yellow remains the shade most people picture. Not every successful choice in business comes from planning.

sections.key: Innovation needs both a technology and someone who finds the right problem, and trying a product can persuade better than advertising.
sections.b:
The Post-it story shows how innovation often really works. It was not a single flash of genius. It needed a technology nobody had a use for, a scientist stubborn enough to keep promoting it, a colleague with a real everyday problem, and a company culture that allowed time for side projects.

It also shows a marketing truth: a genuinely new product can fail if customers cannot picture using it, and letting people try it can be more persuasive than any advertisement. Silver and Fry both received recognition for the invention, and Post-it Notes are now among the most recognisable office products ever made.

quiz.q: Why did Spencer Silver's adhesive seem like a failure at first?
o: It was too strong to peel away from paper
It lost its stickiness within a few hours
It gripped lightly, though it could be reused
It could only be applied to wood or metal
quiz.e: It missed the goal of a very strong glue, but its light, clean grip later proved valuable.

quiz.q: What turned the weak adhesive into a product idea?
o: A customer asked for a stronger office glue
A colleague wanted bookmarks that would stay put
A competitor launched a similar adhesive
A government contract for removable labels
quiz.e: A real everyday problem matched a technology that had been looking for a use.

quiz.q: What turned weak early sales around?
o: Cutting the price in all four test cities
Running television advertisements nationwide
Changing the notes to a stronger adhesive
Giving out free samples so people could try them
quiz.e: Customers could not imagine needing the product until they used it.

quiz.q: Why are Post-it Notes yellow?
o: The team happened to use yellow scrap paper
Market research showed yellow sold best
Yellow was the cheapest dye available
Yellow matched the company's logo
quiz.e: The colour came from paper at hand and then proved practical because it stands out.

quiz.q: What does the Post-it story suggest about innovation?
o: It comes from one inventor's sudden flash of genius
It needs a technology, persistence and a real problem
It depends on advertising more than the product
It works best when side projects are banned
quiz.e: Many people, a patient scientist and a culture of experimenting all contributed.

LESSONS.push: A glue that failed to stick properly ended up on every desk. How?

LESSONS.title: IKEA and the genius of the flat pack
LESSONS.hook: A teenager selling pens by mail order in rural Sweden built the world's biggest furniture retailer. The secret involved taking the legs off a table.

sections.key: Ingvar Kamprad founded IKEA at seventeen, and the name comes from his initials and his home.
sections.b:
Ingvar Kamprad grew up on a farm called Elmtaryd near the village of Agunnaryd, in Småland, a region of southern Sweden known for poor, stony soil and thrifty people. As a boy he sold matches, then seeds, Christmas cards and pencils. In 1943, aged seventeen, he registered his own company. He named it by combining his initials with the first letters of his farm and village: Ingvar Kamprad, Elmtaryd, Agunnaryd, or IKEA.

At first it sold pens, wallets and picture frames by mail order. In the late 1940s Kamprad added furniture made by local manufacturers, and before long furniture was the main business.

sections.key: Furniture packed flat is cheaper to store and ship, and IKEA designs everything around a low target price.
sections.b:
In 1956 IKEA employee Gillis Lundgren was trying to fit a table into a car after a photo shoot. It would not go in, so he took the legs off. The company realised that flat-packed furniture is cheaper to store and ship and less likely to be damaged, and customers could carry it home and assemble it with simple tools. Flat packing was not entirely new, but IKEA made it the heart of its business. Lundgren went on to design many products, including the Billy bookcase in 1979.

Thrift is built into the strategy. Designers often start with a target price and work backwards, choosing materials, shapes and packaging to save money. A bookcase that packs a few centimetres flatter means more fit on a truck.

sections.key: When Swedish rivals tried to shut IKEA out, it found cheaper suppliers abroad and became even cheaper.
sections.b:
IKEA's low prices made established Swedish furniture retailers furious. In the 1950s they pressured local manufacturers to stop supplying the upstart, and IKEA was even barred from some furniture trade fairs. Rather than give in, Kamprad looked further afield. In the early 1960s IKEA began having furniture made in Poland, where production costs were much lower.

The boycott, meant to crush the company, pushed it to build its own international supply chain and design more of its own products. That made IKEA cheaper still and gave it control over how its furniture was made and packed. It is a classic case of turning a threat into an advantage by changing the approach rather than the goal.

sections.key: IKEA lowers prices by having shoppers pick up, transport and assemble their own furniture.
sections.b:
IKEA's first store opened in Älmhult in 1958, and the model has been refined ever since. It rests on a simple bargain: the customer does part of the work and pays a lower price. In a traditional shop, staff fetched items, delivered them and assembled them. At IKEA, shoppers browse a showroom, note product codes, collect flat boxes from a self-serve warehouse, take them home and build the furniture themselves.

Even the winding one-way path through the showroom is designed to show customers as much of the range as possible. Restaurants, play areas and cheap snacks encourage families to stay longer, and longer visits tend to mean bigger purchases. Today IKEA has hundreds of stores in dozens of countries, including several in Australia.

sections.key: People value things more when they have built them themselves, provided they finish the job.
sections.b:
Assembling furniture can be frustrating, but it may also make people like it more. In a study published in 2012, researchers Michael Norton, Daniel Mochon and Dan Ariely asked people to assemble simple IKEA storage boxes, fold origami or build Lego models. Those who had built the item were willing to pay noticeably more for it than people offered an identical item already assembled.

The researchers called this the IKEA effect: labour leads to love. When participants failed to finish building something, the effect faded. Businesses use the idea widely, from build-your-own toy shops to apps that let you customise your profile.

quiz.q: How did Ingvar Kamprad come up with the name IKEA?
o: From the Swedish word for home furnishing
From the town where the first store opened
From his initials and his farm and village
From the surname of its first designer
quiz.e: Ingvar Kamprad, Elmtaryd and Agunnaryd gave I-K-E-A.

quiz.q: Why is flat-packed furniture so valuable to IKEA's business?
o: It is cheaper to store, ship and protect
It makes furniture stronger when assembled
It lets customers return items more easily
It allows furniture to be sold without a showroom
quiz.e: Packing flat cuts costs at every step, so the savings reach the shopper.

quiz.q: How did the Swedish boycott end up helping IKEA?
o: It forced IKEA to raise its prices at home
It pushed IKEA to find cheaper suppliers abroad
It stopped IKEA selling any furniture in Sweden
It led rivals to copy IKEA's flat packs
quiz.e: IKEA changed its approach, not its goal, and the threat became an advantage.

quiz.q: What is the bargain at the heart of IKEA's model?
o: Customers pay more for faster delivery
Staff assemble furniture for free at home
Customers order everything online first
Customers do some of the work for a lower price
quiz.e: Self-service collection, transport and assembly remove costs that a traditional shop must cover.

quiz.q: What is the IKEA effect?
o: People value things more when they built them
People prefer cheap furniture to expensive furniture
People enjoy shopping in large showrooms
People trust products with Scandinavian names
quiz.e: Effort creates attachment, as long as the task is completed successfully.

LESSONS.push: A table with its legs removed built a global retail empire.

LESSONS.title: The 80/20 rule: the vital few
LESSONS.hook: A few customers bring most of the sales, a few problems cause most of the headaches. The 80/20 rule is one of the most useful ideas in business, and one of the most misunderstood.

sections.key: Pareto noticed unequal wealth in Italy, and Joseph Juran later turned the idea into a general management rule.
sections.b:
Vilfredo Pareto, an Italian engineer turned economist, studied data on wealth and income in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. He noticed that a small fraction of people owned a very large share of the land. In Italy, roughly 80 per cent of the land was held by about 20 per cent of the population, and he found similar patterns elsewhere. A tale about pea pods in his garden is hard to verify.

Pareto never proposed a universal rule. That came decades later from Joseph Juran, a quality pioneer who found a few causes produced most manufacturing defects. He called them the vital few, as opposed to the trivial many (later the useful many), and named the idea after Pareto. He later acknowledged he had stretched Pareto's work.

sections.key: In many situations a minority of causes produces a majority of the effects, and 80/20 is shorthand, not a law.
sections.b:
At heart the Pareto principle is a simple observation: inputs and outputs are often unequal. A minority of causes frequently produces most of the results. In a typical business, a small group of customers may account for most of the revenue, a few products for most of the profit, or a handful of recurring faults for most of the complaints.

The numbers 80 and 20 are a memorable shorthand, not a law of nature. The real split might be 70/30, 90/10 or 95/5. The two numbers also do not have to add up to 100, because they measure different things: one is the share of causes, the other the share of effects.

sections.key: The principle helps you decide where to look first and focus effort where it matters most.
sections.b:
The practical power of the Pareto principle is in deciding where to look first. Quality engineers use a Pareto chart, a bar chart that sorts problems from most to least frequent, to show which few causes deserve attention. A cafe owner might find that a handful of menu items make most of the money, and simplify the rest. A support team might find that most calls are about a few common issues, and fix those with clearer instructions.

In personal work, it suggests asking which tasks truly move a project forward, and doing those before polishing the details. The question is not how to do everything, but which few things matter most.

sections.key: The 80/20 rule is a pattern to check, not a guarantee, and the useful many still matter.
sections.b:
Because it is catchy, the principle is often misused. Some people treat 80/20 as an exact law and assume the numbers without measuring anything. Others conclude the remaining 80 per cent of customers, tasks or products can simply be dropped. That can be a serious mistake. Small customers may become large ones, cheap products may draw people into a store, and routine tasks such as paperwork, safety checks and maintenance can have serious consequences if neglected.

Juran's later phrase, the useful many, was a deliberate correction. The principle works best as a prompt to gather data and look for imbalances, not as an excuse to ignore everything outside the top fifth.

sections.key: Systems where success builds on success naturally produce uneven outcomes, so averages can mislead.
sections.b:
Why do so many things follow this lopsided pattern? One reason is that success compounds. A popular product gets better shelf space, more reviews and more word of mouth, which makes it more popular still. A big customer may grow faster because it already has scale. In networks such as cities, websites and social media, a few hubs attract a large share of the connections.

Mathematicians describe such distributions as heavy-tailed or power laws, and they appear in fields from earthquakes to book sales. This helps explain why averages can mislead. When a few cases dominate the total, the typical case may look very different from the average one.

quiz.q: What did Joseph Juran add to Pareto's observation?
o: He proved that exactly 80 per cent of land is held by 20 per cent
He showed wealth is spread evenly in most countries
He generalised it into a rule that a few causes drive most problems
He replaced it with the idea of the trivial many only
quiz.e: Juran took a pattern in wealth and applied it to causes and effects in quality management.

quiz.q: Which statement about the 80 and 20 figures is correct?
o: They are shorthand, and the real split varies
They are a fixed law that always holds
They must always add up to 100
They apply only to wealth and land
quiz.e: Real splits might be 70/30 or 90/10, and the numbers measure different things.

quiz.q: How might a support team use the Pareto principle?
o: Answer calls in the order they arrive
Fix the few issues behind most of the calls
Hire more staff for every kind of call
Ignore the issues that cause the fewest calls
quiz.e: Sorting problems by frequency shows where effort will make the biggest difference.

quiz.q: Why is it a mistake to drop everything outside the top 20 per cent?
o: The bottom 80 per cent always makes most of the profit
The rule says every item matters exactly the same
Cutting them always raises overall costs
Small customers can grow, and neglected tasks can cause harm
quiz.e: The useful many still matter, so the rule should prompt measurement, not neglect.

quiz.q: Why do many systems end up lopsided?
o: Everything is shared out evenly over time
Random chance cancels out in the long run
Success compounds, so winners attract still more success
Large groups always behave like their average member
quiz.e: A popular product or hub keeps gaining advantages, which is why a few cases dominate the total.

LESSONS.push: Twenty per cent of the effort often drives most of the results. Is that true?

LESSONS.title: Psychological safety: why the best teams admit mistakes
LESSONS.hook: A researcher expected the best hospital teams to make the fewest errors. Her data said the opposite, and that surprise changed how we think about teamwork.

sections.key: Amy Edmondson found that better hospital teams reported more errors, because they felt safe to speak up.
sections.b:
In the 1990s researcher Amy Edmondson studied medication errors in hospital teams. She expected teams with better leadership and stronger relationships to make fewer mistakes. The data seemed to show the reverse: the better teams reported more errors.

Then she realised what might be happening. The best teams were probably not making more mistakes. They were more willing to talk about them, while in teams where people feared blame, errors were hidden. That insight led to psychological safety, which Edmondson, later a Harvard Business School professor, defines as a shared belief in a team that it is safe to take interpersonal risks, such as asking a question, admitting a mistake or raising a concern.

sections.key: Google found that how a team works together mattered more than who was on it, and safety mattered most.
sections.b:
In 2012 Google launched Project Aristotle to find out what made some of its teams more effective than others. Researchers studied around 180 teams, expecting the right mix of skills, personalities or backgrounds to explain success. Those factors mattered far less than expected. What mattered most was how team members interacted.

When Google published its findings in 2015, it listed five key dynamics: psychological safety, dependability, structure and clarity, meaning, and impact. Psychological safety was described as by far the most important, the foundation the others depended on. The findings drew wide attention and brought Edmondson's work to a far larger audience.

sections.key: Psychological safety works best when it is combined with high standards.
sections.b:
A common misunderstanding is that psychological safety means lowering expectations or avoiding criticism. Edmondson is clear that it does not. It also does not mean everyone agrees. It describes the climate of a group, not one person's confidence: the same person might speak freely in one team and stay silent in another. It means honest disagreement and bad news surface early, while there is still time to act.

She describes a grid. Low safety and low standards produce apathy. High safety with low standards is comfortable but unstretching. High standards with low safety produces anxiety, and people hide problems. The goal is high standards with high safety, her learning zone. Candour and kindness are not opposites.

sections.key: Fear does not stop problems; it mostly stops leaders hearing about them until they are bigger.
sections.b:
The cost of silence can be enormous. Investigations into accidents in aviation, healthcare and engineering have often found that someone saw a warning sign but hesitated to raise it with a more senior person. From around the 1980s aviation responded with crew resource management training, which teaches junior crew to voice concerns clearly and captains to invite them.

In business the costs are usually quieter but still real: a flawed product nobody challenged, a project everyone privately doubted, a safety shortcut nobody reported. Fear does not stop problems happening. It mostly stops leaders hearing about them until they are much bigger and more expensive to fix.

sections.key: Leaders build psychological safety by inviting input, admitting their limits and responding well to bad news.
sections.b:
Psychological safety can be built, and leaders have the biggest influence. Edmondson suggests three broad practices. First, frame the work as a learning problem rather than simple execution, being honest that there is uncertainty and that everyone's input is needed. Second, acknowledge your own fallibility, with something as simple as saying you might be missing something. Third, model curiosity by asking genuine questions.

Just as important is how you react when someone speaks up. Thanking a person for raising a problem, even unwelcome news, encourages others to do the same. Reacting with anger teaches the whole team to stay quiet. Trust is built slowly and can be damaged very quickly.

quiz.q: Why did the better hospital teams report more errors?
o: They made far more mistakes than other teams
They were more willing to talk about mistakes
They had fewer staff checking the work
They were required to report everything by law
quiz.e: Teams without fear of blame surface errors, while fearful teams hide them.

quiz.q: What did Google's Project Aristotle find mattered most for team effectiveness?
o: The mix of skills and personalities on the team
The seniority of the team's manager
The size of the team's annual budget
How members interacted, led by psychological safety
quiz.e: Team dynamics mattered more than who was on the team, with safety as the foundation.

quiz.q: How does Edmondson's 'learning zone' combine safety and standards?
o: Low standards with high safety
High standards with low safety
High standards with high safety
Low standards with low safety
quiz.e: People are pushed to excel and feel able to say when something is going wrong.

quiz.q: What is the main danger of a team where people stay silent?
o: Leaders hear about problems only once they have grown
Meetings become much longer than planned
Teams disagree too often to make decisions
Staff stop working to high standards deliberately
quiz.e: Silence does not prevent problems; it delays the warning that could prevent them.

quiz.q: How should a leader respond when someone raises unwelcome news?
o: Ask who else knew about it before the meeting
Thank them, so others feel safe to speak up too
Move on quickly without comment
Show disappointment so the mistake is not repeated
quiz.e: How leaders react teaches the whole team whether speaking up is safe.

LESSONS.push: The best hospital teams reported the most errors. Why would that be good?

LESSONS.title: Unit economics: does each sale actually make money?
LESSONS.hook: A business can grow fast, win millions of customers and still be heading for ruin. Unit economics is the simple maths that tells you which kind of business you have.

sections.key: Unit economics asks whether one sale makes money after its variable costs, before fixed costs are covered.
sections.b:
Company accounts can hide a lot. Revenue may soar while losses grow faster. Unit economics asks a simple question: looking at one unit, such as a cup of coffee, a delivery, a subscription or a customer, does the business make or lose money? If each unit loses money, growth just loses money faster.

Imagine a coffee cart selling coffee at five dollars a cup. Beans, milk, cup and lid cost about one dollar seventy, and card fees add ten cents. These variable costs rise with every cup. What is left, roughly three dollars twenty, is the contribution margin, the amount each sale contributes to fixed costs and profit. If fixed costs such as permits, insurance and the owner's wage are 800 dollars a week, the cart must sell about 250 cups to break even.

sections.key: Customer acquisition cost is everything you spend to gain one new customer, and it tends to rise as you grow.
sections.b:
For many businesses, especially subscriptions and online services, the biggest cost is not making the product but finding the customer. Customer acquisition cost, or CAC, is the total spent on marketing and sales in a period divided by the new customers gained. If a business spends 10,000 dollars on advertising and wins 200 customers, its CAC is 50 dollars each.

The number is easy to underestimate. Free trials, discounts, sales staff wages and referral rewards all count. CAC also tends to rise as a business grows, because the easiest and most enthusiastic customers are won first, and later ones take more effort and money to persuade.

sections.key: Customer lifetime value estimates the profit, not revenue, a customer brings over the whole relationship.
sections.b:
The partner to CAC is customer lifetime value, or LTV. It estimates how much profit, not just revenue, a typical customer generates over the whole time they stay. A simple version multiplies the margin per period by how many periods customers usually remain. A gym member who pays 20 dollars a week, of which 12 dollars is margin, and stays about a year on average, is worth roughly 600 dollars in margin.

Investors often compare the two numbers. A common rule of thumb says LTV should be around three times CAC or more, and that the acquisition cost should be earned back within a reasonable time. It is a guide, not a law.

sections.key: MoviePass grew rapidly by paying cinemas more per customer than it charged them, and collapsed.
sections.b:
MoviePass is one of the best-known examples of broken unit economics. In 2017 the American service cut its subscription to about ten US dollars a month, letting members see up to one movie in a cinema every day. The catch was that MoviePass paid cinemas close to the full ticket price for each film. A single ticket could cost more than a month's subscription.

Customers loved it, and membership soared into the millions within a year. But every enthusiastic moviegoer deepened the losses. The company tried restrictions, price changes and limits, which angered customers. The service shut down in 2019, and its parent company filed for bankruptcy in early 2020.

sections.key: Strong unit economics turn growth into an advantage instead of a threat.
sections.b:
Unit economics is useful whether you run a market stall or assess a startup. The key questions are simple. What is the price, and what are the true variable costs of each sale? How much does it cost to win a customer, and how long do they stay? How long until a new customer pays back what it cost to win them?

Some businesses deliberately lose money on early customers, expecting costs to fall with scale or customers to buy more later. Occasionally that works. Often it does not, and the plan rests on hope rather than evidence. The healthiest businesses can show that each unit makes money now, so every extra sale makes the company stronger.

quiz.q: In the coffee cart example, what is the contribution margin?
o: 5 dollars, the full price of each cup
About 1 dollar 80, the variable cost per cup
About 3 dollars 20, the price less variable costs
800 dollars, the weekly fixed cost
quiz.e: Price minus variable costs is what each sale contributes towards fixed costs and profit.

quiz.q: Why does customer acquisition cost often rise as a business grows?
o: Advertising becomes cheaper per customer over time
Existing customers stop paying their bills
Staff wages fall as a business gets bigger
The easiest, most enthusiastic customers are won first
quiz.e: Later customers take more effort and money to persuade.

quiz.q: What does customer lifetime value measure?
o: Profit from a customer over the whole relationship
Revenue from a customer's very first purchase
What it costs to win one new customer
The total number of customers a business has
quiz.e: LTV counts profit over time, which can then be compared with what it cost to win the customer.

quiz.q: Why did MoviePass lose money as it grew?
o: It charged members too much for tickets
It paid cinemas more per film than members paid
It had too few members to cover its costs
It spent too little on advertising
quiz.e: With negative unit economics, each extra enthusiastic customer deepened the losses.

quiz.q: What do healthy unit economics let a company do?
o: Skip fixed costs such as rent and wages
Rely on future customers to cover losses
Grow so each extra sale makes it stronger
Stop tracking how long customers stay
quiz.e: When each unit makes money now, growth is an advantage rather than a threat.

LESSONS.push: A business can win millions of customers and still head for ruin. Here's the maths.

LESSONS.title: Tupperware, Brownie Wise and the home party
LESSONS.hook: A clever plastic container was gathering dust on shop shelves. Then a single mother from Detroit worked out how to sell it, and changed direct selling for good.

sections.key: Tupperware's clever airtight seal sold poorly in shops because customers did not understand it.
sections.b:
Earl Tupper, an American inventor from New Hampshire, worked for DuPont in the late 1930s and became interested in polyethylene, a new plastic. He developed ways to purify and mould it into containers that were light, unbreakable and flexible, unlike the brittle plastics of the time. His real breakthrough was the lid. Inspired by paint tin lids, he designed a seal that snapped on and could be made airtight by pressing out a little air, the famous burp. Tupperware went on sale after the Second World War.

But in hardware and department stores it sat on shelves. Plastic was a novelty, and the seal was not obvious from a container on a shelf. Many people could not work out how to close the lids. The product needed to be shown.

sections.key: Brownie Wise discovered that Tupperware sold brilliantly when shown at home parties, and Tupper put her in charge.
sections.b:
Some saleswomen working for home-selling companies such as Stanley Home Products had begun demonstrating Tupperware at gatherings in people's homes, with far better results than shops. One was Brownie Wise. Born in Georgia, she was a divorced single mother raising her son in Detroit. She found Tupperware sold brilliantly when women could see it, touch it and watch the lid seal.

Wise built a network of dealers and moved to Florida, and her group's results caught Tupper's attention. In 1951 he pulled Tupperware out of shops altogether and committed to home parties. He put Wise in charge of the new sales operation, Tupperware Home Parties, with the title of vice-president.

sections.key: The home party combined demonstration, social connection and the trust of friends.
sections.b:
The home party model was simple but powerful. A host invited friends and neighbours to her house. A dealer demonstrated the products, often with games and a playful show of how the seal kept food fresh or how a sealed bowl full of liquid could be tossed without spilling. Guests could handle everything and place orders, and the host received a gift for organising it.

Buying from a friend in a relaxed social setting created a sense of trust and obligation that a shop counter could not match. For many women in the 1950s, who were largely excluded from business careers, becoming a dealer offered independent income, flexible hours and the chance to rise through a sales organisation.

sections.key: Wise built a culture of celebration and became a business celebrity, then was dismissed in 1958.
sections.b:
Wise understood motivation. At the Florida headquarters she held lavish annual events, called jubilees, where top sellers won prizes ranging from appliances to cars and boats. Recognition mattered as much as money. Sales grew rapidly, and in 1954 Wise became the first woman on the cover of the American magazine Business Week.

But her fame and independence led to clashes with Tupper, who reportedly resented her growing profile. In 1958 he dismissed her. That same year he sold the company to the Rexall Drug Company for about sixteen million US dollars. Wise received a modest payout, and for years her role was largely left out of the company's official history.

sections.key: The party plan spread to many products, and its core lesson is that a product customers do not understand will not sell.
sections.b:
Tupperware became a global brand, and the party plan was copied by companies selling cosmetics, kitchenware, candles, jewellery and more. It works because it combines demonstration with personal relationships, though critics note that social pressure to buy from a friend can be uncomfortable.

Times changed. As more women worked outside the home and shopping moved online, the party model struggled, and Tupperware's sales declined for years. In 2024 the company filed for bankruptcy protection in the United States. Yet the core lesson remains sharp. A product that customers do not understand will not sell, however good it is. Finding the right way to show it can matter as much as inventing it.

quiz.q: Why did Tupperware sell poorly in shops?
o: The containers were too expensive for most people
Shoppers could not see how the airtight seal worked
The plastic cracked easily in transport
Shops refused to stock plastic goods
quiz.e: The product needed to be shown and handled, which a shelf could not do.

quiz.q: What did Brownie Wise discover about selling Tupperware?
o: It sold best when heavily discounted in shops
It sold only to people who already owned it
It needed television advertising to succeed
It sold well when people could see and handle it
quiz.e: Seeing and touching the product, and watching the lid seal, made the difference.

quiz.q: Why did the home party model work so well?
o: Demonstrations plus the trust of friends
Prices well below what any shop charged
Pressure on every guest to buy something
Free home delivery for every guest's order
quiz.e: It combined hands-on demonstration with personal trust in a social setting.

quiz.q: How did Wise's career end at Tupperware?
o: She retired after the company was sold
She was promoted to run the whole company
Tupper dismissed her in 1958 after a clash
She resigned to start a rival company
quiz.e: Her fame and independence clashed with Tupper, and her contribution was long overlooked.

quiz.q: What is the core lesson of the Tupperware story?
o: A product people do not understand will not sell
Plastic products always sell better than others
Home parties remain the best way to sell anything
Low prices matter more than clear demonstrations
quiz.e: Finding the right way to show a product can matter as much as inventing it.

LESSONS.push: A brilliant container sat unsold until one woman showed people how to use it.

LESSONS.title: What is a business worth? Valuation explained
LESSONS.hook: Two experts can look at the same company and arrive at prices billions apart. Valuation is part maths, part judgement, and understanding it changes how you see every price tag in the market.

sections.key: The price of a business is what someone pays; its value is an estimate of the cash it can produce for its owners.
sections.b:
Price is what you pay; value is what you get. Warren Buffett, a student of the investor Benjamin Graham, put it that way. A price is a fact, such as the latest share price or an agreed sale. Value is an estimate of what the business is really worth to its owners, and estimates differ. A buyer and a seller can disagree sharply, both in good faith.

Most serious valuation rests on one idea: a business is worth the cash it will generate for its owners over its remaining life. Everything else, from complex spreadsheets to rules of thumb, is a way of estimating that cash and what it is worth today.

sections.key: A dollar in the future is worth less than a dollar now, so analysts discount future cash back to the present.
sections.b:
Would you rather have 100 dollars today or in a year? Almost everyone says today. Money in hand can be invested, it avoids the risk of a broken promise, and inflation can erode what future money buys. So analysts discount future amounts back to the present. If you could earn 10 per cent elsewhere, 100 dollars in a year is worth about 90.91 dollars today, because that sum grows to 100 at 10 per cent.

This is the base of discounted cash flow (DCF). An analyst forecasts the free cash flow in each future year, meaning cash left after running the business and making necessary investments. Each year is discounted to today's dollars, then the results are added up.

sections.key: Riskier cash flows are discounted at higher rates, and small changes in the rate can swing a valuation sharply.
sections.b:
Nobody can forecast forever, so analysts model five or ten years in detail, then add one terminal value for everything after. A common method treats the business as growing steadily for ever: next year's cash flow divided by the discount rate minus the growth rate. Often this is most of the total.

The discount rate is where judgement and risk enter. It is the return investors require for backing this business instead of another. A stable utility earns a lower rate than an uncertain young technology firm. Small changes matter. One million dollars of cash flow growing 2 per cent for ever is worth 12.5 million at a 10 per cent rate, but about 14.3 million at 9 per cent.

sections.key: Multiples value a business by comparing it with similar ones, and equity value is what remains for shareholders after debt.
sections.b:
DCF is rigorous but laborious, so analysts also use multiples, much like valuing a house from recent sales nearby. The price to earnings ratio compares share price with profit per share. Enterprise value to EBITDA compares the whole business, debt included, with earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation. If similar firms trade at ten times EBITDA, a business earning five million might be worth about fifty million. Multiples are quick and market-based, but if the whole market is overpriced they copy the error.

Enterprise value is the whole operating business. Equity value is roughly that minus net debt (debt less spare cash). An 800,000 dollar house with a 500,000 dollar mortgage gives you only 300,000 of equity.

sections.key: A valuation is only as good as its assumptions, so test them and use a range rather than trusting one number.
sections.b:
Valuation models look precise, with numbers to the last dollar, but they rest on forecasts of growth, margins and risk that nobody can know. As the example showed, a one percentage point change in the discount rate can shift a valuation by more than ten per cent. The long-term growth rate has a similar effect.

Careful analysts therefore present a range, test pessimistic and optimistic scenarios, and check the answer against multiples. Many experienced investors also want a margin of safety, another idea linked to Graham: buy only when the price is comfortably below their estimate of value, so that errors in their assumptions do not ruin them.

quiz.q: According to most serious valuation, what is a business worth?
o: The average price of its recent share trades
The cash it will produce for its owners over time
The total cost of its buildings and equipment
Whatever the seller originally paid for it
quiz.e: Valuation estimates the cash a business will produce for its owners and what that cash is worth today.

quiz.q: Why is 100 dollars received in a year worth less than 100 dollars today?
o: Banks refuse to hold money for longer than a year
Prices always fall over the following twelve months
Tax is charged only on money received later
Money now can be invested and avoids risk and inflation
quiz.e: Return, risk and inflation all make money in hand more valuable, so future cash is discounted.

quiz.q: What happens to value when a higher discount rate is applied to the same cash flows?
o: It rises, because the cash looks more certain
It stays the same, because the cash flows have not changed
It falls, because riskier cash is worth less today
It doubles, because the future is weighted more heavily
quiz.e: A higher required return shrinks the present value of future cash, so risky businesses are worth less today.

quiz.q: Why can two businesses with identical operations have different equity values?
o: One may carry more debt, leaving less for shareholders
Equity value ignores the debt each business carries
Enterprise value is always lower than equity value
Equity value is set by each company's revenue alone
quiz.e: Equity value is roughly enterprise value minus net debt, so heavy borrowing leaves less for owners.

quiz.q: Why do careful analysts present a range of values instead of a single figure?
o: Regulators require analysts to give a range
Forecasts are uncertain and small changes matter
A range makes the price easier to negotiate down
A single figure suits only private businesses
quiz.e: Because small assumption changes move the answer a lot, testing scenarios is more honest than one precise number.

LESSONS.push: Two experts can value the same company billions apart. Here's how.

LESSONS.title: Anger: why letting off steam backfires
LESSONS.hook: Punch a pillow, scream into the void, smash plates in a rage room. It feels like it should help. The research says it usually makes things worse.

sections.key: Anger is an emotion built to confront perceived wrongs, and the trouble lies in what we do with it.
sections.b:
Anger has a bad reputation, but it exists for a reason. It flares when we feel wronged, blocked or treated unfairly, and it prepares the body to push back. Heart rate and blood pressure rise, adrenaline surges, muscles tense and attention narrows onto the problem. In our evolutionary past that energy helped people defend food, territory or family.

Today it can still be useful. Anger signals that something matters, it can give us courage to stand up for ourselves or others, and it has fuelled many campaigns against injustice. The trouble is not feeling anger. It is what we do next, and one of the most popular answers is wrong.

sections.key: The idea that anger builds up like pressure and must be released is old and intuitive, but largely mistaken.
sections.b:
Aristotle wrote about catharsis, the purging of emotions, when he described how audiences felt after watching tragedy. Centuries later Sigmund Freud and others pictured emotions as fluid or steam in a closed system. Bottle it up and the pressure grows until it bursts out somewhere harmful. Let it out safely and you return to calm.

This hydraulic picture shaped twentieth century advice: hit a punching bag, scream into a pillow, play violent games to get aggression out of your system. It lives on in rage rooms, where customers pay to smash crockery and old televisions. The picture feels right because anger feels like pressure. But feelings are not steam, and the brain is not a kettle.

sections.key: People who hit a punching bag while thinking about their insulter became more aggressive, while those who sat quietly were calmest.
sections.b:
In 2002 psychologist Brad Bushman tested catharsis on about 600 university students. Each wrote an essay and received harsh feedback, supposedly from another student, including that it was one of the worst essays the reader had seen. One group then hit a punching bag while thinking about the person who insulted them. A second hit the bag while thinking about getting fit. A third sat quietly for a couple of minutes.

Afterwards everyone could blast their insulter with unpleasant noise through headphones. The group who vented while focused on their anger felt the most anger and were the most aggressive. The quiet group were the least angry and least aggressive. Doing nothing beat letting off steam.

sections.key: Venting is practice: it keeps the body aroused and the grievance fresh, so calming down works better.
sections.b:
Venting fails because it is rehearsal. Replaying an insult, ranting about it or acting out hitting someone keeps the alarm system switched on and the offence at the front of your mind. Psychologists call the mental version rumination, one of the strongest predictors of anger lasting longer and spilling onto innocent targets. A revved-up body is also primed to read new frustrations as further attacks.

In 2021 Sophie Kjærvik and Brad Bushman pooled more than 150 studies. Activities that lower arousal, such as slow breathing, relaxation, mindfulness, yoga and simply pausing, reliably reduced anger. Hitting things, and in some studies vigorous exercise straight after a provocation, generally did not. Regular exercise is still good for mood and health. When you are boiling, though, cool the body first: breathe out longer than you breathe in, step away, or delay your reply.

sections.key: The goal is neither suppressing nor venting anger but expressing it clearly, without aggression, once you have calmed down.
sections.b:
Stuffing anger down has costs too, including strain on relationships and health. The skill lies between exploding and bottling. Once the first surge settles, ask what the anger points to. Was a boundary crossed? Is something unfair? Then say so plainly, focusing on the behaviour and its effect rather than attacking the person. 'I was embarrassed when the mistake was raised in front of everyone' invites a conversation. 'You always humiliate me' invites a fight.

Talking helps only when it moves towards understanding or solving the problem. Anger that is understood can lead to useful change. Anger that is merely released usually leads to more anger.

If anger often arrives too fast and hard, harms relationships, or has been linked to violence, see a GP for a referral. In immediate danger, call 000.

quiz.q: What is the main problem with anger according to this lesson?
o: Feeling it at all, since it has no useful purpose
What we do with it, because the feeling can be useful
Its effect on blood pressure, which is always harmful
Its link to evolution, which makes it outdated
quiz.e: Anger signals that something matters; the harm comes from what we do with it.

quiz.q: What does the 'steam engine' theory of anger claim?
o: Anger fades fastest when you ignore it completely
Anger is caused by heat and fatigue in the body
Anger builds like pressure and must be released
Anger is learned only by watching violence
quiz.e: The theory treats anger as pressure in a closed system, but feelings do not work like steam.

quiz.q: In the punching bag study, which group ended up least angry and least aggressive?
o: Those who hit the bag while thinking about getting fit
Those who hit the bag while thinking about their insulter
Those who wrote a second essay
Those who sat quietly for a couple of minutes
quiz.e: Venting while focused on the anger made things worse; doing nothing beat letting off steam.

quiz.q: What should you do first when you are boiling with anger?
o: Calm your body by breathing slowly or stepping away
Hit something safe to burn off the energy
Write a long message to the person immediately
Go for a sprint straight after the argument
quiz.e: Calming activities reduce anger, while arousing ones usually do not help in the moment.

quiz.q: What is the healthiest way to deal with anger once it settles?
o: Pretend it is not there and wait for it to fade
Calmly say what happened and how it affected you
Rant with friends who will take your side
Wait for the person to apologise first
quiz.e: Clear, specific expression of the behaviour and its effect invites conversation rather than a fight.

LESSONS.push: Doing nothing beat hitting a punching bag. Why venting backfires.

LESSONS.title: Why we cry
LESSONS.hook: Humans are, as far as scientists can tell, the only animals that shed tears because they feel something. So why did evolution give us such a strange and visible signal?

sections.key: Your eyes make basal tears all the time, reflex tears for irritants and emotional tears when feelings run high.
sections.b:
Your eyes are never truly dry. Small glands keep them coated with basal tears, which wash away dust, feed the cornea and contain proteins that help fight infection. Every blink spreads a fresh layer.

Reflex tears flood in when something irritates the eye, such as smoke, grit or a chopped onion. Cutting an onion releases a volatile sulphur compound that irritates nerves in the eye, so the eye flushes it away.

The third type, emotional tears, are the mysterious ones. Nothing touches the eye. Sadness, grief, frustration, relief, joy or being deeply moved triggers them. Humans are, as far as scientists can tell, the only animals that clearly cry for emotional reasons, and thinkers have puzzled over why for centuries.

sections.key: Tears are made by glands above each eye and drain into your nose, which is why crying makes your nose run.
sections.b:
The main tear-making organ is the lacrimal gland, tucked under the bony brow above the outer corner of each eye. Tiny ducts release fluid onto the eye, and blinking sweeps it towards the inner corner. There, two little openings called puncta, one on each eyelid, act like drains. They lead to a channel that empties into the nasal cavity.

Normally this system handles the gentle flow of basal tears unnoticed. When you cry hard, tears are made faster than the drains can cope with, so they spill over the lower lid and down your cheeks. The extra fluid pouring into your nose explains the sniffing and runny nose that come with a good cry.

sections.key: Darwin saw emotional tears as a by-product, but many researchers now see them as a visible signal that draws help.
sections.b:
In his 1872 book The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals, Charles Darwin studied crying closely, watching his own children among others. He concluded that weeping was probably incidental, a result of muscles squeezing around the eyes during screaming, rather than useful in itself.

Many later researchers disagree. Dutch psychologist Ad Vingerhoets, who has studied crying for decades, argues that tears are above all a signal to other people. Unlike a sob, which anyone nearby can hear, tears are visible mainly up close, to those we are most likely to trust. They say someone is hurting, overwhelmed or vulnerable, and they tend to draw comfort and help.

Tears may also signal no threat, since blurry eyes and a crumpled face are hard to fight with.

sections.key: Visible tears make a face look sadder and more in need of support, which explains why tears are so moving.
sections.b:
In 2009 psychologist Robert Provine and colleagues showed people photos of tearful faces, then the same photos with the tears digitally removed. With tears, the faces were rated clearly sad. Without them, many looked far less sad, and some were read as puzzled, concerned or neutral. Other studies find that people who see tearful faces feel more inclined to help or comfort.

This supports the signal idea. Adult tears tend to appear in moments of helplessness, and we can find them powerfully moving even in strangers on a screen.

Crying changes across life, too. Newborns cry loudly from birth, often with few tears at first, because their tear system is still maturing. Adult triggers shift towards loss, conflict, powerlessness and being moved by kindness or reunion.

sections.key: Crying helps most when you are comforted and understood, and the idea that tears flush out stress chemicals is poorly supported.
sections.b:
Ask people whether crying helps and most say yes. Yet in laboratories, people watching sad films often feel a little worse straight afterwards. Some research suggests the lift arrives later, as feelings recover over the following hour or so.

What matters most is what happens around the tears. People who are comforted or feel understood are more likely to say crying helped. Those who feel ashamed or judged often feel worse. A popular claim says tears flush stress chemicals from the body. Emotional tears differ slightly in make-up, but there is little evidence that so small a volume removes enough of anything to matter.

Crying that rarely stops, or being unable to cry for a long time after a major loss, is worth raising with a GP.

quiz.q: What triggers emotional tears, unlike reflex tears?
o: Smoke, grit or onion vapour irritating the eye
Feelings such as grief, relief, joy or being moved
The blink that spreads fluid across the eye
Dry air that dries out the surface of the eye
quiz.e: Reflex tears respond to irritants, while emotional tears come from feelings rather than anything touching the eye.

quiz.q: Why does crying hard make your nose run?
o: Tears drain through small openings into the nose
The sinuses swell in response to stress hormones
The nose makes extra mucus to replace lost fluid
Tears are made in glands inside the nose
quiz.e: Tears drain through the puncta into the nose, and extra tears overload this system.

quiz.q: What do many researchers now think emotional tears are mainly for?
o: Washing dust from the eye after stress
Lowering blood pressure during distress
Signalling vulnerability and drawing comfort
Removing waste chemicals from the body
quiz.e: Tears are visible mainly up close, so they work as a signal to people we trust.

quiz.q: What did Provine's photo experiment show when tears were digitally removed?
o: Faces were judged just as sad as before
Faces looked less sad, and sometimes neutral
Faces looked more distressed than before
Faces looked angrier to most viewers
quiz.e: Tears make a face read as clearly sad and encourage others to help.

quiz.q: What best predicts whether people feel better after crying?
o: How many tears they shed
How long they spend crying in total
Whether they cried alone in a quiet room
Whether they felt comforted and understood
quiz.e: Support around the tears matters most, while the chemical flushing claim has little evidence.

LESSONS.push: Your eyes make three kinds of tears. Only one is still a puzzle.

LESSONS.title: Laughter: it's not really about jokes
LESSONS.hook: We think we laugh because something is funny. One scientist spent years eavesdropping on laughing strangers and found that most laughter has nothing to do with humour at all.

sections.key: Studies of everyday conversation found most laughter follows ordinary remarks, because it works as a social signal.
sections.b:
In the 1990s neuroscientist Robert Provine, of the University of Maryland, Baltimore County, took a simple approach. Rather than showing people comedy in a lab, he and his students hung around shopping centres, campuses and city streets, noting what people had just said when someone laughed.

Across more than a thousand episodes, only around 10 to 20 per cent of laughs followed anything like a joke. Most came after lines such as 'I'll see you guys later' or 'Are you sure?' Speakers also laughed more than their listeners.

Laughter, Provine concluded, is less a reaction to comedy than a social signal: a way of saying we are friendly, relaxed and on the same side.

sections.key: People laugh far more with others than alone, and laughter spreads, which is why laugh tracks work.
sections.b:
If laughter were just about funny things, you would laugh as much alone as with friends. You don't. In diary studies, Provine found people laughed about 30 times more often in social situations than alone, and much of what they laughed at alone came from television or radio, which supply a kind of company.

Laughter is also contagious. Hearing others laugh makes us more likely to laugh, which is why television producers began adding canned laughter in the 1950s, using a machine nicknamed the 'laff box', invented by sound engineer Charley Douglass. Most people say they dislike laugh tracks, yet studies have found they can make people laugh more at the same jokes.

sections.key: Laughter grew out of the panting play sounds of our ape ancestors and seems to signal that rough play is just play.
sections.b:
Laughter is far older than language. Chimpanzees, bonobos, gorillas and orangutans make breathy panting sounds when they play-wrestle or are tickled. Researchers who compared these sounds found a family tree of laughter that matches the apes' evolutionary relationships. Ape laughter pants in and out with each breath, while human laughter chops a single outward breath into rhythmic 'ha-ha-ha' bursts.

The roots may go deeper. In the late 1990s neuroscientist Jaak Panksepp found that rats make high-pitched chirps, too high for human ears, when tickled, and tickled rats chase the researcher's hand for more. In mammals, laughter seems to have begun as a signal that rough play is only play.

sections.key: Listeners can often tell spontaneous laughs and smiles from deliberate ones, but neither is a foolproof lie detector.
sections.b:
Neuroscientist Sophie Scott, of University College London, separates spontaneous laughter, which bursts out of us, from volitional laughter, the polite laugh we produce on purpose. Brain imaging shows partly different areas respond to each, and people can usually tell them apart. In a 2014 study by Gregory Bryant and Athena Aktipis, sped-up spontaneous laughs began to sound like animal calls, while deliberate ones still sounded human. That suggests real laughter relies on an older vocal system than speech does. Deliberate laughter is not dishonest; it is often a kind, useful signal.

Smiles work similarly. Guillaume Duchenne, a nineteenth century French neurologist, noted that real joy also tightens the muscle around the eye, creating crow's feet. But many people can fake this, so it is not a foolproof test.

sections.key: Shared laughter builds closeness and eases pain, but claims that laughter cures disease go beyond the evidence.
sections.b:
Social laughter does something useful. In 2012 a team led by evolutionary psychologist Robin Dunbar found that people who laughed together at comedy videos could tolerate more pain than those who watched dull films. They linked this to the brain's own opioid-like chemicals. Shared laughter helps people feel closer, soothes tension and makes tough situations bearable, as anyone in a hard job with dark humour knows.

But claims that laughter cures disease, or that a set number of laughs replaces exercise, go far beyond the evidence.

Contagion can reach extremes. In 1962 at a girls' school in Kashasha, Tanganyika (now Tanzania), uncontrollable laughing spread to villages and affected roughly a thousand people over months. No infection or poison was found; it is described as mass psychogenic illness, a physical response spreading through a group under stress.

quiz.q: What did Provine's street observations find about what people laughed at?
o: Most laughs followed ordinary remarks, not jokes
Most laughs followed jokes told by strangers
Most laughs followed comedy on television
Most laughs followed teasing and insults
quiz.e: Only about 10 to 20 per cent of laughs followed anything like a joke, so laughter is mainly a social signal.

quiz.q: Why does laughter in a group tend to increase?
o: People laugh to cover up boredom or awkwardness
Laughter is contagious, so it spreads between people
Groups tell funnier jokes than people alone do
Being alone makes people avoid laughing on purpose
quiz.e: Laughter spreads between people, which is why we laugh far more in company and laugh tracks work.

quiz.q: What does the evidence about apes and tickled rats suggest laughter began as?
o: A warning cry about a nearby threat
A way of attracting a possible mate
A signal that rough play is friendly
An early form of simple speech
quiz.e: Play sounds in apes and rats suggest laughter began as a signal that rough play is friendly.

quiz.q: What did sped-up recordings reveal about spontaneous laughs?
o: They sounded just as human as deliberate laughs
They sounded more like nonhuman animal calls
They became impossible to tell from speech
They sounded more polite and controlled
quiz.e: Real laughter seems to rely on an older vocal system than the one we use for speech.

quiz.q: What is a fair claim about laughter and health?
o: Laughing a set number of times daily replaces exercise
Laughter cures many serious diseases
Shared laughter can raise pain tolerance and build closeness
Laughter has no social benefits at all
quiz.e: Shared laughter has real social and short-term benefits, but wider health claims are exaggerated.

LESSONS.push: Most laughter follows ordinary remarks, not jokes. So what is it for?

LESSONS.title: Self-compassion: being on your own side
LESSONS.hook: Many of us talk to ourselves in ways we would never talk to a friend. Research suggests that harsh inner critic is not the motivator we think it is.

sections.key: Constant self-attack makes people more anxious and less willing to learn from mistakes, rather than more motivated.
sections.b:
Picture a friend who has just botched a job interview. You would probably say interviews are nerve-racking, one bad day does not define them, and they will do better next time. Now picture yourself in the same position. Many people's inner voice says something like 'You idiot, you always choke.'

We tend to believe this harshness keeps us sharp, and that going easy on ourselves would make us lazy. Psychologists who study self-compassion argue the opposite is often true. Constant self-attack tends to make people more anxious, more afraid of failure and less willing to look honestly at their mistakes, which makes learning from them harder.

sections.key: Self-compassion means self-kindness, remembering common humanity and mindful awareness, and it differs from self-esteem.
sections.b:
The modern science took off in 2003, when psychologist Kristin Neff defined self-compassion and built a way to measure it. It has three parts. Self-kindness means answering your own pain and failures with warmth, not harsh judgement. Common humanity means remembering that struggle and imperfection are part of being human. Mindfulness means noticing painful feelings clearly, without ignoring them or being swept away. In short, treat yourself in hard moments as a good friend or coach would.

It is not self-esteem. From the 1980s a self-esteem movement spread through schools, even a California task force in 1986. A major 2003 review led by Roy Baumeister found that boosting self-esteem did little for school or work results. Self-esteem often rests on judging yourself above average, so it collapses when you fail. Self-compassion holds steady either way.

sections.key: Experiments suggest self-compassion makes people more willing to improve after failure, not less.
sections.b:
In 2012 psychologists Juliana Breines and Serena Chen, at the University of California, Berkeley, tested whether self-compassion breeds complacency. Students sat a difficult vocabulary test designed so most would do poorly. Afterwards some were encouraged to be understanding towards themselves, some got a self-esteem boost telling them they must be intelligent, and others got no message.

Offered the chance to study before a second test, the self-compassion group studied longer than either other group. In other studies, people prompted towards self-compassion were more willing to take responsibility for a past wrong and try not to repeat it. Kindness towards yourself seems to make facing your flaws feel safer.

sections.key: Self-compassion is not self-pity or self-indulgence, and it works by calming the body's threat response.
sections.b:
Critics worry that self-compassion is a polite word for excuses. It is not. Self-pity dwells on how unfair life is to me in particular, the opposite of common humanity. Self-indulgence grabs short-term comfort, like another night on the couch instead of training. A compassionate response is often the tougher one: the good coach who says 'that hurt, it's understandable, now let's work out what went wrong.' You can hold high standards and still speak to yourself decently.

Psychologist Paul Gilbert describes a threat system, a drive system and a soothing system. Self-attack fires up the threat system, with racing heart, tension and urge to hide. Self-compassion is thought to engage the soothing system. Higher self-compassion is linked to lower anxiety and depression, though much of this research is correlational.

sections.key: Simple habits, like talking to yourself as you would to a friend, build self-compassion over time.
sections.b:
Self-compassion is a skill that improves with practice. One simple method is the friend test. When you notice a spiral of criticism, ask what you would say to a mate in the same situation, then say that to yourself, even if it feels awkward.

Neff suggests a short self-compassion break in tough moments that runs through her three parts: acknowledge that this is hard, remind yourself that others struggle with this too, and offer yourself a kind word. Some people find a physical gesture helps, such as a hand on the chest. Writing a letter to yourself from the point of view of a kind, wise friend is another exercise used in research.

None of this replaces professional help when you need it, but it is a good daily habit.

quiz.q: What do psychologists say about harsh self-criticism?
o: It keeps people sharp and motivated to improve
It tends to increase anxiety and fear of failure
It has little effect on how people learn
It helps most when the mistake is serious
quiz.e: Constant self-attack tends to increase fear of failure and make honest reflection harder.

quiz.q: Why does self-esteem often fail when you need it most?
o: It rests on being above average, so failure topples it
It is built from other people's kindness, which fades
It is only available to people who succeed regularly
It needs hours of meditation to maintain
quiz.e: Self-compassion does not depend on being special or successful, so it holds steady after failure.

quiz.q: In the Breines and Chen experiments, what did the self-compassion group do before the second test?
o: They skipped studying because they felt reassured
They studied for the same time as everyone else
They studied longer than the other two groups
They asked to be excused from the second test
quiz.e: Self-compassion made students more willing to improve, not complacent.

quiz.q: Which description fits self-compassion rather than self-indulgence?
o: Choosing comfort tonight and training later
Dwelling on how unfair life has been to you
Telling yourself mistakes do not matter
Admitting the pain, then working out what to fix
quiz.e: A compassionate response keeps high standards but speaks to yourself decently.

quiz.q: What is the 'friend test' for building self-compassion?
o: Say to yourself what you would say to a friend
Ask a friend to judge your performance
Compare yourself with your friends' results
Avoid the problem until a friend raises it
quiz.e: Speaking to yourself as you would to a mate shifts the inner voice from attack to support.

LESSONS.push: Being kind to yourself after failure may make you try harder, not less.

LESSONS.title: Love languages: what the science says
LESSONS.hook: Words, time, gifts, help or touch: millions of couples have sorted themselves into love languages. Relationship scientists have now put the idea to the test.

sections.key: Gary Chapman proposed in 1992 that people give and receive love in different ways, and couples flounder when they mismatch.
sections.b:
Gary Chapman, a Baptist pastor and marriage counsellor in North Carolina, noticed a pattern. Partners often loved each other but felt unloved, because each expressed affection in a way the other did not register. In 1992 he published The Five Love Languages, arguing that people give and receive love through different channels.

The book became one of the best-selling relationship books ever, with versions for parents, workplaces and teenagers. Online quizzes let people find their primary language, and the terms have entered everyday speech.

The five are words of affirmation, quality time, receiving gifts, acts of service and physical touch. Chapman's central claim is that each person has one or two primary languages, and that speaking your partner's is the key to them feeling loved.

sections.key: Research finds little support for the idea that matching love languages makes couples happier.
sections.b:
If Chapman were right, couples whose languages match should be noticeably more satisfied. Studies have tested this and the results are underwhelming. A 2017 study by Bunt and Hazelwood found that matching love languages did not predict relationship satisfaction, while partners' broader self-regulation did.

People also often do not fit one primary language; many value all five quite highly. Questionnaires force artificial choices, such as asking whether you would rather receive a hug or a compliment, when most people would happily take both. Psychologists have also questioned whether five is the right number at all.

sections.key: Love is better thought of as a balanced diet needing many nutrients than as a single language.
sections.b:
In 2024 psychologists Emily Impett, Haeyoung Gideon Park and Amy Muise reviewed love languages against decades of relationship science. They found three core assumptions lacked strong evidence: that people have a single primary love language, that there are exactly five, and that matched couples are happier.

Rather than discarding the idea, they offered a different metaphor. Love is less like a language you either speak or do not, and more like a balanced diet. Most people need affection, attention, support, appreciation and closeness in some mix, and that mix can change over a lifetime or even week to week. A partner recovering from surgery may crave practical help; one facing a big exam may need encouragement.

sections.key: Treated as a conversation starter rather than a personality type, love languages can help you ask what your partner values.
sections.b:
None of this makes love languages useless. The core insight, that people notice and value different gestures and that you should not simply give the love you would like to receive, is sound advice. Many couples find the vocabulary helps start conversations they might otherwise avoid, such as 'I feel closest to you when we spend time together, not when you buy me things.'

The risk comes when the label becomes a rule or an excuse. Someone says 'my language is gifts' and feels entitled to presents, or 'touch isn't my language' and dismisses a partner's need for affection. Used as a conversation starter instead of a type, the idea can do good.

sections.key: Responsiveness, turning towards small bids for connection and showing appreciation predict happy couples better than any type.
sections.b:
Relationship scientists point to patterns that matter more than categories. One is perceived partner responsiveness, studied by Harry Reis and others: the sense that your partner understands you, values you and cares for your needs.

Another comes from John Gottman's research, which describes everyday 'bids' for connection, such as pointing out a bird outside or sighing about a hard day. Couples who regularly turn towards these bids, responding with interest rather than ignoring them, tend to stay together and stay happier. Expressing gratitude, sharing good news and celebrating each other's wins also predict closeness.

In short, happy couples pay attention to each other's changing needs and keep showing up, whatever form the love takes.

quiz.q: What was Chapman's central claim about love languages?
o: Everyone expresses and receives love in the same way
Each person has one or two primary love languages
Couples should avoid expressing love through gifts
Only physical touch creates lasting relationships
quiz.e: Chapman argued that couples flounder when they speak different languages of love.

quiz.q: What did research find about couples whose love languages match?
o: They were far more satisfied than other couples
They were far less satisfied than other couples
Matching did not predict relationship satisfaction
They stayed together longer in every study
quiz.e: Studies have found little support for the idea that matching love languages makes couples happier.

quiz.q: How did the 2024 review suggest thinking about love instead?
o: As a balanced diet of needs that changes over time
As a fixed personality type set in childhood
As one language that can be learned in a weekend
As a ranking of which partner loves more
quiz.e: Most people need a mix of needs met, and the mix can shift even from week to week.

quiz.q: What is the best way to use the love languages idea?
o: As a rule that your partner is obliged to follow
As an excuse to ignore your partner's other needs
As a quiz result that fixes your personality for life
As a conversation starter about what each of you values
quiz.e: The vocabulary helps start conversations, but turning it into a label can become a rule or an excuse.

quiz.q: What does the research say predicts happy couples better than love-language types?
o: Having the same hobbies and interests as your partner
Responding to small bids for connection, and appreciation
Avoiding all disagreements between partners
Giving your partner the most expensive gifts
quiz.e: Responsiveness and turning towards bids matter more than any category.

LESSONS.push: Millions have a 'love language'. The research is less convinced.

LESSONS.title: Regret: the things we didn't do
LESSONS.hook: In the short term we regret our mistakes. Over a lifetime, research suggests, the chances we never took weigh far more heavily.

sections.key: Regret comes from imagining a better alternative you feel responsible for, which is why it stings and why it is useful.
sections.b:
Regret is a thinking emotion. To feel it, you must imagine an alternative version of events, the one where you spoke up, studied harder, stayed, left, or did not hit send, and compare it with reality. Psychologists call this counterfactual thinking. It sets regret apart from disappointment: you can be disappointed by the weather, but you regret things you feel responsible for.

That sense of responsibility is why regret stings, and also why it can be useful. In 2005 psychologists Neal Roese and Amy Summerville reviewed studies of what people regret most and found the top areas were education, career, romance and parenting. These are areas where choices are significant and change still feels possible.

sections.key: How we feel about an outcome depends heavily on what we imagine instead, as Olympic bronze medallists show.
sections.b:
In a well-known 1995 study, psychologists Victoria Medvec, Scott Madey and Thomas Gilovich showed volunteers footage of medallists at the 1992 Barcelona Olympics and asked them to rate how happy each looked. Bronze medallists appeared happier than silver medallists, both just after their events and on the podium.

The researchers pointed to counterfactual thinking. Silver medallists compare upwards, with the gold they nearly won. Bronze medallists compare downwards, with finishing fourth and going home with nothing. Later studies often find similar patterns, though not always, since expectations matter: a silver can delight an athlete who never expected a medal. The lesson is broader than sport.

sections.key: Over a lifetime we regret what we did not do more than what we did, because missed chances stay open-ended.
sections.b:
Gilovich and Medvec noticed a striking pattern. About a recent decision, people regret actions more: the rash comment or bad purchase stings. But looking back over a whole life, the pattern reverses and the biggest regrets are mostly things not done, such as not pursuing education, not taking a chance on a relationship, not spending time with family.

They suggested why. Regrets of action get repaired: we apologise, fix the problem or find a silver lining. Inactions are open-ended. A bad action has a known outcome, but a path not taken can be imagined endlessly, and it often turns out wonderfully in our heads. We also forget the real reasons we held back, such as money, family duties or genuine risk, so past caution looks like cowardice.

sections.key: Bronnie Ware's observations of dying patients match the research on regrets of inaction, though they are not a scientific study.
sections.b:
Australian palliative care worker Bronnie Ware spent several years caring for people in the last weeks of their lives. In 2009 she wrote a blog post about the regrets they shared, later expanded into a book. The most common was wishing they had had the courage to live a life true to themselves rather than the one others expected. Others included wishing they had not worked so hard, had expressed their feelings, had stayed in touch with friends and had let themselves be happier.

Her list is personal observation rather than a scientific study, and should be read that way. Still, it lines up strikingly well with the research on regrets of inaction.

sections.key: Regrets fall into foundation, boldness, moral and connection types, and examined kindly they point to what you value.
sections.b:
Writer Daniel Pink gathered regrets from thousands of people in many countries for his 2022 book The Power of Regret and sorted them into four types. Foundation regrets: failing to build a stable base, like not saving or not finishing study. Boldness regrets: chances not taken. Moral regrets: doing the wrong thing, such as cheating or betraying someone. Connection regrets: relationships allowed to drift.

Each type shows something you deeply value. Handled well, regret is useful. Writing or talking about it shrinks it. Treating your past self kindly, remembering what you knew then, helps you learn rather than punish yourself. Imagining advice to a friend, or the view from ten years on, makes the lesson clearer. And when unsure, the bolder choice is often the one you will not regret.

quiz.q: What separates regret from simple disappointment?
o: It lasts much longer than disappointment
Imagining a better outcome you were responsible for
It only happens after a financial loss
It is felt only about other people's choices
quiz.e: Regret depends on counterfactual thinking and a sense of responsibility.

quiz.q: Why did bronze medallists often look happier than silver medallists?
o: They trained harder and enjoyed the process more
They received larger prizes and sponsorships
They compared themselves with fourth place, not gold
They had lower expectations of every competition
quiz.e: Our feelings depend on what we imagine instead: upward comparison hurts, downward comparison soothes.

quiz.q: Over a whole lifetime, which regrets tend to dominate?
o: Impulsive purchases and rash comments
Chances we never took or things left undone
Mistakes that were quickly fixed
Decisions made under pressure from others
quiz.e: Action regrets get repaired or explained away, while missed chances remain open-ended and imagined as wonderful.

quiz.q: How should Bronnie Ware's list of dying regrets be understood?
o: As a controlled experiment with a large sample
As proof that working hard always causes regret
As a medical study from an Australian hospital
As personal observations, not a scientific study
quiz.e: Her list is not scientific, but it lines up well with findings about regrets of inaction.

quiz.q: What does a 'boldness' regret involve?
o: A chance not taken, like a trip never made
Failing to save money or finish study
Betraying or cheating another person
Letting an old friendship drift apart
quiz.e: Pink's four types are foundation, boldness, moral and connection regrets, and boldness regrets are missed chances.

LESSONS.push: Over a lifetime, which regrets weigh more: what we did, or didn't do?

LESSONS.title: Fear: how your brain keeps you alive
LESSONS.hook: A snake-shaped stick on a bush track can make you leap before you know why. Fear is fast, ancient and occasionally wrong, by design.

sections.key: Fear triggers a rapid, automatic set of bodily changes, including freezing, that prepare you to survive danger.
sections.b:
