When you sense a threat, your body changes in a fraction of a second. The sympathetic nervous system and adrenaline raise your heart rate and blood pressure and speed up breathing. Blood is diverted to large muscles and away from digestion, which is why fear can bring a churning stomach or dry mouth. Pupils widen, sugar is released for energy and sweating increases. Goosebumps are a leftover from ancestors whose fur stood on end to look bigger.

The phrase 'fight or flight' was popularised by physiologist Walter Cannon in the early twentieth century. Researchers now add freezing, since stillness makes animals harder to spot. Freezing is an involuntary reflex, not a choice or a sign of weakness, so people who froze in a crisis should not blame themselves.

sections.key: The amygdala can trigger defensive reactions before the cortex has worked out what the threat is.
sections.b:
Deep in each temporal lobe sits an almond-shaped cluster of neurons called the amygdala, named from the Greek word for almond. Studying rats from the 1980s, neuroscientist Joseph LeDoux traced how threat signals reach it. A quick, rough 'low road' runs from the thalamus, a sensory relay station, straight to the amygdala. A slower 'high road' passes through the cortex, which analyses the scene in detail.

The low road lets you jump at a stick that looks like a snake before your cortex has decided it is a stick. Mistakes are cheap and missing a real snake is not. LeDoux has since stressed that the amygdala drives defensive reactions, not necessarily the conscious feeling of fear.

sections.key: A patient with damage to both amygdalae showed little fear of snakes or haunted houses, yet panicked when breathing carbon dioxide.
sections.b:
Some of the most striking evidence comes from a woman known in research as S.M. A rare genetic condition, Urbach-Wiethe disease, damaged the amygdala on both sides of her brain. In a 2011 study led by Justin Feinstein, she handled snakes at an exotic pet shop and had to be stopped from touching dangerous ones. At a haunted house attraction she laughed at the performers and even startled one. She also struggled to recognise fear in other people's faces.

There is a twist. In a later study, breathing air enriched with carbon dioxide, which creates a feeling of suffocation, brought on a panic attack. Threats from inside the body, it seems, can trigger fear without the amygdala.

sections.key: Evolution may prepare us to learn some fears quickly, but which fears we develop depends heavily on experience.
sections.b:
Why do so many people fear snakes and spiders, which rarely harm anyone in cities, but not cars or power points, which kill far more? Psychologist Martin Seligman proposed in 1971 that evolution has 'prepared' us to learn certain fears quickly.

Experiments by Susan Mineka and colleagues supported this. Laboratory-raised rhesus monkeys showed little fear of snakes at first, but after watching videos of other monkeys reacting fearfully to snakes, they quickly developed the fear. When the videos were edited so the monkeys seemed to fear flowers, the watchers did not learn to fear flowers.

Humans also pick up fears by watching others, especially parents. Some fears may be prepared, but which ones a person develops depends heavily on experience.

sections.key: Fear answers a present threat and anxiety an uncertain future one; both are normal, and treatable when they get out of proportion.
sections.b:
Fear responds to a specific, present danger, such as a car swerving towards you, and fades once the threat passes. Anxiety is a drawn-out apprehension about things that might happen, like a medical result or next week's interview. Both are useful in moderation; mild anxiety can sharpen preparation. Problems arise when they are out of proportion to the danger, last long or interfere with life. Anxiety disorders are among the most common mental health conditions, and effective treatments exist, especially exposure-based therapy, which helps people safely face what they fear. A GP is a good first step.

Many people also enjoy fear when they know they are safe. Researchers at Aarhus University's Recreational Fear Lab, studying visitors to a haunted house, found enjoyment peaked at moderate levels of fear.

quiz.q: Why should someone who froze during a crisis not blame themselves?
o: Freezing is an involuntary reflex, not a weakness
Freezing only happens to people who are poorly trained
Freezing means the danger was never real
Freezing is a habit that can be easily unlearned
quiz.e: Freezing is a normal reflex that makes animals harder to spot.

quiz.q: Why can you jump at a stick that looks like a snake?
o: The cortex always analyses the scene before the body reacts
A fast route to the amygdala reacts before the cortex checks
The eyes send a false signal when light is poor
Snakes release a scent that triggers the response
quiz.e: The low road is fast but rough, because a false alarm is cheap and a missed snake is not.

quiz.q: What did patient S.M. reveal about fear?
o: Fear cannot be produced by the body in any way
Fear depends on seeing a threat with your eyes
Fear is entirely learned from watching parents
Body alarms can cause fear without the amygdala
quiz.e: S.M. felt little fear of snakes yet panicked when breathing carbon dioxide.

quiz.q: What did the monkey experiments suggest about fears of snakes versus flowers?
o: Monkeys never learn fears by watching others
Monkeys learned to fear both about equally
Monkeys learned fear of snakes, not of flowers
Monkeys learned fear of flowers more easily
quiz.e: Evolution may prepare us to learn some fears quickly, but experience still shapes which ones we develop.

quiz.q: What best distinguishes anxiety from fear?
o: Anxiety is always a disorder, but fear never is
Anxiety concerns a possible threat; fear a present one
Anxiety is caused by genes, while fear is learned
Anxiety fades within a few seconds, unlike fear
quiz.e: Fear fades once the threat passes, while anxiety is drawn out and about what might happen.

LESSONS.push: Why your body can jump before your brain knows what it saw.

LESSONS.title: The power of touch
LESSONS.hook: Your skin has nerve fibres that seem to exist mainly to register a caring stroke. Touch is one of the first languages we learn, and one we never stop needing.

sections.key: Touch develops first and is central to how babies bond, grow and survive, as kangaroo care shows.
sections.b:
Touch is the first sense to develop in the womb, and for a newborn it is a primary way of experiencing the world. Being held, rocked and stroked helps regulate a baby's temperature, breathing and heart rate, and calms distress. In the 1950s Harry Harlow's infant rhesus monkeys clung to a soft cloth mother rather than a wire one that provided milk. The experiments are now considered cruel, but they helped overturn the idea that babies attach to carers simply because carers feed them.

In 1978 in Bogotá, Colombia, paediatrician Edgar Rey Sanabria faced an incubator shortage and began having mothers hold premature babies skin-to-skin on their chests. Called kangaroo mother care, it can improve survival, warmth, breathing, feeding and weight gain. The World Health Organization recommends it, and skin-to-skin contact is common in Australian hospitals.

sections.key: Special nerve fibres in hairy skin respond best to slow, gentle stroking, giving us a dedicated channel for affectionate touch.
sections.b:
Skin is packed with sensors for pressure, vibration, temperature and pain. In the late twentieth century, Scandinavian researchers including Åke Vallbo and Håkan Olausson studied a slow-conducting nerve fibre in human hairy skin, such as the arm and back, called C-tactile afferents. These respond most strongly to gentle stroking at roughly the speed of a caress, a few centimetres per second, and at about skin temperature.

They seem linked to the pleasant, emotional feeling of touch rather than to identifying textures or shapes. In one striking case, a patient who had lost the large nerve fibres that carry ordinary touch information could still faintly detect gentle stroking and report it as pleasant. Our bodies appear to have a dedicated channel for affectionate touch.

sections.key: People can communicate distinct emotions through touch alone, and small touches can shift behaviour.
sections.b:
In a 2006 study led by psychologist Matthew Hertenstein, pairs of strangers sat either side of a barrier, unable to see each other. One put an arm through, and the other tried to communicate specific emotions only by touching the forearm. Receivers identified anger, fear, disgust, love, gratitude and sympathy well above chance. Each had a typical touch: love was often stroking, sympathy patting, gratitude shaking hands, and anger hitting or squeezing.

Brief touches can also shift behaviour. In a 1984 restaurant experiment by April Crusco and Christopher Wetzel, diners lightly touched on the hand or shoulder by a waitress tended to leave larger tips than those not touched.

sections.key: Supportive touch is linked with a calmer stress response, though research cannot yet prove hugs themselves protect health.
sections.b:
Touch from a trusted person can damp the body's stress response. In experiments where women faced the threat of a mild electric shock in a brain scanner, holding their husband's hand reduced activity in threat-related brain regions, and the effect was stronger in happier marriages.

In a 2015 study led by psychologist Sheldon Cohen, around 400 healthy adults reported how often they were hugged, then were deliberately exposed to a common cold virus and monitored in quarantine. Those who received more frequent hugs and had more social support tended to have less severe symptoms if they got sick. The study cannot prove hugs caused this, since huggers may differ in other ways, but it fits a wider pattern linking warm contact with health.

sections.key: Good touch is always welcome touch, and many people who get little caring contact can find safe ways to add some.
sections.b:
Norms around touch differ widely. In an often-quoted informal 1960s study, psychologist Sidney Jourard counted café couples touching in an hour: very high in San Juan and Paris, very low in Florida and none in London. It was small, but later research also finds big differences between countries and relationships. Whatever the culture, touch helps only when wanted. Unwanted touch triggers stress, and people, including children, may decline a hug. Asking 'Do you want a hug?' costs nothing.

Some people, especially those who live alone, older people and the isolated, go weeks without kind touch. 'Touch starvation' is an everyday phrase, not a diagnosis, but surveys link lack of touch with loneliness. Welcome hugs, holding hands, massage, sport, dancing, patting a pet or a hand on the chest can all help.

quiz.q: What did Harlow's monkey experiments help overturn?
o: The idea that touch develops last of the senses
The idea that babies bond with carers only for food
The idea that premature babies need incubators
The idea that mothers are more important than fathers
quiz.e: Infant monkeys preferred a soft cloth mother to a wire one with milk, showing that contact matters in its own right.

quiz.q: What are C-tactile afferents specialised to detect?
o: Sharp pain from cuts and burns on the skin
Slow, gentle stroking at about skin temperature
Heavy pressure from a firm grip or squeeze
Fast vibration from rough or textured objects
quiz.e: These slow nerve fibres respond best to caress-like stroking and are linked to the pleasant feeling of touch.

quiz.q: What did Hertenstein's barrier experiment show?
o: Strangers cannot recognise emotions without seeing a face
Only love can be communicated by touch
Touch communicates emotions only between close family
People can convey distinct emotions through touch alone
quiz.e: Receivers identified emotions such as love, gratitude and anger from forearm touch alone, well above chance.

quiz.q: Why can't the hug and cold study prove hugs protect health?
o: Nobody in the study was exposed to the virus
The adults were too young to catch colds
People who are hugged more may differ in other ways
Hugs were only counted during the quarantine
quiz.e: The study shows a link, not cause, which still fits a wider pattern linking warm contact with health.

quiz.q: What is the key condition for touch to be beneficial?
o: That it lasts at least a full minute
That the other person is a total stranger
That it takes place somewhere private
That the person receiving it wants it
quiz.e: Unwanted touch triggers stress rather than comfort, so asking first makes the gesture safer.

LESSONS.push: Your skin has nerves tuned to a caress. Here's what they're for.

LESSONS.title: Emotional contagion: how moods spread
LESSONS.hook: One grumpy person can sour a whole meeting; one cheerful barista can lift a queue. Emotions pass between people almost like a cold, and mostly without our noticing.

sections.key: Emotional contagion is the automatic tendency to pick up others' emotions, and it begins in infancy.
sections.b:
You walk into a tense room and feel your shoulders tighten before anyone speaks. You chat with an excited friend and leave in a better mood. Psychologists call this emotional contagion. The term was popularised by Elaine Hatfield, John Cacioppo and Richard Rapson in their 1994 book Emotional Contagion.

It starts remarkably early. In studies from the 1970s, newborn babies only a day or two old were more likely to cry when they heard another baby crying than when they heard other noises of the same loudness. Long before we can talk, we are tuned in to the feelings of others.

sections.key: We automatically copy others' expressions, and this copying may nudge our own feelings, though the effect is modest.
sections.b:
The main mechanism appears to be mimicry. In conversation we copy each other's expressions, tone, speech rhythm and posture, mostly unaware. Swedish psychologist Ulf Dimberg measured tiny electrical signals in facial muscles while people viewed faces. Smiling faces triggered slight activity in smiling muscles, and angry faces in frowning muscles, within a fraction of a second, even when faces were flashed too briefly to be consciously seen.

Copying a face may nudge feeling through facial feedback. A famous 1988 pen-in-teeth study claimed smilers found cartoons funnier, but a 2016 replication across 17 labs found no effect. The 2022 Many Smiles project found that mimicking or posing a smile could make people feel slightly happier, though the pen method did not reliably work. Facial feedback seems real, but modest.

sections.key: One person's mood can ripple through a team, and leaders' moods are especially contagious.
sections.b:
In a 2002 study, organisational psychologist Sigal Barsade of the Yale School of Management had volunteers negotiate how to share a pool of money. Unknown to them, one member was a trained actor who behaved with cheerful enthusiasm, warm calm, irritable hostility or depressed sluggishness. The actor's mood spread to the others, and groups with a cheerful actor reported more cooperation and less conflict.

Other research has found that leaders' moods are especially contagious, since people watch those in charge closely. This matters in offices, hospital wards and building sites, where a calm supervisor can steady a tense shift. Emotions are not just private states; they are part of a team's working conditions.

sections.key: Moods may spread through networks and online feeds, but the size of the effects is debated.
sections.b:
In 2008 Nicholas Christakis and James Fowler analysed Framingham Heart Study data, which also recorded who was friends, neighbours or relatives. They reported that happiness was linked among friends, friends' friends and even friends' friends' friends. Critics noted that people befriend others like themselves and share environments such as suburb or job market, which can make happiness cluster without anything spreading. The size of these network effects is still debated.

In a 2014 Facebook and Cornell study of about 689,000 users, news feeds were quietly tweaked for one week in 2012 to show fewer positive or fewer negative posts. Users seeing fewer positive posts wrote slightly fewer positive words and more negative ones, and the reverse held too. Effects were tiny, but contagion seemed possible through text alone. The study sparked criticism because users had not knowingly agreed.

sections.key: Knowing about contagion lets you choose what you catch and what you pass on.
sections.b:
Emotional contagion is not a flaw. It helps us connect, empathise and coordinate. But knowing about it gives you choices. Notice when your mood shifts after time with certain people, places or feeds, and ask whether the feeling is yours or you have simply caught it.

People in caring and frontline roles, such as nurses, teachers, paramedics and police, are constantly exposed to others' distress and anger. Deliberate decompression after a shift, through exercise, a chat with a trusted mate or time outdoors, can stop it piling up.

Contagion also works in your favour. A calm voice can lower the temperature of a tense room, and spending time with steady, warm people is one of the simplest ways to borrow some of their steadiness.

quiz.q: What did the studies of newborn babies show?
o: Babies cried more at any loud noise
More often at another baby's cry than at other sounds
Babies only respond to their mother's voice
Babies cannot respond to emotions before six months
quiz.e: Even a day-old baby responds to another baby's distress, so we are tuned to others' feelings from the start.

quiz.q: What is the main mechanism behind emotional contagion?
o: Mimicry of expressions, voices and posture
Reading other people's thoughts
Learning from explicit instruction
Sharing the same food and sleep patterns
quiz.e: We copy others' faces and voices automatically, often within a fraction of a second.

quiz.q: What happened in Barsade's group negotiation study when the actor was cheerful?
o: Groups worked more slowly
The actor was quickly identified by the group
Groups reported more cooperation and less conflict
Nothing changed, as moods did not spread
quiz.e: One person's mood spread to the others and shaped how well the team worked together.

quiz.q: Why do critics doubt that happiness 'spreads' through friendship networks?
o: The data came only from online posts
People befriend similar others and share surroundings
Happiness cannot be measured at all
The study excluded neighbours and relatives
quiz.e: Similarity and shared surroundings can produce clusters without any contagion, so the size of the effect is debated.

quiz.q: How can people in frontline roles stop other people's distress piling up?
o: Push down every feeling until the shift is over
Decompress after a shift with exercise or time outdoors
Only ever work alongside calm and cheerful colleagues
Stop caring about the distress of the people they help
quiz.e: Deliberate decompression and noticing where a mood came from help you choose what you carry.

LESSONS.push: Newborns cry when they hear other babies cry. Moods spread like this.

LESSONS.title: Emotional labour: when feelings are part of the job
LESSONS.hook: Flight attendants smile through turbulence; debt collectors scowl on cue. In 1983 a sociologist showed that many jobs sell not just our time and effort, but our feelings.

sections.key: Emotional labour is managing your own feelings as part of paid work, so that customers feel a certain way.
sections.b:
In 1983 sociologist Arlie Hochschild published The Managed Heart. Her idea: many jobs demand more than physical or mental effort. Workers must also produce particular emotions in themselves and, through them, in customers. She called this emotional labour. A nurse stays composed in front of frightened families. A funeral director offers quiet sympathy, day after day.

Hochschild studied Delta Air Lines flight attendants, who were trained to treat the cabin as their living room and to imagine a rude passenger might simply be frightened of flying. Debt collectors faced the opposite task: suppressing sympathy and projecting sternness. In both cases, feelings had become part of what the employer sells, and so something to train and monitor.

sections.key: Workers can fake the expected emotion on the outside, or work to genuinely feel it, and sometimes it comes naturally.
sections.b:
Hochschild borrowed two ideas from the theatre. In surface acting, you put on the expected expression without changing what you feel, smiling at a rude customer while seething inside. In deep acting, you try to summon the feeling itself, perhaps by reframing the customer as anxious rather than nasty, or by recalling something warm.

Later researchers added a third case: sometimes workers simply feel what the job requires, such as real compassion for a patient, so no acting is needed. Hochschild also described feeling rules, the often unspoken norms about what we should feel in a situation, such as joy at a wedding or grief at a funeral.

sections.key: Surface acting is linked to exhaustion and lower job satisfaction, while autonomy, support and genuine time off make emotional work more sustainable.
sections.b:
Hochschild worried that long-term emotional labour could leave people unsure which feelings were really theirs. Researchers describe emotional dissonance: the gap between what you feel and what you must display. Pooled workplace studies, including a 2011 meta-analysis, link surface acting fairly consistently with emotional exhaustion, lower job satisfaction and more stress symptoms. Deep acting shows weaker, more mixed links with strain.

Emotional labour is not inherently harmful, and many people find meaning in comforting others. It is easier to sustain with some freedom over how you express yourself, supportive colleagues and managers, and a workplace that backs staff against abusive customers. Genuinely switching off during time off also helps recovery.

sections.key: Emotional labour is concentrated in service, care and frontline jobs, where lower-status workers are often expected to absorb rudeness.
sections.b:
Hochschild estimated that about a third of American workers had jobs involving substantial emotional labour, and about half of working women, reflecting how many women worked in service and caring roles. Examples include retail and hospitality staff, call centre workers, nurses, teachers, childcare workers, paramedics, police and social workers.

The demands differ. Some roles require constant positivity, others composure amid distress or hostility, and corrections or security work means projecting calm authority while staying alert to danger. Status matters too: workers lower in the hierarchy are often expected to absorb rudeness without responding. Customer mistreatment is a significant stressor for frontline staff, especially when they cannot set limits.

sections.key: "Emotional labour" now often means unpaid relationship and household work, a stretch that Hochschild herself has questioned.
sections.b:
In the 2010s the phrase escaped academic journals. People began using it for the unpaid work of remembering birthdays, organising family schedules, noticing what the household is running out of, and soothing everyone's moods. This load is often carried disproportionately by women. Related terms such as the mental load describe the invisible planning behind running a home.

These are real and important issues, and research on the division of household labour is extensive. But Hochschild has said in interviews that the term has sometimes been stretched to cover almost any chore, blurring her original focus on managing feelings, especially for a wage. When you meet the phrase, it helps to ask which meaning is intended.

quiz.q: What did Hochschild mean by emotional labour?
o: Doing physically tiring work for long hours without any breaks
Managing your own feelings at work so customers feel a certain way
Feeling stressed because of an unusually heavy workload
Listening to colleagues talk about their personal problems
quiz.e: Hochschild showed that in many jobs, feelings become part of what the employer sells.

quiz.q: What is the difference between surface acting and deep acting?
o: Surface acting fakes the expression; deep acting tries to feel it
Surface acting is for customers; deep acting is for managers
Surface acting uses words only; deep acting uses body language
Surface acting is rehearsed; deep acting is always improvised
quiz.e: Surface acting changes only what you show, while deep acting tries to change what you feel.

quiz.q: What does research link to regular surface acting?
o: Stronger friendships with workmates and customers
Faster career progress and higher pay
Better physical health and a steadier mood
Emotional exhaustion and lower job satisfaction
quiz.e: Faking an emotion you do not feel takes effort, and the cost shows up as exhaustion and lower satisfaction.

quiz.q: Who is most likely to do heavy emotional labour at work?
o: Machine operators working alone on a factory floor
Warehouse staff who rarely deal with anyone else
Frontline and care workers, such as nurses and teachers
Software developers working on solo projects
quiz.e: Emotional labour is concentrated in jobs that involve dealing directly with people's feelings.

quiz.q: Why does Hochschild question the modern use of "emotional labour"?
o: It was meant to describe only the work of flight attendants
It has been stretched to cover almost any chore
It now refers only to physical tasks done around the house
It was never meant to apply to paid work at all
quiz.e: The original idea was about managing feelings, especially in paid work, so it helps to ask which meaning is intended.

LESSONS.push: Some jobs sell your smile. What does it cost the person behind it?

LESSONS.title: Shackleton and the Endurance
LESSONS.hook: His ship was crushed by ice and his men were stranded at the bottom of the world. What happened next became the most famous survival story in polar history.

sections.key: Shackleton planned the first crossing of Antarctica and chose his crew for temperament as well as skill.
sections.b:
By 1914 Amundsen had reached the South Pole and Scott had died returning from it. Ernest Shackleton wanted a new prize: the first crossing of Antarctica on foot, from the Weddell Sea to the Ross Sea, about 2,900 kilometres. His ship Endurance sailed from England in August 1914, just as the First World War began. The Admiralty told him to carry on.

The famous "Men wanted for hazardous journey" advertisement is almost certainly a myth: researchers have found no trace of it in the archives. In reality thousands reportedly applied, and Shackleton chose men through quick, quirky interviews, valuing cheerfulness under strain as much as skill.

sections.key: Endurance was frozen into the pack ice and crushed, leaving the crew camped on drifting floes with one goal: getting home alive.
sections.b:
In January 1915, still short of the Antarctic coast, Weddell Sea pack ice closed around Endurance. The 28 men played football on the floes and held concerts while the ship drifted through the polar winter. Then the pressure grew and the hull buckled. In October Shackleton ordered everyone onto the ice, and in November Endurance sank. The goal became getting every man home alive.

The crew camped on moving ice with three lifeboats, and the sled dogs had to be shot. Photographer Frank Hurley, an Australian, kept a few glass plate photographs and smashed the rest so he would not be tempted to go back. In April 1916 the ice broke up and they took to the boats.

sections.key: With no hope of discovery on Elephant Island, Shackleton and five men sailed a small lifeboat 1,300 kilometres to South Georgia.
sections.b:
After about a week at sea the boats reached Elephant Island in mid April 1916, the first solid ground in about 16 months. But it lay far from any shipping route and nobody knew they were there. So Shackleton took five men in the James Caird, a lifeboat under 7 metres long that the ship's carpenter had strengthened and partly decked over. The other 22, led by Frank Wild, sheltered under two upturned boats and ate penguins and seals.

On 24 April the six set out for South Georgia, 1,300 kilometres away. Frank Worsley navigated with only a handful of sun sightings. The men were soaked, chipped ice off the boat and survived a hurricane force storm. After about 16 days they landed.

sections.key: Shackleton crossed South Georgia's unmapped interior to raise the alarm, and all 22 men on Elephant Island were eventually rescued.
sections.b:
They had landed on the wrong side of South Georgia, and the whaling stations lay on the far coast. The boat was too battered to sail around. So Shackleton, Worsley and Tom Crean crossed the island's unmapped glaciers and mountains, with screws in their boots for grip, a rope and almost no rest. After about 36 hours they reached the Stromness whaling station in May 1916.

Shackleton then made several attempts to reach Elephant Island, but ice turned him back. On 30 August 1916 the Chilean tug Yelcho, commanded by Luis Pardo, finally got through. All 22 men were alive. Sadly, the expedition's separate Ross Sea party, on the far side of Antarctica, lost three men.

sections.key: Shackleton's expedition failed at its goals but is remembered for leadership, and in 2022 Endurance was found, well preserved, about 3,000 metres down.
sections.b:
For over a century Endurance lay somewhere beneath the Weddell Sea, so choked with ice that searching seemed nearly impossible. In March 2022 an expedition using an icebreaker and underwater robots located the wreck about 3,000 metres down. The wooden hull was largely intact, and the name ENDURANCE could still be read across the stern. Cold water and the absence of the wood-eating creatures found in warmer seas had protected it.

The wreck is a protected historic site under the Antarctic Treaty and is being left undisturbed. Shackleton's expedition failed at everything it set out to do, yet it is remembered for something rarer: a leader who brought every man of Endurance home.

quiz.q: What is the truth about the "Men wanted for hazardous journey" advertisement?
o: It ran in newspapers for a year and drew thousands of replies
It was written by Shackleton at the request of the Admiralty
No trace of it exists in the archives, so it is probably a myth
It was real, but it was only ever posted in port towns
quiz.e: The famous advert is a wonderful piece of writing, but no original has ever turned up.

quiz.q: Why did the expedition's goal change in 1915?
o: Endurance was crushed and sank, so survival became the goal
The war ended and the Admiralty recalled the ship
The crew ran out of fuel at South Georgia
Amundsen announced he would make the crossing first
quiz.e: Once the ship was lost, survival replaced the crossing as the goal.

quiz.q: Why did Shackleton sail the James Caird to South Georgia?
o: The island had no food, so the men had to leave
The Admiralty had ordered them to meet a ship there
The men on the island had grown tired of waiting
Nobody knew they were there, far from any shipping route
quiz.e: Waiting for rescue on Elephant Island meant almost certain death, so help had to be fetched.

quiz.q: Why did Shackleton cross South Georgia's mountains on foot?
o: The crew wanted to map the unexplored interior
They had landed on the wrong side and the boat was too battered
The James Caird had been left behind on Elephant Island
The whalers had told them a ship waited inland
quiz.e: The only way to reach the whaling station was across unmapped glaciers and peaks.

quiz.q: Why was the Endurance wreck so well preserved?
o: It was buried deep under thick layers of mud and sand
It lay in shallow water covered by permanent sea ice
Cold water and no wood-eating creatures, unlike warmer seas
Divers had recovered and restored it after 1915
quiz.e: The cold, ice-choked Weddell Sea kept the wooden hull largely intact for over a century.

LESSONS.push: The famous Shackleton recruiting advert probably never existed.

LESSONS.title: The safety lift: how Otis made skyscrapers possible
LESSONS.hook: Lifting people up a shaft was easy. Convincing them they would not plunge to their deaths was the hard part, and one man did it by cutting his own rope.

sections.key: People hoisted loads for thousands of years but avoided riding them, because a snapped rope meant a straight fall.
sections.b:
Lifting with ropes and pulleys is ancient. Builders hauled stone, mines raised ore, and in Rome's Colosseum, wooden lifts worked by teams of men raised wild animals into the arena. By the early nineteenth century, steam-powered hoists moved goods between factory floors.

People rarely rode them. Hemp ropes wore out and snapped, and when they did, the platform and everything on it fell straight down the shaft. A broken rope on a goods hoist meant smashed crates. On a passenger lift it would mean funerals. Building a lift that people would trust was the real challenge.

sections.key: Elisha Otis's 1852 brake used a spring and ratchet teeth to catch the platform the moment its rope went slack.
sections.b:
Elisha Otis was an American mechanic from Vermont who had tried businesses from wagon building to running a sawmill. In 1852 he was working at a bedstead factory in Yonkers, New York, and was asked to help install a hoist to lift heavy equipment. Worried about what would happen if the rope failed, he devised a safety brake.

He attached a strong wagon spring to the top of the platform, linked to the hoisting rope. While the rope was taut, the spring was held in. If the rope broke and the tension vanished, the spring snapped outwards and its ends caught in ratchet teeth cut into the guide rails on either side of the shaft.

sections.key: Otis won public trust by having his own rope cut in front of a crowd, and the first passenger safety lift opened in 1857.
sections.b:
A clever brake is useless if nobody trusts it, and Otis understood showmanship. At an exhibition in New York's Crystal Palace in 1854, he rode an open platform high above the crowd, then had an assistant cut the only rope with an axe. The platform dropped a few centimetres and stopped dead. Otis is said to have announced, "All safe, gentlemen, all safe." Whether or not those were his exact words, the stunt worked, and orders arrived.

In March 1857 the first commercial passenger safety lift opened in the E. V. Haughwout Building, a five storey store on Broadway. Steam-powered, it climbed about twelve metres a minute. Otis died in 1861, but his sons built the company into a giant, with lifts around the world, including the Eiffel Tower.

sections.key: Safe lifts and steel frames made skyscrapers possible and turned top floors from the cheapest into the most prestigious.
sections.b:
Before lifts, buildings were limited by how many stairs people would climb, usually five or six storeys. The top floors were the least desirable, often rented cheaply to servants, poor tenants or struggling artists. Safe lifts changed that. Combined with steel frames, which carry far more weight than thick masonry walls, they let cities build upwards, and the skyscraper was born. Chicago's ten storey Home Insurance Building, finished in 1885, is often called the first.

Electric lifts soon replaced steam and hydraulic ones; Werner von Siemens demonstrated one in Germany in 1880. The view, the quiet and the distance from street noise made the top floors the most prestigious addresses in town.

sections.key: Modern lifts layer several independent protections, so deadly falls are extremely rare, and if you are stuck you should stay inside and wait for help.
sections.b:
Modern traction lifts hang from several steel cables, each strong enough alone to hold the car. A counterweight balances the car, so the motor lifts only the difference. If the car goes too fast, an overspeed governor triggers brakes that clamp onto the guide rails, a descendant of Otis's idea. Buffers cushion the car at the bottom. In 1945, after a bomber hit the Empire State Building, operator Betty Lou Oliver survived a fall of about 75 storeys, partly because trailing cables and compressed air slowed it.

Supertall towers use sky lobbies, where passengers change lifts, and lighter carbon fibre cables. If you ever get stuck, press the alarm or intercom button, stay inside and wait for trained help. Never try to climb out. For a medical emergency, call 000.

quiz.q: Why did people avoid riding hoists before Otis?
o: Steam engines regularly exploded inside the shaft
Hoists were far too weak to carry more than a crate
A snapped rope sent the platform plunging down the shaft
Hoists were too slow to be worth the trouble
quiz.e: Rope failure on a passenger hoist would have been fatal, so hoists carried only goods.

quiz.q: How did Otis's safety brake work?
o: A spring snapped out and caught ratchet teeth in the guide rails
A heavy counterweight pulled the platform back up if it fell
A second rope took over automatically when the first one broke
Air trapped in the shaft cushioned the platform's fall
quiz.e: The brake stayed disengaged while the rope was taut and snapped into the rails the moment tension vanished.

quiz.q: Why did Otis have his rope cut in front of a crowd?
o: To test the strength of a new type of rope
To show how quickly a lift could be repaired
To win a prize for the fastest descent
To prove his brake worked and win public trust
quiz.e: The public demonstration built the trust that turned an invention into orders.

quiz.q: How did safe lifts change the value of upper floors?
o: Lower floors became cheaper because of the street noise
Top floors went from the cheapest to the most prestigious
Rents rose evenly on every floor of a building
Upper floors stayed cheap because lifts were slow
quiz.e: Once climbing stairs was unnecessary, the view and quiet made the top the best address.

quiz.q: What should you do if you get stuck in a lift?
o: Press the alarm or intercom, stay inside and wait for trained help
Force the doors open and climb out to the nearest floor
Press every button so that the lift restarts
Climb through the roof hatch to reach the shaft ladder
quiz.e: The car is the safest place to be, and trained help will get you out.

LESSONS.push: He cut his own rope in front of a crowd. Why he lived, and what it built.

LESSONS.title: The tin can: food that keeps
LESSONS.hook: An army needed food that would not rot, so a French government offered a prize. The answer sits in your pantry today, and for decades nobody knew why it worked.

sections.key: France offered a prize for preserving food, and Nicolas Appert won it in 1810 by heating food sealed in glass bottles.
sections.b:
For most of history, people preserved food by drying, salting, smoking, pickling or packing it in sugar. These methods changed taste and texture, and armies on the move still ate poorly. In the 1790s the French government offered a prize for a practical solution. ("An army marches on its stomach" is usually attributed to Napoleon, though nobody can prove he said it.)

Parisian confectioner Nicolas Appert spent about fifteen years experimenting. He packed food into thick glass bottles, sealed them with cork and wax, and heated them in boiling water for a carefully judged time. Samples sent to sea with the navy came back still edible months later. In 1810 he won 12,000 francs, on condition he published his method. His business is often called the first commercial cannery, though his containers were bottles, not cans.

sections.key: Appert's method worked because heat kills microbes and a seal keeps new ones out, which Pasteur's work explained decades later.
sections.b:
Appert believed that heat drove out a corrupting quality in the air, and that sealing kept it from returning. He had the method right and the reason wrong. About half a century later, Louis Pasteur and others showed that food spoils mainly because of microorganisms: bacteria, yeasts and moulds. Heating kills most of them, and a proper seal stops new ones getting in. Without microbes, the food inside can last for years.

This is a lovely example of technology running ahead of science. People often learn that something works long before anyone can explain it. The explanation then lets engineers improve the method, for example by working out the precise temperatures and times different foods need.

sections.key: Tin-plated iron cans began replacing fragile glass from 1810, but the can opener arrived almost fifty years later.
sections.b:
Glass was heavy and broke easily on ships and battlefields. In 1810, the year Appert won, Englishman Peter Durand was granted a patent for preserving food in containers including tin-plated iron canisters. Bryan Donkin and partners set up a London canning works around 1812, supplying the Royal Navy and polar explorers. The cans were really iron, later steel, with a thin tin coating to stop rust, each soldered shut by hand.

Oddly, the can opener lagged behind. Early cans were so thick that instructions reportedly suggested a hammer and chisel, and soldiers reportedly used bayonets or even gunfire. Ezra Warner patented the first US opener in 1858, and William Lyman's rotating wheel followed in 1870, once thinner steel cans made openers practical.

sections.key: Canned food fed explorers and armies, though lead solder in early cans may have harmed some and was later phased out.
sections.b:
Canned food went wherever fresh supplies were scarce. Polar expeditions packed it in huge quantities. Sir John Franklin's doomed 1845 Arctic expedition carried thousands of cans, and some researchers suggest lead from the soldered seams contributed to the crew's decline, though historians debate how much it mattered compared with cold, scurvy and starvation.

During the American Civil War, canned food reached soldiers on a large scale, and many took the habit home. By the late nineteenth century, factories using machines and pressure cookers called retorts turned out cans by the million. Lead solder was eventually phased out, and modern cans are often lined to protect both the food and the metal. Ring-pull lids came in the twentieth century.

sections.key: Canned food is safe and nutritious, but discard cans that are swollen, leaking, badly dented or that spurt when opened.
sections.b:
Today canned food is among the safest and cheapest ways to store nutritious food for long periods, and it keeps many nutrients surprisingly well. Canned tomatoes, beans and fish are kitchen staples around the world. Most cans are steel or aluminium, and both are highly recyclable.

The one serious danger is a rare bacterium, Clostridium botulinum, which can grow without oxygen if a can is poorly processed or damaged. So the advice is simple: do not use cans that are swollen, bulging, leaking, badly dented along the seams, or that spurt when opened. In a suspected case of food poisoning with serious symptoms, such as trouble breathing or swallowing, call 000.

quiz.q: What were the key steps in Appert's method?
o: Pack food in salt and store the jars in cool cellars
Dry food in the sun, then seal it in wax
Seal food in glass bottles, then heat them in boiling water
Boil food, then pour it into open jars
quiz.e: Heating the sealed bottles for a judged time was the heart of Appert's preserving method.

quiz.q: Why does sealed, heated food keep without spoiling?
o: Heat kills most microbes and the seal stops new ones getting in
Heat drives out a corrupting quality in the air, as Appert believed
The tin coating gives off a natural preservative
Heat removes all moisture, and the seal keeps it out
quiz.e: Appert had the method right but the reason wrong; Pasteur's work showed microbes cause spoilage.

quiz.q: Why did the can opener arrive so long after the can?
o: Soldiers preferred bayonets and refused to use new tools
Early cans were thick; openers needed thinner steel
Patent offices rejected opener designs for decades
Early cans were opened with a simple ring pull
quiz.e: Opener design followed can design: thinner steel made a simple opener workable.

quiz.q: What risk did early cans carry?
o: The tin coating dissolved into the food as a poison
Rust from the iron caused rapid food spoilage
Pressure cookers left the food undercooked
Lead from soldered seams could get into the food
quiz.e: Lead solder was eventually phased out and modern cans are often lined.

quiz.q: What should you do with a swollen or leaking can?
o: Cook it for longer to kill any bacteria inside
Use it quickly before the food spoils further
Throw it out, as it may harbour dangerous bacteria
Keep it, since swelling only affects the lid
quiz.e: Damaged cans can harbour Clostridium botulinum, so safe practice is to discard them.

LESSONS.push: Food was sealed in cans for decades before anyone knew why it stayed fresh.

LESSONS.title: Spectacles: the invention that extended working lives
LESSONS.hook: Nobody knows who invented glasses, and one famous inventor turns out to be a fake. But this medieval gadget quietly changed what people could do after forty.

sections.key: From the mid forties the eye's lens stiffens and close focus fails, which reading stones only partly solved before spectacles.
sections.b:
Inside your eye, a flexible lens changes shape to focus at different distances. With age it stiffens, and by the mid forties most people find small print blurs unless held at arm's length. This is presbyopia, from the Greek for "old eye". Before spectacles, a scribe, jeweller or weaver could see their working life cut short at the peak of their skill.

The magnifying power of curved glass was known early. The Arab scholar Ibn al-Haytham studied optics around the year 1000, and his work was later translated into Latin. Medieval readers used "reading stones", rounded glass or rock crystal laid on the page. They helped, but you had to slide them along the line, and they were no use for sewing or carving.

sections.key: Spectacles appeared in northern Italy in the 1280s, their inventor is unknown, and the Salvino degli Armati story rests on a fabricated inscription.
sections.b:
The best early evidence is a sermon. In 1306 the Dominican friar Giordano da Pisa told a Florentine congregation that eyeglasses had been invented less than twenty years earlier, and that he had met the maker, but he did not record the name. That points to northern Italy in the 1280s, where Venice had skilled glassworkers. The first spectacles had two convex lenses, thicker in the middle, in riveted frames perched on the nose.

Many books once named Salvino degli Armati of Florence as the inventor. The evidence was a tomb inscription, which historians concluded was a seventeenth-century fabrication meant to give Florence the credit. No reliable earlier record exists. A satisfying story with a name and a plaque can travel for centuries, even when the honest answer is that we do not know.

sections.key: Concave lenses for short sight came later, and in 1604 Kepler explained that spectacles shift where light focuses on the retina.
sections.b:
The first spectacles helped with close work, which is why they spread among older readers. Short-sighted people, who struggle with distant objects, needed concave lenses, thinner in the middle, which spread light out before it enters the eye. Clear evidence of these appears by the fifteenth century.

Spectacle makers worked largely by trial and error. A proper theory came in 1604, when the astronomer Johannes Kepler showed that the eye forms an image on the retina at the back, and that spectacles work by shifting where light comes to a focus so it lands on the retina properly. Lens makers' skills also fed directly into the invention of the telescope and microscope.

sections.key: Side arms, bifocals and contact lenses each solved a practical problem with wearing glasses.
sections.b:
For centuries, the hardest part of wearing glasses was keeping them on. People tried ribbons, leather straps and frames that pinched the nose. Rigid side arms resting on the ears became common in the eighteenth century, and the London optician Edward Scarlett is often credited with popularising them in the first half of the 1700s.

Benjamin Franklin, tired of swapping between two pairs, described his "double spectacles" in a 1784 letter, with each lens split into a top half for distance and a bottom half for reading. These became known as bifocals. In 1888 the German doctor Adolf Fick described glass lenses placed directly on the eye. Comfortable soft contact lenses arrived in the 1960s, thanks to the Czech chemist Otto Wichterle.

sections.key: Glasses extended skilled working lives and remain one of the most effective health tools, yet about a billion people have vision impairment that is preventable or unaddressed.
sections.b:
It is easy to overlook glasses because they are everywhere, but their effect has been enormous. In medieval and early modern Europe, they let scholars, clerks, merchants and craftspeople keep doing detailed work for decades longer. Some historians argue this gave a small but real boost to learning and productivity, especially after the printing press made books cheaper and reading more common.

The need is still huge. The World Health Organization estimates that around a billion people worldwide have vision impairment that could have been prevented or has yet to be addressed, much of it simple short sight or presbyopia. A cheap pair of reading glasses can still keep someone working, reading and independent, just as it did seven centuries ago.

quiz.q: Why did spectacles matter so much to skilled workers?
o: They protected the eyes from dust and splinters of wood
Ageing eyes lose close focus; glasses restored working years
They allowed craftspeople to work comfortably in dim light
They improved the distance vision of scribes and merchants
quiz.e: Presbyopia could end a craft career early, and spectacles removed that limit.

quiz.q: What should we conclude about the supposed inventor Salvino degli Armati?
o: He is well documented, but his workshop records were lost
He invented concave lenses rather than spectacles
He copied Ibn al-Haytham's design in Florence
His only evidence is a fabricated tomb inscription
quiz.e: A tidy story with a name and a plaque can be false; the honest answer is that we do not know.

quiz.q: What do concave lenses correct, and how?
o: Short sight, by spreading light out before it enters the eye
Presbyopia, by thickening the eye's flexible lens
Long sight, by bringing light to a single point
Blurred reading, by simply magnifying the letters
quiz.e: Concave lenses are thinner in the middle and suit people who struggle with distant objects.

quiz.q: Which problem did bifocals solve?
o: Glasses sliding off the nose
Lenses fogging up in cold weather
Swapping pairs for distance and reading
Frames pinching the bridge of the nose
quiz.e: Each bifocal lens has a distance half on top and a reading half below.

quiz.q: What does the World Health Organization's estimate of a billion people show?
o: Most people now wear glasses by the age of thirty
Many vision problems, often simple ones, go unaddressed
Glasses cause more vision problems than they solve
Almost all vision impairment comes from untreatable disease
quiz.e: Glasses are a cheap, effective health tool, and many people who need them still go without.

LESSONS.push: Nobody knows who invented glasses, and the best-known name rests on a forgery.

LESSONS.title: Matthew Flinders: the man who named Australia
LESSONS.hook: He sailed all the way around the continent, was locked up for six and a half years, and published his great work the day before he died. Then his grave was lost under a railway station.

sections.key: Flinders joined the navy at fifteen and, with George Bass, proved in 1798 and 1799 that Tasmania is an island.
sections.b:
Matthew Flinders, born in 1774 in Lincolnshire, said Robinson Crusoe made him want to go to sea. He joined the Royal Navy at fifteen and sharpened his navigation and chart making under William Bligh on Bligh's second breadfruit voyage. In 1795 he reached the young colony of New South Wales and befriended the ship's surgeon George Bass, who shared his appetite for exploring the coast in tiny boats.

Europeans had long wondered whether Van Diemen's Land (Tasmania) joined the mainland. In 1798 and 1799 Flinders and Bass sailed the sloop Norfolk all the way around it, settling the question. The passage became Bass Strait, at Flinders' suggestion, giving ships from Britain a shorter if stormy route to Sydney.

sections.key: In 1801 to 1803 Flinders made the first known circumnavigation of Australia, with Bungaree and a ship's cat called Trim aboard.
sections.b:
Flinders persuaded Sir Joseph Banks and the Admiralty to back a survey of the continent's coastline. He sailed in 1801 in HMS Investigator with scientists and artists, including botanist Robert Brown and botanical artist Ferdinand Bauer. He charted the south coast, then the east, rounding Cape York into the Gulf of Carpentaria. The ship was rotting so badly that he cut the survey short. He reached Sydney in June 1803, completing the first known voyage all the way around Australia.

Bungaree, a Kuring-gai man from the Broken Bay area, sailed with him and helped communicate with Aboriginal groups. He is regarded as the first Australian-born person to circumnavigate the continent. So did Trim, Flinders' clever black cat with white paws, who has statues near Flinders' own, including outside the State Library of NSW.

sections.key: After being wrecked on a reef in 1803, Flinders was detained by the French on Mauritius for six and a half years.
sections.b:
In 1803 Flinders set off for England as a passenger aboard HMS Porpoise, which struck a reef off the Queensland coast, now called Wreck Reef. The survivors camped on a sandbank while Flinders took a ship's cutter, a small open boat, back to Sydney to organise a rescue. He then continued towards England in the tiny, badly leaking schooner Cumberland, and in December 1803 put in at Mauritius, then a French colony.

Britain and France were at war again, and the governor, Charles Decaen, suspected him of spying. Flinders was detained for six and a half years, and used the time to work on his charts and journals. Trim, who had stayed with him, vanished on the island.

sections.key: Flinders championed the name Australia, and Governor Macquarie began using it officially in 1817.
sections.b:
Released in 1810, Flinders reached England in poor health and spent his last years preparing his account of the voyages. The continent was known by names including New Holland and Terra Australis, the "southern land". Flinders preferred a shorter form, Australia, which he found more pleasing to the ear. He was not the first to use the word, but he was its most influential champion.

His book, A Voyage to Terra Australis, used Australia in its text, though his publishers kept the older name in the title. Governor Lachlan Macquarie read it and began using Australia in official correspondence from 1817. The book was published on 18 July 1814. Flinders died the next day, aged forty.

sections.key: Flinders' grave was lost for more than two centuries until archaeologists found it near London's Euston station in 2019.
sections.b:
Flinders was buried in a London cemetery, but over the following decades the burial ground was cleared and built over during the expansion of Euston railway station. His exact resting place was lost, and a story grew that he lay beneath one of the platforms.

In 2019, archaeologists excavating for the High Speed 2 rail project found a coffin with a lead breastplate bearing his name, among tens of thousands of burials. In 2024 his remains were reburied in his home village of Donington, Lincolnshire. In Australia his name lives on in places such as Flinders Street in Melbourne, the Flinders Ranges and Flinders University.

quiz.q: What did Flinders and Bass prove in 1798 and 1799?
o: A river route led from Sydney to an inland sea
Tasmania is an island, separated from the mainland by a strait
Van Diemen's Land was joined to Victoria by a narrow isthmus
New Holland and New South Wales were separate landmasses
quiz.e: Sailing around Van Diemen's Land settled the question and opened a shorter route through Bass Strait.

quiz.q: What did the Investigator voyage achieve?
o: The first known voyage all the way around the Australian continent
The discovery of a new sea route between Sydney and Britain
The first survey of Tasmania's coastline
The founding of the first settlement in the north
quiz.e: Flinders completed the circuit when he reached Sydney in June 1803.

quiz.q: Why was Flinders held on Mauritius for six and a half years?
o: He had been convicted of damaging a French ship
He was held until he handed over his charts
Britain and France were at war, and the governor suspected spying
His leaking schooner was seized for unpaid port fees
quiz.e: Wartime suspicion, not any crime, kept him detained.

quiz.q: What was Flinders' role in how Australia got its name?
o: He invented the word, and the Admiralty adopted it in 1814
He argued against it and kept Terra Australis
Macquarie coined it after reading Bass's journals
He championed the shorter name, which Macquarie used from 1817
quiz.e: Flinders was not the first to use the word, but he was its most influential champion.

quiz.q: How was Flinders' lost grave found?
o: Archaeologists on a rail project found a coffin with his name
Descendants found his burial record in a Lincolnshire church
A ground survey of a Donington churchyard located it
Builders at a Melbourne station dug up his remains
quiz.e: Station expansion buried the cemetery, and the 2019 excavation uncovered his identifiable coffin.

LESSONS.push: Matthew Flinders mapped a continent. His grave was lost under a railway station.

LESSONS.title: Zheng He and the treasure fleets
LESSONS.hook: Decades before Columbus, a Chinese admiral led some of the largest fleets the world had ever seen across the Indian Ocean. Then China stopped sending them.

sections.key: Zheng He, a Muslim captive from Yunnan, rose through the household of Prince Zhu Di to command the Ming treasure fleets.
sections.b:
Zheng He was born around 1371 in Yunnan, southwest China, into a Muslim family named Ma. His father and grandfather had reportedly made the pilgrimage to Mecca. When Ming armies conquered Yunnan, the boy was captured, castrated, as was common for captive boys entering royal service, and sent to serve the prince Zhu Di.

He grew into a tall, capable soldier and adviser and helped Zhu Di win a bloody civil war and seize the throne in 1402. Zhu Di became the Yongle Emperor, one of the most ambitious rulers in Chinese history. He rewarded his loyal eunuch with the surname Zheng, and later gave him command of an enterprise on a scale the world had rarely seen.

sections.key: Between 1405 and 1433 Zheng He led seven voyages with fleets of hundreds of ships across the Indian Ocean, though the size of the biggest ships is debated.
sections.b:
The first voyage set out in 1405. Chinese records describe over 300 ships carrying around 27,000 people: sailors, soldiers, interpreters, doctors, craftsmen and officials. Across seven voyages, ending in 1433, the fleets visited Vietnam, Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand and Sri Lanka, then India's Calicut and Hormuz at the entrance to the Persian Gulf. Later voyages reached Arabia and East Africa, including Mogadishu and Malindi, and some crew visited Mecca. They sailed with the seasonal monsoon winds.

The largest "treasure ships" are described in a later Ming source as roughly 120 to 140 metres long. Some historians accept this; many doubt wooden hulls could be so long, and suggest 60 to 75 metres, still enormous. Nobody disputes the fleets were vast and well organised.

sections.key: The voyages displayed Ming power and drew rulers into China's tribute system, backed by force when needed, and one result was a giraffe at the Chinese court.
sections.b:
The fleets did not set out to found colonies. Their main purpose was to show the new emperor's might and wealth, gather tribute, and bring foreign rulers into a system in which they acknowledged his supremacy and received gifts and trade in return. But the voyages were not entirely peaceful. Soldiers fought a pirate leader near Palembang in Sumatra, and in Sri Lanka a local king was captured and taken to China.

One charming result was a giraffe. In 1414 envoys from Bengal brought one to China, originally from Malindi. Courtiers declared it a qilin, a gentle creature of legend whose appearance signalled a wise and virtuous ruler. For an emperor who had taken power violently, heaven's approval walking into the palace on four long legs had obvious political value.

sections.key: After about 1433 China stopped sending fleets on that scale, for reasons of cost, frontier threats and hostile officials that historians still debate.
sections.b:
Zheng He probably died around 1433, during or soon after the seventh voyage, and he may have been buried at sea. No fleet on that scale ever sailed again. Historians point to several reasons. The voyages were extremely expensive, and the court faced costly pressures on land, especially from Mongol forces on the northern frontier and the building of the new capital at Beijing.

Confucian officials were often hostile to the powerful palace eunuchs who ran the voyages, and saw them as a wasteful vanity. Later Ming governments also restricted private overseas trade for long periods. A story says officials deliberately destroyed the voyage records, though how much was lost and why is still debated.

sections.key: Zheng He did not reach America, as a 2002 book claimed; he is honoured across Asia as a symbol of seafaring and cultural exchange.
sections.b:
Zheng He's story has attracted wild claims. A popular book published in 2002 argued that his fleets discovered America and sailed around the world in 1421. Historians have firmly rejected this: there is no credible evidence for it in Chinese or other records, or in archaeology. The real story needs no exaggeration.

Around Southeast Asia, temples and shrines remember him, including in Malacca, Semarang and Surabaya, and he is respected by both Chinese and Muslim communities. In modern China he is a symbol of peaceful maritime exchange. Decades before Portuguese ships reached India, Chinese fleets had crossed the same ocean, and then chose not to come back.

quiz.q: How did Zheng He come to command the fleets?
o: He was a Ming admiral trained in the imperial navy
He was a captive who helped Prince Zhu Di win the throne
He was a merchant who funded the fleet himself
He inherited the command from his father
quiz.e: Zhu Di became the Yongle Emperor and rewarded his loyal eunuch with command.

quiz.q: What is debated about the treasure ships?
o: Whether any ships left China at all
Whether the fleets used the monsoon winds
Whether the biggest reached 120 metres or more
Whether the fleets ever visited Africa
quiz.e: Wooden hulls that long would flex and leak, so many historians think the figures are exaggerated.

quiz.q: What was the main purpose of the voyages?
o: To display Ming power and gather tribute
To found colonies along the Indian Ocean coast
To search for a sea route to Europe
To spread the emperor's religion abroad
quiz.e: The fleets were floating diplomacy, backed by force when needed.

quiz.q: Why did China's great ocean voyages end?
o: A storm destroyed the whole fleet in 1433
Portuguese ships blocked the Indian Ocean
The monsoon winds stopped reversing
Cost, hostile officials and pressures on land
quiz.e: Historians point to expense, frontier threats and opposition at court, though the details are debated.

quiz.q: What do historians say about the claim that Zheng He's fleets reached America in 1421?
o: Chinese records confirm it, but only for some trips
Historians reject it: no credible evidence exists
Wrecks found on the Pacific coast prove it
It rests on a hidden set of official Ming maps
quiz.e: The real story of the fleets needs no exaggeration.

LESSONS.push: A fleet of hundreds of Chinese ships crossed the Indian Ocean in 1405. Then it stopped.

LESSONS.title: How railways invented time zones
LESSONS.hook: Once every town set its clocks by its own sun. Then trains arrived, timetables turned into chaos, and the world had to agree on what time it was.

sections.key: Each town once kept its own solar noon, and fast trains with precise timetables made that confusing and dangerous.
sections.b:
For most of history, time was local. Noon was when the Sun stood highest, and because the Earth turns, that moment arrives later the further west you go. Bristol's clocks ran about ten minutes behind London's. By horse and coach, nobody cared.

Railways changed the scale. People covered in hours what once took days, and timetables had to be precise to the minute. With every station on local time, passengers missed connections, and on single track lines confusion over time could cause collisions. The telegraph made a solution possible, because a time signal could travel along wires almost instantly. Railway companies became the keepers of the clock and ran their whole networks on one standard time.

sections.key: Railways, not governments, pushed Britain and North America onto standard time: Greenwich time in the 1840s and the day of two noons in 1883.
sections.b:
In Britain, the Great Western Railway adopted London time in 1840, and by about 1848 most railways used Greenwich Mean Time. Some towns kept two times for a while, with public clocks given two minute hands. In 1880 Parliament made GMT the legal time across Great Britain.

North America had a bigger problem: dozens of railway times, with big stations showing several clocks. On 18 November 1883 the railways of the United States and Canada switched to standard time zones about an hour apart. In many towns clocks were reset at noon, so people lived through noon twice, which is why it is remembered as the day of two noons. The railways, not the government, organised it. US federal law made time zones official only in 1918.

sections.key: In 1884 an international conference chose Greenwich as zero longitude, giving countries a shared reference on which to build time zones.
sections.b:
Standard zones need a starting point. In 1884 delegates from about twenty five countries met in Washington DC for the International Meridian Conference. They chose the meridian through the Royal Observatory at Greenwich as zero degrees longitude. Practical reasons favoured it, as most of the world's shipping already used charts based on Greenwich.

The Canadian railway engineer Sandford Fleming was one of the great champions of a worldwide system of time based on a single meridian. Not everyone agreed: France abstained in the vote and kept using the Paris meridian for its own purposes for decades. The conference did not impose time zones around the world, but it gave countries a shared reference to build their own on.

sections.key: The Australian colonies adopted standard time in 1895, and today daylight saving differences leave the mainland on five different times in summer.
sections.b:
In Australia, each colony had kept its own local time, and travellers crossing borders by train faced the same headaches as everyone else. In 1895 the colonies agreed on standard times based on Greenwich: Eastern, Central and Western. South Australia first chose nine hours ahead of Greenwich, but in 1899 moved to nine and a half hours, a choice that has been debated ever since. The Northern Territory, then administered by South Australia, followed.

Half-hour zones are unusual but not unique: India uses one, and Nepal goes further with a quarter-hour offset. Daylight saving complicates things today. Queensland, Western Australia and the Northern Territory don't use it, so in summer the mainland runs on five different times.

sections.key: Modern time is set by atomic clocks, but time zones remain a mix of geography and politics.
sections.b:
Greenwich Mean Time has largely been replaced as the world's reference by Coordinated Universal Time, or UTC, kept by a network of highly accurate atomic clocks. Because the Earth's spin is slightly irregular, leap seconds have occasionally been added to keep UTC close to the Sun, but in 2022 international scientists voted to stop adding them by 2035.

Time zones themselves are decided by governments, and politics often beats geography. China, which spans the width of five standard zones, uses just one official time, so in its far west the Sun can rise very late by the clock. Spain sits mostly west of Greenwich but uses Central European Time. The railway engineers' solution still governs every phone and laptop.

quiz.q: Why did local solar time become a problem?
o: Towns began setting their clocks by different calendars
Fast trains and timetables made differing town times unsafe
Clocks stopped being accurate once railways opened
Church bells could no longer be heard from stations
quiz.e: Local time was harmless at horse speed, but trains needed one shared clock.

quiz.q: Why is 18 November 1883 remembered as the day of two noons?
o: Clocks were reset at noon, so noon came twice
Railways ran a second set of trains at noon that day
The Sun appeared to stand still over the continent
Governments declared a second midday holiday
quiz.e: Railways switched North America to standard zones, and many towns reset their clocks at noon.

quiz.q: What did the 1884 International Meridian Conference achieve?
o: It imposed one set of time zones on every country
It abolished local solar time in all member nations
It moved the prime meridian from Paris to Washington
It chose Greenwich as zero longitude for time zones
quiz.e: The conference gave countries a common starting line, but left them to build their own zones.

quiz.q: Why does the Australian mainland run on five times in summer?
o: Each state sets its own calendar year
Some places use daylight saving and others do not
The 1884 conference fixed five Australian zones
Sunrise varies too much to use fewer zones in summer
quiz.e: Zone differences plus daylight saving choices produce five different clock times.

quiz.q: Why does China use a single time zone across its whole width?
o: Atomic clocks drift unevenly across big countries
UTC requires large countries to use fewer zones
Governments decide zones, and politics often beats geography
The Earth spins more slowly in the east
quiz.e: Time zones are political choices, as China's one zone and Spain's Central European Time show.

LESSONS.push: In 1883, many towns lived through noon twice. Here's why.

LESSONS.title: Lewis and Clark: across a continent
LESSONS.hook: In 1804 a small army party set out to cross North America to the Pacific and back. They found no easy river route, but they mapped a continent and depended on the people who already lived there.

sections.key: After the Louisiana Purchase, President Jefferson sent Lewis and Clark to explore the west and find a water route to the Pacific.
sections.b:
In 1803 the United States bought the Louisiana Territory from France for about fifteen million dollars, roughly doubling the young country. President Jefferson wanted to know what the land held, from plants and rivers to the Native nations living there. Above all he hoped for a practical water route linking the Missouri to the Pacific. He chose his secretary, army captain Meriwether Lewis, to lead.

Lewis asked his former army comrade William Clark to share command, and the two worked as genuine equals. Lewis spent months studying botany, astronomy and medicine and buying supplies, including gifts for Native leaders. The Corps of Discovery, thirty to forty soldiers and boatmen, with York, an enslaved man owned by Clark, and Lewis's dog Seaman, left near St Louis in May 1804.

sections.key: The Corps wintered with the Mandan and Hidatsa, where Sacagawea joined; she was an interpreter and a sign of peace, not the guide.
sections.b:
By late 1804 the Corps had travelled over two thousand kilometres up the Missouri to the Mandan and Hidatsa villages in what is now North Dakota, and built a fort to survive the winter. Only one member died on the whole journey, Sergeant Charles Floyd. There they hired the trader Toussaint Charbonneau, whose wife Sacagawea was a young Shoshone woman captured by Hidatsa raiders as a girl. Her baby son travelled with them.

Sacagawea is often pictured as the guide, but she was not hired as one and did not know most of the route. Her value lay elsewhere: she spoke Shoshone, recognised landmarks near her home, and her presence signalled peaceful intent, since war parties did not travel with women. In August 1805 the Shoshone chief Cameahwait proved to be her brother, which helped secure horses.

sections.key: The Rocky Mountains were far wider and harder than Jefferson expected, ending the dream of an easy water route across the continent.
sections.b:
The first great obstacle was the Great Falls of the Missouri, where it took about a month to carry boats and supplies around a series of waterfalls. Then came the Rockies. Jefferson had hoped for a short portage between rivers, but the mountains were range after range. In September 1805 the Corps crossed the Bitterroot Mountains on a steep trail in early snow, with little game. They were reduced to eating candles and some of their horses.

Starving and sick, they came down into the lands of the Nez Perce, who fed them and helped them build canoes. They paddled down the Snake and Columbia rivers and in November 1805 reached the Pacific. The crossing ended the dream of an easy water route.

sections.key: At the Pacific the captains let the whole party vote on where to winter, including York and Sacagawea, though it changed nothing about their status.
sections.b:
The Corps had to decide where to spend the winter, and the captains put the question to the whole party. York's view and Sacagawea's were recorded alongside the soldiers', an extraordinary moment for an enslaved man and a Native woman in that era, though it changed nothing about their status afterwards.

They built Fort Clatsop, near today's Astoria in Oregon, and endured a wet, miserable winter, with rain on most days. In March 1806 they started for home. The return journey included a deadly clash with Blackfeet warriors, the only fight of the journey in which people were killed.

sections.key: The Corps' maps and descriptions of over a hundred new species transformed knowledge of the west, but the expedition opened a painful chapter for Native nations.
sections.b:
The Corps reached St Louis in September 1806, after more than two years away, to a public that had largely given them up for dead. Their journals and Clark's maps transformed knowledge of the west, and they described well over a hundred animals and plants new to science, including the grizzly bear and prairie dog.

But the expedition also opened the way for fur traders, settlers and the US government, and over the following century Native nations along the route lost much of their land and many lives. The travellers' fates were mixed. Lewis died of gunshot wounds in 1809, widely believed to be suicide. Clark did not free York for around a decade. Sacagawea is thought to have died young, around 1812, though some Shoshone traditions say she lived into old age.

quiz.q: What did Jefferson most hope the expedition would find?
o: A chain of sites for forts to defend the territory
A water route linking the Missouri River to the Pacific
Gold deposits to fund the new government
A treaty line separating the territory from Spain
quiz.e: The hoped-for water route was the expedition's central geographic goal.

quiz.q: What was Sacagawea's real value to the expedition?
o: She spoke Shoshone and her presence signalled peaceful intent
She knew the full route and guided the Corps across the Rockies
She was an army scout hired to hunt food
She was a trained mapmaker who drew the charts
quiz.e: The popular picture of Sacagawea as guide is a myth; her skills and presence mattered in other ways.

quiz.q: What did the Rocky Mountains show about the hoped-for route?
o: A short portage linked the rivers, as Jefferson expected
The Missouri flowed straight through to the Pacific
A pass known to Native guides gave an easy crossing
No easy route existed; the mountains were far wider than hoped
quiz.e: Range after range of mountains ended the dream of a simple river passage.

quiz.q: What made the vote on where to winter remarkable?
o: It was the only time the captains gave up command
Native leaders chose the site of Fort Clatsop
An enslaved man and a Native woman had their views recorded
The whole party voted to head home early
quiz.e: Recording their views was extraordinary for the era, even though it changed nothing for them afterwards.

quiz.q: What was the expedition's lasting effect on Native nations?
o: It secured permanent protection for Native lands
It opened the way for settlers, and nations lost land and lives
It had little effect, since the Corps left no maps
It ended contact for decades as the route was too hard
quiz.e: The maps and knowledge brought by the Corps served expansion that cost Native nations dearly.

LESSONS.push: She was not the guide. The real story of Sacagawea is more interesting.

LESSONS.title: Into the Challenger Deep
LESSONS.hook: The deepest point in the ocean lies nearly 11 kilometres down, under pressure that could crush a submarine. Two men first reached it in 1960 in a craft held up by petrol.

sections.key: The Challenger Deep is nearly 11 kilometres down, where pressure is over a thousand times that at the surface.
sections.b:
In the western Pacific lies the Mariana Trench, a scar on the seafloor over 2,500 kilometres long, formed where one tectonic plate dives beneath another. At its southern end is the Challenger Deep, the deepest known place in the oceans, about 10,900 metres down by most recent measurements. Put Mount Everest at the bottom and its summit would still sit more than two kilometres underwater. It is named after HMS Challenger, whose 1870s scientific voyage took a sounding there.

Every ten metres of seawater adds roughly one atmosphere of pressure, so at the bottom it is more than a thousand times that at sea level, over a tonne on every square centimetre. An ordinary submarine would be crushed.

sections.key: Piccard's bathyscaphe paired a thick crew sphere with a petrol-filled float, because petrol is lighter than water and barely compresses.
sections.b:
A crewed vessel needs a thick sphere, which spreads pressure evenly, but such a sphere sinks like a stone. The question was how to float back up. The solution came from the Swiss physicist Auguste Piccard, who had flown balloons into the stratosphere. His bathyscaphe, meaning "deep boat", was essentially an underwater balloon: a large petrol-filled float above a small, thick steel crew sphere.

Petrol is lighter than water and compresses very little, so it keeps providing lift under enormous pressure. To descend, the craft carried tonnes of iron pellets as ballast, held by electromagnets. To rise, the crew released the pellets. Auguste and his son Jacques built the Trieste in Italy in the 1950s, and the US Navy later bought it.
