sections.key: In 1960 Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh reached the bottom of the Challenger Deep in the Trieste, staying about twenty minutes.
sections.b:
On 23 January 1960, Jacques Piccard and US Navy lieutenant Don Walsh squeezed into the Trieste's cramped sphere, only about two metres across inside. The descent took nearly five hours. Partway down they heard a loud crack, and later found that an outer window had fractured, though the inner structure held.

They settled onto the seabed, nearly 11 kilometres down, and spent only around twenty minutes there. Their landing stirred up fine sediment that made photographs impossible. Piccard reported seeing a flatfish through the porthole, but many biologists now doubt this, since fish are not thought to survive at that depth. The ascent took over three hours, and both men returned to a hero's welcome.

sections.key: No one returned for 52 years, until James Cameron's 2012 solo dive in a submersible built mostly in Sydney using buoyant foam.
sections.b:
After the Trieste, no human went back for fifty-two years. Uncrewed vehicles such as Japan's Kaiko reached the deep in the 1990s, while crewed submersibles like Alvin explored shallower sites. Attention flowed to the Space Race, and it was said that more people had walked on the Moon than visited the deepest ocean.

On 26 March 2012 filmmaker James Cameron dived alone in Deepsea Challenger, a vertical, torpedo-like submersible designed and built mostly in Sydney, with Australian engineer Ron Allum. It used syntactic foam, packed with tiny hollow glass spheres, for buoyancy instead of a petrol float. The descent took about two and a half hours, and he spent around three hours at the bottom before a hydraulic fault cut his time short. He described a lunar-like, desolate landscape.

sections.key: Since 2019 a reusable submersible has taken many people to the bottom, and has found plastic debris even there.
sections.b:
In 2019 the American explorer Victor Vescovo began repeated dives in the Limiting Factor, a titanium-hulled submersible designed to reach the bottom of any ocean again and again. On his Five Deeps Expedition he reached the deepest points of all five oceans. Over the following years the craft took a number of people to the Challenger Deep. In June 2020, Kathryn Sullivan, a former NASA astronaut and the first American woman to walk in space, became the first woman to reach it.

Dives have also brought sobering news, as researchers have reported plastic debris and human-made pollutants even in the deepest trenches. The bottom of the world is no longer out of reach, and neither, it turns out, is our rubbish.

quiz.q: Why can't an ordinary submarine reach the Challenger Deep?
o: Its engines would overheat in the cold water
The trench is too narrow for a submarine to enter
Pressure over a thousand times sea level would crush it
It would lose all navigation without sunlight
quiz.e: Pressure rises by about one atmosphere every ten metres, so the bottom is crushing.

quiz.q: Why is petrol used in a bathyscaphe's float?
o: It is lighter than water and barely compresses
It burns to push the craft upwards
It is denser than seawater and keeps the craft stable
It insulates the crew sphere from the cold
quiz.e: Lift that survives enormous pressure is what lets the craft return to the surface.

quiz.q: What happened during the Trieste's 1960 descent?
o: The petrol float leaked and had to be replaced
An outer window cracked, though the inner structure held
The iron ballast jammed and slowed the dive
The crew sphere briefly flooded
quiz.e: The dive succeeded despite the crack, and the crew still reached the bottom.

quiz.q: How did Deepsea Challenger differ from the Trieste?
o: It used buoyant foam instead of a petrol float
It was lowered on a long cable from a ship
It carried two crew in a spherical cabin
It descended using iron pellet ballast
quiz.e: Syntactic foam, packed with hollow glass spheres, gave buoyancy at full ocean depth.

quiz.q: What have recent dives found in the deepest trenches?
o: No sign of any life at all
Large shipwrecks from the Second World War
Sunlight reaching the seabed from vents
Plastic debris and human-made pollutants
quiz.e: Even the bottom of the ocean now shows human impact.

LESSONS.push: The deepest point of the ocean sat unvisited for 52 years after 1960.

LESSONS.title: Scurvy: the cure that kept getting lost
LESSONS.hook: For centuries a disease killed more sailors than storms and battles. The cure was found, forgotten and found again, and the final answer turned on a lucky choice of guinea pig.

sections.key: Scurvy, caused by a lack of vitamin C, killed huge numbers of sailors by weakening the collagen that holds the body together.
sections.b:
After a couple of months on salted meat and ship's biscuit, sailors grew exhausted. Their gums swelled and bled, teeth loosened, bruises appeared from nowhere and old wounds reopened. Even long-healed fractures could come apart. Untreated, scurvy killed. On George Anson's voyage around the world in the 1740s, about 1,900 men set out and only a few hundred returned, with disease, mostly scurvy, killing far more than enemy action. Vasco da Gama also lost many men to it.

The cause is a lack of vitamin C, which helps build collagen, the protein that holds skin, vessels, gums and scars together. Without it, tiny vessels leak and wounds cannot knit. Humans, other apes, guinea pigs and some bats and birds cannot make vitamin C, so we must eat it.

sections.key: In 1747 James Lind ran an early controlled trial showing citrus cured scurvy, but the lesson did not stick.
sections.b:
In 1747 the naval surgeon James Lind chose twelve sailors with scurvy and split them into six pairs. On the same basic diet, each pair received a different remedy: cider, dilute sulphuric acid, vinegar, seawater, a spice and garlic paste, or two oranges and a lemon daily. The citrus pair improved dramatically, one being fit for duty within about a week. Comparing treatments side by side in similar patients makes this a landmark of medicine.

Yet Lind treated citrus as one remedy among many. He also boiled juice into a concentrate, and vitamin C breaks down with heat, so it was far weaker than fresh fruit. Nobody knew why citrus worked, and James Cook credited several remedies, including sauerkraut. His fresh food from ashore probably mattered more.

sections.key: The Royal Navy's lemon juice largely ended scurvy from 1795, but a later switch to weaker limes let it return.
sections.b:
Urged on by the physician Gilbert Blane and others, the Royal Navy began issuing lemon juice to all sailors in 1795, usually in the daily grog. Scurvy largely vanished from the fleet. Then the cure was quietly undermined. In the mid nineteenth century the navy switched to cheaper limes from the West Indies. Limes contain considerably less vitamin C than lemons, and processing the juice could destroy more.

British sailors earned the nickname limeys, but on long Arctic expeditions in the 1870s scurvy struck men who had taken their lime juice. Many experts wrongly concluded that citrus did not work. Others blamed bacteria or poisons in tinned meat.

sections.key: In 1907 guinea pigs, which like us cannot make vitamin C, developed scurvy, and that opened the way to identifying the vitamin.
sections.b:
The breakthrough came in 1907. The Norwegian scientists Axel Holst and Theodor Frølich were studying beriberi and fed guinea pigs a grain-only diet. Instead the animals developed scurvy. It was luck: rats and mice make their own vitamin C and would have shown nothing. Now scurvy could be studied in the lab and foods could be tested for their power to prevent it.

In the late 1920s Albert Szent-Györgyi isolated a compound that, in the early 1930s, he showed prevented scurvy. It was renamed ascorbic acid, meaning "against scurvy". Norman Haworth worked out its structure and helped synthesise it, and in 1937 Szent-Györgyi and Haworth won Nobel Prizes.

sections.key: Scurvy is rare but not gone, and its history shows a cure is only as good as our understanding of why it works.
sections.b:
With vitamin C cheap and plentiful in fruit and vegetables, scurvy is rare in wealthy countries, but it has not disappeared. Doctors still see it in people with severely limited diets, such as some older people living alone, people with alcohol dependence or certain eating disorders, and occasionally children with very selective eating. Because it is now unusual, it can be missed: bleeding gums and bruising have many causes. Treatment with vitamin C, guided by a doctor, usually brings rapid improvement.

The story carries a lasting lesson. Lind found strong evidence in 1747, yet confusion, cost-cutting and wrong theories meant sailors kept dying for generations. A cure is only as good as our understanding of why it works.

quiz.q: Why does a lack of vitamin C cause bleeding gums and slow-healing wounds?
o: Collagen forms poorly, so tissues and vessels break down
The blood cannot carry enough iron to the gums
Bacteria multiply unchecked in the mouth
The skin loses its natural oils and dries out
quiz.e: Vitamin C helps build collagen, and without it tissues, vessels and scars fall apart.

quiz.q: What made Lind's 1747 experiment a landmark?
o: It compared treatments side by side in similar patients
It tested one remedy on an entire ship's crew
It identified vitamin C as the active ingredient
It ended scurvy in the navy within a year
quiz.e: Fair side-by-side comparison is the core of a controlled trial, even in a very small one.

quiz.q: Why did scurvy return after the navy switched from lemon to lime juice?
o: Sailors refused to drink the lime juice
Limes cause a different disease
Limes held less vitamin C than lemons
Limes were never issued on long voyages
quiz.e: Limes contain considerably less vitamin C than lemons, so the cure quietly weakened.

quiz.q: Why was the choice of guinea pigs so lucky for researchers?
o: Guinea pigs are the only animals that eat grain
They develop beriberi within days
They reproduce faster than rats and mice
Like humans, they cannot make their own vitamin C
quiz.e: Animals that make their own vitamin C, like rats and mice, would not have developed scurvy.

quiz.q: What lasting lesson does the history of scurvy offer?
o: Evidence is enough on its own for a cure to be adopted
A cure is only as good as our understanding of why it works
New treatments should never be tested on small groups
Diet matters less than medicine for deadly diseases
quiz.e: Lind had strong evidence in 1747, but without understanding the reason, the cure was lost and sailors kept dying.

LESSONS.push: A cure for a deadly disease was found, lost and found again. Why?

LESSONS.title: Salt: the rock that built civilisations
LESSONS.hook: Empires taxed it, armies guarded it and whole cities grew rich on it. The humble white crystal on your table has one of the biggest stories in food.

sections.key: Our bodies need sodium for nerves, muscles and water balance, which is why people and animals have always sought out salt.
sections.b:
Salt is mostly sodium chloride, and sodium is essential. Your nerves use it to fire signals, your muscles need it to contract, and your kidneys use it to manage the water in your body. Hunter-gatherers who ate plenty of meat got enough from their food, but once people farmed grain, they needed extra. Animals feel the same pull, and grazing animals wear tracks to natural salt licks. Many ancient roads and settlements grew up along such routes.

Today the problem has flipped. Most Australians eat more salt than health authorities recommend, and much of it is hidden in bread, sauces and processed meats.

sections.key: Salt has been mined, boiled from springs, dried from sea water and pumped from deep wells.
sections.b:
There are three classic sources. Rock salt is mined from ancient seas that dried out and were buried. At Hallstatt in the Austrian Alps, people have mined it since the Bronze Age, and the region grew rich enough that an early European culture is named after it. Brine from salty springs is boiled down, as across Europe and China. Sea water is dried by sun and wind in shallow ponds. Australia is a major producer this way, with huge salt fields near Dampier in Western Australia, mostly shipped to Asia for industry.

In Sichuan, workers drilled narrow wells with heavy bits on bamboo cables. In 1835 the Shenhai well at Zigong passed 1,000 metres, and natural gas from such wells fuelled the fires that boiled the brine.

sections.key: Because everyone needs salt, governments taxed and controlled it, and those taxes became symbols of injustice.
sections.b:
Salt was big business for the state. Under the Han dynasty in the 110s BC, China's government took control of salt and iron production, and a court debate in 81 BC, recorded as the Discourses on Salt and Iron, argued whether the state should profit from necessities.

A salt tax is hard to dodge. France's gabelle was uneven, some regions paying many times more than others and some people required to buy a minimum amount. Smugglers were punished harshly, and the gabelle was one grievance of the French Revolution, abolished in 1790. In 1930, Gandhi walked to the sea at Dandi and picked up natural salt in defiance of the British Indian salt monopoly.

The word salary comes from the Latin salarium, related to sal, meaning salt. But there is no clear evidence that Roman soldiers were paid in salt.

sections.key: Salt preserves food by drawing water out of it, leaving too little free water for most microbes to grow.
sections.b:
Before refrigeration, salt was a main way to stop food rotting. It works through osmosis. Salt pulls water out of the food's cells and out of any bacteria, and the water left is so tightly bound to dissolved salt that most microbes cannot use it. That is how salted cod, cured ham, anchovies and corned beef were made. Salt cod became a huge international trade and is still loved in Portugal, Spain and the Caribbean.

Salt also steers fermentation. In sauerkraut, kimchi and pickles, the right amount holds back spoilage organisms while helpful lactic acid bacteria do their sour, flavourful work.

sections.key: Nearly all cooking salts are chemically similar, and what matters most is crystal size and added iodine.
sections.b:
Sea salt, rock salt, pink Himalayan salt and table salt are overwhelmingly sodium chloride. Trace minerals tint some salts, but in the amounts you eat they make little nutritional difference. What changes is the crystal. Big flakes dissolve slowly and crunch on top of food, while fine salt packs densely, so a teaspoon of fine salt is noticeably saltier than a teaspoon of flakes. That is why a recipe calling for a teaspoon of salt can come out differently.

Iodine is the other difference. Deficiency can cause goitre and affect brain development, so many countries add iodine to salt. Since 2009, Australian bakers have been required to use iodised salt in most bread, a quiet public health measure.

quiz.q: Why did early farmers need extra salt that hunter-gatherers often did not?
o: Grain supplies little sodium, unlike a meat-rich diet
Farming made their bodies lose sodium faster
Wild animals had eaten all the natural salt
Grain contains compounds that block sodium
quiz.e: Meat supplies sodium, so people who settled to farm grain had to find salt elsewhere.

quiz.q: How is salt produced by solar evaporation?
o: Sea water is dried by sun and wind in shallow ponds
Brine from springs is boiled over gas fires
Rock salt is crushed and washed in the sun
Deep wells pump out dry crystals
quiz.e: Solar evaporation lets sun and wind do the work, as on Western Australia's coast.

quiz.q: Why did salt taxes become symbols of injustice?
o: Salt was a luxury, so only wealthy households could be taxed
Everyone needed salt, so the tax was hard to avoid and unfair
Governments banned salt, so ordinary people had to smuggle it
The tax was paid only by foreign merchants and their agents
quiz.e: A necessity cannot be avoided, so heavy or uneven salt taxes provoked lasting anger.

quiz.q: How does salt help preserve food?
o: It kills microbes by heating the food
It makes food too acidic for bacteria
It draws water out so microbes cannot grow
It coats the food in a layer of oil
quiz.e: Through osmosis, salt removes the free water microbes need to grow.

quiz.q: What really differs between sea salt, rock salt and table salt?
o: Their basic chemical makeup, which differs a lot
Mainly crystal size and whether iodine is added
How much sodium each contains in every gram
The trace minerals, which make a big nutritional difference
quiz.e: All are mostly sodium chloride, so crystal size and added iodine matter most.

LESSONS.push: Empires taxed it and a famous march defied it. Why was salt worth that much?

LESSONS.title: Bananas: the fruit of clones
LESSONS.hook: The banana in your lunchbox is almost certainly a genetic copy of nearly every other banana in the shop. That makes it cheap, convenient and surprisingly fragile.

sections.key: The banana plant is a giant herb with a trunk made of leaves, and its fruit is botanically a berry.
sections.b:
A banana plantation looks like a forest, but banana plants are not trees. They have no wood. What looks like a trunk is a pseudostem of tightly wrapped leaf bases, and the true stem stays mostly underground as a fleshy corm. Some plants grow taller than a house, making them among the largest herbaceous plants in the world. Each pseudostem flowers once, bears one large bunch and dies back, while new shoots called suckers rise from the base.

Botanically, the fruit is a berry, because it develops from a single flower's ovary and has its seeds inside the flesh. Strawberries, confusingly, do not count as true berries.

sections.key: Cultivated bananas are sterile and seedless, so every new plant is grown from a piece of its parent: a clone.
sections.b:
Wild bananas, which grow across South-East Asia and the western Pacific, are full of hard seeds. Evidence from Kuk Swamp in Papua New Guinea suggests people cultivated bananas there around 7,000 years ago. Traders and migrants carried them to India, Africa and the Pacific, and they reached the Americas after European contact in the early sixteenth century. Sweet bananas are eaten raw, while plantains and cooking bananas are boiled or fried, and in parts of East Africa they are a daily staple.

Our bananas come from rare plants with three sets of chromosomes, which makes them sterile. The dark specks inside are undeveloped seeds. Farmers plant suckers, cuttings or laboratory plantlets, so each plant is identical to its parent.

sections.key: Because export bananas are clones, a soil fungus destroyed the Gros Michel and the Cavendish took its place.
sections.b:
Until the mid-twentieth century, the banana in Western shops was mostly the Gros Michel, or Big Mike. It was large and creamy, and its thick skin survived long shipping. But it was vulnerable to Panama disease, a wilt caused by a soil fungus that blocks the plant's water vessels and can persist in soil for decades. Every Gros Michel was a clone, so none had resistance. Plantations across Central America and the Caribbean were devastated. By the 1960s, exporters had switched to the Cavendish, which resisted that strain.

The Cavendish has an English story. In the 1830s, the Duke of Devonshire's gardener Joseph Paxton, who later designed the Crystal Palace, coaxed one into fruit in the Chatsworth House hothouses and named it after his employer. It was more delicate, so exporters began packing bananas in boxes.

sections.key: Bananas are picked green and ripen as the gas ethylene turns starch into sugar.
sections.b:
Shop bananas are harvested hard and green, because ripe fruit bruises easily. Like apples, tomatoes and avocados, bananas are climacteric fruit: they keep ripening after picking. The trigger is ethylene, a simple gas the fruit produces itself. Distributors use ripening rooms and add a little ethylene to start the fruit off evenly.

As a banana ripens, starch converts to sugars, the flesh softens and the green chlorophyll in the skin breaks down, revealing yellow pigments. Brown spots mean it is very ripe. A paper bag with an apple traps ethylene and speeds ripening, while refrigeration blackens the skin but leaves the flesh fine.

sections.key: Banana money shaped Central American politics, and Australia protects its own industry with strict biosecurity.
sections.b:
In the early twentieth century, American companies such as United Fruit owned plantations, railways and ports in Central America. In 1904 O. Henry used the phrase "banana republic" for a country dominated by foreign business. In 1928 Colombian troops fired on striking banana workers, and in 1954 a CIA-backed coup removed Guatemala's elected government, whose land reforms threatened United Fruit.

Most Australian bananas grow in far north Queensland, around Tully and Innisfail. Cavendish dominates, and the small, sweet Lady Finger is a local favourite. Fresh bananas are not imported, so cyclones such as Larry in 2006 and Yasi in 2011 sent prices soaring. The biggest threat is Tropical Race 4, a Panama disease strain that attacks Cavendish and was found in Queensland in 2015.

quiz.q: Why is a banana plant not a tree?
o: It has no wood; its trunk is wrapped leaf bases
It grows only in tropical soil, never in cooler places
It produces no flowers, only fruit
Its fruit grows underground like a root
quiz.e: The pseudostem is made of tightly wrapped leaf bases, not wood.

quiz.q: Why is every plant in a banana plantation genetically alike?
o: Wild bananas have no variation
Pollen from one plant fertilises all the rest
Sterile plants are grown from cuttings
Farmers breed them in laboratories from seed
quiz.e: Cultivated bananas cannot breed normally, so each new plant is a clone of its parent.

quiz.q: Why did Panama disease devastate the Gros Michel?
o: It was grown only in cold climates
Every plant was a clone, so none had resistance
The fungus spread through shipping boxes
Its skin was too thin to protect it
quiz.e: A uniform crop has no genetic variety, so one disease can sweep through all of it.

quiz.q: What triggers a banana to ripen?
o: Cold air in the display fridge
Ethylene, a gas the fruit makes itself
Direct sunlight falling on the skin
Moisture building up inside the peel
quiz.e: Ethylene starts the conversion of starch to sugar, and extra ethylene speeds the process.

quiz.q: Why is Tropical Race 4 a worry for Queensland growers?
o: It attacks the Cavendish, the main variety grown
It makes the fruit unsafe to eat after harvest
It spreads only through cyclone winds and rain
It only affects bananas imported from overseas
quiz.e: Tropical Race 4 is a Panama disease strain that threatens the Cavendish, so hygiene helps contain it.

LESSONS.push: The banana in your lunchbox is a copy. Why that makes it so fragile.

LESSONS.title: The potato: from the Andes to everywhere
LESSONS.hook: A knobbly tuber from the high Andes fed empires, sparked suspicion in Europe, and became one of the world's most important foods.

sections.key: The potato was domesticated in the high Andes, and Andean peoples developed thousands of varieties and a way to store it for years.
sections.b:
The potato we eat was domesticated in the Andes, near Lake Titicaca in southern Peru and northern Bolivia, perhaps 7,000 to 10,000 years ago. Farmers grew food above 3,000 metres, with frost, thin air and short seasons. They bred thousands of varieties, from purple and red to gold and near black, each suited to particular soils, heights and uses. The International Potato Center in Lima keeps a huge collection as insurance for the future.

Fresh potatoes rot, so Andean peoples invented chuño. Potatoes freeze overnight on the ground, thaw in the sun and are trodden to squeeze out water. The light, hard result lasts for years, and the Inca state stored it in roadside warehouses.

sections.key: Europeans distrusted the potato at first, but its high yields eventually won farmers over, helped by Parmentier's promotion in France.
sections.b:
Spanish soldiers met the potato in the 1530s, and by the 1560s and 1570s it had crossed the Atlantic. Europeans were wary. It belongs to the nightshade family, and its leaves and green parts really do contain toxic glycoalkaloids, including solanine. Gradually farmers noticed that potatoes gave far more calories per hectare than wheat or rye, grew in poor soil and cool climates, and could stay in the ground until needed.

In France, the army pharmacist Antoine-Augustin Parmentier had survived on potatoes as a prisoner of war. He promoted them tirelessly, and in 1772 the Paris Faculty of Medicine declared them fit to eat. A story says he guarded a potato field by day but not by night, so locals would steal it. That tale may be embellished.

sections.key: Relying on one potato variety left Ireland exposed when blight struck in 1845.
sections.b:
By the 1840s, much of Ireland's rural poor relied on potatoes for most of their food. Many grew a single high-yielding variety, the Lumper, so the crop was genetically very uniform. In 1845 late blight, caused by the fungus-like Phytophthora infestans, turned potatoes black and rotten in the ground, and it returned in following years.

Roughly a million people died of starvation and disease, and more than a million emigrated, many to North America, Britain and Australia. Political choices made it worse: food continued to be exported from Ireland, and relief was inadequate. The famine is a lasting lesson about the danger of depending on a single crop.

sections.key: Potatoes feed the world efficiently and are more nutritious than their reputation, if not deep fried and loaded with fat and salt.
sections.b:
The potato spread across Europe, Asia and Africa, and is now one of the most important food crops on Earth. As of the mid-2020s, China grows the most, followed by India. Potatoes give more food per hectare than most grains and need less water, which matters as populations grow and the climate changes.

They are also more nutritious than their reputation. A potato provides energy as starch, along with fibre, potassium and a useful amount of vitamin C, with much of the fibre in the skin. It is usually what we do to potatoes, such as deep frying and adding salt, butter and cream, that makes them less healthy, not the potato itself.

sections.key: Starchy potatoes suit mash and chips, waxy ones suit salads, and green or bitter potatoes should be trimmed or thrown out.
sections.b:
Potatoes fall into two camps. Floury or starchy varieties, such as russets, break apart when cooked and suit fluffy mash, roasts and chips. Waxy varieties, such as kipflers and small new potatoes, hold their shape for salads and boiling. The difference comes from starch content and how the cells hold together.

Store potatoes somewhere cool, dark and dry. Light turns them green as they make chlorophyll, and alongside it they can make more glycoalkaloids, which taste bitter and can cause illness in large amounts. Cut away green patches and sprouts generously, and throw out potatoes that are very green or taste bitter. Keeping them out of the light is the simplest fix.

quiz.q: How does chuño preserve potatoes?
o: They are smoked over open fires for several weeks
They are buried in damp soil until they ferment
They are salted and then dried in the shade
They are frozen overnight, thawed in sun and trodden dry
quiz.e: Repeated freezing, thawing and treading removes water, giving a potato that lasts for years.

quiz.q: Why did farmers eventually adopt the potato despite their suspicion?
o: It produced far more calories per hectare, even in poor soil
It was cheaper to import than wheat from the colonies
It had no toxic parts, so cooks trusted it
It tasted better than bread to most Europeans
quiz.e: High yields in poor soils and cool climates outweighed Europeans' early wariness.

quiz.q: What made Ireland so vulnerable to potato blight in 1845?
o: Heavy reliance on one genetically uniform potato variety
Poor soil that could grow nothing else
A shortage of farmers after heavy emigration
A ban on growing other vegetables
quiz.e: A uniform crop has no variety to resist disease, so dependence on it was dangerous.

quiz.q: What usually makes potato dishes less healthy?
o: The starch that is found inside the potato
How they are prepared, such as deep frying
Their lack of fibre and other nutrients
The vitamin C that sits in their skin
quiz.e: Potatoes themselves offer starch, fibre, potassium and vitamin C. Preparation is the issue.

quiz.q: What should you do with a potato that has green patches?
o: Peel off only the brown spots and cook as normal
Boil it for longer to neutralise the toxins
Cut away the green generously, or bin very green ones
Freeze it until the green fades to white
quiz.e: Green patches can signal more glycoalkaloids, which can cause illness in large amounts.

LESSONS.push: Europe feared it, then one crop's failure killed a million. The potato's story.

LESSONS.title: Rice: the grain that feeds billions
LESSONS.hook: Billions of people eat rice every day. Its story runs from ancient Chinese wetlands to a ‘miracle rice’ and paddies in the New South Wales Riverina.

sections.key: Asian and African rice were domesticated separately, and flooding paddies helps rice outcompete weeds.
sections.b:
Most rice is Asian rice, Oryza sativa, domesticated in the Yangtze region of China roughly 9,000 years ago, though researchers still debate how japonica and indica arose. Farmers selected plants whose grains stayed on the stalk, easing harvest. Separately, West Africans domesticated African rice, Oryza glaberrima, in the Niger River delta around 3,000 years ago. It is hardy and still grown, though Asian rice has largely replaced it.

Rice does not need to be underwater, but it tolerates flooding because air channels carry oxygen to its roots. Weeds struggle in flooded soil, so farmers flood paddies to control them. The downside is methane from microbes in flooded soil, which farmers try to cut by alternate wetting and drying.

sections.key: The texture of cooked rice depends mainly on two starches, amylose and amylopectin.
sections.b:
Rice starch comes in two forms. Amylose is a straight chain, and rices high in it, such as many long-grain varieties, cook up firm with separate grains. Amylopectin is highly branched and makes rice soft and sticky. Japanese short-grain rice has relatively little amylose, so it clumps nicely for sushi. Risotto rices such as arborio release creamy starch when stirred. Sticky or glutinous rice, used in Thai and Lao cooking, is almost entirely amylopectin and contains no gluten; glutinous means glue-like. Jasmine tends to be softer and stickier than basmati. Rinsing removes surface starch and gives looser grains.

There are two classic methods: absorption, where grains soak up a measured amount of water, and boiling in plenty of water that is drained. Electric rice cookers have been popular in Japan since the mid-1950s.

sections.key: Polishing rice removes the vitamins in its bran, and studying the resulting disease helped reveal that vitamins exist.
sections.b:
Brown rice keeps its bran and germ, which hold fibre, oils, minerals and B vitamins. White rice has them polished away, so it cooks faster and lasts longer but is less nutritious. As steam-powered mills spread polished rice across Asia in the late nineteenth century, beriberi became widespread, causing nerve damage, weakness and heart failure.

In the Dutch East Indies, now Indonesia, the physician Christiaan Eijkman noticed in the 1890s that chickens fed polished rice developed similar symptoms and recovered on unpolished rice. His work helped show that tiny amounts of certain substances in food are essential. The missing substance proved to be thiamine, vitamin B1, and Eijkman shared the 1929 Nobel Prize.

sections.key: Short, sturdy IR8 rice boosted yields across Asia, but modern rice farming also strains water and the environment.
sections.b:
In the 1960s, experts feared mass famine in Asia as populations outgrew harvests. At the International Rice Research Institute in the Philippines, breeders crossed a tall Indonesian variety with a Taiwanese dwarf. The result, IR8, released in 1966, had short, stiff stems. Tall varieties fell over under heavy fertiliser, but IR8 carried heavy heads of grain and often yielded far more. Known as "miracle rice", it was central to the Green Revolution. The costs included heavier use of fertiliser, pesticides and water, and the loss of many traditional varieties.

Australia has grown rice commercially for about a century, mainly in the Riverina, on Murrumbidgee and Murray water. Growers achieve some of the world's highest yields, but the crop swings with drought, collapsing in very dry years.

sections.key: Cooked rice must be cooled quickly and refrigerated because heat-resistant Bacillus cereus spores can make toxins.
sections.b:
Rice can carry spores of Bacillus cereus, which survive cooking. If cooked rice sits warm for hours, the spores grow and make toxins that reheating will not destroy, causing vomiting.

So cool leftover rice quickly, refrigerate it within an hour or so, eat it within a day or so and reheat it until steaming hot. Spreading rice on a tray helps it cool faster. The risk comes from the time the rice spends warm, not from the rice itself, which is a safe, healthy staple for billions of people when handled sensibly.

quiz.q: Why do rice paddies work well as flooded fields?
o: Rice cannot grow without being fully underwater
Water makes rice grains heavier and easier to harvest
Weeds struggle in flooded soil, but rice tolerates it
Flooding adds nutrients that other crops need
quiz.e: Air channels let rice tolerate flooding, which helps it outcompete weeds.

quiz.q: What makes sticky rice sticky?
o: It contains a lot of gluten
It is almost entirely amylopectin
It is never rinsed or soaked
It is very high in amylose
quiz.e: Highly branched amylopectin makes rice soft and clumpy, and sticky rice has no gluten.

quiz.q: What caused beriberi to spread with polished rice?
o: Polishing removed the bran, which held thiamine
Steam mills contaminated the rice with bacteria
White rice was too high in starch
Polishing added toxins to the grain
quiz.e: The bran holds vitamin B1, so polished rice left people short of thiamine.

quiz.q: Why did IR8 rice raise yields so much?
o: Short, stiff stems let it carry heavy grain upright
It was grown in flooded fields all year round
It needed far less water than older varieties
It had tall stalks that caught more sunlight
quiz.e: Short stems let IR8 take heavy fertiliser and carry more grain.

quiz.q: Why should leftover rice be cooled and refrigerated quickly?
o: Cold rice quickly loses most of its vitamins
Reheating cooked rice makes the grains hard
Spores survive cooking and make toxins in warm rice
Rice absorbs smells from other food in the fridge
quiz.e: The toxins from Bacillus cereus survive reheating, so limiting time warm is the key.

LESSONS.push: One grain feeds billions, and one pan of leftovers can make you ill. Why?

LESSONS.title: Pots and pans: what your cookware is doing
LESSONS.hook: Cast iron, stainless steel, non-stick and copper each handle heat differently. Know their personalities and your cooking gets easier overnight.

sections.key: Good cookware spreads heat evenly and holds enough of it that cold food does not crash the pan's temperature.
sections.b:
A pan has two main heat jobs. The first is conducting heat sideways from the burner, so the whole base is evenly hot instead of scorching in the middle with cool edges. Metals vary hugely: copper conducts roughly twenty-five times better than stainless steel, and aluminium is not far behind copper.

The second job is storing heat. A thick, heavy pan holds more energy, so when you drop in a cold steak the temperature does not crash and you still get a good sear. Cast iron is a poor conductor but a great heat store. No single material does everything perfectly, which is why cooks collect a few different pans for different tasks.

sections.key: Cast iron and carbon steel heat slowly, hold heat well, and gain a non-stick seasoning of baked-on oil.
sections.b:
Cast iron is heavy, nearly indestructible and can last for generations. It heats slowly and unevenly, so preheat it gently for several minutes. Once hot it holds heat beautifully, ideal for searing and frying. Its seasoning is not grime. When thin layers of oil are heated past their smoke point, the oil polymerises into a hard, slick coating bonded to the metal.

A popular myth says never to use detergent. Modern dishwashing liquid is mild and will not strip well-polymerised seasoning, although soaking or a dishwasher can cause rust. Dry the pan straight away and wipe on a little oil.

Carbon steel is close to cast iron in chemistry but rolled thinner, so it heats faster and is much lighter. Woks and omelette pans are often carbon steel, and are seasoned too.

sections.key: Stainless steel is tough and non-reactive but needs an aluminium or copper core to heat evenly.
sections.b:
Stainless steel resists rust, does not react with acidic foods like tomato or wine, and can go from stovetop to oven. On its own it conducts heat poorly, so good pans are clad, with aluminium or copper sandwiched between steel. Food sticks when the pan is not hot enough, because proteins bond to the metal. Flick in a drop of water: if it skitters as a bead, the pan is hot, thanks to the Leidenfrost effect, where a cushion of steam holds the droplet up. Then add oil and food.

Copper is the most responsive metal, heating and cooling almost instantly, and is usually lined with tin or stainless steel because it reacts with some foods. Plain aluminium is light, cheap and conductive but reacts with acidic foods and dents easily. Hard-anodised aluminium is tougher.

sections.key: Non-stick coatings are stable at normal cooking temperatures, but an empty pan overheated on high can release harmful fumes.
sections.b:
In 1938 the DuPont chemist Roy Plunkett was experimenting with refrigerant gases. One cylinder seemed empty, but cut open it held a waxy white solid: the gas had polymerised into PTFE, a material so slippery and unreactive that almost nothing sticks to it. In the 1950s the French engineer Marc Grégoire bonded PTFE to aluminium, reportedly at his wife Colette's suggestion, creating Tefal.

At ordinary temperatures PTFE is inert. Above roughly 260 degrees Celsius it breaks down, releasing fumes that can cause flu-like symptoms in people and can kill pet birds. An empty pan on high can get that hot within minutes, so cook on low to medium heat and replace badly scratched pans. PFOA, a chemical once used to make PTFE, raised health and environmental concerns and has been phased out.

sections.key: Induction cooktops need magnetic pans, and a few well-chosen pieces beat a large matching set.
sections.b:
An induction cooktop does not heat a coil or flame. A rapidly changing magnetic field makes electric currents flow inside the pan's base, so the pan itself becomes the heat source. That works only with magnetic metals such as cast iron, carbon steel and many stainless steels. Plain aluminium, copper and glass will not work without a magnetic base. A quick test is whether a fridge magnet sticks firmly to the bottom.

When building a kitchen, a few good pieces usually beat a big boxed set. A heavy frying pan in cast iron or carbon steel, a non-stick pan for eggs, a clad stainless saucepan and a big pot for stock and pasta cover most cooking.

quiz.q: Why does a heavy pan help when you add a cold steak?
o: It conducts heat sideways faster than copper
It holds more heat, so it stays hot
It stops the steak from sticking
It reflects heat back into the food
quiz.e: A thick pan holds more energy, so cold food does not cool it much and you still get a good sear.

quiz.q: What is cast iron seasoning?
o: A mineral salt rubbed into the surface
Burnt food residue that builds up over time
A layer of oil baked into a hard coating
A factory-applied plastic film
quiz.e: Oil heated past its smoke point polymerises into a hard, slick coating, not grime.

quiz.q: Why are good stainless steel pans clad with aluminium or copper?
o: Stainless steel conducts heat poorly on its own
Stainless steel rusts quickly
Stainless steel is too light to hold heat
Stainless steel reacts with tomato
quiz.e: The aluminium or copper core spreads heat evenly through a pan that is otherwise a poor conductor.

quiz.q: What is the main safety risk with non-stick pans?
o: Small flakes of coating are toxic if swallowed
The coating dissolves in acidic foods
Cooking on medium heat damages the coating
An empty pan on high heat can release fumes
quiz.e: PTFE is stable at normal temperatures but breaks down above roughly 260 degrees Celsius.

quiz.q: How can you check if a pan will work on an induction cooktop?
o: See whether it is heavier than a kilogram
Check that it has a non-stick coating
Look for a copper base
Check that a magnet sticks to its base
quiz.e: Induction needs a magnetic base, and a magnet sticking firmly shows it has one.

LESSONS.push: Left empty on high, a non-stick pan can turn hazardous in minutes. Why?

LESSONS.title: Sugar: a sweet substance with a bitter past
LESSONS.hook: Sugar began as a rare spice and a medicine. Its rise to everyday sweetness was driven by slavery, wars and, in Queensland, a painful chapter of Australian history.

sections.key: Sugarcane, first domesticated in New Guinea, became a rare spice and medicine before Europe's supplies grew and it turned into an everyday staple.
sections.b:
Sugarcane is a giant grass first domesticated in New Guinea thousands of years ago. People chewed the stalks for their sweet juice. In India, they learned to boil the juice down into crystals, at least by the early centuries AD. The word sugar descends from the Sanskrit sharkara, and candy from khanda. Greek writers who met Alexander the Great's forces in India described a reed that made honey without bees.

Arab and Persian cultivators spread cane and refining across the Mediterranean, and to medieval Europeans sugar was a luxury used in medicine and feasts. That changed when Europeans grew cane on Atlantic islands such as Madeira, then in the Americas: Columbus took it to Hispaniola in 1493. Prices fell and demand soared, and in Britain sweetened tea became part of daily life.

sections.key: Sugar plantations ran on the enslavement of millions of Africans, and British consumers eventually boycotted slave-grown sugar.
sections.b:
Sugar was hard, dangerous work. Cane had to be crushed and boiled quickly after cutting, so mills and boiling houses ran around the clock. Brazil and then Caribbean islands such as Barbados and Jamaica became huge producers, and owners met their labour demand through the transatlantic slave trade. Millions of enslaved Africans were shipped to the Americas, many to sugar colonies where death rates were terrible. Historians see sugar as a central engine of the slave economy.

In the early 1790s, British pamphlets urged families to stop buying slave-grown sugar, and around 300,000 people took part. Women, who largely controlled household shopping but could not vote, were central. Britain abolished its slave trade in 1807 and slavery in most colonies from 1834. The boycott is an early example of ethical consumption.

sections.key: Sugar from beets is chemically identical to cane sugar, and war-time blockades turned beet sugar into a major industry.
sections.b:
In 1747 the German chemist Andreas Marggraf showed that sugar crystals from beets were identical to cane sugar. His student Franz Achard bred beets with more sugar and opened the first beet sugar factory in Silesia in 1801.

War made the difference. During the Napoleonic Wars, the British naval blockade cut France off from Caribbean cane sugar. Napoleon backed beet sugar with land grants, funding and decrees in the early 1810s, and factories sprang up. The industry survived the war, and a significant share of the world's sugar now comes from beets grown in cooler climates. Chemically, white sugar from cane and from beet is the same molecule: sucrose.

sections.key: Queensland's sugar industry relied on tens of thousands of Pacific Islander labourers, many tricked or forced into coming.
sections.b:
Sugar became a major Queensland industry from the 1860s. Planters wanted cheap labour for hot, punishing work, and between 1863 and 1904 around 60,000 people from Pacific islands, especially today's Vanuatu and Solomon Islands, were brought to Queensland under labour contracts. Some came willingly, but many were tricked, coerced or kidnapped, a practice known as blackbirding. Wages were low, conditions harsh and death rates high.

After Federation, the Pacific Island Labourers Act of 1901 led to the deportation of most Islanders, as part of the White Australia policy. Some stayed, and their descendants form the Australian South Sea Islander community, formally recognised by the Commonwealth in 1994. The cane toad was also introduced in 1935 to fight cane beetles.

sections.key: Sugar is not poison, but the World Health Organization advises keeping free sugars below 10 percent of daily energy.
sections.b:
Table sugar, sucrose, is one glucose and one fructose unit joined together, and your gut quickly splits it apart. Honey, maple syrup, coconut sugar and raw sugar are mostly the same simple sugars in slightly different proportions, with only trace amounts of anything else, so they are not much healthier.

The World Health Organization recommends keeping free sugars below 10 percent of daily energy, and suggests below 5 percent brings further benefits. Free sugars are those added to food, plus those in honey, syrups and juices. Sugars naturally inside whole fruit, milk and vegetables are not counted. Sugary drinks are the biggest single source for many people, and they are strongly linked to tooth decay and weight gain.

quiz.q: Why did sugar change from a rare luxury to an everyday staple in Europe?
o: More cane grown in the Americas lowered prices
Cheaper Asian imports arrived by overland routes
Sugar stopped being used in medicine and feasts
Arab traders began selling it more cheaply
quiz.e: As cane growing expanded in the Atlantic and Americas, prices fell and demand soared.

quiz.q: What did the British sugar boycott of the 1790s show?
o: Women could organise only through voting
Sugar could not be produced without slavery
Households could act by changing what they bought
Slavery ended in the colonies immediately
quiz.e: Households, especially women, used shopping choices to oppose slavery, an early form of ethical consumption.

quiz.q: Why did the Napoleonic Wars boost beet sugar?
o: Beet sugar was chemically better than cane
The British blockade cut France off from cane
Cane sugar was banned across Europe
Beets were easier to carry on ships
quiz.e: Cut off from cane, France backed beet sugar, and the industry outlasted the war.

quiz.q: What was blackbirding?
o: A law banning the burning of cane fields
A trade in tropical bird feathers
Tricking or forcing Pacific Islanders into labour
A tax on sugar sold in Queensland
quiz.e: Many Islanders brought to Queensland's cane fields were tricked, coerced or kidnapped.

quiz.q: Why are honey and raw sugar not much healthier than table sugar?
o: They contain more sucrose than cane sugar
They are mostly the same simple sugars
The World Health Organization does not count them
They are digested more slowly
quiz.e: These sweeteners are mostly the same sugars, and honey is counted as free sugar.

LESSONS.push: Sugar once sat with spices in a pharmacy. How did it become so common?

LESSONS.title: Escoffier: the chef who organised the kitchen
LESSONS.hook: Every time a cook answers ‘Yes, chef’, they echo one man. Auguste Escoffier turned chaotic kitchens into disciplined teams, and named a dessert after an Australian soprano.

sections.key: Before Escoffier, grand kitchens were hot, disorganised places where cooks duplicated work.
sections.b:
Georges Auguste Escoffier was born in 1846 in Villeneuve-Loubet, near Nice. At around thirteen he began an apprenticeship in his uncle's restaurant, then worked his way up through Paris kitchens. During the Franco-Prussian War of 1870 he cooked for the French army, an experience of feeding large numbers under pressure that many writers think shaped his ideas about organisation.

Kitchens of the time were brutal. Coal-fired ranges made them extremely hot, ventilation was poor and cooks often drank heavily through long shifts. One cook might spend hours making a whole dish while another did nearly the same beside him. Service à la russe, with courses brought out one after another, was replacing service à la française, with many dishes placed on the table together, and it demanded tighter timing.

sections.key: Escoffier organised kitchens into specialised stations in a clear chain of command, so complex dishes could be assembled in minutes.
sections.b:
Escoffier's lasting innovation was the brigade de cuisine, a kitchen run like a well-drilled team. At the top sits the chef de cuisine, with a sous chef second in command. Each station is led by a chef de partie: the saucier handles sauces and sautéed dishes, the rôtisseur roasts, the poissonnier cooks fish, the entremetier handles vegetables and soups, the garde manger prepares cold foods and the pâtissier makes pastry and desserts. Junior cooks, called commis, work under each leader.

Because stations prepare components in parallel, a complex dish can be assembled in minutes rather than hours. He also pushed for calmer behaviour, discouraging shouting, drinking and smoking on duty, and insisting on clean uniforms. The structure and its French titles are still used worldwide, including in Australia.

sections.key: Escoffier's partnership with hotelier César Ritz made dining out in elegant hotels fashionable, including for women.
sections.b:
In Monte Carlo, Escoffier met the Swiss hotelier César Ritz, and the two formed one of history's great hospitality partnerships. In 1890 they took charge of London's new Savoy Hotel, where Escoffier's cooking drew royalty, aristocrats and celebrities. They helped make dining in an elegant hotel restaurant fashionable, including for well-to-do women, who had been less likely to dine in public.

The Savoy partnership ended in 1898, when Ritz and Escoffier were dismissed amid a dispute with the owners over alleged financial irregularities. They moved on quickly. Ritz opened his famous Paris hotel that year, with Escoffier running the kitchen, and the pair then opened the Carlton Hotel in London, where Escoffier cooked for many years.

sections.key: Escoffier created Peach Melba to honour Australian soprano Nellie Melba, one of the great opera stars of her day.
sections.b:
Escoffier liked to name dishes after famous guests, and his best-known tribute was to an Australian. Nellie Melba, born Helen Porter Mitchell in Melbourne, took her stage name from her home city and became one of the most celebrated sopranos of her time. While she performed in London in the 1890s, Escoffier created a dessert in her honour: poached peaches served on vanilla ice cream.

An early presentation was reportedly served in a swan carved from ice, a nod to the opera Lohengrin. Raspberry sauce joined the classic recipe a few years later. Melba toast, crisp thin slices of dry toast, is also traditionally linked to the singer and Escoffier's kitchens.

sections.key: Escoffier's Le Guide Culinaire simplified French cooking into a system, and his kitchen model still runs restaurants today.
sections.b:
In 1903 Escoffier published Le Guide Culinaire, written with colleagues, which gathered thousands of recipes into a single reference still read by chefs. Marie-Antoine Carême had earlier grouped French sauces. Escoffier's system is usually summarised as five mother sauces: béchamel, velouté, espagnole, hollandaise and tomato. Learn these and you can make hundreds of variations. He also championed simplicity over towering decoration, his motto often given as "faites simple", focused on flavour rather than display.

He supported charities for retired cooks and worked to make cooking respected as a skilled career. He was later made a knight of the Legion of Honour and died in 1935, aged 88. His influence lives on in stations, titles and the call-and-response of "Yes, chef", and in the idea that a kitchen should run calmly, cleanly and on time.

quiz.q: What problem did Escoffier face in nineteenth century kitchens?
o: Too few cooks to prepare meals
Cooks unfamiliar with French recipes
Banned use of coal-fired stoves
Hot, chaotic kitchens with duplicated work
quiz.e: Work was loosely organised, so cooks overlapped and service suffered.

quiz.q: Why does the brigade system speed up service?
o: Stations prepare parts of a dish in parallel
One cook makes each dish from start to finish
Dishes are cooked ahead of time and then reheated
Customers choose from a much shorter menu
quiz.e: Specialised stations working at once turn hours of work into minutes.

quiz.q: What did Escoffier and Ritz help change about dining out?
o: They moved fine dining out of hotels
They made hotel dining fashionable, women included
They replaced restaurants with banquets
They made meals cheaper for ordinary people
quiz.e: Their Savoy partnership made hotel restaurants a stylish place for society to dine.

quiz.q: What is Peach Melba made of?
o: Raspberry sauce over toast
Poached peaches on vanilla ice cream
Peaches baked in pastry
Sugar-coated peaches in cream
quiz.e: Escoffier created the dessert of peaches on vanilla ice cream for the soprano Nellie Melba.

quiz.q: What is the idea behind the mother sauces?
o: A few base sauces can be varied into hundreds
Every dish needs its own separate sauce
Sauces should be left out of simple cooking
Each chef must invent their own signature sauce
quiz.e: Five base sauces can be varied with added ingredients to produce many others.

LESSONS.push: Why every kitchen shouts the same reply, and who put it there.

LESSONS.title: Kitchen myths, busted
LESSONS.hook: Searing seals in juices. Alcohol burns off. Oil stops pasta sticking. These ideas get passed from cook to cook, and many of them are simply wrong.

sections.key: Searing adds flavour but does not seal in juices; keeping meat juicy comes from not overcooking it.
sections.b:
The idea that searing ‘seals in the juices’ goes back to the German chemist Justus von Liebig in the mid-1800s and spread through cookbooks for a century. Experiments have repeatedly shown it is wrong. A seared crust is not waterproof, and seared meat loses about as much moisture as unseared meat cooked to the same internal temperature, sometimes more. The sizzle in the pan is moisture boiling away.

Searing is still worth doing, because the Maillard reaction creates deep browned flavour and appealing colour. What keeps meat juicy is not overcooking it, which is why a thermometer matters far more than a dramatic sear.

sections.key: A surprising share of alcohol can remain in cooked food, depending on time and method.
sections.b:
Many people believe all the alcohol in wine or spirits disappears as soon as a dish is heated. United States Department of Agriculture measurements show otherwise. When alcohol was added to a boiling liquid and removed from the heat, most of it remained. Flaming a dish left around three-quarters. After 15 minutes of simmering, about 40 percent was still there, and even after two and a half hours, around 5 percent remained.

Alcohol and water evaporate together, so it never vanishes all at once. The amounts per serve are usually small, but it matters for people who avoid alcohol completely for health, religious or recovery reasons, and for young children.

sections.key: Oil in pasta water does little, and salt gives flavour rather than faster boiling.
sections.b:
Pouring oil into pasta water ‘to stop it sticking’ does almost nothing. Oil and water do not mix, so the oil sits on the surface while the pasta tumbles below. Pasta sticks in the first couple of minutes, when surface starch turns gluey. Use plenty of water at a rolling boil and stir well early on. Oil that coats drained pasta can make sauce slide off. Save a cup of the starchy water instead, which helps sauces turn glossy.

Salt does not make water boil faster either. Dissolved salt slightly raises the boiling point, but at cooking amounts the change is a fraction of a degree. The burst of bubbles when salt hits hot water is crystals giving gases a place to form. The real reason to salt is flavour: food absorbs salt as it cooks, seasoning it from within.

sections.key: Microwaves heat only the outer centimetre or two of food, and quick microwaving often keeps vitamins well.
sections.b:
A popular belief says microwaves cook from the inside out. In fact they penetrate only a centimetre or two into most foods, making water molecules jiggle and generate heat. The centre of a large item warms as heat spreads inwards, just as in an oven, only from a thicker starting layer. That is why recipes include standing time to let heat even out, and why stirring and rotating help avoid cold spots, which matter for food safety when reheating.

Another myth is that microwaving destroys nutrients. Because cooking is quick and uses little water, microwaving vegetables often keeps water-soluble vitamins, such as vitamin C, as well as or better than boiling.

sections.key: Bacteria can transfer to dropped food in under a second, and frozen produce can be as nutritious as fresh.
sections.b:
The five-second rule claims food is safe if picked up quickly. In 2016, food scientist Donald Schaffner's team at Rutgers University contaminated surfaces including stainless steel, tile, wood and carpet with bacteria, then dropped watermelon, bread, buttered bread and gummy lollies. Transfer could happen in under a second. Longer contact meant more bacteria, but speed alone did not make food safe. Moisture mattered most: watermelon picked up the most, dry lollies the least. Carpet transferred fewer bacteria than tile or steel.

Fresh is not always better than frozen either. Fresh vegetables can spend days in transport and your fridge, losing vitamins. Frozen vegetables are blanched and frozen soon after harvest, and studies generally find similar nutrients. Frozen peas, berries and spinach are cheap and waste less, while fresh often wins on texture and taste.

quiz.q: What actually keeps a steak juicy?
o: Searing it first to seal the surface
Resting it in oil before cooking
Not overcooking it
Cooking it at the highest heat possible
quiz.e: Searing does not seal in juices, so avoiding overcooking is what matters.

quiz.q: What happens to alcohol when you simmer it in a dish?
o: Some remains, even after long cooking
It all evaporates within a few minutes
It turns into sugar as it heats
It stays at the same level however long you cook
quiz.e: Even after two and a half hours of simmering, around 5 percent of alcohol remained.

quiz.q: What is the real reason to salt pasta water?
o: It seasons the pasta as it cooks
It makes the water boil faster
It stops the pasta sticking
It stops the water boiling over
quiz.e: Salt raises the boiling point only slightly, so its job is seasoning from within.

quiz.q: Why do microwave recipes include standing time?
o: The food keeps cooking from the inside out
Heat spreads inwards from the outer layer and evens out
The microwaves keep working after the oven stops
The food needs to cool before it is safe to eat
quiz.e: Microwaves heat only the outer layer, and the centre warms as that heat spreads inwards.

quiz.q: What did the Rutgers study find about the five-second rule?
o: Dry foods are always safe if picked up quickly
Bacteria transfer only after several seconds
Carpet always transferred the most bacteria
Transfer takes under a second, and wet foods pick up most
quiz.e: Speed does not make dropped food safe; moisture mattered most.

LESSONS.push: Searing doesn't seal in juices. What does keep meat moist?

LESSONS.title: Pavlova, lamingtons and pies: Australia's food icons
LESSONS.hook: Who really invented the pavlova? Why can't you sell an ‘Anzac cookie’? The stories behind Australia's favourite foods are full of rivalries, legends and law.

sections.key: Pavlova and lamingtons are Australian icons whose true origins are disputed or unknown.
sections.b:
The pavlova is named after the Russian ballerina Anna Pavlova, who toured Australia and New Zealand in 1926 and 1929. Australians long credited Bert Sachse of Perth's Esplanade Hotel with creating it in 1935. But the New Zealand food historian Helen Leach found New Zealand recipes called pavlova from the late 1920s. She also found similar meringue cakes in Europe and the United States long before either country named one after a dancer. The friendly argument is unlikely ever to end.

The lamington is a sponge square dipped in chocolate icing and rolled in desiccated coconut. It is named after Lord Lamington, Governor of Queensland from 1896 to 1901. The popular story credits his French-born chef, Armand Galland, with inventing it to use up stale sponge, but historians cannot confirm it.

sections.key: The word Anzac is protected by Australian law, and Anzac biscuits may only be sold under strict conditions.
sections.b:
Anzac biscuits are made from rolled oats, flour, sugar, butter, golden syrup and usually desiccated coconut, with no eggs. They are linked to the First World War, but historians think oat biscuits were mainly baked and sold at home to raise money for the war effort, not standard soldiers' food. Troops were issued a notoriously hard ration biscuit, jokingly called an Anzac tile or wafer.

The name Anzac itself is protected under Australian law, and using it commercially needs approval from the Minister for Veterans' Affairs. Products may be sold as Anzac biscuits if they stick to the traditional recipe and shape. Calling them ‘Anzac cookies’ is not normally allowed, because of the American association.

sections.key: The hand-held meat pie arrived from Britain and became an Australian favourite, with regional variations such as the pie floater.
sections.b:
Australians are devoted to the meat pie: minced or chunky beef in gravy inside a pastry case, eaten by hand at football games, bakeries and service stations. The tradition came from Britain, but Australians made it their own, with brands, bakery competitions and fierce local loyalties.

Variations abound, including curry pies, steak and kidney, and the pie with tomato sauce on top. Adelaide is famous for the pie floater, a meat pie served upside down in a bowl of thick green pea soup, often topped with tomato sauce and once sold from late-night pie carts. Debates about the right pastry, gravy and filling still run hot, and many bakeries now offer gourmet and vegetarian versions.

sections.key: The Chiko Roll, dim sim and Tim Tam show Australian food borrowing from other cuisines and making something new.
sections.b:
In 1951 the Bendigo boilermaker Frank McEncroe launched the Chiko Roll at the Wagga Wagga Agricultural Show. Inspired by Chinese spring rolls, it wrapped cabbage, celery, barley, carrot, beef and seasonings in thick, deep-fried pastry, tough enough to eat on the move. The Australian dim sim, loosely based on Cantonese dumplings such as siu mai, is usually credited to Melbourne's Wing Lee restaurant in the 1940s. It is larger and meatier, steamed or deep fried, and often eaten with soy sauce.

In the 1950s, Arnott's food technologist Ian Norris came across Britain's Penguin biscuit overseas. In 1964 Arnott's launched the Tim Tam, named after the racehorse that won the 1958 Kentucky Derby. Fans invented the ‘Tim Tam slam’, using the biscuit as a straw for hot drinks.

sections.key: National foods usually have many borrowed roots and legendary origin stories; what makes them iconic is the pride people build around them.
sections.b:
Look closely at almost any national dish and you find borrowing. Meat pies came from Britain, pavlova from a long European meringue tradition, the Chiko Roll and dim sim from Chinese cooking, and the flat white from a cafe culture shaped by Italian and other migrants. Long before any of this, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples ate a rich range of native foods, an older story still.

Origin tales tend to be colourful and hard to verify: a chef inventing a cake for unexpected guests, a dessert created in one inspired moment. Historians who dig into old cookbooks and newspapers often find gradual change rather than one inventor. What makes a food iconic is less its birth than the memories, rituals and pride people build around it.

quiz.q: What does the evidence suggest about the pavlova's origin?
o: Earlier recipes exist in New Zealand and Europe
It was invented in Perth in 1935 and nowhere earlier
It was first made in Russia for the ballerina herself
It was created by a Queensland governor's chef
quiz.e: Earlier New Zealand recipes and older meringue cakes mean the Perth claim is not the whole story.

quiz.q: Why can't you normally sell ‘Anzac cookies’ in Australia?
o: The name is protected, and ‘cookie’ is American
Cookies cannot legally contain oats
The traditional recipe is a closely guarded secret
Cookies must be approved by the army before sale
quiz.e: Anzac biscuits may use the protected name only if they follow the traditional recipe and shape.

quiz.q: What is a pie floater?
o: A pie with a thick gravy topping
A meat pie served in thick green pea soup
A pie baked inside a loaf of bread
A pie cooked in boiling water
quiz.e: Adelaide's pie floater is served upside down in a bowl of pea soup, often topped with tomato sauce.

quiz.q: What do the Chiko Roll and dim sim show about Australian food?
o: They were copied exactly from overseas
They borrowed ideas and made them local
They were created by the army
They were designed to be eaten cold
quiz.e: Both took inspiration from Chinese food and became something distinctly Australian.

quiz.q: What usually makes a food an icon, according to the lesson?
o: A single inventor and a documented date
A secret recipe protected by strict law
The memories and pride people build around it
A famous chef serving it in fine restaurants
quiz.e: Foods become iconic through the meaning people give them, not because of a single origin.

LESSONS.push: Two countries claim the pavlova. The evidence may surprise both.

LESSONS.title: Cooking by degrees: the science of precise temperature
LESSONS.hook: A few degrees can turn silky meat into shoe leather. Understanding exactly what heat does to proteins explains sous vide, perfect eggs and why chefs swear by thermometers.

sections.key: Heat changes the shape of proteins, and each protein sets at its own temperature, often only a few degrees apart.
sections.b:
Proteins are long chains folded into specific shapes. Heat makes them vibrate until the weak bonds holding their shape give way. They unfold (denaturation), then tangle with their neighbours (coagulation). That is what turns runny egg white solid and translucent prawn flesh firm and opaque.

The crucial detail is that different proteins set at different temperatures. In an egg, ovotransferrin starts setting near 62 degrees, the yolk thickens around 65, and ovalbumin needs close to 80. Hold an egg at 63 to 65 degrees for about an hour and you get a custard-like yolk and a barely set white, as in Japanese onsen tamago, cooked in hot springs. Boiling water at 100 degrees overshoots everything.

sections.key: Meat firms as its proteins set, dries out as they squeeze out juice, and turns tender only as collagen melts into gelatine.
sections.b:
Meat is mostly water held inside muscle proteins and wrapped in connective tissue made largely of collagen. The muscle protein myosin begins to set at around 50 degrees, so the meat firms but stays juicy. That is roughly the rare range.

Through the 60s, other proteins, including actin at about 66 degrees or above, contract and squeeze out moisture, and the meat turns noticeably drier. Collagen behaves differently. It shrinks at around 60 degrees, but given enough time at higher temperatures it slowly breaks down into gelatine. That gives braised meat its silky, falling-apart texture. Hence the cook's dilemma: tender cuts want low temperatures, while tough, collagen-rich cuts need long cooking.

sections.key: Sous vide cooks sealed food in water held at the exact target temperature, so it cannot overcook the usual way.
sections.b:
Sous vide is French for 'under vacuum'. Food is sealed in a bag and cooked in a water bath held at an exact temperature. Its culinary use is usually traced to 1974, when chef Georges Pralus used it for foie gras, which lost far less fat under gentle heat. Food scientist Bruno Goussault later trained chefs in it. Home circulators became affordable in the 2010s.

Water carries heat much faster than air, which is why you can briefly put a hand in a 200 degree oven but not in boiling water. Set the bath to 56 degrees for medium-rare steak and the food can never get hotter. It cooks evenly from edge to centre, with no grey band. Cooks then add a quick, hot sear for browning.

sections.key: Bacteria die according to both temperature and time, so a lower temperature held longer can be as effective as a brief higher one.
sections.b:
Food safety guidance usually gives one number, such as cooking poultry until the centre reaches 75 degrees, which kills bacteria like Salmonella almost instantly. But bacterial death really depends on temperature and time together. At lower temperatures bacteria still die, just more slowly.

Food scientists have published tables showing that holding food at a lower temperature for long enough achieves the same reduction as a brief moment at a higher one. That is how sous vide cooks can safely serve juicier chicken. These methods need accurate equipment, correct holding times and an understanding of the science. For everyday home cooking, follow the official temperature guidance and check with a probe thermometer.

sections.key: Low temperature cooking carries real food safety risks, and a probe thermometer is the simplest tool for cooking precisely.
sections.b:
Precise low temperature cooking has risks that conventional cooking avoids. In a sealed, airless bag, bacteria that thrive without oxygen, such as Clostridium botulinum, can become a hazard if food is held too long at too low a temperature or cooled slowly afterwards. Cooking below about 55 degrees for long periods is particularly risky. Eat cooked food promptly, or chill it quickly in iced water and refrigerate it.

Pregnant people, young children, older adults and those with weakened immunity are generally advised to avoid lightly cooked meat, fish and eggs. For any cook, the best tool is a probe thermometer. Once you know the internal temperature, you are no longer guessing, and dry chicken and overcooked steak become far rarer.

quiz.q: Why does an egg held at about 64 degrees have a custardy yolk and a soft white?
o: Each protein sets at its own temperature
The shell blocks most of the heat
Low heat draws water out of the yolk
The white contains no protein to set
quiz.e: Some white proteins and the yolk set around 62 to 65 degrees, while ovalbumin needs nearer 80.

quiz.q: Why do tough, collagen-rich cuts need long, slow cooking?
o: Myosin needs several hours of heat to set
Collagen turns to gelatine only after hours of heat
Long cooking adds moisture to the meat
Collagen is a fat that must melt out
quiz.e: Collagen slowly turns to gelatine, which gives braises their silky, tender texture.

quiz.q: Why can't food overcook in a sous vide bath in the usual sense?
o: The vacuum bag stops heat reaching the edges
Food cooks from the inside out as the bath circulates
The bath is set to the target, so food cannot get hotter
Ice is added to the water as the food cooks
quiz.e: The bath is held at the target temperature, so the whole piece reaches that doneness and no further.

quiz.q: How can a lower cooking temperature still make food safe?
o: Bacteria cannot survive in a vacuum bag
Low temperatures make bacteria harmless
Only a temperature of 100 degrees ever kills bacteria
A longer hold kills as many bacteria as brief high heat
quiz.e: Bacterial death depends on time and temperature together, so lower temperatures need longer holding times.

quiz.q: What is the most practical way for a home cook to cook precisely and safely?
o: Check with a probe thermometer
Cook by timing alone at a low heat
Taste the food as it cooks
Judge doneness by colour
quiz.e: A probe thermometer takes the guesswork out, avoiding both dry food and unsafe undercooking.

LESSONS.push: A few degrees turn a silky egg yolk into chalk. Find out why.

LESSONS.title: 1816: the year without a summer
LESSONS.hook: A mountain in Indonesia blew itself apart, and a year later it snowed in New England in June. Here is how one eruption chilled half the world.

sections.key: In April 1815 Mount Tambora in Indonesia produced the largest eruption in recorded history.
sections.b:
Mount Tambora sits on Sumbawa, in what is now Indonesia. After days of rumbling, it exploded with enormous force around 10 and 11 April 1815. The blasts were heard more than 2,000 kilometres away, and some colonial officials reportedly mistook them for cannon fire and sent troops to investigate.

Ash and rock rose into the stratosphere, and glowing avalanches of hot gas and debris swept down the slopes. The mountain lost well over a kilometre of height, leaving a caldera about six kilometres wide. Volcanologists rate it a 7 on the Volcanic Explosivity Index, a level reached only a handful of times in the past few thousand years.

sections.key: The eruption and the famine that followed killed tens of thousands of people.
sections.b:
The eruption itself killed many thousands of people on Sumbawa, buried under ash or caught by scorching flows. The larger toll came afterwards. Ash smothered crops and fouled water across Sumbawa and neighbouring Lombok, and livestock died in great numbers. Starvation and disease followed for months.

Exact numbers are impossible to know because regional records were patchy. Estimates of the total death toll commonly run to tens of thousands, and some researchers argue it was higher. The small kingdom of Tambora, its people and language, was largely wiped out. Archaeologists later found houses, pottery and human remains under the ash, earning the site the nickname 'Pompeii of the East'.

sections.key: Sulphur gas, not ash, cooled the planet, by forming a haze high in the stratosphere that reflected sunlight.
sections.b:
Ash falls out of the air within days or weeks, so it was not ash that changed the world's weather. The real culprit was sulphur dioxide. Tambora blasted huge amounts of it into the stratosphere, more than ten kilometres up, where there is no rain to wash it out.

There it reacted with water to form tiny droplets of sulphuric acid, called sulphate aerosols. Winds spread this haze around the globe over the following months. The droplets reflected some incoming sunlight back into space, so less warmth reached the ground. Global average temperatures dropped by somewhere around half a degree. That sounds small, but it was enough to upset growing seasons across the Northern Hemisphere for a year or more.

sections.key: In 1816 summer frosts and cold rain ruined harvests in North America and Europe, and no one knew why.
sections.b:
In New England and eastern Canada, snow fell in early June, and killing frosts returned in July and August, destroying corn and other crops. Farmers who replanted several times watched each attempt fail.

In western Europe the summer was cold and relentlessly wet. Harvests failed across Britain, Ireland, France and the German lands, grain prices soared and food riots broke out in several countries. Switzerland suffered severe hunger, and 1816 is remembered as one of its worst years in modern times. Typhus spread through a weakened Irish population. Many New England families gave up their rocky farms and moved west. People at the time had no idea why the weather had turned so savage.

The cold also had an unexpected literary legacy.

sections.key: Ice cores later linked Tambora to the cold of 1816, though the full story also involved an earlier eruption and a quiet Sun.
sections.b:
In June 1816 a group of English writers, including Lord Byron, Percy Shelley and Mary Godwin (soon to be Mary Shelley), holidayed beside Lake Geneva. Endless rain kept them indoors, so Byron proposed a ghost story contest. Mary's idea became Frankenstein; Byron's doctor, John Polidori, wrote The Vampyre.

For a long time the cold itself was a puzzle. In the early twentieth century William Humphreys argued that volcanic dust and gases could cool the climate. Ice cores from Greenland and Antarctica later clinched it, showing a sharp sulphate spike in layers from about 1815 and 1816. But another large eruption, still unidentified, occurred around 1808 or 1809, and the Sun was quiet, so Tambora struck an already cool world.

quiz.q: How do volcanologists rate Tambora's 1815 eruption on the Volcanic Explosivity Index?
o: A 5, like Mount St Helens in 1980
A 6, like Pinatubo in 1991
A 7, a rarity in recent millennia
An 8, the top of the scale
quiz.e: Tambora rates a 7, among the largest eruptions of the past few thousand years.

quiz.q: Why is the true death toll from Tambora hard to know?
o: Records were patchy, and famine caused most deaths
The eruption killed no one directly
Everyone on the island survived and later moved
The deaths were never connected to the eruption
quiz.e: The larger toll came from starvation and disease, and records were patchy, so estimates run to tens of thousands or more.

quiz.q: What actually cooled the climate after Tambora erupted?
o: Ash blocking sunlight for several years
Steam from the eruption forming thick clouds
Sulphate droplets reflecting sunlight
Lava cooling the surrounding ocean
quiz.e: Sulphur dioxide reached the stratosphere and formed aerosols that reflected sunlight, whereas ash falls out within days or weeks.

quiz.q: What happened in New England in 1816?
o: Record drought and heat ruined the crops
June snow, then frosts in July and August
The summer was normal but winter was harsh
Floods washed away the farms
quiz.e: Cold and frost destroyed crops in North America, while western Europe had a cold, wet summer and failed harvests.

quiz.q: What does the evidence in ice cores show about the cold years?
o: Layers of volcanic glass from Indonesia
Unusually thick annual snow layers
Trapped bubbles of volcanic steam
A sulphate spike in layers from 1815 and 1816
quiz.e: Sulphate from the eruption fell as acid snow at both poles, leaving a chemical fingerprint in the ice.

LESSONS.push: A volcano in Indonesia once brought June snow to New England. How?

LESSONS.title: Reading the clouds
LESSONS.hook: Every cloud has a name, and most have a message about the weather to come. A young pharmacist worked out how to read them over two hundred years ago.

sections.key: Luke Howard's simple Latin cloud names, proposed in 1802, are still the basis of cloud naming today.
sections.b:
Before the early 1800s, clouds were thought too fleeting to classify.
