Then English pharmacist and amateur weather watcher Luke Howard gave a talk in London in 1802, published the next year, called On the Modifications of Clouds. Borrowing from naturalists who sorted plants and animals into families, he proposed a few Latin names. Cirrus is a curl or wisp of hair. Cumulus is a heap. Stratus is a layer or sheet. Nimbus refers to rain.

They could be combined, so a heaped rain cloud became cumulonimbus. The scheme was so clear that it spread across Europe, and the writer Goethe admired Howard enough to write poems in his honour.

sections.key: Clouds form when rising air cools until its water vapour condenses onto tiny particles, then stays aloft because the droplets are so small.
sections.b:
Air always holds some invisible water vapour, and warm air holds more. When air rises, the pressure drops, so it expands and cools. At its dew point it can no longer hold all its vapour, and the excess condenses into droplets or ice crystals around microscopic specks of sea salt, dust, smoke and pollen. Air can be forced up by the Sun heating the ground, wind pushing it over mountains, or cold air sliding under warm.

A small fair weather cumulus about a kilometre across holds roughly 500 tonnes of water, about a hundred elephants. It floats because that weight is spread over billions of tiny droplets, which fall so slowly that gentle updrafts hold them up.

sections.key: Clouds are grouped by height and by whether they spread in sheets or pile up in heaps.
sections.b:
The World Meteorological Organization's International Cloud Atlas recognises ten main cloud types, grouped by height. High clouds, roughly five kilometres up or more, are made of ice crystals: wispy cirrus, patchy cirrocumulus and milky cirrostratus.

Middle clouds take the prefix alto. Altocumulus forms rows of puffy patches, and altostratus is a grey veil through which the Sun looks like a smudged coin. Low clouds include stratus, a flat grey blanket that can sit on hilltops as fog, stratocumulus in lumpy layers, and nimbostratus, the thick, dark sheet behind a long day of steady rain. Cumulus and cumulonimbus are special because they can stretch from low levels to great heights.

sections.key: Cumulonimbus is the thunderstorm cloud, towering more than ten kilometres high and flattening into an anvil at the top.
sections.b:
On a hot, humid afternoon, a small cumulus can keep growing as warm, moist air surges upwards inside it. Condensing vapour releases heat, which makes the air rise even faster. A towering cloud like this is cumulus congestus. If it keeps going, it becomes a cumulonimbus, whose top can reach twelve kilometres or more, and higher in the tropics.

When the rising air hits the stable layer at the base of the stratosphere, it cannot rise further and spreads sideways into a flat anvil. Inside, strong updrafts and downdrafts toss raindrops and ice about, building hail and separating electrical charges. Cumulonimbus brings downpours, damaging winds, lightning and, occasionally, tornadoes.

sections.key: Watching how clouds change over a few hours can tell you what weather is coming.
sections.b:
Clouds are not perfect forecasters, but their patterns carry real information. High cirrus streaks that thicken into a pale sheet of cirrostratus, sometimes with a halo around the Sun or Moon, often mean a warm front and its rain are approaching within a day or so. Small, flat-topped cumulus on a sunny morning suggest a settled day, but cumulus that swell into tall, cauliflower towers by midday warn of afternoon storms. Lens-shaped lenticular clouds near mountains signal strong winds aloft.

Clouds still hold surprises. In 2017 the Atlas added asperitas, a dramatic, wave-like underside first championed by members of the public in the Cloud Appreciation Society.

quiz.q: What does the cloud name 'cumulus' mean?
o: Layer or sheet
Rain
Curl of hair
Heap
quiz.e: Cumulus is Latin for heap, for puffy, piled-up clouds. Stratus means layer and cirrus a curl of hair.

quiz.q: Why does a cloud holding hundreds of tonnes of water not fall?
o: Clouds are made of steam, which is lighter than air
The Earth's magnetic field supports them
It is spread over billions of tiny droplets
Clouds are hollow, like balloons
quiz.e: Each droplet is minute, so it sinks extremely slowly and gentle updrafts keep it aloft.

quiz.q: How are the ten main cloud types mainly grouped?
o: By their colour and brightness
By height, and by sheet or heap shape
By the season they appear in
By how much rain they hold
quiz.e: High, middle and low clouds are further described as layered (stratus) or heaped (cumulus).

quiz.q: What causes the flat 'anvil' top of a thunderstorm cloud?
o: Strong upper winds slicing off the top of the cloud
Ice crystals melting and collapsing at the top
Rising air meets the stable stratosphere and spreads out
The cloud cooling quickly after sunset
quiz.e: Updrafts cannot push far into the stable stratosphere, so the cloud spreads out into an anvil.

quiz.q: What does thin cirrus thickening into cirrostratus, perhaps with a halo, often signal?
o: A week of settled, fine weather
A warm front and rain approaching
A sudden cold snap with frost
Snow within the next hour
quiz.e: Thickening high cloud is a classic sign that a warm front and its rain are on the way, often within a day or so.

LESSONS.push: A fluffy cloud can weigh as much as a hundred elephants. Why doesn't it fall?

LESSONS.title: Tornadoes: the most violent winds on Earth
LESSONS.hook: Tornadoes produce the fastest winds measured near the ground, yet they are small, brief and still not fully understood. Here is what we do know.

sections.key: A tornado is a violently rotating column of air from a storm cloud to the ground, and the strongest come from supercells.
sections.b:
A tornado is a column of rapidly spinning air touching both the ground and the base of a thunderstorm. Many show as a funnel because falling pressure condenses moisture and dust thickens the shape. Most last a few minutes and travel a few kilometres, but a few become monsters, hundreds of metres wide and tens of kilometres long.

The powerful ones form in supercells. Warm, moist air near the ground, cooler, drier air above, a lifting trigger and wind shear (winds changing speed and direction with height) set the lower atmosphere rolling horizontally. A strong updraft tilts that roll upright, so the updraft rotates. This broad column is a mesocyclone. Why only some supercells produce tornadoes is still being researched.

sections.key: The United States has more tornadoes than anywhere else because contrasting air masses collide over its flat central plains.
sections.b:
The United States records on the order of a thousand or more tornadoes in a typical year, far more than any other country. Warm, humid air flows north from the Gulf of Mexico, dry air descends from the Rockies and south west deserts, and cold air sweeps down from Canada. They meet over flat plains, with no east to west mountain range to keep them apart.

The region from Texas to South Dakota is nicknamed Tornado Alley, and the south east sees many deadly tornadoes too. The Tri-State Tornado of 1925 killed nearly 700 people across Missouri, Illinois and Indiana. Bangladesh, however, suffered the deadliest tornado on record, in 1989.

sections.key: Tornadoes are rated by the damage they cause, because their winds are rarely measured directly.
sections.b:
Ordinary instruments are usually destroyed by a tornado, or simply not in the right place. In 1971 the meteorologist Ted Fujita created a scale that estimated wind speed from the damage left behind. The United States replaced it in 2007 with the Enhanced Fujita scale, which runs from EF0, peeling shingles and breaking branches, to EF5, where well built houses are swept off their foundations. EF5 winds are estimated at over 320 kilometres per hour.

Portable Doppler radar has since let scientists chase storms and measure winds inside them. During the Oklahoma outbreak of May 1999, a truck-mounted radar recorded winds of around 480 kilometres per hour, among the highest ever measured on Earth.

sections.key: Australia gets tornadoes too, usually weaker than in America, and the outback willy-willy is a different thing.
sections.b:
Many Australians are surprised to learn tornadoes happen here. They are reported every year, most often in the south west of Western Australia, along the eastern seaboard and in parts of inland New South Wales and Queensland, and some are spawned by tropical cyclones coming ashore. Most are short-lived and weak, but destructive ones occur, such as the tornado that tore through Bucca in Queensland in 1992.

A common confusion is worth clearing up. The 'willy-willy' of outback folklore is usually a dust devil, a spinning column of air that forms on hot, clear days from heated ground, not from a storm. Dust devils are mostly harmless curiosities, while true tornadoes need a thunderstorm overhead.

sections.key: Shelter low, inside and away from windows; opening windows to equalise pressure is a myth.
sections.b:
Take warnings seriously. In Australia, follow the Bureau of Meteorology's severe thunderstorm warnings, and call 000 in a life-threatening emergency. If a tornado approaches, go to the lowest floor of a sturdy building and into a small interior room, such as a bathroom or hallway, with as many walls as possible between you and the outside. Stay away from windows, and cover your head and neck. Cars and caravans offer poor protection.

One old myth deserves retiring. People were once told to open windows so the house would not explode from low pressure. In fact, houses are destroyed by wind and flying debris, and time spent opening windows is time not spent sheltering.

quiz.q: What is a mesocyclone?
o: A small tornado over water
A cyclone that forms in the mid-latitudes
The calm eye of a tornado
A rotating updraft in a supercell storm
quiz.e: Wind shear tilted upright by a strong updraft makes the updraft rotate, and strong tornadoes can form beneath it.

quiz.q: Why does the central United States get so many tornadoes?
o: It has the hottest summers on Earth
It lies on a tectonic plate boundary
Contrasting air masses meet over flat plains
Its forests channel the wind
quiz.e: Humid Gulf air, dry western air and cold Canadian air collide over the plains, ideal for supercells.

quiz.q: How is a tornado's Enhanced Fujita rating usually decided?
o: By the damage it causes
By measuring its funnel width
By counting how long it lasts
By the colour of the funnel
quiz.e: Winds are rarely measured directly, so ratings are estimated from the damage left behind.

quiz.q: What is the outback 'willy-willy' usually?
o: A small tornado from a thunderstorm
A tropical cyclone in miniature
A dust devil formed over hot ground
A type of thunderstorm cloud
quiz.e: Willy-willies are usually dust devils, which form on hot, clear days. True tornadoes need a thunderstorm above.

quiz.q: Why should you not open windows when a tornado approaches?
o: It lets the tornado come inside the house
It makes the tornado grow stronger
It increases the risk of lightning strikes
Pressure is not the danger; wind and debris are
quiz.e: The pressure idea is a myth. Get to a small interior room on the lowest floor, away from windows.

LESSONS.push: The fastest winds ever measured near the ground are brief and tiny. Here's why.

LESSONS.title: Antarctica: the continent of extremes
LESSONS.hook: The coldest, windiest, highest and driest continent holds most of the world's ice, and lakes hidden kilometres beneath it.

sections.key: Antarctica is almost twice the size of Australia and holds about 90 per cent of the world's ice.
sections.b:
Antarctica covers about 14 million square kilometres, nearly twice the area of Australia. Almost all of it lies under an ice sheet averaging around two kilometres thick, and more than four kilometres deep in places. That ice holds roughly 90 per cent of all the ice on Earth and about 70 per cent of its fresh water. If it all melted, which would take many thousands of years, global sea levels would rise by close to 60 metres.

The ice is so heavy it presses the land beneath it downward, yet the ice sheet's thickness gives Antarctica the highest average elevation of any continent. Beneath it lie mountain ranges, valleys and even volcanoes.

sections.key: Antarctica holds the record for the lowest air temperature, and its interior is a desert with very little snowfall.
sections.b:
On 21 July 1983, at Russia's Vostok Station on the high East Antarctic plateau, thermometers recorded -89.2 degrees Celsius, the coldest air temperature ever measured directly. Satellites have since detected snow surfaces below -90 degrees. Antarctica is colder than the Arctic because it is a high landmass rather than a frozen ocean, its white surface reflects most sunlight, and for months each winter the Sun does not rise over much of it.

Cold air holds little moisture, so the interior receives only a few centimetres of water equivalent a year. It counts as a desert. The ice built up because almost nothing melts. The McMurdo Dry Valleys, largely free of ice and snow, are used to test equipment and ideas for exploring Mars.

sections.key: Cold, heavy air flowing downhill off the ice plateau creates some of the strongest winds on the planet.
sections.b:
Antarctica's interior is a vast dome of ice, and the air above it becomes intensely cold and dense. Gravity pulls this heavy air downhill towards the coast, where it can accelerate into ferocious katabatic winds, from a Greek word meaning going down. Some coastal places are battered almost constantly.

The Australian geologist Douglas Mawson found this out during his Australasian Antarctic Expedition of 1911 to 1914. His base at Cape Denison in Commonwealth Bay was so wind-lashed that he titled his account The Home of the Blizzard. Expedition members learned to walk bent almost horizontally into the gusts. The same expedition saw Mawson's harrowing solo trek back to base after both his companions died.

sections.key: The Antarctic Treaty of 1959 set the continent aside for peace and science, and its claims are effectively frozen.
sections.b:
Seven countries, including Australia, claim parts of Antarctica. Australia's claim, the Australian Antarctic Territory, is the largest at about 42 per cent of the continent. Yet these claims are effectively frozen.

In 1959, at the height of the Cold War, twelve nations signed the Antarctic Treaty, which came into force in 1961. It bans military activity and nuclear explosions, guarantees freedom of scientific research and requires countries to share their findings. The Madrid Protocol of 1991 later banned mining and set strict environmental rules. More than fifty countries have now joined. Australia runs three permanent research stations on the continent, Casey, Davis and Mawson, and a fourth on sub-Antarctic Macquarie Island.

sections.key: Hundreds of liquid lakes lie beneath the ice, and the largest permanent land animal is a tiny wingless midge.
sections.b:
Liquid water lies far beneath the ice. Radar surveys have found hundreds of subglacial lakes, kept from freezing by the insulating ice above and by heat rising from the Earth below. The largest known, Lake Vostok, lies under about four kilometres of ice, which Russian drillers reached in 2012. Some lakes are linked by rivers flowing under the ice sheet.

On the surface, life clings mostly to the coasts. Penguins, seals and seabirds feed in the rich surrounding ocean, and emperor penguins breed through the dark winter on the sea ice. There are no native land mammals. The largest animal living permanently on land is a wingless midge only a few millimetres long.

quiz.q: Roughly how far would sea levels rise if all of Antarctica's ice melted?
o: About 6 metres
About 600 metres
About 60 metres
About 2 metres
quiz.e: The ice sheet holds enough water to raise sea levels by close to 60 metres, though melting would take many thousands of years.

quiz.q: Why is Antarctica colder than the Arctic?
o: It is a high landmass, not a frozen ocean
It is farther from the Sun than the Arctic
It has more volcanoes cooling the air
It spins faster than the North Pole
quiz.e: The Arctic is an ocean warmed slightly by the sea beneath, while Antarctica is a high, reflective continent.

quiz.q: What are katabatic winds?
o: Warm winds blowing in from the ocean
Winds caused by the Earth's rotation alone
Gusts produced by melting icebergs
Cold, dense air flowing downhill off the ice
quiz.e: Katabatic means going down. Heavy cold air drains off the high interior towards the coast, sometimes at great speed.

quiz.q: What does the Antarctic Treaty system do?
o: Divides Antarctica equally among all nations
Bans military activity and protects science
Gives Australia full ownership of the continent
Allows oil drilling with a permit
quiz.e: The 1959 treaty bans military activity and guarantees scientific freedom, and the 1991 Madrid Protocol bans mining.

quiz.q: What is the largest animal living permanently on land in Antarctica?
o: The emperor penguin
The leopard seal
The Weddell seal
A tiny wingless midge
quiz.e: Penguins and seals depend on the sea. The largest true land-dweller is a tiny flightless midge.

LESSONS.push: The coldest continent is also a desert. Why so little snow?

LESSONS.title: Everest: the roof of the world
LESSONS.hook: The highest mountain on Earth is still rising, and its summit is made of rock that formed at the bottom of an ancient sea.

sections.key: Everest's official height is 8,848.86 metres, agreed by Nepal and China in 2020, and the air there holds about a third of the oxygen at sea level.
sections.b:
Mount Everest sits on the border between Nepal and the Tibet region of China. Measuring it has always been tricky, partly because its snow cap changes depth, and partly because the two countries used different methods and quoted slightly different figures for decades. In December 2020 they jointly announced a new official height of 8,848.86 metres, based on satellite positioning and surveyors carrying equipment to the summit.

At that height the air pressure is only about a third of that at sea level, so each breath delivers far less oxygen. Above about 8,000 metres lies what climbers call the death zone, where the body slowly deteriorates and cannot acclimatise.

sections.key: Everest's summit rock formed on an ancient sea floor and was pushed skyward when India collided with Asia.
sections.b:
The top of Everest is limestone that formed hundreds of millions of years ago on the floor of a shallow sea. Geologists have found fossils of marine creatures such as trilobites and crinoids (sea lilies) in it. How did a seabed end up nearly nine kilometres in the sky?

The answer is plate tectonics. India was once a separate landmass drifting north across the Tethys Ocean. When it collided with Asia, sediments from the ocean floor were crumpled, stacked and pushed upwards. The Himalaya are the result of that crash, which began around 50 million years ago, though geologists debate the exact timing. India still pushes north by a few centimetres every year.

sections.key: The Himalaya are pushed up a few millimetres a year while erosion wears them down, so their height is a constant tug of war.
sections.b:
The collision has not stopped. Precise satellite measurements show parts of the Himalaya rising by a few millimetres each year. At the same time, ice, landslides, rivers and frost shatter the rock and carry it away, so the height we see is a constant tug of war between uplift and erosion.

Earthquakes are part of the same process. The devastating Nepal earthquake of April 2015 was caused by the Indian plate sliding beneath Asia. It also shifted the land around Everest slightly, one reason the mountain was measured again a few years later.

sections.key: Everest was named after a surveyor who reportedly objected, and was first climbed on 29 May 1953 by Hillary and Tenzing.
sections.b:
The mountain has local names: Chomolungma in Tibetan, often translated as goddess mother of the world, and Sagarmatha in Nepali. British surveyors called it Peak XV until calculations around 1852, in which Radhanath Sikdar is often credited with a key role, showed it to be the highest on Earth. Surveyor General Andrew Waugh proposed naming it after his predecessor, Sir George Everest, who reportedly objected that locals could not easily write or say it. The name was adopted in 1865 anyway.

In 1924 George Mallory and Andrew Irvine vanished near the top, and whether they summited is unknown. On 29 May 1953, Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay stood on the summit. Hundreds have died trying since.

sections.key: Mauna Kea is taller from base to peak and Chimborazo's summit is farthest from Earth's centre, so which is biggest depends on the question.
sections.b:
Everest's summit is the highest point above sea level, but there are other ways to measure a mountain. Mauna Kea in Hawaii rises about 4,200 metres above the sea, yet most of the volcano is underwater. Measured from its base on the ocean floor, it stands around 10,000 metres, taller than Everest.

Then there is Chimborazo, a volcano in Ecuador only about 6,260 metres above sea level. Because the Earth spins, it bulges slightly at the equator, and Chimborazo sits near the top of that bulge. Its summit is therefore the point on Earth's surface farthest from the planet's centre, roughly two kilometres farther out than Everest's. Which mountain is biggest depends on the question you ask.

quiz.q: Why does each breath deliver so little oxygen near Everest's summit?
o: The air contains no oxygen above 8,000 metres
Air pressure there is about a third of sea level
Snow and ice absorb the oxygen around climbers
Climbers breathe more slowly in the cold
quiz.e: Low air pressure means each breath carries far less oxygen, which is why the death zone is so punishing.

quiz.q: Why are there marine fossils near the summit of Everest?
o: Floods carried them up from the lowlands
Sea levels were once nine kilometres higher
It formed on the seabed and was uplifted
Glaciers dragged them up from the coast
quiz.e: The summit limestone formed in the Tethys Ocean, and the India-Asia collision lifted it into the sky.

quiz.q: What is happening to the height of the Himalaya today?
o: They are sinking under their own weight
They still rise slowly as erosion wears them
They stopped changing millions of years ago
They are rising by several metres a year
quiz.e: India still pushes into Asia, lifting the range slowly, while erosion constantly removes rock.

quiz.q: What is still unknown about the 1924 attempt on Everest?
o: Which country sponsored the expedition
Whether Mallory and Irvine reached the top
Whether the mountain had been surveyed
Which route they took up the mountain
quiz.e: Mallory and Irvine vanished high on the mountain, and the camera that might settle it has never been found.

quiz.q: Why is Chimborazo's summit farther from Earth's centre than Everest's?
o: It is taller above sea level than Everest
It is a volcano that is still growing
It is near the equator, where Earth bulges
It stands on a base far below sea level
quiz.e: The spinning Earth bulges at the equator, so Chimborazo's summit is the farthest point from the planet's centre.

LESSONS.push: The summit of Everest is made of seabed. Here's how it got there.

LESSONS.title: Kati Thanda–Lake Eyre: Australia's sometimes sea
LESSONS.hook: For most of its life it is a blinding sheet of salt. Then, every so often, distant floods turn it into Australia's largest lake and birds arrive from hundreds of kilometres away.

sections.key: Kati Thanda-Lake Eyre lies about 15 metres below sea level in outback South Australia and is usually a dry salt crust.
sections.b:
In the arid north of South Australia lies Kati Thanda-Lake Eyre, the lowest natural point on the Australian continent, about 15 metres below sea level. Kati Thanda comes from the Arabana people, the traditional owners, for whom the lake holds deep cultural significance. The dual name was formally adopted in 2012. Lake Eyre honours the English-born explorer Edward John Eyre, who saw parts of it in 1840.

Most of the time the lake is dry, a vast flat crust of salt that glares white under the sun. It has two main parts, Lake Eyre North, much the larger, and Lake Eyre South, joined by a narrow channel.

sections.key: The lake sits at the bottom of one of the world's largest internally draining basins, where no water ever reaches the sea.
sections.b:
Water flows downhill, and in central Australia much of it flows towards Kati Thanda. Its catchment, the Lake Eyre Basin, covers about 1.2 million square kilometres, roughly one sixth of Australia, across parts of Queensland, the Northern Territory, South Australia and New South Wales.

It is one of the largest internally draining basins in the world, meaning none of its water ever reaches the sea. Rivers such as the Diamantina, the Georgina and Cooper Creek wander slowly across a vast, flat landscape known as the Channel Country. Floodwater can take months to travel from Queensland to the lake, and most of it evaporates or soaks into the ground on the way.

sections.key: The lake fills close to capacity only a few times a century, and even then it is shallow and turns saltier as it spreads.
sections.b:
The basin is so dry and evaporation so intense that it takes exceptional rain to deliver serious water to Kati Thanda. Small floods reach the lake fairly often, and a significant filling happens only every several years. Filling close to capacity happens only a few times in a century. The great floods of the 1950s and 1974 were among the biggest on record.

When full, it is the largest lake in Australia, covering around 9,500 square kilometres. Even then it is mostly just a few metres deep. As the water spreads over the salt crust, it dissolves salt and turns saltier, and the shallow water can glow pink from salt-loving algae and microbes.

sections.key: Floods trigger a boom of shrimp, fish and waterbirds, but breeding is a race against the shrinking, saltier lake.
sections.b:
When water arrives, the desert erupts with life. Eggs of tiny crustaceans such as brine shrimp, dormant in the dry mud, hatch within days. Fish washed down the rivers multiply in the fresher water. Then the birds come. Pelicans, silver gulls, terns, ducks and other waterbirds arrive in huge numbers, many to breed on islands in the lake.

Australian pelicans appear to fly hundreds of kilometres from the coast, and exactly how they detect that the lake has filled remains a mystery. Breeding is a race against time. As the lake shrinks and salt rises, fish die off and food runs out, and colonies may be abandoned before all the chicks fledge.

sections.key: Lake Eyre's unregulated river system still floods in natural cycles, and in 1964 its dry bed hosted a land speed record.
sections.b:
In 1964 British driver Donald Campbell brought his jet-turbine car, Bluebird CN7, to Lake Eyre. Unusual rain softened the salt and delayed his runs for weeks. On 17 July 1964, on a surface still damp, he set a land speed record of about 648 kilometres per hour (403 miles per hour). Later that year he set a water speed record in Western Australia, the only person to break both records in a year.

The basin itself is one of the largest unregulated dryland river systems left on Earth, flowing in irregular boom and bust cycles that drive fish breeding and green the Channel Country pastures. Scientists, pastoralists and Aboriginal communities who have cared for it for tens of thousands of years work to protect it.

quiz.q: Roughly how far below sea level is the lowest part of Kati Thanda-Lake Eyre?
o: About 150 metres
About 15 metres
About 1.5 metres
About 400 metres
quiz.e: The lake's lowest point is about 15 metres below sea level, the lowest natural point in Australia.

quiz.q: What does it mean that the Lake Eyre Basin is 'internally draining'?
o: Its water flows underground to the ocean
It drains into the Murray River
Its water never reaches the sea
It is fed only by rain falling on the lake itself
quiz.e: Water in the basin flows towards the lake and then evaporates or soaks away, never reaching the ocean.

quiz.q: How often does the lake fill close to its full capacity?
o: Only a few times a century
Every summer
Every two years
Never in recorded history
quiz.e: Small floods reach the lake fairly often, but near-full filling happens only a few times each century.

quiz.q: What happens to the lake's birds and fish as the floodwater shrinks?
o: They multiply because the water is clearer
Salt rises, fish die off and food runs out
They migrate back upstream
Nothing changes until the next flood
quiz.e: As the lake shrinks and turns saltier, food runs out, so breeding is a race against time.

quiz.q: Why does the Lake Eyre Basin flood in irregular boom and bust cycles?
o: Its rivers are dammed and released on a schedule
Tides push seawater in from Spencer Gulf
Its rivers are largely natural and rain-fed
Underground springs overflow each year
quiz.e: Few dams or irrigation works interfere, so the rivers still flow as they always have, driving fish breeding and green pastures.

LESSONS.push: A salt crust the size of a small country sometimes becomes a lake. Why?

LESSONS.title: Supervolcanoes: the truth about Yellowstone
LESSONS.hook: A few volcanoes have erupted on a scale that dwarfs anything in recorded history. Are they overdue to do it again? The real answer is calmer than the headlines.

sections.key: A supereruption ejects more than 1,000 cubic kilometres of material, leaving a vast collapsed caldera.
sections.b:
Volcanologists measure eruptions on the Volcanic Explosivity Index, from 0 to 8. Each step up means roughly ten times more material. A VEI 8 eruption blasts out more than 1,000 cubic kilometres of ash, pumice and rock. For comparison, Mount St Helens in 1980 produced around one cubic kilometre.

A volcano capable of this is called a supervolcano, a popular rather than strictly scientific term that spread through television documentaries around the year 2000. Supervolcanoes rarely look like classic cones. Their eruptions empty such a vast underground magma reservoir that the ground collapses, leaving an enormous depression called a caldera.

sections.key: Yellowstone has had three giant caldera-forming eruptions in 2.1 million years, and it sits over a moving hotspot.
sections.b:
Yellowstone, mostly in Wyoming, has produced three huge caldera-forming eruptions in 2.1 million years. The first, about 2.1 million years ago, was the largest, at around 2,500 cubic kilometres. The second, about 1.3 million years ago, was much smaller. The third, about 631,000 years ago, produced around 1,000 cubic kilometres and formed today's caldera. Since then it has mostly produced slow lava flows, the latest about 70,000 years ago.

Why is it volcanic, far from any plate boundary? A hotspot, a plume of hot rock rising from the mantle, stays put while the North American plate slides south west over it. Older calderas trail across Idaho's Snake River Plain. Yellowstone holds more than half of the world's active geysers, including Old Faithful.

sections.key: No: volcanoes do not erupt on a timetable, and the chance of a supereruption in any given year is very small.
sections.b:
A common claim online is that Yellowstone is overdue, because its big eruptions average about 700,000 years apart. This reasoning fails. Three events are far too few to establish a pattern, the gaps were quite different, and volcanoes are not clocks.

Studies of the magma beneath Yellowstone suggest the reservoir is mostly solid crystal mush, with only a modest fraction of molten rock, far less than a supereruption would likely need. The United States Geological Survey monitors the area closely with seismometers, GPS and gas sensors. It considers a future supereruption possible but highly unlikely in any given year, and judges smaller lava flows or steam explosions much more likely.

sections.key: The Toba supereruption, about 74,000 years ago, was once blamed for nearly wiping out humanity, but newer evidence weakens that idea.
sections.b:
The largest eruption of the past couple of million years happened at Toba, on Sumatra, about 74,000 years ago. It ejected something like 2,800 cubic kilometres and left a caldera now filled by Lake Toba, about 100 kilometres long.

In the 1990s some researchers proposed that Toba caused a volcanic winter so severe it pushed early humans to the brink of extinction, a genetic bottleneck. The idea became famous, but newer evidence has weakened it. Archaeological sites in India and South Africa suggest people carried on making tools and finding food through the eruption. Many scientists now think Toba's climate effects were real but shorter or more patchy than once feared.

sections.key: New Zealand's Lake Taupō fills the caldera of the youngest known supereruption, about 25,500 years ago.
sections.b:
The world's most recent supereruption happened not far from Australia. About 25,500 years ago, the Taupō volcano in New Zealand's North Island produced the Oruanui eruption, ejecting more than 1,000 cubic kilometres of material. Ash fell over much of New Zealand and as far as the Chatham Islands. Lake Taupō, New Zealand's largest lake, now fills part of the collapsed caldera.

Taupō erupted again around 232 CE in the Hatepe eruption, one of the most violent of the past few thousand years, though not on a super scale. It remains an active system that scientists watch carefully. Like Yellowstone, its quiet beauty, with hot springs and steaming vents, sits on top of an extraordinary history.

quiz.q: What defines a supereruption on the Volcanic Explosivity Index?
o: Any eruption lasting more than a year
An eruption that produces lava flows over 100 kilometres long
An eruption ejecting more than 1,000 cubic kilometres of material
Any eruption that kills more than 10,000 people
quiz.e: A VEI 8 eruption ejects more than 1,000 cubic kilometres, about a thousand times more than Mount St Helens in 1980.

quiz.q: Why is there a line of old calderas across southern Idaho?
o: Yellowstone was once several volcanoes on a plate boundary
The North American plate has moved over a stationary hotspot
Glaciers carried volcanic rock there
Rivers carved out the calderas
quiz.e: As the plate drifted south west over the mantle hotspot, activity appeared to move north east, leaving older calderas behind.

quiz.q: Why is the claim that Yellowstone is 'overdue' misleading?
o: Yellowstone erupted in 1980
Its eruptions happen exactly every 100,000 years
Yellowstone is extinct
Volcanoes do not erupt on a schedule
quiz.e: Eruption gaps vary, volcanoes are not clocks, and the magma reservoir appears mostly solid crystal mush.

quiz.q: What has newer evidence suggested about Toba's effect on humans?
o: It wiped out most humans outside Africa
Archaeology suggests people carried on through it
It caused humans to migrate to Australia
It had no effect on climate at all
quiz.e: Archaeological sites suggest people coped, weakening the idea of a near-extinction bottleneck.

quiz.q: Where was the world's most recent known supereruption?
o: Yellowstone, USA
Toba, Indonesia
Mount Vesuvius, Italy
Taupō, New Zealand
quiz.e: The Oruanui eruption at Taupō, about 25,500 years ago, is the youngest known supereruption.

LESSONS.push: Is Yellowstone overdue to blow? The answer is calmer than the headlines.

LESSONS.title: When the Sahara was green
LESSONS.hook: Ten thousand years ago, people fished, swam and herded cattle across land that is now the world's largest hot desert. A wobble in Earth's orbit explains how.

sections.key: Rock art, fossils and ancient shorelines show the Sahara once had lakes, grasslands and large animals.
sections.b:
The Sahara covers around nine million square kilometres of North Africa, larger than Australia, and much of it gets almost no rain. Yet clues to a different past are scattered across it. Rock paintings and engravings at places like Tassili n'Ajjer in Algeria show giraffes, elephants, rhinoceroses, hippopotamuses and herds of cattle. Fossilised crocodile and fish bones lie in bare sand, and ancient shorelines mark vanished lakes. Mega-Lake Chad once covered hundreds of thousands of square kilometres.

Scientists call this wetter time the African Humid Period, lasting roughly from 15,000 to 5,000 years ago. In 1933 explorer László Almásy found the Cave of Swimmers in Egypt's Gilf Kebir, whose figures appear to swim, though some researchers think they may be spiritual rather than literal.

sections.key: Slow changes in Earth's orbit strengthened summer sunshine and pulled the monsoon rains north.
sections.b:
The main driver was astronomical. Earth's axis slowly wobbles, like a spinning top, in a cycle of roughly 20,000 to 26,000 years called precession. This changes the time of year when Earth is closest to the Sun. Around 10,000 years ago the Northern Hemisphere was closest during its summer, so North Africa received noticeably more summer sunshine than today.

Stronger heating over the land drew the West African monsoon much further north, carrying rain deep into what is now desert. Feedbacks amplified the change: plants and lakes darkened the landscape and recycled moisture into the air, helping the rains persist. The opposite process eventually dried the region out.

sections.key: Fishers and herders lived across the wet Sahara, leaving graves, pottery and harpoons behind.
sections.b:
People moved into the Sahara as it greened. At Gobero, in Niger, archaeologists working from 2000 onwards uncovered graves of communities who lived beside an ancient lake. Their remains lay with bone harpoons, fish hooks and pottery, along with bones of fish, turtles and crocodiles. One moving burial held a woman and two children, apparently laid to rest together.

Across the region people made some of the world's early pottery and, later, took up cattle herding as conditions became drier and less predictable. Rock art shows people with herds and dogs. This was not a single culture but many groups, adapting over thousands of years to a landscape that kept changing around them.

sections.key: The Sahara became desert again around 5,000 years ago, though how fast is still debated.
sections.b:
As Earth's orbit continued its slow cycle, summer sunshine in North Africa weakened and the monsoon retreated south. The lakes shrank, the grasslands thinned and the Sahara became desert again around 5,000 years ago.

Scientists still debate how quickly. Ocean sediments, which record dust blown off Africa, suggest a fairly abrupt shift over a few centuries. Lake and pollen records suggest a more gradual drying that varied by place. The people there had to adapt, and many appear to have moved towards more reliable water, including the Nile Valley. Some archaeologists suggest this migration played a part in the rise of early Egyptian civilisation, though that link remains a hypothesis.

sections.key: The Sahara has swung between green and desert many times, and its dust still fertilises the Amazon.
sections.b:
The green period was not unique. Sediment records show the Sahara has swung between desert and grassland many times over hundreds of thousands of years, roughly in step with the precession cycle. These green corridors may have opened routes for animals and early humans to move out of Africa.

Even as a desert, the Sahara shapes the planet. Winds lift hundreds of millions of tonnes of dust each year and carry it across the Atlantic. Much comes from the Bodele Depression in Chad, the dried bed of the old mega-lake. Satellite studies suggest this dust delivers phosphorus and other nutrients to the Amazon rainforest, helping fertilise one of Earth's richest ecosystems.

quiz.q: Which of these is evidence that the Sahara was once green?
o: Ancient tree rings in the sand
Records written by Roman travellers
Coal deposits under the dunes
Rock art showing hippos and cattle
quiz.e: Rock art at sites like Tassili n'Ajjer, plus fossils of crocodiles and fish, show the Sahara once had water and grasslands.

quiz.q: What mainly caused the green Sahara?
o: A sudden rise in ocean salt levels
An orbital wobble strengthening the monsoon
A long series of volcanic eruptions
Early farmers planting large forests
quiz.e: Precession gave North Africa stronger summer sunshine, drawing the West African monsoon far further north.

quiz.q: What did archaeologists find at Gobero in Niger?
o: A buried city with pyramids and temples
The ruins of a Roman fort and its road
Lakeside graves with harpoons, hooks and pottery
Fossilised nests of dinosaur eggs
quiz.e: Gobero's burials sat beside an ancient lake and included fishing tools and bones of fish, turtles and crocodiles.

quiz.q: What do scientists still debate about the end of the green Sahara?
o: Whether it ever happened
Whether the Moon caused it
Whether it ended within the last century
How quickly the drying occurred
quiz.e: Some records suggest an abrupt shift over centuries, others a gradual drying that varied by place.

quiz.q: How does Saharan dust affect South America today?
o: It causes frequent dust storms in Brazil
It blocks rainfall over the Amazon
It helps fertilise the Amazon rainforest
It has no effect because it never crosses the Atlantic
quiz.e: Dust, much of it from Chad's Bodele Depression, crosses the Atlantic and delivers nutrients to the Amazon.

LESSONS.push: People once swam and herded cattle where the Sahara now lies. What changed?

LESSONS.title: Monsoons: the seasons of rain
LESSONS.hook: For billions of people, the most important weather event of the year is the arrival of the monsoon. Its rains decide harvests, rivers and even history.

sections.key: A monsoon is a seasonal reversal of winds that brings a wet season and a dry season, and the word means season.
sections.b:
The word monsoon comes, through Portuguese and Dutch, from the Arabic mawsim, meaning season. People often use it to mean heavy rain, but strictly a monsoon is a pattern of winds that reverses direction with the seasons. For part of the year, winds blow in from the ocean, carrying moisture and bringing a long wet season. For the rest, they blow from the land, bringing dry weather.

Monsoons affect South Asia, East and South East Asia, West Africa, northern Australia and parts of the Americas. The South Asian monsoon is the largest and most famous, and it shapes the lives and livelihoods of well over a billion people.

sections.key: Land heats faster than sea, so in summer hot land draws moist ocean air inland where it rises and falls as rain.
sections.b:
The basic driver is simple. Land heats and cools much faster than the ocean. In late spring and summer the land warms strongly, and the hot air above it rises, creating lower pressure near the ground. Cooler, moist air flows in from the ocean to replace it. As that humid air is lifted, by heating or by mountains, it cools and drops its moisture as rain. In winter the pattern reverses, as the land becomes cooler than the sea.

The real picture is more complicated. The monsoon is also tied to the seasonal migration of the tropical rain belt, the Intertropical Convergence Zone, which follows the Sun's strongest heating north and south through the year.

sections.key: The South West monsoon reaches Kerala around 1 June and brings roughly three quarters of India's yearly rain.
sections.b:
Each year the India Meteorological Department watches for the monsoon to arrive on the coast of Kerala, at India's southern tip, typically around 1 June. Over the following weeks the rains push north and usually cover almost the whole country by early to mid-July. The South West monsoon delivers roughly three quarters of India's annual rainfall in just four months.

The Himalaya and the high Tibetan Plateau play a crucial role. The plateau heats strongly in summer, helping power the circulation, while the mountains keep the moisture over the subcontinent. A good monsoon fills reservoirs, recharges groundwater and feeds rice and other crops. A weak one can mean drought, falling harvests and rising food prices.

sections.key: Monsoon winds forced up steep hills in north east India produce some of the highest rainfall ever recorded.
sections.b:
Some of the wettest places on Earth are in the Khasi Hills of Meghalaya, in north east India. Monsoon winds loaded with moisture from the Bay of Bengal are forced up steep slopes and wring out torrential rain. The village of Mawsynram averages close to 12 metres of rain a year, among the highest averages anywhere. Nearby Cherrapunji holds a famous record: in the twelve months from August 1860 to July 1861 it received more than 26 metres.

People have adapted in remarkable ways. Some Khasi villages have grown living bridges by training the roots of rubber fig trees across rivers over many years, creating structures that grow stronger with age.

sections.key: Reliable monsoon winds shaped Indian Ocean trade for centuries, and northern Australia has its own monsoon.
sections.b:
Because monsoon winds blow reliably one way for part of the year and the other way later, a ship could sail across the Arabian Sea and return when the winds reversed. Arab, Indian, Persian, African, and later Greek and Roman merchants used this to trade spices, pepper, textiles, gems and gold between East Africa, Arabia, India and South East Asia. A first century Greek guidebook, the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, describes these routes.

Australia has a monsoon too. Across the Top End, the Kimberley and Cape York, the wet season runs roughly November or December to March, with north westerly winds, heavy rain and humidity, arriving in active bursts and breaks. First Nations peoples of the north recognise many more seasons than two, based on detailed knowledge of weather, plants and animals.

quiz.q: Strictly speaking, what is a monsoon?
o: Any spell of very heavy rain
Winds that reverse with the seasons
A powerful tropical cyclone
A steady wind off the sea
quiz.e: The word comes from the Arabic for season, because the winds reverse with the seasons.

quiz.q: What is the basic driver of a summer monsoon?
o: Strong tides pulled by the Moon
Volcanic heat beneath the land
Cold air sinking over the ocean
Land heating faster than the sea
quiz.e: Hot land creates low pressure, and moist ocean air flows in, rises and drops its rain.

quiz.q: Roughly what share of India's annual rainfall comes from the South West monsoon?
o: About a tenth
About a quarter
About half
About three quarters
quiz.e: The South West monsoon delivers roughly three quarters of India's annual rain in about four months.

quiz.q: Why are places like Mawsynram and Cherrapunji so wet?
o: They sit at sea level beside the ocean
Moist winds are forced up steep hills
They lie directly on the equator
Glacier meltwater floods them each year
quiz.e: Moisture from the Bay of Bengal is pushed up the Khasi Hills, wringing out enormous rainfall.

quiz.q: How did monsoon winds help ancient trade?
o: They pushed fleets across the Pacific Ocean
They kept the Indian Ocean calm all year
Seasonal reversals let ships sail out and home
They blew ships straight to Europe in weeks
quiz.e: Sailors timed voyages so the winds carried them one way, then waited for the reversal to sail home.

LESSONS.push: For a billion people, one wind decides the year. How does it turn around?

LESSONS.title: Ice cores: reading Earth's frozen diary
LESSONS.hook: Drill deep into Antarctica and you pull up ancient air, volcanic fallout and the planet's temperature history, layer by layer, going back 800,000 years.

sections.key: Snow that never melts compresses into ice, forming a dated archive with the oldest layers at the bottom.
sections.b:
In the coldest parts of Greenland and Antarctica, snow falls and never melts. Each year's snow buries the last, compressing into granular firn and then solid ice. The youngest ice sits on top and the oldest near the bedrock, sometimes more than three kilometres down. Scientists drill out cores about ten centimetres wide and ship them frozen to laboratories.

Where snowfall is heavy, each year leaves a distinct layer, so layers can be counted like tree rings for tens of thousands of years. Deeper down, the ice thins and flows, so ages come from flow models and volcanic markers. Eruptions such as Tambora in 1815 leave sulphate spikes in both Greenland and Antarctic ice, tying the records to one calendar.

sections.key: Bubbles sealed in ice are real samples of the past atmosphere, though the air is younger than the ice around it.
sections.b:
The most remarkable treasure in ice cores is air. As firn turns to ice, the spaces between grains close off and trap tiny bubbles of atmosphere. In the laboratory, scientists crush or melt samples under vacuum and measure gases such as carbon dioxide and methane.

There is one subtlety. Air keeps circulating through the porous firn until it is sealed, typically several tens of metres down. So the trapped air is younger than the ice around it, sometimes by thousands of years where snowfall is slow. Scientists correct for the gap. Australian researchers contributed greatly with cores from Law Dome, near Casey Station, where high snowfall gives a detailed record of carbon dioxide over the past two thousand years.

sections.key: The ratio of heavy to light water molecules in each layer of ice reveals how cold it was when the snow fell.
sections.b:
Ice itself records temperature. Some water molecules contain heavier isotopes, such as oxygen-18 instead of oxygen-16, or deuterium, a heavy form of hydrogen. As moist air travels towards the poles and cools, the heavier molecules tend to fall out as rain or snow first.

So the colder the conditions, the fewer heavy molecules remain in the snow that finally lands on the ice sheet. By measuring the ratio of heavy to light isotopes in each layer, scientists can reconstruct how temperature changed over time. This isotope thermometer, developed largely by Danish scientist Willi Dansgaard from the 1950s, is a foundation of modern climate science.

sections.key: Antarctic cores show eight ice-age cycles in which carbon dioxide and temperature rose and fell together.
sections.b:
The longest continuous ice core record comes from Dome C, high on the East Antarctic plateau, drilled by the European project EPICA. It reaches back about 800,000 years and shows eight full cycles of ice ages and warmer interglacial periods.

Through all of them, carbon dioxide and temperature rise and fall together. In cold glacial periods carbon dioxide sat around 180 parts per million. In warm interglacials it rose to around 280 to 300. Changes in Earth's orbit pace the cycles, with carbon dioxide acting as a powerful amplifier. By the mid-2020s atmospheric carbon dioxide had passed 420 parts per million, far outside the range of the entire ice core record.

sections.key: Greenland ice shows climate can shift by many degrees within decades, and scientists are now hunting for ice over a million years old.
sections.b:
Greenland cores revealed something unsettling. In the last ice age, temperatures there repeatedly jumped by several degrees, sometimes ten or more, within decades. These Dansgaard–Oeschger events showed that climate can change abruptly. The ice also records human history: lead from Roman mining and smelting settled in the snow, and dipped in times of war and plague. Wildfires and dust storms leave traces too.

A puzzle remains. About a million years ago, ice-age cycles lengthened from roughly 41,000 to about 100,000 years, and nobody is sure why. In early 2025 the Beyond EPICA project reached bedrock at Little Dome C, recovering ice believed to be well over a million years old.

quiz.q: How do scientists date ice too deep for its yearly layers to be counted?
o: By drilling a second hole beside the first
By measuring the ice's temperature at depth
By using ice-flow models and volcanic markers
By counting the bubbles in each metre of core
quiz.e: Deep ice is squeezed thin, so ages come from flow models tied to markers like volcanic sulphate spikes.

quiz.q: Why is the air in ice core bubbles younger than the ice around it?
o: Bubbles slowly rise through the solid ice
Air circulates through porous firn until sealed
Modern air leaks into cores during drilling
Bacteria make new gases inside the ice
quiz.e: Air stays mobile in the firn until it seals off, so the trapped sample is younger than the ice, and scientists correct for the gap.

quiz.q: How do isotope ratios in ice reveal past temperatures?
o: Warmer snow always contains more salt
Colder conditions leave fewer heavy molecules in snow
Heavy isotopes glow under ultraviolet light
Colder ice forms thicker layers every year
quiz.e: Heavier molecules fall out first as air cools on its way to the poles, so colder snow holds fewer of them.

quiz.q: What does the 800,000-year record show about carbon dioxide and temperature?
o: They moved independently throughout the record
They rose and fell together across eight cycles
Carbon dioxide stayed constant for 800,000 years
Carbon dioxide rose only when ice sheets grew
quiz.e: Across eight cycles carbon dioxide tracked temperature between about 180 and 300 parts per million, well below today's level.

quiz.q: What did Dansgaard–Oeschger events show?
o: That ice ages always end very gradually
That Greenland was never covered in thick ice
That volcanoes are the main cause of ice ages
That climate can shift abruptly within decades
quiz.e: Greenland ice showed that climate can change suddenly, not only slowly.

LESSONS.push: Antarctic ice holds air from 800,000 years ago, and it's still telling us things.

LESSONS.title: Ireland's Great Hunger, 1845–1852
LESSONS.hook: A microscopic organism destroyed one crop, and within a few years Ireland had lost a quarter of its people. The blight was natural. The scale of the disaster was not.

sections.key: Ireland's poorest depended almost entirely on one fragile potato crop, so when blight struck, there was nothing to fall back on.
sections.b:
By the 1840s Ireland had about eight and a half million people, many renting tiny plots from landlords. Wheat, oats, cattle and butter were grown for rent and sale, but the poorest lived on potatoes. An acre could feed a family for much of a year, and a labourer might eat several kilograms a day. Many relied on one high-yielding but vulnerable variety, the ‘lumper’.

In 1845 Phytophthora infestans, a fungus-like water mould probably from the Americas, arrived. Leaves blackened and potatoes rotted in the ground. Roughly a third to a half of the 1845 crop was lost, and 1846 was worse. Other countries had blight too, but nowhere else was so large a share of people so dependent on the crop.

sections.key: Government relief existed but was shaped by a belief that the market and local taxes should carry the burden.
sections.b:
Prime Minister Robert Peel's government quietly bought American maize in 1845 to sell cheaply. From 1846 Lord John Russell's government leaned on the idea that the state should not interfere with trade. The starving were offered work on public projects such as roads, often for wages too low to buy food, and sometimes on roads that led nowhere.

In 1847 soup kitchens briefly fed around three million people a day, and they worked. Yet they were wound down within months, and responsibility shifted to workhouses and local property taxes. The Gregory clause denied relief to anyone holding more than a quarter acre, forcing many to give up their homes to qualify.

sections.key: Ireland kept exporting food during the famine, but historians see the deeper failure as one of political choices, not supply.
sections.b:
One of the most painful facts of the famine is that grain, cattle and butter kept leaving Ireland while people starved. Landlords needed rent, farmers sold crops to pay it, and armed guards sometimes escorted food convoys past hungry crowds.

Historians debate how much difference keeping that food would have made. From 1847 more grain was coming in than going out, and the loss of the potato was too vast for exports alone to fill. But most agree the deeper problem was choice, not supply. A wealthy empire could have kept people alive and instead treated the crisis as a chance to reform Irish agriculture. Charles Trevelyan, a senior Treasury official, came to symbolise that outlook.

sections.key: Most famine victims died of diseases that spread among weakened, homeless people, and about a million died in all.
sections.b:
Hunger made people vulnerable, and disease did much of the killing. Typhus, relapsing fever and dysentery swept through crowded workhouses, roadsides and cabins. Scurvy appeared as diets collapsed.

Landlords, facing unpaid rents and rising local taxes, evicted hundreds of thousands of tenants, often tearing down cottages so families could not return. Whole communities in the west, in counties such as Mayo, Galway and Cork, were devastated. Around one million people died between 1845 and 1852, though exact numbers are uncertain because so many deaths went unrecorded. Irish speakers called it An Gorta Mór, the Great Hunger. The worst year, 1847, became known as Black ’47, and mass graves from that time are still being identified.

sections.key: Over a million people emigrated, Ireland's population kept falling for decades, and the famine reshaped Irish identity worldwide.
sections.b:
For many families the only hope was to leave. Well over a million emigrated, mostly to Britain, the United States and Canada, some on overcrowded ‘coffin ships’. At the quarantine station on Grosse Île in Canada, thousands died of typhus in 1847 alone. Between 1848 and 1850 an assisted scheme brought more than four thousand Irish orphan girls to Sydney, Melbourne and Adelaide.

Ireland's population kept falling for decades and the island still holds fewer people than before the famine. The Irish language declined, bitterness towards British rule hardened, and Irish communities abroad kept the memory alive. In 1847 the Choctaw Nation, recently forced from their own lands, sent money to help, honoured today by a sculpture in County Cork. Most historians see a natural disaster made far deadlier by poverty, a harsh land system and government decisions.

quiz.q: Why were so many Irish people exposed when the blight struck?
o: Ireland had never grown potatoes before
The poorest relied almost entirely on one potato crop
Ireland imported nearly all of its potatoes
Potatoes were reserved for the landlords
quiz.e: With one fragile crop as their main food, the poorest had nothing to fall back on when it failed.

quiz.q: Why did government relief fall short?
o: Free-trade beliefs left costs to local taxes
Most Irish people declined the aid offered
Britain lacked ships to carry any food
Landlords blocked all relief from arriving
quiz.e: Soup kitchens worked but were closed within months, and the policy relied on markets and local taxes.

quiz.q: What do most historians conclude about food exports during the famine?
o: Exports alone explain the whole famine
Exports were not enough; policy made it worse
Exports stopped entirely before the famine
Exports were seized by the army at ports
quiz.e: The deeper problem was political choice, not a lack of supply.

quiz.q: What killed most famine victims?
o: Violence between tenants and landlords
Freezing winters in the western counties
Typhus and dysentery among weakened people
Shipwrecks on the crossing to Canada
quiz.e: Hunger weakened people, and fevers and dysentery spread through workhouses, roadsides and cabins.

quiz.q: What happened to Ireland's population after the famine?
o: It recovered fully within about a decade
It kept falling for decades and is still lower
It doubled because of immigration
It stayed the same throughout the century
quiz.e: Emigration became a habit that lasted generations.

LESSONS.push: A mould ruined one crop. Why did so many Irish people die?

LESSONS.title: The Christmas Truce of 1914
LESSONS.hook: Five months into the most industrial war yet fought, enemy soldiers climbed out of their trenches, shook hands and sang carols together. Then they went back to killing each other.

sections.key: Soldiers in trenches only metres apart began informal understandings to hold fire, which made the Christmas truce possible.
sections.b:
In August 1914 many expected the war to be over by Christmas. Instead, the German advance was stopped at the Marne and both armies dug in. By winter trenches ran from the Belgian coast to the Swiss border, sometimes only fifty to a few hundred metres apart. Men lived in freezing water among rats and the unburied dead. Yet the closeness let them hear the enemy talking, coughing and singing.

Small unofficial understandings grew. Each side might spare the other at breakfast, or let men fetch water or bring in wounded. Historians call it ‘live and let live’. In December Pope Benedict XV called for a Christmas pause, but governments ignored him.

sections.key: The truce began with ordinary soldiers, not leaders, as German trenches lit candles and British soldiers answered in song.
sections.b:
On Christmas Eve 1914, British soldiers in several sectors were astonished to see lights along the German trenches. German troops had placed small Christmas trees, decorated with candles, on their parapets. Then came singing, including ‘Stille Nacht’, Silent Night. The British replied with their own carols, and each side applauded the other across no man's land.

Shouted conversations followed, helped by Germans who had worked in Britain and spoke English. A few brave men walked out unarmed. When nobody fired, others followed. By Christmas morning, along stretches of the front, men who had been trying to kill each other days earlier stood together in the frozen mud.

sections.key: Soldiers swapped gifts, buried their dead together and probably kicked balls about, though no organised match is proven.
sections.b:
Letters home describe an extraordinary day. Men exchanged cigarettes, chocolate, plum puddings, buttons and badges, and showed each other photographs of their families. Barbers cut enemy hair. Most importantly, both sides used the calm to recover and bury the bodies lying between the lines, sometimes with joint services.

Football is the most famous part of the story. Several soldiers wrote of kickabouts with the enemy, sometimes with a makeshift ball, and these accounts seem genuine. But a single organised match with a final score is much harder to prove. Historians think informal games happened in a few places, not one grand fixture across the front.

sections.key: The truce was patchy and brief, and in many places the shooting never stopped.
sections.b:
It is easy to imagine the whole front falling silent, but that did not happen. The truce was strongest where British and German troops faced each other, especially around Ypres in Belgium. It occurred in some French and Belgian sectors too, but less often, perhaps because those soldiers were fighting on their own invaded soil.

Elsewhere fighting continued and men were killed on Christmas Day. Some truces lasted only hours, others until New Year or beyond. By some estimates around one hundred thousand soldiers took part, but nobody knows the true figure. Many soldiers felt uneasy, some officers were furious, and not every man who wrote home that week described peace.

sections.key: Commanders banned fraternisation to stop a repeat, but the truce remains proof that shared humanity can survive even total war.
sections.b:
High commands saw the truce as a threat to discipline. If soldiers came to like their enemies, how could they be ordered to kill them? In following years strict orders forbade fraternisation, and bombardments were sometimes scheduled for Christmas. Small local pauses still happened in 1915, but nothing like 1914. The war grew more brutal, with poison gas, the Somme and Verdun.

When British newspapers printed soldiers' letters and photographs in January 1915, readers were amazed. Some retellings are romanticised, but the core is well documented in hundreds of letters and diaries. The truce did not shorten the war. Its power lies in an uncomfortable question: if the men in the trenches could stop, why couldn't those in charge?

quiz.q: What was the ‘live and let live’ system?
o: An official peace treaty between the armies
Informal habits of holding fire on quiet sectors
A medical programme for wounded soldiers
A prisoner exchange scheme at Christmas
quiz.e: Close trenches and shared misery led soldiers to quietly ease the killing, long before the famous truce.

quiz.q: Who started the Christmas truce?
o: Ordinary soldiers, who sang and walked out
Generals who signed a Christmas ceasefire
Governments responding to the Pope's appeal
Chaplains ordered to negotiate with the enemy
quiz.e: The truce came from soldiers acting on their own, not from leaders.

quiz.q: What do historians conclude about football during the truce?
o: There was one official match with a recorded score
Informal kickabouts probably happened in places
No football was ever played along the front
Games were organised by senior officers
quiz.e: Soldiers' letters support casual games, but a single organised match is hard to prove.

quiz.q: Which statement about the truce is accurate?
o: It covered the whole front until the war ended
It occurred only on the French side
It was patchy, and fighting continued in some places
It was ordered by senior British officers
quiz.e: The truce was strongest between British and German troops around Ypres, but far from universal.

quiz.q: Why did commanders work to prevent another truce?
o: Friendly soldiers might refuse to fight
The winter weather had finally improved
Newspapers had banned all stories about it
The Pope had forbidden any repeat
quiz.e: Armies depend on soldiers seeing the other side as an enemy, so fraternisation was forbidden.

LESSONS.push: In 1914, enemies climbed out of their trenches on Christmas. How did it start?

LESSONS.title: The Titanic: one night that changed the sea
LESSONS.hook: On a calm, moonless night in April 1912, the largest ship afloat struck an iceberg and sank in under three hours. The rules that keep ships safe today were written in its wake.

sections.key: Titanic was built for size and comfort, and the claim that it was advertised as unsinkable is mostly a later exaggeration.
sections.b:
RMS Titanic was built in Belfast by Harland and Wolff for the White Star Line and launched in 1911. About 269 metres long, it was briefly the largest ship in the world. White Star competed with Cunard on size and luxury, not speed. First class had a swimming pool, a gymnasium and Turkish baths. The hull was divided into sixteen watertight compartments, and the ship could float with any two flooded, or the first four.

A trade journal called such ships ‘practically unsinkable’, but it was not a central advertising slogan. The boldest versions of the claim spread after the disaster. Still, confidence in modern ships was real, and it contributed to too few lifeboats and ignored ice warnings.

sections.key: Titanic received several ice warnings yet kept up a high speed through a calm, moonless night.
sections.b:
Titanic left Southampton on 10 April 1912, called at Cherbourg and Queenstown, and headed for New York with over two thousand people aboard. On 14 April the Marconi wireless operators received several warnings about ice ahead. Not all reached the bridge, partly because the operators were busy sending passengers' private messages.

Captain Edward Smith altered course slightly but kept the ship at about 22 knots, close to its top speed, as was normal practice then. The sea was flat calm with no moon, so no waves broke around the base of icebergs to reveal them. The lookouts in the crow's nest had no binoculars.

sections.key: The iceberg opened too many compartments, and water spilled from one to the next until Titanic sank in about two hours and forty minutes.
sections.b:
At about 11.40 pm on 14 April, lookout Frederick Fleet spotted an iceberg dead ahead. The officer on watch ordered a hard turn, but too late. The iceberg scraped along the starboard side below the waterline, buckling plates and popping rivets along a long stretch of hull. It was not one huge gash but a series of openings.

Water poured into the first five or six compartments, more than the design could survive. Thomas Andrews, the ship's designer, who was aboard, told the captain the ship would sink. As the bow went down, water spilled over the tops of the bulkheads from one compartment into the next. At about 2.20 am on 15 April, Titanic broke apart and sank.

sections.key: Titanic carried lifeboats for only about half of those aboard, and the nearest ship never came.
sections.b:
Titanic carried twenty lifeboats with room for about 1,178 people. That exceeded the outdated British rules, which were based on a ship's weight, but it covered only about half of the roughly 2,200 aboard. Early boats left well under capacity. More than 1,500 people died, many in water near minus two degrees. Most first class passengers survived; around three quarters of third class did not.

The liner Carpathia, roughly 90 kilometres away, steamed through the ice and picked up around 700 survivors. The Californian, much closer, had stopped for the night. Its crew saw rockets but did not understand them, and its only wireless operator had gone to bed.

sections.key: The disaster led to international rules on lifeboats, round-the-clock radio watches and ice patrols that still shape shipping.
sections.b:
Inquiries in the United States and Britain led to the first International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea, known as SOLAS, agreed in London in 1914. Ships had to carry lifeboat places for everyone aboard and hold lifeboat drills. Wireless rooms on passenger ships were to be staffed around the clock, so no distress call went unheard.

The International Ice Patrol was created to track icebergs in the North Atlantic, and it still operates. The wreck lay undiscovered until 1985, when a team led by Robert Ballard and Jean-Louis Michel found it nearly four kilometres down, broken in two. Its slow decay reminds us how a confident age learned humility the hard way.

quiz.q: What is the truth about the ‘unsinkable’ claim?
o: It was White Star's main advertising slogan
The captain announced it at departure
A trade journal used it and the boast grew
It was invented after the wreck was found
quiz.e: The strongest versions of the claim spread after the sinking, though real confidence in modern ships mattered.

quiz.q: Why was the iceberg so hard to spot?
o: Fog covered the whole North Atlantic
Calm, moonless water, and no binoculars
The lookouts had fallen asleep at their posts
The ship's lights had been switched off
quiz.e: Flat water and no moon hid the berg until it was close.

quiz.q: Why did Titanic sink even though it could survive some flooding?
o: One enormous gash split the hull in two
Too many compartments flooded and overflowed
A large hole opened in the upper deck
The rudder snapped off in the collision
quiz.e: The design could survive four flooded compartments, but the iceberg opened five or six.

quiz.q: Why did Titanic have so few lifeboats for the people aboard?
o: Lifeboats had not yet been invented
Outdated rules based boat numbers on weight
Passengers voted against carrying more boats
The owners removed boats to save weight
quiz.e: The ship met the old rules, which fell far short of what its 2,200 people needed.

quiz.q: What change helped ensure distress calls would not go unheard?
o: Round-the-clock radio watches on liners
Banning night sailing across the Atlantic
Fitting every liner with searchlights
Limiting ships to a top speed of 15 knots
quiz.e: Californian's operator was asleep, so SOLAS required continuous radio watches.

LESSONS.push: The Titanic's famous ‘unsinkable’ boast is mostly a myth. The real story differs.

LESSONS.title: Dunkirk: the miracle of 1940
LESSONS.hook: In nine days in 1940, an army that seemed doomed was carried home across the English Channel. Britain called it a miracle. Churchill warned that wars are not won by evacuations.

sections.key: A fast German breakthrough trapped the Allied armies against the sea, and a three-day halt order gave them time to defend Dunkirk.
sections.b:
On 10 May 1940 Germany attacked the Netherlands, Belgium and France. Allied commanders sent their best troops, including most of the British Expeditionary Force, north into Belgium. But German tanks came through the hilly Ardennes, which the French thought too difficult for armour, crossed the Meuse and reached the Channel on 20 May. Hundreds of thousands of Allied soldiers were caught in a shrinking pocket.

On 24 May the German advance halted, confirmed by Hitler. Tank maintenance, marshy ground, fear of counterattack and Göring's claim that the Luftwaffe could finish the job may all have played a part. The pause lasted around three days, giving the Allies time to strengthen the perimeter, where French troops held out.

sections.key: Operation Dynamo, planned beneath Dover Castle, began hoping to save 45,000 men under terrible conditions.
sections.b:
Vice-Admiral Bertram Ramsay organised the rescue from rooms deep in the cliffs below Dover Castle. The codename, Operation Dynamo, is said to come from a room that once housed an electrical generator. When it began on 26 May, planners hoped to save perhaps 45,000 men in two days.

Conditions were terrible. Bombing had wrecked Dunkirk's docks, oil tanks burned and black smoke hung over the town. The beaches sloped so gently that large ships could not get close. Men waited for days on the sand under air attack, in long lines into the sea. Ramsay's staff worked almost without sleep, improvising hour by hour.

sections.key: Most soldiers left from a harbour breakwater, while the famous little ships ferried men from the beaches to larger vessels.
sections.b:
The famous image of Dunkirk is a flotilla of pleasure boats, fishing vessels and yachts crossing the Channel. These ‘little ships’ were real and heroic, many crewed by naval reservists or their owners, and vital for carrying men from the shallow beaches to larger ships offshore.

But most soldiers were taken off from the East Mole, a long concrete and timber breakwater protecting the harbour. It was never designed for ships to tie up against, yet destroyers and passenger ferries came alongside and loaded thousands of men at a time. Many hundreds of vessels took part, from warships to Thames barges. The Royal Navy's destroyers did the heaviest lifting, and several were sunk.

sections.key: The RAF's inland air battle and the French rearguard made the escape possible, often unseen by men on the beach.
sections.b:
Soldiers on the beaches were bombed and strafed, and many angrily asked where the Royal Air Force was. In fact the RAF was flying hard, but much of its fighting took place inland or above the cloud, intercepting bombers before they reached the coast. It lost many aircraft and pilots.

On the ground, defending the perimeter mattered just as much. British units fought delaying actions, and French troops held the line until the end, letting others escape. When the evacuation finished on 4 June, tens of thousands of French soldiers who had protected the beaches were left behind and taken prisoner. Their sacrifice is often forgotten in the British telling.

sections.key: About 338,000 troops were rescued, but Churchill insisted that wars are not won by evacuations.
sections.b:
Around 338,000 Allied soldiers were carried to England, including well over 100,000 French troops, many quickly shipped back to fight in France. Against the original hope of 45,000, it seemed a miracle. But many ships were sunk, and the British army abandoned almost all its heavy equipment: tens of thousands of vehicles, hundreds of tanks, guns and ammunition. France signed an armistice on 22 June. Yet Britain kept the core of a trained army, later the backbone of forces in Africa, Italy and Normandy.

On 4 June Churchill told the Commons that wars are not won by evacuations and called the campaign a colossal military disaster. He ended with his promise to fight on the beaches and never surrender.

quiz.q: How did German forces trap the Allied armies?
o: With a naval blockade of the Channel
By bombing the Belgian army into surrender
By capturing Dunkirk before anyone arrived
By driving tanks through the Ardennes
quiz.e: The armour crossed terrain the French thought impassable and cut off the armies in the north.

quiz.q: Why was getting men off the beaches so difficult?
o: Shallow beaches and a wrecked harbour
The Channel was frozen across its whole width
Soldiers refused to board the waiting ships
No ships were available to be sent across
quiz.e: Bombing ruined the harbour and shallow beaches kept big ships far offshore.

quiz.q: Where were most soldiers actually taken off?
o: By flying boats from the harbour
From the East Mole, a harbour breakwater
From a port further along the coast
From an airfield outside the town
quiz.e: The little ships were vital, but most men boarded destroyers and ferries at the mole.

quiz.q: How did the RAF and French troops contribute to the escape?
o: They sank the German invasion fleet
They negotiated a local ceasefire
The RAF fought inland and French troops held on
They ferried soldiers across the Channel
quiz.e: Both fought out of sight of the beaches, and many French troops were captured as a result.

quiz.q: How did Churchill describe the campaign on 4 June?
o: As a complete and glorious victory
As a failure caused by France alone
As a miracle with no losses
As a colossal military disaster
quiz.e: He praised the deliverance but warned that wars are not won by evacuations.

LESSONS.push: Why did German tanks stop outside Dunkirk? Historians still argue about it.

LESSONS.title: The Panama Canal: cutting a continent in two
LESSONS.hook: For centuries people dreamed of a shortcut between the Atlantic and Pacific. The first attempt ended in disaster. The second succeeded only after doctors worked out what was really killing the workers.

sections.key: A canal would save around 13,000 kilometres of sailing, but the first attempt failed because of terrain, a flawed design and disease.
sections.b:
Panama is a narrow strip of land, at its slimmest under 80 kilometres wide. A ship sailing from New York to San Francisco had to go around Cape Horn, a voyage of more than 20,000 kilometres. A canal would cut roughly 13,000 kilometres from it.

In 1881 a French company led by Ferdinand de Lesseps, hero of the Suez Canal, began digging. He insisted on a sea-level canal with no locks. But Panama was nothing like flat Egyptian desert: mountains, landslides, heavy rains and the flooding Chagres River defeated the plan. Yellow fever and malaria killed workers in huge numbers, around 20,000 during the French years, many of them Caribbean labourers. By 1889 the company was bankrupt, and the half-dug ditches were left to the jungle.

sections.key: The United States backed Panama's independence from Colombia in 1903 to secure the canal route.
sections.b:
At the start of the twentieth century, the United States wanted a canal for trade and to move its navy quickly between oceans. President Theodore Roosevelt bought the French company's assets, but Colombia, which then ruled Panama, rejected the treaty terms.
