In November 1903 a revolt in Panama declared independence, and US warships made sure Colombian troops could not land to stop it. Within about two weeks the new government's representative, a Frenchman named Philippe Bunau-Varilla, signed a treaty giving the United States control of a Canal Zone across the country, in perpetuity. Many Panamanians resented the deal from the start, and it became a source of tension in Latin America for decades.

sections.key: Controlling the mosquitoes that spread yellow fever and malaria made the canal possible.
sections.b:
Work began in 1904, and at first yellow fever returned and workers fled. The breakthrough came from medicine. Building on Carlos Finlay's theory and Walter Reed's experiments in Cuba, doctors had confirmed that yellow fever was spread by mosquitoes, while malaria was carried by a different mosquito.

Dr William Gorgas, the chief sanitary officer, launched a vast campaign. Teams drained swamps, spread oil on standing water, fumigated buildings, screened windows and installed piped water so people no longer stored it in open barrels. By 1906 yellow fever had been eliminated from the zone, and malaria deaths fell sharply. It was one of the great public health victories in history, and without it the canal would likely have failed again.

sections.key: Engineers lifted ships over the land with locks and a huge lake, using Caribbean labour paid under a segregated system.
sections.b:
Chief engineers John Stevens and later George Goethals abandoned the sea-level idea. They dammed the Chagres River at Gatun, creating then the largest artificial lake in the world. Ships climb through giant locks, cross the lake about 26 metres above sea level, then descend through more locks. The hardest work was the Culebra Cut through the mountainous spine of the isthmus, where landslides repeatedly buried months of digging. On 15 August 1914 the cargo ship SS Ancon made the first official transit.

Most labour came from the Caribbean, especially Barbados and Jamaica, doing the most dangerous jobs. White Americans were paid in gold, most other workers in silver, with poorer housing and food. Over 5,000 workers died in the American years.

sections.key: Panama took full control of the canal at the end of 1999, but the canal still depends on rain to work.
sections.b:
Resentment of the Canal Zone, a slice of US-run territory cutting through the middle of Panama, grew through the twentieth century. In 1964 riots over flying the Panamanian flag in the zone left more than twenty people dead. In 1977 US President Jimmy Carter and Panama's leader Omar Torrijos signed treaties to transfer the canal. On 31 December 1999 Panama took full control.

Since then it has run the canal profitably and opened larger locks in 2016 to take bigger ships. The canal still depends on rain to fill Gatun Lake, and in 2023 a severe drought forced limits on the number of ships that could pass, a reminder that even great engineering relies on nature.

quiz.q: Why did the French effort to build the canal fail?
o: They ran out of steel for the locks
Landslides, floods and fever overwhelmed it
The United States invaded the work site
Panama refused to allow any digging
quiz.e: Landslides, floods and fever defeated de Lesseps' plan.

quiz.q: How did the United States gain control of the canal route?
o: It bought the land outright from Spain
It conquered Panama in a short war
Colombia freely gave up the route to it
It backed Panama's revolt, then won a treaty
quiz.e: After Colombia rejected the deal, the US supported a revolt and then secured the zone by treaty.

quiz.q: What breakthrough made construction possible?
o: Controlling disease-carrying mosquitoes
Developing much stronger dynamite
Building faster ocean steamships
Finding a cheaper source of steel
quiz.e: Draining swamps and screening homes cut disease, which was the main killer.

quiz.q: How do ships cross the high ground of Panama?
o: Through a long tunnel under the hills
Up through locks to a lake and back down
On a giant railway across the isthmus
By sailing at sea level the whole way
quiz.e: The locks lift ships to Gatun Lake and lower them on the other side.

quiz.q: Why did a drought in 2023 limit ships using the canal?
o: The locks depend on rain-fed Gatun Lake
Sea levels dropped below the canal floor
Panama closed it for a major upgrade
Fuel shortages stopped the locks working
quiz.e: Even great engineering depends on nature.

LESSONS.push: The Panama Canal was only possible after doctors beat a tiny enemy. Which one?

LESSONS.title: Bismarck and the making of Germany
LESSONS.hook: In 1860 there was no country called Germany, just dozens of separate states. Eleven years later a German empire was proclaimed in a French palace, built by one man's three wars.

sections.key: Bismarck argued that Germany would be united by force rather than speeches and votes, the supposed mistake of 1848.
sections.b:
After 1815 the German lands formed a loose Confederation of 39 states, from great powers like Austria and Prussia to tiny free cities like Hamburg. Prussia grew rich through industry and the Zollverein, a customs union that excluded Austria. In 1848 an elected parliament in Frankfurt tried to unite Germany, and failed.

In 1862 King Wilhelm I was stuck in a fight with parliament over funding for a bigger army. He appointed Otto von Bismarck, a ruthless Junker diplomat, who simply carried on collecting taxes without approval. He declared that the great questions of the day would be decided not by speeches and majority votes, but by iron and blood. The phrase came to define his career.

sections.key: Bismarck won short wars against Denmark, Austria and France by isolating each enemy first.
sections.b:
Bismarck's genius lay in fighting one enemy at a time, ensuring no other power joined in. In 1864 Prussia and Austria together defeated Denmark over Schleswig and Holstein. Bismarck then used disputes over running those duchies to provoke Austria.

In 1866 the Prussian army, using railways, telegraphs and fast-firing breech-loading rifles, crushed Austria at Königgrätz in a war lasting only weeks. Bismarck insisted on mild terms so Austria would not seek revenge, but it was pushed out of German affairs. Prussia annexed several states and formed the North German Confederation. Only the southern states, including Bavaria, remained outside. Bismarck believed a war with France would bring them in.

sections.key: Bismarck edited a royal telegram to provoke France into war, then saw the German Empire proclaimed at Versailles.
sections.b:
In 1870 a relative of the Prussian king was offered the Spanish throne. France protested and it was withdrawn, but France pressed further, demanding at Ems a promise it would never be renewed. Wilhelm politely declined and telegraphed Bismarck. Bismarck shortened the message so the king seemed to have curtly snubbed the ambassador. The French public was outraged and France declared war, appearing the aggressor. The southern states, bound by defensive alliances, joined Prussia.

At Sedan Napoleon III was captured. On 18 January 1871, with Paris besieged, Wilhelm I was proclaimed Kaiser in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles, a deliberate humiliation. France paid an indemnity and gave up Alsace and much of Lorraine.

sections.key: Bismarck repressed Catholics and socialists, yet created the world's first national social insurance to win workers over.
sections.b:
As chancellor, Bismarck saw enemies of the new empire everywhere. In the 1870s he waged the Kulturkampf against the power of the Catholic Church, which backfired by strengthening Catholic political loyalty. He then turned on the socialist movement, banning its organisations from 1878.

Yet alongside repression came a remarkable innovation. To win workers away from socialism, he introduced national health insurance in 1883, accident insurance in 1884, and old age and disability pensions in 1889. Workers, employers and the state shared the costs. It was the first system of its kind in the world and became a model for many other countries. His motives were conservative, but the legacy proved lasting.

sections.key: Bismarck kept the peace through a web of alliances that his successors let fall apart.
sections.b:
After 1871 Bismarck declared Germany satisfied. His aim was to prevent a war that could destroy what he had built, especially a two-front war against France and Russia. He presented himself as an honest broker at the Congress of Berlin in 1878, and wove a network of treaties: the Dual Alliance with Austria-Hungary in 1879, later the Triple Alliance with Italy, and a secret Reinsurance Treaty with Russia in 1887.

In 1888 the young Wilhelm II came to the throne and clashed with the old chancellor, who was forced to resign in 1890. The treaty with Russia was not renewed, and Russia soon allied with France. The isolation Bismarck feared was beginning to take shape, setting the stage for 1914.

quiz.q: What did Bismarck mean by ‘iron and blood’?
o: That Germany needed more steel mills
That long parliamentary debate would decide
That force, not votes, would settle it
That Austria should lead unification
quiz.e: He believed the 1848 parliamentarians had failed because they relied on words, not power.

quiz.q: What made Bismarck's three wars so effective?
o: He fought all his enemies at the same time
He relied almost entirely on naval power
He kept his army away from railways
He isolated each enemy and fought short wars
quiz.e: One enemy at a time, with no outside help, kept the wars quick and decisive.

quiz.q: What did Bismarck do with the Ems Telegram?
o: He destroyed it before it reached anyone
He edited it so the king seemed to insult France
He sent it to Russia as a warning
He had it translated into French for the press
quiz.e: The edit inflamed French opinion, so France appeared to be the aggressor.

quiz.q: Why did Bismarck introduce national social insurance?
o: To win workers away from socialism
Because Austria insisted on it
To help pay for the new army
To copy a system used in Britain
quiz.e: His motives were conservative, but he created the world's first system of its kind.

quiz.q: What happened after Bismarck was forced out in 1890?
o: Germany shrank its army to avoid another war
The Russian treaty lapsed and Russia chose France
Germany joined France against Austria-Hungary
Wilhelm II abdicated less than a year later
quiz.e: The isolation he had feared began to take shape.

LESSONS.push: Bismarck edited one telegram and helped start a war. Here's how.

LESSONS.title: 1848: the year Europe caught fire
LESSONS.hook: In a few weeks of 1848, revolutions broke out in dozens of cities across Europe. Kings fled, ministers resigned and constitutions were promised. Within two years almost all of it had been undone.

sections.key: Repressive rule, new ideas and a hunger crisis combined to make Europe ready to explode in 1848.
sections.b:
After 1815, Europe's great powers tried to restore order under conservative monarchs. Austria's Prince Metternich symbolised the system of censorship, secret police and suspicion of change. Beneath the surface pressures were building. Liberals wanted constitutions, elected parliaments and a free press. Nationalists wanted peoples such as Germans, Italians, Hungarians and Poles to govern themselves. Industrialisation was creating a new urban working class in grim conditions.

Then, in the mid 1840s, potato blight and poor grain harvests sent food prices soaring, followed by a financial crisis and mass unemployment in 1847. Hungry, angry crowds and frustrated middle class reformers were a combustible mix.

sections.key: The overthrow of France's king in February 1848 set off revolutions in city after city within weeks.
sections.b:
A revolt in Palermo came first, in January, but Paris ignited the continent. King Louis-Philippe banned political banquets used by reformers. In February protests turned into street fighting, soldiers fired on a crowd, and within days the king fled to England. The Second Republic gave all adult men the vote, abolished slavery in French colonies and created national workshops for the unemployed.

News travelled fast by rail, telegraph and newspaper. In March Metternich resigned and fled Vienna. In Berlin, after deadly barricade fighting, King Frederick William IV promised a constitution. Milan drove out the Austrians, and Hungary under Lajos Kossuth won sweeping self-government. In weeks, governments that seemed immovable gave way to demands that a year earlier meant prison.

sections.key: German liberals elected a national parliament to unite Germany, but it had no army, no money and no ruler willing to accept its crown.
sections.b:
In May 1848 an elected assembly met in St Paul's Church in Frankfurt to create a united, constitutional Germany. Its members were mostly lawyers, professors and civil servants. They debated long and earnestly, drawing up basic rights including freedom of speech and equality before the law.

But they faced hard questions. Should Germany include German-speaking Austria and its many non-German peoples? And the parliament had no army or money of its own. In 1849 it offered the crown of a united Germany to Frederick William IV of Prussia. He refused a crown offered by an elected assembly rather than by fellow princes. The parliament soon dissolved, and its remnant was dispersed by troops.

sections.key: Revolutionaries divided among themselves while the armies stayed loyal to the old rulers.
sections.b:
The revolutions failed for several connected reasons. Middle class liberals wanted constitutions and order, while workers wanted jobs and social change, and the two soon feared each other. In Paris, closing the national workshops sparked the bloody June Days uprising, crushed by the army with thousands killed.

Nationalities quarrelled too: Hungarians demanded freedom from Austria while denying it to Croats and Romanians within Hungary. Above all, the armies mostly stayed loyal to their monarchs. In late 1848 Austrian troops retook Vienna, and young Franz Joseph became emperor. In 1849 Russian troops helped crush Hungary. In France, voters elected Louis-Napoleon Bonaparte president, and in 1851 he seized power and soon declared himself emperor.

sections.key: Though defeated, 1848 freed Austria's peasants, spread constitutions and sent exiled Forty-Eighters across the world.
sections.b:
Some changes endured. In the Austrian Empire, peasants were freed from compulsory labour owed to landlords, and this was never reversed. Prussia kept a limited constitution and parliament. Denmark became a constitutional monarchy in 1849, the Netherlands liberalised its constitution, and Switzerland adopted a federal constitution. Piedmont-Sardinia kept its constitution and later led Italian unification. Rulers learned that ignoring public opinion was dangerous, and increasingly used nationalism for their own ends, as Bismarck later did.

Thousands of exiled Germans, the Forty-Eighters, emigrated to the United States, some later fighting for the Union. Britain's Chartists held a huge London meeting in April 1848 but fizzled out. The Communist Manifesto appeared in February 1848 but had little influence that year.

quiz.q: What economic troubles helped trigger the revolutions?
o: A gold rush that drained workers from farms
A sudden boom in wages and employment
Failed harvests and a financial crisis
A ban on trade with the Americas
quiz.e: Hunger and unemployment turned discontent into revolt.

quiz.q: Why did the Paris revolution of February 1848 matter so much?
o: It ended every monarchy in Europe at once
It proved a king could be overthrown
It was won with help from foreign armies
It gave women the vote across Europe
quiz.e: News travelled fast, and liberals elsewhere concluded that if Paris could do it, so could they.

quiz.q: Why did the Frankfurt Parliament fail to unite Germany?
o: France invaded Frankfurt and shut it down
It had no army, and Prussia's king refused it
Voters rejected its constitution in a referendum
Its members refused to meet after the first week
quiz.e: Without power of its own, it relied on rulers who then rejected it.

quiz.q: Which factor most helped the old rulers regain control?
o: Railways stopped carrying news
Armies stayed loyal to their monarchs
Britain invaded to restore the kings
The revolutionaries lost every election
quiz.e: Divided revolutionaries could not match loyal armies.

quiz.q: Which change in the Austrian Empire outlasted the revolutions?
o: A republic ruled by elected leaders
Independence for Hungary from Austria
The end of forced peasant labour dues
Votes for every adult in the empire
quiz.e: Peasants stayed free of the old labour dues even after the revolution was crushed.

LESSONS.push: In 1848 kings fell across Europe in weeks. Why did so little of it last?

LESSONS.title: Australia's Vietnam War
LESSONS.hook: It was Australia's longest war of the twentieth century and its most divisive. Young men were chosen for it by a lottery of birthdays, and many came home to silence.

sections.key: Fear of communism spreading through Asia, and the wish to keep the United States close, drew Australia into Vietnam.
sections.b:
After the Second World War, Australian leaders feared communism in Asia, especially after China's communist victory in 1949 and the Korean War. The domino theory held that if one country fell, its neighbours would follow until the threat reached Australia. Vietnam was divided in 1954 into a communist North and non-communist South, and an insurgency grew in the South. Australia also wanted to strengthen its alliance with the United States, formalised in the ANZUS treaty of 1951. In 1962 it sent thirty military advisers.

In April 1965 Prime Minister Robert Menzies announced an infantry battalion, saying South Vietnam had requested help, a claim later questioned. From 1966 the 1st Australian Task Force at Nui Dat focused on patient jungle patrolling.

sections.key: National service selected twenty-year-old men by drawing birth dates, and conscripts could be sent to Vietnam.
sections.b:
In 1964 the government introduced national service. Twenty-year-old men had to register, and a lottery drew birth dates from a barrel. If yours was drawn, you could be called up for two years. From 1965 these conscripts, often called nashos, could be sent overseas, including to Vietnam.

Around 15,000 national servicemen served there, and some were killed. The randomness troubled many Australians. A young man's future, and perhaps his life, could depend on whether a marble bearing his birth date came out of a barrel. Some refused to register or serve, and a few were jailed. The ballot made the war deeply personal for families across the country.

sections.key: In August 1966 a single Australian company held off a much larger enemy force in a rubber plantation.
sections.b:
On 18 August 1966, D Company of the 6th Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment, about 105 men, was patrolling near Nui Dat in a rubber plantation called Long Tan. In a tropical downpour they met a far larger force of Viet Cong and North Vietnamese troops.

For several hours the Australians, with three New Zealand artillery observers, fought off repeated attacks, helped by intense artillery fire from the base and an ammunition drop by helicopter. As darkness fell, armoured personnel carriers arrived and the attackers withdrew. Eighteen Australians were killed. Enemy losses were far higher, though exact numbers are disputed. Long Tan became the best-known Australian action of the war, and 18 August is now Vietnam Veterans Day.

sections.key: As the war dragged on without victory, opposition grew into some of the largest protests in Australian history.
sections.b:
At first many Australians supported the war, but doubts grew as it dragged on, particularly after the Tet Offensive of 1968 showed the enemy was far from beaten. Television brought images of the fighting into lounge rooms. Groups such as Save Our Sons, formed by mothers of possible conscripts, campaigned against the ballot.

In May 1970 the Moratorium marches brought huge crowds into cities around Australia. In Melbourne, led by Labor politician Jim Cairns, estimates ranged from 70,000 to 100,000. Supporters of the war saw protesters as disloyal; many protesters saw the government sending young men to die for an unwinnable cause. The divide split families, churches and friendships.

sections.key: Australian troops withdrew by 1972, but many veterans came home to indifference and were recognised only years later.
sections.b:
As the United States reduced its forces, Australia followed. The task force left Phuoc Tuy in late 1971. In December 1972 the Whitlam government ended conscription and freed men jailed for refusing to serve. Almost 60,000 Australians served and around 520 died. Vietnamese deaths ran into the millions. Saigon fell in April 1975, and Australia later resettled tens of thousands of Vietnamese refugees.

Most veterans came home individually, often quietly, expected to slip back into ordinary life. Some were abused by protesters, and some older veterans' groups were slow to welcome them. Many struggled with post-traumatic stress, and concerns grew about Agent Orange, investigated by a Royal Commission in the 1980s. In October 1987 tens of thousands marched in Sydney's Welcome Home parade, and a national memorial opened in Canberra in 1992.

quiz.q: What was the domino theory?
o: A plan to build railways across Asia
A strategy for winning Australian elections
Falling countries would drag down neighbours
A theory about growth in Asian economies
quiz.e: Australian leaders feared communism would spread south until it reached Australia.

quiz.q: How were national servicemen selected?
o: By exam results
By height and weight
By volunteering only
By a ballot of birth dates
quiz.e: A lottery of birthdays decided which twenty-year-olds were called up.

quiz.q: How did the outnumbered Australians hold on at Long Tan?
o: A tank squadron arrived within minutes
Artillery fire and an ammunition drop
The enemy withdrew at first contact
Navy gunfire from the coast supported them
quiz.e: Support from the base kept them fighting until armoured carriers arrived.

quiz.q: Why did support for the war erode?
o: Conscription was dropped before troops arrived
Television was banned from the battlefield
The enemy proved far from beaten after Tet
The United States asked Australia to leave
quiz.e: Doubts grew as victory seemed out of reach.

quiz.q: What did many veterans face when they returned?
o: A national parade on the day they landed
Indifference, then recognition years later
Immediate pensions and honours for all
Official bans on talking about service
quiz.e: Recognition came slowly, culminating in the 1987 Welcome Home parade.

LESSONS.push: Australia chose conscripts by drawing birthdays from a barrel. Here's how it worked.

LESSONS.title: Apartheid: rise and fall
LESSONS.hook: For more than four decades, South Africa's laws sorted every person by race and decided where they could live, work, love and vote. Then, against most predictions, the system was dismantled without the all-out civil war many had feared.

sections.key: After 1948, South Africa's government turned long-standing discrimination into a total legal system that classified everyone by race.
sections.b:
Discrimination long predated apartheid. When the Union of South Africa formed in 1910, most black people were denied the vote. The Natives Land Act of 1913 restricted black land ownership, and pass laws controlled travel and work. In 1912 black leaders founded what became the African National Congress. The word apartheid, Afrikaans for apartness, entered politics in the 1940s.

In 1948 the National Party won office and built the system. The Population Registration Act of 1950 classified everyone as white, coloured, Indian or black. Cross-racial marriage was banned. The Group Areas Act created separate residential areas, and communities such as District Six and Sophiatown were bulldozed. Separate and unequal schools, hospitals and beaches followed, and Bantu Education prepared black children for labouring lives.

sections.key: Apartheid's planners tried to strip black South Africans of citizenship by assigning them to separate ‘homelands’.
sections.b:
The most ambitious part of apartheid was the homeland system. The government divided black South Africans into ethnic groups and assigned each to a territory, or Bantustan, often scattered fragments of poor land. The aim was to declare these homelands independent, so black people would become citizens of them rather than of South Africa, leaving a white-ruled state with no black citizens at all.

Four homelands, including Transkei, were declared independent, though almost no other country recognised them. Millions were forcibly moved there in the 1960s and 1970s, often to places with few jobs or services. Workers who needed city jobs became migrants in their own country, living in hostels far from their families.

sections.key: Peaceful protest was met with bullets and bans, pushing the resistance towards armed struggle and a new generation of youth revolt.
sections.b:
Through the 1950s the ANC led nonviolent campaigns and in 1955 adopted the Freedom Charter. On 21 March 1960 at Sharpeville, police opened fire on a pass-law protest, killing 69 people. The ANC was banned. Nelson Mandela and others concluded that peaceful protest was failing, and in 1961 Umkhonto we Sizwe began sabotage. After the Rivonia trial in 1964 Mandela was sentenced to life.

On 16 June 1976 thousands of Soweto students marched against being taught some subjects in Afrikaans. Police opened fire, and a photograph of dying twelve-year-old Hector Pieterson travelled the world. Hundreds were killed in the unrest. Steve Biko's Black Consciousness movement urged pride; he died in police custody in 1977. In the 1980s protests and boycotts led to states of emergency.

sections.key: Sanctions and boycotts isolated South Africa, though historians debate how much they mattered compared with internal resistance.
sections.b:
International pressure grew steadily. The United Nations condemned apartheid, and many countries imposed trade, arms and financial sanctions, especially in the 1980s. Banks refused new loans and companies pulled out, damaging an already struggling economy.

Sport mattered deeply to many white South Africans, and sporting boycotts struck at their sense of belonging in the world. South Africa was excluded from the Olympics for decades. In Australia, a 1971 tour by the Springbok rugby team sparked large protests and clashes, and later governments of both major parties took strong anti-apartheid positions in the Commonwealth. Historians debate how much sanctions alone forced change compared with internal resistance and economic decline, but together they made apartheid increasingly costly to keep.

sections.key: Despite violence, negotiations led to South Africa's first fully democratic election in 1994 and Mandela's presidency.
sections.b:
By the late 1980s many in government realised apartheid could not survive. On 2 February 1990 President F. W. de Klerk announced the ANC would be legalised. On 11 February Nelson Mandela walked out of prison after 27 years. Negotiations were interrupted by violence that killed thousands. In 1993 the assassination of ANC leader Chris Hani brought the country to the brink, but Mandela's appeal for calm held. He and de Klerk shared the Nobel Peace Prize.

On 27 April 1994 South Africans of every race voted together for the first time, many queueing for hours. The ANC won about 62 per cent, and Mandela became president of a government of national unity. A Truth and Reconciliation Commission heard testimony. Apartheid law was gone, but its economic legacy of deep inequality remains.

quiz.q: What did the Population Registration Act of 1950 do?
o: Gave every adult South African the vote
Created a national register of farms
Placed each person in a racial group
Abolished the pass laws across the country
quiz.e: Racial classification was the foundation for the rest of the apartheid system.

quiz.q: What was the goal of the homeland system?
o: To give black South Africans far more farmland
To remove their South African citizenship
To build new cities shared by all races
To end the pass laws within a generation
quiz.e: Independent homelands would have left a white-ruled state with no black citizens.

quiz.q: Why did leaders such as Mandela turn to armed struggle?
o: They had just won a national election
Peaceful protest met bullets and bans
The United Nations had formally ordered it
Sanctions had failed to have any effect
quiz.e: After the ANC was banned, they concluded peaceful protest alone was failing.

quiz.q: What do historians say about sanctions and boycotts?
o: They had almost no effect on South Africa
They alone ended apartheid in 1990
They worked only in sport and in Australia
They added to other pressures on apartheid
quiz.e: Historians debate sanctions' share, but all pressures together made apartheid costly to keep.

quiz.q: What helped South Africa avoid civil war during the transition?
o: Foreign troops took control of the country
Negotiations, and Mandela's call for calm
The army seized power for several years
Apartheid laws were kept by agreement
quiz.e: Tense negotiations continued despite violence, and calm held.

LESSONS.push: A system of racial laws ended in 1994 without the civil war many predicted. Why?

LESSONS.title: Mao's China: the Great Leap and the Cultural Revolution
LESSONS.hook: Mao Zedong set out to transform China into a modern socialist power within a generation. Two of his campaigns caused one of the deadliest famines in history and a decade of political terror.

sections.key: After winning power in 1949, Mao remade society by force, then punished the people who criticised him.
sections.b:
On 1 October 1949, Mao Zedong proclaimed the People's Republic of China after the Communists beat Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalists, who retreated to Taiwan. Many welcomed peace after decades of invasion, warlords and civil war. Land reform gave land to peasants through public ‘struggle sessions’ in which many landlords were killed. Estimates of deaths in these campaigns range from several hundred thousand to several million. Private businesses were nationalised.

In 1956 Mao invited criticism: ‘let a hundred flowers bloom’. When it turned to the party's right to rule, he reversed course. The 1957 Anti-Rightist Campaign labelled about 550,000 people, many of them teachers, writers and scientists, as ‘rightists’, and many were sent to labour camps. Honest criticism became dangerous, and that silence had disastrous consequences.

sections.key: From 1958, Mao tried to turn China into an industrial power almost overnight through mass mobilisation.
sections.b:
In 1958 Mao launched the Great Leap Forward, aiming to overtake Britain in steel production within about fifteen years and to prove that mass enthusiasm could beat Soviet-style caution. Hundreds of millions of peasants were organised into vast people's communes, where private plots were abolished and families ate in communal canteens.

Millions of backyard furnaces consumed pots, pans and tools, and much of the steel they made was useless. Farmers were pulled from the fields to work on furnaces and dams. Pseudo-scientific methods such as very close planting and deep ploughing were imposed. A campaign against the Four Pests killed huge numbers of sparrows, and crop-eating insects flourished.

sections.key: Inflated harvest reports led the state to seize grain that villagers needed, causing one of history's deadliest famines.
sections.b:
Local officials, terrified of being labelled rightists, reported fantastic harvests that never existed. The state took grain based on those false figures, leaving many villages with little or nothing to eat, while China continued to export grain. In 1959 Defence Minister Peng Dehuai privately criticised the Leap in a letter to Mao. Mao purged him, and the campaign was pushed even harder.

The famine of 1959 to 1961 followed. Estimates of excess deaths range from around fifteen million to more than forty million, and many demographers put it near thirty million. It was largely caused by policy. By the early 1960s, Liu Shaoqi and Deng Xiaoping quietly allowed private plots and markets again, and food production slowly recovered.

sections.key: In 1966 Mao unleashed young Red Guards against officials, teachers and tradition, and turned on his own colleagues.
sections.b:
Mao stepped back from running the economy but grew suspicious. He believed the party was becoming a privileged elite, that the Soviet Union showed how a revolution could decay, and he resented his lost authority. His cult of personality grew, helped by Defence Minister Lin Biao, whose army published the Little Red Book.

In 1966 Mao launched the Cultural Revolution, calling on young people to attack ‘bourgeois’ influences. Red Guards waved the Little Red Book at huge Tiananmen Square rallies. They humiliated, beat and sometimes killed teachers and officials, and destroyed books, temples and historic sites in a campaign against the ‘Four Olds’: old customs, culture, habits and ideas. Liu Shaoqi was purged and died in custody in 1969. Deng Xiaoping was sent to work in a tractor factory. Rival factions fought, and the army restored order.

sections.key: Political violence lasted a decade, and China's leaders later gave a carefully limited verdict on Mao's rule.
sections.b:
From 1968 Mao sent an estimated sixteen to seventeen million urban youths ‘down to the countryside’ to learn from peasants. Many lost their education, an experience that shaped a generation, including Xi Jinping. In 1971 Lin Biao, Mao's chosen successor, died in a plane crash in Mongolia after apparently fleeing a failed plot, though details remain murky. Estimates of deaths in the Cultural Revolution range from hundreds of thousands to two million or more.

Mao died on 9 September 1976, and within a month the Gang of Four, including his widow Jiang Qing, were arrested. Deng Xiaoping then opened China to markets. A 1981 party resolution called the Cultural Revolution a catastrophe but said Mao's contributions outweighed his errors. Research remains restricted, so estimates still vary.

quiz.q: What lesson did people take from the Anti-Rightist Campaign?
o: Open criticism of the party was dangerous
Intellectuals would now run policy
Landlords could safely return
Foreign advice should be sought
quiz.e: Punishing those who spoke up taught everyone to stay silent, which proved disastrous later.

quiz.q: Why did the Great Leap Forward's steel drive and farming methods backfire?
o: Backyard furnaces made high-quality steel cheaply
Communes raised private plots for every family
Killing sparrows helped crops to flourish
Labour left farms and the steel was useless
quiz.e: Labour was pulled from farming into poor-quality projects, and harmful methods were imposed from above.

quiz.q: How did false harvest reports help cause the famine?
o: Farmers were told to sell grain at a loss
Officials hid grain to share it later
The state took grain using inflated figures
Imports were cut after the reports
quiz.e: Grain taken on the basis of imaginary harvests left villages with too little to eat.

quiz.q: What did Mao call on young people to do in 1966?
o: Rebuild the economy under local officials
Return quietly to their classrooms
Attack ‘bourgeois’ ideas and old customs
Defend the party's older leaders
quiz.e: The Cultural Revolution turned Red Guards against officials, teachers and tradition.

quiz.q: Why do estimates of the Cultural Revolution's human toll vary so widely?
o: Records were published in full but disputed
Archives are restricted and research limited
The campaign lasted only a few months
Most of those affected later left China
quiz.e: Limited access to archives and research leaves historians working with uncertain evidence.

LESSONS.push: Officials reported harvests that never existed. What followed was sobering.

LESSONS.title: Backing up: never lose your photos again
LESSONS.hook: In 1998, a single mistyped command wiped out most of Pixar's Toy Story 2. What saved the film was a backup nobody knew existed.

sections.key: Data is lost through ordinary accidents and failures, even at world-class studios, so it can happen to you.
sections.b:
In 1998, while Pixar was making Toy Story 2, someone ran a command that began deleting the film's files from the shared drives. Characters, sets and animation disappeared as staff watched. The studio's regular backups turned out not to be working properly. The film was rescued because technical director Galyn Susman, working from home after having a baby, had a fairly recent copy on her home computer. It was carefully driven back to the studio and most of the work was restored.

Data vanishes in ordinary ways: a phone dropped in the surf, a stolen laptop, a drive that quietly fails, an accidental delete, a fire or flood. Every drive eventually fails. The question is not whether something will go wrong, but whether you will lose anything when it does.

sections.key: Keep three copies of what matters, on two kinds of storage, with one copy offsite.
sections.b:
A widely quoted rule of thumb, popularised by photographer Peter Krogh, is 3-2-1. Keep at least three copies of anything important: the original plus two backups. Store them on at least two different kinds of storage, such as your computer's internal drive and an external drive, so one type of failure cannot take them all.

Keep at least one copy offsite, somewhere physically separate, so a fire, flood or burglary at home leaves something behind. Today that is usually a cloud backup service, but a drive kept at a relative's house or your workplace also counts. The rule is not magic, but it makes you think about every way your data could be destroyed at once.

sections.key: Sync copies your mistakes everywhere, so keep a backup that mistakes and malware cannot reach.
sections.b:
Many people assume their files are safe in iCloud, Google Drive, OneDrive or Dropbox. Most of these are built mainly to sync, keeping files identical across devices. So a deleted folder or overwritten document can spread to every device within seconds. Many keep deleted files and older versions for a limited time, so learn how long and how to restore them.

Ransomware is software that encrypts your files and demands payment, often in cryptocurrency, for the key. Paying guarantees nothing and funds criminals. A drive that is permanently plugged in can be encrypted too. Keep a backup drive unplugged except during backups, or use a cloud service that keeps older versions. The Australian Cyber Security Centre lists regular backups among its essential strategies.

sections.key: Your phone probably holds your most irreplaceable memories, so check that it really backs itself up.
sections.b:
For many people the irreplaceable files are photos and videos of children, travels and people who are no longer here. Most now live on a phone, which is easy to lose, drop or break. iPhones and Android phones can both back up automatically to the cloud, but the free storage is often small. Once it fills up, backups can silently stop.

Check your phone's settings to see when it last backed up successfully. Paying a few dollars a month for more storage is cheap insurance. Every so often, download your photo library to a computer or external drive as well, so your memories do not depend on a single company or account login.

sections.key: A backup you have never restored from is only a hope, and the one that runs by itself is the one that happens.
sections.b:
Pixar's backups were running, or so everyone thought, until the day they were needed. Every few months, pick a random file or photo and try to recover it from each backup. Check that it opens. Make sure you know your cloud password and have two-factor authentication sorted, or your backup may be locked behind a login you cannot remember on the day your phone is lost.

Nobody remembers to copy files by hand every week, so automate. Turn on automatic phone backups, use Time Machine on a Mac or File History on Windows with an external drive, and add a cloud service for the offsite copy. Start with photos, important documents and tax records. Any backup is infinitely better than none.

quiz.q: What does the Toy Story 2 story show about backups?
o: Backups are only needed for large companies
Even top studios can nearly lose everything
Home computers are safer than shared drives
Deleted files can always be recovered easily
quiz.e: If a world-class studio nearly lost its film, ordinary people can lose their photos too.

quiz.q: Why does the 3-2-1 rule include an offsite copy?
o: Home disasters such as fire cannot reach it
It speeds up the copying process
Offsite copies never need to be tested
It replaces the need for a second copy
quiz.e: A physically separate copy survives disasters that destroy everything kept in one place.

quiz.q: Why is a syncing service not a true backup on its own?
o: It cannot store photos or documents
It only works on one device at a time
It deletes files after a fixed number of days
A deletion or overwrite can spread everywhere
quiz.e: Sync keeps devices identical, so mistakes copy everywhere unless older versions are kept.

quiz.q: What can quietly stop a phone's cloud backup from working?
o: Changing the phone's ringtone
Turning the screen off overnight
Updating the phone's apps
Free storage filling up
quiz.e: When storage is full, backups can silently stop, so check the date of the last successful backup.

quiz.q: Why should you restore a random file from your backup every few months?
o: To free up space on your drive
To make the next backup run faster
To check it works before you need it
To avoid paying for cloud storage
quiz.e: Only a tested restore proves you have the copies you believe you have.

LESSONS.push: A mistyped command wiped out a Pixar film. Something unexpected saved it.

LESSONS.title: Six knots worth knowing
LESSONS.hook: Most people know one knot and use it for everything. Sailors, climbers and truckies know better, and a handful of knots will cover almost anything you need.

sections.key: Learn the basic rope terms, and remember the reef knot suits bandages and parcels but not joining ropes under load.
sections.b:
Knot instructions use a small vocabulary. The working end is the end you move to tie the knot. The standing part is the rest of the rope, often the part under load. A bight is a U-shaped fold, and a loop is a bight where the rope crosses itself. Almost every knot weakens a rope, so climbing or lifting people needs proper training.

The reef knot, or square knot, is right over left, then left over right. It lies flat, so it suits bandages, slings and parcels. Get the second step wrong and you have a granny knot, which slips. To join two ropes under strain, a sheet bend is far more secure, because a reef knot can capsize.

sections.key: The bowline makes a fixed loop that will not slip and stays easy to untie, even after a heavy load.
sections.b:
Pronounced ‘boh-lin’, the bowline has been called the king of knots. It forms a loop at the end of a rope that does not tighten or slide. That makes it useful for tying a rope around a tree or post, or, in a rescue, a person. Children learn it with a story: make a small loop, then the rabbit (the working end) comes up out of the hole, around the tree and back down the hole.

After taking a heavy load, a bowline can still be loosened by pushing the collar. Its weakness is that it can work loose when not under load, so climbers usually prefer a figure-eight loop.

sections.key: A clove hitch is quick but can slip, while a round turn and two half hitches holds even under strain.
sections.b:
The clove hitch is two turns around a pole, the second crossing over the first and tucked under itself. It is fast to tie and easy to adjust and undo. It secures boat fenders, starts lashings and ties off tent lines and garden stakes. It is not set-and-forget: if the post rotates or the load changes direction, it can work loose. For a long-term tie, add half hitches.

If a rope is already under tension, perhaps from a boat drifting away, use a round turn and two half hitches. Pass the rope around the object twice, so friction takes most of the load. Then make a half hitch around the standing part, and repeat it in the same direction. It is strong, secure and easy to untie after a strain. Boaties use it for mooring.

sections.key: A figure-eight stops a rope escaping, and a trucker's hitch lets you pull a load down tight.
sections.b:
A stopper knot keeps a rope from escaping. An overhand knot works but can jam tight. The figure-eight is better: make a loop, pass the end around the standing part, then back through the loop. It is bulkier, so it is less likely to pull through, and easier to untie. Sailors use it on lines, and it suits drawstrings and clotheslines. Threaded back along itself, it forms the loop climbers rely on.

The trucker's hitch works like a simple pulley. Make a fixed loop partway along the rope, pass the working end around an anchor point such as a tie-down hook, then back through the loop. The mechanical advantage is theoretically about three to one, though friction reduces it. Pinch it, secure with two half hitches, and recheck the load after a few kilometres.

sections.key: Knots are learned by the hands, not the eyes, so practise until you can tie them without thinking.
sections.b:
Reading about knots is a little like reading about swimming. It only sticks once you have done it many times. Keep a short length of rope near the couch and tie each knot while watching television until you can do it without looking.

Then practise in awkward conditions: with the rope behind a post, in the dark, or with cold hands. That is when you will actually need it, while a tarp flaps in a storm or a boat drifts from the jetty. Start with the bowline, the clove hitch and the round turn with two half hitches. Those three alone will handle most everyday jobs.

quiz.q: What is the reef knot's main weakness?
o: It is too bulky to use on bandages
It takes far too long to tie
It can capsize if ropes are pulled hard
It cannot be tied with thick rope
quiz.e: For joining ropes under strain, a sheet bend is more secure than a reef knot.

quiz.q: Why is the bowline so useful?
o: It tightens down hard on whatever it holds
It makes a fixed loop that stays easy to untie
It joins two ropes of different thickness
It stays secure even when left completely slack
quiz.e: The bowline's loop stays fixed under load and can still be loosened afterwards.

quiz.q: Why use a round turn and two half hitches on a rope already under tension?
o: Friction from the wraps holds the strain
It is quicker to tie than a clove hitch
It suits only thin, slippery rope
It gives you a three-to-one pull
quiz.e: Friction from the round turn holds the strain, giving you time to tie the hitches.

quiz.q: What does the trucker's hitch give you?
o: A simple pulley effect to tension a load
A knot that cannot be untied
A loop that never changes size
A stopper for the end of a line
quiz.e: It multiplies your pull, so you can tension the rope more than you could by hand.

quiz.q: What is the best way to learn knots so they work when needed?
o: Read instructions until you remember them
Watch animations once and rely on memory
Learn as many knots as possible at once
Practise by hand until it is automatic
quiz.e: Hands learn knots through repetition, so practise until it needs no thought.

LESSONS.push: The reef knot is famous, yet it can fail under strain. Why?

LESSONS.title: Mending clothes: buttons, seams and holes
LESSONS.hook: A missing button or a split seam sends a lot of good clothing to landfill. Ten minutes with a needle and thread can save it.

sections.key: Mending was once ordinary and is returning, and a small tin of supplies covers most repairs.
sections.b:
During the Second World War, clothing in Britain was rationed, and in 1943 the government published a booklet called Make Do and Mend. It taught people to darn socks, patch elbows and make clothes last, as people always had. Today clothing is cheap and huge amounts end up in landfill, often for faults that take minutes to fix. Mending is returning to save money, reduce waste and, for many people, to calm the mind.

A useful kit fits in a small tin: hand-sewing needles, thread in black, white, navy, grey and beige, pins, small sharp scissors, safety pins and spare buttons. A seam ripper makes unpicking easy. If unsure of a colour, choose slightly darker thread, which shows less.

sections.key: Use doubled thread with a secure knot, and leave slack under a button so it sits neatly.
sections.b:
Cut thread about as long as your arm, as longer lengths tangle. For jobs that take strain, pull the thread through until the ends meet and knot them, so you sew with a double strand. Finish with a few small stitches in the same spot to lock it.

To sew on a button, start from the back so the knot is hidden. Go up through one hole and down the opposite one several times. Here is the trick most people miss: lay a toothpick or matchstick across the button and sew over it. Remove it, bring the needle up under the button and wind thread around the stitches. This forms a shank, so the button sits neatly without puckering.

sections.key: Sew a split seam along its original stitch line, and use a slip stitch for hems so little shows.
sections.b:
A split seam, perhaps under an arm, is often the quickest fix. Turn the garment inside out and pin the edges together along the old stitch line. Start a little before the gap, where the stitching is sound, and sew a backstitch: bring the needle up a short way ahead, then go back down at the end of the previous stitch. This makes a strong, continuous line. Carry on past the gap and lock off.

For a dropped hem, fold it back along its crease and pin it. With a slip stitch, hide the thread inside the fold and pick up just one or two threads of the main fabric each time. Keep stitches small and not too tight. Iron-on hemming tape is a quick fix that may not survive many washes.

sections.key: Darning weaves new threads across a hole, and visible mending turns the repair into decoration.
sections.b:
Darning is the traditional repair for socks and knitwear. Stretch the area over something rounded, such as a darning mushroom or a light bulb. Sew rows of thread across the hole, then weave more threads through them at right angles, creating a small patch of new fabric. For woven clothes like jeans, a patch on the inside or outside works well.

Many menders now celebrate their repairs rather than hiding them. Sashiko, a Japanese stitching tradition whose name means roughly ‘little stabs’, uses rows of small running stitches, often white on indigo, to reinforce worn cloth. Patched and repatched Japanese textiles called boro, once a sign of poverty, are now admired as art.

sections.key: Many zip faults can be fixed cheaply, and part of the skill is knowing which jobs to pay for.
sections.b:
Zips cause a lot of unnecessary clothing deaths. If a zip sticks, rub a graphite pencil, a bar of soap or a little candle wax along the teeth, then work the slider gently back and forth. If the teeth keep separating behind the slider, it has often widened with wear. Squeezing its sides very gently with pliers, a little at a time, can make it grip again.

If a pull tab snaps off, a small key ring or paperclip makes a serviceable replacement. Some repairs, such as replacing a whole zip in a coat, are fiddly enough that a tailor or alterations shop is worth the money. Knowing which jobs to do yourself and which to pay for is part of the skill.

quiz.q: Why is mending making a comeback?
o: Clothing has become far more expensive
Sewing is now taught in every workplace
Fashion brands now offer free mending
It saves money, cuts waste and is calming
quiz.e: Cheap clothing fills landfill, and simple repairs offer savings, less waste and calm.

quiz.q: What does laying a toothpick across a button while sewing achieve?
o: It stops the thread from tangling
It keeps the button from ever coming off
It leaves slack so a shank can form
It hides the knot at the back
quiz.e: The slack becomes a thread shank, letting the button sit on the buttonhole without puckering.

quiz.q: Where should you sew when repairing a split seam?
o: Across the fabric a few centimetres from the seam
Along the original stitch line, starting before the gap
Only on the outside with a loose stitch
Along a new line cut beside the old one
quiz.e: Rejoining the original stitch line, from sound stitching, gives the strongest and neatest repair.

quiz.q: What is visible mending?
o: Hiding a hole with iron-on tape
Making the repair a feature, like sashiko
Using a darning mushroom to hide the patch
Replacing damaged clothing with new
quiz.e: Visible mending celebrates repairs rather than hiding them, as in sashiko and boro.

quiz.q: What can often free a sticking zip?
o: Rubbing graphite or wax along the teeth
Cutting away the fabric that is stuck
Pulling the slider hard with pliers
Washing the garment in hot water
quiz.e: A little lubricant on the teeth and a gentle wiggle fixes many zip problems.

LESSONS.push: Ten minutes with a needle can save a garment. Most people miss one button trick.

LESSONS.title: The emergency department: how it really works
LESSONS.hook: Why does someone who arrived after you get seen first? The answer goes back to Napoleon's battlefields, and understanding it makes a hospital visit far less frustrating.

sections.key: Triage means treating the sickest first, an idea that began in Napoleonic battlefield medicine.
sections.b:
For much of history, wounded soldiers were treated according to rank, or not until the fighting ended. Dominique-Jean Larrey, a surgeon in Napoleon's armies, changed that. He introduced light, fast horse-drawn ‘flying ambulances’ to reach the wounded during battle, and insisted the most dangerously injured be treated first, whatever their rank or even their side.

The word triage comes from the French trier, meaning to sort. The idea spread through military medicine and, in the twentieth century, into civilian hospitals. The principle is the same today. An emergency department is not a queue. It is a sorting system designed to make sure the person most likely to die without help is seen first.

sections.key: A triage nurse decides how long you can safely wait, using five categories with maximum times to be seen.
sections.b:
At an Australian emergency department you will usually speak first with a triage nurse. In a couple of minutes they ask what has happened, check key signs such as breathing and pulse, and look for danger. They are not diagnosing you. They are deciding how long you can safely wait. Be clear and specific, and neither exaggerate nor play things down.

Australian and New Zealand departments use the Australasian Triage Scale, in place in various forms since the 1990s. Category 1 is immediately life-threatening, seen immediately. Category 2, such as severe chest pain, within 10 minutes. Category 3 within 30 minutes, Category 4 within an hour and Category 5 within two hours. These are the maximum times for assessment and treatment to begin, not for the whole visit. Busy departments sometimes miss targets.

sections.key: Long waits usually mean sicker people have arrived or the hospital's wards are full.
sections.b:
Waiting rooms can be maddening, especially when others are called ahead of you. Usually someone more urgent has come in, perhaps by ambulance through a different door. Arriving by ambulance does not jump the queue. Ambulance patients are triaged too, so a less urgent one may still wait.

Another major cause of delay is access block. When patients who need admission cannot move to a ward because no beds are free, they stay in emergency, occupying cubicles and staff time. That is why waits often reflect pressure across the whole hospital rather than slow work in the department itself.

sections.key: Call 000 for emergencies, use a GP or urgent care for the rest, and bring your details if you go.
sections.b:
Always call Triple Zero (000) or go to emergency for chest pain, difficulty breathing, signs of stroke such as a drooping face or slurred speech, severe bleeding, a serious head injury, seizures, severe burns, or someone unconscious or unresponsive. If in doubt, call 000. For a sprain, minor cut or ear infection, a GP, after-hours GP or urgent care clinic may see you faster, and pharmacists and nurse-staffed advice lines can help you decide.

If you go, bring your Medicare card, a list of medicines and allergies, and details of your doctor. Ask staff before you eat or drink, as you may need surgery or tests. A friend can listen and speak up for you. If your condition worsens while you wait, tell the triage nurse straight away. You can be reassessed and moved up.

sections.key: Public emergency care is free for Medicare-eligible patients, though ambulance costs vary by state.
sections.b:
If you are eligible for Medicare, treatment as a public patient in a public hospital emergency department costs nothing. Ambulances are different. Some states and territories cover their own residents, while others can charge substantial fees unless you have ambulance cover through a state scheme or private health insurance. Check your situation before you need one, though cost should never stop you calling 000 in an emergency.

When you are discharged, ask for a copy of your discharge summary, make sure you understand any new medicines and warning signs, and book a follow-up with your GP. The emergency department fixes the crisis. Your GP handles what comes after.

quiz.q: What principle does triage follow?
o: The most seriously ill patient is seen first
Patients are seen in order of arrival
Patients are seen according to rank
Those who wait longest are seen first
quiz.e: An emergency department is a sorting system, not a queue.

quiz.q: What is the triage nurse's job?
o: Diagnose your condition fully
Decide whether you pay
Book your follow-up with a GP
Decide how long you can safely wait
quiz.e: Triage sets urgency, not a diagnosis, so give clear and honest information.

quiz.q: What is access block?
o: A delay caused by locked doors
A limit on visitors in treatment areas
Admitted patients waiting in emergency for a bed
Patients refused admission at the front desk
quiz.e: Long waits often reflect pressure across the whole hospital, not slow work in emergency.

quiz.q: What should you do if your condition worsens while you wait?
o: Wait until your name is called
Leave and return later
Tell the triage nurse straight away
Ask another patient to check
quiz.e: You can be reassessed and moved up, and staff would rather hear early.

quiz.q: Who pays for treatment in a public hospital emergency department?
o: You, unless you have private insurance
Nobody, for Medicare-eligible patients
Your GP, then you repay them
Your state ambulance service
quiz.e: Public emergency care is free for Medicare-eligible patients, though ambulance fees vary.

LESSONS.push: Why the person who arrived after you is seen first, and why that is fair.

LESSONS.title: Small talk that isn't so small
LESSONS.hook: Most of us avoid chatting with strangers because we expect it to be awkward. Experiments suggest we have badly misjudged both them and ourselves.

sections.key: We expect talking to strangers to be unpleasant and underestimate how much they like us, and we are wrong on both counts.
sections.b:
In a 2014 study, psychologists Nicholas Epley and Juliana Schroeder asked Chicago train and bus commuters to talk to a stranger, keep to themselves or commute as usual. Beforehand, people predicted talking would be the least pleasant. Afterwards, those who chatted reported the most positive journeys. Those approached were generally happy to talk. The effects were modest, not life-changing.

A 2018 study led by Erica Boothby found the liking gap: after chatting, people underestimated how much their partner liked them. We replay our own awkward moments, while the other person just found us pleasant. The gap appeared in labs, among university housemates and in public workshops. If you leave thinking you were boring, they very probably did not.

sections.key: Brief friendly exchanges with acquaintances and strangers lift your mood and can open up opportunities.
sections.b:
Close friends and family are central to wellbeing, but casual connections count too. Gillian Sandstrom and Elizabeth Dunn found that people felt happier on days with more interactions with weak ties, such as classmates, neighbours and the person who makes their coffee. In another study, customers asked to have a genuine, friendly exchange with a barista left in a better mood than those told to be efficient.

Weak ties also bring practical benefits. Mark Granovetter's classic research suggested that new opportunities, including jobs, often come through acquaintances rather than close friends, because they move in different circles and hear about different things.

sections.key: Open with a shared situation, then ask follow-up questions, which make people like you more.
sections.b:
Most people overthink the first sentence. You need a door, not wit. Comment on your shared situation: the weather, the queue, the food. ‘Have you been to one of these before?’ works at most gatherings. Open questions give the other person room to talk. A popular memory aid is FORD: family, occupation, recreation and dreams. Read the cues, though: someone with headphones on and eyes on a book may not want company.

A 2017 Harvard study led by Karen Huang analysed thousands of conversations, including speed dating. People who asked more questions were better liked, and follow-up questions mattered most. If someone mentions Tasmania, ‘What was the highlight?’ shows you heard them, which switching to your own holiday does not. People tend to ask fewer questions than ideal.

sections.key: People enjoy meaningful conversations with strangers more than they expect to.
sections.b:
Small talk is a warm-up, not a destination. Research by Michael Kardas, Amit Kumar and Nicholas Epley, published in 2022, found that people expected deep conversations with strangers to feel more awkward and less enjoyable than they actually were. Participants who answered more personal, meaningful questions consistently felt more connected than they had predicted.

You do not need to leap to intimate subjects. Moving from ‘What do you do?’ to ‘What do you enjoy most about it?’ or ‘How did you end up doing that?’ invites a real answer. Offering something genuine about yourself in return helps the other person feel safe going further.

sections.key: Conversations rarely end when both people want them to, so a warm and clear exit is a kindness.
sections.b:
Ending a conversation can feel harder than starting one. A 2021 study led by Adam Mastroianni asked people how long they had wanted their conversations to last. Conversations almost never ended when both people wanted them to. Often both wanted to stop earlier, or one wanted more and the other less, and neither could tell.

So a graceful exit helps. Summarise something from the chat, thank them and give a reason, even a simple one: ‘I'll let you get back to your evening. It was great hearing about the trip.’ If you would like to meet again, say so specifically. A clean, warm ending leaves both people with a good final impression.

quiz.q: What is the ‘liking gap’?
o: People like strangers less than friends
People underrate how much others like them
Conversations are shorter than expected
People overestimate how interesting they are
quiz.e: We replay our awkward moments, while the other person usually found us perfectly pleasant.

quiz.q: Why can acquaintances be valuable for finding new opportunities?
o: They move in different social circles
They know us better than our close friends
They are far more likely to offer us a job
They give us more honest advice than family
quiz.e: Weak ties connect us to information that our close circle does not have.

quiz.q: Which kind of question makes people like you more?
o: Questions that quickly move the subject to you
Yes-or-no questions that keep things brief
Questions about their income and work
Follow-up questions that build on their answer
quiz.e: Follow-ups show you were listening, which is what most of us want from a conversation.

quiz.q: How do deeper conversations with strangers tend to go compared with expectations?
o: More awkward than people predicted
About as awkward as predicted
Shorter than people predicted
More enjoyable than people predicted
quiz.e: People expected awkwardness but felt more connected after meaningful questions.

quiz.q: Why is a clear, warm exit a kindness?
o: People enjoy long goodbyes
Most people want conversations to last longer
Few end when both people want them to
Exits are only needed in business
quiz.e: Neither person usually knows when the other wants to stop, so a clear exit helps both.

LESSONS.push: We expect talking to strangers to be awkward. The evidence says otherwise.

LESSONS.title: Flat battery, flat tyre: getting yourself going
LESSONS.hook: The two most common reasons cars get stuck are a dead battery and a flat tyre. Both are fixable by the roadside, if you know the order of things and put safety first.

sections.key: Get well off the road, turn on your hazard lights, and only do the job yourself if it is genuinely safe.
sections.b:
Before you touch a jack or a jumper lead, think about traffic, the biggest danger at any roadside breakdown. Pull off as far from moving cars as you can, onto firm, level ground if possible, and turn on your hazard lights. Put the handbrake on and switch off the engine.

On a busy highway or freeway, on a bend or in poor light, it is often safer to get out on the side away from traffic, stand well back behind a barrier if there is one, and call roadside assistance instead of attempting the job. If anyone is injured, there is a fire or fuel leak, or you are in danger, call Triple Zero (000).

sections.key: Connect red to positive on both cars, black to the good battery, and the last black clamp to bare metal away from the battery.
sections.b:
A flat battery announces itself with rapid clicking, a slow laboured crank, or nothing, often with dim dashboard lights. Common causes are lights left on, short trips, weeks of disuse, age and Australian heat. If it is cracked, leaking, bulging or smells strongly of rotten eggs, do not jump it. Call for help.

Check both manuals. Park the cars close but not touching, with both engines off and both batteries 12 volts. Connect red to the flat battery's positive, the other red to the good battery's positive, then black to the good battery's negative. The last black clamp goes on bare, unpainted metal on the flat car's engine or body, away from the battery. Batteries can give off hydrogen gas, and this keeps any final spark away from it.

sections.key: Run the donor car, start the flat one, remove leads in reverse, then drive and get the battery tested.
sections.b:
Start the donor car and let it run for a few minutes to put charge into the flat battery. Then try the stranded car. If it does not start after a few short attempts, wait, as long cranking can overheat the starter motor. Once it runs, remove the leads in exactly the reverse order: black from the metal point, black from the good battery, red from the good battery, red from the formerly flat one. Never let clamps touch each other. Drive for a decent stretch, then have the battery tested soon.

Compact lithium jump starter packs can start most petrol cars alone; keep one charged. Hybrids and EVs have a small 12-volt battery that powers the electronics. Manufacturers have specific procedures, so follow the manual.

sections.key: Loosen the wheel nuts while the wheel is on the ground, jack only at the marked point, and never go under the car.
sections.b:
If a tyre is deflating, slow down gently and pull over as soon as it is safe. Driving on a flat ruins the tyre and can damage the wheel. Once safely stopped, find the spare, jack, wheel brace and locking wheel nut key. On a slope, put something heavy against the wheel diagonally opposite the flat. Before lifting, loosen each wheel nut about half a turn, usually anticlockwise, while the wheel can't spin.

Place the jack at the jacking point in the owner's manual and raise the car just until the tyre is clear. Never put any part of your body under a car held only by a jack. Fit the spare, snug the nuts by hand in a star pattern, lower the car, then tighten fully. Recheck the nuts after a short distance.

sections.key: A space-saver spare is for getting you to a tyre shop at reduced speed, not for everyday driving.
sections.b:
Many cars carry a space-saver spare, a narrow temporary wheel that saves boot space and weight. It is designed to get you to a tyre shop, not for weeks of driving. Most carry a maximum speed label, often 80 kilometres per hour, and they reduce braking and cornering grip, so drive gently.

Some newer cars have no spare, only a tyre repair kit with sealant and a small compressor. These can fix small punctures in the tread, such as from a nail, but not sidewall cuts or major damage. Find out what your car carries, and practise once at home. A calm driveway lesson beats a first attempt on a highway at night.

quiz.q: What is the biggest danger at a roadside breakdown?
o: Overheating tyres
A flat battery
Passing traffic
Running out of fuel
quiz.e: Think about traffic first, and call roadside assistance if the location is unsafe.

quiz.q: Why does the final black clamp go on bare metal away from the battery?
o: To save time when connecting the last lead
To keep any spark away from battery hydrogen gas
Because battery terminals are always painted
To charge the car body as well as the battery
quiz.e: Placing the last connection away from the battery avoids a spark near explosive gas.

quiz.q: What should you do after the car starts?
o: Remove leads in reverse, then drive and test it
Switch the engine off straight away to rest it
Leave the leads attached until the morning
Reconnect the leads to double-check the charge
quiz.e: A battery that went flat once may be on its way out, so test it soon.

quiz.q: Why loosen the wheel nuts before lifting the car?
o: The wheel cannot spin while it is on the ground
The jack can then lift the car faster
The spare then fits onto the studs more easily
It lets hot brakes cool before lifting
quiz.e: With the tyre on the ground, you can apply force without the wheel turning.

quiz.q: What is a space-saver spare designed for?
o: Everyday driving for several weeks or months
Towing a trailer on a long highway trip
Replacing all four tyres on a long journey
Getting you to a tyre shop at reduced speed
quiz.e: It is a temporary wheel with reduced grip, so drive gently and replace it promptly.

LESSONS.push: Which cable goes on last matters more than you'd think. Here's why.

LESSONS.title: Reading a map and compass
LESSONS.hook: Phones die, satellites drop out and screens are hard to read in the rain. A paper map and a compass need no battery, and the skills to use them are surprisingly learnable.

sections.key: A paper map and compass never run out of battery, and a map's scale tells you real distances.
sections.b:
Phone navigation is brilliant until the battery goes flat in the cold, the screen cracks or you lose signal in a deep valley. Bushwalking clubs and search and rescue groups in Australia still advise carrying a paper map and compass, and knowing how to use them, as a backup. Navigating with a map also makes you read the land and notice ridges and creeks. People following a blue dot often have little idea of their surroundings.

Walking maps are usually topographic, with scales such as 1:25,000 or 1:50,000. On a 1:25,000 map, one centimetre is 250 metres; on a 1:50,000 map, 500 metres. The larger the second number, the more ground the map covers and the less detail. Map distance is flat, so a steep kilometre takes longer than a level one.

sections.key: Contour lines reveal the shape of the land, and grid references give a location with eastings first, then northings.
sections.b:
Each contour line joins points of the same height, and the contour interval is in the legend. Close lines mean steep ground; wide spacing means gentle ground. Stacked closed rings mark a hill or peak. V or U shapes pointing uphill show a valley or gully, often with a creek. Pointing downhill, they show a spur, a ridge running down from higher ground.

A grid reference describes a location precisely, perhaps to rescuers. Australian topographic maps use the Map Grid of Australia, with vertical lines called eastings and horizontal lines called northings. Give the easting first, then the northing: ‘along the corridor, then up the stairs’. A four-figure reference identifies a grid square, usually one kilometre across. Six figures estimate tenths within it, to about 100 metres.

sections.key: Compasses point to magnetic north, so you must correct a map bearing for declination.
sections.b:
True north is the geographic North Pole. Grid north follows the map's vertical grid lines and is very close to true north. Magnetic north is where your compass points. The difference is magnetic declination. In Australia it ranges from near zero in parts of Western Australia to over ten degrees east in the south-east. Maps print the declination. A ten-degree error over five kilometres puts you almost a kilometre off course.

To take a bearing, lay a baseplate compass's edge on the map joining where you are to where you are going, with its arrow pointing to the destination. Turn the dial until the orienting lines parallel the grid lines, with the orienting arrow to the top of the map. Read the bearing, then correct for declination: where it is east, subtract it.

sections.key: Turn your body until the red needle sits in the orienting arrow, then walk from landmark to landmark.
sections.b:
Hold the compass flat with the direction-of-travel arrow pointing ahead. Turn your whole body until the red, north end of the needle sits inside the orienting arrow, often remembered as ‘red in the shed’. The arrow now points along your bearing. Rather than staring at the compass, pick a distinct landmark in that direction, walk to it, then repeat.

Keep the compass away from metal, phones, car bodies and power lines, which can pull the needle. Another technique is aiming off: when heading for a point on a creek or track, deliberately aim to one side so you know which way to turn on arrival.

sections.key: Compasses are balanced for different zones, so use one suited to Australia and practise somewhere safe first.
sections.b:
Earth's magnetic field also dips downward at an angle that changes with latitude. A compass needle is weighted to cancel that dip in the region where it will be used. A compass balanced for Europe or North America may tilt, drag on its housing and read sluggishly in Australia. Check it is balanced for the southern hemisphere or Australian zone, or choose a global needle.

Practise somewhere safe and familiar, such as a local park or well-marked track, before relying on your skills in remote country. And always tell someone your plans and carry an emergency beacon where there is no phone coverage.

quiz.q: On a 1:50,000 map, what does one centimetre represent?
o: 50 metres
250 metres
5 kilometres
500 metres
quiz.e: One unit on the map equals 50,000 on the ground, so a centimetre is 500 metres.

quiz.q: What do closely spaced contour lines show?
o: Gentle ground
A flat plain
Steep ground
A walking track
quiz.e: Close contours mean the height changes quickly over a short distance.

quiz.q: Why must you correct for magnetic declination?
o: The map's grid lines are printed wrongly each year
Your compass points to magnetic north, not grid north
Compasses read too slowly on a steep slope
True north moves a few degrees every year
quiz.e: Without correction, a ten-degree error over five kilometres puts you almost a kilometre off course.

quiz.q: What is the point of aiming off?
o: It saves distance by cutting across a corner
You know which way to turn on reaching a creek
It avoids magnetic interference from metal objects
It lets you skip choosing landmarks to walk to
quiz.e: Deliberately aiming to one side removes the guesswork when you arrive at a linear feature.

quiz.q: Why should a compass match your region?
o: Magnetic dip varies, so a mismatched needle drags
Compasses only work properly in one hemisphere
Mismatched compasses always read true north
Locally made compasses are always much cheaper
quiz.e: Needles are weighted for a magnetic zone, so choose one balanced for Australia or a global model.

LESSONS.push: Your compass needle doesn't point to true north. Here's the gap and why it matters.

LESSONS.title: Hiring a tradie without regrets
LESSONS.hook: Most tradies are honest, skilled and busy. A few simple checks help you find them, and avoid the small number who leave a trail of half-finished jobs.

sections.key: Check a tradie's licence on the official register and choose people through trusted recommendations.
sections.b:
In every Australian state and territory, electrical work must be done by a licensed electrician, and gas fitting and most plumbing by licensed tradespeople. Building work above a certain value also generally requires a licensed builder. Faulty wiring, gas leaks and structural mistakes can kill. Each state's regulator runs a free online register where you can check a licence is current, what it covers and any disciplinary actions. Ask for the number and check it yourself. Also confirm public liability insurance.

The best leads come from neighbours, friends and family who had similar work recently. Choose detailed reviews and be wary of a burst of short, glowing ones. Ask about similar jobs, who will do the work and whether subcontractors are involved. Someone vague, who never returns calls or will not put things in writing is unlikely to change.

sections.key: Compare written quotes for the same scope, and expect a written contract and limited deposit on bigger jobs.
sections.b:
For more than a small job, get at least three written quotes. A quote sets out the work, materials, total price, whether GST is included and how long it is valid. An estimate is only a best guess, and the bill can legitimately end up higher. Make sure every quote covers the same scope. The cheapest may leave out rubbish removal or quality materials. Agree changes in writing, with the price, before they are done.

Above certain values, a written contract is generally required, setting out the work, price, timeframes and dispute handling. Read it before signing. Several states cap the deposit a builder can ask for on domestic work, commonly at around 10 per cent or less. For bigger projects, tie payments to completed stages, not calendar dates, which matters if the business collapses partway.

sections.key: Home warranty insurance is a last-resort safety net if the builder dies, disappears or goes broke.
sections.b:
Most states require builders to take out home warranty insurance, known by different names, on residential jobs above a set value. It typically covers you if the builder dies, disappears or becomes insolvent and cannot finish the work or fix defects.
