The builder must usually give you the certificate before taking a deposit or starting work, so ask to see it.

Separately, tell your own home and contents insurer about major renovations, as some policies change cover while building work is under way. The tradie's public liability insurance covers damage they cause to your property or injuries to other people, so check that it is current too.

sections.key: Door knockers after storms, pressure to decide now and demands for big cash payments are warning signs.
sections.b:
Be very wary of anyone who knocks uninvited, especially after a storm or flood, claiming your roof or gutters urgently need work. Under consumer law, agreements made after an uninvited approach generally come with a cooling-off period of 10 business days.

Other red flags include pressure to sign today, a quote far below everyone else's, no ABN, no fixed address, refusal to give a written quote and a request for most of the money up front, especially in cash. Cash with no invoice leaves you with no proof of what was agreed. Pay by traceable methods, keep every receipt and never hand over the full amount before the job is finished.

sections.key: Raise problems early and in writing, then escalate to your state's fair trading or building regulator if needed.
sections.b:
Under the Australian Consumer Law, services must be provided with due care and skill, be fit for any purpose you made clear, and be delivered within a reasonable time if no deadline was agreed. If something is not right, raise it calmly and promptly, ideally while the tradie is on site, then follow up in writing with photos. Give them a fair chance to fix it, because most will.

If they will not, contact your state's fair trading office or building regulator, which can often help resolve disputes. Some states run building dispute services, and civil tribunals can decide claims. Keep a folder of quotes, contracts, messages, invoices and photos from the start. Good records are your strongest tool.

quiz.q: How should you check a tradie's licence?
o: Look it up on your state regulator's free register
Take their word because they sound confident
Ask a neighbour whether the card looks real
Check only that they hold liability insurance
quiz.e: The register shows whether a licence is current, what it covers and any disciplinary actions.

quiz.q: What is the difference between a quote and an estimate?
o: A quote is always cheaper than an estimate
An estimate is legally binding on the tradie
A quote never includes the cost of materials
A quote is a firm price; an estimate is a guess
quiz.e: With only an estimate, the final bill can legitimately end up higher.

quiz.q: What does home warranty insurance protect you against?
o: Damage you cause to your own property
Injuries to the tradie while on site
The builder dying, disappearing or going broke
Rising material prices during the job
quiz.e: It is a last-resort safety net, and you should ask to see the certificate before work starts.

quiz.q: What generally applies when you agree to work after an uninvited approach?
o: No right to change your mind
A full refund after any delay
A short cooling-off period
A mandatory cash deposit
quiz.e: Consumer law gives you time to reconsider an agreement made after an uninvited approach.

quiz.q: What should you do first if a job is not right?
o: Withhold payment without telling the tradie
Raise it promptly, then follow up in writing
Post an online review before speaking to them
Wait until the whole job is finished
quiz.e: Early, documented communication gives them a fair chance to fix it and builds your records.

LESSONS.push: Before you sign anything, there is a free check most people skip.

LESSONS.title: When someone dies: the practical steps
LESSONS.hook: In the middle of grief come phone calls, forms and decisions nobody prepares you for. Knowing the order of things can lift some of the weight.

sections.key: Call 000 for a sudden death, but an expected death needs no rush, and some deaths must go to the coroner.
sections.b:
If someone dies suddenly or unexpectedly, or you are unsure whether they have died, call Triple Zero (000) straight away. Operators will guide you, and paramedics and often police will attend. If the death was expected, for example someone in palliative care at home, there is no need for an ambulance. Contact their doctor or palliative care team, who will arrange for the death to be confirmed. There is generally no requirement to have the body taken away immediately, so you can take time to sit with the person and call family.

Before a funeral, a doctor must complete a medical certificate stating the cause of death. Sudden, unexpected, violent, accidental or unexplained deaths must be reported to the coroner, who may order a post-mortem or an inquest. Coronial staff can explain each step.

sections.key: The funeral director usually registers the death, and a meaningful farewell need not be expensive.
sections.b:
Most families engage a funeral director, who collects the person, helps arrange the service and usually lodges the details to register the death with the state or territory Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages. The registry then issues the official death certificate, which differs from the doctor's medical certificate. You will need it, or certified copies, for banks, super funds and insurers.

Check whether the person left wishes about burial, cremation or music. A funeral can be religious or secular, large or small. Funerals can cost many thousands of dollars, and grieving families may overspend out of love or guilt. Get more than one quote, ask for itemised prices and consider simpler options such as direct cremation followed by a memorial gathering. A calmer friend can join the meetings.

sections.key: Many organisations need to know, and a free national service can notify several at once.
sections.b:
A surprising number of organisations need to be told: Services Australia for Centrelink and Medicare, the Australian Taxation Office, banks, super funds, insurers, employers, utility and phone companies, and more. The free Australian Death Notification Service, run with the state registries, lets you notify a number of participating organisations in one go once the death is registered.

Keep a list of who you have contacted, when and what they said. Many banks and large companies have dedicated bereavement teams who can make it gentler. Redirecting mail and closing unused accounts also helps protect against criminals who misuse the identities of people who have died.

sections.key: The executor manages the estate, so do not distribute belongings until it is clear who has legal authority.
sections.b:
If there is a will, the executor it names manages the estate: gathering assets, paying debts and distributing what remains. If there is no will, a close relative can apply to the court to be appointed administrator. Until it is clear who has the authority, avoid giving away belongings or money, however obvious the wishes seem.

Some things move outside the estate. Jointly held bank accounts and property usually pass straight to the surviving owner, and super is paid by the fund's trustee, often following the member's nominations. Many banks will pay funeral invoices directly from the deceased's account. A final tax return is often needed, and solicitors and public trustees can help.

sections.key: Very little must happen immediately, so accept help, take things in order and be kind to yourself.
sections.b:
In the first weeks the to-do list can feel endless, but very little has to happen immediately. Prioritise the essentials, such as the funeral and anything protecting the estate, and let the rest wait. Accept practical offers such as cooking, making calls or minding children, and consider putting one organised friend or relative in charge of the paperwork list.

Grief comes in waves and can bring exhaustion, poor sleep and forgetfulness. Talk with your GP if you are struggling, and know that grief support services and helplines exist. If you are ever worried about your safety or someone else's, call 000. Being kind to yourself is part of the work.

quiz.q: What should you do first if a death is sudden or unexpected?
o: Contact a funeral director
Call Triple Zero (000)
Wait for a doctor's visit next day
Notify the bank
quiz.e: Emergency operators guide you, and paramedics and often police attend.

quiz.q: How does the official death certificate differ from the doctor's medical certificate?
o: It is issued by the state registry
It is signed by the funeral director
It states the cause of death only
It is needed before the doctor certifies
quiz.e: You need the registry's death certificate or certified copies to deal with banks, super funds and insurers.

quiz.q: What does the Australian Death Notification Service do?
o: Arranges and pays for the funeral service
Pays the deceased's remaining debts
Appoints the executor named in a will
Lets you notify several organisations at once
quiz.e: It is free and saves repeating the same notification to many organisations.

quiz.q: Why avoid giving away belongings early?
o: The belongings must all be sold first
Beneficiaries must be paid only in cash
The funeral director owns them temporarily
It may not yet be clear who has legal authority
quiz.e: Only the executor or administrator has authority to distribute the estate.

quiz.q: What is a sound approach to the paperwork in the first weeks?
o: Finish every task within the first week
Handle it all alone to avoid burdening others
Do the essentials, accept help, let the rest wait
Put it aside entirely for a year
quiz.e: Very little has to happen immediately, and help and rest are part of coping.

LESSONS.push: Most of what must happen after a death can wait. Here is what cannot.

LESSONS.title: Buying a home: from inspection to settlement
LESSONS.hook: Buying a home is the biggest purchase most people ever make, and the process is full of unfamiliar words and quiet traps. Here is the path from first inspection to handing over the keys.

sections.key: Pre-approval is only an indication of what a lender may offer, and the costs on top of the price add up quickly.
sections.b:
Find out what you can spend before you fall for a house. Pre-approval, sometimes called conditional approval, is a lender's indication of how much it may lend. It is not a guarantee: the lender still assesses the property and your circumstances.

Then add the costs on top of the price. Stamp duty (transfer duty) is often the biggest. Others include conveyancing, inspections, loan fees, possibly lenders mortgage insurance, moving and repairs.

First home buyers can get help. Most states offer duty concessions or exemptions, and federal guarantees have let eligible buyers purchase with a five per cent deposit and no lenders mortgage insurance. The First Home Super Saver Scheme, running since 2017, lets you save a deposit through voluntary super contributions, within limits. Rules change often, so check current ones.

sections.key: A building and pest inspection, plus a strata report for units, can reveal problems you cannot see on an open-home visit.
sections.b:
A home that looks lovely at an open inspection can hide serious problems. A professional building inspection checks for structural defects, roof damage, rising damp, cracking and safety issues. Termites are a real threat in much of Australia, so a pest inspection is usually done at the same time.

For an apartment or townhouse in a strata scheme, a strata report matters just as much. It shows the owners corporation's finances, including savings for future major works, any special levies charged or planned, building defects, disputes and the by-laws, which may restrict pets, renovations or short-term letting.

An inspection costs a few hundred dollars. Missing a structural problem can cost tens of thousands.

sections.key: Have a conveyancer or solicitor review the contract before you sign, and know that auctions are unconditional while private sales may not be.
sections.b:
Conveyancing transfers ownership from seller to buyer. Hire a licensed conveyancer or solicitor before you make an offer, not after. They review the contract of sale and the seller's disclosure documents, which vary by state. They look for easements, which give others rights over part of the land, and covenants, which can restrict what you build. They also check special conditions that may favour the seller.

In a private sale, you can make an offer subject to conditions such as finance approval or a satisfactory inspection. Most states also allow a short cooling-off period, often a few business days, in which you can withdraw by paying a small fee. At auction there is generally no cooling-off period, and the winning bidder is committed on the spot. Finance, inspections and legal review must be finished before auction day.

sections.key: Once contracts are exchanged you are legally bound and pay a deposit, so use the weeks before settlement to finalise the loan, insurance and a final inspection.
sections.b:
When both sides sign the contract, and in many states exchange copies, the sale becomes legally binding, subject to any cooling-off period or conditions. You then pay a deposit, commonly 10 per cent, though a smaller one can sometimes be negotiated, or a deposit bond used. It is usually held in trust. If you fail to complete without a valid reason, you can lose it and face further costs.

Settlement is commonly 30 to 90 days later. Your lender finalises the loan, and your conveyancer completes searches and adjusts council rates and water charges. In some states the property is at your risk from the contract date, so ask when to arrange building insurance. A final inspection is usually allowed before settlement. Avoid new loans or job changes, which can complicate final approval.

sections.key: Settlement now mostly happens electronically, after which the title is yours and the agent releases the keys.
sections.b:
On settlement day you usually do not need to be anywhere special. Settlement in Australia now mostly happens on electronic platforms, where the lawyers, conveyancers and banks for both sides complete the exchange of money and documents online. Funds move, the title is transferred into your name and the seller's loan is paid out.

Your conveyancer confirms when it is done, and the agent then releases the keys. Switch on utilities in your name, update your address and check your insurance is active.

Keep the settlement statement and contract with your important records. They matter when you eventually sell, and for capital gains tax if the property is ever rented out or is no longer your main residence.

quiz.q: What does pre-approval from a lender tell you?
o: About how much a lender may lend
The exact loan you will receive
That the property has passed valuation
That stamp duty will be waived
quiz.e: Pre-approval is an indication only; the lender still assesses the property and your circumstances.

quiz.q: Why is a pest inspection usually done with a building inspection?
o: It is required by law before every sale
It replaces the need for a strata report
Pests are visible at any open home
Termites are a real threat in much of Australia
quiz.e: Termites can cause serious hidden damage, so a pest check is usually done alongside the building inspection.

quiz.q: What is the key difference between buying at auction and by private sale?
o: Auction buyers get a longer cooling-off period
Auction wins are generally unconditional
Private sales cannot include conditions
Auctions do not need a contract
quiz.e: Because an auction win is binding on the spot, finance, inspections and legal checks must come first.

quiz.q: Why should you ask about building insurance soon after signing?
o: Insurance is only needed after you move in
The lender pays for it until settlement
In some states, risk passes to you at contract
Insurance is included in the deposit
quiz.e: Risk can pass to the buyer at contract, so insurance should not wait until you move in.

quiz.q: Why keep your settlement statement and contract afterwards?
o: The agent requires them each year
They prove your loan rate to the bank
They record your costs, which matter for tax
They must be lodged with council rates
quiz.e: Records of what you paid help with tax calculations, including capital gains tax if the property is ever rented out or is not your main residence.

LESSONS.push: Your offer is not the real price of a house. Here is what else you pay.

LESSONS.title: Alice in Wonderland: the story told on a river
LESSONS.hook: On a summer afternoon in 1862, a shy maths lecturer made up a story to entertain three bored girls in a rowing boat. It became one of the most translated books ever written.

sections.key: Alice began as a tale improvised on a rowing trip in 1862 for a ten-year-old girl who asked for it to be written down.
sections.b:
On 4 July 1862, Charles Dodgson, a mathematics lecturer at Christ Church, Oxford, rowed up the Thames towards Godstow. With him were his friend Robinson Duckworth and the three daughters of the college dean, Henry Liddell: Lorina, Alice and Edith. Alice was ten.

To pass the time, Dodgson spun a tale about a girl named Alice who tumbles down a rabbit hole into a world where nothing behaves sensibly. Duckworth later remembered asking if he was inventing it on the spot, and Dodgson said yes. At the end of the day, Alice Liddell asked him to write it down for her. He took the request seriously, though it took him more than two years to finish.

sections.key: A handwritten gift grew into a published novel, and the author invented the pen name Lewis Carroll.
sections.b:
Dodgson wrote the story out by hand, added his own pen drawings, and in November 1864 gave Alice a small volume titled Alice's Adventures Under Ground. Friends who read it, including the writer George MacDonald, whose children loved it, urged him to publish.

He expanded the tale, adding episodes such as the Mad Tea-Party and the Cheshire Cat. He also built a pen name from his own: Charles Lutwidge became Carolus Ludovicus, then was reversed and anglicised into Lewis Carroll.

He hired John Tenniel, the leading cartoonist of Punch, and paid for the illustrations himself. Alice's Adventures in Wonderland appeared from Macmillan in 1865, and Tenniel's drawings have shaped how readers picture Alice ever since.

sections.key: The first print run was withdrawn over poor picture quality, which made the few surviving copies enormously valuable.
sections.b:
Tenniel was unhappy with the first printing of 2,000 copies in 1865, complaining that the pictures were badly printed. Dodgson agreed to withdraw the edition and pay for a new one. The reprint, dated 1866, is the edition most Victorian readers knew.

Many unbound sheets from the rejected run were sold to an American publisher and issued in the United States. The few bound copies already given away became extreme rarities. Only around two dozen copies of the original 1865 edition are known to survive, mostly in libraries, and one can sell for well over a million dollars at auction.

A perfectionist's fussing over ink and paper created one of the most sought-after books in the world.

sections.key: Wonderland's absurdity is built from logic pushed to extremes, along with parody and wordplay, and the Mad Hatter is not named that in the book.
sections.b:
Wonderland feels chaotic, but much of its humour is logic pushed to ridiculous extremes, as you might expect from a mathematician. Characters take words literally, argue over definitions and follow rules that make no sense. Many of Alice's poems parody the moralising verses Victorian children had to memorise.

The Hatter asks why a raven is like a writing desk and admits he has no idea. For years Carroll gave no answer, and only in a later edition did he suggest a playful one.

The book never actually calls him the Mad Hatter. He is simply the Hatter, though the Cheshire Cat assures Alice that everyone there is mad. The famous nickname came from readers and later adaptations.

sections.key: Popular stories about Queen Victoria and mercury-poisoned hatters are unproven or false, while the original manuscript did return to Britain as a gift.
sections.b:
One legend says Queen Victoria loved Alice and asked for Carroll's next book, receiving a dry mathematical treatise. Carroll publicly denied this in 1896. Another claim says the Hatter was inspired by hat makers poisoned by the mercury used on felt. That poisoning was real, and the phrase mad as a hatter predates the book, but there is no evidence Carroll was making that point. His family's relationship with the Liddells cooled in 1863 for reasons nobody fully knows, because the relevant diary pages were later cut out.

In 1928 Alice, by then Mrs Hargreaves, sold the manuscript at auction in London, and it went to the United States. In 1948 American donors led by Luther Evans, the Librarian of Congress, bought and returned it to Britain in thanks for its wartime role. It is now in the British Library.

quiz.q: How did the story of Alice first come into being?
o: It was drafted as a school lesson
It was commissioned by a publisher
It was improvised aloud on a rowing trip
It was adapted from an older folk tale
quiz.e: Dodgson invented it on the spot for the Liddell girls, and only wrote it down at Alice's request.

quiz.q: How was the pen name Lewis Carroll created?
o: It was the name of an Oxford colleague
It was chosen by the publisher
His name was Latinised, then reversed
It came from a character in the story
quiz.e: Charles Lutwidge became Carolus Ludovicus and then Lewis Carroll.

quiz.q: Why are surviving copies of the 1865 edition so valuable?
o: The print run was recalled, so few survive
It contains handwritten notes by Carroll
It was printed in a signed limited run
It was the only edition with colour plates
quiz.e: Because the run was recalled over print quality, only around two dozen copies are known.

quiz.q: What is true of the Mad Hatter in the book?
o: He is named the Mad Hatter on his first appearance
He solves the raven riddle in the story
He is based on a real Oxford hat maker
He is only ever called the Hatter
quiz.e: The nickname Mad Hatter came from readers and adaptations, not from the text.

quiz.q: What is the evidence that the Hatter was inspired by mercury poisoning?
o: Carroll wrote about it in his diary
None; the link is only speculation
Tenniel said he drew it from a patient
The Liddell family confirmed it
quiz.e: Mercury poisoning in hat making was real, but nothing shows Carroll meant to refer to it.

LESSONS.push: A rowing trip, a ten-year-old and an invented story. Why one copy fetches millions.

LESSONS.title: Ern Malley: the poet who never lived
LESSONS.hook: In 1944 an Australian magazine hailed the discovery of a brilliant dead poet. He had been invented in a single afternoon by two bored soldiers.

sections.key: In the 1940s Australian modernists around Angry Penguins argued for a break with old forms, and traditionalist critics thought the new poetry was nonsense.
sections.b:
In the early 1940s, Australian art and literature were split between traditionalists and a younger crowd excited by modernism, the experimental style of writers such as T. S. Eliot and painters like Picasso.

At the centre of the avant-garde was Angry Penguins, a magazine co-founded in Adelaide in 1940 by Max Harris, who was still a teenager. Melbourne patrons John and Sunday Reed backed it, and their circle included the painters Sidney Nolan and Albert Tucker. It published surrealist-influenced poetry and argued that Australia needed to break with old forms.

To its critics, much of this poetry looked like pretentious nonsense that anyone could produce. Two of them decided to test that idea.

sections.key: James McAuley and Harold Stewart stitched random phrases into poems and invented a dead poet to sign them.
sections.b:
James McAuley and Harold Stewart were young poets who disliked modernism and preferred traditional craft. In 1943 both were serving in the army in Melbourne. By their own account, they wrote a whole body of work in a single afternoon.

They opened books at random, including a dictionary, a collected Shakespeare, a dictionary of quotations and an American report on draining swamps to control mosquitoes, and wove the phrases into sixteen poems. They deliberately included nonsense, false allusions and clumsy lines.

Then they invented an author: Ern Malley, a mechanic and insurance salesman who had supposedly died young in 1943, leaving his poems unpublished. They titled the collection The Darkening Ecliptic.

sections.key: Max Harris believed he had found a lost genius and devoted a special issue to him, until the press exposed the hoax.
sections.b:
The poems reached Harris with a covering letter from Ethel Malley, Ern's supposedly grieving sister, who said she did not understand them but wondered if they were any good.

Harris was thrilled. He believed he had found a major poet who had died unrecognised, and in 1944 he devoted a special issue of Angry Penguins to Ern Malley, with a cover painting by Sidney Nolan inspired by the poems. Some readers suspected a joke from the start.

Within weeks, journalists began investigating who Ethel and Ern really were. In June 1944 the press revealed the truth, and McAuley and Stewart explained their experiment, declaring that the poems were deliberately meaningless.

sections.key: The hoax made Harris a national laughing stock and led to an obscenity conviction that seemed to prove the hoaxers right.
sections.b:
The story was a sensation, and newspapers across the country mocked Harris and modernism together. Worse followed. South Australian police charged Harris with publishing indecent material, pointing to lines in the Ern Malley poems and other contributions to the magazine.

The trial in Adelaide in 1944 became famous for its absurdity. A police detective was asked to explain why certain words and images were immoral, and admitted he did not know what some of them meant. Harris was convicted and fined five pounds.

Angry Penguins survived only a few more years. For a while the episode seemed to prove what the hoaxers intended: that modernist poetry could not tell genuine art from random words.

sections.key: Many readers later judged the fake poems genuinely good, which raises lasting questions about authorship, intention and meaning.
sections.b:
Then something unexpected happened. Over the following decades, many critics and poets argued that the poems were striking, with vivid images and an odd emotional power, however they were made. Sidney Nolan returned to Ern Malley in his art for years, and the American poet John Ashbery was among the admirers. Some suggested the hoaxers had, despite themselves, poured real talent and feeling into the work. The poems have stayed in print ever since, and the hoax inspired later writing, including Peter Carey's 2003 novel My Life as a Fake.

Does a poem's value depend on what its author intended? Meaning kept appearing where the authors said there was none. Some historians argue the hoax set Australian modernism back by years. Max Harris went on to a long career as a bookseller, publisher and columnist, and never fully disowned Ern.

quiz.q: What did the hoaxers believe about modernist poetry?
o: That it was too traditional for Australia's readers
That it copied older poets far too closely
That it was pretentious nonsense anyone could write
That it was too costly for small magazines to publish
quiz.e: The hoaxers doubted modernists could tell real poetry from nonsense, and built the hoax to test that.

quiz.q: How were the Ern Malley poems actually made?
o: By weaving together phrases from random books
By copying the notes of a real poet who had died
By translating poems from French into English
By reworking the early verse of Max Harris
quiz.e: The poems were stitched from random phrases and deliberately included nonsense.

quiz.q: Why did Max Harris publish Ern Malley so lavishly?
o: He had been told it was a joke
He wanted to expose a rival magazine
He was paid by the Malley family
He thought he had found a lost genius
quiz.e: Harris was convinced he had discovered a lost genius, so he dedicated a special issue to him.

quiz.q: What happened to Harris after the hoax was revealed?
o: He was banned from publishing for life
He was prosecuted for indecency and fined
He was sued by the hoaxers
He closed the magazine immediately
quiz.e: A South Australian court convicted him of publishing indecent material and fined him five pounds.

quiz.q: Why does the Ern Malley affair still interest critics?
o: It proved modernism had no value
It showed the poems were plagiarised
Poems meant as nonsense won admirers
It uncovered a true dead poet
quiz.e: The poems' lasting appeal raises the question of whether intention or reading gives a work its value.

LESSONS.push: Two soldiers wrote a famous poet in one afternoon. The poems outlived the joke.

LESSONS.title: Pen names: why writers hide
LESSONS.hook: George Orwell, Mark Twain and George Eliot were not real names. Behind every pen name is a reason, from prejudice to privacy to a bit of mischief.

sections.key: A pen name is an invented name an author publishes under, and writers have long used them for reasons from prejudice to privacy.
sections.b:
A pen name, also called a pseudonym or nom de plume, is a name an author publishes under instead of their own. The practice is ancient and widespread. Voltaire was born François-Marie Arouet. Lewis Carroll was Charles Dodgson. George Orwell was Eric Arthur Blair. Australian readers know Henry Handel Richardson, author of The Fortunes of Richard Mahony, but the writer was in fact Ethel Florence Lindesay Richardson.

Writers have adopted pen names to escape prejudice, to protect their families, to keep a day job, to separate different kinds of writing, or simply because they liked the sound of something better. Each disguise tells a small story about the pressures writers faced in their time.

sections.key: The Brontë sisters and Mary Ann Evans chose male-sounding names so their books would be judged seriously.
sections.b:
In 1846 three sisters in a Yorkshire parsonage published poems as Currer, Ellis and Acton Bell. In 1847 Jane Eyre by Currer Bell became a sensation, and Wuthering Heights and Agnes Grey followed. The authors were Charlotte, Emily and Anne Brontë. They chose names that were not obviously female because, Charlotte later explained, critics treated women writers with prejudice. Charlotte and Anne revealed themselves to their publisher in 1848.

Mary Ann Evans, a respected editor and translator, turned to fiction in the 1850s as George Eliot. She wanted her work judged as serious literature, not light romance. She also lived openly with the married writer George Henry Lewes, a scandal in Victorian England. A male name kept attention on the books. Her identity soon leaked, but she kept the name.

sections.key: Some pen names carry hidden meanings from the writer's life, such as a riverboat depth call or a Suffolk river.
sections.b:
Samuel Clemens worked as a Mississippi riverboat pilot before he became a writer. On the river, crew called out depth readings, and mark twain meant the second mark on the line: two fathoms, about 3.7 metres, deep enough for a steamboat to pass safely. Clemens began signing his newspaper writing Mark Twain in 1863.

Eric Blair adopted the name George Orwell in 1933 for his first book, Down and Out in Paris and London, partly to spare his family embarrassment about his time living in poverty. George was a solidly English name, and the River Orwell in Suffolk was one he knew.

Both disguises became so famous that the real names now sound like the pseudonyms.

sections.key: Established authors sometimes take new names to escape their own fame, and a leak can transform a book's sales overnight.
sections.b:
Pen names are not only for beginners. Stephen King published several novels as Richard Bachman, partly because publishers then believed more than about one book a year by the same author would saturate the market. A bookshop worker noticed similarities and researched copyright records, and King was exposed in 1985.

J. K. Rowling's initials were themselves a kind of disguise. Her publisher suggested boys might be reluctant to read a book by a woman, and she borrowed the K from her grandmother Kathleen. In 2013 she published a crime novel, The Cuckoo's Calling, as Robert Galbraith. It had modest sales until her authorship leaked, after which it shot up the bestseller lists overnight.

The Galbraith episode suggests that names strongly influence sales, if not quality.

sections.key: Some modern authors use pen names to keep the focus on the work, or so loyal readers know what to expect.
sections.b:
The Italian novelist who writes as Elena Ferrante has kept her real identity officially private since her first novel in 1992, even as her Neapolitan novels became international bestsellers. She has said that books, once written, do not need their authors. Journalists have tried to unmask her, prompting fierce debate about whether readers have any right to know.

Pen names raise interesting questions. Does knowing an author's gender, background or reputation change how we read?

Today, pen names are also common in genre fiction, where authors may write romance under one name and thrillers under another so that loyal readers know what to expect.

quiz.q: Why have writers adopted pen names?
o: Because the law requires a registered name
Because publishers always insist on it
To avoid prejudice or protect privacy
Only to sound more impressive
quiz.e: Writers have used pseudonyms for many reasons, from prejudice and privacy to keeping a day job.

quiz.q: Why did Mary Ann Evans publish as George Eliot?
o: Because a male name was legally required
To hide that she was a translator
To be taken seriously and protect her privacy
Because her publisher invented it
quiz.e: A male name stopped her being typecast as a romance writer and kept attention off her unconventional life.

quiz.q: What does the name Mark Twain refer to?
o: A riverboat depth call meaning two fathoms
A character from his first novel
A mining term from the goldfields
A nickname given by his publisher
quiz.e: On the Mississippi, mark twain meant two fathoms, deep enough for a steamboat.

quiz.q: What happened to The Cuckoo's Calling when Rowling's authorship leaked?
o: It was withdrawn from sale
It sold the same as before
The publisher cancelled the series
Its sales rose sharply overnight
quiz.e: The book had modest sales as Robert Galbraith, then shot up the bestseller lists once the author was known.

quiz.q: Why do some genre authors use several pen names?
o: Because tax rules require a new name
So loyal readers know what to expect
To avoid competing with their publisher
Because bookshops require separate names
quiz.e: A name signals a style, so a writer of romance and thrillers can keep each audience's expectations clear.

LESSONS.push: Her name on the cover could have cost her readers. Why writers choose a disguise.

LESSONS.title: Dracula: the theatre manager's monster
LESSONS.hook: The world's most famous vampire was created by a busy Irish theatre manager who never set foot in Transylvania. Much of what we think we know about Dracula isn't in the book.

sections.key: Bram Stoker spent most of his career managing a London theatre and wrote fiction in his spare time.
sections.b:
Abraham 'Bram' Stoker was born in Dublin in 1847. As a small child he was so ill that he could barely walk, and he later wrote that he spent his early years in bed listening to his mother's stories, including grim memories of a cholera epidemic. He recovered completely and became a champion athlete at Trinity College Dublin.

He worked as a civil servant at Dublin Castle while writing theatre reviews for free. One review praised the actor Henry Irving, the two became friends, and in 1878 Stoker moved to London to become business manager of Irving's Lyceum Theatre. He held the job for around 27 years, handling everything from finances to tours, and wrote fiction in the gaps.

sections.key: Stoker built on a century of vampire folklore and fiction and added scale, research and method.
sections.b:
Vampires did not begin with Stoker. Eastern European folklore told of the restless dead returning to harm the living, and vampire panics in the 1700s spread across Europe. In 1819 John Polidori's story The Vampyre gave the creature an aristocratic, seductive character. In the 1840s the cheap serial Varney the Vampire thrilled readers for years. In 1872 Sheridan Le Fanu published Carmilla, about a female vampire, which scholars widely see as an influence on Stoker.

What Stoker added was scale and method. He spent several years researching and planning, filling notebooks with ideas, and fused folklore, modern technology and Victorian anxieties into one sweeping thriller that would overshadow everything before it.

sections.key: Stoker's villain began as Count Wampyr and took the name Dracula from a library book he found in Whitby.
sections.b:
Stoker's surviving working notes show his vampire began as Count Wampyr. In 1890 he holidayed in Whitby, a Yorkshire fishing town with a ruined abbey on the cliff. In the local library he read an 1820 book about Wallachia and Moldavia that mentioned a ruler called Dracula and claimed the word meant devil in the local language. Stoker seized the name.

The historical figure behind it was Vlad III of Wallachia, known as Vlad the Impaler, but scholars point out that Stoker seems to have known very little about him beyond the name.

Whitby itself found its way into the novel. Dracula comes ashore there when a ship runs aground in a storm, and he leaps onto land in the shape of a large dog.

sections.key: Dracula is told through diaries, letters and recordings, and its heroes beat an ancient monster with modern technology and teamwork.
sections.b:
Dracula, published in May 1897, has no single narrator. It is assembled from journals, letters, newspaper cuttings, a ship's log and telegrams. This form, called an epistolary novel, makes the story feel like a case file of real evidence.

It was also strikingly modern. Dr Seward records his diary on a phonograph, and Mina Harker types up and organises the documents on a typewriter, cross-referencing them to track the Count. The heroes use trains, telegrams and blood transfusions.

Stoker set an ancient monster against the newest technology of the 1890s, and much of the tension comes from that clash. The heroes win less through strength than through information, teamwork and careful paperwork.

sections.key: Several famous vampire rules come from films, not the novel, and Florence Stoker's lawsuit nearly destroyed the unauthorised Nosferatu.
sections.b:
Readers who come to the novel from films are often surprised. Stoker's Count walks around London in daylight; the sun weakens his powers but does not destroy him. Sunlight as a killer was popularised by the 1922 German silent film Nosferatu. The novel's Count is first an old man with a long white moustache who grows younger as he feeds. The suave figure in evening dress owes much to stage adaptations and Bela Lugosi's 1931 Hollywood performance. Garlic, crucifixes and a stake through the heart do appear, but Stoker freely mixed his rules.

Stoker died in 1912 with modest means. Nosferatu was an unauthorised adaptation that renamed the Count as Orlok. His widow Florence sued, and a German court ordered copies destroyed. Some prints survived abroad, and the film is now considered a masterpiece.

quiz.q: What was Bram Stoker's main career?
o: Full-time novelist and magazine writer
Lecturer at Trinity College Dublin
Business manager of a London theatre
Newspaper editor in his home city
quiz.e: Stoker managed Henry Irving's Lyceum Theatre for around 27 years and wrote fiction in spare moments.

quiz.q: What did Stoker add to earlier vampire stories?
o: The first ever female vampire character
The idea of vampires as aristocrats
Years of research and careful planning
A factual account of the vampire panics
quiz.e: Others had written about vampires, but Stoker planned and fused folklore and modern concerns at scale.

quiz.q: Where did the name Dracula come from?
o: A library book he read in Whitby
A Romanian friend of Irving
A real prince he visited in Wallachia
His mother's childhood stories
quiz.e: Stoker's notes began with Count Wampyr, and he took Dracula from a book he found in Whitby.

quiz.q: How do the characters defeat Dracula in the novel?
o: By physical strength and combat alone
By relying only on old folklore
By avoiding modern technology entirely
Information, teamwork and careful records
quiz.e: The heroes use phonographs, typewriters, trains and telegrams to organise and share what they know.

quiz.q: Which popular idea about vampires is not in Stoker's novel?
o: A stake through the heart can kill them
Sunlight destroys them
Garlic can ward them off
They can appear as a dog, a bat or a wolf
quiz.e: In the book the Count walks about in daylight, and the sunlight kill came from Nosferatu.

LESSONS.push: The most famous vampire never burned in sunlight in his own book.

LESSONS.title: Charles Dickens and the cliffhanger
LESSONS.hook: Dickens wrote his novels a few chapters at a time, while readers waited for each new instalment. A secret childhood trauma shaped much of what he wrote.

sections.key: A painful childhood spent pasting labels in a warehouse gave Dickens a lifelong sympathy for poor children.
sections.b:
Charles Dickens was born in Portsmouth in 1812, the son of a navy pay clerk who was hopeless with money. In 1824, when Charles was twelve, his father was imprisoned for debt in London's Marshalsea prison, and much of the family moved in with him, as was common then.

Charles was sent to work in a warehouse near the Thames, pasting labels onto pots of boot blacking for about ten hours a day. The job lasted perhaps a year, but he felt abandoned and humiliated. He told almost no one. The full story became public only after his death, when his friend John Forster published his biography.

The echoes run through his novels, which are full of orphans, debtors and cruel institutions.

sections.key: Dickens's training as a shorthand reporter sharpened his ear, and a comic serial made him Britain's most popular author in his mid-twenties.
sections.b:
Dickens had little formal schooling, but he taught himself shorthand and became a fast, skilled reporter, including in the press gallery of parliament. He watched people closely and listened to how they spoke. His humorous sketches of London life appeared under the pen name Boz.

In 1836 a publisher asked him to write text to accompany a series of comic sporting illustrations. Dickens took control of the project, which became The Pickwick Papers. Sales started slowly, but when the witty Cockney servant Sam Weller appeared, the story took off. By the end of its run, each monthly part was selling tens of thousands of copies. Dickens was in his mid-twenties and already the most popular author in Britain.

sections.key: Publishing in cheap instalments let Dickens write a few chapters ahead, end on suspense and respond to readers.
sections.b:
Most of Dickens's novels first appeared in parts rather than as complete books. The typical format was a monthly instalment of about 32 pages with two illustrations, costing one shilling, usually running for nineteen or twenty months. Some novels, such as Oliver Twist, ran in magazines.

This made fiction affordable for more people, since buying a part a month was easier than paying for a whole book. It also shaped how Dickens wrote. He often stayed only a few instalments ahead of publication, ended parts on moments of suspense and could adjust stories in response to readers' reactions.

Families and neighbours gathered to read new instalments aloud, so a single copy might reach many listeners.

sections.key: Readers grieved openly for Dickens's characters, and A Christmas Carol helped shape the modern idea of Christmas while piracy cost him income.
sections.b:
The Old Curiosity Shop, published weekly in 1840 and 1841, followed the doomed child Little Nell. As her death approached, readers begged Dickens to spare her. A famous story says crowds on a New York wharf shouted to arriving ships asking whether she was dead, but historians note the tale is poorly documented and may be embellished. What is certain is that many readers grieved openly.

In 1843, short of money, Dickens wrote A Christmas Carol in about six weeks. He insisted on an expensive edition with gilt edges and colour illustrations at a low price, so his profits disappointed. The story helped popularise a Christmas of family, generosity and feasting.

He also fought piracy. American publishers could reprint British books without paying the author, and the United States did not protect foreign authors meaningfully until 1891.

sections.key: Dickens became a star performer on paid reading tours, which earned a fortune but exhausted him.
sections.b:
From the late 1850s, Dickens gave paid public readings of his work, playing every character with different voices and gestures. Audiences in Britain and America packed halls to see him. The tours earned him a fortune but exhausted him, especially his violent reading of the murder of Nancy from Oliver Twist.

In June 1865 he survived a serious railway accident at Staplehurst in Kent, when his train crashed on a bridge under repair. He helped tend the injured and dying, then remembered his manuscript and climbed back into the carriage to retrieve it. He was shaken for the rest of his life.

He died in 1870, five years to the day after the crash, leaving The Mystery of Edwin Drood unfinished.

quiz.q: How did Dickens's childhood shape his novels?
o: He wrote only about wealthy families and clergy
His long schooling gave him a classical style
Child labour after his father's imprisonment
His father's navy career inspired his plots
quiz.e: His humiliating factory job left a lasting sympathy for orphans, debtors and the poor.

quiz.q: What skill from reporting helped make Dickens a writer?
o: Listening closely to how people spoke
Writing very long and detailed reports
Sketching the scenes he reported on
Translating news from foreign papers
quiz.e: Years as a shorthand reporter trained him to watch and listen to people closely.

quiz.q: Why did serial publication change how Dickens wrote?
o: He finished every novel before publishing it
He wrote only short stories for magazines
He ignored reader reactions as he wrote
He wrote as he went, ending parts on suspense
quiz.e: Writing as he went let him build suspense and adjust stories in response to readers.

quiz.q: Why did A Christmas Carol disappoint Dickens financially?
o: Most readers waited for a cheaper edition
Its lavish production cost left little profit
He sold the rights before it was published
The printer failed to deliver the books on time
quiz.e: His insistence on an expensive-looking edition at a low price squeezed his profits.

quiz.q: What did Dickens's reading tours cost him?
o: They made him a financial loss overall
They ended his career as a novelist
They earned a fortune but left him exhausted
They were only ever held at home in London
quiz.e: Performing every character was draining, especially the murder of Nancy.

LESSONS.push: He pasted labels on boot polish at twelve and never told anyone. It shaped his novels.

LESSONS.title: Invented languages: from Esperanto to Klingon
LESSONS.hook: People have built entire languages from scratch, hoping to unite the world, deepen a fantasy, or just for fun. Most failed. A few took on lives of their own.

sections.key: People have invented languages for nearly nine centuries, for logic, communication or fiction.
sections.b:
Constructed languages, often called conlangs, are designed by a person rather than evolving naturally in a community. One of the earliest recorded is the Lingua Ignota, or unknown language, created by the German abbess Hildegard of Bingen in the twelfth century, with around a thousand invented words.

In the 1600s, philosophers such as John Wilkins in England tried to build perfectly logical languages, where every word's form would reveal its meaning by sorting all of reality into categories. These schemes were brilliant and unusable.

Historians have counted hundreds of attempts. Their makers have had three main motives: to help people from different nations communicate, to explore ideas about logic and thought, or to bring a fictional world to life.

sections.key: Volapük boomed and split because its creator held on to control, and the simpler Esperanto took over.
sections.b:
In 1879 Johann Martin Schleyer, a Catholic priest in southern Germany, published Volapük, an international language. In the 1880s it spread astonishingly fast, with clubs, journals and congresses, and supporters claimed a very large following, though such numbers are hard to verify. But Volapük was difficult, with complex grammar and words so altered from their sources that they were hard to recognise. When reformers proposed simplifying it, Schleyer insisted on keeping control, and the movement split. Within a few years most followers had moved to a rival.

That rival was Esperanto, published in 1887 by Ludwik Zamenhof, an eye doctor from Białystok, then part of the Russian Empire. He believed a neutral shared language could reduce the mistrust between the Poles, Jews, Germans and Russians around him. Spelling is phonetic and grammar has very few exceptions.

sections.key: Esperanto survived dictators and the rise of English, and remains the most successful international language ever created.
sections.b:
Esperanto's internationalism made authoritarian regimes suspicious. In Nazi Germany it was attacked as a Jewish conspiracy, partly because Zamenhof was Jewish, and the movement was suppressed. In Stalin's Soviet Union, many Esperantists were arrested in the purges of the late 1930s, accused of contact with foreigners. Zamenhof's own children were killed in the Holocaust.

Even so, the language survived, holding world congresses, publishing original literature and translations, and later thriving online. Estimates of speakers vary enormously, from tens of thousands of fluent users to perhaps a couple of million with some knowledge.

It never became the global second language its founder hoped for. English largely took that role, for reasons of power and economics rather than design. Still, it remains the most successful international language ever created.

sections.key: Tolkien invented languages first and then built a world and mythology for them to live in.
sections.b:
J. R. R. Tolkien was a professional philologist, an expert in the history of languages, and he invented languages from his teenage years onwards. He called the hobby his secret vice in a 1931 lecture.

For Tolkien, the languages came before the stories. He later explained that he built his mythology partly to give his languages a world and a history in which they could exist.

His two main Elvish languages were modelled on real ones he loved. Quenya drew on the sounds of Finnish, while Sindarin was influenced by Welsh. He also worked out how they had changed over thousands of years of imagined history. That depth helps explain why Middle-earth feels so ancient: its names carry the weight of invented centuries.

sections.key: Film and television turned language invention into a career, with consistent grammar that fans can actually learn.
sections.b:
In 1984 the linguist Marc Okrand developed the Klingon language for the film Star Trek III, building on a few words used earlier in the series. He deliberately gave it unusual features to sound alien, including a basic word order of object, verb, subject, which is rare among human languages. The Klingon Dictionary followed in 1985, and devoted fans have since translated works including Hamlet.

Later, the linguist David J. Peterson created Dothraki and High Valyrian for the television series Game of Thrones, and languages for many other productions. These languages have consistent grammar and vocabulary, which is why fans can learn them. Some have even appeared in mainstream language learning apps, a sign of how seriously the art is now taken.

quiz.q: What did philosophers like John Wilkins try to build?
o: A secret language for use by the church
Logical languages where words reveal meaning
A simplified form of everyday Latin
A trade language for merchants and sailors
quiz.e: Their schemes sorted reality into categories, which made them brilliant but unusable.

quiz.q: Why did Volapük collapse?
o: It was banned by European governments
It was quickly replaced by English
It was hard, and its creator resisted change
It never had any printed materials
quiz.e: Its complexity and Schleyer's insistence on control split the movement, and followers moved to Esperanto.

quiz.q: Why was Esperanto persecuted by dictatorships?
o: It threatened their national languages
It was spoken only by wealthy elites
Its internationalism made it seem suspicious
It was taught only in universities
quiz.e: Regimes attacked Esperanto because it was international and connected people across borders.

quiz.q: What was unusual about how Tolkien worked?
o: He built his world to house his languages
He wrote the stories first and added words later
He translated his stories from Old Norse
He took his languages from older fantasy
quiz.e: Tolkien built his world partly to give his invented languages a place and a history.

quiz.q: Why can fans actually learn Klingon and Dothraki?
o: They are copied from real languages
They are simple versions of English
They have only a few hundred words
They have consistent grammar and vocabulary
quiz.e: Professional language creators give these languages systematic rules, so they work like real languages.

LESSONS.push: Most invented languages died young. Why a few became real communities.

LESSONS.title: Sign languages: real languages, not gestures
LESSONS.hook: Sign languages have their own grammar, history and even accents. They are not universal, and they are not English on the hands.

sections.key: Sign languages are many separate natural languages with their own grammar, not universal gestures or spoken words spelled on the hands.
sections.b:
Many hearing people assume sign language is one universal system of gestures, or a spoken language spelled out with the hands. Neither is true. There are many sign languages around the world, and one widely used reference catalogue lists well over a hundred.

They arise naturally wherever deaf people form communities, and they differ from each other as spoken languages do. British Sign Language and American Sign Language are not mutually intelligible, even though both countries speak English. Each has its own vocabulary and grammar, which are not copied from the spoken language around it.

Fingerspelling, where words are spelled letter by letter, exists but is used mainly for names and borrowed terms, not everyday conversation.

sections.key: American Sign Language differs from British because it descends largely from French Sign Language through a historical accident.
sections.b:
Why is American Sign Language so different from British? The answer is a historical accident. In 1815 Thomas Hopkins Gallaudet, an American minister, travelled to Britain to learn how to teach deaf children, but the schools he visited were secretive about their methods. Instead he met teachers from the Paris school for the deaf, which welcomed him, and studied there with Laurent Clerc, a deaf teacher.

Clerc agreed to come to America, and in 1817 they founded what is now the American School for the Deaf in Hartford, Connecticut. The French signs Clerc brought mixed with local sign systems used by American deaf people. The result was ASL, which still shares many signs with French Sign Language. Gallaudet University in Washington, DC, is named in his honour.

sections.key: On Martha's Vineyard hearing and deaf people shared a sign language, suggesting deafness becomes a disability when society cannot communicate.
sections.b:
On Martha's Vineyard, off Massachusetts, a hereditary form of deafness was unusually common from the 1700s into the early 1900s, especially in certain villages. A local sign language developed, and many hearing islanders learnt it too.

Deaf people married, worked, voted and joined community life much like anyone else, and hearing residents sometimes signed to each other even when no deaf person was present. The anthropologist Nora Ellen Groce documented this history in a 1985 book whose title reports what older residents told her: that everyone there spoke sign language.

The case suggests that deafness becomes a disability largely when society cannot communicate with deaf people. As the island became less isolated, the local sign language died out.

sections.key: A hearing-led congress banned sign language from deaf classrooms in 1880, yet sign languages survived through deaf communities.
sections.b:
In 1880, an international congress of educators of the deaf met in Milan. Almost all delegates were hearing, and they voted overwhelmingly for oralism, teaching deaf children only through speech and lip-reading, and against sign language in classrooms.

Over the following decades, schools in many countries followed this approach. Deaf children were often punished for signing, and some deaf teachers lost their jobs. Many deaf adults later described their schooling as deeply damaging, with years spent drilling speech instead of learning.

Yet sign languages survived in dormitories, playgrounds and deaf clubs, passed from child to child. In 2010 an international congress on deaf education, held in Vancouver, formally rejected the Milan resolutions and apologised for their effects.

sections.key: Research showed that signs have structure like spoken words, and Auslan belongs to the same family as British and New Zealand Sign Language.
sections.b:
For a long time even scholars thought sign was mere gesture. In 1960 William Stokoe, a hearing English teacher at Gallaudet College, showed that ASL signs break into meaningful building blocks, such as handshape, location and movement, much as spoken words are built from sounds. Change one element and the meaning changes. Later work found rich grammar, including space used to track who did what to whom, and raised eyebrows marking a yes or no question.

Australia's sign language is Auslan, a name that came into wide use in the 1980s. It descends mainly from British Sign Language, with some Irish influence, and is closely related to New Zealand Sign Language. Auslan users fingerspell with two hands, while ASL uses one. It was recognised in the 1987 national language policy.

quiz.q: Which statement about sign languages is accurate?
o: They are all mutually understandable
They copy the grammar of spoken languages
Each has its own vocabulary and grammar
They rely mainly on fingerspelling
quiz.e: Sign languages arise naturally in deaf communities and differ from each other as spoken languages do.

quiz.q: Why does American Sign Language differ so much from British?
o: It was invented from scratch in Hartford
It copies English word order
It descends largely from French Sign Language
British schools refused deaf students
quiz.e: Gallaudet learned from Paris teachers, and Clerc's French signs mixed with local American signs.

quiz.q: What does the Martha's Vineyard story suggest?
o: Disability often comes from social barriers
Deafness is easily cured in isolated places
Sign languages cannot survive for long
Hearing people learn signing with difficulty
quiz.e: Where everyone could sign, deaf islanders took part fully in community life.

quiz.q: What did the 1880 Milan congress decide?
o: Sign language should be taught in every school
Deaf teachers should lead all classes
Schools should use fingerspelling only
Deaf children should be taught by speech alone
quiz.e: The oralist ruling harmed many deaf students, though sign languages survived outside classrooms.

quiz.q: What did Stokoe's 1960 research show about ASL?
o: Signs are mostly pictures drawn in the air
Signs have parts, such as handshape and movement
Signs follow the grammar of spoken English
Signs have no consistent rules at all
quiz.e: Signs break into building blocks, just as words break into sounds, so sign is a true language.

LESSONS.push: In some places everyone signed, whether or not they were deaf. How that happened.

LESSONS.title: What your eyes and brain do when you read
LESSONS.hook: Reading feels smooth and effortless, but your eyes are jumping, stopping and skipping all the time. And your brain is using circuits that evolved for something else.

sections.key: Writing is too recent for evolution to have built a reading brain, so reading repurposes circuits that evolved for other tasks.
sections.b:
Humans have been speaking for at least tens of thousands of years, probably far longer, but writing was invented only around 5,000 years ago, and mass literacy is barely a few centuries old. That is far too recent for evolution to have produced a brain built for reading.

So how do we do it? The neuroscientist Stanislas Dehaene proposed a theory called neuronal recycling. Learning to read repurposes circuits that evolved for other jobs, such as recognising objects and faces, and links them to the brain's language areas.

In children learning to read, scans show a region on the underside of the left hemisphere becoming increasingly tuned to written letters and words. It is often called the visual word form area. In skilled readers it responds strongly to letters in a familiar script, and much less to unfamiliar symbols.

sections.key: One brain region becomes specialised in recognising written words, and damage to it can leave a person able to write but unable to read.
sections.b:
The visual word form area sits in the left fusiform gyrus, near areas that respond to faces and objects. It helps us recognise a word whether it is written in capitals, lower case or different fonts, an impressive feat of pattern recognition.

Damage to this area, for example from a stroke, can cause a condition in which a person can still write but struggles to read back what they have just written.

Research also suggests that learning to read changes the brain in other ways, including how it processes spoken sounds. This partly explains why reading and phonics are so closely linked.

sections.key: Your eyes read in quick jumps and pauses, and the brain stitches them into what feels like smooth reading.
sections.b:
Watch someone's eyes as they read and you will see they do not move smoothly along the line. They make quick jumps called saccades, separated by brief pauses called fixations. In English, a typical fixation lasts roughly a quarter of a second, and a typical jump covers around seven to nine letters.

During the jump itself, you take in almost no useful visual information. The brain stitches the pauses together so that reading feels continuous.

Readers skip many short, predictable words, such as the and of, and land more often on longer content words. About one jump in ten or so goes backwards as the reader checks something. Researchers study all this with eye trackers, which record exactly where and when the eyes stop.

sections.key: You see only a few letters clearly at a time, and your window of attention extends ahead in your reading direction.
sections.b:
Sharp vision covers only a tiny part of what your eyes see, so at each fixation you can identify only a handful of letters clearly. Experiments in which on-screen text changes depending on where the reader is looking have measured this window.

For English readers it extends roughly three or four letters to the left of the fixation point and about fourteen or fifteen to the right, because that is where the next words are. For readers of Hebrew, which runs right to left, the window is reversed.

Information at the edge of the window helps the brain plan the next jump and get a head start on the next word. Reading, in short, is constant prediction.

sections.key: Reading much faster usually means understanding much less, and the famous scrambled-letters meme is not Cambridge research.
sections.b:
Typical silent reading speeds for adults are roughly 200 to 300 words per minute. A major 2016 review led by the eye-movement scientist Keith Rayner concluded that speed reading claims of thousands of words per minute do not hold up. The limit is the brain's speed in recognising words and understanding language, not the eyes. Pushing faster means comprehension drops. Speed reading is essentially skimming, a useful skill for finding information but no shortcut to deep understanding. Faster reading comes mainly from reading more.

The scrambled-letters meme claims research at Cambridge shows letter order does not matter if the first and last letters are right. Matt Davis, a Cambridge scientist, found no such study. The text works partly because many words are short, function words are intact, and letters stay near their correct positions. Jumbled text still slows readers down.

quiz.q: How does the brain manage to read despite writing being so recent?
o: It uses a dedicated reading organ
It copies speech centres entirely
It relies on memory alone
It repurposes circuits from other tasks
quiz.e: Neuronal recycling adapts older circuits, such as those for recognising objects and faces, for reading.

quiz.q: What can damage to the visual word form area cause?
o: Losing the ability to speak
Being able to write but not read it back
Forgetting how to recognise faces
Being unable to hear sounds
quiz.e: This region is specialised for recognising written words, so damage can disrupt reading while writing survives.

quiz.q: What do your eyes actually do while you read?
o: Glide smoothly along each line
Scan every letter one by one
Jump and pause, seeing little mid-jump
Fix on each word for a full second
quiz.e: Saccades and fixations are stitched together by the brain so that reading feels continuous.

quiz.q: Why does the attention window reach further in your reading direction?
o: The eyes see better on one side
Letters ahead are larger
The next words to be read lie ahead
Words behind need more checking
quiz.e: Information ahead helps the brain plan the next jump, so reading is constant prediction.

quiz.q: What does research say about speed reading?
o: Much faster reading usually reduces comprehension
It can double comprehension with practice
It works if you stop hearing words in your head
It is possible with special eye training
quiz.e: The brain's word recognition is the limit, so very fast reading is really skimming.

LESSONS.push: Your eyes never glide across a page. What they do instead may surprise you.

LESSONS.title: Banned books: the trials that changed what we can read
LESSONS.hook: Popes, customs officers and courts have all tried to stop people reading certain books. Again and again, the ban made the book more famous.

sections.key: For four centuries the Catholic Church kept an official list of forbidden books, which grew from fear of the printing press.
sections.b:
In 1559, under Pope Paul IV, the Catholic Church published the Index Librorum Prohibitorum, the Index of Prohibited Books. Catholics were forbidden to read or own listed works without permission.

The Index grew out of anxiety about the printing press and the Protestant Reformation, which spread new ideas faster than authorities could control them. Over time it included works by figures such as the astronomer Galileo and the philosopher René Descartes. Galileo's Dialogue, which defended the idea that the Earth moves around the Sun, stayed on the list for around two centuries.

The final edition appeared in 1948, and the Index was formally abolished in 1966, ending its legal force.

sections.key: Landmark trials in 1933 and 1960 won the right to publish frank novels by judging a book as a whole and weighing its literary merit.
sections.b:
James Joyce's Ulysses broke many rules, including frank descriptions of sex and the body. The full book appeared in Paris in 1922, then was smuggled and seized by customs. In 1933 Random House arranged a seizure to provoke a test case. Judge John M. Woolsey ruled the book, read as a whole, was not obscene, and it was published legally in the United States in 1934.

D. H. Lawrence's Lady Chatterley's Lover stayed banned in Britain in full for decades. A 1959 law allowed literary merit as a defence, and Penguin tested it in 1960 with a cheap, unabridged paperback. The prosecutor asked jurors if it was a book they would want their wives or servants to read, which sounded hopelessly out of touch. The jury acquitted Penguin.

sections.key: For much of the twentieth century Australia ran one of the strictest censorship regimes in the Western world, until pressure in the 1960s and 1970s forced reform.
sections.b:
Australian censorship ran largely through customs, which seized imported books at the border, alongside state obscenity laws. For long periods the list of banned titles was itself kept confidential, so readers often did not know what they were missing.

Works by Joyce, Lawrence and many others were banned at various times, as were political works judged subversive. Lady Chatterley's Lover stayed banned in Australia for several years after the British trial.

Pressure for change grew through the 1960s. In 1970, Penguin Australia secretly printed Philip Roth's banned novel Portnoy's Complaint locally and distributed it, provoking prosecutions in several states. Around the same time, the federal customs minister Don Chipp began dramatically loosening the system, moving toward a classification approach.

sections.key: Censorship has sometimes gone beyond bans into book burning and violence against authors and translators.
sections.b:
On 10 May 1933, Nazi-organised students in Berlin and other German cities burnt tens of thousands of books by Jewish, left-wing and other authors deemed un-German. More than a century earlier the poet Heinrich Heine, whose own works were burnt, had written in a play that where books are burnt, people will eventually be burnt too.

In 1989 Iran's supreme leader, Ayatollah Khomeini, issued a fatwa calling for the death of Salman Rushdie over his novel The Satanic Verses, which many Muslims considered blasphemous. Rushdie spent years in hiding. His Japanese translator, Hitoshi Igarashi, was murdered in 1991.

In 2022, Rushdie himself was stabbed at a public lecture in New York state and lost the sight of one eye.

sections.key: Banning a book often advertises it, and today's challenges target library shelves rather than customs lists.
sections.b:
Censors face a stubborn problem: forbidding a book advertises it. The Lady Chatterley trial turned a little-read novel into a bestseller, and Ulysses gained a glamorous reputation partly because readers had to smuggle it.

Today, book bans more often take the form of challenges to books in school and public libraries, where parents or groups ask for titles to be removed. Organisations such as the American Library Association track these challenges, which in recent years have frequently targeted books about race, gender and sexuality.

People still argue about where the line falls between protecting children and restricting ideas. Many libraries celebrate an annual Banned Books Week, inviting readers to discover the books others tried to keep from them.

quiz.q: What prompted the Church to create the Index of Prohibited Books?
o: A shortage of paper for printing books
A dispute over translations of the Bible
A rise in book smuggling from overseas
Fear of new ideas spreading in print
quiz.e: The printing press spread new ideas faster than authorities could control them.

quiz.q: What did the 1933 Ulysses ruling establish?
o: All books must be approved by customs
Books must be judged as a whole
Foreign books cannot be sold
Publishers must remove frank scenes
quiz.e: Judge Woolsey found Ulysses, read as a whole, was not obscene, opening the way to publication.

quiz.q: How did Australian book censorship largely operate?
o: By local parish licences alone
Through publisher self-regulation
Customs seizures and secret lists
By boards run by universities
quiz.e: Customs checked imports at the border, and readers often could not see the lists of banned titles.

quiz.q: What was the Nazi book burning aimed at?
o: Only books that attacked the Church
Foreign newspapers and magazines only
Authors the regime called un-German
Scientific and technical textbooks
quiz.e: The burnings of 1933 targeted authors the regime judged un-German.

quiz.q: Why do bans often backfire?
o: A ban makes people curious about the book
Banned books are cheaper to print
Authors write more when they are censored
Libraries stock more copies of them
quiz.e: A ban advertises the book, as the Lady Chatterley trial and the smuggling of Ulysses showed.

LESSONS.push: A ban meant to silence a book tends to do the opposite. Four famous cases.

LESSONS.title: Does your language shape how you think?
LESSONS.hook: Do Inuit really have hundreds of words for snow? Does a language without left and right change how you see the world? The truth is stranger and more subtle than the myths.

sections.key: Language may nudge what we notice and remember, but it does not set the limits of what we can think.
sections.b:
Benjamin Lee Whorf was a chemical engineer who worked for a fire insurance company in Connecticut and studied linguistics in his spare time, partly under Edward Sapir. He noticed workers being careless near drums labelled ‘empty’ that still held explosive vapour. The word, he suggested, was shaping their behaviour. In the 1930s he argued that speakers of very different languages think differently. This became the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis, though neither man stated it formally.

The strong version says language sets the limits of thought. It is almost certainly false: babies and animals reason without words, and we keep inventing words for new ideas. The weak version, linguistic relativity, says language nudges what you notice and remember.

sections.key: The Hopi no-time claim and the Inuit snow-words claim are both exaggerations that careful linguists debunked.
sections.b:
Whorf claimed the Hopi language of Arizona had no words or grammar for time as we understand it. In 1983 the linguist Ekkehart Malotki documented extensive Hopi time expressions, including words for days, seasons and units of time.

The claim that Inuit have dozens or hundreds of words for snow grew from a modest remark by the anthropologist Franz Boas, who mentioned four root words. It swelled with each retelling until Laura Martin and Geoffrey Pullum debunked it in the 1980s. Inuit languages build long words from many parts, so counting words misleads, and English has plenty of snow words too.

sections.key: Guugu Yimithirr speakers use compass directions instead of left and right, and keep track of direction at all times.
sections.b:
Some of the strongest evidence for linguistic relativity comes from Australia. Speakers of Guugu Yimithirr, from Cape York in Queensland, do not use words like left, right, in front or behind to say where things are. They use cardinal directions, even at small scales: there is an ant on your northern leg.

John Haviland and Stephen Levinson found that speakers kept remarkably accurate track of direction at all times, even indoors or after travelling, because their language demands it. When people turned around and recreated arrangements of objects, such speakers preserved compass direction. English and Dutch speakers preserved left and right.

sections.key: Language can sharpen colour distinctions, supply tools such as number words, and shape how people picture time.
sections.b:
Russian has separate basic words for lighter blue (goluboy) and darker blue (siniy). In a 2007 study, Russian speakers were slightly faster at telling two shades apart across that boundary, but not when they silently repeated numbers, which suggests language was involved.

The Pirahã of the Amazon have no exact number words. In several experiments they struggled with exact quantities beyond about three, though results varied. Number words may be a cognitive tool for exactness.

English speakers lay time out left to right, Hebrew and Arabic speakers often right to left, and Kuuk Thaayorre speakers on Cape York east to west, whichever way they face. Aymara links the past with the front, since you can see it.

sections.key: Most researchers accept a modest form of linguistic relativity, with caution about the headline findings.
sections.b:
Most researchers now accept a modest form of relativity. Language does not trap anyone's mind, but it guides attention, makes some distinctions easier to notice and remember, and provides tools like number words.

Caution is still essential. Some well-publicised findings, such as grammatical gender changing how people describe objects, have proved hard to replicate. Claims linking grammar to behaviour like saving money remain contested. Critics such as the psychologist Steven Pinker argue that thought runs on something deeper than any particular language. Learning another language may not rewire your mind, but it can show you distinctions you never noticed.

quiz.q: Why is the strong version of the Sapir-Whorf idea almost certainly false?
o: Translation between languages is never possible
People can think about things they have no words for
Children learn grammar before they hear any words
Words never influence what people pay attention to
quiz.e: People, babies and animals can reason without words, so language does not set the limits of thought.

quiz.q: How did the claim that Inuit have hundreds of words for snow arise?
o: Linguists counted them in a large survey
A study of Hopi time words was misapplied
A modest remark about four root words was exaggerated
Inuit grammar has a separate form for each snowfall
quiz.e: The claim grew from a small observation that was inflated with every retelling.

quiz.q: Why do Guugu Yimithirr speakers keep such accurate track of direction?
o: Everyday descriptions require compass directions
They carry maps and compasses everywhere
They avoid travelling away from home
Their language has no words for place
quiz.e: A language that demands compass directions trains its speakers to know them at all times.

quiz.q: What did the Pirahã number studies suggest?
o: Numbers are an inborn human sense
Exact number words may be a tool for exact quantities
People cannot learn to count as adults
Large quantities cannot be estimated at all
quiz.e: Without number words, exact quantities beyond about three became hard, so number words extend what we can do.

quiz.q: What do most researchers now accept about language and thought?
o: Language guides attention without trapping the mind
Language fully determines what people can think
Language has no effect on thinking at all
Grammatical gender reliably changes perception
quiz.e: A modest form of relativity holds: language nudges attention and offers tools, but it does not limit thought.

LESSONS.push: Does the word for something change how you see it? The truth is subtler than myth.

LESSONS.title: The pigeonhole principle: the simplest idea that proves surprising things
