LESSONS.hook: If you have more pigeons than holes, some hole holds two pigeons. That is the whole idea, and it can prove that two people in Sydney have exactly the same number of hairs.

sections.key: If more items go into fewer boxes, some box must hold two, which proves something exists without finding it.
sections.b:
Ten pigeons fly home to nine pigeonholes. However they arrange themselves, at least one hole must hold two birds. There is no trick, no probability and no calculation. It cannot be otherwise. This is the pigeonhole principle, perhaps the most obvious statement in all of mathematics.

Mathematicians love it because it proves something must exist without ever finding it. You need not know which hole is crowded, only that one is. Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet used the idea in the 1830s and 1840s, and in German it became the Schubfachprinzip, the drawer principle. The English name probably refers to small desk or mail-sorter compartments, not actual birds.

sections.key: When items outnumber the possible categories, a match is certain, even if you can never find it.
sections.b:
Black and grey socks sit jumbled in a dark drawer. How many must you grab to be certain of a pair? Three. Two socks might be one of each, but a third must match one. The colours are the holes and the socks are the pigeons. Likewise, among 367 people two must share a birthday, since there are only 366 dates. Certainty differs from likelihood: a shared birthday is likely with 23 people, but only 367 guarantees it.

Sydney has over five million people. A head holds roughly 100,000 hairs, perhaps up to 150,000, and nobody has a million. Make a hole for every count from zero to one million, and at least two Sydneysiders must have exactly the same number. In fact at least five share one.

sections.key: Divide the items by the boxes and round up to find the fewest that must share a box.
sections.b:
A stronger version tells you how crowded a box must be. Suppose 100 people at a conference are each born on one of the seven days of the week. Dividing 100 by 7 gives about 14.3, so at least one weekday is the birthday of 15 or more of them.

The rule is to divide the number of items by the number of boxes and round up. With 10 pigeons and 3 holes, some hole has at least 4. This is how you can prove that among any 13 people, at least two were born in the same month, and among any 25, at least three were.

sections.key: The pigeonhole trick is to show there are fewer real options than there appear to be.
sections.b:
At a party, guests shake hands with some others, never with themselves or twice with the same person. Prove that two guests shook exactly the same number of hands.

Say there are 20 guests. Each person's count could be anything from 0 to 19, which looks like 20 values for 20 people, just enough to all differ. But look closer. If someone shook nobody's hand, then nobody can have shaken all 19 others. So 0 and 19 cannot both appear. That leaves only 19 usable holes for 20 guests, and two people must share a count. The trick is common: first show there are fewer real options than there seem.

sections.key: Counting possibilities against items shows what is impossible, from universal compression to collision-free fingerprints.
sections.b:
The principle sets hard limits in computing. Could a clever program shrink every possible file, even by one bit? Counting says no. There are 1,024 different files exactly 10 bits long but only 1,023 shorter ones, including the empty file. If every 10-bit file shrank, two would share a compressed version and the program could not know which to restore. Real compression works because everyday files are full of patterns; truly random data cannot be squeezed.

The same logic explains why hash functions, which turn any data into a short fingerprint, must sometimes give two inputs the same fingerprint. Security depends on making such collisions extraordinarily hard to find. The principle guarantees only that a match exists, not where it is.

quiz.q: What can the pigeonhole principle prove?
o: How many boxes are crowded
That some box must be shared
Which specific box holds two items
The probability of a shared box
quiz.e: It guarantees that some box is shared, even though it says nothing about which one.

quiz.q: Why must two Sydney residents have exactly the same number of hairs?
o: Hair counts are always whole thousands
Most people have the same hair colour
Residents outnumber the possible hair counts
Hair counts never change over time
quiz.e: With more than five million people and only about a million possible counts, some count must repeat.

quiz.q: If 10 pigeons go into 3 holes, what can you say for certain?
o: Some hole has at least 4 pigeons
Every hole has exactly 3 pigeons
No hole has more than 3 pigeons
Some hole is left empty
quiz.e: Ten divided by three is about 3.3, and rounding up means some hole holds at least 4.

quiz.q: In the 20-guest handshake puzzle, why are there only 19 usable counts?
o: Guests cannot shake their own hands
Nobody shakes hands more than once
Counts of 0 and 19 cannot both occur
Two guests always shake no hands
quiz.e: Someone with 19 handshakes met everyone, so nobody can have 0, which leaves fewer options than guests.

quiz.q: Why can no lossless program shrink every possible file?
o: Shorter files are fewer than longer ones
Programs cannot read files bit by bit
Shorter files are always less accurate
Compression only works on text files
quiz.e: There are not enough shorter files to give each longer file its own compressed version.

LESSONS.push: Two people in Sydney have exactly the same number of hairs. Here's how we know.

LESSONS.title: The clever maths hiding in A4 paper
LESSONS.hook: Fold an A4 sheet in half and you get a smaller sheet of exactly the same shape. That is no accident: it rests on a single number, the square root of 2.

sections.key: Only a rectangle with sides in the ratio of the square root of 2 keeps its shape every time it is halved.
sections.b:
Cut most rectangles in half and the halves change shape. A square becomes two long strips; a sheet twice as long as wide becomes two squares. That is a nuisance for printers, because pages will not shrink neatly onto the next size down.

Call the short side 1 and the long side r. Fold the sheet and the old short side becomes the new long side, while the new short side is r divided by 2. For the shape to stay the same, r over 1 must equal 1 over r/2. So r squared is 2, and r is the square root of 2, about 1.414. A4 measures 210 by 297 millimetres, and 297 divided by 210 is 1.414. Fold it for A5, 148 by 210, with the same proportions.

sections.key: Each size in the A series has half the area of the one before, so enlarging or reducing scales each side by the square root of 2.
sections.b:
A0 has an area of one square metre, measuring 841 by 1,189 millimetres. Halve it for A1, then A2, A3 and A4, which is one sixteenth of a square metre. So a standard 80 gram sheet of A4 weighs 5 grams, handy for estimating the weight of a letter.

The photocopier's odd settings, 141% and 71%, are the square root of 2 in disguise. To enlarge A4 to A3 the area must double, so each side grows by 1.414, or 141%. Shrinking A4 to A5 scales each side by 0.707, or 71%. Because every sheet has the same shape, copies fit with no white strip down one side.

sections.key: The square root of 2 shape was noticed in 1786, but took until the twentieth century to become an international standard.
sections.b:
In 1786 the German scientist Georg Christoph Lichtenberg noted in a letter that a sheet with sides in the ratio of the square root of 2 could be halved again and again without changing shape. Revolutionary France, busy rationalising everything from weights to calendars, used the same ratio for some official paper in a 1798 stamp duty law.

The idea then faded until the German engineer Walter Porstmann built a full system around it, starting from one square metre. Germany adopted it as DIN 476 in 1922, and in 1975 it became the international standard ISO 216. Australia uses it, as do most nations. The United States and Canada mostly keep older inch-based sizes such as Letter.

sections.key: The B and C series fit between the A sizes, so a whole family of sheets and envelopes fits together.
sections.b:
The system has two companion series. B sizes sit between A sizes. B4, at 250 by 353 millimetres, is larger than A4 but smaller than A3, and each side is the geometric mean of its neighbours: multiply them and take the square root. B sizes suit posters, passports and some books.

The C series, mostly for envelopes, sits between A and B, so a C envelope is just larger than the matching A sheet. A C4 envelope holds an A4 sheet flat, while a C5 takes A4 folded once. The popular DL envelope, 110 by 220 millimetres, suits A4 folded into thirds. One number holds the whole family together.

sections.key: Only the square root of 2 survives halving, which is why paper uses it rather than the golden ratio.
sections.b:
People often assume elegant rectangles follow the golden ratio, about 1.618, though many claims of it in art and architecture are exaggerated. A golden rectangle has its own neat trick: cut a square off one end and what remains is another golden rectangle.

That is beautiful mathematics, but it is not what paper needs. When you fold a sheet you halve it, rather than trim off a square, and only the square root of 2 survives halving. US Letter, 8.5 by 11 inches, has a ratio of about 1.29, and folding it in half changes its shape noticeably. A4 is a quiet reminder that a simple equation, solved properly, can make countless everyday jobs easier.

quiz.q: What is the ratio of the long side to the short side of A4 paper?
o: About 1.618
About 1.414
About 1.29
About 2.0
quiz.e: The square root of 2, about 1.414, is the only ratio that stays the same when a sheet is halved.

quiz.q: Why does a photocopier use 141% to enlarge A4 onto A3?
o: Doubling the area scales each side by 1.414
The paper must be one and a half times longer
Each side must double in length
Copiers always add a 41% margin
quiz.e: Doubling the area means scaling each side by the square root of 2, about 141%.

quiz.q: What did Lichtenberg notice about sheets with sides in the ratio of the square root of 2?
o: They halve again and again without changing shape
They were the most pleasing rectangle
They always had an area of one square metre
They fitted any envelope without folding
quiz.e: Because halving preserves the shape, such sheets can be divided again and again.

quiz.q: Which envelope is designed for A4 folded into thirds?
o: C4
C5
B4
DL
quiz.e: The DL envelope, 110 by 220 millimetres, is made for an A4 sheet folded in three.

quiz.q: Why does paper use the square root of 2 rather than the golden ratio?
o: The golden ratio cannot be measured
Only the square root of 2 survives halving
Golden rectangles are too narrow to print
The golden ratio is only used in the United States
quiz.e: A sheet is halved, not trimmed by a square, and only the square root of 2 keeps its shape when halved.

LESSONS.push: Fold A4 in half and the shape stays the same. One number makes that possible.

LESSONS.title: Every shuffle is history: the astonishing size of 52!
LESSONS.hook: Shuffle a pack of cards properly and you have almost certainly created an order that no one in history has ever held. The maths behind that claim is simple and staggering.

sections.key: A pack of 52 cards can be ordered in about 8 followed by 67 zeros ways, far more than all shuffles ever made.
sections.b:
Three books can be arranged 3 × 2 × 1 = 6 ways; four, 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 24. This multiplying-down pattern is a factorial, written 4!. Christian Kramp introduced the notation in 1808. Ten books give 3,628,800 orders, and twenty give more than two quintillion.

For a pack of 52 cards, 52! is roughly 8 × 10⁶⁷, a number 68 digits long that begins 8065. Imagine all eight billion people alive today shuffling once a second since the Big Bang, about 13.8 billion years ago. They would have made roughly 3.5 × 10²⁷ decks, less than a billionth of a billionth of a billionth of all possible orders.

sections.key: A thoroughly shuffled deck is almost certainly in a new order, and about seven riffle shuffles are enough to get there.
sections.b:
A well-shuffled deck is almost certainly in an order that has never existed before. The catch is the word ‘well’. A new pack comes in set order, and a couple of lazy shuffles leave much of it intact. Uniqueness applies only when all 52! orders are equally likely.

How many shuffles is enough? In 1992 Dave Bayer and Persi Diaconis analysed the riffle shuffle, where you split the deck and let the halves fall together. The deck stays noticeably ordered at first, then becomes well mixed quite suddenly at around seven shuffles. More adds little. The overhand shuffle is far weaker: one analysis suggested thousands. Diaconis left home as a teenager to travel as a magician before becoming a professor of statistics.

sections.key: A perfectly precise shuffle is not random, and repeating a fixed rearrangement eventually returns you to the start.
sections.b:
Skilled magicians can cut a deck into two exact halves of 26 and interleave them perfectly, one card from each side in turn. In the out-shuffle, the top card stays on top. Do it once and the deck looks mixed. Keep going and something surprising happens: after exactly eight perfect out-shuffles, a 52-card deck returns to its original order.

Magicians use this predictability to make a pack look mixed while knowing where every card is. The lesson is that mixing depends on randomness. A shuffle that is too precise is just a permutation, a fixed rearrangement, and repeating a fixed rearrangement enough times brings you back to where you began.

sections.key: Divide by the number of ways to rearrange a selection when the order of its items makes no difference.
sections.b:
Sometimes order does not matter. A five-card poker hand is the same hand whatever order you pick the cards up in. To count hands, start with 52 × 51 × 50 × 49 × 48 ordered ways to deal five cards, then divide by 5!, the 120 ways of rearranging the same five. That gives 2,598,960 possible hands.

The same idea measures lotteries. A game where you choose 6 numbers from 45 has 8,145,060 combinations, so one entry has about a one in eight million chance of the top prize. This kind of counting is called combinatorics. It tells you plainly how long the odds are, and why a lottery ticket is entertainment, not a plan.

sections.key: When you want something hard to guess, length and genuine randomness matter far more than clever substitutions.
sections.b:
Explosive growth in possibilities protects you every day. A four-digit PIN has only 10,000 possibilities, which is why banks lock a card after a few wrong guesses. A long password made of several random words has vastly more, because each extra word multiplies the total.

Modern encryption relies on keys chosen from so many possibilities that trying them all would take longer than the age of the universe, even with enormous computing power. The same principle that makes a shuffled deck unique makes a properly chosen key unguessable.

The practical takeaway: length and genuine randomness matter far more than clever substitutions, such as swapping the letter o for a zero.

quiz.q: Why does a pack of 52 cards have so many possible orders?
o: Choices shrink: 52, then 51, then 50 …
Each card can face up or down
Cards can be dealt in any of 52 suits
Every shuffle adds a new card
quiz.e: Multiplying the shrinking number of choices for each position gives 52!, an enormous total.

quiz.q: Why is a well-shuffled deck almost certainly in a unique order?
o: Casinos never reuse a deck
Possible orders vastly outnumber shuffles ever made
Every shuffle changes the order of the cards
Cards keep their order after any shuffle
quiz.e: The number of possible orders dwarfs the number of shuffles that have taken place.

quiz.q: What happens after eight perfect out-shuffles of a 52-card deck?
o: The deck is fully random
The deck is completely reversed
The deck returns to its original order
The deck ends in alternating colours
quiz.e: A perfect shuffle is a fixed rearrangement, so repeating it enough times cycles back to the start.

quiz.q: Why divide by 5! when counting poker hands?
o: The order of the five cards does not matter
Five cards are dealt face down
Only five suits are used
Hands with matching suits are removed
quiz.e: Each hand can be picked up in 120 orders, so dividing removes the repeats.

quiz.q: What makes a password or key hard to guess?
o: Swapping letters for similar-looking numbers
Using a familiar phrase with a capital letter
Length and genuine randomness
Changing it every day
quiz.e: Each extra random element multiplies the possibilities, while predictable substitutions add little.

LESSONS.push: Your last shuffle probably produced an order that has never existed before. Here's why.

LESSONS.title: The averaging trap: when rates don't add up
LESSONS.hook: Drive somewhere at 60 km/h and back at 40, and your average speed is not 50. Averages of rates fool almost everyone, and the mistake shows up in fuel bills, class sizes and bus stops.

sections.key: Average speed is total distance divided by total time, so averaging the speeds themselves gives the wrong answer.
sections.b:
You drive 60 km to a friend at 60 km/h, then crawl home through roadworks at 40 km/h. Your average speed is not 50 km/h. The trip there took one hour. The trip home took 1.5 hours. You covered 120 km in 2.5 hours, which is 48 km/h. The slow leg counts for more because you spend longer on it. Averaging the speeds gives both legs equal weight.

For equal distances, the proper tool is the harmonic mean: 2 divided by (1/60 + 1/40) is 48. It is never above the ordinary average and leans towards the smaller number. The simple rule: add up the totals, then divide, rather than averaging the rates.

sections.key: Translate rates back into real quantities such as distance and time before averaging anything.
sections.b:
A cyclist rides one kilometre up a steep hill at 30 km/h and wants to average 60 km/h over the two-kilometre round trip. How fast must she go downhill? Intuition says 90 km/h, to balance the 30.

But to average 60 km/h over two kilometres, the whole trip must take two minutes. The climb alone, one kilometre at 30 km/h, has already used those two minutes. She would have to descend in no time at all, which means infinite speed. The target is impossible. Puzzles like this show why it pays to turn rates back into distances and times before averaging.

sections.key: Miles per gallon hides savings: swapping a thirsty car for a modest one saves more fuel than upgrading an efficient one.
sections.b:
In 2008 Richard Larrick and Jack Soll published a study in Science on the ‘MPG illusion’. People assume that a bigger improvement in miles per gallon saves more fuel. Australia mostly uses litres per 100 kilometres, which avoids the trap.

Compare two upgrades. Replacing a car that uses 20 litres per 100 kilometres with one using 15 saves 5 litres every 100 kilometres. Replacing an efficient car using 6 litres with one using 4 saves only 2. In kilometres per litre, the first goes from 5 to about 6.7, while the second leaps from about 16.7 to 25. The second looks far more impressive, yet the first saves more than twice as much fuel.

sections.key: Averages depend on who is counting: people tend to land in the bigger classes and the longer gaps.
sections.b:
A small college has two classes, one of 10 students and one of 90. It can truthfully report an average class size of 50. But ask each student. Ten answer 10 and ninety answer 90, which averages 82. Both are correct, yet most students sit in the crowded class. The friendship paradox is similar: on average, your friends have more friends than you do, because popular people appear in many friend lists.

Buses average one every 10 minutes, but suppose gaps alternate between 5 and 15 minutes. A random arrival is three times as likely to land in a 15-minute gap. Your expected wait is 6.25 minutes, not 5. This is the inspection paradox: longer things are more likely to be the ones you find.

sections.key: An average only means something if you know what it is an average of.
sections.b:
These traps share a cause: an average is only meaningful if you know what it is an average of. Three questions protect you.

First, are you averaging rates? If so, go back to the totals, such as distance and time, or fuel and kilometres, and divide those instead.

Second, who is doing the counting? An average across classes, buses or businesses can differ wildly from the average experienced by the people inside them.

Third, would a different unit tell a different story? Kilometres per litre and litres per 100 kilometres carry identical information, but one makes savings easy to see. None of this needs advanced maths, just the patience to ask what lies behind a number before trusting it.

quiz.q: You drive 60 km at 60 km/h and return the same 60 km at 40 km/h. What is your average speed?
o: 50 km/h
48 km/h
52 km/h
45 km/h
quiz.e: You cover 120 km in 2.5 hours, and the slower leg takes more of the time.

quiz.q: Why can a cyclist never average 60 km/h over a 2 km round trip after climbing 1 km at 30 km/h?
o: Downhill speed cannot exceed 90 km/h
Climbing always costs twice as much time
The climb alone uses up all the time allowed
Round trips must be measured in whole minutes
quiz.e: At 60 km/h the whole trip takes two minutes, and the climb has already used them.

quiz.q: Which car swap saves more fuel over 100 km?
o: From 20 to 15 litres per 100 km
From 6 to 4 litres per 100 km
From 12 to 9 litres per 100 km
From 8 to 7 litres per 100 km
quiz.e: The first saves 5 litres and the second only 2, even though the second looks bigger in km per litre.

quiz.q: A college has classes of 10 and 90 students. What class size does the average student experience?
quiz.e: Most students sit in the large class, so their typical experience is far more crowded than the official average.

quiz.q: What should you do first when you need to average rates?
o: Average the rates directly
Take the highest of the rates
Round each rate to a tidy number
Go back to the totals and divide
quiz.e: Dividing total distance by total time, or total fuel by total distance, avoids giving unequal legs equal weight.

LESSONS.push: Drive there at 60 and back at 40, and your average isn't 50. Find out why.

LESSONS.title: The doomsday rule: find the weekday of any date in your head
LESSONS.hook: A mathematician named John Conway could tell you the day of the week for any modern date in a couple of seconds. His method is easy to learn, and it starts with 4 April.

sections.key: In any year, a set of memorable dates share one weekday, called the doomsday, which anchors every other date.
sections.b:
In the early 1970s the British mathematician John Horton Conway, famous for inventing the Game of Life, devised a way to work out the weekday of any date mentally. He built on an earlier method by Lewis Carroll, the author of Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, who was also a mathematician.

The trick rests on a striking fact. In any given year, a whole collection of memorable dates always land on the same weekday. Conway called that weekday the year's ‘doomsday’. The name is not sinister. It simply means the anchor day for that year.

sections.key: Memorable anchor dates always share the doomsday weekday, so any date is only a short count away.
sections.b:
The even months are easy: 4 April, 6 June, 8 August, 10 October and 12 December (4/4, 6/6, 8/8, 10/10, 12/12). For the odd months, the mnemonic ‘I work 9 to 5 at 7-Eleven’ gives 9 May, 5 September, 11 July and 7 November. The last day of February is always a doomsday, as is 14 March. For January, use 3 January in ordinary years and 4 January in leap years.

In 2026 all of these are Saturdays. Christmas? The nearest anchor is 12 December, a Saturday, so 19 and 26 December are too, making Christmas a Friday. Australia Day: 3 January is Saturday, so 31 January is too, making 26 January a Monday.

sections.key: Each ordinary year moves the doomsday forward one weekday and each leap year two, starting from a century anchor.
sections.b:
A normal year has 365 days, which is 52 weeks and one day, so the doomsday moves forward by one weekday. A leap year adds a day, so the jump after 29 February is two. In 2026 the doomsday is Saturday. In 2027 it is Sunday. In 2028, a leap year, it jumps two places to Tuesday.

To handle any year in a century, start from a known anchor: Wednesday for the 1900s and Tuesday for the 2000s. Add the number of years past the century, plus the number of leap years in that stretch, and count forward that many weekdays, ignoring complete weeks.

sections.key: Weekdays repeat every seven days, so only the remainder after removing complete weeks matters.
sections.b:
Test the method on Neil Armstrong's Moon step on 20 July 1969, by American time. The 1900s anchor is Wednesday. The year is 69 years into the century, which includes 17 leap years, since 69 divided by 4 is 17 with some left over. Add them: 69 plus 17 is 86.

Remove complete weeks: 86 divided by 7 is 12 weeks with 2 left over. Two days on from Wednesday makes 1969's doomsday a Friday. The July anchor is 11 July, a Friday, and so is 18 July. That makes 20 July a Sunday. In eastern Australia it was already the next day, so viewers here watched on Monday 21 July.

sections.key: The Gregorian calendar repeats exactly every 400 years, and weekday cycles are modular arithmetic, the arithmetic of remainders.
sections.b:
The method works because the calendar follows fixed rules. Pope Gregory XIII introduced the Gregorian calendar in 1582. A year is a leap year if divisible by 4, except century years, which must be divisible by 400. So 1900 was not a leap year but 2000 was. The 400-year cycle holds 146,097 days, exactly 20,871 weeks, so the calendar repeats perfectly, and the 13th falls on a Friday slightly more often than any other weekday.

Conway reportedly had his computer quiz him with random dates when he logged in. He died in April 2020. To learn the method, start with the current year's anchors. It teaches modular arithmetic: weekdays cycle every seven, as hours cycle every twelve.

quiz.q: What is a year's ‘doomsday’?
o: The weekday shared by 4/4, 6/6 and 8/8
The final Saturday in each year
The weekday on which 1 January falls
The weekday that 29 February falls on
quiz.e: Memorable dates in a year all share one weekday, which anchors every other date.

quiz.q: If 12 December 2026 is a Saturday, what day is 25 December 2026?
o: Thursday
Friday
Saturday
Sunday
quiz.e: Add two weeks to reach 26 December, a Saturday, then Christmas is the day before.

quiz.q: Why does the doomsday jump from Sunday in 2027 to Tuesday in 2028?
o: 2028 is a leap year, so it moves two days
The 2028 calendar starts on a Tuesday
Doomsdays always move by two days
Calendars are reset every decade
quiz.e: A leap year adds 29 February, which pushes the doomsday on by two weekdays instead of one.

quiz.q: Why can you remove complete weeks in the Moon landing calculation?
o: Weekdays repeat every seven days
Weeks are always 86 days long
Leap years only count whole weeks
Each year has exactly 52 weeks
quiz.e: Because weekdays cycle every seven days, 86 days forward is the same as 2 days forward.

quiz.q: Why does the Gregorian calendar repeat every 400 years?
o: Every century year is a leap year
Pope Gregory fixed the weekdays
400 years hold a whole number of weeks
Leap years only happen every 400 years
quiz.e: 146,097 days is exactly 20,871 weeks, so every date lands on the same weekday after 400 years.

LESSONS.push: Name any modern date and the weekday follows in seconds, starting from 4 April.

LESSONS.title: Logarithms: the invention that turned multiplying into adding
LESSONS.hook: In 1614 a Scottish nobleman published tables that saved astronomers years of drudgery. For the next 350 years, his idea sat in the pocket of every engineer as the slide rule.

sections.key: Adding is easy and multiplying is hard, and patterns in powers hint at a way to turn one into the other.
sections.b:
Picture an astronomer around 1600 working out a planet's orbit. Each step means multiplying and dividing numbers of seven or more digits, and one slip ruins weeks of work. Navigators and surveyors faced the same burden. Adding large numbers is quick and fairly safe, but multiplying by hand means rows of partial products and lots of carrying.

Mathematicians wondered whether hard multiplication could become easy addition. A clue came from powers. Since 2 × 2 × 2 is 8 and 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 is 16, multiplying 8 by 16 means adding the counts of twos, 3 plus 4, to get 7 twos. That is 128.

sections.key: A logarithm is a power, so adding logarithms multiplies numbers and subtracting them divides.
sections.b:
John Napier was the Laird of Merchiston near Edinburgh, who also wrote a fiercely argued book on the Book of Revelation. Mathematics was his passion. He spent around two decades developing logarithms, a word built from Greek roots meaning ratio and number, and published them in 1614. His tables paired numbers with their logarithms. Napier's version differs from today's, but the essential trick was there.

With base 10, the logarithm of 100 is 2 and of 1,000 is 3. The logarithm of 2 is about 0.301 and of 8 about 0.903. Add them to get 1.204, look up the number with that logarithm, and you find 16, which is 2 × 8. Division becomes subtraction, powers become multiplication, and square roots become halving.

sections.key: Base 10 tables and Kepler's planetary tables put logarithms to work across science.
sections.b:
The English mathematician Henry Briggs travelled to Scotland in 1615 to meet Napier. They agreed that logarithms would be more convenient in base 10, so the logarithm of 10 was 1 and of 100 was 2. Napier died in 1617. Briggs calculated the new tables by hand, including a large volume in 1624. These common logarithms stayed in classrooms, including Australian ones, until cheap electronic calculators arrived in the 1970s.

The astronomer Johannes Kepler seized on logarithms early. He used them in completing the Rudolphine Tables, published in 1627, which predicted planetary positions far more accurately than anything before. Logarithms did not create the scientific revolution, but they made its endless calculations bearable.

sections.key: Sliding two logarithmic scales against each other adds lengths, which multiplies numbers.
sections.b:
Soon after Napier, the English mathematician Edmund Gunter drew a ruler marked with a logarithmic scale, so distances along it represented logarithms. Using dividers, users could add lengths and so multiply numbers. In the 1620s and 1630s the clergyman William Oughtred slid two such scales against each other, which did the adding automatically. This was the slide rule.

For centuries it was the engineer's constant companion, helping design bridges, ships, aircraft and, at NASA, the rockets of the Apollo programme. A good slide rule gave about three significant figures, accurate enough for most engineering. Pocket calculators replaced it almost overnight in the 1970s.

sections.key: Logarithms are the natural way to measure quantities that span huge ranges or grow by multiplying.
sections.b:
Calculators made log tables obsolete, but logarithms are everywhere. The decibel scale for sound is logarithmic: every 10 decibels means ten times the sound intensity. Earthquake magnitude scales are logarithmic, as is the pH scale, where each step is a tenfold change. In finance and biology, logarithms describe compound growth and halving.

Your senses seem to work roughly logarithmically too, noticing proportional changes rather than absolute ones. An extra candle brightens a dark room far more than a sunny one. The idea Napier spent twenty years refining still shapes how scientists see the world, long after its original purpose disappeared.

quiz.q: Using powers of 2, why does 8 × 16 equal 128?
o: Three twos and four twos make seven twos
Sixteen is the square of eight
Multiplying always means adding the two numbers
Doubling sixteen twice gives 128
quiz.e: Multiplying powers of a number means adding their counts, which is the idea behind logarithms.

quiz.q: If the logarithm of 2 is about 0.301 and of 8 about 0.903, what number has a logarithm of about 1.204?
quiz.e: Adding the logarithms gives 1.204, and the number with that logarithm is 2 × 8 = 16.

quiz.q: What change did Briggs and Napier agree would make logarithms more convenient?
o: Using base 10, so log 10 equals 1
Using tables with fewer entries
Replacing numbers with ratios
Printing tables in a Latin book
quiz.e: With base 10, the logarithms of 10, 100 and 1,000 become 1, 2 and 3.

quiz.q: How does a slide rule multiply numbers?
o: By counting beads on rods
Sliding two log scales to add lengths
By turning a crank with gears
By reading a table of products
quiz.e: Adding lengths on logarithmic scales is the same as multiplying the numbers.

quiz.q: What does a rise of 10 decibels mean?
o: Ten times the sound intensity
Ten more units of sound
Double the sound intensity
Ten per cent more sound
quiz.e: The decibel scale is logarithmic, so equal steps mean multiplying the intensity.

LESSONS.push: A Scottish laird spent twenty years on a shortcut that engineers used for 350 years.

LESSONS.title: Ramanujan: the clerk who wrote to Cambridge
LESSONS.hook: A largely self-taught clerk in Madras posted pages of strange formulas to a famous English mathematician. They were so astonishing that they changed both men's lives.

sections.key: Ramanujan taught himself mathematics from a book of results with few proofs, at the cost of his formal education.
sections.b:
Srinivasa Ramanujan was born on 22 December 1887 in Erode, in southern India, and grew up in Kumbakonam. As a teenager he found a book by George Shoobridge Carr, a summary of several thousand mathematical results, mostly given without proofs. He worked through it alone, filling notebooks with his own discoveries.

His obsession had a cost. He won a college scholarship but neglected his other subjects, failed his exams and lost it. For several years he lived in poverty, working with little guidance. Eventually supporters who recognised his talent helped him find a job as a clerk at the Madras Port Trust in 1912, giving him a small wage and time to keep working.

sections.key: Hardy recognised the genius in Ramanujan's unproven formulas and brought him to Cambridge to teach him proof.
sections.b:
In January 1913 Ramanujan wrote to Godfrey Harold Hardy, a leading mathematician at Trinity College, Cambridge, enclosing pages of formulas, many about infinite series, without proof. Hardy got many letters from cranks and was tempted to dismiss it. But he and John Littlewood realised the pages were remarkable: some results known, a few wrong, many new and astonishing. Hardy said some must be true, because no one would have had the imagination to invent them otherwise.

Ramanujan sailed for England in 1914. Hardy insisted on rigorous proofs, while Ramanujan reached results by intuition, saying some came from his family goddess Namagiri. Wartime Cambridge was hard for a strict vegetarian far from home, yet in 1918 he became a Fellow of the Royal Society, one of the first Indians so honoured.

sections.key: Ramanujan seemed to know individual numbers the way other people know old friends.
sections.b:
The most famous story comes from Hardy. Visiting his friend in hospital, Hardy remarked that he had arrived in taxi number 1729, which seemed a rather dull number. Ramanujan replied that, on the contrary, it was very interesting. It is the smallest number that can be written as the sum of two cubes in two different ways.

Check it: 1 cubed plus 12 cubed is 1 + 1,728, which is 1,729. And 9 cubed plus 10 cubed is 729 + 1,000, which is also 1,729. Numbers with this property are now called taxicab numbers. The story captures something real about Ramanujan, who knew individual numbers like old friends.

sections.key: Hardy and Ramanujan found a formula that estimates the number of partitions of a whole number with astonishing accuracy.
sections.b:
One of their greatest achievements concerns partitions, the ways to write a whole number as a sum of positive whole numbers. The number 4 has five: 4, 3+1, 2+2, 2+1+1 and 1+1+1+1. Counts explode as numbers grow. The number 200 has 3,972,999,029,388, a figure Percy MacMahon worked out painstakingly by hand.

Hardy and Ramanujan found a formula that estimated such values with astonishing accuracy, later refined into an exact formula. Ramanujan also spotted hidden patterns. The partition counts of 4, 9, 14, 19, 24 and so on, every fifth number, are always divisible by 5. Those counts begin 5, 30, 135, 490 and 1,575.

sections.key: Ramanujan died at 32, but his notebooks still inspire mathematics and show how easily talent can be missed.
sections.b:
By 1917 Ramanujan was seriously ill. Doctors suspected tuberculosis, though the cause is still debated and some studies suggest a liver infection, amoebiasis. He returned to India in 1919, still working on ‘mock theta functions’, and died on 26 April 1920, aged 32. In 1976 George Andrews found a bundle of later papers, the ‘lost notebook’, in Trinity's library. Researchers spent decades proving its results, and some ideas have found uses in modern physics.

His fast formulas for pi, published in 1914, were used by computer scientists in the 1980s to compute millions of digits. India celebrates 22 December as National Mathematics Day. His story is also a warning: he was found partly by luck, through supporters and one letter that reached the right reader. Hardy wondered how much more he might have achieved with an earlier, fuller education.

quiz.q: Why did Ramanujan lose his college scholarship?
o: He failed exams in his other subjects
He left college to work as a clerk
He could not afford the fees
He refused to study mathematics
quiz.e: His obsession with mathematics cost him his other subjects, his exams and the scholarship.

quiz.q: What did Hardy conclude about some of Ramanujan's formulas?
o: They were copied from a textbook
They were wrong but cleverly disguised
They could be proved by a simple trick
No one would invent them if false
quiz.e: Hardy judged that no one would have the imagination to invent such formulas if they were false.

quiz.q: Which pair of cube sums shows why 1729 is special?
quiz.e: 1,729 is the smallest number that is the sum of two cubes in two different ways.

quiz.q: Which pattern did Ramanujan spot in partition counts?
o: Every partition count is an even number
Counts for 4, 9, 14 and so on divide by 5
Counts double whenever the number grows
Every partition count is a prime number
quiz.e: Every fifth partition count, starting at 4, is divisible by 5, such as 5, 30, 135 and 490.

quiz.q: Why is Ramanujan's story called a warning about lost talent?
o: He was found partly by chance, via one letter
He never published any of his results
His results were all later proved wrong
He refused help from Cambridge mathematicians
quiz.e: His talent reached the right reader by chance, so many others may never have been found.

LESSONS.push: A clerk's letter to Cambridge held formulas so strange they had to be true.

LESSONS.title: I cut, you choose: the maths of fair sharing
LESSONS.hook: Two children and one cake have a perfect solution that is thousands of years old. Add more children and mathematicians needed until 2016 to finish the job.

sections.key: Divide and choose works because the cutter gets whichever piece is left, so they have every reason to cut fairly.
sections.b:
Two siblings, one slice of cake, and an argument brewing. The classic solution is simple: one cuts, the other chooses. The cutter has every reason to make the pieces equal in their own eyes, because they get whichever piece is left. The chooser takes the piece they prefer. Neither can reasonably complain.

The idea is ancient. In the Book of Genesis, Abraham proposes dividing the land between himself and Lot, and lets Lot choose. Mathematicians admire it because it works even when people value things differently. One sibling may care about the icing and the other about size. Nobody needs to agree on what fair means or trust anybody else's judgement.

sections.key: Envy-free is stricter than proportional, and the last diminisher method is proportional but not envy-free.
sections.b:
A division is proportional if each of n people gets what they consider at least one nth of the total. It is envy-free if nobody would rather swap their share for another's. For two people these are the same. With three or more they differ: you may think you got a fair third yet feel someone else did better.

In the 1940s Hugo Steinhaus, Stefan Banach and Bronisław Knaster devised the last diminisher method. The first person cuts a slice they think is fair. Anyone who thinks it too big may trim it, and the last person to trim takes it. The rest continue with what remains. It is proportional, but not envy-free.

sections.key: Envy-free sharing was solved for three people around 1960, but for any number of people only in 2016, and not practically.
sections.b:
Around 1960 John Selfridge found an envy-free method for three people, and John Conway independently found it in the early 1990s. It is now called the Selfridge–Conway procedure. Roughly, the first person cuts three equal pieces. The second trims the biggest to tie with the second biggest. The third picks first, the second picks next, and the first takes what remains. A second round shares the trimmings. Nobody prefers anyone else's total, in at most five cuts.

For four or more people it was far harder. In 1995 Steven Brams and Alan Taylor published an envy-free procedure for any number of people, but it had no upper limit on cuts. In 2016 Haris Aziz and Simon Mackenzie found a bounded method, though it needs astronomically many steps. It proves fairness is possible, not that it is practical.

sections.key: Fair division also works for rooms and rent, always allowing prices where each housemate prefers their own room.
sections.b:
Fair division is not just about cake. Housemates sharing a place with a big sunny room, a small room and a room near the noisy road must divide a rent bill as well as the rooms. In 1999 the mathematician Francis Su published a method, building on others' work, that uses a result called Sperner's lemma. It shows there is always a way to set the rents so that each person prefers their own room at its price.

Online tools now use these ideas to split rent, chores and shared costs. Fairness flips when the thing shared is unpleasant. With chores, the cutter divides the jobs into two loads they find equally heavy, and the chooser takes the lighter one.

sections.key: A nursery rule has become a tool of diplomacy: good mechanisms, not trust, make sharing work.
sections.b:
The most surprising use of divide-and-choose may be international law. Under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, agreed in 1982, a company or country wanting to mine the deep seabed beyond national borders proposes an area large enough for two mining operations, split into two parts of similar estimated value.

The International Seabed Authority then chooses one part to reserve for itself or for developing countries, and the applicant may work the other. The applicant has every reason to divide fairly, just like the child cutting the cake. A nursery rule has become a tool of diplomacy, showing that good mechanisms, rather than trust or goodwill, can make sharing work.

quiz.q: Why does ‘I cut, you choose’ encourage the cutter to be fair?
o: The chooser can punish an unfair cut
Cutters are always more skilled
The cutter gets whichever piece is left
Both pieces are always exactly equal
quiz.e: Since the cutter takes what the chooser leaves, an even split is their best option.

quiz.q: What does it mean for a division to be envy-free?
o: Everyone gets an identical share
The shares are cut by a neutral person
Each person gets exactly one nth of the total
Nobody would rather have someone else's share
quiz.e: Envy-free is stricter than proportional because it removes any wish to swap.

quiz.q: What did the 2016 result by Aziz and Mackenzie achieve?
o: A bounded envy-free method for any number of people
A practical rule for splitting a cake at parties
A proof that envy-free sharing is impossible
An envy-free method for three people only
quiz.e: It showed envy-free sharing can always finish in a fixed number of steps, though far too many to use.

quiz.q: What does Su's rent method show for housemates?
o: The biggest room should cost the most
Some set of rents leaves nobody envious
Rent should be split equally
Housemates should draw lots for rooms
quiz.e: A way always exists to set the rents so that nobody envies another's room at its price.

quiz.q: In deep-sea mining, why does the applicant divide the area into two parts of similar value?
o: The other party picks which part to reserve
Mining is only allowed on equal-sized areas
The applicant keeps both parts
Both parts are shared with the public
quiz.e: Since the Authority chooses, the applicant has every reason to make the halves fair, as in cut and choose.

LESSONS.push: Why a fair cake split for three people took mathematicians until around 1960.

LESSONS.title: The maths of queues: why lines get long so suddenly
LESSONS.hook: A café that is busy most of the time can run smoothly, then a few extra customers turn it into a long wait. Queueing theory explains why, and how to fix it.

sections.key: Queues form from variability in arrivals and service times, even when a server has spare capacity on average.
sections.b:
In the early 1900s telephone companies faced an expensive puzzle: too few lines and callers heard a busy signal; too many and costly equipment sat idle. The Danish mathematician Agner Krarup Erlang, working for the Copenhagen Telephone Company, tackled it with probability. His 1909 paper began queueing theory, the mathematics of waiting. The erlang, a unit of telephone traffic, is named after him. The same maths now runs call centres, emergency departments, checkouts, traffic lights and internet servers.

A coffee cart serves 30 customers an hour and 24 arrive on average. Yet customers arrive in clumps, and orders vary in complexity. Idle time in quiet moments cannot be saved for later. Variability, not just average workload, creates waiting.

sections.key: Waiting stays modest until utilisation nears full capacity, then climbs steeply.
sections.b:
In a classic model of one server with random arrivals and service times, the average wait depends on utilisation, the fraction of time the server is busy. At 50 per cent utilisation the average wait equals about one typical service time. At 80 per cent it is four service times. At 90 per cent it is nine, and at 95 per cent it is nineteen.

Plotted on a graph, the line stays fairly flat, then bends sharply upward like a hockey stick. That is why a café can cope well for most of the morning, then be swamped when a few extra customers arrive. A system run near full capacity, with no slack, is fragile.

sections.key: Pooling several servers behind one line usually shortens and evens out the average wait.
sections.b:
At a supermarket with a separate line at every checkout, the person in front of you has a price problem while the next line races ahead. A bank or airport instead uses one snaking queue feeding several counters, with the front person going to whichever frees up first.

The average wait is usually shorter with a single queue, and the waits are far more even. Nobody gets stuck behind one slow transaction while other servers sit idle. Mathematicians call this the benefit of pooling. Separate lines can still make sense when space is tight or when express lanes speed up small purchases, but pooling is one of the most reliable lessons of queueing theory.

sections.key: On average, the number of items in a stable system equals the arrival rate multiplied by the time each stays.
sections.b:
One of the most useful results is beautifully simple. Little's law, proved by John Little in 1961, says the average number of items in a stable system equals the rate at which they arrive multiplied by the average time each one stays.

If a café gets 20 customers an hour and each stays half an hour, then on average 20 × 0.5, or 10 customers are inside at any moment. The law works almost regardless of the details. It applies to shoppers, patients in a hospital ward, cars on a motorway or tasks waiting on a computer. Managers use it in reverse too: knowing how many people are typically present and how fast they arrive tells you how long each stays.

sections.key: Slack, smoother demand and a fair, informed wait make systems and people cope better with queues.
sections.b:
People judge waits by how they feel. In 1985 David Maister wrote an influential essay noting that unoccupied time feels longer than occupied time, uncertain waits feel longer than known ones, unexplained waits feel longer, and so do unfair ones, such as watching someone push in. That is why theme parks post estimated waits, apps show your position in a queue, and businesses put screens where people line up.

The maths applies to your week too. A schedule packed to 95 per cent of your time collapses at the first delay. Slack is not laziness. Staggering appointments smooths out bunching, and sharing one inbox spreads work. A long line is rarely about one slow person. It is usually mathematics at work.

quiz.q: Why can a queue form even when a server has spare capacity on average?
o: Servers always work slower when busy
Variability, and idle time cannot be banked
Customers prefer to wait together
Average capacity is always overstated
quiz.e: Clumped arrivals create waiting, and the idle time during quiet moments is lost for good.

quiz.q: In the classic single-server model, how does the average wait at 90% utilisation compare with 50%?
o: About nine times as long
About twice as long
About the same
About 90% longer
quiz.e: The wait rises from one service time at 50% to nine at 90%, the steep end of the hockey stick.

quiz.q: Why is a single queue feeding several counters usually fairer than separate lines?
o: It makes each transaction faster
It evens out waits between customers
It needs fewer staff in every case
It removes the need for express lanes
quiz.e: Pooling means the next person goes to whichever server frees up first, reducing both the average and the unevenness.

quiz.q: A clinic sees 6 patients an hour and each stays 2 hours on average. By Little's law, how many are there on average?
quiz.e: Arrival rate times average stay is 6 × 2, so about 12 patients are present at any time.

quiz.q: Why does a week scheduled to 95 per cent of your time tend to go wrong?
o: Small delays snowball with no slack
Busy people always work faster
Appointments never run to time
People forget what they scheduled
quiz.e: Near full capacity there is no slack to absorb variability, just as the hockey-stick curve predicts.

LESSONS.push: A café with spare capacity can still have a long queue. The maths explains why.

LESSONS.title: Calculus without fear: the maths of change
LESSONS.hook: Calculus has a fearsome reputation, but its two big ideas can be grasped with a speedometer and an odometer. Its invention also sparked one of the bitterest feuds in science.

sections.key: Calculus answers two questions: how fast something is changing right now, and how much has built up over time.
sections.b: Strip away the symbols and calculus asks two questions. How fast is something changing at this exact moment? And if you know how fast it is changing, how much has it added up to over time? Every car shows both ideas. The speedometer reports how fast your distance is changing right now. The odometer adds up all those changing speeds into a total distance. The first idea is differentiation, which gives a derivative. The second is integration, which gives an integral. Together they sit at the heart of physics, engineering, economics and biology, anywhere things change smoothly. Ordinary arithmetic copes with fixed values. Calculus copes with constant change.

sections.key: Zeno's paradoxes showed that infinitely small steps are tricky, and Archimedes trapped answers between ever-finer approximations.
sections.b: Long before anyone named calculus, the Greeks wrestled with its core difficulty. Around the fifth century BCE, Zeno of Elea argued that swift Achilles can never catch a tortoise with a head start, since each time he reaches where it was, it has moved on. How can infinitely many steps add up to a finite result? Today we can answer: a half, a quarter, an eighth and so on forever totals exactly 1. In the third century BCE, Archimedes squeezed a circle between polygons inside and outside it. With 96 sides, he showed pi lies between 223/71 and 22/7, about 3.1408 and 3.1429. He used similar reasoning for the area under a parabola and the volume of a sphere. He lacked a general method.

sections.key: Newton and Leibniz invented calculus independently, and a bitter dispute over who came first followed.
sections.b: In the mid-1660s, with Cambridge closed by plague, young Isaac Newton developed his method of fluxions but kept it largely to himself. In Germany, Gottfried Leibniz developed his own version in the 1670s and published first, in 1684. A bitter priority dispute followed, with Newton's supporters accusing Leibniz of plagiarism. In 1712 the Royal Society, which Newton led as president, ruled in Newton's favour in a report he secretly drafted much of himself. Historians now agree the two men invented calculus independently. Leibniz's notation, such as dy/dx and the long S for an integral, proved clearer and won out. British mathematicians, loyal to Newton's dots, fell behind continental Europe for decades.

sections.key: A derivative zooms in to find the rate of change at an instant; an integral adds up thin slices to find a total.
sections.b:
Drop a ball and it falls about 4.9 × t² metres in t seconds, ignoring air resistance. How fast is it moving at exactly one second? From 1 to 1.1 seconds, the average speed is 10.29 metres per second. From 1 to 1.01, it is about 9.85. As the interval shrinks, the average closes in on exactly 9.8. That limit is the derivative: the slope of a curve at a single point.

Integration runs the other way. A steady 60 km/h for two hours is a rectangle on a speed graph, 60 high and 2 wide, so 120 kilometres. For varying speed, slice the area into thin strips and add them up. Infinitely thin strips give the exact answer. Engineers use this for forces on dams and volumes of fuel tanks.

sections.key: The fundamental theorem links the two halves of calculus, and nineteenth-century limits finally made it rigorous.
sections.b:
The deepest discovery is that the two halves undo each other. Integrate a speed to get distance, differentiate that, and you get the speed back. This is the fundamental theorem of calculus. Isaac Barrow, Newton's teacher, had glimpsed it, but Newton and Leibniz made it a working method. Instead of adding thousands of strips, you find a formula whose derivative matches your curve, and the area follows almost instantly.

Yet the foundations were shaky. In 1734 George Berkeley mocked vanishing quantities as ‘ghosts of departed quantities’. In the nineteenth century, Cauchy and Weierstrass rebuilt calculus on precisely defined limits, answering Zeno at last. Today it underpins weather forecasts, rocket trajectories, medical scanners and AI training, which follows derivatives downhill to reduce errors.

quiz.q: In the car picture of calculus, what does the odometer represent?
o: Finding speed at a single instant
Measuring how quickly speed is changing
Adding up changing speeds into a total distance
Estimating fuel used per kilometre
quiz.e: The odometer accumulates speed over time, which is what integration does; the speedometer shows differentiation.

quiz.q: What does adding a half, a quarter, an eighth and so on forever show?
o: Fractions can never be added together
An infinite sum can have a finite value
Achilles really cannot catch the tortoise
Infinite sums always grow without limit
quiz.e: The total approaches exactly 1, which is how we answer Zeno's worry about infinite steps.

quiz.q: How do historians now view the invention of calculus?
o: Newton invented it and Leibniz copied it
Leibniz invented it and Newton copied it
Archimedes had already completed it
Newton and Leibniz each invented it independently
quiz.e: Both men reached calculus on their own, though their supporters fought bitterly over priority.

quiz.q: As the time interval around one second shrinks, what happens to the falling ball's average speed?
o: It approaches 9.8 m/s
It rises without limit
It falls towards zero
It stays at 10.29 m/s
quiz.e: A derivative is the limit that average speed approaches as the interval shrinks towards zero.

quiz.q: What does the fundamental theorem of calculus say?
o: Every curve is a straight line up close
Infinitely small quantities are always zero
Differentiation and integration undo each other
Calculus only works for circles and spheres
quiz.e: Because the two operations are opposites, hard area problems can often be solved by finding a formula instead of adding strips.

LESSONS.push: You can grasp calculus with a car dashboard. Its inventors spent years at war.

LESSONS.title: Dollar Bill and the day Australia went decimal
LESSONS.hook: On one Monday in 1966, a whole nation swapped pounds, shillings and pence for dollars and cents. The government's first choice of name, the royal, was so unpopular it was dropped.

sections.key: Before 1966 Australians did their sums in a system of twelves and twenties, and a 1959 committee recommended going decimal.
sections.b: For most of its history Australia counted money the British way. A pound was worth 20 shillings, and each shilling was worth 12 pence, so a pound held 240 pennies. Prices were written as £2 7s 6d, and totalling a shopping bill meant constant carrying of twelves and twenties. Australia had issued its own pound since 1910, but the arithmetic was inherited from medieval England. By the 1950s businesses, banks and schools were complaining. Children spent hours converting pence to shillings, and new adding machines and early computers suited tens far better. Many countries had already gone decimal, and a government committee set up in 1959 recommended Australia follow.

sections.key: The government's first choice of name, the royal, was so unpopular that it was quietly dropped for the dollar.
sections.b: Choosing a name proved harder than the maths. The public sent in thousands of suggestions, from the austral and the kanga to the emu and the ming, a cheeky nod to Prime Minister Robert Menzies' nickname. In 1963 the government announced the new unit would be called the royal. The reaction was swift and scornful. Newspapers mocked it, and many felt it sounded old-fashioned for a young country building its own identity. Before the changeover the government backed down and settled on the dollar, a name already used in the United States, Canada and elsewhere, and easy to say. The fuss is a reminder that money is not just maths. It carries national pride.

sections.key: The switch happened on a single day, backed by one of Australia's biggest public education campaigns.
sections.b: The changeover was set for Monday 14 February 1966, nicknamed C-Day. To prepare people, the Decimal Currency Board ran one of the biggest public information campaigns Australia had seen. Its star was a cartoon character called Dollar Bill, and a catchy jingle sung to the tune of the bush ballad ‘Click Go the Shears’ explained the change on radio and television. The conversion rule was simple: ten shillings became one dollar, so one pound became two dollars. Thousands of cash registers and machines had to be converted or replaced. Old and new money circulated side by side for a while, with shopkeepers giving change in decimal currency to drain the old coins from circulation.

sections.key: The new coins carried Australian wildlife, but the first round fifty cent coin held so much silver it was worth hoarding.
sections.b:
Designer Stuart Devlin, a young Australian who later became a famous silversmith in London, put native animals on the coins instead of kings and coats of arms. The one cent showed a feathertail glider, the two cent a frilled-neck lizard, the five cent an echidna, the ten cent a lyrebird and the twenty cent a platypus. The fifty cent carried the coat of arms. The monarch stayed on the other side.

One coin did not last. The round 1966 fifty cent piece was 80 per cent silver, and as the silver price climbed, the metal became worth more than fifty cents. People hoarded it. In 1969 it was replaced by the twelve-sided copper-nickel coin still used today.

sections.key: Australia kept innovating, pioneering polymer banknotes and later scrapping its smallest coins.
sections.b:
The story did not stop in 1966. In 1988, for the bicentenary of European settlement, the Reserve Bank issued a ten dollar note printed on plastic polymer instead of paper. It was developed in Australia partly to defeat counterfeiters, since a clear window and other features were very hard to copy. By 1996 Australia had become the first country with a full series of polymer notes, and the technology has since spread to many countries.

Meanwhile inflation slowly shrank the value of small coins. In 1992 the one and two cent coins were withdrawn, and cash totals have been rounded to the nearest five cents ever since. Card payments are still charged to the exact cent.

quiz.q: Why was the old pounds, shillings and pence system hard to use?
o: Twelves and twenties made adding up slow
It had no coins smaller than a shilling
Each state used different units
Prices could not be written down
quiz.e: Twelves and twenties made everyday arithmetic slow, and tens suited adding machines and computers far better.

quiz.q: Why did the government drop the name ‘royal’ for the new currency?
o: Another country already used it
It was widely mocked as old-fashioned
It was too difficult to pronounce
Banks refused to put it on notes
quiz.e: The name felt out of step with national identity, which shows money carries pride as well as value.

quiz.q: What was the conversion rule on C-Day?
o: One pound became one dollar
Ten shillings became one dollar
One penny became one cent
One shilling became one dollar
quiz.e: The simple rule of ten shillings to a dollar made the switch easy to explain to the public.

quiz.q: Why did people hoard the original round fifty cent coin?
o: It carried the national coat of arms
Its silver was worth over fifty cents
It was only ever issued for one year
Shops were forbidden to accept it
quiz.e: When a coin's metal is worth more than its face value, people keep it and spend cheaper money instead.

quiz.q: What happened to the one and two cent coins in 1992?
o: They were redesigned with new animals
They were replaced by plastic coins
They became collectors' gold coins
They were withdrawn from circulation
quiz.e: Inflation shrank the value of small coins until they were no longer worth making.

LESSONS.push: Almost nobody wanted this name for Australia's new money. Here's what we got instead.

LESSONS.title: Why the Aussie dollar rises and falls
LESSONS.hook: In 2001 an Australian dollar bought less than 50 US cents. A decade later it bought more than a US dollar. Here is what moves a currency.

sections.key: An exchange rate is simply the price of one currency in terms of another, set by supply and demand.
sections.b: When you hear that the Australian dollar is ‘at 65 US cents’, it means one Australian dollar can be swapped for 65 American cents. An exchange rate is a price, and like other prices it is set by supply and demand. Every day, importers, exporters, tourists, investors and banks buy and sell currencies. Trading is enormous, measured in trillions of US dollars a day worldwide. If more people want Australian dollars, perhaps to buy Australian iron ore or bonds, the price rises. If more want to sell them, it falls. The Australian dollar, nicknamed the Aussie, is one of the most heavily traded currencies in the world.

sections.key: Australia let its currency float in December 1983, one of the biggest economic reforms in its history.
sections.b: It was not always this way. For decades Australia's currency was pegged, first to the British pound, then to the US dollar, and from 1974 to a basket of currencies that officials adjusted. The government and Reserve Bank effectively decided the rate, and strict controls limited how much money could flow in or out. Defending the peg became harder as money sloshed around the world. In December 1983 the Hawke government, with Treasurer Paul Keating, floated the dollar and removed most exchange controls, letting the market set the price. Since then the Reserve Bank has only occasionally stepped into the market, usually during severe disorder.

sections.key: The Aussie tends to rise with commodity prices and with higher Australian interest rates, and to fall in global panics.
sections.b:
Australia sells vast quantities of iron ore, coal, gas, gold, wheat and beef. When those prices climb, foreign buyers need more Australian dollars, so the currency tends to rise. That is why traders call it a commodity currency. In the 2000s, China's industrialisation lifted the dollar from under 48 US cents in 2001 to above parity in late 2010, peaking in 2011. When commodity prices later fell, so did the dollar.

Interest rates matter too. If Australian rates exceed those in the United States or Japan, investors buy Australian dollars to earn more. The carry trade borrows in a low-rate currency, such as the yen, to invest in a higher-rate one. It can unwind suddenly, which is why the Aussie often falls in global crises.

sections.key: A strong dollar helps importers and travellers, while a weak one helps exporters and tourism.
sections.b: Whether a high dollar is good news depends on who you are. When the Aussie is strong, overseas holidays are cheaper, imported cars and electronics cost less, and Australians can buy foreign shares more cheaply. But exporters suffer, because their goods become more expensive for foreign buyers, and local manufacturers struggle against cheaper imports. Universities and tourism operators also feel it, since Australia becomes a pricier place to study or visit. A weak dollar flips these effects. Overseas trips hurt, but farmers, miners and tour operators gain. This makes the exchange rate a kind of shock absorber for the economy, cushioning the blow when commodity prices or global conditions change.

sections.key: Comparing burger prices is a playful way to ask whether a currency is overvalued.
sections.b:
If a currency is fairly priced, the same basket of goods should cost roughly the same everywhere once you convert the money. Economists call this idea purchasing power parity. In 1986 The Economist magazine turned it into a light-hearted gauge called the Big Mac index. If a Big Mac costs much more in Switzerland than in the United States after conversion, the Swiss franc looks overvalued by burger logic.

The index is deliberately simple, since local wages, rents and taxes all affect burger prices. But it captures a real idea. In the long run, exchange rates tend to drift towards levels that make prices broadly comparable, even if they stray widely in the short term.

quiz.q: What is an exchange rate?
o: A tax charged on overseas travel
The interest rate the central bank sets
A fixed rate set by the United Nations
The price of one currency in another
quiz.e: Like any price, an exchange rate moves with supply and demand.

quiz.q: What changed when Australia floated the dollar in December 1983?
o: The market, not officials, set its price
It was pegged to the US dollar
It was linked to the price of gold
It replaced the British pound
quiz.e: Floating removed the official peg and most exchange controls, so supply and demand set the rate.

quiz.q: Why does the Aussie often rise when iron ore and coal prices climb?
o: Buyers need more Australian dollars
It is backed by gold reserves
The Reserve Bank must buy the ore
Investors always prefer commodities to cash
quiz.e: Higher export earnings mean more demand for Australian dollars, which is why it is called a commodity currency.

quiz.q: Who generally benefits when the Australian dollar is weak?
o: Australians holidaying overseas
Importers of foreign cars
Exporters and tourism operators
People buying foreign shares
quiz.e: A weak dollar makes Australian goods and holidays cheaper for foreign buyers, but overseas purchases cost more.

quiz.q: What does the Big Mac index suggest if a burger costs far more in one country after conversion?
o: Its burgers are better quality
Its currency may be overvalued
Its wages must be falling
Its central bank has failed
quiz.e: The index applies purchasing power parity: over time, exchange rates tend to drift towards levels that equalise prices.

LESSONS.push: In 2001 it bought under 50 US cents. A decade later, more than a dollar. What changed?

LESSONS.title: Bank runs: when everyone wants their money at once
LESSONS.hook: Your bank does not keep your savings in a vault. Usually that is fine. When everyone turns up at once, it can be catastrophic.

sections.key: Banks lend out most deposits and keep only a fraction on hand, which makes even healthy banks fragile.
sections.b: When you deposit money in a bank, it does not sit in a box with your name on it. Banks take deposits that customers can withdraw at any moment and use them to fund loans that will not be repaid for years, such as mortgages and business loans. They keep only a small portion as cash and reserves, betting, sensibly, that not everyone will want their money on the same day. This arrangement is the heart of banking, turning idle savings into homes and businesses. But it creates a built-in fragility. A bank can be perfectly sound, with good loans that will be repaid, and still be unable to hand everyone their money back immediately.

sections.key: A run can topple a healthy bank simply because people fear it will fall.
sections.b: Imagine a rumour spreads that your bank is in trouble. Even if you think it is false, you have a problem. If others believe it and withdraw their money, the bank may run out of cash, and those who wait could lose out. So the rational move is to join the queue. Everyone reasons the same way, and the fear becomes reality. Economists Douglas Diamond and Philip Dybvig described this trap in a famous 1983 model, showing a bank run can be a self-fulfilling prophecy. Their work helped earn them a share of the 2022 Nobel Prize in economics, alongside Ben Bernanke, who studied how bank failures deepened the Great Depression.

sections.key: Australia suffered one of history's great banking crises after a property bubble burst.
sections.b: Australia knows this story well. In the 1880s Melbourne boomed on gold wealth and borrowed British money, and land prices soared in a speculative frenzy. Dozens of building societies and land banks lent freely against property. When the bubble burst at the end of the decade, borrowers defaulted and many of these institutions collapsed. In 1893 the crisis reached the major banks. Depositors rushed to withdraw their money, and many of the colonies' major banks suspended payments within a few weeks. Some reopened after being reorganised, but savings were frozen or lost, and the colonies plunged into a deep depression that lasted much of the decade. Melbourne took years to recover.

sections.key: Central banks, calm explanation and deposit insurance give savers no reason to run.
sections.b:
In the film It's a Wonderful Life (1946), George Bailey calms panicked customers by explaining that their money is not in a safe. It is in the neighbours' houses, lent out so they could buy homes. Real banks rely on something more powerful: a central bank willing to lend them cash against good assets in an emergency, acting as a lender of last resort.

The most effective cure has been deposit insurance. After thousands of American banks failed in the early 1930s, the United States created the FDIC in 1933. Australia introduced its Financial Claims Scheme in 2008. As of the mid-2020s it protects deposits up to 250,000 dollars per account holder at each authorised institution. Because the guarantee exists, the need to use it is far less likely. Confidence itself is the protection.

sections.key: Modern runs can happen within hours, driven by phones and social media.
sections.b: Runs have not disappeared. In September 2007 queues formed outside Britain's Northern Rock, one of the first visible signs of the global financial crisis and the first run on a British bank in well over a century. In March 2023 California's Silicon Valley Bank collapsed in a run of startling speed. Many customers were tech firms with deposits far above the insured limit. As worries spread through group chats and social media, they tried to pull tens of billions of dollars in a single day using banking apps. There were no queues outside, just a flood of online transfers. Regulators closed the bank within roughly two days, showing how quickly modern panic can spread.

quiz.q: Why can a sound bank still be unable to repay all depositors at once?
o: It keeps all deposits in gold
Banks are not allowed to hold cash
Most deposits are lent out for years
The government holds the deposits
quiz.e: Banks fund years-long loans with deposits that can be withdrawn at any time, so they cannot repay everyone immediately.

quiz.q: What did Diamond and Dybvig show about bank runs?
o: They only happen to badly run banks
They can be self-fulfilling, toppling even healthy banks
They are caused only by high interest rates
They cannot happen once a country has a central bank
quiz.e: If enough people fear a failure and withdraw, the fear itself can cause the failure.

quiz.q: What turned Melbourne's 1880s boom into the crisis of the 1890s?
o: A property bubble that burst
A ban on British investment
A shortage of gold coins
A law forcing banks to close
quiz.e: Reckless lending against rising land prices collapsed when the bubble burst, and the crisis reached the major banks in 1893.

quiz.q: What is the role of a central bank as lender of last resort?
o: Setting the price of everyday goods
Shutting down banks that lose money
Lending cash to sound banks in an emergency
Guaranteeing every loan a bank makes
quiz.e: Emergency cash lets a solid bank survive a run without selling its good loans in a panic.

quiz.q: What made the 2023 run on Silicon Valley Bank so unusual?
o: It dragged on over several years
It involved only paper cheques
It was stopped by deposit insurance alone
It played out in hours, via banking apps
quiz.e: Digital banking let customers move tens of billions in a day, so the run played out in hours instead of weeks.

LESSONS.push: Your bank is not holding your savings in a vault. So what happens if everyone asks?

LESSONS.title: The Medici: the bankers who built a Renaissance
LESSONS.hook: A family of Florentine money-changers became bankers to the Pope, patrons of genius and rulers of a city. Their tricks still shape finance today.

sections.key: Banking in Renaissance Italy began with money-changers working at benches in the street.
sections.b: In the 1300s Italian cities such as Florence, Venice and Genoa were the trading hubs of Europe, awash with coins from dozens of states. Merchants needed someone to weigh, test and swap these coins, and to move money safely over long distances. Money-changers set up at tables, and the Italian word for such a bench, banco, gave us the word bank. A banker who could not pay was said to be banca rotta, a broken bench, the root of our word bankrupt. In 1397 Giovanni di Bicci de' Medici founded the Medici Bank in Florence. Within a few decades it would become the most powerful bank in Europe.

sections.key: The Medici grew rich managing the Church's money, and avoided the ban on interest through bills of exchange.
sections.b:
The Medici's greatest client was the papacy. The Church collected revenue from England to Poland and needed to move it to Rome without carting silver across the Alps. The Medici's network of trusted agents could do it, and for long stretches of the 1400s they were the Pope's main bankers. Later family members became popes, including Leo X and Clement VII.

There was an awkward problem. The Church condemned usury, meaning interest on a loan. The answer was the bill of exchange. A Florentine merchant handed over florins and received a document payable months later in another currency, say in Bruges or London. The rates were set so the banker profited, but on paper it was a currency exchange, not a loan. In practice, interest was hidden inside the exchange.

sections.key: The Medici ran semi-independent branches across Europe, an early model for modern firms.
sections.b: At its height the Medici Bank had branches in Rome, Venice, Milan, Geneva, Avignon, Bruges and London, among other places. Each was run by a manager who often held a share of the profits, giving him a reason to work hard, while the family in Florence kept overall control. Branches were set up as separate partnerships, so a disaster in one city would not automatically drag down the rest. The Medici and other Italian merchants also kept careful accounts using double-entry bookkeeping, recording every transaction as both a debit and a credit so errors stood out. The method was spreading among Italian traders by the 1300s, and the friar Luca Pacioli described it in print in 1494.

sections.key: Medici wealth funded some of the greatest art and architecture of the Renaissance.
sections.b: Giovanni's son Cosimo de' Medici used the bank's fortune to become the unofficial ruler of Florence from 1434, steering politics through allies rather than holding a crown. He was also a generous patron. He funded churches, the library of the monastery of San Marco and artists such as Donatello, and supported scholars who translated ancient Greek philosophy. His grandson Lorenzo the Magnificent continued the tradition, and the young Michelangelo spent time in his household. Part of this giving was genuine love of learning and beauty. Part of it was likely an attempt to win public support, and perhaps to ease consciences troubled by the Church's teaching on wealth. Either way, Florence was transformed.

sections.key: Bad loans to rulers and weaker management brought the bank down in 1494.
sections.b: Under Lorenzo, who was more interested in politics and poetry than ledgers, the bank weakened. Some branch managers made reckless loans to princes, who were powerful, unpredictable and hard to sue. The London branch lent heavily to King Edward IV during the Wars of the Roses and suffered heavy losses. The Bruges branch, under Tommaso Portinari, lent to Charles the Bold, Duke of Burgundy, who was killed in battle in 1477. One by one, branches closed. In 1494, when the Medici were driven out of Florence, the bank collapsed. The lesson echoes through financial history: lending to the mighty can feel safe until the mighty decide, or are unable, to pay.
