quiz.q: Where does the word ‘bank’ come from?
o: The Latin word for gold
The name of a German banking family
The Italian word banco, meaning bench
The banks of the river Arno
quiz.e: Early money-changers worked at benches, and the Italian word for bench gave us ‘bank’.

quiz.q: How did bankers earn a return despite the Church's ban on usury?
o: By charging entry fees to churches
By building profit into bills of exchange
By selling indulgences to clients
By ignoring the ban openly
quiz.e: On paper a bill of exchange was a currency swap, so the interest stayed hidden in the exchange rates.

quiz.q: Why were Medici branches set up as separate partnerships?
o: To avoid paying tax in any city
So each branch could issue its own coins
So one failing branch would not sink the rest
Because the Pope demanded the split
quiz.e: Separate partnerships limited the damage of any single failure, an idea modern firms still use.

quiz.q: Why did the Medici spend so much on art and scholarship?
o: Because the Church required it of them
Genuine love of learning, and public favour
Because they had no other use for money
Because artists paid them for the honour
quiz.e: Patronage mixed genuine passion with a bid for popularity, and it transformed Florence.

quiz.q: What helped bring down the Medici Bank?
o: A Florentine stock market crash
The invention of paper money
A ban on double-entry bookkeeping
Risky loans to powerful rulers
quiz.e: Rulers are powerful and hard to sue, so lending to them can end in losses the lender cannot recover.

LESSONS.push: The word bank comes from a street bench. This family turned it into an empire.

LESSONS.title: Behavioural economics: why we're not rational with money
LESSONS.hook: Traditional economics imagined people as cool calculators. Then psychologists started running experiments, and the calculators turned out to be human.

sections.key: Classic economics assumed people calculate every choice logically, but real people do not.
sections.b: For much of the twentieth century, economic theory leaned on a convenient character sometimes nicknamed Homo economicus. This imaginary person knows what they want, calculates costs and benefits precisely, never gets tired or tempted, and always chooses the option that serves them best. The assumption made the maths workable, and it still explains a great deal about how markets behave. But anyone who has bought something on impulse, kept a gym membership they never use or put off saving for retirement knows real people are different. Behavioural economics grew from testing how people actually decide, using experiments borrowed from psychology, and building those findings back into economics.

sections.key: Losing something tends to hurt more than gaining the same thing feels good, so people overvalue what they own.
sections.b:
In 1979 psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky published prospect theory. One central idea is loss aversion: in many experiments, losing 100 dollars hurts roughly twice as much as winning 100 dollars pleases, though estimates vary and some researchers argue the effect is smaller. It helps explain why investors hang on to falling shares, and why ‘don't miss out’ marketing works. Kahneman won the 2002 Nobel Prize in economics; Tversky had died in 1996.

In a 1990 study, mugs were handed to half a class. Owners typically demanded about twice what buyers would pay. This is the endowment effect, and it explains why sellers overprice their homes and free trials work. Later research debates its strength.

sections.key: We treat money differently depending on where it came from or what we have labelled it for.
sections.b: In theory a dollar is a dollar. In practice we sort money into mental jars. Economist Richard Thaler called this mental accounting. Someone might carry credit card debt at a high interest rate while keeping savings in a holiday fund earning far less, because the holiday money feels untouchable. A tax refund or a win at the races often gets spent more freely than wages, as if it were not quite real money. Mental accounting is not always bad. Labelling money for bills or emergencies can stop you overspending. But it can also lead to choices that cost money, so it helps to ask occasionally whether your jars still make sense together.

sections.key: We tend to grab rewards now and push costs into the future, even against our own plans.
sections.b: Ask people whether they would prefer 100 dollars in a year or 110 dollars in a year and a week, and most will wait the extra week. Ask whether they want 100 dollars today or 110 dollars next week, and many grab the money now. The gap is the same, but the present has a special pull. Economists call this present bias. It shows up in spending, saving, diets and procrastination, and it explains why buy now, pay later deals are so tempting. The future self who has to pay feels like a stranger. One response is to make good choices automatic, so your present self does not have to win the argument every time.

sections.key: Small changes to how choices are presented, such as defaults, can change behaviour without banning anything.
sections.b: If people are predictably irrational, can choices be designed to help them? In their 2008 book Nudge, Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein argued that defaults matter enormously. If workers are automatically enrolled in a retirement plan and must opt out, far more end up saving than if they must opt in. Thaler and Shlomo Benartzi designed Save More Tomorrow, in which workers commit in advance to saving part of future pay rises, sidestepping both present bias and loss aversion. Thaler received the Nobel Prize in 2017. Australia's compulsory superannuation, introduced in 1992, goes further than a nudge, since employers must contribute, but it rests on a similar insight about how hard saving is.

quiz.q: What did behavioural economics add to the idea of the perfectly rational ‘Homo economicus’?
o: Evidence from experiments on real choices
A legal ban on all impulse purchases
Proof that free markets never work well
A new form of currency for traders
quiz.e: It tests real behaviour using psychology experiments, then builds the findings back into economics.

quiz.q: What is loss aversion?
o: Refusing to make any risky investment
Preferring to save rather than spend
Feeling a loss more than an equal gain
Fearing the loss of a wallet or purse
quiz.e: Losses tend to hurt more than equal gains please, which also helps explain why people overvalue what they own.

quiz.q: Someone keeps a holiday fund while paying high interest on a credit card. Which idea does this illustrate?
o: The endowment effect
Mental accounting
Present bias
Loss aversion
quiz.e: Labelling money for a purpose can make it feel untouchable, even when that costs more in interest.

quiz.q: Why do buy now, pay later deals appeal so strongly?
o: They always cost less than paying cash
They automatically improve your credit score
Rewards now feel bigger than later costs
Retailers are required by law to offer them
quiz.e: The present has a special pull, so the cost that arrives later feels like someone else's problem.

quiz.q: According to Thaler and Sunstein, what does automatic enrolment with an opt-out do?
o: It makes little difference to saving
It greatly increases how many people save
It forces everyone to stay in the plan
It lowers what employers must contribute
quiz.e: Defaults matter because most people stick with the pre-set choice, so the right default helps them save.

LESSONS.push: People often value a mug twice as highly the moment it becomes theirs. Why?

LESSONS.title: The gold standard and the end of Bretton Woods
LESSONS.hook: For generations, money was promised to be as good as gold. Then on a Sunday night in 1971, an American president broke the link with a television address.

sections.key: Under the gold standard a currency could be swapped for a fixed amount of gold, which kept inflation low but tied governments' hands.
sections.b: Under the gold standard a government promised that its paper money could be exchanged for a fixed weight of gold on demand. Britain led the way. The pound was effectively linked to gold from the early 1700s, partly through a gold price set in 1717 while Isaac Newton was Master of the Mint, and formally from 1821. By the 1870s Germany, the United States and many others had joined. Because each currency was fixed to gold, they were fixed to each other, making trade and lending more predictable. Governments could not simply print money, so long-run inflation stayed low. The classical gold standard lasted until the First World War.

sections.key: The money supply depended on gold, not on what the economy needed, so downturns were hard to fight.
sections.b: The discipline came at a cost. The money supply depended on how much gold a country held, not on what the economy needed. When gold flowed out, a country often had to raise interest rates and squeeze its economy, even in a slump. Prices could fall for years, making debts harder to repay. The system also depended on new gold discoveries. Gold rushes in California, Australia and South Africa expanded the world's money supply in ways that had nothing to do with economic policy.

sections.key: Countries that abandoned gold earlier generally recovered from the Great Depression sooner.
sections.b: After the First World War, countries tried to rebuild the gold standard. In 1925 Britain, with Winston Churchill as Chancellor of the Exchequer, returned to gold at the pre-war rate, which most economists now agree overvalued the pound and hurt British industry. John Maynard Keynes attacked the decision in a pamphlet called The Economic Consequences of Mr Churchill. When the Great Depression struck, the gold standard helped spread deflation from country to country, as central banks raised rates to defend their gold. Britain left gold in 1931 and the United States effectively devalued in 1933. Research by economic historians, including Barry Eichengreen and Ben Bernanke, found that countries leaving gold earlier tended to recover faster.

sections.key: The post-war system pegged currencies to the dollar, but its design slowly undermined faith in the gold promise.
sections.b:
In July 1944, delegates from 44 Allied nations met at Bretton Woods, New Hampshire, led by Keynes for Britain and Harry Dexter White for the United States. Other currencies were pegged to the US dollar, and the dollar was convertible into gold at 35 dollars an ounce, but only for foreign governments and central banks. The conference also created the IMF and what became the World Bank.

Around 1960, economist Robert Triffin spotted a hidden contradiction. The world needed a growing supply of dollars for trade, which came from American spending abroad. But the more dollars piled up overseas, the less likely America held enough gold to honour them. Vietnam war spending widened the gap, and France under de Gaulle began converting dollars into gold.

sections.key: In August 1971 the US suspended the dollar's convertibility into gold, ending the gold link for good.
sections.b: On Sunday 15 August 1971, President Richard Nixon went on television and announced that the United States would temporarily stop converting dollars into gold for foreign governments. He also imposed wage and price controls and a surcharge on imports. The suspension was never lifted. Attempts to patch together new fixed rates collapsed, and by 1973 the major currencies were floating against each other. Since then, the world's money has been fiat money, valuable because governments declare it legal tender and people trust it, not because it can be exchanged for metal. Some still call for a return to gold, but most economists argue that flexibility in crises is worth the loss of the golden anchor.

quiz.q: Under a gold standard, what could you do with paper money?
o: Exchange it for a fixed amount of gold
Spend it only within your own city
Swap it for shares in the central bank
Nothing apart from buying everyday goods
quiz.e: A fixed link to gold limited money printing and kept currencies stable against each other.

quiz.q: What was the main drawback of tying the money supply to gold?
o: Gold was too heavy to ship between nations
The money supply was set by gold holdings
It caused very high long-run inflation
Banks were banned from making any loans
quiz.e: A country losing gold often had to squeeze its economy even in a slump.

quiz.q: What did economic historians find about countries that left gold early in the Great Depression?
o: They suffered longer depressions
They saw no difference
They tended to recover sooner
They were shut out of trade
quiz.e: Leaving gold freed central banks to ease policy instead of defending the gold link.

quiz.q: What was the Triffin dilemma?
o: Gold supplies grew faster than trade
Exchange rates changed every day
The IMF had too little money to lend
More dollars abroad meant weaker gold backing
quiz.e: Supplying the world with dollars meant issuing more than America's gold could cover at 35 dollars an ounce.

quiz.q: What did President Nixon announce on 15 August 1971?
o: A permanent return to the gold standard
The launch of a new world currency
Suspending dollar-to-gold convertibility
The founding of the World Bank and IMF
quiz.e: The suspension was never lifted, and by 1973 major currencies floated against each other.

LESSONS.push: Money was once promised to be as good as gold. One Sunday night changed that.

LESSONS.title: The global financial crisis of 2008
LESSONS.hook: It began with American home loans that should never have been made. Within months, some of the world's biggest banks were failing and governments were scrambling to stop a second Great Depression.

sections.key: In the early 2000s, easy loans to risky borrowers drove US house prices up, on the assumption they would keep rising.
sections.b: In the early 2000s American house prices rose rapidly for years. Interest rates were low after the dot-com crash, and lenders competed fiercely for business. Many began offering subprime mortgages to borrowers with weak credit histories, sometimes with little checking of income at all, and often with low introductory rates that would jump later. The thinking was that rising house prices would bail everyone out: a struggling borrower could refinance or sell at a profit. Buyers, lenders and investors all assumed prices would keep climbing, or at least would not fall across the whole country at once. When prices peaked around 2006 and began to fall, that assumption collapsed, and defaults began to climb.

sections.key: Mortgages were bundled into complex securities, and heavily borrowed banks could be wiped out by small losses.
sections.b:
Many lenders did not keep the loans they made. Banks bundled thousands of mortgages into securities and sold them to investors, a process called securitisation. These were repackaged into more complex products, such as collateralised debt obligations, which split the income into layers of risk. Rating agencies gave many top layers their highest AAA rating. Pension funds, banks and councils worldwide bought them. Lenders who could sell loans on had less reason to care whether borrowers could repay, and few investors understood where the risk sat.

Leverage magnified the danger. Many investment banks borrowed around thirty dollars or more for every dollar of their own capital, much of it short term. A small fall in asset values could wipe them out.

sections.key: The collapse of Lehman Brothers triggered a global panic and frozen credit markets.
sections.b: In March 2008 the investment bank Bear Stearns was rescued through a sale to JPMorgan Chase, with support from the US Federal Reserve. Then, in September, the authorities chose not to rescue Lehman Brothers, a 158-year-old investment bank. On 15 September it filed for bankruptcy, the largest in US history, with assets of more than 600 billion dollars. Within days the insurer AIG, which had sold huge amounts of protection against mortgage defaults, needed a massive government rescue. A large money market fund that held Lehman debt ‘broke the buck’, sparking runs on similar funds. Lending between banks almost seized up, and share markets plunged. Governments responded with unprecedented measures, including the 700 billion dollar US rescue program known as TARP.

sections.key: Fast stimulus, sharp rate cuts, sound banks and Chinese demand helped Australia avoid a recession.
sections.b: Australia came through better than almost any other advanced economy. Its big banks had less exposure to American subprime securities and were closely supervised. The Reserve Bank cut the cash rate from 7.25 per cent in September 2008 to 3 per cent by April 2009. The government guaranteed bank deposits and wholesale funding, and spent heavily on stimulus, including cash payments to households and a large school building program. Meanwhile China launched its own enormous stimulus, keeping demand for Australian iron ore and coal strong. The economy shrank in only one quarter, at the end of 2008, so it avoided the technical definition of a recession: two consecutive quarters of decline.

sections.key: The crisis led to tougher bank rules and years of low interest rates and slow growth.
sections.b: Elsewhere, the damage lasted years. Millions of Americans lost their homes, US unemployment reached around 10 per cent, and parts of Europe slid into a debt crisis from 2010, with Greece the most severe case. Central banks cut interest rates to near zero and bought bonds on a vast scale. Regulators responded with new rules. The international Basel III standards required banks to hold more and better quality capital and more liquid assets, and the US passed the Dodd-Frank Act in 2010. Debate continues over whether the reforms went far enough, and over the fairness of rescuing banks while many ordinary people bore the costs. The crisis also fuelled lasting public anger at finance.

quiz.q: What were subprime mortgages?
o: Loans only for commercial property
Mortgages guaranteed by the government
Home loans to weak-credit borrowers
Home loans with no interest charged
quiz.e: Lenders assumed rising house prices would rescue risky borrowers, and that assumption failed when prices fell.

quiz.q: What is securitisation?
o: Hiring extra security staff for banks
Bundling loans into tradeable securities
Insuring customer deposits with the state
Raising interest rates on home loans
quiz.e: Selling loans on spread the risk around the world and weakened lenders' reason to check borrowers.

quiz.q: Why did leverage make banks so vulnerable?
o: Small losses could wipe out capital
They had too few customers
They were banned from lending
Their shares were too expensive
quiz.e: With around thirty dollars borrowed for every dollar of capital, thin cushions vanished quickly.

quiz.q: What happened after Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy in September 2008?
o: Credit markets calmed within days
Bank lending seized up and shares fell
House prices began to recover quickly
Governments stopped all further rescues
quiz.e: Lehman's failure turned a crisis into a global panic, forcing governments into unprecedented rescues.

quiz.q: Which of these helped Australia avoid recession during the crisis?
o: Sharp interest rate rises
Heavy holdings of US subprime debt
A collapse in Chinese demand
Fast rate cuts and government stimulus
quiz.e: Sound banks, fast policy action and China's demand for Australian resources softened the blow.

LESSONS.push: A 158-year-old bank was allowed to fail. The world's credit froze within days.

LESSONS.title: The market for lemons: when sellers know more than buyers
LESSONS.hook: A short paper about dodgy used cars was rejected by several journals. It went on to win a Nobel Prize and explain why some markets break down.

sections.key: When sellers know far more than buyers, good products can be driven out of a market.
sections.b: In the United States a defective car is called a lemon, and a good one a peach. In 1970 economist George Akerlof used used cars to explore a powerful idea. The seller knows the car's history. The buyer usually does not. Economists call this asymmetric information. If buyers cannot tell peaches from lemons, they offer only an average price. To the owner of a genuine peach, that is too low, so many decide not to sell. That leaves more lemons, buyers lower their offers further, and more good cars leave. In the extreme, the market collapses until only lemons remain, or no trade happens at all, even though buyers would gladly pay a fair price for a good car.

sections.key: Akerlof's paper was turned down several times before it became a classic.
sections.b: The paper had a rocky start. Akerlof later recounted that several leading journals rejected it, with reviewers suggesting it was too trivial or, alternatively, that if it were correct, economics would be different. It was eventually published in the Quarterly Journal of Economics in 1970. Over time it became one of the most cited papers in the field, because the idea applied far beyond cars. In 2001 Akerlof shared the Nobel Prize in economics with Michael Spence and Joseph Stiglitz, who had developed related ideas about how markets cope with hidden information. Together their work helped launch the economics of information, which now underpins thinking about insurance, lending and online trade.

sections.key: People who expect to claim are keener to buy insurance, which can push premiums up.
sections.b: Insurance shows the lemons problem in reverse. The buyer of health insurance often knows more about their own health than the insurer does. If premiums are set at an average level, people who expect to need lots of care find the deal attractive, while healthy people may decide it is not worth it. As the healthy leave, the insured pool gets sicker and more expensive, premiums rise and still more healthy people drop out. This spiral is called adverse selection. Australia's Lifetime Health Cover, introduced in 2000, tackles it by adding a loading to private hospital cover premiums for people who first take out cover later in life, from their early thirties on, encouraging people to join while young and healthy.

sections.key: Markets fight back with warranties, credentials and checks that reveal hidden quality.
sections.b: Markets are not helpless. Michael Spence showed how the informed side can send a signal, an action that is costly for low-quality sellers to fake. A dealer who offers a long warranty on a used car signals confidence, since honouring it on a lemon would be expensive. Spence's best-known example was education: a degree may signal persistence and ability to employers, whatever its direct usefulness. Joseph Stiglitz showed how the less informed side can screen, for instance by offering a menu of insurance policies with different excesses, so customers reveal their own risk by what they choose. Brand reputations, independent inspections and vehicle history reports all do the same job, making hidden quality visible.

sections.key: Much of modern commerce, from online reviews to consumer law, exists to close information gaps.
sections.b: Once you see the lemons problem, it appears everywhere. Online marketplaces rely on ratings and reviews so strangers can trust each other, and fake reviews are damaging precisely because they poison those signals. Lenders check credit histories because borrowers know more about their own finances. Employers ask for references. Consumer protection laws, including statutory guarantees that goods must be of acceptable quality, give buyers some assurance and reduce the advantage of sellers who hide defects. Akerlof's insight was that missing information is not a minor detail. It can stop a market working at all. Much of the machinery of modern commerce, from warranties to watchdogs, exists to close that gap.

quiz.q: In Akerlof's model, why might good cars disappear from the market?
o: Buyers start to prefer older cars
The government bans them from sale
Average prices are too low for their owners
Good cars are always exported abroad
quiz.e: When buyers cannot tell quality, the average price drives out the best sellers, leaving mostly lemons.

quiz.q: What is asymmetric information?
o: When two countries charge different prices
When one party knows much more than the other
When both sides hold exactly the same facts
When information is protected by copyright
quiz.e: The gap between what sellers and buyers know is what makes the lemons problem possible.

quiz.q: What is adverse selection in insurance?
o: Insurers choosing only healthy customers
Buying the wrong policy by honest mistake
A rule that bans cover for young people
Likely claimants being keenest to buy cover
quiz.e: As healthier people drop out, the pool gets costlier, which is why schemes like Lifetime Health Cover reward early joiners.

quiz.q: Why can a long warranty work as a signal?
o: Sellers are required by law to offer one
A lemon would cost the seller dearly
It always lowers the price of the car
It hides the car's history from buyers
quiz.e: A signal works when low-quality sellers cannot afford to fake it.

quiz.q: Why do online marketplaces rely on ratings and reviews?
o: They help strangers judge unseen quality
They replace the need to set any prices
The law requires every seller to have them
They stop sellers from advertising widely
quiz.e: Reviews close the information gap between buyers and sellers, which is why fake reviews do so much damage.

LESSONS.push: A paper about dodgy used cars was rejected again and again. Then it won a Nobel.

LESSONS.title: Inequality: how the gap between rich and poor is measured
LESSONS.hook: Is the gap between rich and poor growing? The answer depends on what you measure, and economists have been arguing about it for more than a century.

sections.key: Income is what flows in each year; wealth is what you own, and it is usually far more unequal.
sections.b: Talk about inequality often blurs two different things. Income is money that comes in over a period, from wages, business profits, interest, rent or government payments. Wealth is the stock of what you own minus what you owe: a house, superannuation, shares, savings and a car, less any mortgage or debts. A young doctor might have a high income but little wealth, while a retired farmer could have modest income and substantial wealth in land. Across almost every country, wealth is far more unequally distributed than income. Wealth builds up over a lifetime, earns its own returns and can be passed on, so differences tend to compound over time.

sections.key: A single number from 0 to 1, drawn from the Lorenz curve, summarises how unequally income or wealth is shared.
sections.b: In 1905 the American economist Max Lorenz proposed a neat way to picture inequality. Line everyone up from poorest to richest and plot what share of total income the bottom 10 per cent, 20 per cent and so on receive. If everyone earned the same, the line would be perfectly straight. The more it sags, the more unequal the society. In 1912 the Italian statistician Corrado Gini turned this into a single number. A Gini coefficient of 0 means perfect equality, and 1 means one person has everything. Most developed countries have income Gini figures between roughly 0.25 and 0.40, and wealth figures that are considerably higher.

sections.key: Wealth concentrates at the top in a similar pattern everywhere, so the median says more than the mean.
sections.b:
Around 1900, Italian economist Vilfredo Pareto studied tax and property records from several countries and centuries. He found the top of the distribution followed a similar pattern again and again, with a small share of people holding a large share of the total. The popular 80/20 rule was named after him, though it is far looser than his mathematics. This power law still describes the top of wealth distributions well.

It means averages can mislead. If a billionaire walks into a pub, the average wealth soars, yet nobody else is richer. Economists often prefer the median, the person exactly in the middle, to the mean. They also compare the 90th and 10th percentiles, or track the top 1 per cent's income share.

sections.key: Economists disagree about whether growth naturally narrows or widens inequality.
sections.b: In 1955 economist Simon Kuznets suggested that inequality rises as countries industrialise and then falls as they mature, an upside-down U called the Kuznets curve. The mid-twentieth century seemed to prove him right, as gaps narrowed in many rich countries. Then, from around 1980, top income shares rose again in the United States, Britain and elsewhere. In 2013 French economist Thomas Piketty published Capital in the Twenty-First Century, arguing that when the return on capital exceeds the growth rate of the economy, wealth tends to concentrate. His book became a surprise bestseller and drew strong criticism, with economists still debating his data, his theory and his proposed wealth taxes.

sections.key: How easily people move up or down the income ladder matters as much as the size of the gap.
sections.b: A snapshot of inequality does not say whether the same people stay at the top or bottom. Economic mobility asks how strongly your adult income is linked to your parents' income. Research led by economist Miles Corak found that countries with higher inequality tend to have lower mobility between generations, a link dubbed the Great Gatsby curve by Alan Krueger in 2012. It is a correlation, and researchers debate what drives it, from education and housing to social networks. Measured mobility in Australia has generally been found to be higher than in the United States, though comparing countries is tricky. Many people care less about the gap itself than about whether the ladder is climbable.

quiz.q: Why is wealth usually more unequal than income?
o: Wealth is counted in a different currency
It compounds over time and can be inherited
Income is capped by law in most countries
Wealth only counts cash held at banks
quiz.e: Wealth compounds over time and passes between generations, so gaps widen.

quiz.q: What does a Gini coefficient of 0 mean?
o: One person has everything
The data are missing
The economy is not growing
Everyone has exactly the same
quiz.e: The Gini runs from 0, perfect equality, to 1, where one person holds everything.

quiz.q: Why do economists often prefer the median to the mean when describing typical wealth?
o: A few very rich people can inflate the mean
Medians are required in official reports
The mean cannot be worked out for wealth
The median always rises faster over time
quiz.e: One billionaire in a pub lifts the average without making anyone else richer; the median is unmoved.

quiz.q: What did Thomas Piketty argue in Capital in the Twenty-First Century?
o: Inequality always falls as economies grow richer
Money should be fully backed by gold reserves
Wealth concentrates when capital outgrows the economy
Inequality is too hard to measure reliably
quiz.e: If capital grows faster than the economy, those who own it pull ahead, though economists still debate his case.

quiz.q: What does the Great Gatsby curve describe?
o: Rising house prices in New York
The spending habits of the very rich
The shape of the Lorenz curve
Higher inequality tied to lower mobility
quiz.e: Where gaps are larger, children's incomes tend to depend more on their parents' incomes, though the causes are debated.

LESSONS.push: Why a billionaire walking into a pub makes the average drinker look richer.

LESSONS.title: Quantitative easing: what central banks do when rates hit zero
LESSONS.hook: When interest rates can fall no further, central banks reach for a stranger tool: creating money to buy bonds. Australia tried it in 2020, with mixed results.

sections.key: Central banks steer the economy with interest rates, but cutting them stops working once they approach zero.
sections.b: Normally the Reserve Bank of Australia steers the economy with its cash rate, the overnight rate at which banks lend to each other. Cutting it makes borrowing cheaper and encourages spending and investment. But there is a floor. Near zero, further cuts become difficult, because people and banks could simply hold cash, which pays nothing but never charges you either. Economists call this the zero lower bound. A few central banks in Europe and Japan pushed rates slightly negative, but not by much. When a severe downturn hits and rates are already near zero, central banks need another tool. The best known is quantitative easing, or QE.

sections.key: A central bank creates new reserves to buy bonds, which pushes longer-term interest rates down.
sections.b: Under QE, a central bank buys large amounts of financial assets, mainly government bonds, from banks and investors. It pays with newly created reserves: electronic money in the accounts that commercial banks hold at the central bank. Despite the popular phrase, no banknotes are printed. The buying pushes bond prices up, and because prices and yields move in opposite directions, longer-term interest rates fall. That feeds through to mortgages and business loans. Sellers also receive cash they may put into corporate bonds or shares, an effect called portfolio rebalancing. QE also signals that the bank intends to keep rates low for a long time.

sections.key: Japan pioneered QE in 2001, and other major central banks adopted it after the 2008 financial crisis.
sections.b: Japan tried modern QE first. After its asset bubble burst in the early 1990s, it endured years of weak growth and falling prices. From 2001 to 2006 the Bank of Japan bought government bonds to expand bank reserves, and it later revived the approach on a far larger scale. The 2008 financial crisis made QE mainstream. The US Federal Reserve bought trillions of dollars of bonds and mortgage-backed securities, the Bank of England began in 2009 and the European Central Bank in 2015. Related tools exist too. The Fed capped bond yields from the Second World War until 1951, and the Bank of Japan adopted a version in 2016.

sections.key: The RBA bought bonds and targeted yields in 2020, then abandoned its yield target abruptly in 2021.
sections.b:
Australia skipped QE in the global financial crisis because its rates were well above zero. The pandemic changed that. In March 2020 the RBA cut the cash rate to 0.25 per cent, set the same target for three-year government bond yields and offered banks cheap funding. In November 2020 it cut both to 0.1 per cent and began a $100 billion Bond Purchase Program, later extended to roughly $280 billion in total.

The yield target ended badly. In 2021 the recovery was faster than expected and inflation rose, so markets bet on earlier rate rises than the bank's guidance of low rates until 2024. The RBA abandoned the target in November 2021, and later reviews acknowledged the disorderly exit damaged its credibility.

sections.key: QE probably helped steady markets in crises, but its wider effects are hard to measure and its side effects are debated.
sections.b: Most central bank research finds QE lowered long-term interest rates and helped steady markets in crises. Its effect on jobs and growth is much harder to measure, because nobody can rerun history without it. Critics raise three concerns. By lifting the prices of bonds, shares and property, QE may have widened wealth gaps, since wealthier people own most of those assets. It can blur the line between monetary policy and government financing. And when rates later rose, central banks faced large losses on the bonds they held. The RBA has reported negative equity as a result, though central banks can keep operating normally in that situation.

quiz.q: Why do central banks struggle to cut interest rates much below zero?
o: Banks refuse to lend at very low rates
Holding cash pays nothing but costs nothing
Governments ban negative rates by law
Cutting rates always triggers immediate inflation
quiz.e: Near zero, holding cash becomes a rival to deposits, so further cuts lose their force.

quiz.q: How does buying bonds under QE push longer-term interest rates down?
o: The central bank lifts the cash rate in step
Newly printed banknotes flood into mortgages
Purchases lift bond prices, which lowers yields
Banks are required to cut their loan rates
quiz.e: Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions, so heavy buying lowers longer-term rates.

quiz.q: How did QE change after the 2008 financial crisis?
o: Japan and the US dropped it after one trial
Only small developing economies adopted it
Deeply negative rates replaced it everywhere
It became a standard tool of major central banks
quiz.e: An emergency experiment became a normal part of the central bank toolkit.

quiz.q: Why did the RBA's yield target collapse in 2021?
o: Markets expected earlier rate rises than signalled
Banks refused to buy any more government bonds
The RBA ran out of reserves it could create
Federal government debt had been fully repaid
quiz.e: Markets bet against the RBA's guidance, and the bank dropped the target, which damaged its credibility.

quiz.q: Why do critics say QE may have widened wealth gaps?
o: It sharply cut wages for lower-paid workers
It lifted asset prices, which wealthier people mostly own
It raised taxes on ordinary household savings
It gave newly created money directly to banks' owners
quiz.e: Higher asset prices mainly benefit those who already own the assets.

LESSONS.push: Central banks can create money to buy bonds. Why isn't that just printing cash?

LESSONS.title: Cane toads: the pest that conquered the north
LESSONS.hook: In 1935 a hundred-odd toads were shipped to Queensland to save the sugar crop. They ignored the beetles they were meant to eat and set off across a continent.

sections.key: Cane toads were brought to Queensland in 1935 to eat cane beetles, but they could not reach them.
sections.b:
In the early 1930s, grubs of native cane beetles were chewing the roots of Queensland's sugar crop. The cane toad, a hardy amphibian from Central and South America, had a reputation for eating plantation pests elsewhere. In June 1935, 102 toads were brought from Hawaii to Gordonvale, near Cairns. They bred fast, and thousands of young toads were soon released around the cane fields. Some scientists warned that releasing an untested predator was reckless. They were ignored.

The plan had a basic flaw. Adult beetles sit high on the cane stalks and their grubs live underground, but toads are heavy ground hunters that cannot climb. There is no good evidence they dented beetle numbers. They ate almost everything else instead.

sections.key: Huge clutches of eggs, a tough body and few natural enemies let cane toads spread across northern Australia.
sections.b: Cane toads have almost every trait an invader needs. A female can lay tens of thousands of eggs in one clutch, in long strings of jelly in still water. Tadpoles develop quickly, and adults tolerate heat, drought and habitats from wetlands to suburban backyards. In their native range, parasites, diseases and predators that evolved alongside them keep numbers in check. In Australia almost none of those controls exist. The countryside around the cane farms offered insects, frogs, small mammals and pet food. Toads spread south into New South Wales and west across the Northern Territory, reaching the Kimberley by the late 2000s. They now cover well over a million square kilometres, and the western front is still moving.

sections.key: Toads at the invasion front have evolved to travel faster, which speeds up the spread.
sections.b: The invasion is accelerating. In the early decades the front advanced about ten kilometres a year. By the 2000s, toads in the Northern Territory were advancing at more than five times that rate. Biologist Rick Shine and colleagues found why. The toads leading the charge had longer legs than those in older populations, and they travelled further each night in straighter lines. The reason is simple selection. The fastest toads reach new ground first, where food is plentiful and competitors are few, and they breed with other fast toads. Generation after generation, the front became a population of athletes. It is one of the clearest examples of evolution within living memory.

sections.key: Cane toad toxin kills many native predators that never evolved to cope with it.
sections.b: Large parotoid glands behind a toad's head hold a poison of chemicals called bufadienolides, which attack the heart. Every life stage is toxic, including eggs and tadpoles. Predators in the toads' native range have had millions of years to adapt, but Australian predators had never met one. Goannas, freshwater crocodiles, northern quolls, some snakes and pet dogs die after biting or swallowing a toad. When the front reaches a new area, some goanna populations can crash dramatically. Not every native animal loses, though. Crows and kites have learned to flip toads over and eat the safer innards, and native water rats have been seen doing something similar.

sections.key: Since toads cannot be removed, scientists now work to reduce harm and teach predators to avoid them.
sections.b: Nobody has found a way to remove cane toads from Australia, so the focus is on limiting the damage. One clever idea uses the toads' own biology. Cane toad tadpoles are strongly attracted to a chemical from toad toxin, because they hunt and eat newly laid toad eggs. Traps baited with that chemical catch huge numbers of tadpoles while leaving native tadpoles largely alone. Another approach is taste aversion training. Northern quolls and goannas have been fed small toads or toad sausages that make them sick but do not kill them, so they learn to avoid toads before the invasion arrives. If you catch toads at home, wildlife authorities recommend humane methods, such as cooling them in a fridge and then freezing them.

quiz.q: Why did the cane toads fail to control the cane beetles?
o: The beetles were poisonous to the toads
The beetles lived where toads could not reach
Toads hibernated through the beetle season
Farmers killed the toads before they bred
quiz.e: Heavy, ground-dwelling toads could not climb the stalks or dig to the grubs, so they ate other things.

quiz.q: Why did cane toads spread so quickly across Australia?
o: A cooler, wetter climate than their homeland suited them
Huge egg clutches, hardiness and few natural enemies
Farmers kept moving them north by truck
They fed only on native cane pests
quiz.e: A tough body, huge clutches of eggs and the lack of parasites and predators let numbers surge.

quiz.q: Why are toads at the invasion front faster than toads in older populations?
o: They eat a much richer diet on fresh ground
Warmer weather in the north speeds them up
The fastest toads arrive first and breed together
They belong to a separate, faster species
quiz.e: Selection favours speed at the front, so each generation there runs faster than the last.

quiz.q: Why do native predators such as goannas die after eating cane toads?
o: Toads carry a parasite that spreads to them
Toad spines badly injure their throats
Toad meat is far too tough to digest
They have no evolved resistance to the poison
quiz.e: Australian predators had never met a toad, so they have no defence against its toxin.

quiz.q: How do tadpole traps help control cane toads?
o: A lure of toad toxin attracts toad tadpoles
Bright lights draw tadpoles in at night
They poison all the water around them
They play recordings of male toad calls
quiz.e: Toad tadpoles are drawn to the toxin chemical because they eat toad eggs, so traps largely spare native tadpoles.

LESSONS.push: They were shipped in to guard a crop and ignored the pest. What did they do instead?

LESSONS.title: Living light: the glow of bioluminescence
LESSONS.hook: In the darkest places on Earth, animals make their own light. They use it to hunt, hide, flirt and even call the police on their attackers.

sections.key: Bioluminescence is cold light made by a chemical reaction in a living thing, and most of it happens in the sea.
sections.b:
Bioluminescence is cold light made by life. Usually a molecule called luciferin reacts with oxygen, helped by an enzyme called luciferase, and the energy comes out as light rather than heat. Different groups evolved their own versions, so glowing has arisen independently dozens of times. Some animals make the light themselves. Many deep-sea fish instead house glowing bacteria in special organs.

The sea is where it thrives. Off California, researchers found roughly three-quarters of the deep-water animals they observed could make light. Most is blue or blue-green, which travels furthest in sea water. Reds fade within metres. Some dragonfish make red light near their eyes and can see it, a private searchlight for prey that cannot.

sections.key: Some animals glow on their undersides to erase their own shadow, a trick called counter-illumination.
sections.b: In the ocean's twilight zone, faint light filters down from above. Any animal swimming there casts a dark silhouette that predators below can spot. Many fish, squid and shrimps solve this by lighting up their undersides to match the glow overhead, so their outline disappears. This is called counter-illumination. Hatchetfish use rows of light organs along their bellies. The Hawaiian bobtail squid uses glowing bacteria called Vibrio fischeri, held in a light organ. Each morning it expels most of them and regrows the colony, and it can adjust its brightness to match moonlight. It is invisibility achieved by adding light rather than taking it away.

sections.key: Light can be used as bait, as a burglar alarm, or as a smoke screen to confuse a predator.
sections.b: The deep-sea anglerfish dangles a bacteria-lit lure from a modified fin spine on its head and swallows whatever comes to investigate. Light also serves defence. Tiny plankton flash when disturbed, and biologists have proposed a burglar alarm effect: the flash may attract larger predators that attack whatever is attacking the plankton. Certain jellyfish give off pinwheels of light when grabbed, perhaps for the same reason. Others use light as a smoke screen. Some deep-sea shrimps and squid squirt glowing fluid instead of dark ink, and the vampire squid can release sticky, glowing mucus. A predator lunging at the bright cloud may miss the animal slipping away into the dark.

sections.key: On land, glowing insects use light to find mates or to trap food.
sections.b:
Fireflies are actually beetles, and their flashes are a courtship language. Males flash species-specific patterns in flight, and females answer from the ground with timed signals. Some females exploit this. In North America, females of the genus Photuris mimic the replies of another genus, lure in eager males and eat them.

Australia and New Zealand have a different light show. The glow-worms of caves and damp gullies, such as Springbrook in Queensland or Waitomo in New Zealand, are not worms but the larvae of fungus gnats. They hang sticky silk threads from the ceiling and glow blue to attract small flying insects, which become trapped and are reeled in.

sections.key: Glowing plankton light up beaches, and borrowed glowing proteins have transformed biology.
sections.b:
Sometimes the glow comes to the shore. Tiny single-celled plankton called dinoflagellates flash when disturbed, so breaking waves, paddling feet and kayak strokes can light up electric blue. Beaches in Tasmania, Jervis Bay and many places overseas occasionally put on this display. Some fungi glow too, including Australia's ghost fungus, which shines a faint green on rotting wood at night.

Scientists have borrowed nature's lights. Firefly luciferase is used in laboratories to detect chemical activity, and a green fluorescent protein from a jellyfish became a revolutionary tool for tagging cells and genes, earning the 2008 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. A glow first noticed in the sea now helps researchers watch diseases develop.

quiz.q: What usually produces the light in bioluminescence?
o: Waste heat released from the animal's body
Electricity stored in special skin cells
Luciferin reacting with oxygen and an enzyme
Moonlight reflected off special scales
quiz.e: The energy of the reaction is released as light rather than heat, which makes the glow remarkably efficient.

quiz.q: What is counter-illumination?
o: Flashing to warn others of danger
Glowing underneath to hide your silhouette
Using light to attract mates
Squirting clouds of glowing fluid
quiz.e: By matching the faint light from above, an animal's shadow disappears to predators looking up.

quiz.q: Why might a flash from disturbed plankton help protect them?
o: It blinds the attacker for good
It warms the water so predators leave
It may call bigger predators to the attacker
It tells nearby plankton to breed
quiz.e: This burglar alarm idea suggests the flash calls in bigger predators that turn on the attacker.

quiz.q: What are the glow-worms of Australian and New Zealand caves, and why do they glow?
o: Firefly larvae that glow to find mates
Earthworms that glow to warn predators
Fungus gnat larvae that glow to lure prey
Beetle larvae that glow to scare off birds
quiz.e: They are fungus gnat larvae that glow blue to draw small flying insects into silk threads.

quiz.q: What causes the glowing waves seen on some beaches?
o: Tiny plankton that flash when disturbed
Radioactive minerals in the wet sand
Phosphorus washing off coastal rocks
Jellyfish stinging in the shallows
quiz.e: Dinoflagellates flash when the water moves, so waves and footsteps light up blue.

LESSONS.push: In the dark deep sea, glowing is common. Why would an animal glow to turn invisible?

LESSONS.title: Elephants: memory, matriarchs and the meaning of death
LESSONS.hook: Elephants live in families led by wise old females, talk in rumbles too low for us to hear, and pay strange attention to their dead.

sections.key: There are three living elephant species: African savanna, African forest and Asian elephants.
sections.b: Genetic studies show Africa holds two elephant species, not one. The savanna elephant is the largest land animal alive, with big males up to about four metres at the shoulder and six tonnes or more. The forest elephant is smaller, with straighter, downward-pointing tusks, and lives in central and west African rainforest. The IUCN began assessing them separately in 2021. The Asian elephant, with smaller ears and a domed head, is a different branch again, more closely related to the extinct woolly mammoth than to either African species. Elephants eat well over a hundred kilograms a day and can live into their sixties. They dig waterholes, open thick bush and, in forests, spread seeds in their dung.

sections.key: Elephant families are led by an older female, and her experience can mean life or death.
sections.b: Elephant society is built around females. A family of related mothers, daughters, sisters and young is led by an older matriarch. Young males leave in their early to mid teens. Pregnancy lasts around 22 months, the longest of any land mammal, and the calf, about a hundred kilograms at birth, is helped by aunts and older sisters. Research in Kenya's Amboseli National Park showed why the matriarch matters. Families led by older females were better at telling familiar calls from strangers' and reacted most strongly to the most dangerous lion roars. Older matriarchs also remember routes to water in drought. When poaching kills them, a lifetime of knowledge is lost.

sections.key: Elephants communicate with deep rumbles, some below the range of human hearing, and may sense vibrations through the ground.
sections.b: Elephants trumpet, but much of their conversation is quieter to our ears. They use deep rumbles, part of which are infrasound, frequencies too low for humans to hear. These sounds travel far, helping scattered groups keep in touch and males find females ready to mate. Researchers have also found evidence that elephants detect vibrations travelling through the ground. Their feet and trunks are packed with sensitive nerve endings, and elephants sometimes freeze, lean forward and press a foot down as if listening. The trunk is a marvel too: a boneless organ of muscle that can pluck a single blade of grass, suck up litres of water or lift a heavy log, with an extraordinary sense of smell.

sections.key: Elephants seem to recognise themselves in mirrors and show unusual interest in their dead, though elephant graveyards are a myth.
sections.b:
Elephants are among the few animals that seem to recognise themselves in a mirror. In 2006 an Asian elephant named Happy at the Bronx Zoo repeatedly touched a painted mark on her head that she could see only in her reflection. Elephants also cooperate on tasks, swat flies with branches and remember individuals for years.

They treat their dead unusually too. They touch bodies, stand quietly beside them and return over several days. In Amboseli, elephants showed far more interest in elephant skulls and ivory than in other skulls or wood. Whether this is grief is still debated. The old story of elephant graveyards is a myth, though bones can gather near water where weak animals linger.

sections.key: Heavy poaching in Gorongosa left far more tuskless females, a clear case of evolution driven by hunting.
sections.b: Humans have shaped elephants too. Ivory poaching targets animals with tusks. In Mozambique's Gorongosa National Park, heavy poaching during the civil war from 1977 to 1992 left a population with a far higher share of tuskless females, because tuskless animals were more likely to survive and breed. Genetic research published in 2021 confirmed this was evolution driven by hunting. It is a sobering reminder of how quickly human pressure can change a species, and of the knowledge lost whenever older elephants are killed.

quiz.q: Why are elephants now generally counted as three species rather than two?
o: Asian elephants were found to be two species
Genetic studies show two distinct African species
Forest elephants are just young savanna elephants
Savanna elephants vary a lot in size by country
quiz.e: African savanna, African forest and Asian elephants are now treated as three distinct species.

quiz.q: What did research in Amboseli show about older matriarchs?
o: They are more aggressive towards all visitors
They leave the family once they grow old
Their families respond better to real threats
They stop communicating with the herd
quiz.e: Families led by older matriarchs were better at judging which calls and lion roars were genuinely dangerous.

quiz.q: How do elephants keep in touch over long distances?
o: High-pitched trumpets carrying for kilometres
Chemical signals left in their dung trails
Tapping their tusks against large trees
Deep rumbles, partly too low for us to hear
quiz.e: Low sounds travel well over long distances, so rumbles help scattered groups stay in contact.

quiz.q: What is true of the so-called elephant graveyards?
o: They are documented sites elephants walk to before dying
They are a myth, though bones may gather near water
They are protected by law in Kenya
They are used only by Asian elephants
quiz.e: There are no special graveyards; bones may build up near water where weak animals linger.

quiz.q: Why does Gorongosa National Park have many tuskless female elephants?
o: A disease weakened and destroyed their tusks
Poaching favoured the tuskless survivors
They were bred that way in captivity
Tusks wear away in hot, dry climates
quiz.e: Poaching killed tusked elephants, so tuskless ones survived to breed, and genetic work confirmed the shift.

LESSONS.push: Elephants talk in sounds we cannot hear, and they notice the dead. What else do they do?

LESSONS.title: Emperor penguins: fathers of the Antarctic winter
LESSONS.hook: While most birds leave the Antarctic winter behind, emperor penguins walk into it to breed. The fathers then stand in the dark for two months with an egg on their feet.

sections.key: Emperor penguins are the largest penguins and the only penguins that breed through the Antarctic winter.
sections.b: Emperor penguins stand a little over a metre tall and can weigh more than 30 kilograms when well fed, making them the largest living penguins. They live only around Antarctica and spend most of their lives at sea, hunting fish, krill and squid. What makes them unique is their timing. Most Antarctic animals breed in the brief summer, when food is plentiful and temperatures are mild. Emperors do the opposite. In autumn they march, waddle and toboggan on their bellies across the sea ice to traditional breeding sites, sometimes many kilometres from open water. There, in the coldest, darkest season on the planet, they court, pair up and raise a single chick.

sections.key: The female passes her single egg to the male, who incubates it for about two months without eating.
sections.b:
After courtship, around May or June, the female lays one large egg. Weakened by fasting, she must return to the sea to feed, so the egg is passed to her partner. This is delicate: if it rolls onto the ice, it can freeze and the embryo dies. The male balances it on his feet under a warm brood pouch, and she sets off on her long trek.

For about 65 days he stands through the polar night, in temperatures that can fall below minus 40 degrees Celsius, eating nothing. Counting courtship, he may fast around four months, living on stored fat and moving as little as possible. If his partner is late, he can produce a nourishing throat secretion for the newly hatched chick.

sections.key: Thousands of penguins huddle and slowly shuffle so that everyone takes a turn in the warmth.
sections.b: Alone, a male emperor would struggle to survive the winter. Together they manage it. In the worst weather, males press tightly into huddles of thousands of birds. Inside a dense huddle the temperature can climb above 30 degrees Celsius, so warm that birds sometimes break away to cool down. Huddles are not static. Researchers filming colonies found the birds shuffle in small, coordinated steps, sending slow waves through the group, so the huddle gradually moves and reorganises. Birds on the windy edge work inwards while others drift outwards. The result is a remarkably fair system, in which no bird stays in the warm centre or on the freezing edge for too long.

sections.key: Explorers once risked their lives in the polar winter to collect emperor eggs.
sections.b: The emperors' winter breeding was so mysterious that scientists once took terrible risks to study it. In 1911, on Robert Falcon Scott's Antarctic expedition, Edward Wilson, Henry Bowers and Apsley Cherry-Garrard set out in the winter darkness for the emperor colony at Cape Crozier. They hoped the embryos would reveal clues to how birds evolved from reptiles. In temperatures below minus 50 degrees Celsius, they man-hauled sledges for weeks, lost their tent in a blizzard and nearly died. They returned with three eggs. Wilson and Bowers later perished with Scott on the return from the South Pole. Cherry-Garrard told the story in his classic book The Worst Journey in the World.

sections.key: Satellites now count emperor colonies, and shrinking sea ice is their greatest threat.
sections.b: Colonies are remote, so scientists now find many from space. The birds leave large brown stains of guano on the white ice, visible in satellite images, and high-resolution pictures can help estimate numbers. Surveys have revealed colonies no one knew existed. The same technology shows the danger. Emperors need stable sea ice from autumn until their chicks grow waterproof feathers in summer. In 2022, early sea ice break-up in one region of west Antarctica likely killed almost all chicks in several colonies. Because sea ice is shrinking as the climate warms, many scientists warn that emperor numbers could fall steeply this century.

quiz.q: What makes the breeding of emperor penguins unusual?
o: They breed on sea ice in winter
They breed only on rocky islands
They lay their eggs in the water
They breed only once every five years
quiz.e: Emperors are unique in breeding through the Antarctic winter on sea ice, not in summer.

quiz.q: How does the male survive about two months of incubation?
o: He eats snow and ice for energy
He takes shifts at sea with other males
He lives off stored fat and barely moves
He feeds on fish kept in his brood pouch
quiz.e: He eats nothing for around 65 days, living on stored fat while keeping the egg off the ice.

quiz.q: How do emperor huddles stay fair to all the birds?
o: The strongest birds stay in the middle
Birds shuffle so positions slowly rotate
Females push males out of the centre
Huddles only form for a few minutes
quiz.e: Small coordinated movements send waves through the huddle, moving birds between the edge and the warm centre.

quiz.q: What did the 1911 winter journey hope to learn from emperor embryos?
o: How penguins survive in water
How colonies find their way home
How birds evolved from reptiles
How the cold affects egg size
quiz.e: Scientists believed the embryos might reveal how birds evolved from reptiles, which made them worth a deadly trek.

quiz.q: Why does shrinking sea ice threaten emperor penguins?
o: Chicks need stable ice until fully feathered
Eggs hatch too early in warmer water
Colonies become too crowded to breed
Adults cannot find mates without it
quiz.e: Early break-up in 2022 likely killed almost all chicks in several colonies.

LESSONS.push: Most Antarctic birds leave for winter. Why do emperors breed through it?

LESSONS.title: Hibernation: the art of switching off
LESSONS.hook: Some animals survive hard times by turning their bodies almost all the way down. A few cool themselves to below freezing and still wake up.

sections.key: Hibernation is a controlled, reversible shutdown of metabolism, and many small animals use shorter daily torpor.
sections.b:
We say animals sleep through winter, but hibernation is different. A hibernator deliberately lowers its metabolism, the rate its body burns energy, to a tiny fraction of normal. Body temperature drops, breathing slows and a ground squirrel's heart may fall from hundreds of beats a minute to a handful. Biologists call this state torpor. Hibernation is long torpor, lasting weeks or months, and the body controls it and can reverse it.

Many small animals use shorter daily torpor. Hummingbirds burn energy so fast that a cold night without food could kill them, so some let their body temperature fall overnight and warm up at dawn. Small Australian marsupials such as dunnarts, some possums and gliders, and many microbats do the same.

sections.key: Arctic ground squirrels cool their bodies to below zero without freezing solid.
sections.b: The Arctic ground squirrel of Alaska and northern Canada holds a remarkable record. During hibernation its body temperature can fall to almost minus three degrees Celsius, the lowest core temperature measured in a mammal. Its body fluids do not freeze, because they are supercooled, staying liquid below the usual freezing point. Even so, the squirrel cannot stay that cold all winter. Like most small hibernators, it wakes every week or few, rewarming to normal temperature for a short time before dropping again. These arousals burn a large share of its stored energy. Scientists still debate why they are needed, with ideas including resetting the immune system or restoring the brain.

sections.key: Bears stay fairly warm in winter but go months without eating, drinking or passing waste.
sections.b: Bears were once said not to be true hibernators, because their body temperature drops only a few degrees. Today most biologists count them as hibernators of a special kind. A black or brown bear in its den slows its metabolism dramatically while staying relatively warm, which helps a mother give birth and nurse tiny cubs in mid-winter. The astonishing part is what bears do without. They can go for months without eating, drinking, urinating or defecating. Their bodies recycle waste products into new protein, and they lose surprisingly little bone or muscle despite lying still. Medical researchers study bears closely, hoping to help bedridden patients or people with kidney disease.

sections.key: Echidnas and the mountain pygmy possum are among Australia's true hibernators.
sections.b: Australia might not seem like hibernation country, but some of its animals do it. Short-beaked echidnas in cooler regions, such as Tasmania and the alpine high country, can hibernate for several months, letting their body temperature fall close to their surroundings. The mountain pygmy possum, a small, endangered marsupial found only in the alpine areas of Victoria and New South Wales, hibernates for months beneath the winter snowpack among boulder fields. In spring and summer it feasts on Bogong moths, which migrate to the mountains, and builds fat for the long sleep. Fewer moths in recent years has worried researchers, because the possums depend on that rich food supply to survive winter.

sections.key: Hibernation turns up in unexpected animals, and learning how it works may one day help medicine.
sections.b: Hibernation has surprised scientists more than once. In 1946 naturalist Edmund Jaeger found a common poorwill, a North American nightbird, torpid in a rock crevice in winter, showing that at least one bird could hibernate. In 2004 researchers reported that the fat-tailed dwarf lemur of Madagascar hibernates for months in tree holes, the first primate known to do so. These discoveries have sparked medical interest. If doctors could safely slow a human's metabolism, it might protect organs during surgery, buy time for trauma or stroke patients, or one day help astronauts on very long journeys. For now that remains research, not reality. Hibernators remind us that bodies can be far more flexible than we assume.

quiz.q: What best describes hibernation?
o: A very deep, ordinary kind of sleep
A faint caused by extreme cold
Simply staying in a burrow all winter
A controlled, reversible drop in metabolism
quiz.e: Hibernation is long-lasting torpor, an actively managed shutdown rather than just deep sleep.

quiz.q: How can an Arctic ground squirrel's body fall below zero without freezing?
o: Its body fluids supercool and stay liquid
Its blood is swapped for plain antifreeze
Its thick fur stops the cold reaching it
Its heart beats faster to keep it warm
quiz.e: Supercooled fluids stay liquid below the usual freezing point, giving the lowest core temperature recorded in a mammal.

quiz.q: What can hibernating bears go without for months?
o: Any heartbeat or breathing at all
Staying even slightly warm
Eating, drinking and passing waste
Any change in their metabolism
quiz.e: Bears go months without food, water or passing waste, recycling waste products into protein.

quiz.q: Why does the mountain pygmy possum depend on Bogong moths?
o: The moths help it build its winter nest
They give it the rich food that builds fat
They keep predators away from its burrow
The moths signal the start of each spring
quiz.e: The possum feasts on migrating Bogong moths in spring and summer, so fewer moths threaten its winter survival.

quiz.q: Why are doctors interested in hibernation?
o: It could replace most surgical procedures
Hibernators never suffer from any disease
Humans will soon be able to hibernate
It might protect organs in surgery or trauma
quiz.e: The idea is still research, but slowed metabolism could buy time and protect organs.

LESSONS.push: One mammal can cool to below freezing and wake up. How does it avoid turning to ice?

LESSONS.title: The wolves of Yellowstone
LESSONS.hook: When wolves returned to Yellowstone in 1995, they became the centre of one of ecology's most famous stories. The truth is messier, and more interesting.

sections.key: Some species have effects on their ecosystem far larger than their numbers suggest.
sections.b: In the 1960s American ecologist Robert Paine ran a simple experiment on the rocky shore of Washington State. He repeatedly removed a predatory sea star from one stretch of rocks and left a neighbouring stretch alone. Without the sea star, mussels took over, crowding out other species, and the shore's diversity collapsed. Paine called such a species a keystone, after the stone at the top of an arch that holds the rest in place. The idea that predators can shape whole ecosystems through a chain of effects called a trophic cascade became hugely influential. Sea otters, for instance, protect kelp forests by eating sea urchins. Wolves in Yellowstone became the most famous test case of all.

sections.key: Wolves were deliberately wiped out of Yellowstone by the 1920s, then returned from Canada in 1995 and 1996.
sections.b: Yellowstone, established in 1872, was the world's first national park, but early managers saw wolves as vermin that killed livestock and the elk and deer visitors liked to see. Government hunters shot, trapped and poisoned them, and by the mid-1920s they were gone. Elk numbers rose, and managers worried about heavy browsing of young aspen, willow and cottonwood. Rangers at times culled elk themselves. Attitudes changed, and after the wolf was listed as endangered, plans to restore it gained momentum despite fierce opposition from ranchers. In 1995 and 1996, 31 wolves from Canada were released into the park, and more went to central Idaho. They thrived, settling at roughly one hundred inside the park, and became a major attraction in the Lamar Valley.

sections.key: A popular account says wolves restored trees, beavers and even the shape of rivers.
sections.b: As the wolves settled in, elk numbers on the northern range fell sharply, from around 19,000 in the mid-1990s to a fraction of that within two decades. Some researchers reported willows and aspens growing taller in places, and beaver colonies increased. A powerful story took shape. Wolves, it was said, not only ate elk but frightened them away from exposed valleys and riverbanks, creating a landscape of fear. Freed from browsing, trees recovered, beavers returned, songbirds followed and riverbanks stabilised. A short online video in 2014, How Wolves Change Rivers, spread this story to many millions of viewers. It is a beautiful narrative of nature healing itself, and parts of it are supported by real evidence.

sections.key: The strength of Yellowstone's trophic cascade is still debated by researchers.
sections.b: Many ecologists think the popular story is too tidy. Elk declined for several reasons at once, including predation by cougars and bears as well as wolves, hunting outside the park and drought. Some studies found elk did not avoid risky places as strongly as the landscape of fear idea suggested, and that aspen often failed to recover even where wolves were common. Other work found willow recovery was patchy and modest. One reason is that when beavers vanished, their dams collapsed, streams cut deeper channels and the water table dropped. Willows on those drier banks struggle however few elk there are. Researchers still disagree on how much of Yellowstone's change can truly be credited to wolves.

sections.key: Wolves clearly changed Yellowstone, but ecosystems rarely follow a simple chain of cause and effect.
sections.b: Decades of radio-collar data make Yellowstone's wolves among the most studied large predators on Earth. Some effects are well established. Their kills feed ravens, eagles, magpies, bears and coyotes through winter, and wolves have reshaped the behaviour and numbers of other predators. Elk herds are smaller and behave differently. What remains contested is how far those changes flowed down to trees, rivers and the wider landscape. The debate is not a failure of science but science working, as researchers test an appealing idea against messy data. The broader lesson is valuable. Removing a top predator can change an ecosystem for a century, and putting it back does not simply rewind the clock.

quiz.q: What is a keystone species?
o: One with outsized effects for its numbers
The most numerous species in an ecosystem
A species that lives only on rocky shores
The largest animal in its ecosystem
quiz.e: Removing Paine's sea star collapsed the shore's diversity, showing how one predator can hold a community together.

quiz.q: Why did managers worry after wolves were removed from Yellowstone?
o: Visitor numbers fell sharply after the wolves went
Elk numbers rose and browsing harmed young trees
Livestock on nearby ranches began to die
Coyotes disappeared from the whole park
quiz.e: Without their main predator, elk increased and browsed young trees heavily.

quiz.q: What is the 'landscape of fear' idea?
o: Visitors keep away from areas with wolves
Wolves keep away from people and roads
Elk avoid risky places where wolves hunt
Rivers flood when wolves are present
quiz.e: Fear of wolves is said to change where elk feed, easing browsing pressure on exposed valleys and riverbanks.

quiz.q: Why do many ecologists think the popular wolf story is too tidy?
o: Wolves were never actually in Yellowstone
The video was filmed in a different park
Elk numbers did not change after wolves returned
Several factors cut elk, and recovery was patchy
quiz.e: Cougars, bears, hunting and drought all affected elk, and the loss of beaver dams limited willow recovery.

quiz.q: What does the Yellowstone debate teach about removing top predators?
o: Putting a predator back does not simply rewind the clock
Returning a predator always restores an ecosystem quickly
Predators have little effect on ecosystems
Scientific disagreement shows the research has failed
quiz.e: Ecosystems rarely follow a simple chain of cause and effect, so some damage repairs along its own path.

LESSONS.push: The story of wolves reshaping rivers is famous. Scientists say it is more complicated.

LESSONS.title: Spider silk: nature's super-material
LESSONS.hook: Weight for weight, some spider silk is stronger than steel and tougher than Kevlar. Spiders make it at room temperature from water and protein, and we still cannot copy it properly.

sections.key: Spider silk is a protein stored as liquid and turned into solid thread as it is drawn out, and one spider can make several kinds.
sections.b:
Silk is made of proteins called spidroins, stored in the spider's abdomen as a thick liquid. As the spider draws it out through tiny spinnerets, changes in acidity and water content, plus the stretching force of pulling, make the molecules line up and lock into a solid fibre. It happens at normal temperature with water as the solvent, while human factories making strong fibres often need high heat and harsh chemicals.

Orb-weavers, which build wheel-shaped webs, can have up to seven types of silk gland. Strong dragline silk forms the frame and safety line. The sticky capture spiral is stretchier and coated with glue droplets, so a fast insect is slowed rather than bouncing off. Other silks wrap prey, cement threads down and case eggs.

sections.key: Dragline silk combines strength with stretch, making it exceptionally tough for its weight.
sections.b: The claim that spider silk is stronger than steel is often repeated, so let us be precise. Steel and good dragline silk have broadly similar strength per thickness, but silk is far lighter, so weight for weight silk comes out ahead. Its real superpower is toughness, the energy a material can absorb before breaking. Because dragline silk both resists pulling and stretches a good deal, it absorbs more energy than Kevlar, the fibre used in protective vests. The toughest silk known comes from Darwin's bark spider of Madagascar, described in 2010. It builds enormous webs over rivers, anchored by bridge lines that can stretch around 25 metres across the water.

sections.key: Young spiders and some adults travel huge distances by floating on silk threads.
sections.b: Silk lets spiders fly. In a behaviour called ballooning, a spider climbs to a high point, raises its abdomen and releases fine threads into the air until it lifts off. Spiders have been found drifting thousands of metres up and landing on ships far out at sea, which helps explain how they are among the first animals to colonise new islands. Scientists long assumed ballooning depended only on wind. Research published in 2018 showed spiders also respond to the atmosphere's natural electric field, which can lift their charged silk. In parts of Australia, mass ballooning occasionally blankets paddocks in shimmering silk, sometimes nicknamed angel hair.

sections.key: Spider silk can be woven, but it is painstaking to harvest because spiders cannot be farmed like silkworms.
sections.b: People have long dreamed of spider silk cloth, but spiders are territorial and often cannibalistic, so they cannot be packed together like silkworms. A famous project in Madagascar showed what it takes. Textile maker Simon Peers and designer Nicholas Godley had workers collect more than a million golden orb-weaver spiders over several years, gently draw silk from each with a hand-cranked device, then return them to the wild. The naturally golden textiles, including a cape shown at London's Victoria and Albert Museum in 2012, are among the rarest fabrics in the world. Long before that, fine spider silk served as crosshairs in optical instruments such as telescope and gun sights, because it was thin, strong and even.

sections.key: Engineers can make spider silk proteins in other organisms, but spinning them into fibre as good as the real thing remains hard.
sections.b: Since spiders cannot be farmed, scientists have tried to make silk without them. Researchers have inserted spider silk genes into bacteria, yeast, silkworms and plants, and in one well-known project, into goats whose milk contained silk proteins. Making the protein is the easier half. Spinning it into fibre as good as a spider's is very hard, because the spider's duct performs its chemistry and stretching with remarkable precision. Some companies have launched products using artificial silk proteins, but none yet matches natural dragline silk at large scale. Possible uses include medical sutures, artificial ligaments, lightweight protective gear and biodegradable materials. For now the humble garden spider still out-engineers the laboratory.

quiz.q: How does liquid silk protein become a solid thread?
o: It is heated up inside the spider's abdomen
Acidity changes and pulling align proteins
It dries hard in sunlight after release
It reacts with oxygen in the air like glue
quiz.e: Changes in acidity and water, combined with stretching as it is drawn out, make the proteins lock into a solid fibre.

quiz.q: What is the main strength of dragline silk compared with Kevlar?
o: Far greater resistance to very high heat
It is completely rigid and never stretches
Toughness: energy absorbed before breaking
Natural magnetic properties that repel metal
quiz.e: Silk resists pulling and stretches, so it absorbs more energy than Kevlar before breaking.

quiz.q: What did the 2018 research add to our understanding of ballooning?
o: Spiders flap their front legs to take off
Only fully grown spiders are able to balloon
Ballooning only ever happens after dark
Electric fields in the air can help lift them
quiz.e: Spiders sense electric fields that can provide lift, not just wind.

quiz.q: Why can't spiders be farmed like silkworms?
o: Their silk is poisonous to the touch
They are territorial and often cannibalistic
They die within hours of being captured
Farming spiders is illegal in most countries
