quiz.e: Crowded spiders attack and eat each other, so silk must be collected from individual spiders by hand.

quiz.q: Why has artificial spider silk not matched the natural fibre?
o: Scientists cannot make any spider silk protein
Spider genes cannot be put into other organisms
Spinning the protein into a fibre is very hard
Artificial silk always dissolves in water
quiz.e: The spider's duct controls chemistry and stretching so precisely that it has proven very hard to copy.

LESSONS.push: Spider silk is made from water and protein at room temperature. Why can't we copy it?

LESSONS.title: Termite mounds: cities without architects
LESSONS.hook: Millions of tiny, mostly blind insects build towers taller than a person, without plans or a boss. The way those towers breathe has even fooled scientists.

sections.key: Termites are social cockroaches, not ants, and they digest wood with help from microbes in their guts.
sections.b:
Termites are not ants. Genetic studies show they are specialised cockroaches that became social. Like ants, they have a strict division of labour: a king and queen produce the young, workers gather food and build, and soldiers defend, some with huge jaws and others with snouts that squirt sticky chemicals. Workers include both males and females, and young grow gradually without a pupa stage.

Termites can live on wood and dead grass, even though cellulose is very hard to break down, because they have partners in their guts: bacteria and, in some groups, single-celled organisms. African and Asian Macrotermes go further, growing a fungus on chewed plant material inside their mounds and eating it. By recycling dead plants, termites enrich and loosen dry soils much as earthworms do in wetter ones.

sections.key: Mounds emerge from simple rules followed by individual termites, a process called stigmergy.
sections.b: No termite knows what the finished mound will look like. Most workers are blind, and none is in charge. So how do they build such complex structures? In the 1950s French biologist Pierre-Paul Grassé proposed an idea he called stigmergy. Each insect responds to the work already done around it. A termite drops a mud pellet laced with scent, which makes other termites more likely to drop pellets in the same spot. Small piles grow into pillars, pillars bend towards each other and arches form. Local cues such as humidity, airflow and carbon dioxide also guide where they dig and build. The grand structure emerges from millions of tiny decisions, with no plan anywhere in the colony.

sections.key: In the Northern Territory, so-called magnetic termites build thin mounds aligned north to south, which helps control temperature.
sections.b: Some of the world's most striking mounds are in northern Australia. In Litchfield National Park, near Darwin, fields of thin, slab-like mounds stand like gravestones, all aligned roughly north to south. They are built by so-called magnetic termites, a name that suggests a compass. Their broad faces catch the gentle morning and late-afternoon sun, while the thin edge faces the fierce midday sun, which helps keep the mound's temperature steadier through the day. Heat control is the best-supported reason for the alignment, though some experiments suggest the termites may also sense the Earth's magnetic field. Nearby, the giant cathedral mounds of other termite species can tower several metres high, among the largest structures built by any animal apart from humans.

sections.key: Mounds were long thought to work like chimneys, but research shows a more complex, lung-like system.
sections.b: A big colony uses lots of oxygen and produces carbon dioxide and heat, so its mound must exchange air with the outside. For decades the textbook explanation was a chimney: warm air from the colony rises up a central shaft and is drawn out, pulling fresh air in. Later work, notably by physiologist J. Scott Turner and colleagues, found this was too simple. Many mounds are closed structures with porous walls, more like a lung than a chimney. Research has shown that daily temperature swings, with the outer walls heating and cooling faster than the core, drive air around the channels, while wind gusts also push gases through the walls. Scientists are still refining the details.

sections.key: A Zimbabwean building borrowed ideas from termite mounds to save energy.
sections.b: The best-known example of termite-inspired design is the Eastgate Centre in Harare, Zimbabwe, an office and shopping complex completed in 1996. Architect Mick Pearce, working with engineers, designed it to stay cool without conventional air conditioning. Thick walls store heat, fans move cool night air through the building and chimneys release warm air. It uses far less energy for cooling than comparable buildings. There is an irony: the design drew on the chimney model of termite ventilation, which biologists have since revised. Nature still holds plenty of lessons. In Brazil, scientists reported in 2018 a vast field of termite mounds covering an area around the size of Great Britain, some estimated to be about four thousand years old.

quiz.q: How do termites digest tough plant material such as wood?
o: With stomach acid that dissolves cellulose
With help from gut microbes, and some farm fungus
By soaking it in water until it softens
By eating only the sap inside the wood
quiz.e: Gut bacteria and other microbes break down cellulose, and Macrotermes also grow a fungus on chewed plants.

quiz.q: What is stigmergy?
o: A queen termite giving building orders
A poison sprayed by soldier termites
Each termite reacting to earlier building
The chemical that hardens termite mud
quiz.e: Each termite reacts to cues like scented mud pellets, and the mound emerges from millions of local decisions.

quiz.q: Why are magnetic termite mounds aligned north to south?
o: To follow underground water
To block the prevailing winds
To mark the colony's borders
To avoid the hottest midday sun
quiz.e: The alignment helps keep the mound's temperature steadier by limiting midday heating.

quiz.q: How does current research suggest many termite mounds ventilate?
o: Like a simple chimney with a constant updraft
Heat swings and wind push air through the walls
Worker termites fanning air with their wings
They stay sealed and need no fresh air
quiz.e: Work by Turner and others showed mounds act more like lungs than chimneys.

quiz.q: How does the Eastgate Centre stay cool without conventional air conditioning?
o: Thick walls, night fans and warm-air chimneys
Water is sprayed over the roof all day long
Large ice stores underground hold winter cold
Its windows are sealed and tinted very dark
quiz.e: The design borrowed from the termite mound idea of moving air through a structure, using ventilation chimneys.

LESSONS.push: Termite towers have no architect and no plan. How do they get built?

LESSONS.title: Island evolution: giants, dwarfs and the dodo
LESSONS.hook: Strand animals on an island and strange things happen. Elephants shrink, rats grow huge and birds forget how to fly.

sections.key: Islands isolate living things, and Galapagos finches show how fast evolution can run there.
sections.b:
Islands have taught biologists more about evolution than almost anywhere. Colonists that drift, fly or blow in are cut off from their relatives, often with few competitors and no large predators, and over generations they can change dramatically. Darwin's 1835 visit to the Galapagos helped shape his thinking, and Wallace developed similar ideas in the Malay Archipelago.

Galapagos finches show adaptive radiation, where one ancestor spreads into many forms. Over about two million years, one colonising group became more than a dozen species, with beaks for crushing seeds, probing cactus flowers, catching insects or even drinking seabird blood. After a severe drought in 1977 left only large, hard seeds on Daphne Major, Peter and Rosemary Grant found that bigger-beaked birds survived better and the next generation had larger beaks. Evolution can be measured within years.

sections.key: On islands, large animals often shrink while small animals often grow larger.
sections.b: Biologists have noticed a broad tendency nicknamed the island rule. Large mammals stranded on islands often become smaller over generations, perhaps because food is limited and there are fewer predators to outgrow. Small animals such as rodents often become larger, perhaps because they no longer need to hide from predators and face less competition. The fossil record is full of examples. Dwarf elephants, some about the size of a large pig, once lived on Mediterranean islands including Sicily, Malta and Crete. On the Indonesian island of Flores, there were dwarf relatives of elephants alongside giant rats. The rule is a tendency rather than a law, and scientists still debate how consistent it is, but the examples are striking.

sections.key: A small human species lived on Flores, and how it became so small is still debated.
sections.b: In 2003 researchers excavating Liang Bua cave on Flores found the skeleton of an adult human relative who stood about a metre tall. It was named Homo floresiensis and quickly nicknamed the hobbit. Its brain was about the size of a chimpanzee's, yet stone tools were found in the same cave layers. Later work dated the remains to between roughly 100,000 and 60,000 years ago. How the hobbits came to be so small is still debated. One idea is that they descended from Homo erectus and shrank under island conditions, like the island's elephants. Another is that they came from an older, already small-bodied lineage. Either way, island life shaped human evolution too.

sections.key: Without ground predators, island birds often lose flight, which leaves them defenceless when people arrive.
sections.b: Flying is expensive. It needs big muscles and a light, demanding body. On islands without ground predators, many birds evolved to give it up. The dodo of Mauritius was a large, flightless relative of pigeons, and its closest living relative is the Nicobar pigeon. New Zealand, with no native land mammals other than bats, became a kingdom of birds, including the giant moa, the kiwi and the kakapo, a heavy, flightless, nocturnal parrot. Losing flight was sensible until humans arrived with rats, cats, pigs and hunting. The dodo was gone within a century of Dutch sailors landing in 1598, with the last widely accepted sighting in 1662. The moa vanished within a few centuries of people reaching New Zealand.

sections.key: Island species are especially vulnerable to newcomers, but the Lord Howe stick insect shows they can be rescued.
sections.b: Island species often evolve without defences against newcomers, so they are especially vulnerable. A large share of recorded animal extinctions in the past five centuries have been island species, many caused by introduced rats, cats and other invaders. Australia has a famous case. On Lord Howe Island, a large, flightless stick insect disappeared after black rats came ashore from a shipwreck in 1918. In 2001, researchers found a tiny surviving population on Ball's Pyramid, a sheer volcanic spire in the ocean nearby. Captive breeding programs have since raised many more. In 2019 a major operation began to eradicate rodents from Lord Howe, opening the possibility of returning the insect home. Islands show both how easily species are lost and how they can be saved.

quiz.q: What did Peter and Rosemary Grant observe after the 1977 drought on Daphne Major?
o: All of the finches died out
The beaks became smaller overall
The next generation had larger beaks
Finches stopped breeding for years
quiz.e: With only large, hard seeds left, bigger-beaked birds survived better and passed on larger beaks.

quiz.q: According to the island rule, what tends to happen to large mammals on islands?
o: They grow larger
They become smaller
They become flightless
They stay the same
quiz.e: Large mammals often shrink on islands, as seen in the dwarf elephants of the Mediterranean and Flores.

quiz.q: Which statement about Homo floresiensis is accurate?
o: It was a modern human with a rare disease
Its small size is fully explained and agreed
It lived mainly on the island of Madagascar
Its origins and small size are still debated
quiz.e: Whether through island dwarfing or an older small lineage, its origins are still debated.

quiz.q: Why did many island birds lose the ability to fly?
o: Flying is costly, and nothing on land hunted them
Island winds were too strong for them to fly in
Their wings were damaged by constant salt water
Early humans bred them to be flightless
quiz.e: Flying needs big muscles and a light body, so birds gave it up where nothing hunted them on the ground.

quiz.q: Why are island species so vulnerable to introduced animals such as rats?
o: They breed too slowly to matter much
They are always much smaller than invaders
They evolved with no defences against them
Introduced animals mostly eat only plants
quiz.e: Island species often have no defences against predators they have never met, which is why so many have gone extinct.

LESSONS.push: On islands, elephants shrink and rats grow huge. What does that say about evolution?

LESSONS.title: Symbiosis: the partnerships that built life
LESSONS.hook: Nearly every cell in your body contains descendants of ancient bacteria. Life on Earth is less a war of all against all than a tangle of deals, partnerships and double-crosses.

sections.key: Symbiosis is a spectrum of close partnerships, from mutual benefit to parasitism, renegotiated as conditions change.
sections.b:
Biologists sort close living-together relationships by who benefits. In mutualism, both partners gain: bees collect nectar while pollinating flowers. In commensalism, one gains while the other is barely affected, like barnacles riding on a whale. In parasitism, one gains at the other's expense. The German botanist Anton de Bary coined the word symbiosis in 1879.

These boxes are useful, but nature rarely respects them. A relationship can turn from helpful to harmful as conditions change, and each partner is under pressure to take a little more than it gives. Symbiosis is best seen as a spectrum of bargains, constantly renegotiated by evolution.

sections.key: Mitochondria and chloroplasts descend from free-living bacteria that were engulfed over a billion years ago.
sections.b:
Life's most important partnership began well over a billion years ago. A single-celled organism took in a bacterium and, instead of digesting it, came to depend on it. That bacterium became the mitochondrion, which powers our cells using oxygen. Later, an early cell took in a photosynthetic bacterium, which became the chloroplast in plants and algae.

In the 1960s, the American biologist Lynn Margulis championed this idea, called endosymbiosis, against widespread scepticism. The evidence now backs her. Mitochondria and chloroplasts have their own small circular DNA, bacteria-like ribosomes and double membranes, and they divide by splitting in two. Complex life, including us, is a partnership at its core.

sections.key: Lichens and corals are partnerships between very different organisms, and corals lose theirs when the water gets too hot.
sections.b:
A lichen looks like a single organism, but it is a fungus living with an alga or a cyanobacterium. The fungus provides structure and shelter, and its partner makes food from sunlight. Together they colonise bare rock, tree bark and frozen tundra where neither could live alone. In 2016, researchers found that many lichens also contain a yeast, a third partner that went unnoticed for over a century.

Reef-building corals work similarly. Their cells house microscopic algae that photosynthesise and pass much of their food to the coral. When the water becomes too hot, the partnership breaks down. The coral expels the algae and turns white, an event known as coral bleaching.

sections.key: Tight partnerships such as figs and fig wasps invite cheats, as cleaner fish and their mimics show.
sections.b:
A fig starts as an enclosed cluster of tiny flowers, and only a fig wasp, usually specialised to one or a few fig species, can pollinate it. A female squeezes in, often losing her wings, pollinates some flowers, lays eggs in others and dies. Her offspring mate inside, and the females leave carrying pollen. Neither partner can reproduce without the other, and the bond is tens of millions of years old.

Partnerships invite cheating. Bluestreak cleaner wrasse remove parasites from larger fish, but would often rather nibble their protective mucus. Clients chase cheats away, and cleaners behave better when other fish are watching. The sabre-toothed blenny goes further: it mimics a cleaner, then bites chunks from fish.

sections.key: Our own species has partners too: honeyguide birds lead people to honey, and gut microbes and Wolbachia bacteria shape our health.
sections.b:
In parts of Africa, the greater honeyguide leads people to wild bees' nests, then eats the wax left once humans open the hive. Yao honey hunters in northern Mozambique summon the bird with a special trilling call, and a 2016 study found it responded to that call far more than to other sounds.

Our microbes matter too. Trillions of bacteria, mostly in the gut, help digest food, train the immune system and fend off germs. The claim that they outnumber our cells ten to one is a myth: a 2016 study put the ratio closer to one to one. Wolbachia bacteria introduced into Aedes aegypti mosquitoes reduce their ability to spread dengue. The World Mosquito Program, which began in Australia, released them in north Queensland, where local outbreaks have since become very rare.

quiz.q: What is commensalism?
o: One partner gains at the other's expense
One partner benefits, the other barely affected
Both partners gain from the relationship
Neither partner is affected by the other
quiz.e: In commensalism one partner benefits while the other is barely affected, unlike mutualism, where both gain.

quiz.q: What evidence supports the idea that mitochondria were once free-living bacteria?
o: They are found only in plant cells
They are made of the same material as cell walls
They have their own circular DNA, like bacteria
They can still survive outside cells today
quiz.e: Mitochondria keep bacteria-like features: their own small circular DNA, ribosomes, double membranes and division by splitting.

quiz.q: What happens to a coral during bleaching?
o: It expels the algae living in its cells
It grows a thick white shell
It starts to photosynthesise by itself
It is buried under drifting sand
quiz.e: When the water is too hot, the coral-algae partnership breaks down and the coral expels its algae, turning white.

quiz.q: What does the sabre-toothed blenny do?
o: It cleans parasites off larger fish
It guards coral from hungry predators
It pollinates sea grass in shallow bays
It mimics a cleaner, then bites clients
quiz.e: Every successful partnership creates an opening for cheats, and the blenny exploits the cleaner's good reputation.

quiz.q: What is true of the claim that bacteria outnumber our own cells ten to one?
o: It is accurate and well established
It is a myth; the ratio is closer to one to one
It is a myth; our own cells outnumber bacteria a hundred to one
It is accurate for the gut only
quiz.e: A 2016 study estimated roughly equal numbers of bacterial and human cells, debunking the old ten-to-one figure.

LESSONS.push: Nearly every cell in your body hosts descendants of ancient bacteria. How?

LESSONS.title: The ring of Gyges: would you be good if no one could see?
LESSONS.hook: A shepherd finds a ring that makes him invisible, and soon he has seduced a queen and murdered a king. Plato used the story to ask the most uncomfortable question in ethics.

sections.key: In Plato's Republic, a shepherd finds a ring of invisibility and uses it to seize a kingdom.
sections.b:
Early in Plato's Republic, written around 375 BC, a young man named Glaucon tells a story. A shepherd called Gyges is tending his flock in Lydia, in what is now western Turkey, when an earthquake splits the ground. In the chasm he finds a hollow bronze horse holding the body of a giant, wearing only a gold ring. Gyges takes it.

Later he discovers that turning the ring's setting towards his palm makes him invisible, and turning it back makes him visible again. He wastes no time. He gets himself sent to the palace as a messenger, seduces the queen, kills the king with her help and takes the throne.

sections.key: Glaucon argues that people are just only because they fear being caught, and asks whether justice is worth having once every reward is removed.
sections.b:
Glaucon, one of Plato's older brothers, imagines two such rings: one given to a just man, one to an unjust man. He bets that both would behave the same way, taking whatever they pleased. Nobody is so iron-willed, he says, as to resist when there is no risk. If so, justice is not valued for itself. It is a compromise: we avoid harming each other because we fear being harmed.

He then raises the stakes. A perfectly unjust man with a spotless reputation grows rich and admired, while a perfectly just man branded wicked is whipped, imprisoned and executed. Which life is better? Glaucon and his brother Adeimantus ask Socrates to prove that justice benefits the just person even when every outside reward is stripped away.

sections.key: Plato's reply is that justice is the health of the soul, with reason ruling over spirit and appetite.
sections.b:
Answering the challenge takes up most of the rest of the Republic. Socrates argues that the soul has three parts: reason, which seeks truth; spirit, which feels pride, anger and honour; and appetite, which craves food, sex and money.

In a just person, reason rules, spirit supports it and appetite is kept in its place. In an unjust person, the parts are at war, and appetite or ambition takes control. The unjust ruler with the magic ring is therefore not free at all. He is a slave to cravings that can never be satisfied: restless, suspicious and alone. Justice, Plato concludes, is to the soul what health is to the body, and no amount of wealth makes up for a sick soul.

sections.key: Herodotus tells an older, ring-free version in which the queen forces Gyges to choose between killing the king and dying.
sections.b:
Gyges may have been a real person. A king of Lydia by that name ruled in the 7th century BC and founded a dynasty that later included the famously wealthy Croesus.

The historian Herodotus, writing in the 5th century BC, tells a very different tale of his rise. King Candaules is so proud of his wife's beauty that he insists his bodyguard Gyges hide in the royal bedroom to see her undressed. The queen spots him and gives him a stark choice: kill the king and marry her, or die. He chooses the throne. There is no magic ring in Herodotus, but both stories share hidden watching and power gained by stealth.

sections.key: The ring tests whether you would act the same way when no one is watching.
sections.b:
Readers often compare Gyges' ring to the One Ring in Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings, which also grants invisibility and corrupts its wearer. Whether Tolkien had Plato in mind is uncertain. Today many people carry a weaker version in their pockets: anonymous accounts, deleted messages and private browsing offer a taste of acting unseen.

The thought experiment lasts because it is so personal. It asks not what rules a society needs, but what you would do if consequences vanished. Try a small ring: a mistake in your favour at the till, an unwatched moment at work. Some philosophers say Plato's answer merely redefines justice as inner balance. Even so, the old saying holds: integrity is doing the right thing when no one is watching.

quiz.q: How does Gyges use the ring once he discovers its power?
o: He hands it to the king as a loyal gift
He returns it to the chasm and forgets it
He seduces the queen and takes the throne
He uses it only to guard his flock at night
quiz.e: Gyges uses invisibility for personal gain, showing what Glaucon thinks anyone would do without fear of being caught.

quiz.q: What is Glaucon's main claim about justice?
o: People are just mainly out of fear of being caught
Justice is a gift handed to humans by the gods
Only kings and rulers are ever truly just
Justice is too vague an idea to define at all
quiz.e: Glaucon argues justice is a compromise born of fear: give anyone a ring of invisibility and they would behave unjustly.

quiz.q: According to Socrates in the Republic, what is justice in a person?
o: Following the laws of the city as exactly as possible
Keeping a spotless reputation among fellow citizens
Reason ruling spirit and appetite, as in a healthy soul
Giving away your wealth to help the poor and sick
quiz.e: Plato describes justice as the right order of the soul's three parts, comparable to health in the body.

quiz.q: How does Herodotus' version of Gyges differ from Plato's?
o: Gyges refuses the throne and leaves Lydia
The tale is set in Egypt rather than Lydia
Gyges is revealed to be a god, not a man
There is no ring; the queen forces him to act
quiz.e: In Herodotus, the queen gives Gyges a choice of killing the king or dying, and no magic is involved.

quiz.q: What does the ring of Gyges ask you to consider?
o: Whether invisibility will ever be possible
Whether you act the same when no one is watching
Whether kings should be elected by citizens
Whether ancient myths are literally true
quiz.e: The thought experiment asks what you would do if consequences vanished, which shows whether your goodness is genuinely your own.

LESSONS.push: A shepherd finds a ring and soon becomes king. Would you do the same?

LESSONS.title: Diogenes: the philosopher who lived in a jar
LESSONS.hook: He slept in a storage jar, carried a lamp in daylight and reportedly told Alexander the Great to get out of his sunlight. Behind the stunts was a serious idea about what we really need.

sections.key: Diogenes turned an exile over defaced coins into a motto: challenge the false values society stamps onto things.
sections.b:
Diogenes was born around 412 BC in Sinope, a Greek trading city on the Black Sea. Almost everything we know comes from stories gathered centuries later, especially by the biographer Diogenes Laertius, so many details are legend.

By these accounts, Diogenes or his father, who was in charge of the city's money, was caught defacing the coinage, and Diogenes was exiled. He turned the incident into a motto: deface the currency. He meant challenging the false values society stamps onto things, such as wealth, status, fashion and good manners. Arriving in Athens, he set about testing which values were genuine and which were counterfeit.

sections.key: Diogenes lived with almost nothing to show how little a person needs, and the insult 'dog' gave the Cynics their name.
sections.b:
In Athens, Diogenes lived in a large ceramic storage jar near the marketplace. He owned a cloak, a staff and a bag, and little else. One story says he had a drinking cup until he saw a boy drinking from his cupped hands. He threw the cup away, declaring that a child had beaten him in simplicity.

He ate, slept and did everything else in public, scandalising respectable citizens. They called him kyon, meaning dog. He embraced the insult, and his followers became known as Cynics, from the Greek for doglike. Their aim was to live according to nature, free of needless wants.

sections.key: Diogenes' stunts were pointed lessons, and his reply to Alexander shows that a person who wants nothing cannot be bought.
sections.b:
Diogenes was a performer as much as a thinker. He reportedly walked the streets in daylight with a lit lamp, saying he was looking for a human being, meaning an honest one. When Plato defined a human as a featherless creature that walks on two legs, Diogenes supposedly plucked a chicken and announced, 'Here is Plato's human.'

In the most famous tale, Alexander the Great found him lying in the sun in Corinth and asked if he could do anything for him. 'Yes,' said Diogenes, 'stand out of my sunlight.' Alexander reportedly said that if he were not Alexander, he would wish to be Diogenes. Historians cannot confirm the meeting. Its point still strikes: someone who wants nothing cannot be bribed, flattered or threatened.

sections.key: Diogenes called himself a citizen of the world, an idea the Stoics later developed.
sections.b:
Asked where he came from, Diogenes reportedly said he was a kosmopolites, a citizen of the world, the origin of our word cosmopolitan. In ancient Greece this was radical: identity was bound to one's city, and exile was among the worst punishments. If what matters is living well according to nature, Diogenes implied, the borders and customs of any one city are secondary.

The idea travelled. Crates of Thebes, his most important follower, gave away a fortune to live as a Cynic. He married Hipparchia, a wealthy woman who chose that life and became one of the few women philosophers of ancient Greece whose name survives. Crates taught Zeno, founder of the Stoics, who developed the idea into all humans belonging to one community of reason.

sections.key: Diogenes asks which of our wants are real needs and which are only what society tells us to want.
sections.b:
Diogenes died in Corinth, traditionally in 323 BC, the same year as Alexander, though the dates are uncertain. The Cynics were street philosophers with no building or fixed curriculum. Their legacy was two ideas: virtue is enough for happiness, and most social conventions are optional.

Few people would want to live as he did, but his challenge holds up. How many of our wants are real needs, and how many are what society tells us to want? Modern minimalism and the urge to declutter echo him. A simple test: of any possession or ambition, ask whether losing it would leave you truly worse off, or only less admired.

quiz.q: What did Diogenes mean by his motto 'deface the currency'?
o: He wanted to abolish money entirely
He wanted to design better coins
He wanted to challenge society's false values
He was confessing to a crime in public
quiz.e: The motto came from a coin scandal, but Diogenes used it to expose counterfeit values such as status and wealth.

quiz.q: Why did Diogenes live with almost nothing?
o: He had lost his fortune in exile
To show how little a person really needs
He had taken a religious vow of silence
The Athenians had banned him from owning property
quiz.e: He deliberately lived simply, free of needless wants, to prove that a person needs very little.

quiz.q: What does Diogenes' reply to Alexander, 'stand out of my sunlight', illustrate?
o: Someone who wants nothing cannot be bought
Kings should be honoured above all other people
Sunlight is a gift that comes from the gods
Philosophers should serve their rulers loyally
quiz.e: Because Diogenes wanted nothing from Alexander, even the most powerful man in the world had nothing to offer him.

quiz.q: What did Diogenes imply by calling himself a 'citizen of the world'?
o: He had visited every single city in Greece
Living well matters more than city borders
He rejected all friendship and family ties
Only Athenians were truly civilised citizens
quiz.e: If the aim is living well according to nature, the laws and borders of any one city are secondary.

quiz.q: Which question reflects the test inspired by Diogenes?
o: How can I make this possession last for many years?
How does my version of this compare with what others own?
What will this ambition or possession be worth in ten years?
Would losing this really leave me worse off, or only less admired?
quiz.e: The test separates real needs from wants that society has taught us to chase.

LESSONS.push: He lived in a jar and told the world's most powerful man to move. Why?

LESSONS.title: The drowning child: Peter Singer’s challenge
LESSONS.hook: You would ruin your shoes to save a child drowning in front of you. An Australian philosopher asked why distance should make any difference, and the question changed how millions think about giving.

sections.key: Singer's principle: if we can prevent something very bad without sacrificing anything of comparable moral importance, we ought to.
sections.b:
Imagine you are walking past a shallow pond and see a child drowning. You could wade in, but you would ruin your clothes. Almost everyone agrees you must save the child. Peter Singer, a philosopher born in Melbourne in 1946, used this scene in his 1972 essay Famine, Affluence, and Morality. The cost there was muddy clothes; later retellings added expensive shoes.

He wrote it during the 1971 crisis in East Pakistan, now Bangladesh, where war, a devastating cyclone and mass displacement left millions of refugees facing hunger and disease. Aid from rich nations fell far short. His principle: if we can prevent something very bad without sacrificing anything of comparable moral importance, we ought to do it.

sections.key: Singer argues that neither distance nor the inaction of others reduces our duty to help.
sections.b:
The argument's power lies in the next step. If you must ruin your clothes to save the child in the pond, why not spend the same amount to save a child dying of a preventable disease far away? Singer argued that distance in itself has no moral weight. A child's life is not worth less because it is further from you. Nearness makes suffering more vivid, not more important.

Another objection is that millions of people could help, so the burden cannot fall on me. Singer imagined several adults standing around the pond, all ignoring the child. That does not make it acceptable for you to walk past too. Others' failure does not cancel your duty, so giving is an obligation, not just generosity.

sections.key: Taken strictly, Singer's principle asks a great deal, so he offered weaker versions and realistic guidelines.
sections.b:
Followed to its conclusion, Singer's principle is extremely demanding. If you should give whenever it costs you nothing of comparable importance, you should keep giving until giving more would harm you or your dependants as much as it helps others.

Singer accepted this but also offered a weaker version: we should at least prevent bad outcomes when the cost to us is genuinely insignificant, such as a new jacket we do not need. In later books, including The Life You Can Save in 2009, he suggested more modest guidelines based on income. A realistic standard that most people actually meet, he argued, does more good than a perfect one they ignore.

sections.key: Effective altruism asks us to use evidence to find where giving does the most good.
sections.b:
Singer's ideas helped shape the effective altruism movement, which emerged in the late 2000s. Its central claim is that if we give, we should use evidence to find where our money or time does the most good.

In 2009, the Oxford philosophers Toby Ord and William MacAskill helped found Giving What We Can, whose members pledge to give at least 10 per cent of their income to highly effective charities. Charity evaluators compare causes such as malaria prevention and deworming by estimating their cost per life improved. The movement has drawn both admiration and controversy, especially after the 2022 collapse of the crypto exchange FTX, whose founder had been a prominent supporter.

sections.key: Many philosophers accept part of Singer's argument but reject its most demanding form.
sections.b:
Critics have pushed back in several ways. Following the English philosopher Bernard Williams, some argue that a morality demanding constant sacrifice leaves no room for the personal projects, friendships and commitments that give life meaning.

Others say the pond is too simple: a single rescue is certain and immediate, while aid to distant countries is uncertain, can be misdirected, and does not tackle the political causes of poverty. Still others defend special duties to family and community. Yet even many critics concede Singer's basic point that wealthy people can do a great deal of good at little cost to themselves. More than fifty years on, the shallow pond remains a test many readers find hard to walk past.

quiz.q: What is the core of Singer's principle?
o: Charity is admirable but entirely optional
We should prevent great harm if the cost is minor
Only governments have any duty to help others
We should give away absolutely everything we own
quiz.e: The pond case shows we accept this principle when the child is near, so Singer asks why it should change with distance.

quiz.q: What is Singer's view of physical distance?
o: Distance makes our duty stronger
Distance in itself has no moral weight
We owe nothing to people outside our country
Distance matters for adults but not for children
quiz.e: A child's life is not worth less because the child is far away, even though nearby suffering feels more vivid.

quiz.q: Why did Singer suggest modest guidelines based on income?
o: He thought charity should be avoided altogether
He wanted only the very richest people to give
A realistic standard is more likely to be followed
He decided the pond example was misleading
quiz.e: Singer accepted that his strict principle is very demanding, so he proposed guidelines most people could realistically follow.

quiz.q: What is the core idea of effective altruism?
o: Giving only to causes close to your own community
Giving only through religious organisations
Delaying all giving until you are quite wealthy
Using evidence to find where giving helps most
quiz.e: Effective altruism asks people to compare causes carefully so their money or time helps as many people as possible.

quiz.q: What is one criticism of Singer's demanding view of giving?
o: It leaves no room for personal commitments
Wealthy people can do very little good by giving
Distant suffering is not real suffering at all
The pond example is far too complicated to follow
quiz.e: Critics such as Bernard Williams argue a morality that demands constant sacrifice crowds out friendships and personal projects.

LESSONS.push: You would ruin your shoes to save a child. An Australian asked why distance matters.

LESSONS.title: The experience machine: would you plug in?
LESSONS.hook: Imagine a machine that could give you any life you wanted, every moment indistinguishable from reality. Most people say they would refuse, and that refusal tells us something surprising about happiness.

sections.key: Robert Nozick imagined a machine that could give you any experiences you wanted, indistinguishable from real life.
sections.b:
In 1974, the American philosopher Robert Nozick described a thought experiment in his book Anarchy, State, and Utopia. Suppose brilliant neuroscientists could build a machine that stimulates your brain so you would think and feel you were writing a great novel, making a friend or reading an interesting book. All the while you would actually be floating in a tank with electrodes attached to your head.

You could choose your experiences from a vast library, and you would not know you were plugged in. Every moment would feel completely real. Nozick even allowed for occasional breaks to choose the next stretch. Then he asked: should you plug in for life?

sections.key: Most people refuse the machine, which suggests we value more than pleasant experience and challenges hedonism.
sections.b:
Many people, when first asked, say they would not plug in, even though the machine promises delight, achievement and love. That reaction matters because of Nozick's target: hedonism, the view that pleasant experience is the only thing good in itself. The 18th-century English philosopher Jeremy Bentham built his utilitarianism on the idea that pleasure and pain are all that ultimately matter.

If hedonism were true, the machine would be an easy choice, since it can deliver better feelings than real life ever could. Hesitation suggests we value something beyond our own experiences. If you feel a real but imperfect life beats a perfect simulated one, you are not a pure hedonist. It became one of the most discussed thought experiments of the 20th century.

sections.key: Nozick gave three reasons the machine falls short: we want to do things, to be a certain kind of person, and to touch reality.
sections.b:
Nozick suggested three things the machine cannot give us. First, we want to actually do certain things, not just have the experience of doing them. We want to really write the novel, not merely feel as if we had.

Second, we want to be a certain kind of person. In the tank you would be, as Nozick put it, an indeterminate blob, with no genuine courage, kindness or wit, because you never act. Third, the machine limits us to a man-made reality, a world no deeper than its programmers imagined. Plugging in, he wrote, is a kind of suicide. Together these points suggest a good life involves real contact with the world and real achievement, not just good feelings.

sections.key: Later philosophers asked whether our refusal reflects deep truth or only a bias towards the familiar.
sections.b:
Not everyone accepts Nozick's conclusion. Some philosophers argue that our reluctance to plug in might reflect a bias towards the familiar, sometimes called status quo bias, rather than a deep truth about value.

To test this, the philosopher Felipe De Brigard reversed the scenario in a 2010 study. He asked people to imagine discovering that they were already in an experience machine, and that their real life outside was very different. Would they unplug? Many said they would rather stay. If people prefer to keep the life they know, real or simulated, then the original intuition may be less about reality and more about fear of losing what is familiar. The debate continues.

sections.key: The machine separates feeling good from doing good, which helps you see what you believe makes a life go well.
sections.b:
When The Matrix appeared in 1999, many viewers recognised Nozick's idea. The character Cypher bites into a steak he knows is not real and decides he would rather return to the comfortable illusion. Today virtual reality, immersive games and feeds tuned to our preferences offer partial versions of the machine. None comes close, but each asks how much of your time you want to spend in experiences rather than reality.

The machine is useful because it separates what ordinary life bundles together: feeling good and doing good. Some philosophers say well-being includes real relationships, knowledge and authenticity; others defend hedonism. Either way, ask yourself: would you plug in? If not, what would you miss? Your answer summarises what you think life is for.

quiz.q: What does Nozick's experience machine do?
o: Records your memories to replay later
Lets you travel back through time
Makes chosen experiences feel real
Reads the thoughts of other people
quiz.e: The machine creates experiences indistinguishable from reality while you float in a tank, unaware you are plugged in.

quiz.q: What does widespread refusal to plug in suggest?
o: We value things beyond pleasant experience
Pleasure is the only thing that matters
People fear technology
Real life is always better than any simulation
quiz.e: If pleasant experience were all that mattered, plugging in would be an easy choice, so hesitation hints at other values.

quiz.q: Which is one of Nozick's reasons for refusing the machine?
o: The machine might break down and leave us stranded
We would miss real food, sleep and fresh air
We want to really do things, not merely feel we did
It would cost far more than most people could afford
quiz.e: Nozick argued we want to act, to be a certain kind of person and to be in contact with a reality deeper than a programmed one.

quiz.q: What did Felipe De Brigard's reversed scenario suggest?
o: Everyone always prefers real life to illusion
Nobody would ever use such a machine at all
Refusal may partly reflect liking the familiar
Pleasure turns out to be completely meaningless
quiz.e: Many people told they were already in a machine chose to stay, hinting that status quo bias may shape the original intuition.

quiz.q: Why is the experience machine a useful thought experiment?
o: It proves that hedonism is correct
It predicts which technology will succeed
It separates feeling good from doing good
It shows that virtual reality is harmful
quiz.e: By pulling apart feeling good and doing good, the machine forces you to say what you think makes a life go well.

LESSONS.push: A machine offers a perfect life you could never tell was fake. Most refuse. Why?

LESSONS.title: Zeno’s paradoxes: why Achilles can never win
LESSONS.hook: Around 2,500 years ago, a Greek thinker ‘proved’ that a runner can never catch a tortoise and that a flying arrow never moves. It took mathematicians two thousand years to say clearly what was wrong.

sections.key: Zeno devised his paradoxes to defend his teacher's claim that change and motion are illusions.
sections.b:
Zeno lived in Elea, a Greek colony in southern Italy, in the 5th century BC. He followed the philosopher Parmenides, who argued that reality is a single, unchanging whole and that motion and change are illusions of the senses. Most people found this absurd.

Zeno's response was clever. Rather than prove Parmenides directly, he showed that the ordinary belief in motion leads to absurdities of its own. He reportedly wrote a book of around forty such arguments, but it has not survived. We know his most famous paradoxes mainly through Aristotle, who described them in his Physics in order to refute them. Plato's dialogue Parmenides depicts Zeno visiting Athens with his teacher.

sections.key: Zeno argued that dividing a journey into endless stages makes catching a tortoise, or even starting to walk, seem impossible.
sections.b:
Achilles, the swiftest hero of Greek legend, races a tortoise given a head start. When Achilles reaches where the tortoise began, it has crept ahead a little. When he reaches that point, it has moved again, by less. This continues forever, so Zeno concluded Achilles can never catch it. Real runners overtake slower ones all the time. The challenge is to explain exactly where the reasoning goes wrong.

The dichotomy is stranger still. To reach a door, you must first walk halfway, before that a quarter, before that an eighth, without end. With no first step, it seems you can never start. A later story says Diogenes answered by simply walking across the room, which shows motion happens but not why the argument fails.

sections.key: Zeno argued that an arrow is at rest at every instant, so it seems it can never move.
sections.b:
The arrow paradox works differently. Picture an arrow in flight. At any single instant, it occupies a space exactly equal to its own length. In that instant it is not moving, because an instant has no duration in which movement could happen.

But the whole flight is made up of instants. If the arrow is at rest in every one of them, when does it actually move? Zeno concluded that motion is impossible. The paradox puzzled thinkers for centuries because it seems to attack the very idea of something moving at a particular moment. Aristotle replied that time is not made of indivisible instants, just as a line is not made of points laid end to end.

sections.key: Infinitely many shrinking steps can add up to a finite distance, covered in a finite time.
sections.b:
Much of the modern answer lies in mathematics. Add a half, a quarter, an eighth, a sixteenth and so on forever, and the total never exceeds one. It gets closer and closer to one, and mathematicians say the infinite sum equals exactly one.

So infinitely many steps can add up to a finite distance. If each step takes proportionally less time, they can be completed in a finite time, and Achilles catches the tortoise at a precise, calculable point. Ancient mathematicians glimpsed this idea, but the rigorous theory of limits that makes it precise was developed in the 19th century by mathematicians including Augustin-Louis Cauchy and Karl Weierstrass. Calculus also defines speed at an instant as a limit.

sections.key: Zeno shows that when a valid-looking argument reaches an absurd conclusion, a hidden assumption deserves a closer look.
sections.b:
Most mathematicians regard the paradoxes as resolved. Some philosophers are less sure. The mathematics shows the infinite sum has a finite value, but critics ask how anyone can complete an infinite sequence of distinct tasks one after another. Thought experiments about supertasks ask whether a lamp switched on and off infinitely many times in two minutes is on or off at the end. Physics adds a twist: it is an open question whether space and time are infinitely divisible.

Zeno did not change anyone's mind about whether things move. He showed that our ideas about space, time and infinity were less clear than we thought. Bertrand Russell praised his arguments as immeasurably subtle and profound.

quiz.q: Why did Zeno create his paradoxes?
o: To prove that the gods control every motion
To prepare an entry for a famous running race
To defend his teacher's denial of motion
To invent a new kind of mathematics for traders
quiz.e: Zeno aimed to show that belief in motion leads to absurdities, supporting his teacher's claim that reality is unchanging.

quiz.q: In the Achilles paradox, why can Achilles supposedly never catch the tortoise?
o: Each time he arrives, it has moved ahead
The tortoise is secretly faster than he is
Achilles tires before he reaches the finish
The track is infinitely long in total
quiz.e: Zeno splits the race into endless catching-up stages, each leaving the tortoise slightly ahead.

quiz.q: What is the arrow paradox's central claim?
o: Arrows always miss their intended target
Arrows travel faster than the speed of sound
At every instant the arrow is at rest
An arrow can be in two places at once
quiz.e: An instant has no duration for movement, so an arrow made of resting instants seems unable to move at all.

quiz.q: What does the sum of a half, a quarter, an eighth and so on forever equal?
o: Infinity
One half
Zero
One
quiz.e: The series converges to exactly one, so infinitely many shrinking steps can add up to a finite distance.

quiz.q: What lesson does Zeno offer for good thinking?
o: Absurd conclusions should simply be accepted as true
Arguments that seem valid should always be ignored
Reasoning about infinity should never be trusted
Check the assumptions behind an absurd conclusion
quiz.e: Finding the flaw in Zeno's reasoning took centuries and taught us a great deal about infinity and limits.

LESSONS.push: A runner can never catch a tortoise, or so a Greek thinker 'proved'. Where's the flaw?

LESSONS.title: Pascal’s wager: betting on God
LESSONS.hook: A brilliant 17th-century mathematician argued that believing in God is simply the smart bet. His reasoning helped invent decision theory, and its flaws are as instructive as its strengths.

sections.key: Pascal's wager comes from notes for an unfinished book by a mathematical genius who underwent a profound religious conversion.
sections.b:
Blaise Pascal was born in France in 1623. As a teenager he wrote a notable work on conic sections, and at around nineteen he began building one of the first mechanical calculators to help his father with tax accounts. In 1654 he exchanged letters with Pierre de Fermat about dividing the stakes in an unfinished game of chance, helping lay the foundations of probability theory. That year, on 23 November, he had an intense religious experience, which he recorded on a paper he kept sewn into his coat.

He planned a great defence of Christianity, but died in 1662 aged 39, leaving fragments. Published in 1670 as the Pensées, they include the wager.

sections.key: Pascal argued that we cannot avoid the choice, and that an infinite reward outweighs any finite cost, however small the chance.
sections.b:
Pascal did not claim to prove that God exists; he thought reason alone could not settle it. He asked instead: given that we cannot be certain, what is the rational way to live? We cannot sit on the fence, he said, because living as though God does not exist is itself a bet.

He then weighed the outcomes. Bet on God and God exists: eternal happiness, an infinite reward. Bet on God and God does not exist: you lose little, perhaps some worldly pleasures. Bet against God and God exists: you lose the infinite reward. Bet against and God does not exist: you gain only a finite amount. So any chance at all makes belief the rational bet. This is an early use of expected value: weighing each outcome by both its size and its probability.

sections.key: Pascal admitted that belief cannot be switched on at will, and suggested acting as believers do.
sections.b:
An obvious objection is that you cannot choose to believe something just because it would be useful. Pascal anticipated this. He suggested that a person who wanted to believe but could not should begin by acting as believers do: attending Mass, taking holy water and following religious practice. Over time, he thought, habit would shape the heart and belief would follow.

Critics find this troubling, since it seems to cultivate belief through habit rather than evidence. Defenders reply that Pascal was being psychologically realistic. Many of our deepest attitudes, from confidence to kindness, grow from repeated action rather than argument alone.

sections.key: The strongest criticism is that the wager does not say which god to bet on, and that huge payoffs can justify almost anything.
sections.b:
The most famous objection is that Pascal framed the choice as a simple pair: the Christian God or no god. But there are many religions with different demands, and some imagined gods might punish exactly the beliefs that others reward. Once all these possibilities are included, the wager no longer points clearly in one direction.

Other critics question whether a god would reward belief adopted as a calculated bet, and whether infinite values can be handled sensibly in such calculations. A related puzzle, Pascal's mugging, has a stranger demanding money by promising an astronomically large reward. Tiny probabilities multiplied by huge payoffs can justify almost anything.

sections.key: Whatever its flaws, the wager pioneered a way of thinking about decisions under uncertainty.
sections.b:
Few philosophers today think the wager settles whether one should believe in God. But its influence reaches far beyond religion. The philosopher of science Ian Hacking argued it was one of the earliest examples of decision theory, the study of how to choose rationally when outcomes are uncertain.

Its structure of listing options, outcomes and probabilities, then weighing them, is now used in fields from insurance and medicine to public policy and climate planning. Debates about rare but catastrophic risks often echo Pascal's reasoning. When the stakes are high and the facts uncertain, how we frame a decision can matter as much as the evidence.

quiz.q: What question was Pascal's wager designed to answer?
o: Whether God's existence can be proven by logic
Which of the world's religions is the oldest
How to choose rationally without certainty
Whether science and faith are in conflict
quiz.e: Pascal believed reason could not settle the question, so he asked how to choose wisely under uncertainty.

quiz.q: What is the key reason Pascal gives for betting on God?
o: Most people already believe in God
An infinite reward outweighs any finite cost
The Church commands everyone to believe
Reason has proven that God exists
quiz.e: With an infinite payoff on one side and only finite pleasures on the other, belief seems the rational bet.

quiz.q: How did Pascal suggest someone who cannot believe should proceed?
o: Give up the attempt altogether
Read more about science and nature
Debate priests until he is convinced
Act as believers do and let belief follow
quiz.e: He recommended religious practice, trusting that habit would gradually shape belief.

quiz.q: What is the 'many gods' objection?
o: It does not say which of many gods to bet on
There are too many churches to choose from
Gods are not interested in human belief
Pascal himself believed in several gods
quiz.e: Once all possible religions and gods are included, the wager no longer points clearly to one choice.

quiz.q: Why does the wager matter beyond religion?
o: It proved that probability theory is wrong
It is an early example of decision theory
It showed that all gambling is rational
It settled the old debate about belief
quiz.e: Pascal's method of weighing outcomes by size and likelihood is now used in insurance, medicine and public policy.

LESSONS.push: A famous mathematician said believing in God is simply the smart bet. Is it?

LESSONS.title: What is knowledge? The three-page paper that broke a definition
LESSONS.hook: For a long time, a neat definition of knowledge seemed good enough. Then, in 1963, a little-known philosopher published three pages that sent the field scrambling.

sections.key: Knowledge was long defined as justified true belief, because a lucky guess can be true without being knowledge.
sections.b:
Suppose you believe it will rain tomorrow, and it does. Did you know? If you checked a reliable forecast, perhaps yes. If you had a hunch, you were only lucky. Epistemology, from the Greek word for knowledge, studies questions like this. Knowledge cannot be mere true belief, because a lucky guess can be true.

Ideas reaching back to Plato's Theaetetus suggested an answer, which many 20th-century philosophers settled on: justified true belief. To know something, you must believe it, it must be true, and you must have good reasons or evidence. The forecast reader has justification; the hunch follower does not. For a long time this was treated as a neat standard definition.

sections.key: Edmund Gettier showed in a three-page paper that a belief can be justified and true yet still not be knowledge.
sections.b:
In 1963, Edmund Gettier, a young philosopher at Wayne State University in Detroit, published a paper in the journal Analysis titled Is Justified True Belief Knowledge? It ran to about three pages, and it is now one of the most widely cited articles in modern philosophy. Stories say he wrote it partly under pressure to publish, and he published little else.

In his first case, Smith has strong evidence that Jones will get a job, and has counted ten coins in Jones's pocket. He concludes that the successful applicant has ten coins. But Smith gets the job himself, and also has ten coins. His belief is true and justified, yet he did not know. He was right by coincidence.

sections.key: Similar examples appeared long before Gettier, in India and in Bertrand Russell's writing.
sections.b:
Gettier was not the first to notice the problem. In the 8th century, the Indian Buddhist philosopher Dharmottara described a traveller who sees a shimmering mirage, believes there is water ahead, and finds water hidden under a rock at that very spot.

In 1948, Bertrand Russell described someone who looks at a stopped clock that happens to show the right time. They form a justified true belief about the time, but do not really know it. Roderick Chisholm later offered a person who sees what looks like a sheep in a field. It is really a dog, but a genuine sheep happens to be out of sight elsewhere in the field. In each case, luck breaks the link between justification and truth.

sections.key: Philosophers proposed many repairs, but each seemed to meet new counterexamples.
sections.b:
Gettier's paper set off decades of attempts to fix the definition. One proposal added a fourth condition: the belief must not be reasoned from anything false. Smith's reasoning depended on the false belief that Jones would get the job. But critics found cases without obvious false steps, such as someone who looks at the one real barn in a district full of convincing fake barn fronts.

The causal theory said the fact must cause the belief in the right way. Reliabilism said knowledge comes from reliable belief-forming processes. Each approach handled some cases and stumbled on others. In 1994, Linda Zagzebski argued that as long as justification can fall short of guaranteeing truth, a clever enough counterexample can always be built.

sections.key: There is still no agreed definition of knowledge, and the lesson is that being right and knowing why are different.
sections.b:
Today there is no universally accepted definition of knowledge. Timothy Williamson at Oxford argues that knowledge cannot be broken into simpler parts and should be treated as a basic concept in its own right. Others keep refining definitions. Experimental philosophers have tested Gettier cases on people from different cultures and found that many share the intuition that these lucky believers lack knowledge, though how widely is still debated.

The puzzle has practical echoes. In science, journalism and everyday life we often reach correct conclusions for the wrong reasons. Being right and knowing why are not the same thing.

quiz.q: Why is true belief alone not enough for knowledge?
o: Beliefs can never be true in the first place
A lucky guess can be true without being knowledge
Only trained scientists can ever have knowledge
Knowledge must always be written down first
quiz.e: A hunch that happens to be correct is a true belief, but most people would not call it knowledge.

quiz.q: What did Gettier's 1963 paper show?
o: Knowledge is impossible for any human mind
Plato's account of knowledge was entirely right
Only scientific methods can produce knowledge
A justified true belief may not be knowledge
quiz.e: Gettier described cases that are true and justified but only by luck, so the classic definition was incomplete.

quiz.q: Why does the person in Russell's stopped-clock example not know the time?
o: They cannot read the clock face properly
The clock is running slightly too fast
The clock is stopped but happens to be right
They are dreaming about the time
quiz.e: Their belief is true and justified, but only by coincidence, because the clock is not working.

quiz.q: What did Linda Zagzebski argue about attempts to fix the definition?
o: They have all finally succeeded in the end
Justification turns out to be unnecessary
Knowledge should be settled by majority vote
Clever new counterexamples can always be built
quiz.e: Any definition that allows a gap between justification and truth leaves room for luck, and so for new Gettier cases.

quiz.q: What practical lesson does Gettier's puzzle offer?
o: Being right differs from knowing why
Evidence matters less than confidence
Experts are always right about the facts
A guess is as good as real knowledge
quiz.e: We often reach correct conclusions for the wrong reasons, so being right is not the same as knowing.

LESSONS.push: You can be right, have good reasons, and still not know. How is that possible?

LESSONS.title: Machiavelli: the man behind ‘The Prince’
LESSONS.hook: His name became a byword for cunning and ruthlessness. But the real Niccolò Machiavelli was a tortured civil servant, a lover of republics and perhaps the first modern political scientist.

sections.key: Machiavelli spent fourteen years as a senior official of the Florentine Republic before being dismissed and tortured when the Medici returned.
sections.b:
Niccolò Machiavelli was born in Florence in 1469. In 1498, four years after the Medici were driven out, he became a senior official of the new Florentine Republic, serving as secretary of its Second Chancery. For fourteen years he handled diplomacy and military affairs, visiting the courts of the French king, the pope and other rulers, and watching how power was gained and lost. He also organised a citizen militia, believing Florence should not rely on hired mercenaries.

In 1512, Spanish troops helped restore the Medici, and he lost his post. Early in 1513 his name appeared on a list of plotters and he was arrested. He endured the strappado, hoisting by the wrists tied behind the back, reportedly without confessing. A general amnesty freed him weeks later.

sections.key: Machiavelli wrote The Prince in 1513 in enforced retirement, hoping to win back favour.
sections.b:
Machiavelli retired, impoverished, to his small farm outside Florence. In a famous letter to his friend Francesco Vettori in December 1513, he described his days. He snared birds, chatted with locals and played cards at the inn.

But in the evening he went to his study, took off his muddy clothes and put on formal robes. Then, as he put it, he entered the ancient courts of ancient men and asked them the reasons for their actions. From those conversations with history he composed a little work on principalities. That work was The Prince, written hoping to win back favour and employment. It was dedicated to a member of the Medici family, but it was not published until 1532, five years after his death in 1527.

sections.key: The Prince describes politics as it is, arguing that a ruler must sometimes act against conventional morality but must avoid being hated.
sections.b:
The Prince shocked readers because it described politics as it is, not as it ought to be. Earlier advice books urged rulers to be generous, merciful and honest. Machiavelli argued that a ruler who always tried to be good would be ruined among so many who are not.

It is best to be both loved and feared, he wrote, but if one must choose, it is safer to be feared. Crucially, a ruler must avoid being hated, which usually means leaving subjects' property and families alone. A ruler should be both a fox, to recognise traps, and a lion, to frighten wolves.

His model was Cesare Borgia, who had his harsh deputy Remirro de Orco killed and displayed in Cesena. Machiavelli's point: cruelty well used is applied once, for security, and then stops.

sections.key: Machiavelli believed skill and boldness could partly master the power of luck.
sections.b:
Two words run through Machiavelli's writing: fortuna and virtù. Fortuna is luck or circumstance, the unpredictable force that can raise or ruin anyone. Virtù does not mean moral virtue. It means skill, energy and boldness, the capacity to seize opportunities and adapt.

Machiavelli compared fortune to a violent river that floods the plains. When it rages, nothing can stop it, but in calm times people can build dykes and embankments to control it. He guessed that fortune governs about half of our actions and leaves the other half to us. A wise ruler prepares in good times and adapts quickly when circumstances change, rather than clinging to one way of acting.

sections.key: Machiavelli's longer work shows that he actually preferred republics to princes.
sections.b:
The common image of Machiavelli as a cheerleader for tyranny is incomplete. His longer book, the Discourses on Livy, praises the Roman Republic and argues that free republics, where citizens share power and laws restrain ambition, are generally more stable and successful than principalities.

Even the phrase 'the ends justify the means' does not appear in his writings, although he did argue that rulers are judged by results. In 1559 the Catholic Church placed his works on its Index of Prohibited Books, and Machiavellian came to mean scheming. Yet many modern scholars see him as a founder of political science, one of the first to study power by observing what actually happens.

quiz.q: What did Machiavelli's years as a Florentine official give him?
o: A fortune from his dealings with the Medici
An inside view of how power is won and lost
A reputation as a successful army general
A place in the royal court of France
quiz.e: Fourteen years of diplomacy and military affairs let him watch closely how rulers won and lost power.

quiz.q: Why did Machiavelli write The Prince?
o: He wanted to overthrow the Medici family
He was commissioned by the pope himself
He hoped to win back favour and employment
He wanted to promote a free republic
quiz.e: After losing his post and being tortured, he wrote a short book from history's lessons hoping to regain employment.

quiz.q: What did Machiavelli say about being feared or loved?
o: If you must choose, fear is safer, but avoid hatred
It is always better to be loved than to be feared
Fear works best when the ruler is also hated
A ruler should avoid both fear and love entirely
quiz.e: Fear is more reliable than love, but hatred is dangerous, which a ruler avoids by respecting subjects' property and families.

quiz.q: In Machiavelli's writing, what does 'virtù' mean?
o: Moral goodness in a ruler's public life
Religious faith and devotion to the Church
Wealth and high status at a royal court
Skill and boldness in seizing opportunities
quiz.e: Virtù is the capacity to seize opportunities and adapt, which lets a person partly master fortune.

quiz.q: What does the Discourses on Livy reveal about Machiavelli?
o: He wanted all of Italy ruled by the pope
He preferred free republics, such as Rome, to princes
He rejected every form of government as corrupt
He hoped to be made a prince himself one day
quiz.e: In the Discourses he praises the Roman Republic and argues free republics are generally more stable and successful.

LESSONS.push: His name means cunning, yet he loved republics and was tortured for it. Who was he?

LESSONS.title: Nietzsche: the most misunderstood philosopher
LESSONS.hook: He is quoted on gym walls and was claimed by the Nazis, yet he despised antisemites and warned against blind nationalism. The real Friedrich Nietzsche is stranger and more interesting than his legend.

sections.key: Nietzsche was a brilliant young scholar who broke with Wagner over nationalism and antisemitism.
sections.b:
Friedrich Nietzsche was born in 1844 in Röcken, in Prussia, the son of a Lutheran pastor who died when he was four. In 1869, at just twenty-four, he became professor of classical philology at the University of Basel, before completing the usual doctoral requirements. His first book, The Birth of Tragedy, appeared in 1872. Severe headaches, eye problems and stomach troubles dogged him, and in 1879 he resigned and lived modestly in boarding houses across Europe, writing furiously.

As a young man he admired the composer Richard Wagner, but grew disillusioned with his German nationalism, his Christian themes in Parsifal and the surrounding antisemitism. Nietzsche repeatedly mocked nationalism and expressed contempt for antisemites.

sections.key: After Nietzsche's collapse his sister shaped his image, and later scholars worked to separate him from Nazi propaganda.
sections.b:
In January 1889, in Turin, Nietzsche suffered a sudden mental collapse. A famous story says it followed his embracing a horse being whipped, though that may be embellished. He never recovered, and died in Weimar in 1900, cared for by his mother and then his sister Elisabeth.

Elisabeth, whose husband Bernhard Förster was an antisemitic agitator, controlled his manuscripts. She edited his letters selectively and assembled The Will to Power from his notes to suit her own views. She later welcomed the Nazis, who made selective use of phrases like the Übermensch while ignoring his contempt for antisemitism and nationalism. After the war, scholars such as Walter Kaufmann restored his reputation. Nietzsche's writing does contain harsh and elitist passages, but most scholars agree he was no proto-Nazi.

sections.key: Nietzsche asked whether you could bear to live your exact life again, forever, as a test of how fully you affirm it.
sections.b:
One of Nietzsche's most famous ideas appears in The Gay Science, published in 1882. He imagines a demon creeping into your loneliest loneliness and telling you that you must live your life again, exactly as it has been, every pain and joy in the same order, infinitely many times.

Would you curse the demon, he asks, or call it divine? Nietzsche used this as a test of how fully you affirm your life. Scholars disagree about whether he meant it as a literal theory of the universe or as a thought experiment. Most read it as the latter: a way of asking whether you are living in a way you would choose again and again.

sections.key: Nietzsche's ideal, amor fati, was to love life's suffering rather than wish it away.
sections.b:
Closely linked to eternal recurrence is amor fati, Latin for love of fate. Nietzsche wrote that his formula for greatness was wanting nothing to be different, not forwards, not backwards, not in all eternity, and not merely to bear what is necessary but to love it. This has much in common with Stoicism, though he criticised the Stoics on other points.

It also connects to his best-known line, from Twilight of the Idols in 1888: what does not kill me makes me stronger. Out of context it sounds like a motivational slogan. Nietzsche lived with chronic pain, and meant something more personal: suffering can be turned into a source of growth.

sections.key: Nietzsche's deepest concern was how to create meaning after traditional values lost their grip.
sections.b:
Nietzsche's statement that God is dead was not a triumphant boast but a warning. He feared that as religious belief faded in Europe, people would lose the foundation for their values and slide into nihilism, the sense that nothing matters.

His Übermensch was not a racial ideal but an image of a person who creates their own values and affirms life without outside guarantees. He also argued that there are no facts free of perspective, a view called perspectivism. His aphorisms, irony and exaggeration make him easy to quote and easy to misread. Reading him in full, rather than on a poster, reveals a restless, searching mind wrestling with problems that still feel modern.

quiz.q: Why did Nietzsche break with Richard Wagner?
o: Wagner refused to perform his music at Bayreuth
They quarrelled bitterly over money and credit
Wagner publicly insulted his mother and sister
He disliked Wagner's nationalism and antisemitism
quiz.e: Nietzsche became disillusioned with Wagner's German nationalism, Christian themes and the antisemitism in his circle.

quiz.q: Why is the Nazi image of Nietzsche misleading?
o: He mocked antisemites; his sister edited his notes
He openly supported the Nazis' political aims
He never wrote anything about power or politics
His books were never published until the 1930s
quiz.e: Elisabeth edited his work selectively and promoted a distorted image, while Nietzsche himself mocked nationalism and antisemites.

quiz.q: What does the idea of eternal recurrence ask?
o: Whether history repeats itself every few centuries
Whether souls are reborn as different animals
Whether you would happily relive your life forever
Whether time travel is physically possible
quiz.e: A demon announcing you must relive your life endlessly is a test of how fully you affirm the life you have.

quiz.q: What does 'amor fati' mean?
o: Fear of fate
Escape from fate
Change your fate
Love of fate
quiz.e: Amor fati is Nietzsche's ideal of embracing everything that happens, even suffering, rather than wishing it otherwise.

quiz.q: What was Nietzsche's 'God is dead' statement meant as?
o: A triumphant boast about the rise of atheism
A warning that losing faith could lead to nihilism
A call for governments to ban religion
A prediction that science would end suffering
quiz.e: Nietzsche feared that as faith faded, people would lose meaning, which is why he asked how to create it ourselves.

LESSONS.push: Quoted on gym walls, claimed by Nazis, yet he despised their ideas. What did he mean?

LESSONS.title: The paradox of the heap: where do boundaries go?
LESSONS.hook: One grain of sand is not a heap. Adding a single grain never turns a non-heap into a heap. So, it seems, there are no heaps at all. This ancient puzzle about vagueness still divides logicians today.

sections.key: Tiny, harmless steps can seem to prove an absurd conclusion about a vague word like heap.
sections.b:
One grain of sand is not a heap. Adding a single grain to something that is not a heap never makes it a heap. So two grains is not a heap, nor three, nor a million. Yet a million grains clearly is a heap. Each premise looks true and each step looks valid, but the conclusion is absurd.

This is the sorites paradox, named from soros, the Greek word for heap. It is credited to Eubulides of Miletus, a 4th-century BC philosopher also linked to the liar paradox. A matching version, the bald man, runs the other way: removing one hair never turns a man who is not bald into a bald one.

sections.key: The sorites paradox arises with almost any word that has borderline cases, so it challenges how logic handles ordinary language.
sections.b:
The sorites is not really about sand. It arises with any vague term: a word with borderline cases where it is unclear whether it applies. Tall, old, rich, red, child and crowd are all vague.

Someone 190 centimetres tall is clearly tall and someone 150 centimetres is not, but what about 175? There seems to be no single millimetre at which a person becomes tall. Yet if no small change can make a difference, the same reasoning concludes that nobody is tall. Most everyday words are vague, so this is no mere curiosity. It asks whether ordinary logic, built for sharp categories, can handle ordinary language.

sections.key: Epistemicism holds that vague words have sharp boundaries that we can never know.
sections.b:
The Stoic Chrysippus, a great logician of the ancient world, is reported to have advised a wise person to fall silent somewhere before the doubtful cases and decline to answer. Critics mocked this. But some modern scholars think he may have meant that a boundary exists and cannot be known.

That is close to epistemicism, defended by the British philosopher Timothy Williamson in his 1994 book Vagueness. It says there is a precise number of grains at which a pile becomes a heap. We cannot know it, because meaning is fixed by patterns of use too complex to survey. This keeps classical logic intact, but many find it unbelievable that one grain could make the difference.

sections.key: Other theories change how truth works, but they all struggle to say where borderline cases begin.
sections.b:
Supervaluationism, developed in a 1975 paper by the philosopher Kit Fine, imagines every acceptable way of making a vague word precise. A statement is true if it is true on every sharpening, false if false on every one, and neither otherwise.

Another approach uses degrees of truth, drawing on fuzzy logic introduced by the engineer Lotfi Zadeh in 1965. On this view, 'this pile is a heap' might be true to degree 0.7. Critics note that both theories face higher-order vagueness: where exactly do the borderline cases begin?

The American philosopher Peter Unger went further and accepted the paradox's conclusion, arguing that ordinary vague objects such as heaps do not strictly exist.

sections.key: When boundaries are blurred, societies draw arbitrary but useful lines, and clear thinking means knowing when to rely on them.
sections.b:
In practice we handle vagueness with bright lines. Childhood fades into adulthood gradually, yet laws set fixed ages for voting, driving and drinking. Nobody changes overnight on their eighteenth birthday, but a clear rule is fairer and easier to apply than case-by-case judgement. Speed limits, blood alcohol thresholds and pass marks work the same way.

The sorites also underlies slippery slope arguments, which claim that because no clear line separates a small step from an extreme outcome, we should not take the first step.
