Recognising the structure helps you judge when such arguments hold. Medical definitions, legal standards like reasonable care and debates about when life begins all lack sharp edges. Sometimes clear thinking means living with blurred boundaries.

quiz.q: What makes the heap argument a paradox?
o: The premises are obviously false from the start
It relies on a mistake in basic arithmetic
Each step seems valid, yet the result is absurd
Its conclusion is true but nobody can prove it
quiz.e: Plausible premises and apparently valid steps lead to a conclusion we know to be wrong, which is what makes it a paradox.

quiz.q: Why does the paradox matter beyond sand and hair?
o: It arises with any vague word, such as tall or old
It only affects words used in mathematics
It applies only to words naming physical objects
It shows that large collections cannot be counted
quiz.e: Most everyday words are vague, so the problem challenges how logic copes with ordinary language.

quiz.q: What does epistemicism claim about vague words?
o: They have no boundaries at all
Their boundaries shift with each speaker's mood
They are meaningless and should be avoided
They have sharp boundaries that we cannot know
quiz.e: Epistemicism keeps classical logic by saying the lines are real but hidden from us.

quiz.q: On the supervaluationist view, when is a vague statement true?
o: When it is true on most people's personal definitions of the word
When it is true on every acceptable way of making the word precise
When it is true to a degree of at least one half or higher
When it can be verified by measuring the object directly
quiz.e: A statement true on some sharpenings and false on others is treated as neither true nor false.

quiz.q: Why do laws set fixed ages for voting or driving, even though people mature gradually?
o: Everyone truly changes overnight at that age
Vague concepts cannot be regulated by law
A clear rule is fairer and easier to apply
Judges may never consider individual cases
quiz.e: Bright lines are arbitrary but practical ways of handling gradual change.

LESSONS.push: One grain is not a heap. Neither are two. So where do heaps come from?

LESSONS.title: Phineas Gage: the man with an iron rod through his head
LESSONS.hook: In 1848 a metre-long iron bar shot clean through a young man's skull, and he lived. What happened to his personality afterwards became one of the most retold, and most exaggerated, stories in psychology.

sections.key: In 1848 an explosion drove an iron rod through Phineas Gage's head, and he survived.
sections.b:
On 13 September 1848, Phineas Gage, a 25-year-old railway foreman near Cavendish, Vermont, was packing gunpowder into a drilled hole with a tamping iron. Something went wrong, possibly because the sand had not yet been added. The powder ignited and fired the rod upward like a spear. It was about 1.1 metres long, more than 3 centimetres thick and weighed around six kilograms. It entered under his left cheekbone, passed behind his left eye and burst out through the top of his skull.

Astonishingly, Gage was speaking within minutes and rode to town sitting upright in an ox cart. The physician John Martyn Harlow kept him alive through a dangerous infection, and by early 1849 Gage was walking about.

sections.key: Harlow's report suggested that the front of the brain helps govern personality, judgement and self control.
sections.b:
Before the accident, Harlow wrote, Gage had been a shrewd, energetic and well balanced worker, the most efficient foreman his employers had. Afterwards he was 'fitful, irreverent', impatient of advice and full of plans he abandoned as quickly as he made them. Friends said he was 'no longer Gage', and his employers would not take him back.

Harlow's report, published in full in 1868, became a landmark. It suggested that parts of the brain at the front of the head have something to do with personality, judgement and self control, not just with movement or the senses. For a young science of the brain, it was dramatic evidence.

sections.key: Later writers filled the gaps in a thin record with unsupported tales of a ruined man.
sections.b:
Here is where the story goes wrong. Harlow's notes were fairly brief, and Gage left no account of his own. Into that gap, later writers poured colour. In books and lectures Gage became a drunk, a brawler, a wife beater, a drifter who could never hold a job.

Almost none of this is supported by evidence. Gage was never married, and there is no good record of heavy drinking or violence. He did spend a short time showing himself and his iron to paying audiences. The exaggerations tended to grow whenever someone needed a vivid example of the frontal lobes going wrong.

sections.key: Gage drove a coach in Chile for about seven years, which suggests a substantial recovery.
sections.b:
The Australian psychologist Malcolm Macmillan spent decades tracking down every scrap of evidence about Gage. In the early 1850s Gage went to Chile, where for roughly seven years he drove a coach between Valparaíso and Santiago. That is a demanding job: handling a team of horses on rough mountain roads, keeping to a schedule and dealing with passengers.

Macmillan argued that Gage's changes were probably most severe in the first months, and that he then rebuilt a working life, perhaps helped by a job with clear routines. In 2009 two collectors identified the first known photograph of Gage, showing a well-dressed man proudly holding his iron.

sections.key: Gage shows how the frontal lobes shape behaviour, and how one thinly recorded case can be bent into a myth.
sections.b:
In poor health, Gage left Chile in 1859 to join his family in San Francisco. He began having epileptic seizures, very likely a late consequence of his injury, and died in May 1860, aged 36. His skull and tamping iron are now in Harvard's Warren Anatomical Museum. Most scans suggest the damage was concentrated in the left frontal lobe.

Later cases confirmed that this region helps us plan, hold back impulses and behave appropriately with others. The second lesson is quieter: a single dramatic case is easy to bend into whatever shape a writer needs. The real Gage changed for a time, then appears to have recovered far more than most retellings admit.

quiz.q: What was remarkable about Gage's accident?
o: He survived and was talking within minutes
He was unharmed as the rod missed his brain
He lost consciousness for several months
He was unable to speak for several weeks
quiz.e: Gage was conscious and talking soon after the injury, and he lived for another twelve years.

quiz.q: What did Harlow's report suggest about the front of the brain?
o: It is responsible only for vision and hearing
It controls only the movement of the legs
It plays no role in behaviour or thought
It helps govern personality and self control
quiz.e: The reported personality change was dramatic early evidence that the frontal lobes shape behaviour.

quiz.q: Why is much of the 'ruined Gage' story unreliable?
o: Harlow kept exhaustive daily notes that contradict the tales
The record was thin, so later writers added unsupported detail
Gage himself published a detailed denial of the stories
Gage's family confirmed every detail of the retellings
quiz.e: With little recorded, exaggerations grew whenever a vivid example of frontal lobe damage was wanted.

quiz.q: What does Gage's work as a coach driver in Chile suggest?
o: He never recovered any function at all
He lived the rest of his life in hospital
He recovered enough to hold a demanding job
He could not hold down any job for long
quiz.e: Handling horses on mountain roads and keeping to a schedule points to a substantial recovery.

quiz.q: What is the quieter lesson of Gage's story?
o: Brain injuries never change behaviour
Every retelling of a famous case is accurate
One thinly recorded case is easily bent into a myth
Science is best built on one dramatic example
quiz.e: Treat vivid single cases with caution, because retellings tend to bend them to fit the story.

LESSONS.push: A metre-long rod went through his skull. The story of what came next is mostly wrong.

LESSONS.title: Patient H.M.: the man who lived in the present
LESSONS.hook: After a brain operation in 1953, Henry Molaison could no longer form new long-term memories. For more than fifty years he met the scientists studying him as if for the first time, and he changed what we know about memory.

sections.key: Surgery that eased Henry Molaison's seizures left him unable to form new long-term memories.
sections.b:
Henry Molaison was born in 1926 in Connecticut. His childhood seizures became so frequent and severe that he could barely work. Some accounts link the epilepsy to a bicycle accident, though the cause was never certain. Drugs did not help enough.

In 1953, aged 27, he was referred to the neurosurgeon William Beecher Scoville, who removed parts of the medial temporal lobe on both sides of his brain. This included most of the hippocampus and the amygdala. His seizures eased, but he could no longer remember the staff he saw every day, and he would read the same magazine repeatedly with fresh interest. His intelligence, personality, language and much of his earlier life were intact. Scoville later warned other surgeons never to repeat the procedure on both sides.

sections.key: Henry's case showed that specific brain structures, such as the hippocampus, are crucial for forming new memories.
sections.b:
From 1955, the young psychologist Brenda Milner began testing Henry. In 1957 she and Scoville published a paper that overturned a common belief of the time: that memory was spread evenly across the brain, so no single area was essential.

Henry's case showed that the hippocampus and its neighbours were crucial for forming new long-term memories of facts and events. Yet they were not the store where old memories lived, because Henry could recall much of his childhood. To protect his privacy, he was known in hundreds of scientific papers only by his initials, H.M. Few people outside research knew his name until he died.

sections.key: Henry could learn new skills without remembering that he had practised them, so there is more than one kind of memory.
sections.b:
Milner's most famous experiment asked Henry to trace a star shape while seeing his hand and the paper only in a mirror, a task almost everyone finds awkward at first. Over three days of practice, Henry improved steadily, just like anyone else. But each day he insisted he had never done the task before.

The result was profound. It showed there is more than one kind of memory. Remembering facts and events, called declarative memory, depended on the structures Henry had lost. Learning skills and habits, called procedural memory, relied on other brain systems that still worked.

sections.key: Henry's working memory was intact, so he could converse, but information vanished once his attention moved on.
sections.b:
Henry could repeat a list of numbers or hold a thought for a short while, so long as he kept rehearsing it. His working memory was largely normal, and he could follow a conversation and be polite and witty. But once his attention shifted, the information was gone. The neuroscientist Suzanne Corkin, who studied him for over four decades, said he never learned to recognise her.

He understood in a general way that his memory was poor. He was often described as gentle, patient and fond of crossword puzzles, which drew on vocabulary he had learned before the operation. A few scraps stuck, such as the floor plan of his new home. He took part in research willingly, and many scientists have written of the ethical questions his case raises about consent.

sections.key: After his death in 2008, Henry's brain was sliced and digitised, and his case shaped modern ideas of memory.
sections.b:
Henry Molaison died in December 2008, aged 82. With consent arranged years earlier, his brain was preserved and scanned. In 2009 it was cut into 2,401 extremely thin slices at the University of California, San Diego, in a procedure streamed online. The slices were digitised so researchers anywhere could examine what had been removed and what remained.

Modern ideas about the types of memory, the role of the hippocampus, and how memories are consolidated all trace back to him. He never remembered the scientists who studied him, but generations of students now learn his name.

quiz.q: What was the main result of Henry's operation?
o: His memory improved dramatically after surgery
He lost all memories from before the surgery
His intelligence and language were severely damaged
Seizures eased, but he could not form new memories
quiz.e: The surgery removed structures needed to turn new experiences into lasting memories.

quiz.q: What belief did Henry's case overturn?
o: That the brain is divided into two separate hemispheres
That memory is spread evenly, with no one essential area
That epilepsy can never be treated by any surgery
That the hippocampus is mainly responsible for vision
quiz.e: Henry showed that the hippocampus and its neighbours are crucial for forming new memories.

quiz.q: What did the mirror drawing experiment show?
o: Henry was unable to learn any new task
Declarative memory is the only kind of memory
There is more than one kind of memory
Practice has no effect on how well skills develop
quiz.e: Procedural memory relied on brain systems Henry still had, unlike memory for facts and events.

quiz.q: Why could Henry hold a conversation despite his amnesia?
o: He had learned to write everything down
He remembered each person from earlier visits
His working memory was largely normal
His entire long-term memory was intact
quiz.e: Information held in working memory vanished once his attention shifted.

quiz.q: Why was Henry's brain sliced and digitised after his death?
o: So researchers could study it in detail worldwide
To prove the original operation had failed
Because the law required every brain to be sliced
To compare it with a healthy brain from his family
quiz.e: The digitised slices keep his case available for research on memory worldwide.

LESSONS.push: For fifty years he met his own researchers as strangers. What he taught us about memory.

LESSONS.title: Split brain: two minds in one head?
LESSONS.hook: When surgeons cut the bridge between the brain's two halves, patients seemed perfectly normal. Then clever experiments revealed that each half could know things the other did not.

sections.key: Surgeons cut the corpus callosum to stop severe seizures, and patients seemed surprisingly normal afterwards.
sections.b:
Your brain has two hemispheres, joined mainly by the corpus callosum, a band of roughly 200 million nerve fibres. Each hemisphere mainly handles the opposite side of the body: the left controls the right hand and receives the right side of what you see. In most people the left also does most of the work of producing speech.

Some epilepsy involves electrical storms that sweep across both hemispheres. In the 1940s and again in the 1960s, surgeons cut the corpus callosum in patients whose seizures could not be controlled otherwise. For many it helped, and the patients could talk, walk and joke as before. Early observers concluded the corpus callosum might do very little. Careful testing showed otherwise.

sections.key: Showing information to only one hemisphere revealed that each side could know things the other did not.
sections.b:
In the 1960s the neurobiologist Roger Sperry and his student Michael Gazzaniga, working at Caltech, designed a clever test. A patient stared at a dot on a screen while a word or picture flashed briefly to its left or right, too fast for the eyes to move.

An image on the right went only to the left hemisphere, and the patient could easily name it. An image on the left went only to the right hemisphere, and the patient typically said they had seen nothing. Yet if they reached behind a screen with the left hand, controlled by the right hemisphere, they could pick out the very object shown. One half knew; the half that did the talking did not.

sections.key: The hemispheres do differ, but the idea of 'left brained' and 'right brained' people is a myth.
sections.b:
The experiments suggested that the left hemisphere usually dominates language, while the right is often better at some spatial tasks, such as arranging blocks or recognising faces. Sperry shared the 1981 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for this work.

But the findings were stretched into a popular myth: that people are either logical 'left brained' types or creative 'right brained' types. There is no good evidence for this. A large brain imaging study published in 2013 found no sign that individuals have a stronger left or right side overall. In a healthy brain, almost every complex activity, including creativity and logic, draws on both hemispheres working together through the corpus callosum.

sections.key: The speaking left hemisphere confidently invents explanations, and ordinary people do much the same.
sections.b:
Gazzaniga showed a patient known as P.S. a chicken's claw to the left hemisphere and a snowy scene to the right. Asked to pick matching pictures, his right hand chose a chicken and his left hand chose a shovel. Asked why, his speaking left hemisphere, which had never seen the snow, did not hesitate: you need a shovel to clean out the chicken shed. The answer was fluent, confident and made up. He was not lying. He believed it.

Gazzaniga proposed that the left hemisphere houses an 'interpreter' that weaves our actions and feelings into a coherent story. Many studies show ordinary people also give confident reasons for choices influenced by things they never noticed. We rarely feel the difference between knowing and guessing.

sections.key: Whether a split-brain patient has one consciousness or two is still debated.
sections.b:
If each hemisphere can perceive, decide and act without the other knowing, is a split-brain patient one person or two? Some early reports described conflict between the hands, such as one doing up buttons while the other undid them, though such episodes seem rare and mostly occur soon after surgery.

In 2017 a Dutch-led team reported that two patients could respond accurately to images on either side using either hand. They argued that consciousness may stay unified even when perception is split. Others dispute that reading. Today the operation is performed far less often because better treatments exist, so researchers have fewer patients to learn from.

quiz.q: Why was the corpus callosum cut in some epilepsy patients?
o: To improve their memory and learning ability
To stop seizures spreading across the brain
To increase their creativity and lift mood
To lower the pressure inside the skull
quiz.e: Severing the link was meant to keep a seizure in one half from sweeping across the whole brain.

quiz.q: What happened when a word was flashed only to the right hemisphere?
o: They named the object at once and described it fully
They could not pick it out with either hand afterwards
They denied seeing it, yet the left hand picked it out
They named it aloud while pointing with the right hand
quiz.e: The right hemisphere knew the object but lacked the speech needed to say so.

quiz.q: What does brain imaging say about 'left brained' and 'right brained' people?
o: Most people favour the left side for everything
Creative people use only the right hemisphere
People show no overall preference for one side
Logical people use only the left hemisphere
quiz.e: Complex activities, including creativity and logic, use both hemispheres working together.

quiz.q: Why did P.S. say you need a shovel to clean out the chicken shed?
o: His speaking hemisphere made up a plausible reason
He remembered cleaning out a shed the day before
He was deliberately lying to mislead the researchers
He had clearly seen the snowy picture as well
quiz.e: The interpreter builds a confident story even without the facts, and ordinary people do this too.

quiz.q: Why can't researchers settle whether a split-brain patient has one mind or two?
o: The question was settled and is no longer debated
The surgery has become more common than ever
Patients refuse to take part in any research
The evidence is open to more than one reading
quiz.e: The 2017 findings suggest unified consciousness, but others dispute that interpretation.

LESSONS.push: Cut the bridge between the brain's halves, and one half knows what the other does not.

LESSONS.title: Learned helplessness, and the twist fifty years later
LESSONS.hook: A famous experiment seemed to show that animals could learn to give up. Half a century on, the scientist who made it famous admitted they had got it backwards.

sections.key: Dogs given shocks they could not control often failed to escape later, when escape was easy.
sections.b:
In 1967 Martin Seligman and Steven Maier at the University of Pennsylvania gave dogs mild but unpleasant shocks. Some could stop the shocks by pressing a panel with their heads. Others received exactly the same shocks but could do nothing. Later, all the dogs were put in a box where they could escape a shock simply by jumping a low barrier.

Most dogs that had controlled the earlier shocks, or had none, quickly learned to jump. Most of those that had faced inescapable shocks lay down and whimpered. The researchers called this learned helplessness: the dogs had apparently learned that nothing they did mattered. The key was not the pain but the lack of control. Such experiments would face far tougher ethical scrutiny today.

sections.key: Studies with people linked helplessness to depression and to how we explain setbacks.
sections.b:
Studies with people used milder discomforts such as noise or unsolvable puzzles. Those who faced noise they could not switch off were often slower to find the solution later. Seligman proposed that learned helplessness could help explain depression, in which people feel that nothing they do will make a difference.

But not everyone became helpless. In 1978 Seligman and colleagues revised the theory to focus on how people explain bad events. Those most at risk saw setbacks as permanent, pervasive and personal. Those who saw them as temporary, limited and partly due to circumstances bounced back more readily. This work fed into learned optimism, positive psychology and cognitive therapies that help people question their automatic explanations.

sections.key: In 2016 the original scientists concluded that passivity is the brain's default, and what animals learn is control.
sections.b:
Steven Maier, by then a neuroscientist, traced the brain circuits behind the original effect. In 2016 he and Seligman published a paper looking back at fifty years of work. They reported that the original theory had the mechanism backwards.

Passivity in the face of prolonged bad events is not learned. It is the brain's default response, driven by a deep brainstem region called the dorsal raphe nucleus. What can be learned is control. When an animal discovers that its actions work, a region of the prefrontal cortex detects this and switches off the default passivity. In other words, it is not helplessness we learn, but hope.

sections.key: Experiences of control may protect against later stress, though most evidence comes from animals.
sections.b:
Maier's experiments in rats found that animals that first experienced controllable stress were later more resilient, even when facing stress they could not control. The experience of mastery seemed to leave a lasting protective effect, at least in those studies.

The findings are mainly from animals, so care is needed in applying them to people. Still, they fit human research suggesting that a sense of agency matters for wellbeing. They suggest the best defence against hopelessness may not be avoiding hardship altogether, but building genuine experiences of effort paying off, so the brain has evidence that what we do can make a difference.

sections.key: The basic observation held up, while the explanation changed, and small wins matter in everyday life.
sections.b:
The phrase learned helplessness is now part of everyday language, and the basic observation has held up well: repeated uncontrollable setbacks can sap motivation. What changed was the explanation of why. It is a fine example of science working properly, with the original scientists revising their own famous theory when better evidence arrived.

The practical message is encouraging. If giving up is the default, small, achievable wins are not trivial. Breaking a big problem into manageable steps, noticing what you can influence, and questioning explanations that are permanent, pervasive and personal are all ways of teaching the brain, again and again, that effort matters.

quiz.q: What mattered most in the original dog experiments?
o: The strength and duration of the shocks
The breed and size of the dogs
Lack of control over the shocks
How hungry the dogs were at the time
quiz.e: Both groups of shocked dogs received identical shocks, so the difference was control.

quiz.q: Which style of explaining setbacks put people most at risk of helplessness?
o: Seeing them as temporary, limited and partly due to circumstances
Ignoring them completely
Seeing them as permanent, pervasive and personal
Seeing them as a useful challenge
quiz.e: How people explain bad events shapes whether they bounce back.

quiz.q: What did Maier and Seligman conclude in 2016?
o: Passivity is the default, and control is what is learned
Helplessness is learned through repeated exposure to pain
Dogs cannot learn anything from their experiences
The original experiments have been entirely discredited
quiz.e: Experiencing that actions work lets the prefrontal cortex switch off the default passivity.

quiz.q: What did Maier's rat experiments suggest about controllable stress?
o: It makes animals permanently fearful of any stress
It has no lasting effect on later behaviour
It makes later stress feel considerably worse
It may make animals more resilient to later stress
quiz.e: Experiences of mastery seemed to leave a lasting protective effect, though evidence is mainly from animals.

quiz.q: What practical step follows if giving up is the brain's default?
o: Avoid all hardship wherever you possibly can
Build small wins that show effort makes a difference
Wait until motivation arrives on its own
Treat every setback as permanent and personal
quiz.e: Small wins and manageable steps teach the brain, again and again, that effort matters.

LESSONS.push: Fifty years on, the scientist behind a famous experiment said it was backwards.

LESSONS.title: Earworms: why songs get stuck in your head
LESSONS.hook: Almost everyone has had a few seconds of a song loop endlessly in their mind. Researchers have studied which tunes stick, why, and what actually helps get rid of them.

sections.key: An earworm is a short fragment of music that replays in your mind unbidden, and nearly everyone gets them.
sections.b:
The word earworm translates the German Ohrwurm, and psychologists call it involuntary musical imagery. It is usually not a whole song but a fragment, often the chorus or a catchy hook, that repeats on a loop. In some large surveys, around nine in ten people say they get earworms at least weekly.

Most are mildly annoying or even pleasant, and fade within minutes or hours. The most obvious trigger is hearing a song recently, especially more than once. Memories can trigger them too: a word, place or person linked to a song can set it going years later. People report more earworms when tired, stressed or doing tasks that need little thought, such as showering or chores. Heavy music listeners and musically trained people report them more often.

sections.key: Songs that become earworms tend to be fast, with a familiar shape plus something unusual.
sections.b:
A study led by Kelly Jakubowski of Goldsmiths, University of London, analysed reports from around 3,000 people about songs that most often got stuck. Compared with similarly popular songs that rarely stuck, the earworms tended to have faster tempos and melodies with a fairly common overall shape, the rising and falling pattern found in many nursery rhymes.

But they also had something distinctive, such as unusual leaps between notes or repeated phrases. Frequently named songs included Lady Gaga's 'Bad Romance' and Kylie Minogue's well named 'Can't Get You Out of My Head'. Familiar enough to be easy, unusual enough to grab attention.

sections.key: Nobody knows exactly why earworms loop, and trying hard to suppress one can keep it going.
sections.b:
No one is entirely sure why earworms happen. Musical memories may be especially easy to replay, because melody and rhythm bind them together. Another idea links to the Zeigarnik effect, from Bluma Zeigarnik's 1920s report that people remembered interrupted tasks better. Later attempts to repeat it have given mixed results, so treat it as a hypothesis. What is clear is that earworms thrive when the mind is idle and wanders, and fade when it is occupied.

Trying to banish one by force of will can backfire. Daniel Wegner's 'white bear' studies found that people told not to think of a white bear kept thinking of it. The more you check whether the song has gone, the more you remind yourself of it.

sections.key: Chewing gum and moderately demanding tasks have some evidence behind them.
sections.b:
A few strategies have been tested. In a 2015 study at the University of Reading, people who chewed gum after hearing catchy songs reported fewer intrusive thoughts of them. The likely reason is that chewing ties up some of the mental machinery used to imagine speaking or singing to yourself.

Other research suggests a moderately challenging task, such as an anagram or a sudoku, can crowd out an earworm. The key word is moderately: tasks that are too easy leave room for the song, while tasks that are too hard make the mind wander. Some people swear by listening to the whole song through, to give it an ending, but evidence for that is thinner. Often, accepting the earworm and letting your attention move on works as well as anything.

sections.key: Earworms may be the flip side of a memory system built to rehearse and keep sound patterns.
sections.b:
Before writing, much of human culture was carried in songs, chants and rhymes, because melody and rhythm make words easier to remember. Advertisers exploit the same quirk with jingles, and teachers use it with songs for the alphabet or times tables. The brain's tendency to replay sound patterns, even uninvited, may be the flip side of a powerful system for learning and keeping them.

For most people earworms are harmless. Hearing music that seems to come from outside your head is not an earworm, and is worth mentioning to a doctor. If intrusive music or thoughts become constant and distressing, talk to a GP, as occasionally it can be part of a broader issue such as obsessive compulsive disorder.

quiz.q: What is an earworm?
o: A song you deliberately practise until it is learned
Music that seems to come from outside your head
A fragment of music that replays in your mind unbidden
A detailed memory of an entire concert
quiz.e: Earworms are usually a chorus or hook on a loop, and they feel like your own inner voice.

quiz.q: Which feature do the stickiest songs tend to share?
o: A fast tempo with a familiar but distinctive shape
A slow tempo with a plain, forgettable melody
Complex rhythms with no repeated phrases at all
A very quiet, unremarkable melody with no hook
quiz.e: Earworms are familiar enough to be easy, yet unusual enough to grab attention.

quiz.q: Why can trying hard not to think of a song backfire?
o: Concentrating makes the song physically louder
Songs always grow stronger when they are ignored
The brain cannot forget anything it has heard
Trying to suppress a thought can bring it back
quiz.e: As in the white bear studies, checking whether the song has gone reminds you of it.

quiz.q: Why does a moderately demanding task help against an earworm?
o: Any hard task silences the song instantly and for good
Too easy leaves room for the song; too hard lets the mind wander
Very easy tasks work best of all
The task must always involve listening to music
quiz.e: A task that occupies the mind without overwhelming it crowds out the song.

quiz.q: When is it worth talking to a GP about intrusive music or thoughts?
o: Whenever you get a tune stuck for a day
Only if the song is one you dislike
When they become constant and distressing
Never, because earworms are always harmless
quiz.e: Most earworms are harmless, but constant distress may signal a broader issue that needs professional help.

LESSONS.push: Nine in ten of us have one most weeks. Why a few seconds of music won't let go.

LESSONS.title: Sleep paralysis: the demon on your chest
LESSONS.hook: You wake in the dark, unable to move, and you are certain someone is in the room. For centuries people blamed witches and demons. The real explanation lies in a brief mix-up between sleep and waking.

sections.key: Sleep paralysis is being awake but unable to move, often with a sense of a presence in the room.
sections.b:
Sleep paralysis usually happens as you fall asleep or wake. You are aware of your surroundings and can usually open your eyes, but you cannot move your arms, legs or head, and may struggle to speak. Episodes last from a few seconds to a couple of minutes, though they can feel much longer.

What makes many episodes frightening is what comes with them: a powerful sense that someone is in the room, pressure on the chest, and sometimes vivid sights, sounds or the sensation of being touched. Then it ends. It is more common than people think. A widely cited 2011 review by Brian Sharpless and Jacques Barber estimated that about 8 per cent of people have had at least one episode, though estimates vary.

sections.key: The paralysis is the normal muscle shutdown of dream sleep, lingering while you are partly awake.
sections.b:
The explanation lies in rapid eye movement, or REM, sleep, the stage when most vivid dreaming happens. During REM sleep, the brain actively switches off most of the body's voluntary muscles, leaving only the eyes and breathing muscles working. This is protective, because it stops you acting out your dreams.

Normally the switch flips back the moment you wake. In sleep paralysis, the transition goes slightly wrong. Your conscious mind comes online while the muscle shutdown of REM is still in force. You are, in effect, partly awake and partly still in a dreaming state, which is why the experience feels so real and so strange.

sections.key: Dream imagery leaking into waking awareness explains the sense of a menacing presence that cultures have long described.
sections.b:
If part of your brain is still in dream mode, dream imagery can spill into what you perceive with your eyes open. That is why people see shadowy figures, hear footsteps or feel hands upon them. The sense of threat may be sharpened because the brain's alarm systems are active during REM. The weight on the chest may be partly because breathing is automatic and shallow in REM, so a deliberate deep breath is hard.

Because the experience is so similar everywhere, many cultures have their own explanations. In Newfoundland it is being 'hagged'. In Japan it is kanashibari, roughly 'bound in metal'. The word nightmare originally meant a 'mare', a spirit that sat on sleepers. Henry Fuseli's 1781 painting The Nightmare shows a demon on a sleeping woman's chest.

sections.key: Sleep deprivation, irregular hours and stress are among the most common triggers.
sections.b:
Perhaps the most important factors are not getting enough sleep and having an irregular sleep schedule. That is one reason shift workers, new parents, students during exams and long haul travellers can be more prone to it. Stress and anxiety appear to raise the risk, and it is more common among people with post traumatic stress disorder.

Some studies suggest sleeping on your back may make episodes more likely, though the evidence is limited. Frequent sleep paralysis can also be one feature of narcolepsy, a sleep disorder that causes overwhelming daytime sleepiness. For most people, though, an occasional episode is simply a harmless glitch.

sections.key: Understanding what is happening, staying calm and keeping regular sleep habits all help.
sections.b:
Simply understanding sleep paralysis can take away much of its power. Many people find that reminding themselves 'this is sleep paralysis, it is harmless and it will pass' makes episodes far less frightening. Some find that focusing on slow breathing, or trying to move something small such as a finger or toe, helps break the spell, although evidence for specific techniques is limited.

Over the longer term, the most useful steps are getting enough sleep and keeping a regular sleep routine where possible. If episodes are frequent or distressing, or come with extreme sleepiness during the day, talk to a GP, who may refer you to a sleep specialist.

quiz.q: What is sleep paralysis?
o: Being awake but briefly unable to move, often with hallucinations
A sleep disorder that causes people to walk about at night
Falling asleep suddenly and without warning during the day
A dream so vivid that you cannot remember it
quiz.e: The person is aware but cannot move, and often senses a presence in the room.

quiz.q: Why does the paralysis happen?
o: The body is damaged by a lack of oxygen overnight
The muscles are exhausted from the day's activity
A malicious spirit presses down on the sleeper
The muscle shutdown of REM sleep lingers after you wake
quiz.e: The brain normally switches off voluntary muscles in REM to stop you acting out dreams.

quiz.q: Why do people sense an intruder?
o: The bedroom is genuinely haunted by a spirit
Dream imagery spills into waking perception
Real intruders tend to enter at night
The condition damages the eyes during sleep
quiz.e: Dream imagery spills into waking awareness, and the brain's alarm systems add a sense of threat.

quiz.q: Which factors make sleep paralysis more likely?
o: Drinking too much water by day
Exercising in the morning
Too little or irregular sleep
Eating a late dinner
quiz.e: Shift workers, new parents and exam students are more prone because of irregular, short sleep.

quiz.q: What helps most over the long term?
o: Staying awake as late as possible each night
Avoiding any thought of it during the day
Getting enough sleep and keeping a regular routine
Sleeping only during the daytime hours
quiz.e: Good sleep habits reduce episodes, and a GP can help if they are frequent or distressing.

LESSONS.push: You wake, can't move, and sense someone is there. The cause is a glitch in dream sleep.

LESSONS.title: Why time flies, and why it drags
LESSONS.hook: An hour in a dentist's waiting room crawls, while a week on holiday vanishes. Yet looking back, the holiday feels longer. Your sense of time is not a clock. It is a story your brain tells.

sections.key: The brain has no organ for time, and paying attention to time passing makes it seem to slow.
sections.b:
We have eyes for light and ears for sound, but no dedicated sense organ for time. The brain builds duration from many sources: neural rhythms, attention, emotion and how many new events we take in. For intervals of a second or less, people are surprisingly precise. For longer stretches, judgements are easily pushed around.

Psychologists distinguish between judging time as it passes, called prospective timing, and judging it afterwards, called retrospective timing. While waiting for a kettle to boil, your attention keeps returning to time, and each check stretches the interval. That is the grain of truth in 'a watched pot never boils'. When absorbed, little attention is left for tracking time, and it flies. Fear and anxiety can stretch time, while enjoyable focus shrinks it.

sections.key: A holiday flies by while it happens but feels long in memory, because it is full of new experiences.
sections.b:
A week of new sights on holiday seems to rush past, yet looking back it feels longer than a routine week at work. The psychologist and broadcaster Claudia Hammond named this the holiday paradox.

The likely explanation is that, in hindsight, we judge durations partly by how many distinct memories we have from that period. A holiday packed with novel experiences leaves many memories, so it seems long. A routine week leaves few, and blurs into its neighbours. The reverse happens with boredom: a dull afternoon drags while you live through it, then shrinks to almost nothing in memory.

sections.key: Frightening moments are remembered in rich detail rather than seen in slow motion, and perception is edited before you notice.
sections.b:
Many people describe crashes or falls as happening in slow motion. In a 2007 study, the neuroscientist David Eagleman and colleagues had volunteers fall backwards from a tall tower into a safety net at a Texas amusement park. They estimated their own fall lasted roughly a third longer than falls they watched. But a wrist display flashed numbers too fast to read normally, and falling volunteers could not read them. Frightening moments are not perceived in slow motion; they are remembered in rich detail, which makes them feel longer afterwards.

Chronostasis is a small cousin: after your eyes jump to an analogue clock, the second hand can seem to freeze for longer than a second, because the brain backdates what you see after the movement.

sections.key: The feeling that years pass faster with age is real for long stretches, but the evidence is more mixed than the saying suggests.
sections.b:
A common complaint of adulthood is that the years rush by. One popular explanation is that each year is a smaller fraction of your life, though this is hard to test. A more research friendly idea links back to the holiday paradox: childhood and youth are full of firsts, while adult life often settles into routine, leaving fewer distinctive memories per year.

Surveys find that older people often say the last decade went quickly. But studies asking about the past week or month show weaker age differences than you might expect. The feeling seems to apply mostly to long stretches of time looked back upon.

sections.key: Novelty and variety are the best tools for making life feel longer in memory.
sections.b:
If remembered time depends on distinct memories, there are practical ways to make life feel fuller. Breaking routines with small changes, such as a new walking route, a different weekend activity or learning a skill, gives memory more distinct markers to hold onto. Travel, even locally, can do the same.

Paying deliberate attention, such as noticing details or recalling the day's events at the end of it, may also help experiences stick. None of this makes the clock tick slower. But since our sense of how long we have lived is built from memories rather than minutes, filling time with variety is the closest thing we have to stretching it.

quiz.q: Why does a kettle seem to take forever when you watch it?
o: The brain's clock runs slower when you stand still
Kettles heat water more slowly under observation
Waiting damages your sense of timing
Checking on time passing makes the interval seem longer
quiz.e: Attention to time passing stretches how long an interval feels.

quiz.q: Why does a holiday feel long in memory but short while it happens?
o: Days away from home are physically a little longer
It leaves many distinct memories from new experiences
Time genuinely slows down while you are travelling
You forget most of what happens on holiday
quiz.e: In hindsight, more distinct memories make a period seem longer.

quiz.q: What did the free fall experiment suggest about slow motion in a crisis?
o: Time really does slow down for the brain in danger
Fear makes our eyesight sharper in an emergency
Frightening moments are remembered in rich detail
People never misjudge time when they are in danger
quiz.e: Falling volunteers could not read the flashing numbers, so perception had not sped up.

quiz.q: According to the lesson, what best explains why years can seem to speed up?
o: Adult days are physically shorter than childhood days
Routine adult life leaves fewer distinctive memories
Older people sleep through a larger share of each year
Clocks and calendars are less accurate in later life
quiz.e: Fewer new experiences per year means fewer markers when looking back.

quiz.q: How can you make life feel longer in memory?
o: Add novelty and variety, and notice details
Repeat the same daily routine as precisely as possible
Count the hours more often during the day
Avoid travel and any kind of change
quiz.e: Variety gives memory more distinct markers, so time looks fuller in hindsight.

LESSONS.push: A holiday vanishes while it happens, yet feels long afterwards. Your brain keeps odd time.

LESSONS.title: Why you can't tickle yourself
LESSONS.hook: Try it now: tickle the sole of your own foot. Almost nothing. The reason reveals one of the brain's cleverest tricks, a system that predicts the future a fraction of a second ahead.

sections.key: Light and laughter-producing tickles are different, and the second almost always needs another person.
sections.b:
People have puzzled over this for more than two thousand years. The Problems, a collection of ancient Greek writings traditionally attributed to Aristotle, asks why you cannot tickle yourself. Charles Darwin also noticed that tickling depends on the touch being unexpected. The skin receives much the same stimulation either way, so the difference must lie in the brain.

In 1897 the psychologists Granville Stanley Hall and Arthur Allin described two sensations. One is a light, feathery touch that causes an itchy, crawling feeling, which they called knismesis. The other is the heavier touch to the ribs, armpits and feet that makes people squirm and laugh, which they called gargalesis. People can sometimes give themselves the first, but the laughter producing kind almost always needs someone else, and tickling is strongly social.

sections.key: Your brain predicts the sensations of its own movements and turns them down.
sections.b:
Every time your brain sends a command to your muscles, it also makes a copy of that command, sometimes called an efference copy. Using this copy, the brain predicts what you should feel. When the actual sensations arrive, they are compared with the prediction. Anything that matches is treated as expected and turned down in intensity. Anything that does not match stands out.

This system is constantly at work. It helps you tell the difference between touching something and being touched, and lets your brain focus on surprises in the world rather than the predictable results of your own actions. When you try to tickle yourself, your brain knows exactly what is coming.

sections.key: Adding a small delay to a self-produced touch made it feel far more ticklish.
sections.b:
In the late 1990s Sarah Jayne Blakemore, Daniel Wolpert and Chris Frith at University College London tested this idea. Participants moved a handle with one hand, and a robot copied the movement, stroking soft foam across the palm of their other hand.

When the robot copied the movement exactly and instantly, it did not feel very ticklish. When the researchers added a delay of a fraction of a second, or changed the direction of the stroke, participants rated the sensation as increasingly ticklish. The more the sensation failed to match the prediction, the stronger it felt.

sections.key: Because we feel our own force less, people tend to push back harder than they were pushed.
sections.b:
This prediction system has a curious side effect. In a 2003 study published in Science, pairs of volunteers took turns pressing on each other's finger, each told to press back with exactly the same force they had just felt. Neither intended to escalate, yet the force rose sharply round after round, by roughly 40 per cent each turn.

Because each person felt their own press as weaker than it really was, they pushed harder to match what they had received. The researchers suggested this may help explain why physical scuffles, such as children's tit for tat shoving, so often escalate. Each side genuinely feels it is only responding in kind.

sections.key: Accurate prediction helps us sort sensations caused by us from those caused by the world.
sections.b:
If the brain fails to predict the consequences of its own actions properly, self produced sensations might feel as though they come from outside. Researchers have explored whether this could help explain symptoms of schizophrenia, such as hearing one's own inner speech as an external voice. A study by Blakemore and colleagues published in 2000 found that people with such symptoms rated self tickling as more intense than other participants did. This is an active area of research and the full picture is complex.

The failure to tickle yourself points to something deep. Your brain constantly predicts what it will feel, and uses those predictions to sort sensations into those caused by you and those caused by the world.

quiz.q: Which kind of tickling almost always needs another person?
o: A light, feathery touch that makes skin itch
A firm touch that makes you squirm and laugh
A slow stroke with something cold or wet
Any touch limited to the hands or feet
quiz.e: People can sometimes produce the light itch themselves, but laughter-producing tickling is social.

quiz.q: Why does your own touch feel less ticklish?
o: Your skin is less sensitive to your own hands
Your muscles absorb the pressure
Your brain predicts it and turns the sensation down
You touch with less force
quiz.e: Sensations that match the brain's prediction are treated as expected and dampened.

quiz.q: What happened when the tickling robot added a delay?
o: It felt weaker because the robot was slower and softer
Participants felt nothing at all through the foam
It felt more ticklish because it no longer matched the prediction
The robot became much easier for people to control
quiz.e: The more the sensation failed to match the prediction, the stronger it felt.

quiz.q: Why does tit for tat shoving escalate?
o: Each side feels its own push as weaker and pushes harder
Each person deliberately wants to win the exchange
The skin grows more sensitive with every push
Pain makes both people forget the rules of the game
quiz.e: Each side genuinely believes it is only matching what it received.

quiz.q: How does the brain tell sensations caused by you from those caused by the world?
o: By judging how strong each sensation feels
By ignoring touch and relying on vision alone
By waiting to see whether the sensation repeats
By predicting what its own actions will produce
quiz.e: When predictions fail, self produced sensations may feel as though they come from outside.

LESSONS.push: Why your own fingers can't make you laugh, and the brain trick behind it.

LESSONS.title: Phantom limbs: feeling a hand that isn't there
LESSONS.hook: Most people who lose a limb continue to feel it, sometimes for decades. The phantom can itch, clench and ache, and it has taught scientists that the body you feel is a model built by the brain.

sections.key: Most amputees feel the missing limb, and the pain it can cause is very real.
sections.b:
Doctors have recorded this for centuries. The sixteenth century French surgeon Ambroise Paré described soldiers in pain in limbs that had been removed. The American neurologist Silas Weir Mitchell coined 'phantom limb' in 1871, after treating Civil War amputees. Most amputees, by many estimates well over half, feel phantom sensations at some point. The phantom can feel warm, itchy or tingling, and can seem to move or grip. Phantoms have even been reported after the loss of a breast or a tooth.

For many people it is a strange but tolerable presence. For a large number it hurts, sometimes as a hand clenched so tightly the nails seem to dig in. Such pain was once dismissed as imagination. Today it is understood to be fully real, produced by the nervous system. All pain is produced by the brain.

sections.key: The brain holds a map of the body, and the area for a lost limb does not simply go blank.
sections.b:
In the 1930s and 1940s the Canadian neurosurgeon Wilder Penfield stimulated the surface of patients' brains during surgery and found that touch from different body parts is mapped in an orderly strip called the somatosensory cortex. It is often drawn as a distorted figure, the homunculus, with enormous hands and lips.

The area for the hand sits right beside the area for the face. In the early 1990s V. S. Ramachandran stroked the face of a young man who had lost his arm. A touch to the cheek was felt on his cheek and on his missing thumb. Ramachandran proposed that the hand area, deprived of input, had been invaded by signals from the face area. Imaging shows maps can reorganise, though newer studies suggest the hand area may keep its map, and the link to pain is debated.

sections.key: A mirror can make a phantom appear to move, sometimes easing a clenched or painful phantom.
sections.b:
Ramachandran asked: what if the brain could be shown the limb moving? In the mid 1990s he built a simple box with a vertical mirror in the middle. A patient placed their intact arm on one side and looked into the mirror, so the reflection appeared where the missing arm should be. When they moved the real hand, it looked as though the phantom moved too.

Some patients reported that the phantom suddenly felt as though it moved, and that cramping eased. The approach became known as mirror therapy, and it is now used in some rehabilitation settings, often alongside other treatments.

sections.key: Mirror therapy helps some people, but trials are small and results are mixed.
sections.b:
Mirror therapy captured public imagination because it is cheap and elegant. The scientific picture is more modest. Clinical trials have generally been small, and systematic reviews describe the evidence as limited, with benefits that vary between people. Some patients find it very helpful, others feel little change.

Researchers, including the Australian pain scientist Lorimer Moseley, have developed related approaches such as graded motor imagery. It works through stages: recognising left and right limbs in pictures, imagining movements, and then mirror work. Phantom pain is usually managed by a medical team with a combination of approaches, and anyone experiencing it should seek specialist advice.

sections.key: You feel the brain's model of your body, which can be fooled even without amputation.
sections.b:
Phantom limbs reveal something true of everyone. You do not feel your body directly. You feel the brain's model of it, built from touch, vision, the sense of where your limbs are, and expectations.

In the rubber hand illusion, first reported in 1998 by Matthew Botvinick and Jonathan Cohen, a person's real hand is hidden while a fake rubber hand sits in view. When both are stroked at the same time with a brush, many people begin to feel the touch on the rubber hand, and some even flinch when it is threatened. Seen this way, a phantom is the brain's body model carrying on after the body itself has changed.

quiz.q: How is phantom limb pain now understood?
o: As imagination that patients should ignore
As damage left behind in the missing limb
As real pain generated by the nervous system
As an after-effect of the anaesthetic used
quiz.e: All pain is produced by the brain, so it can be felt in a limb that no longer exists.

quiz.q: What did Ramachandran propose to explain touches on the face being felt in a phantom thumb?
o: Nerves from the face run down to the missing thumb
The man was imagining the sensation of being touched
Signals from the face area spread into the hand area
His thumb had been touched by accident at the same time
quiz.e: Deprived of input, the hand region of the brain's body map may have been taken over by the neighbouring face region.

quiz.q: How does a mirror box work?
o: The reflection of the good limb appears where the missing one was
It numbs the phantom using focused beams of light
It stimulates the nerves of the stump with electricity
It hides the intact limb from view completely
quiz.e: Seeing the phantom apparently move can ease a clenched or painful position.

quiz.q: How strong is the evidence for mirror therapy?
o: Proven in large trials to cure phantom pain
Shown to be useless in every trial so far
Never tested in any scientific study at all
Helpful for some, but trials are small and mixed
quiz.e: Reviews describe the evidence as limited, so specialist advice matters.

quiz.q: What does the rubber hand illusion show?
o: The brain cannot learn to accept new body parts
The body you feel is a model built by the brain
Rubber is as sensitive to touch as human skin
People always know exactly where their hands are
quiz.e: Matching touch and vision can shift where you feel your own hand.

LESSONS.push: The hand is gone, but it itches. What a vanished limb reveals about the body you feel.

LESSONS.title: Stockholm syndrome: the story behind a famous label
LESSONS.hook: In 1973 four bank hostages in Sweden seemed to side with their captors, and a new psychological condition was born. But one hostage's own account of those six days tells a different story.

sections.key: The 1973 Stockholm siege became famous because the hostages seemed to fear the police more than their captors.
sections.b:
On 23 August 1973, Jan-Erik Olsson walked into a Kreditbanken branch on Norrmalmstorg square in central Stockholm, fired a gun and took bank staff hostage. He demanded that a well-known criminal, Clark Olofsson, be brought from prison to join him, and the authorities agreed. For six days the two men held four employees in the vault. The siege ended on 28 August when police pumped tear gas into the vault. No hostage was seriously injured.

What puzzled observers was the hostages' behaviour. They seemed to fear the police more than the robbers. After release, some stayed in contact with Olofsson.

sections.key: Psychiatrist Nils Bejerot called the hostages' attitude a psychological reaction to captivity, and the media turned it into a famous syndrome.
sections.b:
Nils Bejerot, a Swedish psychiatrist who advised police during the siege, suggested the hostages' attitude was a psychological reaction caused by captivity. The media called it 'Norrmalmstorg syndrome', soon known abroad as Stockholm syndrome. In the popular version, captives become attached to their captors and take their side.

The label became hugely famous the following year, when American heiress Patty Hearst was kidnapped and later took part in a bank robbery with her kidnappers. At her 1976 trial the defence argued she had been coerced and brainwashed. She was convicted, but her sentence was commuted and she was eventually pardoned.

sections.key: Kristin Enmark argued her reaction was a rational response to a risky police operation, not a disorder.
sections.b:
Hostage Kristin Enmark spoke by phone with Prime Minister Olof Palme during the siege. She pleaded to be allowed to leave with the robbers, saying she trusted them and feared the police would get everyone killed. In later interviews, she has said the police seemed willing to risk the hostages' lives, while the robbers were the people physically present who could keep her safe minute by minute.

Seen that way, staying on good terms with them looks less like a disorder and more like a survival strategy. Critics say the label shifted attention from the authorities' decisions to a young woman's supposed psychology.

sections.key: Stockholm syndrome is not a recognised psychiatric diagnosis, and there is little systematic evidence for it.
sections.b:
Despite its fame, Stockholm syndrome does not appear in the major psychiatric diagnostic manuals, the DSM and the ICD. There are no agreed diagnostic criteria. Researchers who have reviewed the literature found remarkably little systematic evidence for it, and much of what is written relies on a handful of famous cases and media reports.

Studies of hostage situations suggest strong positive bonds with captors are uncommon. That doesn't mean captives never feel complicated emotions towards the people holding them. But the popular idea of a well-defined syndrome, in which victims are reliably 'converted', rests on a thin foundation.

sections.key: Being agreeable to someone who holds power over you is often a survival strategy, and the label can unfairly blame victims.
sections.b:
Many researchers now describe these reactions as survival strategies. Being compliant, calm and friendly towards someone who controls whether you live can reduce the chance of violence. Small kindnesses from a captor can produce real gratitude in a person under extreme stress. Calling that a syndrome implies the victim's mind malfunctioned, when it may have been working hard to keep them alive.

Today the phrase is often applied to people who stay in abusive relationships. Critics, including researchers working with survivors of family violence, say this suggests victims are irrational, ignoring the fear, isolation and financial pressure that make leaving hard. In Australia, call 000 in immediate danger, or 1800RESPECT on 1800 737 732.

quiz.q: What puzzled observers about the hostages in the 1973 siege?
o: They refused to speak to anyone after being released
They seemed to fear the police more than their captors
They tried repeatedly to escape from the vault
They were badly hurt by the tear gas attack
quiz.e: The hostages' apparent trust in the robbers and fear of police is what made the case seem so strange.

quiz.q: In the popular version of Stockholm syndrome, what is supposed to happen to captives?
o: They forget the details of their time in captivity
They become openly hostile towards other victims
They recover quickly with no lasting effects
They grow attached to their captors and take their side
quiz.e: The popular idea is that captives bond with their captors, which is exactly the claim the evidence struggles to support.

quiz.q: How does Kristin Enmark's account reframe her behaviour?
o: As a rational response to a risky police operation
As a symptom of a diagnosed mental illness
As a deliberate plan to help the robbers escape
As the result of a bribe from the captors
quiz.e: Her reaction looks like a sensible attempt to stay safe, not a disorder.

quiz.q: What is the status of Stockholm syndrome in psychiatry?
o: It is a standard diagnosis in the DSM and ICD
It is proven to affect most people taken hostage
It is not a recognised diagnosis, with little evidence
It is recognised only for cases that involve banks
quiz.e: There are no agreed criteria and little systematic evidence, so it is a label rather than an established syndrome.

quiz.q: Why do critics object to using the label for abusive relationships?
o: It makes abuse seem less common than it really is
It implies victims are irrational and ignores barriers
It is too technical for most people to understand
It applies only to crimes committed by strangers
quiz.e: Fear, isolation and financial pressure explain why people stay, so a catchy label can wrongly blame victims.

LESSONS.push: A famous psychological condition that may never have existed. Start with a bank vault.

LESSONS.title: Choking: back blows and chest thrusts
LESSONS.hook: Most people picture the Heimlich manoeuvre. Australian first aid guidelines teach something different, and the reason is a surprising story about evidence.

sections.key: Severe choking is usually silent, because a fully blocked airway leaves no air to speak, cough or breathe.
sections.b:
Movies make choking loud, but a person with a fully blocked airway usually can't speak, cough or breathe. They may clutch their throat, look panicked, and their lips and face may turn blue or grey. The brain is starved of oxygen within minutes, so the response must be fast.

Choking is a risk at every age. Toddlers explore with their mouths, and grapes, nuts, popcorn and hard lollies are common culprits. Older adults are at risk too, especially when swallowing has weakened after a stroke or with conditions such as dementia. Meat is a classic cause in adults.

sections.key: If the person can cough forcefully, encourage them to keep coughing and stay with them.
sections.b:
The simplest test is whether the person can cough effectively. A strong, noisy cough means air is still moving, and coughing is the body's best tool for clearing the airway. Encourage them to keep coughing. Don't slap their back or give them water while they cough well.

Stay with them and watch closely, because a partial blockage can become a complete one. If coughing doesn't clear it, call Triple Zero (000). A weak, silent or ineffective cough, difficulty breathing or an inability to speak signals a severe blockage. Then you act and call for help at the same time.

sections.key: For severe choking in a conscious person, call 000 and give up to five sharp back blows, checking after each one.
sections.b:
Under Australian guidelines from the Australian and New Zealand Committee on Resuscitation (ANZCOR), the first step for a conscious adult or child with severe choking is back blows. Call 000, or have someone else call.

Stand slightly behind the person, support their chest with one hand and bend them well forward, so gravity helps. With the heel of your other hand, give a sharp blow between the shoulder blades. Check after each blow whether the object has come out, rather than automatically delivering all five. The aim is a sudden jolt that loosens the blockage so it falls forward out of the mouth, not deeper.

sections.key: If back blows fail, give up to five chest thrusts, then keep alternating the two methods.
sections.b:
If five back blows haven't cleared the airway, switch to chest thrusts. Support the person's back with one hand. Place the heel of your other hand on the lower half of the breastbone, the same spot used for CPR, and push in sharply. Chest thrusts are slower and sharper than CPR compressions. Each one squeezes a burst of air out of the lungs, like a cough you create for them.

Check after each thrust. If the blockage remains after five, go back to five back blows, and keep alternating until the object comes out, help arrives, or the person becomes unresponsive.

sections.key: Australian guidelines don't recommend abdominal thrusts, and babies get head-down back blows and two-finger chest thrusts.
sections.b:
In 1974 the American surgeon Henry Heimlich popularised abdominal thrusts. They are still taught in places such as the United Kingdom and United States, though advice varies. ANZCOR's guideline says abdominal thrusts are not recommended, citing reports of life-threatening complications such as injured organs, and finds back blows and chest thrusts work with low risk. If you live in Australia, learn the local method.

For babies under one, call 000 and lay the baby face down and head-down along your thigh or forearm, supporting the head and jaw. Give up to five back blows, then turn them over for up to five two-finger chest thrusts, and keep alternating.

If anyone collapses and stops breathing normally, start CPR.

quiz.q: Why is severe choking often silent?
o: Most people faint before they can make a sound
No air can pass, so they can't speak or cough
The person is too embarrassed to make a noise
The throat swells shut within a few seconds
quiz.e: With no air moving, the person can't shout, cough or breathe, so you must watch for the signs.

quiz.q: If a choking person is coughing forcefully, what should you do?
o: Give them a drink of water to ease the cough
Give sharp back blows straight away
Lay them flat on their back to rest
Encourage them to keep coughing and stay with them
quiz.e: A strong cough is the body's best tool for clearing the airway, so let it work and watch closely.

quiz.q: How should you position someone for back blows?
o: Lying flat on their back on the floor
Sitting upright and leaning back in a chair
Leaning well forward so gravity helps
Lying on their side with knees drawn up
quiz.e: Bending forward lets gravity help, so the object moves out rather than deeper.

quiz.q: What is the correct sequence if back blows don't work?
o: Abdominal thrusts until the object clears
Up to five chest thrusts, then alternate
More back blows only, as hard as possible
Offer sips of water to wash it down
quiz.e: Alternating back blows and chest thrusts continues until the object clears, help arrives or the person collapses.

quiz.q: Why do Australian guidelines not recommend abdominal thrusts?
o: They have been shown never to work at all
They are thought to work only on children
They can cause serious injuries to organs
They need special equipment to be done safely
quiz.e: Reports of serious injuries led Australia to favour back blows and chest thrusts, which work with low risk.

LESSONS.push: Most people picture the Heimlich. Australian guidelines teach something else.

LESSONS.title: Stopping severe bleeding
LESSONS.hook: A person can lose a dangerous amount of blood in minutes. The most powerful tool for stopping it is something everyone already owns: their hands.

sections.key: Severe bleeding can become life-threatening within minutes, so act while you call 000.
sections.b:
An adult holds roughly five litres of blood. A wound to a major vessel in the arm, leg, neck or groin can bleed heavily enough to become life-threatening within minutes. Paramedics are fast, but not always fast enough, so the person beside the injured one matters most.

Bleeding is life-threatening if blood is spurting or pulsing, flowing steadily, pooling on the ground, or soaking through clothing and bandages. First check for danger to yourself. Then call Triple Zero (000), or ask someone else to call while you act. Put the phone on speaker so the operator can coach you.

sections.key: Firm, direct pressure on the wound is usually the quickest and most effective way to stop bleeding.
sections.b:
Australian first aid guidelines are clear: direct pressure is usually the quickest and most effective way to stop bleeding. Put a pad, such as folded cloth, gauze or a clean T-shirt, on the wound and press down hard with both hands. If nothing is available, use bare hands. Infection can be treated in hospital, but blood loss cannot be undone.

Lean in and use your body weight. Keep the pressure steady rather than lifting to check, because each peek can let a fragile clot break. Wear gloves if you have them, but don't waste time hunting for them.

sections.key: If blood soaks through, leave the first pad in place and put another on top.
sections.b:
The instinct is to peel away a blood-soaked dressing and replace it. Resist it. Removing the first pad can tear away the clot forming underneath and restart the bleeding. Place a second pad over the first and bind it firmly with a bandage, or keep pressing.

Help the person lie down, especially if the bleeding is from a leg or is severe, and keep the injured part still. Lying down reduces the risk of fainting and helps blood reach the brain.

If an object such as a knife or glass is stuck in the wound, leave it. It may be plugging the hole. Pad around it and press on the pads either side, then call 000.

sections.key: For life-threatening limb bleeding that pressure cannot stop, a trained first aider can use a tourniquet.
sections.b:
A tourniquet is a tight band around an arm or leg, above a wound, that cuts off blood flow to the limb. Old first aid courses taught people to fear them. Military experience, including in Iraq and Afghanistan, showed they save lives in catastrophic limb bleeding.

Australian guidelines now say to use one for life-threatening limb bleeding that direct pressure cannot control, if one is available and you are trained. Place it a short distance above the wound, not over a joint or the wound itself, following the product's instructions, and tighten until the bleeding stops. Note the time it was applied and tell paramedics. Never loosen it yourself.

sections.key: Pale, clammy skin and a fast pulse can signal shock, and most everyday bleeding is minor and easily managed.
sections.b:
Even after bleeding is controlled, the body may struggle. Shock is a dangerous drop in blood flow to the organs. Signs include pale, cold, clammy skin, a rapid weak pulse, fast breathing, anxiety, confusion and drowsiness. Keep the person lying down, reassure them and cover them to stop heat loss. Give no food or drink, since they may need surgery. If they become unresponsive and stop breathing normally, start CPR.

Most bleeding is minor. Rinse small cuts, press with a clean cloth and cover. For a nosebleed, sit up, lean forward and pinch the soft part of the nose for at least ten minutes. Tilting the head back is wrong, as blood runs down the throat.

quiz.q: Why does the person next to an injured person matter most in severe bleeding?
o: Only bystanders are allowed to touch a wound
Ambulances do not attend bleeding injuries
Help may not arrive before the blood loss is critical
Bleeding stops on its own after a few minutes
quiz.e: Serious bleeding can become fatal within minutes, so bystander action is what buys time.

quiz.q: What is the quickest and most effective way to control severe bleeding?
o: Washing the wound thoroughly first
Raising the arm above the head and waiting
Applying a bandage loosely to avoid pain
Firm, direct pressure with a pad or hands
quiz.e: Pressing hard and steadily controls the bleeding while help is on the way.

quiz.q: What should you do if blood soaks through the first pad?
o: Remove it and put on a fresh pad
Leave it there and add another pad on top
Stop pressing so the wound can breathe
Rinse the pad under running water
quiz.e: Removing the pad can tear away the forming clot and restart the bleeding.

quiz.q: When is a tourniquet appropriate under Australian guidelines?
o: For limb bleeding that pressure cannot control
For any cut on an arm or a leg that bleeds
For nosebleeds that last several minutes
For bleeding from the neck or the head
quiz.e: A tourniquet is a last resort for life-threatening limb bleeding that pressure alone cannot stop, used by someone trained.

quiz.q: What is the correct way to treat a nosebleed?
o: Tilt the head back and pinch the bridge
Lie flat and wait for it to stop
Push tissue deep into the nostril
Sit up, lean forward and pinch the soft part
quiz.e: Leaning forward keeps blood from running down the throat, and sustained pinching lets a clot form.

LESSONS.push: Severe bleeding can turn critical in minutes. Your own hands are the best first tool.

LESSONS.title: Seizures: what to do and what not to do
LESSONS.hook: Watching someone have a seizure is frightening, and the most famous piece of advice about it is completely wrong. The right response is calm, simple and mostly about keeping them safe.

sections.key: A seizure is a sudden burst of abnormal electrical activity in the brain, and it has many possible causes.
sections.b:
The brain runs on electrical signals passed between billions of nerve cells. During a seizure, a sudden burst of abnormal, synchronised activity disrupts that traffic. What happens depends on where it starts and how far it spreads.

Epilepsy is a tendency to have recurring seizures. But seizures can also be triggered by a high fever in young children, a head injury, very low blood sugar, alcohol withdrawal, some drugs, or an illness affecting the brain. Seizures are more common than many people think, and many of us will witness one, so basic seizure first aid is worth knowing.

sections.key: Some seizures cause convulsions, while others look like staring, confusion or odd repeated movements.
sections.b:
The type most people picture is a tonic-clonic seizure, once called grand mal. The person may cry out, stiffen, fall and jerk rhythmically, sometimes with noisy breathing, drooling or loss of bladder control. Most stop on their own within a few minutes.

Many seizures look nothing like this. In a focal seizure, a person may seem dazed, pluck at clothes, smack their lips, wander or not respond properly. An absence seizure, most common in children, can look like a few seconds of blank staring, easily mistaken for daydreaming. Someone having a quieter seizure may be misjudged as drunk or rude when they actually need patience and protection.

sections.key: Note the time, move dangers away, cushion the head and don't restrain the person.
sections.b:
Stay with the person and stay calm. Check the time straight away, because how long the seizure lasts is one of the most important things to know. Move hard or sharp objects away and put something soft, like a folded jacket, under their head. If it's safe, loosen anything tight around the neck.

Don't hold them down or try to stop the movements. Restraint can injure both of you and won't end the seizure. Don't move them unless they are in danger, such as near traffic, water, stairs or fire. Ask onlookers to give them space and privacy.

sections.key: Never put anything in a person's mouth during a seizure, because it is impossible to swallow your tongue.
sections.b:
For generations, people were told to force something between the teeth of a person having a seizure, to stop them swallowing their tongue. This is a harmful myth. The tongue is anchored to the floor of the mouth and cannot be swallowed.

Pushing a spoon, wallet or fingers into the mouth can break teeth, injure the jaw, cause choking on fragments and get your fingers badly bitten. A person may bite their tongue or cheek, which can bleed, but this usually heals and is far less dangerous than what well-meaning bystanders cause.

When the movements stop, roll the person onto their side into the recovery position. Give no food or drink until they are fully awake and able to swallow.

sections.key: Stay with the person as they recover, and call 000 if the seizure is long, repeated, in water or causes injury or breathing trouble.
sections.b:
Confusion, drowsiness or upset can last several minutes or longer after a seizure. Speak calmly, tell them where they are and stay until they're alert. Some people carry an identification card, wear a medical bracelet or have a seizure management plan.

Many people with known epilepsy don't need an ambulance for a typical short seizure. But Epilepsy Action Australia advises calling 000 if it lasts over five minutes, another follows before recovery, or they don't wake up. Call too if they are injured, have trouble breathing, are pregnant or diabetic, it's their first seizure, or you're unsure. Any seizure in water is an emergency. Febrile seizures in young children are usually harmless, but have a doctor check a first one.

quiz.q: What is a seizure?
o: A blockage of blood flow to the brain
A reaction that occurs only in epilepsy
A burst of abnormal electrical activity in the brain
A loss of muscle strength from low blood sugar
quiz.e: Seizures come from abnormal brain activity and can have causes other than epilepsy.

quiz.q: Which statement about seizures is correct?
o: All seizures involve falling and jerking
Seizures happen only to people with epilepsy
Some look like staring or confusion, not convulsions
A seizure always lasts longer than ten minutes
quiz.e: Absence seizures are easily mistaken for daydreaming, so not every seizure involves convulsions.

quiz.q: What should you do during a convulsive seizure?
o: Hold the person still to stop the movements
Note the time, clear hazards and cushion the head
Move them to a quiet room straight away
