Pour cold water over their face
quiz.e: Timing the seizure and protecting from injury is the core of first aid, and restraint can cause harm.

quiz.q: Why should you never put anything in a seizing person's mouth?
o: It helps keep the airway open for the person
The seizure will last longer if they bite down
It is only dangerous when the person is a child
Tongues can't be swallowed, and objects cause injury
quiz.e: Swallowing the tongue is a myth, and forcing objects in breaks teeth and risks choking.

quiz.q: When should you call 000 for a seizure?
o: Only if the person has not been diagnosed with epilepsy
Only if they bite their tongue during the seizure
If it lasts over five minutes, repeats or is in water
Whenever the person falls asleep once it is over
quiz.e: Long, repeated, first-time or in-water seizures carry higher risk and need an ambulance.

LESSONS.push: You cannot swallow your tongue. So why was that advice believed for generations?

LESSONS.title: Electricity: the danger you can't see
LESSONS.hook: Electricity gives no warning: no smell, no sound, nothing to see. A few simple rules, and one small switch in your meter box, stand between ordinary life and a fatal shock.

sections.key: Electric current can stop the heart and cause deep burns that look small from outside.
sections.b:
Current crossing the chest can throw the heart into a chaotic rhythm called ventricular fibrillation, where it quivers instead of pumping. That is cardiac arrest. Current can also make muscles contract so strongly a person can't let go of what they're holding. And as it passes through tissue, it generates heat and burns along its path.

Entry and exit wounds can look small while muscles, nerves and blood vessels inside are badly damaged. Anyone who has had a significant shock or electrical burn should be checked by a doctor, even if they feel fine.

sections.key: A safety switch (RCD) cuts power in a fraction of a second when current leaks, and it's one of the home's great lifesavers.
sections.b:
A residual current device, called a safety switch in Australia, constantly compares the current going out along the active wire with the current returning along the neutral. If they don't match, current is leaking somewhere, possibly through a person. The switch cuts the power within a fraction of a second, fast enough to greatly reduce the risk of death.

Safety switches differ from circuit breakers and fuses, which mainly protect wiring from overload. Newer homes must have them, but many older homes have them on only some circuits, or none. Most have a test button worth pressing regularly.

sections.key: Electrical wiring work in Australia must be done by a licensed electrician, and simple habits prevent most home hazards.
sections.b:
Across Australia, it's illegal for an unlicensed person to do electrical wiring work, such as installing power points, replacing light switches or running cables. Faulty wiring can kill, sometimes years later and for someone else entirely, and a loose connection can start a fire inside a wall.

At home, the habits are simple. Don't use appliances with frayed or damaged cords. Don't overload power boards or daisy-chain them. Keep appliances away from water and never touch switches with wet hands. Never fish toast from a plugged-in toaster with a knife. If a switch or power point feels warm or smells of burning, get it checked.

sections.key: Treat every fallen powerline as live and stay at least eight metres away, even if you're in a car.
sections.b:
After storms, crashes and bushfires, powerlines can lie on the ground, fences, cars or trees. Treat every fallen line as live, even if it isn't sparking, because it may be re-energised automatically. Distributors advise staying at least eight metres away, about two car lengths. Electricity can travel through wet ground, puddles, fences and metal, so you needn't touch the line to be hurt. Call 000 if someone is injured or there's a fire.

If a line falls on your car, stay inside unless it's on fire. If you must leave, jump clear with your feet together, never touching the car and ground at the same time, then shuffle away with small steps.

sections.key: Never touch someone in contact with electricity, switch off the power first, and look up before raising anything tall.
sections.b:
If someone is being electrocuted, don't grab them. The current can flow into you too. Switch off the power at the switchboard or wall, or unplug the appliance if safe. For powerlines and high voltage, don't approach: call 000 and wait for the electricity company. Once power is off, check them using DRSABCD, start CPR if needed, send for a defibrillator and cool burns under cool running water for twenty minutes.

Many serious accidents happen outdoors when tall objects meet overhead lines: ladders, tipper trays, boat masts. Electricity can also arc across a gap. Look up before raising anything tall, carry long objects horizontally, and never climb poles, towers or train roofs.

quiz.q: Why should anyone with a significant electric shock see a doctor even if they feel fine?
o: Electric shocks always cause infections
The heart always stops after a shock
Doctors must check every shock by law
Skin wounds can hide serious internal damage
quiz.e: The damage inside muscles, nerves and vessels can be far worse than the burn on the skin suggests.

quiz.q: How does a safety switch protect you?
o: It stops wiring overheating under load
It cuts the power fast when current leaks
It lowers your household power bill
It stores power for use in emergencies
quiz.e: By spotting a mismatch between outgoing and returning current, it shuts off power before a shock becomes fatal.

quiz.q: Who may legally carry out electrical wiring work in Australia?
o: Any adult following a manual
A homeowner doing a small job
Only a licensed electrician
Anyone supervised by a friend
quiz.e: Faulty wiring can kill or start a fire years later, which is why the work is restricted.

quiz.q: What should you do if a powerline lands on your car?
o: Get out and run to the nearest building
Open the door and hold the metal frame
Drive away as quickly as possible
Stay inside unless it's on fire, and call 000
quiz.e: The safest place is usually inside, unless fire forces you out.

quiz.q: What is the first step when helping someone being electrocuted?
o: Switch off the power before touching them
Pull them clear with your bare hands
Splash water on them to cool them
Wait for them to let go on their own
quiz.e: Touching them while they're still in contact with power can make you a second casualty.

LESSONS.push: No smell, no sound, nothing to see. What stands between you and a fatal shock?

LESSONS.title: Poisons at home: one number to remember
LESSONS.hook: Most poisonings happen not in labs or crime novels but in ordinary kitchens, bathrooms and handbags. Knowing one phone number, and one danger hiding in your remote control, could save a child's life.

sections.key: Most poisonings are ordinary accidents at home, and children under five are the most at risk.
sections.b:
Poisoning sounds like something from a detective story, but most cases are home accidents. Children under five are especially vulnerable because they explore with their mouths, copy adults and move fast. A child can climb onto a bench, open a handbag or find a dropped tablet in seconds.

Common culprits include medicines, cleaning products, dishwasher and laundry pods, essential oils, cosmetics, garden chemicals and some plants. Adults are poisoned too, often through medication mix-ups like a double dose, or chemicals kept in the wrong containers. A few habits prevent most of it.

sections.key: Save 13 11 26, the Poisons Information Centre, and call 000 first if the person is collapsed, seizing, struggling to breathe or very drowsy.
sections.b:
Australia's national poisoning advice number is 13 11 26, the Poisons Information Centre. It's answered around the clock, every day, from anywhere. Specialists can tell you whether a substance and amount is likely to be harmful, what to do now and whether to go to hospital. Many calls end with reassurance. Save the number in your phone and put it on the fridge.

But if the person has collapsed, is having a seizure, is having trouble breathing or is very drowsy, call Triple Zero (000) first.

Don't make them vomit, or give milk, unless the Poisons line or a doctor says so. Vomiting can burn corrosives twice or draw petroleum products into the lungs. Rinse skin and eyes with running water. Keep the container.

sections.key: A swallowed button battery can burn through tissue within two hours, so go straight to hospital.
sections.b:
Small coin-shaped lithium batteries are in car keys, remote controls, kitchen scales, thermometers, toys and musical greeting cards. If a child swallows one and it lodges in the oesophagus, it reacts with saliva and body fluids to produce a strongly alkaline chemical that can burn through tissue, sometimes within two hours. The damage can reach major blood vessels. Children have died in Australia this way.

Symptoms may be vague or absent at first, so don't wait for them. If you suspect a child has swallowed a button battery, or put one in their nose or ear, call 000 or go straight to a hospital emergency department, and call 13 11 26 for advice.

sections.key: After children died, Australia introduced mandatory button battery standards in 2022, but older products and spare batteries remain a risk.
sections.b:
In 2013, four-year-old Summer Steer of Queensland died after swallowing a button battery no one knew she had found. Her death and others led to campaigns by families, doctors and consumer groups. In 2022, Australia introduced mandatory safety standards, enforced by the ACCC. Products with button batteries must have secure compartments young children can't easily open, batteries must be in child-resistant packaging, and warnings are required. Australia was among the first countries to introduce mandatory rules like this.

Still, older products, cheap imports and spare batteries in drawers remain a risk. Store them up high and dispose of used ones safely.

sections.key: Safe storage prevents most poisonings, and wild mushrooms should never be eaten unless an expert has identified them.
sections.b:
Keep medicines, including vitamins and pain relievers, in a locked or child-resistant cupboard at least 1.5 metres off the ground, not in handbags or on bedside tables. Put them away straight after use, even while answering the door. Never store chemicals in drink bottles. Keep products in original labelled containers. Ask visitors to keep bags out of reach. Give medicines with the lights on, reading the label.

Some of the most dangerous poisons are natural. The death cap mushroom, introduced to Australia, grows around Canberra and Melbourne, often under oaks. Cooking doesn't destroy its toxins, and part of one can cause liver failure, with symptoms delayed for many hours. Never eat wild mushrooms unless an expert is certain. After eating an unknown mushroom or plant, call 13 11 26 at once and keep a sample.

quiz.q: Why are children under five most at risk of poisoning?
o: They are given more medicines than adults
They explore with their mouths and move quickly
They are naturally resistant to bitter tastes
They spend more time outdoors than adults
quiz.e: Curiosity, mimicry and speed combine to make small children especially vulnerable.

quiz.q: When should you call 000 instead of 13 11 26?
o: When you are unsure what the product was
When a child has only touched the product
When the person has collapsed or is seizing
When the label says 'keep out of reach'
quiz.e: Emergencies come first. The Poisons line is for advice when the person is still alert.

quiz.q: Why are swallowed button batteries so dangerous?
o: They explode as soon as they are swallowed
They release heavy metals that cause slow illness
They always cause immediate, obvious choking
They react with body fluids and burn tissue quickly
quiz.e: The chemical burn can start quickly, so act without waiting for symptoms.

quiz.q: What problem remains despite Australia's 2022 battery standards?
o: Older products and spare batteries are still a risk
Batteries can no longer be sold in shops
Battery compartments are now too hard for adults
Warnings are no longer required on products
quiz.e: Standards cover new products, so loose and older batteries still need safe storage.

quiz.q: What is the safest rule about wild mushrooms?
o: Cook them thoroughly for several minutes first
Never eat one unless an expert has identified it
Eat only a small amount the first time you try
Avoid only the ones growing under oak trees
quiz.e: Death cap toxins survive cooking, and symptoms can be delayed for hours.

LESSONS.push: The most dangerous thing in your remote control isn't what you'd expect.

LESSONS.title: Carbon monoxide: the invisible killer
LESSONS.hook: It has no colour, no smell and no taste, and its symptoms feel like the flu. Here is how an ordinary heater can quietly poison a home, and how to stop it.

sections.key: Two young brothers died in 2010 from a faulty gas heater, with no smoke, smell or alarm to warn them.
sections.b:
In May 2010, two brothers, Chase and Tyler Robinson, died in their sleep at their rented home in Shepparton, Victoria. The cause was carbon monoxide from a faulty gas heater. Nothing had seemed wrong: no smoke, no strange smell, and no alarm, because the home had no carbon monoxide detector.

A coronial inquest examined who was responsible for maintaining the heater. Their mother, Vanessa Robinson, became a prominent campaigner for gas heater safety, and the case helped drive change, including regular gas safety checks in Victorian rental homes. It is a painful reminder that the most dangerous hazards may be ones we cannot sense.

sections.key: Carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin far more strongly than oxygen does, pushing oxygen out of your blood.
sections.b:
Carbon monoxide is made when fuels such as gas, wood, charcoal, petrol or diesel burn without enough oxygen. Red blood cells carry oxygen using haemoglobin. Carbon monoxide binds to it roughly two hundred times more strongly than oxygen does, so even small amounts steadily push oxygen out of the blood. The brain and heart suffer first.

The gas is colourless, odourless and tasteless, so people breathe it unaware. High levels can cause unconsciousness and death within minutes. Lower levels over hours or days can cause lasting brain and heart damage.

sections.key: Early signs look like flu, so clues such as several people feeling sick at home are what give it away.
sections.b:
Early symptoms are ordinary: headache, dizziness, nausea, vomiting, tiredness, weakness, breathlessness and confusion. People assume flu, migraine or a stomach bug. Clues point to carbon monoxide instead. Several people, or pets, feel sick at once. Symptoms are worse at home or with a heater running, and improve outside.

People who are asleep or have been drinking may lose consciousness before noticing, so night-time poisoning is especially dangerous. Babies, older people, pregnant women and people with heart or lung disease are more vulnerable.

sections.key: Faulty gas heaters and indoor barbecues or generators are common sources, so service heaters with a licensed gasfitter.
sections.b:
A major source in Australian homes is gas space heaters, especially older or poorly maintained ones. An open-flued heater should send fumes out through a flue, but a blocked or faulty flue, or exhaust fans pulling air the wrong way, can spill carbon monoxide inside. Unflued heaters release fumes into the room and need good ventilation. Other causes are barbecues, camping stoves, patio heaters or charcoal used indoors, in tents, caravans or garages, generators near open windows, and engines running in closed garages.

Have gas heaters serviced by a licensed gasfitter, generally at least every two years or as the manufacturer recommends. Warning signs include a yellow or orange flame, soot or stains, and a stuffy room. If you rent, ask when the heater was last checked.

sections.key: Smoke alarms can't detect carbon monoxide, so fit a separate alarm, and if you suspect poisoning, get everyone out and call 000.
sections.b:
Smoke alarms don't detect carbon monoxide. A separate alarm from a hardware store warns you when levels rise. Place it per the instructions, typically near fuel-burning appliances and sleeping areas, and test it regularly. Requirements for them vary by state and territory, but regulators encourage them, especially with gas heating. An alarm is a backstop, not a substitute for servicing.

If you suspect poisoning, get everyone, including pets, into fresh air. If quick and safe, switch off the appliance and open doors on your way out. Call 000. Start CPR if someone isn't breathing normally. Don't return until a licensed gasfitter has checked the source. Treatment is high-concentration oxygen, and everyone should be assessed.

quiz.q: What made the Shepparton heater so dangerous?
o: It produced thick smoke that filled the house
It caused a fire that spread silently overnight
The gas gives no smoke, smell or taste to warn you
It released a strong gas smell that was ignored
quiz.e: The home had no detector, and the gas itself is undetectable by the senses.

quiz.q: How does carbon monoxide harm the body?
o: It burns the delicate lining of the lungs
It binds to haemoglobin and pushes oxygen out
It thickens the blood so it cannot flow properly
It paralyses the muscles used for breathing
quiz.e: It binds far more strongly than oxygen, starving the brain and heart first.

quiz.q: Which clue most suggests carbon monoxide rather than flu?
o: Symptoms appear only after eating a meal
Only one person in the house has a headache
A high fever develops over a day or two
Several people and pets feel worse at home
quiz.e: Group symptoms that ease away from home point to a shared environmental cause.

quiz.q: How often should gas heaters generally be serviced by a licensed gasfitter?
o: Only when they stop heating the room properly
Every ten years, before the coldest winter
At least every two years, or as the maker says
Only before they are used for the first time
quiz.e: Regular servicing and a carbon monoxide test catch leaks before they harm anyone.

quiz.q: Why can't a smoke alarm protect you from carbon monoxide?
o: It only works during daylight hours
Smoke alarms don't detect the gas at all
It detects the gas but sounds too quietly
It is switched off while a heater is running
quiz.e: A dedicated carbon monoxide alarm is the only warning device, and it supplements regular servicing.

LESSONS.push: It has no colour, smell or taste, and it feels like the flu. Meet the invisible danger.

LESSONS.title: Croc country: staying safe in the north
LESSONS.hook: Northern Australia is home to the largest reptile on Earth, an ambush hunter that has been perfecting its technique for millions of years. The rules for living alongside it are simple, and they work.

sections.key: Saltwater crocodiles are the largest living reptile and ambush hunters across northern Australia.
sections.b:
The estuarine or saltwater crocodile, Crocodylus porosus, is the largest living reptile. Large males can grow beyond five metres and weigh many hundreds of kilograms, while females are considerably smaller. In Australia they live across the tropical north, from the Kimberley through the Northern Territory to Queensland, down the east coast into central Queensland.

They are ambush predators. A crocodile can lie almost submerged with only its eyes and nostrils showing, wait a long time for an animal to come to the water's edge, then lunge with astonishing speed. Australia's other species, the freshwater crocodile, is smaller and far less dangerous, though it can still bite.

sections.key: Protection brought crocodiles back strongly, so more big animals now share waterways with people.
sections.b:
After the Second World War, saltwater crocodiles were hunted intensively for their skins, and populations crashed. Western Australia, the Northern Territory and Queensland introduced protection between about 1970 and 1974. Numbers have since bounced back strongly, especially in the Northern Territory, where the wild population is estimated at around one hundred thousand.

It's one of conservation's great success stories, but it has a consequence. More and larger crocodiles now share rivers, beaches and boat ramps with growing numbers of residents and tourists. Fatal attacks remain rare in Australia, a few at most each year, and nearly all involve people in or right beside the water.

sections.key: Salties live well beyond the sea, so assume any northern water may hold a crocodile, sign or not.
sections.b:
The name is misleading. Salties live in tidal rivers, mangroves and estuaries, but also in freshwater billabongs, swamps, waterholes and rivers far from the coast. They swim along the coast and can turn up on popular beaches and around islands. A clear, inviting waterhole with no sign may still hold one.

Crocodiles are hard to spot. Muddy water, reflections and camouflage mean even locals can miss a large animal a few metres away. They're regularly seen in waterways near Darwin, Cairns and Townsville. Wildlife authorities give one rule: in croc country, assume any water may contain crocodiles, and don't swim unless you are certain it's safe.

sections.key: Keep well back from the water, don't leave food or scraps near it, and don't repeat routines at the water's edge.
sections.b:
CrocWise guidance and similar advice from the Northern Territory and Western Australia dramatically reduces risk. Obey warning signs, but never assume water without signs is safe. Don't swim, paddle or wade where crocodiles may live. Stand a few metres back when fishing, and never on overhanging logs. Don't clean fish or leave scraps, bait or food near the water, boat ramps or campsites. Never feed crocodiles. Be extra alert at night and during the roughly September to April breeding season.

Camp at least fifty metres from the water and well above the high water mark. Collect water in a bucket from a distance. Crocodiles learn routines, so vary your spot. In boats, keep limbs inside. Canoes and kayaks aren't recommended.

sections.key: Zigzag running is a myth; the real risk is the lunge from the water, so keep your distance and report sightings.
sections.b:
The popular idea is to run in a zigzag because crocodiles can't turn quickly. Experts regard this as a myth. Crocodiles are fast over short distances but rarely chase people away from water. The real risk is the sudden lunge at someone on the bank, wading or swimming. Keep your distance in the first place.

Each state and territory with crocodiles has a way to report sightings, which helps officers decide whether one needs to be removed. Report crocodiles that act aggressively, approach people or boats, or turn up in towns. If someone is attacked, call 000. Don't enter the water yourself. Once they're out, control bleeding with firm direct pressure, keep them warm and lying down, and follow DRSABCD.

quiz.q: How do saltwater crocodiles typically hunt?
o: Chasing prey over long distances on land
Hunting in coordinated packs in open water
Lurking almost submerged, then lunging at the bank
Stalking prey on open ground around midday
quiz.e: Their ambush technique makes the water's edge the danger zone.

quiz.q: What is a consequence of the saltwater crocodile's recovery?
o: Fatal attacks now happen across the north every week
They are now found only in remote wilderness areas
They have disappeared from most northern rivers
More large crocodiles now share waterways with people
quiz.e: Protection worked, so people and crocodiles now meet more often at rivers, beaches and boat ramps.

quiz.q: What is the best rule for water in croc country?
o: Swim only if there are no warning signs
Assume any water may hold a crocodile, sign or not
Swim only in water with a clear bottom
Swim only in freshwater, never in salt water
quiz.e: Salties live in fresh and salt water, and are hard to see, so signs alone aren't enough.

quiz.q: How far from the water should campers set up, according to CrocWise?
o: At least fifty metres back from the water's edge
Within about ten metres, for easy access to water
Right on the sloping bank for a good view of the water
Anywhere, as long as there are no warning signs nearby
quiz.e: Staying back reduces the chance of a crocodile learning your routines or ambushing you.

quiz.q: What do experts say about the zigzag running advice?
o: It is the best way to escape a chasing crocodile
It works only against freshwater crocodiles
It works only when running on soft ground
It is a myth, as the real risk is the lunge
quiz.e: Crocodiles rarely chase people away from water, so prevention beats escape tactics.

LESSONS.push: It's the largest reptile on Earth, and it's not only found where you'd think.

LESSONS.title: Cold water and hypothermia
LESSONS.hook: Many people who die in cold water drown before hypothermia ever sets in. The first minute is the most dangerous, and the instinct to swim hard can be exactly the wrong one.

sections.key: Hypothermia is an Australian risk too, and water pulls heat from the body far faster than air.
sections.b:
Hypothermia isn't only for polar explorers. In Australia, people get into trouble with cold regularly: bushwalkers in Tasmania caught by sudden storms, even in summer, skiers and hikers in the Alps, rock fishers swept into winter seas, and kayakers and boaters who capsize in cold rivers and lakes.

Water is the great accelerator, drawing heat from the body far faster than air at the same temperature. Wind and wet clothing do something similar on land. Add rain, tiredness and inadequate clothing, and a person can become dangerously cold on a seemingly mild day, especially in the mountains, where weather can change within an hour.

sections.key: Falling into cold water triggers an involuntary gasp and rapid breathing that can cause drowning within the first minute.
sections.b:
When a person suddenly falls into cold water, the shock on the skin triggers an involuntary gasp, followed by rapid, uncontrollable breathing, a racing heart and a spike in blood pressure. This cold shock response peaks in the first minute or so.

If your head is underwater during that first gasp, you can inhale water and drown almost immediately, long before the body cools. The racing heart can also trigger heart problems in people at risk. That is why many cold water deaths happen close to shore or a boat, and why even strong swimmers can drown quickly after an unexpected fall.

sections.key: After falling in, float on your back until the cold shock passes, rather than swimming hard.
sections.b:
The instinct is to thrash and swim hard. But swimming and panicking during cold shock makes breathing harder to control and raises the risk of inhaling water. Water safety groups, including Britain's Royal National Lifeboat Institution, now teach: float first.

Lean back, spread your arms and legs, and keep your face out of the water, moving your hands gently if needed, until the gasping and fast breathing settle, typically within a minute or two. Then you can think clearly: signal for help, grab something that floats, or swim to safety if it's close. A lifejacket makes all of this far easier.

The 1-10-1 rule of thumb sums up the timing: roughly one minute to control your breathing, ten minutes of meaningful movement, and an hour or more before unconsciousness.

sections.key: Hypothermia is a core temperature below about 35 degrees, and the person needs shelter, dry layers, gentle handling and a 000 call.
sections.b:
Hypothermia means core temperature has dropped below about 35 degrees Celsius, from a normal of around 37. Early signs are intense shivering, cold pale skin and fumbling hands. Then come the 'umbles': stumbling, mumbling, fumbling and grumbling, with slurred speech and slow, confused thinking. In severe cases shivering stops, a dangerous sign rather than a good one. Watch each other closely, because judgement fades early.

Call 000 for anything beyond mild hypothermia. Move them out of wind, rain or water and handle them gently. Replace wet clothes with dry layers or wrap them in blankets, including head and neck, and insulate from the ground. If alert, give warm sweet drinks, never alcohol. Don't rub limbs or use a hot bath. Start CPR if they stop breathing normally.

sections.key: Don't enter the water to rescue someone: call 000 and reach or throw them something that floats.
sections.b:
Each year people drown trying to rescue others, often family members, including children and dogs. The safest approach is reach or throw, don't go.

Call 000. Then reach the person from a safe position with a pole, branch, rope or towel, lying down on the bank for balance, or throw something that floats, such as a lifebuoy, an esky, a bodyboard or a ball. Tell them to float on their back and keep calm. Only trained rescuers with proper equipment should enter the water, especially if it's cold or fast-flowing.

Prevention is simpler: wear a lifejacket when boating or rock fishing, dress in layers, check the forecast and tell someone where you're going.

quiz.q: Why does cold water chill the body so much faster than air?
o: It is always colder than the air around it
It stops the body from shivering properly
It draws heat from the body far faster than air
It reacts with the natural oils on the skin
quiz.e: Water pulls heat out quickly, so cold water is dangerous even on a mild day.

quiz.q: What makes cold water shock so deadly in the first minute?
o: Core temperature plunges within seconds
An involuntary gasp can let you inhale water
Blood stops flowing to the brain at once
The muscles lock up the instant you land
quiz.e: The gasp reflex can cause drowning long before the body cools.

quiz.q: What should you do first after falling into cold water?
o: Swim hard straight towards the nearest shore
Take off your heavy clothes straight away
Tread water with your head tilted forward
Float on your back until your breathing settles
quiz.e: Floating lets the cold shock pass so you can think and act clearly.

quiz.q: Why is it a dangerous sign when a hypothermic person stops shivering?
o: It can mean hypothermia has become severe
It means the person is starting to warm up
It shows the cold shock has now passed
It means they should be given cold drinks
quiz.e: Shivering stopping can signal that the body is losing its ability to cope with the cold.

quiz.q: How should you help someone in trouble in cold water?
o: Swim out and carry them back to shore
Jump in with a rope tied around yourself
Call 000, then reach or throw them a float
Wait for them to swim to shore themselves
quiz.e: Reach or throw, don't go, because rescuers often drown too.

LESSONS.push: Many cold water deaths come before the body cools. The first minute is the danger.

LESSONS.title: First on the scene of a car crash
LESSONS.hook: One day you may be the first person to arrive at a crash. What you do in the first few minutes, starting with protecting yourself, can decide how many people go home.

sections.key: Make yourself safe before approaching a crash, because the scene is often dangerous for rescuers.
sections.b: The instinct is to rush to the wreckage. But traffic is still moving, drivers are distracted, and visibility may be poor. Rescuers are sometimes struck by other vehicles. Start by making yourself safe. Slow down and park well clear of the crash, ideally off the road. Turn on your hazard lights. If it's dark, wear something bright or use a torch, and set up a reflective triangle well back if you have one. Keep children and passengers in your car or well away from the road. Then assess the scene before approaching.

sections.key: Call 000 early and give your location first, then describe the crash and stay on the line.
sections.b:
Call Triple Zero (000) as early as possible, or ask a bystander to call while you check on people. The most important information is where you are. Look for road names, cross streets, kilometre markers, landmarks or direction of travel. The free Emergency+ app, developed by Australia's emergency services, shows your GPS coordinates to read out.

Then describe the crash: how many vehicles, how many injured, whether anyone is trapped, unconscious or bleeding badly, and whether there's fuel leaking, smoke or fire. Stay on the line; the operator can guide you through first aid.

sections.key: Look for fuel, fire, powerlines and unstable cars before approaching, and leave high-voltage parts to the crews.
sections.b:
Before approaching, look for dangers. Is there spilt fuel, smoke or fire? Fallen powerlines, which could make the vehicle and ground dangerous? Is the car unstable, on its side or on a slope? Is traffic still flowing?

If it's safe, ask occupants to turn off the ignition, or do it yourself if you can without risk, and make sure nobody smokes nearby. Don't approach a vehicle with powerlines on it; stay at least eight metres away and warn others. Electric and hybrid vehicles can carry high-voltage components, so leave anything beyond basic first aid to emergency crews. If you can't make it safe, stay back and wait.

sections.key: Leave injured people where they are unless there's immediate danger, but keep the airway open for anyone unresponsive.
sections.b:
People in a crash may have hidden neck or spine injuries, and movement could make them worse. As a rule, leave injured people where they are and keep them still. Support their head if they're conscious and it's comfortable. Reassure them that help is coming and ask them not to move their head. The exception is immediate danger: fire, rising water or traffic. Then getting them out matters more. Keep head, neck and body aligned as best you can.

If someone is unresponsive, the airway is often the biggest threat. Australian guidelines say keeping it open outranks the possibility of spinal injury. Follow DRSABCD. If they're breathing, support the airway and roll them onto their side if needed. If not, they need CPR.

sections.key: Leave a motorcyclist's helmet on unless it blocks airway management, and remember that drivers involved must stop and help.
sections.b:
Should you remove a motorcyclist's helmet? Generally, leave it on. It may support a neck injury, and incorrect removal could cause harm. If the rider is conscious and breathing, open the visor, talk to them and keep them still. The helmet only comes off if it stops you managing their airway or breathing, for example with vomiting or CPR. Ideally two people do it: one supports the head and neck, the other gently spreads the helmet and eases it off.

Australian road rules require drivers in a crash to stop, help anyone injured and exchange details. Witnesses are not usually obliged to stay, but their account helps. It's normal to feel shaken afterwards. A first aid course is the best preparation.

quiz.q: Why should you park well clear of a crash and turn on hazard lights?
o: It stops fuel leaking from the crashed cars
It warns approaching drivers and protects rescuers
It switches off the crashed cars' engines
It makes the scene easier to photograph
quiz.e: Protecting yourself first means you can help without becoming another casualty.

quiz.q: What is the most important information to give the 000 operator?
o: The make of the cars
Who caused the crash
Exactly where you are
The number plates
quiz.e: Responders can't help until they know where to go.

quiz.q: Why should you stay well back from a vehicle with a powerline on it?
o: Its doors lock to trap anyone close by
The fuel inside will certainly ignite
The line's weight could crush the vehicle
The car and the ground near it may be live
quiz.e: Fallen lines can energise the vehicle and the ground around it, so stay at least eight metres away.

quiz.q: When should you move an injured person from a crash?
o: As soon as you reach them and check them
When fire or traffic puts them in danger
Whenever they say they feel able to sit up
Only once the police have arrived on scene
quiz.e: Escaping an immediate threat outweighs the risk from a possible spinal injury.

quiz.q: What is the general advice for an injured motorcyclist's helmet?
o: Always take it off straight away
Cut it off as the very first step
Leave it on unless it blocks their airway
Remove it only after the ambulance arrives
quiz.e: The helmet may support a neck injury, so remove it only when airway care requires it.

LESSONS.push: The first minutes at a car crash may depend on a step most people skip.

LESSONS.title: How people really behave in disasters
LESSONS.hook: We imagine stampedes and mass panic. Decades of research tell a stranger story: in a crisis, the real danger is often that people stay calm, slow and polite for far too long.

sections.key: Mass panic is rare in disasters; people mostly stay calm and help each other.
sections.b:
Films show crowds screaming and trampling one another. Real disasters rarely look like that. From the 1950s, sociologists such as Enrico Quarantelli studied fires, floods, earthquakes and bombings and found that true mass panic, meaning wild, selfish flight, is uncommon. Most people stay orderly. Strangers help strangers, families stick together, and survivors are usually the first rescuers, pulling neighbours from rubble long before professionals arrive.

Fatal crowd crushes do happen, but investigators usually blame overcrowding and poor crowd management, not people losing their minds. The myth does harm too, because it can make authorities reluctant to share frightening information quickly.

sections.key: The real danger in a crisis is delay: we explain warnings away, then wait for others to act first.
sections.b:
If panic is not the problem, delay is. When an alarm sounds or smoke appears, we first assume a drill, a false alarm or burnt toast. This is normalcy bias. It usually serves us well, because most alarms are false, but in a real emergency those minutes matter. People in burning buildings have finished meals and waited for lifts.

Even once we accept something is wrong, we seek information first: phoning family, asking colleagues, scanning social media. Researchers call this milling. If everyone waits for everyone else, each person reads the calm around them as proof of safety. Studies of the World Trade Center evacuation on 11 September 2001 found many survivors delayed leaving to make calls or gather belongings.

sections.key: Under extreme stress some people freeze, and clear, loud, simple instructions often get them moving.
sections.b:
A third response is freezing. Under sudden, overwhelming stress, some people become stuck, unable to decide or move. This is not cowardice. It reflects the brain struggling to process an unfamiliar situation quickly enough. Survivors of plane crashes and shipwrecks describe fellow passengers sitting motionless as fire or water approached.

The British psychologist John Leach, who studied survival behaviour, has suggested that only a minority of people respond quickly and effectively in a sudden crisis, that most are bewildered for a time, and that a small minority behave in counterproductive ways. The exact proportions are debated, but the pattern is widely recognised. The practical lesson is that people who freeze often respond well to clear, loud, simple instructions from someone else.

sections.key: Rehearsal and following instructions save lives, because under stress the brain falls back on what it has practised.
sections.b:
Rick Rescorla, a former soldier, headed security for Morgan Stanley at the World Trade Center. After the 1993 bombing he was sure the towers would be attacked again, so he made staff practise stairwell evacuations despite their grumbling. On 11 September 2001 he ignored advice to stay put and ordered them out of the South Tower. Almost all of the firm's roughly 2,700 staff there survived. He went back inside to help others and was killed when the tower collapsed.

Aircraft are designed to be emptied in about 90 seconds, but only if people carry nothing. On 2 January 2024 at Tokyo's Haneda Airport, all 379 people escaped a burning Japan Airlines A350, widely credited to crew training and passengers leaving their bags behind.

sections.key: Know your exits, decide what you will do in advance, and act early on any warning.
sections.b:
A few habits help. When you enter a hotel, theatre, plane or new workplace, notice the nearest exits and count the rows or doors to them, because smoke makes it hard to see. Decide in advance, while calm: if a fire alarm sounds, you leave immediately; on a severe bushfire day, you leave early rather than wait and see. Practise household fire escape plans.

Treat any warning as real until proven otherwise. An unnecessary evacuation costs little, while a late one can cost everything. Your phone and bag can be replaced. And in a crisis, be the person who says, clearly and calmly, we need to go now.

quiz.q: What have disaster researchers found about mass panic?
o: It is the main cause of deaths in disasters
It is rare, and most people stay calm and help others
It happens in nearly every fire, but only briefly
It is common in crowds but rare among families
quiz.e: Studies of real disasters show calm, cooperative behaviour is far more common than wild, selfish flight.

quiz.q: Why can milling be dangerous in an emergency?
o: It makes people run in circles and trample each other
Everyone waits on others, and calm looks like safety
It sends crowds towards the nearest exit all at once
It spreads rumours that can set off a stampede
quiz.e: When no one moves, each person takes the group's calm as evidence that there is no danger.

quiz.q: What often helps a person who has frozen during a crisis?
o: Being left alone to calm down
Waiting quietly until they decide for themselves
Clear, loud, simple instructions from someone else
A detailed explanation of what is happening
quiz.e: Freezing reflects a brain struggling to process the situation, so short, direct instructions can break it.

quiz.q: Why did regular evacuation drills help Morgan Stanley's staff on 11 September 2001?
o: People under stress fall back on what they have practised
Drills made the stairwells wider and safer
Drills taught staff to wait for official advice
Practice removes all fear in an emergency
quiz.e: Rehearsal turns a confusing emergency into a routine the brain can follow.

quiz.q: What is the best response when a fire alarm sounds in a building?
o: Check social media first to confirm it is real
Finish what you are doing, then leave if it continues
Treat it as real and leave at once
Wait for others nearby to start moving
quiz.e: An unnecessary evacuation costs little, while a late one can cost everything.

LESSONS.push: Panic is rare in disasters. The real danger is something much quieter.

LESSONS.title: Solid, liquid, gas … and stranger things
LESSONS.hook: School taught us three states of matter. Nature has more, including one that fills the stars and one that was only made in a lab in 1995.

sections.key: Solids, liquids and gases differ in how freely their particles move.
sections.b: Everything is made of atoms and molecules that never stop moving. In a solid, they are locked in place and can only vibrate, which is why a brick keeps its shape. In a liquid, they are still packed closely but can slide past one another, so water takes the shape of its container. In a gas, they fly about freely, bouncing off each other and the walls, with mostly empty space between them. The molecules in the air you are breathing travel at roughly 500 metres per second, faster than a passenger jet, colliding with each other billions of times every second.

sections.key: Substances melt, boil or sublimate when their particles gain enough energy to break free, and boiling depends on air pressure.
sections.b:
Heat a solid and its particles vibrate harder until they break out of their fixed places and it melts. Keep heating and some escape as a gas. While ice melts, its temperature stays at 0°C, because the energy goes into breaking the bonds holding particles in place rather than making them move faster.

Boiling also depends on the air pressure above. Water boils at 100°C at sea level but only around 70°C on the summit of Mount Everest, which makes a decent cup of tea surprisingly hard. Some substances skip the liquid stage. Dry ice, which is frozen carbon dioxide, turns straight into gas, a change called sublimation.

sections.key: Glass is a rigid amorphous solid that does not flow, whereas pitch really is an extremely slow liquid.
sections.b:
Glass has jumbled atoms like a liquid yet is rigid, so scientists call it an amorphous solid. The story that old windows are thicker at the bottom because glass flowed over centuries is a myth. Old panes were spun or blown unevenly, and glaziers often fitted the thick edge down. At room temperature, glass would take far longer than the age of the universe to sag visibly.

Pitch, a tar-like substance that shatters under a hammer, truly flows. In 1927 Professor Thomas Parnell at the University of Queensland poured heated pitch into a funnel and, three years later, cut its stem open. A drop takes the best part of a decade to fall, and fewer than a dozen have. A camera set up in 2000 failed at the crucial moment.

sections.key: Plasma is a gas so hot its atoms are torn apart, while a Bose–Einstein condensate forms just above absolute zero.
sections.b:
Heat a gas enough and collisions knock electrons off their atoms. The result is plasma, a mix of free electrons and positive ions that conducts electricity and responds strongly to magnetic fields. Lightning, neon signs, auroras and every star, including the Sun, are plasma, so most of the ordinary visible matter in the universe is thought to be in this state.

At the other extreme, Bose and Einstein predicted in the 1920s that atoms cooled near absolute zero would fall into one quantum state and act as a single giant wave. In 1995 Eric Cornell and Carl Wieman in Colorado cooled rubidium atoms to around 170 billionths of a degree above absolute zero and made one. They shared the 2001 Nobel Prize in Physics with Wolfgang Ketterle.

sections.key: Solid, liquid and gas are human labels, and many materials refuse to fit neatly into one.
sections.b: Mix cornflour with water and you get oobleck, a goo that pours like a liquid but turns firm when you punch it or run across it. Scientists call it a non-Newtonian fluid, because its thickness changes with the force applied. Liquid crystals flow like a liquid but line up in an orderly way like a crystal, and turning them with electric fields is how many screens control light. Sand and grain can pour through a funnel like water, yet hold up a person standing on a beach. Nature is under no obligation to follow the labels people invented.

quiz.q: In which state are particles packed closely but able to slide past one another?
o: Solid
Liquid
Gas
Plasma
quiz.e: Liquid particles touch but are not locked in place, so liquids take the shape of their container.

quiz.q: Why does water boil at a lower temperature on top of Mount Everest?
o: The air pressure is much lower
The water there is purer
The air contains less oxygen
The mountain's rocks are colder
quiz.e: Boiling depends on the pressure above the liquid, and the air at that height presses far less.

quiz.q: Why are some old window panes thicker at the bottom?
o: Glass slowly flows downwards over centuries
Gravity gradually compresses glass over time
They were made unevenly and fitted thick edge down
Rain leaves mineral deposits along the bottom edge
quiz.e: Glass at room temperature does not flow noticeably, so the uneven thickness came from how old panes were made.

quiz.q: What is plasma?
o: A thick liquid found inside stars
A gas so hot its atoms split into ions
A solid with no regular crystal pattern
A gas cooled close to absolute zero
quiz.e: Extreme heat strips electrons from atoms, and the charged mixture behaves unlike an ordinary gas.

quiz.q: Why does oobleck count as an in-between material?
o: It melts at room temperature
It is made from only one type of atom
Its thickness changes with applied force
It alternates between a gas and a solid
quiz.e: A non-Newtonian fluid like oobleck pours like a liquid but turns firm under sudden force.

LESSONS.push: Ice stays at 0 degrees while it melts, even as you heat it. Where does the energy go?

LESSONS.title: Air pressure: the weight of the sky
LESSONS.hook: Right now the air is pressing on you with the weight of about ten tonnes on every square metre. Here's why you don't notice, and how people first worked it out.

sections.key: Air has weight, and the atmosphere presses on everything, but we are not crushed because the pressure is balanced.
sections.b: Air feels like nothing, but it is made of real molecules with real mass, and there are many kilometres of it stacked above your head. At sea level, that weight presses on every surface with a force of roughly ten tonnes per square metre, about 101 kilopascals. So why aren't we flattened? Because air pressure pushes in every direction at once, not just downward, and the fluids and air inside your body push back outward with equal force. Everything is balanced. You only notice when that balance is suddenly upset, for example when your ears pop in a lift, or when a sealed packet of chips puffs up on a flight.

sections.key: Torricelli showed that the weight of the air can hold up a column of mercury, which led to the barometer.
sections.b: In the early 1600s, well diggers and engineers knew a frustrating fact. Suction pumps could not raise water more than about ten metres, however well they were built. Evangelista Torricelli, a former assistant to Galileo, suspected the weight of the air was the answer. In 1643 he filled a long glass tube with mercury, which is about 13.6 times denser than water, covered the open end and turned it upside down into a dish of mercury. The column dropped until it stood about 76 centimetres high, leaving an empty space at the top. The air pressing on the dish was holding the mercury up. Torricelli had made the first barometer, and he noticed the height changed slightly from day to day.

sections.key: A barometer carried up a mountain showed lower pressure at height, proving that pressure comes from the air above.
sections.b: The French thinker Blaise Pascal reasoned that if the atmosphere really had weight, less of it should press down at the top of a mountain. In 1648 he persuaded his brother-in-law, Florin Périer, to test the idea on the Puy de Dôme, a volcanic peak in central France. Périer left one mercury tube at the bottom with a watcher and carried another to the summit, about a kilometre higher. At the top, the mercury column was several centimetres shorter. Coming down, it rose again. It was a beautifully simple experiment that settled the question. Today the unit of pressure, the pascal, honours Pascal, and aircraft altimeters still work by measuring this same fall in pressure with height.

sections.key: What looks like suction is really the atmosphere pushing, because a vacuum cannot pull anything.
sections.b:
Around 1650, Otto von Guericke, scientist and mayor of Magdeburg, built one of the first air pumps. He fitted two copper hemispheres about half a metre across together with only a greased rim between them, then pumped out the air. The atmosphere outside clamped the halves together. Accounts describe two teams of horses failing to pull the sphere apart, yet when air was let back in, the halves simply fell open.

It is the same when you drink through a straw. You lower the pressure inside your mouth, and the normal air pressure on the drink's surface pushes it up. Suction cups work the same way. That also explains the old pump puzzle: the atmosphere can push water up only about ten metres, because that is the height of water column it can balance.

sections.key: Differences in air pressure drive the weather, speed up cooking and shape how aircraft cabins work.
sections.b:
Air pressure changes from place to place, and those differences drive the weather. High pressure usually brings sinking air and settled, clear skies, while low pressure brings rising air, cloud and often rain. Wind is air moving from higher pressure towards lower, which is why the curved lines on a weather map, called isobars, are so useful.

Pressure also changes how we cook. A pressure cooker traps steam, raising the pressure so water boils at around 120°C and food cooks much faster. And at an airliner's cruising height, the outside air is far too thin to breathe for long, so cabins are pressurised to a level similar to being on a mountain a couple of kilometres high.

quiz.q: Why aren't we crushed by the weight of the atmosphere?
o: Air is too light to matter at ground level
Gravity cancels most of the air pressure out
Our skin is strong enough to resist the force
Air pushes all ways and we push back
quiz.e: Pressure inside and outside the body is balanced, so we feel nothing until that balance is upset.

quiz.q: What did Torricelli's mercury tube experiment show?
o: Air has no weight near ground level
Air has weight and supports mercury
Mercury turns to gas in a vacuum
Water is denser than liquid mercury
quiz.e: The mercury stayed up because the atmosphere pressed on the dish, which made the first barometer.

quiz.q: What happened to the mercury column at the top of the Puy de Dôme?
o: It was taller, as the air was colder there
It stayed exactly the same
It was shorter, with less air above
It froze solid in the cold
quiz.e: Less atmosphere above means lower pressure, which holds up a shorter mercury column.

quiz.q: What actually moves a drink up a straw?
o: Your mouth pulling the drink upward
Air pressure pushing on the drink's surface
The vacuum attracting the liquid
Surface tension inside the straw
quiz.e: A vacuum cannot pull, so the surrounding atmosphere does the pushing.

quiz.q: What does low air pressure usually bring?
o: Sinking air and clear, settled skies
Stronger winds that blow only upward
Rising air, cloud and often rain
Lower boiling points in kitchens
quiz.e: Low pressure means rising air, which tends to form cloud and rain.

LESSONS.push: Ten tonnes of air press on every square metre around you. Why aren't you flattened?

LESSONS.title: Viruses: life's tiny hijackers
LESSONS.hook: They can't eat, grow or reproduce on their own, yet they outnumber the stars in the observable universe and have left their fingerprints all over your DNA.

sections.key: A virus is genetic instructions in a protein coat that hijacks a cell to copy itself.
sections.b:
A virus is astonishingly simple: a short set of genetic instructions, in DNA or RNA, inside a protein shell called a capsid. Some, like flu and coronaviruses, add a fatty envelope taken from the last cell they infected. It has no machinery to make energy, build proteins or copy itself, and most are far smaller than bacteria, measured in tens to hundreds of nanometres.

So it hijacks a cell. Surface proteins fit particular receptors on particular cells, like a key in a lock. The COVID-19 virus uses its spike protein to latch onto a receptor called ACE2. Inside, the cell reads the viral genes as its own and builds new viruses, which burst out or bud off, ready to infect neighbours. One cell can release thousands.

sections.key: Viruses were discovered because they passed through filters fine enough to trap bacteria.
sections.b: In 1892, the Russian scientist Dmitri Ivanovsky studied a disease that left tobacco leaves blotchy. He passed sap from sick plants through a fine porcelain filter meant to trap bacteria. To his surprise, the filtered sap could still infect healthy plants. In 1898 the Dutch microbiologist Martinus Beijerinck repeated the work and concluded that something new was at play, an infectious agent much smaller than any bacterium that could only multiply inside living cells. He used the Latin word virus, meaning poison or slimy liquid. Tobacco mosaic virus became the first virus identified, and later one of the first photographed, once electron microscopes produced clear images in the late 1930s.

sections.key: Viruses evolve like living things but cannot metabolise or reproduce alone, so scientists still debate whether they are alive.
sections.b:
Outside a cell, a virus is inert. It doesn't eat, breathe, grow or respond to anything, and some can sit on a surface like a speck of dust. Many textbook definitions of life require an organism to run its own metabolism and reproduce by itself, and viruses fail both tests.

Yet inside a cell they multiply furiously, and they clearly evolve by natural selection, the hallmark of living systems. Their genes mutate, and the versions best at spreading come to dominate, which is why new flu vaccines are needed most years. Some biologists place viruses on the edge of life, while others argue they deserve a branch of their own. There is no single agreed answer.

sections.key: Most viruses on Earth infect bacteria, and a few giant viruses are bigger than some bacteria.
sections.b:
The vast majority of viruses infect bacteria, not us. These are called bacteriophages, meaning bacteria eaters, and many look like tiny lunar landers, with a head and spidery legs that inject DNA into a bacterium. Scientists estimate there are around ten million trillion trillion viruses on Earth, far more than the stars in the observable universe. Most float in the oceans, where they kill a large share of marine bacteria every day, releasing nutrients that feed other life.

Then there are the giants. Mimivirus, identified in 2003 inside amoebae, was so large that researchers first mistook it for a bacterium. It even carries genes once thought unique to cellular life.

sections.key: About eight per cent of human DNA is viral leftovers, while vaccines and antivirals, not antibiotics, protect us from viruses.
sections.b:
Retroviruses, such as HIV, insert their genes into the DNA of the cells they infect. When ancestors' egg or sperm cells were infected, those genes passed to every later generation. Roughly eight per cent of the human genome is now these viral fossils, far more than the small fraction that codes for proteins. Most are silent, but a retrovirus-derived gene called syncytin helps form a key layer of the placenta.

Antibiotics attack structures that bacteria have and viruses lack, so they do nothing against a cold or flu, and taking them needlessly can encourage resistant bacteria. Instead we rely on the immune system, vaccines and antiviral drugs. Smallpox, which killed hundreds of millions of people in the twentieth century, was declared eradicated in 1980.

quiz.q: Why can't a virus reproduce on its own?
o: It lacks genetic material of its own
It cannot make energy or proteins itself
It is too large to enter a cell
It is destroyed whenever it meets air
quiz.e: A virus carries instructions only, so it must borrow a cell's machinery to make copies.

quiz.q: What first suggested to scientists that something smaller than bacteria could cause disease?
o: It was seen under a light microscope
It glowed under ultraviolet light
It grew on a dish of nutrient jelly
Filtered sap could still infect healthy plants
quiz.e: The infectious agent passed through a filter fine enough to stop bacteria, so it had to be smaller.

quiz.q: Why do many scientists hesitate to call viruses fully alive?
o: They cannot mutate or evolve in any way
They carry no genetic material of any kind
They need a host to metabolise or multiply
They are never found inside living cells
quiz.e: Viruses evolve like living things but depend entirely on a host cell to function and reproduce.

quiz.q: Which kind of virus is by far the most common on Earth?
o: Those that infect bacteria
Those that infect humans
Those that infect plants
Those that infect fish
quiz.e: Bacteriophages vastly outnumber viruses that infect animals, and they shape marine life.

quiz.q: Why won't antibiotics cure the flu?
o: Flu is too mild for any treatment to work
Flu viruses are too big for the drugs
Viruses lack what antibiotics attack
Antibiotics only work against fungi
quiz.e: Antibiotics target features of bacteria, so against viruses they do nothing and encourage resistance.

LESSONS.push: Viruses may not be alive, yet they've left their mark in your DNA. Here's how.

LESSONS.title: Why things float
LESSONS.hook: A steel ship weighing tens of thousands of tonnes floats, yet a small pebble sinks. The explanation goes back to a Greek genius, and possibly a bath.

sections.key: The famous bath story is probably more legend than history, but the principle behind it is real.
sections.b:
The tale goes that King Hiero II of Syracuse suspected his goldsmith had mixed silver into a gold crown. He asked Archimedes to find out without damaging it. Stepping into a bath, Archimedes noticed the water rise, realised he could measure the crown's volume by the water it displaced, and ran through the streets shouting ‘Eureka’, meaning ‘I have found it’.

The trouble is that the Roman architect Vitruvius wrote the story down about two centuries after Archimedes died, and some historians doubt it. Galileo pointed out that the overflow method would be too imprecise for a crown, and suggested Archimedes more likely used a balance and his principle of buoyancy. Either way, the principle is enormously useful.

sections.key: An object in a fluid is pushed up by a force equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces.
sections.b: Archimedes wrote a treatise called On Floating Bodies, and its central idea is now known as Archimedes' principle. When an object sits in water, it pushes some water out of the way. The surrounding water pushes back, creating an upward force called buoyancy, equal to the weight of the water displaced. If the object weighs less than the water it can displace, it floats. If it weighs more, it sinks, though it still feels lighter, which is why you can lift a friend easily in a swimming pool. The principle works for any fluid, liquid or gas. It explains why a log bobs on a river and why a helium balloon rises through the heavier air around it.

sections.key: A ship floats because its hull encloses air and displaces a volume of water that weighs as much as the ship.
sections.b:
Steel is about eight times denser than water, so a solid block of it sinks instantly. Hammer the same steel into a bowl shape, though, and it can float. The hull encloses a huge volume of air. As the ship settles into the water, it pushes aside water and sinks lower until the weight of the water displaced exactly equals the ship's own weight. At that point it floats.

This is also why a ship sits lower when loaded with cargo, because it must push aside more water to balance the extra weight. Punch a hole in the hull and let water replace the air, and the balance is lost.

sections.key: The denser the water, the easier it is to float, which is why ships carry several load lines.
sections.b:
In nineteenth-century Britain, some owners overloaded old, overinsured ships so heavily that they sank with their crews. Sailors called them coffin ships. MP Samuel Plimsoll campaigned against the practice, and the Merchant Shipping Act of 1876 made load line markings compulsory. The Plimsoll line shows how deep a ship may safely sit. Modern versions have several marks because fresh water is less dense than seawater, and warm water is less dense than cold.

The same idea explains why you float more easily in the sea than in a pool, and why an egg sinks in tap water but floats in very salty water. The Dead Sea, on the border of Israel, Jordan and the West Bank, is several times saltier than the ocean, so swimmers bob like they're lying on a lilo.

sections.key: Machines and animals rise and sink by changing their density through ballast, swim bladders or heated air.
sections.b:
A submarine floats on the surface until it opens its ballast tanks and lets seawater in. Heavier now, it sinks. To rise, it uses compressed air to blow the water back out. Many bony fish manage the same trick with a swim bladder, a gas-filled sac they inflate or deflate to hover at a chosen depth without constantly swimming.

Buoyancy works in air too. Heating air makes it expand and become less dense, so a hot air balloon is pushed upward by the cooler, denser air around it. On 21 November 1783, a balloon built by the Montgolfier brothers carried two men across Paris, in the first free flight with people on board. Your own body is close to the density of water, which is why a deep breath of air helps you float.

quiz.q: Why do some historians doubt the famous ‘Eureka’ story?
o: It was recorded about two centuries later
Baths did not exist in ancient Greece
Archimedes never lived in Syracuse
Gold crowns were never made in that era
quiz.e: The earliest account comes long after the event, and a crown's volume is hard to measure by overflow.

quiz.q: According to Archimedes' principle, the upward force on an object in a fluid equals what?
o: The volume of the object itself
The weight of the fluid it displaces
The depth of the water around it
The surface area of the object
quiz.e: Buoyancy equals the weight of fluid pushed aside, so an object floats if it weighs less than that.

quiz.q: Why can a steel ship float when a solid steel block sinks?
o: Ship steel is lighter than ordinary steel
Seawater is denser than any steel
Its hull holds air and displaces much water
Its engines hold it up in the water
quiz.e: Shape spreads the ship's weight over enough displaced water to balance it.

quiz.q: Why does a ship's Plimsoll line have several marks?
o: Water density varies with salt and warmth
Different cargoes each need their own mark
Crew numbers change how low a ship sits
The time of day changes how deep a ship floats
quiz.e: Fresh and warm water are less dense than salty or cold water, so a ship sits lower in them.

quiz.q: How does a submarine dive?
o: By spinning its propeller backwards
By flooding its ballast tanks
By pumping air into its tanks
By cooling its outer hull
quiz.e: Adding water makes the submarine heavier than the water it displaces, so it sinks.

LESSONS.push: A steel ship floats while a pebble sinks. The answer is about shape, not weight.

LESSONS.title: Static electricity: sparks from nowhere
LESSONS.hook: That zap from a car door or a supermarket trolley is the same force that gave electricity its name, and it runs the printer in your office.

sections.key: The word electricity comes from the Greek word for amber, which attracts small objects when rubbed.
sections.b: Ancient Greeks noticed that amber, the golden fossilised tree resin, attracted bits of straw, feathers and dust when rubbed with fur or wool. Tradition credits the philosopher Thales of Miletus, around 600 BC, with describing this, though nothing he wrote survives. The Greek word for amber was elektron. Almost two thousand years later, in 1600, the English physician William Gilbert showed in a book on magnetism that many other materials, like glass and sulfur, behaved the same way. He called them electricus, Latin for like amber. From that root came the word electricity, so every power point in your home carries an echo of a lump of ancient resin.

sections.key: Rubbing two materials moves electrons from one to the other, and the charged objects then attract or repel.
sections.b:
Atoms contain positive protons and negative electrons, normally in balance. When two different materials touch and rub, electrons can transfer from one to the other. The one that gains electrons becomes negative and the other positive. Scientists rank materials by this tendency in the triboelectric series. Opposite charges attract and like charges repel.

Rub a balloon on your jumper and it sticks to a wall, even though the wall is neutral. The negative balloon pushes electrons in the wall's surface slightly away and draws positive charge closer, and the nearer attraction wins. This is induction. Put your hand on a Van de Graaff generator and your hairs all share one charge, repel and stand up. Physicists still don't fully understand how charge moves in contact.

sections.key: Static shocks happen when built-up charge jumps to a conductor, and they are worse in dry air.
sections.b:
Walking across carpet in rubber-soled shoes, or sliding across a car seat, can build up several thousand volts on your body. Nothing happens until you reach for something metal, like a door handle. Then the charge jumps the gap in a tiny spark, and you feel the zap. Despite the high voltage, the shock is harmless because the amount of charge is tiny and the current lasts a fraction of a second.

Shocks are far more common in dry conditions, such as cold winter days or air-conditioned offices. In humid air, a thin film of moisture lets charge leak away before it can build up. A simple trick is to touch metal with a key first, so the spark jumps from the key.

sections.key: Photocopiers, laser printers, pollution filters and paint sprayers all use static electricity.
sections.b:
In 1938, American patent lawyer Chester Carlson, tired of copying documents by hand, made the first dry copy using static electricity in a makeshift lab in Queens, New York. His process, later called xerography, took years to find a backer but became the basis of the photocopier and the laser printer. Inside, light creates a pattern of charge on a drum, powdery toner sticks only to the charged areas, and heat fuses it onto paper.

Static also cleans the air. Electrostatic precipitators, developed in the early twentieth century, charge smoke particles in chimneys so they are drawn onto collecting plates. Car makers use the same idea to spray paint evenly onto charged car bodies.

sections.key: A tiny static spark can ignite fuel vapour or dust and can quietly destroy electronics.
sections.b:
Most shocks are merely annoying, but a spark in the wrong place can start a fire. Petrol gives off flammable vapour, and fuel stations warn people not to get back into their car while refuelling, because sliding across the seat can build up charge that may spark at the nozzle. Touching the metal body of the car before handling the nozzle helps discharge you safely. If a fire starts, move away and call 000.

Fine dust from flour, sugar or grain can explode if a spark ignites a dense cloud of it, which is why factories and silos manage static carefully. Electronics are vulnerable too. A discharge too small for you to feel can still damage a microchip, so technicians often wear grounding wrist straps.

quiz.q: Where does the word electricity come from?
o: The Greek word for amber
The Latin word for lightning
The Greek word for spark
The English word for charge
quiz.e: Amber attracted small objects when rubbed, and the Greek word for it gave electricity its name.

quiz.q: Why does a charged balloon stick to a neutral wall?
o: The wall carries the opposite charge permanently
Static electricity works like glue on smooth walls
The wall's electrons all jump onto the balloon
Charges in the wall shift and attract the balloon
quiz.e: Induction shifts charges inside the wall, leaving opposite charge nearest the balloon.

quiz.q: Why are static shocks more common in dry air?
o: Moisture in humid air drains charge away
Dry air carries more electrons
Cold air makes metal hold more charge
Dry air is a better conductor of charge
quiz.e: A thin film of moisture on surfaces drains charge before it can build up into a spark.

quiz.q: How does a laser printer put toner on the page?
o: Heat makes the toner stick to the drum
Toner clings to charged areas of the drum
A magnet pulls the toner onto the paper
The toner is dissolved in a wet ink
quiz.e: Light makes a charge pattern on the drum, and charged areas pick up toner, which heat then fuses to paper.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid sliding across your car seat while refuelling?
o: It can scratch the seat and the fuel gauge
It can build up a spark near petrol vapour
It makes the pump deliver fuel too fast
It can damage the car's electronic systems
quiz.e: A small spark near flammable vapour can start a fire, so touch the car's metal body before handling the nozzle.

LESSONS.push: The word electricity comes from a lump of golden resin. Here is the story.

LESSONS.title: Plastics: the miracle material
LESSONS.hook: Plastics went from a Victorian curiosity to something found in the deepest ocean trench in barely a century. It's a story of long molecules, lucky accidents and an unsolved problem.

sections.key: Plastics are polymers, giant molecules built from thousands of small repeating units, which chemists can tune.
sections.b:
The word polymer comes from Greek for ‘many parts’. A polymer is a giant molecule made by linking small building blocks, called monomers, into long chains, often thousands of units long. Polyethylene, the plastic in shopping bags and milk bottles, is the small molecule ethylene joined end to end over and over.

Nature made polymers long before chemists did. Silk, rubber, wool, the cellulose in wood and paper, and even your own DNA are polymers. What makes synthetic plastics so useful is that chemists can tune them. By choosing different monomers, chain lengths and links between chains, they can make materials that are soft or rigid, clear or coloured, stretchy or tough.

sections.key: Plastics began with altered natural materials in the 1860s, and several key ones were found by accident before World War II.
sections.b:
The first plastics were chemically altered natural materials. Alexander Parkes showed Parkesine, made from cellulose, in London in 1862. John Wesley Hyatt developed celluloid around 1870, partly in a search for an ivory substitute for billiard balls, and it later became early film, though it was dangerously flammable. In 1907 Leo Baekeland created Bakelite, the first fully synthetic plastic: hard, heat resistant and insulating, it went into radios and telephones.

In 1933, ICI chemists Eric Fawcett and Reginald Gibson found a waxy solid, polyethylene, in a high-pressure vessel; it soon insulated wartime radar cables. In 1938 Roy Plunkett at DuPont found a slippery powder in an apparently empty cylinder, which became Teflon. Wallace Carothers' nylon stockings sensationally went on sale in 1940, then went to war as parachutes and ropes.

sections.key: Thermoplastics can be melted and reshaped, thermosets cannot, and the number in the recycling triangle is not a promise of recycling.
sections.b:
Thermoplastics have long tangled chains that slide past one another when heated, so they soften and can be moulded again. Polyethylene, polypropylene, PVC and PET (drink bottles) are thermoplastics, which makes recycling by melting possible. Thermosets, such as Bakelite, epoxy glue and fibreglass resin, form chemical cross-links as they set into one rigid network. They char rather than melt, which makes them tough and very hard to recycle.

The number from 1 to 7 inside a triangle of arrows, introduced in the United States in 1988, only identifies the plastic: 1 is PET, 2 is high-density polyethylene, 5 is polypropylene, 7 is everything else. It is not a recycling promise. What can be recycled depends on local facilities, so check your council's guidelines.

sections.key: Plastic is cheap and durable, so it builds up in the environment and only a small share has ever been recycled.
sections.b:
Global plastic production has grown from almost nothing in 1950 to roughly 400 million tonnes a year by the 2020s. A widely cited 2017 study estimated that of all plastic waste generated up to 2015, only around 9 per cent had been recycled, and the rest was burned, buried or left in the environment.

Part of the problem is chemistry. The same strong carbon chains that make plastics durable mean few microbes can digest them, so most do not biodegrade in any useful timeframe. Sunlight and waves slowly break them into smaller fragments instead. Recycling has limits too, because many plastics get shorter chains and weaker each time they are melted and reprocessed.

sections.key: Microplastics are now found almost everywhere, but their health effects are still uncertain.
sections.b:
Plastic pieces smaller than five millimetres are called microplastics. Some are made small, like the microbeads once common in face scrubs, but most come from larger items breaking down, tyres wearing on roads and synthetic fibres shed in the wash. They have been found in Arctic snow, on remote mountaintops and in the deepest part of the ocean, the Mariana Trench. Studies have also detected them in human blood and organs.

What that means for health is genuinely uncertain. Researchers are still developing reliable ways to measure such tiny particles and to work out whether, and at what levels, they cause harm. Read early headlines with care.

quiz.q: What makes synthetic plastics so versatile?
o: They contain no carbon atoms at all
Their building blocks and chains can be tuned
They are all made from one natural resin
Their molecules are all the same length
quiz.e: Adjusting the building blocks and chain structure produces materials from soft to rigid and clear to coloured.

quiz.q: Why was Bakelite a turning point in plastics?
o: It was the first fully synthetic plastic
It was the first plastic that could float
It was the first plastic to replace ivory
It was the first plastic found by accident
quiz.e: Bakelite showed plastics did not have to start from natural materials, and its heat resistance suited electrical fittings.

quiz.q: What does the number inside the recycling triangle tell you?
o: That your council will recycle the item
How many times the item can be recycled
How safe the plastic is to eat from
What type of plastic the item is made of
quiz.e: The code identifies the plastic, while actual recycling depends on local facilities.

quiz.q: Why do most plastics persist in the environment for so long?
o: Few microbes can digest their carbon chains
Sunlight makes them tougher as they age
They are chemically identical to rock
Salt in seawater preserves them for ages
quiz.e: Durable carbon chains resist biological breakdown, so sunlight and waves only fragment plastics.

quiz.q: What is the best way to treat headlines about microplastics and health?
o: As proof that they are harmless at any level
As settled fact that they cause specific diseases
As rumours with no basis in research
As early, uncertain findings from ongoing research
quiz.e: Scientists are still working out how to measure these particles and whether they cause harm.

LESSONS.push: That recycling triangle on plastic doesn't mean what most people think it does.

LESSONS.title: Measuring the world: the metric story
LESSONS.hook: Revolutionaries once set out to measure the planet to define the metre. Today a metre, a second and a kilogram are fixed by the laws of nature themselves.

sections.key: The metric system replaced confusing local units with a metre based on the size of the Earth.
sections.b:
In eighteenth-century France, units of length, weight and volume varied from region to region and even market to market, so merchants and tax collectors could exploit the confusion. After the Revolution of 1789, reformers wanted a rational system based on nature, belonging to no nation: for all times and all peoples.

In 1791 the French Academy of Sciences decided the metre would be one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator through Paris.
