From 1792, astronomers Delambre and Méchain spent around seven years surveying from Dunkirk to Barcelona, through revolution and war. Because of small errors and the Earth's imperfect shape, the official metre came out about 0.2 millimetres short of the intention. It was close enough, and it stuck.

sections.key: Metric units link to one another and scale in powers of ten, so conversion is just moving a decimal point.
sections.b:
The genius of the metric system is that its units connect. A litre is the volume of a cube ten centimetres on each side, and the kilogram was originally defined as the mass of one litre of water. Everything scales by tens, so converting is a matter of moving a decimal point, and prefixes like kilo, centi and milli work the same way for every unit.

Temperature joined in too. The Celsius scale puts 0 at the freezing point of water and 100 at its boiling point, though the Swedish astronomer Anders Celsius originally set it the other way around in 1742, with 100 for freezing and 0 for boiling. It was flipped shortly after his death.

sections.key: Standards moved from metal objects to constants of nature, with the kilogram the last to change in 2019.
sections.b:
In 1889 the standard kilogram became a platinum-iridium cylinder, about 39 millimetres tall, kept under three glass bell jars in a vault at Sèvres near Paris. It was called Le Grand K, and by definition it weighed exactly one kilogram. Over decades, copies and original drifted apart by tens of micrograms, roughly a grain of sand, and nobody could say which had changed.

So scientists chose constants that never change. In 1967 the second became 9,192,631,770 oscillations of radiation from a caesium atom. In 1983 the metre became the distance light travels in a vacuum in 1/299,792,458 of a second. On 20 May 2019 the kilogram was redefined using the Planck constant, measured with devices called Kibble balances, and Le Grand K retired. Any well-equipped laboratory can now reproduce a kilogram.

sections.key: Australia moved to metric in the 1970s, though some imperial units linger in everyday life.
sections.b:
Australia moved to decimal currency in 1966, and the Metric Conversion Act of 1970 set the country on course to change its measurements too. Over the following decade, temperatures, distances, weights and volumes all changed over. One of the most visible moments came on 1 July 1974, when road signs switched from miles to kilometres. Today most of the world uses metric for daily life, with the United States the best-known exception.

Still, older units hang on in Australia in surprising places. Television and phone screens are sold by size in inches, tyre pressures are often given in pounds per square inch, and many people still describe a newborn's weight, or their own height, in imperial units.

sections.key: Mixing up units has destroyed a spacecraft and nearly brought down an airliner.
sections.b:
In 1999, NASA's Mars Climate Orbiter reached Mars and vanished. Software from one team produced thruster data in imperial pound-force seconds, while another team's software expected metric newton-seconds. The small, repeated error steered the probe too close to the planet, where it was destroyed.

In 1983, an Air Canada Boeing 767 ran out of fuel at cruising height, partly because a fuel calculation had mixed up pounds and kilograms during the airline's switch to metric. The aircraft carried far less fuel than the crew believed. The pilots glided the powerless jet to a disused airbase at Gimli, in Manitoba, and everyone on board survived. It became known as the Gimli Glider.

quiz.q: What was the original aim for the length of the metre?
o: One ten-millionth of pole to equator
The length of a French king's foot
The distance light travels in a second
One thousandth of the Earth's width
quiz.e: Reformers tied the metre to the planet itself, so no nation or king owned the unit.

quiz.q: What makes the metric system easy to use?
o: Its units only measure length and mass
Its units are linked and scale in powers of ten
Each unit has its own naming pattern
It relies on local standards that vary by town
quiz.e: Because everything scales by ten, converting means moving a decimal point.

quiz.q: Why was the kilogram redefined in 2019?
o: Its master object was drifting in mass
Le Grand K was destroyed in a vault fire
The old standard had grown too heavy to use
Countries could not agree on which metal to use
quiz.e: Defining the kilogram by the Planck constant lets any laboratory reproduce it without a master object.

quiz.q: Which imperial units still linger in everyday Australian life?
o: Miles on highway signs
Pounds as the unit of money
Gallons on petrol pump prices
Inches for screen sizes
quiz.e: Australia converted in the 1970s, but screens, tyre pressure and baby weights still often use imperial units.

quiz.q: What caused the loss of NASA's Mars Climate Orbiter?
o: A fuel leak during its launch phase
A failure of its solar panels in space
A misplaced decimal in the launch date
A mix-up between imperial and metric units
quiz.e: Mixed units produced a small repeated error that steered the probe too close to Mars.

LESSONS.push: For 130 years, the kilogram was one lump of metal in a French vault. Then it retired.

LESSONS.title: Chaos and the butterfly effect
LESSONS.hook: A weather scientist rounded off a number and went to get a coffee. When he came back, he had discovered why the future can never be fully predicted.

sections.key: After Newton, many scientists believed that perfect knowledge of the present would allow perfect prediction of the future.
sections.b:
After Isaac Newton showed that simple laws could explain the motions of the planets, the universe began to look like a precise machine. In 1814, the French mathematician Pierre-Simon Laplace described an imaginary intellect that knew the position of every particle and every force acting on them. For such a being, he wrote, nothing would be uncertain, and the future would be as clear as the past. Later writers called it Laplace's demon.

The idea was not foolish. Astronomers could predict eclipses centuries ahead. It seemed that the only obstacle to predicting anything, including the weather, was gathering enough data and doing enough calculation.

sections.key: Henri Poincaré glimpsed chaos in the 1880s when he found that three bodies under gravity can behave in tangled, unpredictable ways.
sections.b:
In the 1880s, King Oscar II of Sweden offered a prize for proof that the solar system was stable in the long run. The French mathematician Henri Poincaré studied a simplified version, three bodies moving under each other's gravity, and won in 1889.

Then, as his paper was being prepared for publication, a serious error was found. Correcting it, Poincaré realised the three-body problem could behave in extraordinarily tangled ways, with tiny changes leading to vastly different orbits. The printed copies had to be recalled and destroyed, reportedly at a cost greater than the prize money. His corrected work is now seen as an early glimpse of chaos theory.

sections.key: In 1961 Edward Lorenz found that rounding one number made a computer weather forecast diverge completely.
sections.b:
Edward Lorenz was a meteorologist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology who had built a simple weather model on an early computer. In 1961, wanting to look at one run more closely, he restarted it partway through, typing in numbers from an earlier printout. The printout had rounded to three decimal places, so instead of 0.506127 he entered 0.506. The difference was about one part in four thousand.

He went for a coffee while the slow machine worked. When he returned, the new forecast had tracked the old one for a while, then drifted further and further away until the two bore no resemblance. Lorenz realised this was not a computer fault. It was a property of the weather.

sections.key: In chaotic systems, tiny differences grow until they change the outcome completely, even though the rules are exact.
sections.b:
Lorenz published in 1963, but his work reached a wide audience after a 1972 talk. Its title, reportedly suggested by a colleague, asked: ‘Does the flap of a butterfly's wings in Brazil set off a tornado in Texas?’ It was a question, not a claim that butterflies control the weather. By coincidence, a plot of his equations looks like a pair of butterfly wings.

A chaotic system is deterministic: the same start always gives the same result, with no randomness in the rules. The catch is sensitive dependence on initial conditions. Tiny differences grow, roughly doubling again and again, until they swamp everything. Since we can never measure perfectly, predictions eventually fail. Release a double pendulum twice from what looks like the same position and the swings soon diverge wildly.

sections.key: Chaos limits long-range prediction, but forecasters cope by running many slightly different simulations.
sections.b:
Chaos explains why weather forecasts are reliable for a few days, useful for about a week, and of little value beyond about two weeks. Forecasters deal with this honestly through ensembles, running a model many times with slightly different starting conditions. If the runs agree, confidence is high; if they spread out, the outlook is uncertain.

Chaos turns up elsewhere too. In 1976, the Australian-born scientist Robert May showed that a very simple equation for animal populations could swing from steady numbers to wild booms and busts. Even planetary orbits are thought to be chaotic over tens of millions of years. Laplace's demon would need infinitely precise data, and nature never provides that.

quiz.q: What did Laplace's imaginary intellect illustrate?
o: Perfect data would make the future knowable
That weather forecasts would soon be perfect
That eclipses cannot be predicted ahead
That nature follows no fixed laws
quiz.e: It captured the clockwork view that enough data and calculation would make everything predictable.

quiz.q: What did Poincaré realise when he corrected his error?
o: The solar system is perfectly stable
Three bodies can move in tangled, sensitive ways
Gravity does not act between planets
Three bodies always settle into a fixed orbit
quiz.e: Even simple gravity between three bodies can be wildly sensitive to its starting conditions.

quiz.q: What did Lorenz's rounding of a number show?
o: His computer had a hardware fault
Rounding errors always cancel out later
Weather can be forecast years ahead
Tiny changes can grow enormously over time
quiz.e: The divergence was a property of the weather model, not a computer fault.

quiz.q: What does it mean to call a chaotic system deterministic?
o: Its outcomes are random
Its rules contain no randomness
It can always be forecast far ahead
It never changes over time
quiz.e: Chaos is exact rules combined with sensitivity to tiny differences, not randomness.

quiz.q: How do forecasters handle chaos in the weather?
o: They run many simulations with varied starts
They ignore every forecast beyond one day
They replace models with seasonal averages
They wait for better calendars to appear
quiz.e: Agreement across an ensemble means high confidence, while a wide spread signals an uncertain outlook.

LESSONS.push: A rounded number and a coffee break changed how we understand the future.

LESSONS.title: Carbon: the element of everything
LESSONS.hook: The same atom makes a diamond, a pencil, a soccer-ball-shaped molecule and most of you. Carbon's secret is its talent for holding hands.

sections.key: Carbon forms four strong bonds, so it can build the chains and rings that underpin the molecules of life.
sections.b:
Each carbon atom has four electrons available for bonding, so it can link with up to four other atoms. Crucially, it bonds strongly with other carbon atoms, forming long chains, branches and rings that act as frameworks for other elements. That flexibility makes carbon the backbone of proteins, fats, sugars and DNA. The chemistry of carbon compounds is so vast that it has its own branch, organic chemistry, covering many millions of known substances.

Carbon is common too. After hydrogen, helium and oxygen, it is the fourth most abundant element in the universe by mass, and it makes up around a fifth of your body by mass.

sections.key: Carbon is forged in stars by fusing three helium nuclei, a process Fred Hoyle predicted must be unusually efficient.
sections.b: The Big Bang produced almost no carbon. It is forged inside stars, where three helium nuclei fuse into one carbon nucleus. In the early 1950s, the British astronomer Fred Hoyle realised that by the known physics this reaction should be far too rare to make the carbon we see. Since carbon obviously exists, he reasoned, carbon nuclei must have a particular energy state that made the reaction much more likely. In 1953 he persuaded sceptical experimental physicists at Caltech to look for it, and they found it close to where he had predicted. The carbon in your cells was made this way, in stars that lived and died long before the Sun formed.

sections.key: Diamond and graphite are both pure carbon, and only the arrangement of atoms makes one hard and the other soft.
sections.b:
In diamond, each carbon atom is locked to four neighbours in a rigid 3D framework, making it the hardest natural material known. Natural diamonds form over a hundred kilometres down in the mantle, under enormous heat and pressure, and rise in rare volcanic eruptions. In graphite, atoms bond to three neighbours in flat hexagon sheets, stacked like pages and held together weakly, so they slide and graphite is soft and slippery. At the surface graphite is more stable, so diamonds are technically turning into it, far too slowly to notice.

Pencils contain no lead. A pure graphite deposit found at Borrowdale, England, in the sixteenth century looked like lead ore, so it was called black lead. Pencil ‘lead’ is graphite mixed with clay: more clay makes a harder H pencil, more graphite a softer B pencil.

sections.key: Carbon also forms soccer-ball-shaped molecules and single-atom sheets, both discovered in recent decades.
sections.b:
In 1985, Harold Kroto, Robert Curl and Richard Smalley blasted graphite with a laser and found a stable molecule of exactly 60 carbon atoms: a hollow sphere of 12 pentagons and 20 hexagons, like a soccer ball. They named it buckminsterfullerene, after Buckminster Fuller's geodesic domes, or buckyball. The three shared the 1996 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Buckyballs have since been detected in space.

Graphene is a single sheet of graphite, one atom thick. In 2004 at the University of Manchester, Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov pressed sticky tape onto graphite and kept peeling flakes until some were one atom thick. Graphene is strong, flexible, nearly transparent and conducts well. They won the 2010 Nobel Prize in Physics.

sections.key: Carbon cycles between air, oceans, rocks and living things, and burning fossil fuels releases it far faster than nature removes it.
sections.b:
The carbon in your body has been on a long journey. Plants pull carbon dioxide from the air and use sunlight to build it into sugars. Animals eat the plants, and both release carbon dioxide as they breathe and decay. The oceans absorb vast amounts of carbon dioxide, and over millions of years carbon is locked away in limestone and other rocks, then slowly returned by volcanoes.

Fossil fuels such as coal, oil and gas are the remains of ancient living things, carbon buried and stored for millions of years. Burning them releases that carbon into the air far faster than natural processes can remove it, which is the main reason carbon dioxide levels in the atmosphere are rising.

quiz.q: Why is carbon the backbone of the molecules of life?
o: It is the most common element in the universe
It forms strong bonds that build chains and rings
It is the lightest element that can bond
It can only bond with hydrogen atoms
quiz.e: Carbon's four bonds let it build flexible frameworks for proteins, fats, sugars and DNA.

quiz.q: Where is the carbon in your body made?
o: In the Big Bang itself
Deep in the Earth's core
In erupting volcanoes
Inside stars, from helium
quiz.e: The Big Bang made almost no carbon, so it was forged in earlier stars.

quiz.q: What makes diamond hard and graphite soft when both are pure carbon?
o: Diamond contains traces of other elements
Graphite is a different element
The arrangement of the atoms differs
Diamond is much older than graphite
quiz.e: Diamond's rigid 3D bonds resist force, while graphite's weakly held sheets slide past one another.

quiz.q: What is graphene?
o: A hollow cage of 60 carbon atoms
A single-atom-thick sheet of graphite
A mixture of graphite and clay
A form of diamond found in volcanoes
quiz.e: Geim and Novoselov isolated one-atom-thick layers using sticky tape.

quiz.q: Why are atmospheric carbon dioxide levels rising?
o: Plants have stopped absorbing carbon dioxide
Oceans now release more than they absorb
Burning fossil fuels adds carbon too quickly
Volcanoes now erupt far more often than before
quiz.e: Fossil fuels stored carbon for millions of years, and we release it within decades.

LESSONS.push: A diamond and a pencil are made of the same atom. So why are they so different?

LESSONS.title: Antimatter: the universe's missing twin
LESSONS.hook: For every particle there is a mirror-image twin with the opposite charge. When they meet, both vanish in a flash of pure energy. So why is the universe made almost entirely of one kind?

sections.key: Antimatter was predicted by an equation in 1931 and spotted in cosmic-ray tracks in 1932.
sections.b:
In 1928 Paul Dirac combined quantum mechanics with Einstein's special relativity in one equation for the electron. It worked beautifully, but it had a strange feature. Just as the square root of four can be plus or minus two, the equation also gave solutions that seemed to describe electrons with negative energy. Dirac took them seriously. In 1931 he proposed they pointed to a new particle with an electron's mass but a positive charge.

In 1932 Carl Anderson found it. His cloud chamber, sitting in a strong magnet, recorded cosmic rays from space. He photographed a track that curved like an electron's, but the wrong way. A lead plate across the chamber showed which way the particle travelled. He called it the positron, and shared the 1936 Nobel Prize in Physics.

sections.key: When matter meets its antimatter twin, all of their mass turns into energy.
sections.b:
Every particle has an antiparticle with the same mass but opposite charge. Electrons have positrons, and protons have antiprotons. When a particle meets its antiparticle, they annihilate. Their mass becomes energy, usually as gamma rays, following E = mc².

It is the most complete conversion of mass into energy known. Nuclear fission and fusion turn less than one per cent of their fuel's mass into energy. Annihilation converts all of it. The process also runs backwards. A sufficiently energetic gamma ray passing near an atomic nucleus can turn into an electron and a positron. This is called pair production, and it creates matter out of energy.

sections.key: Physicists can make anti-atoms and hold them in magnetic traps, and antihydrogen falls under gravity like ordinary matter.
sections.b:
Emilio Segrè and Owen Chamberlain led the team that created the antiproton at Berkeley in 1955, and won the 1959 Nobel Prize in Physics. In 1995 researchers at CERN, near Geneva, combined an antiproton with a positron to make antihydrogen, the simplest anti-atom. They made only a handful, and the atoms annihilated almost instantly.

Holding antimatter is the hard part, because touching the wall of any container destroys it. In 2010 CERN's ALPHA experiment trapped antihydrogen in a carefully shaped magnetic field, and soon held some for around a quarter of an hour. In 2023 ALPHA showed that antihydrogen falls under gravity, just like ordinary matter.

sections.key: Antimatter helps medical imaging, but making it costs far more energy than it releases, so it cannot be a fuel.
sections.b:
Antimatter already works in hospitals. A PET scan (positron emission tomography) uses a sugar tagged with a radioactive atom. Busy tissue, such as some tumours, takes up more of it. Each emitted positron meets an electron almost at once, and the two annihilate into gamma rays heading in opposite directions. Detectors catch both and map the activity. Positrons also occur naturally, in a very small fraction of potassium-40 decays (found in bananas and in you) and in some thunderstorms.

As fuel, antimatter disappoints. It is made in accelerators one collision at a time, using far more energy than it could ever return, and it must be suspended in a vacuum. CERN has noted that all the antimatter it has made would light one bulb for only minutes.

sections.key: The Big Bang should have made equal matter and antimatter, yet a tiny excess of matter survived and nobody knows why.
sections.b:
Here is the deepest puzzle. Our best theories say the Big Bang should have produced matter and antimatter in equal amounts. They should have annihilated completely, leaving a universe of nothing but light. Instead, there are galaxies, stars and people, all made of matter. A small excess of matter survived, often estimated at about one extra particle for every billion pairs.

In 1967 Andrei Sakharov set out the conditions needed for such an imbalance. Since 1964, experiments have found that some particles and their antiparticles behave slightly differently, but the differences found so far are far too small to explain it. Why anything exists at all is still unsolved.

quiz.q: Why did Dirac propose a new particle?
o: Cosmic rays had already revealed an unknown particle to him
His equation's extra solutions implied a positively charged electron twin
Experiments had shown that electrons can carry positive charge
He needed a heavier particle to explain how atoms hold together
quiz.e: Dirac took the odd negative-energy solutions seriously, and they predicted antimatter.

quiz.q: What happens when a particle meets its antiparticle?
o: They bounce apart with swapped charges
They fuse into a single heavier particle
Their mass turns into energy, as gamma rays
About one per cent of mass becomes energy
quiz.e: Annihilation is the most complete conversion of mass into energy known.

quiz.q: Why is antihydrogen so hard to store?
o: It repels ordinary matter, so it drifts away from any container
Touching any container wall destroys it, so magnetic fields hold it
It is radioactive and quickly melts through any container wall
It decays within a few nanoseconds whatever physicists try
quiz.e: Antimatter annihilates on contact with matter, so it is held in a magnetic trap.

quiz.q: Why is antimatter not a practical fuel?
o: It releases less energy than fission does
It cannot be made in a laboratory at all
It is too stable to react with anything
It costs far more energy to make than it returns
quiz.e: Making antiparticles in accelerators is staggeringly inefficient, so it is a research tool, not an energy source.

quiz.q: What is the puzzle of the missing antimatter?
o: Equal amounts should have formed, yet nearly everything is matter
Antimatter was made in equal amounts but is hidden inside stars
Matter and antimatter both survived in equal amounts today
No physical theory has ever predicted that antimatter exists
quiz.e: Equal amounts would have annihilated, so a small excess of matter must have survived.

LESSONS.push: Every particle has a twin that destroys it. So why does anything exist?

LESSONS.title: The snail in the bottle: how negligence law was born
LESSONS.hook: A woman in a Scottish café sipped a ginger beer and claimed she found a rotting snail in it. Her lawsuit changed the law for almost everyone in the English-speaking world.

sections.key: A woman who said she found a snail in her ginger beer had no contract with anyone, so the old law seemed to leave her without a remedy.
sections.b:
On 26 August 1928, May Donoghue drank ginger beer from a dark, opaque bottle at the Wellmeadow Café in Paisley, near Glasgow. A friend had bought it. When the rest was poured into her ice cream float, she later said, the decomposed remains of a snail slid into her glass. She claimed shock and gastroenteritis.

The trouble was legal. If a faulty product hurt you, your main route was usually to sue the seller for breach of contract. She had no contract with the café owner, who had neither made the drink nor sealed the bottle. She had none with the manufacturer, David Stevenson, either. Earlier cases suggested that a manufacturer owed nothing to a stranger, except for inherently dangerous items.

sections.key: The Lords decided only whether she had a claim in law, not whether the snail was real.
sections.b:
Mrs Donoghue had little money, so she was allowed to sue as a pauper, without paying the usual court costs. Her lawyer, Walter Leechman, took on the manufacturer. The case reached the House of Lords, then Britain's highest court, which ruled in May 1932.

The judges did not decide whether a snail had really been in the bottle. They answered a preliminary question: assuming everything she said was true, did the law give her a claim? By three votes to two, they said yes. A manufacturer who sells a product meant to reach the consumer unchanged owes that consumer a duty to take reasonable care.

sections.key: Lord Atkin's neighbour principle says you owe reasonable care to anyone you can foresee your actions might injure.
sections.b:
The most famous judgment came from Lord Atkin, who reached for the parable of the Good Samaritan, in which a lawyer asks, 'Who is my neighbour?' Atkin gave a legal answer. You must take reasonable care to avoid acts or omissions that you can reasonably foresee would be likely to injure your neighbour. And your neighbour is anyone so closely and directly affected by what you do that you ought to have them in mind.

This was a broad principle, not a narrow rule about ginger beer. A duty of care can exist between strangers wherever harm is foreseeable and the relationship is close enough. Lawyers call it the neighbour principle, and first-year law students still learn it.

sections.key: To win a negligence claim you generally must show a duty of care, a breach of that duty, and harm caused by the breach.
sections.b:
Donoghue v Stevenson gave shape to negligence, the law of careless harm. Broadly, a person suing must show three things. First, the other side owed them a duty of care. Second, the other side breached it by falling below the standard of a reasonable person in their position. Third, the breach actually caused harm of a kind the law recognises.

These ideas now sit behind claims about car crashes, medical mistakes, slippery supermarket floors and unsafe buildings. Courts have spent decades refining where duties begin and end, because a duty that stretched forever would make everyone liable for everything. Many places, including Australian states, have also passed laws limiting some claims and damages.

sections.key: The principle spread across the common law world, though no court ever decided whether the snail existed.
sections.b:
A Scottish decision about a Paisley café could have stayed local. Instead, in the mid-1930s, an Australian case reached the Privy Council in London, then Australia's final court of appeal. Dr Richard Grant had developed severe dermatitis from woollen underwear made by Australian Knitting Mills, which contained irritating chemicals left from manufacturing. Relying on Donoghue v Stevenson, the Privy Council held the manufacturer liable. Courts in Canada and New Zealand followed, and governments later built consumer protection laws on these foundations.

Here is the twist. David Stevenson died before the trial on the facts, and the claim was settled out of court. No judge ever ruled on whether the snail existed. A memorial now marks the café site.

quiz.q: Why did Mrs Donoghue seem to have no legal claim?
o: Snails in drinks were not considered harmful by the courts
She had no contract with the seller or the maker of the drink
The café had closed before she could bring a legal action
Ginger beer was exempt from the product laws of the time
quiz.e: Under the old law, a stranger who used a faulty product could not sue the maker.

quiz.q: What did the House of Lords decide?
o: That a snail had really been in the bottle, so she won
That only the café owner could be sued for the harm
If her story was true, manufacturers owed her reasonable care
That she must wait for Parliament to pass a new product law
quiz.e: The Lords answered a question of law, not of fact, and created a duty of care for manufacturers.

quiz.q: What does the neighbour principle say?
o: You owe care only to people you have a contract with
You owe care only to family and close friends
You owe care only to people who are paying you
You owe care to anyone you can foresee you might harm
quiz.e: Duty of care extends to anyone so closely affected that you ought to have them in mind.

quiz.q: What must you generally show to win a negligence claim?
o: A duty of care, its breach, and resulting harm
A contract, a payment and a written complaint
Intent, motive and a full confession
A witness, a receipt and a medical report
quiz.e: Negligence needs a duty, a failure to meet the reasonable standard, and resulting harm.

quiz.q: Why do we not know whether the snail was real?
o: The bottle was lost before the trial could take place
The Lords ruled that the snail had never existed at all
The maker died and the claim was settled out of court
The jury could not reach a verdict on the evidence given
quiz.e: The case is remembered for its legal principle, not its facts.

LESSONS.push: A woman, a bottle and a possibly imaginary snail changed the law.

LESSONS.title: Habeas corpus: the right not to simply vanish
LESSONS.hook: Two Latin words protect you from being locked away without reason. They have stood up to kings, slave owners and presidents.

sections.key: Habeas corpus is a court order demanding that a jailer justify why a person is being held.
sections.b:
Habeas corpus is Latin for 'you shall have the body'. It is the name of a writ, a formal court order, directed at whoever is holding a prisoner, whether a jailer, a soldier or a government official. The writ commands them to bring the person before the court and show a lawful reason for the detention. If they cannot, the judge can order the prisoner released.

It does not decide whether someone is guilty. It asks a more basic question: is there any legal authority to hold this person at all? That makes it a check on power itself. Without it, a government could make people disappear into cells with no charge, no trial and no end date.

sections.key: English courts and Parliament turned the writ into a real check on the Crown, ending with the Habeas Corpus Act of 1679.
sections.b:
Versions of the writ existed in English courts by the 1200s, at first mostly to bring people to court. Judges later used it to test whether detentions were lawful, drawing strength from Magna Carta of 1215: no free man to be imprisoned except by the lawful judgment of his peers or the law of the land.

In 1627 Charles I jailed knights who refused a forced loan demanded without Parliament's consent. The jailer's only answer was that they were held by the king's special command, and the court refused to release them. Outrage helped produce the Petition of Right in 1628, declaring such imprisonment unlawful. In 1679 Parliament passed the Habeas Corpus Act, setting deadlines and penalties to stop officials dodging the writ.

sections.key: In 1772 the writ stopped an enslaved man being shipped away by force, a landmark in the struggle against slavery.
sections.b:
In 1772 the writ was used in a dramatic case. James Somerset had been enslaved in Virginia and brought to England by Charles Stewart, a customs official. Somerset escaped, was recaptured and was put aboard a ship bound for Jamaica, where he would be sold.

Supporters, including the campaigner Granville Sharp, sought habeas corpus. Lord Mansfield, the senior judge of the King's Bench, ruled that no law in England allowed a master to force Somerset out of the country, and Somerset was freed. The decision did not abolish slavery, which continued in British colonies for decades. But it was widely celebrated and became a landmark in the long struggle against slavery.

sections.key: Governments in crisis have suspended habeas corpus, and each time it has been controversial.
sections.b:
Because habeas corpus limits government power, governments under pressure have sometimes tried to switch it off. Britain's Parliament suspended it several times, for example in the 1790s amid fears of revolution spreading from France.

The framers of the United States Constitution included the writ but allowed suspension only in cases of rebellion or invasion when public safety required it. In 1861, at the start of the Civil War, President Abraham Lincoln suspended it in some areas. Chief Justice Roger Taney argued in the Merryman case that only Congress had that power, and Lincoln largely ignored him. Congress later authorised suspension. Lawyers and historians still debate how far emergencies justify setting aside this ancient safeguard.

sections.key: Habeas corpus remains part of the law in Australia and across the common law world, and matters most when other protections fail.
sections.b:
English colonists carried habeas corpus around the world. It remains part of the law in countries including Australia, New Zealand, Canada, India and the United States. In Australia, superior courts such as the state Supreme Courts and the High Court can issue it.

In practice, many detentions are now reviewed through other routes, such as bail hearings, appeals and judicial review, so the old writ is used less often than its fame suggests. But it still matters most when other protections fail. It has been invoked over immigration detention, mental health detention and wartime imprisonment. Its message endures: power must always answer one question in court. By what lawful authority is this person being held?

quiz.q: What question does habeas corpus force a jailer to answer?
o: Whether the prisoner is guilty or innocent
What lawful authority justifies the detention
How long the sentence should be served
Who first reported the crime to police
quiz.e: The writ tests the legality of the detention, not guilt or innocence.

quiz.q: How did the 1679 Habeas Corpus Act strengthen the writ?
o: It abolished the Crown's power to arrest anyone
It limited the writ to use by nobles only
It set deadlines and penalties for officials
It replaced the writ with trial by jury
quiz.e: Parliament added deadlines and penalties so officials could not simply ignore the court.

quiz.q: What did the Somerset case show?
o: It stopped a forced removal from England, though slavery continued
It abolished slavery across the British Empire in the year 1772
It showed that judges could not interfere with ship captains
It showed the writ applied only to British-born subjects
quiz.e: Habeas corpus freed Somerset, and the decision became a landmark in the struggle against slavery.

quiz.q: Why is suspending habeas corpus so controversial?
o: It makes courts hear far more cases than they can handle
It lengthens the sentences of prisoners already convicted
It removes the writ only for visitors from foreign countries
It lets authorities hold people without justifying it to a court
quiz.e: The writ is a check on government power, so switching it off removes that check.

quiz.q: Why is the writ used less often today?
o: Most countries have formally abolished it in recent years
Governments have permanently suspended it in peacetime
Other routes review many detentions, but it backs them up
It can only ever be used during a declared war
quiz.e: Bail, appeals and judicial review handle most cases, leaving habeas corpus as the safeguard of last resort.

LESSONS.push: Two Latin words stand between you and a cell with no end date. What do they demand?

LESSONS.title: The 1967 referendum: what it really changed
LESSONS.hook: More than 90 per cent of Australians voted Yes in 1967, the biggest win in referendum history. Yet many people still believe it did things it never did.

sections.key: The 1967 referendum won about 91 per cent of the vote after a decade of campaigning by Aboriginal and non-Aboriginal Australians.
sections.b:
On 27 May 1967, about 91 per cent of Australians voted Yes to a question about Aboriginal people, and every state agreed. It is the biggest Yes in referendum history, in a country where change is hard. A proposal needs a majority of voters nationally and majorities in at least four of six states, and only a handful of more than 40 proposals have passed.

The result came from a decade of campaigning. The Federal Council for the Advancement of Aborigines and Torres Strait Islanders gathered petitions, with leaders including Faith Bandler and Joe McGinness. The 1965 Freedom Ride, led by Charles Perkins and students, exposed segregation in country New South Wales. By the vote, the major parties backed Yes and there was almost no organised No case.

sections.key: The referendum deleted a phrase from the race power and removed section 127, and those two changes were its entire legal effect.
sections.b:
The 1901 Constitution mentioned Aboriginal people only twice, and both times to exclude them. Section 51 lists the subjects the federal Parliament can make laws about. It gave power over 'the people of any race, other than the aboriginal race in any State', which left laws about Aboriginal people to the states. Section 127 said that in reckoning the numbers of the people of the Commonwealth, 'aboriginal natives shall not be counted'.

The 1967 referendum removed the words 'other than the aboriginal race in any State' from section 51, and deleted section 127 altogether. That was the entire legal effect of the vote.

sections.key: The referendum did not give Aboriginal people the vote, because voting rights come from ordinary laws passed earlier.
sections.b:
One of the most common beliefs about 1967 is that it gave Aboriginal people the right to vote. It did not. Voting rights are set mainly by ordinary laws passed by parliaments, not by the Constitution.

Some Aboriginal people could vote in a few colonies from the 1850s and 1890s, although many were later excluded. In 1962 the Commonwealth Electoral Act was amended to give all Aboriginal people the right to vote in federal elections. The states moved at different speeds, and Queensland was the last to grant state voting rights, in 1965. So by the referendum, Aboriginal Australians had the right to vote everywhere, even though many still faced real barriers in practice.

sections.key: The vote did not create citizenship, and no law ever classed Aboriginal people as flora and fauna.
sections.b:
Another myth is that the referendum made Aboriginal people citizens. Australian citizenship was created in 1949, and Aboriginal people born in Australia were covered by it. In practice, many were still denied rights by state laws controlling where they lived, worked and married.

A third myth says Aboriginal people were managed under a 'Flora and Fauna Act' until 1967. Historians and fact checkers have found no such law, at federal or state level. The myth probably spread because it captured how dehumanising the real treatment felt, but it is not accurate. Correcting these myths does not shrink the referendum's importance. It shows that its power was partly symbolic, and partly about which government held responsibility.

sections.key: The referendum let the federal Parliament make laws for Aboriginal people, but progress came more slowly than many hoped.
sections.b:
Removing the exclusion from section 51 meant the Commonwealth, not just the states, could now make laws specifically for Aboriginal people. The federal government went on to create new agencies and programs, and in 1976 Parliament passed the Aboriginal Land Rights (Northern Territory) Act. Deleting section 127 meant Aboriginal people would be included in official population counts.

Yet the change was neutral on its face. The race power covers people of any race, and courts have since debated whether laws made under it must benefit the group. Many campaigners felt real progress came more slowly than the 1967 hope promised. Even so, the vote remains a landmark, and its date now marks the start of National Reconciliation Week.

quiz.q: What made the 1967 result so unusual?
o: It was the first referendum ever held in Australia
It passed by only a single vote in a close national count
About 91 per cent voted Yes and every state agreed
The major parties campaigned hard against the proposal
quiz.e: Years of campaigning and broad political support produced the biggest Yes in referendum history.

quiz.q: What did the referendum change in the Constitution?
o: It deleted words in the race power and removed section 127
It gave Aboriginal people the right to vote in federal elections
It created Australian citizenship for Aboriginal people
It returned all Indigenous affairs to the state governments
quiz.e: Those two changes were the entire legal effect of the vote.

quiz.q: Why is 'the 1967 referendum gave Aboriginal people the vote' a myth?
o: Aboriginal people were never allowed to vote until 1975
The Constitution already gave all adults the vote
Only Aboriginal men gained the vote in 1967
Earlier ordinary laws had already granted the vote
quiz.e: Federal voting rights came in 1962 and Queensland followed in 1965, before the referendum.

quiz.q: What is true of the claim that a 'Flora and Fauna Act' governed Aboriginal people?
o: It was repealed in 1967
It applied only in Queensland
No such law has ever been found
It was replaced by 1949 citizenship laws
quiz.e: The myth captures how dehumanising treatment felt, but no such law existed.

quiz.q: What new power did the change give the federal Parliament?
o: To abolish the state parliaments and govern directly
To grant Australian citizenship to Aboriginal people
To make laws specifically for Aboriginal people, not only the states
To set the national voting age for all federal elections
quiz.e: Removing the exclusion from section 51 opened a new era of national policy.

LESSONS.push: The biggest Yes in Australian history. What many people wrongly think it did.

LESSONS.title: Gerrymandering: winning by drawing the lines
LESSONS.hook: You can lose the popular vote and still win the election, if someone has drawn the map cleverly enough. Meet the strange art of the gerrymander.

sections.key: The word 'gerrymander' comes from an 1812 cartoon mocking a district shaped like a monster.
sections.b:
In 1812 the Massachusetts legislature redrew its state senate districts to help the governing party, and Governor Elbridge Gerry signed the map into law. One district north of Boston twisted so strangely that critics said it looked like a salamander. The Boston Gazette published a cartoon turning it into a winged, clawed beast and named it the 'Gerry-mander'.

The insult stuck. Gerry's name was pronounced with a hard G, like Gary, but the word is now almost always said with a soft G, like Jerry. Gerry himself reportedly disliked the plan, yet his name is forever attached to it.

sections.key: Gerrymanders work by packing opponents into a few seats or cracking them thinly across many.
sections.b:
Where each electorate elects one member, boundaries matter enormously. Imagine a region with ten seats, where two parties each have half the voters. Draw the lines one way and each party wins five seats. Draw them another way and one party can win seven or eight.

There are two classic tricks. Packing means cramming as many of your opponent's supporters as possible into a few seats, which they win by huge, wasteful margins. Cracking means splitting the rest thinly across many seats, so they fall just short everywhere. Their votes are not taken away. They are arranged so that many make no difference. With modern data and computers, these techniques can be applied with remarkable precision.

sections.key: When seats hold unequal numbers of voters, some votes count for more, and Australia has its own examples.
sections.b:
A cousin of the gerrymander is malapportionment, where some electorates hold many more voters than others. If country seats have half the voters of city seats, each country vote counts roughly double. It sometimes reflected a belief that rural areas needed extra representation, and sometimes it simply helped whoever drew the map. Britain's 'rotten boroughs' were tiny constituencies with a handful of voters that still elected MPs, until reforms from 1832 began to sweep them away.

In South Australia, heavily weighted rural seats kept Thomas Playford's government in power for decades, a system nicknamed the Playmander. Queensland's zonal system, introduced under Labor in 1949 and later reshaped by Country and National Party governments, was nicknamed the Bjelkemander after Premier Joh Bjelke-Petersen. Both let parties win government with fewer votes than their rivals.

sections.key: Australia moved boundary drawing to independent bodies, with electorates of roughly equal size.
sections.b:
After the Fitzgerald Inquiry into corruption in the late 1980s, Queensland moved to boundaries drawn by an independent commission with roughly equal enrolments. Other states have also moved towards equal weighting over time.

Today federal boundaries are drawn by the Australian Electoral Commission, an independent statutory body, not by politicians. When population shifts or a state's number of seats changes, a redistribution is held. Committees propose boundaries, the public and parties can lodge objections, and an independent commission makes the final decision. The law requires electorates in a state to have close to the same number of voters, within set tolerances, while also considering communities of interest, transport links and physical features. States and territories run similar independent processes. Parties still argue about decisions, but the pencil is out of the hands of those who benefit.

sections.key: In many US states legislators still draw the lines, and federal courts will not rule on partisan gerrymanders.
sections.b:
In the United States, district lines are usually drawn by state legislatures, so whichever party controls a state can shape its map. Both major parties have been accused of gerrymandering where they hold power. Some states have handed the job to independent or bipartisan commissions, often after citizen ballot initiatives.

US Supreme Court decisions in the 1960s, especially Reynolds v Sims in 1964, required state legislative districts to have roughly equal populations, a principle known as one person, one vote. Courts also hear challenges over racial discrimination. But in 2019, in Rucho v Common Cause, the Court held that partisan gerrymandering claims are political questions federal courts cannot resolve. Researchers use measures such as the efficiency gap, which counts wasted votes, to detect unfair maps.

quiz.q: What is a gerrymander?
o: Drawing electoral boundaries to favour one party
Counting votes in a different order
Giving some voters two ballots
Changing the voting age to suit a party
quiz.e: The name comes from a district drawn to help one party win.

quiz.q: What is 'cracking'?
o: Cramming opponents into a few seats they win by huge margins
Removing opponents from the electoral roll
Spreading opponents thinly across many seats so they fall short
Redrawing every seat after each election
quiz.e: Cracking wastes the opponent's votes by spreading them, while packing wastes them by concentrating them.

quiz.q: Why does malapportionment distort election results?
o: It changes the way the votes are counted afterwards
Votes in seats with fewer voters count for more
It lets voters choose which electorate they join
It removes some voters from the electoral roll
quiz.e: If a country seat has half the voters of a city seat, each country vote counts about double.

quiz.q: Why are Australian federal boundaries considered fairer?
o: The governing party draws them and the High Court approves
Each state draws its own with no oversight at all
An independent commission draws them with near-equal voter numbers
They were fixed at Federation and have never changed
quiz.e: Independent redistributions keep the pencil away from those who benefit.

quiz.q: Why are partisan maps still common in the United States?
o: State legislatures usually draw them, and courts avoid partisan claims
Federal law requires the major parties to draw them together
Independent commissions are banned in every single state
Courts reject all challenges, including racial discrimination
quiz.e: Control of the legislature means control of the map, and the courts have left partisan claims to states and Congress.

LESSONS.push: A cartoon salamander gave us a word for winning by redrawing the map.

LESSONS.title: Diplomatic immunity: why ambassadors can't be arrested
LESSONS.hook: A diplomat can park illegally, refuse to answer police and walk free from a courtroom. There is a surprisingly old and sensible reason why.

sections.key: Protecting envoys is one of the oldest rules of international relations, because without it no one could negotiate.
sections.b:
Rulers have always needed to talk to their rivals, even during wars. That only works if messengers can travel safely. Ancient Greek heralds, Roman envoys and ambassadors in many other civilisations were protected, often with religious overtones.

In the early 1200s, Mongol envoys sent by Genghis Khan to the Khwarazmian Empire in Central Asia were mistreated, and at least one was executed. Genghis Khan responded with a devastating invasion from 1219. The lesson has been learned again and again. If envoys can be arrested, jailed or killed, diplomacy collapses, and the only remaining way to settle disputes is force.

sections.key: Britain passed a law protecting diplomats after Russia's ambassador was dragged from his coach over debts.
sections.b:
In 1708, Andrey Matveyev, the ambassador of Tsar Peter the Great, was about to leave London when he was dragged from his coach and briefly locked up over unpaid debts to local merchants. Peter was furious and demanded that the offenders be severely punished.

The British government was embarrassed, but under English law the creditors had done nothing illegal. To repair the relationship, Parliament passed the Diplomatic Privileges Act, which made it unlawful to arrest ambassadors or seize their goods, and Queen Anne's government sent a formal apology to Moscow. It shows how international law often grows: an awkward incident exposes a gap, and states create rules so it does not happen again.

sections.key: Modern diplomatic immunity comes from a 1961 treaty almost every country has joined.
sections.b:
The main rules are in the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations of 1961, one of the most widely accepted treaties in the world. Australia gives effect to it through its Diplomatic Privileges and Immunities Act of 1967.

Under the convention, diplomatic agents cannot be arrested or detained, and they are immune from the host country's criminal courts. They are also immune from most civil and administrative cases, with exceptions such as private property deals or business unrelated to their official work. Their families generally share these protections. The diplomatic bag, used to send documents and items between an embassy and its home government, must not be opened or detained. A separate, narrower 1963 convention protects consular officials.

sections.key: An embassy remains part of the host country, but local officials cannot enter without the mission head's consent.
sections.b:
Films often say that stepping into an embassy means stepping onto foreign soil. That is a myth. An embassy in Canberra stands on Australian territory, and in general Australian law applies there.

What the Vienna Convention does is make the premises inviolable. Police and other officials of the host country may not enter without the consent of the head of the mission, even with a warrant, and the host country must protect the building from intrusion or damage. That is why people sometimes seek refuge inside embassies. They have not left the country, but local authorities cannot simply walk in and take them. The effect can look similar, but the legal reasoning is quite different.

sections.key: Immunity is not impunity: abusers can be expelled, and every country gains from protecting envoys.
sections.b:
Diplomats must respect local laws. When they break them, the host country can ask the sending country to waive immunity so the person can be prosecuted, or declare the diplomat persona non grata, an unwelcome person, who must then leave. In April 1984, shots fired from the Libyan embassy in London killed Police Constable Yvonne Fletcher during a protest. Britain could not enter or prosecute, so after a siege it expelled the diplomats and broke off relations.

Why keep the system? Reciprocity. Every country has diplomats abroad, sometimes in places with hostile governments. If a host could arrest them on real or invented charges, they could become hostages. Immunity lets envoys report honestly and deliver unwelcome messages without fear.

quiz.q: Why have societies long protected envoys?
o: Envoys were always members of the royal family
Armies needed envoys to carry supplies to the front
Without safe messengers, rivals cannot negotiate
Rulers wanted to profit from the trade envoys carried
quiz.e: Protecting envoys keeps channels open that can prevent war.

quiz.q: What does the arrest of Russia's ambassador in London show about how international law grows?
o: An awkward incident exposes a gap, then states make new rules
Treaties are always written before any incident happens
Only full-scale wars have ever created new international rules
Courts invent the rules without any state agreeing to them
quiz.e: Parliament protected ambassadors by statute after the embarrassing arrest.

quiz.q: Under the Vienna Convention, what protection does a diplomat generally have?
o: Freedom from any obligation to respect local laws
Immunity from arrest and from criminal courts
Immunity from being expelled by the host country
The right to be tried only inside their own embassy
quiz.e: Diplomats are immune from arrest and criminal courts, but they can still be expelled.

quiz.q: What is the legal status of an embassy?
o: It is foreign soil where only the sending country's laws apply
It is open to police who arrive carrying a warrant
It is host territory, but officials need the mission head's consent
It is owned and administered by the United Nations
quiz.e: Inviolability, not foreign soil, is what keeps local authorities out.

quiz.q: Why do nearly all countries respect diplomatic immunity?
o: An international police force enforces the rules everywhere
They earn income from the trade that diplomats bring
Each state has envoys abroad it wants protected, so all gain
Diplomats pay a fee to their host countries for it
quiz.e: Reciprocity makes the occasional injustice the price of keeping diplomacy safe.

LESSONS.push: A diplomat can ignore a police summons. The reason is older and wiser than it looks.

LESSONS.title: The Geneva Conventions: rules for the worst of times
LESSONS.hook: Even war has laws. They began with a Swiss businessman who stumbled onto a battlefield and could not forget what he saw.

sections.key: One businessman's horror at a battlefield led to the Red Cross and the first Geneva Convention.
sections.b:
In June 1859, Swiss businessman Henry Dunant travelled to northern Italy hoping to meet Napoleon III about a business venture. He arrived just after the Battle of Solferino. Tens of thousands lay dead or wounded, with little medical help. Dunant organised local villagers, many of them women, to care for the wounded of both sides.

His 1862 book, A Memory of Solferino, proposed trained volunteer relief groups and an international agreement protecting the wounded and their carers. In 1863 he and four other Genevans formed the committee that became the International Committee of the Red Cross. In 1864 twelve states signed the first Geneva Convention. Wounded and sick soldiers had to be cared for on either side, and ambulances, hospitals and medical staff were protected, marked by a red cross on white, the reverse of the Swiss flag.

sections.key: Dunant ended his life in poverty and obscurity, but was later awarded the first Nobel Peace Prize.
sections.b:
Dunant's own story did not end happily for many years. His business ventures in Algeria failed, he went bankrupt in the 1860s, and the scandal forced him out of the organisation he had helped create. He drifted through Europe in poverty and eventually settled in the small Swiss town of Heiden, where he lived quietly in a hospital home.

In the 1890s a journalist rediscovered him, and his story spread again. In 1901 Dunant shared the very first Nobel Peace Prize with the French peace campaigner Frédéric Passy. He died in 1910. His birthday, 8 May, is now celebrated as World Red Cross and Red Crescent Day.

sections.key: After the Second World War, states agreed four new conventions in 1949, including one to protect civilians.
sections.b:
The original treaty was updated in 1906 and 1929, but the Second World War exposed its limits. Millions of prisoners of war died in captivity, and civilians suffered mass killings, deportations and starvation under occupation.

In 1949 states agreed on four new Geneva Conventions. The first protects wounded and sick soldiers on land. The second does the same for those wounded, sick or shipwrecked at sea. The third sets out how prisoners of war must be treated, including humane conditions and protection from torture and public curiosity. The fourth, entirely new, protects civilians in enemy hands and in occupied territory. Every country in the world has ratified the 1949 conventions, which makes them truly universal.

sections.key: Humanitarian law rests on distinction, proportionality and humane treatment, and applies equally to all sides.
sections.b:
Two Additional Protocols in 1977 strengthened protections for civilians and for victims of civil wars. Together with other treaties, such as the Hague Conventions on weapons and tactics, they form international humanitarian law.

A few principles run through it. Distinction means combatants must tell military targets from civilians, and may only target the former. Proportionality means an attack is unlawful if the expected harm to civilians would be excessive compared with the concrete military advantage. People who are no longer fighting, such as the wounded, the sick and those who surrender, must be treated humanely. These rules do not decide whether a war is justified. They apply equally to all sides, whatever the cause.

sections.key: Grave breaches are war crimes that any state must pursue, though enforcement remains the hardest part.
sections.b:
The red cross emblem is protected by law and must not be misused, even for decoration or advertising. The red crescent has been used since the 1870s, and in 2005 states adopted a third emblem, the red crystal, with no religious or national associations.

Enforcement is the hardest part. The conventions require states to search for and prosecute people accused of grave breaches, such as wilful killing, torture or taking hostages, whatever their nationality. Australia does this through its own legislation, including the Geneva Conventions Act 1957. Since the 1990s, international tribunals and the International Criminal Court have also tried war crimes. Violations still happen far too often, but the rules give victims a standard and the world a way to judge.

quiz.q: What did the first Geneva Convention require?
o: Prisoners of war to be released as soon as a battle ended
Wounded and sick soldiers to be cared for on either side
Armies to stop fighting at night and on holy days
Civilians to be moved away from every battlefield
quiz.e: Neutrality and protection for the wounded and their carers was the revolutionary idea.

quiz.q: What happened to Dunant after founding the Red Cross?
o: He fell into poverty, but later won the first Nobel Peace Prize
He led the Red Cross for the rest of his long life
He became a wealthy banker in Geneva and a public figure
He was forgotten and never received any public honour
quiz.e: Dunant's idea outlasted his own fortunes, and he was finally honoured in 1901.

quiz.q: What did the fourth 1949 convention add?
o: Rules covering only naval battles and ship crews
Limits on which weapons armies were allowed to build
Protection for civilians in enemy hands and occupied territory
Rules on the circumstances in which wars may begin
quiz.e: The Second World War showed that civilians needed their own treaty.

quiz.q: What does the principle of proportionality mean?
o: Both sides must field equal numbers of troops
Civilians may be targeted if the cause is a just one
Civilian harm must not be excessive for the gain
Attacks are lawful whenever a senior general approves them
quiz.e: Proportionality limits harm to civilians even when a target is legitimate.

quiz.q: Who can pursue people accused of grave breaches?
o: Every state must search for and prosecute them
Only the country where the breach occurred may do so
Only the Red Cross may bring such people to account
Only the accused person's own country may do so
quiz.e: The conventions make grave breaches a matter for all states, not just the combatants.

LESSONS.push: A businessman went to meet an emperor and ended up writing rules for war.

LESSONS.title: Lindy Chamberlain and the dingo: a wrongful conviction
LESSONS.hook: A baby vanished from a tent near Uluru, and her mother was convicted of murder. It took decades, and a chance discovery, to prove the truth.

sections.key: Azaria Chamberlain vanished from a tent in 1980, and public suspicion turned on her parents.
sections.b:
On 17 August 1980, Michael and Lindy Chamberlain, a pastor and his wife from Mount Isa, were camping near Uluru. Their nine-week-old daughter Azaria was asleep in the tent. Lindy heard a cry, went to check and saw a dingo leaving. Azaria was gone. She was never found, though some of her clothing turned up near a dingo den a week later.

Many Australians found the story hard to believe. Rumours spread about the family's Seventh-day Adventist faith, including the false claim that Azaria's name meant 'sacrifice in the wilderness'. Lindy's calm in public was read as coldness. A 1981 inquest found a dingo took the baby, but police kept investigating a murder theory.

sections.key: The prosecution relied on confident forensic evidence that was later shown to be badly flawed.
sections.b:
A second inquest led to Lindy being charged with murder and Michael with being an accessory after the fact. There was no body, no confession, no clear motive and no witness to any killing. The case rested heavily on science. Experts testified that tests found foetal blood in the family's car, including a spray pattern under the dashboard. A forensic expert argued that marks on the jumpsuit looked like a bloody handprint and that its damage was made by a cutting instrument, not a dingo's teeth. The prosecution suggested Lindy had cut Azaria's throat in the car.

The Darwin jury, faced with confident experts, convicted. In October 1982 Lindy was sentenced to life imprisonment with hard labour, and Michael received a suspended sentence. Appeals, including to the High Court, failed.

sections.key: In 1986 a missing piece of clothing was found by chance, and a Royal Commission dismantled the forensic evidence.
sections.b:
Lindy had always said Azaria wore a small matinee jacket, which had never been found. In early 1986, an English tourist, David Brett, fell to his death while climbing Uluru. Searching for his remains, police found the jacket half buried near a dingo lair, in an area not easily reached. It supported Lindy's account. Within days she was released, having served more than three years.

The government set up a Royal Commission, led by Justice Trevor Morling. His 1987 report found serious problems with the forensic evidence. Most strikingly, the supposed spray of foetal blood under the dashboard was shown to be a sound deadening compound applied when the car was made.

sections.key: The convictions were quashed in 1988, but a coroner only confirmed in 2012 that a dingo took Azaria.
sections.b:
Morling concluded that the convictions could not be justified on the evidence. In September 1988 the Northern Territory Court of Criminal Appeal quashed the convictions of both Lindy and Michael. In 1992 the Chamberlains received compensation of about 1.3 million dollars for their wrongful imprisonment and legal costs.

Yet the official cause of death remained uncertain. A third inquest, in 1995, returned an open finding. Only at a fourth inquest, in June 2012, did the Northern Territory coroner, Elizabeth Morris, formally find that Azaria had been taken and killed by a dingo, and the death certificate was changed. More than 30 years after that night, the family's account was finally recognised in law.

sections.key: A conviction is only as strong as its evidence, and confident experts and public prejudice can mislead.
sections.b:
The case is now studied as a warning about wrongful convictions. Experts presented uncertain results with too much confidence, and some tests were poorly done or misread. The jury had little way to know.

In the years that followed, Australian forensic science moved towards stricter standards, accreditation and more careful presentation of evidence in court. The case also showed how media coverage and public prejudice can shape a trial, as people judged Lindy by her manner and religion rather than the facts. Later dingo attacks on children, including a fatal attack on Fraser Island, now K'gari, in 2001, ended any lingering doubt that dingoes can be dangerous. Above all, a conviction is only as strong as its evidence.

quiz.q: What fed public suspicion of the Chamberlains?
o: A confession Lindy gave to police early on
Rumours about their faith and Lindy's calm manner
Evidence that Azaria had been seen alive later
A clear motive uncovered by the investigators
quiz.e: People judged Lindy by her manner and faith rather than by the facts.

quiz.q: What did the prosecution's case rest on?
o: Several eyewitnesses who saw the killing take place
A signed confession from Michael to the police
Forensic evidence that experts presented confidently
Proof that dingoes never enter campgrounds near Uluru
quiz.e: Jurors trusted confident experts, whose results were later shown to be flawed.

quiz.q: What did the jacket and the Royal Commission reveal?
o: The jacket backed Lindy; the 'blood' was car sound deadener
The jacket proved Lindy had been lying to police all along
The blood tests were correct but the jury misread them
The dashboard stain was confirmed to come from the baby
quiz.e: New evidence and a review showed the forensic case could not stand.

quiz.q: Why did the coroner only confirm a dingo took Azaria in 2012?
o: Earlier findings left the cause of death unsettled or open
The family never asked for any further inquest until 2012
The jacket was lost again and no new evidence emerged
Police refused to reopen the case until the year 2012
quiz.e: Clearing the Chamberlains came in stages, and the cause of death was formally settled last.

quiz.q: What is the main lesson of the case?
o: Confident experts can mislead, so evidence needs scrutiny
Dingoes are harmless to children, as the case proved
Juries should never be allowed to hear forensic evidence
Media coverage cannot influence the outcome of a trial
quiz.e: The case pushed Australian forensic science towards stricter standards and more careful evidence.

LESSONS.push: Australia convicted a mother over a missing baby. Then a jacket turned up.

LESSONS.title: Marbury v Madison: how courts got the power to strike down laws
LESSONS.hook: A row over an undelivered job letter gave judges one of the greatest powers in modern government. The judge who did it managed to win by appearing to lose.

sections.key: An undelivered job letter from the outgoing president took William Marbury straight to the Supreme Court.
sections.b:
John Adams and the Federalists lost the 1800 election to Thomas Jefferson. Before handing over in March 1801, Adams created new judicial posts and filled them with Federalists, whom critics called the midnight judges. One was William Marbury, named a justice of the peace for the District of Columbia. His commission was signed and sealed, but in the last-minute rush the Secretary of State's office failed to deliver it. That Secretary of State was John Marshall, who had just become Chief Justice.

When Jefferson took office, his Secretary of State, James Madison, refused to hand it over. Marbury sued directly in the Supreme Court, seeking a writ of mandamus, an order commanding an official to do his legal duty.

sections.key: Marshall found that Marbury was owed his job, but that the Court could not order it, because the law was unconstitutional.
sections.b:
The case was a trap. If Marshall ordered Madison to deliver the commission, the administration would probably ignore him, exposing the young Court as powerless. If he backed down, he would seem to concede that the executive could ignore the law.

In February 1803, Marshall ruled that Marbury had a right to his commission and the law should provide a remedy. But the Supreme Court could not provide it. The section of the Judiciary Act that let Marbury come directly to the Court tried to expand its original jurisdiction beyond what the Constitution allowed. When an ordinary law conflicts with the Constitution, the Constitution must win. So Marbury lost, and Jefferson got his result. But the Court had claimed something far bigger: the power to declare acts of Congress unconstitutional.

sections.key: Judicial review is the power of courts to strike down laws that breach the constitution.
sections.b:
Marshall's reasoning was straightforward. A written constitution is the supreme law, deliberately placed above ordinary laws. If Congress could pass any law regardless of the Constitution, its limits would be meaningless. Someone must decide whether a law conflicts with it, and Marshall argued that this job belonged to judges. In one of the most quoted lines in American law, he wrote that it is emphatically the province and duty of the judicial department to say what the law is.

This is judicial review. The Constitution had not spelled it out clearly, though some founders had discussed the idea. Marshall made it settled doctrine, using a case where his ruling gave his political opponents a short-term win.

sections.key: The Court did not strike down another federal law for over half a century, a reminder that judicial review can be used badly.
sections.b:
For such an important power, judicial review was used sparingly at first. After Marbury, the Supreme Court did not strike down another act of Congress until 1857, in the infamous Dred Scott decision. It held that Black Americans could not be citizens and helped push the country towards civil war. Judicial review is a tool, and courts can use it badly as well as wisely.

Over time the power grew. In the 20th century, the Court struck down laws on everything from segregated schools to campaign spending. Because judges are unelected, debates continue about how boldly they should use this power, and when they should defer to elected lawmakers. Those debates are as old as the decision itself.

sections.key: Australia's High Court has long used judicial review, while British courts traditionally cannot strike down Acts of Parliament.
sections.b:
The idea spread to many countries with written constitutions. Australia's framers built a federal system in which the Commonwealth's powers are limited, so it was taken for granted that the High Court would decide whether laws stayed within those limits. In the 1951 Communist Party case, Justice Fullagar wrote that in our system the principle of Marbury v Madison is accepted as axiomatic, meaning self-evident.

The United Kingdom is different. Under parliamentary sovereignty, British courts cannot strike down an Act of Parliament. Since the Human Rights Act 1998 they can declare a law incompatible with protected rights, but Parliament decides whether to change it. Different systems, different answers to the question of who has the final word.

quiz.q: Why was Marshall in a political trap?
o: He had already promised Jefferson a win in return
Ordering it risked defiance; refusing risked looking weak
Congress had banned the Court from hearing such cases
He had no real way of reading the Constitution
quiz.e: Either choice risked weakening the young Court.

quiz.q: How did Marshall's ruling lose the case but win something bigger?
o: Marbury lost, but the Court gained the power to void laws
Marbury won, and Jefferson was ordered to resign
The Court claimed the power to appoint all federal judges
The Court gave Congress more power over the judges
quiz.e: By striking down a law, the Court established that it could.

quiz.q: What is judicial review?
o: The power of judges to write new laws for Parliament
A parliamentary review of a judge's conduct
Courts striking down laws that breach the constitution
The right of a losing party to appeal to a higher court
quiz.e: A constitution's limits mean little unless someone can enforce them.

quiz.q: What does the Dred Scott decision show about judicial review?
o: Courts should never use it
It is only ever used to protect rights
It was used often before 1850
It can be used badly as well as wisely
quiz.e: Judicial review depends on how judges choose to use it.

quiz.q: How do British courts differ from Australia's High Court on striking down laws?
o: They strike down laws more often than the High Court does
They cannot strike down Acts, only declare them incompatible
They cannot interpret statutes passed by Parliament at all
They answer to Australia's High Court on constitutional matters
quiz.e: Parliament keeps the final word in the United Kingdom.

LESSONS.push: A letter that never arrived gave judges the power to strike down laws.

LESSONS.title: Common law and civil law: the world's two great legal families
LESSONS.hook: Most of the world's legal systems descend from one of two ancestors: medieval English judges, or the law books of ancient Rome. Which one you live under shapes how courts work.

sections.key: Most legal systems descend from either the common law or the civil law tradition, and 'civil law' has two meanings.
sections.b:
Arrested in Sydney, Paris, Tokyo or Chicago, you would meet courtrooms that work differently. Much of the difference is history. Common law grew from medieval England and spread with the British Empire, to Australia, the United States, Canada, New Zealand and India. Civil law grew from Roman law, revived in medieval Europe and organised into national codes. It covers most of continental Europe, Latin America and much of Asia and Africa, so by number of countries it is more widespread.

Beware the vocabulary. In everyday Australian use, civil law means non-criminal disputes, such as contracts and negligence. Here it names a whole tradition built on written codes, and civil law countries have criminal cases too. Lawyers often say 'civilian systems' for clarity.

sections.key: The common law grew case by case from the rulings of royal judges, bound by precedent.
sections.b:
After the Norman conquest of 1066, English kings gradually built a national system of royal courts. Under Henry II, who reigned from 1154 to 1189, royal judges travelled on circuits around the country, hearing cases in the king's name. Over time they developed rules that applied across the whole realm, a law common to all of England, which is where the name comes from.

Rather than starting from a grand written code, the common law grew case by case. Judges looked at how earlier cases had been decided and followed them. This principle, called precedent, means a decision of a higher court binds lower courts in similar cases. Parliament can override judge-made law with statutes, but much of the law began in courtrooms.

sections.key: Civil law grew from Justinian's law books, rediscovered in medieval Italy and later turned into national codes.
sections.b:
In the 530s, the Eastern Roman emperor Justinian ordered his lawyers to collect and organise centuries of Roman law. The result, later called the Corpus Juris Civilis, or Body of Civil Law, was a vast compilation of legal rules and expert opinions. For centuries it was largely forgotten in Western Europe.

Then, in the late 1000s, scholars in Bologna, Italy, began studying it closely, and Roman law became the basis of university legal education across Europe. Many centuries later, nations turned these ideas into tidy national codes. The most influential was France's Civil Code of 1804, often called the Napoleonic Code. Germany's Civil Code of 1900 was another giant, later influencing countries as different as Japan and Greece.

sections.key: Common law trials are usually adversarial, while civil law trials are more inquisitorial, with judges leading the inquiry.
sections.b:
The traditions also differ in how trials work. Common law systems are usually adversarial. Two sides, each with its own lawyers, present evidence and question witnesses, while a judge acts like an umpire and, in serious criminal cases, a jury often decides the facts.

Civil law systems are usually more inquisitorial. Judges, sometimes including an investigating judge before trial, take a more active role in gathering evidence and questioning witnesses, and written files matter more. Juries are less common, although some countries use lay judges who sit alongside professionals. Judges in civil law countries are often career officials trained for the role, rather than experienced lawyers appointed later in life, as is common in Australia.

sections.key: Many places mix traditions, and the two families have grown closer over time.
sections.b:
Real legal systems are rarely pure. Scotland and South Africa have mixed systems combining civil law roots with common law influences. In Canada, Quebec uses a civil code for private law, while the other provinces follow common law. Louisiana's private law shows its French and Spanish heritage. Many countries also blend in religious or customary law.

The two great families have also drifted closer. Common law countries now rely on huge volumes of statutes, so much of their law is written down much like a code. Meanwhile, courts in civil law countries often follow earlier decisions of higher courts in practice, even where they are not formally bound. Two old family trees, with branches increasingly intertwined.

quiz.q: What does 'civil law' mean in the phrase 'civil law tradition'?
o: A legal tradition built on Roman law and written codes
The law dealing only with contracts and negligence
The law governing a country's public servants
Law developed case by case by royal judges
quiz.e: In this sense civil law is a whole legal family, and it includes criminal law too.

quiz.q: What is precedent in the common law?
o: A judge's personal preference in each case
