A statute passed by Parliament to override judges
A higher court's ruling that lower courts must follow
A rule that each case starts from a written code
quiz.e: Judges follow how earlier cases were decided, which is how the common law grew.

quiz.q: Where does civil law come from?
o: Royal judges travelling circuits around medieval England
Roman law compiled under Justinian and later turned into codes
A single treaty signed by the states of medieval Europe
The customs and administration of the British Empire
quiz.e: The Corpus Juris Civilis, rediscovered in Bologna, shaped the codes of France and Germany.

quiz.q: How do common law and civil law trials typically differ?
o: Common law lacks lawyers, while civil law always uses them
Civil law relies on juries, common law on career judges
They are identical in how trials are run and who leads
Common law is adversarial, civil law more inquisitorial
quiz.e: The traditions differ in who drives the search for evidence.

quiz.q: How have the two traditions changed over time?
o: They have drawn closer, as each borrows from the other
They have grown further apart over the past century
One has completely replaced the other around the world
They no longer share any features at all
quiz.e: Common law is increasingly codified, while civil law courts follow precedent in practice.

LESSONS.push: Two ancient legal families decide how most of the world's courts work. Which is yours?

LESSONS.title: The Communist Party case: when the High Court said no
LESSONS.hook: In 1950, at the height of the Cold War, the Australian Parliament banned the Communist Party. Within months, the High Court struck the law down, in one of its most important decisions.

sections.key: In 1950 the Menzies government passed a law to dissolve the Communist Party of Australia, and it was challenged almost at once.
sections.b:
By 1950 the Cold War was deepening. The Soviet Union had tested an atomic bomb, communists had won China's civil war, and the Korean War began in June, with Australian forces soon involved. At home, a major coal strike in 1949 sharpened fears of communist influence in the unions.

Robert Menzies' Liberal and Country Party coalition won the 1949 election promising to ban the Communist Party, then a legal party. Parliament passed the Communist Party Dissolution Act in 1950. Labor, which controlled the Senate, was divided but let it pass. Almost as soon as the act took effect in October, it was challenged in the High Court.

sections.key: The act dissolved the party, let the government declare other groups and people unlawful, and relied on Parliament's own statements of fact.
sections.b:
The act declared the Communist Party dissolved and its property forfeited to the Commonwealth. On government advice, the Governor-General could also declare other organisations unlawful if they were linked to communism and judged a threat to security or defence. Individuals could be declared too, which barred them from Commonwealth jobs and from office in certain unions.

Crucially, the act opened with recitals: statements in which Parliament itself declared that communists were working to overthrow the government by violence, and that the law was needed for defence. People who were declared had only limited ability to challenge the government's conclusions in court.

sections.key: Six of the seven judges held that Parliament cannot make its own law valid by declaring the facts that would justify it.
sections.b:
The Communist Party and several unions argued the act exceeded federal power. Dr H. V. Evatt, Labor's deputy leader and a former High Court judge, appeared for the Waterside Workers' Federation, a controversial choice. The Commonwealth relied mainly on the defence power in section 51 of the Constitution. The central question was whether Parliament could simply declare a threat to exist, and so give itself the power to act.

In March 1951 the High Court struck the act down by six votes to one, with Chief Justice Latham dissenting. Whether a law falls within a head of power is for the courts to decide. As Justice Fullagar put it, a stream cannot rise higher than its source. Australia was not formally at war, so the defence power could not support such measures.

sections.key: Justice Dixon wrote that the Constitution assumes the rule of law, so the limits on government power are for judges to decide.
sections.b:
The most celebrated judgment came from Justice Owen Dixon, later Chief Justice and widely regarded as one of Australia's greatest judges. He observed that history, and not only ancient history, shows that governments as well as private groups can undermine democratic institutions. He added that the Constitution was framed on traditional conceptions, some of which it simply assumes, and that the rule of law is one of them.

In other words, the Constitution takes for granted that government is subject to law, enforced by independent courts. Dixon's words are quoted in many later cases. They help explain why Australian courts insist that judges, not ministers, set the limits of government power.

sections.key: After the court said no, voters narrowly refused to give Parliament the power, a second check on government.
sections.b:
The Menzies government took the question to the people. After winning a double dissolution election in April 1951, it held a referendum in September asking voters to give the Commonwealth power over communists and communism. Evatt, by then Labor leader, campaigned against it as a threat to civil liberties. Early polls favoured Yes, but support fell during the campaign.

Just under half of voters said Yes, and only Queensland, Western Australia and Tasmania carried it, short of the double majority required. The Communist Party stayed legal, never became a major electoral force, and dissolved itself in the early 1990s.

The case is still cited when courts weigh security laws, because the same question returns: who decides the limits of government?

quiz.q: What was the main aim of the Communist Party Dissolution Act of 1950?
o: To ban strikes in the coal industry
To dissolve the Communist Party of Australia
To bring Australia into the Korean War
To give the Senate new powers
quiz.e: The Menzies government wanted to ban the then-legal Communist Party, driven by Cold War fears.

quiz.q: What role did the 'recitals' play in the act?
o: Parliament's own declarations that communists were a threat
They listed the penalties for joining the party and its unions
They gave the High Court special powers to review the act
They named every party member who would be declared
quiz.e: The recitals tried to make the law valid by having Parliament declare the facts that justified it.

quiz.q: What did Fullagar mean by 'a stream cannot rise higher than its source'?
o: Courts must defer to Parliament on matters of security
Parliament cannot create its own power by declaring facts
Federal laws always override conflicting state laws
Every law must pass both houses in a fixed order
quiz.e: Whether a law falls within Parliament's powers is for the courts to decide, not for Parliament to declare.

quiz.q: What did Justice Dixon say the Constitution assumes?
o: That Parliament is supreme over the courts
That emergency powers may be used in peacetime
That political parties are protected
That government is subject to the rule of law
quiz.e: The Constitution takes for granted that government must obey the law, enforced by independent courts.

quiz.q: What happened at the 1951 referendum on communism?
o: It passed in every state of the Commonwealth
It was cancelled after the High Court ruling
It narrowly failed, carrying only three states
It passed, but the government never used it
quiz.e: Voters acted as a second check, refusing the power the courts had said Parliament lacked.

LESSONS.push: Parliament banned a political party, then six judges said it couldn't. Why?

LESSONS.title: Eclipses: the cosmic coincidence
LESSONS.hook: For a few minutes, day turns to night, the temperature drops and stars appear at noon. It happens because of one of the luckiest coincidences in the solar system.

sections.key: The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon but also about 400 times farther away, so they look almost the same size.
sections.b:
Hold your thumb at arm's length and it can hide a whole building. The Moon does the same trick with the Sun. The Sun is roughly 400 times the Moon's diameter, yet it also sits roughly 400 times farther from us. Both discs therefore look almost exactly the same size in our sky, about half a degree across.

No other planet has a moon that fits its sun so neatly. When the Moon passes directly between Earth and the Sun, it can cover the blinding disc completely and leave the faint outer atmosphere, the corona, glowing like a silver crown. It is an accident of geometry, and we happen to live in the right era to enjoy it.

sections.key: Because the Moon's orbit is slightly oval, some solar eclipses are total, some leave a ring of fire, and most people see only a partial one.
sections.b:
The Moon's orbit is not a perfect circle. If an eclipse happens when the Moon is near its closest point, it looks big enough to cover the Sun entirely, giving a total eclipse. Near its farthest point, the Moon looks slightly too small and a bright ring of sunlight surrounds it. That is an annular eclipse, from the Latin annulus, meaning ring.

Anyone outside the narrow central path sees only a partial eclipse, with a bite taken out of the Sun. The path of totality is usually only about 100 to 200 kilometres wide and races across Earth's surface faster than a jet airliner. That is why eclipse chasers travel the world to stand in exactly the right strip of land.

sections.key: The Moon's orbit is tilted about five degrees, so eclipses only happen when the Sun, Moon and Earth line up at the crossing points.
sections.b:
The Moon circles Earth roughly once a month, so you might expect an eclipse at every new moon. The catch is that its orbit is tilted about five degrees compared with Earth's path around the Sun. Most months the new moon slides just above or below the Sun in our sky and nothing happens.

Eclipses can only occur when a new or full moon lines up with one of the two points where the orbits cross. These alignments arrive in eclipse seasons, roughly every six months. Ancient Babylonian astronomers noticed that eclipses repeat in a cycle of about 18 years and 11 days, now called the saros. It let them predict eclipses long before anyone understood orbits.

sections.key: In a total lunar eclipse the Moon turns red because Earth's atmosphere bends sunset-coloured light onto it.
sections.b:
In a lunar eclipse, Earth passes between the Sun and the full Moon, and our planet's shadow falls across the lunar surface. You might expect the Moon to vanish, but it usually glows deep copper or blood red. The reason is our atmosphere. Sunlight skimming past the edge of Earth is bent inwards towards the Moon, and most of its blue light is scattered out on the way, the same process that makes sunsets red. In effect, the Moon is lit by every sunrise and sunset on Earth at once.

Unlike solar eclipses, lunar eclipses can be seen by anyone on the night side of the planet, and they are completely safe to watch with the naked eye.

sections.key: Only totality is safe to view directly; at every other stage of a solar eclipse you need certified eclipse glasses or an indirect method.
sections.b:
Even when most of the Sun is covered, the remaining sliver is intense enough to damage the retina. The retina has no pain receptors, so you may not notice until afterwards. Ordinary sunglasses are nowhere near dark enough.

Safe options include certified eclipse glasses or solar viewers meeting the ISO 12312-2 standard, or an indirect method such as a pinhole projector, where you look at an image of the Sun cast onto paper. Never look through binoculars, a camera or a telescope without a proper solar filter fitted to the front. The one exception is the brief period of totality, when the Sun is completely hidden. The moment the first bead of sunlight reappears, the glasses go back on.

Australia's turn comes on 22 July 2028, when totality crosses the country, including Sydney.

quiz.q: Why do the Sun and Moon look almost the same size from Earth?
o: Earth's atmosphere magnifies the Moon's disc
The Sun is 400 times larger but 400 times farther away
The Moon sits closer to the Sun than Earth does
They really are almost exactly the same size
quiz.e: The Sun's far greater size is cancelled out by its far greater distance.

quiz.q: What causes an annular eclipse, with a ring of sunlight around the Moon?
o: Clouds covering part of the Sun during the eclipse
Earth's shadow falling partly on the Moon
The Moon being near the far point of its orbit
The Moon being much closer to Earth than usual
quiz.e: The Moon's oval orbit means it sometimes looks too small to cover the whole Sun.

quiz.q: Why don't we see a solar eclipse at every new moon?
o: The Moon is moving too fast to line up most months
The Moon only passes in front of the Sun twice a year
Earth's rotation keeps pulling the Moon out of line
The Moon's orbit is tilted, so it usually misses the Sun
quiz.e: A roughly five-degree tilt means the alignment only works near the points where the orbits cross.

quiz.q: Why does the Moon often turn red during a total lunar eclipse?
o: Earth's air bends reddened sunset light onto it
Red dust on the Moon reflects the shadow's light
The Moon heats up and glows red in the shadow
Light reflects from Mars onto its surface
quiz.e: Blue light is scattered out as sunlight passes through our air, leaving red light to reach the Moon.

quiz.q: When is it safe to look at a solar eclipse without eye protection?
o: During the partial phases, if most of the Sun is covered
Only during totality, when the Sun is completely covered
At any time, if you also wear dark sunglasses
Any time the Sun is low in the sky near sunset
quiz.e: Any sliver of exposed Sun can damage the retina painlessly, so only totality is safe.

LESSONS.push: For a few minutes at noon, stars appear. It hinges on a lucky ratio of 400.

LESSONS.title: Comets: dirty snowballs from the deep
LESSONS.hook: For thousands of years comets were seen as omens of doom. Then one astronomer predicted a comet's return, died before he could see it, and was proved right.

sections.key: Before science explained them, comets were widely feared as signs of disaster, and even Aristotle misjudged what they were.
sections.b:
A comet appears suddenly, hangs in the sky for weeks with a ghostly tail, then fades. To many ancient cultures that unpredictability was frightening. Chinese astronomers kept careful comet records for more than two thousand years, often linking them to political upheaval. In 1066 a bright comet appeared over Europe shortly before the Norman conquest of England, and the Bayeux Tapestry shows people pointing at it in alarm.

The word comet comes from the Greek for 'long-haired', describing the streaming tail. Aristotle believed comets were something happening in Earth's upper atmosphere, not objects travelling through space. It took many centuries, and better telescopes, to prove him wrong.

sections.key: Edmond Halley realised that several historical comets were one object returning, and predicted its comeback decades ahead.
sections.b:
In the early 1700s, the English astronomer Edmond Halley studied records of bright comets and noticed that those seen in 1531, 1607 and 1682 had remarkably similar paths. Using his friend Isaac Newton's new laws of gravity, he argued they were a single comet on a long oval orbit, returning roughly every 75 to 76 years. He predicted it would reappear around 1758.

Halley died in 1742 and never saw the result. On Christmas night 1758, a German farmer and amateur astronomer, Johann Palitzsch, spotted the comet right on cue. It was a triumph for Newton's physics, and the comet has carried Halley's name ever since. It last passed in 1986 and is due back in 2061.

sections.key: A comet's core is a small, dark lump of ice, dust and rock, and the glorious display comes from the cloud it releases.
sections.b:
In 1950 the American astronomer Fred Whipple proposed that a comet's heart, its nucleus, is a 'dirty snowball' of frozen water, carbon dioxide, ammonia and other ices mixed with dust and rock. Space missions have since confirmed the basic idea, though many comets turned out to be more dust than ice.

A typical nucleus is only a few kilometres wide and surprisingly dark, reflecting about as much light as charcoal. When the European probe Giotto flew past Halley's Comet in 1986, it photographed a lumpy, peanut-shaped nucleus roughly 15 kilometres long, jetting gas from its sunlit side. The display we see from Earth comes not from this tiny core but from the vast cloud it releases when warmed.

sections.key: A comet grows a curved dust tail and a straight gas tail, and both point away from the Sun, not behind the comet.
sections.b:
Far from the Sun a comet is frozen and inactive. As it swings closer, sunlight warms the surface and the ices turn straight into gas, dragging dust out with them. This builds a fuzzy atmosphere called the coma, which can be larger than Jupiter.

Then the tails form. The dust tail is pushed gently by sunlight, curves along the comet's path and shines yellowish white. The ion tail is made of electrically charged gas swept away by the solar wind, so it runs straight and often glows blue.

Here is the surprise: both tails point away from the Sun, not behind the comet. When a comet heads back out into the solar system, it travels tail first.

sections.key: Comets are frozen leftovers from the solar system's birth, and in 2014 Rosetta's Philae became the first lander to touch one.
sections.b:
Comets are leftovers from the formation of the solar system about 4.6 billion years ago. Those returning in under 200 years mostly come from the Kuiper Belt, a ring of icy bodies beyond Neptune. Comets with orbits of thousands or millions of years are thought to come from the Oort Cloud, a vast shell of icy objects. No one has directly seen it; it is inferred from the orbits of comets.

The European Space Agency's Rosetta reached comet 67P, a rubber-duck-shaped body about four kilometres long, after a ten-year chase. In November 2014 it released the Philae lander. Its harpoons failed to fire, and it bounced twice into a cliff's shadow, yet sent data for about 60 hours. Rosetta found 67P's water differs chemically from Earth's oceans.

quiz.q: What did Aristotle wrongly believe about comets?
o: That they were distant stars like the others
That they were pieces broken off the Moon
That they were a phenomenon of Earth's atmosphere
That they were fixed in the sky all year
quiz.e: Better telescopes and observation later showed that comets travel through space.

quiz.q: Why was Halley's prediction such a triumph for science?
o: It proved comets are born inside Earth's atmosphere
It showed comets never return once they have passed
It proved comets are fragments of the Moon
Newton's laws predicted its return after Halley's death
quiz.e: The comet's return showed that gravity governs comets, as it does planets.

quiz.q: What is a comet's nucleus mostly made of?
o: Molten rock and metal
Ice, dust and rock
Glowing gas
Pure water ice
quiz.e: The nucleus is a small, dark mix of ices, dust and rock; the bright show comes from the cloud it releases.

quiz.q: Which way do a comet's tails point?
o: Always behind the comet along its path
Towards the Sun
Towards Earth
Away from the Sun
quiz.e: Sunlight and the solar wind push the tails away from the Sun, so an outbound comet travels tail first.

quiz.q: Where are long-period comets thought to come from?
o: The asteroid belt
The Kuiper Belt only
The Oort Cloud
Jupiter's moons
quiz.e: The Oort Cloud is a vast shell of icy objects, known only from the orbits of the comets it sends inwards.

LESSONS.push: Two tails, yet a comet can fly tail first. How does that work?

LESSONS.title: Voyager: the longest journey
LESSONS.hook: Two spacecraft launched in 1977 with a tiny fraction of a modern smartphone's computing power are still talking to Earth from interstellar space.

sections.key: A rare lineup of the outer planets let one spacecraft swing from planet to planet, using each one's gravity as a slingshot.
sections.b:
In the 1960s, NASA engineer Gary Flandro noticed that in the late 1970s Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune would line up in a way that happens only about once every 175 years. A spacecraft could fly past one planet and use its gravity to slingshot towards the next, saving years of travel and enormous amounts of fuel. This 'gravity assist' turned an impossible grand tour into a practical one.

NASA built two identical spacecraft, Voyager 1 and Voyager 2. Confusingly, Voyager 2 launched first, on 20 August 1977, followed by Voyager 1 on 5 September. Voyager 1 was on a faster path, so it overtook its twin and reached Jupiter first.

sections.key: The Voyagers turned the giant planets' moons from dots of light into worlds, and Voyager 2 alone visited Uranus and Neptune.
sections.b:
Before the Voyagers, the giant planets' moons were little more than dots of light. At Jupiter in 1979, the probes found active volcanoes on the moon Io, the first ever seen beyond Earth. They imaged Europa's cracked icy crust, hinting at an ocean beneath, and found thin rings around Jupiter. At Saturn in 1980 and 1981 they revealed intricate structure in the rings and studied the hazy moon Titan.

Voyager 1 was then bent up and out of the plane of the planets for a close look at Titan. Voyager 2 carried on alone, becoming the only spacecraft ever to visit Uranus, in 1986, and Neptune, in 1989.

sections.key: Voyager 1 photographed Earth as a speck from six billion kilometres, and each Voyager carries a golden record of life on Earth.
sections.b:
On 14 February 1990, at the urging of astronomer Carl Sagan, Voyager 1 turned its camera back towards home from about six billion kilometres away. Earth appears as a speck less than a pixel wide, suspended in a beam of sunlight. The photo became famous for its perspective, not its detail. Soon afterwards the cameras were switched off for good to save power.

Each Voyager also carries a gold-plated copper record, with contents chosen by a committee chaired by Sagan. It holds greetings in 55 languages, sounds of rain, surf, whales and a mother's kiss, 115 images, and music from Bach to Chuck Berry. The cover shows how to play it and the Sun's position among pulsars. Finding it is very unlikely; it is partly a message to ourselves.

sections.key: Voyager 1 crossed the heliopause into interstellar space in 2012 and Voyager 2 followed in 2018, though both remain under the Sun's gravity.
sections.b:
The Sun blows a constant stream of charged particles, the solar wind, which inflates a vast bubble around the solar system called the heliosphere. Its outer boundary, the heliopause, is where the solar wind gives way to the thin gas between the stars.

In August 2012 Voyager 1 crossed that boundary, becoming the first human-made object to reach interstellar space. Voyager 2 crossed in November 2018. Neither has left the solar system in every sense, because the Sun's gravity still rules a region far beyond, including the Oort Cloud of comets.

Voyager 1 is now more than 24 billion kilometres away, so far that its radio signals take nearly a full day to reach us.

sections.key: Engineers keep the Voyagers running by rationing power and patching old software, and only the Canberra dish can command Voyager 2.
sections.b:
Each Voyager runs on generators that turn the heat of decaying plutonium into electricity. Output drops by a few watts a year, so engineers have switched off heaters and instruments one by one. The transmitters use roughly the power of a refrigerator light bulb. In 2023 Voyager 1 began sending gibberish because of a failed memory chip. A small team spent months diagnosing it from over 20 light-hours away, moved the affected code elsewhere, and restored contact in 2024.

After Neptune, Voyager 2 was flung south, out of view of the Deep Space Network's stations in California and Spain. Only the 70-metre dish at Tidbinbilla near Canberra can send it commands. When that dish was offline for upgrades in 2020, Voyager 2 could be heard but not commanded for months.

quiz.q: What made the Voyagers' grand tour of the outer planets practical?
o: A new kind of nuclear-powered rocket engine
A rare planetary lineup allowing gravity assists
Refuelling stops at Jupiter and Saturn on the way
A launch from a base on the far side of the Moon
quiz.e: Each planet's gravity flung the craft onward, saving years of travel and huge amounts of fuel.

quiz.q: Which planets has only Voyager 2 visited?
o: Jupiter and Saturn
Mars and Venus
Pluto and Neptune
Uranus and Neptune
quiz.e: Voyager 2 continued alone after Saturn, reaching Uranus in 1986 and Neptune in 1989.

quiz.q: Why is the Pale Blue Dot photograph so famous?
o: It shows how small Earth looks from deep space
It was the sharpest image of Earth ever taken
It was the first picture of Earth's continents
It showed signs of life on Earth
quiz.e: Its power lies in the perspective: everyone who has ever lived spent their life on that speck.

quiz.q: Why is Voyager 1 not considered to have left the solar system entirely?
o: Its radio signals can still be received on Earth
The Sun's gravity still dominates a region far beyond
It remains inside the heliosphere bubble
It is still in orbit around Neptune
quiz.e: Crossing the heliopause means leaving the solar wind's bubble, not the Sun's gravitational reach.

quiz.q: Why can only the Canberra station send commands to Voyager 2?
o: It has the oldest dish of the three stations
The other two stations have been permanently switched off
It headed south, out of view of the northern stations
Voyager 2 was built and launched in Australia
quiz.e: Voyager 2 sits deep in the southern sky, where only the Tidbinbilla dish can see it and transmit.

LESSONS.push: Still talking after nearly 50 years, on less power than a fridge bulb.

LESSONS.title: Venus: Earth's hellish twin
LESSONS.hook: It is almost the same size as Earth and the brightest planet in our sky. Land on it, though, and you would be crushed, cooked and dissolved within hours.

sections.key: Venus is the brightest natural object in the night sky after the Moon, and it only appears around twilight.
sections.b:
If you have ever noticed a brilliant 'star' low in the west after sunset or in the east before dawn, it was probably Venus. It orbits closer to the Sun than we do, so it never strays far from the Sun in our sky and shows only around twilight.

Its thick, bright clouds reflect about three quarters of the sunlight that hits them, making it dazzling. Ancient peoples sometimes thought the morning and evening appearances were two different objects; the Greeks called them Phosphorus and Hesperus before realising they were the same planet. Venus is so bright that it is regularly reported as a UFO, and under very dark skies it can even cast a faint shadow.

sections.key: Venus is nearly Earth's size and mass, but its dense carbon dioxide atmosphere and acid clouds made it a completely different world.
sections.b:
On paper, Venus looks like Earth's sibling. Its diameter is about 95 percent of Earth's, its mass about 80 percent, and it is made of similar rock. For a long time people imagined steamy swamps or oceans under its permanent clouds, and early science fiction filled it with jungles. The truth only emerged with radio telescopes and spacecraft in the 1960s.

Venus's atmosphere is about 96 percent carbon dioxide, and so dense that surface pressure is around 90 times Earth's, like being nearly a kilometre deep in the ocean. Above sit thick clouds of sulfuric acid droplets. Whatever the two planets shared at birth, they took very different paths.

sections.key: A runaway greenhouse effect makes Venus's surface about 465°C, hotter than Mercury and hot enough to melt lead.
sections.b:
Mercury is much closer to the Sun, yet Venus is the hottest planet in the solar system. Its surface sits at roughly 465°C, day and night, from pole to equator. The cause is a runaway greenhouse effect. Sunlight that gets through the clouds warms the ground, but the dense carbon dioxide traps the heat trying to escape to space.

Many scientists think Venus may once have been cooler, possibly with shallow oceans. As the young Sun brightened, the water evaporated, adding more heat-trapping vapour until the oceans were lost. That history is still debated, but Venus shows how powerfully an atmosphere can control a planet's temperature.

sections.key: Venus spins backwards and so slowly that one rotation takes longer than one orbit of the Sun.
sections.b:
Venus takes about 225 Earth days to orbit the Sun but about 243 to spin once on its axis, so its day is longer than its year. It also rotates in the opposite direction to most planets, so the Sun would rise in the west and set in the east, if you could see it through the clouds.

Nobody is certain why. Ideas include a giant collision early in its history, or the slow effect of the Sun's tides on its heavy atmosphere. Oddly, while the planet itself turns at a crawl, its upper atmosphere races around the whole planet in about four Earth days, driven by hurricane-force winds.

sections.key: Soviet Venera probes landed on Venus and sent back pictures, and a Venus transit in 1769 sent Captain Cook towards Australia.
sections.b:
Landing on Venus is brutally hard, yet the Soviet Union did it repeatedly. Venera 7 sent faint signals from the surface in December 1970, the first data from the surface of another planet. In 1975 Venera 9 and 10 returned the first pictures of the ground. In 1982 Venera 13 sent colour images and survived about two hours. NASA's Magellan orbiter later mapped almost the whole planet by radar through the clouds, revealing volcanoes and lava plains.

Occasionally Venus crosses the Sun's face, a transit. Timing one from distant places could reveal the Earth-Sun distance, so Britain sent Lieutenant James Cook to Tahiti for the June 1769 transit. His sealed orders then led to New Zealand and, in 1770, Australia's east coast. The next transit is in 2117.

quiz.q: Why is Venus only seen around dawn or dusk?
o: It only reflects enough sunlight at those times
Earth's shadow hides it for most of the night
Its orbit is inside Earth's, so it stays near the Sun
It moves too fast to be seen later in the night
quiz.e: A planet inside Earth's orbit can never appear far from the Sun in our sky.

quiz.q: What is Venus's atmosphere mostly made of?
o: Mostly nitrogen, as on Earth
Mostly carbon dioxide
Mostly oxygen and water vapour
Mostly hydrogen and helium
quiz.e: A dense carbon dioxide atmosphere, with acid clouds above, makes Venus very unlike Earth.

quiz.q: Why is Venus hotter than Mercury, which is closer to the Sun?
o: Its core is much hotter than Mercury's
It has more volcanoes than any other planet
It is closer to the Sun than Earth is
A runaway greenhouse effect traps its heat
quiz.e: Dense carbon dioxide traps heat, so atmosphere matters more than distance here.

quiz.q: What is unusual about Venus's rotation?
o: It spins backwards, so its day outlasts its year
It spins faster than any other planet does
It rotates once per orbit, always facing the Sun
It rotates on its side, like Uranus does
quiz.e: A turn takes about 243 Earth days, but an orbit takes only about 225.

quiz.q: Why did Britain send James Cook to Tahiti in 1769?
o: To claim Tahiti for the British Crown before France
To trade for spices and provisions with the islanders
To time a Venus transit and measure the Sun's distance
To map the coast of South America for the navy
quiz.e: Timing the transit from far-apart places let astronomers measure the Sun's distance.

LESSONS.push: Earth's twin has a day that lasts longer than its year.

LESSONS.title: Pluto and the dwarf planets
LESSONS.hook: In 2006 Pluto was voted out of the planet club. The real story is less about Pluto being demoted and more about discovering it had a lot of company.

sections.key: Clyde Tombaugh found Pluto in 1930 by comparing photographs of the sky, partly through luck and mostly through patience.
sections.b:
In the early 1900s, astronomer Percival Lowell was convinced an unknown 'Planet X' lay beyond Neptune, and his observatory in Flagstaff, Arizona, kept searching after his death. In 1929 it hired Clyde Tombaugh, a 22-year-old Kansas farm boy with no university degree, who had impressed staff with drawings from his homemade telescope.

Tombaugh photographed the same patches of sky several nights apart and flicked between the plates with a blink comparator, looking for a dot that moved against the background stars. On 18 February 1930 he found one. The calculations that inspired the hunt later proved wrong, so finding Pluto was partly luck, combined with enormous patience.

sections.key: The name Pluto was suggested by 11-year-old Venetia Burney from Oxford, and it honoured Percival Lowell too.
sections.b:
News of the new planet spread worldwide, and name suggestions poured in. In Oxford, England, 11-year-old Venetia Burney heard about it over breakfast and suggested Pluto, the Roman god of the underworld, fitting for a cold, dark world at the edge of the solar system. Her grandfather passed the idea to an astronomer friend, who sent it to the Lowell Observatory.

Staff there voted unanimously in favour, partly because the first two letters, P and L, honoured Percival Lowell. Venetia reportedly received a five-pound note as a reward. Soon after, Walt Disney introduced a cartoon dog named Pluto. Decades later, an instrument on the New Horizons spacecraft was named in her honour.

sections.key: Each new measurement shrank Pluto, until it proved far smaller than first thought, and smaller even than our Moon.
sections.b:
At discovery, Pluto was assumed to be roughly Earth-sized, because it was thought to be disturbing Neptune's orbit. Each new measurement shrank it. In 1978 astronomers discovered its largest moon, Charon, which allowed Pluto's mass to be calculated precisely. It was tiny: only about a fifth of our Moon's mass.

Pluto is about 2,380 kilometres across, narrower than Australia is wide. Charon is about half Pluto's diameter, so large that the two swing around a shared point in the space between them. Pluto's orbit is also odd: stretched and tilted, and between 1979 and 1999 it came closer to the Sun than Neptune did.

sections.key: Pluto is one of the largest members of the Kuiper Belt, and the discovery of Eris forced a formal definition of a planet.
sections.b:
In 1992 astronomers found another small icy body beyond Neptune, the first known member of what is now called the Kuiper Belt. Hundreds, then thousands more followed. Pluto was not a lonely ninth planet but one of the largest of a vast belt of frozen leftovers.

The crisis came in 2005, when a team led by Mike Brown announced Eris, first thought larger than Pluto. Later measurements showed it is very slightly smaller in diameter but about a quarter more massive. If Pluto was a planet, Eris had to be one too, and possibly dozens more.

In August 2006 the International Astronomical Union defined a planet in Prague: it orbits the Sun, is massive enough to be round, and has cleared the neighbourhood around its orbit.

sections.key: Pluto failed the 'cleared its neighbourhood' test and became a dwarf planet, yet New Horizons found a surprisingly active world.
sections.b:
Pluto passes the first two tests but fails the third, because it shares its region with countless Kuiper Belt objects. It became a dwarf planet, alongside Eris and the asteroid Ceres, with Haumea and Makemake added later. Some planetary scientists still argue for a definition based on a body's own properties, not its surroundings.

NASA's New Horizons flew past Pluto on 14 July 2015, nine and a half years after launch. Expectations were modest: an old, cratered ball of ice. Instead it found a pale heart-shaped region, Tombaugh Regio, holding Sputnik Planitia, a young plain of nitrogen ice that flows like glaciers and has almost no craters. There were also water-ice mountains kilometres high and a blue haze. Some of Tombaugh's ashes were aboard.

quiz.q: How did Clyde Tombaugh find Pluto?
o: Using a large radio telescope in Arizona
By mathematical predictions from Lowell alone
By comparing photographs for a dot that moved
By sending a space probe out beyond Neptune
quiz.e: Careful, patient comparison of photographic plates revealed a moving object.

quiz.q: Why was the name Pluto chosen?
o: It honoured the farm where the discoverer grew up
A fitting Roman god, and P and L honour Percival Lowell
It was named after a cartoon dog from a Disney film
It was chosen by a public vote held in Britain
quiz.e: The Lowell staff liked the god's fit and the initials of Percival Lowell.

quiz.q: What let astronomers measure Pluto's mass precisely and show it was tiny?
o: Landing a probe on its icy surface
Watching it pass in front of Neptune
Tracking the orbit of its moon Charon
Counting its craters from Earth
quiz.e: A moon's orbit reveals the mass of the body it circles, and Pluto proved far smaller than expected.

quiz.q: Why did the discovery of Eris force a new definition of a planet?
o: Eris was discovered to be larger than Neptune
If Pluto were a planet, Eris and others would be too
Eris turned out not to orbit the Sun at all
Eris was found inside the orbit of Earth
quiz.e: Pluto is one of many Kuiper Belt worlds, so a clear rule was needed.

quiz.q: Which test of the 2006 planet definition does Pluto fail?
o: Orbiting the Sun in its own path
Being massive enough to be round
Holding at least one moon in orbit
Clearing the area around its orbit
quiz.e: Pluto shares its region with countless Kuiper Belt objects, so it does not dominate its path.

LESSONS.push: Pluto lost its planet status, but not for the reason most people think.

LESSONS.title: Jupiter and Saturn: the giants
LESSONS.hook: Jupiter could swallow every other planet with room to spare, and Saturn is light enough, in a sense, to float. Meet the two kings of the solar system.

sections.key: Jupiter has more than twice the mass of all the other planets combined, and its moons helped overturn the Earth-centred universe.
sections.b:
Jupiter is about 11 times wider than Earth and roughly 318 times more massive. Put all the other planets together and Jupiter still outweighs them more than twice over. Despite its size, it spins faster than any other planet, a day lasting just under 10 hours, which visibly flattens it at the poles.

When Galileo pointed his telescope at it in January 1610, he saw four small points of light that changed position night after night. They were moons circling Jupiter: Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto. It was powerful evidence that not everything in the heavens orbits Earth, and it helped undermine the old Earth-centred view. Ganymede is larger than the planet Mercury.

sections.key: Jupiter is not a failed star, since it would need roughly 80 times more mass to ignite fusion.
sections.b:
Jupiter is often called a 'failed star' because it is mostly hydrogen and helium, like the Sun. The label misleads. To ignite hydrogen fusion in its core, an object needs roughly 80 times Jupiter's mass, and Jupiter was never close. It gives off more heat than it receives from the Sun, left over from its formation and slow contraction, but it does not shine by fusion.

Its interior is extraordinary all the same. Under crushing pressure, hydrogen is thought to become an electrically conducting fluid called metallic hydrogen. Swirling currents in it probably generate Jupiter's enormous magnetic field, the strongest of any planet, which traps radiation lethal to unshielded spacecraft electronics.

sections.key: Jupiter's Great Red Spot is a storm wider than Earth that has been tracked for about two centuries, and it reaches hundreds of kilometres deep.
sections.b:
Jupiter's colourful stripes are bands of cloud driven by powerful jet streams flowing east and west. Its most famous feature is the Great Red Spot, a high-pressure storm that spins anticlockwise and is wider than Earth. Astronomers have tracked it continuously since at least the 1830s. Giovanni Cassini described a spot in 1665, but historians are unsure whether it was the same storm.

The spot has been shrinking over the past century and has become rounder, though it is still enormous. NASA's Juno spacecraft, orbiting Jupiter since 2016, has measured that the storm reaches hundreds of kilometres down into the atmosphere. Nobody is quite sure why it has lasted so long or what gives it its reddish colour.

sections.key: Saturn's rings are mostly water ice, vast but very thin, and Saturn is the only planet less dense than water.
sections.b:
Saturn's rings are countless pieces of ice, from tiny grains to house-sized chunks, each orbiting like a miniature moon. The main rings span roughly 280,000 kilometres, about three quarters of the distance to the Moon, yet are often only about ten metres thick. Galileo saw them in 1610 but his blurry telescope made him think Saturn had 'ears'; Christiaan Huygens worked out in the 1650s that they were a ring. Whether they formed with Saturn or are much younger is still debated.

Saturn's average density is about 0.7 grams per cubic centimetre, less than water's 1.0, so it would float in a big enough bathtub. The idea falls apart quickly, since Saturn has no solid surface. Its low density and fast spin make it the most flattened planet. At its north pole sits a six-sided jet stream wider than Earth.

sections.key: Cassini studied Saturn for 13 years, then plunged into it deliberately in 2017 to protect moons that might host life.
sections.b:
The Cassini-Huygens mission, a partnership between NASA, the European Space Agency and the Italian Space Agency, arrived at Saturn in 2004. Its Huygens probe parachuted onto Titan in January 2005, the most distant landing ever made, revealing riverbeds and lakes of liquid methane and ethane. Cassini also found jets of water vapour spraying from the small moon Enceladus, evidence of a hidden ocean.

By 2017 the spacecraft was almost out of fuel. To avoid any risk of it crashing into, and contaminating, a moon that might host life, controllers steered it through the gap between Saturn and its rings 22 times. Then, on 15 September 2017, they sent it plunging into Saturn's atmosphere. It transmitted data until the very end.

quiz.q: Why were the four moons Galileo saw around Jupiter so important?
o: They proved Jupiter had a set of rings
They showed not everything orbits Earth
They proved Jupiter was really a small star
They revealed the Great Red Spot
quiz.e: Moons circling Jupiter undermined the idea that everything orbits Earth.

quiz.q: Why is calling Jupiter a 'failed star' misleading?
o: It is made mostly of rock and metal, not gas
It was once a star that burned itself out
It would need about 80 times more mass to ignite
It is far too cold to ever shine at all
quiz.e: Jupiter was never close to the mass needed for fusion.

quiz.q: What is Jupiter's Great Red Spot?
o: A giant storm wider than Earth
A shadow cast by one of its moons
A giant volcano that erupts on its surface
A huge crater left by an old impact
quiz.e: It is a high-pressure storm that reaches hundreds of kilometres down.

quiz.q: What is unusual about Saturn's average density?
o: It is the densest planet
It is greater than Earth's
It equals Jupiter's
It is lower than water's
quiz.e: Saturn is mostly hydrogen and helium, so it is less dense than water, though it has no solid surface to float.

quiz.q: Why was Cassini deliberately sent into Saturn?
o: To test a new engine in Saturn's atmosphere
To protect moons that might host life
Because it had lost contact with Earth
To photograph Saturn's core up close
quiz.e: Controllers wanted to eliminate any risk of crashing into a moon such as Enceladus or Titan.

LESSONS.push: One of the giants is light enough, in a sense, to float. Which one?

LESSONS.title: Planetary defence: dodging asteroids
LESSONS.hook: The dinosaurs had no space program. We do, and in 2022 humanity knocked an asteroid off course for the very first time.

sections.key: Space rocks strike Earth all the time, and an asteroid impact is the one natural disaster we could see coming years ahead and prevent.
sections.b:
Tonnes of space dust and small rocks fall on Earth every day, mostly burning up as shooting stars. Larger impacts are rarer but real. About 66 million years ago an asteroid roughly ten kilometres wide struck near Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula, and the resulting global catastrophe wiped out the non-bird dinosaurs. Impacts on that scale are thought to happen only every hundred million years or so. Smaller ones are far more frequent and can still devastate a city or region.

The good news is that, of all natural disasters, an asteroid impact is the only one we can, in principle, see coming years ahead and prevent entirely. That is the job of planetary defence.

sections.key: Airbursts over Russia in 1908 and 2013 show what relatively small asteroids can do, and what to do if you see a fireball.
sections.b:
On 30 June 1908, something exploded in the air above Tunguska in Siberia, flattening an estimated 80 million trees across about 2,000 square kilometres. Most scientists think it was a stony asteroid or comet fragment perhaps 50 to 60 metres across. The area was so remote that very few people were hurt.

On 15 February 2013, a rock about 20 metres wide burst over the Russian city of Chelyabinsk. Its blast wave arrived well after the flash, shattering windows across the city, and about 1,500 people were injured, mostly by flying glass. Many had rushed to windows to look.

Experts now advise treating a very bright fireball like lightning: move away from windows and wait for the boom. Such events are extremely rare. If anyone is injured, call 000.

sections.key: Survey telescopes have found over 90 percent of the largest near-Earth asteroids, and none is on a collision course.
sections.b:
Since the 1990s, telescopes have systematically scanned the sky for near-Earth objects, asteroids and comets whose orbits bring them close to ours. Surveys such as Catalina, Pan-STARRS and ATLAS photograph the sky night after night, looking for moving dots, and astronomers then calculate each orbit decades ahead.

Scientists believe more than 90 percent of near-Earth asteroids larger than a kilometre, the kind that could cause global disaster, have been found, and none poses a known threat for at least the next century. Smaller objects, still big enough to destroy a city, are far less complete. New facilities, including the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile and planned space telescopes, should find many more.

sections.key: New asteroids sometimes show a small impact chance that vanishes as their orbits are measured more precisely.
sections.b:
When an asteroid is first spotted, its path is uncertain, like predicting where a thrown ball will land from a split-second glimpse. Sometimes Earth falls inside the early range of possibilities, so the odds look worrying, then drop to zero as observations accumulate.

In 2004 the asteroid Apophis, about 340 metres wide, briefly showed a chance of nearly 3 percent of hitting Earth in 2029. Further tracking ruled out any impact in 2029 and for at least the next century. Instead, on 13 April 2029 it will pass within about 32,000 kilometres of Earth, closer than many communications satellites, and may be visible to the naked eye from parts of the world. In early 2025, asteroid 2024 YR4 followed a similar pattern before being ruled out as a threat to Earth.

sections.key: In 2022 NASA deliberately crashed a spacecraft into an asteroid moonlet and measurably changed its orbit.
sections.b:
Finding a dangerous asteroid is only half the problem; we also need a way to move it. The simplest idea is a kinetic impactor: hit it hard with a spacecraft, years ahead, so a tiny change in speed grows into a miss by the time it reaches Earth.

NASA's Double Asteroid Redirection Test, or DART, tried this on a harmless target. Dimorphos is a moonlet about 160 metres wide, orbiting a larger asteroid called Didymos. On 26 September 2022, DART slammed into it at over 20,000 kilometres per hour. Dimorphos had orbited Didymos in about 11 hours and 55 minutes; afterwards its orbit was about 32 minutes shorter, far more than the minimum mission goal. The European Space Agency's Hera mission is following up.

quiz.q: Why is an asteroid impact unlike other natural disasters?
o: It is far more frequent than any other disaster
It always destroys a whole continent
It can be seen coming years in advance
It only ever happens over the oceans
quiz.e: We can find and track asteroids long before they arrive, which makes prevention possible in principle.

quiz.q: If you see an extremely bright fireball, what is sensible advice?
o: Rush to the window for a better look
Go outside straight away to find the meteorite
Stay clear of windows until any blast passes
Switch off the power at the meter box
quiz.e: The blast arrives well after the flash, and flying glass injured most people at Chelyabinsk.

quiz.q: Roughly what share of near-Earth asteroids over one kilometre wide have been found?
o: More than 90 percent
About half
About 10 percent
Almost none so far
quiz.e: The biggest threats are well mapped, though smaller city-destroying objects are far less complete.

quiz.q: Why do some newly found asteroids show a worrying impact chance that later vanishes?
o: Their orbits shift suddenly while they travel
Early data leaves the path uncertain until refined
They hide behind the Sun for several months
They break apart as they near Earth
quiz.e: Early path estimates have a wide range, and more observations usually shrink it until Earth falls outside.

quiz.q: What did the DART mission achieve?
o: It landed astronauts on an asteroid
It destroyed a dangerous asteroid in space
It brought back samples from an asteroid
It shifted the orbit of an asteroid moonlet
quiz.e: A deliberate impact shortened Dimorphos's orbit by about 32 minutes, proving the technique can work.

LESSONS.push: Humanity moved a space rock on purpose once. It was easier than expected.

LESSONS.title: Australia's place in space
LESSONS.hook: A sheep paddock dish carried Apollo 11's moonwalk to the world, and a quiet desert range launched a satellite in 1967. Australia's space story is bigger than most people know.

sections.key: Woomera, a remote rocket range in South Australia, launched Australia's first satellite, WRESAT, in 1967.
sections.b:
In 1947, Britain and Australia agreed to build a long-range weapons testing site in the South Australian outback. The town of Woomera, named after an Aboriginal spear-thrower, grew up to support it. The range stretched well over a thousand kilometres across the desert, giving room to fire rockets far from populated areas.

In the mid-1960s the United States offered Australia a spare Redstone rocket. Scientists in Salisbury, South Australia, built a small satellite, WRESAT, in under a year. It launched from Woomera on 29 November 1967, making Australia one of the first handful of nations to launch a satellite from its own territory. It measured the Sun's radiation and the upper atmosphere before burning up in January 1968. Britain's only satellite on a British rocket, Prospero, followed from Woomera in 1971.

sections.key: The 64-metre Parkes radio telescope supplied most of the television pictures of the Apollo 11 moonwalk.
sections.b:
The Parkes radio telescope opened in 1961 among the sheep paddocks of central western New South Wales, its 64-metre dish among the most advanced in the world. In July 1969, when Neil Armstrong stepped onto the Moon, it was high over Australia.

The first minutes of television were received by NASA's Honeysuckle Creek station near Canberra, which captured Armstrong climbing down the ladder. Parkes then took over and supplied the pictures for most of the roughly two-and-a-half-hour moonwalk, despite strong winds that pushed the dish close to its safety limits. The 2000 film The Dish dramatised the story, with some liberties. In 2020 the telescope also received the Wiradjuri name Murriyang.

sections.key: Canberra hosts one of NASA's three Deep Space Network stations, and Parkes found the first fast radio burst in its archives.
sections.b:
To keep in touch with distant spacecraft as Earth rotates, NASA built three tracking stations roughly a third of the way around the globe from one another: Goldstone in California, Madrid in Spain, and Tidbinbilla near Canberra. At any moment at least one can see a given spacecraft.

The Canberra Deep Space Communication Complex, run on NASA's behalf by Australia's national science agency CSIRO, has helped communicate with missions such as Voyager, the Mars rovers and New Horizons.

Parkes has made discoveries of its own. In 2007, astronomers searching its archived data found the first known fast radio burst, a millisecond flash of radio waves from far beyond our galaxy, opening up an entirely new field of astronomy.

sections.key: When Skylab fell over Western Australia in 1979, the local shire jokingly fined NASA for littering.
sections.b:
Skylab, America's first space station, re-entered the atmosphere in July 1979, earlier than planned, and broke up over the Indian Ocean and southern Western Australia. Debris rained down around the town of Esperance and across the Nullarbor, though no one was hurt.

The Shire of Esperance issued NASA a light-hearted 400-dollar fine for littering. A San Francisco newspaper offered 10,000 dollars for the first piece of Skylab delivered to its office. It was claimed by a 17-year-old from Esperance, Stan Thornton, who flew to the United States with fragments.

The fine went unpaid for 30 years, until a Californian radio host raised the money from listeners and paid it in 2009.

sections.key: Australians have flown with NASA, and Australia now has its own space agency and a landing site for asteroid samples.
sections.b:
Paul Scully-Power, an Australian-born oceanographer, flew aboard the Space Shuttle Challenger in 1984 as a payload specialist. Adelaide-born engineer Andy Thomas became a NASA astronaut and flew four missions, including a long stay on the Russian space station Mir in 1998.

In 2024 Katherine Bennell-Pegg became the first astronaut to graduate from training under the Australian flag, completing the European Space Agency's basic astronaut training. Australia established its own Australian Space Agency in 2018.

Its deserts remain useful too. In 2010 and 2020, Japanese Hayabusa capsules carrying samples from asteroids parachuted down near Woomera, bringing pieces of other worlds to Australian soil. The remote outback that suited rocket tests also suits recovering spacecraft.

quiz.q: Why was Woomera chosen as a rocket range?
o: It was close to Sydney and its workforce
It was the coldest place in Australia
It already had a large jet airport
It was remote, with room to fire rockets
quiz.e: Vast, empty desert let rockets be tested far from populated areas.

quiz.q: What role did Parkes play in the Apollo 11 broadcast?
o: It supplied pictures for most of the moonwalk
It sent the landing commands to the crew
It tracked the Saturn V rocket after launch
It recorded the astronauts' heart rates
quiz.e: Honeysuckle Creek caught the first minutes; Parkes then carried most of the moonwalk to the world.

quiz.q: Why does NASA have three Deep Space Network stations around the globe?
o: Each one is assigned to a different planet
So one can always see a spacecraft as Earth rotates
Three stations cost less than a single large one
To follow different spacecraft in different seasons
quiz.e: Spacing them about a third of the way round keeps every spacecraft in view of one station.

quiz.q: How did the Shire of Esperance respond to Skylab debris landing in 1979?
o: It sued the United States for the damage
It built a museum and charged NASA entry
It fined NASA 400 dollars for littering
It banned future space stations from the area
quiz.e: The light-hearted fine went unpaid for 30 years, until a radio host paid it in 2009.

quiz.q: Why do Japanese asteroid sample capsules land near Woomera?
o: It is the closest launch site to Japan
The remote desert is a safe, empty landing zone
Australian engineers built the capsules for Japan
The capsules were launched from Woomera originally
quiz.e: Hayabusa capsules parachuted into the same remote outback that suited rocket testing.

LESSONS.push: A sheep paddock dish helped the world watch a moonwalk. Here's the story.

LESSONS.title: Reading starlight: what stars are made of
LESSONS.hook: In 1835 a famous philosopher declared that we could never know what the stars are made of. Within a few decades, scientists were doing exactly that, using rainbows.

sections.key: In 1835 Auguste Comte called the chemistry of the stars forever unknowable, a reminder that 'impossible' is a dangerous word.
sections.b:
The French philosopher Auguste Comte, founder of positivism, wanted science to stick to what could be observed. In 1835 he gave an example of knowledge forever beyond reach: we could study the stars' shapes, distances and motions, but never their chemical composition, since no one could visit them or take a sample.

It seemed reasonable. Chemistry meant handling substances in a laboratory, and the stars were unreachably far away. Yet within about 25 years, scientists found a way to identify elements in the Sun from Earth. Comte's claim is now often quoted as a warning that 'impossible' can be a dangerous word. The key had already been found, in a ray of sunlight split by glass.

sections.key: Fraunhofer found hundreds of dark lines crossing the Sun's spectrum, and Kirchhoff and Bunsen showed each element makes its own pattern.
sections.b:
Isaac Newton showed in the 1660s that a prism splits sunlight into a rainbow, a spectrum. In 1814, German optician Joseph von Fraunhofer built instruments precise enough to magnify it and found hundreds of thin dark lines, as if exact colours were missing. He mapped about 570 and labelled the strongest with letters, a system still used. He could not explain them.

Around 1859 in Heidelberg, physicist Gustav Kirchhoff and chemist Robert Bunsen heated substances in a flame and studied the light through a prism. Each element gave its own set of bright lines, like a barcode. Sodium's two yellow lines matched two of Fraunhofer's dark lines. Cooler gas in the Sun's outer layers absorbs those same colours, so dark lines reveal which elements are present.

sections.key: Helium was identified in the Sun's spectrum in 1868, decades before anyone found it on Earth.
sections.b:
During a total solar eclipse in 1868, astronomers studying the Sun's glowing outer layers saw a bright yellow line that matched no known element. Jules Janssen observed it from India, and Norman Lockyer studied it soon afterwards. Lockyer, working with chemist Edward Frankland, concluded it belonged to a new element and named it helium, after Helios, the Greek god of the Sun.

Many chemists were sceptical of an element known only from a distant star. Then in 1895 Scottish chemist William Ramsay detected the same spectral line from gas released by a uranium mineral. Helium, the second most common element in the universe, had first been discovered 150 million kilometres away. The method also found two new elements on Earth, caesium and rubidium.

sections.key: In 1925 Cecilia Payne showed that stars are made overwhelmingly of hydrogen and helium, overturning expert opinion.
sections.b:
In the early 1900s astronomers assumed stars had about the same make-up as Earth's crust, rich in heavier elements like iron. Cecilia Payne, a young British astronomer who moved to Harvard because women had few prospects in astronomy in England, applied new atomic physics to stellar spectra.

Her 1925 doctoral thesis concluded that stars are overwhelmingly hydrogen and helium, in vastly greater amounts than anyone expected. The senior astronomer Henry Norris Russell persuaded her to describe the result as almost certainly not real. A few years later Russell reached the same conclusion himself.

Payne was right: hydrogen and helium make up about 98 percent of the ordinary matter in stars. Her thesis is now considered among the most important in astronomy.

sections.key: A star's spectrum also reveals its temperature and whether it is moving towards or away from us.
sections.b:
Spectra hold far more than a list of ingredients. A star's colour reveals its surface temperature: red stars are relatively cool, around 3,000°C, while blue-white stars can exceed 20,000°C. In the early 1900s, Annie Jump Cannon at Harvard classified hundreds of thousands of stars by spectrum into the sequence O, B, A, F, G, K and M, from hottest to coolest, which astronomers still use.

Spectra also reveal motion through the Doppler effect. Light from an object moving away is stretched towards the red end, while light from one approaching is squeezed towards blue. Measuring these tiny shifts showed that distant galaxies are rushing away from us, the evidence for an expanding universe, and it still helps detect planets around other stars.

quiz.q: What lesson is Auguste Comte's 1835 claim often used to illustrate?
o: Philosophers make the best scientists
Stars are made of fire
Light travels instantly
Calling something unknowable can prove wrong
quiz.e: Within about 25 years, scientists were identifying the Sun's elements from Earth.

quiz.q: What did Kirchhoff and Bunsen realise about the Sun's dark lines?
o: Each element has its own unique pattern of colours
They were flaws in the glass of the prism
They were caused only by Earth's atmosphere
They showed how fast the Sun rotates
quiz.e: A star's dark lines work like a barcode revealing which elements are present.

quiz.q: Why was the discovery of helium remarkable?
o: It was first isolated from volcanic gas on Earth
It was the first element chemists made artificially
It was seen in the Sun's light decades before Earth
It was first detected in a fallen meteorite
quiz.e: A mystery yellow line in sunlight pointed to a new element, which was found on Earth only in 1895.

quiz.q: What did Cecilia Payne's 1925 thesis show about stars?
o: They are mostly iron
They are made like Earth's crust
They are mostly carbon
They are overwhelmingly hydrogen and helium
quiz.e: Her spectral analysis overturned the assumption that stars resemble Earth's crust.

quiz.q: What can the Doppler shift in a star's light tell us?
o: The star's age in millions of years
Whether it is moving towards or away from us
The exact mix of elements inside it
How wide the star is across
quiz.e: Light stretched towards red means moving away; squeezed towards blue means approaching.

LESSONS.push: A philosopher said we'd never know what stars are made of. A rainbow disagreed.

LESSONS.title: Dark matter and dark energy
LESSONS.hook: Everything we have ever seen, every star, planet and person, makes up only about 5 percent of the universe. The rest is a mystery with a name but no explanation.

sections.key: Galaxies spin and cluster as if they hold far more mass than their visible stars and gas supply.
sections.b:
In 1933 Swiss astronomer Fritz Zwicky measured the speeds of galaxies in the Coma Cluster. They moved so fast that the cluster should have flown apart, unless it held far more mass than its light suggested. He called the hidden material 'dunkle Materie', German for dark matter. His estimate was far too large, since distances were badly underestimated then, but the puzzle was real.

In the 1970s Vera Rubin and Kent Ford measured spiral galaxies such as Andromeda. In a solar system, outer planets orbit slowly. In these galaxies the outer stars did not slow down. The simplest explanation was a vast, invisible halo of extra mass around each galaxy.

sections.key: Gravitational lensing maps where dark matter sits, and colliding clusters show it is a real substance.
sections.b:
Dark matter gives off no light, but it has gravity, and gravity bends light. Massive galaxy clusters act as giant warped lenses, stretching the images of more distant galaxies into arcs. By measuring that distortion, astronomers can map where the mass actually is.

The Bullet Cluster is two galaxy clusters that collided. In 2006 researchers showed that most of the ordinary matter, hot gas, had been slowed and piled up in the middle. Most of the mass, revealed by lensing, had passed straight through. This was widely seen as strong evidence that dark matter is a real substance, separate from ordinary matter.

sections.key: Dark matter is probably an unknown kind of particle that barely interacts with anything, and none has yet been detected.
sections.b:
Dark matter is not simply dim stars, dust or black holes. Observations rule out ordinary matter making up more than a small fraction of it. Most physicists think it is a particle outside the standard model of particle physics, one that interacts with almost nothing except through gravity. Candidates include weakly interacting massive particles, nicknamed WIMPs, and extremely light particles called axions.

Experiments deep underground, shielded from cosmic rays, wait for a dark matter particle to bump into an atom. Australia's Stawell Underground Physics Laboratory, in a Victorian gold mine, hosts one. So far there is no confirmed detection, and a minority of scientists suspect gravity itself needs modifying.

sections.key: In 1998 two teams found that distant supernovae were fainter than expected, so the universe's expansion is accelerating.
sections.b:
Astronomers have known since the 1920s that the universe is expanding. The natural assumption was that gravity would slow it. In the 1990s two rival teams set out to measure the slowdown using Type Ia supernovae, exploding white dwarfs with a predictable peak brightness that work as cosmic distance markers.

Saul Perlmutter led one team in the United States. Brian Schmidt led the other, the High-Z Supernova Search Team, at the Australian National University's Mount Stromlo Observatory, with Adam Riess making key analyses. In 1998 both found the same startling result: distant supernovae were fainter than expected, so the expansion is accelerating. The three shared the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics.

sections.key: Dark energy is the name for whatever drives the acceleration, and it makes up about 68 percent of the universe.
sections.b:
Something seems to be pushing space apart. Physicists call it dark energy, a name for the effect rather than an explanation. The leading idea is that empty space carries a small, constant energy, like the cosmological constant Einstein added to his equations and later abandoned. Yet quantum theory predicts a value wildly larger than observed, one of science's biggest mismatches.

The universe's budget appears to be about 68 percent dark energy, 27 percent dark matter and only 5 percent ordinary matter. Recent results from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument in Arizona hint that dark energy may be weakening, but they are not yet conclusive. We can measure the universe precisely and still not say what most of it is.

quiz.q: What did Vera Rubin find in spiral galaxies?
o: Outer stars orbit nearly as fast as inner ones, implying extra unseen mass
Outer stars orbit much slower, as planets do in a solar system
Stars at the edge are moving away from the galaxy centre
Galaxies spin faster the fewer stars they contain
quiz.e: Flat orbital speeds far from the centre point to an invisible halo of extra mass.

quiz.q: What did the Bullet Cluster collision suggest about dark matter?
o: Most of the mass passed through, separate from the slowed gas
It is made of the hot gas left in the middle
It was destroyed when the clusters collided
It is just dim stars hidden behind the clusters
quiz.e: Mass revealed by lensing separated from the gas, so dark matter behaves like a real substance.

quiz.q: What do most physicists think dark matter is?
o: Dim stars, dust and black holes we have not yet counted
A particle outside the standard model that barely interacts
A form of light too faint for telescopes to see
Ordinary matter that is simply very cold gas
quiz.e: Ordinary objects are ruled out as the main part, so an unknown particle is the leading idea.

quiz.q: Why did faint distant supernovae surprise astronomers in 1998?
o: They showed the universe's expansion is speeding up
They proved the expansion had stopped altogether
They showed supernovae are not reliable distance markers
They showed gravity was slowing expansion faster than expected
quiz.e: Supernovae fainter than expected meant they were further away, so expansion has accelerated.

quiz.q: Roughly how much of the universe is ordinary matter?
o: About 68 percent
About 27 percent
About 5 percent
About 50 percent
quiz.e: Stars, planets and people are only about 5 percent, with dark matter 27 and dark energy 68.

LESSONS.push: Everything we can see is only about 5 percent of the universe. What is the rest?

LESSONS.title: Barcodes and QR codes: reading the stripes
LESSONS.hook: Lines drawn in beach sand, a pack of chewing gum in Ohio and a Japanese board game all helped create the codes you scan every day.

sections.key: The barcode began as an idea sketched in beach sand in 1948, but took decades to become practical.
sections.b:
In 1948 the head of an American food chain reportedly asked a Drexel Institute dean whether checkouts could be automated. Graduate student Bernard Silver overheard and told his friend Norman Joseph Woodland. Woodland recalled the breakthrough on a Miami beach. Thinking of the Morse code he learned as a Boy Scout, he dragged his fingers through the sand, turning dots and dashes into thin and thick lines.

The pair filed a patent in 1949, granted in 1952, including a circular 'bullseye' version readable from any direction. But nothing could read it cheaply. Practical barcodes had to wait more than two decades for lasers and microchips.

sections.key: The 1974 scan of a chewing gum pack launched the barcode age, which paid off once enough products carried codes.
sections.b:
In the early 1970s American grocers agreed on one standard, the Universal Product Code, or UPC. The winning design came from IBM, where Woodland then worked. It used straight vertical bars, since the bullseye tended to smudge on fast printing presses.

On 26 June 1974, at a Marsh supermarket in Troy, Ohio, a cashier scanned a ten-pack of Wrigley's Juicy Fruit gum. Take-up was slow, because shops needed expensive scanners and manufacturers had to print codes on everything. Once enough products carried them, the benefits snowballed: faster queues, fewer pricing errors and detailed data on what sold and when. Europe adopted a compatible 13-digit system, which Australia uses too.

sections.key: A scanner reads the pattern of light and dark bars as a product number, and the shop's computer looks up the price.
sections.b:
A barcode is a message written in light and shadow. The scanner shines light across the stripes, traditionally a red laser, though many modern scanners use a small camera. Black bars absorb light and white spaces reflect it, so a sensor sees a rapidly changing pattern. Each digit is a particular combination of bar and space widths. Guard patterns at the start, middle and end show where the code begins and whether it is being read upside down.

The number rarely contains the price. It identifies the product, and the shop's computer looks up the current price in its database. That is why a price change does not mean relabelling every item.

sections.key: Denso Wave's QR code stores far more than a barcode by using a grid, with finder squares to spot it quickly.
sections.b:
An ordinary barcode holds only a short number, and Japanese car factories scanned many for every box of parts. At Denso Wave, then part of the car-parts maker Denso, engineer Masahiro Hara led a team to design something better. He has said the idea came while playing Go, whose black and white stones on a grid suggested storing information in two dimensions.

Released in 1994, the Quick Response code could hold thousands of characters, including Japanese kanji. The hardest puzzle was making it instantly recognisable among printed clutter. The team studied printed material to find a shape that almost never appears by chance, and settled on the nested squares now in three corners of every QR code.

sections.key: QR codes survive damage thanks to error correction, but each one is a link you cannot read, so check before trusting it.
sections.b:
The three large squares are finder patterns. Wherever the code sits in an image, the scanner spots them and works out which way is up. The rest of the grid holds data plus error correction, based on mathematics published by Irving Reed and Gustave Solomon in 1960, also used on CDs and in spacecraft communication. At the highest of four protection levels, roughly 30 per cent of the code can be dirty or covered and still be recovered. That is why a logo can sit over the middle of a code.

Denso Wave pledged not to enforce its patent, so anyone can use QR codes freely. Scammers exploit that, sticking fake codes over real ones. Check the web address before entering anything.

quiz.q: Why did the first barcode patent not lead to scanners straight away?
o: Shops refused to print any kind of code on products
The bullseye design could only be read from one direction
Cheap readers needed lasers and microchips, not yet built
Grocers had already agreed on a different standard
quiz.e: The idea was sound, but practical scanners needed laser and microchip technology that came decades later.

quiz.q: Why did barcodes spread slowly after the first scan in 1974?
o: The code could not be read by early scanners at all
Customers disliked having prices removed from items
Printing presses could not produce straight bars
Scanners were costly and products needed codes printed
quiz.e: Benefits snowballed only once enough products carried codes to justify the scanners.

quiz.q: What does the number in a barcode usually identify?
o: The current price of the item
The shop where the item was made
The date the item was packed
The product itself, not its price
quiz.e: Prices live in the shop's database, so they can change without relabelling products.

quiz.q: Why was the QR code developed for car factories?
o: Barcodes could not be printed on car parts
A barcode held too little data for their needs
Factories wanted codes that could be read only by machines
Workers needed codes that could be read in the dark
quiz.e: Storing data in two dimensions lets a single code hold thousands of characters.

quiz.q: Why can a QR code still scan with a logo printed over its middle?
o: The scanner only reads the three corner squares
Logos are printed in an ink the camera ignores
Built-in error correction can recover the hidden data
The data is repeated in every corner square
quiz.e: Extra error-correction data lets up to about 30 per cent of a code be damaged and still read.

LESSONS.push: A pack of chewing gum made history in 1974. Find out how stripes learned to carry data.

LESSONS.title: Y2K: the disaster that didn't happen
LESSONS.hook: As 1999 drew to a close, the world braced for computers to think it was 1900. Midnight came and almost nothing broke. Was it all hype, or one of history's great quiet successes?

sections.key: Programmers wrote years as two digits to save scarce memory, leaving old software that might read 2000 as 1900.
sections.b:
In the 1960s and 1970s computer memory and storage were astonishingly expensive, and a standard punch card had only 80 columns. Programmers saved space by writing years as two digits: 68 instead of 1968. Few expected the programs to last decades, yet many did. Banking, payroll, airline and government systems were built in layers on old code, often in COBOL, and rarely replaced.

By the 1990s vast amounts of software assumed every year began with 19. When the calendar ticked over to 2000, the year 00 might be read as 1900. The problem became known as Y2K, short for Year 2000.

sections.key: The danger was date arithmetic going wrong in many connected systems at once, including hidden embedded chips.
sections.b:
The fear was never that computers would explode. It was arithmetic. If a system works out age by subtracting birth year from the current year, 00 minus 65 gives minus 65. Interest, card expiry dates, warranties and record deletion all rely on comparing dates, and a sorted list might put 2000 before 1999. Some programs also failed to treat 2000 as a leap year, because century years are leap years only if divisible by 400.

Tiny processors sit in lifts, power stations and medical devices, and nobody had a full list of which tracked dates. Most did not, but organisations could not know without testing. The worry was many failures at once, in connected systems.

sections.key: Armies of programmers spent years fixing old code, and the cost is often estimated in the hundreds of billions of dollars.
sections.b:
Through the late 1990s, programmers combed through old code line by line, and retired COBOL experts were in demand again. Common fixes were expanding years to four digits, or 'windowing', where a program treats two-digit years below a cut-off, say 50, as 20xx and the rest as 19xx.

Worldwide cost estimates vary widely, often falling between 300 and 600 billion US dollars. Australia, like many countries, ran national awareness and readiness programs, and governments set up command centres to monitor the changeover. Some critics said much of the money went to overcautious consultants. Others noted that the work also cleaned up and documented ageing systems that needed attention anyway.

sections.key: The changeover brought only minor glitches, which left many people asking whether the warnings had been hype.
sections.b:
Australia and the Pacific reached midnight hours before Europe and North America, so the world watched them for early signs of trouble. None came on a large scale. There were glitches. Some websites showed the year as 19100, because programs added 1900 to the year, and a few ticketing and payment machines misbehaved. In Japan some monitoring equipment at nuclear plants reported errors, without any danger to safety. A US military satellite intelligence system had several hours of problems.

Most faults were fixed quickly and passed almost unnoticed. Within days, some newspapers that had warned of chaos were asking whether it had all been a beat-up.

sections.key: When prevention works, the absence of disaster can make the warning look foolish, and time bugs still lurk.
sections.b:
Y2K is a classic case of the preparedness paradox: fix a problem before it bites, and the lack of disaster can make the warning look silly. Experts still debate how bad things would have been. Some countries that spent little also had few problems, partly because they relied less on old systems. Yet many who did the work insist they found serious faults that would have caused real damage.

Date bugs have not gone away. Many systems count seconds since 1 January 1970, and where that count is stored as a 32-bit number it will overflow on 19 January 2038. Much software has been updated, but the next deadline is ticking.
