quiz.q: Why did programmers write years with only two digits?
o: Memory and storage were expensive, so they saved space
Four-digit years could not be stored in any language
Early computers could not count past 99
Punch cards had no room for numbers
quiz.e: Saving two digits per date added up when storage was scarce, and nobody expected the code to last.

quiz.q: What was the real danger of Y2K?
o: Computers physically failing at midnight
Wrong date calculations in many linked systems
Clocks stopping on every device
Software deleting itself deliberately
quiz.e: Wrong date arithmetic, in many systems at once, was the concern rather than anything exploding.

quiz.q: What does 'windowing' do to fix Y2K?
o: Treats two-digit years below a cut-off as 20xx
Replaces every old computer with a newer model
Stores each year as a word instead of digits
Blocks dates after 1999 from being entered
quiz.e: Windowing was a quick repair that avoided rewriting every date field to four digits.

quiz.q: What happened when midnight arrived in 2000?
o: Banks and power grids failed around the world
Only minor glitches occurred, mostly fixed quickly
Nothing at all went wrong anywhere in the world
Air travel was shut down worldwide for a week
quiz.e: Small faults appeared, but there was no large-scale breakdown.

quiz.q: What is the preparedness paradox?
o: Preparing for a problem always makes it worse
Good prevention can make the warning look needless
Warnings are always exaggerated by the media
Problems solved early are always more expensive
quiz.e: When prevention works, nothing happens, which can make the effort seem like hype.

LESSONS.push: The world feared computers would think it was 1900. Why did almost nothing happen?

LESSONS.title: How a search engine finds anything
LESSONS.hook: Type a few words and, in a fraction of a second, the right page appears out of billions. It is not searching the internet when you press Enter. It did that long before.

sections.key: The early web outgrew hand-built directories and simple word matching, so search needed a smarter way to judge pages.
sections.b:
When the World Wide Web opened to the public in the early 1990s there were only a handful of websites, and people kept lists. Within a few years there were millions of pages, written by anyone and linked every which way, with no central catalogue.

Early helpers took two approaches. Yahoo began in 1994 as a hand-built directory, with people sorting sites into categories like a library. Others, such as AltaVista, used software to read pages automatically and match the words you typed. Directories could not keep up with the web's growth, and word-matching was easily fooled: a page repeating a word hundreds of times could jump to the top. Search needed a better way to judge which pages were worth showing.

sections.key: Crawlers read the web ahead of time and build an index, so your search looks up a prepared list rather than scanning the internet.
sections.b:
Behind every search engine is a crawler, also called a spider or bot. It starts with known web addresses, downloads each page, notes every link and adds the new addresses to its list. This reaches much of the public web, but never all of it: pages behind logins are left out, and a small file called robots.txt, a convention from 1994, lets sites ask crawlers to stay away.

A search engine does not scan the internet when you press Enter. It has already built an index, like the one in a textbook, listing for each word the pages that contain it. Searching 'koala habitat' finds pages on both lists. This inverted index runs to well over a hundred million gigabytes, so answers return in a fraction of a second.

sections.key: PageRank treated links as citations, so a page linked by many important pages ranked higher.
sections.b:
In 1996 two Stanford PhD students, Larry Page and Sergey Brin, began a research project nicknamed BackRub. Their insight came from academic publishing, where an important paper is one that many others cite. They treated a link from one page to another as a citation. A page linked by many others was probably useful, and a link from an important page counted for more than one from an obscure page.

They called the measure PageRank, a pun on Page's surname. Their company, launched in 1998 as Google, took its name from 'googol', the number 1 followed by 100 zeros, with a change of spelling. Its results were noticeably better than rivals', and within a few years it dominated web search.

sections.key: Modern ranking weighs many signals, including meaning, freshness and your location, not just links.
sections.b:
PageRank still matters, but it is now one ingredient among many. Search engines try to work out what you meant, not just what you typed, so a search for 'how tall is Uluru' can surface a page saying 'Uluru rises 348 metres above the plain'. They also consider how recent a page is, whether it works on phones, your language and where you are, which is why 'pizza near me' gives different answers in Perth and Hobart.

Machine learning increasingly helps interpret meaning. How signals are combined is a closely guarded secret, partly for competitive reasons and partly to stop people gaming the system. A whole industry, search engine optimisation, exists to help sites climb the rankings.

sections.key: Search is free because advertisers pay for clicks, so it pays to tell ads from results.
sections.b:
Running a search engine costs a fortune, yet you pay nothing. The money comes mainly from advertising. When you search for 'running shoes', advertisers compete in an automated auction, run in a split second, for the chance to show you a link, and they typically pay only when someone clicks. A search is a powerful moment for advertisers, because you are telling the engine exactly what you want right now.

This model explains a few things. Sponsored results often appear above ordinary ones, marked with a small label. Engines also learn from what people click. Notice the difference between an ad and a result, and remember the top link is not automatically the best one.

quiz.q: Why did simple word-matching search fail on the early web?
o: Pages could repeat a word to jump to the top
Software could not read pages automatically
The web had too few pages to search
Directories were too slow to build by hand
quiz.e: Word counts were easy to game, so search needed a better way to judge quality.

quiz.q: Why do search results appear so quickly?
o: The engine scans the internet live when you press Enter
A prebuilt index lists which pages contain each word
Websites send their pages to you directly
Results are saved from the last person who searched
quiz.e: The crawling happens in advance, so your search is just a fast lookup in an index.

quiz.q: What was the key idea behind PageRank?
o: Pages with the most repeated words should rank highest
Links from important pages should count for more
Pages should be ranked purely by their newest content
Pages with the shortest addresses should rank first
quiz.e: Treating links like citations let quality, not repetition, drive ranking.

quiz.q: Why can 'pizza near me' give different results in Perth and Hobart?
o: Search engines consider where you are searching from
Perth has more pizza shops than any other city
The engine ignores what you typed
Results are chosen at random for each city
quiz.e: Modern ranking uses many signals, including location, language and meaning.

quiz.q: How do search engines mainly earn money?
o: Charging users a monthly fee
Selling the pages they have crawled
Advertisers paying, usually per click
Taking a share of every purchase you make
quiz.e: Ads are bought in a split-second auction, so sponsored results can appear above ordinary ones.

LESSONS.push: It does not search the internet when you press Enter. Here is what it does instead.

LESSONS.title: How a mobile call finds you
LESSONS.hook: Your phone is a radio, quietly chatting with towers you never notice. Here is how a call reaches you, even on a moving train.

sections.key: Your phone talks by radio only to the nearest base station, and the rest of the call travels by cable and fibre.
sections.b:
When you call a friend across the street, your phones do not talk directly. Your phone sends radio signals to the nearest base station, usually antennas on a tower, rooftop or pole. From there the call travels over cables and optical fibre through the operator's network, then back out through the base station near your friend. Radio is only the first and last link.

Phones transmit at low power to save battery, so base stations must be spread across the landscape, often only a few hundred metres apart in busy cities. The central problem for engineers was letting millions of people share a limited range of radio frequencies at once without drowning each other out.

sections.key: Dividing an area into small cells lets frequencies be reused, and handover keeps your call going as you move.
sections.b:
The answer, proposed at Bell Labs in 1947 by Douglas Ring and W. Rae Young, was to divide an area into small zones called cells, each with its own base station. Neighbouring cells use different frequencies, but distant cells can reuse the same ones. Planners draw hexagon honeycombs, though real cells are messy shapes bent by hills and buildings. Capacity grows as cells shrink, which is why cities have many small ones. Hence 'cellular', and why Americans say cell phones.

Calls survive moving between cells through handover. Your phone constantly measures nearby signals, and the network switches your call to the new cell in a fraction of a second. With no neighbouring cell, as on a remote highway, the call drops.

sections.key: A SIM proves who you are by answering a secret-key challenge, which stops others from cloning your phone.
sections.b:
The SIM card, or its built-in digital version, the eSIM, is a tiny secure computer. It stores an identity number linked to your account and a secret key designed never to leave the chip. When your phone connects, the network sends a random challenge. The SIM combines it with the secret key to produce an answer, and the network, holding a copy of the key, checks the result. A match lets you in.

This lets the network bill the right person and makes it hard to impersonate someone else. Older analogue phones had no such protection: calls could be overheard with a radio scanner, and identities cloned to run up bills on another person's account. Even idle, your phone checks in so the network knows roughly where you are.

sections.key: Each mobile generation added something new, from digital voice and texting to video, and 5G needs many more small cells.
sections.b:
1G arrived in the 1980s, carrying voice as analogue radio signals. Australia's first cellular network opened in 1987. 2G, in the early 1990s, went digital, improving security and making room for text messages. The first text was sent on 3 December 1992, when engineer Neil Papworth typed 'Merry Christmas' from a computer to a colleague's phone in Britain. Messages were capped at 160 characters, a limit that shaped how a generation wrote.

3G, from the early 2000s, made mobile internet practical, and 4G, from around 2010, made video streaming and apps routine. 5G adds higher speeds and shorter delays, partly by using higher frequencies with a shorter range, which means many more small cells.

sections.key: Old networks are switched off to reuse their frequencies, and 000 works from any mobile.
sections.b:
Radio spectrum is limited, so operators periodically switch off old networks to reuse their frequencies. Australia closed its analogue network around 2000, its 2G networks during the 2010s, and its 3G networks during 2024. Some older phones that relied on 3G for voice calls suddenly could not call anyone, including emergency services. If you or an older relative are unsure whether a phone still works properly, your provider can check it.

In an emergency, call 000 from any mobile. If your own network has no coverage but another does, your emergency call can be carried on that other network. The number 112 also works from mobiles, but 000 remains Australia's main emergency number.

quiz.q: What is the main job of the radio link in a mobile call?
o: Carrying the whole call from phone to phone
Connecting your phone to the nearest base station
Storing your call until the other person answers
Sending the call directly to your friend's phone
quiz.e: Radio covers only the first and last link, with the rest carried over cable and fibre.

quiz.q: Why are mobile networks divided into cells?
o: So the same frequencies can be reused by distant cells
So each phone can have its own private frequency
So signals travel further than a single tower allows
So hills and buildings stop interfering with signals
quiz.e: Reusing frequencies in cells far apart lets millions share limited spectrum.

quiz.q: How does a SIM prove your identity to the network?
o: It sends its secret key straight to the network
It combines a random challenge with a secret key
It displays your phone number to the tower
It uses your voice to confirm who you are
quiz.e: The key never leaves the chip, so the network can check the answer without exposing the secret.

quiz.q: Why does 5G need many more small cells?
o: Its higher frequencies travel shorter distances
It carries only voice calls instead of data
It needs a separate tower for every phone
It reuses analogue signals from 1G
quiz.e: Higher frequencies give more speed but cover less distance.

quiz.q: What can you do if your own network has no coverage in an emergency?
o: Wait until your own signal returns
Call 000, as it can use another network
Text a family member and wait for a reply
Ring your provider to switch networks
quiz.e: A 000 call can use any available network, so it can work even without your own coverage.

LESSONS.push: Your phone is quietly chatting with towers you never notice. Here is how a call finds you.

LESSONS.title: How screens make pictures
LESSONS.hook: Everything on your screen, from a sunset photo to this sentence, is built from millions of tiny lights in just three colours.

sections.key: Every screen is a grid of pixels, each mixing red, green and blue light to make any colour.
sections.b:
Look at a screen through a magnifying glass, or a drop of water, and the illusion falls apart. The image is really a grid of tiny dots called pixels. A 4K television has 3840 pixels across and 2160 down, more than eight million in all. A modern phone packs in several hundred per inch, so the dots are invisible at normal distance.

Each pixel is usually made of three subpixels: red, green and blue. Varying their brightness produces millions of colours. Red and green together look yellow, all three at full strength look white, and all off look black. This is additive mixing, the opposite of paint. It works because the retina has three types of cone cells, and a screen simply stimulates them in the right proportions.

sections.key: An LCD shines a constant backlight through filters and liquid crystals that twist to let more or less light through.
sections.b:
Most monitors and many televisions use liquid crystal displays, or LCDs. Behind the panel is a backlight, today usually LEDs, that shines white light the whole time. In front are two polarising filters set at angles to each other, with a thin layer of liquid crystal between them. Liquid crystals can flow like a liquid yet line up in order, like a crystal.

A small voltage twists or untwists them, changing how much light gets through the second filter. Each subpixel has its own colour filter and tiny transistor. The weakness is that the backlight stays on behind everything, so dark scenes can look slightly grey rather than truly black.

sections.key: OLED pixels make their own light, so black is simply off, though the materials age and can burn in.
sections.b:
OLED stands for organic light-emitting diode. There is no backlight. Each subpixel is a thin sandwich of carbon-based materials that glow when current passes through. To show black, a pixel simply turns off, giving deep blacks and strong contrast, and saving battery on phones when much of the screen is dark. OLED panels can be thin and flexible, which makes folding phones possible.

The trade-offs are cost and ageing. The organic materials slowly lose brightness, and blue ones fade fastest. An image left on screen for very long periods, such as a news ticker or game scoreboard, can leave a faint permanent ghost called burn-in. Manufacturers fight it with tricks such as subtly shifting the image.

sections.key: A screen shows rapid still frames, and a higher refresh rate makes motion feel smoother.
sections.b:
A screen never shows true motion. It shows a rapid series of still images, like a flipbook. The number of redraws each second is the refresh rate, measured in hertz. Many screens refresh 60 times a second, while newer phones, gaming monitors and televisions reach 120 hertz or more, making scrolling and fast games feel smoother.

Films are traditionally shot at only 24 frames per second, so a screen often shows each movie frame more than once. Some phones change their refresh rate on the fly, dropping as low as one hertz for a still image to save battery, then jumping back up as soon as you scroll. The faster your finger moves, the more those extra frames matter.

sections.key: Beyond a certain pixel density your eye cannot see extra detail, so more pixels are not always better.
sections.b:
More pixels are not always better. Whether you can see the difference depends on pixel size, screen size and viewing distance. The eye can only resolve detail down to a certain fineness, and once pixels are smaller than that at your distance, adding more brings little visible gain.

Apple built its 'Retina' marketing in 2010 around exactly this idea: pixels too small to pick out individually at a typical viewing distance. It also explains why, for most people watching from the couch, an 8K television offers only a modest improvement over 4K. Contrast, brightness, colour accuracy and how cleanly the screen handles fast motion often matter more to how good a picture actually looks.

quiz.q: How does a screen produce yellow?
o: It uses a dedicated yellow subpixel
It turns all three subpixels fully off
It lights red and green subpixels together
It lights blue and green subpixels together
quiz.e: Red and green light mixed together stimulate our cones the way yellow does.

quiz.q: Why can dark scenes look grey on an LCD?
o: The liquid crystals make their own grey light
The backlight stays on behind every pixel
The colour filters turn white into grey
LCD panels use fewer pixels in dark areas
quiz.e: Filters cannot block all the always-on backlight, so black is rarely fully black.

quiz.q: What causes burn-in on an OLED screen?
o: The backlight overheating over time
Dust trapped between the polarising filters
Using the screen at a high refresh rate
Static images ageing some pixels faster than others
quiz.e: Organic materials fade with use, so pixels showing the same image wear differently.

quiz.q: Why might a phone drop its refresh rate to one hertz?
o: To make scrolling feel smoother
To save battery when showing a still image
To match the 24 frames of a film
To reduce burn-in on the display
quiz.e: There is no need to redraw an unchanged image, so slowing the refresh saves power.

quiz.q: Why does an 8K television often look only slightly better than 4K from the couch?
o: 8K screens use a lower refresh rate
8K panels have fewer colours available
Your eye cannot make out the extra detail
The extra pixels are hidden behind the backlight
quiz.e: Past the eye's limit at a given distance, extra pixels bring little visible gain.

LESSONS.push: Everything on your screen is built from just three colours of light. How?

LESSONS.title: The transistor: the switch that changed everything
LESSONS.hook: In 1947 two physicists built a clumsy contraption of gold foil, plastic and germanium. Its descendants now number in the billions inside your phone.

sections.key: Vacuum tubes made early electronics possible but were bulky, hot and unreliable, so Bell Labs sought a solid replacement.
sections.b:
In the first half of the twentieth century, electronics meant vacuum tubes, known in Australia and Britain as valves. These glass bulbs could amplify a signal or switch a current, making radio, television and early computers possible. But they were bulky, hot and power hungry, and their filaments burned out like light globes.

ENIAC, an American computer completed in 1945, used around 17,500 of them, filled a large room and drew about 150 kilowatts. Tubes failed regularly, and finding the dead one took time. AT&T, whose network relied on huge numbers of tubes and mechanical switches, wanted something better. Its research arm, Bell Labs, went looking for a solid replacement.

sections.key: In December 1947 Bardeen and Brattain built the first transistor, and Shockley soon designed a sturdier version.
sections.b:
Bell Labs assembled a team to study semiconductors, materials such as germanium and silicon that conduct better than an insulator but worse than a metal. In December 1947, John Bardeen and Walter Brattain pressed two closely spaced gold contacts onto a slab of germanium and found that a small current through one controlled a larger current through the other. The device amplified a signal. They demonstrated it on 23 December. It was awkward, held together with a plastic wedge and a spring, but it worked.

Their group leader, William Shockley, was reportedly frustrated at not being directly involved. Within weeks he worked out a sturdier design, the junction transistor, which became the basis for practical devices.

sections.key: A transistor can amplify and act as a switch with no moving parts, and switches are the foundation of computing.
sections.b:
A transistor does two jobs. It can amplify, turning a weak signal into a stronger copy, which made pocket transistor radios possible. And it can act as a switch with no moving parts: a small voltage on one terminal turns a larger current on or off.

That second job is the foundation of computing. Computers represent information as on and off, one and zero. A few transistors make a logic gate, a circuit whose output is on only if both inputs are on, or if either is. Combine gates and you can add, compare and store numbers. Because transistors switch billions of times a second using very little power, enormous numbers can work together on a single chip.

sections.key: A walkout from Shockley's lab seeded Silicon Valley, and the integrated circuit put whole circuits on one chip.
sections.b:
Bardeen, Brattain and Shockley shared the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics. Shockley had by then set up a lab in Mountain View, California, but his suspicious management drove eight young scientists to walk out in 1957. The 'traitorous eight' founded Fairchild Semiconductor, a seedbed for Silicon Valley. Robert Noyce and Gordon Moore later founded Intel in 1968. Bardeen won a second Nobel in 1972 for superconductivity, the only person to win the physics prize twice.

Wiring individual transistors by hand became the problem. In 1958 Jack Kilby at Texas Instruments built a circuit in a single piece of germanium. Soon after, Noyce proposed a more practical silicon design using the planar process of Jean Hoerni. Both are credited with the integrated circuit.

sections.key: Moore's law is an observation that chip transistor counts roughly double every two years, a trend now slowing.
sections.b:
In 1965 Gordon Moore, then at Fairchild, wrote a magazine article noting that components on a chip had been doubling every year, and predicted this would continue for at least a decade. In 1975 he revised the pace to roughly every two years. This became Moore's law, though it is an observation about engineering and economics, not a law of nature. It held remarkably well for about half a century, partly because the industry treated it as a target.

Modern chips contain tens of billions of transistors, each far smaller than a bacterium. Progress has slowed as parts of transistors shrink to just a few atoms thick, and engineers debate how much longer the trend can continue.

quiz.q: Why did engineers want to replace vacuum tubes?
o: They were too cheap for large companies to trust
They could only handle signals from radio stations
They were bulky, hot and prone to burning out
They needed a new kind of glass that was scarce
quiz.e: Tubes were large and power hungry, and frequent failures made big machines like ENIAC hard to keep running.

quiz.q: What did the first transistor do?
o: Stored information as a magnetic pattern
Let a small current control a larger one
Produced light from an electric current
Converted heat directly into electricity
quiz.e: One current controlling another is what let it amplify signals and switch.

quiz.q: Why are transistors the foundation of computing?
o: They store data on tiny spinning magnetic discs
They turn digital signals into radio waves
They can only be built from rare precious metals
They can switch on and off without moving parts
quiz.e: On and off states represent one and zero, and gates built from them can add, compare and store numbers.

quiz.q: What problem did the integrated circuit solve?
o: The tangle of wiring separate transistors by hand
The shortage of germanium for early transistors
The weak signal from point-contact transistors
The high price of gold for the contacts
quiz.e: Making components and connections together on one piece turned electronics into something like printing.

quiz.q: What is Moore's law?
o: An observation that transistor counts double every two years or so
A physical law limiting how small a transistor can be
A rule that chip prices must double every year
A rule that chips should use half the power each year
quiz.e: It is an engineering and economic trend, not a law of nature, and it is slowing.

LESSONS.push: Two physicists built a clumsy gadget in 1947. Now billions sit in your pocket.

LESSONS.title: How your phone camera takes a photo
LESSONS.hook: A phone camera's lens is smaller than a pea, yet it can rival cameras costing thousands of dollars. The secret is less about glass and more about software.

sections.key: A camera sensor counts photons in millions of tiny photosites, and software later guesses the missing colours.
sections.b:
A digital camera uses an image sensor, a silicon chip covered in millions of light-sensitive sites called photosites. Each works like a bucket left out in the rain. During an exposure, photons strike the silicon and knock electrons loose, and the photosite collects them. Brighter light means more charge. Afterwards the charge is measured and turned into a number. Almost all phones use CMOS sensors, built like computer chips, which made them cheap and power-efficient.

A photosite counts light but cannot see colour. Most sensors put a red, green or blue filter over each one, in a checkerboard patented by Kodak's Bryce Bayer in 1976, with twice as many green as red or blue. Software estimates the two missing colours at each point from its neighbours, called demosaicing.

sections.key: Small phone sensors catch few photons in dim light, producing noise, and more megapixels can make this worse.
sections.b:
Phones are thin, so their sensors and lenses must be small. A full-frame professional sensor is about 36 by 24 millimetres, and most phone sensors are a fraction of that area. A smaller sensor gathers less light, so in a dim room each photosite may collect only a few photons.

Light arrives randomly, so with few photons the counts fluctuate from one photosite to the next, and the image fills with grainy speckles called noise. The electronics add a little of their own. This is a physical limit, not a manufacturing fault, and explains why phone photos once looked so poor indoors and at night. Cramming in more megapixels can make it worse, because each photosite becomes smaller still.

sections.key: Computational photography merges several frames into one photo, cancelling noise and keeping detail in light and dark areas.
sections.b:
The breakthrough was computational photography. A modern phone is often already capturing frames before you press the shutter, and combines several into one picture. Averaging many frames cancels much of the random noise, much as averaging many people's guesses cancels individual errors.

Combining shorter and longer exposures keeps detail in both a bright sky and dark shadows, a technique called high dynamic range, or HDR. Night modes capture frames over a second or more and align them to correct for shaky hands. All this happens in moments on dedicated processors. The photo you see is not a single instant of light but a carefully assembled composite.

sections.key: After merging, the phone edits the picture, so different brands can render the same scene very differently.
sections.b:
After merging frames, the phone keeps editing. It adjusts white balance so a white shirt looks white under orange indoor light, sharpens edges, smooths skin and boosts colours to look pleasing. Many phones recognise what is in the scene, such as food, faces or sky, and treat each part differently.

Portrait mode imitates the soft background blur of a large lens. A tiny lens produces little natural blur, so software estimates how far away each part of the scene is, using two cameras, depth sensors or machine learning, then blurs the background artificially. Look closely at hair or glasses edges and you can sometimes spot mistakes. Different brands make different choices, which is why the same scene can look noticeably different on two phones.

sections.key: A phone photo is the camera's best estimate of a scene, and heavy processing can blur capturing and creating.
sections.b:
All cameras interpret the world. Film chemistry favoured some colours over others, and photographers have always chosen exposure and framing. But phones push interpretation much further, and the line between capturing and creating has blurred. Some features can erase unwanted people from the background, or combine the best expressions from several shots of a group.

A well-known controversy arose in 2023 over phone photos of the Moon. A tester showed that one brand's processing added lunar detail missing from a deliberately blurred original, drawing on a model trained on what the Moon looks like. Most processing is harmless and simply produces better pictures. Still, a modern phone photo is best seen as the camera's best estimate of a scene, not a perfect copy.

quiz.q: How does a phone sensor get colour information?
o: Each photosite measures red, green and blue at once
Filters over photosites, with software filling the gaps
A prism splits light before it reaches the sensor
Photosites change colour as brightness increases
quiz.e: Each photosite sees one colour, so software fills in the other two from neighbouring points.

quiz.q: Why do small sensors produce noisy photos in dim light?
o: The colour filters add random speckles of their own
Small lenses cannot focus light in dim rooms
Few photons per photosite, so chance variation shows
Dim light makes the sensor overheat and misfire
quiz.e: With few photons, random fluctuations between photosites appear as grain.

quiz.q: How does combining many frames improve a photo?
o: It averages out noise and keeps light and dark detail
It makes the lens collect more light each frame
It speeds up the shutter so every frame is sharper
It swaps the sensor's colour filters for better ones
quiz.e: Random errors cancel when frames are averaged, and mixing exposures handles bright and dark areas.

quiz.q: How does portrait mode create background blur?
o: The tiny lens produces strong blur naturally
Software estimates depth and blurs the background
A second lens physically defocuses the background
The sensor moves back and forth during the shot
quiz.e: A small lens gives little natural blur, so software imitates a large lens.

quiz.q: What does the 2023 Moon controversy show about phone photos?
o: The Moon is too bright for any phone sensor
Phones always show the Moon exactly as it is
The Moon looks different on every phone sensor
Processing can add detail the sensor never captured
quiz.e: A phone photo is an estimate of a scene, which can include detail added by a trained model.

LESSONS.push: A lens smaller than a pea rivals pricey cameras. The secret is mostly software.

LESSONS.title: How computers store letters and emoji
LESSONS.hook: Computers only understand numbers. So how does a letter, a Chinese character or a laughing-crying face survive the trip from your phone to someone else's?

sections.key: Computers store text as numbers using a shared table, and ASCII was the first widely successful one, though only for English.
sections.b:
Inside a computer there are no letters, only binary numbers. To store text, everyone must agree on a table mapping each character to a number. Send 65 and a receiving computer using the same table shows a capital A. Early computers each had their own tables, so text from one machine could turn to gibberish on another.

In 1963 American standards bodies published the first version of ASCII, the American Standard Code for Information Interchange, refined over the following years. It used 7 bits, allowing 128 codes: English letters in upper and lower case, digits, punctuation and control codes, such as a 'bell' code that rang a bell on teleprinters. ASCII was a huge success, but it was designed for English and left out most of the world's writing.

sections.key: Competing extensions of ASCII caused garbled text, known in Japan as mojibake, whenever the wrong table was used.
sections.b:
Computers usually store data in bytes of eight bits, which hold 256 values, so many systems used the spare 128 slots for accented letters, symbols or other alphabets. But different countries and companies filled the slots differently. Greek, Russian, Hebrew and Western European text each had their own versions, and Chinese and Japanese, with thousands of characters, needed more complex schemes.

Open a document using the wrong table and the numbers came out as the wrong characters. Japanese users had a word for the jumble: mojibake, roughly 'character transformation'. Anyone who has seen an apostrophe turn into a string like â€™ on a web page has met the same problem.

sections.key: Unicode gives every character in every writing system a unique number, keeping ASCII's values for compatibility.
sections.b:
In the late 1980s, engineers including Joe Becker of Xerox and Lee Collins and Mark Davis of Apple began working on a universal solution. The Unicode Consortium was founded in 1991 and published the first version of the standard that year. Its goal: one number, called a code point, for every character in every writing system, past and present.

Capital A is still 65, for compatibility with ASCII, and is written in Unicode as U+0041. Unicode now covers well over 150,000 characters across more than 160 scripts, including Arabic, Devanagari, Cherokee, Egyptian hieroglyphs and cuneiform. New characters are added through a formal proposal process, and the standard is updated roughly once a year.

sections.key: UTF-8 stores Unicode in one to four bytes while leaving plain English text identical to ASCII.
sections.b:
Giving characters numbers is only half the job; you also need a way to store them as bytes. One evening in September 1992, computer scientists Ken Thompson and Rob Pike, then at Bell Labs, sketched a scheme on a placemat in a New Jersey diner. It became UTF-8.

Its elegance is that ordinary English text is stored exactly as in ASCII, one byte per character, so old files and programs keep working. Other characters use two, three or four bytes, with bit patterns that clearly mark where each character starts, so software never mistakes part of one character for another. UTF-8 spread steadily, and today the great majority of web pages use it, a quiet but enormous victory for compatibility.

sections.key: Emoji are Unicode characters whose artwork varies by platform, and many are built by joining several code points.
sections.b:
Emoji come from Japan: e means picture and moji means character. The resemblance to 'emotion' is a coincidence. In 1999 Shigetaka Kurita created 176 simple 12 by 12 pixel designs for NTT Docomo's mobile internet service, now held by New York's Museum of Modern Art, though another carrier had offered picture symbols slightly earlier. Each carrier used its own codes, so emoji broke between networks. Pressure from companies including Google and Apple led to emoji joining Unicode in 2010.

Unicode gives each emoji a code point and name, such as U+1F602, 'face with tears of joy', but not the artwork, so Apple, Google and others draw their own. Skin tones attach as modifiers, and family emoji join several with an invisible zero-width joiner, so one picture can use seven or more code points.

quiz.q: Why did early text often turn to gibberish between computers?
o: Letters cannot be stored in binary
Text was too long to send over wires
Each machine used a different character table
The first computers could only show numbers
quiz.e: Without a shared table, the same number could mean different characters on different machines.

quiz.q: What causes mojibake?
o: Reading text with the wrong table
Using too many emoji in one message
A damaged hard drive
Sending text across time zones
quiz.e: The numbers are correct but get interpreted through the wrong table, giving the wrong characters.

quiz.q: What is Unicode's main goal?
o: A faster way to type English letters
A single code covering every writing system
A smaller set of characters for the web
A separate code for each country
quiz.e: A single universal code point per character ends the clash between competing tables.

quiz.q: Why was UTF-8's design so useful?
o: It uses exactly two bytes for every character
It removes the need for Unicode
It only supports emoji and symbols
It stores plain English text exactly like ASCII
quiz.e: Compatibility with ASCII let old files and programs keep working.

quiz.q: Why can the same emoji look different on two phones?
o: Unicode sets the code point and name, not the artwork
Each phone stores emoji as small photographs
Phone makers assign their own numbers to each emoji
Screens redraw emoji differently each time they load
quiz.e: Each company draws its own designs for the same Unicode code point.

LESSONS.push: Computers only understand numbers. So how does a laughing face reach your friend's phone?

LESSONS.title: Open source: the free code running the world
LESSONS.hook: Much of the digital world runs on software written in the open and given away. In 2024, one engineer's curiosity about a half-second delay showed both the strength and the fragility of that system.

sections.key: Open source software publishes its source code so anyone can study, change and share it under a licence.
sections.b:
Software begins as source code, instructions written in a programming language. Most commercial programs are distributed only in compiled form, which computers can run but humans can barely read, so the recipe stays secret. Open source software publishes the recipe. Anyone can study it, fix it, improve it or build on it, under a licence that sets the rules. Some licences let you do almost anything; others require you to share your changes too.

Open source does not mean nobody is paid. Many developers are employed by companies that rely on the software. But the code itself is shared, and it is everywhere: phones, cars, televisions, routers and the servers behind most websites.

sections.key: Frustration with locked-up software led Stallman to start free software, and Torvalds' hobby kernel completed it.
sections.b:
By the late 1970s software was increasingly locked up as a commercial product. Richard Stallman, an MIT programmer, later described a formative frustration: a jamming laser printer he could not fix because the maker would not share the source code. In 1983 he announced the GNU project to build a complete operating system of free software, and in 1985 founded the Free Software Foundation. 'Free' meant freedom, not price. His GNU General Public License required shared changes to stay free, a twist nicknamed copyleft.

GNU still lacked a kernel. In August 1991 Linus Torvalds, a 21-year-old Helsinki student, posted that he was writing a free operating system, just a hobby, not big and professional like GNU. Programmers worldwide sent improvements, and Linux was born. He later created Git too.

sections.key: Linux and other open source projects underpin phones, servers, supercomputers and online security.
sections.b:
Linux is far more widespread than most people realise. Android, the world's most popular phone system, is built on the Linux kernel. Linux runs most of the servers behind websites and cloud services, and since 2017 every one of the 500 fastest supercomputers on the TOP500 list has run it. Open source also supplies browser engines, databases, programming languages and the encryption libraries protecting online banking.

Companies build on this shared foundation rather than writing everything from scratch. Even firms that once feared open source came around. Microsoft's chief executive Steve Ballmer called Linux 'a cancer' in 2001; Microsoft later became one of open source's biggest contributors.

sections.key: Widely used open source code can depend on a few underfunded volunteers, which makes serious flaws a shared risk.
sections.b:
Shared code has a weakness: everyone uses it, but no one in particular is responsible for it. In 2014 researchers discovered Heartbleed, a serious flaw in OpenSSL, encryption software used by a large share of secure web servers. The project was run by a handful of people, with only one working on it full time, and received only around 2000 US dollars a year in donations.

In 2021 another severe flaw, Log4Shell, turned up in Log4j, a widely used logging tool maintained largely by volunteers. Each crisis pushed companies and governments to fund critical projects more seriously. A popular web cartoon sums up the worry: digital infrastructure balanced on one small project that a lone volunteer has thanklessly maintained for years.

sections.key: A tiny delay noticed by one engineer exposed a backdoor planted in xz Utils after two years of trust-building.
sections.b:
In March 2024 Andres Freund, a Microsoft engineer who works on the PostgreSQL database, noticed something odd: logging in to a test machine used more processor time than it should, adding about half a second. Curious, he traced the delay to xz Utils, a small compression tool in many Linux systems. Someone had hidden a backdoor in it that could have let an attacker take control of affected servers.

The culprit, using the name Jia Tan, had spent around two years earning the trust of the project's overstretched volunteer maintainer before gaining the access to slip it in. It was caught before reaching the stable versions of major Linux distributions. Who was behind it remains unknown, though many security experts suspect a well-resourced, possibly state-backed group.

quiz.q: What makes software open source?
o: Its source code is public to study and change
It is always free of charge to the user
It is written only by volunteers
It can only run on Linux
quiz.e: Open source means the recipe is shared under a licence, not that nobody gets paid.

quiz.q: What did Stallman mean by 'free' software?
o: It never costs the user any money
It can never be sold by anyone
Users are free to study and change it
It comes with no licence or rules
quiz.e: The point was freedom, free as in free speech, not free as in free beer.

quiz.q: Where is Linux commonly used today?
o: Only on home desktop computers and laptops
Only in specialist research laboratories
Almost nowhere outside hobbyist computers
Android phones, web servers and supercomputers
quiz.e: Linux quietly powers much of the digital world, from phones to supercomputers.

quiz.q: What did Heartbleed reveal about open source?
o: Vital shared code can rely on a few underfunded people
Open source is always less secure than commercial code
Encryption software cannot be fixed
Volunteers refuse to maintain code
quiz.e: Everyone relies on the code, yet few fund or maintain it, so flaws carry shared risk.

quiz.q: How was the xz Utils backdoor discovered?
o: A routine government audit
A security alarm at a major bank
An engineer chasing a login delay
A public report from the attacker
quiz.e: Careful curiosity about a small slowdown uncovered a hidden attack.

LESSONS.push: A half-second delay on one test machine uncovered a plot against the internet.

LESSONS.title: Turing and the problems no computer can solve
LESSONS.hook: Before electronic computers existed, a 23-year-old mathematician proved there are questions no computer, however powerful, will ever be able to answer.

sections.key: Turing answered Hilbert's decision problem by first defining exactly what a mechanical procedure is.
sections.b: In 1928 David Hilbert and Wilhelm Ackermann posed the Entscheidungsproblem, or ‘decision problem’. Could a definite step-by-step procedure decide whether any statement in formal logic is provable? If so, mathematics could in principle be mechanised. In 1931 Kurt Gödel had shown that any consistent system rich enough for arithmetic contains true statements it cannot prove, but the decision problem was a separate question. Answering it needed a precise definition of ‘mechanical procedure’. In 1936 Alan Turing, a 23-year-old fellow of King's College, Cambridge, supplied one. He imagined a simple machine: an endless tape of squares, a head that reads, writes or erases one symbol at a time and moves left or right, and a finite table of rules. Anything that can be calculated by a precise procedure, he argued, such a machine can calculate.

sections.key: A universal machine can run any other machine's rules, which is the idea behind every modern computer.
sections.b: Turing's paper, ‘On Computable Numbers’, held a second startling idea. The rule table of any Turing machine can itself be written down as symbols on a tape. So a universal machine, given a description of any other machine plus its input, can simulate it step by step and produce the same result. One machine can do the work of every machine, if it is handed the right instructions. That is exactly what a modern computer is. Your laptop needs no different hardware to be a word processor, a game or a calculator; it simply loads a different program. Historians debate how directly Turing's abstract idea influenced the engineers who built the first stored-program computers in the late 1940s, but the concept existed in 1936.

sections.key: The halting problem asks whether a perfect checker could tell, in advance, if any program will finish or run forever.
sections.b: Anyone who has watched a frozen app knows that programs can get stuck in endless loops. A perfect checker, able to examine any program and its input and say in advance whether it will stop or run forever, would be enormously useful. Some cases are easy: a program that counts from one to ten halts, while ‘repeat forever’ does not. Others are fiendish. Imagine a program that searches for an even number greater than 2 that is not the sum of two primes, and stops only if it finds one. Whether it ever halts depends on Goldbach's conjecture, unsolved since 1742. A perfect halting checker would settle such questions instantly. This is the halting problem.

sections.key: No general halting checker can exist, because any such checker could be made to contradict itself.
sections.b: Suppose someone claims to have built a perfect checker, called H. In the form usually taught today, the argument runs like this. Build a program called Contrary that takes any program, asks H whether it halts when given its own code, and then does the opposite. If H says it halts, Contrary loops forever; if H says it loops, Contrary stops. Now feed Contrary its own code. Whatever H predicts, Contrary does the reverse, so H is wrong. No such H can exist. Turing used reasoning of this kind to answer Hilbert: no general mechanical procedure can decide every mathematical question. The American logician Alonzo Church reached the same conclusion independently, by a different route, shortly before.

sections.key: Because some questions are undecidable, no virus scanner or bug checker can ever be perfect.
sections.b: The halting problem is no quirk of old mathematics. A later result, Rice's theorem, extends it: no program can perfectly decide, for every possible program, any meaningful property of how that program behaves, such as whether it will ever leak a password. That is why no antivirus software can be guaranteed to catch every piece of malicious code, and why tools that check programs for bugs must accept limits. They can miss problems, raise false alarms or give up on some cases. In practice, engineers work around this with time limits, careful restrictions and checkers that are right most of the time. Turing's 1936 insight remains a humbling boundary. Some questions are not merely hard for computers. They are impossible.

quiz.q: Why did Turing need to describe his imaginary machine to answer Hilbert?
o: Computers were already built and needed testing
A 'mechanical procedure' had to be defined first
Gödel had already answered the decision problem
He planned to build it from vacuum tubes
quiz.e: To prove what no procedure can do, Turing first had to define exactly what a procedure is.

quiz.q: What makes a universal machine the idea behind modern computers?
o: It is faster than any machine built for one task
It stores all its data on an endless tape
One machine can do any job if given instructions
It keeps running without ever being switched off
quiz.e: A computer needs no new hardware for each job, only a different program.

quiz.q: Why is a program that hunts for a Goldbach counterexample a hard test for a halting checker?
o: It always runs for exactly one second each time
It needs more memory than any computer could hold
It is too short for a checker to analyse properly
Its halting depends on an unsolved maths problem
quiz.e: A perfect checker would have to settle open mathematical questions, which hints at how demanding the task is.

quiz.q: What does the Contrary argument show?
o: A perfect checker must be wrong about Contrary
Loops should never be used in any program
Computers reason more slowly than people do
A halting checker is possible but very slow
quiz.e: Whatever H predicts about Contrary, Contrary does the opposite, so no perfect H can exist.

quiz.q: What practical consequence follows from undecidability?
o: Computers cannot reliably add very large numbers
No antivirus can be guaranteed to catch all malware
Programs cannot be copied without errors
Internet speeds have a fixed upper limit
quiz.e: Perfectly judging what any program will do is impossible, so checkers must accept limits.

LESSONS.push: In 1936, before computers existed, a young mathematician proved what they could never do.

LESSONS.title: The illusory truth effect: why repetition feels like proof
LESSONS.hook: Hear something often enough and it starts to feel true, even when you know better. Here's why your brain falls for it, and how to fight back.

sections.key: Hearing a claim again makes it feel truer, because familiar ideas are easier for the brain to process.
sections.b: In 1977 psychologists Lynn Hasher, David Goldstein and Thomas Toppino had students rate trivia statements for truth over three sessions, two weeks apart. Some statements returned every session; others were new each time. The repeated ones were rated more likely to be true each time, whether they were true or not. Nothing about the evidence had changed. Only familiarity had. The leading explanation is processing fluency: a statement you have met before is easier to read and understand, and the brain treats that ease as a sign of accuracy. It is often a decent clue, but fluency can come from almost anywhere. Easier-to-read colours, and rhymes such as ‘woes unite foes’, also make statements seem truer.

sections.key: Repetition can nudge belief even in claims that contradict what you already know.
sections.b: It is tempting to think this only works on topics you know nothing about. In a 2015 study led by Lisa Fazio, participants read statements such as ‘A sari is the name of the short pleated skirt worn by Scots’, which contradicts something most of them knew: that skirt is a kilt. Even so, reading a false statement more than once made people rate it as somewhat more true than they otherwise would. Knowledge helped, but it didn't switch the effect off. People often failed to bring what they knew to mind and relied on the feeling of familiarity instead. The biggest jump in belief tends to come from the second exposure, with smaller gains after that.

sections.key: Even a single earlier glimpse of a false headline can make it seem more accurate later, warning label or not.
sections.b: In 2018 Gordon Pennycook, Tyrone Cannon and David Rand showed people real fake-news headlines styled as they would appear in a feed. Headlines people had seen before were rated as more accurate than new ones, after just one earlier exposure. Strikingly, the effect still appeared when the headlines had carried a warning label saying they were disputed by fact-checkers. This matters because online platforms are repetition machines. A claim can reach you through a friend's post, a meme, a video and a comment thread in the same afternoon, and each one makes it feel a little more familiar. Advertisers and propagandists have understood the power of repetition for a very long time.

sections.key: Correct a myth by leading with the truth, so the fact rather than the myth becomes the familiar thing.
sections.b: Correcting a falsehood is a headache. A typical myth-busting article repeats the myth, sometimes in large type, then explains why it's wrong. Readers may later remember the familiar claim and forget the correction. Researchers once worried that corrections might routinely ‘backfire’ and strengthen false beliefs, but later work found this is rare; corrections generally help. Still, how you correct matters. A widely recommended approach, sometimes called a ‘truth sandwich’, starts with the accurate fact, mentions the myth once and clearly labels it false, explains why it's wrong, then finishes by repeating the truth. That way the fact gets the repetition and becomes the familiar one.

sections.key: Treat ‘I've heard that before’ as a cue to check the evidence, not as a conclusion.
sections.b: You can't stop repetition from affecting you, but you can make it work less well. Notice the feeling of ‘I've heard that before’ and treat it as a cue, not a conclusion. Ask where you heard it, whether the source was reliable, and whether you have ever seen actual evidence. Some studies suggest that prompting people to focus on accuracy, or to think about how they know a claim is true, reduces the effect, especially for claims they have the knowledge to check. It also helps to be careful about what you repeat yourself. Every time you pass on a dubious claim, even as a joke, you add one more exposure to someone else's sense that it's true.

quiz.q: Why does a repeated statement tend to feel more true?
o: Each repeat gives the brain fresh evidence for it
People tend to repeat only claims that are true
Familiar claims feel easy to process, so seem true
Repetition makes people check the facts more carefully
quiz.e: Processing fluency makes familiar claims feel smooth, and the brain reads smoothness as truth.

quiz.q: What happened when people repeatedly read false statements that contradicted their own knowledge?
o: Repetition still made them seem somewhat more true
They rejected them more firmly each time
They grew sceptical of every statement they read
They permanently forgot the correct fact
quiz.e: Knowing better helps, but familiarity can still nudge belief when we fail to bring our knowledge to mind.

quiz.q: Why are online platforms a good environment for the illusory truth effect?
o: They only show claims that have been checked
Warning labels completely cancel the effect
People rarely see the same claim more than once
A claim can reach you many times in one afternoon
quiz.e: Feeds repeat claims constantly, and even a disputed label does not stop familiarity from working.

quiz.q: What is the ‘truth sandwich’ approach to correcting a myth?
o: Repeat the myth several times so people notice it
Open with the fact, name the myth once, end with the fact
Ignore the myth and hope people forget it
Point out how foolish believers of the myth are
quiz.e: Putting the truth at the start and end makes the fact, not the myth, the thing that gets repeated.

quiz.q: What is a good response to the feeling of ‘I've heard that before’?
o: Ask where you heard it and look for evidence
Treat it as proof the claim is true
Ignore all claims you have heard before
Repeat the claim to test it on others
quiz.e: Familiarity is a cue to check the source and evidence, not a conclusion.

LESSONS.push: Why a claim you've heard a few times feels truer, even when you know better.

LESSONS.title: Confirmation bias: the puzzle almost everyone gets wrong
LESSONS.hook: Three numbers, one hidden rule, and a mistake that reveals how we all hunt for proof we're right rather than for the truth.

sections.key: Most people test a rule only with examples that fit their theory, so they never see it fail.
sections.b: In 1960 the British psychologist Peter Wason, at University College London, gave volunteers three numbers: 2, 4, 6. The sequence followed a rule he had in mind, and their job was to discover it. They could propose their own sets of three numbers, and he would say whether each fitted. Most people quickly formed a theory, such as ‘even numbers going up by two’, and tested it with sets like 8, 10, 12. Every one earned a yes, so they announced their rule, and many were told they were wrong. The real rule was simply ‘any three numbers in increasing order’. Tests like 8, 10, 12 fit both the theory and the real rule, so they could never reveal the mistake. Those who succeeded tried sequences their theory said should fail, such as 1, 2, 3.

sections.key: In Wason's selection task, most people turn over the wrong cards, because they look for confirmation rather than a possible break.
sections.b: Wason's most famous puzzle followed in 1966. Four cards each have a letter on one side and a number on the other. You can see E, K, 4 and 7. The rule is: ‘If a card has a vowel on one side, it has an even number on the other.’ Which cards must you turn over to check whether the rule is being broken? Most people pick E, and often 4 as well. E is right. But 4 tells you nothing, because the rule says nothing about what must be behind an even number. The card you need is 7: if a vowel is hiding behind it, the rule is broken. In many studies, only around one person in ten chooses correctly.

sections.key: The same logic becomes simple when the puzzle is about catching rule-breakers in a familiar setting.
sections.b: Here's the strange part. Researchers later rewrote the puzzle in familiar terms. Imagine you are checking a bar where the rule is: ‘If someone is drinking beer, they must be over 18.’ The four cards show: drinking beer, drinking cola, age 25 and age 16. Which do you check? Most people quickly pick the beer drinker and the 16-year-old, which is logically the same answer as E and 7. Studies by Richard Griggs and James Cox in 1982 found that versions like this are solved far more often than the abstract one. Psychologists still debate why. Some argue our minds are tuned to spot social cheating; others say familiar situations simply make it obvious which cases could break the rule.

sections.key: Confirmation bias is the habit of seeking, noticing and remembering information that supports what we already believe.
sections.b: Wason's puzzles became classic demonstrations of confirmation bias: the tendency to search for, interpret and remember information in ways that support what we already think. It shows up far beyond the laboratory. A detective who settles on a suspect early may give extra weight to clues that point their way. Someone convinced a colleague dislikes them reads every short email as proof. Investors can seek out news that flatters the shares they already own. Online, search engines and feeds make it easy to find something that agrees with almost any belief. The bias isn't stupidity. Holding on to a working theory saves effort, and often the theory is right. The danger is that we rarely notice when it isn't.

sections.key: The best test of a belief is one that could prove it wrong.
sections.b: The lesson from Wason is practical. When you have a theory, ask: what would I expect to see if I were wrong, and have I looked for it? Scientists build this into their method by designing experiments that could fail. You can do a small version in daily life. Before a big purchase, read the worst reviews, not just the best. Before deciding someone is untrustworthy, list the evidence that points the other way. In a 1984 study, Charles Lord and colleagues found that asking people to deliberately consider the opposite reduced biased judgements more effectively than simply telling them to be fair and unbiased. Testing your ideas like this feels uncomfortable, but it's the quickest route to the truth.

quiz.q: Why did testing a set like 8, 10, 12 fail to help people in the 2-4-6 task?
o: The numbers were too large to judge fairly
Wason gave misleading answers to some tests
It fitted both their theory and the true rule
It was rejected because it broke the real rule
quiz.e: A test that your theory and the true rule both pass cannot tell them apart.

quiz.q: In the card task showing E, K, 4 and 7, which cards must be turned over to check the rule?
o: E and 4
E and 7
K and 4
4 and 7
quiz.e: Only E and 7 could reveal a vowel paired with an odd number; 4 cannot break the rule.

quiz.q: Why is the drinking-age version of the card puzzle so interesting?
o: Same logic, yet people solve it far more easily
It uses a completely different kind of logic
Hardly anyone ever solves it correctly
It shows people are better at maths when relaxed
quiz.e: The logic is the same as E and 7, but a familiar setting makes the cases that could break the rule obvious.

quiz.q: What is confirmation bias?
o: Changing your mind whenever someone disagrees
Trusting only what recognised experts say
Avoiding strong opinions on every subject
Favouring information that backs your existing beliefs
quiz.e: We search for, interpret and remember evidence in ways that back up our existing views.

quiz.q: According to the 1984 study by Lord and colleagues, what helped reduce biased judgements?
o: Being told to be fair
Reading more evidence that supports your view
Deliberately considering the opposite
Deciding more quickly
quiz.e: Actively imagining you could be wrong works better than simply promising to be unbiased.

LESSONS.push: Three numbers and a hidden rule. Almost everyone makes the same mistake.

LESSONS.title: Outcome bias: why good decisions can end badly
LESSONS.hook: A coach made one of the most criticised calls in sport, and a poker player says we judged it all wrong. Learn to tell a smart choice from a lucky one.

sections.key: Judging a decision only by how it turned out, which poker players call ‘resulting’, is a mistake.
sections.b: In February 2015 the Seattle Seahawks were seconds from winning the Super Bowl. Trailing the New England Patriots by four points, they had the ball about a metre from the line with 26 seconds left. Most fans expected a handoff to their powerful running back. Instead, coach Pete Carroll called a pass. It was intercepted, and the Patriots won. Headlines called it one of the worst calls in the game's history. Yet some analysts argued it was reasonable: interceptions that close to the line are rare, and an incomplete pass would stop the clock. Former poker player Annie Duke, in her 2018 book Thinking in Bets, calls judging by results alone ‘resulting’. In poker you can play a hand perfectly and still lose to the last card. In life there are fewer hands and messier information.

sections.key: People rate the very same decision as worse, and the decision-maker as less competent, when it turns out badly.
sections.b: In 1988 the psychologists Jonathan Baron and John Hershey gave volunteers descriptions of decisions made under uncertainty, such as a doctor's choice about whether to go ahead with a risky operation. Everyone received the same information that had been available to the decision-maker at the time. The only thing that changed was the outcome: in some versions the patient lived, and in others the patient died. People rated the decision itself as worse, and the decision-maker as less competent, when the outcome was bad. Yet the choice had been made with exactly the same knowledge. Baron and Hershey called this outcome bias.

sections.key: Every outcome mixes decision quality with luck, and a bad decision that works out well is the most dangerous combination.
sections.b: Picture a simple grid. A good decision with a good outcome is a deserved success. A good decision with a bad outcome is bad luck. A bad decision with a bad outcome is a predictable failure. And a bad decision with a good outcome is a lucky escape, which may be the most dangerous of all. Think of someone who drives home after too many drinks and arrives safely. The outcome teaches them nothing useful, or worse, teaches them it was fine. Each lucky escape can make the next risky choice feel safer. Outcome bias collapses these four boxes into two: it worked, so it was right; it failed, so it was wrong.

sections.key: Once we know how things turned out, we overestimate how predictable they were.
sections.b: Outcome bias has a close relative: hindsight bias, the feeling that we ‘knew it all along’. In the 1970s the psychologist Baruch Fischhoff showed that once people learnt how an event turned out, they judged that outcome to have been more predictable than people who hadn't been told. Their memories of what they had predicted earlier also shifted towards what actually happened. Together these biases make the world seem more orderly than it really is. They also make us unfair judges. Workers, doctors, pilots and leaders can be blamed for bad outcomes they could not reasonably have foreseen, while people who took foolish risks and got away with them can be rewarded and promoted.

sections.key: To learn from experience, review how a decision was made, not just how it turned out.
sections.b: The fix is to judge decisions by the process behind them. Ask: what did we know at the time? What options did we consider? Did we think about the risks and how likely they were? Was there information we could reasonably have gathered but didn't? Armies, hospitals and airlines have long used structured reviews after events, and these work best when they examine successes and failures with the same honesty. A simple personal tool is a decision journal. Before an important choice, write down what you expect to happen and why. Later, compare that with what actually happened. Over time you'll see whether your judgement is sound, or whether you've simply been lucky.

quiz.q: What does ‘resulting’ mean?
o: Recording the score after each game
Judging a choice only by its result
Making decisions much too quickly
Betting only on the likely winners
quiz.e: Resulting ignores luck and judges the choice by its outcome alone.

quiz.q: In Baron and Hershey's study, what changed between versions of each scenario?
o: The information available to the doctor
The doctor's experience
The type of operation
Only the outcome
quiz.e: With identical information, a bad outcome alone made people judge the decision and the decision-maker more harshly.

quiz.q: Why might a bad decision with a good outcome be especially dangerous?
o: It always leads to a later punishment
It is impossible for anyone to notice
It can teach people a risky choice was fine
It makes people far too cautious
quiz.e: A lucky escape rewards the risk, making the next risky choice feel safer.

quiz.q: What is hindsight bias?
o: Forgetting which decisions you made last year
Thinking an outcome was obvious once you know it
Planning so far ahead that plans stop working
Trusting experts less after one mistake
quiz.e: Knowing the result makes it seem obvious, so we judge past decisions unfairly.

quiz.q: What is a good way to learn from a decision?
o: Review what you knew and what you weighed
Judge it only by how it turned out
Avoid reviewing decisions that worked
Blame whoever was in charge at the time
quiz.e: Reviewing the process, for example with a decision journal, separates skill from luck.

LESSONS.push: A coach made the most criticised call in sport. Was it actually a bad decision?

LESSONS.title: N-rays: the rays only believers could see
LESSONS.hook: In 1903 a respected French physicist discovered a new kind of radiation, and other scientists soon confirmed it. There was just one problem: it didn't exist.

sections.key: After X-rays and radioactivity, physicists were primed to believe new rays existed, and N-rays were judged by eye.
sections.b: At the end of the 1800s physics was full of astonishing discoveries. In 1895 Wilhelm Röntgen found X-rays. The next year Henri Becquerel found that uranium gave off its own radiation, and soon Marie and Pierre Curie were isolating new radioactive elements. In 1903 René Blondlot, a respected physicist at the University of Nancy, announced another kind, which he named N-rays after his home city. The claim seemed like the next exciting chapter. N-rays supposedly made a small spark or a faintly glowing screen grow slightly brighter, and observers judged this by eye in a darkened room. That is a very weak signal: in dim light the eye struggles to judge small differences in brightness, and tiny flickers are easy to read as meaningful. Still, other scientists reported observations of their own.

sections.key: When a result can only be seen by believers, and failures are blamed on the observer, the claim is very hard to test.
sections.b: Not everyone was convinced. Physicists in Germany and Britain, among them some of the most skilled experimenters of the day, set up the apparatus and saw nothing. Supporters had an answer ready: perhaps the sceptics' eyes were not sensitive enough, or they lacked the right technique. This is a warning sign worth remembering. When a result can only be seen by people who already believe in it, and failures are explained away as the observer's fault, the claim has become very difficult to test. A real effect should show up for careful researchers whether or not they hope to find it. The disagreement rumbled on, until a visiting American physicist decided to investigate for himself.

sections.key: In 1904 Robert Wood secretly removed a vital part of the equipment, and the readings carried on.
sections.b: In 1904 the American physicist Robert W. Wood, of Johns Hopkins University, visited Blondlot's laboratory. Blondlot demonstrated how an aluminium prism supposedly spread N-rays into a spectrum, with readings taken in a darkened room. While the room was dark, Wood quietly removed the prism and kept it out of sight. Blondlot carried on reading out measurements as if nothing had changed. Wood also reported other secret checks in which observers kept seeing effects that should have vanished. He published his account in the journal Nature later that year. Without accusing anyone of dishonesty, the report made it clear that the observations depended on what the observers expected, not on any real rays.

sections.key: Blondlot almost certainly believed what he saw, because expectation shapes perception.
sections.b: There is no good evidence that Blondlot set out to deceive anyone. He was an accomplished scientist who had done respected earlier work measuring the speed of electrical waves. What went wrong was more ordinary and more unsettling: he and others genuinely perceived what they expected to perceive. After Wood's report, interest in N-rays faded quickly, especially outside France, though Blondlot is said to have kept believing in them. The episode is now a classic case study in how expectation shapes observation. The chemist Irving Langmuir later popularised the phrase ‘pathological science’ for cases like this, where researchers fool themselves with effects so faint they sit right at the edge of what can be detected.

sections.key: Good science guards against expectation by keeping observers from knowing what to expect.
sections.b: A similar lesson came from a horse. In early 1900s Berlin, a horse called Clever Hans appeared to answer arithmetic questions by tapping his hoof. In 1907 the psychologist Oskar Pfungst showed that Hans was responding to tiny, unconscious cues from the people around him, who tensed and relaxed as he neared the right answer. When the questioner didn't know the answer, or Hans couldn't see them, his skill vanished. The solution to both stories is blinding. In a well-run modern trial, the people measuring results don't know which participants received the treatment. Wood, in effect, ran a blind test. Whenever you can, test a claim in a way that stops the tester's hopes from steering the result.

quiz.q: Why did N-rays seem believable in 1903?
o: They were bright enough to see in daylight
They had been predicted decades earlier
Recent finds such as X-rays made new rays plausible
Every laboratory in Europe had detected them
quiz.e: Recent discoveries of invisible rays primed physicists to accept one more kind.

quiz.q: What warning sign appeared when other laboratories couldn't find N-rays?
o: The sceptics refused to try the experiment
The equipment was too expensive to build
The sceptics were not trained physicists
Failures were blamed on the sceptics' eyes
quiz.e: A claim that only believers can confirm, with failures excused, is very hard to test.

quiz.q: What happened when Robert Wood secretly removed the prism?
o: The readings stopped at once
The readings carried on as before
Blondlot spotted the missing prism
The rays seemed to grow stronger
quiz.e: Readings that continue without the key part show the observations depended on expectation.

quiz.q: How did Blondlot come to ‘see’ rays that weren't there?
o: He deliberately forged the readings
His expectations shaped what he sincerely saw
His instruments gave faulty readings
He copied results from other laboratories
quiz.e: Expectation shaped observation, so he sincerely saw what he hoped to see.

quiz.q: What does ‘blinding’ mean in an experiment?
o: Running the experiment in complete darkness
Keeping the final results from the public
Testing only on animals, never people
Keeping testers unaware of key details
quiz.e: If testers don't know what to expect, their hopes can't steer the result.

LESSONS.push: A respected scientist found rays that other labs couldn't. A visitor spotted why.

LESSONS.title: Deduction, induction and abduction: three ways to reason
LESSONS.hook: Sherlock Holmes called it deduction, but he was usually doing something else. Learn the three basic kinds of reasoning, and what each can and can't prove.

sections.key: Holmes's first meeting with Watson shows reasoning from small clues to a big conclusion, though not strictly deduction.
sections.b: In A Study in Scarlet, published in 1887, Sherlock Holmes shakes hands with Dr John Watson and says, ‘You have been in Afghanistan, I perceive.’ Watson is astonished. Holmes later explains his chain of thought. Here was a gentleman of a medical type with a military air, so probably an army doctor. His face was tanned but his wrists were pale, so he had recently come from the tropics. He looked haggard and held his left arm stiffly, suggesting illness and an injury. Where might an English army doctor recently have suffered such hardship? Afghanistan. Holmes called this the science of deduction. Logicians would say he was mostly doing something different. To see why, we need three kinds of reasoning.

sections.key: In a valid deduction, if the premises are true, the conclusion must be true.
sections.b: Deduction moves from general statements to a conclusion that follows necessarily. All humans are mortal; Socrates is human; therefore Socrates is mortal. If both starting statements, called premises, are true, the conclusion cannot be false. That is deduction's great strength: certainty. Its weakness is that the conclusion contains nothing that wasn't already packed inside the premises. Deduction also depends completely on the premises being right. An argument can be valid in structure and still reach a false conclusion if a premise is wrong: all birds can fly; penguins are birds; therefore penguins can fly. Logicians call an argument ‘sound’ only when it is valid and its premises are actually true.

sections.key: Induction generalises from experience, which is useful but never completely certain.
sections.b: Induction works the other way, from particular observations to general conclusions. The sun has risen every morning in recorded history, so it will rise tomorrow. Every swan Europeans had ever seen was white, so all swans must be white. Most of our everyday knowledge, and much of science, rests on reasoning like this, and usually it serves us well. But an inductive conclusion can always be overturned by new evidence. In 1697 the Dutch explorer Willem de Vlamingh and his crew saw black swans on a river in what is now Western Australia, which became known as the Swan River. A belief backed by countless observations was undone by a single flock of birds. Induction also fails when we generalise from too few cases, such as judging a whole city on one rude waiter.

sections.key: Abduction reasons from evidence to the most likely explanation, but it can miss better alternatives.
sections.b: The American philosopher Charles Sanders Peirce named a third kind, abduction. It starts with a surprising observation and asks what would best explain it. The lawn is wet this morning. Did it rain, did the sprinkler run, or did dew form? A bone-dry footpath points to the sprinkler. This is also called inference to the best explanation, and it is what Holmes was really doing with Watson. Doctors diagnosing from symptoms and mechanics tracing an engine noise do the same. It is risky, because the best explanation you can think of may not be true: perhaps Watson was tanned from a holiday and hurt his arm falling off a horse. Treating abduction as deduction is a known fallacy, affirming the consequent: ‘If it rained, the lawn would be wet. The lawn is wet. Therefore it rained.’

sections.key: Good thinking cycles through explanation, prediction and testing.
sections.b: In practice the three kinds of reasoning work as a team, and science is a good model. A researcher notices something odd and uses abduction to propose a likely explanation, called a hypothesis. They then use deduction to work out what should happen if that explanation is true: if this fertiliser helps plants grow, then plants given it should grow taller than identical plants without it. Finally they gather observations and use induction to judge whether the evidence supports the idea. Then the cycle starts again. You can do the same with everyday puzzles.
