When you land on an explanation, ask what else could explain the facts, what your idea predicts, and whether you've checked.

quiz.q: Which kind of reasoning was Holmes mostly using when he guessed Watson had been in Afghanistan?
o: Deduction
Abduction
Induction
Pure intuition
quiz.e: Holmes chose the most plausible explanation for the clues, which is abduction.

quiz.q: What makes a deductive argument ‘sound’?
o: It is convincing to most people
It is based on many observations
It has a surprising conclusion
It is valid and its premises are true
quiz.e: A valid structure only guarantees a true conclusion when the premises are true as well.

quiz.q: What did the black swans seen in 1697 show about induction?
o: Strong evidence can still be overturned
Induction always leads to false conclusions
Swans migrate to Australia each year
Deduction is more reliable than observation
quiz.e: Induction is useful but never certain, because new evidence can always overturn it.

quiz.q: ‘If it rained, the lawn would be wet. The lawn is wet, so it rained.’ What's wrong with this?
o: Nothing, it is a perfectly valid deduction
It wrongly assumes that rain is rare
It treats one possible cause as the only one
It relies on far too few observations
quiz.e: A wet lawn has other possible explanations, so the conclusion is only a guess at the best one.

quiz.q: In the scientific cycle, what role does deduction usually play?
o: Coming up with the first explanation
Predicting what follows if the idea is true
Collecting and counting observations
Making further testing unnecessary
quiz.e: Deduction turns a hypothesis into a testable prediction.

LESSONS.push: Sherlock Holmes called it deduction. Logicians say he was doing something else.

LESSONS.title: The framing effect: same facts, different choices
LESSONS.hook: Would you choose a treatment with a 90 per cent survival rate? What about one with a 10 per cent death rate? They're identical, yet the wording changes what people choose.

sections.key: Describing identical options as lives saved or lives lost flips people's choices.
sections.b: In 1981 the psychologists Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman published a now-famous problem. Imagine a disease outbreak expected to kill 600 people. One group chose between two programs. With Program A, 200 people will be saved. With Program B, there's a one-third chance all 600 are saved and a two-thirds chance no-one is saved. Most chose A, the sure thing. A second group got the same choice in different words. With Program C, 400 people will die. With Program D, there's a one-third chance nobody dies and a two-thirds chance all 600 die. Now most chose D, the gamble. Yet A and C describe exactly the same outcome, as do B and D.

sections.key: People avoid risk when outcomes are framed as gains, and gamble to avoid sure losses.
sections.b: The outbreak problem revealed a pattern that Kahneman and Tversky built into their prospect theory. When outcomes are described as gains, such as lives saved, people tend to be cautious and prefer a certain result. When the same outcomes are described as losses, such as deaths, people become more willing to gamble to avoid a sure loss. Part of the reason is loss aversion: losses tend to feel more painful than equivalent gains feel good, with many studies putting the ratio at roughly two to one, though estimates vary. Logically, the wording should make no difference. Psychologically, the frame sets the reference point against which everything else is judged.

sections.key: Even physicians' choices shifted depending on whether outcomes were framed as survival or death.
sections.b: You might hope experts would see through framing. In a 1982 study in the New England Journal of Medicine, Barbara McNeil and colleagues, including Tversky, asked people to choose between surgery and radiation therapy for lung cancer. Surgery carried a higher risk of dying during or soon after treatment, but better long-term survival. When the results were presented as chances of surviving, surgery looked more attractive than when the very same results were described as chances of dying. The effect appeared among patients, among students, and among physicians. Since then, many guides to communicating medical risk have encouraged presenting figures in more than one way, for example giving both survival and death rates together.

sections.key: Highlighting the positive side of the same facts, or one aspect of an issue, shifts judgements and opinions.
sections.b: In a 1988 study, Irwin Levin and Gary Gaeth asked people to evaluate minced beef described as either ‘75 per cent lean’ or ‘25 per cent fat’. Same meat, but the ‘lean’ version was rated better quality and less greasy. The gap shrank when people tasted the beef, though it didn't vanish. Yoghurt is ‘95 per cent fat free’ rather than ‘5 per cent fat’. A fee is a ‘discount for paying cash’ rather than a ‘surcharge for paying by card’. A broader kind of framing highlights different aspects of an issue. In a 1997 study, readers of a news story about a planned Ku Klux Klan rally were more tolerant of it when it was framed as free speech than as a threat to public order. Is a policy ‘tax relief’ or a ‘cut to services’?

sections.key: Restate choices in more than one way and convert percentages into real numbers before deciding.
sections.b: You can't avoid frames, because every description has to start somewhere. But you can learn to notice them. When you face an important choice, deliberately flip the wording: if you're told nine out of ten customers are satisfied, remind yourself that one in ten isn't. If a deal is framed as avoiding a loss, ask how it looks as a plain gain. Turn percentages into concrete counts, such as ‘out of 100 people like me, how many?’ This makes risks much easier to compare. Be especially wary when someone else has chosen the frame for you and stands to gain from your decision. And when you present information to others, giving both frames is often the fairest thing you can do.

quiz.q: In the outbreak problem, why is the switch in people's choices surprising?
o: The programs had genuinely different outcomes
The second group was given more information
Programs A and C described exactly the same outcome
The participants were all doctors
quiz.e: Only the wording changed, from lives saved to lives lost, yet the choices flipped.

quiz.q: When outcomes are framed as losses, people tend to:
o: Become more cautious
Become more willing to gamble
Choose whichever option is listed first
Ignore the numbers entirely
quiz.e: Because losses feel painful, people will take a risk to avoid a sure one.

quiz.q: Who was influenced by framing in the 1982 lung cancer study?
o: Only students
Only patients without medical training
Patients, students and physicians alike
Nobody, once the numbers were explained
quiz.e: Medical expertise did not protect against framing, so presenting figures both ways is wise.

quiz.q: What happened in the minced beef study when people actually tasted the meat?
o: The effect became much stronger
The effect shrank but did not vanish
People preferred the ‘fat’ label
Tasting made them reject both samples
quiz.e: Direct experience reduced the effect, but the label still coloured the judgement.

quiz.q: Which is a good way to defuse a frame?
o: Go with your first gut reaction every time
Trust only the positive descriptions
Avoid numbers and rely on instinct
Flip the wording and use real counts
quiz.e: Flipping the wording and using real counts reveals what the frame was hiding.

LESSONS.push: Ninety per cent survival and ten per cent death mean the same. Why do choices differ?

LESSONS.title: The wisdom of crowds: when many guesses beat experts
LESSONS.hook: In 1906 hundreds of people guessed the weight of an ox. Hardly anyone was spot on, but together they were astonishingly close. Here's why, and when crowds turn foolish.

sections.key: A crowd's middle guess of an ox's weight in 1906 came within about one per cent of the truth.
sections.b: In 1906 the scientist Francis Galton visited a livestock fair in Plymouth, England. Visitors could pay a small fee to guess the weight of an ox once it had been slaughtered and dressed, with prizes for the closest entries. Galton, who was not a great admirer of ordinary people's judgement, collected the 787 legible tickets and analysed them. The guesses were all over the place. But the middle value, the median, was 1,207 pounds, about 547 kilograms. The actual weight was 1,198 pounds, so the crowd was out by less than one per cent. Later analyses found the average was even closer. Galton published the result in Nature in 1907 under the title ‘Vox Populi’, the voice of the people.

sections.key: When people's mistakes are independent, overestimates and underestimates tend to cancel, so the average beats most individuals.
sections.b: How can a crowd of non-experts beat almost every individual in it? Each guess contains some genuine information and some error. One person overestimates because the ox looks bulky; another underestimates because they're thinking of a smaller breed. If those errors point in different directions, they cancel out when averaged, while the useful information adds up. The result is often better than most individual guesses, and sometimes better than an expert's. James Surowiecki popularised the idea in his 2004 book The Wisdom of Crowds. By his account, on Who Wants to Be a Millionaire? the contestants' chosen friends gave the right answer about 65 per cent of the time, while the studio audience's most popular answer was right about 91 per cent of the time.

sections.key: Crowds are wise when they are diverse, independent, decentralised and properly combined.
sections.b: Surowiecki argued that wise crowds need four ingredients. Diversity: people should bring different information and perspectives, not all the same views. Independence: each person's judgement should be their own, rather than copied from those around them. Decentralisation: people should be able to draw on local and specialised knowledge. And aggregation: there must be some way of combining all the private judgements into one answer, such as an average, a vote or a market price. Take away any of these and the magic fades. The same principles underpin tools from averaged economic forecasts to pooled product ratings. A room of people who all read the same article, or who call out their guesses one after another, is less a crowd of independent minds than one opinion repeated many times.

sections.key: Social influence can make a crowd more confident without making it more accurate.
sections.b: Independence is the fragile ingredient. In a 2011 study, Jan Lorenz and colleagues in Switzerland asked groups to estimate factual quantities, such as crime figures, over several rounds. Some groups were shown what the others had guessed before answering again. Seeing others' answers narrowed the range of guesses and made people more confident, but the group's estimates did not become more accurate. The crowd had lost its diversity without gaining any wisdom. On a larger scale, similar dynamics help explain stock market bubbles, fads and panic buying, where people react to each other rather than to independent information. A crowd that copies itself doesn't cancel out its errors. It can amplify them.

sections.key: Averaging two separate guesses of your own can be more accurate than either one, especially if you wait between them.
sections.b: You can even borrow the effect for yourself. In 2008 Edward Vul and Harold Pashler asked people to answer factual questions, then unexpectedly asked them to guess again. The average of a person's two guesses was more accurate than either guess alone, and the benefit was larger when the second guess came three weeks later rather than straight away. The delay helped because it made the second guess more independent of the first. Researchers call this the crowd within. A practical version: when you estimate something important, such as how long a job will take, make a guess, then assume your first answer was wrong, think about why, and make a second estimate. Then average the two.

quiz.q: What was striking about the guesses at the Plymouth fair?
o: Most individuals guessed almost exactly right
The butchers' guesses were by far the best
Nobody guessed within 100 pounds of the weight
The crowd's median was about one per cent out
quiz.e: Individual guesses were scattered, yet the crowd's middle value was remarkably accurate.

quiz.q: Why does averaging many guesses work?
o: Independent errors tend to cancel out
Crowds always contain an expert
People guess more carefully in groups
Large numbers are easier to estimate
quiz.e: Overestimates and underestimates offset each other while the real information adds up.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT one of Surowiecki's conditions for a wise crowd?
o: Diversity
Independence
Unanimity
Aggregation
quiz.e: Wise crowds need diverse, independent views that are combined, not everyone agreeing.

quiz.q: What happened when people in Lorenz's study saw others' guesses?
o: Accuracy improved sharply as guesses converged
Guesses spread out much more widely than before
Most people refused to guess a second time
Guesses narrowed, but accuracy did not improve
quiz.e: Copying reduces diversity and independence, so the crowd gets surer without getting wiser.

quiz.q: Why did a second guess made weeks later help more than an immediate one?
o: People simply remembered the answer better
The second guess was more independent
The first guess was nearly always wrong
Waiting made people far more confident
quiz.e: Independence is what lets errors cancel, and a delay supplies some of it.

LESSONS.push: Hundreds of people guessed an ox's weight. Why the crowd beat almost every individual.

LESSONS.title: Small samples, big surprises: the law of small numbers
LESSONS.hook: The places with the lowest cancer rates and the highest ones share the same surprising feature. Understanding why will change how you read every ranking and review.

sections.key: The places that look healthiest and unhealthiest are often the least populated, because small samples swing to extremes.
sections.b: Imagine a map of the United States showing kidney cancer rates by county. The counties with the lowest rates are mostly rural and sparsely populated. Fresh air, clean water, active lives? Now look at the counties with the highest rates. They are also mostly rural and sparsely populated. Rural life can't be both protective and harmful. The statistician Howard Wainer, and later Daniel Kahneman in Thinking, Fast and Slow, explained why: small counties have small populations, and small numbers bounce around far more. Toss a fair coin four times and all heads happens about one time in sixteen. Toss it 400 times and it is practically impossible. Small samples crowd both the top and the bottom of any ranking.

sections.key: Even people trained in statistics tend to ignore sample size when it matters.
sections.b: In the early 1970s Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman posed a question. A town has two hospitals. In the larger one about 45 babies are born each day, and in the smaller one about 15. Roughly half of all babies are boys, but the exact share varies from day to day. Over a year, each hospital records the days when more than 60 per cent of the babies born were boys. Which hospital recorded more such days? Most people said about the same. The right answer is the smaller hospital, because with only 15 births a day, lopsided results are much more common. In an earlier paper titled ‘Belief in the law of small numbers’, they had shown that even research psychologists trusted small samples too much.

sections.key: To halve the uncertainty in an average, you need four times as much data.
sections.b: The maths traces back to the 1700s and the French-born mathematician Abraham de Moivre. In modern terms, the typical wobble in an average shrinks in proportion to the square root of the number of things being averaged. That has a sobering consequence. To halve the uncertainty in an estimate, you don't need twice as much data; you need four times as much. To cut it to a tenth, you need a hundred times more. Howard Wainer has called this ‘the most dangerous equation’, not because it's complicated, but because ignoring it has led to so many costly mistakes. It explains why tiny trials, small surveys and short track records can be so misleading.

sections.key: Policies built on small-sample rankings can end up chasing noise.
sections.b: Wainer's favourite cautionary tale involves American education. From the late 1990s, reformers noticed that small schools were overrepresented among the top performers on test results. Major funders, including the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, invested heavily in creating smaller schools and breaking up big ones. But as Wainer and colleagues pointed out, small schools were also overrepresented among the worst performers. Their results were simply more variable, because each year's scores came from fewer students. Evaluations of the small-schools push produced mixed results, and the Gates Foundation later shifted its education strategy. Whatever the other merits of smaller schools, the striking rankings had been at least partly an illusion created by sample size.

sections.key: Before trusting an extreme result, check how many cases it is based on.
sections.b: Once you know this, you'll see it everywhere. A new café with five reviews averaging five stars may be no better than an established one averaging 4.6 from 2,000 reviews. A footballer who scores in each of their first three games isn't necessarily a star. A small study reporting a dramatic effect is more likely to be a fluke than a large study reporting a modest one. A useful habit is to mentally pull extreme results from small samples back towards the average until more evidence comes in. Statisticians have formal versions of this idea, sometimes called shrinkage. And when you hear that a small town is the best or worst place for something, your first question should be: how many people live there?

quiz.q: Why do US counties with the lowest and the highest kidney cancer rates often share small populations?
o: Small counties are close to large cities
Small populations swing to extremes by chance
Small counties share the same water supply
Rural life is both protective and harmful
quiz.e: Small samples swing widely, so they fill both ends of a ranking.

quiz.q: In the hospital problem, which hospital records more days when over 60 per cent of babies are boys?
o: The larger hospital
Both about the same
It depends on the season
The smaller hospital
quiz.e: With fewer births per day, lopsided results are much more common.

quiz.q: To halve the uncertainty in an average, roughly how much more data do you need?
o: Twice as much
Ten times as much
Four times as much
Half as much
quiz.e: Uncertainty shrinks with the square root of the sample size, so halving it takes four times the data.

quiz.q: Why were small schools overrepresented among the top performers?
o: Fewer students made their results swing more
Their teachers were consistently better
They received far more funding per pupil
They were given much easier tests
quiz.e: The same variability also put small schools among the worst performers, so the pattern was largely noise.

quiz.q: A new café has five reviews, all five stars. What's the most sensible view?
o: It's definitely the best café in town
Five-star ratings are usually fake
Too few reviews to judge it with confidence
Ignore all online reviews from now on
quiz.e: Extreme results from small samples should be tempered until more evidence arrives.

LESSONS.push: The healthiest and unhealthiest places on the map share one odd feature.

LESSONS.title: Piltdown Man: the fake fossil that fooled science for 40 years
LESSONS.hook: For four decades, a skull from an English gravel pit was hailed as a key link in human evolution. It was a forgery, and the reasons experts believed it are the real lesson.

sections.key: In 1912 bones from a Sussex gravel pit were announced as a vital human ancestor.
sections.b: In December 1912 Charles Dawson, a solicitor and keen amateur fossil collector, and Arthur Smith Woodward, a leading geologist at the British Museum (Natural History), presented a sensational find to the Geological Society of London. From a gravel pit near Piltdown in Sussex came fragments of a skull and part of a jawbone with two worn teeth, along with animal fossils and crude stone tools. Woodward's reconstruction showed a creature with a large, humanlike braincase and an apelike jaw. It was named Eoanthropus dawsoni, ‘Dawson's dawn man’. Newspapers celebrated the earliest Englishman, and many experts accepted Piltdown as a vital link between apes and humans.

sections.key: Piltdown told experts what they wanted to hear, and the evidence that could have exposed it was missing or hard to reach.
sections.b: Piltdown confirmed what many scientists already thought: that a large brain evolved before other human features. National pride played a part too. Germany had the Neanderthal remains and the Heidelberg jaw, and France had Cro-Magnon skeletons, but Britain had little of comparable importance. There were warning signs. The jaw was broken exactly where it would have shown whether it belonged with the skull: the joint and the chin were missing. Some scientists, especially in the United States and France, argued early that skull and jaw came from different creatures. But most researchers saw only plaster casts, which could not show tool marks or staining. Later finds, including a canine tooth in 1913, seemed to settle the debate.

sections.key: Because Piltdown seemed authentic, a genuine African fossil was sidelined for decades.
sections.b: The forgery did real damage. In 1924 the Australian-born anatomist Raymond Dart, working in South Africa, identified a small fossil skull from a quarry at Taung. In 1925 he argued in Nature that this ‘Taung Child’ belonged to an early human relative, which he named Australopithecus africanus. It had the opposite combination to Piltdown: a small, apelike brain but humanlike teeth and signs of upright posture. Many leading experts dismissed it, partly because it clashed with Piltdown's big-brain-first story. It took more than two decades, and many further fossil discoveries in Africa, before Dart's view was widely accepted. We now know that upright walking came long before large brains.

sections.key: New dating methods and careful examination proved the bones were a recent fake, probably by Dawson.
sections.b: As genuine fossils emerged, Piltdown looked out of place. In 1949 Kenneth Oakley applied a new fluorine test, which helps estimate how long bones have been buried. The Piltdown bones contained surprisingly little fluorine, suggesting they were far younger than claimed. In 1953 Oakley, with Joseph Weiner and Wilfrid Le Gros Clark, announced the truth. The jaw came from an orangutan, its teeth filed down to look humanlike. The skull belonged to a modern human who had lived only centuries earlier. The bones had been stained to look ancient. For decades people argued over who did it, with suspects including Woodward and even Arthur Conan Doyle. A 2016 study using DNA analysis and CT scanning pointed to a single forger, and Dawson was by far the most likely.

sections.key: Be most careful with evidence that tells you exactly what you hoped to hear.
sections.b: Piltdown wasn't exposed because science is infallible; it was exposed because science keeps testing. Better methods and new evidence eventually revealed what expectation had hidden. But the story offers lessons well beyond fossils. Be extra careful with evidence that confirms exactly what you, your team or your country hoped to find. Ask whether anyone has examined the original data, rather than a summary or a copy. Notice when crucial pieces of evidence are conveniently missing. And remember that the anomaly that doesn't fit, like the Taung Child, may turn out to be the real discovery. When an idea seems to explain everything you expected, that's a moment to look harder, not to relax.

quiz.q: What did Woodward's reconstruction of Piltdown Man show?
o: A small brain with a humanlike jaw
A large, humanlike braincase with an apelike jaw
A complete skeleton walking upright
A skull identical to a Neanderthal
quiz.e: This big-brain, ape-jaw combination looked like a missing link.

quiz.q: Why were most researchers unable to spot the forgery early on?

Most only saw plaster casts, not the originals
The bones were locked in a foreign museum
No-one was allowed to publish about them
quiz.e: Casts hid tool marks and staining, and the missing joint and chin hid the mismatch.

quiz.q: What was Raymond Dart's Taung Child?
o: Another forgery by the same hoaxer
A Neanderthal skull from South Africa
A real early human relative, long dismissed
An orangutan skull with filed teeth
quiz.e: Its small brain and humanlike teeth clashed with Piltdown's story, so a real ancestor was sidelined.

LESSONS.push: For 40 years a fossil fooled experts. What they wanted to believe was the real trap.

LESSONS.title: The lady tasting tea: how to design a fair test
LESSONS.hook: A scientist claimed she could taste whether the milk or the tea went into the cup first. Working out how to test her claim properly helped shape the modern experiment.

sections.key: A casual claim at afternoon tea led Ronald Fisher to ask how to test any claim fairly.
sections.b:
In the early 1920s, at the Rothamsted agricultural research station north of London, the statistician Ronald Fisher offered a colleague a cup of tea. Dr Muriel Bristol, a scientist who studied algae, declined because he had poured the milk in after the tea. She preferred milk first, and insisted she could taste the difference.

Fisher was sceptical. According to later accounts from people who were there, a test was quickly arranged, and she reportedly identified the cups correctly. Fisher used the story to open a chapter of his 1935 book The Design of Experiments. Behind a light-hearted example lay a serious question: how do you fairly test a claim?

sections.key: A fair test starts by assuming pure guessing, the null hypothesis, and working out how often guessing would succeed.
sections.b:
Fisher's key move was to assume the claim is false. Suppose Bristol has no ability and is simply guessing. This assumption is now called the null hypothesis. Then ask whether her actual performance would be surprising by comparison.

His design used eight cups, four milk-first and four tea-first, in random order. She would pick out the four milk-first cups. There are 70 ways to choose four cups from eight, and only one is fully correct. A guesser has a 1 in 70 chance of a perfect score, about 1.4 per cent. Three right and one wrong can happen 16 ways, so scoring at least three out of four by luck is 17 in 70, about 24 per cent. That's too common to prove anything. Decide what counts as convincing before you run the test.

sections.key: Random order stops hidden patterns or clues from being mistaken for skill.
sections.b:
Why serve the cups in random order? Imagine the four milk-first cups were all prepared and served first. They might be slightly cooler, or the taster might notice a pattern. Any success could then come from those clues rather than from tasting the milk.

Fisher argued that randomisation is the most reliable protection against hidden factors like these, including ones nobody has thought of. He also stressed keeping everything else the same: the same cups, the same tea and the same amount of milk. He developed these ideas through crop experiments at Rothamsted, where treatments were assigned to plots of land at random so that differences in soil couldn't bias the results.

sections.key: A test that is too small can never give convincing evidence, however genuine the skill.
sections.b:
Fisher's framework also shows why the number of trials matters. With six cups, three of each, there are only 20 ways to choose, so even a perfect score has a 1 in 20 chance of happening by luck, or five per cent. With just four cups, two of each, a guesser gets a perfect score one time in six. A test that small could never convince anyone, however good the taster.

Fisher suggested treating results that would happen by chance less than about one time in 20 as worth taking seriously. That convention later hardened into the famous 0.05 threshold for statistical significance. He saw it as a rough guide to which results deserve attention, not a magic line between truth and falsehood.

sections.key: Fisher's principles underpin modern trials and A/B tests, but a good method doesn't cure wishful thinking.
sections.b:
Fisher's ideas now run through modern research. Drug trials assign patients to treatment or placebo at random and ask how likely the results would be if the drug did nothing. Farmers test crop varieties in randomised plots. Technology companies run A/B tests, randomly showing different web page versions to different users. Three questions travel well. What would I expect to see if this claim were false? Could something else explain the result? Was the test big enough to tell?

Yet Fisher himself erred. In the late 1950s he argued that the smoking and lung cancer link might not be causal, suggesting an inherited factor could explain both. Asking about hidden causes is legitimate, but the evidence against smoking became overwhelming. Fisher was a keen pipe smoker and had consulted for the tobacco industry.

quiz.q: What question did the tea story lead Fisher to explore?
o: How to fairly test whether a claim is true
How to brew tea consistently
Whether milk affects the taste of algae
How to measure a taster's experience
quiz.e: The light-hearted example opened a serious inquiry into how to test any claim fairly.

quiz.q: What is the null hypothesis in the tea test?
o: That she can always tell the difference
That milk-first tea tastes better
That she has no ability and is simply guessing
That the cups were poured incorrectly
quiz.e: A fair test starts by assuming guessing, then asks whether the result would be surprising under that assumption.

quiz.q: Why should the cups be served in random order?
o: To make the test quicker to run
So hidden patterns can't pass for skill
To reduce the number of cups needed
So the taster drinks less tea overall
quiz.e: Randomisation protects against hidden factors, including ones nobody has thought of.

quiz.q: Why would a test with only four cups, two of each, be unconvincing?
o: The tea would go cold before the end
Small tests always favour the poorest taster
A guesser gets a perfect score one time in six
Fisher's method only works with eight cups
quiz.e: When luck alone succeeds this often, even a perfect score proves nothing, so test size matters.

quiz.q: What does Fisher's smoking argument show?
o: Randomised trials are generally unreliable
Smoking was never linked to lung cancer
Statisticians can't ask about hidden causes
Good methods don't cure wishful thinking
quiz.e: Even the method's inventor let what he wanted to be true colour his judgement.

LESSONS.push: She said she could taste which went in first. How do you test that fairly?
