The business claimed the unpaid invoice as a tax write-off.
WORDS.origin: From write off, meaning to cancel a debt in an accounting ledger.
WORDS.blank: The insurer ruled the flooded car a total ___.

WORDS.def: Illegal, dishonest or immoral behaviour.
ex: The audit found no evidence of wrongdoing by staff.
He denied any wrongdoing throughout the trial.
WORDS.origin: From wrong and doing, Old English.
WORDS.blank: The company was cleared of any ___ after the investigation.

WORDS.def: Unjust, unlawful or contrary to what is fair or right.
ex: She sued the company for wrongful dismissal.
The report examined dozens of wrongful convictions over the decade.
WORDS.origin: From wrong and the suffix -ful.
WORDS.blank: He was awarded compensation after a ___ arrest.

WORDS.def: Showing dry, ironic humour, often through a slight, knowing expression.
ex: He gave a wry smile when asked if the plan had worked.
Her wry commentary made even the boring meetings bearable.
WORDS.origin: From Old English wrigian, 'to turn, twist'.
WORDS.blank: She offered a ___ comment about the traffic before hanging up.

WORDS.def: A fear, dislike or distrust of people from other countries or cultures.
ex: The historian traced how xenophobia rose during past economic downturns.
The campaign aimed to counter xenophobia with community events.
WORDS.origin: From Greek xenos, 'stranger, foreigner', and phobos, 'fear'.
WORDS.blank: Sociologists study how ___ can spike during periods of uncertainty.

WORDS.def: A plant adapted to live and thrive in a very dry environment with little water.
ex: Cacti are classic xerophytes, storing water in their thick stems.
The botanist's garden was full of xerophytes suited to the dry climate.
WORDS.origin: From Greek xeros, 'dry', and phyton, 'plant'.
WORDS.blank: Spinifex is a native ___ that copes well with the outback's dry heat.

WORDS.def: A standard or measure used to judge or compare the quality or level of something.
ex: Exam results are often used as a yardstick for school performance.
Customer satisfaction is the main yardstick the company uses to judge success.
WORDS.origin: Originally a literal stick, one yard long, used for measuring.
WORDS.blank: Profit alone shouldn't be the only ___ for judging a company's success.

WORDS.def: To have an intense feeling of longing for something or someone.
ex: After months overseas, she yearned for a good flat white.
He yearned to see his grandchildren again before the year was out.
WORDS.origin: From Old English giernan, 'to desire'.
WORDS.blank: After years in the city, he would often ___ for the quiet of the farm.

WORDS.def: The amount of profit or return produced by an investment, or, as a verb, to produce a result or to give way.
ex: The term deposit offers a decent yield compared to a regular savings account.
The talks finally began to yield results after weeks of stalemate.
WORDS.origin: From Old English gieldan, 'to pay, repay'.
WORDS.blank: Investors were disappointed by the fund's low ___ last quarter.

WORDS.def: A wooden frame used to join two draught animals for pulling, or, figuratively, something that binds or burdens a person.
ex: The bullocks were fitted with a wooden yoke to pull the cart.
She finally felt free of the yoke of her old job.
WORDS.origin: From Old English geoc, related to Latin iugum.
WORDS.blank: The colony eventually threw off the ___ of foreign rule.

WORDS.def: Occurring every day; ordinary and commonplace to the point of dullness.
ex: She found poetry in the quotidian rhythm of the 7:42 train into Flinders Street.
The novel lingers on quotidian details: burnt toast, school lunches, the bins on a Tuesday night.
WORDS.origin: From Latin quotidianus, from quotidie 'every day' (quot 'how many' + dies 'day').
WORDS.blank: After a month of travel, he was oddly glad to return to the ___ routine of commuting, cooking and sleeping.

WORDS.def: Showing a casual, carefree lack of concern, especially where worry would be expected.
ex: He strolled into the exam ten minutes late with an insouciant grin.
Her insouciant shrug suggested the parking fine was the least of her worries.
WORDS.origin: From French, in- 'not' + soucier 'to worry, care', from Latin sollicitare 'to disturb'.
WORDS.blank: Despite the storm warnings, the surfer remained ___, waxing his board as the sky turned black.

WORDS.def: A manuscript page scraped or washed and written over, with traces of the earlier text still visible; by extension, anything bearing layers of its own history.
ex: Multispectral imaging revealed lost works of Archimedes hidden beneath the prayers of a medieval palimpsest.
The old terrace in Fitzroy is a palimpsest of painted signs, each fading through the next.
WORDS.origin: Via Latin from Greek palimpsestos 'scraped again', from palin 'again' + psen 'to rub smooth'.
WORDS.blank: Under ultraviolet light the parchment proved to be a ___, with an older Greek text beneath the Latin.

WORDS.def: Having a strong spiritual or religious quality; suggesting the presence of something divine or awe-inspiring.
ex: At dawn, Uluru glowing red felt almost numinous to the silent crowd.
The cathedral's vast, dim nave produced a numinous hush.
WORDS.origin: From Latin numen, numinis 'divine power, nod of the gods'; popularised by Rudolf Otto's Das Heilige (1917), published in English as The Idea of the Holy.
WORDS.blank: Standing alone among the ancient redwoods, she felt a ___ sense of being in the presence of something holy.

WORDS.def: Impossible to escape or avoid, however hard one struggles.
ex: Rising sea levels are an ineluctable concern for low-lying Pacific nations.
The tragedy moves with ineluctable logic towards its final scene.
WORDS.origin: From Latin ineluctabilis, from in- 'not' + eluctari 'to struggle out of'.
WORDS.blank: Ageing is ___: no diet, cream or surgery can hold it off forever.

WORDS.def: An unfilled space or gap, especially a missing section in a manuscript, argument or body of knowledge.
ex: The thesis fills a lacuna in research on early colonial Tasmania.
A water-damaged lacuna in the diary leaves three crucial days unexplained.
WORDS.origin: From Latin lacuna 'pool, pit, gap', from lacus 'lake'.
WORDS.blank: Scholars have long puzzled over the ___ in the poem, where an entire stanza was torn from the page.

WORDS.def: Deliberately faithless and treacherous; betraying trust.
ex: The perfidious adviser sold the campaign's strategy to the rival party.
'Perfidious Albion' was a long-standing French jibe at supposed English treachery.
WORDS.origin: From Latin perfidiosus, from perfidia 'treachery', from per- 'away from' + fides 'faith'.
WORDS.blank: The ___ ally signed the treaty in the morning and invaded by nightfall.

WORDS.def: The appearance of being true or real, especially in fiction or art.
ex: The film's verisimilitude owes much to shooting on location in outback Queensland.
Small, precise details lend a story verisimilitude.
WORDS.origin: From Latin verisimilitudo, from verisimilis 'probable', literally 'like the truth' (verum 'true' + similis 'like').
WORDS.blank: The novelist interviewed retired detectives to give her crime scenes greater ___.

WORDS.def: Deliberately inoffensive and bland, so as to avoid provoking any reaction; (originally) relieving pain.
ex: The press release was a page of anodyne corporate phrases that said nothing at all.
He gave an anodyne answer about 'learning from the process'.
WORDS.origin: Via Latin from Greek anodunos 'painless', from an- 'without' + odune 'pain'.
WORDS.blank: Fearing a backlash, the minister replaced her fiery speech with a few ___ remarks about working together.

WORDS.def: Denoting a past period remembered as idyllically happy and peaceful.
ex: He spoke wistfully of the halcyon summers of his youth on the Mornington Peninsula.
Those were the halcyon days before mortgages and deadlines.
WORDS.origin: From Greek alkuon 'kingfisher'; in legend the bird calmed the sea to nest on it around the winter solstice, the 'halcyon days'.
WORDS.blank: Grandma still talks about the ___ days of the 1960s, when the whole street left their doors unlocked.

WORDS.def: (Especially of fabric) so light, delicate and fine that it is almost transparent.
ex: A diaphanous curtain stirred in the sea breeze.
The dragonfly's diaphanous wings caught the afternoon light.
WORDS.origin: From medieval Latin diaphanus, from Greek diaphanes 'see-through', from dia 'through' + phainein 'to show'.
WORDS.blank: The bride wore a ___ veil of silk so fine you could read print through it.

WORDS.def: Vanishing gradually from sight or memory; fading away almost as soon as it appears.
ex: The evanescent glow of the aurora australis faded before she could find her camera.
Fame on social media is evanescent.
WORDS.origin: From Latin evanescere 'to disappear', from e- 'out' + vanescere 'to vanish' (vanus 'empty').
WORDS.blank: The scent of the jasmine was ___, gone the moment the wind changed.

WORDS.def: A person who is self-indulgently devoted to luxury and sensual pleasure.
ex: A true sybarite, he booked the spa, the degustation and the penthouse in a single weekend.
The resort markets itself to sybarites who never want to lift a finger.
WORDS.origin: From Sybaris, an ancient Greek city in southern Italy whose citizens were famed for their luxury.
WORDS.blank: Only a committed ___ would insist on silk sheets and champagne while camping.

WORDS.def: Travelling from place to place, especially working or living in a series of locations for short periods.
ex: As a peripatetic music teacher, she visits six schools across the Riverina each week.
His peripatetic childhood, following his father's mining jobs, meant nine schools in ten years.
WORDS.origin: From Greek peripatetikos, from peripatein 'to walk up and down'; applied to Aristotle's school, which taught in a covered walkway of the Lyceum.
WORDS.blank: The ___ surgeon flew between remote clinics in the Kimberley, never staying more than a week.

WORDS.def: A person who confidently gives opinions on matters beyond their knowledge or expertise.
ex: The comment section was full of ultracrepidarians explaining virology to virologists.
A celebrity turned ultracrepidarian, he now lectures economists on monetary policy.
WORDS.origin: From Latin ultra crepidam 'beyond the sandal', from Pliny's story of the painter Apelles telling a cobbler who criticised more than a sandal to stick to his trade; used by William Hazlitt in 1819.
WORDS.blank: The footballer was an ___, offering his views on quantum physics and climate science with equal confidence.

WORDS.def: A state of disuse, especially of a law or custom that is no longer observed or enforced.
ex: The old statute against Sunday trading had long fallen into desuetude.
The tradition of formal calling cards has passed into desuetude.
WORDS.origin: From Latin desuetudo, from desuescere 'to become unaccustomed', from de- 'away' + suescere 'to grow used to'.
WORDS.blank: No one had been prosecuted under the archaic law for a century, and judges agreed it had fallen into ___.

WORDS.def: The legal right to use and enjoy the income or produce of another's property, without owning it and without damaging or diminishing its substance.
ex: Under the will, she held a usufruct of the farm for life, after which it passed to her nephews.
The usufruct let him keep the rents from the building but not sell it.
WORDS.origin: From Latin usufructus, from usus et fructus 'use and enjoyment (of the fruits)'.
WORDS.blank: He could harvest the orchard's apples under his ___, but he could not fell the trees or sell the land.

WORDS.def: A paid position that requires little or no work but brings status or income.
ex: Critics called the ambassadorship a sinecure for retired politicians.
His board seat was a sinecure: four meetings a year and a generous fee.
WORDS.origin: From Latin sine cura 'without care', originally a church benefice without the 'cure' (care) of souls.
WORDS.blank: The so-called advisory role was a ___, paying a full salary for one lunch a month.

WORDS.def: (Of speech or writing) using too many words and therefore tediously long.
ex: The judge criticised the prolix submissions, which ran to four hundred pages.
Her early drafts were prolix, but the editor cut them to the bone.
WORDS.origin: From Latin prolixus 'poured forth, extended', from pro- 'forward' + liquere 'to be liquid'.
WORDS.blank: The report was so ___ that its key finding was buried on page ninety.

WORDS.def: A state of serene calm and freedom from mental disturbance, prized as the goal of life by Epicureans and Sceptics.
ex: Epicurus taught that ataraxia comes from limiting desires and banishing fear of the gods.
After a week offline in the Daintree, he felt something close to ataraxia.
WORDS.origin: From Greek ataraxia 'impassiveness', from a- 'not' + tarassein 'to disturb'.
WORDS.blank: The Epicureans sought ___, an untroubled calm of mind, rather than wild pleasure.

WORDS.def: A person or thing that is the centre of attention or admiration.
ex: The young Matilda was the cynosure of every scout at the national championships.
Her gold gown made her the cynosure of the Logies red carpet.
WORDS.origin: Via Latin from Greek kunosoura 'dog's tail', the name for the constellation Ursa Minor, which contains the Pole Star used for guidance.
WORDS.blank: The moment the champion walked in, she became the ___ of the room, every eye turning to her.

WORDS.def: A confused, jumbled mixture of things, often used scornfully of ideas or claims.
ex: The defence's story was a farrago of half-truths and invented alibis.
The website was a farrago of conspiracy theories and miracle cures.
WORDS.origin: From Latin farrago 'mixed fodder for cattle', from far 'spelt, grain'.
WORDS.blank: The so-called evidence was a ___ of rumours, misquotes and outright fabrications.

WORDS.def: Only just begun and so not yet fully formed or developed; rudimentary.
ex: The policy was still inchoate, a few bullet points on a whiteboard.
Her inchoate fears took shape only when the letter arrived.
WORDS.origin: From Latin inchoatus, past participle of incohare 'to begin'.
WORDS.blank: At this stage the plan is ___, more a vague ambition than a strategy.

WORDS.def: Serving no practical purpose or result; superfluous.
ex: Once the new law passed, the old clause became otiose.
The editor struck out every otiose adjective.
WORDS.origin: From Latin otiosus 'at leisure, unemployed', from otium 'leisure'.
WORDS.blank: With automatic backups in place, the nightly manual copy is now ___ and can be dropped.

WORDS.def: Written or said to promote a particular point of view, especially a controversial one, rather than to present the facts fairly.
ex: The documentary's tendentious editing left out every inconvenient interview.
Reviewers dismissed the history as tendentious, more pamphlet than scholarship.
WORDS.origin: Early 20th century, from 'tendency' modelled on German tendenziös; ultimately from Latin tendere 'to stretch, aim'.
WORDS.blank: The so-called independent review was ___, written to justify a decision already made.

WORDS.def: The near-straight-line alignment of three celestial bodies, such as the Sun, Earth and Moon at new or full moon.
ex: Spring tides occur at syzygy, when the pulls of the Sun and Moon combine.
A total solar eclipse is a particularly precise syzygy.
WORDS.origin: Via late Latin from Greek suzugia 'a yoking together', from suzugos 'yoked'.
WORDS.blank: Eclipses can happen only at ___, when the Sun, Earth and Moon fall into line.

WORDS.def: The moment in a drama when a character makes a critical discovery or recognises the truth of their situation.
ex: Oedipus's anagnorisis, realising he has killed his father, is the model Aristotle admired.
The film's anagnorisis comes when the detective sees her own handwriting on the note.
WORDS.origin: From Greek anagnorisis 'recognition', from anagnorizein 'to recognise'; analysed in Aristotle's Poetics.
WORDS.blank: In Aristotle's terms, the play's ___ comes when the king finally recognises the beggar as his lost son.

WORDS.def: Showing steady, careful and persevering diligence.
ex: Years of sedulous practice turned a shy student into a concert pianist.
The archivist's sedulous cataloguing saved the collection from chaos.
WORDS.origin: From Latin sedulus 'zealous, careful', perhaps from se dolo 'without guile'.
WORDS.blank: Thanks to her ___ attention to every receipt, the audit found nothing amiss.

WORDS.def: Unattractive and objectionable; off-putting and repellent.
ex: His rebarbative manner alienated even his allies.
The brutalist car park was condemned as rebarbative.
WORDS.origin: From French rebarbatif, from se rebarber 'to face each other beard to beard', from barbe 'beard'.
WORDS.blank: Critics found the building ___: a grim slab of raw concrete that seemed designed to repel visitors.

WORDS.def: A salary, fee or other payment received from employment or holding an office.
ex: The directors' emoluments are disclosed in the annual report.
Judges' emoluments are set by an independent tribunal.
WORDS.origin: From Latin emolumentum, probably originally 'payment to a miller for grinding corn', from emolere 'to grind out'.
WORDS.blank: The annual report lists each director's ___, including salary, bonus and superannuation.

WORDS.def: Relating to or consisting of money.
ex: Members of parliament must declare any pecuniary interest in matters they vote on.
The penalty was purely pecuniary: a fine, with no jail time.
WORDS.origin: From Latin pecuniarius, from pecunia 'money', from pecu 'cattle', the earliest form of wealth.
WORDS.blank: Councillors with a ___ interest in the development, such as shares in the builder, had to leave the room.

WORDS.def: The misappropriation of money by a person entrusted with looking after it, such as a trustee or treasurer.
ex: The club treasurer's defalcation came to light during the annual audit.
The trustee was removed after a defalcation that drained the family fund.
WORDS.origin: From medieval Latin defalcare 'to lop off', from falx, falcis 'sickle'.
WORDS.blank: The trustee's ___ left the estate $2 million short when the beneficiaries finally checked the accounts.

WORDS.def: A literary or artistic assistant, especially one who writes from dictation or copies manuscripts.
ex: Blind by then, Milton dictated Paradise Lost to a series of amanuenses.
She served as the composer's amanuensis, writing out the scores he sang to her.
WORDS.origin: From Latin (servus) a manu 'slave at hand(writing)' + -ensis 'belonging to'.
WORDS.blank: Unable to hold a pen after the stroke, the novelist dictated her final book to an ___.

WORDS.def: A self-taught person, especially one who has mastered a subject without formal instruction.
ex: An autodidact, he learned Mandarin from library books and podcasts.
Ramanujan was largely an autodidact before he wrote to Hardy.
WORDS.origin: From Greek autodidaktos 'self-taught', from autos 'self' + didaskein 'to teach'.
WORDS.blank: Never having attended university, the brilliant ___ taught herself calculus from secondhand textbooks.

WORDS.def: Having the iridescent, shimmering lustre of mother-of-pearl.
ex: The inside of the abalone shell was smooth and nacreous.
Nacreous clouds glow in pastel colours high in the polar stratosphere after sunset.
WORDS.origin: From nacre 'mother-of-pearl', via French from Italian naccaro, probably of Arabic origin.
WORDS.blank: Polar stratospheric clouds are also called ___ clouds for their shimmering mother-of-pearl colours.

WORDS.def: Stubbornly or wilfully disobedient to authority, especially to the orders of a court.
ex: The judge found the witness contumacious for refusing three times to answer.
A contumacious refusal to pay the fine led to a warrant.
WORDS.origin: From Latin contumax, contumacis 'stubborn, insolent'.
WORDS.blank: Having ignored three court orders to produce the documents, the director was held in contempt for ___ conduct.

questions.q: What is the only positive whole number that is exactly twice the sum of its digits?
Which war did the Peace of Westphalia (1648) bring to an end?
o: The Hundred Years' War
The Thirty Years' War
The Wars of the Roses
The Seven Years' War
questions.e: It also helped establish the modern idea of sovereign states.

questions.q: What does the Chandrasekhar limit describe?
o: The maximum mass of a stable white dwarf
The speed at which galaxies recede
The size of the observable universe
The minimum mass of a planet
questions.e: The limit is about 1.4 solar masses. Above it, a white dwarf can't support itself against gravity.

questions.q: Which language family does Finnish belong to?
o: Indo-European
Uralic
Turkic
Germanic
questions.e: It is related to Estonian and Hungarian, unlike most European languages.

questions.q: Fermat's Last Theorem resisted proof for over 350 years until 1994. What does it claim?
o: Every even number above 2 is the sum of two primes
aⁿ + bⁿ = cⁿ has no positive integer solutions for n > 2
There are infinitely many pairs of twin primes
Every whole number has exactly one prime factorisation
questions.e: Andrew Wiles announced a proof in 1993 and completed it in 1994.

questions.q: What do Gödel's incompleteness theorems show?
o: Every true statement can be proved
Some true statements cannot be proved
Mathematics is inconsistent
Infinity doesn't exist
questions.e: This holds for any consistent system capable of basic arithmetic. Published by Kurt Gödel in 1931.

questions.q: Which enzyme unwinds the DNA double helix during replication?
o: Ligase
Helicase
Polymerase
Amylase
questions.e: Polymerase builds the new strands; ligase joins fragments.

questions.q: In 1952 Michael Ventris deciphered the Linear B script. What language did it turn out to record?
o: Egyptian
An early form of Greek
Latin
Phoenician
questions.e: The clay tablets were Mycenaean palace records, written centuries before Homer.

questions.q: What does Gresham's law state?
o: Prices rise with demand
Bad money drives out good
Taxes reduce spending
Trade benefits both sides
questions.e: People hoard more valuable coins and spend debased ones.

questions.q: What are telomeres?
o: Enzymes that copy DNA
Protective caps on chromosome ends
Pores in the cell membrane
Proteins that fold RNA
questions.e: They shorten as cells divide. Hobart-born Elizabeth Blackburn shared the 2009 Nobel Prize in Medicine for discovering how they are protected.

questions.q: What is a Lagrange point?
o: The point where a black hole's gravity is strongest
A point where gravity and orbit balance for a small object
The lowest point of an orbit around a planet
The outer boundary of the solar system
questions.e: Every pair, such as the Sun and Earth, has five. Space telescopes are often parked near them.

questions.q: Why did the 1913 Paris premiere of Stravinsky's The Rite of Spring cause a near-riot?
o: Its jarring music and choreography shocked the audience
The orchestra stopped playing partway through
The performance was staged without any music
Its libretto was considered politically offensive
questions.e: The dissonant score and unconventional choreography were unlike anything the audience expected.

questions.q: Which metal has the highest melting point?
o: Iron
Titanium
Tungsten
Platinum
questions.e: About 3,422°C, which is why it is used in rocket nozzles and was used for light-bulb filaments.

questions.q: What is a 'hapax legomenon'?
o: A type of Greek poem
A word that occurs only once in a text
A binding legal precedent
An unproven mathematical claim
questions.e: They can make ancient words very hard to translate.

questions.q: Which of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World stood at Alexandria?
o: The Colossus
The Lighthouse (Pharos)
The Hanging Gardens
The Mausoleum
questions.e: It stood over 100 metres tall by some estimates.

questions.q: What is the most abundant protein in the human body?
o: Keratin
Collagen
Haemoglobin
Insulin
questions.e: It's a major component of skin, bone, tendons and ligaments.

questions.q: Which moon of Saturn has a thick nitrogen-rich atmosphere and liquid methane lakes?
o: Europa
Titan
Enceladus
Io
questions.e: Europa and Io orbit Jupiter.

questions.q: In what year was the Treaty of Waitangi signed in New Zealand?
questions.e: Between the British Crown and many Māori chiefs.

questions.q: Who painted The Garden of Earthly Delights?
o: Pieter Bruegel
Hieronymus Bosch
Jan van Eyck
Albrecht Dürer
questions.e: A strange, crowded triptych from around 1500.

questions.q: Which mineral sits at 1, the softest, on the Mohs hardness scale?
o: Gypsum
Talc
Calcite
Quartz
questions.e: Diamond sits at 10.

questions.q: What does the Drake equation estimate?
o: The age of the universe
The number of alien civilisations in our galaxy
The mass of a black hole
The speed of continental drift
questions.e: Frank Drake wrote it in 1961. Most of its factors, like how often life arises, are still unknown.

questions.q: Which philosopher wrote the Critique of Pure Reason (1781)?
o: Hegel
Immanuel Kant
David Hume
Descartes
questions.e: Kant was 'awakened from his dogmatic slumber' by Hume.

questions.q: In economics, what is a 'Giffen good'?
o: A good whose price is fixed by law
A good whose demand rises as its price rises
A good that is free for everyone to use
A good that is traded across borders
questions.e: A rare exception to the usual law of demand.

questions.q: Leonhard Euler's 1736 solution to the Seven Bridges of Königsberg problem founded which branch of maths?
o: Calculus
Graph theory
Probability
Number theory
questions.e: He proved no walk could cross each of the city's seven bridges exactly once, by reducing the map to points and lines.

questions.q: Which is the only sea with no coastline?
o: The Sargasso Sea
The Coral Sea
The Caspian Sea
The Tasman Sea
questions.e: It lies in the North Atlantic, bounded by ocean currents rather than land, and is named after its floating Sargassum seaweed.

questions.q: What does the Latin legal phrase 'habeas corpus' literally mean?
o: Let the buyer beware
You shall have the body
In good faith
The thing speaks for itself
questions.e: It protects against unlawful detention.

questions.q: The Hanseatic League, a powerful medieval trading network, was centred on which sea?
o: The Mediterranean
The Baltic
The Black Sea
The Caspian
questions.e: Merchant towns such as Lübeck, Hamburg and Riga dominated northern European trade from the 1200s to the 1400s.

questions.q: What is the smallest prime number greater than 100?
questions.e: 101 has no divisors other than 1 and itself.

questions.q: Which physicist's 1928 equation, combining quantum mechanics and relativity, led him to predict antimatter?
o: Paul Dirac
Enrico Fermi
Richard Feynman
Niels Bohr
questions.e: The positron, the electron's antimatter twin, was found by Carl Anderson in 1932.

questions.q: The Voynich manuscript is famous for what?
o: Being the oldest printed book
Being written in an undeciphered script
Containing da Vinci's secret notes
Being the first English dictionary
questions.e: Its vellum dates to the early 1400s. The strange text and drawings of unknown plants still baffle cryptographers.

questions.q: How many prime numbers are there below 100?
questions.e: There are 168 primes below 1,000, and they thin out steadily as numbers grow.

questions.q: What is special about 1729, the 'taxicab number'?
o: It is the first number whose digits sum to a perfect cube
It is the largest perfect number below 10,000
It is the smallest number divisible by every number from 1 to 12
It is the smallest sum of two positive cubes in two different ways
questions.e: 1729 = 1³ + 12³ = 9³ + 10³, as Ramanujan pointed out when G. H. Hardy arrived in taxi number 1729.

questions.q: What is the Riemann hypothesis about?
o: Where the non-trivial zeros of the zeta function lie
How many dimensions a sphere can be smoothly bent into
Whether there are infinitely many twin primes
Whether every even number above 2 is the sum of two primes
questions.e: Posed in 1859, it would pin down how the primes are distributed, and it is one of the Clay Millennium Prize problems.

questions.q: Why was the proof of the four colour theorem (1976) a landmark?
o: It was proved wrong after being accepted for a century
It was the first major proof to depend on a computer check
It showed that three colours are enough for any map
It was the first proof co-authored by two mathematicians
questions.e: Kenneth Appel and Wolfgang Haken had a computer check almost 2,000 configurations, which sparked debate about what counts as a proof.

questions.q: How many regular convex polyhedra (Platonic solids) exist?
o: Infinitely many
questions.e: Tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron and icosahedron: Euclid's Elements ends by proving there can be no others.

questions.q: Does the harmonic series 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/4 + ... add up to a finite number?
o: Yes, about 2.718
Yes, exactly 2
Yes, exactly pi squared over 6
No, it grows without limit
questions.e: It grows incredibly slowly: the first million terms add up to only about 14.4.

questions.q: Which book, written in 1202, helped bring Hindu-Arabic numerals into use in Europe?
o: Fibonacci's Liber Abaci
Euclid's Elements
Newton's Principia
Al-Khwarizmi's Algebra
questions.e: It also contains the rabbit-breeding puzzle that gives us the Fibonacci sequence.

questions.q: What does Emmy Noether's theorem (1918) connect?
o: Symmetries in nature with conservation laws
Temperature with entropy
Electricity with magnetism
Mass with energy
questions.e: For example, the laws of physics not changing over time is exactly why energy is conserved.

questions.q: Since 1983, how has the metre been defined?
o: By a platinum-iridium bar kept near Paris
By the distance light travels in a vacuum in 1/299,792,458 of a second
As one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator
By a wavelength of light from krypton-86
questions.e: Fixing the speed of light as an exact number made the metre depend on the second.

questions.q: What is Cherenkov radiation?
o: Light emitted by a charged particle outpacing light in a medium
Heat radiated from the edge of black holes
Radio waves produced by lightning strikes
X-rays emitted when fast electrons slow down
questions.e: It causes the eerie blue glow in the water around nuclear reactor cores.

questions.q: What does the Pauli exclusion principle state?
o: You cannot know a particle's position and momentum exactly at once
Every action has an equal and opposite reaction
Energy can be neither created nor destroyed
No two identical fermions can occupy the same quantum state at once
questions.e: It forces electrons into successive shells, which gives the periodic table its structure and keeps matter from collapsing.

questions.q: What is the SI unit of magnetic flux density?
o: The weber
The tesla
The henry
The gauss
questions.e: The gauss is the older CGS unit: 1 tesla equals 10,000 gauss, and an MRI scanner typically runs at 1.5 to 3 tesla.

questions.q: What did the Michelson-Morley experiment of 1887 famously fail to detect?
o: The electron
Gravitational waves
Earth's motion through the 'luminiferous aether'
The bending of starlight by the Sun
questions.e: Its null result was later explained by special relativity: light's speed is the same for every observer.

questions.q: Albert Einstein received the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics chiefly for what?
o: The equation E = mc²
General relativity
Special relativity
His explanation of the photoelectric effect
questions.e: The 1921 prize was formally awarded in 1922. His work showed light comes in discrete packets, a foundation of quantum theory.

questions.q: Which element has the highest electronegativity?
o: Oxygen
Fluorine
Chlorine
Helium
questions.e: On the Pauling scale fluorine scores about 3.98, which is why it reacts with almost everything.

questions.q: Mendeleev predicted the properties of 'eka-silicon' before it was discovered. What is it called today?
o: Gallium
Selenium
Germanium
Tin
questions.e: Clemens Winkler found it in 1886, and its measured properties closely matched Mendeleev's forecast.

questions.q: What does it mean for a molecule to be 'chiral'?
o: It conducts electricity when dissolved
It cannot be superimposed on its mirror image
It contains a ring of six carbon atoms
It has no overall electric charge
questions.e: The word comes from the Greek for hand, since left and right hands are the classic example.

questions.q: What does the Haber-Bosch process manufacture?
o: Nitroglycerin
Steel
Ammonia
Sulfuric acid
questions.e: By fixing nitrogen from the air for fertiliser, it now helps feed a large share of the world's population.

questions.q: In 1807, Humphry Davy used electrolysis to isolate which two elements for the first time?
o: Calcium and magnesium
Potassium and sodium
Oxygen and hydrogen
Chlorine and fluorine
questions.e: He went on to isolate several more, including calcium and magnesium, the following year.

questions.q: Photo 51, the X-ray image that revealed DNA's helical shape, was made in whose lab?
o: Francis Crick's
Rosalind Franklin's
Linus Pauling's
Gregor Mendel's
questions.e: It was taken in 1952 by her PhD student Raymond Gosling, and Watson saw it without her knowledge.

questions.q: Which enzyme copies RNA into DNA, the trick used by retroviruses like HIV?
o: Reverse transcriptase
Helicase
DNA ligase
RNA polymerase
questions.e: It was discovered independently by Howard Temin and David Baltimore in 1970.

questions.q: What are Okazaki fragments?
o: Short stretches of DNA made on the lagging strand during replication
Fragments of cell membrane left after cell division
Tiny RNA molecules that silence genes
Pieces of broken chromosome that cause mutations
questions.e: DNA polymerase can only build in one direction, so one strand must be copied in pieces, later joined by DNA ligase.

questions.q: Where in a eukaryotic cell does the Krebs (citric acid) cycle take place?
o: The nucleus
The Golgi apparatus
The mitochondrial matrix
The cytoplasm
questions.e: Glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm, then its products move into mitochondria to be fully broken down.

questions.q: Genetically, fungi are more closely related to which group?
o: Plants
Animals
Algae
Bacteria
questions.e: Fungi and animals share a common ancestor, and fungal cell walls are made of chitin, like insect exoskeletons, not cellulose.

questions.q: In 1796, Edward Jenner showed he could protect against smallpox using material from which disease?
o: Rabies
Chickenpox
Cowpox
Measles
questions.e: The word vaccine comes from vacca, Latin for cow.

questions.q: In the 1840s, Ignaz Semmelweis sharply cut deaths from childbed fever in Vienna by introducing what?
o: Open windows in maternity wards
Ether anaesthesia
Boiling of surgical instruments
Handwashing between patients
questions.e: Many doctors rejected his idea, and it only won acceptance after germ theory arrived decades later.

questions.q: Which organ produces most of the hormone erythropoietin, which drives red blood cell production?
o: The liver
The thyroid
The spleen
The kidneys
questions.e: This is why people with serious kidney disease often develop anaemia.

questions.q: Howard Florey, who shared the 1945 Nobel Prize for turning penicillin into a usable drug, was born in which country?
o: Australia
Canada
New Zealand
Scotland
questions.e: Born in Adelaide in 1898, he shared the prize with Alexander Fleming and Ernst Chain.

questions.q: John Snow's 1854 study, which traced an outbreak to the Broad Street pump in London, concerned which disease?
o: Typhoid
Cholera
Bubonic plague
Smallpox
questions.e: He persuaded officials to remove the pump's handle, and his maps helped found modern epidemiology.

questions.q: Which Ottoman sultan captured Constantinople in 1453?
o: Mehmed II
Suleiman the Magnificent
Osman I
Selim I
questions.e: He was only 21, and he made the city his new capital.

questions.q: Which Carthaginian general crossed the Alps with war elephants in 218 BCE?
o: Hamilcar
Hasdrubal the Fair
Hannibal
Scipio
questions.e: It was an opening move of the Second Punic War, and he then won crushing victories in Italy, including Cannae.

questions.q: Which female pharaoh of Egypt's 18th Dynasty built the great temple at Deir el-Bahari?
o: Cleopatra VII
Ankhesenamun
Nefertiti
Hatshepsut
questions.e: She was often shown with a false beard, the traditional symbol of a pharaoh's authority.

questions.q: Who led the Haitian Revolution until his capture by the French in 1802?
o: Jean-Jacques Dessalines
Toussaint Louverture
Henri Christophe
Simón Bolívar
questions.e: He died in a French prison in 1803, the year before Haiti declared independence.

questions.q: The Congress of Vienna (1814-15) redrew the map of Europe after the defeat of whom?
o: Frederick the Great
Kaiser Wilhelm II
Louis XIV
Napoleon
questions.e: Its balance of power helped Europe avoid a general war for about a century.

questions.q: The Taiping Rebellion (1850-1864), one of the deadliest civil wars in history, was fought in which country?
o: India
Japan
China
Russia
questions.e: Its leader, Hong Xiuquan, claimed to be the younger brother of Jesus, and the war killed tens of millions.

questions.q: In which year was the last Western Roman emperor, Romulus Augustulus, deposed?
o: 527 CE
395 CE
476 CE
410 CE
questions.e: The Germanic general Odoacer deposed him, while the Eastern Roman Empire carried on for nearly another thousand years.

questions.q: The Treaty of Tordesillas (1494) divided newly claimed lands outside Europe between which two powers?
o: Spain and Portugal
Spain and England
England and France
Portugal and the Netherlands
questions.e: Its dividing line is the reason Brazil speaks Portuguese while most of Latin America speaks Spanish.

questions.q: Whose book Leviathan (1651) described life without government as 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short'?
o: John Locke
Jean-Jacques Rousseau
Thomas Hobbes
Niccolò Machiavelli
questions.e: He wrote it in exile in Paris during the upheaval of the English Civil War, arguing that people accept a strong ruler in exchange for security.

questions.q: In which language did the Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius write his Meditations?
o: Greek
Aramaic
Etruscan
Latin
questions.e: Greek was the language of philosophy for educated Romans, and he wrote the notes for himself, not for publication.

questions.q: Which philosopher, a follower of Jeremy Bentham, wrote the essay Utilitarianism?
o: John Stuart Mill
David Hume
Henry Sidgwick
Adam Smith
questions.e: Mill refined Bentham's idea by arguing some pleasures, like those of the intellect, are higher than others.

questions.q: Which school of philosophy did Zeno of Citium found in Athens around 300 BCE?
o: Epicureanism
Cynicism
Stoicism
Scepticism
questions.e: It is named after the Stoa Poikile, the painted porch where Zeno taught.

questions.q: Who wrote The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money (1936)?
o: John Maynard Keynes
Friedrich Hayek
Alfred Marshall
Milton Friedman
questions.e: It argued governments could spend to fight unemployment during a slump, reshaping economics after the Great Depression.

questions.q: In game theory, what is a Nash equilibrium?
o: The outcome that gives all players the greatest total reward
A situation where every player picks a strategy at random
A game in which one player's gain exactly equals another's loss
A set of strategies where no player gains by switching alone
questions.e: The prisoner's dilemma shows it can leave everyone worse off than if they had cooperated.

questions.q: When economists say demand for a product is 'price elastic', what do they mean?
o: The price can rise without any change in sales
Sales change by a larger proportion than price
Buyers switch products only when prices fall
Demand rises and falls with the seasons
questions.e: Luxuries and goods with close substitutes tend to be elastic, while essentials like petrol tend to be inelastic in the short run.

questions.q: What does 'quantitative easing' involve?
o: A country fixing its currency to the US dollar
A government cutting taxes to boost spending
A bank reducing its lending to control inflation
A central bank creating money to buy bonds
questions.e: It is used when interest rates are already near zero, and the Reserve Bank of Australia used it from 2020.

questions.q: The Great Vowel Shift, from about 1400 to 1700, changed the pronunciation of which language?
o: French
English
Spanish
German
questions.e: Spelling had largely settled before it finished, which is why English vowels rarely sound the way they are written.

questions.q: Which language of Spain and France is a 'language isolate', with no proven relatives?
o: Galician
Occitan
Basque
Catalan
questions.e: It is widely thought to predate the arrival of Indo-European languages in western Europe.

questions.q: In linguistics, what is a 'phoneme'?
o: A word borrowed from another language
The smallest sound that changes a word
A letter that is written but not spoken
The smallest unit of meaning in a word
questions.e: In English, /p/ and /b/ are separate phonemes because 'pat' and 'bat' mean different things.

questions.q: What does Grimm's law describe?
o: Why irregular verbs survive longest
Regular consonant shifts into Germanic languages
The order in which children learn speech sounds
How fairy tales spread between cultures
questions.e: It explains pairs like Latin pater and English father, where p shifted to f. Jacob Grimm, the fairy-tale collector, stated it in 1822.

questions.q: What is a 'creole' language?
o: A former pidgin now spoken as a first language
A language with no written form or grammar rules
A language invented by traders to hide meaning
A dialect that is spoken only inside large cities
questions.e: Kriol, spoken by many Aboriginal people across northern Australia, is an example.

questions.q: Who painted Las Meninas (1656)?
o: El Greco
Francisco Goya
Diego Velázquez
Bartolomé Murillo
questions.e: The painter included himself at his easel, and the king and queen appear only as a reflection in a mirror.

questions.q: What is true fresco (buon fresco)?
o: Painting outdoors straight from the natural landscape
Painting in oils on a stretched canvas surface
Painting in pigment on wet plaster that sets into the wall
Painting with egg-yolk paint on wooden panels
questions.e: Fresco is Italian for fresh, and Michelangelo painted the Sistine Chapel ceiling this way.

questions.q: Who sculpted The Ecstasy of Saint Teresa in Rome?
o: Gian Lorenzo Bernini
Donatello
Michelangelo
Antonio Canova
questions.e: The marble figure sits in a theatrical chapel lit by a hidden window, a showpiece of Baroque drama.

questions.q: Hokusai's The Great Wave off Kanagawa comes from which print series?
o: Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji
One Hundred Famous Views of Edo
The Fifty-three Stations of the Tōkaidō
The Tale of the Heike
questions.e: Mount Fuji sits small in the background, dwarfed by the wave. The series used the imported pigment Prussian blue.

questions.q: How many semitones make up a perfect fifth?
questions.e: The two notes vibrate in a frequency ratio of roughly 3:2, one of the most consonant intervals.

questions.q: Which composer developed the twelve-tone technique in the early 1920s?
o: Claude Debussy
Arnold Schoenberg
Gustav Mahler
Igor Stravinsky
questions.e: It treats all twelve notes of the chromatic scale as equals, arranged in a fixed series called a tone row.

questions.q: Who composed The Well-Tempered Clavier?
o: George Frideric Handel
Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart
Antonio Vivaldi
Johann Sebastian Bach
questions.e: Its two books each contain a prelude and fugue in all 24 major and minor keys.

questions.q: Which Russian writer's comic novel Dead Souls follows a swindler buying up the names of dead serfs?
o: Ivan Turgenev
Nikolai Gogol
Anton Chekhov
Leo Tolstoy
questions.e: Chichikov plans to mortgage the 'souls' as if they were still alive. Gogol burned much of the second volume shortly before he died in 1852.

questions.q: Who guides Dante through Hell and Purgatory in the Divine Comedy?
o: Beatrice
Homer
Saint Peter
Virgil
questions.e: Beatrice takes over at the summit of Purgatory and leads him through Paradise, since Virgil, as a pagan, cannot enter Heaven.

questions.q: James Joyce's Ulysses takes place over a single day in Dublin. Which one?
o: 23 April 1922
1 January 1900
17 March 1916
16 June 1904
questions.e: It is said to be the day of Joyce's first outing with Nora Barnacle, and fans celebrate it each year as Bloomsday.

questions.q: Which novel opens: 'Happy families are all alike; every unhappy family is unhappy in its own way'?
o: Madame Bovary
The Brothers Karamazov
Anna Karenina
War and Peace
questions.e: Leo Tolstoy published it in instalments in the 1870s.

questions.q: In which Shakespeare play does Portia say 'The quality of mercy is not strained'?
o: Measure for Measure
The Merchant of Venice
Much Ado About Nothing
Julius Caesar
questions.e: She says it while disguised as a young lawyer, pleading with Shylock in court.

questions.q: What is the longest continental mountain range in the world?
o: The Himalayas
The Andes
The Great Dividing Range
The Rocky Mountains
questions.e: It runs about 7,000 km, though the mostly underwater mid-ocean ridge system is far longer.

questions.q: About how deep is the Challenger Deep, the deepest known point in the ocean?
o: About 11 km
About 14 km
About 5 km
About 8 km
questions.e: It lies in the Mariana Trench, and Mount Everest placed inside it would still sit about 2 km underwater.

questions.q: Which is the largest landlocked country in the world?
o: Bolivia
Chad
Mongolia
Kazakhstan
questions.e: It is the ninth-largest country overall and borders the Caspian Sea, which is itself landlocked.

questions.q: Which river flows through or along the borders of more countries than any other?
o: The Danube
The Rhine
The Mekong
The Volga
questions.e: It touches 10 countries on its way from Germany's Black Forest to the Black Sea, passing four capital cities.

questions.q: In criminal law, what does 'mens rea' mean?
o: Let the matter speak for itself
A guilty act
Beyond reasonable doubt
A guilty mind
questions.e: Most crimes need both mens rea and actus reus, the guilty act.

questions.q: Which legal doctrine did the High Court of Australia overturn in Mabo v Queensland (No 2) in 1992?
o: Parliamentary sovereignty
Double jeopardy
Terra nullius
Separation of powers
questions.e: It recognised native title for the Meriam people of Mer (Murray Island) in the Torres Strait.

questions.q: What does the legal principle of 'stare decisis' require?
o: Courts follow the precedents set by earlier decisions
The accused is presumed innocent until proven guilty
Both sides must be heard before judgement
A person cannot be tried twice for the same crime
questions.e: The Latin means roughly 'to stand by things decided', and it is central to common law systems.

questions.q: In AD 212, which Roman emperor granted citizenship to almost all free men across the empire?
o: Hadrian
Caracalla
Constantine
Marcus Aurelius
questions.e: The historian Cassius Dio claimed it was partly a tax grab, since only citizens paid the inheritance tax.

riddles.q: A man looks at a portrait and says: 'Brothers and sisters I have none, but that man's father is my father's son.' Who is in the portrait?
o: Himself
His son
His father
His nephew
riddles.e: 'My father's son' is himself, so the man's father is him: it's his son.
Each term describes the one before: 111221 is 'three 1s, two 2s, one 1', so 312211.

riddles.q: How many times do a clock's hour and minute hands overlap in a full 24-hour day?
riddles.e: The minute hand laps the hour hand 11 times every 12 hours, not 12, so 22 times a day.

riddles.q: Eight identical-looking balls include one that is slightly heavier. What is the fewest weighings on a balance scale that guarantees finding it?
riddles.e: Weigh 3 against 3. If they balance, weigh the last 2 against each other. If not, take the heavier 3 and weigh 1 against 1.

riddles.q: On an island, knights always tell the truth and knaves always lie. A says: 'We are both knaves.' What are A and B?
o: Both knaves
A is a knave, B is a knight
Both knights
A is a knight, B is a knave
riddles.e: A knight couldn't say it, so A lies; then 'both knaves' is false, so B is a knight.

riddles.q: Four cards show A, K, 4 and 7. Each has a letter on one side and a number on the other. To test the rule 'If a card has a vowel on one side, it has an even number on the other', which cards must you turn over?
o: A and 4
A and 7
A only
A, 4 and 7
riddles.e: Turn A (it must hide an even number) and 7 (it must not hide a vowel). The 4 can't break the rule whatever is behind it.

riddles.q: Which English word contains all five vowels, a, e, i, o and u, exactly once and in alphabetical order?
o: Education
Sequoia
Facetious
Questionable
riddles.e: Abstemious is the other well-known example.

riddles.q: Which English word sounds exactly the same after you remove four of its five letters?
o: Tough
Eight
Queue
Yacht
riddles.e: Remove u, e, u, e and you are left with Q, pronounced the same.

riddles.q: What letter comes next: M, V, E, M, J, S, U, ?
o: O
S
P
N
riddles.e: They are the planets in order from the Sun, ending with Neptune.

riddles.q: What letter comes next: T, F, S, E, T, ?
o: E
N
F
T
riddles.e: Two, four, six, eight, ten, twelve: the first letters of the even numbers.

riddles.q: A game show has three doors: a car behind one, goats behind two. You pick a door. The host, who knows where the car is and always opens an unpicked goat door, opens one and offers you a switch. If you always switch, what is your chance of winning the car?
riddles.e: Your first pick is right 1/3 of the time, so switching loses then; the other 2/3 of the time the host's forced reveal leaves the car behind the remaining door, so switching wins 2/3.

riddles.q: Consider all two-child families that have at least one boy. Assuming each child is independently equally likely to be a boy or a girl, what fraction of those families have two boys?
riddles.e: The equally likely families are BB, BG, GB and GG; ruling out GG leaves three, and only one of them (BB) has two boys.

riddles.q: Ignoring leap years and assuming all 365 birthdays are equally likely, what is the smallest group in which the chance that at least two people share a birthday exceeds 50%?
riddles.e: With 23 people there are 253 possible pairs, and the probability that all birthdays differ drops to about 49.3%, so a shared birthday is slightly more likely than not.

riddles.q: On an island, knights always tell the truth and knaves always lie. A says: 'B is a knave.' B says: 'A and I are the same type.' What are they?
o: A is a knave, B is a knight
A is a knight, B is a knave
Both are knaves
Both are knights
riddles.e: If A were a knave, B would be a knight, but then B's true statement would make them the same type, a contradiction. So A is a knight and B a knave, whose claim of 'same type' is duly false.

riddles.q: Exactly one of three suspects is guilty, and exactly one of their statements is true. A: 'I am innocent.' B: 'A is guilty.' C: 'I am innocent.' Who is guilty?
o: A
B
C
It cannot be determined
riddles.e: If A were guilty, B and C would both be telling the truth; if B were guilty, A and C would both be truthful. Only C guilty leaves exactly one true statement (A's).

riddles.q: Two guards stand at a fork: one road is safe. One guard always tells the truth, the other always lies, and you don't know which is which. With one question to one guard, what is a sure way to choose the safe road?
o: Ask 'Which road is safe?' and take it
Ask 'Are you the truthful guard?' and decide from the answer
Ask 'Which road would the other guard say is safe?' and take that one
Ask 'Which road would the other guard say is safe?' and take the other one
riddles.e: Whichever guard you ask, the answer passes through exactly one lie, so it always names the dangerous road; take the opposite one.

riddles.q: Among 12 identical-looking coins, one is counterfeit and is either heavier or lighter, you don't know which. What is the minimum number of uses of a balance scale that guarantees finding the fake and whether it is heavy or light?
riddles.e: There are 24 possibilities (12 coins times heavy or light). Two weighings give only 3 x 3 = 9 outcomes, while three give 27, and a known scheme does it in three.

riddles.q: Using a balance scale where weights may go in either pan, what is the fewest whole-kilogram weights needed to weigh every whole number of kilograms from 1 to 40?
riddles.e: Weights of 1, 3, 9 and 27 kg work, since each can sit on the load side, the other side, or off the scale. Three weights can reach at most (3^3 minus 1) / 2 = 13 kg, far short of 40.

riddles.q: A farmer must ferry a wolf, a goat and a cabbage across a river. The boat carries him plus one item. Left alone, the wolf eats the goat and the goat eats the cabbage. What is the minimum number of one-way crossings?
riddles.e: Goat over, return, wolf over, bring the goat back, cabbage over, return, goat over: 7 crossings. Fewer is impossible because the goat must be brought back once.

riddles.q: Four people must cross a bridge at night with one torch. At most two cross at once, carrying the torch, at the slower person's pace. They take 1, 2, 5 and 10 minutes. What is the shortest total time?
o: 19 minutes
18 minutes
16 minutes
17 minutes
riddles.e: 1 and 2 cross (2), 1 returns (1), 5 and 10 cross together (10), 2 returns (2), 1 and 2 cross (2): 17. Having the 1-minute person escort everyone takes 19.

riddles.q: What is the angle between the hour and minute hands of an analogue clock at exactly 3:15?
o: 0 degrees
7.5 degrees
15 degrees
22.5 degrees
riddles.e: The minute hand points at the 3 (90 degrees), but the hour hand has moved a quarter of the way from 3 to 4, an extra 7.5 degrees, to 97.5 degrees.

riddles.q: A clock takes 5 seconds to strike six o'clock, timed from the first chime to the last. At the same rate, how long does it take to strike twelve?
o: 10 seconds
12 seconds
11 seconds
13 seconds
riddles.e: Six chimes have five gaps, so each gap is 1 second. Twelve chimes have eleven gaps, taking 11 seconds.

riddles.q: In a non-leap year, 1 January falls on a Monday. On what day does 31 December fall?
o: Monday
Tuesday
Sunday
Wednesday
riddles.e: 365 days is 52 weeks plus 1 day, so day 365 is the same weekday as day 1. The next 1 January is then a Tuesday.

riddles.q: What is the greatest number of Friday the 13ths that can occur in a single calendar year?
riddles.e: Every year has at least one and at most three. For example, a common year starting on a Thursday has them in February, March and November.

riddles.q: What number comes next: 2, 3, 5, 9, 17, 33, ?
riddles.e: Each term is double the previous one minus 1 (equivalently, the gaps double: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32), so 33 x 2 minus 1 = 65.

riddles.q: What number comes next: 61, 52, 63, 94, 46, ?
riddles.e: These are the squares 16, 25, 36, 49 and 64 written backwards. The next square, 81, reversed is 18.

riddles.q: Why are the digits arranged in this order: 8, 5, 4, 9, 1, 7, 6, 3, 2, 0?
o: They follow the order of keys on a phone keypad
Their English names are in alphabetical order
Each is the previous one minus 3, wrapping round
They are ordered by how many strokes it takes to write them
riddles.e: Eight, five, four, nine, one, seven, six, three, two, zero: the English names run in alphabetical order.

riddles.q: A bat and a ball cost $1.10 in total. The bat costs $1.00 more than the ball. How much does the ball cost?
o: 10 cents
1 cent
5 cents
55 cents
riddles.e: If the ball is x, the bat is x + 1.00, so 2x + 1.00 = 1.10 and x = 0.05. A 10-cent ball would make the bat $1.10 and the total $1.20.

riddles.q: A patch of lily pads doubles in size every day. It takes 48 days to cover the whole lake. On which day did it cover half the lake?
o: Day 24
Day 47
Day 46
Day 36
riddles.e: It doubles each day, so it was half the size the day before it was full: day 47.

riddles.q: If 5 machines take 5 minutes to make 5 widgets, how long would 100 machines take to make 100 widgets?
o: 100 minutes
20 minutes
1 minute
5 minutes
riddles.e: Each machine makes one widget in 5 minutes, so 100 machines working in parallel make 100 widgets in the same 5 minutes.

riddles.q: Three guests pay $30 for a room. The manager realises it costs $25 and sends the porter with $5. The porter keeps $2 and gives each guest $1 back. Each has now paid $9: 3 x $9 = $27, plus the porter's $2 makes $29. Where is the missing dollar?
o: The manager kept it back
It vanished in the rounding
None; the sum is misleading
The porter really kept $3
riddles.e: The guests' $27 equals the $25 room plus the porter's $2. The $2 should be subtracted from $27, not added; $27 + $3 refunded = $30 is the correct tally.

riddles.q: Which common English word contains three consecutive pairs of double letters?
o: Committee
Mississippi
Balloon
Bookkeeper
riddles.e: Book-keeper: oo, kk, ee appear back to back. Committee and Mississippi have double letters, but never three pairs in a row.

riddles.q: Which nine-letter word can lose one letter at a time, staying a real English word at every step, all the way down to a single letter?
o: Something
Startling
Stretched
Stringent
riddles.e: Startling, starting, staring, string, sting, sing, sin, in, I.

riddles.q: Consider all rolls of two fair dice that show at least one six. What fraction of those rolls show two sixes?
riddles.e: Of the 36 equally likely outcomes, 11 contain at least one six (6 + 6 minus the double-counted 6 and 6), and only one of them is a double six.

riddles.q: Three boxes hold two gold coins, two silver coins, and one of each. You pick a box at random and draw a coin at random from it: it is gold. What is the probability the other coin in that box is gold?
riddles.e: There are three equally likely gold coins you could have drawn, and two of them sit in the gold-gold box, so the chance is 2/3, not 1/2.

riddles.q: Three logicians walk into a bar. The bartender asks: 'Does everyone want a drink?' The first says 'I don't know.' The second says 'I don't know.' The third says 'Yes!' What can you conclude?
o: All three want a drink
Only the third wants a drink
None of them knows what the others want
The first two do not want a drink
riddles.e: If the first didn't want one, he would answer 'No'; 'I don't know' shows he does. The same goes for the second, so the third, who also wants one, can answer 'Yes'.

riddles.q: A dark drawer holds 10 black socks and 10 white socks. What is the fewest you must take out, without looking, to be certain of getting a pair of black socks?
riddles.e: In the worst case you draw all 10 white socks first, then need 2 black ones: 12 in total. Three guarantees a matching pair, but not a black one.

CLAIMS.c: Humans only use 10% of their brains.
CLAIMS.e: Brain scans show activity across virtually the whole brain over a day.

CLAIMS.c: If you touch a baby bird, its parents will reject it.
CLAIMS.e: Most birds have a weak sense of smell and won't abandon a chick because a human handled it. If it's uninjured, pop it back in the nest.

CLAIMS.c: You can see the Great Wall of China from space with the naked eye.
CLAIMS.e: It's very long but only a few metres wide. Astronauts say it's extremely hard, if not impossible, to spot unaided from orbit.

CLAIMS.c: Lightning never strikes the same place twice.
CLAIMS.e: Tall structures get hit again and again. The Empire State Building is struck around 20 times a year.

CLAIMS.c: Porcupines can shoot their quills at attackers.
CLAIMS.e: They can't. The quills detach easily when something touches them, then their barbed tips work their way into the skin.

CLAIMS.c: Venus takes longer to spin once on its axis than to orbit the Sun.
CLAIMS.e: Venus spins once every 243 Earth days but orbits the Sun in 225.

CLAIMS.c: Sea otters hold hands while they sleep.
CLAIMS.e: Resting sea otters often link paws, or wrap themselves in kelp, so they don't drift apart.

CLAIMS.c: Honey can stay edible for thousands of years.
CLAIMS.e: Its low water content and acidity stop microbes growing. Pots of honey thousands of years old have been found in ancient Egyptian tombs.

CLAIMS.c: Bananas are berries, but strawberries aren't.
CLAIMS.e: Botanically, a berry grows from one flower's ovary with seeds inside. Bananas fit; strawberries don't.

CLAIMS.c: Napoleon was unusually short.
CLAIMS.e: He was about 1.69 m, average for a Frenchman of his time. Old French inches and British cartoons fed the myth.

CLAIMS.c: Cracking your knuckles causes arthritis.
CLAIMS.e: Studies have found no link. The pop is gas bubbles in the joint fluid.

CLAIMS.c: People swallow about eight spiders a year in their sleep.
CLAIMS.e: There's no evidence for this. Spiders avoid breathing, snoring humans.

CLAIMS.c: A living tree is older than the Great Pyramid of Giza.
CLAIMS.e: 'Methuselah', a bristlecone pine in California, is about 4,800 years old. The Great Pyramid was finished around 4,500 years ago.

CLAIMS.c: Ancient Greek marble statues were originally plain white.
CLAIMS.e: Traces of pigment show many were brightly painted, with coloured skin, clothing and eyes. The paint wore away over the centuries.

CLAIMS.c: Chameleons change colour mainly to blend in with their background.
CLAIMS.e: They change colour mostly to signal mood and to control their temperature.

CLAIMS.c: Sugar makes children hyperactive.
CLAIMS.e: Double-blind studies found no effect on behaviour. Parents who think their child had sugar rate them as more hyperactive.

CLAIMS.c: Oxford University is older than the Aztec Empire.
CLAIMS.e: Teaching at Oxford existed by 1096. The Aztec capital, Tenochtitlan, was founded in 1325.

CLAIMS.c: You can drive across the Amazon River on a bridge.
CLAIMS.e: No bridge crosses the main Amazon. It runs mostly through thinly populated rainforest with soft, flood-prone banks, so ferries do the job.

CLAIMS.c: A group of flamingos is called a flamboyance.
CLAIMS.e: Yes, really. Flamingos often rest standing on one leg, which scientists think helps them save energy.

CLAIMS.c: Water swirls down the drain the opposite way in the Southern Hemisphere.
CLAIMS.e: The Coriolis effect is far too weak at sink size. The shape of the basin and how the water was poured matter more.

CLAIMS.c: A coin dropped from a skyscraper could kill someone.
CLAIMS.e: A small flat coin tumbles and hits a low top speed. It would sting, not kill.

CLAIMS.c: Platypuses glow under ultraviolet light.
CLAIMS.e: Scientists reported in 2020 that platypus fur absorbs UV light and gives off a blue-green glow. Why it happens is still a mystery.

CLAIMS.c: Hair and fingernails keep growing after death.
CLAIMS.e: The skin dries and pulls back, which makes them look longer.

CLAIMS.c: Einstein failed maths at school.
CLAIMS.e: He excelled at maths and had mastered calculus by about 15.

CLAIMS.c: There are more trees on Earth than stars in the Milky Way.
CLAIMS.e: Earth has about 3 trillion trees; the Milky Way has roughly 100 to 400 billion stars.

CLAIMS.c: The shortest war in recorded history lasted less than an hour.
CLAIMS.e: The Anglo-Zanzibar War of 1896 lasted roughly 40 minutes before the sultan's forces gave up.

CLAIMS.c: Daddy long-legs spiders are highly venomous, but their fangs are too weak to bite us.
CLAIMS.e: They can bite, but their venom is weak and barely affects humans. The claim is an old internet myth.

CLAIMS.c: A stiff drink warms you up in the cold.
CLAIMS.e: Alcohol makes you feel warm by widening blood vessels near the skin, but that actually lowers your core temperature.

CLAIMS.c: Eating carrots gives you night vision.
CLAIMS.e: Carrots are healthy, but the myth was spread by British propaganda in World War II to hide radar technology.

CLAIMS.c: Swallowed chewing gum stays in your stomach for seven years.
CLAIMS.e: Your body can't digest gum base, but it passes through your gut and out within a few days, like other things you can't digest.

CLAIMS.c: The Eiffel Tower can grow around 15 cm taller in hot weather.
CLAIMS.e: Iron expands when heated, so the tower's height changes with the temperature.

CLAIMS.c: Mosquitoes kill more people each year than any other animal.
CLAIMS.e: They spread malaria, dengue and other diseases that kill hundreds of thousands of people a year.

CLAIMS.c: You lose most of your body heat through your head.
CLAIMS.e: Your head loses heat roughly in proportion to its surface area, only around 10%. Cover up everywhere.

CLAIMS.c: Australia is wider than the Moon.
CLAIMS.e: Australia is about 4,000 km from east to west; the Moon is about 3,475 km across.

CLAIMS.c: Elephants drink through their trunks like a straw.
CLAIMS.e: They suck several litres of water up into the trunk, then squirt it into their mouths.

CLAIMS.c: Ostriches bury their heads in the sand when scared.
CLAIMS.e: They lie flat or run. They do turn their eggs in ground nests, which may have started the myth.

CLAIMS.c: Tomatoes are fruits.
CLAIMS.e: Botanically, a fruit contains seeds. Cooks treat tomatoes as vegetables.

CLAIMS.c: Dogs can only see in black and white.
CLAIMS.e: Dogs see some colours, mainly blues and yellows, but not reds and greens the way we do.

CLAIMS.c: Old windows are thicker at the bottom because glass slowly flows.
CLAIMS.e: Old glass was made unevenly, and builders often put the thick edge at the bottom. Glass doesn't flow noticeably.

CLAIMS.c: Fortune cookies were invented in China.
CLAIMS.e: They were popularised in California in the early 1900s, probably adapted from a Japanese cracker, and are rarely seen in China.

CLAIMS.c: You should wait 30 minutes after eating before swimming.
CLAIMS.e: There's no good evidence that eating before swimming causes dangerous cramps.

CLAIMS.c: Shaving makes hair grow back thicker and darker.
CLAIMS.e: Shaving cuts hair at a blunt angle so it feels coarser, but it doesn't change thickness, colour or growth rate.

CLAIMS.c: Touching a toad gives you warts.
CLAIMS.e: Warts are caused by a human virus (HPV). A toad's bumpy skin can't pass them on, though some toads, like cane toads, have toxins, so wash your hands.

CLAIMS.c: Sound travels faster through water than through air.
CLAIMS.e: About four times faster, because water is far harder to compress than air, so pressure waves pass through it more quickly.

CLAIMS.c: A lightning bolt is hotter than the surface of the Sun.
CLAIMS.e: Lightning can heat the air to around 30,000°C; the Sun's surface is about 5,500°C.

CLAIMS.c: Most of the oxygen we breathe comes from the Amazon rainforest.
CLAIMS.e: Ocean plankton produce around half of Earth's oxygen, and the Amazon uses up most of what it produces.

CLAIMS.c: Going out with wet hair in the cold gives you a cold.
CLAIMS.e: Colds are caused by viruses, so you can't catch one without being exposed. Some research suggests a chill may help a virus you already carry take hold, and cold weather keeps people indoors together, where viruses spread.

CLAIMS.c: The Atlantic Ocean is saltier than the Pacific.
CLAIMS.e: On average, yes. Winds carry moisture evaporated from the Atlantic across Central America, where it falls as rain on the Pacific.

CLAIMS.c: An Australian turtle can breathe through its bottom.
CLAIMS.e: The Fitzroy River turtle in Queensland absorbs oxygen from water through its cloaca, letting it stay underwater for long periods.

CLAIMS.c: Reading in dim light permanently damages your eyesight.
CLAIMS.e: It can cause temporary eye strain, but there's no evidence of lasting damage.

CLAIMS.c: The Moon has no gravity.
CLAIMS.e: The Moon's gravity is about one-sixth of Earth's. It's also the main cause of our ocean tides.

CLAIMS.c: Diamonds are made of carbon, the same element as pencil graphite.
CLAIMS.e: The difference is how the carbon atoms are arranged.

CLAIMS.c: The Sun is yellow.
CLAIMS.e: The Sun gives off all colours of light, which mix to make white. From space it looks white; our air scatters blue light, making it look yellowish from the ground.

CLAIMS.c: Crocodiles can't stick their tongues out.
CLAIMS.e: A crocodile's tongue is held in place by a membrane along the floor of its mouth.

CLAIMS.c: All sharks must keep swimming or they'll suffocate.
CLAIMS.e: Some species must, but many, like the Port Jackson shark and wobbegongs, pump water over their gills while resting.

CLAIMS.c: Your blood is blue until it touches air.
CLAIMS.e: Blood is always red: darker when low in oxygen. Veins only look blue because of how light passes through skin.

CLAIMS.c: Olympic gold medals are made mostly of silver.
CLAIMS.e: Rules require at least 92.5% silver, plated with at least 6 grams of gold.

CLAIMS.c: Coffee dehydrates you, so it doesn't count towards your fluid intake.
CLAIMS.e: For regular drinkers, moderate coffee adds to your daily fluids. The mild diuretic effect doesn't cancel it out.

CLAIMS.c: Stainless steel can still rust.
CLAIMS.e: Chromium in the steel forms a thin, invisible layer that resists rust, but salt water, scratches or harsh cleaners can still cause rust spots.

CLAIMS.c: The cells lining your stomach are replaced every few days.
CLAIMS.e: The surface lining is constantly renewed, which helps protect it from its own acid.

CLAIMS.c: You need to drink eight glasses of water a day on top of everything else.
CLAIMS.e: There's no solid science behind the eight-glass rule. Food, tea, coffee and other drinks all count, and for most healthy people thirst is a reliable guide.

CLAIMS.c: If you stop exercising, your muscle turns into fat.
CLAIMS.e: Muscle and fat are different tissues, so one can't become the other. Without exercise muscles shrink, and if you eat the same amount, fat can build up.

CLAIMS.c: You can sweat out toxins.
CLAIMS.e: Sweat is mostly water with a little salt, and its job is cooling you down. Your liver and kidneys do the real work of clearing waste.

CLAIMS.c: People having a seizure can swallow their tongue.
CLAIMS.e: It's physically impossible to swallow your tongue. Never put anything in the person's mouth: time the seizure, cushion their head and call 000 if needed.

CLAIMS.c: Weeing on a jellyfish sting eases the pain.
CLAIMS.e: Urine doesn't help and may make a sting worse. For tropical box jellyfish, call 000 and pour on vinegar; for bluebottles, soak the area in hot water.

CLAIMS.c: Earwax should be cleaned out with cotton buds.
CLAIMS.e: Ears clean themselves: wax slowly moves outwards on its own. Cotton buds tend to push wax deeper and can damage the eardrum.

CLAIMS.c: You can't get sunburnt on a cloudy day.
CLAIMS.e: Much of the Sun's UV gets through cloud, so you can still burn. In Australia, check the daily UV index rather than the sky.

CLAIMS.c: A suntan is a healthy way to protect your skin from burning.
CLAIMS.e: A tan is a sign your skin cells have already been damaged by UV. It gives only very weak protection, far less than sunscreen.

CLAIMS.c: SPF 50 sunscreen blocks twice as much UV as SPF 25.
CLAIMS.e: SPF 25 blocks about 96% of UVB and SPF 50 about 98%. The bigger difference comes from applying enough and reapplying often.

CLAIMS.c: Antibacterial soap is needed to properly clean your hands.
CLAIMS.e: Studies have found plain soap and water works just as well for everyday handwashing. Soap lifts germs off your skin so they rinse away.

CLAIMS.c: Taking extra vitamins is always harmless, because your body gets rid of what it doesn't need.
CLAIMS.e: Some vitamins, like A and D, are stored in the body and can build up to harmful levels. More is not always better.

CLAIMS.c: Sugar itself eats holes in your teeth.
CLAIMS.e: Bacteria in your mouth feed on sugar and produce acid, and it's the acid that wears away tooth enamel. That's why brushing and less frequent snacking both help.

CLAIMS.c: Your heart stops when you sneeze.
CLAIMS.e: A sneeze can briefly change pressure in your chest and alter your heartbeat rhythm, but your heart keeps beating.

CLAIMS.c: You're slightly taller in the morning than at night.
CLAIMS.e: During the day, gravity squashes the soft discs between the bones of your spine. By evening you can be about 1 cm shorter, and you get it back overnight while lying down.

CLAIMS.c: Your small intestine is much longer than your large intestine.
CLAIMS.e: The small intestine is about 6 metres long and the large intestine about 1.5 metres. The names refer to how wide they are, not how long.

CLAIMS.c: Your inner ears help you keep your balance.
CLAIMS.e: Fluid-filled canals in your inner ear sense how your head moves. That's why an ear infection can make you feel dizzy.

CLAIMS.c: Your left lung is smaller than your right lung.
CLAIMS.e: The left lung is smaller to make room for your heart. It has two sections, called lobes, while the right lung has three.

CLAIMS.c: Fingernails grow faster than toenails.
CLAIMS.e: Fingernails grow roughly two to three times faster than toenails. A lost fingernail takes about six months to grow back fully.

CLAIMS.c: Fresh sweat has almost no smell.
CLAIMS.e: Body odour comes from bacteria on the skin breaking down sweat, mostly from glands in the armpits. That's why washing makes such a difference.

CLAIMS.c: Most people have a dominant eye.
CLAIMS.e: Just as you favour one hand, your brain relies slightly more on one eye. Frame a distant object between your hands and close each eye in turn to find yours.

CLAIMS.c: Natural and herbal remedies are always safe because they come from plants.
CLAIMS.e: Many strong medicines and poisons come from plants. Herbal products can also interact with prescription medicines, so tell your doctor or pharmacist what you take.

CLAIMS.c: Cutting an earthworm in half creates two worms.
CLAIMS.e: In some species the head end can survive and regrow a tail, but the tail end usually dies. You never get two whole worms.

CLAIMS.c: One dog year equals seven human years.
CLAIMS.e: Dogs age very fast in their first year or two, then more slowly. Size matters too: large breeds tend to age faster than small ones.

CLAIMS.c: Koalas are a type of bear.
CLAIMS.e: Koalas are marsupials, carrying their young in a pouch. The 'koala bear' name came from early European settlers.

CLAIMS.c: All bees die after they sting.
CLAIMS.e: Honeybee workers usually die after stinging a mammal because their barbed sting gets stuck. Most other bees, and wasps, can sting again and again.

CLAIMS.c: Only female mosquitoes bite.
CLAIMS.e: Females need protein from blood to develop their eggs. Males feed on nectar and plant juices instead.

CLAIMS.c: Wombats do cube-shaped poo.
CLAIMS.e: Parts of a wombat's intestine walls stretch differently, which shapes its droppings into cubes. Wombats leave them on rocks and logs to mark their territory.

CLAIMS.c: Cheetahs can't roar.
CLAIMS.e: Cheetahs chirp, purr and hiss, but they lack the voice box structure that lets lions and tigers roar.

CLAIMS.c: Koalas have fingerprints very like ours.
CLAIMS.e: Koala fingerprints have loops and whorls so similar to human ones that they are hard to tell apart, even under a microscope.

CLAIMS.c: Penguins only live in icy places.
CLAIMS.e: The Galápagos penguin lives near the equator, and little penguins live along southern Australia's coast. Phillip Island in Victoria is famous for them.

CLAIMS.c: Polar bears have black skin under their fur.
CLAIMS.e: Their fur hairs are actually clear and hollow, and they look white because they scatter light. The black skin underneath helps soak up warmth.

CLAIMS.c: Rats laugh when they're tickled.
CLAIMS.e: Researchers found rats make high-pitched chirps when tickled, too high for humans to hear. Tickled rats even chase the researcher's hand for more.

CLAIMS.c: Flamingos are born pink.
CLAIMS.e: Flamingo chicks hatch grey or white. Their pink colour comes from pigments in the algae and shrimp they eat.

CLAIMS.c: Snails have teeth.
CLAIMS.e: A snail's tongue-like ribbon, called a radula, is covered in thousands of microscopic teeth. It uses them to scrape up food.

CLAIMS.c: Bulls are made angry by the colour red.
CLAIMS.e: Bulls can't tell red from green. It's the movement of the matador's cape that makes them charge, not its colour.

CLAIMS.c: Sharks have skeletons made of bone.
CLAIMS.e: A shark's skeleton is made of cartilage, the same bendy material in your ears and nose. It's lighter than bone, which helps sharks stay buoyant.

CLAIMS.c: Cats can't taste sweetness.
CLAIMS.e: Cats lack a working version of the gene for the sweet taste receptor. As strict meat-eaters, they don't need it.

CLAIMS.c: Chocolate is poisonous to dogs.
CLAIMS.e: Chocolate contains theobromine, which dogs process very slowly. Dark chocolate and cooking chocolate are the most dangerous.

CLAIMS.c: Redback spider bites often kill people in Australia.
CLAIMS.e: No one in Australia is known to have died from a redback bite since antivenom arrived in the 1950s. Bites can still be very painful, so seek medical help.

CLAIMS.c: Australia's wild rabbit plague began with about two dozen rabbits released for hunting.
CLAIMS.e: In 1859, Thomas Austin released 24 rabbits on his property near Geelong. Within decades there were hundreds of millions across the country.

CLAIMS.c: Most of Australia's native mammals are found nowhere else on Earth.
CLAIMS.e: More than 80% of Australia's mammals are endemic, including kangaroos, koalas, wombats and platypuses. Long isolation let them evolve separately.

CLAIMS.c: A wombat can sprint at up to about 40 km/h.
CLAIMS.e: Despite their stocky build and short legs, wombats can briefly outrun most people over a short distance.

CLAIMS.c: Giant pandas have the digestive system of a meat-eater.
CLAIMS.e: Pandas are classed as carnivores, but they eat mostly bamboo. Their gut digests it poorly, so they spend up to around 14 hours a day eating.

CLAIMS.c: Dingoes arrived in Australia long after the first people.
CLAIMS.e: The oldest known dingo remains are around 3,500 years old, while people have lived in Australia for tens of thousands of years. Dingoes were probably brought by seafaring visitors.

CLAIMS.c: Adult elephants can't jump.
CLAIMS.e: Elephants are very heavy and their leg bones point straight down, so they can't push off the ground with all four feet at once. They can still walk surprisingly fast.

CLAIMS.c: Some ants farm other insects.
CLAIMS.e: Many ants protect aphids and 'milk' them for the sweet honeydew they produce. The ants guard them from predators in return.

CLAIMS.c: Killer whales are actually a type of dolphin.
CLAIMS.e: Orcas are the largest member of the ocean dolphin family. The name 'killer whale' likely came from sailors who saw them hunting whales.

CLAIMS.c: Astronauts float on the space station because there's no gravity there.
CLAIMS.e: At the station's height, gravity is still about 90% as strong as on the ground. Astronauts float because they and the station are always falling around Earth together.

CLAIMS.c: Footprints left on the Moon could last for millions of years.
CLAIMS.e: The Moon has no wind or rain to wear them away, so the Apollo astronauts' footprints could last millions of years unless small space rocks disturb them.

CLAIMS.c: The Moon looks bigger near the horizon because it's closer to us then.
CLAIMS.e: It's an illusion: the Moon is actually slightly further away when rising. Measure it with a coin at arm's length and it's the same size.

CLAIMS.c: Earth is a perfect sphere.
CLAIMS.e: Earth bulges slightly at the equator because it spins. It's about 43 km wider across the equator than from pole to pole.
