CLAIMS.c: Black holes suck in everything around them like cosmic vacuum cleaners.
CLAIMS.e: From a distance, a black hole pulls just like any object of the same mass. If the Sun were swapped for a black hole of equal mass, Earth would keep the same orbit.

CLAIMS.c: Venus spins in the opposite direction to most planets.
CLAIMS.e: On Venus, the Sun rises in the west and sets in the east. Uranus also has an unusual spin, tipped over on its side.

CLAIMS.c: You can see the International Space Station without a telescope.
CLAIMS.e: It reflects sunlight and looks like a bright, steady star gliding across the sky in a few minutes, usually just after sunset or before sunrise.

CLAIMS.c: Heavier objects fall faster than lighter ones.
CLAIMS.e: Without air resistance, everything falls at the same rate. An Apollo 15 astronaut dropped a hammer and a feather on the Moon and they landed together.

CLAIMS.c: Pure water is a good conductor of electricity.
CLAIMS.e: Pure water conducts electricity poorly. It's the salts and minerals dissolved in everyday water that carry the current, which is why water and electricity are still a deadly mix.

CLAIMS.c: Raindrops are shaped like teardrops.
CLAIMS.e: Small raindrops are round, and larger ones flatten on the bottom as they fall, a bit like a hamburger bun.

CLAIMS.c: Greenland is bigger than Australia.
CLAIMS.e: Australia is more than three times bigger. Common world maps stretch areas near the poles, which makes Greenland look huge.

CLAIMS.c: Rubber tyres protect you from lightning when you're in a car.
CLAIMS.e: A few centimetres of rubber can't stop lightning. A hard-topped car protects you because its metal body carries the current around you to the ground.

CLAIMS.c: Your body contains enough iron to make a small nail.
CLAIMS.e: An adult has about 3 to 4 grams of iron, mostly in the haemoglobin that carries oxygen in your blood.

CLAIMS.c: Most of Earth's fresh water is frozen.
CLAIMS.e: Around two-thirds of the world's fresh water is locked up in ice caps and glaciers, mostly in Antarctica and Greenland.

CLAIMS.c: Australia is the driest inhabited continent.
CLAIMS.e: Only Antarctica is drier. Much of inland Australia gets less than 250 mm of rain a year.

CLAIMS.c: Cooking always burns off all the alcohol in a dish.
CLAIMS.e: Plenty can remain, depending on the method and time. Studies found a dish simmered for 30 minutes can still hold about a third of its alcohol.

CLAIMS.c: Most 'wasabi' served outside Japan is actually horseradish.
CLAIMS.e: Real wasabi is expensive and hard to grow. Most of the green paste is horseradish mixed with mustard and green colouring.

CLAIMS.c: Each cashew nut grows on the outside of a fruit.
CLAIMS.e: A cashew hangs from the bottom of a fleshy 'cashew apple'. The nut sits inside a shell containing an irritating oil, so it has to be processed carefully.

CLAIMS.c: Bananas grow on trees.
CLAIMS.e: Banana plants look like trees, but they have no wooden trunk. Botanically, they're giant herbs.

CLAIMS.c: Almonds are closely related to peaches.
CLAIMS.e: Both belong to the same plant group, Prunus, along with plums and cherries. The almond we eat is the seed inside the fruit's stone.

CLAIMS.c: A very fresh egg will sink in a glass of water.
CLAIMS.e: As an egg ages, moisture escapes through the shell and the air pocket inside grows. Older eggs tilt upwards or float.

CLAIMS.c: You should wash raw chicken before cooking it.
CLAIMS.e: Washing chicken can splash bacteria around your sink and kitchen. Proper cooking kills the germs anyway.

CLAIMS.c: Worcestershire sauce is made with fish.
CLAIMS.e: Traditional Worcestershire sauce contains fermented anchovies, along with vinegar, molasses, tamarind and spices.

CLAIMS.c: Brown eggs are more nutritious than white eggs.
CLAIMS.e: Shell colour depends on the breed of hen. Inside, brown and white eggs are nutritionally the same.

CLAIMS.c: Apples float in water because they contain lots of air.
CLAIMS.e: About a quarter of an apple's volume is air trapped between its cells. That makes them less dense than water, which is why apple bobbing works.

CLAIMS.c: Vanilla comes from an orchid.
CLAIMS.e: Vanilla beans are the seed pods of a climbing orchid. Each flower must usually be hand-pollinated, which helps explain vanilla's high price.

CLAIMS.c: Moving into a higher tax bracket means all your income is taxed at the higher rate.
CLAIMS.e: Australia uses marginal rates: only the income above each threshold is taxed at that bracket's rate. Tipping into a higher bracket only affects the extra dollars.

CLAIMS.c: Checking your own credit score lowers it.
CLAIMS.e: Checking your own score is a 'soft' enquiry that doesn't affect it. Applications for new credit are what show up on your file.

CLAIMS.c: If an investment falls 50%, it needs to rise 50% to get back to where it started.
CLAIMS.e: It needs to double, a 100% gain. $100 that drops to $50 must gain another $50, which is 100% of $50.

CLAIMS.c: Australian shops must accept any number of coins as payment.
CLAIMS.e: Coins are only legal tender up to set limits. For example, 5c to 50c coins only have to be accepted up to $5 in total in a single payment.

CLAIMS.c: Australia's 1c and 2c coins were taken out of circulation in the early 1990s.
CLAIMS.e: They were withdrawn in 1992. Cash totals are now rounded to the nearest 5 cents, while card payments are still charged to the exact cent.

CLAIMS.c: The colony of New South Wales's first official coins were made by punching holes in Spanish dollars.
CLAIMS.e: In 1813, Governor Macquarie had the centres punched out of Spanish silver dollars. The ring became the 'holey dollar' and the centre the 'dump', giving the colony two coins.

CLAIMS.c: The Australian $2 coin is smaller than the $1 coin.
CLAIMS.e: The $2 coin replaced the $2 note in 1988. It is worth more than the $1 coin but is noticeably smaller.

CLAIMS.c: The numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 are less likely to win Lotto than a random mix.
CLAIMS.e: Every combination has exactly the same chance. The only catch is that many people pick those numbers, so you'd share the prize.

CLAIMS.c: Australian lenders advertising a home loan interest rate must also show a 'comparison rate'.
CLAIMS.e: The comparison rate combines the interest rate with most fees and charges into one figure. It makes the true cost of different loans easier to compare.

CLAIMS.c: The word 'mortgage' literally means 'death pledge'.
CLAIMS.e: It comes from Old French. The pledge 'dies' when the debt is paid off, or when the borrower fails to pay and loses the property.

CLAIMS.c: Listening to Mozart makes babies smarter.
CLAIMS.e: The 'Mozart effect' came from a small 1993 study of adults, showing only a brief boost on one type of task. Later research didn't support lasting effects.

CLAIMS.c: Lie detector tests reliably catch liars.
CLAIMS.e: Polygraphs measure signs of stress, like heart rate and sweating, not lies. Honest people can fail from nerves, which is why courts rarely accept them.

CLAIMS.c: A famous 1957 experiment proved hidden 'Eat popcorn' messages in films boosted sales.
CLAIMS.e: The marketer behind it, James Vicary, later admitted the results were made up. Attempts to repeat it failed.

CLAIMS.c: Your memory records events like a video camera.
CLAIMS.e: Each time you recall something, your brain rebuilds it. Details can shift or be added without you noticing.

CLAIMS.c: Humans now have a shorter attention span than a goldfish.
CLAIMS.e: That widely shared claim has no scientific source behind it. Attention depends heavily on the task and how interested you are.

CLAIMS.c: Liars usually avoid eye contact.
CLAIMS.e: Large reviews of deception research show gaze aversion isn't a reliable sign of lying. Many liars hold eye contact deliberately.

CLAIMS.c: Hospitals get busier during a full moon.
CLAIMS.e: Studies of emergency departments and hospital admissions have found no link to the full moon. We just tend to notice busy nights that fit the story.

CLAIMS.c: Your handwriting reveals your personality.
CLAIMS.e: Graphology, the practice of reading personality from handwriting, has failed scientific tests. It performs no better than chance.

CLAIMS.c: Noticing something everywhere right after you learn about it has a name.
CLAIMS.e: It's called the frequency illusion, or Baader-Meinhof phenomenon. The thing isn't more common: your attention is now tuned to spot it.

CLAIMS.c: 'Goodbye' comes from 'God be with ye'.
CLAIMS.e: Over centuries the phrase was shortened to 'godbwye'. 'Good' later replaced 'God', perhaps influenced by 'good day'.

CLAIMS.c: 'Posh' comes from 'Port Out, Starboard Home', about the best cabins on ships to India.
CLAIMS.e: There's no evidence for this story, and no tickets stamped 'POSH' have been found. The word's real origin is unknown.

CLAIMS.c: The word 'quiz' was invented as a bet by a Dublin theatre owner.
CLAIMS.e: The tale of a man paying children to scrawl 'quiz' around Dublin only appeared decades later. The word was already in use before the supposed bet.

CLAIMS.c: 'Sincere' comes from the Latin 'sine cera', meaning 'without wax'.
CLAIMS.e: This popular story about sculptors hiding cracks with wax is a folk tale. The word comes from the Latin 'sincerus', meaning pure or clean.

CLAIMS.c: The word 'nice' once meant 'foolish'.
CLAIMS.e: It comes from the Latin 'nescius', meaning ignorant. Over centuries it shifted through meanings like 'fussy' and 'precise' before becoming 'pleasant'.

CLAIMS.c: The word 'muscle' comes from the Latin for 'little mouse'.
CLAIMS.e: Romans thought a flexing muscle looked like a mouse moving under the skin, so they called it 'musculus'.

CLAIMS.c: The word 'alphabet' comes from the first two Greek letters.
CLAIMS.e: Alpha and beta are the first two letters of the Greek alphabet. In English we have a similar name: learning your 'ABCs'.

CLAIMS.c: The word 'checkmate' comes from Persian.
CLAIMS.e: It comes from the Persian 'shāh māt', usually translated as 'the king is helpless' or 'the king is defeated'. Chess reached Europe through Persia and the Arab world.

CLAIMS.c: Sign language is the same all over the world.
CLAIMS.e: There are hundreds of sign languages. Australia's is Auslan, which is closer to British Sign Language than to American Sign Language.

CLAIMS.c: 'Emoji' comes from the English word 'emotion'.
CLAIMS.e: It's Japanese: 'e' means picture and 'moji' means character. The resemblance to 'emotion' is a coincidence.

CLAIMS.c: The word 'clue' comes from a ball of thread.
CLAIMS.e: A 'clew' was a ball of yarn. In Greek myth, Theseus used a thread to find his way out of the Labyrinth, so a clew came to mean something that guides you to an answer.

CLAIMS.c: The word 'disaster' literally means 'bad star'.
CLAIMS.e: It comes from the Italian 'disastro', from 'dis' (bad) and 'astro' (star). Bad events were once blamed on unlucky positions of the stars and planets.

CLAIMS.c: The English word 'girl' once meant a child of either sex.
CLAIMS.e: In Middle English, 'girl' could mean any young person. Boys were sometimes called 'knave girls'.

CLAIMS.c: The abbreviation 'lb' for pound comes from Latin.
CLAIMS.e: It stands for 'libra', an ancient Roman unit of weight. In Latin 'libra' also meant scales, which is where the star sign Libra gets its name.

CLAIMS.c: Uluru has two official names.
CLAIMS.e: Since 1993 it has had a dual name, and since 2002 it has been officially 'Uluru / Ayers Rock'. Uluru is its Anangu name.

CLAIMS.c: The first programmers of the ENIAC computer were women.
CLAIMS.e: Six women programmed ENIAC, one of the first general-purpose electronic computers, in the 1940s. They worked it out largely from wiring diagrams.

CLAIMS.c: The first computer mouse was made of wood.
CLAIMS.e: Douglas Engelbart's team built it in the 1960s from a wooden block with two metal wheels underneath.

CLAIMS.c: Bluetooth is named after a Viking-era king.
CLAIMS.e: Harald 'Bluetooth' Gormsson united parts of Denmark and Norway. The technology was meant to unite devices, and its logo combines his initials in runes.

CLAIMS.c: The first text message ever sent said 'Merry Christmas'.
CLAIMS.e: Engineer Neil Papworth sent it from a computer to a mobile phone in the UK in December 1992.

CLAIMS.c: Deleting a file immediately wipes it from your computer's drive.
CLAIMS.e: Usually the computer just marks the space as free to reuse. Until it's written over, the data can often be recovered, so use proper wiping tools for sensitive files.

CLAIMS.c: The internet and the World Wide Web are the same thing.
CLAIMS.e: The internet is the global network connecting computers. The Web, invented by Tim Berners-Lee around 1989, is one service that runs on it, alongside things like email.

CLAIMS.c: reCAPTCHA puzzles once helped digitise old books.
CLAIMS.e: When you typed hard-to-read words, you were often helping computers read scanned books and newspaper archives that software couldn't decipher.

CLAIMS.c: Email is older than the World Wide Web.
CLAIMS.e: Ray Tomlinson sent the first network email between computers in 1971, about two decades before the Web appeared. It ran on ARPANET, a US research network that grew into the internet.

CLAIMS.c: Junk email is called 'spam' because of a Monty Python sketch.
CLAIMS.e: In the 1970 sketch, Vikings in a café drown out conversation by singing about Spam. Early internet users borrowed it for floods of unwanted messages.

CLAIMS.c: People convicted in the Salem witch trials were burnt at the stake.
CLAIMS.e: In Salem in 1692, those executed were hanged, and one man was pressed to death with stones. Burning was used for witchcraft in parts of Europe, not in colonial Massachusetts.

CLAIMS.c: In the Middle Ages, most people died by about 30.
CLAIMS.e: Average lifespans were low mainly because so many children died young. People who survived childhood often lived into their 50s, 60s or beyond.

CLAIMS.c: Iron maidens were a common medieval torture device.
CLAIMS.e: There's no good evidence they were used in the Middle Ages. Most surviving examples were put together in the 1700s and 1800s for display.

CLAIMS.c: An apple falling on Isaac Newton's head inspired his theory of gravity.
CLAIMS.e: Newton said watching an apple fall in a garden got him thinking about gravity. There's no evidence it hit him on the head.

CLAIMS.c: George Washington had wooden false teeth.
CLAIMS.e: His dentures were made from materials like ivory, metal, and human and animal teeth. Stains in the ivory may have made them look like wood grain.

CLAIMS.c: Roman gladiators nearly always fought to the death.
CLAIMS.e: Gladiators were expensive to train and feed, so many bouts ended without a death. A defeated fighter could be spared.

CLAIMS.c: Medieval knights in armour had to be lifted onto their horses with cranes.
CLAIMS.e: Plate armour weighed about 15 to 25 kg, spread across the body. Knights could mount horses, run and even do acrobatics in it.

CLAIMS.c: Viking warriors wore horned helmets into battle.
CLAIMS.e: No horned helmet has ever been found from a Viking-age warrior. The image became popular in the 1800s, helped by costumes for Wagner's operas.

CLAIMS.c: Julius Caesar was born by caesarean section.
CLAIMS.e: His mother Aurelia lived for decades after his birth, which would have been very unlikely after the surgery in Roman times. The name's origin is uncertain.

CLAIMS.c: Marco Polo brought pasta to Italy from China.
CLAIMS.e: Pasta was already known in Italy before Polo returned in 1295. The story was spread by a 1920s American pasta industry magazine.

CLAIMS.c: Harvard University is older than calculus.
CLAIMS.e: Harvard was founded in 1636. Newton and Leibniz developed calculus independently several decades later.

CLAIMS.c: The fax machine was invented before the telephone.
CLAIMS.e: Scottish inventor Alexander Bain patented an early fax design in 1843, more than 30 years before Bell's 1876 telephone patent.

CLAIMS.c: Albert Einstein was offered the presidency of Israel.
CLAIMS.e: In 1952 he was invited to become Israel's president, a largely ceremonial role. He politely declined, saying he lacked the right skills.

CLAIMS.c: The First Fleet set up its settlement at Botany Bay.
CLAIMS.e: The fleet arrived at Botany Bay in January 1788, but found it unsuitable. They moved north to Port Jackson and landed at Sydney Cove on 26 January.

CLAIMS.c: All boomerangs are designed to come back.
CLAIMS.e: Most boomerangs used for hunting and fighting were non-returning and flew long and straight. Returning boomerangs were mostly used for sport and play.

CLAIMS.c: Galileo invented the telescope.
CLAIMS.e: The first known telescope patent was sought by a Dutch spectacle maker in 1608. Galileo built improved versions and was among the first to study the sky with one.

CLAIMS.c: Christopher Columbus never set foot on the mainland of what is now the United States.
CLAIMS.e: On his four voyages he reached Caribbean islands, including Puerto Rico, now a US territory, and the coasts of Central and South America, but never the North American mainland.

CLAIMS.c: Napoleon's soldiers shot the nose off the Great Sphinx.
CLAIMS.e: Drawings from decades before Napoleon's 1798 arrival already show the Sphinx without its nose. Marks suggest it was deliberately chiselled off centuries earlier.

CLAIMS.c: The Olympic torch relay dates back to ancient Greece.
CLAIMS.e: The ancient Games had sacred flames, but the torch relay to the host city was introduced for the 1936 Berlin Olympics.

CLAIMS.c: A man on horseback cut the ribbon before the official opening of the Sydney Harbour Bridge.
CLAIMS.e: In 1932, Francis de Groot rode forward and slashed the ribbon with his sword before the Premier could cut it. The ribbon was retied and cut again.

CLAIMS.c: The largest alluvial gold nugget ever found was dug up in Victoria.
CLAIMS.e: The 'Welcome Stranger' was found near Moliagul in 1869, just below the surface. It held about 70 kg of gold.

CLAIMS.c: Most convicts sent to Australia were serious violent criminals.
CLAIMS.e: Most were transported for theft and other property crimes, often fairly minor. Many sentences were seven years.

CLAIMS.c: The Sydney Opera House roof is covered in more than a million tiles.
CLAIMS.e: About 1,056,000 glazed tiles cover the sails. They were made in Sweden and designed to be self-cleaning in the rain.

CLAIMS.c: Australia has more than 10,000 beaches.
CLAIMS.e: Coastal scientists have counted more than 10,000 beaches around Australia's coast. You could visit a new one every day for over 27 years.

PUZZLES.q: A bat and a ball cost $1.10 in total. The bat costs $1.00 more than the ball. How much does the ball cost?
o: 10 cents
5 cents
1 cent
55 cents
PUZZLES.e: If the ball is 5c, the bat is $1.05, and together they're $1.10. The quick answer, 10c, would make the total $1.20.

PUZZLES.q: If 5 machines take 5 minutes to make 5 widgets, how long would 100 machines take to make 100 widgets?
o: 100 minutes
20 minutes
5 minutes
1 minute
PUZZLES.e: Each machine makes one widget in 5 minutes, so 100 machines make 100 widgets in the same 5 minutes.

PUZZLES.q: A patch of lily pads doubles in size every day. It takes 48 days to cover the whole lake. How long does it take to cover half?
o: 24 days
36 days
46 days
47 days
PUZZLES.e: It doubles daily, so the day before it's full, it was half: day 47.

PUZZLES.q: In a race, you overtake the person in second place. What place are you in now?
o: First
Second
Third
PUZZLES.e: You've taken their spot, so you're second.

PUZZLES.q: A farmer has 17 sheep. All but 9 run away. How many are left?
PUZZLES.e: 'All but 9' means 9 stay behind.

PUZZLES.q: Mary's father has five daughters: Nana, Nene, Nini and Nono. What is the fifth daughter's name?
o: Nunu
Mary
Nina
PUZZLES.e: It's Mary: she's one of her father's daughters.

PUZZLES.q: A clock shows 3:15. What is the angle between the hour and minute hands?
PUZZLES.e: The minute hand is on the 3. The hour hand has moved a quarter of the way from 3 to 4, which is a quarter of 30°: 7.5°.

PUZZLES.q: You have a 3-litre jug and a 5-litre jug and a tap. Can you measure exactly 4 litres?
o: Yes
No
PUZZLES.e: Fill the 5, pour into the 3 (2 left). Empty the 3, pour the 2 in. Fill the 5 again and top up the 3 (needs 1). You're left with 4.

PUZZLES.q: Some months have 31 days. How many have 28 days?
o: All 12
PUZZLES.e: Every month has at least 28 days.

PUZZLES.q: Two fathers and two sons go fishing. Each catches one fish, but they only bring home three. Nothing was lost. How?
o: One fish was eaten
They're a grandfather, father and son
One person didn't fish
It's impossible
PUZZLES.e: Three people: the father is also a son, so there are two fathers and two sons.

PUZZLES.q: A shop cuts a price by 20%, then raises the new price by 20%. Compared with the original price, it's now...
o: The same
4% lower
4% higher
2% lower
PUZZLES.e: 0.8 × 1.2 = 0.96, so it's 4% below the original.

PUZZLES.q: What comes next: 2, 6, 12, 20, 30, ?
PUZZLES.e: The gaps grow by 2 each time (4, 6, 8, 10, 12), so the next is 42.

PUZZLES.q: What gets wetter the more it dries?
o: A sponge
A towel
The sun
PUZZLES.e: A towel gets wetter as it dries you.

PUZZLES.q: Which weighs more: a kilogram of feathers or a kilogram of bricks?
o: Feathers
Bricks
They weigh the same
PUZZLES.e: A kilogram is a kilogram.

PUZZLES.q: A doctor gives you three pills and says to take one every half hour. How long until they're all gone?
o: 30 minutes
1 hour
90 minutes
2 hours
PUZZLES.e: Take one now, one at 30 minutes and the last at 60 minutes.

PUZZLES.q: If 3 people take 3 hours to dig 3 holes, how long does 1 person take to dig 1 hole?
o: 1 hour
3 hours
9 hours
20 minutes
PUZZLES.e: Each person digs one hole in 3 hours.

PUZZLES.q: What comes next: 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, ?
PUZZLES.e: Each number is the sum of the two before it: 5 + 8 = 13. It's the Fibonacci sequence.

PUZZLES.q: A snail is at the bottom of a 10-metre well. Each day it climbs 3 m; each night it slips back 2 m. On which day does it reach the top?
o: Day 7
Day 8
Day 10
Never
PUZZLES.e: After 7 days it's at 7 m. On day 8 it climbs 3 m and reaches the top before slipping.

PUZZLES.q: A rope ladder hangs over the side of a boat, with rungs 30 cm apart. The tide rises 1 metre. How many extra rungs go underwater?
o: None
PUZZLES.e: The boat floats, so it rises with the tide and the ladder stays at the same level against the water.

PUZZLES.q: Jess is taller than Sam. Sam is taller than Ali. Who is the shortest?
o: Jess
Sam
Ali
Can't tell
PUZZLES.e: Jess > Sam > Ali, so Ali is shortest.

PUZZLES.q: Cutting a log into 3 pieces takes 6 minutes. At the same speed, how long does it take to cut an identical log into 4 pieces?
o: 8 minutes
9 minutes
10 minutes
12 minutes
PUZZLES.e: 3 pieces need only 2 cuts, so each cut takes 3 minutes. 4 pieces need 3 cuts: 9 minutes.

PUZZLES.q: A train leaves at 11:50 and the trip takes 45 minutes. When does it arrive?
PUZZLES.e: 10 minutes gets you to 12:00, then 35 more minutes: 12:35.

PUZZLES.q: You have one match and walk into a dark room with a candle, a heater and a lamp. What do you light first?
o: The candle
The heater
The lamp
The match
PUZZLES.e: You have to light the match before anything else.

PUZZLES.q: Anna can paint a fence in 3 hours. Ben can paint the same fence in 6 hours. Working together, how long will it take them?
o: 4.5 hours
2 hours
3 hours
1.5 hours
PUZZLES.e: Anna paints 1/3 of the fence per hour and Ben 1/6, so together they do 1/3 + 1/6 = 1/2 per hour. Half a fence an hour means 2 hours. Averaging the two times (4.5 hours) is the classic trap.

PUZZLES.q: A tap fills an empty tank in 4 hours. A drain empties a full tank in 6 hours. If both are open, how long does the empty tank take to fill?
o: 12 hours
2 hours
10 hours
24 hours
PUZZLES.e: Each hour the tap adds 1/4 of the tank and the drain removes 1/6, a net gain of 3/12 - 2/12 = 1/12. So it takes 12 hours to fill.

PUZZLES.q: A mother is three times as old as her daughter. In 12 years, she will be exactly twice as old. How old is the daughter now?
PUZZLES.e: If the daughter is d, then 3d + 12 = 2(d + 12), so d = 12. Check: 12 and 36 now, then 24 and 48 in 12 years.

PUZZLES.q: A car travels at a steady 90 km/h. How far does it go in 20 minutes?
o: 18 km
45 km
30 km
20 km
PUZZLES.e: 20 minutes is one third of an hour, and one third of 90 km is 30 km.

PUZZLES.q: You roll one ordinary six-sided die. What is the chance of rolling a number greater than 4?
o: 1 in 2
1 in 3
1 in 6
2 in 3
PUZZLES.e: Only 5 and 6 are greater than 4. That's 2 of the 6 faces, which is 1 in 3.

PUZZLES.q: A bat and a ball cost $1.10 in total. The bat costs $1.00 more than the ball. How much does the ball cost?
o: 10 cents
1 cent
5 cents
15 cents
PUZZLES.e: If the ball costs x, the bat costs x + $1.00, so 2x + $1.00 = $1.10 and x = 5 cents. Check: 5 cents + $1.05 = $1.10. Answering 10 cents is the intuitive trap, because then the bat would be $1.10 and the total $1.20.

PUZZLES.q: What comes next: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, ?
PUZZLES.e: These are the prime numbers, which divide evenly only by 1 and themselves. 15 and 16 aren't prime, and 17 comes before 19.

PUZZLES.q: What comes next: 1, 2, 4, 7, 11, 16, ?
PUZZLES.e: The gaps grow by one each time: +1, +2, +3, +4, +5, so the next step is +6, and 16 + 6 = 22.

PUZZLES.q: What comes next: 1, 8, 27, 64, ?
PUZZLES.e: These are cubes: 1x1x1, 2x2x2, 3x3x3, 4x4x4. Next is 5 x 5 x 5 = 125.

PUZZLES.q: What comes next: 3, 6, 11, 18, 27, ?
PUZZLES.e: The gaps are 3, 5, 7, 9, so the next is 11, giving 38. Each term is also a square number plus 2 (36 + 2 = 38).

PUZZLES.q: What comes next: Z, X, V, T, R, ?
o: Q
O
S
P
PUZZLES.e: The pattern goes backwards through the alphabet, skipping one letter each time. After R, skip Q and land on P.

PUZZLES.q: What comes next: 1, 2, 6, 24, 120, ?
PUZZLES.e: Each number is multiplied by the next whole number: x2, x3, x4, x5. So 120 x 6 = 720. These are called factorials.

PUZZLES.q: All bloops are razzies. All razzies are lazzies. Are all bloops definitely lazzies?
o: No, never
Yes, definitely
Only some of them
There's no way to tell
PUZZLES.e: If every bloop is inside the razzie group, and every razzie is inside the lazzie group, then every bloop must be a lazzie too. The made-up words stop you relying on what you already know.

PUZZLES.q: 'If it rains, the grass gets wet.' You look out and the grass is wet. What can you be sure of?
o: Nothing about whether it rained
It definitely rained
It definitely didn't rain
It will rain soon
PUZZLES.e: A sprinkler or morning dew could also wet the grass. Reasoning backwards like this is a common error called 'affirming the consequent'.

PUZZLES.q: On an island, knights always tell the truth and knaves always lie. A says: 'B is a knave.' B says: 'A and I are the same type.' What are they?
o: Both are knights
Both are knaves
A is a knave, B is a knight
A is a knight, B is a knave
PUZZLES.e: If A were a knave, B would be a knight, but then B's claim that they match would be false, which a knight can't say. So A is a knight, B is a knave, and B's claim is a lie, as it should be.

PUZZLES.q: Someone ate the last biscuit. Amy says: 'Ben ate it.' Ben says: 'Cal ate it.' Cal says: 'Ben is lying.' Exactly one of them is lying. Who ate it?
o: Amy
Cal
Ben
It's impossible to tell
PUZZLES.e: If Ben ate it, Amy tells the truth, Ben lies and Cal (who says Ben is lying) tells the truth: exactly one liar. Testing Amy or Cal as the eater gives two liars each time.

PUZZLES.q: Four friends stand in a queue. Kim is ahead of Nia. Nia is ahead of Lee. Max is behind Lee. Who is second in line?
o: Kim
Nia
Lee
Max
PUZZLES.e: Put the clues together and the only possible order is Kim, Nia, Lee, Max. So Nia is second.

PUZZLES.q: You have a balance scale and just three weights: 1 kg, 3 kg and 9 kg. Weights can go on either pan. What is the heaviest whole-kilogram load you can weigh exactly?
o: 13 kg
9 kg
12 kg
15 kg
PUZZLES.e: All three together make 1 + 3 + 9 = 13 kg. Putting weights on the load's pan fills every gap below that too, for example 2 kg = 3 kg on one side against 1 kg plus the load on the other.

PUZZLES.q: There are 10 bags of coins. Real coins weigh 10 g, but one whole bag holds fakes weighing 11 g each. With a digital scale, what is the fewest weighings needed to find the fake bag?
PUZZLES.e: Take 1 coin from bag 1, 2 from bag 2, and so on up to 10 from bag 10, and weigh them all at once. Every extra gram over 550 g points to a bag: 3 extra grams means bag 3.

PUZZLES.q: An adult and two children must cross a river. The boat carries either one adult alone, or up to two children. What is the fewest one-way crossings needed to get everyone across?
PUZZLES.e: Both children cross (1), one rows back (2), the adult crosses (3), the other child rows back (4), and both children cross again (5). The boat always needs a child on the far side to bring it back.

PUZZLES.q: What is the smallest number of people you need in a room to be certain that at least two share a birth month?
PUZZLES.e: With 12 people, everyone could be born in a different month. The 13th person must match someone. This is the 'pigeonhole principle'.

PUZZLES.q: You draw cards from a shuffled 52-card deck without looking. How many must you draw to be certain of getting two of the same suit?
PUZZLES.e: There are only 4 suits, so 4 cards could all be different. The 5th card must match one of them.

PUZZLES.q: A clock loses 10 minutes every hour. It is set correctly at noon. What does it show when the real time is 6:00 pm?
PUZZLES.e: Six hours pass, and the clock loses 10 minutes in each, 60 minutes in total. So it is a full hour behind.

PUZZLES.q: You glance at an ordinary clock in a mirror. The reflection seems to show 3:00. What is the real time?
PUZZLES.e: A mirror flips left and right. The hour hand that appears to point right (at 3) really points left (at 9), while the minute hand at 12 looks the same.

PUZZLES.q: Today is Wednesday. What day of the week will it be in 100 days?
o: Thursday
Friday
Saturday
Monday
PUZZLES.e: 100 days is 14 full weeks (98 days) plus 2 days. Full weeks change nothing, so it's two days after Wednesday.

PUZZLES.q: Today is Monday. What day was it three days before the day after tomorrow?
o: Sunday
Saturday
Monday
Friday
PUZZLES.e: The day after tomorrow is Wednesday. Three days before Wednesday is Sunday.

PUZZLES.q: You buy an old book for $12 and sell it for $15. Then you buy it back for $18 and sell it again for $21. Overall, how much money did you make?
PUZZLES.e: Treat it as two separate deals: $3 profit on the first and $3 profit on the second, $6 in total. Adding up all money in and out gives the same: 15 + 21 - 12 - 18 = 6.

PUZZLES.q: You can walk to work at 5 km/h in 36 minutes. How long would the same trip take by bike at 15 km/h?
o: 18 minutes
24 minutes
12 minutes
10 minutes
PUZZLES.e: The bike is three times as fast, so it takes a third of the time. (36 minutes at 5 km/h is a 3 km trip, and 3 km at 15 km/h is 12 minutes.)

PUZZLES.q: A 200-metre train travels at 72 km/h through a 400-metre tunnel. How long from the moment its front enters until its back leaves?
o: 20 seconds
30 seconds
10 seconds
60 seconds
PUZZLES.e: 72 km/h is 20 metres per second. The front must travel the tunnel's 400 m plus the train's own 200 m, so 600 m at 20 m/s takes 30 seconds.

PUZZLES.q: A hen and a half lays an egg and a half in a day and a half. At that rate, how many eggs does one hen lay in 6 days?
PUZZLES.e: Two-thirds of the hens lay two-thirds of the eggs in the same time, so one hen lays one egg in a day and a half. Six days holds four lots of a day and a half, so four eggs.

PUZZLES.q: Your average after four tests is 80. What do you need on the fifth test to lift your average to 82?
PUZZLES.e: Four tests at 80 total 320. An average of 82 over five tests needs 410 points, so the fifth must be 410 - 320 = 90.

PUZZLES.q: Count carefully: how many letters are in the two words 'the alphabet'?
PUZZLES.e: Count the letters in the actual words: 'the' has 3 and 'alphabet' has 8, which makes 11.

PUZZLES.q: An electric train is travelling north. A strong wind is blowing from the west. Which way does the train's smoke blow?
o: To the east
There is no smoke
To the north-east
To the south
PUZZLES.e: Electric trains draw power from overhead wires or a live rail and don't burn fuel, so there's no smoke.

PUZZLES.q: What can you hold in your right hand, but never in your left hand?
o: Your left elbow
Your right elbow
A pencil
Your nose
PUZZLES.e: Your right hand can cup your left elbow, but your left hand can never reach its own elbow. Try it.

PUZZLES.q: Before Mount Everest was measured and recognised, what was the highest mountain on Earth?
o: K2
Kangchenjunga
Mont Blanc
Mount Everest
PUZZLES.e: The mountain was always the tallest; people just hadn't measured it yet. British surveyors identified it as the highest peak in the 1850s.

PUZZLES.q: A man lives on the 10th floor. Each morning he takes the lift all the way down. Coming home, he rides only to the 7th floor and walks the rest, unless it's raining. Why?
o: He is avoiding a neighbour on floor 8
The lift is broken above floor 7
He's too short, but his umbrella reaches
He visits a friend on floor 7
PUZZLES.e: Only the umbrella explains the rain rule: on wet days he can use it to press the '10' button. Lateral puzzles reward finding the one detail every answer must explain.

PUZZLES.q: I'm a two-digit number. My digits add up to 9, and my tens digit is twice my ones digit. What number am I?
PUZZLES.e: Pairs adding to 9 are 9-0, 8-1, 7-2, 6-3 and 5-4. Only in 63 is the first digit twice the second.

PUZZLES.q: Think of any number. Double it, add 10, halve the result, then subtract the number you first thought of. What do you get?
o: It depends on your number
PUZZLES.e: Doubling and halving cancel out, and so do adding and subtracting your number. All that survives is half of the 10 you added.

PUZZLES.q: If you write out every whole number from 1 to 100, how many times do you write the digit 7?
PUZZLES.e: There are ten 7s in the ones place (7, 17, ... 97) and ten in the tens place (70 to 79). 77 lands in both groups, which is right, because it contains two 7s.

PUZZLES.q: How many zeros are at the end of 1 x 2 x 3 x ... x 20 (every whole number from 1 to 20 multiplied together)?
PUZZLES.e: Each zero needs a 10, which is 2 x 5. There are plenty of 2s but only four 5s (from 5, 10, 15 and 20), so there are four zeros.

PUZZLES.q: What is the last digit of 2 multiplied by itself 100 times (2 to the power of 100)?
PUZZLES.e: Powers of 2 end in a repeating cycle: 2, 4, 8, 6, 2, 4, 8, 6 ... The cycle length is 4 and 100 divides exactly by 4, so it lands on the last one, 6.

PUZZLES.q: A bag holds 3 red marbles and 1 blue marble. You pull out two without looking. What is the chance both are red?
o: 1 in 2
1 in 4
3 in 4
9 in 16
PUZZLES.e: The first is red 3/4 of the time, then the second is red 2/3 of the time, and 3/4 x 2/3 = 1/2. Another way: of the 6 possible pairs, 3 are both red.

PUZZLES.q: You flip a fair coin three times. What is the chance of getting at least one head?
o: 1 in 2
3 in 4
1 in 8
7 in 8
PUZZLES.e: The only way to get no heads is tails three times, a 1/2 x 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/8 chance. Everything else has a head, so 7/8.

PUZZLES.q: A game costs $2 to play. You roll a die and win as many dollars as the number shown. If you play many times, what happens on average?
o: You break even
You gain $1.50 per game
You lose 50 cents per game
You gain $3.50 per game
PUZZLES.e: The average roll is (1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6) / 6 = 3.5, so you win $3.50 on average for a $2 fee, a gain of $1.50 per game.

PUZZLES.q: A girl points at a boy and says: 'That boy's mother is my mother's only daughter.' Who is the boy?
o: Her son
Her brother
Her cousin
Her nephew
PUZZLES.e: Her mother's only daughter must be the girl herself. So she is the boy's mother.

PUZZLES.q: Tom's grandfather has 3 children, and each of them has exactly 2 children. How many cousins does Tom have on that side of the family?
PUZZLES.e: There are 6 grandchildren in total. Tom is one, and his only sibling is another, which leaves 4 cousins.

PUZZLES.q: What is the most pieces you can cut a flat round pizza into with 3 straight cuts, without moving any pieces?
PUZZLES.e: Cuts through the centre give only 6. Each new cut adds one piece, plus one more for every earlier cut it crosses inside the pizza: 2, then 4, then 7.

PUZZLES.q: Walking up the stairs from floor 1 to floor 3 takes 30 seconds. At the same pace, how long from floor 1 to floor 6?
o: 60 seconds
75 seconds
90 seconds
45 seconds
PUZZLES.e: Floor 1 to 3 is only 2 flights, so each flight takes 15 seconds. Floor 1 to 6 is 5 flights: 75 seconds.

PUZZLES.q: What is the fewest straight cuts needed to divide a round cake into 8 equal pieces, if you can't move pieces between cuts?
PUZZLES.e: Two cuts from above in a cross make 4 quarters, then one horizontal cut through the middle of the cake's height turns them into 8. Four cuts from above would also work, but 3 is fewer.

PUZZLES.q: In 3 years, Emma will be twice as old as she was 3 years ago. How old is Emma now?
PUZZLES.e: If Emma is x, then x + 3 = 2(x - 3), so x = 9. Check: in 3 years she'll be 12, and 3 years ago she was 6.

PUZZLES.q: When I was 6, my brother was half my age. Now I'm 40. How old is my brother?
PUZZLES.e: When I was 6 he was 3, so he's 3 years younger. The gap never changes, so he's 37. Halving 40 is the trap.

PUZZLES.q: Three boxes. One holds gold. Box A says 'The gold is here.' Box B says 'The gold is not here.' Box C says 'The gold is not in A.' Only one label is true. Where is the gold?
o: Box B
Box A
Box C
It can't be worked out
PUZZLES.e: Try each box. Gold in A makes the A and B labels true; gold in C makes the B and C labels true. Only gold in B leaves exactly one true label (C's).

PUZZLES.q: Using only addition and exactly eight 8s, which of these makes 1,000?
PUZZLES.e: 888 + 88 = 976, and three more 8s add 24 to reach exactly 1,000. Count the digits: 3 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 8.

PUZZLES.q: Divide 30 by a half, then add 10. What do you get?
PUZZLES.e: Dividing by a half means asking how many halves fit into 30, which is 60. Add 10 to get 70. Dividing by 2 would give 15 + 10 = 25.

PUZZLES.q: A leaky tap drips once every second. About 20 drops make 1 millilitre. Roughly how much water is wasted in a day?
o: About 0.4 litres
About 4 litres
About 40 litres
About 400 litres
PUZZLES.e: A day has 86,400 seconds, and 86,400 / 20 = 4,320 mL, or about 4.3 litres. Over a year that's more than 1,500 litres.

PUZZLES.q: You want to average 60 km/h over a 2 km lap. You drive the first kilometre at 30 km/h. How fast must you drive the second kilometre?
o: It can't be done
90 km/h
120 km/h
180 km/h
PUZZLES.e: Averaging 60 km/h over 2 km means finishing in 2 minutes. At 30 km/h the first kilometre alone takes 2 minutes, so there's no time left at all.

PUZZLES.q: A shirt costs $40 after a 20% discount. What was the original price?
PUZZLES.e: After 20% off you pay 80% of the original. If 80% is $40, then 10% is $5 and 100% is $50. Adding 20% to $40 gives the wrong answer of $48.

PUZZLES.q: A 100 kg watermelon is 99% water. After drying in the sun it is 98% water. What does it weigh now?
o: 98 kg
99 kg
50 kg
75 kg
PUZZLES.e: The solid part is 1 kg and doesn't change. At first it's 1% of the weight; afterwards it's 2%, so the total must have halved to 50 kg.

PUZZLES.q: In a queue, you are 7th from the front and 7th from the back. How many people are in the queue?
PUZZLES.e: There are 6 people in front of you and 6 behind you, plus you: 13. Adding 7 + 7 counts you twice.

PUZZLES.q: Two volumes of an encyclopedia sit side by side on a shelf, in order, spines facing out. Each has 4 cm of pages and a 2 mm cover on each side. A bookworm chews from page 1 of Volume 1 to the last page of Volume 2. How far does it travel?
o: 4 mm
8 cm
8.4 cm
8.8 cm
PUZZLES.e: With spines facing you, page 1 of Volume 1 sits on its right side, next to Volume 2, and the last page of Volume 2 sits on its left side. The worm only chews through two covers: 2 mm + 2 mm.

PUZZLES.q: On a standard die, opposite faces always add up to 7. If the top face shows 2, what's on the bottom?
PUZZLES.e: The pairs are 1 and 6, 2 and 5, and 3 and 4. So 2 on top means 5 underneath.

PUZZLES.q: A frog is 1 metre from a wall. Each jump carries it exactly half of the remaining distance. After how many jumps does it touch the wall?
o: Never
PUZZLES.e: After each jump some distance remains (a half, a quarter, an eighth ...), so it gets endlessly closer without arriving. After 10 jumps it's less than 1 mm away.

PUZZLES.q: Two people played 5 games of chess. Each won 3 games and there were no draws. How is that possible?
o: One game was replayed
They didn't play each other
They counted a draw as a win
It isn't possible
PUZZLES.e: Nothing says they were opponents. Each could have played other people, winning 3 and losing 2.

PUZZLES.q: You have 10 fingers. How many fingers are on 10 hands?
PUZZLES.e: Each hand has 5 fingers (counting the thumb), so 10 hands have 50. The mention of your 10 fingers is there to lure you into saying 100.

PUZZLES.q: Which is bigger: 2 to the power of 10, or 10 to the power of 3?
o: 10 to the power of 3
They're exactly equal
It depends on the order
2 to the power of 10
PUZZLES.e: 2 to the power of 10 is 1,024, and 10 x 10 x 10 is 1,000. That's why a 'kilobyte' was traditionally 1,024 bytes.

PUZZLES.q: Which fraction is larger: 3/7 or 4/9?
o: They're equal
It can't be told without a calculator
PUZZLES.e: Cross-multiply: 4 x 7 = 28 and 3 x 9 = 27, so 4/9 is a touch bigger. As decimals they're about 0.444 and 0.429.

PUZZLES.q: You draw one card from a shuffled 52-card deck. What is the chance it is a heart or a king (or both)?
o: 4 in 13
1 in 4
1 in 13
PUZZLES.e: There are 13 hearts and 4 kings, but the king of hearts is in both groups. That's 16 different cards out of 52, which simplifies to 4 in 13.

PUZZLES.q: You roll two dice. What is the chance at least one of them shows a six?
o: 1 in 3
1 in 6
1 in 36
PUZZLES.e: The chance neither shows a six is 5/6 x 5/6 = 25/36, so at least one six is 11/36. Adding 1/6 + 1/6 = 12/36 counts double sixes twice.

PUZZLES.q: On average, how many times do you need to roll a fair die to get your first six?
PUZZLES.e: When something has a 1 in 6 chance each try, it takes 6 tries on average. Some runs are much shorter and some much longer.

PUZZLES.q: A bag holds two coins: one normal and one with heads on both sides. You pick one at random, flip it, and it lands heads. What is the chance it's the double-headed coin?
o: 1 in 2
3 in 4
2 in 3
1 in 3
PUZZLES.e: There are three equally likely heads you could be seeing: two from the double-headed coin and one from the normal coin. Two of those three belong to the double-headed coin.

PUZZLES.q: A knockout tennis tournament starts with 64 players. How many matches are played to find the champion?
PUZZLES.e: Every match knocks out exactly one player, and 63 players must be knocked out to leave one champion. The same trick works for any number of players, byes included.

PUZZLES.q: A chocolate bar is a 4 x 6 grid of squares. Each snap breaks one piece into two along a line. How many snaps are needed to get all 24 squares apart?
PUZZLES.e: Each snap adds exactly one piece. Going from 1 piece to 24 pieces therefore always takes 23 snaps, whatever order you break it in.

PUZZLES.q: You have 10 litres of juice that is 20% concentrate. How much water must you add to make it 10% concentrate?
o: 2 litres
5 litres
20 litres
10 litres
PUZZLES.e: The mix contains 2 litres of concentrate. For that to be 10% of the drink, the total must be 20 litres, so add 10 litres of water.

SCENARIOS.q: Towns that sell more ice cream have more drownings. What's the best explanation?
o: Ice cream causes drowning
Hot weather drives both
Drowning makes people buy ice cream
It's pure coincidence
SCENARIOS.e: A third factor, hot weather, increases both swimming and ice-cream sales. That's a confounding variable.

SCENARIOS.q: A study finds that people who drink coffee live longer. What can you actually conclude?
o: Coffee makes you live longer
There's an association, but other factors could explain it
Coffee is harmful
Nothing at all
SCENARIOS.e: An observational study shows a link, not a cause. Coffee drinkers might differ in income, health or habits.

SCENARIOS.q: A new supplement worked for 4 out of 5 people in a trial. How convincing is that?
o: Very convincing: 80% success
Not very: the sample is far too small
It proves it works for 80% of people
It proves it doesn't work
SCENARIOS.e: With only five people, chance and placebo effects can easily explain the result.

SCENARIOS.q: Linda is 31, outspoken and studied philosophy, with a passion for social justice. Which is more likely?
o: Linda is a bank teller
Linda is a bank teller and active in the feminist movement
Both are equally likely
There's no way to compare them
SCENARIOS.e: Two things both being true can never be more likely than one of them alone. The detailed version just feels more fitting. That's the conjunction fallacy.

SCENARIOS.q: "You can't trust his argument about tax. He failed maths at school." Which fallacy is this?
o: Ad hominem
Straw man
Slippery slope
False dilemma
SCENARIOS.e: Ad hominem attacks the person instead of the argument.

SCENARIOS.q: "You can't tell me to quit smoking. You smoked for 20 years!" What's wrong with this reply?
o: Nothing, it's a fair point
Tu quoque: it dodges by pointing to hypocrisy
Straw man: it twists the argument
Slippery slope: it predicts a chain of events
SCENARIOS.e: Pointing out hypocrisy dodges the argument. Smoking is just as harmful whoever warns you about it.

SCENARIOS.q: "If we lower the speed limit to 40, next they'll ban cars altogether." Which fallacy?
o: Slippery slope
Ad hominem
Red herring
False cause
SCENARIOS.e: It leaps to an extreme outcome without showing why each step would follow. Every link in a chain like that needs evidence.

SCENARIOS.q: "Either you support this policy, or you don't care about children." Which fallacy?
o: Straw man
False dilemma
Appeal to emotion
Hasty generalisation
SCENARIOS.e: A false dilemma presents only two options when more exist.

SCENARIOS.q: "Millions of people use this remedy, so it must work." What's wrong with this reasoning?
o: Nothing, popularity proves it
It's an appeal to popularity
It's a straw man
It's circular
SCENARIOS.e: Popularity isn't evidence. Many popular beliefs have been wrong.

SCENARIOS.q: "Every successful founder I've read about dropped out of uni, so dropping out helps you succeed." What's the flaw?
o: No flaw
Survivorship bias: you don't hear about dropouts who failed
Confirmation bias about unis
Anchoring on famous names
SCENARIOS.e: Survivorship bias looks only at the winners. Most dropouts who failed never get written about.

SCENARIOS.q: Which is the strongest evidence that a medicine works?
o: A celebrity recommending it
One patient's success story
A large randomised controlled trial
The company's press release
SCENARIOS.e: Randomised controlled trials compare similar groups and reduce bias. Anecdotes and marketing don't.

SCENARIOS.q: "My grandad smoked every day and lived to 95, so smoking isn't that bad." What's the problem?
o: It's anecdotal: one case doesn't outweigh data from millions
Nothing, it's real evidence
Grandad was probably lying
It's an appeal to authority
SCENARIOS.e: Individual exceptions exist, but large studies show smoking greatly raises the risk of disease and early death.

SCENARIOS.q: After a terrible game, the coach yelled at the team. Next game they played much better. What's the most likely explanation?
o: Yelling works
Performance tends to return to average after an extreme result
The other team was weaker
The players were scared
SCENARIOS.e: Regression to the mean: an unusually bad result is usually followed by a more typical one, with or without yelling.

SCENARIOS.q: The schools with the very best average results in a league table are mostly small schools. Should parents conclude small schools teach better?
o: Yes, small schools clearly teach better
Not necessarily: small groups vary more
Only if they are private
Yes, averages never lie
SCENARIOS.e: With fewer students, a few very strong or weak ones swing the average. Small schools turn up at both extremes.

SCENARIOS.q: You roll two dice and add them. Which total comes up most often?
o: All totals are equally likely
SCENARIOS.e: Six combinations make 7 (1 and 6, 2 and 5, 3 and 4, each either way round), more than any other total. 2 and 12 can each be made only one way.

SCENARIOS.q: Your last three home projects each ran well over budget, but you're sure this one will come in on time. What's the likely trap?
o: Anchoring
The planning fallacy
Survivorship bias
The sunk cost fallacy
SCENARIOS.e: The planning fallacy is underestimating time and cost despite past experience. Start from your own track record, or how long similar projects really took.

SCENARIOS.q: A jacket is labelled 'Was $400, now $199'. Why does $199 feel like a bargain?
o: It's always a bargain
The $400 acts as an anchor that shapes your sense of value
Jackets are cheap
Sales are regulated
SCENARIOS.e: Anchoring: the first number you see sets the reference point. Ask what the jacket is worth to you, not what it 'was'.

SCENARIOS.q: You're convinced a diet works, so you only read articles that praise it. What's this called?
o: Critical thinking
Confirmation bias
Peer review
The placebo effect
SCENARIOS.e: Confirmation bias is seeking out information that supports what you already believe. Look for the best case against it.

SCENARIOS.q: You paid $60 for a concert ticket, but you're exhausted and would rather stay home. What's the smartest way to decide?
o: Go, or the $60 is wasted
Ignore the $60, because it's spent either way, and choose what you'd enjoy more now
Go, but leave early so you get some value from the ticket
Always stay home
SCENARIOS.e: The $60 is a sunk cost. It's gone whatever you do, so it shouldn't drive the decision.

SCENARIOS.q: In a street, nine people earn $60,000 and one earns $10 million. Which better describes a typical income there?
o: The mean (about $1 million)
The median ($60,000)
The highest income
They're the same
SCENARIOS.e: One extreme value drags the average up. The median, the middle value, better describes a typical person.

SCENARIOS.q: A headline says crime in a small town is 'up 100%'. It rose from 2 incidents to 4. What's the best takeaway?
o: The town is now dangerous
With tiny numbers, percentages can sound alarming but mean little
Crime doubled everywhere
Police are failing
SCENARIOS.e: Always ask for the raw numbers. A big percentage change on a small base is often just noise.

SCENARIOS.q: An online poll on a car website finds 80% of people want lower petrol taxes. Why be cautious?
o: Online polls are always right
People chose to take part, and the audience is mainly drivers, so it's not representative
80% is too low
Petrol isn't taxed
SCENARIOS.e: Self-selected samples reflect who shows up, not the whole population.

SCENARIOS.q: A headline says 'Scientists say chocolate helps weight loss'. What should you check first?
o: Whether you like chocolate
How big the study was, whether it was in people, and who funded it
The journalist's name
Nothing: scientists said it
SCENARIOS.e: Small, animal or industry-funded studies are often overhyped. One study rarely settles anything.

SCENARIOS.q: An email from 'your bank' says your account is locked and gives you a link to log in. What's the safest move?
o: Click the link quickly
Reply with your details
Ignore the link and contact the bank through its official app or a number you look up yourself
Forward it to friends
SCENARIOS.e: Banks won't ask you to log in through an email link. Scammers rely on urgency to rush you.

SCENARIOS.q: You invest $1,000 at 7% a year and reinvest the returns. Roughly what is it worth after 10 years?
o: About $2,000
SCENARIOS.e: About $1,967. The rule of 72: divide 72 by the rate (72 ÷ 7 ≈ 10) to find how many years it takes to double.

SCENARIOS.q: Two $20,000 loans both charge 6% interest. Loan A runs 5 years; loan B runs 10 years with lower repayments. Which costs more interest overall?
o: Loan A
Loan B
They cost the same
Neither charges interest
SCENARIOS.e: Lower repayments feel easier, but you pay interest for twice as long. Loan B costs roughly twice as much in interest.

SCENARIOS.q: "This herbal remedy is completely natural, so it can't do any harm." What's the flaw?
o: No flaw in the argument
Appeal to nature
Straw man
Circular reasoning
SCENARIOS.e: Being natural does not make something safe or effective. Arsenic, death cap mushrooms and snake venom are all natural, and some herbal remedies interact with prescription medicines.

SCENARIOS.q: A famous actor recommends a vitamin supplement in an ad. Why isn't that strong evidence it works?
o: Actors can't take vitamins
They're not an expert in medicine and are being paid
Ads are illegal
It is strong evidence
SCENARIOS.e: That's an appeal to (false) authority. Fame in one field doesn't make someone an expert in another.

SCENARIOS.q: Shark attacks get heavy news coverage. For Australian beachgoers, how does the risk of dying from a shark compare with drowning?
o: Sharks are far riskier
About the same
Drowning is far more common
Neither ever happens
SCENARIOS.e: Around 100 or more people drown on Australia's coast each year; fatal shark bites are typically a handful. Vivid news makes rare risks feel common.

SCENARIOS.q: Children from homes with lots of books tend to get better school results. A council plans to post free books to every family, expecting grades to jump. What's the flaw?
o: Other factors, like income, may explain both
Nothing: more books will clearly raise grades
Books may actually be lowering grades overall
Grades cause families to buy books, so it will backfire
SCENARIOS.e: A confounding variable can sit behind a correlation. A fair test would compare otherwise similar families, some given books and some not.

SCENARIOS.q: People who went to hospital this year were more likely to die this year than people who didn't. Should you avoid hospitals?
o: Yes: hospitals are clearly dangerous places
No: sicker people are the ones who go in
Yes, but only during the winter months
Yes: hospitals cause the illnesses people die of
SCENARIOS.e: This is selection by illness, a form of confounding. Comparing patients with healthy people who stayed home is not a fair comparison.

SCENARIOS.q: The more firefighters sent to a fire, the more damage the fire tends to cause. What's the best explanation?
o: Firefighters cause much of the damage
Fewer firefighters would reduce the damage
Bigger fires cause both damage and call-outs
It's pure coincidence with no explanation
SCENARIOS.e: The size of the fire is a common cause of both. Mixing up which way cause runs, or missing a common cause, is a classic trap.

SCENARIOS.q: Suburbs with lots of trendy cafes have higher house prices. Will opening a new cafe on your street raise your home's value?
o: Yes, cafes directly raise house prices
Yes, by roughly 10% within a year
No, cafes always lower nearby prices
Unlikely: wealthy areas attract both
SCENARIOS.e: Local wealth is the likely common cause. Cafes tend to follow money into an area rather than create it.

SCENARIOS.q: Students who use a school's free tutoring get lower marks, on average, than students who don't. Does tutoring make students worse?
o: Probably not: struggling students sign up
Yes, tutoring clearly harms learning
Yes, so the service should be closed
It proves the tutors are poorly trained
SCENARIOS.e: This is selection bias with possible reverse causation: low marks lead to tutoring, not the other way round. A fair test compares similar students.

SCENARIOS.q: People who carry a cigarette lighter are more likely to develop lung cancer. What explains this?
o: Lighters give off cancer-causing fumes
Smokers carry lighters and get cancer more
Lung cancer makes people buy lighters
It shows lighters should be banned
SCENARIOS.e: Smoking is the confounding variable. The lighter is a marker of the real cause, not the cause itself.

SCENARIOS.q: Teams that got new standing desks report higher productivity, but those teams were also the newest and best-funded. What would best test whether the desks cause the boost?
o: Ask the teams if they like the desks
Buy standing desks for everyone and watch
Randomly assign desks to some teams
Look only at the single most productive team
SCENARIOS.e: Random assignment spreads other differences evenly between groups. It's the main way to turn a correlation into evidence of cause.

SCENARIOS.q: A study found countries that eat more chocolate per person have won more Nobel Prizes per person. What's the sensible takeaway?
o: Chocolate makes people much smarter
Winning Nobel Prizes makes people eat chocolate
Scientists should eat a lot more chocolate
Rich countries buy more chocolate and research
SCENARIOS.e: This real finding appeared in a medical journal in 2012 and is now a classic teaching example of spurious correlation. Comparing whole countries hides countless other differences.

SCENARIOS.q: A headline says a new compound 'cures cancer'. The study was done in mice. What's the best response?
o: Be cautious: results may not carry over
Ask your doctor to prescribe it tomorrow
Accept it: mice and humans are very similar
Dismiss it outright as fake news
SCENARIOS.e: Animal studies are an early step, not proof. Only a small share of drugs that look promising in early research end up approved for people.

SCENARIOS.q: A gadget online has twelve 5-star reviews, all posted in the same week with very similar wording. What should you conclude?
o: It must be an excellent product
They may be fake; check elsewhere
Twelve reviews is plenty of evidence
Similar wording shows buyers agree
SCENARIOS.e: Clusters of glowing reviews with matching phrasing are a common sign of review manipulation. Independent sources carry more weight.

SCENARIOS.q: Which usually gives the most reliable overall picture of whether a treatment works?
o: A single small trial with a striking result
A news story about a patient
A systematic review of many trials
An expert's personal opinion
SCENARIOS.e: Systematic reviews look at all the relevant studies, so one lucky or flawed result carries less weight.

SCENARIOS.q: An article claims 'a study shows' walking backwards boosts memory, but gives no link, author or journal. What's the smartest approach?
o: Trust it, because it mentions a study
Share it so others can decide for themselves
Assume the study is completely made up
Treat it as unverified until sourced
SCENARIOS.e: A claim is only as good as its source. Many viral 'studies' turn out to be misreported, very small or nonexistent.

SCENARIOS.q: In a trial of a supplement for back pain, 70% of people felt better after six weeks. There was no comparison group. What's the problem?
o: Pain often eases by itself anyway
No problem: 70% is a strong result
Six weeks is far too long to wait
Supplements can't ever affect pain
SCENARIOS.e: A control group shows what would have happened anyway. Natural recovery and the placebo effect can make useless treatments look effective.

SCENARIOS.q: A study praising a breakfast cereal was funded by the company that makes it. What's the most sensible view?
o: It must be false because of the funding
Not automatically wrong, but seek independent studies
Funding never affects the research
It's more trustworthy, as they know the product best
SCENARIOS.e: Conflicts of interest raise the bar for evidence. Independent replication is the best check.

SCENARIOS.q: A roulette wheel has landed on red eight times in a row. What are the chances of black on the next spin?
o: Much higher, black is due
Lower, red is on a streak
The same as any spin
Exactly 100%
SCENARIOS.e: Believing a result is 'due' is the gambler's fallacy. Each spin is independent, and the green zero means black is always slightly under 50%.

SCENARIOS.q: A condition affects 1 in 1,000 people. A test catches every real case but also wrongly flags 5% of healthy people. You test positive. Roughly how likely is it you have the condition?
o: About 95%
About 50%
Exactly 100%
About 2%
SCENARIOS.e: Out of 1,000 people, about 1 true case tests positive alongside about 50 false alarms, so only about 1 in 51. This is base rate neglect.

SCENARIOS.q: The forecast said 30% chance of rain, and it stayed dry. Was the forecast wrong?
o: No: it should rain on 3 days in 10
Yes, it was completely wrong
Yes, it should have said 0% instead
It means 30% of the area gets rain for sure
SCENARIOS.e: A single outcome can't prove a probability wrong. Forecasts are judged by how well they match reality over many days.

SCENARIOS.q: There are 23 people in a room. Roughly what's the chance at least two share a birthday?
o: About 6%
About 50%
About 23%
Almost zero
SCENARIOS.e: This is the birthday paradox. With 23 people there are 253 possible pairs, which is why a match is far more likely than it feels.

SCENARIOS.q: You roll a standard die four times. Roughly what's the chance of getting at least one six?
o: About 67% (four times one-sixth)
About 17%
About 52%
SCENARIOS.e: You can't simply add the chances. Work out the chance of no sixes, (5/6) to the power of 4, about 48%, and subtract from 100%.

SCENARIOS.q: A raffle sells 1,000 tickets at $10 each for a single $5,000 prize. On average, what is each ticket worth?
o: $10, so you break even
$5,000, the full prize amount
$50 per ticket
$5, a loss of $5 per ticket
SCENARIOS.e: Expected value is the prize times the chance of winning: $5,000 x 1/1,000 = $5. Fine for a good cause, but it's a donation, not an investment.

SCENARIOS.q: A '1-in-100-year flood' hit a town last year. What's the chance of another one this year?
o: Still about 1% a year, not a schedule
Zero, as it won't recur for 99 years
Higher, because floods tend to come in pairs
Certain, as another is now overdue
SCENARIOS.e: Over a 30-year home loan, a 1% yearly chance adds up to roughly a 26% chance of at least one such flood.

SCENARIOS.q: You think of an old friend and, minutes later, they call you. What's the most likely explanation?
o: You predicted it
Coincidence: such things happen
Your friend sensed your thoughts
It proves the call was meant to be
SCENARIOS.e: The law of truly large numbers: with enough chances, rare coincidences become almost certain. We remember the hits and forget the misses.

SCENARIOS.q: Sam: "We should cut back on sugary drinks in school canteens." Alex: "So you want kids never to enjoy a treat again?" What has Alex done?
o: A fair summary of Sam's view
An ad hominem attack on Sam
A straw man: distorting Sam's point
An appeal to popularity
SCENARIOS.e: A straw man swaps the real argument for a weaker, exaggerated one. Restating someone's view fairly is the first step to disagreeing well.

SCENARIOS.q: "Nobody has proven this fuel-saving gadget doesn't work, so it must work." What's wrong with this?
o: Nothing, it's perfectly sound reasoning
It's a slippery slope argument
It's a false dilemma fallacy
Appeal to ignorance: no disproof isn't proof
SCENARIOS.e: The burden of proof sits with whoever makes the claim. Independent tests of many fuel-saving gadgets have found little or no benefit.

SCENARIOS.q: "I started taking vitamin C, and a week later my cold was gone. So it cured my cold." What's the flaw?
o: Post hoc: most colds clear in a week anyway
No flaw: the timing proves it worked
It's a straw man argument
It's circular reasoning, nothing more
SCENARIOS.e: Post hoc ergo propter hoc means 'after this, therefore because of this'. Something happening first doesn't mean it caused what followed.

SCENARIOS.q: After several news stories about home break-ins, you guess burglary is far more common than official figures show. What's likely going on?
o: Survivorship bias in the news
The availability heuristic
The official figures must be wrong
Anchoring on the first story
SCENARIOS.e: We judge how likely something is by how easily examples come to mind. News coverage makes rare events very easy to recall.

SCENARIOS.q: A surgeon says an operation has a '90% survival rate'. Another says it has a '10% death rate'. Many patients prefer the first. Why?
o: The first operation is genuinely safer
The second surgeon is less skilled
The framing effect: same fact reworded
Confirmation bias in patients
SCENARIOS.e: Both statements are identical. Try restating a figure the other way round before deciding.

SCENARIOS.q: Most people stay in whatever super investment option they were put in when they started a job, without ever checking it. What explains this?
o: Defaults are always the best choice
The halo effect in action
Hindsight bias in action
Status quo bias: sticking with defaults
SCENARIOS.e: Defaults are powerful because changing takes effort. Checking fees and options occasionally can make a real difference over decades.

SCENARIOS.q: After the share market drops, a friend says, "I knew that was going to happen." They didn't sell anything beforehand. What's this?
o: Hindsight bias: it seems obvious now
Good forecasting by your friend
Loss aversion after the fall
The framing effect at work
SCENARIOS.e: Once we know the outcome, we rewrite our memory of how certain we felt. A useful check: did they act on it at the time?

SCENARIOS.q: An interviewer is impressed by a candidate's confident, polished manner and rates their spreadsheet skills highly too, without testing them. What's the bias?
o: Anchoring on first impressions
The halo effect: one trait colours others
Survivorship bias in hiring
No bias: confident people are skilled
SCENARIOS.e: The halo effect is why structured interviews and practical tests are used. They judge each skill on its own evidence.

SCENARIOS.q: Surveys often find most drivers rate themselves as above average. What does this show?
o: Most drivers really are above average
The surveys must be rigged
Overconfidence: we can't all be above average
The availability heuristic at work
SCENARIOS.e: This is sometimes called illusory superiority. We know our own good intentions but judge others by their mistakes.

SCENARIOS.q: An ad says a medicine 'halves your risk of a heart attack'. The risk falls from 2 in 1,000 to 1 in 1,000. What's the fuller picture?
o: Half of all heart attacks are prevented
Risk falls by 50 percentage points
It prevents 500 heart attacks per 1,000
A 50% relative drop; 1 fewer per 1,000
SCENARIOS.e: Relative risk sounds dramatic; absolute risk shows the real size of the change. Always ask 'out of how many?'

SCENARIOS.q: A company's bar chart shows its profits towering over a rival's. The vertical axis starts at 95 instead of 0. What should you notice?
o: The axis exaggerates a possibly small gap
The company is far more profitable
Charts can never be misleading
Axes always start at 95
SCENARIOS.e: A truncated axis magnifies small gaps. Check the numbers on the axis, not just the height of the bars.

SCENARIOS.q: A poll shows 51% support for a plan and 49% against, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3 points. What's the best conclusion?
o: The plan clearly has majority support
Too close to call: could go either way
The poll is useless and should be ignored
Exactly 51% of people support it
SCENARIOS.e: The margin of error means support could plausibly be anywhere from about 48% to 54%. Small leads inside it are not meaningful.

SCENARIOS.q: A loan's interest rate rises from 4% to 5%. Which description is accurate?
o: It's up exactly 1 per cent
It's up 5 per cent in total
1 percentage point, or 25% higher
It's up 25 percentage points
SCENARIOS.e: Percentage points measure the gap between two percentages; per cent measures relative change. Headlines often mix them up.

SCENARIOS.q: A stat says most car crashes happen within 5 km of home. Does that mean driving near home is especially dangerous?
o: Yes, local roads are the most dangerous
Yes, people drive worse near home
It means long trips never have crashes
Not necessarily: most driving is local
SCENARIOS.e: This is a denominator problem. You'd need crashes per kilometre driven to compare how risky each kind of trip is.

SCENARIOS.q: You could drive 40 minutes each way across town to save $20 on a toaster. What's the smartest way to think about it?
o: Count fuel and time too
Always go: $20 is $20
Never go: saving money is pointless
Go, but only if you can haggle
SCENARIOS.e: This is opportunity cost: every choice uses time and money that could go elsewhere. Price alone rarely tells the whole story.

SCENARIOS.q: You're choosing a paint colour for a room, and separately deciding whether to sell your house. How should your effort differ?
o: Treat both exactly the same way
Take more care with the sale
Spend most of your time on the paint
Decide both on gut feel in seconds
SCENARIOS.e: Reversible decisions can be made quickly and fixed later. Irreversible ones deserve slow, careful thought.

SCENARIOS.q: Your team is about to launch a project and everyone is upbeat. What's a good technique to uncover hidden problems?
o: Ask only the most positive person
Skip planning to save some time
A pre-mortem: imagine it failed
Launch first and check it later
SCENARIOS.e: Imagining failure makes it easier to voice doubts that optimism hides. Psychologist Gary Klein popularised the method.

SCENARIOS.q: You've spent three weeks comparing 40 kettles and still can't choose. What's the most sensible approach?
o: Keep researching until you find the perfect one
Buy all 40 and return the rest
Give up on buying a kettle at all
Set a few must-haves and buy the first match
SCENARIOS.e: This is satisficing: choosing 'good enough' instead of the best possible. Research suggests satisficers are often happier with their choices.

SCENARIOS.q: At the cinema: small popcorn $5, medium $8.50, large $9. What's the medium most likely there to do?
o: Make the large look like a bargain
Give the best value for money
Suit most people's appetite
Nothing, it's just another size
SCENARIOS.e: This is the decoy effect. Decide how much you actually want before comparing prices.

SCENARIOS.q: After a heated argument with your manager, you want to email your resignation right now. What's the smartest move?
o: Send it immediately while you feel strongly
Wait until you're calm, then decide
Post about it online first
Resign by text instead
SCENARIOS.e: Strong emotion narrows thinking and makes the present feel permanent. Big, hard-to-reverse choices are best made with a cool head.

SCENARIOS.q: In a meeting, the boss states their view first and everyone quickly agrees. How could the group make a better decision?
o: Let the boss make the decision alone
Take a vote after the boss has spoken
Have people write views down first
Only invite people who will agree
SCENARIOS.e: This helps avoid groupthink, where the wish for harmony overrides honest assessment. Early, independent views bring more information to the table.

SCENARIOS.q: You want to save more but always seem to spend what's in your account. What's a proven strategy?
o: Rely on willpower each week
Save whatever is left at month's end
Check your balance less often
Auto-transfer to savings on payday
SCENARIOS.e: This is a commitment device: deciding once, in advance, removes the daily temptation. 'Pay yourself first' is the classic version.

SCENARIOS.q: You're offered either a guaranteed $500 or a coin flip for $1,200 or nothing. Which has the higher expected value?
o: The coin flip: $600 on average
The guaranteed $500 payment
They're exactly equal
Neither has an expected value
SCENARIOS.e: Expected value is each outcome times its chance: 50% of $1,200 is $600. Many people still take the sure thing, which is reasonable if you can't afford to get nothing.

SCENARIOS.q: A caller says they're from the ATO, that you owe tax, and that police will arrest you today unless you pay in gift cards. What should you do?
o: Buy the gift cards just to be safe
Hang up and call the ATO's official number
Give your tax file number to prove identity
Ask them to call back tomorrow
SCENARIOS.e: The ATO doesn't threaten immediate arrest or ask for payment in gift cards or cryptocurrency. Pressure and unusual payment methods are hallmarks of a scam.

SCENARIOS.q: You get a text saying your myGov account is suspended, with a link to 'verify your details'. What's the smartest response?
o: Tap it quickly before the account is deleted
Reply STOP with your details
Don't tap it; go to myGov yourself
Forward it to family to check
SCENARIOS.e: Government impersonation texts rely on fear and urgency. Going to the official site yourself sidesteps the fake link entirely.

SCENARIOS.q: A text says Australia Post couldn't deliver your parcel and asks you to pay a $2.99 redelivery fee through a link. What's really going on?
o: A normal fee for redelivering a parcel
A tracking service for your parcel
Harmless, since it's only $2.99
Likely a scam to steal card details
SCENARIOS.e: The small fee lowers your guard. The real goal is your card number, which can then be used for much bigger purchases.

SCENARIOS.q: A message from an unknown number says, "Hi Mum, I dropped my phone, this is my new number. Can you pay a bill for me urgently?" What's the safest move?
o: Call their old number to check
Pay it: they sound stressed
Reply asking which bill they mean
Transfer a smaller amount first
SCENARIOS.e: This 'Hi Mum' scam relies on love and urgency. Verifying through a channel you already trust stops it cold.

SCENARIOS.q: An online ad shows a famous Australian endorsing a crypto platform that 'guarantees' 20% returns a month. What's the smartest conclusion?
o: A rare opportunity worth trying
A scam: guarantees are a red flag
Safe, because a celebrity backs it
Fine if you only invest a little
SCENARIOS.e: Scammers use fake news pages and deepfake videos of well-known people. ASIC's Moneysmart website lists common warning signs and companies to avoid.

SCENARIOS.q: A pop-up on your computer says it's infected and tells you to call a 'Microsoft support' number. What should you do?
o: Call and let them fix it remotely
Pay for the virus removal they offer
Close the browser window and never call
Enter your password to unlock it
SCENARIOS.e: Real tech companies don't use pop-ups asking you to call them. Remote access lets scammers into your bank accounts and files.

SCENARIOS.q: At work, a supplier emails saying their bank details have changed and asks you to pay the next invoice to the new account. What's the safest step?
o: Reply to the email to confirm
Pay it, since the email looks genuine
Pay half to each account
Phone them on a number you already have
SCENARIOS.e: This is business email compromise. Scammers hack or copy real email accounts, so the check must use a separate, trusted channel.

SCENARIOS.q: A cold caller offers to help you access your super early to pay off debts, for a fee. What's the smartest response?
o: Accept, since it's your money
Decline, as it's likely an illegal scheme
Give them your fund details to check eligibility
Ask for a discount on the fee
SCENARIOS.e: Super can only be released early in limited legal circumstances. Illegal early release schemes can leave you with drained super and tax penalties. Your fund or the ATO can explain the genuine rules.

SCENARIOS.q: You're selling a couch online. A buyer says they've paid by PayID, then sends an email saying you must pay a fee to 'upgrade to a business account' before you receive it. What's happening?
o: A normal bank process
A scam: you never pay to receive money
The buyer is being generous
You should pay, then ask for a refund
SCENARIOS.e: Fake PayID emails are a common marketplace scam. Check your actual bank account for the money before handing anything over.

SCENARIOS.q: A credit card has a $3,000 balance at 20% interest a year. If the balance stayed the same all year, roughly how much interest would you pay?
o: About $60
About $200
About $600
About $3,000
SCENARIOS.e: 20% of $3,000 is $600. Paying only the minimum each month means much of each payment goes to interest, so debts can take years to clear.

SCENARIOS.q: Someone has $5,000 in savings earning 4.5% and a $5,000 credit card debt at 20%. Using the savings to clear the card changes their yearly position by how much?
o: Costs more than it saves
Makes no difference
Saves about $225 a year
Saves about $775 a year
SCENARIOS.e: The card costs about $1,000 a year in interest, while the savings earn about $225, a net gain of about $775. Paying off high-interest debt is like earning a guaranteed return equal to its rate. Many people keep a small emergency buffer as well.

SCENARIOS.q: Your savings earn 2% interest a year while prices rise 4% a year. What's happening to what your money can buy?
o: It's shrinking by roughly 2% a year
It's growing by 2% a year
It's growing by 6% a year
It stays exactly the same
SCENARIOS.e: The real return is roughly interest minus inflation. A bigger number in your account doesn't always mean more buying power.

SCENARIOS.q: Two home loans advertise 5.8% and 5.9% interest. The 5.8% loan has much higher fees. What helps compare them fairly?
o: The advertised rate alone
The comparison rate, with fees
The lender's brand recognition
The number of branches
SCENARIOS.e: Australian lenders must show a comparison rate next to advertised rates. It's based on a standard loan amount, so your own costs may differ a little.

SCENARIOS.q: Super fund A charges 1% of your balance a year in fees; fund B charges 0.5%. On a $100,000 balance, what's the yearly difference?
SCENARIOS.e: 1% is $1,000 and 0.5% is $500. Over decades that gap compounds as well, so small fee differences can add up to a lot.

SCENARIOS.q: Rice costs $4.00 for a 500 g bag or $5.40 for a 750 g bag. Which is cheaper per kilogram?
o: The 500 g bag
They cost the same per kg
You can't compare them
The 750 g bag
SCENARIOS.e: Unit pricing shows cost per 100 g or per kg, and big Australian supermarkets must display it. Bigger packs are often, but not always, cheaper per unit.

SCENARIOS.q: An investment of $100 falls 10%, then rises 10%. What is it worth now?
SCENARIOS.e: $100 falls to $90, and 10% of $90 is only $9. A percentage fall needs a bigger percentage rise to recover.

SCENARIOS.q: Instead of paying a loan monthly, someone pays half the monthly amount every fortnight. Why does this usually pay the loan off faster?
o: Fortnightly payments have no interest
It makes 13 monthly payments a year
Banks give a fortnightly discount
It lowers the interest rate
SCENARIOS.e: The extra payment each year goes straight to reducing the balance, which also cuts future interest. It's a common general strategy, not a lender trick.

SCENARIOS.q: Choosing car insurance, you can lower your premium by picking a higher excess. What's the key question to ask?
o: Which option has the lowest premium?
Which insurer advertises the most?
Could I comfortably pay the excess?
Can I avoid ever claiming?
SCENARIOS.e: The excess is what you pay towards each claim. A higher excess trades a lower regular cost for a bigger bill when something goes wrong.

SCENARIOS.q: After news of a plane crash, a friend decides to drive interstate instead of flying 'to be safe'. What's the reality?
o: Driving is far safer than flying
They are about equally safe
Flying risk doubles after a crash
Driving is riskier per kilometre
